## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

[Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with a number of manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority and importance for ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately evident to the reader which Fathers commented on the texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which places in their works they did so. An edition of the greatest accuracy, easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection—one, systematic, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but assembled for the first time in our library from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.]

# The Complete Works of Saint Maximus of Turin

## [Column 0009]

### Pope Pius VI to His Illustrious Son in Christ, Victor Amadeus, King of Sardinia: Greeting and Apostolic Blessing

The distinguished esteem that we had long conceived in our mind for the eloquence, learning, and virtue of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, grew daily stronger and increased greatly; and at last it led us to consider the task of illuminating his works and bringing them once more into the light of day. Although we were pressed by anxiety over many matters, and matters of the greatest importance, we nevertheless thought that our cares ought also to be directed to this undertaking. Accordingly, we ordered and diligently arranged that a new edition of the Homilies, Sermons, and Treatises of this same holy bishop should be prepared—an accurate and elegant edition, insofar as that could be achieved.

We wished this edition, once completed and supplied in all its parts, to bear the royal name of Your Majesty, because we judged that it was owed, if to anyone, certainly and above all to you alone. For since you were born, raised, and educated in that city, and now rule it—that city over which Maximus himself long presided as bishop, and which he instructed and fortified with the precepts and institutions of orthodox religion—and since you are descended from ancestors who cultivated that same doctrine and those same institutions with such holiness, as though they had learned them from Maximus himself, and who were so devoted and bound to the Apostolic See that you regard it as destined always to be counted among your solid and genuine glories that you imitate them: who could deny that whatever originated with that bishop and belongs to him, you may indeed, and ought by a certain right of your own, claim for yourself?

Now, since the people of Turin had been taught by Maximus that care must be taken lest the faith suffer harm [Note: [Col. 0009] Sermon 87, p. 620; 88, p. 624; 96 and following, p. 655 and following; and Homily 45, p. 140; 47, p. 146, etc.], and that they must therefore remain in the ship at whose helm Peter sits, holding together the entire structure and mass of the Christian work [Note: [Col. 0009] Homily 54, p. 169 and following, and Sermon 94, p. 640 and following], the counts, dukes, and kings of the House of Savoy—of whom you yourself are the august offspring and heir not only of their rule but also of their virtue and piety—judged that they must strive and labor with the utmost effort to ensure that error should have no place to establish itself anywhere in their dominions, and that the orthodox religion guarded and proclaimed by the chair of Peter should remain whole and uncorrupted.

For this reason they were not merely a help and protection to those governors and defenders who fought for the truth of Christian doctrine, for the unity of the Church, and for the dignity and authority of the pontiffs. They also raised great armies to drive from their territories, as a pestilence, the heresies that factions of sectarians had introduced both earlier [Note: [Col. 0009] See the letters of Martin V to the Duke of Savoy, A.D. 1430, in *Preuves de l’Histoire généalogique de la royale maison de Savoie*, p. 274, Lyon edition, 1660, and vol. I, pp. 461, 467, 479] and in the sixteenth century. [Column 0010] They established the equestrian Order of Saints Maurice and Lazarus, with the approval of the Supreme Pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0010] See the letters of Pope Gregory XIII, in the same work, pp. 524 and following, 526 and following, and 529; and the letters of Pope Clement VIII, in the same work, pp. 553 and following], investing immense sums of money for the use of the knights [Note: [Col. 0010] Gregory XIII, in a letter of A.D. 1572, preserved in the same work, p. 524].

They presided over that order with such title, dignity, power, and virtue as grand masters that no one can doubt that examples of vigilance, courage, zeal, and energy in enlarging the commonwealth of the Christian people, safeguarding and advancing the doctrine of the Catholic faith, and defending the primacy of the Roman chair ought to be sought from them. At the same time, everyone must acknowledge that each of them individually acquired for himself the glory of a defender of religion, which he had already inherited from his ancestors.

[Column 0011] Nor is this merely our own persuasion; it is the ancient, perpetual, and constant conviction of the earlier pontiffs. When we recall the past, Clement VIII immediately comes to mind. Speaking of Charles Emmanuel I—the duke who, as is known, suppressed the Calvinist heresy when it attempted to break into central Italy and confined it to narrow mountain ridges—he declared that he could truly and solemnly affirm that this prince had joined to the splendor of his lineage, which he derived from illustrious and august emperors, a devotion to the Church; and that with the greatest resources and with unconquerable greatness, constancy, and firmness of spirit he had fought so vigorously for the See of Peter and for the faith that he preserved the ancient reputation of his forebears and retained forever, whole and undiminished, their inheritance of virtue and glory [Note: [Col. 0011] In a letter written in A.D. 1605, in the same work, p. 555].

To this same conclusion lead the testimonies given in earlier times by Alexander IV, Innocent VI, and Eugene IV—for why should we mention them all? The first, as early as the year 1260 [Note: [Col. 0011] In a letter to Eleanor, Queen of England, in the same work, p. 90], and the second in 1362 [Note: [Col. 0011] Letter to Count Amadeus, in the same work, p. 204. See Samuel Guichenon, *Histoire généalogique de la royale maison de Savoie*, book I, chapter 10, p. 92, vol. I, Lyon edition, 1660], called the counts of the House of Savoy devoted sons of the Church, whose devotion had always burned around the Apostolic See, and called them its constant zealots, champions, and athletes of the Lord. The third is an authoritative witness that the counts themselves, and those who succeeded them as dukes, had often undertaken the patronage and defense of the Church, especially when its affairs were harassed and afflicted; and that they had been so effective by their counsel, zeal, virtue, and work that they not only restored the Church’s fortunes but also increased them wonderfully:

“They supported the peace, tranquility, and unity of the Church of God and of the Apostolic See with their counsels, assistance, and even their own persons, and they helped to extend the Catholic faith over broad regions and frontiers, also destroying by the sword the fiercest enemies who had attempted to darken its glory” [Note: [Col. 0011] Compare this letter of his in the same work, p. 301].

The distinguished records of the deeds performed in this sphere with particular courage and excellence by Humbert [Note: [Col. 0011] See Guichenon, *Histoire généalogique*, etc., vol. I, 1660 edition, pp. 191, 215, 235, and 239], Amadeus [Note: [Col. 0011] Compare what Baron relates concerning Amadeus II under the year 1068, and Guichenon, p. 209 and following, relying on the records of the Supreme Pontiffs. Concerning Amadeus III, see Guichenon himself, in the same work, p. 227 and following; concerning the others, in the same work, pp. 348, 413, 418, 421, 427], Philip [Note: [Col. 0011] Concerning Philip, see Guichenon, in the same work, p. 296, where he cites Matthew Paris as a witness in the reign of Henry III], Charles [Note: [Col. 0011] See Guichenon, in the same work, pp. 577, 610, and 613], Philibert [Note: [Col. 0011] Consult the same author, in the same work, pp. 680, 687, and 690], and Charles Emmanuel [Note: [Col. 0011] In the same work, pp. 729, 730, 765, and 791] are preserved in illustrious documents.

We know of the wars against the Saracens undertaken, begun, sometimes renewed, and for the most part concluded with favorable battles by those same rulers [Note: [Col. 0011] Guichenon, book I, chapter 10, p. 92, and book XI, chapter 8; on Thomas, p. 246; on Amadeus V, chapter 20, p. 362; and on Amadeus VI, chapter 23, p. 417 and following]. We know of the assistance sent to Christians struggling in the East and exposed to the danger of losing their freedom [Note: [Col. 0012] Guichenon, book II, chapter 28, on Amadeus IX, p. 556]; [Column 0012] of Rhodes, freed by their forces from a violent assault and a long siege while some were considering surrender, after the enemies of the holy religion had been driven away [Note: [Col. 0012] Guichenon, book II, chapter 20, on Amadeus V, under the year 1315, vol. I, p. 362. Compare the writers whom he lists there, and chapter 38, on Charles Emmanuel II, p. 1026]; of treaties entered into with powerful princes for the sake of sustaining and asserting evangelical truth; of bishoprics enlarged or established [Note: [Col. 0012] Guichenon, book II, on Amadeus II, chapter 5, p. 209; chapter 23, on Amadeus VI, pp. 420 and 422; and chapter 25, pp. 461, 464, and 467] [Note: [Col. 0012] See what Guichenon reports concerning Humbert II under 1034, p. 190; concerning Odo I, in the same work, pp. 201 and 202; and concerning Charles Emmanuel II, p. 865. The deeds performed in this sphere by Victor Amadeus, who now happily rules, are well known]; of benefices increased at great expense [Note: [Col. 0012] Guichenon, vol. I, pp. 191, 222, 244, 248, 270, 426, 427, etc.]; of teachers summoned by the offer of generous rewards [Note: [Col. 0012] Guichenon must be consulted, in the same work, pp. 656 and 765, where he discusses Charles Emmanuel. Yet in this matter the work of Victor Amadeus and Charles Emmanuel was much more distinguished, as is also that of the prince who now reigns], so that the people might not only be kept in the faith and in their duty but might also be strengthened in them to the highest degree.

We know of nearly innumerable other achievements of the same kind accomplished by the princes of the House of Savoy. Their examples of defending and enlarging the Catholic name now live on with you and under your rule.

But since Maximus’s devotion toward the Apostle Peter was so great [Note: [Col. 0012] Compare his Homilies 68 and following, p. 215 and following, and Sermons 61 and following, p. 566 and following], that he not only offered him honors, worship, and prayers himself, but also urged his hearers to venerate him as the teacher and father of the martyrs [Note: [Col. 0012] Homily 70, p. 226, and Homily 71, p. 228], who could doubt that the veneration which that apostle has had and still has at Turin has passed from there into the hearts of the princes of the House of Savoy?

The evidence of this is preserved in the charters of Humbert II [Note: [Col. 0012] Guichenon, vol. II, *Preuves*, etc., p. 28], [Column 0013] Amadeus II [Note: [Col. 0013] Guichenon, vol. II, *Preuves*, etc., p. 33], Amadeus III [Note: [Col. 0013] The same work, p. 34], and the others who later ruled there. To follow these records one by one would certainly carry us beyond the proper length of a letter.

Now, concerning the cultivation of discipline and the retention of the pontiffs’ decrees: what is there in the charters of the counts and dukes that is not entirely consonant with the precepts of Maximus? If the opinion that this bishop expressed when consulted on such matters at the Roman synod under Pope Hilary is compared [Note: [Col. 0013] A.D. 465, vol. II of the Councils, p. 801, Paris edition, 1714] with what had been done, or was to be done, by Adelaide [Note: [Col. 0013] Guichenon, vol. II, *Preuves*, etc., pp. 19 and 24], by the Humberts, by the Amadeuses [Note: [Col. 0013] The same work, p. 31 and following. See the constitution of Pope Honorius II, in the same work, pp. 32 and 42 and following]—especially by Amadeus IX [Note: [Col. 0013] Guichenon, vol. I, p. 556], who was enrolled among the blessed because of his heroic virtues—and finally by the other princes of Savoy who flourished afterward, as had been foreseen by the distinguished men Anselm of Canterbury and Peter Damian, eminent in learning and holiness, everyone will have to judge that those princes had undertaken nothing which did not appear to conform to the decisions of that same holy bishop.

Especially worthy of remembrance is what Anselm wrote in a letter to Count Humbert II. The holy man testifies that he respected and honored him because he had observed and fully understood his life, integrity, and resolve to uphold the institutions of the Roman Church; and because he knew that, in preserving peace and justice, Humbert exercised the power of his principality with piety [Note: [Col. 0013] Book III, letter 65, p. 391, Paris edition of the *Works*, 1675].

Of Peter Damian we shall say this briefly: he saw how that glory and ornament of your lineage, Adelaide, was a devoted guardian, vigorous champion, and defender of ecclesiastical discipline. After comparing her with Deborah because of the firmness and greatness of her spirit, he urged her to be a refuge and aid to bishops striving to correct their clergy and bring them back to their duty. But in this matter [as Maximus had previously taught [Note: [Col. 0013] Sermon 109, p. 675]] he observed that severity must be tempered with gentleness, so that neither of the two should become excessive: immoderate gentleness does not remove vices but nourishes them, while immoderate severity frightens sick souls and turns them away from the cultivation of virtue [Note: [Col. 0013] Letter to Adelaide, in Guichenon, vol. II, *Preuves*, etc., p. 10 and following].

But what need is there to produce all the splendid evidence in this sphere supplied by that princely woman and by the later counts and dukes, evidence so widely known that it requires no one’s speech? Nevertheless, I do not think we should omit the matter of generosity exercised toward sacred buildings and the poor. This virtue was commended by Maximus in many sermons [Note: [Col. 0013] Homilies 85, p. 288; 86, p. 292; 88, p. 297; 91, p. 308; 93, p. 315; 94, p. 319 and following; 96, p. 325; 97, p. 327; 98, p. 331; and Sermon 99, p. 645], and was always cultivated and observed by the counts, dukes, and kings of the House of Savoy, so that it appears to have been and still to be a characteristic of your blood.

In this virtue of beneficence Adelaide [Note: [Col. 0013] See Peter Damian’s letter to Adelaide, in Guichenon, vol. II, *Preuves*, etc., p. 12; and Adelaide’s charters, in the same work, pp. 14 and following and [Column 0014] 17 and following, and in Guichenon’s vol. I, pp. 185, 201, and 202], Amadeus I [Note: [Col. 0014] The same work, p. 194], Humbert II [Note: [Col. 0014] The same work, p. 214], Amadeus III [Note: [Col. 0014] The same work, pp. 224, 225, 227, and 229], Humbert III [Note: [Col. 0014] The same work, p. 234 and following], Thomas [Note: [Col. 0014] The same work, p. 244 and following, 248], Amadeus IV [Note: [Col. 0014] The same work, p. 270 and following], Peter and his daughter Agnes [Note: [Col. 0014] In the same author, vol. II, *Preuves*, etc., p. 21 and following], Beatrice [Note: [Col. 0014] The same work, p. 64 and following], Amadeus V [Note: [Col. 0014] In the same author, vol. I, p. 362 and following], Aymon [Note: [Col. 0014] The same work, p. 390 and following], Amadeus VI [Note: [Col. 0014] The same work, pp. 410 and 426 and following], Amadeus IX [Note: [Col. 0014] The same work, p. 555 and following], Emmanuel Philibert [Note: [Col. 0014] Concerning Charles II, Philibert, Charles III, and Emmanuel Philibert, see the same work, p. 580 and following]—who professed that he would freely devote all his strength and resources to the defense of the Catholic religion—Charles Emmanuel, and the others excelled [Note: [Col. 0014] The same work, pp. 864 and following, 910, etc.].

Among the many glorious and magnificent deeds performed at home and in war by your grandfather, the unconquered King Victor Amadeus, this certainly deserves mention: in the most difficult times for the state, when the treasury was under extreme pressure, he not only did not allow anything to be taken away from the churches, but also relieved, with truly royal generosity, the calamities of those afflicted by poverty.

Following his example, your father, King Charles Emmanuel, took such careful concern for the poor that, for their nourishment and relief, while preserving the resources of the churches and religious colleges, he founded, enlarged, and endowed houses for the support of the poor, orphanages, and hospitals; and whenever the need arose—and it arose [Column 0015] very often—he generously distributed money among citizens crushed by poverty.

When we speak of these deeds of your ancestors, King Victor Amadeus, we speak also of you. So many proofs of your religion, piety, and constancy in upholding discipline are celebrated, as well as of your clemency, beneficence, and generosity, especially toward the unfortunate, that you seem never to have endured being surpassed in virtue by any of them.

Yet we shall not undertake to address and describe these matters individually and in detail, because your well-known and well-tested exceptional modesty prevents us. We would rather deprive you of the testimony you deserve than risk injuring that modesty.

Meanwhile, you see where this entire discourse of ours leads. Since the sound instruction of religion and moral discipline was transmitted to posterity through the vigilance, diligence, labor, and work of Saint Maximus, and since it has passed through your ancestors to you yourself in such a way that it has always been preserved whole and unharmed, and continues to be preserved, with the greatest care, assistance, and zeal, the only thing remaining is that the monuments of the bishop’s genius, learning, and wisdom which he left behind should be regarded as belonging by right to you.

Accordingly, all of those works that have so far been found, illuminated by our command with annotations, explanations, and a preface, collected into a single volume and committed to print—and although it may appear that we are sending them to you not so much as a gift as restoring them to you—we are nevertheless assured by your exceptional graciousness and your outstanding goodwill and reverence toward the Apostolic See that Your Majesty will receive this act, whether restoration or gift, as a certain token of our supreme devotion and benevolence toward you.

Since we are fully persuaded of this, we most lovingly bestow the apostolic blessing upon you and upon your entire royal family, while praying earnestly for your welfare.

Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, on 10 July 1784, in the tenth year of our pontificate.

## [Column 0015]

# Preface

## [Column 0015] [XIII]

### I

The esteem and renown in which the homilies, sermons, and other minor works of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, were held can be understood above all from this: scarcely had he exchanged this mortal life for immortality in the fullness of glory when the writer Gennadius—distinguished both for his reputation for learning and as a contemporary of that age—in his book entitled *On Illustrious Men*, not merely listed these works but also commended them, as having proceeded from a teacher who had been sufficiently attentive to the divine Scriptures and sufficiently capable of teaching the people extemporaneously.

Gennadius specifically mentioned a considerable number of these homilies, sermons, and minor works, indicating their titles and contents; he referred to the remainder in general terms because he had indeed read them at some time but had not retained them at all closely.

### II

Afterward, a large part of these works began to be copied separately, for the convenience of the churches, and gathered into codices together with homilies and sermons of various other Fathers, long before the age of Albinus Flaccus, or Alcuin, the Benedictine monk. It consequently happened, partly through the carelessness and partly through the ignorance of scribes, that the works were either circulated without any author’s name or were assigned in their headings to authors other than Maximus.

In distinguishing these works, separating them from those belonging to others, and restoring them to Maximus, it can scarcely be said how much time and labor I have expended.

# Part I  
## The Scholarly and Manuscript Resources Used, and the Order in Which This Edition Was Completed

## [Column 0015]

### III

First of all, I considered it of the utmost importance to determine what had been done by those who had previously undertaken the burden and care of publishing the works of the holy bishop, and on what monuments and arguments they had relied when judging that some of them should be counted among the genuine works, while others should be rejected as doubtful or spurious.

Accordingly, I obtained for my use all the editions of Maximus’s works that had so far been prepared—not only those containing all the homilies and sermons that could then be found by investigation, but also those presenting certain homilies or several sermons that had either been omitted by others or had been included in some ancient collection which earlier editors had either never seen or had published from an old codex with insufficient accuracy.

When I learned that one Damian, a Benedictine monk of Asciennes, had devoted a long period of work to collecting the homilies of this holy bishop—the first of all to publish them in print—and discovered that his collection, which death had prevented him from issuing, had eventually been edited by John Gymnicus and published at Cologne in 1535, I turned to it and examined it carefully.

In reading it, I observed that it contained none of Damian’s annotations, but that he was mentioned [Column 0017] with the highest praise only in the dedicatory letter, because he had enriched the Church with the works of Saint Maximus of Turin.

After that, I examined with the greatest diligence the editions of Galesinius, Theophilus Raynaudus, and Gallandius. I also spent day and night handling the works in which Combefis, John Mabillon, Ludovico Antonio Muratori, Edmund Martène—and why should I mention them all?—had published separate monuments of the genius of this same Maximus.

Then I applied myself to reading the writings of distinguished men skilled in history and critical scholarship. These men had certainly not merely discussed the minor works of that holy bishop; they had also determined what should be judged to be done concerning them.

### IV

Among these, after Gennadius and Honorius of Autun, were John Trithemius, Erasmus of Rotterdam, Sixtus of Siena, Latino Latini, Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, Cardinal Caesar Baronius, Philip Labbe, the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur who edited the works of Saints Ambrose and Augustine, Natalis Alexander, John Albert Fabricius, William Cave, Louis Ellies Dupin, Casimir Oudin, [XV] Sebastian Tillemont, Remy Ceillier, the brothers Peter and Jerome Ballerini, and many others whom there is not even time to name. I gladly and gratefully acknowledge that their labors benefited me greatly.

First, their general agreement in attributing these minor works to Maximus caused me to decide that more homilies and sermons ought to be credited to him. Second, these writers persuaded me to attribute certain works only recently discovered to that same holy bishop: although they had not seen them, they had learned from their predecessors and stated clearly enough that they should be assigned to Maximus.

Third, I confess that from these same writers I learned how exceptional was the ability of the holy Bishop of Turin to deliver sermons extemporaneously. It is therefore not surprising if there is such a large quantity and abundance of sermons and homilies bearing the name of this same Maximus.

Fourth, I testify that with the assistance of these writers I corrected many passages of our holy bishop that had previously been shamefully corrupted. In this respect I benefited especially from the labors of Erasmus, Latino Latini of Viterbo, the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, and the Ballerini brothers.

The diligence of Erasmus in distinguishing Maximus’s minor works and testing them against manuscript codices can be understood from many other sources, and especially from Casimir Oudin. In the second volume of his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, published at Frankfurt in 1722, Oudin discusses the Rotterdam edition of the works of Saint Ambrose, begun by Erasmus himself and completed by Custerus in 1527. Among other things he says:

> “It contains brief orations, letters, and addresses to the people. Erasmus has no doubt that the last of these are spurious, since he says that they contain nothing of the Ambrosian vein. John Custerus likewise, in his edition of the works of Saint Ambrose, attributes all of them to Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, both on the authority of manuscript codices and on that of printed editions.”

I shall say this briefly about Latino Latini. After completing his edition of Tertullian’s works, in collecting and illuminating which he had devoted prolonged and diligent labor, he turned, in obedience to Pope Gregory XIII, to preparing for publication, accurately and in orderly fashion, the treatises and letters of Saint Cyprian.

As a result, he gained extensive opportunities to read, examine, and explain the writings that many other Fathers had committed to literature. He recorded many observations that he had made in them in his *Commentaries*, which were finally published in 1576 under the title *Sacred and Profane Library*.

In this *Library*, he restored to Maximus certain homilies that either lacked titles or bore pseudonymous titles. He also corrected others, which had been corrupted in various places through the fault of copyists, in accordance with the authority of superior manuscript codices. In this way he enabled them to emerge into public view after recovering their genuine brilliance.

Afterward, the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, in the appendices to the works of Saint Ambrose and to volume V of the works of Saint Augustine, not only arranged for whatever homilies and sermons of Maximus they had brought together to be printed as accurately as they could, but also, by adding various readings that they had discovered in ancient codices, showed which readings they themselves judged preferable.

In this respect I see that the diligence of the Ballerini brothers in their appendix to the sermons of Saint Leo was equal.

### V

Although, as I have said, I owe very much to the writers whom I have named above, I nevertheless did not think that I should rely on them so exclusively that I would not myself search for, discover, read, and compare manuscript codices with one another. Where such codices existed in the libraries of cities separated from us by great distances, I arranged for them to be examined by men whose reputation in these studies was exceptional, and for anything discovered in those codices that differed from the printed editions to be reported to us.

I learned that three codices in particular were of this kind.

[Column 0019] The first belonged to the monastery of Saint Gall in Switzerland. Concerning this codex, Father Dom Magnus Hungenblykerus, prefect of the library of Saint Gall and a monk of outstanding learning, wrote to us courteously, as was his custom, on 5 January 1779. He stated that he agreed with John Mabillon, a man of immortal memory, and with Martin Gerbert, the most learned abbot and prince of Saint Blaise, that this parchment codex in folio, written in Lombard characters, was no later than the eighth century.

He said that it falsely bore the name of Saint Augustine. Nothing in it, he maintained, consisted of homilies or sermons that could be attributed to Augustine. This was evident, he said, from another ninth-century codex belonging to the same library, also written in Lombard characters, which bore the following heading:

> “A very ancient volume of the homilies of Maximus, bishop, on various feasts throughout the year.”

Since precisely the same homilies were contained both in this codex and in the older one, this ought certainly to be strong evidence that the scribe had made a serious mistake in declaring Augustine the author of Maximus’s minor works.

He further differed from Mabillon in that he counted no more than ninety homilies of Maximus in both codices, whereas Mabillon counted ninety-seven. But the sole reason for Mabillon’s judgment, he said, was that he had thought there were as many homilies of Maximus as there are books *On the Sacraments*—seven books that, in my opinion, are less correctly ascribed to Ambrose.

I shall discuss this matter at the appropriate place.

## VI

The second of the principal codices which I mentioned is the codex of the former monastery of Nonantola in the territory of Modena, now belonging to the Roman library of the Cistercian monks of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme. This codex too is a parchment volume in folio, marked with the number 90, as its outer cover shows, although inside, on page 1, it bears the number 134. In antiquity, as in the more careful execution and integrity of its writing, it surpasses the other codices of that library, and belongs to the seventh, or at latest the eighth, century of the Church. The formation of its letters is Roman, tending slightly, as they say, toward the Lombardic script of the second period.

From pages 129 to 169 it contains sixty items, partly homilies and partly sermons. Concerning these, the eminent Cardinal Besutius stated the following in the catalogue of the library of Santa Croce: “I am certain that they have Saint Maximus as their author.”

When I saw this codex celebrated by Mabillon and Blanchini, I read it with the greatest care. With the assistance of the most learned and most courteous Father Dom Cyprian Travacato, professor of Greek in the monastery of Santa Croce, and prefect of the library established through the zeal and work of the learned Father Abbot Rancati, I collated it with another parchment codex in quarto belonging to the same library. This second codex is written in an elegant, rounded Roman script; it is numbered 94, although inside it bears the number 67, and, according to Cardinal Besutius, belongs to the twelfth century of the Church.

This second codex is certainly more recent, but nevertheless deserving of the highest regard. At the beginning it contains exorcisms over the possessed; next, two letters of the supreme pontiff A.—that is, as I believe, Alexander III—the first addressed to the monks of San Benedetto Padilironense, the second to A., bishop of Reggio. Both letters were written to settle a dispute that had arisen concerning the estate of Saint Caesarius between those monks of Padilirone and the monks of Nonantola. Finally, from page 5 to page 163, it contains ninety-six homilies or sermons of Saint Maximus.

Among these are forty-eight sermons in which scarcely anything differing from the texts presented by codex 90 can be detected. Since both codices moreover have the same titles of the sermons and the same beginnings, there can be no doubt that Maximus ought to be regarded as their author. This too was the opinion of Cardinal Besutius, a man highly skilled in antiquarian matters; and the passages read before the homilies and sermons in the second codex clearly confirm it. For first there are these verses:

> Behold a book full, and joyful with the highest nectar,  
>   
> Rich in the sayings of Maximus, for through them it shines fruitful.  
>   
> Here the prudent reader, finder of virtue in conduct,  
>   
> Is nourished by food rich in the milk of children,  
>   
> And by solid food, certainly worthy of the mature.  
>   
> If at first a vigorous treatment should seem to appear,  
>   
> Yet let him not avoid it, if he keeps his eyelids from falling;  
>   
> Finally, if he studies, if his mind does not nod, drunken,  
>   
> He will draw from here great things suited to many virtues.

These barbarous verses are immediately followed by a preface, after which comes the title: “Here begin the sermons of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin.”

## VII

Since we have begun speaking of the codices of the library of Santa Croce, it does not seem out of place briefly to discuss the two lectionary books preserved there. They are parchment volumes in folio, written in rather large semi-Gothic letters, as they are called. They contain altogether twelve sermons of Saint Maximus. From them I extracted several passages full of usefulness and entirely worthy of being transferred into our present collection.

## VIII

It remains for me to speak of the codex which, as I noted above, must be considered the third among the principal codices. It belongs to the Ambrosian Library of Milan, is written in Lombardic letters, dates from the eighth century of the Christian era, and is marked with the letter C, number 98.

I understand that this codex was held in very high esteem by eminent men, especially by Mabillon and Muratori. It is therefore all the more regrettable that it is defective in many places and lacks both its beginning and its final pages. The consequence has been that certain works contained in the same codex could not be brought to light without being reduced by many large portions of their text.

When I inquired about this codex from Giovanni Battista Branca, a truly learned and diligent man who, with great distinction, holds the office of acting prefect of the library, I learned the following: the codex once belonged to the monastery of Bobbio; it subsequently disappeared from there; and long afterward it was acquired at a high price by the eminent man, outstanding in learning and virtue, Cardinal Federico Borromeo, who brought it into the celebrated Ambrosian Library—an illustrious ornament not merely of Milan but of all Italy.

Several sermons can be seen in the same codex, but most of them are lamentably torn apart and curtailed. Some bear the names of their authors; others do not. Some of them are attributed to Maximus. Those who praise and defend the reliability of so ancient and excellent a codex do not consider it sufficiently trustworthy for its authority alone to determine and establish to which of the Fathers each sermon ought to be attributed.

Ludovico Antonio Muratori copied seventy-seven sermons from it, and inserted in the fourth volume of his *Anecdota* several that had not previously been published. Enough has now been said about codex 98 of the Ambrosian Library.

I shall next discuss the remaining codices that were of great use to me, and I shall do so as briefly as possible. First I shall mention the one recently acquired by the Ambrosian Library itself, which we have learned was written in the eleventh century. It is a parchment codex containing a homily attributed to Maximus, *On the Tradition of the Creed*. Canon Giovanni Battista Branca, whom I have just mentioned, copied it and took care to send it to us together with the variant readings of codex 98. I mention this so that everyone may know how grateful we are to a man endowed with such exceptional learning and courtesy.

Let the reader understand the following concerning the other Milanese codices. As Canon Antonio Francesco Frisius, theologian of the imperial basilica of Monza, an illustrious man of brilliant talent and refined learning, informed us, there were formerly in the Ambrosian Basilica two parchment volumes in folio, copied in the year 1514 by Canon Casula. One still survives; the other has perished through the injury of time. Yet Casula’s copy of the latter is extant.

From both, Frisius extracted several homilies bearing the name of Maximus. In my view, the foremost place among them belongs to the homily entitled *On the Restoration of the Greater Church of Milan*, for it contributes substantially to establishing the date of Maximus. I shall discuss the others in the admonitions which I shall appropriately place before each homily and sermon in due course.

Frisius also consulted three codices altogether written in the eleventh century. The first two belonged to the chapter of Monza; the third belonged to the library of the metropolitan church of Milan. Whatever he found in them worthy of our work and labor, he diligently arranged to have transcribed and safely conveyed to us. But enough has now been said about the Milanese and Monzan codices.

## IX

Now for the Subalpine codices. Information about several of them was conveyed to us through the good offices of Joseph Vernazza of Alba, a nobleman and most devoted student of antiquity. As soon as he learned that Pope Pius VI had imposed upon us the task of collecting and publishing the works of Saint Maximus, he persuaded his friend Francesco Meyranesius, theologian of the Academy of Turin and highly skilled in Christian antiquities, not to hesitate to place at our disposal what he had acquired through long study for the purpose of illuminating the monuments of the holy bishop.

Meyranesius had already examined four codices and had compared them thoughtfully and carefully with the published texts. From them he had drawn much that could contribute both usefulness and distinction to an edition, if a more accurate one should eventually be prepared. Wishing to perform an act agreeable to his friend and beneficial to the Church, he generously shared these materials with us.

Of those four codices, the first is from Turin; the second and third formerly belonged to the monastery of Saint Dalmatianus of Pedona; and the fourth belonged to the priory of Appannum, which was situated in the territory of Saluzzo.

The first bears the following inscription, added by a more recent hand: “For the use of the greater church of Turin.” It contains 122 items, partly homilies and partly sermons of Maximus, many of which have not yet seen the light of publication. I shall later provide a catalogue of them and describe the titles and beginnings of each homily and sermon. At the same time I shall show that many more discourses were delivered by Maximus, which perished through the envious ravages of time.

For the present I shall note this: in this first codex, as in the other three, the forms of most of the letters have been wholly or almost wholly effaced, so that scarcely certain fragments remain, which an experienced reader can readily understand or supply without great difficulty. The codex is a parchment volume in folio. Since it was written as early as the eleventh century of the Christian era for the use of the Church of Turin, there is certainly nothing to prevent us from believing that it was copied from excellent exemplars. Its distinctive feature is a continuous sequence and a sufficiently exact arrangement of the homilies, together with their accompanying titles.

The second codex, which we said belonged to the monastery of Saint Dalmatian the Martyr in the district of Pedona, is likewise a parchment volume in folio. That district, after the city of Pedona—once situated at the foot of the Alps—had been destroyed, was assigned by the authority of the Apostolic See to the bishop of Mondovì.

Although this codex too is mutilated in many parts, the numbers written in it clearly show that it once contained 242 homilies and 20 sermons. The catalogue is missing, and I believe that it was removed and torn away from the volume.

At the head of the first homily, in capital letters, is written:

> In the name of Christ. Amen. Here begin the homilies of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin.

The first homily bears the title:

> At the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.

It begins as follows:

> How great is the joy, and how great the gathering.

The homilies that followed concerned the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany, the Baptism of Christ, Lent, Easter, the Ascension of the Lord, and Pentecost. These are followed by sermons, which we mentioned shortly before.

The period in which this codex was written can be learned from what I shall now add, which can be read at the very end of the codex:

> Receive, O martyr Dalmatian, the little gift that I offer,  
>   
> From the monk Atpertus, in your monastery,  
>   
> In the holy monastery of the city of Pedona.  
>   
> Maximus, bishop of the city of Turin, once wrote this . . .  
>   
> We too copied [lacuna] by command of our venerable abbot Ratpertus . . . while our lord Charles, king of the Lombards and Franks, was reigning, in the year . . .

This codex must therefore be assigned to the eighth century. For it is established from other evidence that Ratpertus presided over the monastery of Pedona at the time when Charlemagne held power. He began to reign in 768 and was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III in the year 800, on the birthday of Christ the Savior.

The third codex, which we established had belonged to the same monastery of Pedona, was written by a monk named Joseph while Abbot Henry governed the monastery and King Henry held sovereignty in Italy. At the end of the codex we read:

> Joseph, a monastic librarian and skilled  
>   
> Scribe, copied the book which you see, O greatest bishop of the city of Turin,  
>   
> At Pedona, while Henry was abbot,  
>   
> Continually building up the library with many other books,  
>   
> While King Henry too was reigning.

It is therefore easily understood that this codex must be assigned to the eleventh century. It too is a parchment volume, in quarto. Although not arranged in order, it contains 170 homilies and 40 sermons. On its front is written, in large vermilion capitals, the name of Saint Maximus.

At the beginning it presents a homily whose opening is:

> A few days ago I had warned your Charity, brothers, that, as religious and holy men, you should avoid every pollution of idols, etc.

Muratori published this homily in the fourth volume of his *Anecdota*. The final homily begins:

> A few days ago we not inappropriately discussed this priestly office, etc.

Mabillon copied this homily from a codex at Saint Gall and included it in the first volume of the *Museum Italicum*.

I come now to the fourth codex. It too is a parchment volume, but in small folio. As I noted above, it formerly belonged to the priory of the monks of Appannum. By a later decree of the pontiffs, possession of the buildings and estates of that priory was granted to the bishop of Saluzzo.

It contains, as is clear from the numbers attached to the surviving sermons and homilies, 31 sermons and 70 homilies. But by the savage hand of some unknown and unlearned person, many leaves were torn out and removed, with the result that the public literary heritage suffered a great loss of a substantial part of these homilies and sermons.

At the beginning of the codex there is an inscription written in red letters:

> In the name of Christ. Amen. Homilies of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin.

At the end of the final leaf we read:

> Receive the collected little book which you requested,  
> Of Maximus of Turin, containing the homilies he had written,  
> So that you may read . . . Waldo, the monk, copied it . . .  
> [lacuna]  
> In our library . . .  
> [lacuna]  
> And I shall copy the remaining things again.  
> Under the rule of our lord Lothair.

This codex therefore belongs to the ninth century of the Church, or at the latest to the tenth. The forms of the letters clearly show that it is not more recent. It is uncertain, however, whether it was written under Lothair I, son of Louis the Pious, who ruled in 841, or under the other Lothair, who gained the imperial power in 947.

Since these four codices are of remarkable antiquity and display an extraordinary agreement in assigning the homilies to their author Maximus, there was certainly no reason for me to doubt that certain unpublished works bearing the name of that same Maximus in these codices ought to be attributed to Maximus himself. Among them are three excellent treatises *On Baptism*, which I shall present after the homilies and sermons as a specimen not only of Maximian doctrine but also of his knowledge of sacred rites.

## X

The Vercelli codices must be included among these Subalpine codices. Canon Antonio Francesco Frisius, whom we have already mentioned with praise, examined and thoroughly reviewed three of them with the greatest care. Whatever he found in them worthy of notice, he committed to writing and diligently arranged to share with me.

The first is a homiliary, codex number 66, in very large folio, dating from the twelfth or thirteenth century. It is preserved intact, together with other codices of which the cathedral archive possesses a notable abundance. In this codex is found a homily of our holy bishop entitled *On Miracles*. It is immediately followed by five sermons on Saint Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli, and then by two sermons on the feast of Saint Laurence the Martyr.

The second codex, seventh in the series of the Vercelli cathedral archive, is likewise a parchment volume in very large folio and belongs to the eleventh century. It contains one homily bearing the name of Saint Maximus, with the title:

> On the Octave of the Lord, that is, the Kalends of January.

Gymnicus and others later published it.

Regarding the third, I wish to note that it too is a parchment codex, belongs to the same eleventh century, and contains eighteen homilies. Although these had long since been published in print, this codex nevertheless confirms to a remarkable degree that they ought to be attributed to Maximus.

## XI

The same Frisius informed us that, in addition to the Subalpine codices, he had seen four other homiliary books in the library of the cathedral church of Novara. From them, as from springs, he had drawn much that he foresaw would provide great distinction and usefulness to this edition of ours. I shall briefly explain what sort of codices they are.

The first is a parchment volume in folio and is number seven in the series of the manuscripts of that church. It contains two homilies of Saint Maximus entitled *On the Common Feast of Many Martyrs*. The beginning of the first is:

> The crown of all the martyrs shines, etc.

The beginning of the second is:

> It ought to be enough for the advancement of our salvation, etc.

Both are extant in various manuscript codices, which differ from this Vercelli codex in certain places, as we shall duly note when the time requires.

The second codex, likewise a parchment volume in folio of the same twelfth century, contains that one homily whose beginning we have mentioned:

> It ought to be enough for us, etc.

The third is older, likewise a parchment volume in folio, marked number 27 and adorned with initials beautifully and skillfully painted in various colors. It belongs to the ninth century of the Church, or at the latest to the tenth. It contains nothing but homilies and discourses of Maximus.

At the beginning it presents those delivered before the Nativity of the Lord; next, several of those concerning the other mysteries of Christ the Savior. Although all of these had previously been published, they can nevertheless be greatly illuminated with the help of this codex and attributed to Maximus with greater security.

The fourth codex is comparable to it, though not in age—for it was written in the eleventh century—but in the elegance of its paintings and letters and in the arrangement of its collection of homilies and sermons. It too is a parchment volume in folio and has supplied us with considerable assistance in preparing this edition with greater accuracy.

Let this suffice concerning the Subalpine and Novara codices.

## XII

The course of the work now requires me to discuss the Florentine codices. I should like the reader briefly to learn what first impelled me to examine them.

When I was staying in Florence in 1778, letters were unexpectedly delivered to me—although I had not even suspected anything of the kind—written on the fifth of April by order of Pope Pius VI. I was informed that I should undertake the task of collecting and publishing the works of Saint Maximus of Turin.

Although I knew that I was unequal to the burden, and not only acknowledged but also openly professed my inability to bear it, I was nevertheless urged by further letters to undertake so great a work. At last I obeyed, and reflected that what I did not trust myself to accomplish through talent or experience, especially in this branch of study, I might perhaps achieve through diligence.

Accordingly, after surveying in my mind everything that might contribute to the completion of the work, and deciding above all that attention must be given to ancient manuscript codices, I considered that I would deserve blame if, while living in a city distinguished by an abundance of such codices—most of them preserved with the greatest care in the Laurentian Library—I did not also go there and seek assistance for the work and undertaking I had planned.

There is no reason for me here to pursue the glories of that library by praising them, since the most learned men—Mabillon, Montfaucon, Pearson, Vossius, Lambecius, and almost countless others—long ago fulfilled that task, and their testimony has been entrusted to the everlasting memory of mankind.

I shall say only this in brief: the library had been enriched by the Medici, the great dukes of Etruria, with many distinguished codices of elegance and antiquity, through their supreme generosity for the benefit of the public literary heritage. It was subsequently enlarged by Francis I, the Pious and Most Fortunate, through the addition of the Gaddian codices, which he had acquired for himself at enormous expense. Finally, it was expanded in a wondrous manner by Peter Leopold, Archduke of Austria and great duke of Etruria, who transferred to it a very large number of codices that had previously been scattered and hidden, as though in darkness, in certain lesser-known libraries.

Although I had collected much before beginning my examination of the Laurentian codices, I still remained uncertain whether the numerous homilies and sermons should be attributed to Maximus or to some other Father. In certain codices, some of these homilies and sermons bore no author’s name; some bore the name of Maximus; others bore the names of different authors.

But after I had been granted permission to read the codices of that library, and had found, examined, and collated them with the help of the extremely accurate catalogue prepared and completed with the greatest zeal by Angelo Maria Bandini, a truly learned man, canon of the Laurentian Basilica and prefect of the library, the result was as I had hoped. I restored to Maximus a considerable number of discourses that had been wrongly attributed to others through the error of copyists; and I relegated to the class of doubtful or spurious works others that bore the name of Maximus less securely or falsely.

Almost all these Laurentian codices are homiliaries—that is, they contain homilies of the saints which were customarily read on Sundays, on saints’ birthdays and feasts possessing proper Gospels, at Easter, and at Pentecost, together with those for the weekdays.

> **[Note: [Col. 0025]** See Du Cange, *Glossarium mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, s.v. “HOMILIARIUS,” p. 1093, Venetian edition of 1738, vol. III.]

These homilies of the Fathers were customarily read publicly and were sometimes even translated into the vernacular, so that everyone might more easily understand what was being said.

> **[Note: [Col. 0025]** Synod of Tours, A.D. 813, canon 17, p. 1025, vol. IV of the *Councils*, Paris edition of 1714; and Synod of Mainz, A.D. 847, canon 2, p. 8, vol. V of the same *Councils*.]

In the sixth century and thereafter, homiliary codices belonged not only to cathedral churches but also to parish and monastic churches; indeed, in at least some regions every priest had his own homiliary codices.

With regard to parish churches, a passage from the Synod of Vaison, held in the year 529, is particularly noteworthy.

> **[Note: [Col. 0026]** Canon 2, p. 1105, vol. II of the same edition of the *Councils*.]

For monastic homiliaries, our foremost example will be the Florentine codex of Santa Croce, now the Laurentian codex, which contains homilies of certain Fathers for the entire year. It is divided into two parts. The first bears the following inscription:

> **BOOK OF THE MOST HOLY TRINITY OF THE HERMITAGE, part 1.**  
> Homilies from the First Sunday of Advent to the Easter of the Resurrection.

The second bears this inscription:

> Homilies from the Easter of the Resurrection to the Last Sunday after Pentecost.

As for the homiliary books belonging to individual priests, it will be sufficient to consult the *Capitulary* of Haito, bishop of Basel, who lived in the ninth century of the Church.

> **[Note: [Col. 0026]** Canon 6, vol. IV of the *Councils*, p. 1241.]

Since there must have been such a great abundance of these codices, why should it seem surprising that not all were written by skilled scribes, that many fell into the hands of unlearned copyists, and that they are consequently full of defective titles and false attributions?

Nevertheless, several are of the finest quality. Such are:

1. The codex of Santa Croce just mentioned, which in my judgment belongs to the eleventh century;

2. The codex that first belonged to the Church of Meaux and now belongs to the Laurentian Library;

3. Two codices of the Church of Florence, which I believe were prepared for choral use and which display, in their initial letters, various emblems of the Christian religion, beautifully painted. These two codices now belong to the Laurentian Library;

4. A fourteenth-century codex in which the homilies are distributed in the same series and order as those presented in codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, which I remember discussing above.

As for the Lucchese codices and those of the monastery of the monks of Saint Savior of Monte Amiata—formerly Cistercian—in the territory of Siena, from which our collection at various times obtained some illumination, I shall speak elsewhere.

## XIII

The course of the work now requires me to discuss the Roman codices. As soon as it was announced and made public that Pope Pius VI had instructed us to devote all our study and labor to illuminating and publishing the works of Saint Maximus, it is difficult to imagine how many men distinguished for their learning united in bringing us assistance, wishing to make the matter both especially pleasing to so great a pontiff and particularly useful to the Christian commonwealth.

Among them, Peter Aloysius Galletti, a Benedictine monk of the Cassinese Congregation, now bishop of Cyrene, distinguished for his learning and famous for the many books he has published, conferred upon us a gift of extraordinary kindness, courtesy, and generosity. He gave us various readings which he had extracted from the codices of the Vatican Library, together with several sermons which he had copied from them with the greatest care and diligence.

Although this kind of gift was so useful to me that I can scarcely, or perhaps not at all, express how much I owe on that account to the distinguished bishop, I nevertheless understood that very much remained to be done both in that same Vatican Library, certainly the richest of all, and in the archive of the Basilica of Saint Peter. Had I failed to examine and investigate these collections thoroughly, I would certainly have fallen short both of the work I had undertaken and of the public benefit.

Accordingly, after obtaining from Pope Pius VI permission for both those sanctuaries of venerable antiquity to be opened to me, I began to visit the Vatican Library frequently. When I found more than thirty homiliary codices there, whose oldest examples seemed assignable to the beginning of the eighth century—for they are written in square Roman characters—I could not restrain myself from reading them eagerly and simultaneously investigating whether they agreed with one another or differed in any place.

Almost all these codices have been preserved intact. Some once belonged to Cardinal Sirleto, most renowned for his learning, who wrote certain annotations in them in his own hand; some belonged to Christina, Queen of Sweden, distinguished no less by her literary than by her royal glory; and some finally belonged to Cardinal Pietro Ottoboni.

In the archive of the Basilica of Saint Peter I likewise saw, examined, and collated seven homiliary codices. Added to the Vatican codices, they proved astonishingly useful for correcting readings and supplied assistance not only for defending with greater security the attribution to Maximus of many homilies and sermons, but also for completing them wherever they had been diminished, whether in printed editions or in other handwritten volumes, through the carelessness or ignorance of copyists.

I shall add this exceptional point concerning both the Vatican codices and those of the Basilica of Saint Peter: they ought to be preferred to all the others both for the corrected quality of their text and for the brightness and elegance of their script and the harmony of their arrangement. I shall describe their form and indicate their age in the catalogue of codices which I shall shortly place before the eyes of readers engraved in copperplate.

## XIV

I shall add the Lateran codices to those of the Vatican. In the archive of that basilica I found four homiliary codices, likewise written with considerable exactness in the eleventh century, as I have convinced myself, and worthy of being compared with the better Vatican codices.

All are parchment volumes in very large folio, written in sufficiently bright and elegant characters. Among them are two larger codices which, according to the inscription on the first page, were prepared by Secundinus, Bishop of Taormina.

From these I extracted several previously unpublished works of our Maximus. With their help I also either established more firmly the attribution to their author of certain works published long ago or corrected their text.

## XV

Three homiliary codices were shown to me from the Chisian Library, which, as is widely known and attested, abounds in manuscript codices of exceptional quality. Two belong to the eleventh century and the third to the fifteenth. They formerly belonged to the Church of Anagni.

From them I extracted several variant readings and certain works of Saint Maximus of Turin that had not yet been published. I shall bring them forth later, when the appropriate time requires.

## XVI

The library of the Fathers of the Oratory at the Vallicella is also remarkably rich in an abundance of manuscript codices. Among them are fifteen well-preserved parchment volumes, some belonging to the twelfth century and others to the thirteenth.

In these I found fifty discourses bearing the name of Maximus, which I collated with the exemplar of the works of Saint Maximus that I customarily used. The extent of the benefit and assistance I derived from them may be understood from our admonitions, which precede the homilies and sermons, and from the observations that I took care to place beneath almost every page.

As for the reputation and value of these codices, I prefer that they be learned from the commentaries of the distinguished man Joseph Blanchini rather than from any praise of mine. They are of such importance that they have no need of our eloquence.

Meanwhile, I wish to testify that I owe much more than I can express in words to Father Simone de Magistris, a priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of Saint Philip, for the zeal, diligence, and prolonged labor with which he assisted me while I was collating these codices.

## XVII

Since I have spoken above of the codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, I shall refrain from discussing them, lest I repeat what has already been done.

Concerning the libraries of the Colonna, Conti, Barberini, and Albani families, I shall mention only this: I did visit them and examine with my own eyes all their codices containing anything pertaining to our Maximus, but I found nothing that had not already been thoroughly treated by earlier editors or widely published.

In the Casanatense Library I saw two parchment homiliary codices in very large folio, written in an elegant and clear Roman script and sufficiently ancient, for they belong to the eleventh century of the Church. I shall show in the admonitions what I obtained from them.

## XVIII

The eminent Cardinal de Zelada, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, greatly enlarged and enriched our collection. He not only showed me a large parchment codex in folio of the tenth century, belonging to his extremely well-equipped private library and given to him by the canons of the cathedral church of Orvieto, but also ordered it to be lent to me. In this way he wished to perform an act pleasing to Pope Pius VI, who had deserved so well of him through his beneficence, and enabled me, whenever I had leisure, to collate the codex at my discretion with the exemplar of Maximus’s works that I customarily used.

The additions made to this edition through the assistance of this codex and of two others, both of which are older than the fourteenth century and which the same eminent cardinal also generously placed at my disposal, will be shown at the appropriate time by our admonitions and annotations. At the same time, they will enable everyone to recognize how closely that great man has bound us to himself by so substantial a benefit.

## XIX

Let the final codex be that which formerly belonged to the Church of Esztergom and which, not many years ago, came into the possession of Francesco Carrara, a most distinguished and learned bishop who is secretary of the Sacred Congregation of the Council.

It is made entirely of exceptionally white parchment. Written in a wonderfully bright and elegant script, it dates from approximately the beginning of the sixteenth century of the Church. It was ornamented by Giovanni Boccardino, a Florentine citizen, with paintings in which red vermilion and tawny gold are splendidly varied, depicting the principal mysteries of the Christian religion.

That painter’s exceptional ability in this genre is demonstrated not only by this codex but also by several books in the Florentine Laurentian Library, as well as by the choir books of the Benedictines of Saint Peter of Perugia.

I return to the Carrara codex, which contains the Breviary of the Church of Esztergom. As I examined it, I came upon exactly seven homilies of Saint Maximus. Their character and the variant readings they offer have been duly noted by us in their proper places.

Here I ought to speak at length, as would be fitting and as I should, of the many and great benefits conferred upon me by Bishop Francesco Carrara, and of his merits, were I not restrained by his modesty and afraid that, while attempting to magnify the glory of so great a man, I might instead diminish it.

I believe that enough has now been said about the Roman codices.

## XX

Now I shall proceed farther and speak of those manuscripts that exist in the libraries or archives of monasteries and cities within the Papal States.

First, the very ancient monastery of Subiaco supplied us with several items from the manuscripts that voracious antiquity has allowed it to retain. What these are, and what benefits they have brought to this edition of the works of Saint Maximus, I shall explain carefully in the appropriate notes, as the subject requires.

Our discussion of the manuscripts of Farfa, likewise renowned for its ancient foundation and celebrated in the speech of so many people—not merely private persons, but emperors and pontiffs as well—will not be much longer. In its archive, which Muratori and other most learned men have rightly valued so highly, there exist, among other things, two homiliaries written with Roman letter-forms, with exceptional care, elegance, and clarity. The most eminent man, Cardinal Tamburini of the Holy Roman Church, judged them to belong to the eleventh century, and I see no reason not to agree with him very strongly.

In these I came upon fourteen homilies bearing the name of Saint Maximus. The antiquity and authority of such distinguished monuments establish and confirm that these homilies, already long ago printed and published, ought certainly to be ascribed to Maximus himself.

But concerning the manuscripts of the monastery of Farfa, and concerning the homilies of Maximus contained in them, more elsewhere.

Stefano Borgia, a prelate distinguished both by his rank and by his great intelligence, his great zeal for the best arts, and the liberal and worthy learning and erudition of a nobleman, examined the Beneventan manuscripts. From them he extracted much and communicated it to me—at the express desire of Pius VI, the greatest and wisest pontiff. Our notes and annotations will reveal in due time how valuable these materials are.

## XXI

Far beyond the archives of the other monasteries, both in the extent of its site and in the excellence and abundance of its manuscripts, stands the archive of the monastery of Cassino, from which the distinguished congregation of Benedictine monks derived its noble origin and illustrious name.

I shall not pursue its praises at greater length than I both wish and am able to do. The reputation and renown of the great Christian writers Christianus Lupus, Jean Mabillon, Bernard de Montfaucon, and others deter me: they have so splendidly illuminated the monastery in their writings that anyone who undertook to discuss it again would seem less willing to add ornaments to a magnificent work than to remove them.

I shall therefore confine myself to those manuscripts in its archive that contain something capable of enlarging, expanding, or completing the edition of Maximus’s works.

First of all, however, I want the readers to know this. The keeper of that archive, P. D. Placidus Federici, a monk of the renowned Order of Saint Benedict, outstanding for his exact learning and singular expertise in critical scholarship, learned from the prelate Stefano Borgia—whom I again name here in honor—that it was very much the concern of Pius VI, pontiff of the whole Christian world, that the homilies and sermons of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, should be diligently collected and brought once more into public view in as correct a form as possible.

Federici therefore considered nothing more important than to examine, with every diligence, labor, and effort, the manuscripts entrusted to his care and fidelity; to extract from them many materials, notable both for their number and for their antiquity, integrity, and excellence; and to send them to Rome, dedicated to the name and majesty of that same pontiff, where they would be useful to us.

When these materials had been delivered to the pontiff, and he had recognized, with his supreme wisdom and insight, the great usefulness contained in the Casinensian monuments both for reclaiming and confirming certain minor works as Maximus’s and for adorning—and even enlarging—our collection, he ordered me, as soon as I could and might, to travel to Cassino, taking with me the exemplar of the works of that same Bishop of Turin which I habitually used, and to compare it carefully with the manuscripts in the archive.

I obeyed him promptly and cheerfully as a prince, and willingly as one commanding me for Maximus’s sake.

When I had arrived at Cassino, investigated everything that seemed likely to contribute to the work already undertaken, and set aside the manuscripts that I foresaw would often and greatly serve my purposes, I further asked the monks not to hesitate to assist me in comparing those manuscripts with the exemplar I had brought. Because of their benevolence and courtesy toward me, I easily obtained this: several monks who took pleasure in these studies and were well versed in the works and teachings of the Fathers promised us their assistance.

Among them was P. D. Claudius Trevisanius, a monk outstanding in his knowledge of ecclesiastical history and doctrine. With the assistance of him and his companions—Federici, however, was absent—three or four manuscripts were compared at the same time with my written exemplar. From this I gained so much benefit that I became fully confident that I could not only safely attribute sixty homilies and sermons to Maximus, but also illuminate them with the new and valuable light of variant readings.

I noticed something else in these same manuscripts that is plainly worthy of record: they generally agree so closely with the Vatican manuscripts that it is scarcely possible to detect any difference between them.

The following circumstance is even more noteworthy. The homily *On the Evangelical Fishing*, together with the fourth sermon and the seventieth sermon, *On the Nativity of Saint Lawrence*, could not have been ascribed to Maximus except on the basis of the heading of a single manuscript in the Laurentian Medicean Library. Yet the inscription of another Casinensian manuscript of excellent quality made it possible for us to attribute them to that same holy bishop with much greater certainty.

No one should be surprised that we rejected into the appendix certain sermons bearing the name of Saint Maximus in some manuscripts of the monastery of Cassino. When I perceived that they were very far removed from Maximus’s manner of speaking and style, I did not think authority and credibility should be granted to manuscripts that I knew had been written in periods when nothing was less flourishing than expertise in critical scholarship.

Nor did the benefits that reached our collection of Maximus’s works from the Casinensian congregation of monks consist only of those I have just mentioned. Rather, they were increased and extended much more widely through the care and diligence of the most reverend P. D. Dominicus Favilla, who was then the congregation’s abbot general.

When he learned from the tenth-century catalogue of the library of the ancient and celebrated monastery of Bobbio of Saint Columbanus, published by Muratori [Note: [Col. 0031] Volume III of *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, p. 819], that certain manuscripts in that monastery’s library contained minor works of our Saint, the Bishop of Turin, he ordered the abbot of Bobbio to investigate those manuscripts and report back to him.

The abbot immediately complied with Favilla’s request. But, after searching, he failed to find the manuscripts and consequently came to believe either that they had perished completely or that they had been removed and carried elsewhere, where they lay hidden, as if in darkness, in some archive or library. He therefore informed Favilla by letter that he and his associates had undertaken the search for those manuscripts in vain.

He did report, however, that among the manuscripts still preserved in his monastery eight sermons had been found bearing the name of Saint Maximus, and he arranged for them to be copied and sent to us in Rome.

When five of these sermons had been delivered to us, we discovered that they had already long before been published. The others—the first *On the Nativity of the Lord*, and the second and third *On the Praises of the Blessed Virgin Mary*—we rejected into the appendix of spurious works, because their dry and humble style seemed unworthy of so great an orator.

Let this suffice concerning the manuscripts of Bobbio. I would have omitted discussion of them had they not returned to my memory while I was proclaiming the merits of the Casinensian monks in relation to this edition.

## XXII

After the Casinensian manuscripts, it is appropriate to mention the others preserved in the libraries of the Kingdom of Naples that contributed some assistance and support to the preparation and completion of our collection of Maximus’s works.

First there present themselves the manuscripts that Angelus Maria Bandini, whom I remember having mentioned above, discovered in the library of Monte Oliveto at Naples. They are three in number, all homiliaries, and contain several orations attributed to Maximus.

We rejected five of these into the class of spurious works because they were written with less polish and were less suited to Maximus’s style.

One of these manuscripts contains a sermon beginning:

> “It has often been impressed upon your ears, brothers, etc.”

The manuscript is a parchment volume in very large folio, written in Roman script, and belongs to the eleventh century. Its testimony will therefore establish more firmly that this sermon too is Maximus’s.

A second manuscript is very similar to the first. The third is a paper volume in smaller folio, more recent, from the fourteenth century. It contains the sermon *On the Advent of the Lord*, which begins:

> “With the Godhead propitious, …”

Although this sermon bears Maximus’s name in this manuscript, it bears the name of Ambrose in many other manuscripts, especially printed ones. Let the learned decide to which of these two holy bishops it ought to be attributed. For my part, I fear that it belongs wholly to neither. But, so that I might not appear to have acted rashly, I included it among Maximus’s doubtful works.

At Naples, in the distinguished library of the Augustinians of Saint John of Carbonara, Bandini likewise read a parchment volume in medium folio, written approximately in the middle of the thirteenth century. He observed that several sermons in it were ascribed to Saint Maximus. The agreement of a large number of other manuscripts confirms and establishes that these are genuine productions of that same Saint.

The distinguished scholar extracted much from this manuscript. How much it has helped us to illuminate the edition undertaken by us will be entirely clear from the notes prefixed to each homily and sermon.

In the meantime, I wish the following to be known and carefully observed: the sermon entitled *On Works of Mercy* in that manuscript, beginning:

> “See, brothers, why you are called beloved, etc.,”

ought, in my judgment, to be removed and expunged from the catalogue of Maximus’s works. I did indeed expunge it and ordered it to be placed in the appendix of spurious works, since I found it written with far less gravity, elegance, and propriety than Maximus’s speech appears capable of bearing.

## XXIII

I now come to the Venetian manuscripts. It is remarkable how much they contributed to making our collection not merely more accurate but also more extensive.

As soon as the Most Serene Republic of Venice learned that Pius VI, the father of fathers, was deeply concerned that a new edition of the works of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin—complete in all its parts and proportions so far as possible, and perfectly finished—should be prepared, it assigned the prefect of the Library of Saint Mark the task of devoting all his labor and effort to seeking out that holy bishop’s homilies, sermons, and other minor works.

If, in the course of his search, he discovered anything unpublished or worthy of annotation, he was to copy it accurately and deliver it to the magistrate whom the Republic had designated.

The prefect, being exceptionally learned and diligent, omitted no vigilance, industry, or effort by which he might fully satisfy the prince who had issued the command. He was so fortunate that he discovered three sermons not yet published and noticed several other items in the manuscripts. These he carefully and methodically committed to writing and delivered to the magistrate.

At the magistrate’s order, all of them were placed in a handsome chest, ornamented with the papal insignia, and sent to Rome to the distinguished Julian, the Venetian Republic’s ambassador to the Holy See. He presented them to the pontiff, who received them with splendid demonstrations and expressions of gratitude, and with great evidence of his affection and devotion toward the Republic itself.

The first of the three sermons, copied from an old manuscript of the Library of Saint Mark, is the one that begins:

> “A few days ago, …”

It is also found in a manuscript of the Laurentian Medicean Library under Maximus’s name, as is clear from Bandini’s catalogue, volume I, p. 81. I shall discuss the others elsewhere, especially in the notes, at greater length.

In addition to the sermons, the same prefect supplied two homilies which, although they had been published, are nevertheless more securely attributed to Maximus by the agreement of the Venetian manuscripts.

The distinguished scholar added variant readings, which I shall not fail to insert at the appropriate places.

Finally, he informed us that only two manuscripts in the Venetian Library of Saint Mark contain sermons of Maximus. One of these is a parchment manuscript, numbered 153 and belonging to the eleventh century of the Church. It is the first part of a homiliary divided into two enormous parchment volumes in folio. These volumes once belonged to Cardinal Bessarion and were later given by that same cardinal, together with his other books, to the Republic of Venice.

The manuscript is written with reasonable accuracy.

The other manuscript is the second part of the other volume of that homiliary. Since it was found in the church of Saint Mark mixed in with a few volumes that Petrarch had donated to that church, it was transferred to the library and marked with the number 508.
