This too is a parchment volume in folio, written in the twelfth century, though not with as much correctness as books intended to be read publicly in church ordinarily require.

Let this brief account suffice concerning the manuscripts in the Library of Saint Mark at Venice.

It remains for me to mention something about the library of the canons at Padua. Its manuscript is from the fifteenth century. The same distinguished prefect of the Venetian Library of Saint Mark copied from it two sermons.

The first begins:

> “To present a sermon to your charity, etc.”

A large part of it is included in the common office of martyrs in the Roman Breviary published at Venice by Jenson in 1478.

The other sermon begins:

> “Rightly and fittingly the Church celebrates the distinctions of the blessed martyrs.”

What sort of sermons these are, and how highly they should be valued, I shall show in the notes when the time and circumstances require.

As for the manuscripts of Brescia and Verona, I shall say briefly this: John Nanni, Bishop of Brescia, and John Morosini, Bishop of Verona—both prelates outstanding for their reputation for learning and scholarship—devoted every care, diligence, and effort to ensuring that whatever existed in the manuscripts of their churches relating to Maximus should be conveyed to us, not only to please Pope Pius VI, but also so that their exertions and labors might redound to the glory of the holy bishop.

Nanni sent several sermons and homilies, together with variant readings of the highest quality. I shall discuss these in their proper places, as the occasion requires.

Morosini ordered that the *Readings*, or *Expositions of the Gospels*, should be copied from the very ancient manuscript of his chapter numbered 49 and delivered to us.

It seems to me highly probable that this is the book of Maximus entitled *On the Chapters of the Gospels*, which is mentioned by Gennadius, Honorius of Autun, and Trithemius, and which, having long been lost from our sight, was thought to have perished completely.

From the same manuscript Morosini also ordered two treatises to be copied. Although they are anonymous, they may nevertheless be considered worthy of attribution to Saint Maximus himself. Weighty reasons moved me to ascribe them to that holy man. But more on this elsewhere.

I shall say only this: through the addition of such previously unpublished works, our collection will become much richer and more excellent than the others.

## XXIV

Although we had sufficiently firm support, we were not content with the Italian manuscripts alone. We also judged that the German manuscripts ought to be consulted and compared.

Accordingly, Pope Pius VI wrote to Joseph Garampi, Bishop of Montefiascone and apostolic nuncio at the imperial court in Vienna, a man distinguished by supreme learning and an extraordinary command of the whole of antiquity. He entrusted to him the task of adorning this particular field of scholarship.

To obey so great a prince, who had deserved so well of him, Garampi himself examined the manuscript books of the Augsburg Library. Since he found none that contained anything of Maximus, he turned to the monks of the Order of Saint Benedict and strongly urged and encouraged the abbots of the monasteries of Regensburg, Göttweig, Lambach, and Reichenau to order searches among the ancient manuscript volumes of their distinguished libraries.

His exhortations were so effective that the outcome could not have been more favorable. The monks eagerly set themselves to the work. They completed very full catalogues of the homilies and sermons of Maximus; they transcribed with the greatest care variant readings of very considerable importance; and they reported the age and quality of the manuscripts in which the minor works appeared, together with the attribution of the name of the holy bishop.

This entire collection of so many excellent monuments, so fruitful and so distinguished, was sent to us by that most wise prelate. Although I can gather in thought how much I owe him, I cannot express it in words.

## XXV

Meanwhile, word had spread among many people that a considerable number of manuscripts of this kind existed in Belgium, especially in monastic libraries.

No one could have been more suitable for investigating the matter than Ignatius Busca, apostolic nuncio and Archbishop of Emesa. The pontiff ordered him to be written to and instructed him to act energetically, to investigate where the manuscripts were, and finally to report what they were like, how old they were, how accurately they had been written, and in what respects they differed from the printed editions.

He acted zealously, as he was bound to do. He entrusted the task to learned men with whom he had formed friendships, asking them to contribute their assistance because he himself, burdened with so many responsibilities, could not personally undertake the labor.

When they had carried out the search diligently, they found two manuscripts in two libraries. One of these libraries belonged to the regular canons of Saint Martin at Louvain; the other to the Cistercian monks of the monastery of Cambron.

When the nuncio learned this, he asked the distinguished canon Vandevelde, prefect of the Louvain library and also a most learned professor of theology, to compare whatever homilies and sermons of Maximus he had found in those manuscripts with the published texts and to record everything they presented that was varied or different.

He complied with the nuncio’s request. He compared the thirty homilies themselves with the edition published at Cologne in 1535 and recorded in notes whatever variations he encountered. He delivered the results to the nuncio, who did not think he should delay in sending them to Rome to the pontiff.

I shall not fail to introduce these variant readings in their proper places.

How highly those manuscripts should be valued, I prefer the readers to learn from Vandevelde’s words rather than from mine:

> “The first manuscript,” he says, “is on parchment, in the format commonly called folio. It presents the homilies *On the Temporal Cycle* and *On the Saints* in two volumes, among which several homilies of Saint Maximus occur. The following words are written inside this manuscript: ‘This book belongs to the library of the monastery of the regular canons of Saint Martin at Louvain, on the Gimstraet.’ Also: ‘We received this part of the homilies from the Florentine house of the brothers at Deventer when this house was founded, around the year of the Lord 1434.’

> “But the manuscript is much older, as is evident from the form of its letters and from the fact that no homilies of Bernard have been inserted in it, although it was admirably suited for use in reading in the refectory, for which these volumes served. All the homilies were evidently excerpted from Saint John, Bishop of Constantinople; Augustine; Pope Leo I; Gregory the Great; Bede; Haymo of Halberstadt; and finally Anselm of Canterbury.

> “The second manuscript is on paper, written in a clear script by Brother John de Waulx in the year 1620, as is noted at the end, in the format called octavo. Its title is: ‘Sermons of Blessed Maximus, Bishop of Turin. In the year 1620, [this manuscript] belongs to the library of the abbey of Cambron of the Cistercian Order in Hainaut.’”

## XXVI

Perhaps someone will wonder why, although I made such a careful enumeration of the Italian, German, and Belgian manuscripts, I did not even briefly mention the French ones.

But when that person sees how cautiously and diligently we have proceeded in examining, weighing, and judging the others, and learns in addition that the catalogue and variant readings of the French manuscripts—although long awaited—have not yet been able to reach Rome, he will not only cease to wonder but will also conclude for himself that, once they arrive, I shall certainly not allow anyone to find my zeal or diligence lacking in counting, assessing, and, as appropriate, honoring them as well.

The principal reason I did not think it necessary to wait longer was that, once it had become widely known that our collection had long since been completed and printed, almost everyone was eager that it should finally be brought into the light of public view.

## XXVII

In judging so many manuscript books, I adopted the following precaution at the outset: in general, I preferred older manuscripts to more recent ones. Next, I placed more correct manuscripts before less carefully corrected ones, even when the latter were older. Finally, I assigned greater weight to those that I knew had been copied from the best exemplars.

To distinguish these matters, I established three rules as aids. The first was the agreement of the greatest number of manuscripts, especially the older and more accurate ones. The second was the authority of ancient monuments and writers. The third was the agreement of historians and experts in critical scholarship.

Fortified by these supports, I rightly claimed many minor works for Maximus, even though some people either denied or doubted that certain of them ought to be attributed to him.

If at times some or nearly all of these supports were lacking, I still could not bring myself to judge that works should be taken away from the holy bishop when the similarity of style and expression, the doctrine, the characteristic Maximian manner of citing passages of Sacred Scripture, and the authority of one or another manuscript together suggested that they had been written by him.

Nor could I be deterred from attributing certain minor works to Maximus merely because their language was humbler than that of the others. I am not unaware that holy bishops, especially those of that period, commonly used loftier and more elegant language when they had distinguished hearers learned in eloquence and doctrine, but humbler language when they addressed sermons to an uneducated crowd.

Honoratus, in his *Life of Saint Hilary, Bishop of Arles*, certainly says:

> “If a crowd of learned hearers was absent, he nourished the hearts of country people with simple speech; but whenever he saw that instructed people had arrived, he stirred them equally by his language and his countenance into an unusual state of grace.”

Although the loftiness and elegance of expression in some of Maximus’s works may not seem entirely equal to that found in many others, the sequence, arrangement, and movement of the words, as well as the manner of citing passages of Sacred Scripture, are nevertheless so similar that one can easily recognize Maximus as the author in both groups.

But when I encountered works written in language so colloquial, humble, base, and confused that they seemed wholly unworthy of Maximus, I unhesitatingly decided that they ought to be rejected into the number of spurious works, even if they bore the name of Maximus in certain manuscripts.

In this matter I followed the example of the monks of the Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur and of other men distinguished for their expertise in critical scholarship, who had labored to examine or publish the works of the holy Fathers.

The monks of Saint Maur, who prepared the edition of Saint Ambrose’s works, judged that several sermons should be removed from Ambrose himself for this one reason: some should be assigned to Augustine, some to Maximus, and some to neither of them, but rather to Caesarius or to certain obscure writers of a later age—writers of whom they had never even heard mentioned.

We see the same procedure followed by those who undertook the task of separating the genuine works of Saint Augustine from the spurious and publishing them anew. In their extremely accurate and painstaking edition, they denied that a great number of sermons once attributed to Augustine were his, because of the dissimilarity of their language.

They assigned some of these sermons to Maximus because they displayed the similarity of Maximian language and style and because the name of Maximus was found written in their titles in certain manuscripts.

Furthermore, the brothers Peter and Jerome Ballerini—who, through the many distinguished books they published, brought no less honor to their native Verona than benefit to the Christian commonwealth—in the edition of the works of Saint Leo the Great, which they prepared with the greatest diligence and glory, knew that six homilies had once been attributed by earlier editors to that same pontiff.

When they saw that these homilies had plainly been written in Maximus’s style and noticed that they bore Maximus’s name in several handwritten manuscripts, they restored them to Maximus himself without hesitation.

The first of these homilies is *On the Epiphany*, beginning:

> “On this celebration, beloved, …”

The second, third, and fourth are *On the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul*. The final two are *On the Nativity of Saint Lawrence, Deacon and Martyr*.

They judged two sermons quite differently. One is *On the Nativity of the Lord*, beginning:

> “Let us rejoice in the Lord, beloved, and let us delight in spiritual joy.”

The other is *On the Epiphany*, beginning:

> “When the previous day had been celebrated, on which inviolate virginity, etc.”

Although they saw that these sermons were attributed to Maximus in several manuscripts, they recognized that they contained nothing characteristic of Maximian expression, that their style was entirely Leonine, and that this was confirmed by other manuscripts. They therefore removed them from Maximus and placed them among the sermons of Leo.

If such was the method of such eminent men in judging the works of the Fathers and separating them from spurious writings, why should I ultimately have neglected it, especially when I saw that substantial benefits had thereby been introduced into the republic of letters?

Thus, when I saw that some people attributed to Peter Chrysologus the homily *On the Healing of the Man with the Withered Hand by the Lord*—that is, on Luke 6—which begins:

> “I believe that you have listened attentively,”

and another homily on a passage in the Gospel of Mark, beginning:

> “Christ performed divine mysteries in human actions, etc.,”

I could not fail to publish both under Maximus’s name, since both the language—which is entirely Maximian in them—and the ancient manuscripts demanded this.

I followed the same procedure in publishing quite a few other homilies and sermons. I took the greatest care not to attribute anything foreign to Maximus or to assign anything belonging to Maximus to anyone else, even if a greater number of manuscripts appeared to require the contrary.

Why should I be troubled by manuscripts in which the negligence or ignorance of scribes has caused works of Greek Fathers to be entered under the names of Latin writers?

Let two sermons serve as examples. One is *On the Confession of Sin*, which the Vallicellian manuscript presents as written by Maximus and which Gymnicus places after the Maximian works on p. 357, as though it had been composed in Greek by John Chrysostom.

This sermon also appears in several editions of the works of Saint John Chrysostom. One is the Paris edition of 1556, volume I, prepared under the direction of Philippus Montanus of Armentières. Another is the Paris edition begun and completed in 1581 by the printers Henri Thierry and Sébastien Nivelle, at the expense of the publishers, volume I, columns 989–990, and elsewhere.

But since later editors of the works of Saint John Chrysostom judged that this kind of sermon had nothing Chrysostomian about it, they omitted it.

The other is the sermon *On the Rich Miser*, or *On the Passage in the Gospel: “The Field of a Certain Rich Man Produced Abundant Crops.”* Rufinus translated this sermon from Greek into Latin. It appears in volume III of the works of Basil the Great, pp. 722 ff., Paris edition of 1722.

This sermon, which belongs to Basil, is attributed in some manuscripts to Ambrose and in others to Maximus.

There are six hundred examples of this kind. They plainly demonstrate how little reliance should be placed on the inscriptions of manuscripts from later periods unless at least some of the supports mentioned above concur to confirm them.

## XXVIII

I shall now briefly explain the order and arrangement in which this collection of Maximus’s homilies, sermons, and other minor works has been organized and completed.

First I presented the homilies, divided into three classes. The first consists of those entitled *On the Temporal Cycle*; the second, of those *On the Saints*; and the third, of those *On Various Matters*.

The homilies *On the Temporal Cycle* are generally understood to be those delivered on movable feast days. Those *On the Saints* are the homilies recited on the solemn feast days of particular holy martyrs or confessors, in praise of them. Finally, those *On Various Matters* relate to the exposition of some passage of Sacred Scripture.

After the homilies, I likewise thought that the sermons should be divided into the same number of classes, marked by the same titles.

In his *Glossary*, Du Cange noted the following distinction between homilies and sermons:

> “Homilies,” he says, “were familiar conferences held by bishops in sacred buildings, in which they both questioned the people and were questioned by the people. Thus Photius distinguishes ὁμιλίαι (*homiliai*, homilies) from λόγος (*logos*, a discourse) in the *Bibliotheca*, codex 172.”

For when a sermon was delivered, the speaker was neither questioned by the people nor did he question the people.

Du Cange also maintains that Latin Fathers customarily called those discourses *popular treatises* which the Greeks called homilies, citing Saint Augustine as his witness. Augustine offers the following passage from his preface to Psalm 118:

> “I decided to carry this out through discourses that are delivered among the peoples, which the Greeks call ὁμιλίαι (*homiliai*).”

For some time now, however, the meaning of the word ὁμιλίαι has changed. We now use the term for discourses composed to explain some passage of the Gospel.

I also arranged for three treatises on Baptism to follow the sermons. The agreement of the Subalpine manuscripts proves that these should be attributed to Maximus.

Next follow two treatises drawn from the Veronese manuscript. One is entitled *Against the Pagans*, the other *Against the Jews*. They bear the name of no author. Nevertheless, since their style does not differ from Maximus’s, and since they were copied from the volume containing other minor works of the holy bishop, I would certainly have acted imprudently if I had thought they ought to be removed from the series of Maximus’s works.

Finally, I added the *Gospel Readings*, or *Chapters of the Gospels*, which, as I noted above, are mentioned by Gennadius and, in more recent times, by Trithemius.

I am not unaware that these Gospel Readings in the Veronese manuscript bear neither Maximus’s name nor the name of anyone else. But the omission of a name is not so important that it can deter me from a judgment confirmed both by weighty conjectures and by the authority of distinguished writers of great antiquity and reputation.

Since many subjects explained by Maximus in his homilies and sermons are treated in these Readings with the same language, style, and method, I do not see why the Readings should not be attributed to the author who plainly wrote those homilies and sermons.

Moreover, since, according to Gennadius, Maximus published a work *On the Chapters of the Gospels*, and since these Readings are arranged in such a way that they may properly be entitled *On the Chapters of the Gospels*, what prevents the Readings themselves from being the same as the *Chapters of the Gospels* published by Maximus?

These are the more important works of Maximus on which our collection chiefly rests.

Although I encountered certain other works that did not seem unworthy of so great an author, I did not have sufficiently weighty arguments at hand to establish that they had proceeded from Maximus alone. I therefore remained uncertain. Since I judged that I ought not to decide the matter rashly, I restrained myself so as neither to affirm nor deny that they belonged to Maximus, and consequently rejected them into the appendix of doubtful works.

But when many considerations prevented me from deciding that certain homilies and sermons should be counted either among Maximus’s certain works or among his doubtful works, I placed those homilies and sermons in a second appendix, that of spurious works.

Neither the renown of certain manuscripts nor the opinion of some learned men, who asserted that those homilies and sermons belonged to Maximus, could move me to do otherwise.

The reasons why I could not agree with them have been sufficiently explained in the preface to that second appendix, and therefore there is no need to explain them again here.

I have already explained above which of Maximus’s previously unpublished works I received from manuscripts. I shall now speak of those already published, and indicate which reading I have followed in republishing them. As for the seventy-four homilies first published by Gymnicus and then by Galesinius, I wish everyone to know that I adhered to Gymnicus’s text, while nevertheless supplying or correcting some passages and bringing them into conformity with the authority of more reliable manuscript codices. In publishing the remainder, I followed the examples of the Paris editions of the works of Saint Ambrose from the years 1569 and 1690, Muratori’s *Anecdota* of 1713, and Mabillon’s *Museum Italicum* of 1724.

Finally, I must warn my readers that whatever of good fruit and distinction there is in this edition of ours should, in whatever measure it possesses such qualities, be credited to the foresight, vigilance, and munificence of Pius VI, the excellent and most wise pontiff. For since nothing lies closer to his heart than to provide whatever may seem capable of contributing greatly to the propagation, illumination, and strengthening of the Catholic religion, and since he clearly recognized how useful the works of Saint Maximus could be for that purpose, he took care—at no small expense of his own funds, and with every kind of solicitude, diligence, and zeal—that they should be collected from every quarter, corrected, illuminated, magnificently printed, and brought forth into the public light. May God, the Creator of all, preserve our most holy lord pontiff for a long life, for the stability of his holy Churches and of the orthodox faith [Note: [Col. 0039] The letter of the bishops of the island of Cyprus to Saint Theodore the pope, preserved in the Acts of the Lateran Council under Saint Martin in the year 649, session 2, p. 731, vol. III of the Councils, Paris edition of 1714: Ὁ Θεὸς, ὁ Δημιουργὸς τῶν ἁπάντων διατηρήσοι μακραίωνα τὸν πανάγιον ἡμῶν δεσπότην, πρὸς σύστασιν τῶν ἁγίων αὐτοῦ Ἐκκλησιῶν, καί τῆς ὀρθοδόξου πίστεως. “May God, the Creator of all, preserve our most holy lord for a long life, for the establishment of his holy Churches and of the orthodox faith.”].

# PART II

Which concerns the doctrine of Maximus and the other matters which we promised to discuss in the *Prolegomena*.

[Col. 0041]

## [XXXIX] I

So much, then, concerning our collection of the works of Maximus, the resources which we prepared for completing it, and the arrangement which we followed in organizing and preparing it. It remains for me to discuss the doctrine of this holy bishop and the other matters which I promised to address in the *Prolegomena*.

What the doctrine of so great a man was—how excellent, how refined, how appropriately adapted to the sacred Scriptures, to tradition, and to the decrees of the Church; how distinctly and explicitly he set it forth against the profane novelties of opinions and expressions—can be known and perceived so clearly from his homilies, sermons, and other works that our own discourse is scarcely needed to illuminate it. I am therefore all the more astonished that a man who had undertaken not to write systematically against heretics but to deliver addresses to the people on the cultivation of virtue and piety should have discussed the loftier mysteries of orthodox religion with such precision, and the perverse inventions and doctrines of heretics with such force, while adapting himself so suitably to the understanding of the people whom he instructed, that nothing seems capable of being desired beyond it.

## II

Now, concerning the mystery of the Trinity, he treats it in such a way that, although he argues much more briefly than Athanasius, Hilary, Basil, Augustine, and the other Fathers who opposed the anti-Trinitarians, he nevertheless argues with equal solidity and accuracy. Thus, in Sermon 48, which is the first on Pentecost, p. 523:

> “Those whose gifts are undivided possess, certainly, an inseparable divinity. But when the Spirit enters those in whom Christ dwells, he does not increase the magnitude of their divinity; rather, he advances them in the faith of unity. . . . This is, as we believe, the dispensation of the incomprehensible Trinity: although the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together perform all things inseparably through the effect of the same divinity, certain things are nevertheless bestowed specially by each one . . . . What the Spirit bestows, the Father also bestows, for the Spirit possesses the whole together with the Father; he always proceeds wholly from the Father. And what the Spirit bestows together with the Father, the Son also bestows, since the Son was born from that same Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds. For Christ says: ‘All things that the Father has are mine.’ If all things that the Father has belong to the Son, then what the Spirit has is also common to the Father and the Son. And therefore, since there is no division in the name of those three, we must believe that their will and power are one in every operation. Thus the Trinity accomplishes the heavenly mysteries in its faithful in such a way that, although the operation appears distinct, the mystery is nevertheless proved undivided.”

One divinity, therefore, belongs to the Son and to the Holy Spirit together with the Father, because just as one could not be born from God unless he were God, so there is no doubt that he who proceeds from God is God. But how the Son, who existed, was born from the one and same Father, and how the Spirit, who was not born, proceeds, is known only to the divinity, which, being alone, knows itself. For no one, as it is written, knows the Father except the Son. Therefore what the Son knows, the Spirit also knows; with the Son and the Father he has one name and one divinity.

The same point is made in what this holy bishop himself continues in Sermon 51, the fourth on Pentecost, p. 530, where he writes that the Son, the Holy Spirit, and indeed the Father reign with undivided majesty; and in Sermon 52, the fifth on Pentecost, p. 532, where he says:

> “They announce one another beforehand by mutual testimony, so that they may be believed to be one, to will one thing, and always to be able to do one thing. . . . We are taught these things by the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures so that the undivided majesty but distinct property of the Persons may be revealed to us. For as far as the unity of the divinity is concerned, the Spirit’s agreement is in the Father’s word, and the Father’s will is in the Spirit’s utterance. Who, unless perhaps an impious heretic or faithless Jew, doubts that the Holy Spirit is God? . . . Who is so insane as to deny him to be God, against whom to blaspheme is so impious and deadly that no forgiveness follows the sin of the blasphemer? This Holy Spirit, I say, proceeding from the Father and promised by the Son, deigned to pour the gifts of his glory upon the apostles of Christ.”

And in Sermon 53, the sixth on Pentecost, p. 535:

> “The Holy Spirit is undivided from the Father and inseparable from the Son; and, as the faithful word of the sacred reading teaches us, there is no difference between them in power. . . . The Savior also says of himself: ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life. I am,’ he says, ‘the truth.’ Therefore, if the Son, who is the truth, asserts that the Spirit is the Spirit of truth, who will be able to deny that he is God, except one who does not believe in truth from truth? Thus the true Spirit is God, whom Christ testifies in the same confession both to proceed from the Father and to be sent by himself. The Son of God sends the Spirit of his Father—not as though he were obedient to a command, but as one who agrees with the mystery. For this reason the Spirit, proceeding from the Father, follows as one sent by the Son, lest he be believed to be something other than the Father is, or to will anything different from what the Son wills. Therefore, brothers, it is unmistakably clear that the will of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one.”

I would be excessive if I wished to set out everything that Maximus has admirably embraced concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity. I turn to the mystery of the Incarnation.

## III

Maximus wrote no less accurately than Cyril of Alexandria, Leo the Great, and the others who fought in the middle of the fifth century against the heresiarchs Nestorius and Eutyches in defense of orthodox doctrine. He clearly, distinctly, and precisely teaches, in accordance with the sacred Scriptures, tradition, the decrees of the synods of Ephesus and Chalcedon, and the letter of Saint Leo to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, that two natures—the divine and the human—were united in the person of the divine Word, or Son [XLI], so that there is one person in Christ and two natures [Col. 0043]. He teaches this not in one or another passage, but in many. It would therefore be too lengthy to pursue everything he says about this doctrine. I shall set out only a very few passages, from which everyone may safely judge and determine what the others contain.

In Homily 6, the first on the Nativity of the Lord, p. 19:

> “Today a man proceeded from the virgin, who had known no intercourse with any man; he is at once God and man. Today one and the same person was born as God without any fleshly conception and became man without any begetter. God begot him from eternity; and in time the chaste virgin received him through the operation of almighty God. He was born from eternity without any beginning of created existence; he arose in time from an immaculate virgin. In the first birth he was born God; in the second he was brought forth as man.”

Relevant also are what Maximus says in Homily 8, the third on the Nativity of the Lord, p. 24, and Homily 9, the fourth on the Nativity of the Lord, p. 24. Again, in Homily 10, the fifth on the Nativity of the Lord, p. 25, and elsewhere:

> “Today the Savior of the world received from his mother the condition of being born, although from the Father he has no temporal beginning of birth. Today the Son of God entered the world through a human being, although by his hand the world was made before humanity. . . . One and the same person was born as God without conception and became man without a creature. We read of two generations in Christ, but in both the power of the incomprehensible divinity is present. There God begot him from himself; here the virgin conceived him through God’s operation. There, without beginning; here, without precedent.”

When he says here that God was born without conception, he clearly means that the Son was begotten and born from the Father, not made, and that he excludes any temporal succession from God himself. Hence in Homily 6 on the Nativity of the Lord, p. 19:

> “He was born from eternity,” he says, “WITHOUT ANY BEGINNING OF CREATED EXISTENCE; HE AROSE IN TIME FROM AN IMMACULATE VIRGIN.”

And in Homily 9, the fourth on the Nativity of the Lord, p. 24:

> “At the end of time he was born as man who, before all ages, proceeds as the Only-Begotten from the Father. Born indeed as man in time, but God from eternity.”

When he adds, “he became man without a creator,” this has no other purpose than to signify that the Son of God became man without the work of a man, that is, without a human begetter. Therefore what he expresses here by the words “without a creator,” he explains, as we saw shortly before, by these other words: “without a begetter.” In this very homily, in place of *without a creator* (*sine creante*), the Vatican codex 1267, p. 90, reads *without a begetter* (*sine generante*).

What of Homily 15, the tenth on the Nativity of the Lord, p. 41, where he expresses *without a begetter* in this way:

> “He was born as a man, not begotten through a man.”

Immediately afterward he adds:

> “Although it may seem new, it is not unbelievable that Christ was conceived in Mary’s womb WITHOUT A BEGETTER, he who proceeded from God the Father without conception.”

Now it is also clear from Homily 23, the tenth on the Epiphany, p. 67, that Maximus’s *without a creator* has the same meaning as *without a procreator* and *without a begetter*. Speaking there of Christ, he says:

> “He goes to the wedding, whom the wedding DID NOT CREATE.”

Although Christ’s human nature was created by God—according to Saint Maximus’s Homily 7, p. 22—so that it cannot be said to have been made without God as creator (compare Saint Thomas, *Summa theologica*, Part III, question 16, article 10), nevertheless Christ cannot properly be called a creature unless this is understood as referring to his human nature. Otherwise someone might suppose that Christ’s person was created, which is an Arian doctrine. The dogma of the Catholic faith, however, is that Christ’s person is divine and therefore uncreated. See Saint Thomas in the same place, article 8.

Maximus continues to write about the mystery of the Incarnation in Homily 13, the eighth on the Nativity of the Lord, p. 35:

> “Christ, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells, taking upon himself the weakness of our flesh, was born as a new man. . . . For he did not suddenly emerge for us from a woman as some temporal being or as one who had not previously existed; rather, he who was always God with the Father and always reigned wished to appear to mortals through the virgin by a new mystery: a new man indeed, but the everlasting Lord.”

There are similar statements in Homily 14, p. 39 and following; Homily 20, p. 55; and Homily 25, p. 73 and following, where he says:

> “A new star revealed that a new man had arrived, and truly one so new that, although he was the Son of God, he put on flesh without carnal generation and had, as man, a time of birth, although as God he had no beginning of birth. . . . For insofar as he is God, he is the creator of the world; insofar as he is man, he is the redeemer of the world. How, then, is Christ not Lord of all by the privilege of BOTH SUBSTANCES, since he subjected all things to himself either by creation or by redemption?”

Homily 26, p. 75, and Homily 27, p. 79, speak in harmony with this:

> “Christ Jesus, coming from the Father as God and born as man from a woman, under the appearance of the worshiping Chaldeans, consecrated the faith of the nations. Although he veiled his divinity by the covering of our body, heaven nevertheless disclosed him to be God, and earth recognized him as such. He came humble yet wondrous, so that in him both the truth of the flesh assumed and the nature of the ineffable divinity might shine forth together.”

Consonant with these are what he teaches in Homily 29, the first on the Baptism of Christ, p. 87 and following; Homily 30, p. 92; and Homily 35, p. 99, where he says:

> “The eternal author of our redemption, the almighty Lord, the Only-Begotten of the living God, always remaining inseparably with the Father, deigned to assume a PERFECT man for our sake; he so emptied himself of what he was as God that he passed through all the sacraments of the legal ordinances. For as soon as he proceeded from the holy womb of his blessed mother, he was dedicated by the sign of circumcision, either to SHOW THE UNDOUBTED REALITY OF HIS FLESH, or lest the Jewish people, nurtured by circumcision, should reject him as a foreigner.”

He says the same in Homily 42, p. 125; Homily 43, p. 129; and Homily 56, p. 177, where, after speaking of Christ’s humanity and of Christ rising from the dead, and of his words to Mary Magdalene—“For I have not yet ascended to the Father”—he says:

> “Let us see how Christ has not yet ascended to the Father, when he himself says: ‘Because the Father is in me, and I am in the Father,’ from whom he has never been separated through THE UNDIVIDED SUBSTANCE OF DIVINITY. For when one remains in one, he signifies that the Father and the Son are always together. Or does the Son say that he ascends to the place where he dwells before he ascends? For the same Lord said: ‘No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.’ Therefore, if the Savior is in heaven when he descends, he is much more in heaven before he ascends. But see whether perhaps this statement is directed as a rebuke to Mary, since shortly before, when she was seeking the Lord among the tombs, she was told: ‘Why do you seek the living among the dead?’ and so forth.”

What he continues in Homily 59, p. 190, and Homily 68, p. 217, does not differ. There he speaks as follows:

> “You, Lord, were made Christ from the flesh of the virgin, although you are the everlasting Son of the living God. You, Lord, were born as man from human beings, although in your inconceivable majesty you are God with God.”

There are corresponding statements in Homily 83, p. 270; Sermon 7 on Time, p. 413; Sermon 10, p. 421; Sermon 12, p. 427; and Sermon 16, p. 438, and elsewhere.

From these outstanding testimonies it is plainly evident that Maximus acknowledges two natures in the one Christ. This can be confirmed to the highest degree by the notable passage contained in Homily 14, p. 40, which is as follows:

> “All creation is astonished at so great a miracle: that ONE AND THE SAME PERSON reigns as God in heaven and is nourished as man on earth.”

Nor is this all. In Homily 17, p. 50, he says:

> “Let us also believe this with our whole heart, brothers: that he himself, although sharing our nature, is nevertheless coequal with the Father’s divine substance.”

And in Homily 19, p. 53:

> “Who could explain why the Only-Begotten Son of God, with whom there is ONE AND THE SAME DIVINITY AND OMNIPOTENCE as with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and for whom to will and to be able are one and the same, nevertheless wished to deign to assume our NATURE, taking up what he did not possess and not abandoning WHAT WAS IN HIMSELF, and so inseparably joined the divine nature to the human that he was at once God and man?”

And in Homily 29, p. 83:

> “A great and fearful mystery: one and the same person is proclaimed God from the Father and man from his mother; one and the same is the Son of a woman and the Son of majesty; one and the same is a participant in humanity and Lord of the angels. . . . He who flees the breasts and nourishes all things, he who from heaven grants the substance of life to every living creature, is nourished with earthly milk for the salvation of those on earth. Let no one, therefore, doubt; let no one hesitate: while Christ lived on earth, he shone in heaven, because he came to the earth without leaving heaven.”

In Homily 77, p. 245, speaking of Peter, he says that Peter himself demonstrated:

> “What was, in ONE AND THE SAME Son of God, the condition of the flesh assumed and the privilege of natural divinity.”

And in Homily 83, p. 270:

> “That Christ was made, although he was the Son, is the dispensation of human redemption; that he is Lord belongs to the property of his nature. He is proclaimed and believed to be the one and Only-Begotten, because he was begotten in such a way that he has no companion in his birth. You hear ‘Son,’ not so that you might suppose him to have been brought forth according to some sex, but so that you might believe that God proceeded from God in incomprehensible majesty, as he himself says: ‘I came forth from the Father and came into this world.’ He was born from the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary. You hear ‘Holy Spirit,’ so that you may recognize that birth as at once wondrous and blameless. . . . For when the necessity of our redemption demanded that the Only-Begotten of God become man, he introduced into his birth the privilege of his own divinity, so that he might be born from a virgin. . . . The Only-Begotten of God, therefore, became the Son of Man, so that he who was the creator of the world might also become its redeemer.”

And in Sermon 8, p. 415:

> “The Lord arranged it . . . so that people might be certain that he whom the virgin had borne was the Son of God, whom divinity recognized,” and so forth.

But at last I must put an end to citing passages from Maximus, since it would be almost endless to pursue them all and entirely unnecessary. The passages already cited demonstrate sufficiently and more than sufficiently that the holy bishop treats the mystery of the Incarnation as Leo the Great does, and as the Fathers of the synods of Ephesus and Chalcedon did.

For whoever writes that the one and same Son of God was born from God the Father from eternity without any beginning of created existence, and arose in time from a virgin; whoever acknowledges that in the first birth he was born God and in the second was brought forth as man; whoever again affirms that in the one and same Christ there is both the fullness of divinity and the nature of man, and that Christ himself is Lord of all by the privilege of both substances, because he subjected all things to himself either by creation or by redemption; whoever says that the same one who was born from God from eternity was born in time from a woman, and that the almighty Lord, the Only-Begotten of the living God, always remains inseparably with the Father, from whom he was never separated through the undivided substance of divinity; whoever says that this Son assumed perfect humanity in time; finally, whoever testifies that the one and same Christ born from the virgin is man, although in his inconceivable majesty he is God with God, and that this very Son of God, with whom there is one and the same divinity, will, and power as with the Father and the Holy Spirit, assumed our nature in such a way that, without abandoning what was in himself, he wondrously joined the divine nature to the human inseparably, so that he is at once God and man, Son of a woman and Son of majesty—whoever, I say, confesses these things must necessarily have confessed one person of Christ, in whom two natures, divine and human, subsist inseparably, without confusion or mixture.

For if two persons were imagined, the one and same person would not be the Son of God and the Son of the virgin; there would instead be two sons, which is contrary to Maximus’s doctrine. What more could be desired for overthrowing the heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches, one of whom posited two persons in Christ, while the other posited one nature after the union? Indeed, whoever compares these explicit statements of Maximus with the doctrine of Cyril of Alexandria and Saint Celestine I against the Nestorians, and with the letter of Saint Leo the Great to Flavian against Eutyches, will certainly discover that the views of Maximus correspond and are so similar to those of Cyril and Leo that an egg could not be more like an egg.

## IV

What if Maximus, by affirming that the Son of God was born from the Virgin Mary and therefore that she herself was the mother of God, utterly overturns the heretical doctrine of the Nestorians, who denied that she was *Theotokos*, the Mother of God? This is clear from the testimonies of the holy bishop which we cited above, and it will become even clearer from those which we shall now present.

In Sermon 36, p. 492:

> “He was born from the virgin Mary according to the flesh, and according to his divinity proceeded from the mouth of God the Father.”

And in Sermon 47, p. 495 and following:

> “Who could doubt that he is ineffably the Son of God and the Son of Man, who was able both to undergo death and, after conquering death, to raise himself from the tomb?” [Note: [Col. 0047] The same point is made by Saint Leo I, Sermon 20, the first on the Nativity of Christ, p. 43, vol. I of the works, Roman edition of 1735: “True God and true man are brought together into the unity of the Lord, so that the one and same mediator of God and humanity might, in accordance with what suited our remedies, be able to die from one nature and rise again from the other.”]

> “For, having assumed flesh from the virgin, lest we suffer any clouding of our confession of faith, throughout the whole time of his preaching HE REVEALED HIMSELF TO BE TRUE GOD, AND SHOWED HIMSELF TO BE PERFECT MAN. . . . Thus, in an incomprehensible manner, flesh was in God and God was in flesh, so that neither would suffering separate God from man, nor would God, through man, be subjected to human sufferings. Since it is proclaimed that the Son of God WAS BORN FROM A VIRGIN, human weakness ought not to waver before so great a miracle, because in this astonishing novelty we confess God as its author, for whom every work is possible. . . . He wished the virgin to give birth, and through the overshadowing of his majesty Christ proceeded from Mary without any harm to virginal modesty. . . . But perhaps a faithless person objects and says: ‘No one has ever been born in this way.’ No one indeed, because no one’s flesh, except his, has been united with God. . . . Christ was born wondrously, and yet in your obstinate unbelief you do not believe him to be God? When the foremost of the apostles calls the redeemer of all things the Son of the living God, he confesses in him the substance of the Father’s divinity; when he declares him to be THE SAME Christ, he asserts the reality of his MOTHER’S body. Thus blessed Peter truly embraced BOTH NATURES in Christ [Note: [Col. 0047] Saint Leo, Letter 25, formerly 24, to Flavian, chapter 5 and following, vol. II, p. 125 and following] under one designation, so that, touching briefly upon the mystery of the ineffable mystery in the shortest possible statement, he NEITHER DIVIDED THEM BY DOUBLING THEM NOR CONFUSED THEM BY UNITING THEM [Note: [Col. 0047] Saint Leo, same place, chapter 2 and following, p. 18 and following].”

So that we might understand more fully that in the Savior man must not be separated from God, nor God from man, the glorious teacher of the faith, the apostle Paul, says:

> “God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law.”

The Son of God was certainly not made in order to be sent; rather, for the purpose for which he was sent, the Son became the Son of man [XLVI]. While preserving the property of the divine [Note: [Col. 0047] See also Saint Leo, same place, chapter 3, p. 119 and following] nature, he assumed human nature in himself, not by a confusion having been made, but by a perfect union [Note: [Col. 0047] See also Saint Maximus, Sermon 38, [Col. 0048] p. 500; Sermon 42, p. 509; Sermon 44, p. 514; Sermon 46, p. 518; and Sermon 51, p. 530].

Compare what follows, which is relevant to our subject and purpose and which Maximus has admirably transmitted and explained. In Sermon 43, p. 511:

> “Through this most sacred mystery of the Incarnation, flesh and the Word came together into one Lord and ONE PERSON [Note: [Col. 0048] Compare Saint Leo’s same letter, chapter 3, p. 119 and following], so that God might be thought to have been born from a woman and man might be believed to have come from heaven, according to what the Lord says: ‘No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.’ . . . He was the Son of Man and the Son of God. We cannot confess separately either man without God or God without man. Does it not appear that man transcended heaven when he was united to the Word of God in the virgin’s womb?”

And in Sermon 46, p. 520:

> “What is the depth of this mystery, what an unfathomable secret of divine operation: that he who proceeded from the Father before the ages, and he who proceeded from a woman at the end of time, became one God? This happened so that, although he was the Only-Begotten inseparable from the Father, man might have fellowship with the Father’s immortality in the Only-Begotten of God.”

And in Sermon 53, p. 533:

> “The Father maintained in the Son the power of a DOUBLE SUBSTANCE, so that, by the majesty of his power, the VENERABLE MOTHER might conceive the ONE AND SAME CHRIST AS GOD AND BEAR HIM AS MAN. Is he not visibly the Son of God who was conceived, when, with carnal generation ceasing, a man is believed to have been formed in a virgin’s womb and he who was born is not doubted to be GOD? Wondrous is the birth of the untouched MOTHER.”

And in Sermon 61, p. 554, where, speaking of the birthday of Saint John the Baptist, he says:

> “To him was granted the glory of so great an honor that the MOTHER OF GOD herself was present at his birth, and by her presence the Creator of the world consecrated his beginning, hidden in the womb.”

And in Sermon 62, p. 558:

> “Christ, the very same Word and flesh, is one Lord, and one and the same eternal and new [Note: [Col. 0048] Saint Leo, same place, chapter 4, p. 121] Lord: eternal from God, new from a woman. There he was incomprehensibly begotten from the unbegotten Father; here he was wondrously born from a virgin. There he was brought forth by the Father’s majesty; here he was formed through the Spirit’s operation. There the nature in the Begetter is simple; here the substance in the Redeemer is DOUBLE. . . . If it was new that God was born on earth, it is much more new that man should reign in heaven,” and so forth.

For, as he writes in Sermon 107, p. 669:

> “In our one and same Redeemer, the operation of divinity and humanity must be considered as distinct [that is, differentiated] [Note: [Col. 0048] See the annotation on p. 671 and following of this collection]; and the error of Eutyches must be detested in every way, since he dares to teach that there is only one operation in Christ. For whoever asserts only one side—either that he was merely man or that he was merely God—will deny something: the one who says he was merely man will deny the glory of the Creator; the one who says he was merely God will deny the mercy of the Redeemer.”

[XLVII]

And in Treatise 2, on Baptism, p. 715:

> “This is the faith of Christian Catholics: that we believe we shall rise again with this soul which we now possess, having as a suitable example of our future resurrection our Lord, the Word of the Father, who, being God and the Son of God—that is, the Word—and, according to the substance of his divinity, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, therefore assumed a man of our nature. According to this human nature he wished to be born from a virgin, afterward to suffer and die, to rise again on the third day, and to ascend into heaven [Note: [Col. 0048] Saint Leo, same place, chapter 5, p. 124 and following], so that he might kindle in us the hope of resurrection.”

There are similar statements in Treatise 5, *Against the Jews*, p. 739, and in *On the Chapters of the Gospels*, p. 759.

Now, since Maximus acknowledges that the Son of God, consubstantial with the Father, was born from the Virgin Mary in time according to his humanity, and since he testifies that the divine and human nature came together, without prejudice to the property of either substance, in the one person of the divine Word, and therefore calls Mary both the mother of Christ God and the Mother of God, why should anyone bring the holy bishop into disrepute, as though he had argued about the mystery of the Incarnation less accurately or less suitably to the synods of Ephesus and Chalcedon against Nestorius and Eutyches, or had said anything that could not easily be reconciled with the doctrine of Saints Cyril, Celestine, and Leo?

I ask the readers’ confidence, so that they may attend, recognize, and observe whether there is anything in the definition of that same synod of Chalcedon which the holy Maximus has not expressed with sufficient distinction and clarity in the passages from his homilies, sermons, and treatises cited immediately above.

Here are the words of the synod:

> “Following the holy Fathers, we all unanimously teach the confession of one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, the same perfect in divinity and the same perfect in humanity, truly God and truly man, the same consisting of a rational soul and a body, consubstantial with us according to his humanity, in all things like us except sin. Before the ages begotten from the Father according to his divinity, but in the last days, for us and for our salvation, the same born according to his humanity from Mary the virgin, the Mother of God; one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, Only-Begotten, acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation; the distinction of the natures in no way removed because of the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved, and both coming together into one person and one subsistence, not divided or separated into two persons, but one and the same Son” [Note: [Col. 0049] Session 5, p. 455, vol. II of the Councils, Paris edition of 1714].

## V

Yet Maximus does indeed mention Christ’s flesh and body; he does not, however, likewise mention a rational soul. As though one who attests that Christ possessed a perfect human nature and that its property remained intact were not thereby also attesting that a rational soul was assumed together with the body by the Word! But what need is there for many words, if Maximus himself writes in Sermon 31, p. 470, as follows?

> “And truly it was fitting that that TRUE substance of body AND SOUL should rejoice forever in heaven together with Christ, since, trampling upon these earthly impediments, it had served him alone on earth.”

### VI

Nevertheless, Maximus writes that Christ simulated hunger in Sermon 15, p. 434:

> “Observe,” he says, “the Lord’s strategy, by which he outwitted his adversary. After many fasts, he pretends to be hungry, so that he may again provoke by hunger the devil whom he had already conquered by fasting. For he in a certain way gives him hope of engaging him on account of the weakness of the flesh; and while the devil engages, as it were, with a feeble opponent, he is defeated all the more gloriously.”

But if, according to Maximus, that hunger was simulated by Christ, why could it not likewise be said, according to the same Maximus, that Christ himself simulated weariness, sighs, sorrows, and death?

Yet when I examine the homilies and sermons of the holy bishop, I plainly see that in them Christ is established as having truly been hungry. In Homily 37, p. 107:

> “The devil,” he says, “was unaware that the nourishment which Christ endured in infancy, and that he was hungry as a human being, was not a sign of bodily weakness but a sacrament of heavenly grace.”

Christ therefore WAS HUNGRY AS A HUMAN BEING, according to Maximus. Again, the same Maximus says in Homily 38, p. 112:

> “How can it be that he who, while fasting for so many days, felt neither hunger nor thirst, afterwards became hungry? HE WAS CLEARLY HUNGRY, AND WE CANNOT DENY THAT HE WAS HUNGRY.”

And in Homily 43, p. 129:

> “For our sake he conquered, who deigned TO BE HUNGRY for us. The devil therefore approaches to tempt Christ. [lacuna] He suspects that he is the Son of God, whom he sees extending his fast through forty successive days; but again he doubts that he possesses a divine nature, since he SEES him, as though weak among other human beings, being hungry. He is astonished at this novelty: that he has no human sin, yet bears the necessity of sinful humanity. But Christ the Lord, our Redeemer, in order to restore lost and weakened humanity to God, TOOK UPON HIMSELF HUNGER, WEARINESS, SORROW, AND ALL THE WEAKNESSES OF THE HUMAN BODY.”

Christ therefore was truly hungry, just as he truly endured weariness, sorrow, and the other weaknesses of the human body; but he was hungry for our sake, namely, in order to restore us to God.

Accordingly, what he said in the preceding Homily 38, p. 112—

> “He was hungry not for human food but for salvation; he did not desire the banquets of earthly nourishment but longed for the holiness of heavenly souls. For Christ’s food is the redemption of peoples; Christ’s food is the accomplishment of the Father’s will”—

has no other meaning than that the Savior of the human race was truly hungry, though he was hungry not so much for human food as for salvation, for the sake of bringing which he had taken upon himself hunger, weariness, and sorrow.

The same Maximus continues in Homily 43, p. 130, to write that Christ was more hungry for human salvation, that is, for this rather than for food:

> “But the almighty Only-Begotten, who WOULD HUNGER MORE FOR OUR SALVATION, confounded his tempter with this reply: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.’ By this reply, dearest brethren, the Lord of immeasurable wisdom made the tempter, who had come as an investigator uncertain of the truth, still more uncertain. HE NEITHER DENIED THAT HE POSSESSED HUNGER, NOR ACKNOWLEDGED THAT HE HAD A NECESSITY OF EATING. ‘Not by bread alone,’ he said,” and so forth.

That is: “Even if I am hungry, bread is nevertheless NOT NECESSARY for me, devil,” and so forth.

Moreover, Homily 49, p. 134, says:

> “Moses was not hungry, so that divinity working in fragile humanity might be demonstrated; THE SON OF GOD WAS HUNGRY, so that by assuming our flesh he might reveal that he had taken upon himself a fragile human being. Moses’ not being hungry is an example of heavenly possibility; Christ’s being hungry is a sacrament of our redemption. The Lord accomplished this mystery in his flesh, so that just as he is believed to be God through divine powers, SO ALSO HE MIGHT BE RECOGNIZED AS HUMAN THROUGH HUMAN WEAKNESSES. Hence Christ is hungry AS A HUMAN BEING, and as God he feeds the hungry. Hence he grows weary from traveling, and grants the lame the power to walk. Hence he loosens his eyes into tears, and wondrously restores sight to the blind. Hence he is sorrowful as death approaches, and raises Lazarus, who has died, from the tomb. All these things, brethren, our Creator and Redeemer performs as God and human being, NOT BECAUSE SUCH A NECESSITY OF BEING BORN WAS IMPOSED UPON HIM, but because he willed such a mystery to reign in heaven and on earth.”

The same point is made in Homily 108, p. 357:

> “What is surprising, brethren? Christ came to take up our weaknesses and to bestow his powers upon us; to seek what is human and provide what is divine; to receive insults and return honors; to bear weariness and restore health. [lacuna] Unless Christ had fulfilled the order of the flesh, the assumption of flesh in him would have been purposeless. Therefore he endured these necessities, so that he might be PROVED A TRUE HUMAN BEING by human necessities.”

Again, in Sermon 42, p. 509, while refuting the pagans who were accustomed to object that Christ had been afraid, he says:

> “Christ was afraid, but, in order either to will or to be able to fear, he assumed this from the weakness of our body. For he was afraid from the same source from which he was hungry, from which he was sorrowful, from which he slept, from which he suffered, and from which he wept. What does this mean? You see Christ afraid to die, and do you not behold him with triumphant hand stripping away the spoils of captive death?”

Who, then, can fail to perceive from the passages of our Maximus cited above how the expression τὸ *esurire se simulat*—“he simulates being hungry”—used by the holy bishop in Sermon 15, p. 434, should be understood?

Here *simulat* does not have the same force as *fingit*, “pretends.” For how, according to Maximus’ own view, could Christ have pretended to be hungry, if Maximus himself plainly teaches that Christ did not pretend at all, but truly suffered hunger, no less than weariness and sorrow?

On this matter I wish the testimonies of that same Maximus, which I transcribed shortly before, to be consulted. To these I shall now add others, which make it entirely clear that Christ truly endured these and other experiences of the same kind as a human being.

In Sermon 38, *On the Season*, p. 500, Maximus says:

> “Did he wish to wail in the cradle for no reason? [lacuna] Did he weep in vain? [lacuna] Was he given vinegar to drink and gall to eat without purpose? [lacuna] Is his suffering empty? [lacuna] Therefore, since we are unable, through the coarseness of our carnal understanding, to comprehend the mysteries of his passion, LET US HOLD FAST, THROUGH THE CREDULITY OF RIGHT FAITH, TO WHAT HE ACCOMPLISHED.”

And in Sermon 43, p. 512:

> “In Christ there was at once the dominion of the one who reigns and the service of the one who serves. For although he was in the form of God, as the apostle Paul teaches, he assumed the form of a servant. Christ truly existed in the form of God when, by changing water into wine, he revealed himself to be Lord of creation. [lacuna] But he was in the form of a servant when, wearied by the fatigue of travel, he sat as though resting beside the mouth of a well. He acted in the form of a servant when the impious, insulting him, threw upon him the spittle of their filthy mouths. He had assumed the form of a servant when he did not turn away his face—which was terrifying for believers to behold—from the palms and blows of those who mocked him; and when he inclined even his shoulders, which he had come to bear our sins, to the hands of those striking him, although for those who truly are servants this was the most disgraceful thing to endure. [lacuna] Therefore, brethren, since one and the same Son of God performed wonders and ENDURED THINGS TO BE WEEPED OVER, one and the same was both servant and Lord. As Lord he could do everything; as servant he endured everything.”

To the same conclusion belong what Maximus teaches in Sermon 37, *On the Season*, pp. 495–496:

> “Having assumed flesh from a virgin, so that we might suffer no clouding of THE CONFESSION OF OUR FAITH, throughout the whole time of his preaching he revealed himself to be true God and SHOWED HIMSELF PERFECTLY HUMAN. He wept, mourning with our sorrow; but, powerful through his own might, he took pity on the darkness of the blind: for some he made eyes that had not yet been formed, for others he restored those they had lost. While sailing with his disciples, HE SLEPT IN THE STERN WITH THE SLEEP OF A HUMAN BEING; but by the command of his conscious majesty he immediately restrained the threatening masses of the rising waves and the menacing winds with serene calm. [lacuna] Insults were heaped upon him as the Son of Man; but, so that ignorant mortality might learn the truth of faith that had not yet been displayed, the Father addressed him from heaven as his only Son.”

“If, then, you believe, O human being, the unworthy things that Christ endured, why do you not believe even more readily the wondrous things that he accomplished? If, therefore, Christ truly wailed in the cradle, truly wept, and was truly given vinegar to drink—not pointlessly, not without purpose, not in vain, and not emptily—according to Maximus, who also acknowledges that these things must be believed through the credulity of right faith, why should it not likewise be held, with that same man’s clear agreement, through the credulity of right faith, that Christ was hungry, since Maximus’ own sufficiently established view—as has been demonstrated above in his words—is that Christ’s sorrow, and therefore his weeping, must be regarded in the same way as his hunger?

Again, does he not affirm that Christ’s exhaustion, or weariness, is of the same kind as his hunger, as we saw shortly before? What reason, then, could anyone have for supposing, on Maximus’ authority, that Christ was truly wearied by travel, but was not truly hungry and only simulated hunger?

Moreover, if, according to Maximus, Christ wept “mourning with our sorrow,” why, I ask, was this so, unless it was in order that he might show himself to be a perfect human being, so that we might suffer no clouding of our confession of faith? And can anyone suppose that this clouding was cast over and obscured our confession of faith by Maximus, when he said that Christ was hungry only in appearance and not truly—by Maximus, I say, who had decided that Christ’s sorrow and hunger were to be understood in the same way?

He says:

> “For our sake he conquered, who deigned to be hungry for us” [Note: See the preface to this work, p. XLVIII.];

and shortly afterward:

> “Christ, in order to restore lost and weakened humanity to God, took upon himself HUNGER, weariness, sorrow, and all the weaknesses of the human body.”

Now, since Maximus affirms that it is established by faith that Christ was a perfect human being, and since he acknowledges that his humanity is discerned through his human weaknesses, let us see which weaknesses he enumerates.

> “The Lord accomplished this kind of mystery in his flesh, so that just as he is believed to be God through divine powers, so also he might be recognized as human through human weaknesses.”

But through which weaknesses, I ask? Maximus immediately adds:

> “Hence it is that [Col. 0053] Christ, as a human being, is hungry.”

What? Will anyone call that hunger simulated by which Christ was recognized to be human? But if it were simulated, what would remain except that Christ’s humanity too must be considered fictitious and simulated rather than real?

And what could be more opposed to Maximus’ teaching than this monstrosity of opinion?

It therefore remains that Christ did not simulate hunger but was truly hungry—not merely with Maximus as witness, but also as preacher and defender of the truth.

You may ask me why, then, Maximus wrote that Christ simulated hunger. I shall answer briefly: as is clear from comparing Maximus’ own statements with one another, τὸ *simulasse*, “to have simulated,” amounts to saying that Christ took up or expressed hunger in himself as a human being, not by necessity but by will.

Christ willed to be hungry; yet, if he had not willed it, he would not have been hungry, even if he had prolonged his fast for six hundred years.

Thus he writes that Christ’s having been hungry was:

> “not a sign of bodily weakness but a sacrament of heavenly grace.”

Indeed, in the same place, speaking of Christ, he says:

> “He endured voluntary hunger.”

Moreover, in that very Sermon 15, p. 434, where he says that Christ simulated hunger, does Maximus not plainly indicate that Christ himself willed to be hungry, in order to confound and drive away the devil from whom he had concealed his incarnation?

> “In order,” he says, “to provoke by hunger the devil whom he had already conquered by fasting. For he gives him in a certain way hope of engaging him on account of the weakness of hunger, and while the devil engages as though with a feeble opponent, he is defeated more gloriously.”

For this is the true victory: since the devil had overthrown Adam, immortal, glorious, and feasting, he is now defeated by a mortal, humble, and HUNGRY human being [Note: See Saint Augustine, Sermon 133, also numbered 41, *On the Words of the Lord*, ch. 2, p. 419, vol. V, Antwerp edition, 1700. I omit the other Fathers, whose opinions are similar and entirely conformable.].

For when the devil sees him hungry, he thinks him a human being and doubts that he is the Savior; therefore he says:

> “If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.”

He suspected, I say, that he was Christ when he demanded that he make bread from a stone; but when he saw him HUNGRY, he thought him merely a human being.

The Savior, however, condemns his cunning with a wondrous reply. [lacuna] He therefore answered him:

> “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.”

That is: “Not by earthly bread, not by material food, by which you first deceived Adam, but by the word of God, in which are the nourishment of heavenly life.” Now the Word of God is Christ the Lord, and so forth.

But enough has been said, on Maximus’ authority, concerning the true hunger of Christ after the prolonged fast of forty days.

### VII

I shall now proceed to discuss the other mysteries of Christ the Savior.

Maximus everywhere proclaims that Christ himself was born from Mary, that she possessed original grace, and that she was a virgin before childbirth, in childbirth, and after childbirth.

There is an illustrious passage on Mary’s original grace in Homily 5, p. 18. It reads:

> “Mary was altogether a suitable dwelling-place for Christ, not on account of the condition of her body but on account of her original grace.”

And in Homily 45, p. 138:

> “Rather, I would call Mary herself manna, because she is subtle, radiant, sweet, and a virgin. As though descending from heaven, she poured forth for all the peoples of the Churches food sweeter than honey; whoever neglects to eat and consume it cannot have life within himself.”

Concerning Mary’s virginity, he teaches the following in Homily 5, pp. 17–18:

> “Christ, the salvation of all, is born; the prophets testify that he is the king of the nations. He is born from a virgin, as Isaiah declares, saying: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,’ which is interpreted, ‘God with us.’
>
> “The order of the Lord’s birth therefore proves the truth. A virgin, ignorant of intercourse with a man, conceived; her womb was filled without being touched by an embrace; and her chaste womb received the Holy Spirit, whom pure limbs preserved and an innocent body carried.
>
> “Behold the miracle of the Lord’s mother: SHE IS A VIRGIN WHEN SHE CONCEIVES, A VIRGIN WHEN SHE GIVES BIRTH, A VIRGIN AFTER CHILDBIRTH. Glorious virginity and splendid fruitfulness! The power of the world is born, and there is no groan of the woman giving birth. The womb is emptied, the infant is received, and virginity is not violated.”

And in Homily 7, pp. 21–22:

> “The Gentiles,” he says—“leaving heretics aside for the moment—dull-minded through carnal arguments, still refuse to believe that Christ could have been born from a virgin, and they mock the priest who teaches this. [lacuna]
>
> “But what is this foolish teaching—or rather, what madness—of the wise men of this age? They believe that God once performed wonders and still performs them now; yet in the most sacred birth of his Son, our Lord, they maintain that he could in no way accomplish this through a virgin?
>
> “For that same God who once created heaven, the heavens of heavens, and each of the things that are in them from nothing by divine art [lacuna], is the one who gave the virgin childbirth and offspring.
>
> “If you believe that God was able to create heaven, the sun, and the stars from nothing [lacuna], why do you insist that he could not, by the operation of that same God’s power, grant a child to an untouched virgin?
>
> “For what greater power of almighty God would there be: to have created from nothing all the things you see in heaven and in the world, or to create a human being in the womb of an undefiled virgin, without any preceding carnal union?”

And so forth.

Compare Homily 8, p. 24; Homily 9, pp. 24–25; Homily 11, pp. 30–31; Homily 12, pp. 34–35; Homily 14, pp. 39–40; Homily 15, p. 42; Homily 20, p. 55; and Homily 22, p. 62, where he says:

> “A new human being in time, but God from eternity; a new Christ, but Lord of all the ages. Today that most blessed Virgin Mary gave birth to a human being whom she did not receive from a human being, and she who was an inviolate virgin before childbirth remained so.
>
> “Blind and foolish paganism laughs at the profundity of so great a mystery. That impious blasphemy also mocks it which, in recent days, dared to diminish and corrupt the virgin’s childbirth and blasphemously declared that Christ the Lord could not be brought forth from a virgin.
>
> “The holy Church of Milan shuddered at this blasphemy; our synodal assembly condemned it with one voice; and the pious imperial authority itself abhorred it. For when anyone dares to equate venerable marriage with virginity, he blasphemes Christ by saying that he COULD NOT BE BORN FROM A VIRGIN, while he does not dare to deny that women, after giving birth to human offspring, can remain virgins.”

These words are entirely consonant with what is contained in the synodal letter of the council of the province of Milan against Jovinian and his companions. For in that same letter, no. 4 [Note: p. 670, vol. I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, Paris edition, 1721.], we read:

> “What madness of those deadly howlings, that they should say that Christ COULD NOT BE BORN FROM A VIRGIN, while they assert that women, after giving birth to human offspring, can remain virgins,” and so forth.

When Maximus writes, “The imperial authority itself abhorred the same blasphemy,” this is taken from what the synod itself pursued in the same letter. The passage is as follows, no. 8 [Note: Ibid., pp. 673–674.]:

> “They received a reward worthy of their faithlessness, those Jovinianists who came here for this reason: so that no place would remain in which they were not condemned, since they truly proved themselves Manichaeans [Note: In Peter Coustant’s note on this letter, p. 673 [Col. 0056], this defective reading is supplied as follows: ‘Not believing that Christ was born from a virgin. But if he was not born from a virgin, then certainly he is not believed to have come.’], not believing that he came from a virgin. What is this madness, equal to that of the new Jews? If he is not believed to have come, he is not believed to have assumed flesh; therefore he appeared in a phantom and was crucified in a phantom.
>
> “But for us he was crucified in truth; in truth he is our Redeemer. He is a Manichaean who denies the truth, who denies Christ’s flesh; and therefore there is no remission of sins for them, but the impiety of the Manichaeans, which even the most merciful emperor abhorred, and from which all who saw them fled as from a kind of contagion.”

But I shall discuss this synod elsewhere.

I return to Maximus’ teaching concerning the virginity of the Mother of God.

Thus, in Homily 25, p. 74, reproving a Jew, he says:

> “With you a virgin conceived, and a stranger recognizes the childbirth of your virgin; the angelic voices cannot persuade you of your salvation, and a single Chaldean star led the Chaldeans to your Christ.”

And in Homily 29, p. 87, he introduces John the Baptist addressing Christ:

> “A natural union of man and woman brought me forth; but you were given to us by revered virginity, while the power of the Most High overshadowed you.”

But why should I linger over these passages, when, if I wished to pursue everything that Maximus included in his homilies and sermons concerning this doctrine, I would scarcely ever bring my writing to an end?

I shall therefore set a limit to this subject and be satisfied with one testimony of the holy bishop, which is found in Sermon 37, p. 497:

> “He willed a virgin to give birth, and through the overshadowing of his majesty Christ came forth from Mary without any loss to virginal modesty.
>
> “For this reason the philosophers of the nations and the wise men of the world, who want everything to be established by their own arguments, while they investigate divine matters with earthly understanding, become foolish through their wisdom and do not attain the fullness of truth.
>
> “Those, therefore, who labor to uphold this teaching—when they cannot comprehend something—contend, swelling with proud spirit, that God either does not rightly will it or cannot do it.
>
> “As the Apostle says: ‘Claiming to be wise, they became fools’; and again: ‘They became futile in their reasonings.’
>
> “For what madman would seek human seed in that virginal conception where a heavenly mystery is being accomplished?”

And so forth.

This concludes what has been said concerning the virginity of blessed Mary.

### VIII

Maximus likewise everywhere celebrates Mary’s holiness and proclaims that she was filled with grace. Compare Homily 5, pp. 17–18; Homily 7, p. 22; and Homily 8, p. 24.

Nevertheless, there were those who thought that Maximus had imputed blame to the blessed Virgin because she had asked Christ to provide miraculously the wine that the bridegroom lacked at the wedding feast in Cana of Galilee.

How greatly they were mistaken has been demonstrated by us in the annotation appended to Homily 23, p. 67. It is also perfectly clear from that homily itself. There, p. 68, Maximus says that what Mary requested was a matter of timely grace, and that the most kindly Lord was not displeased to provide small things when great things were to come. For this reason, he says, venerable Mary—truly foreknowing that she was to be the Lord’s mother and anticipating the Lord’s will—carefully instructed the servants and said:

> “Whatever he tells you, do.”

The holy Mother also knew that the Lord’s rebuke to her, “What is there between me and you, woman?” was not the offense of an angry man but bore the mystery of compassion.

What? Are we to suppose that she was called to account, merely because she asked for grace, even though it was timely grace? And what grace did Christ provide? Should Mary be blamed because, knowing beforehand what her Son’s will would bring about and what he would grant, she both requested it from the Son himself and commanded the servants to do whatever he ordered?

Now, if τὸ “What is there between me and you, woman?” indicated, in Maximus’ opinion, that some fault attached to Mary, how could that same Maximus have said that the rebuke was not the offense of one who was angry but bore the mystery of compassion?

Since this is so, what remains except that we acknowledge, on Maximus’ authority, that no fault was attributed to the Virgin?

### IX

What the holy bishop wrote concerning Christ’s progress, as Luke says, in wisdom and age, has been explained by us at sufficient length in the annotations to Homily 21, pp. 58–59.

Maximus himself discusses the fast of that same Savior and our Lord Jesus Christ in many passages, and with complete theological clarity. It would be tedious to list every place in which he treats the subject. I shall cite one passage from Homily 44, p. 133, where he says:

> “Moses is the one who published the ancient law; Christ is the founder of the New Testament. Moses fasts in order to instruct one people in the discipline of the legal commandments; Christ fasts in order to redeem all nations. Moses fasts in order to receive the commands of the present life; Christ also fasts in order to establish the sacraments of eternal salvation. Moses fasts in order to see God; Jesus also fasts in order to show, while triumphing over the devil, that he is one with God.
>
> “After his fast, Moses broke the tablets written by the finger of God when the people transgressed; by his fast Christ consecrated the Gospel that would remain throughout the ages.
>
> “But what are we to make of the fact that, although both fasted for forty days, both are not said to have become hungry after the fast?
