Moses certainly was not hungry, so that divinity working in fragile humanity might be demonstrated; the Son of God was hungry, so that by assuming our flesh he might reveal that he had taken upon himself a fragile human being.
>
> “Moses’ not being hungry is an example of heavenly possibility; Christ’s being hungry is a sacrament of our redemption,” and so forth.

What he writes here concerning fragile humanity, in which divinity was at work, amounts to what he included in Homily 12, p. 35:

> “Observe that as a human being he endured WEAKNESSES for the weak, and as God exercised heavenly power.”

And in Homily 13, p. 35:

> “Today Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom the fullness of divinity exists, assuming the WEAKNESSES of our flesh, was born as a new human being.”

And on p. 38:

> “If, because of the weakness of your understanding, it seems less worthy to you to believe that the Son of God was born from a woman, consider that a virgin gave birth. If the rags in which he was wrapped perhaps seem worthless to you, marvel at the angels praising him and at the multitude of the heavenly host. If you despise the manger in which the infant lay, raise your eyes for a little while and behold in heaven the new star proclaiming the Lord’s birth to the world. If you believe the things that are lowly, believe the wondrous things. If you discuss what belongs to humility, revere what is exalted and heavenly. For from the same reporters and the same authorities you have learned both the humble and the glorious things concerning the Lord Savior; the sacred Gospels have handed down to you everything that pertained to the mystery of your salvation. In them you have grounds for believing the Lord Jesus to have been born a human being and for being unable to doubt that he is God.”

### X

Although Maximus observes that Christ’s divinity was manifested by so many indications, he denies—following the tradition of earlier Fathers [Note: St. Ignatius the Martyr, *Letter to the Ephesians*, no. 19, p. 112, vol. II of the *Apostolic Fathers*, London edition, 1746; Origen, *Homily 6 on Luke*, p. 544, vol. III of the works, Venice edition, 1743; the ancient author of the homily on the holy birth of Christ, no. 3, found in the appendix to the works of St. Basil the Great, vol. II, p. 594, Paris edition, 1722; St. John Chrysostom, *Exposition of Psalm XLIX*, no. 2, p. 225, vol. V of the works, Paris edition, 1724; St. Jerome, book I *On Matthew*, ch. 1, p. 13, vol. IX, Leipzig edition, 1684; St. Leo the Great, Sermon 21, the second *On the Nativity of the Lord*, ch. 3, p. 44, vol. I of the works, Rome edition, 1753, where he says: “Does it not appear, dearest ones, that the very fact that Christ chose to be born from a virgin was grounded in the highest reason? Namely, so that the devil might be unaware that the salvation of the human race had been born,” and so forth. To the same effect is what the monk Jobius writes in book VII, preserved by Photius, codex 222. I omit speaking of the author of the commentaries on the Gospels—which circulate under the name of Theophilus of Antioch—of Andrew of Crete, and of Saint Bernard. I shall say this briefly: this has both been the common opinion of the holy Fathers and remains the common opinion of theologians. What? Did God fear the devil? Not at all. Certainly he did not fear Herod—for whom would the Almighty fear?—but in his supreme counsel he willed that the infant Christ should remain hidden from him, be removed from his fury, and be transferred to Egypt, as related in the Gospel according to Matthew, chapter II. Therefore, because the incarnation of the Word was concealed from the devil, there is no reason to fear that any suspicion of fear could fall upon God.] that the mystery of the Incarnation was known to the devil.

For in Homily 37, the first *On Lent*, p. 107, he introduces the devil speaking as follows:

> “What is this birth, so new and powerful? Born among sinners and impious people, and yet having come forth from a mortal mother, he appears purer than all who are born, and even purer to me than heaven itself.
>
> “No root of greed rises up in him; no envy beats in his heart; his tongue knows no falsehood; his eyes admit no desire; he is not softened by any pleasure of the ears. And what more need I say? I find nothing in him that delights me; he renders all my efforts useless.
>
> “What shall I do? Where shall I turn? I sense that he is stronger. I suppose he wishes to reign in my kingdom—unless perhaps this is God, whom no sin can stain.
>
> “But if he were God, how could he endure the indignities of a woman’s childbirth? How could he be content with a cradle and swaddling clothes? Who could believe the cries of infancy in God? To anyone who does not hear them, is it not ridiculous that God should be nourished by a woman’s milk?
>
> “After everything else, behold, he is hungry, although reason certainly persuades us that God cannot be hungry.”

> “The devil was unaware,” Maximus continues, “that the nourishment which Christ endured in infancy, and that he was hungry as a human being, was not bodily weakness but a sacrament of heavenly grace. [lacuna] Behold, after three questions, the tempter accomplishes nothing. He came uncertain and departs still more uncertain.”

To the same subject belong the extensive discussions in Homily 42, the sixth *On Lent*, pp. 125–126; Homily 43, the seventh *On Lent*, pp. 129–130; Homily 23, the seventh *On the Epiphany*, p. 66; and many other passages that need not be listed.

### XI

Concerning Christ’s baptism and the sanctified waters, Homily 22, the sixth *On the Epiphany*, pp. 62–63, discusses the matter excellently. In that passage Maximus also treats the star seen by the Magi and the notable miracle of water changed into wine.

> “Today,” he says, “we celebrate that by which God declared himself through mighty works in a human being: because on this day either the star in heaven announced the news of his birth, or, at Cana of Galilee, at a wedding feast, he changed water into wine, or, in the waters of the Jordan, he consecrated the waters for the restoration of the human race through his baptism.
>
> “In each of these events the mysteries and joys of our salvation are contained. He was born from a Virgin for us, as the star showed. The washing of baptism was granted to us, as he consecrated it in the channel of the Jordan. He also foreshadowed by the miracle of his deed that we would be changed for the better, when he changed water into wine.
>
> “He intimated to us the baptism of his gift through the example of a second birth; and what he wished us to do, he himself did first.
>
> “We read that the Jews had various baptisms under the Law, but none of them could provide a universal remedy against the evil of transgression. Therefore, for the absolution of the whole world, the waters of regeneration needed to be sanctified from heaven.
>
> “And because the sacrament of baptism was necessary for the human race throughout the whole world, he gave a blessing to all waters when, with unique and singular compassion, he descended into the channel of the Jordan.
>
> “Then the water did not wash the Lord Christ; rather, it was washed. Christ came to you by being born; he served you by living; he engaged battle for you by dying. When you see him dead for you, understand that he was baptized for you.
>
> “He was altogether such even before baptism. Therefore his forerunner and Baptist addressed him in this way when he came to him to be baptized: ‘Lord, I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?’
>
> “What could be clearer concerning the purity of Christ before baptism? What could be stronger? ‘I ought to be baptized by you’: that is, ‘You are the fountain of innocence; you need nothing; you know how to give, but you do not know how to receive.’”

He makes the same point in Homily 29, the first *On the Baptism of Christ*, p. 86, where he says:

> “Today the Savior of the human race, revealed by heavenly signs, was worshiped by the Chaldeans. Today Christ, through the ministry of blessed John, consecrated the waters of the Jordan by the blessing of his own baptism. Today also, invited to a wedding, he manifested the power of his divinity by changing water into wine—water, I repeat, into wine: that is, water which he sanctified in baptism he ennobled at the wedding.
>
> “These three things, brethren, we recount as mysteries of one faith, but they were accomplished through one Lord by the condescension of the Trinity. Nor can unity ever be absent from the operation of divine powers, nor can what is undivided in deity ever be separated from one another.
>
> “Finally, when the Savior was baptized, the Father revealed by his voice that he was not absent from the Only-Begotten, and the Spirit revealed the same through the dove.
>
> “Let us not therefore wonder, brethren, since the Trinity is in our faith, that three mysteries consecrated one day for us.
>
> “Today, then, as we have said, the Magi found through the star what the Jew refused to believe through the prophets. Today the Gentile world, taught from heaven, seeks the world’s Redeemer as king, honors him with gifts as a powerful one, and worships him as God. [lacuna]
>
> “See and consider, brethren, how much grace mortality receives from divine condescension. For, so that the most sacred mysteries of our redemption might be confirmed, and so that the eternal Trinity might be revealed to us more clearly, the Son is baptized in the Jordan, the Spirit sanctifies the sacrament, and the Father discloses the truth. [lacuna]
>
> “Today likewise, as the Fathers testify, the Lord Jesus made wine from water at Cana of Galilee. In such wonders, brethren, you must have no hesitation concerning the Creator. For he who at the beginning of the world gave water its existence also made from water, at the end of the world, whatever he willed.”

Yet someone might ask how Maximus can affirm that Christ, although holy, was nevertheless reborn through baptism—both elsewhere and especially in Homily 30, the second on the Baptism of Christ, pp. 89ff.—and even say that he was sanctified. For he writes as follows:

> At one and the same time, the one whose birth people rejoiced over on earth was rejoiced over as sanctified in heaven. . . . New births deserve new services. There, when he is born according to humanity, his mother Mary enfolds him in her embrace; here, when he is **GIGNITUR**—“born” according to the mystery—God the Father embraces him with his voice.

But nothing could be explained more easily. I say that Maximus calls Christ “reborn,” “regenerated,” and “sanctified,” not because Christ himself acquired anything that he had previously lacked, but because he manifested himself to mortals as he truly was—namely, holy—and because that same Christ sanctified the waters, so that those who were baptized with his baptism might themselves be reborn and regenerated.

For in that same Homily 30, p. 90, when Maximus had posed the question, “If he is holy, why did he wish to be baptized?” he answered:

> Hear, then: Christ is baptized, not so that he may be sanctified by the waters, but so that he himself may sanctify the waters and purify, by his own purification, those streams which he touches. For Christ’s consecration is the consecration of the element in a higher sense. When our Savior is washed, all water is already cleansed for our baptism; the spring is purified, so that thereafter the grace of the laver may be supplied to the peoples who will follow. He therefore goes before through baptism, so that Christian peoples may confidently follow after him, and so forth.

And in the preceding homily, numbered 29, the first on the Baptism of Christ, pp. 87ff., he presents John addressing Christ in this manner:

> I certainly ought to be baptized by you, because corruption belongs to me through the transgression of the father, whereas communion belongs to you in the majesty of the Father. . . . I am an earthly creature; you are the Lamb of God. I am mortal under the law of sin, but you, coming against sins, do not know subjection to sin. And, after everything else, I have been made one who must be redeemed by you, whereas you were born to redeem.

Soon afterward he introduces Jesus replying to John in this way:

> Everything you mention is indeed true; but this is the purpose of my coming: since I have been made subject to the law, the lawful order must be fulfilled. I have come not to live for myself, for eternal life is mine with the Father, but to remove the condition of your death. [LIX] . . .

And indeed, brothers, how could Christ not have come to baptism for our sake, for whose sake he also did not avoid the indignity of bodily circumcision? Hence John, recognizing the saving mystery, no longer sanctifies the Son of God as a baptizer, but, as a devoted minister, obeys the commands imposed from heaven. . . .

> See and consider, brothers, how great a grace mortality receives from divine condescension. For, so that the most sacred mysteries of our redemption may be **CONFIRMED**, and so that the eternal Trinity may be revealed to us **MORE MANIFESTLY**, **THE SON IS BAPTIZED IN THE JORDAN**; the Spirit sanctifies the sacrament; the Father discloses the truth.

What then, if in Homily 33, the fifth on the Baptism of Christ, p. 95, he writes that the Baptist was sanctified by Christ, and that Christ himself, who was without **SIN**, came among the crowds of sinners for baptism, sanctifying not only the waters of the Jordan but also the entire substance of the waters that exist everywhere, and establishing the sacrament of the saving laver?

Moreover, in Homily 34, the sixth on the Baptism of Christ, p. 97, he says:

> John preached in the desert a baptism of repentance to a sinful people, not because it removed committed crimes, but so that it might reform those who had gone astray. For the forgiveness of sins was reserved for the grace of Christ. . . . An exceedingly great multitude of all kinds of people flocked to John out of desire for the laver. . . . Among such people was the Lord of the heavenly powers. . . . Jesus Christ does not disdain, in humility and quietness, to hasten to the baptism of his servant. . . . Jesus is baptized **NOT FOR HIMSELF, BUT FOR US**. He is baptized **NOT SO THAT HE MAY BE PURIFIED BY THE WATERS, BUT SO THAT HE HIMSELF MAY SANCTIFY THE WATERS**. The new man is baptized so that he may establish the sacrament of the new baptism. . . . Consider how great a grace has been **REVEALED TO US IN THE BAPTISM OF THE LORD**, and by what subtle mystery the Trinity has revealed itself to humanity today. . . . By what wondrous mystery our Lord Jesus Christ, either through the touch of his body or through the passage of his glory, sanctifies, vivifies, and illumines every creature for a moment, and so forth.

Maximus confirms this to the highest degree in Sermon 10, pp. 421ff., concerning what I noted shortly before about Christ’s manifestation:

> The days of the Epiphanies are so called by a Greek name. What we call “appearance” or “manifestation,” the Greeks call *epiphany*. We say this because today our Lord and Savior appeared on earth according to the flesh. Although he had been born long before from Mary and had completed thirty years of age, he was nevertheless unknown [Col. 0061] to the world. He became known at the time when he came to John the Baptist to be baptized in the Jordan, and the voice of the Father resounded from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” The one whom the Father had pointed out from heaven by his voice, the Holy Spirit, true in the likeness of a dove and sitting upon his head, wished to **DEMONSTRATE** by his touch, so that no one would suppose that another from among the people was the Son of God. . . . He is baptized [LX] by John in the flesh, but he himself washes John in the Spirit. The waters, which had been accustomed to cleanse other things, were cleansed when our Lord washed, and so forth.

He had said similar things in Sermon 9, pp. 418ff., where he writes:

> He appeared not so much to human eyes as for the sake of salvation. For although he had previously been born from a virgin and was visible to bodily eyes, he did not appear, because the eye of faith did not yet know his power. . . . After he had declared his humanity through miracles, appearing to human minds as something new and unexpected, he poured light into certain eyes of the heart, so that the understanding might recognize the one whom sight had not recognized.

And in Sermon 11, p. 424:

> Did he wish to be baptized for his own sake, when he had no sin, as the prophet says? . . . Certainly for our sake, who, burdened by the sins of many crimes, needed to be cleansed in Christ’s baptism. Therefore the Lord came to the laver, **NOT SO THAT HE HIMSELF MIGHT BE PURIFIED** by the waters, but **SO THAT HE MIGHT PURIFY THE STREAMS OF WATER FOR US**. From the moment he immersed himself in the waters, he removed the sins of all believers. It was necessary that he should remove the sins of all, since he bore the sins of all, as the evangelist says: “This is the Lamb of God; this is the one who takes away the sins of the world.” Thus, in a wondrous manner, one is immersed and the salvation of all is restored.
>
> The Father God is present when the Lord is baptized; the Holy Spirit is present. See the Savior’s benevolence: because he alone subjected himself to insults in the Passion, in the laver he alone did not seek grace. He wishes others to share in his glory. The Father, then, is present, as I said; the Holy Spirit is also present. And because God cannot be seen, the Spirit descends in the form of a dove, the Father in the voice; and, what alone was necessary for establishing faith, he **PRESENTS THE SAVIOR**.

And in Sermon 12, p. 427:

> He accomplished all these things plainly for our sake. For what person would consecration be necessary for, when he himself is the sacrament? For what purpose would the solemnity of the mystery be needed in one who is the fullness of the mystery? . . . As the evangelist says: “From his fullness we have all received.” Therefore, since the fullness of divinity was in him, he did not need to be filled through the mysteries of the sacraments. Rather, he wished to fulfill the mystery, not so that he himself might gain advancement, but so that the fullness of the mystery might benefit us.
>
> Finally, when John the Baptist resisted and said, “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” the Lord said to him, “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” He says, “to fulfill all righteousness.” Why, then, is the Lord baptized? Righteousness does not justify Christ; rather, righteousness itself is sanctified by Christ, and incomplete virtue is fulfilled by the one in whom the fullness of virtues resides. . . . For what consecration could John impart to the one from whom he himself desired to receive sanctification?

Therefore, since, according to Maximus’s testimony, Christ was as holy before baptism as he was after receiving baptism, and since he possessed such innocence that he needed nothing—he knew how to give but not how to receive—and since he did not approach baptism in order to be sanctified [LXI] or purified by the waters, for he has eternal life with the Father, but in order to remove the condition of our death; indeed, since he was baptized not for himself but for us, and in order to sanctify and purify the waters, consecrate the streams he touched, and establish a laver of regeneration for all; and since, as the same Maximus acknowledges, consecration was not necessary for Christ’s advancement, because he himself is the sacrament and the fullness of the mystery, but he wished to fulfill the mystery not so that he himself might gain advancement—for no consecration could be imparted to him—but so that the fullness of the mystery might benefit us—since, I say, these things stand thus, with Maximus himself granting the point, what is there to trouble anyone in those statements of that same Maximus concerning the Savior Christ as reborn, regenerated, sanctified, and consecrated by the waters of baptism?

For the one who writes that Christ was baptized for us, not for himself, clearly indicates, by also calling him reborn and regenerated, that Christ is said to have been sanctified, reborn, and regenerated not in himself but in his members—such as we become through baptism.

That same Maximus, in Homily 21, the fifth on the Epiphany, p. 38, explains that Christ is said to have advanced not because Christ’s holiness, which is perfect, advances, but because he is said to advance when he produces an increase of faith in us.

If this is so, why should we not likewise judge that, when he writes elsewhere that Christ was reborn, regenerated, and sanctified, he wrote this for the reason that Christ is called reborn, regenerated, sanctified, and consecrated because he established for us the sacrament by which we are reborn, regenerated, and sanctified?

Because in the waters of the Jordan he consecrated the waters for the regeneration of the human race through his baptism? [Note: Homily 22, p. 62, and Homily 29, p. 87.]

Because the fact that the Lamb of God was baptized dedicated for us the saving gift of the baptism that regenerates? [Note: Homily 23, p. 65, and Homily 30, p. 90.]

Because he was baptized no longer for his own sake but for ours? [Note: Homily 31, p. 91.]

Why could Christ not also have been called “reborn” by Maximus in his mystical body, which is the Church, when the same holy bishop teaches:

> In Christ’s baptism the Church was spiritually reborn, and is reborn daily. For the Church itself passes daily into the life of regeneration whenever it receives catechumens for baptism.

Moreover, why could the manifestation of Christ’s power and holiness not have been called by Maximus Christ’s sanctification and consecration? By Maximus, I say, who denies that Christ approached baptism in order to gain advancement, but affirms that he approached it for our benefit; and who, when indicating in what sense Christ is said to be born through baptism, says:

> When God the Father embraces him with his voice—for he says, “This is my Son, and so forth”—the Father manifests him as one to be worshiped by the nations. [Note: Homily 30, p. 90.]

## XII.

Since we have now dealt, on the basis of Maximus’s teaching, with the baptized Savior Christ and with the institution of baptism, I think it will not be out of place to explain briefly how gravely [Col. 0063] the holy bishop regarded the fact that in his day there were some who postponed initiation into the sacred rites of baptism—either because they confidently believed that they could be immersed in the waters of the Jordan at some later [LXII] time, or because they had persuaded themselves that they would depart more pure into heaven if they delayed baptism until their final day.

Thus, in Sermon 13, which concerns the Grace of Baptism, pp. 430ff., he says:

> Since it is established, as we have explained above, that Jesus Christ was baptized not for his own sake but for ours, we ought—I am speaking to you catechumens—to receive the grace of his baptism **WITH ALL POSSIBLE HASTE** [Note: [Col. 0063] Gregory of Nyssa’s discourse addressed to those who delay baptism is extant in vol. II of his works, p. 224. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 40, which is on holy baptism, p. 647 of the Cologne edition of 1690, says: “As long as you are numbered among the catechumens, you are in the vestibule of piety. You must enter, pass through the forecourt, behold the holy things, look into the Holy of Holies, and be joined to the Trinity. Great are the things against which you are being attacked; you also need great protection. Therefore raise the shield of faith against them. Compare what follows. See also pp. 50ff., where he refutes the excuses of those who did not hesitate to postpone baptism. Related here are the discussions of St. John Chrysostom in Homily 1 on the Acts of the Apostles, no. 6, p. 11, vol. IX of his works, Paris edition of 1731, and Homily 23, no. 4, p. 190. The other holy Fathers held the same position, but there is no room to set out their opinions.]—and to draw from the fountain of the Jordan, which he blessed, the blessing of consecration, taking care that our sins be plunged into that whirlpool into which his holiness was immersed. . . .

> Therefore, brothers, we ought to be baptized in the same whirlpool as the Savior. But, in order to be immersed in the same fountain, we do not need to seek the region of the East [Note: It is understood from Eusebius’s book *On the Hebrew Places*, which St. Jerome [Col. 0064] translated into Latin, p. 181, vol. III of St. Jerome’s works, Leipzig edition of 1684, that there were quite a few who postponed baptism so that they might be baptized in the Jordan. Among those who postponed baptism for that reason Eusebius includes the emperor Constantine Augustus, Book IV of *The Life of Constantine*, chapter 62, p. 599 of the Turin edition of 1746. The emperor Constantius likewise postponed baptism, as Athanasius records in his letter *On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia*, no. 31, vol. I, part II of his works, Padua edition of 1777, p. 597; but the holy teacher does not indicate for what reason. The elder Theodosius also postponed receiving baptism for some time; concerning this, see Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 6, p. 226 of the Turin edition of 1747. Concerning the praetor Arinthaeus, see what St. Basil writes in Letter 269, formerly 186, to the wife of that same Arinthaeus, no. 2, p. 416, vol. III of his works, Paris edition of 1730. Yet although, because of the circumstances of the times, the Fathers did not openly rebuke this practice in some cases, since they nevertheless rebuked it generally and expressly, as we saw above, they sufficiently indicated that, in their judgment, it ought not to be tolerated in anyone.], nor the river of the Jewish land. For wherever Christ is, there too is the Jordan. The same consecration that blessed the rivers of the East sanctifies the streams of the West. Therefore, even if the river has perhaps another name in worldly usage, it nevertheless contains the mystery of the Jordan.

## XIII.

How much superior Christ’s baptism is to John’s baptism Maximus demonstrates in many passages, following the other Fathers and the Scriptures.

In Homily 22, the sixth on the Epiphany, p. 63, he says:

> We read that the Jews had various baptisms under the Law, but none of these could provide a universal remedy against the evil of transgression. Therefore human beings needed the water of regeneration, sanctified from heaven, for the absolution of the whole world. And because the sacrament of baptism was necessary for the human race throughout the whole world, Christ gave his blessing to all waters when, with unique and singular devotion, he descended into the bed of the Jordan. At that time the wave did not so much wash the Lord Christ as itself was washed.
>
> Therefore Christ came to you by being born, served you by living, and fought for you by dying. The one whom you see dead for you, understand to have been baptized for you. He was entirely such even before baptism; and therefore his precursor and Baptist, when he came to him to be baptized, addressed him thus: “Lord, I ought to be baptized by you.” [LXIII]
>
> What could be clearer concerning the purity of Christ before baptism? What could be stronger? “I ought to be baptized by you,” who are the fountain of innocence. . . . “I ought to be baptized by you,” because with you and in you you display and possess the gifts of purity and the sacrament of baptism; and what I shall give, through your generosity, you possess by nature. At his touch the limbs are immersed and the streams enriched. The blessed water marvels that its own fountain descends into it, and in a single moment conceives eternal remedies, and so forth.

In Homily 33, the fifth on the Baptism of Christ, pp. 95ff.:

> The Church grew because on this day the sacrament of the saving laver was also instituted by Christ the Lord. . . . Finally, our Redeemer wished to be baptized in the Jordan and in turn to sanctify his Baptist. Christ is therefore baptized in the Jordan, and on this day he sanctified the waters of the Jordan through his baptism. But why do I say “of the Jordan”? For through his baptism he sanctified the entire substance of the waters that exist everywhere.
>
> Behold, then, how on this most holy day the Church from the Gentiles was gathered through the calling of the Magi, and how, in Christ’s baptism, it was also spiritually reborn and is reborn daily. For the Church itself passes daily into the life of regeneration whenever it receives catechumens for baptism, and so forth.

And in Homily 34, the sixth on the Baptism of Christ, pp. 96ff.:

> Christ is baptized in the streams of the Jordan; the waters are consecrated for our baptism. Therefore, beloved, we must now say something about baptism to your holiness, insofar as the Lord grants it. . . . John preached in the desert a baptism of repentance to a sinful people, not one that removed committed crimes, but one that reformed those who had gone astray. For the forgiveness of sins was reserved for the grace of Christ. . . .
>
> As he hurried toward the river, John suddenly cried out in the presence of the surrounding crowds: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sins of the world.” This means: “Cease now, cease from my baptism, by which repentance is received. Behold the Baptizer through whom crimes are forgiven. Do not continue wishing to be baptized by your fellow servant. The Lord of us all is present, and he baptizes for life. Follow him; believe in him; with your whole mind, as suppliants, ask from him the laver of salvation—from him by whom I myself, your Baptist, desire to be baptized.”
>
> Jesus is baptized not for himself but for us; not so that he may be purified by the waters, but so that he himself may sanctify the waters. The new man is baptized so that he may establish the sacrament of the new baptism.

But, for the sake of brevity, I shall pass over the other passages of Maximus that bear on this subject and shall use, finally, two passages. The first is taken from Sermon 12, p. 427, and reads as follows:

> Therefore Christ wished to fulfill the mystery, not so that he himself might gain advancement, but so that [Col. 0065] the fullness of the mystery might benefit us. . . . John says: “I ought to be baptized by you.” He therefore protests that the Lord was not baptized for his own sake, since, before he was baptized, John demanded rather to be baptized by him. By saying this he demonstrates that there is greater grace in the Lord’s mystery than in John, the minister of the mystery. [LXIV]
>
> For what consecration could he impart to Christ from whom John himself desired to receive sanctification? The minister was inferior in merits to the disciple in holiness. In comparison with Christ, the teacher John was inexperienced, righteousness was incomplete, and the water was turbid. But when the Lord is baptized, through his blessing the teacher also advances, righteousness is fulfilled, and the water is purified.
>
> The water was purified: although it had been lowly and cold, it was enriched by the warmth of the Lord’s blessing, so that what previously had scarcely washed away the stains of worldly things now **PURIFIES THE SPIRITUAL STAINS OF SOULS**.
>
> Nor should you be surprised that we say water—that is, a bodily substance—can reach **THE PURIFICATION OF THE SOUL**. It certainly reaches it; it penetrates every hidden place of conscience. Although water itself is subtle and fine, through Christ’s blessing it is made still more subtle and, through the hidden channels of life, by the dew of the Spirit penetrates to the sins of the soul. **THE FLOW OF BLESSINGS IS FINER THAN THE COURSE OF THE WATERS.**
>
> Therefore we also said that, in the Savior’s baptism, the blessing that flowed down like a particular river permeated the courses of all the pools and the veins of every spring. For it is wondrous, I say, that when Christ was placed in the Jordan, the rivers of water were washed. But the streams of blessings also ran. On one side the bed of the river carried more turbid water; on the other, the Savior’s pure fountain cleansed it. And, in a kind of astonishment, the consecration of baptism rose downward toward the source of the Jordan, while against the river of the waters the river of blessings was carried, and so forth.

The second passage is taken from Sermon 13, which concerns the Grace of Baptism, pp. 429ff., and is as follows:

> Without prejudice to the faith, I would say that, although both baptisms—namely, John’s and Christ’s—belong to the Lord, I consider that baptism by which we are washed more gracious than that by which the Savior is baptized. This one is celebrated through Christ; that one was celebrated through John. In the former the teacher excuses himself; in the latter the Savior invites us. In the former righteousness is incomplete; in the latter the Trinity is perfect. To the former the holy one came and departed holy; to the latter the sinner comes and departs holy. In the former a blessing is bestowed upon the mysteries; in the latter sins are forgiven through the mysteries.

And thus far concerning the comparison of John’s baptism with Christ’s baptism.

### XIV

Now, concerning the miracles and the preaching of Christ the Savior, briefly, insofar as this can be done.

Maximus notes that through his miracles Christ was manifested as God, although he had assumed human nature, subject as it was to our infirmities (homily 17, p. 50):

> “Christ our Lord had been invited to an earthly wedding and came, not to enjoy that banquet, but to demonstrate that he was its author. By sanctifying that wedding, his divine power increased, when he himself gave the wedding guests the wine that had failed them. He did indeed give wine. He himself changed the water-filled jars into wine [LXV] … Seeing so great a miracle, therefore, as the divine sermon relates, his disciples believed in him—no longer merely that he was the Son of Man, but that he was the Son of God, which so great a miracle confirmed. Let us also, brothers, believe this with all our heart: that he, although sharing our nature, is nevertheless coequal with the divine substance of the Father.”

And in homily 23, the seventh on the Epiphany, p. 69:

> “The transformation of water from its own nature into another created thing testified to the power of the present Creator. Nor could anyone convert water to other uses except the one who made it from nothing … Nor should we doubt, beloved, that the one who transformed water into wine is the one who in the beginning created it as snow and hardened it into ice … The disciples believed—not, certainly, what they saw taking place, but what a carnal gaze could not see. They believed, not that Christ Jesus was the son of a virgin, which was known, but that this same one was the Only-begotten of the Most High, which was proved by the deed. Therefore let us also, brothers, believe with all our heart that he whom we confess as the Son of Man is the Son of God. Let us believe that he shares our nature and is coequal with the substance of the Father, since he attended the wedding as a human being and changed water into wine as God.”

To the same conclusion plainly belong what that holy bishop develops in homily 24, p. 70 and following; homily 29, p. 87 and following; and homily 32, the fourth on Christ’s Baptism, p. 93, where he says:

> “The almighty power of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, is clearly gathered from the reading we have just heard. Although his omnipotence—by which in the beginning, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he created heaven and earth from nothing—seemed hidden in the human being whom he had assumed for our redemption, it was nevertheless manifested to his disciples. For when he had come to a wedding of the ancient institution at Cana of Galilee, and suddenly the wine failed those who were dining, he himself, who had not disdained to be present at that wedding, also wished to confirm that wedding by a miracle, and changed water into wine.”

Nor do the things that he pursues in homily 34, p. 96 and following, belong elsewhere.

Now, in sermon 9, the third on the Lord’s Epiphany, p. 418:

> “Because the Savior then first appeared in the world, that day itself was called Epiphany by the same name. Let us inquire, however, how he appeared—not because he had not previously been in the world, since the world was made through him, but because then for the first time Christ God shone through signs and miracles into the hearts of believers, and the splendor of faith came into the darkened consciences of human beings … He appeared not so much to human eyes as for salvation. For although he had previously been born of a virgin and could be seen by carnal eyes, he did not appear, because the sharpness of faith did not yet know his power … After he had manifested his humanity through miracles, appearing to human minds as something new and unexpected, he infused certain eyes of the heart [LXVI], so that perception might recognize him whom the eye had not recognized. Hence it comes about that we contemplate Christ the Lord through faith, although we have never seen him, while the Jews, who looked upon him with their eyes and touched him with their hands, do not see him even today.

> “Let us therefore inquire what sign he performed in order to declare his divinity to the peoples. He is said to have performed this first miracle: that he changed water into wine. It was plainly a great sign, sufficient for believing in the majesty of God. Who would not marvel that the elements were changed into something other than what they had been? For no one can change nature except the Lord of nature [Col. 0067]. From this we must now believe that mortal human beings can be changed into immortality, since a lowly substance was changed into a precious substance.

> “I do not want you, hearer, to look merely at the names ‘wine’ and ‘water’; but if you wish to establish the power, look at the power of the things themselves. For something far greater—I scarcely know what—is demonstrated … It was therefore fitting that the Lord should wish to perform this deed, so that through this earthly sign the heavenly mystery that was to come might already be seen by the wise. For if it is marvelous to supply the wedding guests with wine when theirs had failed, how much more marvelous is it to restore to human beings the life that had been exhausted.”

Concerning the other wonders performed by Christ—such as the sudden healing of the man whose hand was withered, the restoration of health to the paralytic, and Peter’s walking upon the waters through Christ’s power—Maximus writes in homilies 108 and 116. In the latter, p. 383:

> “The Lord Jesus Christ, entering the synagogue on the Sabbath, cured by spiritual medicine the man who had a withered hand—not by applying herbal juices, nor by binding on medicinal compounds, but by commanding with a word, and by issuing his command in anger he restored health to the body … By a word, therefore, he commands that the sap of the veins should flow into the withered right hand. It is not marvelous if the one who created the entire body from withered dust restored a withered right hand, and restored by the command of his word that which, at the beginning, he had established through the operation of creation. The creature, recognizing its author, obeys.”

In homily 108, p. 360, after Maximus has mentioned the Pharisees’ objections and their asking who the man was who had said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven,” since sins cannot be forgiven except by God, and after Christ’s response, “Which is easier to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk,’” and so forth, he continues:

> “The scrutinizer of souls anticipated the wicked counsels of their minds and displayed the power of his divinity by the testimony of his deed, while he reassembled the limbs of the dismembered body, tightened the sinews, joined the bones, filled out the entrails, strengthened the joints, and raised to walking the steps that had already been buried in a living corpse. ‘Take up your bed’—that is, carry the one who carried you—and reverse all the roles, so that what was the testimony of infirmity may be the proof of health,” and so forth.

Concerning Christ’s granting Peter the ability to walk upon the waters, Maximus had said shortly before, on p. 357:

> “Is this not the one who bent the sea’s whirlpools [LXVII] beneath Peter’s feet, so that the liquid path might offer solid obedience to human steps?” and so forth.

In sermon 94, p. 639, he discusses miracles of healing in general; on p. 642, the storm calmed by Christ; in sermon 95, p. 644 and following, the miraculous catch of fish; and in sermon 106, p. 668, the five loaves and two fish with which Christ fed five thousand men:

> “Five loaves were brought in, and twelve baskets of fragments were carried away. Thus those who gather the leftovers find more than the one who brought the food supplied to the banquet. Finally, after the five thousand men had been fed, scarcely twelve apostles carried away twelve baskets—what one boy had brought in his hand before anything had been consumed. Thus bread is multiplied in the Lord’s hand while it is broken; it grows while it is diminished; while it is distributed it increases; and through a more beneficial expenditure the created food nourishes and advances the peoples. What seemed smaller in the hands of those serving grows in the mouths of those eating. Finally, Saint Andrew says: ‘There is one boy here who has five loaves and two fish,’ and so forth.

> “In a wondrous manner, therefore, through the blessing of Christ the Lord, the solid nature of bread flows, abounds, and overflows; and by a kind of irrigation of strength it becomes for those eating not now a spring of water but of food. We read in the prophets that this same Lord brought drink forth for the thirsty from hard rock. Behold, now he has produced streams for the hungry from dry bread.”

Moreover, in sermon 107, while treating the similar wonder of the seven loaves with which Christ fed four thousand men, the deaf and mute man to whom Christ restored the ability to hear and speak, and the healing of the daughter of the Canaanite woman, he writes as follows, p. 669:

> “Our Lord Jesus Christ has shown the loftiness of his divinity and the mercy of his humanity in many and varied ways in the Holy Scriptures, as he is accustomed to do in mysteries and sacraments, so that those who ask may receive, those who seek may find, and to those who knock it may be opened. For all the miracles that he displayed in this world beneath the frailty of our condition benefit us. The Lord did not perform them without cause, or as though uselessly and in vain. Christ is the Word of God, who speaks to human beings not only in words but also in deeds … On either side, whoever says that he was only a human being denies the glory of the Creator; whoever says that he was only God denies the mercy of the Redeemer.

> “That the Lord had compassion on the crowd, lest they fail through hunger or the exertion of a longer journey, we recognize as the feeling and compassion of human frailty. But that he fed four thousand people with seven loaves and a few fish, we believe to be the work of divine power … Having left the Jews, he came into the territory of the Gentiles, where the Canaanite woman … implores the Lord. She continued asking until she received what she sought.

> “After this he again healed the deaf and mute man. Thus, in those days, when a multitude of people had gathered and they had nothing to eat … the Lord said … ‘I do not want to send them away fasting’ … [LXVIII] His disciples said to him: ‘Where could anyone get enough bread to feed these people in the wilderness?’ The apostles were still held by unbelief, until the mysteries were revealed; they did not remember what he had done with the five loaves and two fish. And he asked them how many loaves they had. They said, ‘Seven,’ and he commanded the crowd to sit down upon the ground … They ate, were satisfied, and took up seven baskets full. Those who had eaten were about four thousand, besides women and children … In the earlier reading, with five loaves and two fish he fed five thousand people; here, with seven loaves, he fed four thousand,” and so forth.

And in sermon 43, p. 512:

> “In Christ there was both the dominion of the one who reigns and the ministry of the one who serves … Christ was in the form of God … when, at his command, demons were driven from possessed bodies and from their ancient dwellings, crying out. He was in the form of God when, in the midst of the waves, the solidified water served his venerable footsteps. For he did everything as the Lord was able to do, and endured everything as a servant.

> “But now let us see by what virtues and by what stages he who was a servant confirmed to his disciples that he was God. First of all, when the beloved centurion’s necessary servant was suffering from a fatal illness, at the request of his master, while absent he healed the absent man—as God truly does—by sending health; and [Col. 0069] the sick man, whom he did not see bodily as he lay at some distance, he visited with the eyes of his divinity.

> “Finally, when the only son of a pitiable widow was already being carried on a bier to the grave for burial, he raised him by the command of his life-giving authority and restored him to life and to his mother in the midst of the crowd, with death itself bearing witness. After this, when the ruler of the priests pleaded for the health of his daughter, he who had given life to one being born brought the soul of the dead girl back into her own body.

> “And lest any suspicion remain among the impious because of the miracles involving more recent deaths, and lest they think that those raised so quickly had not truly died, he proceeded to the burial place of blessed Lazarus. Lazarus had been dead four days and was already stinking, and had moreover been bound with bands, as was customary. At the command of Christ, who called him, he leaped forth and immediately became a participant in conversation with his Lord and a guest at his table. All these things were done so that no one might dispute at all his return from the underworld.”

But enough concerning the miracles. The path to all of them would be long. What occurred at Christ’s death, what he subsequently accomplished, and what Maximus treats fully and at length, I shall describe at a suitable time, when the occasion requires it. Now, a few words concerning Christ’s preaching.

I see that what the Savior of the human race taught, either openly and plainly or by using parables, is gathered by Maximus in homily 108, p. 357 and following; 109, p. 361 and following; 111, p. 369 and following; 114, p. 380 and following; 116, p. 383 and following; 117, p. 386 and following; sermon 2, p. 398 and following; and in other places too numerous to count.

I shall give this brief passage, which the holy bishop observes in sermon 37, the ninth on the Solemnity of Easter, p. 495:

> “Having assumed flesh from a virgin, lest we suffer any clouding of the faith of our confession, THROUGHOUT THE WHOLE PERIOD OF HIS PREACHING he revealed himself as truly God and showed himself to be perfect man. For he wept, grieving as though he shared our sorrow; but, powerful through his own might, he pitied the blindness of the blind: for one he made eyes that had not yet been formed, for another he restored eyes that had been lost. While sailing with his disciples, he slept in the stern with the sleep of a human being; but by the command of his conscious majesty he immediately restrained the threatening masses of the rising waves and the menacing winds with tranquil calm. As a human being subject to temporal life, he repeatedly testified that he would die; but as eternal God, when the life-giving spirit had returned to his body, he commanded the dead to return to the light.”

### XV

Maximus teaches that the Savior Christ, finally sold by the traitor Judas, was handed over through the greatest crime, and that for this reason Judas himself was condemned by his own judgment, in homilies 47, p. 144, and 48, p. 147 and following.

In homily 51, p. 157, Maximus compares the thief who confessed Christ on the cross with Judas:

> “The Lord rightly grants paradise to this thief, because what Judas Iscariot sold in the garden, this man confesses on the gallows of the cross. A wondrous thing! The thief confesses the one whom the disciple denied. A wondrous thing, I say! The thief honors the one suffering whom Judas betrayed with a kiss. From the one, the blandishments of peace are sold; from the other, the wounds of the cross are proclaimed.”

And in homily 52, p. 162:

> “After Judas lost faith, he lost the innocence of the apostolate. For he became guilty of every crime after he denied the Lord of every virtue … Thus faith makes even thieves innocent, while treachery makes apostles criminal.”

There is no need to pursue this subject further.

Concerning the trial instituted against Christ by Pilate, the governor of Judaea—a trial indeed full of injury and injustice—Maximus speaks excellently in homily 46, p. 144.

Regarding the Hebrews who accused Christ and brought ruin upon themselves and their descendants, he says in sermon 29, p. 473 and following:

> “By their cruel sentence they consigned their children and descendants to crimes, saying: ‘His blood be upon us and upon our children.’ A cruel sentence of the Jews, who by their crime not only condemned those presently alive but also killed those not yet born. For how many do they call by this utterance to awareness of the crime, although knowledge of the crime did not yet hold them? Cruel, I say, is their impiety, because it calls their descendants to guilt before bringing them into the light, so that those yet to be born would encounter sin before life. Truly bloodstained parents, who became murderers before they became parents; and before they knew whether they could have them as participants in their blood, they made them partners in their crimes. It is therefore not surprising that they were so cruel toward the Savior, since they proved so cruel toward their descendants.”

Maximus observes that Christ kept silent while he was accused [LXX], and that by keeping silent he confirmed his innocence and won the victory. In homily 46, p. 141 and following:

> “It may perhaps seem astonishing, brothers, that the Lord should be accused before the governor Pilate by the chief priests and remain silent, without exposing their wickedness by his answer, since a defense ordinarily follows an accusation in order to refute it. Astonishing, I say, that the Savior should be accused and remain silent. For silence is sometimes taken as consent; he seems to confirm what is alleged when he does not wish to answer what is asked.

> “Does the Lord therefore confirm his accusation by keeping silent? No indeed: he does not confirm his accusation by keeping silent, but despises it by not refuting it. He is rightly silent who has no need of defense. Let the one who fears defeat seek defense. Let the one who fears being conquered hurry to speak. But Christ, when he is condemned, also conquers; when he is judged, he also wins, as the prophet says: ‘So that you may be justified in your words and conquer when you are judged.’

> “Why, then, did he need to speak before the judgment, for whom the judgment itself was a complete victory? For Christ conquers when he is judged, because he is thereby proved innocent. Hence Pilate says: ‘I am innocent of the blood of this just man,’ and so forth.”

For whom, why, and how savagely the Savior of the human race suffered is perfectly clear from what I shall now quote.

In homily 52, p. 162:

> “One suffered for the salvation of all.”

Again, in homily 50, p. 153:

> “The passion of Christ is our redemption; his death is our life. He endured all these evils so that we might experience every good. He chose to have cruelty exercised against himself so that he might bestow mercy upon us. For by the cross he removed the injuries of the human race and consumed them all in his passion.”

The same thought appears in homily 83, p. 270:

> “The Only-begotten Son of God became the Son of Man, so that he who was the creator of the world might also become its redeemer. He was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate [Col. 0071]. Let us feel no shame concerning the cross of Christ, because through his passion we have victory … The immaculate Lamb suffered not for himself but for us … Nor was it an unconsidered or unforeseen event that he was killed, since by the counsel of his divinity he assumed humanity for this very reason: so that he could be killed for humanity. He chose the punishment of the cross so that a harsher punishment might produce a more exalted victory; and he who suffered for the good of the universe might die lifted high before the eyes of the world, so that those who saw the crucified one might at the same time behold the wonders of the Crucified.”

What shall I say about the symbols of the cross, which Maximus reviewed and explained in the same manner as Justin Martyr and the others who later fought for the Christian religion against the pagans had explained them?

Justin, in the First Apology, no. 55, p. 78 of the Venetian edition of 1747, says:

> “Consider in your minds whether anything in the world can be carried on and joined together in commerce [LXXI] without this figure. The sea cannot be cut through unless that trophy called the sail remains intact in the ship. The earth cannot be plowed without it. Diggers cannot work, nor craftsmen and artisans likewise, except with instruments bearing this figure,” and so forth.

Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter 16; Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, p. 302 of the Leiden edition of 1709; and others, to pass over the rest, argue in agreement with these statements.

Now consider whether Maximus does not proceed in the same way in homily 50, p. 254, concerning the ship’s mast, which displays the likeness of a cross and without which the sea cannot be cut through:

> “Great is the sacrament of the cross; and if we understand it, by this sign the world itself is also saved. For when sailors cut through the sea, they first raise the mast and spread the sail, so that, once the Lord’s cross has been formed, the streams of water may be cleft. By this saving sign they seek the harbor of salvation and escape the danger of death. For the suspended sail on the mast is a certain figure of the sacrament, as though Christ had been exalted upon the cross. Just as the Church cannot stand without the cross, so the ship is weak without the mast … The good farmer also, when he prepares to turn the soil and seek the nourishment of life, attempts to do so only through the sign of the cross. For when he places the plowshare beneath the earth, fastens the ears, and sets in place the handle, he imitates the figure of the cross; the joining itself is a certain likeness of the Lord’s Passion.”

Justin continues:

> “The human form differs from irrational living creatures in no other respect than that it is upright and has the extension of the hands … and displays nothing other than the form of a cross.”

Similar passages are found in Tertullian, *Against the Nations*, book I, chapter 12:

> “In our very body there is, by a silent and secret line, the form of a cross.”

Likewise Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, p. 304:

> “Human beings worship God with outstretched hands and a pure mind. Thus either natural reason rests upon the sign of the cross, or your religion is formed by it.”

What does Maximus say? In the same place, p. 155:

> “The very gait of a human being, when he raises his hands, draws a cross.”

For this reason Maximus observes that Christians formerly became accustomed to praying with outstretched hands:

> “Therefore we are commanded to pray with raised hands, so that even by the gesture of our limbs we may confess the Lord’s Passion.”

Tertullian mentions this custom in the book entitled *On Prayer*, chapter 12:

> “We do not merely raise our hands, but also spread them out, imitating the Lord’s Passion; and by praying we confess to Christ.”

And in *Apologeticus*, chapter 30:

> “Looking upward, Christians pray with outstretched hands, because they are harmless; with uncovered head, because they are not ashamed; finally, without an instructor, because they pray from the heart.”

Long before Tertullian, Clement, bishop of Rome, had committed the same matter to writing in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, no. 2, p. 10, volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, Paris edition of Coustantius, 1721.

Hence, in ancient Christian monuments, especially those in the cemeteries, images are displayed of men and women praying with outstretched hands [LXXII].

I return to Maximus. He continues to write about Christ’s cross as follows:

> “The holy Moses also overcame Amalek in this manner when he waged war against him—not with weapons or iron, but with his hands raised to God.”

An ancient author had first presented this example in the Epistle attributed to Saint Barnabas, no. 12, volume I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 61, London edition of 1746.

Justin Martyr imitated this example in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, no. 91, p. 198, where he says:

> “When the people were waging war against Amalek, and the son of Nave, who was called Jesus, was first in the battle line, Moses himself prayed to God with both hands extended. Hur and Aaron supported them throughout the day, lest, when he grew weary, they should be lowered. For whenever he relaxed anything of this sign imitating the cross, the people were defeated, as it is written in the books of Moses. But whenever it remained in this position, Amalek was defeated for as long as it remained so; and whoever excelled in strength excelled through the cross.”

The writings of Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 10, p. 196, and *Against Marcion*, book III, chapter 18, p. 408 of the Venetian edition of 1744; Saint Cyprian, *Testimonies*, book II, chapter 21, p. 46 of the Oxford edition of 1682; Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 448 of the Leiden edition of 1709, issued after Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*; and, to omit the others lest I be excessive in a matter of little necessity, Gregory of Nazianzus, *Poems*, LIII, p. 127 of the Cologne edition of 1690, do not differ from this.

Nor did Maximus confine himself to these figures or symbols. He also recalled to the people that celebrated and memorable event concerning the bronze serpent raised by Moses at God’s command, for the healing of those who had been brought into extreme danger of life by the bites of serpents.

Thus, in homily 49, p. 152:

> “When holy Moses had led the children of Israel out of Egyptian captivity, and the same people were suffering in the wilderness from a severe attack by serpents, while no defense by weapons could resist them, holy Moses, filled with the divine Spirit, raised a bronze serpent fastened to wood in the midst of the dying crowds, and commanded the people to place their hope of healing in that sign. Through this there arose so great a remedy against the bite of the asps that anyone who had been wounded and either looked upon or hoped in that serpent-cross immediately received the remedy of salvation.

> “The Lord also recalled this deed in the Gospel, saying: ‘Just as Moses exalted the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be exalted.’ Therefore, if the serpent fastened to wood brought healing to the children of Israel, how much more does the Lord crucified upon the gallows provide salvation to the peoples [Col. 0073]? And if the mere figure benefited them, how much benefit do we believe the reality provides?

> “The serpent is therefore crucified first—entirely rightly, so that the devil, who first sinned against God, might first be struck by the sentence of the cross. For he is crucified upon wood so that, because humanity had been deceived in paradise through the tree of desire, humanity might now be saved through the tree of wood; and the same material that had been the cause of death might now be the remedy [LXXIII] of healing,” and so forth.

How closely these statements agree with the teaching of the earlier Fathers is remarkable. The ancient author of the Epistle attributed to the apostle Saint Barnabas, no. 12, p. 63, says:

> “Moses makes a figure of Jesus—that he would suffer and himself give life, whom the Jews thought had perished—in the sign of Israel’s fall. For God brought it about that, when serpents bit them and they were dying, since transgression had occurred through the serpent in Eve … Moses should make a bronze serpent and place it gloriously, and summon the people through a herald … Moses said to them: ‘When one of you has been bitten, let him come to the serpent placed upon the wood, believe, and hope that, although that one is dead, it will be able to give life; and immediately he will be saved.’ And so they did. You have here also the glory of Jesus.”

Justin Martyr, in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, no. 91, p. 199; Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 10, p. 396; and Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 13, no. 20, p. 192 of the Paris edition of 1720, have transmitted corresponding teachings. It would be tedious to mention them all.

Enough, then, concerning the figures and symbols of the cross. It remains for me to set forth briefly, insofar as possible, what Maximus embraced in his writings concerning the death of Christ the Savior.

Thus, in homily 51, p. 158, proposing what our devoted faith should hold concerning the death of the same Savior, he says:

> “This is the full devotion of faith: that when the blood flowing from the Lord’s wounds is seen, forgiveness should then be sought from his power; when his humility is seen, his divinity should then be held all the more firmly; when he is thought to have been delivered over to death, then the honor due to the king should be offered to him.”

The holy thief offered him such honor. Maximus bears witness to this in homily 52, p. 163:

> “The thief recognizes the Savior as the Lord of majesty at the very moment when he sees him afflicted by the endurance of humility.”

In homily 54, p. 173:

> “Who is prefigured in Elisha except our Jesus Christ, who grants resurrection from death and effects life while buried?”

Shortly afterward, comparing Christ with the prophet Jonah, whom the sailors had rebuked, he says:

> “Although the sailors were about to cast Jonah away, they nevertheless feared and said: ‘Lord, do not lay innocent blood upon us.’ Does not the sailors’ rebuke seem to you to be Pilate’s confession, since he hands Christ over, yet washes his hands and says: ‘I am clean from the blood of this just man’?

> “Jonah therefore says in his prayer: ‘Take my life, then, Lord, because death is better for me than life.’ Let our Lord Jesus Christ say this more truly: ‘Death is better for me than life’; that is, ‘While alive I could not save the one nation of the Jews; let me die, and let the whole world be saved by ONE DEATH.’

> “The great fish received Jonah after he had been submerged, but he was not swallowed up … Who is this who can be taken into greedy jaws but cannot be consumed …? Who is this who enters the vast depths of danger safely, and, enclosed beneath an immeasurable and deadly depth [LXXIV], is nourished by living air, and, sent down into another nature, wanders in the exile of life while alive, surviving death and announcing the salvation of the world to come? …

> “This is our Lord Jesus Christ, whom savage death, the insatiable beast, seized as its food, yet trembled as a captive before its own prey. It trembled, I say; for although it knew that he had been crucified, since it did not remember him as guilty, it could not hold him condemned, because punishment does not create guilt; the cause does.

> “As its accustomed food, it devoured the human being lost at the origin of the world; but, suffocated, it recognized the great dignity of that food. Therefore the divine word recalls: ‘And the Lord commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto the dry land.’ He commanded the beast; he commanded death, always hungry; he commanded the abysses and the underworld to restore the Savior to the world.

> “‘Vomited’ must be understood to mean that victorious life returned from the innermost entrails of death, and that frustrated destruction, embittered in the deepest recesses of hell, gave him back from within.

> “Thus we see that in the prophet’s sufferings the death and likewise the resurrection of Christ were most clearly prefigured. Therefore, what you see fulfilled in the servant, do not hesitate to believe in the Lord.”

The Savior had foretold that he would be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, just as Jonah had been in the belly of the great fish (Matthew 12:40).

The Fathers often used this symbol of Jonah, whether refuting the Jews or instructing the people by writing and speaking about the Savior’s death and resurrection. One should consult Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*, no. 107; Tertullian, *On Modesty*, chapter 10, where he writes that Jonah is everywhere an example of the Lord’s Passion; Origen, *Commentary on Matthew*, volume XII, p. 277 of the Venetian edition of 1743; Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* 1, p. 43; and Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 14, no. 17 and following, p. 213 and following. I omit Jerome, Augustine, and Cyril of Alexandria, whose testimonies are transcribed by Natalis Alexander, dissertation 10 in *Ecclesiastical History of the Old Testament*, article 5, volume II, p. 169 of the Lucca edition of 1748.

What if the ancient Christians themselves represented Jonah both in relief sculpture and in paintings, so that those looking upon him might remember Christ’s death and resurrection? Compare Aringhi, *Roma subterranea*, book II, chapter 10, pp. 325 and 335; book III, chapter 22, pp. 533, 551, and following, volume I; book IV, chapter 14, pp. 71 and 97, and so forth; and book V, chapter 22, p. 505 and following, volume II; Filippo Buonarroti, *Osservazioni sopra alcuni frammenti di vasi antichi*, plate 1; Bottari, *Roma subterranea*, plate 42, p. 191; and the Chevalier Vittorio, *Opusculum de septem Dormientibus*, pp. 53 and 55.

But I return to the subject from which I digressed: Maximus’s discussion of the death of Christ the Savior and of the miracles performed at that time.

In homily 57, p. 181:

> “At Christ’s resurrection all the elements rejoice. For I also think that the sun itself is brighter on this [LXXV] day than usual. It is necessary that the sun rejoice at the resurrection of the one at whose Passion it grieved, and that it receive with the splendor of brighter light the life of the one whose DEATH it accompanied with a certain mournful darkness.”

But why delay the reader with many words? I shall omit the other passages of Maximus, which are indeed very numerous [Col. 0075] and equally excellent on this subject. We shall be content with one passage from homily 83, p. 270. It is as follows:

> “The Only-begotten Son of God became the Son of Man, so that he who was the creator of the world might also become its redeemer. He was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate. Let us feel no shame concerning the cross of Christ, because through his passion we have victory … He chose the punishment of the cross so that a harsher punishment might produce a more exalted glory; and he who suffered for the good of the universe might die lifted high before the eyes of the world, so that those who saw the Crucified might behold the wonders of the Crucified.

> “The sudden darkening of the sun, the trembling of the earth, the splitting of the rocks, and the resurrection of the dead sufficiently and abundantly display the glory of the one who suffered. How great a testimony it is that the thief who was crucified alongside him also asked that his memory be made in the heavenly kingdom by his companion in punishment!

> “Hence, beloved, we do not lament with sighs the mockeries and insults that Christ endured, his cross, or his DEATH; rather, we celebrate them with continual praises. He was buried, because it followed that the one who had DIED should receive burial … He was buried so that the one who was believed to have TRULY DIED might be believed to have TRULY RETURNED FROM THE DEAD. ‘On the third day,’ he says, ‘he rose from the dead’ … If you have believed concerning Christ WHAT PERTAINS TO DEATH, believe WHAT PERTAINS TO LIFE. For just as in the Passion there is the mystery of piety, so in the resurrection there is the operation of power, as he himself says: ‘I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again.’

> “How, then, could life after DEATH fail to be available to him for whom to DIE was not a condition but a power? … How could he be held by the laws of hell, who for this very reason IS DEAD, so that death might lose its power?”

Yet someone may perhaps wonder how it is that, although Maximus rightly insists that everyone must believe that Christ truly died, he nevertheless seems to turn the fact that the holy thief did not believe this into a point of praise. For he writes in Homily 51, p. 158:

> This faithful thief did not believe that the one whom he announces as destined to reign would die; he does not suppose that the one whom he confesses will reign in heaven is to be subjected to the underworld.

Nevertheless, anyone who carefully considers the sequence of Maximus’s discourse will clearly perceive that the holy bishop does not praise the holy thief on the ground that the thief believed Christ would not die at all, but because he believed that Christ himself would not have died if he had not wished to die. For, as Maximus teaches shortly afterward:

> The thief understood that the Lord’s entire Passion took place by his own will, and that it lay within his power either to hand over his soul to death or to return again to life.

If Maximus had not understood the matter in this way, he would plainly have contradicted himself. What prudent person could persuade himself that he had spoken contradictory things? [LXXVI] As we have seen, he maintains that Christ truly died and that everyone must believe this. Moreover, what he adds—“The thief does not suppose that the one whom he confesses will reign in heaven is to be subjected to the underworld”—certainly does not prevent the thief from having believed that Christ would die. Indeed, it shows and establishes that he believed he would die.

For, as Maximus’s Homily 55, p. 174, says concerning Christ’s not being subjected to the underworld:

> The Lord safely enters the immense recesses of dangers; confined beneath an immeasurable depth and surrounded by deadly conditions, he is nourished by vital air; lowered into the alien condition of things, into the exile of life, he journeys together with life, and, surviving death, announces the coming salvation of the world. This is our Lord Jesus Christ, whom savage Death, that incomprehensible monster, seized as its food, while captive it trembled before its own prey. It trembled, I say; for although it knew that he had been crucified, yet because it did not remember him as guilty, it could not hold him condemned. [lacuna] Therefore the divine word recalls: “And the Lord commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto the dry land.” He therefore commanded the beast; he commanded ever-hungry Death; he commanded the abysses and the underworld to restore the Savior to the world. “It vomited” must be understood in this way: victorious Life returned from the inmost entrails of Death, and ulcerated destruction gave it back from the deepest recesses of the underworld.

In the afflictions of the prophet Jonah we see most clearly prefigured both the death and the resurrection of Christ. Therefore, what you see fulfilled in the servant, do not hesitate to believe in the Lord.

But since mention has arisen of the holy thief, there is certainly reason to satisfy that writer as well who, a few years ago, brought Maximus into disrepute, as though he had thought that the thief himself attained salvation by faith alone. I shall briefly explain what offended that writer.

He had read in Maximus’s Homily 51 that the thief “believed Christ crucified while he was hanging on the cross, and therefore, because he shared in the Passion, he was granted a share in paradise.” The word *credidit* (“believed”), however, so disturbed the man that he supposed Maximus had recognized and conceded no merit or virtue in the thief beyond faith. Yet that writer failed to notice that Maximus acknowledged in the thief repentance for his crimes; that he proclaimed the thief’s merit and his patience in enduring the punishment of his offenses; and that he recalled the thief’s ardent love for God. Who among the orthodox is unaware that love covers a multitude of sins?

If Maximus said that the thief reached glory through faith, he certainly meant perfect faith—that is, faith working through love—not an unformed faith. He meant it no differently from the Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where he says that the saints through faith conquered kingdoms and obtained the promises.

Maximus’s words in Homily 51, pp. 156–157, are as follows:

> For the thief, the cross which he endured was not so much the condemnation of punishment as the opportunity for salvation. [lacuna] While he suffered punishment, [LXXVII] he attained the heavenly kingdom. [lacuna] Recalling his crimes and doing penance, he began to desire more intensely what he hoped for than to feel what he was suffering. [lacuna] He understood that Christ received these wounds for the sins of others; [lacuna] and he knew that, in Christ’s body, the wounds were not Christ’s wounds but the thief’s; and therefore he began to love more intensely after he recognized his own wounds in Christ’s body.

And in Homily 52, p. 162:

> Great, therefore, and perfect was the faith in that thief. Great and admirable was the faith which believed that Christ gloried in being crucified more than he was being punished. [lacuna] The Lord grants both the service of faith and the reward according to faith and merit.

Maximus our writer therefore did not hold the opinion concerning the holy thief that this recent writer has falsely attributed to him.

[Col. 0077] Nor do those who suspect that Maximus was driven to the point of believing that the person of the Word was separated from Christ’s body during the three days of his death inflict any less injustice upon Maximus than does this same recent writer. For not even a trace of such an opinion is found in Maximus’s works.

Now, the fact that the holy man writes in Homily 45, p. 138, that Christ cried out on the cross, “My God, why have you forsaken me?” certainly does not make us suspect that, in his opinion, the body was forsaken by the Word. Who could deny that Maximus wrote these words appropriately in accordance with the Gospel? What? Does anyone suppose that the authority of the Gospel can be used to show that the divine Word dismissed the body which he had assumed for the sake of human salvation? Nothing could be further from the truth.

Yet Maximus adds:

> He said this so that he might reveal that, for our sake, he had been forsaken, since he bore our sins.

But I ask: in what sense, according to Maximus, did Christ say that he had been forsaken for our sake? In the homilies of Maximus I read that, for our sake, Christ was exposed to the insults of the Jews, to blows, sufferings, and death; but nowhere do I read that the body assumed by the person of the Word was forsaken by that person.

Why, then, should we not judge Christ to have been forsaken, according to Maximus, in the same sense in which the holy Leo taught that he was forsaken? In Sermon 66, chapter 2, p. 187 of the Roman edition of 1753, Leo writes:

> Therefore Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, “Why have you forsaken me?”—so that he might make known to all why it was necessary for him not to be rescued or defended, but to be abandoned to the hands of those who raged against him; that is, so that he might become the Savior of the world and the Redeemer of all human beings, not through misery but through mercy; not through the loss of assistance but through the determination to die; and so forth.

What could be more similar to Maximus’s teaching than this? In Homily 46, p. 142, Maximus writes:

> I do not wish justice to be defended in the manner in which iniquity is usually excused. [lacuna] He prefers to establish his case rather than to state it. He lost his own salvation so that he might gain the salvation of all; he preferred to be defeated in himself so that he might be victorious in all.

Maximus goes on, and on p. 144 shows that Pilate was permitted to confirm the sacrilege of the raging Synagogue against Christ the Savior.

And in Homily 50, p. 154:

> His Passion, he says, is our redemption; his death is our life. He endured all these evils [LXXVIII] so that we might experience every good; he preferred cruelty to be exercised against himself so that he might bestow mercy upon us.

But if, according to Maximus, the person of the divine Word had abandoned the body and separated himself from it, how could Maximus have introduced Christ himself as saying:

> Touch me with your hand, and see by faith that there is in me the reality of that body which hung upon the cross and was taken down dead and laid in the tomb, and the property of the Godhead, by which I raised myself, dead and laid in the tomb?

If the soul had already been separated from the body, and if Christ’s divine person had likewise abandoned that body, how could Maximus have said that Christ himself had been buried and that he had afterward raised himself, deposited in the tomb? Therefore, according to Maximus’s opinion, the person of the Word was not separated from Christ’s body during the three days of his death.

### XVI

We have recently seen what our Maximus thought concerning Christ’s burial. He discusses this subject at much greater length in his homilies and sermons, but there is no need to transcribe them, since they return to the passage of Maximus already set out and in the same form, without presenting anything that seems to require fuller elucidation.

I therefore come to the article concerning Christ’s descent into the underworld. Maximus discusses it as follows in Homily 57, p. 182:

> What wonder is it if there are darknesses above, since, when Christ died, the light descended into the underworld?

In Sermon 31, p. 479:

> While pursuing death even to the underworld, he graciously recalled to the everlasting joys of paradise the human being whom he had created and redeemed. He pursued death even to the underworld, made it captive more gloriously in his kingdom, and triumphed over it. Then those dark inner chambers of the underworld were opened. Eternal night marveled at what had never before seen the light of heaven.
