Hence the prophet himself could say: “O death, I shall be your death; O underworld, I shall be your bite.” For the one whom it thought dead, it was compelled to release, and it experienced the liberation of those whom it had already been holding.

In Sermon 43, p. 514:

> All these things were done, beloved, so that no one at all might dispute his return from the underworld, since he had been proved to have raised the dead with such glory. [lacuna] Let us love him who bestows such great benefits upon us and raises the dead; let us venerate him rising from the underworld; let us honor and adore him also as he sits at the right hand of the Father.

Maximus likewise explains why Christ descended to the underworld in Homily 57, p. 180. For he writes:

> The prophet says that he shines in the underworld: “Light has arisen for those who sat in the region and shadow of death.”

And in Homily 60, pp. 189–190:

> How well the prophet describes the Lord’s triumph! [lacuna] Behold, as the Lord goes to heaven, a glorious captivity does not go before him but accompanies him.

To this may also be referred what he sets forth in Sermon 29, p. 476, and Sermon 31, p. 479:

> While Christ pursues death even to the underworld, he graciously recalls to the everlasting joys of paradise [LXXIX] the human being whom he created and redeemed. [lacuna] On this most sacred festival of the resurrection, while the Lord was raising himself, many bodies of the saints were raised and came to life again, and they entered the holy city. For today, when he rose, the Savior raised up his own victims.

And in Sermon 41, p. 507:

> Let our flesh rejoice, for it truly is earth, because, glorified through Christ, it has earned fellowship with the Godhead. “Let the mountains,” he says, “break forth into joy, and the hills into righteousness.” We may appropriately understand these mountains and hills, which are raised up to joy, as the patriarchs, just as we also read in holy David: “You illuminate wondrously from the eternal mountains.” [lacuna] Not without reason, moreover, all the righteous are called mountains and hills, since, leaving behind the lowliness of earthly conduct, they have raised the summit of their faith toward the heights of heavenly life. Most justly, therefore, the venerable patriarchs are exhorted in prophetic language to assume joy; for their offspring—that is, Christ the Lord—through the mystery of his death and resurrection restored the life that had been lost even to the Fathers of the former age. The patriarchs rejoice in every way: the Son of God, born from their stock, wiped away with the new, immaculate blood of his body the entire face of the world, long defiled by diabolical impieties, and so forth.

And in Sermon 42, p. 510:

> He chose to die, not so that the underworld might claim him for itself, but so that he might free the dead from deaths.

And in Sermon 44, p. 515:

> He did not shrink from the underworld; and, after the author of sin himself had been condemned, he carried the human being whom he had assumed into heaven. [Col. 0079] The human being who, humbled under the law of transgression, had bent his neck beneath the devil’s yoke, escaped all the bonds of tyrannical captivity by being captured by the Son of God.

### XVII

Maximus treats the resurrection of Christ the Savior splendidly in Homily 57, pp. 179 ff.; Homily 58, p. 172; and Homily 88, p. 271, where he says:

> On the third day he rose from the dead. If you have believed concerning Christ what belongs to dishonor, believe what belongs to glory. If you have believed what belongs to death, believe what belongs to life. For just as in the Passion there is the mystery of piety, so in the resurrection there is the exercise of power, as he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again.” How, then, could life after death fail to be available to him for whom dying was not a condition but a power? [lacuna] How could he be detained by the laws of the underworld, who died for this very purpose: that death might lose its power? And so forth.

But, so as not to detain readers with many passages, I shall use only the one passage from Sermon 29, p. 472, which plainly demonstrates the truth of Christ’s resurrection, complete with its miracles. It is as follows:

> He who was given over to the Passion for the sins of all rose again for the salvation of all. The Savior therefore rose from the dead. The event is new and wondrous, but this assertion possesses truth. For, to say nothing of the prophecies of the prophets, the ministry of the angels, the opened recesses of the tomb, and the Lord himself speaking, associating [LXXX], and eating with the disciples after his resurrection, and Thomas even touching with his finger the wounds of the nails—to pass over all these things—nevertheless the impiety of the Jews confirms our faith. Their cautious belief is sufficient to make us believe. For the more diligently they guarded the tomb, the more clearly it is established that he rose. The more guards they placed, the more witnesses they left behind. Divine providence arranged this so that testimony to the resurrection would be borne not only by angels and not only by disciples, but also—what is more—by enemies. We therefore accept more readily what they observed so carefully. For we believe that he could have emerged from under guard more quickly than he had died, and that he proceeded from the tomb by the Lord’s right rather than being secretly removed through the fraud of the disciples. Impiety sealed the tomb with such care that no human hand could have prevailed to destroy it, unless the power of the resurrection alone had opened it. Finally, the holy Evangelist says that, when the angel descended, the earth was shaken by a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the tomb were moved; and the guards who had come to guard the dead man were struck with fear and became like dead men. Like dead men, I say—a perfectly fitting judgment, if, when the righteous man rises, the sinner dies; when the innocent comes to life again, his enemy is killed. For this reason they could not see the Lord as he came forth: terror had overwhelmed their criminal minds, since they were not accustomed to endure the radiance of the shining resurrection. The Pharisees therefore guarded the Lord more anxiously when he was dead than they had persecuted him when alive. [lacuna] They guarded him carefully in the tomb, especially because he had said that he would rise on the third day. They guarded him carefully in the tomb because it was necessary for them now to fear him not as teacher but as judge, and so forth.

See also Sermon 35, pp. 491 ff., and Sermon 37, pp. 498 ff.

The same Maximus discusses Christ’s resurrection and ascension into heaven in Sermon 37, pp. 498 ff., as follows:

> It was not through a superfluous or empty will that the Son of God should die on earth amid the shame of such great sufferings in human nature, while he lived in the heavenly kingdom in the Father’s Godhead; rather, the necessity of our remedy demanded that he be born. What has God to do with flesh? What has the immaculate one to do with the cross? What has the eternal one to do with death? The words, wounds, and every disgrace inflicted by the Passion would indeed have to be reckoned to the Son of God, unless the resurrection that immediately followed had healed all that he suffered. Who, then, is so foolish as to presume, by reconsidering the matter, to disfigure the fact that Christ was crucified, when he was made more wondrous by his Passion than by so many powers and such great miracles? Who would dare reproach him with a three-day burial, whose eternity, abiding with the eternal Father, is proclaimed? Indeed, who would not marvel with utter astonishment that he deigned to enter the underworld, who by his own power was able to return to life after death and did not hesitate to ascend into heaven after the underworld? [LXXXI]

Again, in Homily 60, p. 188:

> He is a grain, he says, when he alone suffers the cross; he is fruit when he is surrounded by the faith of very many apostles. For during those forty days after the resurrection, living with the disciples, he taught them with the full maturity of wisdom and turned them toward good fruitfulness with the entire fecundity of his teachings. Then he ascended into heaven, to the Father, carrying before him the fruit of the flesh and leaving in the disciples the seeds of righteousness. The Lord therefore ascended to the Father.

And in Sermon 44, p. 514:

> Transcending the heights of heaven, Christ ascended to the inconceivable majesty of the Father’s throne. The human being whom the envy of the malignant enemy had expelled and cast out from that first habitation of paradise, making him a stranger in the filth of this world, he placed in the angelic homeland; and the exile from paradise he made a citizen of the heavenly beings.

He writes similar things in Sermon 44, pp. 514 ff.; Sermon 45, p. 516; and Sermon 47, p. 519:

> Tartarus grieves over its plunder together with its prince; but the entire heavenly host rejoices over the restoration of its loss. Today the flesh which, through the working power of the Holy Spirit, he had assumed from the virgin mother on earth has been placed at the Father’s right hand, and the natures of all the heavenly spirits have been bowed before it. Today that new way of which the Apostle once spoke has been inaugurated for us, because through that most blessed flesh of Christ the eternal entrance into heaven—through which no flesh had previously passed—has been opened for us. Today that book which no one but the Lamb could open has been unsealed, because in his death the mysteries of that same book have been revealed, and the things written about him in the Law and the Prophets have been completed on this day, the dispensation of his majesty having been accomplished. Christ first descended so that he might become a sharer in our nature; now he ascended so that he might make us sharers in his glory. Descending, in a wondrous manner of association, he delighted infants with miracles visible to them; ascending, he gave gifts to human beings, so that, instructed in faith and educated to manly strength, they would no longer desire his temporal sight, but would strive with their whole soul to follow him wherever he had gone before them.

[Col. 0081] ### XVIII

I shall briefly explain, from Maximus’s teaching, how Christ now sits at the right hand of the Father.

In Homily 83, the first of the homilies *On Various Subjects*, p. 271, he says:

> He sits at the right hand of the Father. That Christ sits is the reward of the victor; that he sits at the right hand of the Father is the privilege of the Godhead and participation in undivided love.

In Homily 62, pp. 197–198:

> We must believe, as David says concerning the Savior, that he sits at God’s right hand, because we see the Holy Spirit, as the Lord promised, rejoicing in the apostles. The prophet of the Psalms says: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.” According to our custom, a seat is offered to someone who arrives after completing some work and is deemed worthy, [LXXXII] as a mark of honor, to sit. Thus also the human being Jesus Christ, having overcome the devil by his Passion and opened the underworld by his resurrection, arrives victorious in heaven as one whose work has been completed and hears from God the Father: “Sit at my right hand.” Nor is it surprising that the Son is offered by the Father a seat on the same throne, since he is of one substance and nature with the Father. But why should the Son be believed to be at the right hand? This may perhaps trouble someone. For although there is no order of rank where the fullness of the Godhead is present, the Son sits at the right hand not so that he may be preferred to the Father, but so that he may not be thought inferior.

[Note: [Col. 0081] See Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 14, nos. 27 ff., pp. 219 ff.; and Saint Augustine, Sermon 212, p. 652, vol. V; and Saint Thomas, Part III, question 58, article 2, where he says: “To sit at the right hand of the Father is nothing other than to possess together with the Father the glory of the Godhead, blessedness, and judicial power, and to possess these immutably and royally. This belongs to the Son of God according to his being God. Hence it is clear that Christ, according to his being God, sits at the right hand of the Father; yet the preposition ‘at’—which is transitive—indicates only the distinction of the persons and the order of origin, not a degree of nature or dignity, for no such degree exists among the divine persons.” [Col. 0082]]

Maximus continues, writing appropriately in accordance with the Holy Scriptures:

> Therefore the Son is at the right hand because, according to the Evangelist, the sheep will be placed at the right hand and the goats at the left. The first Lamb must therefore occupy the place of the sheep, and the immaculate leader must go before the immaculate flock that will follow, as John says in the Apocalypse: “These follow the Lamb,” and so forth.

The prophet David therefore reports: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand”—that is, the Lord the Father offers to the Lord God Christ, his Son, a sublime seat upon his throne and, as a mark of honor, establishes him in an eternal seat at his right hand.

[Note: [Col. 0082] Saint Thomas shows the bearing of this passage, which the other Fathers also pursue, in the same work, article 3, where he says: “Christ, according to his being God, sits at the right hand of the Father—that is, in equality with the Father. But according to his being human, he sits at the right hand of the Father—that is, in the superior paternal goods above all other creatures: in greater blessedness and with judicial power. If, however, the expression ‘according to his being’ signifies the unity of the suppositum, then in this sense also, according to his being human, he sits at the right hand of the Father, insofar as we venerate the Son of God himself with the assumed nature in the same honor, as stated above.”]

We read in the Acts of the Apostles that blessed Stephen, when he was being stoned by the Jews, said:

> Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Lord Jesus standing at the right hand of God.

Let us therefore consider why the same Lord is prophesied by David as sitting, while he is proclaimed by Stephen as standing.

First of all, how can God, who is incorporeal and invisible, sit? Moreover, upon what seat could God sit, who is infinite and immeasurable, and who rather contains within himself the whole of creation? I think that the holy men said these things concerning the Lord not because they contradict one another, but so that at one time his omnipotence and at another his mercy might be described. For he is said to sit in accordance with the power of a king, and he is suggested to stand in accordance with the goodness of an intercessor. For blessed Paul says that we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ. Christ is therefore judge when he sits, and advocate when he rises.

These things accord with what was later set forth by Saint Gregory in Book II, Homily 29 on the Gospels, no. 7, p. 285, vol. V of the Venetian edition of 1769. Gregory’s interpretation is as follows:

> What does it mean that [LXXXIII] Mark testifies that he saw Christ sitting, while Stephen testifies that he saw him standing? But you know, brothers, that sitting belongs to one who judges, whereas standing belongs to one who fights or assists.

One should also consult Saint Thomas, *Summa theologica*, Part III, question 58, article 1, response to objection 1.

But I shall restrain my discourse. I shall not linger longer in explaining and confirming this argument. I shall proceed to those matters concerning the means of salvation, the gifts, and the adornments by which Maximus shows that the entire human race has been enriched—through the benefit of the incarnation, Passion, and death of Christ the Savior—with the greatest and most abundant blessings.

### XIX.

And indeed that holy bishop first observes the point that overturns the Pelagian dogma, namely: that Adam was not created mortal; that by his fault he introduced original sin into the world, or into his descendants, and through sin, death.

Homily 8, which is the third on the Nativity of the Lord, p. 23:

> Today, he says, that new Adam, Christ, by his wondrous birth newly fashioned our nature; and what had been defiled and corrupted by the pitiable fall of the old Adam, by his precious birth and tearful death he restored to life.

Homily 11, p. 30:

> Today Christ has been born, but in his birth our life has its own birthday; because we who lost the privileges of our first birth, when Christ visited us, have been restored through a holier birth.

Homily 29, which is the first on Baptism, p. 87, where he introduces John the Baptist speaking thus to Christ:

> I have corruption from the transgression of the father, while you have communion in the majesty of the Father. . . . I am mortal by the law of sin, but you, coming against sins, do not know how to be subject to sin.

Homily 83, p. 272:

> Above all, brothers, the remission of sins must be believed, because this is the one remedy that absolves the human race from the sentence of perpetual death. Therefore the Only-Begotten of the Most High deigned to assume flesh and embraced the cross, so that you, who could not escape your crimes and sins, might be made innocent by pardon. Therefore the spotless Lamb was slain, so that by his blood the stain of the human race might be wiped away.

And what stain was this? The stain, namely, of original sin. For thus he writes in Sermon 35, p. 489:

> We who had long been condemned to death by the primal guilt of our origin have now been restored to our former innocence by the death of [Col. 0083] Christ. We who by our sins had deserved the punishments of hell have been restored by his most precious death to the joys of eternal blessedness. We who through Adam’s transgression had been vessels of wrath have now, because of his resurrection, become citizens of the saints.

For, as he observes in Homily 15, p. 42:

> The enemy had bound the human race with such great chains, and so massive a weight of monstrous sins had pressed upon us, that there would have been no return for us to salvation unless he had been born who by his own power could return to life after death.

Now in Sermon 61, the fifth on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, p. 554, Maximus not only mentions original sin, but also the remedies—especially circumcision—which in the Old Law were employed to remove the stain and guilt of that sin. For he writes as follows:

> John received circumcision in his flesh together with the Lord; but by receiving it he brought it to an end. And therefore, although he shone forth as the herald of the new grace and its magnificent announcer, he did not need circumcision in order to escape original sin; rather, divine election raised him above the Law and above the order of human condition.

But here I should like to point out that Maximus did not think John escaped original sin in the sense that he had never contracted it. For this is what the holy bishop held: John did indeed escape the evil of original guilt—not by having entirely avoided it, but by being released from it through the benefit of the Redeemer, after he had already been bound by it, while he was still in Elizabeth’s womb.

Accordingly, Maximus likewise maintains that John had corruption from the transgression of his father and had to be redeemed by Christ, whereas Christ was born not to be redeemed but to redeem. Homily 29, p. 87. Moreover, in Sermon 61, p. 554, he teaches that John’s beginning was consecrated by the presence of the Creator of the world, who was hidden in the Virgin’s womb. But more on circumcision later.

Maximus again speaks of original guilt in Sermon 88, p. 625:

> Let us understand, he says, how powerful the Redeemer’s passion was for taking away the sin of the world. Behold: the death of a man is proved to confer innocence and life. From this let us understand how greatly the sacred death of the Son of God benefited the salvation of all. Behold: human blood washes away both personal and original offense, and so forth.

It is moreover clear from the passages of Maximus that we have described thus far:

1. Adam not only fell, and the sentence of death was pronounced against him even though he had been created immortal, but he also brought sin upon his descendants, and through sin, death.

2. Human beings did not fall miserably only into that original and common guilt; since, through the corruption of the same guilt, they are inclined toward evil, they also bind themselves by what we call actual, or personal, sins.

3. Consequently, human beings were vessels of wrath and were condemned to everlasting destruction.

4. In order that they might be freed from both kinds of sin, redeemed, restored, and brought back to innocence and life, a Redeemer was necessary who would be both God and man. Thus the person of the divine Word assumed human nature, entirely free from sin, but in which, for the sake of our salvation, he would endure great hardships, torments, and death.

And in Homily 12, p. 35:

> The fact, says Maximus, that the Son of God deigned to visit his own world was demanded by the necessity of our salvation, namely, so that heavenly generation might at last restore what earthly birth had lost. But perhaps, when you hear that he who is proclaimed as born of a woman was wrapped in lowly cloths, was content to lie in a manger, and resounded with tearful cries, . . . you doubt that he is God? Rather, brother, through these things recognize that as man he endured weakness for the weak, and as God exercised heavenly power.

And in Homily 13, p. 36:

> Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells, assuming the weakness of our flesh, was born as a new man. Today that second Adam shone forth, not as an inhabitant but as the Lord of paradise. . . . Today light has risen in the darkness. . . . A new man, but the eternal Lord; a new Christ, but the king of all ages. . . . This is he who was foretold by the patriarchs and proclaimed by the prophets. . . . You have received the gift which Abraham rejoiced to see in spirit, and so forth.

And in Sermon 14, p. 39:

> Today Christ was born for us according to the flesh, beginning to be what he was not, but not ceasing to be what he was. For the birth of a man could neither diminish nor separate the unity of his undivided majesty. That God proceeded from his Father is the ineffable and enduring secret of his power; that he was born as man from a woman is for the sake of our salvation. There is the glory of nature; here, the mystery of will. . . . Who, then, brothers, can measure the depth of this heavenly counsel: that the Lord of immortality, . . . so that he might receive death in the condition of flesh for mortals, chose to come forth from a woman’s womb under the human law? . . . In the swaddling clothes he shows that he has assumed our weaknesses and our sins. . . . Such an entrance was fitting for the Savior of the world, so that he who came to cleanse the sins of the human race might be born purer than all others. . . . To whom else should the whole earth sing than to him who brought forgiveness of sins and the hope of eternal salvation to the entire world? . . . It is fitting that he be honored especially by the praises of those whom he saved through the suffering of his own body and the outpouring of his blood.

And in Sermon 15, p. 41:

> He is God from the Father and man from his mother; that is, we confess one Lord, both God and man. In his birth we all perceive that we have been born to life. For he became man not to live for himself, since he is the author of life, but so that by his death he might redeem the life of the dead; and there would have been no return for us to salvation unless he had been born who by his own power could return to life after death.

The same point is made in what Maximus teaches in Homily 19, p. 53 and following; Homily 20, p. 55 and following; Homily 25, p. 73 and following; Homily 27, p. 79 and following; Homily 35, p. 100 and following; Homily 37, p. 105 and following; Homily 49, p. 152 and following; and Homily 50, p. 153, where he says:

> His passion is our redemption. His death is our life. He endured all these evils so that we might experience every good. He preferred cruelty to be exercised against himself so that he might bestow mercy upon us. . . . By taking away through the cross the offenses of the human race, [Col. 0085] he consumed them all in his passion.

Countless passages of the same kind may be found in Maximus’s other homilies, sermons, and short works.

That Christ suffered and died for all human beings, and therefore wished to extend mercy to all, Maximus sometimes affirms openly and more often somewhat obscurely; yet he always affirms it so certainly that he leaves no room for doubt about his view.

In Homily 19, p. 54:

> He who had come mercifully to restore all people, so that even the Gentile world itself might not remain forever in its tearful blindness, gave it also a sign: the Jew could see it in the star that announced the birth of so great a king, and the whole world could recognize in it the arrival of the author of the redemption that was present.

And in Homily 20, p. 55 and following:

> Since he had come from heaven not to redeem only the Jewish people, but also all the nations whom he had created with the Father and the Holy Spirit from the beginning of the world, he wished to give a sign in the star, which Judea could see and the whole world recognize. . . . By that visible sign he called everyone to himself; he promised all the gifts of his grace.

Now, when Maximus writes that the Redeemer endured weakness for the weak, that he came because the necessity of our salvation demanded it, and that he endured these things in order to cleanse the sins of the human race, to redeem by his death the life of the dead, and through his passion and the outpouring of his blood to bring forgiveness of sins and an unfailing hope of return to salvation to the entire world—salvation which human beings could not have attained unless he had been born—when, I say, he writes these things and shows that by the expressions “the whole world” and “the human race” all human beings are called by the Redeemer himself to himself, and that the gifts of divine grace promised by him are promised to all those human beings, does he not plainly demonstrate that this same Redeemer was born, suffered, and died for all, that is, for every human being, and prepared the means by which all might receive the gifts of that grace which he promises?

Again, Maximus teaches in Sermon 19, p. 420, that Christ came into the world to provide for the salvation of human beings . . . and to water their souls with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

In Homily 116, p. 384:

> The cause undertaken by the Savior concerns not merely one person, nor is the weakness of one person alone cared for; rather, the weakness of the entire human race is saved.

That God forgets no human being, but is present to all and has prepared aids for them, he indicates in Sermon 16, p. 439:

> How can God forget us, when in the Gospel he says that even the hairs of our head are numbered before him? If he remembers our hairs, much more does he remember our souls. Through numbering we recognize his care and concern for us. No one numbers anything except what he wishes to guard more carefully. . . . Thus the one who is numbered is held under protection. . . . God remembers all; he calls all to mind—unless our sins intervene and bring forgetfulness upon him.

But how can he remember us, or provide care and concern for all, if he does not offer or prepare aids by which human weakness and infirmity may be strengthened? Without these aids and the support of almighty God, human beings cannot accomplish what would enable them to dispose themselves to be watered by the grace of the Holy Spirit and finally attain everlasting salvation and blessedness.

That divine assistance is necessary Maximus teaches in Homily 42, p. 28, and Homily 64, p. 206. He also observes in Homily 20, p. 56, that Christ calls everyone to himself and promises all the gifts of his grace.

Maximus explains the efficacy of grace, by which Christ causes those whom he effectively wills to repent and to do good, in Homily 108, p. 258:

> Truly, brothers, when a physician seeks or considers the wishes of the sick, while the sick person always desires and requests the opposite, this is why the physician now applies iron, now fire, now bitter potions, and administers them to unwilling patients, so that they may experience the healing which, while sick, they could not perceive. And if a human being disregards insults and despises curses in order freely to restore life and health to those wounded by disease, how much more does Christ the physician, by divine goodness, draw to salvation—even against their will and unwillingly—those wounded by the diseases of sins and suffering from the madness of crimes? If only we would wish it, brothers, if only we would wish to examine all the paralysis of our mind, we would see our soul, deprived of virtues, lying on the beds of vices; then it would become clear to us how Christ daily regards our harmful wills and draws and urges us, though unwilling, toward saving remedies.

The expression *pertrahit et perurget invitos*—“draws and urges them, though unwilling”—does not mean that those who are drawn and urged are driven by necessity to act. Rather, it means that they are moved, persuaded, and determined in freedom. What they then do freely may sometimes be bitter to them and may not please them, just as a bitter medicine does not please the sick person, nor does he enjoy swallowing what the physician freely administers to him.

Nor does Maximus understand this otherwise than does the Church in that collect on the fourth Sunday after Pentecost, in which the priest, preparing to celebrate the sacrifice, prays that God in his mercy may compel our rebellious wills toward himself. For what Catholic is there who would suppose that the Church prays for God to impose necessity upon us? Certainly no one; rather, everyone understands it in this way: those who are driven by evil desires resist, but are so moved and finally overcome by grace itself that they freely yield to God as he determines them toward the good, and at the same time determine themselves toward it.

See our annotation on p. 359.

What Maximus means by the expressions “unwilling” and “reluctant” can be clearly learned from his preface to Homily 109, p. 364, in the notes. There he says that he speaks unwillingly because those who heard him were not being corrected and were acting with excessive sluggishness. Did he mean that he was speaking under compulsion? Nothing could be further from the truth. Rather, because he was speaking without fruit, he spoke unwillingly, although he was not permitted to remain silent. From this it is clear that, for Maximus, *invitus* means the same as *non libens*, “not willingly.”

In any case, he consistently affirms that freedom of choice remains unharmed in every mortal, whether that person acts rightly or wrongly.

In the Treatise on the Chapters of the Gospels, chapter 8, p. 761:

> He did not wish again to break the freedom of choice that he had given to man, lest he violate the freedom of the soul that, as we have said, he had recently granted. Therefore he left the matter to each person’s judgment, reserving for himself the examination that will take place, so that the guilty person may be punished, and the one who did not wish to commit a crime, lest he be punished, may be saved.

What, then, if Christ God, when by his [Col. 0087] action he moves and leads his servants, does not take away but perfects their freedom? Maximus bears witness to this in Sermon 40, p. 504.

In Sermon 58, p. 515:

> Blessed is the freedom found in captivity to Christ. . . . See and consider how advantageous it is for us to be Christ’s captives: he not only grants eternal freedom to those whom he has captured, but also bestows upon them ineffable gifts of heavenly blessings. Therefore the patriarch sings elsewhere: “Turn, O Lord, our captivity, like a stream in the south.” He says “turn,” not “take away”; that is, “grant, Lord, that we who have long been captives of the devil may at last deserve to be your captives.” For we know that subjection to the devil is a most bitter condition, while serving you, Lord, is a joy that cannot be exhausted, and so forth.

Thus, when Christ works within us, he perfects our freedom and brings us joy—especially when the same Savior, dwelling in this desert of our body, overcomes all the devil’s forces there and makes it his dwelling, secluded and secure from worldly thoughts. Thus, thereafter, situated within ourselves as though in a wilderness, we look toward nothing but heaven and earth—that is, we think of no one but the Lord of the heavenly kingdom and the author of the earthly resurrection. Sermon 19, p. 446.

Whatever grace was granted to human beings after Adam’s fall, Maximus teaches, following the earlier Fathers and the Scriptures, must be attributed to the power of Christ the Savior. Since every aid to the blessed life that has come to Adam and his descendants from that time onward has flowed from the fountain of redemption, it must certainly have flowed from the power of him whom Scripture and tradition show, and Maximus acknowledges, to be the Redeemer of the ages and of all the nations whom he created from the beginning of the world.

Homily 19, p. 54; Homily 20, p. 55; and Homily 23, pp. 65–67, where he says that in his work he did not remain hidden, so that all everywhere who believed that the Word and flesh were in the Son of God might be saved. He was the one who made the hungry Hebrew people grow fat on angelic bread, as though on heavenly milk. He was the one who accompanied the Hebrews through the parched deserts, while heaven fed them and the rock gave them drink. And who among the orthodox is unaware that the rock signified Christ, according to Paul, the teacher of the nations?

See also Homily 24, p. 72; Homily 25, p. 74; and Sermon 19, p. 445, where he says that the Lord acted so that, because the first Adam, placed in paradise, had lost the glory of immortality through intemperance of appetite, the second Adam, Christ, might restore that same immortality through abstinence. . . . For this is what the Savior accomplished: that sins might be cleansed by the same paths through which they had been committed. . . . Thus the Lord acts so that human beings may be freed from the adverse judgments by which they had been made liable to sin.

In Sermon 20, p. 448, he observes that through the Savior’s mercy the following occurred in the time of Noah: the righteous might escape, and the unrighteous might sin no more.

> We plainly see, he says, that the Flood was an act of mercy, by which, as though through a kind of baptism, the face of the whole world was renewed: so that what had been stained by the crimes of the wicked might flourish in grace through the dwelling of blessed Noah, and what had then been a brothel of iniquity might now become a dwelling place of holiness. That Flood was a likeness of our baptism. For what was then accomplished is now accomplished: as the waves of water overflowed, vices were put in peril and justice alone reigned; sins were submerged in the depths, while holiness was carried near to heaven. Then, as I have said, what is now accomplished in the Church of Christ was being accomplished. For just as Noah’s ark was carried along after all the vices of sinners had been submerged, so the Church, near to heaven, is carried in the baptismal font; and when all the superstitions of idols have been erased, faith reigns on earth, faith that proceeds from the Savior’s ark.

Whatever good, salvation, and supernatural life there has been, is, or will be in human beings comes from our Savior, who, because he is God, assumed our human nature for this purpose.

In Sermon 29, p. 474:

> In our Savior we have all risen, all come back to life, and all passed over to heavenly things. For in Christ the man there is a portion of the flesh and blood of each one of us. Therefore, where my portion reigns, I believe that I reign; where my blood rules, I feel that I rule; where my flesh is glorified, I know that I am glorified. . . . Although our sins exclude us, the communion of nature does not repel us. For because of the goodness of his divinity, the Savior owes us a particular affection: just as our God is in him, so our blood is also in him. . . . The Lord is not so harsh as to forget man and fail to remember the one whom he himself bears, and so forth.

See also Sermon 35, p. 489, and Sermon 36, p. 491, where he says:

> Christ is truly one day, because the eternity of divinity is one in him. “Today” is the name given to what neither ancient age evades nor future ignorance passes by; rather, like the most powerful light, it contains all things and knows all things, and, possessing everything as though in the present, it holds all things, because with him the past does not slip away and the future is not hidden. . . . Just as he promises us life and glory in the future, so even in the past the causes and occasions of our salvation arise; and thus he who is worshiped so that he may have mercy has already shown mercy. Therefore, made and restored by him, let us now rejoice more abundantly in his benefits, and so forth.

### XX.

I see that Maximus held that justice and holiness are either conferred upon us or increased in us through the sacraments.

Before Abraham, although the holy bishop does not explicitly mention sacraments, he does not seem to have doubted that there were certain signs deserving the name of sacraments, by which the holy patriarchs testified to their faith in Christ who was to come, and by which they were sanctified through that faith joined with charity. This is clear from the sacred Scriptures and from the tradition of the Fathers.

Now, although, according to Maximus, the Hebrews escaped original sin through circumcision from the time of Abraham until Christ, as was observed above, the sacrament itself did not possess by its own power the ability to remove sin; it did so through faith.

Thus Maximus writes in Treatise 5 Against the Jews, p. 740 and following:

> Abraham was justified by faith, not by circumcision. For Scripture says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God.” Therefore Abraham was justified not by circumcision but by faith. For he believed the word of God, was justified, received blessing from God, and received it for himself and for the offspring of his faith. Consider, then, lest you think that circumcision is the sign of the [Col. 0089] faithful. Before Abraham all the saints were uncircumcised, pleased the Lord by purity of mind, and showed within themselves more clearly the Christian people. Review the order set forth in the sacred Scriptures, and you will find that all were as we say. First was Adam himself, who was fashioned by the hands of God, and he remained uncircumcised; then righteous Abel, Enosh and Enoch, Noah and Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God—all righteous, and none of them, as we say, circumcised according to the flesh, and so forth.

Under the Law of Moses there were many ceremonies and various baptisms; but none of these could provide a universal remedy against the evil of transgression. Homily 22, p. 63. The grace conferred in their application belonged to the New Testament. Accordingly, the righteous who lived before the incarnation of the Word were nevertheless Christians in faith and truly in charity, and could rightly be called Christians.

Therefore Maximus, comparing the Law with the Gospel in Homily 3, p. 10, says:

> I think that the two millstones signify the two Testaments, that is, the Law of Moses and the Gospel of the Lord. They have been arranged and prepared in such a way that the two Testaments correspond to each other, as the Savior says: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it.” . . . If the Gospel had not been placed above it, the Law would still lie sluggish and heavy upon Jewish soil, covered by the narrowness of a single province. . . . Without the Gospel the Law accomplished what can be done with a single stone. It could crush, but it could not benefit, as the blessed Apostle says: “The Law produces wrath, but does not bestow grace.” When the Law stood, the Gospel was given; placed above the Old Testament, it adorns both and travels throughout the whole world with such speed . . . For the Gospel, like the upper millstone, receives all who believe, welcomes all who come, and, as if through certain channels of its commandments, sends them inward, so that there, with the salutary commands of the two Testaments softening the harshness of paganism, it may bring forth everything that is pure. . . . The synagogue therefore grinds, but grinds uselessly, since it relies on laboring with a single stone; and therefore it does not so much grind as scatter and crush, and so forth.

Homily 39, p. 116:

> The fountain of the Old Law had water, but it did not have sweetness. It was pleasing to the sight, but it was not pure for drinking. When the wood cast in by Moses was added, they drank the sweetness pleasantly; the sacrament of the wood removed the austerity that the harmful water carried.

[Note: [Col. 0089] He calls it “harmful” not because it itself brought about any evil, but because it was heavy and bitter and gave the [Col. 0090] malice of the Hebrews an occasion for transgression.]

> I think that this was done as a figure. I think that the bitter water represents the Law of the Old Testament; before it was tempered by the cross of the Lord, that Law was harsh. . . . This is the bitterness that was changed into sweetness: that is, the austerity of the Law was tempered by the grace of the Gospel. The letter of the Law is bitter without the mystery of the cross, concerning which the Apostle says: “The letter kills”; but when the mysteries of the passion are joined to it, all its bitterness is spiritually seasoned, and the Apostle says of it: “The Spirit gives life.”

And in Homily 116, p. 384, rebuking the scribes and Pharisees who had neglected to offer Christ, both before and after his coming, to their body as food:

> The cause undertaken by the Savior concerns not merely one person, nor is the weakness of one person alone cared for; rather, the weakness of the entire human race is saved. No one doubts that the right hand, or rather the more distinguished part of the body, has the function of supplying daily nourishment to its body and, by a certain providence, feeding and sustaining the other members so that they may enjoy life. Therefore I should say that the scribes, or teachers, are this right hand in the Jewish people. Established by the Lord as the more distinguished portion of the body of the Pharisees, they neglected to nourish their other members with the oracles of the prophets—that is, they refused to offer Christ to their body, according to the oracles of the prophets, as the food of eternal life. Therefore their teaching withered like a weak hand, because it did not seek the fountain of everlasting wisdom. Finally, it happened that, as though its right hand were contracted, it could not hold the key of knowledge. . . . This key is Christ the Lord, by whom the hidden things of our hearts are opened to belief in the faith. The Pharisees lose this key; the apostles find it, and so forth.

But enough concerning the power upon which the sacraments of the Old Law rested. We must now briefly discuss what Maximus teaches concerning the sacraments of the New Testament.

Concerning baptism, although we have already said something above, I thought that the following few passages should be transferred here.

In Sermon 3, p. 402, Maximus calls baptism necessary because in it the remission of sins is granted.

Addressing catechumens in Homily 31, p. 91:

> Without baptism you cannot attain the joys of paradise.

And in Homily 33, p. 96:

> After receiving baptism, the catechumen becomes a believer. . . . Our Redeemer instituted for all the saving bath of regeneration.

In Homily 48, p. 150:

> We are pilgrims in this world and live in this light as guests. . . . We are pilgrims, I say, and a burial purchased at the price of the Savior’s blood has been obtained for us. For, as the Apostle says, we have been buried with him through baptism into death. Baptism, therefore, is our burial: in it we die to sins, are buried with respect to crimes, and, when the consciousness of the old man has been dissolved, we are restored in renewed infancy to another birth. Baptism, I say, is the burial of the Savior for us, because there we lose what we previously lived, and there we receive anew what enables us to live. Great, therefore, is the grace of this burial, in which a beneficial death is imposed upon us and a more beneficial life is granted. Great, I say, is the grace of this burial, which both purifies the sinner and gives life to the dying.

And in Homily 59, p. 185:

> When the mystery of baptism intervenes, we see old men become children again. For renewal consists in ceasing to be what you were and assuming what you previously were not. Renewal, I say, is why they are now called neophytes: because through a certain newness they have cast off the stains of old age and assumed the grace of simplicity. The Apostle says: “Put off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God.”

Thereupon, speaking on p. 186 about the garments that newly baptized neophytes customarily assumed and about their significance, Maximus says:

> Certainly our neophytes, newly baptized, like [Col. 0091] eagles, cast off the garments of old age and assumed new clothing of holiness. As their ancient stains waste away, so they are adorned by the renewed grace of immortality, like eagles with light feathers, so that the sins of old age have grown old in them, while life has not grown old. They have been brought back to infancy like an eagle to its young. They possess knowledge of the world from their former way of life, but through restoration they now possess the security of righteousness.

See Sermon 8, p. 418, and Sermon 11, p. 426, where he says:

> When Christ the Lord was initiating the sacraments of the Church, a dove came down from heaven. I understand the mystery; I also recognize the sacrament. The dove is the same one that now comes to the Church of Christ in baptism, which once hastened to Noah’s ark during the Flood, then announcing security to it by an olive branch, and now bestowing eternity upon this Church as a sign of divinity.

And in Homily 98, p. 329:

> What is that water which consumes flames but is itself not consumed? I think it is the water that, flowing in the bath from Christ’s fountain, is not consumed by sinners but consumes the fires of Gehenna. When it is poured out through baptism, it both extinguishes the heat of hell and itself lives in human beings, as the Lord says: “The water that I will give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up,” and so forth.

> In a marvelous way, therefore, the water of Christ, by one and the same operation, both gives life and extinguishes. It gives life to souls and extinguishes sins. It restores the former through the refreshment of its bath and consumes the latter by the flood of its waters. And, as concerns the greater grace of baptism, the mystery is celebrated among those above, while Gehenna is extinguished among those below. . . . Here a human being is immersed in the font, and there he is liberated from Tartarus.

> Nor is it surprising that hell is opened in the sacrament of baptism, since heaven too is then opened. For these elements are opened so that freedom and grace may come together at Christ’s bath. Freedom is granted to those who will rise again; grace, to those who will reign. . . . Those who were slaves of sin become free for righteousness; those who were held in the narrow confines of the world receive the pleasant places of paradise.

In Christ’s baptism, therefore, the heavens are opened, and Tartarus is opened as well: the heavens so that the Holy Spirit may come, Tartarus so that the Savior’s mercy may enter there.

### XXI.

Moreover, Maximus denies that baptism can be repeated. In Homily 28, p. 33, comparing that sacrament with almsgiving, he says:

> The bath is given once and promises forgiveness once; but whenever you give alms, you merit forgiveness each time.

To show that he had made the statement about almsgiving emphatically—Greek *ἐμφατικῶς*, “emphatically”—he writes that he had spoken in good faith. For Maximus was not one who would have thought that almsgiving possessed the power of a sacrament.

See also Treatise 2 on Baptism, p. 717 and following.

## XXII

Maximus discusses the anointings performed before baptism and certain other rites, together with their significance, in *Treatises 1 and 2 on Baptism*, pp. 710 ff. He likewise reports that it was customary for the Creed to be recited and a profession of faith to be made before baptism, ibid., p. 714. He further writes on p. 713:

> We have shown that, through the oil of sanctification, you were prepared to hear the faith and called to the good fragrance of Christ; you were admonished to renounce everything with your whole heart […].
>
> After you had given the most certain pledge by which you promised to renounce all his pomp, his works, and every form of diabolical fornication, you descended into the sacred font—the font of life, the font of redemption, the font sanctified by heavenly power—and so sanctified that, by washing away many sins, it sanctifies human beings. You must not judge those waters with your eyes, but with your mind. For although the substance of that water belongs to the ordinary nature of water, its effect nevertheless proceeds from the grace and power of God […].
>
> For the Holy Spirit operates in that water, so that those who before baptism were held guilty of various crimes […] after baptism might be deemed worthy to enter the kingdom of heaven […].
>
> In this font, therefore, before we immersed your whole bodies—for baptism was customarily conferred by immersion—we asked: “Do you believe in God the almighty Father?” You answered: “I believe.” Again we asked: “Do you also believe in Jesus Christ, his Son, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary?” Each of you answered: “I believe.” Again we asked: “Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit?” You answered likewise: “I believe.”
>
> We did this according to the command of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior. When he ascended into heaven to the Father, he charged his disciples, that is, the apostles, saying: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.”
>
> But when anyone hears “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit,” let no one think that we profess three gods. May that sacrilege be far removed from our faith, for we have learned, with his own testimony, that there is only one God […].
>
> We therefore hold and believe in three persons, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, of one power, one substance, one eternity, one will, and likewise one divinity; and we venerate the whole Trinity under the designation of one God. To believe in several gods is pagan impiety.
>
> Again: not to believe that the three persons are of one substance within one divinity, and equal or coeternal, is heretical madness, since this authority of Christ, which we have cited, is manifest: “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” […].
>
> After you had promised to believe these things that we have spoken thus far, we immersed your bodies three times in the font. This order of baptism is celebrated with a twofold mystical significance. It was right that you were immersed three times, since you received baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, who rose from the dead on the third day. That repeated threefold immersion expresses the type of the Lord’s burial, through which you were buried with Christ in baptism and rose with Christ in faith, so that, washed from your sins, you might live by imitating Christ in holiness and virtue.

## XXIII

When baptism was customarily conferred at that time, Maximus demonstrates in Homily 61, p. 194:

> At Easter, he says, all nations are customarily baptized.

Our Maximus also treats baptism of blood in Sermon 88, p. 625, where he says:

> While the fury of persecution presses upon them, catechumens are still preparing their souls for heaven; they are regenerated by death, released from condemnation, and consecrated by the sword.

## XXIV

Maximus continues to write in *Treatise 3 on Baptism*, p. 717:

> Now, he says, we shall discuss those things that are completed in the baptized through sacred instruction. After baptism has been completed, we pour chrism—that is, the oil of sanctification—[Col. 0093] over your heads, by which it is shown that the baptized receive from the Lord a royal and priestly dignity. For in the Old Testament those who were chosen for the priesthood or for the sacred kingship were anointed with oil; and through the anointing of the head some received from the Lord the power to reign, others the power to offer sacrifices […].
>
> But in the Old Testament that oil conferred a temporal kingship and a temporal priesthood […]. This chrism, however—that is, this anointing that has been placed upon you—has conferred the dignity of that priesthood which, once bestowed, never comes to an end.
>
> It is surely astonishing what we have said: through that chrism you have attained the kingdom of future glory and the priesthood. Yet it is not I, but the apostle Peter—indeed, Christ through Peter—who declares that this dignity has been conferred upon you. For he speaks thus to the faithful, that is, to those who have been washed in baptism and consecrated with chrism: “But you are a royal and priestly race, a holy nation,” and so forth.
>
> Consider, therefore, the honor you have received in that mystery, and so forth.

[XCV] Who could fail to understand that Maximus, who kept in mindful remembrance what had been received from Christ and the apostles and entrusted by the Fathers to the perpetual memory of human beings, here indicates the sacrament of confirmation, which was chiefly completed by anointing the forehead with chrism?

Saint Cyprian, *Letter 70 to Januarius*, p. 190 of the Oxford edition of 1682, writes:

> It is also necessary that the one who has been baptized should be anointed, so that, having received chrism—that is, anointing—he may be able to be anointed by God and to have within him the grace of Christ.

The following passage from Saint Pacianus, *Letter 1 to Sympronianus*, bears on the same matter:

> If, therefore, the power both of the washing and of the chrism has descended from the bishops through the ancient and far greater charisms […], then neither the chrism nor baptism […] has been entrusted to his authority, because nothing was commanded by private usurpation, and the whole of it flowed from apostolic authority.

Saint Optatus of Milevis has similar statements in *Against Parmenianus*, Book III, chapter 5, p. 62 of the Antwerp edition of 1702, and Book VII, chapter 4, pp. 102 ff.; so also Saint Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book XV, chapter 26, vol. VIII of the works, p. 708 of the Antwerp edition of 1700. There he asserts that Christ was anointed with the Holy Spirit as a human being, not with visible oil, but with the gift of grace, which is signified by the visible ointment with which the Church anoints the baptized.

He says likewise in *Treatise 3 on the First Letter of John*, no. 5, vol. III, part II, p. 616:

> Spiritual anointing, he says, is itself the Holy Spirit, whose sacrament is contained in visible anointing.

But, so as not to delay over many examples, I shall describe one passage found in *Against the Letter of Petilianus*, Book II, chapter 104, p. 199, vol. IX:

> The sacrament of chrism […] is, among visible signs, a sacrament, just as baptism itself is, and so forth.

Saint Leo the Great, Sermon 23, the fourth *On the Nativity of the Lord*, chapter 6, p. 54, vol. I of the works, Roman edition of 1753, likewise teaches the people in a manner entirely consistent with Maximus:

> You, whom I address in no worthier words than those of the blessed apostle Peter, an elect race, a royal priesthood, and so forth: remain steadfast in that faith which you confessed before many witnesses, and in which, reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, you received the saving chrism and the seal of eternal life.

And in Sermon 3, delivered on the anniversary of his assumption to the pontificate, chapter 1, p. 8, he says:

> In the unity of faith and baptism, beloved, we possess an undivided fellowship and a universal dignity, according to the words of the blessed apostle Peter: “But you are an elect race, a royal priesthood,” and so forth. For the sign of the cross makes all who have been reborn in Christ kings, while the anointing of the Holy Spirit consecrates them priests, so that, apart from the particular servitude of our ministry, all spiritual and rational Christians may recognize that they share in the royal race and the priestly office.

I omit what Salvianus of Marseille transmitted concerning the sacrament of chrism in Book III of *On Providence*, as well as what Vigilius of Tapsus wrote in Book III *Against Eutyches*, no. 7; Saint Isidore of Seville in Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 19; and the Venerable Bede in his commentary on Acts, chapter X, and on the First Letter of John, chapter II.

The Greeks held the same view. [XCVI] See the Council of Laodicea, canon 48, p. 789, vol. I of the *Councils*, Paris edition of 1714, and Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 21, which is the third *Mystagogical Catechesis*, entitled **περὶ Χρίσματος**, “On Chrism,” nos. 1 ff., pp. 315 ff. of the Paris edition of 1720.

It should be observed that Antonius Augustinus Toutée, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur, a learned man especially well versed in the teaching of the Greek Fathers, writes in his note to the aforementioned catechesis of Saint Cyril, no. 3, on the same page:

> What the Latins designate by the name of confirmation, the Greeks customarily call chrism, or **μύρον**, “ointment.” For in this sacrament they have always regarded anointing as its principal element.

Saint Basil of Caesarea, Saint Cyril of Alexandria, and others pursue similar arguments. To reproduce their passages would be both too lengthy and perhaps somewhat tedious and wearisome for readers. Anyone who wants more should consult the excellent dissertation of Joseph Augustinus Orsi, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, *On Confirmatory Chrism*, pp. 135 ff., Milan edition of 1733.

It seems to me that one point deserves somewhat more careful investigation: why does Maximus make anointing of the head the principal part of the sacrament of confirmation, while many of the Fathers place it in the anointing and signing of the forehead?

Innocent I, *Letter 25 to Decentius of Gubbio*, no. 6, vol. I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 858, Paris edition of 1721, writes:

> Presbyters, whether a bishop is absent or present, may anoint those whom they baptize with chrism consecrated by the bishop; but they may not sign the forehead with it, since this belongs exclusively to bishops when they impart the Spirit, the Paraclete.

See Coustant’s annotation on this same passage of Saint Innocent.

But since Maximus had undertaken not to write a theological treatise on the mystery of confirmation but to preach a sermon to the people, he did not seem to think that the matter needed to be divided and refined so minutely, or, as they say, dissected to the living tissue. It was enough—as other Fathers sometimes did as well—to mention the head, of which the forehead is certainly a part.

## XXV

That the sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood is offered on the altars of the Church, and that Christ himself is truly present in the sacrament of the Eucharist, is an orthodox doctrine asserted and proclaimed by Maximus.

In Sermon 78, pp. 599 ff., he says:

> What could be said that is more reverent or more honorable than that the martyrs rest beneath [Col. 0095] that altar on which sacrifice is celebrated to God, on which offerings are made, and on which the Lord is priest […]? Christ is placed upon the altar […] the body is offered upon the Lord’s altar […]. There the blood of Christ is poured out for sinners.
>
> It is therefore fitting […] that burial was granted there to the martyrs, where the Lord’s death is celebrated daily, as he himself says: “Whenever you do these things, you will proclaim my death until I come” […].
>
> Not without reason, as though through a certain fellowship, a tomb was established there for those who were slain, where the members of the Lord’s slaughter are placed […].
>
> We read that many of the righteous are cherished in Abraham’s bosom […]; nevertheless, no one deserved to rest more fittingly than the martyrs, where Christ is both sacrifice and priest—so that they might receive both the propitiation obtained from the offering of the sacrifice and the blessing and fulfillment of the priest’s office.

[XCVII] From this it is perfectly clear:

1. that sacrifice is offered on the altars of the Church;
2. that offerings are made;
3. that these offerings are Christ, who is placed upon the altar and whose body is offered upon it;
4. that the blood of Christ is poured out there for sinners, that the members of the Lord’s slaughter are placed there, and that the death of our Savior is proclaimed;
5. that Christ himself is the priest;
6. that the sacrifice is one of propitiation;

and so forth.

These statements are entirely consonant with the teaching of the Fathers. See Saint Thomas, Part III, Question 82, Article 1, where he adduces testimonies from Augustine, Ambrose, and others confirming the same points. See also what the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur cite from Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, and the other Fathers: Maranus, Preface to the works of Justin, chapters 10 and 15; and Massuet, dissertation 3 on the books of Irenaeus, article 7, nos. 76 ff., to pass over the rest, whose catalogue it is neither convenient nor necessary to construct.

As for what Maximus says concerning the propitiation and the priest’s blessing that the martyrs receive, this does not mean that the holy martyrs possess any sin or guilt requiring expiation through propitiation and blessing. Rather, it means that they obtain what they ask. Maximus was not one who thought that those whom he expressly proclaims to be righteous and holy, and to be held in a place of special honor because of the faith for which they struggled, possessed any sin or guilt.

He says that vengeance for blood is requested from the martyrs there, where Christ’s blood is poured out for sinners. That vengeance for blood signifies nothing other than the overthrow of the kingdom of sin; the manifestation of divine justice; God’s becoming gracious toward sinners and, by blessing them, bringing them to repentance; the restoration and glorification of the bodies of the saints; and finally the second coming of Christ.

Maximus also calls the altar or table the Lord’s table in *Treatise 5 against the Jews*, p. 745. He says that a heavenly banquet is prepared upon it, and that we may therefore sing with David:

> The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has settled me there in a place of pasture.

Concerning the manner in which we are nourished by the Eucharist, and the punishment awaiting those who receive it unworthily, Maximus teaches the following in Homily 45, p. 138. He says that this food is sweeter than honey, and that whoever neglects to eat and consume it cannot have life within himself, as the Lord himself says:

> Unless someone has eaten my flesh and drunk my blood, he will not have life within himself.

Rather, that food will be turned into judgment, as the Apostle says:

> Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.

This was subtly prophesied for the children of Israel in the Testament. When they handled the manna contrary to the divine commandments, worms were produced for them—that is, avengers and judges of their disobedience. [XCVIII] This likeness points to the Lord Christ: whoever neglects to receive him as sweet food and pleasant drink will experience him as judge, as he himself says.

## XXVI

Although Maximus did not treat the matter systematically—for he does not happen to have addressed it expressly—he nevertheless shows sufficiently what his view was concerning the confession of sins.

In Homily 115, p. 382, indicating the necessity of confession, he says:

> Every Christian who wishes to conceal his sins is spiritually a fox. For just as a fox remains in hiding places because of its deceitfulness, so the sinner who is silent hides, because of his conscience, in the pits of his sins. And just as the fox does not dare to display the deceitfulness of its ways amid the crowds of human beings, so this person is ashamed to confess the wickedness of his conduct in the middle of the church.

Speaking of repentance and the hope of obtaining pardon in Sermon 39, pp. 501 ff., he says:

> Is it not right for us to rejoice, since through the sacrament of the new mystery sins are taken away, heaven is given, and paradise is restored? […] The one act of confession absolved all the robber’s former crimes, and in a very brief speech erased whatever he had committed over the course of a long life. The blood of his robbery did not condemn him before God, because he believed Christ’s blood to be a kingdom, not a punishment.
>
> There is no doubt, beloved, that this deed benefited the entire human race. For who would despair of God’s grace after the robber was absolved, provided that the robber’s faith followed his supplicating prayer?
>
> We have another magnificent example of the Lord’s compassion, by which, laying aside all fear of deadly despair, we may trust in the ineffable forgiveness of our Redeemer. When Christ, condemned by the impious, hung upon the cross and Jewish fury mocked the crucified one, he himself, the omnipotent Father’s pious intercessor amid his wounds, prayed for his executioners, saying: “Father, forgive them; they do not know what they are doing,” and so forth.

Maximus does not discuss penitents, their various stages, or the remission of sins granted to them by priests—matters on which other Fathers speak—because the opportunity did not arise for the holy bishop, while delivering addresses to the people, to discuss them. Nor does he discuss extreme unction.

## XXVII

Maximus shows what honor should be paid to the priesthood in Homily 85, p. 285. There he says:

> If you listened carefully to the Gospel reading, you can understand what reverence is owed to the ministers and priests of God. For he writes that they have been enriched by the reward of the Holy Spirit and have received the pledge of the Spirit—certainly through ordination, for I cannot even imagine any other means.

For this reason, he observes that they serve the altar; that is, through the authority they have received, they perform the divine service, and therefore ought to live from the altar. He further teaches that the food of God’s word is to be supplied to the people by priests.

[Col. 0097] He confirms that this office belongs especially to bishops, who possess the right not only to teach the people but also to punish the guilty and to exclude them from communion in sacred things. [XCIX]

Concerning the pledge of the Spirit received by priests, and their service at the altar, he states the following in Homily 114, pp. 388 ff.:

> We serve as soldiers for the Lord and God, as the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.” I say that we do not serve as soldiers in loose and flowing tunics; rather, we have the belt of our service, by which our inner chastity is bound. Concerning this belt the Lord says to his apostles: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands.”
>
> We are therefore soldiers of Christ, and we receive pay and a gift from him, as the blessed Apostle says: “He gave us the pledge of the Spirit”—that is, he enriched us with the reward of the Holy Spirit […].
>
> The Catholic cleric is restrained by this saying. For if he is not content with the pay that, by the Lord’s command, he receives from the altar, but conducts business, sells intercessions, and willingly accepts gifts from widows, he may be regarded more as a merchant than as a cleric.

In Homily 12, pp. 371 ff., discussing the preaching of the divine Word and the right belonging to priests to punish the guilty, whom he compares to bees, he says:

> I rightly said “a swarm of priests,” because, just as bees make sweet honey from the little flowers of the divine Scriptures and, through the skill of their mouths, prepare whatever pertains to the healing of souls, so priests are rightly compared to bees. For, just as bees practice bodily chastity, provide the food of heavenly life, and wield the sting of the law, so they are pure for sanctification, sweet for refreshment, and severe for vengeance.
>
> They are indeed to be compared to bees, since they are contained, as it were, in a hive through the grace of Mother Church. There they construct cells of diverse merits with their sweetest preaching, and from the one swarm of the Savior produce many swarms of Christians […].
>
> The priest’s preaching is correction for the people who are to be saved and a warning to those who are to be judged. For before the judgment we warn them of what awaits them in the judgment itself, and so forth.

That a bishop ought to teach, exhort, admonish, and, if necessary, rebuke the people can be clearly understood from Maximus’s Sermon 103. He writes there, p. 659:

> Sometimes, brothers, when we preach, our sermon seems rather harsh to many, and what we pursue according to the rule is received by some as though it were uttered through the severity of our own sternness. They say: “How harshly and bitterly the bishop preached,” not knowing that the priest’s necessity is greater than his inclination.
>
> I say that the necessity of speaking is greater—not because the will to pursue what is true is lacking, but because the penalty established for silence removes the silence of keeping quiet. We endure necessity while we are afraid, and therefore are compelled to do more than we wish; we impose fearsome things upon others while fearing for our own salvation.
>
> This is the condition of the preacher: he must not conceal another’s sins if he wishes to avoid his own sins, and he must correct his brother by rebuking him so that he may not lose the priest within himself. But if he wishes to dissemble, remain silent, and conceal the matter, then by his silence he neither corrects the other nor, by failing to preach, does he respect himself.
>
> It is therefore better to correct sin by rebuking than, through silence, to take upon oneself the offenses of the sinner. For we have been placed in this position so that, if we do not tell those who offend of their crimes, the guilt of their crimes may also involve us.
>
> For thus the Lord says through the prophet: “And you, son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel; you will hear a word from my mouth when I say to the sinner, ‘You will surely die,’ and you do not speak so that the wicked may beware of his way, that wicked person will die in his iniquity; but I will require his blood from your hand.”
>
> This is an evident and manifest judgment: it stains the watchman with the blood of the criminal because he was silent. Nor is it satisfied that iniquity condemns the wicked person unless it also declares guilty the one who refused to rebuke that same iniquity.
>
> See, therefore, how great is the evil of the offender. The offender himself sins, and the priest is accused. The offender strangles himself with his crimes, and blood is required from the bishop’s hand.
>
> We must therefore speak and cry out, lest that same sinner excuse our silence on the day of judgment, and lest the one who pretends to share in holiness then charge us with companionship in error […].
>
> A watchman is so called because, standing as it were in a lofty tower, he looks out over the neighboring people to ensure that no enemy suddenly slips in among them. Concerned for them, he sees to it that the people enjoy the sweetness of peace; and if he suddenly perceives something adverse, he immediately reports it and announces it resolutely, so that the citizen may be prepared to avoid danger and the discovered enemy may flee.
>
> But if, when the enemy presses forward, the watchman dissimulates, remains silent, or neglects his duty, then the people are unexpectedly seized and the enemy, arriving, runs riot. Therefore all the guilt is attributed to the one who refused to speak in order to save many, but preferred to remain silent so that he might perish along with them.
>
> Who, then, are these watchmen established by the Lord, if not the most blessed priests? They are placed, as it were, upon a lofty tower of wisdom for the protection of the people; from a distance they observe the evils that are approaching and, while still far away, contemplate future punishments—not with the sight of bodily eyes, but with the vision of spiritual prudence.
>
> For this reason they cannot remain silent but are compelled to cry out, lest through their silence the devil, the enemy, invade Christ’s flock.

See also Sermon 104, pp. 661 ff.

Concerning the right by which a bishop may prohibit criminals from communion in sacred things and deprive them of it, Maximus speaks briefly but sufficiently clearly in Homily 47, p. 146. He writes:

> By the bishop’s judgment, criminals are expelled from Christian fellowship.

For it belongs to the leaders of sacred things, who have been charged with administering the Gospel, to cut away the filth of the people, just as it belongs to the farmer carrying the knife to cut off the vine-shoots, Homily 37, p. 111.

[CI]

## XXVIII

Concerning marriage, he says in Homily 23, p. 67:

> The Son of God goes to the wedding, in order that those unions which he had formerly established by his power he might then sanctify by the blessing of his presence.

And in Homily 17, p. 50:

> We ought to rejoice no less because, on this most sacred day of the present celebration of the Epiphany—as we are instructed by the tradition of our fathers—Christ our Lord himself, invited to an earthly wedding, came not to take pleasure in that banquet, but to show that he was its author, and, by sanctifying the marriage, to make known his divine power, and so forth.

[Col. 0099]

## XXIX

Imitating the manner of expression used by the Fathers, Maximus writes that the Church flowed from the saving side and wound of Christ the Savior in Homily 55, p. 172, and Sermon 34, p. 486. There he says:

> At the very beginning of the world’s creation, when that mother of all living beings, Eve, was produced from the rib of the sleeping Adam, the Church, mother of all believers, is shown as destined to be born from the side of Christ dying upon the cross.

[Note: See Saint John Chrysostom, *Homily on the Praise of Maximus*, no. 3, p. 215, vol. III of the works, Paris edition of 1721; and Saint Augustine in the passage to be cited shortly.]

These statements are intended to show that the holy Church was signified by the blood and water flowing from Christ’s side.

To the same point belong what Saint Augustine teaches in Sermon 5, formerly Sermon 1, among the Sirmondian sermons, no. 3, vol. V of the works, Antwerp edition of 1700:

> What flowed from his side, he says, except the sacrament received by the faithful? Spirit, blood, and water […].
>
> By that blood and water the Church is signified as having been born. And when did blood and water come out of his side? When Christ was already sleeping upon the cross. For Adam received sleep in paradise, and then Eve was produced from his side.

Why the Church is signified by blood and water is clear from what John Chrysostom observes in the passage cited immediately above. He says:

> The whole Church consists of that water and blood. He himself is witness, saying: “Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven” […].
>
> We are born through the water of baptism, but we are nourished by blood. Do you see how we are of his flesh and of his bones, since we are both born and nourished from that blood and water?

And just as woman was formed while Adam slept, so the Church was made from Christ’s side after Christ had died. Those who constitute the Church are reborn from water and nourished by the Savior’s blood.

The same point is made by Maximus in Homily 55, p. 174.

[Note: Consult Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 3, [Col. 0100] no. 10, p. 44 of the Paris edition of 1720; Catechesis 13, no. 21, p. 193; Saint Ambrose, Book X on the Gospel of Luke, no. 135, vol. II of the works, Venetian edition of 1748; and Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 15, p. 230, Venetian edition of 1744.]

Moreover, Maximus teaches, following Scripture and the tradition of the Fathers, that the Church is like a ship, whose figure was the ark of Noah, on p. 487, in Homily 55, p. 174, and in Sermon 94, p. 641:

> That ship, he says, floats upon the depths of this world in such a way that, while the world perishes, it preserves unharmed all whom it carries. Its figure we already see in the [CII] Old Testament.
>
> For just as Noah’s ark, while the world was suffering shipwreck, preserved unharmed all whom it had received, so Peter’s Church, while the world is consumed by fire, will present unharmed all whom it embraces. And just as, after the flood had passed, the dove brought a sign of peace to Noah’s ark, so, after judgment has passed, Christ brings the joy of peace to Peter’s Church.

By the authority of Scripture it can be shown that Noah’s ark was a symbol or figure of the Church. See the First Letter of Saint Peter, chapter III, verses 20 ff.

The oldest of the Fathers who confirmed the same point was Justin Martyr. See his *Dialogue with Trypho*, no. 88, p. 242 of the Venetian edition of 1747.

Tertullian followed him. In *On Baptism*, chapter 8, p. 227 of the Venetian edition of 1744, he writes:
