> Just as, after the waters of the flood, by which ancient wickedness was cleansed, after the baptism, so to speak, of the world, the dove, the herald of heavenly peace, was sent down from the ark and announced peace to the earth when it returned with the olive branch—a sign that is also held forth among the nations as a symbol of peace—in the same arrangement of spiritual effect, the dove of the Holy Spirit flies to the earth, that is, to our flesh, rising from the washing after its former sins, bringing the peace of God, sent from heaven, where the Church is the ark represented in figure.

Saint Cyprian agrees in *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 109 of the Oxford edition of 1682:

> If anyone could escape who was outside Noah’s ark, then let the one who is outside the Church escape. The Lord warns us and says: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” […].
>
> Whoever gathers anywhere outside the Church scatters, and so forth.

See also Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 17, no. 10, p. 269 of the Paris edition of 1720; Saint Ambrose, *On Noah and the Ark*, chapter 13, no. 25, p. 276, and chapter 15, no. 52, p. 290, vol. I of the Venetian edition of 1748; and Saint Jerome, *Letter to Damasus*, which is Letter 10 among the Damascian letters, no. 2, p. 546 of Coustant’s Paris edition of 1721. Speaking there of the Church of Peter, or the Roman See, he says:

> Whoever eats the lamb outside this house is profane. If anyone is not in Noah’s ark, he will perish while the flood reigns.

Saint John Chrysostom, in his homily *On the Earthquake and Lazarus*, no. 7, vol. I, p. 783 of the Paris edition of 1718, says:

> The things that are narrated were mysteries and figures of future events; they were figures of what would happen. The ark was the Church, Noah was Christ, the dove was the Holy Spirit, and the olive leaf was God’s kindness, and so forth.

Saint Augustine, *On Baptism*, Book V, final chapter, no. 39, p. 108, vol. IX of the works, and *The City of God*, Book XV, chapter 26, p. 310, vol. VII of the Antwerp edition of 1700, writes:

> God commands Noah, a righteous man […], to make an ark in which he, together with his wife, sons, and daughters-in-law, and with the animals that entered the ark at God’s command, would be saved from the devastation of the flood. Beyond doubt this is a figure of the city of God sojourning in this world, that is, of the Church, which is saved through the wood [CIII] on which hung the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

For this reason ancient Christians took care to have this kind of figure painted or sculpted. On this subject one may consult Ciampini, Bonarrota, Maffeius, Boldettus, and others mentioned by Mamachi, vol. I, pp. 78 and 264, and vol. III of *Christian Antiquities*, Book III, part I, chapter 1, section 3, no. 5, pp. 31 ff.

Concerning the ship that likewise represents the Church, and which was therefore customarily painted, engraved, sculpted in stone, and so forth, see Clement of Alexandria, Book III of the *Paedagogus*, chapter 11, p. 245 of the Paris edition of 1641, and Saint Ambrose on Luke, Book IV, nos. 70 ff., p. 848, vol. II.

See also the ancient monuments cited by Hieronymus Alexander the Younger and others whom Mamachi reviews in the book mentioned, [Col. 0101] no. 32, p. 98.

Now, explaining why he calls the Church like a ship, Maximus says in Homily 50, p. 154:

> When the sea is cut through by sailors, the mast is first raised by them and the sail spread, so that, with the Lord’s cross fashioned, the streams of water may be broken, and by this secure sign of the Lord they seek the harbor of salvation and escape the danger of death.
>
> For the suspended sail upon the mast is a certain figure of the sacrament, as though Christ had been exalted upon the cross. Therefore, deriving confidence from the mystery, people disregard the storms of the winds and undertake the vows of their journey.
>
> Just as the Church cannot stand without the cross, so the ship is weak without the mast. Immediately the devil disturbs it, and the wind batters it. But when the sign of the cross is raised, the devil’s wickedness is immediately driven back and the storm of the winds is stilled.

And thus far concerning the symbols of the ark and the ship. Now I shall briefly explain the comparison of the vine and the moon with the Church, and the Church’s own spread and growth through the preaching of the Word of God and the blood shed by the martyrs, as these matters are transmitted by Maximus.

Thus Maximus, homily 30, p. 478:

> “Noah, a husbandman, when he had planted a vineyard . . . signified Christ, who made the Church a vineyard.”

Who, indeed, is so ignorant as not to know that the Church was compared to a vineyard not only by the Fathers but also by Christ the Savior himself in the Gospel?

Maximus, moreover, in homily 101, p. 338, says:

> “The Church shines not by its own light but by that of the Savior, and radiates not with its own brightness but with the Father’s, as the Apostle says: ‘Yet I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me’; and again: ‘That he might be the firstborn among many brethren.’”

The Church is rightly compared to the moon, since it too drenches us with the dew of the laver and gives life to the soil of our body with the dew of baptism. The Church is rightly compared to the moon because it too gains increase and suffers diminution. For it is often diminished and frequently enlarged. It is diminished by persecutions and enlarged by preaching. It wanes when it is diminished in children; it grows when it is crowned with martyrs. The very cause that brings it diminution also supplies its increase: for often those whom it mourns as persecutors it receives as confessors.

[CIV] This was certainly the unanimous voice of all the Fathers. Justin Martyr, in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, no. 110, p. 214 of the Venice edition of his works, 1747:

> “While we are struck with the sword, while we are crucified, while we are handed over to wild beasts, to chains, to fire, and to every other torture, we plainly do not depart from our confession. But the more such things are inflicted upon us, the more others become believers through the name of Jesus Christ. Just as a vine, if someone cuts away the parts that bear fruit, flourishes so as to produce again other branches, flowering and fruitful, so the same thing happens to us.”

These words agree with what Tertullian writes in his *To Scapula*, chapter 4, p. 72:

> “This sect will not fail; rather, you should know that it is built up more when it seems to be cut down.”

And in the final chapter of the *Apology*, p. 40:

> “We become more numerous whenever we are mown down by you. The blood of Christians is seed.”

Similar are the passages embraced by Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 18, no. 27, p. 298; Saint Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration* 23, p. 414, vol. I of the Cologne edition, 1690, where he says:

> “Persecutions made it [the Church] more illustrious and more splendid through sufferings.”

And in poem 11, addressed to the bishops, vol. II, p. 82, he writes:

> For hostile fury too, and every monstrous  
> Torture, had added new strength to our spirits,  
> And faith, more firmly supported by grievous torments, flourished with greater vigor.

Saint Ambrose, Letter 72, no. 14, p. 1173, vol. III of his works, Venice edition, 1751, says that religion has been “increased, not diminished, through the martyrs.”

Saint John Chrysostom, *Against Jews and Gentiles, That Christ Is God*, no. 12, p. 258, vol. I.

Saint Augustine, on Psalm 40, no. 1, p. 258, vol. IV of the Antwerp edition, 1700, says:

> “The devil stirred up persecutions against the Church in order to destroy the name of Christ . . . . In order that Christ might die again, not in the Head but in his body, the martyrs too were killed. The holy blood that was shed served to multiply the Church; the death of the martyrs was added to the sowing. ‘Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.’ Christians multiplied more and more, and what the enemies had said was not fulfilled . . . . The pagans sit and reckon the years for themselves; they hear their fanatics saying that someday there will be no Christians . . . . They still say: ‘When will he die, and his name perish?’ Twice defeated—or, rather, learn wisdom a third time. Christ died, but his name did not perish; the martyrs died, and the Church was multiplied still more. The name of Christ grows among all nations—the one who foretold his death and resurrection, who foretold the deaths of his martyrs and their crown.”

And in Sermon 1 on Psalm 58, no. 5, p. 418:

> “A great and abundant quantity of martyrs’ blood was poured out; when it had been poured out, the Church, like a sown crop, more fruitfully occupied the whole world, as we now see.”

And in Sermon 32 on Psalm 118, no. 6, p. 1021:

> “Who does not see how greatly the blood [CV] of the Church has aided the Church? How great a harvest has risen throughout the whole world from that seed?”

And in book 22 of *The City of God*, chapter 6, p. 499, vol. VII:

> “Fear could not recall from worshiping and even confessing Christ God so great a multitude of martyrs throughout the world—not fear of a slight offense to their minds, but of immense and varied punishments, and of death itself, which is feared more than all the rest. Nor did the city of Christ, although it was still journeying on earth and already possessed the armies of great peoples, fight against its impious persecutors for temporal safety; rather, in order to obtain eternal safety, it did not resist. They were bound, imprisoned, beaten, and multiplied.”

Saint Leo the Great, Sermon 83, which concerns the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, chapter 6, p. 237, vol. I of his works, Rome edition, 1753:

> “The Church is not diminished by persecutions but increased; and the Lord’s field is always clothed with a richer harvest, while the grains that fall singly are born multiplied.”

Following these Fathers, Maximus continues in Sermon 50, p. 528:

> “The Church is afflicted by the hands of bloodstained men, [Col. 0103] not so that it may fail amid sufferings and punishments, but so that, through the manifold titles of its victories, it may be adorned in all its beauty by the blood of its triumphant martyrs.”

That the Church of Christ flourished before Christ was born, Maximus likewise observes in homily 101, p. 338. Concerning this doctrine, to pass over the others, see Augustine, book 1 of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 15 and following, no. 24 and following, vol. IX, p. 62.

Maximus also teaches in the same place that Jamnes and Mambres attempted to overthrow that Church when they resisted Moses. At that time, however, because it was almost confined within the boundaries of Palestine and had not yet been extended to the Gentiles, it was barren.

Homily 93, p. 353:

> “Let us inquire what that city is which suffered from barrenness . . . . We read that the Apostle said concerning the Church: ‘Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail.’ Therefore the Church is that barren city which, before the coming of Christ, endured barrenness because of the corruption of the waters—that is, because of the sacrilege of the Gentile peoples—and could not produce children for God. When Christ came, taking a human body as a clay vessel, he healed the corruption of the waters—that is, he cut away the sacrileges of the peoples. Immediately the Church, which had been barren, began to be fruitful. Hence the Apostle too says: ‘Rejoice, barren woman.’ For the Church that had been barren produced more children through him than the Synagogue [Note: [Col. 0103] See also homily 18, p. 51], which, though confined within the boundaries of Palestine, was fruitful, had received.”

These statements plainly agree with what has been handed down in the written records of the other Fathers, especially by Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 18, nos. 26 and following, p. 298; and by John Chrysostom, on Isaiah chapter 2, no. 3, p. 21 and following, vol. VI, and on chapter 4 of the Epistle to the Galatians, no. 4, vol. X, p. 710 and following. There the holy Doctor says:

> “Which was formerly barren, and which was formerly desolate? Is it not evident [CVI] that this is the Church from the Gentiles, which formerly was deprived of the knowledge of God? And which is that woman who has a husband? Is it not clear that this is the Synagogue? Yet the barren woman surpassed her in the multitude of children, since the latter had only one nation, whereas the children of the Church fill Greece, Barbary, land, sea—in short, the whole world.”

Maximus further affirms that the Church must be believed. How it must be believed he explains in *Treatise 2 on Baptism*, p. 714:

> “When we asked, ‘Do you believe in the holy Church and the remission of sins?’ we did not ask in such a way that, just as one believes in God, so one should believe ‘in the holy Catholic Church.’ It is holy and catholic because it rightly believes in God. Therefore we did not say that you should believe in the Church as though you believed in God; rather, understand that we mean, and have said: ‘That, living in the holy and catholic Church, [Note: [Col. 0103] See Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 18, no. 25, p. 297, where you read: ‘Faith has handed this over to you to hold: “And in one holy, catholic Church,” so that, fleeing their detestable assemblies, you may always cling to the Catholic Church in which you were reborn. And if you should ever be traveling in cities, do not simply ask where the Lord’s house is—for the impious sects and heresies also attempt to dignify their own dens with the name of the Lord’s houses [Col. 0104]—nor simply where the Church is, but where the Catholic Church is. For this is the proper name of this holy Church, the mother of us all.’ Relevant also are the teachings of Saint Augustine, book 4 of *Against the Letter of Manichaeus*, no. 5, p. 110, vol. VIII of his works, Antwerp edition, 1700.] you should believe in God.’”

And in homily 83, p. 272:

> “The holy Church. Truly the Church must be confessed as holy, through which sanctification has been given to mortals, and, as the number of believers increases, the sanctified world rejoices in the praises of God in almost every tongue. Holy is the Church which, after cleansing away the contagion of sins through the sacrament of baptism, conveys the inhabitants of the earth to heaven.”

Here, then, is the manner in which Maximus understands “holy” and “catholic”: holy because it rightly believes in God, because through it sanctification has been given to mortals, and because, after cleansing away the contagion of sins through baptism, it conveys the inhabitants of the earth to heaven; catholic because it has been spread so widely throughout the world that the sanctified world rejoices in the praises of God in almost every tongue.

Likewise, homily 9, p. 26:

> “Clinging with steadfast faith and customary devotion to the priest’s many admonitions, walking along the paths of religious conduct and the tracks of truth which the universal Church holds, trample more and more underfoot the byways of the heretics and the devil’s fabrications.”

Maximus also maintains that true doctrine is always held and taught by the Catholic Church. Homily 45, p. 140:

> “The Lord’s wisdom was not asserted, nor sought out; for he did not learn from a teacher, as the Jews themselves say: ‘How does this man know letters, since he has not learned?’ And he himself says: ‘My teaching is not from this world, but from him who sent me.’ This is what he says concerning the preceding context: with what garment—or with what garments altogether—is the CATHOLIC CHURCH ALWAYS CLOTHED?”

[CVII] XXX. Let us now consider how and for what reason Maximus calls the Catholic Church both the ship and the Church of Peter.

For he writes as follows [Note: [Col. 0104] Sermon 94, p. 640 and following]:

> “Let us see what that little ship of Simon Peter is, which the Lord judged more suitable than the two others for teaching, and which the Lord judged, of the two, more suitable for teaching, and which both protects the Savior from insult and grants utterances of faith to human beings. For we find that the Lord had already sailed in another ship and had been assailed by grievous insults. He sailed with Moses on the Red Sea, when he carried the people of Israel across the currents of the waves; but he was grievously insulted, as he himself says in the Gospel to the Jews: ‘If you believed Moses, you would believe me.’ The Savior’s insult, however, is the unbelief of the Synagogue.

> “Therefore he chose Peter’s ship and abandoned Moses’—that is, he rejected the faithless Synagogue and took up the faithful Church. For two little ships, as it were, were appointed by God to fish for the salvation of human beings in this world, as in a sea . . . . From these two little ships, one is left at the shore empty and vacant, while the other is brought out into the deep, laden or full. The empty Synagogue is left on the shore because it lost Christ together with the utterances of the prophets; but the laden Church is taken into the deep because it received the Lord [Col. 0105] together with the teaching of the apostles.

> “The Synagogue, I say, is left upon the land, as though clinging to earthly works; but the Church is called into the heights, as though examining the profound mysteries of heaven—in fact, into that height of which the Apostle says: ‘O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!’ Therefore it is said to Peter: ‘Put out into the deep’—that is, into the depths of theological disputation [Note: [Col. 0105] See also Sermon 95, p. 644. Compare also Saint Ambrose, book 4 on Luke, no. 71, p. 848, vol. II of the Venice edition, 1748]. For what is as profound as Peter’s saying to the Lord: ‘You are Christ, the Son of the living God’? What is as earthly as what the Jews said about the Lord: ‘Is this not the son of Joseph the carpenter?’ . . . . Hence the Savior says to Peter: ‘Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.’ But to the Pharisees he says: ‘How can you speak good things when you are evil?’

> “Therefore the Lord ascended this ONE SHIP OF THE CHURCH, IN WHICH PETER HAS BEEN APPOINTED TEACHER, THE LORD SAYING: ‘Upon this rock I will build my Church.’ This ship sails upon the deep of this world in such a way that, although the world perishes, it preserves unharmed all whom it receives. We already see its figure in the Old Testament. For just as Noah’s ark, while the world was shipwrecked, preserved unharmed all whom it had received, so THE CHURCH OF PETER, WHEN THE WORLD IS CONSUMED BY FIRE, WILL PRESENT ALL WHOM IT EMBRACES UNHARMED . . . .

> “But since we read in Matthew that this same little ship of Peter, from which the Lord now draws the mysteries of his heavenly teaching, was disturbed while the Lord slept in it and the winds rose, so that all the apostles feared the danger of death, let us see what the reason is that one and the same little ship here gives instruction to the peoples in tranquility, while there it brings fear of death to the disciples in a storm—especially since Simon Peter was also there with the other apostles.

> “[CVIII] This, then, is the cause of the danger: Simon Peter was there, but the traitor Judas was there as well. For although Peter’s faith founded the little ship, Judas’s faithlessness nevertheless disturbed it. There is tranquility [Note: [Col. 0106] Saint Ambrose must be consulted, same place, no. 70, p. 848] where PETER ALONE SAILS; there is a storm where Judas is added . . . .

> “While the disciples were afraid and Peter was anxious, the Lord was sleeping. It may perhaps seem astonishing that, while Peter was anxious, the Lord was sleeping. He slept for Peter, lest he remain awake for Judas . . . . If all the apostles are endangered by the sin of one Judas, let us beware by this example; let us beware of the faithless man, beware of the traitor, lest through one we many be tossed upon the waves. Indeed, let us cast such a person out of the little ship, so that the Lord may not sleep but remain awake in us; and while he is awake, may no storm of spiritual wickedness shake us. For where faith is intact, there the Savior teaches, watches, and rejoices; there are rest, tranquility, and the healing of all. But where faithlessness has been mixed with faith, there Christ . . . sleeps; there are fear and storm, etc.”

That Maximus is speaking of the Catholic Church is beyond doubt. For he sets this Church against the Synagogue and says that it alone is the one which Christ entered. Moreover, that he calls this same Church both the ship and the Church of Peter is so clear from his words that I do not see how anyone who doubts it could fail to doubt whether there is a sun at all.

But why does he do so? Plainly, because Peter has been appointed teacher in it. From what, then, does he demonstrate Peter’s teaching authority? Clearly, from the fact that Christ said: “Upon this rock I will build my Church.”

Maximus teaches that the ship—or the Church of Peter, or the Church in which Peter has been appointed teacher, to whom it was therefore said, “Upon this rock I will build my Church”—preserves unharmed all whom it embraces, like Noah’s ark; and that those who are outside it perish, as though swallowed by the waters of the Flood.

The holy bishop adds that there is tranquility where Peter alone sails, but a storm where people resembling Judas are added. What else can this mean than that there is tranquility where those are found who agree with Peter concerning doctrine and piety, but a storm if there are any who dissent from Peter? For if there is rest where Peter is alone, how could there be a storm where there is complete agreement with Peter?

And since the rock upon which the Church was built is regarded as its foundation, Maximus therefore calls Peter the foundation of the Church in his *Chapters on the Gospels*, p. 778:

> “He was the shepherd of the Church, and moreover the shepherd of the flock. For Jesus says to him: ‘Feed my sheep.’ A disciple, and THE FOUNDATION OF THE CHURCH, and an apostle and martyr, he was crucified head downward at Rome.”

[CIX] That Peter himself is the rock of which Christ speaks when addressing Peter, Maximus likewise attests in homily 54, p. 169:

> “Like a good shepherd, he received THE FLOCK TO BE GUARDED, so that he who had previously been weak for himself might become A SUPPORT FOR ALL; and he who himself had wavered under the testing of interrogation might ESTABLISH THE OTHERS IN THE STABILITY OF FAITH.”

Finally, for the firmness of devotion he is called THE ROCK OF THE CHURCHES, as the Lord says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” He is called a rock because he first laid the foundations of faith among the nations, AND, LIKE AN IMMOVABLE STONE, SUSTAINS THE FRAMEWORK AND MASS OF THE WHOLE CHRISTIAN WORK.

Thus Peter, the shepherd of Christ’s sheep, and likewise the support of all and the rock of the Churches, established the others in the stability of faith, according to Maximus, so that, having been appointed the rock and, like an immovable stone, sustaining the framework and mass of the whole Christian work, he might fulfill this role.

Peter attained through devotion what Christ possesses through power. As the Apostle says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ.” He rightly merits a share in the name who merits A SHARE IN THE WORK as well, etc.

Maximus himself teaches in homily 53, p. 168, that Peter was called the shepherd of the sheep because he had received OTHERS TO GOVERN.

That Peter was appointed the rock because of his confession of Christ’s divinity, that he received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and that he obtained the power of judgment is the constant doctrine of Maximus, as of the other Fathers.

In homily 68, p. 17 and following, he says:

> “To show how great was the magnitude of Peter’s confession, the Savior said to him: ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’ . . . . This confession granted him that he should receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven before he entered through the gates of heaven . . . . The key of heaven is Peter’s tongue, because, judging the merits of individuals, the Apostle [Col. 0107] either closes or opens the kingdom of heaven to each person. This key, therefore, was not fashioned by the hand of a mortal craftsman; it is THE POWER OF JUDGING GIVEN BY CHRIST . . . . This is Peter, to whom Christ the Lord willingly granted a share in his own name. For just as, as the Apostle Paul taught, CHRIST WAS THE ROCK, so through Christ PETER WAS MADE A ROCK, the Lord saying to him [Note: [Col. 0107] See also homily 113, p. 375; Sermon 27, p. 467; and Sermon 37, p. 497 and following]: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.’ For just as, in the desert, water flowed from the rock for the Lord’s thirsty people, so, when the whole world was exhausted by drought, from Peter’s mouth there sprang a fountain of saving confession. This is Peter, to whom Christ, about to ascend to the Father, entrusted his little sheep and lambs to be fed, so that those whom he redeemed through the compassion of piety, Peter might PRESERVE THROUGH THE POWER OF HIS FAITH. And rightly did the Son of God, judge of hidden things, entrust sheep to be fed and guarded to him in whom he knew that neither zeal nor faith was lacking in nurturing the Lord’s flock.”

And in homily 70, p. 224, Maximus says that Peter, having been a fisherman, was made a teacher, and that Peter’s faith is the foundation of doctrine.

He adds on p. 225:

> [CX] “Of how great merit, therefore, was Peter before his God, that after the rowing of a little ship THE GOVERNANCE OF THE WHOLE CHURCH should be entrusted to him? . . . . What shall I say of Peter, whose righteousness was approved by God as so great, and to whom such POWER OF JUDGING was granted, that heavenly judgment was placed in his authority? Consider, then, and assess with what honor the Apostle Peter must be revered by us, WHOSE SENTENCE PRONOUNCED ON EARTH THE EQUITY OF ETERNAL JUDGMENT DOES NOT REJECT. And therefore attend carefully to the greatness of his glory: when THE KEYS OF THE ETERNAL KINGDOM are entrusted to him, he is permitted to close and open heaven.”

Moreover, in homily 72, p. 231, discussing Peter and Paul, he says:

> “Both received keys from the Lord: THIS ONE [Paul] OF KNOWLEDGE, THAT ONE [Peter] OF POWER . . . . Therefore the blessed Peter and Paul stand out among all the apostles and surpass them by a particular prerogative.”

See also homily 107, p. 354, where he says:

> “The most blessed Peter was fulfilling the work of goodness and discipline, both caring for the sick who were brought to him like a truly good physician and, AS THE FOUNDER OF HEAVENLY DISCIPLINE, punishing liars with just retribution”—namely, Ananias and Sapphira.

And Sermon 37, p. 498, where he calls Peter the foremost of the apostles.

And Sermon 66, p. 567 and following, where he says:

> “To Peter he gave the keys of his kingdom; to Paul, the wisdom of the word.”

Nor is this incredible, since the one who brought forth water from the rock FOUNDED THE CHURCH IN PETER . . . . Paul enters heaven for the sake of teaching; Peter receives the power to open heaven by reason of his simplicity.

Finally, in Sermon 69, p. 577 and following, Maximus again speaks of Peter and Paul:

> “We have often said that Peter himself was called ROCK by the Lord, as he himself says: ‘You are Peter,’ etc. If, then, Peter IS THE ROCK UPON WHICH THE CHURCH IS BUILT, he rightly first heals the feet of the lame, so that, just as HE CONTAINS THE FOUNDATION OF FAITH IN THE CHURCH, he may also strengthen the foundations of the limbs in a human being . . . . Paul was named by the Lord a chosen vessel . . . . The excellent names of the apostles are ‘rock’ and ‘vessel,’ both necessary to the Savior’s household. A house is built through the strength of rocks and adorned through the usefulness of vessels. THE ROCK supports peoples in firmness, so that they may not fall; the vessel covers Christians for protection, so that they may not be tempted.”

What Maximus writes concerning the power of judgment divinely conferred upon Peter, the keys, the authority to bind and loose, Peter’s primacy, and Peter himself as the rock, pillar, and foundation of the Church’s doctrine or faith is plainly coherent and consistent with what was said in the ecumenical Council of Ephesus, with no Father dissenting, session 3, vol. I of the *Councils*, Paris edition, 1714, p. 1478:

> “No one doubts—indeed, it has been known in every age—that the holy, most blessed Peter, prince and head of the apostles, pillar of the faith and foundation of the Catholic Church, received the keys of the kingdom from our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior and Redeemer of the human race, [CXI] and that the power of binding and loosing was given to him. He lives to this time and forever in his successors, καὶ δικάζει—‘and judges,’ or exercises judgment.”

And session 2, p. 1471:

> “Your Blessedness is not unaware that the blessed Apostle Peter is the head of the whole faith, or even of the apostles.”

The same doctrine, drawn from the Gospel, was held by all the Fathers from the beginning. Our writers have shown and demonstrated it so truly and clearly that our discourse need not demonstrate it again here. Meanwhile, Mamachi may be consulted, vol. V, part 1 of *Christian Antiquities*, p. 92 and following, p. 131 and following, p. 286 and following, and p. 405 and following.

Again, what Maximus committed to writing concerning Peter, to whom the governance of the whole Church was entrusted and who received the key of power, while Paul received the key of knowledge, wonderfully agrees with the doctrine of the ancients. They not only wrote these same things but also represented them in bronze monuments.

There is preserved in the museum of the archduke, the Grand Duke of Florence, a notable bronze cemetery lamp which bears the form of a ship. It shows Peter seated at the stern and directing the rudder, while Paul stands at the prow preaching. Mamachi discussed this lamp, after the others whom he names, in vol. III of *Christian Antiquities*, p. 99 and following, and vol. V, p. 291 and following.

It would be a long undertaking to visit all the Fathers whose sequence Mamachi presents in vol. V, p. 410 and following. I shall mention only a very few, whose opinion on this matter was so widely and consistently disseminated that in the fifth century Boniface I affirmed what he knew to be approved by everyone:

> “In Peter the governance and supreme authority of the universal Church stand established.”

This is in Letter 14, p. 1037, vol. I of Coustant’s *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*.

Prudentius, in the book *On the Crowns*, hymn 2, which concerns Saint Lawrence, verses 460 and following, writes of Peter and Paul:

> Here indeed now reign the two  
> Princes of the apostles;  
> One is called the apostle of the nations,  
> [Col. 0109] The other, possessing the first chair,  
> Unlocks the entrusted gates  
> Of eternity.

Arator, moreover, a sixth-century writer, sings of Peter in book 1 of the *Apostolic History*, p. 126, vol. X of the Lyon edition of the *Library of the Fathers*:

> First called from a little boat  
> To the apostolic band was Peter, whose hand, having plied the hook,  
> Was transferred to the key . . . to whom the Lamb entrusted  
> The sheep whom he saved through suffering; throughout the whole world  
> He increases this flock through this shepherd, by which office he rises supreme, etc.

Moreover, what Maximus teaches—that the one who, through the ministry of Moses, brought water from the rock in the desert founded the Church in Peter, from whose mouth [CXII] a fountain of saving confession emerged—was so familiar in the speech of our ancestors and so long established and widespread that they not only compared Peter with Moses, as Jerome did in Letter 95 to the monk Rusticus, p. 772, vol. IV, part II of the Paris edition of his works by Martianay, and said that this same Peter had been flooded with such abundant streams from the very fountain of spiritual gifts [Note: [Col. 0109] See Saint Leo, Sermon 3, chapter 2, p. 8, vol. I of his works, Rome edition, 1753], that, although he alone received many things, nothing passed to anyone without his participation . . . . and although there are many priests and many shepherds among the people of God, Peter nevertheless properly governs them all, whom Christ principally governs, etc.; they even represented this same Peter in the cemetery glass vessels in the likeness of Moses, the leader of the Hebrews, bringing water out of the rock. Compare Mamachi, vol. V of *Christian Antiquities*, p. 296.

Finally, what Maximus proposed and explained concerning the keys bestowed upon Peter by Christ, and concerning the foundation of the doctrine of faith which Peter himself contains by Christ’s favor, was not only transmitted and defended by the other Fathers but also recorded and engraved in monuments. This is evident both from the testimonies of those Fathers collected and reported in commentaries by Sander, Bellarmine, Mauclerc, and others, and more recently by Mamachi [Note: [Col. 0109] Vol. V, part I of *Christian Antiquities*, p. 533 and following, and p. 536 and following], and from the silver vessel and the sarcophagi of the ancient Christians discovered in the cemeteries. In these one sees a representation of the Savior handing keys and a book to the prince of the apostles.

Concerning this vessel, compare what was written after Bottari by Mamachi in the same vol. V, part I, p. 518 and following. Concerning the sarcophagi, paintings, mosaics, and so forth, consult what he collected in the same work, p. 297 and p. 519, and vol. I, p. 282.

### XXXI

Why Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom at Rome, Maximus explains in Homily 69, p. 221 ff., where he says:

“These are the most blessed Peter and Paul, who, preaching with one spirit the mystery of the heavenly kingdom, consecrated their teaching with devout blood and a most courageous death on a single day of suffering. Having also been made princes of all the Churches, they went to Rome by heavenly dispensation and laid their most sacred bodies in the citadel of that city, which had obtained supremacy over the whole world, so that Christ, displaying the power of his might, might place the princes of his kingdom where the world had its imperial capital.”

And in Homily 72, p. 231:

“Peter and Paul stand out among all the apostles and surpass them by a certain special prerogative. Yet among the two of them it is uncertain which should be placed before the other. For I think that they are equal in merits, because they are equal in suffering, and that they lived with a similar devotion to the faith, since we see them reach the glory of martyrdom together. We should not think that it happened without reason that, on one day, in one place, they endured the sentence of one tyrant. They suffered on one day so that they might reach Christ together; in one place, so that Rome might not be lacking to either; under one persecutor, so that equal cruelty might constrain both. The day, therefore, I think, was determined by merit, the place by glory, and the persecutor by virtue.

“But in what place, finally, did they suffer martyrdom? In the city of Rome, which holds the primacy and is the capital of the nations—that is, so that where the capital of superstition had been, there the capital of holiness might rest; and where the princes of the Gentiles dwelt, there the princes of the Churches might remain.”

What he wrote in Homily 73, p. 236, does not differ. Entirely consistent with these statements are those gathered by Saint Leo the Great in Sermon 82, otherwise 80, chapter 4, pp. 235 ff. of the Roman edition of 1753. They are as follows:

“Therefore, blessed apostle Peter, you do not fear coming to this city, and, together with the apostle Paul, your companion in glory, who was still occupied with the organization of other Churches, you enter this forest of roaring beasts and this ocean of the most turbulent depths, with greater steadfastness than when you walked upon the sea. Nor do you fear Rome, mistress of the world. . . . You had already instructed the peoples who had believed from the circumcision. . . . You had already filled Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia with the laws of evangelical preaching; and, without doubting the progress of your work . . . you were bringing the trophy of Christ’s cross into the Roman citadel, where the honor of authority and the glory of suffering had preceded you through divine preaching.”

Chapter 6, p. 237:

“To this city your blessed fellow apostle, the chosen vessel, Paul, came to meet you. He was associated with you at the same time when every innocence, every modesty, and every freedom was suffering under Nero’s rule. . . . In the excellence of these Fathers we ought rightly to rejoice with greater exultation, for God’s grace raised them among all the members of the Church to such a height that, in the body whose head is Christ, he established them as though they were a double light for the eyes. Concerning their merits and virtues, which surpass the ability of all speech, we ought to think nothing different or distinct, because election made them equal, labor similar, and their end equal.”

When Leo and Maximus proclaim that Peter and Paul were equal, similar, and alike, so that it cannot be determined which should be placed before the other, this is to be understood not of the dignity and authority in which both acknowledge Peter to have been superior to Paul, but of their marvelous election, virtue, merit, and glory of martyrdom. This is perfectly clear from the very sequence of the words of both holy bishops. Each of them indeed mentions merit, virtue, and martyrdom; but when he mentions greater dignity and authority, he does so in such a way that he attributes these to Peter and not likewise to Paul.

Concerning Peter, Maximus wrote certain things that indicate that they do not apply in the same way to Paul:

“This is Peter,” he says, “to whom Christ the Lord willingly granted a share in his own name. For just as Christ was the rock, so through Christ Peter was made a rock. . . . This is Peter, to whom Christ, as he was about to ascend to the Father, entrusted his lambs and sheep to be fed.”[Note: Homily 68, pp. 217 ff.]

Again concerning Peter:

“To him,” he says, “after the rowing of a small boat, the governance of the whole Church is entrusted.”[Note: Homily 70, p. 225.]

Then, comparing Paul with Peter and describing what is special and proper to each of them, he writes:[Note: p. 226.]

“What is more magnificent than this apostle [Paul], to whom, while he was established among mortals, it was granted to go above the heavens and permitted to return to earth? What is more blessed than this man, who deserved to learn among the secrets of paradise what no human tongue could express and no one could deserve to hear? . . . What, moreover, shall I say about Peter, to whom such great power of judging was assigned that heavenly judgment was placed within his discretion? . . . Consider carefully the greatness of his glory: when the keys of the eternal kingdom are entrusted to him, he is permitted to close and open heaven.”

But, not to prolong the discussion, it will be enough to recall what the same Maximus teaches in Homily 72, pp. 230 ff.:

“To Peter, as to a good steward, he gave the key of the heavenly kingdom.”[Note: Sermon 66, p. 567: “He gave Peter indeed the keys of his kingdom, and Paul the word of wisdom. Nor is this incredible, since he who brought water from the rock founded the Church on Peter. . . .”] “To Paul, as to a suitable teacher, he entrusted the instruction of ecclesiastical formation—namely,” so that those whom the one had instructed for salvation, the other might receive into rest; so that for the souls whose hearts Paul had opened through the teaching of his words, Peter might open the kingdoms of heaven.

“For in a certain manner Paul too received from Christ the key of knowledge. . . .”[Note: Maximus indicates the sacrament of penance in the same place when, speaking of the key, he says: “It must be called a key by which the hardened hearts of sinners are unlocked for faith, the secrets of minds are disclosed, and whatever is held shut within is brought into the open by rational manifestation. I mean a key which both opens the conscience to confession of sin and encloses grace for the eternity of the saving mystery.”]

“Both received keys from the Lord: the one of knowledge, the other of power.”[Note: Homily 70, p. 224: “He says that Paul’s teaching is the fullness of faith, and Peter’s belief is the foundation of doctrine.”] “The one distributes the riches of immortality; the other bestows the treasures of knowledge.”

Compare what I said above about Peter as chief of the apostles, using Maximus as my authority.

Concerning Leo, take the following. In Sermon 2, p. 6, he says:

“The disposition of truth remains, and blessed Peter, persevering in the strength he received as the rock, does not abandon the governance of the Church entrusted to him. For he was appointed before the others in such a way that, since he is called the rock, since he is pronounced the foundation, since he is established as the doorkeeper of the kingdom of heaven and as the arbiter of binding and loosing, he is also placed in charge of judgments whose decisions will remain even in heaven, so that through the very mysteries of his titles we might recognize what kind of fellowship he had with Christ.”

And in Sermon 3, chapter 2, pp. 8 ff.:

“From the whole world one Peter is chosen, and he is both placed before the calling of all the nations and set above all the apostles, so that although there are many priests and many shepherds among God’s people, Peter nevertheless properly governs all those whom Christ principally governs. The divine condescension granted this man a great and marvelous participation in its power; and if it wished something to be common to the other princes together with him, it never granted anything to the others that it had not given through him. . . .

“For this reason it is said to blessed Peter: ‘I will give you the keys,’ etc. The right of this power did indeed pass also to the other apostles, and the ordinance of this decree extended to all the leaders of the Church; but it was not without reason that what was announced to all was entrusted to one. For this was singularly committed to Peter because Peter’s form is set before all the rulers of the Church.

“Peter’s privilege therefore remains wherever judgment is rendered according to his equity. There is neither excessive severity nor excessive leniency when nothing will be bound or loosed except what blessed Peter has either loosed or bound.”

There are some who, contrary to Maximus, who followed most of the ancients, deny that Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom in the same year. I see, however, no reason why their authority should be accepted. On this matter one may consult Pagius under the year 67, no. 3, and Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Historical Memoirs*, *Life of Saint Peter*, note 40. It is unnecessary to mention more. On the day and place of the martyrdom of these same apostles, compare what Tillemont observes in the same work, notes 43 and 44.

What Maximus adds in Homily 72, p. 232—that Simon Magus, lifted into the air by his magical tricks, was cast down and driven headlong through the prayers of blessed Peter, and that Nero therefore raged against the holy apostles—is also recorded in the memory of other ancient writers, whom Tillemont mentions in the thirty-fourth article of the *Life of Saint Peter*.

Finally, concerning the milk and blood said by Maximus to have flowed from the severed head of Saint Paul, I find that no ancient historian whose testimony ordinarily carries faith and authority has commended this account in writing. Tillemont is to be consulted in note 80 to the *Life of Saint Paul*.

### XXXII

That Saint Lawrence served as deacon in the see of the most glorious Peter is attested by Maximus in Homily 74, p. 237. For where some manuscripts read “of Peter the patriarch,” this is erroneous, as the matter itself makes clear. What if Homily 75, p. 239, says: “When the venerable Sixtus was exercising the priesthood of the apostolic see”? A little later he calls this same Sixtus the supreme priest of the Lord:

“Before all others, the pagan fury attacked Xystus, the supreme priest of the Lord, so that, after the ecclesiastical members had been deprived of so powerful a head—as though the protection of heavenly defense had been removed—the bloody persecutor might invade them.”

To call the supreme priest of the Lord, by antonomasia [Greek: ἀντονομασία, substitution of a title or descriptive name], the man who occupies Peter’s Roman apostolic see and is universally the head of the ecclesiastical members—what is this other than to acknowledge the Roman bishop as the head of all Christians? For while he sits at the helm of the ship, or in Peter’s chair, he also governs Peter’s ship—that is, as we have seen Maximus state, the Catholic Church.

Indeed, according to Maximus, the Lord alone entered the ship of the Church:

“He entered the one ship of the Church, in which Peter has been appointed teacher, when the Lord said: ‘Upon this rock I will build my Church.’ This ship floats upon the deep of this age in such a way that, while the world perishes, it preserves unharmed all whom it receives. In this ship there is tranquility, where Peter alone sails.”[Note: Sermon 94, pp. 640 ff.]

To this Peter, certainly, the governance of the whole Church was entrusted by Christ.[Note: Homily 70, p. 225.]

That Maximus both recognized and confessed this dignity and authority in the Roman pontiff is clear from the acts of the Roman council held under Pope Hilary in the year 465. For when the letter of Ascanio, bishop of Tarragona, and of the other bishops of that province addressed to Pope Hilary had been read, it contained the following:

“Even if no necessity of ecclesiastical discipline existed, we ought truly to have desired that privilege of your see by which, after receiving the keys of the kingdom, the singular preaching of the most blessed Peter, after the Savior’s resurrection, provided illumination for all the world. The primacy of whose vicar, just as it is eminent, is therefore to be feared by all and loved.

“Accordingly, adoring God completely in you, whom you serve blamelessly, we have recourse to the faith praised by the apostolic mouth, seeking answers from the place where nothing is commanded through error, nothing through presumption, but only through pontifical deliberation.

“Since these things stand thus, there is nevertheless among us a false brother whose presumption, just as it was not permissible for us to remain silent about it longer, so the necessity of the judgment to come has compelled us to disclose. . . .

“Therefore, because these presumptions, which divide unity, must be opposed quickly, we ask your see that we may be instructed by apostolic words concerning what you wish to be observed in this matter, so that, supported by your authority, we may, with God’s help, understand what ought to be done.

“Your triumph will surely be achieved if, in the days of your apostolate, the Catholic Church hears what the chair of Saint Peter possesses, and if the new seeds of tares have been uprooted.”

When this letter—which demonstrates how great the dignity and authority of the Roman pontiff are—had been read,[Note: *Roman Synod*, vol. II of the *Councils*, Paris edition, 1714, p. 802.] and all the bishops present had unanimously shouted, “Let the apostolic ordinance be preserved inviolate,” Maximus, bishop of the Church of Turin, said:

“In preserving all the disciplines that pertain to sacred ordinations, I declare more effectively by professing my judgment that I shall never do any of those things which are forbidden. Concerning the remaining matters, I judge that whoever does such things, or refuses to remove from the Churches what has been discovered there, will have to render grave accounts before the judgment of the apostolic see, where he must undergo its sentence.”

When the same judgment had been confirmed by the bishops of Embrun, Aquaviva, Atella, and Salpi, and the bishop of Sabina, Tiberius, had added, “I profess that I observe in all things the statutes of the apostolic see,” all the bishops, and therefore Maximus also, said:

“We all follow the judgments of the brethren. . . . Hear us, O Christ. May Hilary live. . . . Through you let what has been wrongly admitted be corrected.”

Moreover, when another letter of the bishops of the province of Tarragona had been read, in which they asked the most blessed Father Hilary, whom they revered in Christ with apostolic reverence, to strengthen by his authority the decree of the synod of Tarragona,[Note: *Ibid.*, p. 801. The same bishops of Tarragona added: “We humbly beseech your apostolate to confirm by your authority the decree of our humility, which appears to have been justly made by us.”] all the bishops, and therefore Maximus also, acclaimed:

“Hear us, O Christ. May Hilary live. . . . Through the Lord Peter we ask that these things be preserved forever. . . . We ask that these things be preserved.”

Finally, when Pope Hilary had said in the synod that no one might, without endangering his own standing, rashly violate either the divine constitutions or the decrees of the apostolic see—for “we who administer the duties of the most eminent priest will be affected by the guilt of such transgressions if we are found negligent in the causes of God”—all the bishops, and consequently Maximus as well, acclaimed:

“We teach these things. These things must be held. These things must be preserved. We give thanks for your teaching,” and so forth.

From these statements everyone will recognize clearly enough how magnificently, and how suitably and appropriately to the teaching of the ancients and of Scripture, Maximus understood the excellence of the dignity and authority of the Roman pontiff.

Thus far concerning the Church, Peter as the head of the Church, and Peter’s successors, who hold the governance of that Church.

### XXXIII

Briefly, concerning the gatherings of Christians in sacred buildings and concerning common prayers.

Maximus calls temples the receptacles of the Church. Homily 94, which concerns the restoration of the Milanese basilica, p. 316:

“God did not command his Church—which truly is the Church—to be consumed by fire; rather, for our correction, he permitted the receptacles of the Church to be burned. For among the peoples no wise and faithful person is unaware that the city is in the people, and the Church is in the common people. Therefore, beloved, you present to our God not timbers and beams, but yourselves as a living Church. . . .

“Thus it is not now the Church that has been restored—for, under God’s protection, it did not perish—but these walls and roofs into which you, who are God’s Church, have been received. For you are, as the Apostle says, the temple of the living God. . . .

“Sometimes, for our fear, when God mercifully grows indignant with us, and heaven thunders with terrifying voices, sacred buildings are struck down by lightning,” and so forth.

He calls temples the receptacles of the Church because the faithful, who constitute the Church, were accustomed—and indeed ought—to gather there, to hold common stations, to pray, to attend the divine service, and to hear the word of God.

For this reason the holy teacher rebukes his sheep because, in his absence, they came only rarely to the sacred building, or divine house. Homily 112, p. 373:

“I have learned, brothers, that during my absence you come to the church so rarely, and proceed in such small numbers, as though, when I departed, you had departed together with me, and as though, when I am dragged away by necessities, necessity itself had dragged you away with me. . . .

“Do you not know that although I am absent from the church, Christ is not absent from his Church, which is everywhere? You come, brother, to the church and do not find there the Bishop of bishops, the Savior? For the Christian who comes to church only when the bishop is present seems to have come not so much for God’s sake as for a human being’s; nor does he appear to have fulfilled the duty of a God-fearing Christian, but rather the service of paying respect to a friend.”

Maximus was especially concerned that the assemblies, or synaxes, should be celebrated with a large attendance of the people, because, according to the consistent teaching of the ancients,[Note: See Saint Basil, Letter 150 to Amphilochius, no. 2, p. 240, vol. III of the Paris edition of the monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur; and Letter 97 to the Tyanaeans, p. 191: “If those who join together are absent, prayers are far weaker than they are in themselves.” And Letter 174 to the Widow, p. 262: “Join everyone to the communion of prayers; for great is the assistance of those who can appease God.” Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 3 to the Antiochene people, no. 2, p. 37, vol. II of Montfaucon’s Paris edition: “The communion of the Church has great power if we utter prayers with a grieving soul and a contrite heart.” The same author, Homily 3 *On the Incomprehensible Nature of God*, no. 1, p. 461, vol. I: “You can also pray at home; but you cannot pray in the same way as in the Church, where there is such a multitude of fathers and where a united cry is sent up to God. You will not be heard in the same way when you pray to God alone by yourself as when you pray with your brothers. Here there is something more: harmony, agreement, the bond of love, and the prayers of priests. For this reason priests preside, so that the weaker prayers of the multitude, joined with these stronger ones, may rise together with them into heaven,” and so forth. Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter 39: “We come together for the assembly and gather together so that, as though forming a united force, we may surround God with prayers. This force is pleasing to God,” and so forth.] common prayers contribute greatly, so that each person may obtain what he rightly seeks.

Thus he says in Homily 1, p. 6:

“What merit belongs to the one who gives, that one person should work alone in the house while the Lord is entreated by many in the Church? What that person perhaps would not dare to ask from the Godhead, he may receive through the prayers of many petitioners—even what he had not hoped for. Referring to our assistance, the blessed Apostle says: ‘So that thanksgiving may be offered for us by many.’ And again: ‘So that our offering may be acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit.’”

Maximus mentions the stations in Homily 40, p. 117. Stations were gatherings that were accustomed to take place during times of fasting.[Note: Tertullian, *On Fasting*, chapters 11, 13, and 14.]

That the word “station” indicated an assembly or congregation of Christ’s faithful has been shown quite explicitly by the holy bishops Cornelius and Cyprian, who were also martyrs: by the former in a letter included among Cyprian’s letters as no. 49, p. 93 of the Oxford edition of 1682, and by the latter in Letter 44, p. 85.[Note: The reason they were called “stations” may be understood from Tertullian’s book entitled *On Prayer*, chapter 14. The term was derived from the likeness of military stations; concerning these, consult, among others, Livy, book XXXVIII, chapter 25, and book XLV, chapter 33.]

But because Christians were accustomed to be at a station while they were fasting, it consequently came about that fasts themselves were called “stations” by some. Thus the ancient author of the book entitled *The Shepherd*, book III, Similitude 5, p. 231, vol. I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, London edition of 1746, when asking what a station is, answers that it is a fast.

Although others followed this way of speaking, Maximus also approved it. For in the passage just cited he says:

“I believe you have understood why, when I compared our present fasts with those encampments in which the people of Israel, positioned as though in battle formation, overcame King Pharaoh through daily labor and defended themselves from their enemies as though from certain camps by remaining at their stations. Thus, whoever among that marching company failed to complete the extent of the day’s station was either overtaken by Pharaoh or overrun by the wilderness.

“Therefore we too must complete with every effort the forty-day journey set before us and fortify ourselves, as though with certain camps, through the devotion of fasting. Our fasts are camps for us; they defend us from the devil’s assault. Finally, they are called stations because, by standing and remaining in them, we repel the enemies lying in ambush.

“Fasts are plainly camps for Christians; and if anyone strays from them, he is attacked by the spiritual Pharaoh,” and so forth.

The stations that Maximus calls by this name in this homily he calls “halting-places” in the preceding homily, Homily 39, p. 114.

### XXXIV

The principal fast of Christians is that which is observed before Easter. Since it is contained within a period of forty days, it was called Lent, and it continues constantly to be so called.

Concerning the origin of this fast, Saint Maximus writes in Homily 38 as follows:

“Previously, when proclaiming the devotion of the holy Lent, we brought forward examples from the sacred Scriptures by which we could demonstrate that this number of forty was not established by human beings, but consecrated by God; that it was not invented by earthly reflection, but commanded by heavenly majesty. Therefore, whoever passes beyond the established number by eating on a single day is accused not merely as a violator of one day, but condemned as a transgressor of the whole of Lent.

“Thus it is good for a person to fast this appointed number without difficulty and likewise obtain the sanctity of the whole of Lent. These are not so much the commands of priests as of God; and therefore the one who despises them does not despise a priest, but Christ, who speaks through his priest.

“Let us therefore see at what time the Lord enjoined this observance upon us. . . . The Lord himself exercised himself through this number of forty, not in order to gain progress himself, but to show the progress of our salvation. . . .

“After these forty days had been completed without interruption, the Lord did not arrange this fast because he was hungry; but the evangelist says that afterward he became hungry. . . . He was plainly hungry, and we cannot deny that he was hungry. For he hungered not for human food, but for salvation.”[Note: This is not intended to deny that Christ was truly hungry, but to indicate that he hungered for the salvation of human beings more than for food. Maximus writes something similar about Peter in Sermon 68, p. 574: “But I think that after prayer Peter hungered not for human food, but for salvation; and that he was afflicted not by bodily hunger, but by the poverty of believers.” Yet who would suppose that Peter was not truly hungry? Maximus observes that Peter hungered for what was especially in his heart, as though Peter had not hungered for food at all.]

And in Homily 39, pp. 113 ff.:

“We have said that the Lord Jesus Christ consecrated this number of fasting, and, receiving no food for continuous days and nights, made one single body of fasting. . . . He had many periods of time available to him, but one day of abstinence, showing us that we ought to fast this entire number so completely that, since we cannot encompass the whole of Lent in one solid and uninterrupted fast, we should at least celebrate it through daily fasts without interruption. Thus, if anyone omits a single day by abstaining, he violates the whole of Lent and, for the sake of a small amount of food, loses the fruit of great labor. . . .

“For it is not a light sin, brothers, for the faithful not to fast the Lent enjoined by the Lord and to dissolve consecrated fasts through the voracity of the belly. . . . What kind of Christian are you in your conscience when, while Christ is hungry for you, you dine? . . . Therefore, as I have said, it is not a light sin to violate the fast that has been enjoined.”

The same point is made in Homily 44, p. 134, and in Sermon 17, p. 442, where he says:

“Above all, let us preserve his commands, especially those concerning the fasts of Lent. Many people, although this most sacred number of fasting is enjoined upon them, violate the divinely appointed period by eating during the intervening weeks. They do not understand that by tasting food against the prohibition they are guilty of no lesser transgression than Adam, who ate against the command; but Christ’s Passion redeemed the transgressions of that man.”

But since Maximus repeatedly proclaims that sins are forgiven through the power of Christ’s Passion, as we shall see shortly, what does he mean by seeming to deny that transgressors will obtain forgiveness after Christ’s Passion? Maximus denies that another redemption will take place after the Passion; he does not deny that forgiveness of sins is granted through the power of Christ’s Passion, by which he redeemed us. Nevertheless, he holds that the person who transgresses after Christ’s Passion is more culpable, because he dared to sin against the one who shed his blood in order to redeem the human race.

In Sermon 18, p. 442, he says:

“Rightly ought we to preserve through fasts this number of forty days, which we read was consecrated by such examples, especially that of Christ.”

From the passages quoted thus far anyone can see that Maximus says that the Lenten fast is not a human institution but a command of heavenly majesty, or divinely established. He does not speak so narrowly and strictly as to say that it was established by God’s direct command; rather, he argues in such a way as to indicate that it was introduced by the command of the leaders of the Church in accordance with the example of Christ, who had fasted for the same number of days. In this way he says that it is not so much the command of priests as of God, so that the person who despises it does not despise a priest, but Christ, who speaks through his priest.

He does, however, teach that this kind of fasting must be observed and guarded with exceptionally diligent and severe care, because it was consecrated by the example of the Savior of the human race and, as is established from other sources, had always been reverently observed throughout the Christian world[Note: Hence Maximus writes in Sermon 26, p. 461, both that the Lenten fast is commanded by the example of Christ and that it was handed down by the authority of the ancients. He declares that those who do not fast during Lent sin because this is a fast enjoined by law. *Ibid.*, p. 462: “Not to fast during Lent is a sin. Those fasts [of fifty days] are voluntary; these are necessary. The former arise from personal choice; the latter from law. We are invited to the former; we are compelled to the latter.” Concerning the apostolic institution of the Lenten fast, see William Beveridge, book III of *Vindications of the Canon Law of the Primitive Church*, chapter 1 ff., vol. II of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 134, edition of 1722.] from the time of the apostles.

Moreover, there can be no doubt that in Maximus’s time the faithful were bound to abstain from eating meat during that forty-day interval.[Note: Maximus speaks universally and nowhere says that this was peculiar to only certain Churches.]

For in Sermon 18, p. 443, he says:

“During these days above all, let us be stirred to fulfill the Lord’s will, when the pleasure of the flesh is especially extinguished through abstinence. . . . There is also this great benefit during the days of Lent: while we abstain even from what is permitted, we are more and more admonished to avoid what is forbidden. For if we abstain from meat, which is permitted on other days; if we abstain from wine, which may be used in moderation; if, therefore, we avoid these things that are sometimes permitted, let us above all flee from sins, which are never permitted.”

Thus, if at other times everyone was permitted to eat meat, but during Lent this was not permitted, what follows except that the faithful of Christ were then bound by law, or command, not to eat meat?

The holy bishop does not write about wine in the same way as about meat. He does not say that wine was then forbidden; he says only: “which may be used in moderation.” Indeed, in Sermon 25, p. 457, he says that those who fast during Lent perhaps do not drink wine. The word “perhaps” sufficiently indicates that this was not prescribed by law.

Furthermore, it can clearly be understood from the same Sermon 25, p. 485, that during periods of fasting Christians came together at the church from the very first light of day, for the purpose of holding a station. Otherwise the holy teacher would not rebuke those who dared to act differently. He says:[Note: Compare also Sermon 26, p. 462, where he mentions those who gathered in the church to pray during times of fasting.]

“Do you think, brothers, that the person fasts who at first light does not keep vigil at the church, does not seek the holy places of the blessed martyrs, but rises, gathers his servants, arranges the nets, brings out the dogs, and searches through the glades and forests—who, I say, drags his servants along with him, perhaps more eager to come to the church,” and so forth.

Finally, it is understood from this same sermon, pp. 458 ff., that those who fasted were accustomed to take food in the evening, or when the sun was declining. Continuing to rebuke those who took excessive delight in hunting, Maximus says:

“Although, brother, if you are such a person, you return home in the evening, although you eat when the sun is already declining, you may appear to have refreshed yourself late, but you have not therefore fasted for the Lord; nor can it be thought that, while exercising your own pleasure, you have fulfilled the Lord’s will.”

### XXXV

Tertullian, in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3, p. 102 of the Venetian edition of his works, 1744, says:

“On Sunday we consider it unlawful to fast or to worship while kneeling. We enjoy the same exemption from Easter until Pentecost.”

Basil the Great records the same practice in the book he entitled *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27, no. 66, vol. III of the Paris edition of his works, 1730, and teaches that it has come down to us by tradition from the time of the apostles. He says:

“On this day”—that is, Sunday—“the Church teaches her children to complete their prayers standing, so that, through constant remembrance of that life which will never end, we may not neglect to prepare provisions for that departure. Indeed, the entire period of fifty days is a reminder of the resurrection that we await in the age to come. For that one first day, multiplied seven times, completes the seven sacred weeks of Pentecost. . . . On that day the customs of the Church have taught us to pray with our bodies upright, evidently reminding us—as though transferring our minds from present things to future things,” and so forth.

The same point is made by Jerome in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, p. 96, vol. II of the Leipzig edition of his works, 1684. But there is no time to mention all the Fathers and the acts of the synods on this subject.

I shall say this: Maximus mentioned this rite, which was still in force in the fifth century, in Homily 61, pp. 191 ff., where he says:

“Your holiness ought to know, brothers, how we observe this sacred day of Pentecost, or why the number of these fifty days is for us a continual and uninterrupted festival: throughout this period we neither prescribe fasts for observance nor bend our knees to entreat God, but, as we usually do on Sunday, we pray standing.”[Note: See also Saint Augustine, Letter to Januarius 55, otherwise 119, chapter 17, no. 32, p. 106, vol. II of the Antwerp edition, 1700; and the First Synod of Nicaea, canon 20, vol. I of the Paris edition of the *Councils*, 1714, p. 332.]

“And we celebrate the Lord’s resurrection in a festive manner. . . . Sunday is venerable and solemn for us because on it the Savior, like the rising sun, having dispersed the darkness of the underworld, shone forth with the light of the resurrection. For this reason the people of the world call that day ‘the day of the sun,’ because Christ, the sun of righteousness, illuminates it at his rising. Therefore the entire span of the fifty days is celebrated as an image of Sunday, and all these days are counted as Sundays.”

Subsequently, however, this practice was changed, and only the six days after Easter were kept as feast days, as is quite clearly evident from the Synod of Mâcon, held in 585, canon 2, pp. 460 ff., and from the Council in Trullo, held in 706, canon 66, p. 1686, vol. III of the Paris edition of the *Councils*, 1714, as well as from other ecclesiastical records.

### XXXVI

Moreover, Maximus reports that Christians were accustomed to assemble in a church in order to celebrate the anniversaries of the saints, especially of those whose city was the same and whose relics were preserved in that church. For he teaches that veneration and worship are to be offered to the saints, and that they are to be invoked because, through their intercession, they can be for us a singular protection. In Homily 81, p. 261 ff., which concerns the holy martyrs of Turin, Octavius, Adventus, and Solutor, he says:

> “Although we ought to celebrate with the utmost devotion the anniversary of all the holy martyrs, nevertheless the solemnity of those who shed their own blood in our homes must especially be observed by us with complete VENERATION. For although all the saints are everywhere and BENEFIT EVERYONE, nevertheless those who endured punishments for us INTERCEDE FOR US. For when a martyr suffers, he suffers not only for himself but also for his fellow citizens. He suffers for himself unto reward, for his fellow citizens unto example. He suffers for himself unto rest, for his fellow citizens unto salvation. From their example we have learned to believe in Christ; we have learned to seek eternal life through insults; we have learned not to fear death . . . ALL MARTYRS, THEREFORE, MUST BE MOST DEVOUTLY HONORED, but those whose relics we possess are especially TO BE VENERATED BY US. They assist us with their PRAYERS, but these also assist us by their SUFFERING . . . Therefore, brothers, LET US VENERATE IN THIS AGE those whom we may have as our defenders in the future,” and so forth.

And in Homily 118, p. 390, rebuking those who had neglected to attend the sacred rites on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, he says:

> “Tell me, if this sin ought not to be mourned: that you were then so forgetful of your salvation that you did not at all render HONOR to the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul . . . and did not wish to celebrate their ANNIVERSARY WITH US in the highest joy, nor to attend that heavenly banquet in which, amid such great rejoicing of the martyrs, the Lord himself supplied us with the substance of life. But do you wish to know of how many good things you have been deprived? Ask the brothers who were present with me at that time how refreshed they departed from the Lord’s table,” and so forth.

Therefore, brothers, whenever we celebrate the memory of the martyrs, we ought, without any hesitation and laying aside all the activities of this world, TO ASSEMBLE, and TO RENDER THEM HONOR, since by the outpouring of their blood they obtained salvation for us. Whoever honors the martyrs honors Christ also; and whoever despises the saints despises the Lord also.

And in Homily 77, which concerns the holy confessor Eusebius of Vercelli, p. 245:

> “Honoring the memories of the holy Fathers in devout assemblies, we marvel in them both at their personal merits and at the divine gifts bestowed upon them. They are VENERABLE to us because, having despised the light of the present life and scorned the torment of their bodies, they conquered the raging world for the love of God. So did this most blessed Father of ours: rising up with fervent spirit in defense of the indisputable divinity, he resisted the impieties of the Arians, pacified the churches of God with the serene tranquility of faith, and won eternal rewards for himself through manifold suffering . . . Truly and deservedly he is to be VENERATED by all posterity: following the solidity of the firmest rock, he triumphed over the enemies of Christ through the strength of wearied endurance.”

[Note: See also Sermon 77, p. 595 ff.; Sermon 78, p. 599; Sermon 81, p. 607; and Sermon 83, p. 611 ff.]

That the honor shown to the saints redounds to Christ is also asserted by Maximus in Homily 68, p. 216, concerning the holy apostles Peter and Paul. He says:

> “Honoring at annual solemnities the most glorious princes of the Christian faith, we venerate with the worship that is due the Lord and our God himself, who is the author of this faith. For the apostles are called *missi*—‘those who have been sent’—in the Latin language. Therefore, whoever honors those who have been sent plainly honors the one who sent them. For the dignity bestowed upon ministers is undoubtedly offered to the one whose ministers they are, as the Savior himself said to his disciples: ‘Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me.’ Truly blessed are the merits of the apostles, in whom Christ declares that he is both received and heard. Blessed likewise are those whose devotion, having been offered to the apostles, returns to Christ . . . Let us honor Peter and Paul, the most reverend Fathers of all the churches, with the most devoted zeal.”

And in Sermon 78, p. 599:

> “Whenever we celebrate the martyrdoms of the saints, we utter the praises of the Savior; and whenever we affirm their suffering, we proclaim the glory of Christ. For we do not admire what they suffered, but for whom they suffered. Therefore, it is not punishment that is praised, but faith that is honored. We magnify the martyrs not because they endured severe punishments, but because they endured those punishments for the sake of righteousness . . . Therefore the blessed martyrs must be held in the highest and most distinguished place because of their faith,” and so forth.

That the Fathers took care to bury the relics of the saints in churches, and that honor was shown to those relics, is a well-attested fact. Maximus teaches this in Sermon 68, p. 599, where he writes that they were placed beneath the altar:

> “What can be said to be more reverent, what more honorable, than to rest beneath that altar upon which sacrifice is celebrated to God, upon which offerings are made, and upon which the Lord is the priest? . . . Therefore the martyrs are rightly placed beneath the altar, because Christ is placed upon the altar . . . Accordingly, and as though by a certain fellowship, burial was decreed for the MARTYRS THERE, WHERE THE LORD’S DEATH IS CELEBRATED DAILY . . . Not without reason, I say, as though by a kind of fellowship, a tomb was established for THOSE WHO HAD BEEN SLAIN there where THE MEMBERS OF THE LORD’S SLAUGHTER are placed,” and so forth.

In Sermon 88, p. 627, he says:

> “I honor in the flesh of the martyr the scars received for the name of Christ. I honor the ashes consecrated by the confession of the Lord. I honor in the ashes the seeds of eternity. I honor the body that showed me how to love my God, that taught me, for God’s sake, not to fear death. Why should I not honor that body which even the demons reverence—those who afflicted it in punishment but glorify it in the tomb?”

Our people therefore took care that the bodies of their own dead should be buried near the relics of the saints. Maximus says the following in Homily 71, p. 263 ff.:

> “Our forefathers provided that we should join our bodies to the bones of the saints, so that, while Tartarus fears them, punishment might not touch us . . . And therefore, brothers, let us venerate in this age those whom we may have as our defenders in the future; and just as we are joined to THE BONES OF OUR PARENTS, so let us be joined to them by imitation of their faith. For we shall be unable to be separated from him himself if we are joined to them both in religion and in BODY.”

Who, then, can fail to understand that, from the time of Maximus onward, it had already become customary to bury the bodies of the faithful departed in churches? But enough has been said, in accordance with the testimony of Maximus, concerning the assemblies of Christians, their common prayers, churches, the relics of the saints, their veneration and worship, and the custom of burying the bodies of the faithful departed in churches.

Since mention was made shortly before of the holy martyrs of Turin, Octavius, Adventus, and Solutor, it does not seem out of place to state briefly who they were, at what time they suffered, and how great their public renown was.

Maximus declares that they were citizens of Turin, and his authority here must certainly be regarded as very weighty. In Homily 81, p. 261, he says:

> “Although, brothers, we ought to celebrate with the utmost devotion the anniversary of all the holy martyrs, nevertheless the solemnity of those who shed their own blood in our homes must especially be observed by us with complete veneration. For although all the saints are everywhere and benefit everyone, nevertheless those who endured punishments for us especially intercede for us. For when a martyr suffers, he suffers not only for himself but also for his FELLOW CITIZENS. He suffers for himself unto reward, for his FELLOW CITIZENS unto example,” and so forth.

That they shed their blood because they steadfastly confessed that they practiced the Christian religion is likewise affirmed for us by Maximus in the same passage:

> “From their example we have learned to believe in Christ; we have learned to seek eternal life through insults; we have learned not to fear death . . . The blessed martyrs, therefore . . . left us an example: by living well, an example of conduct; by enduring bravely, an example of suffering. For this reason the Lord wished martyrs to suffer in various places throughout the world, so that, as suitable witnesses, they might press upon us by a certain PRESENT EXAMPLE OF FAITH the confession they made, so that human frailty—which scarcely believes the Lord’s preaching after hearing it for a long time—might believe the martyrdom of the blessed through the present testimony of its eyes. ALL MARTYRS, therefore, must be most devoutly honored, but those whose relics we possess are especially to be venerated by us.”
