That they suffered martyrdom at Turin can plainly be inferred from the passages of Maximus just cited. For if this were not so, how could Maximus, addressing the citizens of Turin, say that they had shed their own blood in our homes, and so forth?

At what time they suffered, however, Maximus does not indicate, nor does it seem possible to establish the matter with sufficient certainty from the testimony of others. I am not unaware that they are commonly counted among the martyrs of the Theban Legion.

[Note: Compare Ruinart, note to the Acts of Saints Maurice and his Companions, under the year 286, no. 6, p. 240; *Acta martyrum sincera*, Verona edition, 1731; Tillemont, chapter on Saint Maurice, vol. IV, p. 175, and note 4, p. 64; *Monumenta historiae ecclesiasticae*, Brussels edition, 1732; the Bollandists, January 20, p. 252, and February 13, p. 657 ff.; Octavius Felix Baudissonius, *Oratio panegyrica*, a learned oration on the holy martyrs Octavius, Adventus, and Solutor, published in 1778; Francesco Antonio Zaccaria, vol. I of the *Dissertationes*, published in 1780; and P. de Rivaz, *Vindiciae passionis Thebaeorum militum*, Paris, 1779.]

I see no reason, however, to dissent from that view. But whether these same holy martyrs had enlisted in the army or had not done so, Maximus does not say; still less does he say that they belonged to the Theban Legion.

The Acts of their martyrdom, first published by Mombritius, are the foundation of the widely prevailing tradition on this subject. Yet those Acts are later than the time of Maximus. The author of the *Novalesian Chronicle*, published by Duchesne and Muratori, relates that they were written by William, bishop of Turin, who flourished at the beginning of the tenth century.

It is not, however, very probable that the people of Turin, who gloried in the patronage of such great martyrs, had for so long been without an account of their struggle for Christ. Therefore I do not oppose Enschenius when he says that William received these Acts from some more ancient record. Whether that record should be attributed to Victorinus, the bishop who in the year 494 restored the church dedicated to these martyrs, making it larger and more magnificent; or to some monk who served that same church, I do not trouble myself to determine.

I maintain this much: if these martyrs belonged to the Theban Legion, they died in the year 286, or at the latest around the year 297.

Finally, how great their public renown was is clear both from the homily of Maximus mentioned shortly before—

[Note: These are the words of Maximus, from which it can be understood with what diligence and devotion the people of Turin preserved the remains of those martyrs, and how confidently they relied upon their patronage: “Those whose relics we possess are especially to be venerated by us; with them we have familiarity, for they are always with us and dwell with us,” and so forth.]

—and also from the fact that the people of Turin formerly erected a church in their honor and shortly afterward took care to build a monastery as well.

Maximus treats in detail, in Sermons 81 and 82, p. 697 ff., of the holy martyrs Alexander, Martyrius, and Sisinnius, who suffered death for Christ in the village of Anaunia, in the diocese of Trent, in the year 397.

The holy Vigilius, bishop of Trent, relates at length with whose cruelty and for what reason violence was inflicted upon them in the letters he addressed, one to Simplician, bishop of Milan, and the other to John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople. The Bollandists had both letters printed, the first under May 29; they were also printed by those who published at Verona, in 1731, the genuine acts of the holy martyrs collected by Ruinart, p. 534 ff. The same martyrs are mentioned by Saint Gaudentius of Brescia, Saint Augustine, and Gennadius. See the note on the martyrdom of Sisinnius in Ruinart, ibid., p. 533.

Maximus’s Sermon 84, p. 615 ff., concerns the holy martyrs of Aquileia, Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla. How much honor and praise antiquity attributed to them can be understood from the poems of Venantius Fortunatus. Compare Baronius, note in the *Roman Martyrology* under May 31.

### XXXVII

Since it has been demonstrated what Maximus’s teaching contains concerning communion in the sacraments and in the sacred prayers of the Catholic Church, it follows that I should explain how correctly he also thought about the remission of sins.

Thus, in Homily 83, p. 272, he says:

> “The remission of sins must be believed above all, brothers, because this alone is the remedy that releases the human race from the sentence of everlasting death. Therefore the Only-Begotten of the Most High deigned to assume flesh and embraced the cross, so that he might make you innocent through pardon—you who were unable to escape your crimes and sins. Therefore the spotless Lamb was slain, so that by his blood the stain of the human race might be wiped away. See, brothers, the depth of the mystery; see the height of the sacrament, where death restored life and the filth of sinners was washed away by the blood of the innocent. This remission does not nourish you in sin, but warns you to fear sin now, since you understand that you could not have been saved without pardon. For the goodness of God, through the gift of his mercy, does not arm us for guilt but cleanses us for glory.”

That there is in the Church, by the gift of Christ the Savior, a true power to remit sins, Maximus demonstrates in Homily 68, p. 219. Discussing the apostle Peter, he says:

> “The tongue of Peter is the key of heaven, because, judging the merits of individuals, the Apostle either closes or opens the kingdom of heaven to each person. This key, therefore, is not fashioned by the hand of a mortal craftsman; it is the power of judgment given by Christ. Finally, he says to them: ‘Whose sins you forgive are forgiven, and whose sins you retain are retained.’”

And in Homily 72, p. 230:

> “Christ gave Peter, as a good steward, the key of the heavenly kingdom . . . It must be called a key by which hardened hearts of sinners are opened to faith, the secrets of minds are disclosed, and whatever is held closed within is brought forth into public view by rational revelation—a key, I say, which both opens the conscience to confession of sin and encloses grace within the mystery of salvation unto eternity.”

And in Sermon 51, p. 531:

> “Who except the truly omnipotent God could have accomplished these things, so that savage minds might learn religious holiness and barbarous speech might receive heavenly teaching? Let us therefore venerate with divine worship this Spirit, who possesses the full power of regeneration and the authority to forgive sins, as the Lord instructs his disciples when he says: ‘Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’; and elsewhere: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive are forgiven, and whose sins you retain are retained.’”

From these passages of the holy bishop it is perfectly clear that the power of forgiving sins was granted by Christ not to all Christians, but only to the apostles and disciples, and consequently to bishops and priests.

### XXXVIII

It remains for us to see how appropriately Maximus formulated his teaching concerning the resurrection of the flesh in accordance with sacred Scripture and the teaching of the other Fathers.

In Homily 83, p. 273, he says:

> “Who, believing in God, could doubt the resurrection?”

[Note: On this passage, see annotation 2, p. 276.]

And in Sermon 32, p. 482 ff.:

> “If Christ has risen, our hope, who, brothers, could fail to believe that he too will rise? If we believe that he returned from the dead, why should we doubt that we too will rise, when the blessed Apostle says: ‘For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised’? Since Christ, therefore, has risen, the dead also will be raised. Because the Lord has risen, even his servants will live again. For, as the same Apostle says, he is the firstborn from the dead.”

These statements plainly agree with what he writes in Treatise 3 *On Baptism*, p. 719.

Although these matters, like nearly everything else, were treated and explained excellently by Maximus, it nevertheless often happens that men of the greatest intellectual penetration and learning fall into opinions that are not only false but sometimes strongly conflict with one another. No one should therefore be surprised that the holy bishop occasionally let fall something that seems less consistent with the teaching of the other Fathers and with the testimonies of Scripture.

An example of this is what he presents in Sermon 86, p. 620, as a matter worthy of belief: that certain saints rise each year on the solemn day of Easter. This is so only if that sermon is to be attributed to Maximus—a point which, as I understand, some deny or at least doubt, as we observed in the note on that same sermon.

Nor is the statement contained in that sermon concerning Saint John the Evangelist dissimilar: that, when the doors of the tomb had been closed, he was removed by the grace of the resurrection, so that his burial might be established but he might not be found buried.

[Note: These ideas are repeated in the writings of Ephrem, which Photius reports in the *Bibliotheca*, codex 299, p. 797.]

Who, then, can fail to see plainly that these notions are foreign to the judgment of the other Fathers and have been excerpted from the sort of books that Saint Augustine and Saint Gelasius rejected as apocryphal?

[Note: Saint Augustine, Treatise, chapter 24, on John, no. 2, p. 597, vol. III, part II, Antwerp edition, 1700.]

[Note: See the acts of the Roman synod of 494, chapter 11, vol. II of the *Councils*, p. 940, Paris edition, 1714.]

### XXXIX

Finally, I shall briefly complete what Maximus embraced concerning eternal life.

In Sermon 32, p. 484, he says:

> “We must hope in the Lord in FUTURE LIFE.”

He rightly says that the Apostle taught: “Hope that is seen is not hope.” Therefore we must hope in eternal life.

And in Sermon 37, p. 493:

> “The days on which we are reborn for eternal life are better than those on which we are brought forth in this temporal life, since the gifts of grace are greater than those of nature . . . By our first birth we enter earthly things; by our second we are prepared for heavenly things.”

The same point is made in Homily 88, p. 293; Sermon 18, p. 441; Sermon 67, p. 569 ff.; and Homily 89, p. 98. There, after warning Christians to refer everything to the glory of God, in keeping with the Apostle’s earlier words, he says:

> “Therefore, when we rise, we ought to give thanks to God and perform every work of the day under the sign of the Savior . . . Whoever begins to sow under this sign will obtain the fruit of ETERNAL LIFE. Whoever undertakes to travel under this sign will reach heaven. In this name, therefore, all our actions must be directed, and the whole movement of our life must be referred to him.”

That good works are required for our preparation for eternal life is likewise taught by Maximus in Homily 63, p. 201 ff. From this anyone can easily understand how greatly that recent writer is mistaken who thought that the holy bishop held otherwise; I remember having discussed that writer above, p. LXXVI.

These are the words of the holy bishop:

> “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of the flesh, so that we may deserve to receive the Holy Spirit. If we leave this world, we shall receive a Paraclete like the apostles, that is, the Spirit of truth, whom the Father will send to us. For there is no partiality with God the Father, but the promises already made to the apostles benefit us IF WE PERFORM THE WORKS, DESIRES, AND ACTIONS that the apostles performed. But if, by fulfilling his commandments, we complete the law of the Lord, which is spotless and converts souls, we commit ourselves, through the grace of Christ, as heirs of the Lord and co-heirs of Christ to an eternal inheritance and to dwelling with the angels—may he himself grant this, who lives and reigns forever and ever.”

And in Sermon 41, p. 508:

> “Let us put away every leaven of iniquity, so that we may truly share in this joy to which the mountains and hills are summoned by the prophetic voice through the Holy Spirit, and to which heaven and earth are invited. For who is so dull in understanding, who is so blinded in darkened mind with eyes sunk into the earth, that he would not celebrate with all rejoicing these vows of the whole world, in which the remission of sins, the grace of regeneration, the mystery of redemption, the glory of resurrection, and the hope OF ETERNITY smile upon us?”

And in Sermon 38, p. 502:

> “WE SHALL HOLD AND POSSESS HIS GIFTS OF GLORY if faith fortifies our life and LIFE DOES NOT DEPART FROM FAITH. And just as he [Christ] wished to please us by dying, so let us STRIVE NOT TO DISPLEASE HIM BY LIVING, he himself granting this,” and so forth.

Finally, Maximus establishes that eternal life consists chiefly in the vision of God, in Sermon 47, p. 520:

> “Ascending, Christ gave gifts to human beings, so that, instructed in faith and raised to manly strength, they would no longer desire his temporal vision, but would strive with the whole intensity of their soul to follow him wherever he had gone before them. Therefore, since we have been deprived of his temporal presence, LET US HASTEN WITH OUR WHOLE ATTENTION TO HIS ETERNAL VISION, and with the Psalmist let us say to him: ‘My heart has said to you, I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I shall seek; do not turn your face away from me.’ For THE WHOLE MOST HOLY ECONOMY OF CHRIST’S HUMANITY intends and requires nothing else than to direct us toward heavenly things, so that, when the time of our mortality has been completed, he may lead us to the manifest vision of himself and satisfy us with the eternal glory of his face, as the Apostle testifies: ‘Then we shall see him as he is’; and as the Psalmist says: ‘I shall be satisfied when he appears.’ We shall enjoy forever those goods which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—those which God has prepared for those who love him.

“These goods that holy David contemplated with wonder, insofar as it was possible in an enigma, when he said: ‘What have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?’ For he was unable either to explain in words or sufficiently to comprehend in thought the greatness of heavenly glory.

“Let us therefore not merely hunger for these things, but also thirst for them, because for this purpose the high priest, our forerunner, ascended on our behalf into the Holy of Holies and sits at the right hand of his Father, to confirm our hope by the example of his members and to show that the lowliness of the entire flock will one day follow where it believes its shepherd has gone before . . .

“The hunger of the eagles signifies the longing of holy souls: sensing with the nostrils of faith the head . . . they would wish, on the wings of their sweetest hope, to stand in the presence of their Creator and rejoice in the satisfaction of his face . . .

“Let us believe that he reigns at the right hand of his Father, and let us always strive toward him as though on the twin wings of virtue, charity and hope, so that . . . we too may be able to reign with him in ETERNAL LIFE.”

But enough concerning the teaching of Maximus. Concerning it I seem truly able to say what the bishops of the province of Milan once said, though in another context: that it shone forth, gleamed with the full simplicity of faith, radiated a certain brilliance of light and truth through the assertions of the prophets, the authority of the Gospels, and the testimonies of apostolic teaching, and agreed with all the teachings that blessed Ambrose, aroused by the Holy Spirit, inserted in his books.

Letter to Saint Leo the Great, vol. II of the works of that same Saint Leo, p. 280, Rome edition, 1755.

## A Commentary on the Life of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin

### I. The homeland, lineage, and parents of Saint Maximus

What the homeland, lineage, and parents of Saint Maximus were is unknown to us, and the matter lies shrouded in the darkness of antiquity.

There are those who think that he was an Etruscan, noble by birth, born to a father named Quintianus, and the brother of Saint Leo I, supreme pontiff, and of the holy martyr Justus. But this opinion rests upon grave errors. For it depends upon the single testimony of a monk of Novalesa.

[Note: Compare the Bollandists, vol. V, June 25, p. 50 ff.]

That monk lived in the thirteenth century, or perhaps even later, and delighted in old women’s tales. In any case, no surviving monument is older than that monk’s composition in which anything of this kind is read. Nor, even if such a monument existed, could the story be reconciled with the history of Saint Justus, the monk of Novalesa, whom we know to have suffered martyrdom more than four hundred years after the time of Maximus.

Whether Saint Leo was an Etruscan or a Roman is uncertain; whether he had a brother named Maximus seems to us much more uncertain still.

There have therefore been other men distinguished for learning and birth, some of whom maintained that Maximus was born, raised, and educated at Vercelli, while others held that he was born and raised at Turin. Although their opinion is not as certain as they themselves believed, it is nevertheless much more plausible than the fictitious claim of certain recent writers that Volterra in Etruria—the city of Leo and Maximus—was their birthplace.

Some, however, think that there is no reason to hold Maximus to have been born at Vercelli. For in several sermons bearing Maximus’s name there are notes appended that read: “This is Vercelline”; “He shows himself to be a Vercelline.” They vigorously maintain that these notes have no force, since it is perfectly clear that notes of this kind were added only recently, and since the sermons to which they are attached—and in which the author calls himself the son of Saint Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli—differ so greatly from Maximus’s language and style that they must altogether be rejected as spurious works.

Those who think Maximus was from Turin judge their opinion to be closer to the truth because he seems to assert that he is joined to the martyrs Octavius, Adventus, and Solutor by the bones of his parents.

There will certainly be some, however, who judge this evidence slight, since Maximus, addressing his hearers, could have spoken of being joined to “the bones of our parents” not in his own name but in the name of those citizens of Turin who were present.

[Note: Homily 81, p. 264.]

They will also say that the argument drawn from the custom of that age concerning the selection of bishops from the clergy of their native cities is not especially weighty. For it is clear that in the fourth and fifth centuries many men were enrolled in the clergy, and some who had not even been so enrolled became bishops of cities far removed from their homeland. Ambrose, Martin, Paulinus, and others—whose enumeration would be lengthy and wholly unnecessary—belonged to this number.

Because of the extreme scarcity of ancient records, and because the writers disagree so greatly, we must confess that we have no certain knowledge of Maximus’s birthplace or of the cities in which he lived before becoming a bishop.

### II. That Saint Maximus was Bishop of Turin; whether there were two bishops named Maximus, one succeeding the other, or only one bishop of that Church; and, if there was only one, when he began to exercise the episcopate

It is certain and well established that he was bishop of Turin.

But whether two bishops named Maximus, distinguished by that dignity, flourished at Augusta Taurinorum, one succeeding the other, or whether there was only one; and, if there was only one, at what time he first began to exercise the episcopal office—on these questions learned men have engaged in vigorous dispute.

Those who have attempted to place two bishops named Maximus in the Church of Turin support their opinion with the following arguments.

First, they say that Gennadius, who published his book *On Illustrious Men* fifteen years before the beginning of the sixth century, places the death of Maximus of Turin in the period when Honorius and Theodosius the Younger were ruling the Roman people. Honorius died in the year 423. Therefore, they say, the earlier Maximus must have been the one whose life did not extend beyond that year; and the man who took part in the Council of Milan in 451 and the Roman synod in 465 must consequently be regarded as a second Maximus.

They next observe that Maximus attended the Council of Milan held under the presidency of Ambrose in 389 against the heresy of Jovinian. For Maximus wrote as follows in Homily 4 on the Nativity of the Lord:

[Note: p. 25.]

> “Blind and foolish paganism laughs at the depth of so great a mystery—the birth of Christ the Savior from a Virgin. That impious blasphemy also mocks it, the blasphemy which in recent days, when it presumed to diminish and corrupt the Virgin’s childbirth, declared that Christ our Lord could not have been born from a virgin. The holy Church of Milan abhorred this blasphemy; our synodal assembly condemned it with one voice; and the devout imperial power itself detested it.”

These words are plainly similar to those contained by Saint Ambrose in the letter he sent to Pope Siricius after the synod. The letter reads:

[Note: Letter 8 among the Sirician letters, no. 8, p. 174, vol. I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, Paris edition, 1721.]

> “For them”—the followers of Jovinian—“there is no remission of sins, but rather the impiety of the Manichaeans, which even the most merciful emperor detested, and from which all who saw them fled as from a kind of contagion.”

The advocates of two Maximi further point out that Maximus committed to writing the account of the holy Alexander, Martyrius, and Sisinnius, whom rustic idolaters killed in the village of Anaunia in the diocese of Trent in the year 397 on account of their religion.

[Note: Sermon 76, p. 607 ff.]

> “We ought to receive the holy Alexander, Martyrius, and Sisinnius, who suffered in our own time, with complete veneration. For somehow we have greater affection for those whom our own consciousness knows than for those whom history teaches us. We know the former to have been martyrs by reading; the latter by the contemplation of our eyes. We learn of the former’s sufferings through the report of fame; the tortures of the latter we retain through the testimony of their faces.”

[The printed text appears corrupt at this point: *suppucia vuitus*; the sense is rendered cautiously as “the tortures ... through the testimony of their faces.”]

> “Therefore I ought to have greater affection where opinion urges my belief; I ought, I say, to have greater affection where, through what I have seen, I am compelled to believe more devoutly even what I have not seen. For when what I had heard seemed somewhat impossible to me, I began to believe that it could have happened when I saw similar things take place. And therefore the suffering of our own time has granted us this benefit: it has brought present grace and confirmed former faith.

> “We ought therefore to receive the aforesaid blessed men with complete veneration: first, because they deigned to illumine the days of our life with their precious blood; and then because they bestowed upon us no small privilege before God, showing what the faith of Christians was in our age, since martyrs were worthy to arise from their fellowship.”

But when a man who testifies that the martyrs were killed in 397, that they suffered in his own time, that they illumined the days of his life and his age with their precious blood, and that he knew them not by report or by the faith of historians but by his own consciousness, by the testimony of their faces, by sight, and by the contemplation of his eyes—when such a man is considered, they ask, who could believe that he was able in the year 465 to travel to Rome and attend the synod convened by Pope Hilary?

They further point to imperial laws, which Maximus is said to mention as having been recently promulgated, forbidding the retention in cities of shrines or images of false gods. It is clear that these laws were enacted by Valentinian II in the year 391, during the consulship of Aurelius Symmachus and T. Fabius Tatianus.

Finally, they appeal to the sermons of Maximus in which an invasion of barbarians is discussed. They therefore think that these sermons were written near the beginning of the fifth century, when Alaric was bringing all Italy into devastation and destruction, and when, after engaging in battle at Pollentia, he was defeated by Stilicho and compelled to return to Pannonia, from which he had set out.

On the other hand, those who think that one Maximus alone presided over the people of Turin with episcopal dignity, and that he pronounced a judgment against violators of ecclesiastical discipline at the Roman synod of 465, after Pope Hilary, do not trouble themselves over Gennadius’s passage. For they deny that any account should be taken of a statement so plainly in conflict with distinguished, certain, and public records. And, they say, who could doubt that the acts of the Milanese synod of 451 and of the Roman synod of 465 ought to be counted among distinguished, most certain, and public records? [Col. 0130D] In the list of the bishops who were present, the name of Maximus of Turin is read among the subscriptions. It is therefore established by the most certain—and public—records that Maximus continued to exercise the episcopate of the Church of Turin not only in 451 but also in 465.

Gennadius’s passage, then, ought not to trouble anyone: either it has been corrupted through the ignorance of scribes, or it has become entangled in an error of its author, who, while dozing [Col. 0131A]—

[Note: Examples of Gennadius’s *ἁμαρτημάτων*—“errors” arising from carelessness—could be produced from the same catalogue in no small number; but I omit them, lest I seem excessive. Let one example be that of Julian of Eclanum, whom he mistakenly writes to have been bishop of Capua. Another is that of Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, whom he says was the one by whom the Nestorian doctrine was attacked—something that cannot be admitted, since Atticus died long before Nestorius had begun to spread his perverse doctrine.] [Col. 0131D]

—had forgotten the year of Maximus’s death, although it was not very remote from his own time, as sometimes happens even to historians narrating events not far removed from their memory. [Note: He wrote his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men* around the year 484.] [Col. 0132D]

Gennadius’s passage concerning Maximus is as follows: “He died while Honorius and Theodosius the Younger were reigning.” [Note: The Vatican Codex of the ninth century reads as follows: “He died … in the year 420 from the redemption of the world.” From this it may be recognized that scribes rashly laid hands upon Gennadius’s work and added something to it according to their own judgment.]

What, surely, could be more opposed to the acts of the synods I mentioned shortly before? Thus, whether one should read—as Baronius, Pagius, and Fleury thought—*claruit* (“he became distinguished”) in Gennadius in place of *moritur* (“he died”), or whether it should not be read so, is of little importance. Certainly no one will wrest from men skilled in critical scholarship—men who know how much authority resides in the public records of synods—the concession that, because of Gennadius’s passage, Maximus of Turin ceased to live while Honorius Augustus held supreme power in the West. [Col. 0131B]

Nor should the reasoning of those be approved who persuaded themselves that the whole matter could easily be resolved by positing two bishops of Turin named Maximus: one who, as Gennadius reports, died under the emperor Honorius, and another who, more than forty years later, was present at the Roman synod while Hilary governed the Christian commonwealth. For, if there had been two Maximuses, both would certainly have been writers of homilies. Gennadius, therefore, who had undertaken to compose a catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, would have mentioned both.

That Maximus who flourished long after Honorius wrote the sermons is sufficiently clear and established. [CXXXIV] For in them he not only refuted the heresiarch Eutyches [Note: See our preface, no. 3, p. XL and following], but also named him [Note: Ibid., no. 4, p. XLVI]. Yet Eutyches could not have been named by someone who had departed this life while Honorius still possessed the imperial power. For Eutyches first began to give indications of his heretical teaching in 448, when Honorius had already completed his reign and had died in 423. [Col. 0131C]

Now Gennadius mentions one Maximus, not two. If he had learned that there were two, both distinguished by their writings, he would surely have remembered both; or, if he remembered only one, then certainly the one who was nearer to his own time and had attended two councils with such distinction. Since he mentions only one, he must necessarily have judged that one bishop named Maximus had presided over the people of Turin, though he mistakenly wrote that this man had died while Honorius was still emperor. Unless, perhaps, someone wishes to maintain that *claruit*, the word Gennadius had used, was transformed through scribal error into *moritur*. [Col. 0131D]

Again, those who hold that there was only one bishop of Turin named Maximus in the fifth century emphatically deny that it can be concluded from his fourth homily on the Nativity that he should be numbered among the Fathers who rejected Jovinian’s heresy at the Council of Milan in 389. [Col. 0132A] They say that, because the holy bishop writes in that homily that “in former days” there had been people who blasphemously claimed that Christ could not be born of a virgin, this is not sufficient evidence for assigning his presence to that synod. For, they say, *diebus* (“days”) can amount to the same thing as *temporibus* (“times”). “Our days” means the same as “our times,” both in other writers and sometimes also in Maximus; this can plainly be understood from sermon 76, p. 607 and following.

Indeed, *ante dies* (“a few days ago”), which Maximus often uses [Note: Homily 47, p. 143; sermon 77, p. 592; and sermon 82, p. 659], sometimes appears to amount to the same as *ante annum* or *ante annos* (“a year” or “years before”). [Col. 0132B]

As for Maximus’s further statement, “Our synodal assembly condemned that heresy with one voice,” they say that it need not indicate that he himself was present at the Council of Milan, which was convened under the presidency of Ambrose in 389. For Maximus could quite properly have called “our assembly” a synod at which the bishops of the province of Milan had assembled—a province to which the Church of Turin belonged.

We are accustomed to call groups “ours” even when they were held by the earliest Christians, because, although they were not held by us, they were held by people who, despite living long before our time, practiced the same religion as we do.

If Maximus had begun to exercise the episcopate and had published homilies against Jovinian’s heresy from the time of Ambrose of Milan, it would seem implausible that Jerome—who not long afterward had produced a catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, and in it had mentioned his own books written against Jovinian, while remembering not only Ambrose but also certain others who had scarcely published any small works—would have omitted mention of Maximus himself. [Col. 0132C]

But suppose, they add, that Maximus was present at the assembly he describes. What prevents that assembly from having been held more than twenty years after Ambrose’s Milanese synod? It is established that in 412 the bishops appealed to the emperor Honorius, asking him to take action against Jovinian and his followers, who persisted in heresy and did not hesitate to hold assemblies outside the city.

But why would the bishops have lodged such a complaint concerning assemblies of new sectarians outside the city walls, with such unanimity and concerted effort, unless they had gone to Rome in order to determine, in council together with the pope, what ought to be decreed and done against the impiety? [Col. 0132D]

That the bishops brought their complaint before the emperor is likewise confirmed by an especially authoritative witness, the emperor himself. For in Law 53 of the Theodosian Code, book XVI, title 5, *On Heretics* [Note: Volume VI, p. 174, Lyon edition of 1660], Honorius wrote as follows: [Col. 0133A]

“Bishops’ complaint deplores that Jovinian is holding sacrilegious assemblies outside the walls of the most sacred city. Therefore we order that the aforesaid man be arrested and, having been beaten with lead, be restrained in exile together with his other associates and ministers. The contriver himself is to be brought with all speed to the island of Boa; the others, as may be deemed appropriate, provided that their superstitious conspiracy is dissolved through the separation imposed by his exile, are to be deported forever to solitary islands situated at a great distance from one another. If anyone, with stubborn insolence, should repeat what has been forbidden and condemned, let him know that he will suffer a harsher sentence. Issued on the day before the Nones of March, in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius for the ninth time and Theodosius for the fifth time.” [Col. 0133B]

That is, in the year 412. Jacobus Gothofredus appended the following observation to this law:

“There was a time when I thought that, instead of *episcoporum* (‘of the bishops’), one should read *episcopi Romani* (‘of the Roman bishop’), because Jovinian was stirring up these assemblies in the particular diocese of Rome. Nevertheless, nothing should be changed rashly. Indeed, from the fact that Honorius says in this law that he deplored the bishops’ complaint that Jovinian was holding assemblies outside the walls, it may appear possible to infer that at this time a synod of bishops had been held at Rome, just as a synod was held at Carthage in this same year against Caelestius, a member of Jovinian’s flock.”

Fleury’s account in book XXIII of his history comes to the same conclusion [Note: No. 4, under the year 412, where he says: “The bishops whose complaints gave rise to this law may perhaps have been assembled in council at Rome. Jovinian is not [Col. 0134D] mentioned thereafter, except that it is said that he continued his voluptuous life until his death.”] [Col. 0133C]

Now, if a synod against Jovinian was held at Rome in 412, what prevents us from supposing that Maximus went there and attended that synod, just as he later attended the one in 465? What of it? Could someone who began to exercise the episcopate in 412 or 411 not have prolonged his life until 465?

Hosius, certainly, who held the bishopric of Córdoba at the beginning of the fourth century, still possessed sufficient strength in 357 to undertake a journey from Illyricum to Córdoba, where he lived for at least some time, though not a very long time. What of this? According to Gregory of Tours, Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, held the episcopate for more than seventy years. I pass over Simplicianus, the successor of Saint Ambrose; Salvian; and others—of whom there were certainly many—who reached nearly their hundredth year of life. [CXXXV]

There is no reason even to suspect that this should be denied of Maximus, especially since his subscription is read in the acts of the Roman council of 465 immediately after that of Pope Hilary. This indicates that he was older, in the office of the episcopate he had undertaken, than the others who were present. [Col. 0133D]

Now, if Maximus attended the synod held in 412, there was plainly no reason why, in the homily he delivered not long afterward, he could not appropriately say: “Our synodal assembly,” and proclaim that “in former days the heresy of Jovinian had been condemned by the voice of the assembled holy bishops,” and that the same heresy had likewise been execrated by the pious imperial power itself. [Col. 0134A]

Nor does the argument drawn from Maximus’s mention of the Milanese Church, which had abhorred Jovinian’s blasphemy, possess any force. Who does not know that those who lived long afterward often remember the decrees of Churches, and that certain *ῥητά* (“express statements” or “verbal formulations”) are usually repeated and transcribed from those decrees?

It should therefore not seem surprising if Maximus borrowed from the synodal letter of the Milanese council of 389 what he wrote: “Jovinian blasphemes that Christ could not be born of a virgin, although he does not dare deny that virgins remain virgins after giving birth to human offspring from a woman.” The same point is expressed in that letter as follows: [Col. 0134B]

“What madness of deadly barking, that they should say that Christ could not be born of a virgin, while asserting that virgins remain virgins after giving birth to human offspring from a woman.” [CXXXVI] [Note: Ambrose, *Epistle* 42 to Siricius, no. 4, p. 1041, volume III of the works, Venice edition of 1751.]

But someone may say that at the very end of this same synodal letter the name of Maximus the bishop is read among the subscriptions. That is indeed so. But the city of which that Maximus was bishop is not likewise stated. Some maintain that he was bishop of Emona, as he is identified in the Roman edition of Ambrose’s works. There is no reason to prevent us from agreeing with them.

Rather, there is a substantial reason that proves we must not suppose that the man who, according to ancient testimony, was the one and only Maximus to hold the episcopate of Turin in the fifth century, and who is known and established to have come to Rome in 465 and attended the council summoned by Pope Hilary, was present at the Milanese synod of 389. [Col. 0134C]

Once these points have been established, those same men who insist that there was only one Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, turn to the homilies delivered by Maximus himself concerning the holy martyrs Alexander, Martyrius, and Sisinnius. They deny that anything in them conflicts with their position.

Whether, they say, the holy bishop saw those martyrs or not is of little importance. Suppose that he did see them when he was ten years old: what would be unusual if someone who was ten in 397 had lived until 465? He would certainly have lived to the age of seventy-eight. How many people are there, or have there been, who reach or have reached their seventy-eighth year? [Col. 0134D]

Again, let us grant that those homilies were delivered in 420 or 425. Nothing prevents this. The passion of those martyrs, who had died in 397, would then certainly have been recent, and Maximus could rightly have said: “We know them by the contemplation of our eyes; we retain the punishments they endured through the testimony of our countenance,” and so forth. [Col. 0135A]

They say that the objection concerning Alaric’s invasion is much weaker. For Maximus does not indicate that invasion, but the one Attila made into Italy in the middle of the fifth century. In the homily entitled *On the Tumult of War* [Note: Homily 86, p. 287], Maximus is speaking of barbarian enemies who had invaded the regions neighboring Augusta Taurinorum [Note: Page 288: “This proximity of wars,” he says, “shows us that Christ is nearer to us. For that reason I ought not to fear the enemy who is coming, because through these signs I understand that the Savior is rather coming. Although the one inspires temporal fear, the other brings eternal salvation.”] [Col. 0135C]

He then relates that the citizens, thrown into confusion by fear, began to fortify the city gates [Note: Ibid., p. 289: “For while we are vigilant concerning what we see, we become more vigilant concerning what we hope for. A wise man … when he sees, amid this common disturbance, the leading men preparing defenses on the walls, is himself admonished how to prepare a defense for his soul in the future overthrow of the world. We see the city gates being armed; we too must first arm within ourselves the gates of righteousness, of which the holy prophet said: ‘Open to me the gates of righteousness,’ and so forth. The city gate will then be able to be fortified if the gates of righteousness are first fortified within us. For it is useless to secure warfare with fortifications while provoking God by sins. The former is built with iron, stones, and stakes; the latter is armed with mercy, innocence, and chastity. The former is guarded by a multitude of weapons; the latter is defended by constant prayer.”] [Col. 0135D]

—to establish defenses upon the walls; and finally to prepare everything that could contribute to sustaining the war.

In another homily, entitled *On Not Fearing Enemies*, numbered 87, p. 291 and following, the excellent and most holy bishop warns the people of Turin—who were continuing to prepare themselves for defense—that amid such great tribulation they should pray, fast, sing psalms, and show mercy. By these aids Christians usually become victors over their enemies. Those who think they are fortifying the city keep watch in vain if they themselves do not possess the weapons of faith; and the city is fortified when God guards it.

Homilies 89, p. 297 and following; 90, p. 301 and following; and 91, p. 305, likewise belong to the same situation. In the last of these Maximus reproves the citizens because, through fear of the impending devastation and destruction, when the enemies were drawing nearer, they were preparing to flee in order to preserve their money out of avarice, forgetful of their eternal salvation. [CXXXVII] [Col. 0135B]

[Note: Pages 305 and following: “Destruction is inflicted upon a city only on account of the sin of its citizens. Stop sinning, therefore, and the city will not perish. Why do you flee your homeland? If you wish to be safe, flee your sins instead. If you cease to sin, the enemy is defeated … If the righteous are those who save their homeland, then surely the unjust are those who abandon it … In a way, the homeland is a sweet mother, who gave you birth, who nourished you, and who made you rich so that you might be able to flee. For if you did not possess an abundant supply of resources, you would have no means of escape; and therefore, led by avarice, while fearing to lose your riches, you do not hesitate to act impiously toward your mother. Hence we understand that you care more for your money than for your salvation. Tell me, good citizen, why are you planning to flee? Why are you abandoning your homeland? Perhaps you fear captivity, and do not understand how to show mercy? … God says to Abraham that a city can be saved for the sake of ten righteous people. You therefore think ill of yourself, Christian people, if you do not believe that in so great an assembly of ours there are ten righteous people by whose merits the city can be saved. For when you abandon your homeland, you profess that there are not in it people worthy to deliver it by their merits.”] [Col. 0136C]

Even so, while the citizens continued to tremble with fear, Maximus in homily 92, p. 307 and following, and homily 93, p. 311 and following, strongly encouraged them by the example of Elisha not to lose heart and to pray. If they did so, they could be confident that the enemy’s attack would soon be checked. [Col. 0135C]

From this, the reason for the ever-increasing fear of the people of Turin can easily be understood if the reference is applied to Attila’s invasion and movements; but it cannot rightly be understood if applied to Alaric.

Attila, after conquering, plundering, and destroying many cities of Gaul in 451, had raged against their inhabitants with incredible violence. In 452 he assembled a great army, crossed the Julian Alps, and invaded Italy. After besieging, capturing, and destroying Aquileia, and after some of its inhabitants had been killed and others reduced to slavery, he brought the greatest terror not only to the neighboring regions but also to those farther away. [Col. 0136A]

He then advanced and captured Concordia, Ceneta, Altinum, Tarvisium, Patavium, Vicetia, Brixia, and Bergomum. This increased the fear of the people of Turin. For the nearer an implacable enemy comes, the greater fear he customarily arouses among the inhabitants.

After overwhelming these towns, and following the success of his campaign, Attila carried his arms to Milan. In that city, which he had brought under his power, he displayed dreadful examples of barbarian cruelty. From this anyone may infer how great a horror of the advancing armies seized the minds of the people of Turin, and why many of them decided to secure their money and their safety by flight.

Their terror was later diminished when Attila, having departed from Milan to await Pope Leo and the ambassadors of the emperor Valentinian III for negotiations concerning peace, halted not far from the city of Mantua, at the place where the Mincio flows into the Po. [Col. 0136B]

Finally the Italians—and therefore also the people of Turin—ceased to fear when they learned that the barbarian king, deterred by the speech of Pope Leo from the thought of prolonging the war, had decided to cross the Alps again and return to his own people.

This is the view of the most serious writers. Tristanus Calchus, in book III of his *History of Milan*, p. 64, writes as follows:

“Upon Attila’s departure, peace was restored to Italy. But because the other writers, being too hasty, pass over what a great and grievous disaster was suffered, I thought that, in order to make it known, I should append the words of Maximus, bishop of Turin, from a sermon he delivered to the citizens of Milan concerning the restoration of the Church and the city.” [Col. 0136C]

Remigius Ceillier, a Benedictine monk distinguished for his learning, held the same opinion. For, when discussing the homilies of Saint Maximus concerning the *Tumult of War*, he judged that they ought to be assigned to the year 452, when Attila, king of the Huns, after taking possession of Milan, became so emboldened that he threatened to lay waste the rest of Liguria [Note: *General History*, volume XIV, p. 608]. [Col. 0136D]

But there is no time to pursue the matter further. I shall add one brief point: the whole question is settled by Maximus’s homily 94, entitled *On the Restoration of the Milanese Church*, p. 315 and following. In it he writes that Milan had been captured by the barbarians, overthrown, and destroyed, so that it seemed already to have perished. [CXXXVIII] [Col. 0137A]

[Note: “Some interpreters, excessively ignorant, have said: ‘This city has perished; the Church has collapsed; there is now no reason to live.’ On the contrary, there is reason to live more justly and holily, because almighty God, who in his goodness governs all these great events, delivered into the hands of the enemies not the city that is within you, but the buildings of the city; nor did he allow his Church—which truly is the Church—to be consumed by fire, but, for our correction, permitted the repositories of the Church to be burned. Paul the Deacon, book XV, p. 655, Amsterdam edition of 1623, relates that Attila plundered Milan, but nevertheless refrained from fire and sword. Everyone can see how inconsistent this is with the words of Maximus, who was a contemporary witness.”] [Col. 0137D]

It is clear from the testimony and credibility not only of later but also of ancient historians that the city was captured and plundered by Attila. On the other hand, those who in the memory of our ancestors pursued the Gothic invasions of Italy in their narratives described Alaric’s preparations for war, his expeditions and journeys, and his deeds in such a way as to indicate plainly that he not only failed to conquer that metropolis of Insubria, but did not even begin to attack or besiege it. [Note: Compare what Tillemont collected from writers of that period and from near-contemporary authors and reported in the *Life of Honorius Augustus*, volume V of *History of the Emperors*, articles 16 and 18.]

Finally, the objection concerning the imperial laws that ordered the destruction of pagan sacrilege is equally weak. Why could Maximus not have been referring to the law of Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian III issued in 426, in the consulship of the same Theodosius XII and Valentinian IV? [Col. 0137B]

[Note: Theodosian Code, book XVI, title 10, *On Pagan Sacrifices and Temples*, law 25: “We forbid all the detestable sacrifices of victims belonging to the pagan religion of a criminal mind, and all sacrifices condemned by the authority of the ancient sanctions, as well as the rest of what has been prohibited; and we order all their shrines, temples, and sanctuaries—if any still remain intact—to be destroyed by command of the magistrates and purified by the placement of the sign of the venerable Christian religion,” and so forth.] [Col. 0138D]

Let it nevertheless be granted that the holy bishop directed his attention to the law promulgated by Valentinian II in 391. I can readily accept that. But what prevented Maximus from recalling it thirty or even forty years later—while it still retained its force and had been confirmed by a new constitution of Theodosius II and Valentinian III—to those who neglected to carry it out and uphold it as they ought? For the holy bishop did not say, when he addressed the people in sermon 82, that the law he mentioned was recent. [Note: See Maximus’s sermon 82, p. 610.]

If in sermon 101, p. 658, he recalls the laws of the emperors by which it had been provided that gladiatorial games should no longer be held [Note: See the Theodosian Code, book XV, title 12, *On Gladiators*, law 1], he certainly does not mention them as new. [Col. 0137C] [Note: Sermon 101, p. 658: “Just as the public crime of gladiators has been abolished through the religious devotion of the emperors, so these mad gladiators—namely, the priests of Diana of the fields—should be removed from their own dwellings through the observance of Christianity.”] [Col. 0138D]

And even if he had called one of them new in 415 or 420, he would not have said anything that seemed less than true. For a law issued sixteen years earlier can quite reasonably be called recent. The law enacted by Honorius on this matter was issued in 403 or 404. [Note: See Theodoret, book V of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 26, Turin edition of 1748, p. 203; Gothofredus’s annotations on law 1, book XV, title 12 of the Theodosian Code, p. 398, Lyon edition of 1665; and Tillemont, *Life of Honorius*, article 20, volume V of *History of the Emperors*.]

There is therefore nothing to deter us from believing that Maximus was named bishop of Turin only in the fifth century, and not before the year 415, the fourteenth year of Pope Innocent I.

## III. At What Time Maximus Entered the Episcopate

Since Maximus, as we have seen, appears to recall as recent both the synod assembled against the impious sect of Jovinian and the law promulgated by the emperor Honorius against that same sect in 412, [Col. 0138A] there are those who think that this is evidence that the episcopal office was conferred upon him not long afterward. This opinion, as it seems to us also, is closer to the truth.

But whether Maximus was himself the first bishop of Turin is disputed among learned men. For I understand that there were some who, claiming to have read that certain people lived in Augusta Taurinorum even while Maximus was exercising the episcopate—people bound by superstitions concerning empty gods—and that already in the fourth century, when Julian the Apostate held the imperial power, scarcely anyone had enrolled in the Christian army, concluded from this that no one could have been placed over so small a number of Christians with episcopal dignity. [CXXXIX] They therefore supposed that Maximus was the first person in Turin to receive that honor. [Col. 0138B]

The monk of Novalesa, whom we discussed above, held the opposite view. Following some author unknown to me, he says:

“When the bishop of the city of Turin had been removed from this life by death, blessed Maximus was appointed bishop of the Church of Turin by blessed Leo; he was received within the city of Turin with great joy and praise by the people, and was placed upon his episcopal throne.”

I shall not trouble myself over Leo, who is said to have been Maximus’s brother and to have appointed Maximus, while he was living at Rome, over the people of Turin—for the story has the smell of fiction. But concerning Maximus’s predecessor, which the same monk also mentions, I cannot bring myself to regard the statement as false.

For if, because there were idol-worshipers in the territory of Turin in the fifth century, we had to conclude that the people of Turin had lacked a bishop until the time of Maximus, we would ultimately be driven to admit that before Aurelius there had been no bishop of Carthage, and before Liberius or Damasus no one had presided over the Christians of Rome with papal dignity. What could be more absurd than that? [Col. 0138C]

It is evident from numerous other records, as well as from the law of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius [Note: Theodosian Code, book XVI, title 10, law 20], issued in 415, that many people in the territory of Carthage remained attached to pagan superstition while Aurelius was bishop. [Col. 0138D]

At Rome, meanwhile, the insolence of the idolaters rose to such a height that in 384, when Damasus was governing the Church, they demanded from the emperor, in the name of the Senate, the restoration of their rites and the repair of the altar of Victory. [Note: See Symmachus’s letter to Valentinian, reproduced before Ambrose’s Epistle 18, volume III of the Ambrosian works, Venice edition of 1751, p. 871 and following.] [Col. 0139A]

But the fact that the people of Turin, in considerable numbers, worshiped idols after the middle of the fourth century and arranged for a column to be erected to Julian the Apostate is not sufficient to establish that no one possessed the episcopate in that city, where at least some Christians existed. For we know of other cities in Asia, Africa, and even Italy that had bishops although they were full of pagan inhabitants, some of whom formed the senate and retained temples dedicated to idols.

Rome itself, according to Ammianus Marcellinus [Note: Book XXIII, p. 237 and following], sent several senators devoted to the superstition of idols as ambassadors to that same Julian; and it carefully took precautions to prevent the temple of Apollo, which had already begun to burn, from being consumed by the flames. [Col. 0139B]

Moreover, it is difficult to believe that Vercellae, which was not far from Turin, had been provided with a bishop long before, while Augusta Taurinorum had none—especially since our ancestors followed the practice of the apostles [Note: See Saint Clement of Rome, *First Epistle to the Corinthians*, no. 42, volume I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 151, Lyon edition of 1746] and gave bishops even to cities in which only a few people had begun to practice the Christian religion. [Col. 0139D]

The Fathers committed to writing the record that Gregory Thaumaturgus was given as bishop to the Christians of Neocaesarea in Pontus, who numbered no more than eighteen, in the third century of the Church. [Note: Compare what Tillemont cites from ancient writers on this matter in *Life of Gregory of Neocaesarea*, article 6, volume IV of the *Historical Ecclesiastical Monuments*.] [Col. 0140D]

All the more, then, the honor should not be denied to the people of Turin, whose large Christian population is clear from the fact that, when Maximus began to exercise the episcopate, scarcely any remnants of paganism remained except in a few rural districts and villages. [Col. 0139C] I shall discuss this matter later.

What if Maximus himself appears to indicate his episcopal predecessors in homily 16, p. 45? For there he mentions Fathers who had preceded him, and he affirms that the addresses by which those same Fathers had instructed the people of Turin were repeated to the people of Turin by himself.

But the size of this commentary, as well as my haste to set forth what I have resolved to write about Maximus, prevents me from pursuing further the antiquity of the episcopate of Turin.

# [CXL] IV. On Maximus’s zeal, from the time he assumed the episcopate, for instructing the people of Turin and rightly forming them in moral discipline

As soon as he assumed the office of bishop, he devoted all his efforts to rightly instructing his people in doctrine and in moral discipline [Col. 0139D]. Accordingly, he first took care to uproot from their minds whatever superstition might still remain among his sheep. Thus, when he noticed that many of them believed that, by their shouting, they could come to the aid of the failing moon, he severely rebuked them:

“You see,” he said [Note: [Col. 0140D] Homily 100, p. 333], “brothers, how my humility does not cease laboring with every concern on your behalf, and how I hasten with all speed to turn you toward good fruit. Yet the more I labor with you, the more I am put to shame on your account [Col. 0140A]. For when I see that, despite all my admonitions, you make no progress, my labor is no longer a source of rejoicing but of shame. Behold, I feed Christ’s flock, yet I cannot draw forth the fruit of the flock. No sweetness of faith gladdens me from it; rather, whatever flows from it is harsh and bitter. The shepherd of Christ’s flock is nourished by the flock’s milk when he is fed by the brightness of its good works.

“For who among you, brothers, would not take this grievously?—I do not speak of all of you, for there are some among you whom you ought to have as examples in the practice of religion—who, I say, would not be distressed that you are so forgetful of your salvation that you even sin, heaven bearing witness? For when a few days ago I had rebuked many of you concerning your greed for avarice, that very day, toward evening, such a great shouting arose from the people [Col. 0140B] that its irreligion reached heaven. When I asked what this shouting meant, they told me that your outcry was coming to the aid of the laboring moon and assisting its eclipse by your shouts. For you were crying out lest the heavenly element perish while you remained silent. As though it were feeble and weak, it could not, unless aided by your voices, protect the luminaries that God had created.

“Then, mocking and attacking those hearers of his who had committed this offense, he said: ‘This is plainly what Solomon means when he says: “The fool is changed like the moon.” You are changed like the moon: though a fool and senseless, at the movement of the moon you, who had been a Christian, begin to be sacrilegious. For sacrilege is committed against the Creator when weakness is attributed to the creature. You are therefore changed like the moon: you who shortly before shone with the devotion of faith afterward fail through the weakness of faithlessness [Col. 0140C].

“‘Would that, O fool, you were changed like the moon! For it quickly returns to its fullness; may you return, even late, to wisdom. It swiftly gathers again the light it had lost; may you, even slowly, recover the faith you denied. Your change, therefore, is more serious than the moon’s. The moon suffers a failure of light; you suffer a failure of salvation. How well it is written concerning the wise man: “And he will remain with the sun.” The wise man remains with the sun when, through constancy of faith, he remains with the Savior . . . The moon is changed from its state without willing it; you are voluntarily changed from your understanding. It is brought into decline by the condition of its nature; you are dragged into your own ruin by your will,’ and so forth.”

But it was not enough for him to have said this. He did not think he should remain silent until he had seen that this kind of superstition had been uprooted from the very roots. Thus, in Homily 101, p. 337, he says:

“A few days ago, brothers, we spoke against those who thought that the moon could be brought down from heaven by the incantations of magicians, and we refuted the folly of those who suffer no less a failure of mind than that luminary suffers a failure of light. We also urged them, abandoning their pagan error, to return to wisdom as quickly as the moon returns to its fullness.”

Another form of superstition was this: some members of the people, taken in by it, had fabricated omens on the Kalends of January, by which they confidently expected to discover whether everything would turn out adverse or favorable to them in the year they were about to enter. Nor had they merely observed empty omens; they had also held holidays in the pagan manner and had gathered in large numbers for theatrical spectacles, in which it could scarcely be discerned whether there was more indecency or impiety. Maximus strove with every effort to eradicate this kind of superstition as well.

For this reason he often and at length summoned the people to an assembly. His Homily 16 is On the Kalends of January. At its beginning he urges the people not to be annoyed at hearing the same thing so often [Note: [Col. 0141D] P. 45 ff. See also Homily 103, p. 343 ff., and Sermon 6, p. 409 ff.]. He recalls the Apostle’s words: “Brothers, to write the same things to you is not burdensome for me, but necessary for you” [Note: [Col. 0141D] Philippians III]. “And necessary,” he says [Col. 0141B], “not superfluous, do I consider it if, as a holy admonition formerly given, the addresses of our preceding Fathers are repeated to you. Indeed, what weariness or burden is there in often saying and frequently hearing things useful for the advancement of salvation and pleasing to God?

“And therefore, dearest ones, walking with your customary faith and devotion along the paths of the religious way and the tracks of truth, trample ever more and more upon the byways of error and the devil’s fabrications. For a faithful soul that longs for the fellowship of angels ought not to delight in the sport of demons. Nor can there be any communion among God’s servants between light and darkness, truth and falsehood, disgrace and honor.

“Therefore, whoever among believers either is the temple of God or desires to be one, must carefully beware lest, by pursuing dead and empty things, he cease to be the temple of God and become a habitation of darkness, become a monument of the devil [Col. 0141C].

“The great man continues: ‘Everything is insane that, through the devil’s deceptive falsehood, does not possess the power of God; and more grievous and incurable is the sickness of those who, deceived by the madness of superstitions and the pleasure of games, are insane under the appearance of health. Are not all the things performed for them by the ministers of demons on those days false and insane, when a man, with the strength of his manhood softened, breaks himself wholly into a woman, and does so with such elaborate display and art as though he were ashamed to be what he is? Are not all things there false and insane when human beings, formed by God, transform themselves into cattle, wild beasts, or monsters? How could it not be clear to the wise that there is no soundness there where they do and say impious, dishonorable, and utterly shameful things?’

“Certainly their heart is heavy and weighed down by every form of impiety—those who, through sacrilegious jokes mocking divine admonitions, love empty things and pursue falsehoods, and, finally, to complete their offense, call those very days a new year. Yet they do not inappropriately call the year ‘new’ according to their own practice, since through their impious holidays false disgrace and perversity are renewed in place of honor.

“They call it the new year, as though heaven or earth then displayed something new. They call the January Kalends a new year, although they are always sullied by ancient horror and error. They also say that they gather omens, and, judging the condition of their life by empty signs, they investigate the future of the approaching year through uncertain signs of birds and beasts, although knowledge of the future belongs to God alone and the authority of the Law forbids such things, saying: ‘Do not practice augury; do not attend to omens.’

“But wretched and pitiable people, snatched away by the errors of pagans and blinded by a heart lacking foresight, go out from their homes with impiety and return with sacrilege. Or how can one who has seen himself to be a companion of the faithless in such an observance think that he can be or even be called a Christian?”

Maximus had already perceived the abundant fruit of his exhortations. For he led his fellow citizens so completely away from such superstition that he could finally say with justification:

“Thus I have learned clearly that you, dearest ones, have long since ceased both observing and seeking these things. And truly, they are not to be sought out by you who believe in almighty God . . . As you have done until now out of fear of God, abhor empty things, flee falsehoods, and avoid impiety.”

When Maximus had enjoyed such success in driving superstition out of the city, he omitted no exhortation, diligence, or effort to uproot it from the minds of the country people who inhabited the villages and farms. To accomplish this more easily, he began to press and urge the leading citizens of the city through frequent sermons [Col. 0142C], warning them again and again to attend to their salvation.

They were not to think it permissible for a Christian to tolerate idols remaining in his rural estates and fields, or for sacrifices, honors, worship, and prayers to be offered to them by the tenants. They should know that, unless they made every effort, care, and concern to overthrow, crush, and destroy these things, they themselves would be the authors and guilty parties in the impieties and sacrileges with which their servants, ploughmen, and bailiffs polluted themselves.

Some, in order to excuse and clear themselves, said that they should not be blamed for what others did or had done without their orders. But Maximus, teaching them how greatly they were in error and ignorance of the ordinances of religion, said [Note: [Col. 0141D] Sermon 101, p. 656, and Sermon 82, p. 610: “If we see this and remain silent, if we are silent and endure it, we make ourselves guilty—if not by the performance of the crime, at least by the consent of concealment. For just as opposing sacrilege by contradiction justifies a person, so concealing what one has seen stains the silent person. Most wretched people commonly say: ‘I do not know; I did not order it; it is not my concern; it does not affect me.’ But, as I said, every such person speaks either in misery or fear. For he denies that he ordered to be done what he did not wish to order lest it be done. Certainly, when an evil arising from custom is not restrained, it is admitted. ‘It is not my concern,’ he says. You are deceived and ignorant. Do you not know that God’s cause concerns everyone, and that what is committed by one is punished in many?”]:

Whoever understands that sacrileges are being committed on his property and does not forbid what is being done, in a certain sense commands it himself. By remaining silent and failing to rebuke the one who sacrifices, he gives his consent.

This is the certain judgment of the Apostle Paul, pronounced under divine inspiration: that not only those who commit crimes are guilty, but also those who consent to their perpetrators. Therefore, those who knew that their ploughman or manager of their rural property was sacrificing to idols and did not forbid it should know that they share in the impiety. Even if they did not grant permission, they nevertheless encouraged his license by not restraining him.

“Even if,” he says, “there is no order from you, there is nevertheless will in the crime. For while you are silent, you approve what your peasant has done; if he did not do it, perhaps it would displease you. The subordinate does not sin only against himself when he sacrifices, but also against his master, who does not forbid him; for if he forbade him, he would certainly not sin.

“Great, therefore, is the evil of idolatry. It pollutes those who practice it, pollutes those who dwell there, pollutes those who look upon it; it reaches the ministers, reaches those who know of it, reaches those who remain silent. When a peasant sacrifices, the master is defiled. He cannot fail to be polluted in a place where food is consumed that a sacrilegious worshiper has cultivated, where bloodstained earth has produced it, and a foul granary has preserved it. Everything there is polluted; everything is abominable where the devil dwells in houses, fields, and country people. Nothing there is free from crime where everything is engaged in crime.

“When you enter the storeroom, you will find in it pale sods and dead coals—a fitting sacrifice to a demon, when a dead deity is worshiped with dead things. And if you go out into the field, you will see wooden altars and stone images: a corresponding ministry, in which service is rendered to senseless gods at rotting altars.

“When you rise early and see a peasant wounded by wine, you must know that he is, as they say, either a *dianaticus*—that is, a sacrificer of Diana, the empty divinity of the fields—or a soothsayer. An insane deity commonly has a mad priest. For the priests of this sort filled themselves with wine so that, when they inflicted blows upon themselves in order to satisfy the goddess, they might either not feel the pain or might soften and lessen it.

“Such a priest prepares himself with wine for the blows of his goddess, so that, while drunk, he may not feel his own punishment. They do this not only for the sake of temperance but also as a technique, so that their wounds may hurt less while they are thrown about in drunkenness.

“Plainly empty is the prophet who thinks to establish piety through cruelty. To describe briefly the appearance of this prophet: his head is shaggy with false locks; his chest is bare; his legs are half-covered by a cloak; and, equipped for battle in the manner of gladiators, he carries iron in his hands. Yet he is worse than a gladiator, because the gladiator is compelled to fight against another, while this man is compelled to fight against himself. The one seeks another’s entrails; the other tears apart his own limbs. And, if it may be said, the trainer urges the former to cruelty, while the deity urges the latter [Col. 0143D].

“Dressed, therefore, in this costume and bloodied by this slaughter, judge whether he is a gladiator or a priest.”

After the holy bishop had described the savage adornment of such priests, their hostility to human nature, and their dreadful cruelty, he turned his speech to the citizens who were present and vigorously urged them to recall by what law the gladiatorial contest had been abolished by the Emperor Honorius [Col. 0144A]. He therefore urged them to act sternly and firmly, so that these sacrificers, being worse than gladiators, might be expelled from Christian estates.

On other occasions as well, the holy bishop had often reminded his hearers to remember the laws that Christian emperors had enacted on this matter. In Sermon 82, p. 610, he says:

“God commands, and we sleep in the face of his commands. How often has that same God commanded the sacrileges of idols to be destroyed, and yet we never wish to be concerned with this matter? We have always concealed it; we have always despised it. Later the imperial decree admonished us . . . Princes, indeed, as good Christians, promulgate laws on behalf of religion, but the executors do not enforce them properly; and thus, while the prince is freed from blame, the executor remains guilty,” and so forth.

The fruit Maximus obtained from his exhortations and admonitions can be plainly understood from Sermon 102, p. 657 ff. For he addressed those who had assembled for the sermon as follows:

“We believe that you have made no little progress through the subject of the previous Lord’s Day, since by our preaching we have cleansed your hearts from every pollution of idols. Our hearts are cleansed when our conscience, polluted by the filth of the devil, is not retained in that condition.

“But a person does not have a polluted conscience if he does not permit sacrileges to be practiced on his property. On the other hand, whoever knows that sacrifices are offered to idols in his field and does not forbid it—although he himself may live far away in the city—will nevertheless be touched by that abominable pollution; and although a peasant stands beside the altars, the accursed contamination returns to the master. He becomes its participant, if not by conscience, certainly by knowledge.

“We therefore believe that you have made progress when you restrain the worship of sacrilege on your estates. For we say that, as befits a Christian man—that is, a pure man—his estate should be pure. Solomon says: ‘A pure man is a precious possession.’ If, therefore, a pure man is compared with a most precious possession, how much more valuable is that possession if it is sincere and pure and is not cheapened by any contagion of the devil?”

# V. Maximus also took care that no plague of heresy should invade his flock

But while Maximus was waging a fierce battle against pagan superstition, he was at the same time taking care that no plague of heresy should invade his flock. When he learned how much harm the impiety of Mani had brought even into Italy, he considered it necessary to strive and labor with great effort to fortify the minds of the people of Turin against it through knowledge of orthodox doctrine, and to instruct them in such a way that, if they happened to encounter someone who wished to impose that monstrous heresy upon them, they would be able to recognize and avoid him.

For he knew that heretics commonly set secret snares for the ignorant and unwary, against which everyone must guard carefully and vigorously [Note: [Col. 0143D] Homily 115, p. 382 ff.: “I think that all heretics should be compared with foxes. Since they cannot dwell in the house of the Lord, they prepare for themselves certain meeting places, like dark lairs, in which they lie hidden obstinately and lie in wait for the Church, so that, if some innocent soul should happen to come forward, they may swallow it like a chick of the mother hen [Col. 0144D] . . . Let us therefore avoid, brothers, let us avoid the deadly tricks of lurking foxes; let us avoid the death-dealing snares of the most wicked creatures, lest . . . the foxes of perverse doctrines either seize the fruit of our crops through the deception of their ambushes or consume it by the scorching of flames.”].

Accordingly, he observed generally that, since it is customary for lovers of wicked novelty to measure all divine things by one standard and to entangle and obscure them in lengthy arguments [Note: [Col. 0145D] Homily 89, p. 300], an orthodox Christian must take care not to associate with them [Note: [Col. 0145D] Homily 104, p. 346: “We must be concerned about the gift of faith, watchful, and always armed for its protection by the devotion of our minds, nor must we quickly believe deceptive flatteries. The enemy is accustomed to creep in under the pretext of peace; that is, under the name of a Christian, a heretic enters secretly. To deceive simple people, he carries Christ in his mouth and the devil in his heart; he confesses him with his tongue but blasphemes him in his mind. We must therefore avoid him entirely and join ourselves to him in no fellowship,” etc.].

He therefore teaches that it is the duty of his sheep to believe in one God, who created this visible world from nothing [Note: [Col. 0145D] Homily 7, p. 22; Homily 10, p. 28; Homily 82, p. 270; Homily 89, p. 299 ff.; and Homily 116, p. 383], and not to listen to anyone who dares to determine anything about the Creator by reason, or rather by his own arbitrary judgment.

For he says that these matters cannot be investigated by reason alone:

“How was the world made from nothing? From where did the sky shine forth? By what reasoning do the fluidity of the waters and the solidity of the earth subsist? How also did man come from earth, woman from man, and again man through woman? What is that which, after all things, produces light and darkness, which makes life and death?”

Then he says:

“If, therefore, you, O man, cannot comprehend how or from where you yourself and the things that were made for your sake were made [Col. 0145B], with what presumption or what folly do you scrutinize your own Creator and the Creator of all things? . . .

“These things, dearest ones, are blind to reason but manifest to faith. For then we shall be able to investigate in some measure the immensity of his indefinable majesty, if we recognize that we cannot know what kind and how great God is, as the Lord said to Moses: ‘But you cannot see my face’—that is, you cannot behold my divinity with bodily eyes as it truly is.

“For blessed David, contemplating the power of his omnipotence, cried out, saying: ‘Wonderful are your works, O Lord, and my soul knows them exceedingly well.’ The prophetic soul knew very well that God’s works surpass every meditation of the human mind. For this reason the wisest patriarch, confined by the narrow limits of mortal understanding, marveled at what he could not investigate [Col. 0145C] . . . His soul knew that God is incomprehensible; the flesh could not perceive it. Therefore, whoever wishes rather to examine God’s works than to believe them does not follow the understanding of the soul but error” [Note: [Col. 0145D] Homily 10, p. 28].

Maximus further writes that the Old Testament was given by God [Note: [Col. 0145D] Homily 11, p. 31; Homily 13, p. 31; Sermon 18, p. 442], that it has one and the same Spirit as the New Testament, and that it agrees wonderfully with the New Testament itself [Note: [Col. 0146D] Homily 11, p. 31, and Sermon 80, p. 605].

He teaches that the Son of the eternal God the Father, himself eternal God, assumed human nature; and that, as a human being possessing not an apparent but a real body, he truly suffered and died, rose again, and ascended into heaven [Note: [Col. 0146D] See our Preface, no. 3, p. 11 ff., and nos. 4 ff., p. 45 ff., where we show that Maximus believed and called Christ true God and perfect man. Since he acknowledges Christ as a perfect man, he must certainly have confessed that he possessed both a soul and a body. For Maximus says in Sermon 41, p. 567: “A human being consists of soul and body. One without the other, separated and dispersed, is an incomplete nature.” On Christ truly suffering, dying, being restored to life, and rising again, compare what we have excerpted from Maximus in the Preface, no. 6, p. 48 ff.; no. 12, p. 53; and no. 15 ff., p. 49 ff.], and that from there he will come to judge the living and the dead [Note: [Col. 0146D] Compare Treatise 1, On Baptism, p. 711 ff.].
