He likewise says that marriage was established by God and that Christ afterward sanctified it [Note: [Col. 0146D] See our Preface, no. 28, p. 101], or elevated it into the number of the sacraments of the new law [Col. 0146A].

Maximus does not indeed name the Manichaeans, who argued that marriage was evil, that this perceptible world was evil and had been created by an evil principle, and that the Old Testament had been introduced, following Marcion and other plagues of the same kind. But the holy bishop was not so much concerned that his citizens should know the names of the sects as that they should know the doctrines of orthodox religion. Once they knew those doctrines, they could safely detect and repel the sectarians.

For this reason he silently passes over the name of certain heretics who, in his own time, had invaded the neighboring regions and were attempting to deceive the ignorant and unwary. He was content with ensuring that no citizen should be unaware of what their impiety consisted in.

Thus it is unknown who those heretics were. We know that they had leaders whom they called presbyters. These men had been assigned the task of telling the layperson who confessed his sins to them not to repent, nor to detest and mourn his crimes, but merely to pay whatever amount of money they themselves decided ought to be paid for remission.

To prevent these men from deceiving anyone, Maximus summoned an assembly and addressed the people as follows [Note: [Col. 0146D] Homily 104, p. 346 ff.]:

“We ought not to be surprised that heretics of this kind have begun to wander in our region. The wolf that lies in wait always follows the flock of sheep; the devil the deceiver always attacks the Christian heaven. This happens beneficially, so that, through more vigilant guarding, neither the wolf may desert the flock nor the Christian abandon the Church.

“Hence the Apostle also says: ‘There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you.’ It is as though he said: Christians must have a struggle for the faith, so that those who are approved may have a certain victory.

“But, for the moment setting aside their blasphemies, let us disclose their rules of life. Their leaders, whom they call presbyters, are said to have this kind of instruction: if one of the laity confesses that he has committed a crime, the presbyter is not to say to him, ‘Do penance, lament what you have done, mourn your sins,’ but rather, ‘Give me this much for your crime, and it will be forgiven you.’

“Plainly vain and foolish is the presbyter who, when he receives the spoil, thinks that Christ forgives the sin. He does not know that the Savior is accustomed to forgive sins and to demand precious tears, not counted money, for wrongdoing. Hence he himself says: ‘Freely you have received; freely give’ . . .

“The presbyter receives gifts and, by a sort of bargain, promises indulgence from the Savior. Foolish is the agreement in which it is said that the person who has contributed more to the priest has offended the Lord less. Among such teachers the rich are always innocent and the poor always guilty. How can a poor person make satisfaction for an offense when he does not have what he can offer for his sin?”

Maximus likewise prepared strong and substantial defenses of doctrine against the other heresies. For whenever the occasion required, he showed the error and perversity contained in the doctrines of the Arians [Note: [Col. 0147D] See the Preface, no. 2, p. 39 ff.], of the Helvidians and Jovinianists [Note: [Col. 0147D] Ibid., no. 7, p. 53], of Vigilantius, who denied that the relics of the saints ought to be honored [Note: [Col. 0147D] Ibid., no. 36, p. 121], and of the Nestorians and Eutychians [Note: [Col. 0147D] Ibid., no. 3 ff., p. 40 ff.].

Since he knew that the Arians had engaged in fierce controversies with Saint Eusebius of Vercelli, whenever he had to speak about that defender and champion of the divinity of Christ the Savior, he briefly refuted the doctrine of the impious sect and demonstrated how hostile it was to the truth [Note: [Col. 0147D] Homily 78, p. 246]:

“What are you now attempting, heretic,” he says, “when you try to establish a distinction between the Father and his Son, although the Son, teaching us the truth of his own substance, said: ‘I and the Father are one’? He who says both ‘one’ and ‘we are’ neither divides himself by separation nor confuses himself by union. He who is one with the Father differs from the Father neither in eternity nor in power; and although he is one with the Father, he is nevertheless asserted to have been born from the Father, lest, as the impious Arius blasphemes, the Son be thought either some creature or unequal.

“You hear, therefore, O man, that God was born from God; but in this profound mystery you have only faith by which to believe—you have no argument by which to investigate it. You hear that the Son was born from the Father; but lest you be able to search for any bodily sex in divinity, the Son himself is called both Word and light. He is also called the power of God and the wisdom of God, so that you may understand . . . that the Father did not create bodily, but that through the ineffable mystery of majesty, power proceeded from power and light flowed from light.

“Again, lest you should think that the Word itself was not the substance of truth but merely a spoken utterance of the speaking God, he is called the Son, so that in him you might learn that there is both harmony and affection belonging to him who is the Father . . .

“And truly, brothers, just as seeing the Son is seeing the Father, so, when the Father is understood, the Son is understood also. For whoever believes and confesses that the Father is eternal must necessarily believe that the Son is coeternal . . . He says: ‘Whoever sees me sees the Father.’ How could there be one and undivided vision in the Father and his Son unless there were one and undivided substance?

“Christ is therefore God by nature and man by nature; in both he is true, in both perfect, because he truly received humanity from his mother and naturally possesses divinity from the Father. Whoever thus sees the Son sees the Father, because when we confess Christ to be the same God and Lord, we necessarily attribute the passions to the man and the miracles to God, so that the Only-Begotten of God may be understood to be neither unlike the majesty of the Father nor unlike the flesh of the mother.

“By this faith the Arian faithlessness was refuted by our Fathers. Arius, contradicting the Gospel of blessed John, denied that the Word of God was God and was with God. Blinded by the darkness of his faithlessness, he could see neither the Father nor the Son. And while he insisted that the maker of all things was a creature, and attempted to attribute temporal things to the timeless God, confounded by the madness of his presumption, he lost the mystery of both natures in Christ.

“But that venerable Father, Saint Eusebius, who had read that the Lord said, ‘I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,’ knowing that in this teaching there is a distinction of persons but no difference of nature between the Father and his Son—who are not one person but one substance—held and taught their inseparable unity, asserting equally in Christ the Lord both passible flesh and impassible divinity.”

By these teachings he was accustomed to instruct and strengthen the people entrusted to his faith in the decrees and institutions of religion [Note: [Col. 0147D] Homily 9, p. 26: “Therefore, brothers, adhering with unconquerable faith and customary devotion to so many admonitions of the priest, and walking along the paths of the religious way and the tracks of truth which the universal Church holds, trample ever more and more upon the byways of heretics and the devil’s fabrications.”].

Thus he encouraged his people to trample upon the fabrications of heretics if they persevered steadfastly in the paths of truth held by the universal Church. Heretics [Note: [Col. 0147D] Homily 47, p. 146: “This is ordinarily the judgment of the sacrilegious person, and the one conscious of his deed condemns himself, as the Apostle Paul says concerning the heretic: ‘Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment’. For the heretic condemns himself when he casts himself out of the Church and, compelled by no one, departs from the assembly of the saints. He himself shows what he deserves from all, since by his own judgment he separates himself from all. The heretic, I say, condemns himself because, whereas all guilty persons are expelled from Christian fellowship by the bishop’s sentence, the heretic, anticipating everything, is rejected by the sentence of his own will. Therefore the heretic is condemned to the same punishment as Judas, so that he is at once guilty of his own crime and judge of his own vengeance. And rightly so, because the one sold the Lord, while the other blasphemes him; the one handed him over to persecutors, while the other persecutes him every day. For the heretic persecutes the Lord when he diminishes his divinity and asserts that he is a creature.”]—those who abandoned such paths—are ultimately led to this: condemned by their own judgment, they tear themselves away from the Church and, like Judas, prepare eternal destruction for themselves.

For the Church is that ship which Peter pilots; outside it, those who remain perish [Note: [Col. 0148D] See our Preface, no. 30, p. 107]. In it, the ship to which alone the Lord ascended, Peter is the foundation, sustaining the structure and mass of the entire Christian work; he is the divinely appointed governor, judge, and teacher, to whom Christ granted authority to feed the flock. No one who wishes to be safe and unharmed is permitted to leap out of it [Note: [Col. 0148D] Ibid., p. 108].

But if someone, dissenting from Peter while pretending to be a disciple of Christ, should somehow climb into that same ship, Maximus warns him not to flatter himself. He will be like Judas, whose faithlessness disturbs the little ship founded upon the faith of the Apostle Peter [Col. 0149A]. There is calm wherever Peter alone is sailing; but when Judas joins him, there is a storm [Note: [Col. 0149D] Sermon 103, p. 659]. What remains, then, for one who imitates the deeds of Judas except to suffer Judas’s fatal end?

## VI. Maximus was no less diligent in instructing his flock in moral discipline

He wished to speak the truth openly. He took care not to be either excessively severe or excessively indulgent. He saw to it that his citizens were obedient to his word and came together frequently in church. What moral instructions he gave them.—

Maximus was no less diligent in establishing moral discipline among the people. Above all, he considered it the particular duty of priests, especially bishops, to preach the truth openly and, if they recognized that anything wrong was being introduced, to detest and rebuke it and take care that it be completely eradicated. If they preferred to remain silent rather than speak, they would bring their own salvation into the greatest danger. They had to be exceedingly careful not to be either too severe or too indulgent. For the prophet too had asked to know how to distinguish knowingly and wisely the limits of goodness and what measure discipline ought to have, lest perhaps what was unknown be defiled by the fault of excessive laxity, or stricter discipline blush at its own austerity. And whoever wishes to be good toward one who is sinning acts kindly indeed; but, if he is truly to do good, he must employ the rigor of discipline, so that his goodness may advance that person toward salvation. Otherwise that goodness will be harmful to him, because it allows the sinner to perish whom it could itself have saved once corrected. “Again,” he says, “if by excessive rigor of discipline you offer no remedy of healing goodness, then, while the sinner flees your terror, you will not cure the sinner’s illness. And what way of life, what justice, will there finally be, if either looser gentleness provides connivance for the sinner, or immoderate severity does not recall the offender from his fall?” [Note: [Col. 0149D] Homily 107, p. 353 ff.]

Thus he assured the people entrusted to his care and undertook that he himself would imitate the examples of the venerable Fathers in this matter [Note: [Col. 0149D] Ibid., p. 354.]. Therefore, let the sheep listen to him, since God’s ministers are not merely to be honored but also obeyed [Note: [Col. 0149D] Homily 67, p. 215 ff.]. For the dignity bestowed upon ministers is undoubtedly to be shown to the one whose ministers they are. Let them recall in memory Christ’s declaration when he addressed the apostles: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever receives you receives me.”

Although there were some who obeyed the holy bishop [Col. 0149D], there were nevertheless others who refused to be obedient to his word. This was as harmful to themselves as it was grievous and painful to him. Accordingly, he judged that, both to fulfill his own office and to recall them to health by whatever means he could and was permitted, he had to employ exhortation, reproof, and even threats. Addressing these people, he said [Note: [Col. 0150D] Sermon 104, p. 661 ff.]:

“I had often resolved within myself to withhold from you the words of the Lord’s preaching and not to distribute so frequently the mysteries of heavenly discourse. For it is of no benefit to offer food to one who refuses it, or to extend drink to one who is not thirsty, since he does not drink what you offer with willingness but rather, as though it were turbid, returns it with disgust. Thus it comes about that the people’s sincerity is corrupted, and the fastidious drinker finds grounds for sin.

“Therefore, perhaps it is superfluous to press the preaching of the Lord’s cup upon your charity, since your soul, with its inward parts closed, does not drink it with thirst so much as it pours it out dissemblingly. For the one who hears the Lord’s command with his ear but does not retain it in his heart pours it out . . . and thus the one who had left the church laden returns home empty.

“I had often admonished these people to relieve by their generosity the poverty of those whom adverse fortune had afflicted, and to see to it that no idol remained in their estates, and that they did not allow their household servants who were catechumens to remain longer without the grace of baptism [Col. 0150B]. But I had been heard in such a way that all my speech seemed to have been poured out in vain.

“For this reason, I fear that this evangelical reading applies to many of you: ‘We sang to you, and you did not dance; we lamented, and you did not mourn’ [Note: [Col. 0150D] Ibid., p. 663.]. I had therefore intended to withhold from you the words of the Lord’s preaching—not because I would do this in anger, but so that I might observe the evangelical saying. For the Lord says: ‘Whoever has, to him shall be given; and whoever does not have, even what he has shall be taken away from him’ . . . That is, whoever has been rich in good works, let him be enriched still more by evangelical preaching . . . But if you preach to a fornicator that he ought to remain a virgin, and to a miser that he ought to give away all that is his, it is foolishness for him . . . For to preach what is perfect to such people is like wishing to clothe a beggar covered in rags with silk, and so forth.” [Note: [Col. 0150D] Ibid., p. 662 ff.]

[Col. 0150C] He had already urged the people repeatedly and with the greatest insistence to come frequently to church, in order to keep the station during the periods of fasting and, especially on the festal Sundays, to attend the divine service and refresh the strength of their souls with the sacred rites of the Eucharist. Nevertheless, many did not approach the heavenly table or go to church, preferring either to eat at secular banquets or to go hunting through the groves and forests. Maximus took this badly. Accordingly, he attacked them publicly in these words:

“What are we to say about those people? By what name shall we call them before God—those who, on Sunday, despise the heavenly banquet for the sake of a secular meal and abandon Christ’s table while they delight in the table of a human being? For this is the first offense against Christ’s friendship: when he has called everyone to refreshment on Sunday, each person refreshes himself with his own pleasure in wantonness, rather than coming to the place to which he is led by a certain religious obligation. For it is an obligation for a Christian to assemble at church on Sunday.

“On that day the laws are silent and the courts are quiet, so that human salvation might receive a place of devotion; and one might be released not so much from public business as from the crimes of sins. But what is worse, each wretched person assigns to wantonness what was given for his salvation. He not only fails to assemble at church because of his sins, but, devoting himself to vanities, accumulates for himself more serious sins. May almighty God deliver you from them once you have been corrected” [Note: [Col. 0151D] Sermon 93, p. 638.].

Again [Note: [Col. 0151D] Sermon 25, p. 458.]:

“What does it profit,” he says, “to fast in one’s bodily organs and revel in hunting; to abstain from food and wander into sins; to chastise the body with hunger, perhaps not to drink wine, and yet proceed drunk with thoughts of wickedness? . . . Do you think, brothers, that the man fasts who at first light does not keep vigil at church or seek out the holy places of the blessed martyrs, but, rising, gathers his servants, arranges his nets, brings out the dogs, and searches the groves and forests—dragging his servants along with him, although perhaps they would prefer to come to church—and by his pleasures accumulating the sins of others, unaware that he will be held guilty both for his own offense and for the ruin of his servants?

“He spends the whole day hunting . . . rejoicing if he has caught something . . . [Col. 0151B] He pursues it with such zeal, as though the fast had been proclaimed for the purpose of hunting. In these revelries, then, tell me: what worship of God is there, what devotion of mind can there be, in one who fasts for this reason—not to devote himself to God and to prayers, but, idle and free for the whole day, to pursue his own pleasures?

“Although, therefore, you who are such a person, brother, return home in the evening, and although you eat when the sun is already declining, you may seem to have refreshed yourself late, but you have not fasted for the Lord . . .

“We must know, brothers, that this fast is acceptable to God: if we chastise our bodies not only by abstinence but also clothe our souls in humility. Let us be gentle toward our servants, kind toward strangers, merciful toward the poor. Rising at first light, let us hasten to church, give thanks to God, and ask forgiveness for our sins. . . . Let prayer or reading be constant for us throughout the day. Whoever does not know letters should seek out a holy man and feed upon his conversation. Let no worldly activity hinder an act of devotion; let neither the game of tables distract the mind nor the pleasure of dogs dull the senses. . . . For whatever you do apart from God’s command, although you abstain, you are not fasting. For this is the saving fast: just as the body abstains from banquets, so the soul must be restrained from vices.”

Moved by this severe rebuke and these admonitions, almost all the citizens began to hurry to the sacred church with much greater devotion and frequency, especially on the appointed days. For some time this was a consolation to Maximus amid his cares and labors. But as time passed, when the holy man had gone to a synod for the public good and had been absent from home for a longer period, they—[Col. 0151D] as though their overseer had been released from the fear he inspired—allowed themselves so much license that they came to the assembly only rarely. The sluggishness and negligence of the clergy increased this evil.

When Maximus learned of this upon returning to Augusta Taurinorum, he took it bitterly. Not long afterward, therefore, he summoned the people to an assembly and complained gravely. He said that he grieved because, although he had never ceased to admonish them with paternal affection, he seemed to have accomplished nothing. He had indeed hoped that, after returning from the council of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0151D] Homily 112, p. 373 ff.: “I ought, brothers, after these many days, to preach something more abundant and, returning from so great an examination of the priests, refresh you with sweet discourse,” etc.], he would be able to discuss matters that might be both pleasant and welcome to him, useful to the people. But scarcely had he reached [Col. 0152A] Turin when he clearly perceived that all that hope had been empty.

“For I have discovered,” he said, “that during my absence you come to church so rarely and proceed in such small numbers, as though, when I departed, you had departed together with me; and as though, when necessity drags me away, that same necessity had dragged you away with me. We are alike absent from the house of God; but the difference is that necessity makes me absent, whereas your absence is voluntary.

“Do you not know that, even if I am absent from the church, Christ is not absent from his Church, since he is everywhere? You come, brother, to the church and do not find there the bishop of bishops, the Savior? For the Christian who comes to church only when the bishop is present seems to have come not so much for God’s sake as for a human being’s, and not to have fulfilled the duty of a Christian who fears God but the courtesy of a friend who pays his respects.”

Then, turning his address to the clergy, he accused them of negligence. He said that he could not chastise the people’s license when he saw that he could not correct the negligence of those whom he counted among his brothers. He added that he was not speaking about all of them. It was evident and certain to him that some of them carefully practiced piety and acted diligently, but he knew no less certainly that others were negligent. He admonished these latter to consult their conscience and their salvation.

The force of this speech was so great that the people of Turin, although perhaps more sharply than they might have suspected, nevertheless confessed that they had been deservedly rebuked by the holy bishop [CL]. Accordingly, they took care not to give their shepherd any further occasion for reproach in this matter.

Maximus, rejoicing that they had made progress, saw that some had given themselves over to sadness. To end or lessen this sadness, he addressed them as follows:

“Perhaps my preaching last Sunday was more bitter, because I confronted many of your number more sharply with instruction and truth, and pursued matters that brought no comfort to some but caused sadness. Yet this is of no concern to me. For I rejoice, knowing that the disciple’s sadness is the teacher’s joy. The hearer makes progress when the preacher announces sterner things. Salvation is born for him when the sadness of correction is imposed.

“For the blessed Apostle says: ‘The sadness that is according to God produces repentance leading to steadfast salvation.’ Rightly, then, I rejoice, because I work salvation when I rebuke, even though the son grieves at the bitterness of my speech, while I understand that he is making progress through grief.

“The Apostle says: ‘What son is there whom the father does not chastise?’ A father does not always kiss his son; sometimes he also corrects him. Therefore, when the beloved is chastised, affection is being exercised toward him. Love too has its wounds, which are sweeter when they are inflicted more bitterly. Religious chastisement is sweeter than flattering indulgence. Hence the prophet says: ‘The wounds of a friend are sweeter than the voluntary kisses of an enemy.’

“Therefore, brothers, because I believe that, after so many useful words of my rebuke, you have progressed through the kindness of your understanding, we shall discuss some matters from the sacred Scriptures. For just as a spring that does not trickle with its usual flow is stirred with branches and then is found to be more abundant, while turbid water first issues from it so that purer water may follow, so your holiness had indeed been irritated by the austerity of my speech, but has become more devout through the sweetness of piety” [Note: [Col. 0153D] Homily 113, p. 373 ff.].

What Maximus discussed with the people from the sacred Scriptures, and continued afterward to discuss, is evident both from this same homily and from many other short works of his. He drew passages of sacred Scripture—which he was accustomed to use whenever the occasion demanded—either from the old Itala translation as from a fountain, or brought them forth in Latin after translating them himself from Greek.

In the homily most recently mentioned by us, he seized upon an outstanding passage from the sixth and tenth chapters of Matthew’s Gospel—“But you, whom do you say that I am?”—as an opportunity to teach the people that what one believes in the heart must be confessed with the mouth for salvation.

In his other discourses, relying equally upon the authority of the sacred Scriptures, he admonished the citizens:

- No one who clings to the transitory things of this world is led to true joy [Note: [Col. 0153D] Sermon 70, p. 584.].
- Each person must strive to prepare for himself a way to heaven, so that he may attain true joy [Note: [Col. 0153D] Homily 65, p. 209.].
- This way must be prepared by taking care that there be nothing false, pretended, or double in us [Note: [Col. 0153D] Sermon 109, p. 677.].
- No evil may be admitted, for vice cannot coexist with virtue [Note: [Col. 0153D] Ibid.].
- Everyone’s faith in God must be pure, constant, and unwavering [Note: [Col. 0153D] Sermon 38, p. 51 ff.; Sermon 109, p. 676 ff.], his hope firm [Note: [Col. 0153D] Homily 36, p. 106. See the preface, p. 128, no. 39], and his charity faithful and ardent [Note: [Col. 0153D] Homily 76, p. 242, and Sermon 89, p. 628.], remaining toward one’s neighbors in such a way that it is equal to the love we have for ourselves [Note: [Col. 0153D] Homily 64, p. 204.].
- This is the sum of virtue. Whoever rejects it trusts in vain in his almsgiving, equity, and chastity [Note: [Col. 0153D] Ibid.].
- Devotion must be added to charity [Note: [Col. 0153D] Sermon 68, p. 271.].
- One must not trust in one’s own strength [Note: [Col. 0153D] Ibid.].
- All our works must be referred to God [Note: [Col. 0153D] Homily 89, p. 297 ff.].
- We must pray not so much with the mouth as with the heart [Note: [Col. 0153D] Homily 107, p. 352, and Homily 116, p. 340.].
- [CLI] We must faithfully stand by whatever has been promised to God himself [Note: [Col. 0153D] Homily 97, p. 323 ff.] and fulfill our vows [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homily 96, p. 322.].
- Justice must likewise be cultivated [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homily 114, p. 377.], as must temperance and moderation [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homily 2, p. 4, and Homily 4, p. 14.].
- Excessive adornment must be rejected [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homily 6, pp. 17–18.].
- Fasts must be observed faithfully [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homilies 36 ff., pp. 104 ff.; and Sermon 14, pp. 432 ff.; and Sermon 26, pp. 463 ff.].
- The commands of the Church must be obeyed [Note: [Col. 0154D] Sermon 17, p. 439.].
- Generosity must be practiced toward the poor, strangers, and guests [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homily 4, p. 15; Homily 95, p. 319; and Homilies 97 ff., pp. 325, 331, 393, 398, and 647.].
- One must willingly spare those who have injured us [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homily 64, p. 203, and Homily 75, p. 242.].
- The cares of the world must be avoided [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homily 79, p. 258.].
- Whatever adversity befalls us must be endured with equanimity [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homily 85, p. 285.].
- The tongue must be restrained [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homily 105, p. 347.].
- One must attend to oneself, think humbly of oneself, and act modestly [Col. 0154A] [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homily 85, p. 285.].
- Whatever the ruler has known, decreed, or commanded concerning civil affairs must not merely be tolerated but also carefully observed [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homily 114, p. 377.].
- Reverence must be shown to the heads of sacred institutions [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homily 94, p. 315.] and they must be obeyed.
- Both clergy and laity must see to it that each fulfills his own office completely [Note: [Col. 0154D] Homily 114, p. 377 ff.], gives everyone what is his, injures no one, and, in a word, flees vices and cultivates virtue.

Maximus’s short works are full of instructions of this kind. To embrace them all would be a laborious task and, in my judgment, not at all necessary. I shall therefore make an end here and be content with one matter: the daily practice of the Christian.

After Maximus had often attacked those who, although they had been increased and enriched with benefits by God, the giver of all good things, nevertheless neglected to give him thanks and render them to him [Col. 0154B], he again rebuked the same people briefly in Homily 89, p. 297:

“Whoever is a useful Christian,” he says, “must always speak praises to his Father and Lord and procure all things for his glory, as the blessed Apostle says: ‘Whether you eat or drink or do anything else, do all things for the glory of God.’

“. . . Let all our actions, therefore, be carried out with Christ as our companion or witness, in this manner: let us do good things with him as their author, and avoid evil things because of his companionship. For the one who knows that Christ is his participant is ashamed to do evil. Christ, moreover, is a helper in good things.

“Therefore, when we rise at dawn, before we leave our bedroom we ought to give thanks to the Savior and, before all worldly actions, perform acts of piety, because he guarded us while we rested and slept in our beds.

“[Col. 0154C] . . . We ought, therefore, when we rise, to give thanks to God and perform every work of the day under the sign of the Savior. When you were still a pagan, did you not customarily seek signs, and gather with great inquiry which signs were favorable for which matters? Now I do not want you to err in the number. Know that, in the one sign of Christ, the prosperity of all things is secure. Whoever begins to sow under this sign will obtain the fruit of eternal life . . . .

“Under this name, therefore, all our actions must be directed, and the movement of our whole life referred to him, because, as the Apostle says, ‘In him we live, and move, and are.’

“But when evening closes the day, we ought to praise him with the psalter and sing his glory with measured sweetness, so that, when the contest of our works has been completed, we may seek rest as victors, and the forgetfulness of sleep may be a kind of prize for our labor.”

## VII. The basilica at Turin built at the expense of a count

Meanwhile, a basilica was being erected at Augusta Taurinorum for God Almighty at the expense of a count. Vitalianus and Maianus, although obscure men, yet full of religious devotion and piety, contributed to its completion both their own care and whatever money they could provide. When it had been completed and finished, Maximus considered it his duty to speak publicly about the church, built, furnished, and adorned so magnificently, and to pursue the praises of those who had expended so much care, labor, and money on it.

Accordingly, in Sermon 112, p. 683 ff., he says:

“If the centurion who built the synagogue is commended to the Lord, how much more commendable is the man who built a church? . . . If, therefore, the centurion was justified on account of a fragile or earthly work, then our most illustrious and provident count must surely be justified on account of so enduring and heavenly a work. Just as this count is superior to the centurion in rank, so ought he also to be more devoted in faith.

“A wise and religious count, who serves the Savior as much as he serves the emperor in war, and who hastens to rescue captives from the hands of enemies, hastens all the more to free himself from the devil’s sacrilege. . . . Wise, I say, is the man who, just as he is the emperor’s count, so desires to be Christ’s companion. For by acting well and religiously, he wishes his dignity to be everlasting. . . .

“The centurion excuses himself and declares himself unworthy that the Lord should enter under his roof. Behold, our count is worthy, under whose roof the Savior enters today . . . .

“[Col. 0155C] But what shall I say about our brothers, the holy men Vitalianus and Maianus? I know that they do not seek glory from human beings, but from God alone. Nevertheless, even if I remain silent, their works themselves speak their praise. Whatever we praised shortly before in others belongs to their praise as well. For although many constructed this tabernacle, these men provided the expense with one accord. And with what expense, since they are of modest and limited means in the world? With that, namely, of which the Apostle says: ‘The abundance of faith and the riches of simplicity.’

“For holy men themselves are always rich in their poverty. Hence I believe that these blessed men built this church no less with prayers than with expenditures. For it was fitting that Christ’s work should grow more through prayers than through masonry. They spent their entire substance on the construction of this work, and yet they themselves certainly lack nothing.

“[Col. 0155D] This is plainly, as we have said, a rich and wealthy poverty, which spends everything and possesses everything. But it has been blessed by God, like that widow of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘This poor widow has put in more than all the others; for all these gave out of their abundance, but she put in all the living she had.’”

[Col. 0156A]

## VIII. How diligent Maximus was in instructing his flock in the faith against the Pelagians

After Zosimus [Note: [Col. 0155D] Compare what Marius Mercator writes about the gathering of the Fathers under Zosimus, *Commonitorium*, chap. 31; and Garner, Dissertation 2, which concerns the synods against the Pelagians, Synod 9, vol. XII of the works of St. Augustine, Antwerp edition, 1700, and Synod 14, p. 133.], and subsequently under Leo [Note: [Col. 0155D] See Letter 6 of St. Leo, chap. 2, p. 31, vol. II of the works, Rome edition, 1755.], the supreme pontiffs, episcopal gatherings are known to have been held in Italy against the Pelagians. Whether Maximus attended them is unknown. We do know this: no opportunity for instructing his flock was neglected by the holy bishop, so that the flock might readily guard itself even against wolves of this kind.

When the Pelagians had asserted that there was no original sin and that Adam alone had injured himself, not the human race [Note: [Col. 0155D] See the acts of the Synod of Diospolis, vol. I of the *Councils*, p. 2011, Paris edition, 1714, and the Synod of Milevis, canon 2, p. 1217, same volume], Maximus often and at length fortified the people against this false doctrine, as is clear from the passages we cited in no. 19 of our preface.

Again, when those same heretics contended that God’s grace is given according to our merits, the holy bishop, instructing his people, said:

“It must be noted that the grace of the Holy Spirit is not bound by law or held by the bond of necessity, but, just as the Spirit blows where it wills, so he freely distributes his gifts to whom he wills” [Note: [Col. 0156D] Sermon 61, p. 554.].

He added:

“We must take care not to claim for our own virtue and wisdom anything that we do rightly, since the Lord says to his apostles: ‘For without me you can do nothing.’ This saying warns us that we must hope for everything from him. Everything that turns out successfully must also be attributed to his gifts; without him, as he himself says, we can have absolutely no success in any of our desires” [Note: [Col. 0156D] Sermon 67, p. 571.].

He continued to teach that we have been redeemed not by works but by grace itself [Note: [Col. 0156D] Sermon 107, p. 672.]; and that we must complete all our actions with Christ as our companion or witness, in this way: we do good things with him as their author and avoid evil things because of his companionship . . . [Note: [Col. 0156D] Homily 89, p. 297.] Christ, moreover, is a helper in good things and a protector, or agent, in evil things, so that we may avoid them.

We could present many more examples, but a limit must be imposed. With equal diligence he acted against the Nestorian heresy, which arose and was condemned in his own times. On this matter, see what we have included in part II, no. 3 ff., of our preface.

Then, when Eutyches attempted to spread the poison of his error, he was refuted and condemned especially by the celebrated and divine letter of Pope Leo the Great to Flavian, and he deserved that the holy Council of Chalcedon, held in the year 451, should adhere to the sentence already delivered by Leo himself [Note: [Col. 0156D] See Letter 78, formerly 77, of St. Leo to the bishops of Gaul, chap. 4, p. 278, vol. II of the works, Rome edition, 1755.].

When the holy pontiff had informed the bishops of the province of Milan about this matter and, in addition, about the return of the legates of the Apostolic See from Chalcedon, they assembled in synod in that same year. Under the presidency of Eusebius, bishop of Milan, they replied to the pontiff that they had followed the form of his letter and observed the manner of the prescribed arrangement, and so forth [Note: [Col. 0156D] Compare the acts of the synod, chap. 3, ibid., p. 280.].

Maximus was among those bishops. His subscription is read in the acts of that synod:

“I, Maximus, bishop of the Church of Turin, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, pronouncing anathema upon those who have held impious opinions concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation” [Note: [Col. 0157D] Ibid., p. 281.].

## IX. Attila, king of the Huns, invades Italy. Terrified by this, the people of Turin, at Maximus’s urging, take refuge in prayers and fasts and avert the danger

Attila, king of the Huns, as has been demonstrated above, invaded Italy in the year 452. After conquering, plundering, and destroying Aquileia and laying waste the entire surrounding region, he killed some of the inhabitants and reduced others to miserable servitude. When the people of Turin learned of this, they too began to fear for themselves.

Maximus, who saw how great a danger was threatening [Note: [Col. 0157D] Homily 86, p. 287 ff.], urged them, if they wished the enemy’s assault to be turned away from them, to arm and fortify themselves with faith and heavenly weapons. He taught that this alone was a refuge of salvation amid so great a danger.

[Col. 0157B] He urged them to remember David, who overthrew Goliath not with a weapon but by invoking the divine name, and, after cutting off and taking away his head, crushed the Philistines’ boldness.

Not long afterward, when the report spread that Attila was advancing and was everywhere giving examples of his cruelty, the people of Turin, although they had already stationed defenses on the walls and taken care to fortify the city gates [Note: [Col. 0157D] Ibid.], nevertheless, disturbed by an even greater fear, wondered where the approaching enemy would break through.

To raise their spirits and strengthen them in the hope of averting the barbarian fury, Maximus ascended the platform and addressed the assembly. He again recalled the example of David. He ordered them to remember the Psalmist’s declaration: the city’s guards keep watch in vain unless God is willing to be its guardian and defender. Let them open the gates of righteousness. By prayer, fasting, [Col. 0157C] and generous gifts to the needy, let them make God himself favorable to them [Note: [Col. 0157D] Homily 87, p. 291.].

The less the barbarian diminished his fury and cruelty, the more the citizens’ terror increased. Some of them were so disturbed in mind that, believing that our people were being overcome by the Huns through evil arts, they forgot religion and [CLIV] faith and sought from wicked demons a means of salvation.

Maximus summoned the people [Note: [Col. 0158D] Homily 88, p. 253 ff.] and complained that there were men who, although they boasted that they had enrolled themselves in the Christian army, nevertheless, through fear of suffering the loss of their property, were so cast down in spirit that they seemed to prefer their possessions, which might perish, to their own eternal blessedness.

He presented himself to them as the one who urged them not to forget Christ’s words: that they should not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. [Col. 0157D] Why should they distress themselves, or why fear that their cattle, silver, and patrimony would be taken from them—things that plague, robber, or enemy could carry off, and that they themselves would one day lose together with this mortal life?

Let them give themselves to Christ; let them obey him; let him alone occupy their hearts—him whom neither robber can plunder, nor enemy carry away, nor captivity separate from them.

Then, turning his address to those who trusted that wicked demons would be their help, he rebuked them severely. He said that the wretched people did not know what they were doing or saying: even if they did not immediately lose the temporary things they possessed, they would certainly and miserably lose their souls forever. Let them come to their senses. Let them learn, when they rejoice in prosperity, also to bear without complaint whatever adversities might occur; and let them persuade themselves that both kinds of events proceed from the hands of the most beneficent and most powerful God. Let them earnestly and vigorously strive to appease his anger by prayer, fasting, and almsgiving. If they did this, let them hope that thereafter everything would turn out well for them.

But when the barbarians continued advancing farther, Maximus thought that their assault could be delayed by stricter abstinence and the observance of fasts. Accordingly, he preached from the platform. He set before them the example of the Ninevites and urged the people of Turin to imitate them. Thus he proposed that an embassy to God should be sent through fasting [Note: [Col. 0158D] Homily 90, p. 301 ff.].

[Col. 0158B] Nevertheless, the barbarian had already stormed Milan, and within a short time seemed likely to bring his standards into Turin. From this there arose an incredible terror among the people of Turin, a great part of whom, unwilling to see themselves and their families treated with the cruelty that the enemy had inflicted upon the people of Aquileia, were preparing to secure their own safety and that of their possessions by flight. At so critical a time, with the enemy so near and affairs in such confusion, Maximus not only did not lose heart, but also strengthened his fellow citizens and dissuaded them from their resolve to flee. He appointed a day for an address. On that day, when the citizens had assembled in the basilica, he vehemently reproved them because, distrusting God, they were planning to leave their homeland. They should consider those unworthy of the name of children who abandoned a mother brought into peril of her safety. They should not suppose that, if they departed, they or their children would be safer or less unhappy. Wherever they might finally go, they should know that they would suffer the utmost poverty. For whom would they expect to be so generous toward foreigners and exiles as to prefer assisting needy citizens who were strangers to him rather than those who were his own? Let them cease from sinning and implore God’s help. Thus, he assured them: if they acted in good faith, the city would not perish. But if there were some who distrusted themselves, why did they not trust the prayers of their fellow citizens? Did they think so badly of their homeland that they supposed there was not a single well-conducted and pious citizen whom it could nourish? Yet if there were people of distinguished piety, why should they not rightly believe that, if there had been ten just men in Sodom, God would not have destroyed that city; and why should they not believe that Turin would be saved because of its many just men [Note: [Col. 0158D] Homily 91, pp. 305 ff.]?

Let them place their hope in God, and, relying upon it, call to arms—the arms with which he himself commands us to be equipped. Prayers, fasts, and mercy are that kind of arms [Note: [Col. 0158D] Homily 92, pp. 307 ff.]. After he had in this way raised up and revived those who had been almost lifeless with fear, and had induced them, once they had taken up such weapons, to march out under their standards, the outcome of the war demonstrated that he had promised his fellow citizens nothing in vain. For none of the historians of old wrote that the war had been prolonged as far as Turin. Indeed, the resources of the people of Turin were not diminished; rather, they had abundant money with which to enlarge their estates. From this anyone may infer that the barbarians not only refrained from injuring the people of Turin and from wrongdoing, but also withdrew their advance and, not long afterward, returned to their own people in Pannonia.

Some report that Maximus went to Attila and obtained from him a promise that he would neither besiege the city nor ravage the fields of the people of Turin. But although these writers are recent, and perhaps report the truth, they rely upon no ancient record by which they could prove what they relate. This much is certain: the people of Turin bought up the goods which, contrary to human and divine law, the barbarians had seized from neighboring peoples and perhaps also from some of their own citizens. Maximus was deeply troubled by this. Therefore he is said to have addressed them in the following terms [Col. 0159B] [Note: [Col. 0159D] Homily 96, p. 324]:

“Scripture says to the children of Israel: ‘Do not touch what has been seized by a beast,’ etc.; and by this account anyone who takes what the beast has left is worse than the beast. Tell me, then, Christian: why have you taken possession of the booty left behind by bandits? … But perhaps you say that you bought it, and therefore escape the charge of avarice. A purchase and sale is not ordinarily valid in such circumstances. It is good to buy—but in peace, what is sold voluntarily, not in plunder. Consider the origin of the contract, the seller, and the amount of the price, and you will understand that you are more a buyer of plunder than of something sold. For where did the barbarian get necklaces of gold and gems? Where does a skin-clad man get silken garments? Where, I ask, do you obtain Roman slaves? We know that these belong to our provincials or citizens. Let him therefore act as a Christian and a citizen, who bought for the purpose of returning what he bought.”

Thus he reproved those who had enlarged their household goods through the loss of others, and taught that what had been taken from their owners by force and snatched away by the barbarians ought to be restored to them.

### X. Maximus’ compassion for the needy and his other virtues

Scarcely a year, and a little more, had passed since Attila’s return to Pannonia when, because of an extraordinary drought, the people of Italy were reduced to a shortage of grain and crops and seemed unable to endure the famine. It is difficult to estimate how greatly Maximus then displayed compassion and generosity toward his people. For he demonstrated in reality how outstanding he was in that virtue which he had always commended to others in the strongest terms. He hurried to citizens whose poverty was more severe and assisted them with whatever means he could. Nor did he do this only then: he did so continually from the time when he had begun his episcopate, and especially in the year 450, when all Italy had likewise been afflicted by a scarcity of grain.

Moreover, since he was so constituted that he judged himself bound to lead the clergy and people no less by example than by words, he lived in such a way that he excelled in religion, love of God and neighbor, justice, courage, temperance, self-restraint, generosity—in every virtue, finally—and that he appeared never to command by speech anything he had not first accomplished by his own deeds.

[Col. 0160A] ### XI. The Vandal Genseric comes to Italy with an army. Maximus urges the terrified people of Turin to take refuge in God

When the emperor Valentinian III had been treacherously deprived of empire and life in the year 455 by Petronius Maximus, and when this same Petronius had been proclaimed emperor and had reluctantly and against her will married Eudoxia, the widow of Valentinian, she, in order to avenge the injury inflicted upon her and her husband’s death, secretly sent a trusted man to Carthage to Genseric, king of the Vandals, with letters asking him to assemble a large army, march against Rome, and restore her to freedom. Genseric crossed over into Italy with all possible speed, moved no longer by a desire to obey the empress but by the hope of booty, which he knew for certain would be abundant.

When, after this became known, Petronius had been killed by the soldiers and Roman people, and the Vandal had brought the City under his power and plundered it, and had decided to carry the empress away to Africa as a captive, the region was filled with barbarians; and the people of Turin, consequently, had again begun to fear. Then the holy bishop addressed the people in a crowded church as follows [Note: [Col. 0159D] Homily 6, p. 20]:

“Let us approach God with pure acts of worship. And because we are distressed by the clashing weapons of foreigners, stirred up by the discord of kings who are at variance, we ought not therefore to celebrate with joy the mysteries of the Lord’s Nativity; rather, let us venerate those same mysteries with fitting joy, entreating God that in his mercy he may deign to free and preserve us from these dangers.”

[Col. 0160C] ### XII. The principal basilica of the city of Milan, destroyed by the Huns, is restored by Bishop Eusebius. At his summons and request Maximus addresses the people

Meanwhile, the Milanese basilica which the fury of the Huns had destroyed was restored through the care and diligence of Bishop Eusebius. When Maximus had come there for the dedication, summoned and invited at Eusebius’ own request, he delivered an address entitled *On the Restoration of the Milanese Church* [Note: [Col. 0160D] Homily 94, pp. 315 ff.]. In it he treated of God’s justice toward the guilty and of his mercy toward those who repent and do good. He said that the temple of so great a city had been restored, chiefly through the efforts of Eusebius himself. He recalled that Eusebius’ grief had been turned into joy. Finally, he advised the people to pray that, just as the vengeance of the angry God had not been lacking toward the citizens, so the mercy of the propitious God might continue toward them.

After returning from there to Turin, Maximus never allowed any interruption to occur in his instruction and proper formation of the people.

### XIII. Maximus comes to Rome in 465 and takes part in the synod convened by Pope Hilary

In the year 465 he went to Rome and the apostolic see. Since, as is clear from his homilies and sermons [Note: [Col. 0160D] See our preface, no. 32, p. 115], his devotion to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, was outstanding, there can be no doubt that he often approached his tomb to pay worship and honor and to offer prayers.

At that time Hilary was bishop of the holy Roman Church. He had been informed by a letter from Ascan(i)us, bishop of Tarragona, that Silvanus, bishop of Calahorra, had disregarded ecclesiastical laws and the regulations of the apostolic see and, acting on his own authority and without regard for the metropolitan bishop, had imposed hands upon some unwilling and resisting presbyter, and had appointed him bishop over peoples who belonged to another diocese, although they had not even suspected that such a thing was being contemplated.

Therefore, in order to satisfy both his office and Ascanius, who had appealed to the faith commended by the apostolic voice and had earnestly requested that the see of Peter decide what ought to be done in this matter, the same pontiff convened a synod at the church of the blessed Mary, in the consulship of Flavius Basiliscus and Herminericus, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December [Note: [Col. 0161B] *Councils*, vol. II, pp. 799 ff., Paris edition of 1714. See also our preface, no. 32, p. 115].

Maximus was present and, after Hilary, was asked first to give his opinion [Note: [Col. 0161B] Ibid., p. 801, and our preface, no. 32, p. 116]. From this opinion anyone can perceive how wisely, nobly, and truly he understood the authority of the Roman bishop. I shall not pursue this subject at length: both the size of the commentary prevents it and caution counsels me not to discuss again matters that I have treated more fully elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0161B] Our preface, no. 32, p. 26].

### XIV. The death of Saint Maximus

It is uncertain whether Maximus died in that same year or lived longer. Some think that he died on the seventh day before the Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 0161B] The Roman Martyrology, under the seventh day before the Kalends of July; Cardinal Baronius in his notes on the same place in the Roman Martyrology, where he also mentions that Bellini of Padua, of the Order of Hermits of Saint Augustine, assigns the same date in his *Martyrology*, Venice edition. The Bollandists likewise observe that this date is assigned in the Hagenau manuscript and by Johannes Molanus, theologian of Louvain, who published at Louvain in 1573 the *Martyrology of Usuard*, illustrated with his annotations, printed by Hieronymus Vellaeus in 1777. Galesinius does not differ, as is perfectly clear from his *Martyrology* under 25 June, Venetian edition of 1758. See also Ferrarius, *Catalogue of the Saints*, Milan edition of 1613, under 25 June.].

The people of Turin relate, on the basis of what was handed down to them by their ancestors, that the body of the holy bishop was buried in the church of Saint John the Baptist at Collegno, a church which he had frequently visited during his lifetime to pray. That place is five thousand paces from the city of Turin. Yet no monument of Maximus exists there. This should not seem surprising, since that church, once destroyed, was restored only after a long interval.

[Col. 0161]

## TESTIMONIES OF ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS CONCERNING THE WRITINGS OF SAINT MAXIMUS, BISHOP OF TURIN

### GENNADIUS

From the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*

[Col. 0161C]

Maximus, bishop of the Church of Turin, sufficiently devoted to the divine Scriptures and capable of instructing the people extemporaneously, composed treatises in praise of the apostles, a homily on John the Baptist, and a general homily on all the martyrs. He also expounded many passages from the chapters of the Gospels and from the Acts of the Apostles with great wisdom. He composed two treatises on the life of Saint Eusebius, bishop and confessor of Vercelli; and he published a special book on the grace of baptism concerning Saint Cyprian. He wrote on avarice, hospitality, the eclipse of the moon, almsgiving, the passage written in Isaiah, “Your tavern-keepers mix water with wine,” the Passion of the Lord, the fast of the servants of God, [Col. 0161D] the special fast of Lent and the fact that one should not engage in games during it, Judas the betrayer, the cross of the Lord, his tomb and his resurrection, the Lord accused and condemned before Pilate, and the Kalends of January.

He also wrote homilies on the Nativity of the Lord; many homilies on the Theophany, Easter, and Pentecost; on the need not to fear carnal enemies; on giving thanks to God after eating; on the repentance of the Ninevites; and I have read many other homilies of his on various subjects, [Col. 0162C] [Note: [Col. 0161D] The same codex of the Regia Library reads: “which I do not retain.”] which I retain.

He died during the reigns of Honorius and Theodosius the Younger, in the year 420 from the redemption of the world [Note: [Col. 0162D] The same codex reads “during the reign.” It lacks the words “in the year from the world,” etc.].

### HONORIUS OF AUTUN, TWELFTH CENTURY

From *The Lights of the Church*, or *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, book XX, chapter 20

Maximus, bishop of the Church of Turin, a man sufficiently devoted to the divine Scriptures, composed treatises in praise of the apostles, a homily on John the Baptist, and a general homily on all the martyrs. He also expounded many passages from the chapters of the Gospels and from the Acts of the Apostles with great wisdom. He composed two treatises on the conduct of Saint Eusebius, bishop and confessor of Vercelli. He published a book on Saint Stephen and on the grace of baptism, and works on avarice, hospitality, the eclipse of the moon, [Col. 0162D] almsgiving, the Passion of the Lord, the special fast of Lent, and the Kalends of January; many homilies on the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, Easter, and Pentecost; and many other works. He flourished under Theodosius.

[Col. 0163A] Maximus, bishop of Turin, was most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in explaining homilies to the people, second to none in his time. [Col. 0163B] — *On the Words of Isaiah*, book 1. — *On the Fast of Lent*, book 1. — *On the General Fast of the Servants of God*, book 1. — *On Judas the Betrayer*, book 1. — *On the Cross of the Lord*, book 1. — *On the Tomb of the Lord*, book 1. — *On the Office of the Mass*, book 1. — *On the Accusation of the Lord*, book 1. — *Four Homilies on the Resurrection of the Lord*. — *Three Homilies on Saint Lawrence*. — *One Homily on Saint Stephen*. — *One Homily on the Kalends of January*. — *Three Homilies on the Nativity of the Lord*. — *Two Homilies on the Epiphany*. — *Three Homilies on Easter*. — *Three Homilies on Pentecost*. — *One Homily on the Repentance of the Ninevites*. — *One Homily on the Need Not to Fear Carnal Enemies*. — *On Giving Thanks after Eating*.

He also wrote many other works—sermons and treatises, letters and homilies—which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, [Col. 0163C] in the year of the Lord 420, and died under Theodosius the Younger.

The notes state: “Indeed, he was still present at the Roman council in the year of Christ 465.”

### JOHANNES GYMNICUS

To the religious and most learned man Damianus Ascendius, of the Order of Saint Benedict, at Saint Pantaleon in Cologne, in the year 1535

Much will that praiseworthy intention of yours deserve among sincere devotees of true and Christian religion, excellent and most learned Damianus: your intention to seek out and present the monuments of ancient writers, especially of those who can oppose antidotes to the evils which, in the present lamentable condition of affairs, grow one from another. Those who discover rare and new things, sometimes even harmful or at least not very useful, are received with great applause; they win fame among men of letters, and also gratitude, if they exercise their talents in secular studies or in any way benefit them. For who—and who indeed does not eagerly favor those who labor to discover in pagan writers what we seek, even though it may contribute little to Christian piety?

Certainly, people ought not to be deprived of the praise due to them for contributing in some measure to public affairs and to posterity through what they accomplish, whether prompted by a desire for fame or induced by payment, provided only that the common good is obtained. But with how much greater goodwill shall we pursue the efforts, and with how much greater generosity shall we rejoice in the success, of those who judge that they must undertake this labor in order to restore, enrich, and defend that Christian and true philosophy—without which all wisdom is folly!

Would that we were all of such a mind that we doubted no more over what was lost in the works of any pious Christian writer than over what Greece or Latium has lost in its pagan authors; indeed, that we regarded as a greater discovery whatever increases piety than if we had enriched and rescued from destruction some body of knowledge.

Therefore, excellent Damianus, I believe that no small debt is owed to you by all lovers of truth, because you have given us, for the benefit of students, a most learned writer, no less eloquent, anything but a novice—indeed, to say it once and for all, a divine and consummate writer—to be printed: Saint Maximus, bishop and theologian, supreme in both respects. If antiquity commends him—that is, if the approval of the Christian Church over so many years has weight—he holds a place so much below the blessed Jerome and Ambrose only because he lived later than those whom he follows closely.

He is unquestionably a man most worthy of being brought out of the obscurity in which he has hitherto lain. For, besides the purity and sweetness of his language, by which he holds the reader through a certain quality of his own; besides the sharpness of his judgments, in which he is wholly engaged; the abundance and discernment of his citations; the strength of his arguments; and his severity in rebuke and gravity in exhortation—he possesses a singular treasury of refutations and a testimony against the errors of this age.

What could the best and most conscientious people wish more concerning concord among Christians, the worship and veneration of the saints, the authority of the Church, almsgiving, and fasting than what Maximus the bishop has asserted and confirmed, neither lightly nor superstitiously? But I am wasting time praising an author who will himself commend himself so fully to the pious reader that we shall seem to have said nothing about him.

Nor should anyone entertain any doubt that there is nothing spurious in this work, since Gennadius in his catalogue, and Abbot Trithemius after him, number it among his other works; and all these writings agree so well among themselves, and also with those published in earlier years and those still with us awaiting publication, that even if fraud had been committed in the title, the quality of the discourse could expose the deception. On this point we are content with the testimony of the great Erasmus; but if you do not wish to see it through the eyes of others, examine everything for yourself.

Farewell, most learned Damianus, and if any remainder of this writer is in your possession, see that it soon comes to light. For what benefit is there in things hidden away? Students of Christian theology will consider themselves greatly indebted to you. From our printing house in Cologne, in the year 1535 from the Virgin’s birth, on the Ides of May.

### SIXTUS OF SIENA

Maximus, bishop of the Church of Turin, highly skilled in the sacred Scriptures and an admirable extemporaneous preacher, wrote elegant homilies on various passages of both Testaments. He died under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 420.

### ROBERT CARDINAL BELLARMINE

From *On Ecclesiastical Writers from the Year of the Lord 400 to the Year 500*, Venetian edition of 1728, with a dissertation by Philippe Labbe

[Col. 0165A]

Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, flourished and died during the reigns of Honorius and Theodosius the Younger, according to Gennadius in his *Book on Illustrious Men*. His homilies were published at Rome in 1564. The titles of the homilies to be listed below follow.

“We have said,” Bellarmine writes, “that many sermons are attributed both to Saint Ambrose and to Saint Maximus. But it is more credible that even those attributed to Ambrose belong to Saint Maximus. For Gennadius enumerates nearly all of Saint Maximus’ sermons, and among them are some that are attributed to Ambrose, although the error is not a serious one, since both authors [Col. 0165B] are learned, holy, and ancient.”

## PHILOLOGICAL AND HISTORICAL DISSERTATION

Contained in Bellarmine and taken from Philippe Labbe

Saint Maximus of Turin in the Subalpine region flourished under Honorius, who died in 423, and Theodosius the Younger, who died in 450. Chronologists do not agree among themselves concerning the year of his death. Some wish him to have died before 423, or at any rate before 450, because Gennadius, in chapter 40 of his *Catalogue*, said that Maximus died during the reigns of Honorius—or, if that is removed, at least while Theodosius II was reigning.

But Gennadius, in the edition of Miraeus which I use, presents, in place of *moritur* (“he dies”), which occurs in certain other editions, the reading *floruit* (“he flourished”). This does no harm to the commoner and more certain opinion of Baronius and others who think that Maximus took part in the Milanese synod held under the emperor Marcian and in the Roman synod of 465, under Pope Hilary, after whom he signed first.

The Roman Martyrology commemorates him on 25 July. Gennadius, who in the cited passage reports many noteworthy things about him; Honorius, chapter 40, book I, who, without mentioning Honorius, says that he flourished only under Theodosius; Johannes Trithemius, who asserts that he died under Theodosius; Vossius, who thinks that Gennadius should be read as saying “under the reigns of Odoacer and Theodoric”—to say nothing of the others. His homilies were published both separately, at Cologne, Rome, and elsewhere, and in the libraries of the ancient Fathers.

Here I shall present to you, reader, the Paris edition of 1623. Before doing so, I shall expose for universal ridicule the claims of William Parkins and his apes, Robert Cook, Andreas Rivet, Johannes Heinrich Ottinger, and other similar heterodox writers. They reject as spurious, forged, and of no authority—or at least of uncertain authority—the sermons *On the Martyrs of Turin*, sermon 5 *On the Nativity of Peter and Paul*, and certain others. Why, they ask, should this be so? Because they are found inserted by unskilled scribes and certain half-learned compilers among the sermons of Saint Ambrose and Saint Augustine. Indeed—and I shall say nothing more severe—those who reason in this way, when they turn over manuscript codices, show themselves strangers and complete outsiders.

How much more correctly they would have spoken with Bellarmine: even if certain sermons were attributed to Augustine or Ambrose, it would not be a serious error, since each author is learned, ancient, and holy. But enough of those inelegant faultfinders; let us come to the matter promised.

Two homilies on the Advent of the Lord. — One homily on the Vigil of the Nativity. — Six homilies on the Nativity of the Lord.

Gennadius says that he read homilies on the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany, Easter, and Pentecost, as well as many others delivered on various subjects, “which I would not retain.”

The third of these, which begins “On the Advent of the Lord,” and is found as number 11 among Saint Augustine’s sermons *On the Season*, is nevertheless not to be denied to Maximus; such denial is merely the foolish ἀσυλλογιστία—“non sequitur”—of the heterodox.

[CLX] *On the Circumcision of the Lord*, or *A Rebuke on the Kalends of January*, which is mentioned by Gennadius.

Eight homilies *On the Epiphany*, or *Theophany*, of our Lord Jesus Christ, the seventh of which also discusses the baptism of Christ and is sermon 37 *On the Season* among Augustine’s works.

Seventeen homilies *On Lent, Fasting, the Cross and Passion of the Lord, the Thief, the Burial*, and other matters relating to these subjects. The one that begins “It may perhaps seem remarkable” is sermon 118 *On the Season*, although it is clear from Gennadius that Maximus composed the homily *On the Lord Accused and Judged before Pilate*.

Five homilies *On the Paschal Solemnity*, one of which, according to its position, is listed as number 126 among Augustine’s sermons *On the Season*.

*On the Litanies and the Fast of the Ninevites*, which Gennadius calls *On the Repentance of the Ninevites*.

Three homilies *On the Paschal Solemnity*. [Col. 0166C]

One homily *On the Nativity of Saint Stephen*, which is the fifth among Augustine’s sermons *On the Saints*.

One homily *On the Nativity of Saint Agnes, Virgin and Martyr*.

Three homilies *On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist*; Gennadius mentions them.

Five homilies *On the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul*. The first, which begins “Most glorious,” etc., is found among Augustine’s sermons *On the Saints*. Gennadius reports that Maximus composed treatises in praise of the apostles.

Three homilies *On the Nativity of Saint Lawrence the Martyr*; according to Gennadius.

Two homilies *On the Nativity of Saint Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli and Confessor*, on the Kalends of August; according to the same Gennadius.

Two homilies *On the Nativity of Saint Cyprian*; Gennadius mentions them.

[Col. 0166D] *On the Passage That Says, “Who Is the Greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven?”*, read on the feast days of Saint Michael. Gennadius says that Maximus expounded many passages from the chapters of the Gospels and from the Acts of the Apostles.

*On the Nativity of the Holy Martyrs of Turin, Octavius, Adventius, and Solutor.* Gennadius does not mention this explicitly, but of all the works it appears to be Maximus’ own.

*On the Common of Martyrs*: Gennadius calls this a general homily on all the martyrs.

*On the Handing Over of the Creed*, or *On Its Exposition*, one homily.

Two homilies *On Not Fearing Carnal Enemies and on Giving Thanks to God after Eating*, words taken almost exactly from Gennadius.

*On Avoiding Avarice* and *On the Passage That Says, “Everything Was Held in Common among Them.”* This is found among Ambrose’s sermon 24 *On the Words of the Apostle*; yet we learn from Gennadius that it is a genuine homily of Maximus.

A second homily on the same subject.

Two homilies *On Giving Alms*; according to Gennadius.

One *On Hospitality*; according to the same author.

One *On the Eclipse of the Moon*; according to the same author.

*On the Passage Written in Isaiah, Chapter I: “Your Tavern-Keepers Mix Water with Wine.”* Consult Gennadius, who had read almost all those homilies individually; he closes the mouths of our critics and restrains their boldness.

### JOHANNES ALBERTUS FABRICIUS

From the *Ecclesiastical Library*, Antwerp, 1639

[Col. 0167B] Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin in the Piedmontese region, listed in the Martyrology on 25 June, took part in the Milanese synod under Eusebius and in the Roman council convened by Pope Hilary, during the consulship of Basiliscus and Herminericus—that is, in the year 465. Therefore those are mistaken who write that he died during the reigns of Honorius and Theodosius the Younger. For Theodosius the Younger was reigning when Valentinian III and Gennadius Avienus were consuls, as Cassiodorus testifies in his *Chronicle*.

For the rest, the homilies of Saint Maximus had been published at Cologne in 1535 and at Rome in 1564. Among them, not a few were falsely published under Ambrose’s name, as Costerus and Bellarmine observed.

### FRANCISCUS COMBEFISIUS, O.P.

From the *Preaching Library*, Paris, 1662

[Col. 0167C] Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin in the Subalpine region, flourished under the reigns of Honorius and Theodosius the Younger, according to Gennadius as edited by Miraeus. On this calculation there is nothing to prevent his episcopate from being extended back several years, so that he could have taken part in the Milanese synod under the emperor Marcian and in the Roman council of 465 under Pope Hilary—at which, after the pope himself, he signed first, by reason of the privilege of age rather than of episcopal see.

Gennadius listed most of his sermons, and all those that came to his memory. Some of them, however, have been mixed among the sermons of Augustine and Ambrose; I have taken care to note them in their proper places. This occurred in the manner that I explained at greater length in my work on Saint Peter Chrysologus: namely, each Church selected from the collection of sermons those that seemed most useful to it, regardless of the fact that the collection itself bore the name of another writer, whose sermons were more numerous or more highly regarded. Since so many learned and holy men, not very far apart in age, have sermons whose titles vary, little is lost to them through this confusion.

Maximus’ sermons are plainly elegant and polished. I have added a new sermon for the feast of the Nativity of Saint Mary from the codices of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, bearing the title *On the Assumption of the Same Saint*. It seems more appropriate to the feast of the Annunciation; and on this occasion I thought that Cajetan, in his little work *On the Conception of Saint Mary*, ought not to be accused of falsehood for citing a passage from a sermon of Saint Maximus *On the Assumption of Saint Mary*—a sermon that does not survive for us. He may himself have encountered it under that heading, or it may have come from sources used by Capreolus, Vincent Bandellus, and others.

Whatever the truth concerning the authority of that passage or the accuracy of its title—and I do not wish to argue about these matters—I would not dare, even on the basis of an ancient codex, to assert without qualification that the sermon which I have thus produced is by Maximus of Turin.

[CLXI] ### GUILLELMUS CAVE

From *The Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, Nestorian century, Cologne of the Allobroges, 1720, p. 260

Maximus’ place of origin is uncertain. He was bishop of Turin in Subalpine Gaul, which is today called Piedmont. He flourished in the year 422. The same Maximus, apparently, took part in the Council of Orange in 441, at which several canons concerning ecclesiastical discipline were enacted. He also attended the Milanese synod of 451, when the provincial bishops were assembled to confirm by their judgment what Pope Leo had written to Flavian against Eutyches. Finally, he attended the Roman council held on the feast of Pope Hilary in 465, at which the question of bishops appointing their successors and other episcopal matters was treated. At this council our Maximus signed first after the Roman pontiff, in Baron(ius)’s view because of the prerogative of age among the bishops.

He is said to have died the following year. But where several editions of Gennadius read *moritur* (“he dies”) during the reigns of Honorius and Theodosius the Younger, Miraeus, in his edition of Gennadius, decided that *floruit* (“he flourished”) should be substituted for *moritur*; Baronius had already made the same observation before Miraeus, judging that an error had entered the manuscript.
