The homilies of Saint Maximus appeared at Cologne in 1535; at Rome in 1564, together with the works of Leo, Peter Chrysologus, and others; at Paris in 1614 and 1623; at Lyon in 1633 together with the homilies of Chrysologus; and at Cologne in 1678.

Finally, in the *Library of the Fathers* there are four homilies: *On Not Fearing Barbarians, for One Who Fears God*; *On Elisha*; *On the Ninevites*; *On the Kalends of January*; *On the Eclipse of the Moon before the Nativity of the Lord*; *On the Nativity of the Lord our Savior*; *On Heretics Who Sell Sins*; *On the Fact that Clerics Ought Not to Engage in Business*; and *On the Body of the Lord*. The Reverend Father Mabillon recently drew these from ancient codices and presented them as vindicated for our Maximus, in *Museum Italicum*, vol. I, part 2, p. 1. There he also treats at length and, as is his custom, accurately, of other homilies of Maximus that circulate under the names of Ambrose and Augustine.

### JOHANNES MABILLON

From volume I, page 2, of the *Museum Italicum*, Paris, 1687
1. We begin the second part of this volume—which may it be auspicious and fortunate—with certain unpublished homilies of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin. His eloquence and zeal for the Christian cause were so great that his published homilies deserve a clearer light. For they have been so dispersed and obscured by alien colors that even learned men doubt who their legitimate author is: some assigning one group to Ambrose, others another group to Augustine. Yet conjecture concerning them is not so difficult that they cannot eventually be restored to their author—provided someone applies diligent effort—especially under the guidance of Gennadius, who reported their subjects and titles for the most part. It is not our purpose to offer a careful critical judgment on all those homilies, whether they survive under Ambrose’s name, Augustine’s, or Maximus’s own. This task has been undertaken in part by our colleagues: both those who have already purged Augustine’s sermons, through careful selection, of intruded and spurious pieces, and others of our own associates who are preparing a new edition of Ambrose’s works. Here we shall do only what is relevant to our purpose.

2. We found most, if not all, of Maximus’s homilies in three extremely ancient codices. One is preserved at Milan in the Ambrosian Library; another at Rome, in the monastery of Santa Croce, called “in Jerusalem”; the third in the abbey of Saint Gall among the Swiss. This last codex, entirely written in majuscule letters about a thousand years ago, contains ninety-seven homilies under the following title:

“In the name of Christ begin the homilies of Saint Augustine, bishop and confessor,”

with a table of contents prefixed for the individual homilies. Most of these homilies have been published among the works of Ambrose, Augustine, and the aforementioned Maximus; yet they do not all have Ambrose, nor Augustine, as author, but all, or nearly all, have Maximus as author. Twenty-one of them are unpublished. At our request they were copied by the religious and learned Hermann Shenkius, prefect of the library of Saint Gall.

[Col. 0170C]

3. The Ambrosian codex, no less ancient, is written in Lombard script and is defective at the beginning. It contained about eighty homilies, not all the same as those in the Saint Gall codex. Some bear the title: “Of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin,” who is in truth their legitimate author.

4. The Roman codex of Santa Croce, formerly belonging to the monastery of Nonantola and acquired by Abbot Anselm before the year 800, contains seventy-three homilies, most of which are also found in the Saint Gall copy. The author’s name had been written at the front of the codex, but after it was erased, the name of Saint Ambrose was substituted. Nevertheless, the greater part of these homilies are Maximus’s, although certain others by Jerome and Augustine have been inserted under their names.

5. From these three codices, however ancient, no certain and established knowledge of all Saint Maximus’s homilies can be derived. The Saint Gall codex cites them under Augustine’s false title; the codex of Santa Croce, after the author’s name was erased, gives Ambrose’s name; and the one Ambrosian codex assigns certain pieces to Maximus, but only a few, as we shall later see. From other evidence, however—especially from Gennadius—we understand that all, or almost all, particularly those presented in the Saint Gall codex, should be attributed to Maximus. Indeed, they are so interconnected and closely joined that, once the authorship of one is established, the judgment concerning the others follows. For the author of one homily mentions the preceding homily in the next. Most of them, moreover, acknowledge Maximus as their legitimate parent, since Gennadius clearly identified them. Anyone may easily observe from the notes appended below that the homilies we are now bringing to light for the first time belong to this group.

6. Maximus, Bishop of the Church of Turin, wrote homilies on not fearing carnal enemies, as Gennadius testifies. One homily with this title appears among Maximus’s published homilies. The first of the twelve that we are about to publish has the same subject, and refers to the preceding homily in these words:

“I remember that I have often said that we ought by no means to fear these warlike disturbances.”

The homily which appears among the Ambrosian homilies *On the Saints*, number 24, should also be assigned to the same subject. In the Saint Gall codex it is entitled *On Warlike Disturbances*.

It would be easy to determine who those barbarians were, if Maximus’s age were known. But the date of his death is uncertain. If Gennadius is to be trusted, he died during the reigns of Honorius and Theodosius the Younger—that is, before the year 423, when Honorius died. Miraeus replaced *died* with *flourished*. But our extremely ancient Corbie codex, written in French script, gives preference to the earlier reading.

Nevertheless, Maximus, Bishop of Turin, signed the synodical letter of the Milanese Church to Leo the Great in 451; indeed, in 465 he attended the Roman council under Pope Hilary and signed first of all, even before the archbishops of Embrun and Milan. It must therefore be said either that there were two bishops of Turin with the same name in the same century, or, if there was only one, that Gennadius departed from the truth in specifying the date of Maximus’s death, although Gennadius lived in those times. At any rate, from the fact that Maximus signed the Roman synod immediately after the pope, it may be inferred that he was senior in age to the other bishops present at that council.

[Col. 0171C]

7. The two following homilies that we publish require the same author as the first, as is evident from their sequence. These three homilies exist in the Ambrosian and Saint Gall codices.

8. Gennadius attributes to our Maximus homilies on the repentance of the Ninevites. Among the published works there is one *On the Ninevites*, to which our fourth homily refers under these words:

“We said last Sunday about the Ninevites…”

Both are found in the same codices just mentioned.

[Col. 0171D]

9. Homily 5, *On the Kalends of January*, is designated by Gennadius in precisely these words. There is one published homily of the same title and subject; and there is likewise one among Ambrose’s works, homily 11 *On the Liturgical Year*, to which ours corresponds more closely. For the homily attributed to Maximus testifies that its hearers had long since restrained themselves from those vices of the Kalends; whereas both ours and Ambrose’s were delivered at the time in question. Moreover, in the Ambrosian codex ours follows the preceding homilies, and the next homily follows it there as well—the homily which Gennadius also records as *On the Eclipse of the Moon*. The codices of Santa Croce and Saint Gall have a different order.

10. Whether the three homilies *On the Nativity of the Lord*, a title suggested by Gennadius, ought to be preferred to those found under Maximus’s name, or admitted together with them, we prefer to leave to the judgment of others rather than decide ourselves. Nevertheless, our homilies display more substance than the others.

11. Homily 10 among ours, *On Heretics Who Sell Sins*, is found without an author’s name in one Saint Gall codex, which, as we have already said, was written by hand about a thousand years ago. Gennadius suggests no homily of Maximus under this title, unless perhaps he refers confusedly to it in these words:

“I have read many other homilies of his on different subjects, which I do not retain [or perhaps: which I do not mention].”

Since the homilies immediately preceding it in the Saint Gall codex, as well as those following it, have Maximus as author, the same judgment seems appropriate concerning this homily, especially since its style is uniform. Who those heretics were, however, is not clear to us.

[Col. 0172B]

12. Our homily 11, *Against Clerics Who Engage in Commerce*, begins with these words:

“We recently condemned clerics who engage in trade. But if we consider the matter rightly, an office is not truly a business, etc.”

This homily seems to correspond to Ambrose’s homily 56 *On the Liturgical Year*, at whose end we read:

“For a Catholic cleric too is held by this judgment. If he is not content with the stipends that, by God’s command, he receives from the altar, but practices trade, sells intercessions, and gladly accepts the gifts of widows, he may be considered a merchant rather than a cleric.”

If this is so, both homilies must be restored to Maximus. For ours clearly belongs with the homily that stands last among Maximus’s works, on the passage of Isaiah:

“Your tavern-keepers mix water with wine,”

which Gennadius explicitly identified. That homily begins with these words:

“Not inappropriately, a few days ago we explained that this priestly function retains a certain form of business, and that this clerical office is no small source of profit.”

These are the very words of our homily 11, to which this unquestionably Maximinian homily therefore refers.

13. Our homily 12 is by the same author. For Maximus, according to Gennadius, wrote *On the Lord’s Tomb*. The books of Maximus contain two works on this subject. In one of them, *On the Lord’s Cross and Burial*, number 2, words highly appropriate to our homily are reported, beginning:

“But let us consider this very body of the Lord, etc.”

These remarks concern the homilies that we shall publish below, selected from among many others.

14. In the Ambrosian codex there is one homily of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, *On the Nativity of the Holy Martyrs*. It begins as follows:

“As we know, brothers, the festival of the servants of the Lord always follows the vows of their Lord, etc.”

We do not find it among the published works. The codex then contains two homilies on Saints Alexander and Sisinnius, who, according to Paulinus, suffered martyrdom after the death of Saint Ambrose; then a homily of Saint Maximus on Saint Eusebius, martyr and Bishop of Vercelli. It begins:

“To add anything to the praise of Saint Eusebius is to detract from it, etc.”

This wording is more correct in Ambrose’s works than in Maximus’s. It is followed by:

“Likewise, a discourse delivered at Vercelli. When we gather to perform the duties owed to the revered memory of our common father Eusebius, in honor of his confession, etc.”

Then:

“Likewise, on Saint Eusebius and the Maccabees. Although my ignorance and modesty, dearest brothers, hold me back from presenting the discourse owed to your charity, etc.”

Then:

“Likewise, on Saint Eusebius the Confessor and the Maccabees. The devotion of a double festival, dearest brothers, invites us to assemble with complete eagerness for the celebration of this day, etc.”

Finally, another homily follows, beginning:

“Although, beloved brothers, I am an unworthy son and the least servant of our blessed father, the supreme priest and confessor Eusebius, etc.”

In the margin, in extremely ancient script, is written:

“Note that this man is the one from Vercelli.”

Here the catalogues of homilies contained in the three codices mentioned above ought to be presented together with critical judgment. But that would require another occasion and other leisure.

15. It is worth observing in passing that the six published books *On the Sacraments*, which are attributed to Ambrose in the editions, are inserted without an author’s name among the foregoing sermons in the Saint Gall codex, and divided into seven sermons under this title:

“Here begins the first day of Easter.”

Thus each of the six books constitutes a separate sermon for six successive days of the week; and the seventh begins at the end of the sixth book, namely with these words:

“Another of David’s Psalms, although it is a single little book, etc.”

Of perhaps greater importance is the fact that sermon 4—which in the published editions is book 4—reads as follows in the codex:

“You see, then, how effective the word of Christ is. If the word of the Lord Jesus has such power that things began to exist which did not exist, how much more effective is it in making things exist and changing them into something else?”

In the published editions the final clause reads:

“And changing the things that existed into something else.”

From these two readings Berengarius, as reported by Lanfranc in his dialogue against him, combined a single version, introducing him as speaking thus:

“Through the consecration of the altar, bread and wine become the sacrament of religion—not so that they cease to be what they were and are changed into something else, as blessed Ambrose says in the book *On the Sacraments*.”

After explaining this passage as Berengarius presented it, Lanfranc says that in certain codices the aforesaid sentence is found in other words—namely, precisely the words found in the editions just mentioned. By that time, moreover, the aforesaid work *On the Sacraments* had already been divided into six books, and Lanfranc cites it in the same form.

16. I return to Maximus, whose sermons, as they have been published under his name, for the most part have Maximus as their author. Accordingly, all those that are falsely assigned to Ambrose among his works must be restored to Maximus; very few should be attributed to Ambrose, while far more belong to Maximus.

There are also others that we cannot attribute either to Ambrose or to Maximus, but only to later authors. Such are the second and third sermons *On Advent*, sermon 22 *On Septuagesima*, and sermon 23 *On Sexagesima*. These terms were unknown not only in Maximus’s time but even in Ambrose’s; the same is true of the term *Advent* for the definite number of days customarily celebrated before the Nativity of the Lord.

Ambrose or Maximus therefore would not have said what is read at the beginning of the second sermon *On Advent*:

“This period is not improperly called the Advent of the Lord.”

Nor would they have used these words in sermon 22:

“In the whole year no day is called Septuagesima except this one; nor Sexagesima except the following Sunday; nor Quinquagesima except the third day from now.”

Certainly sermon 31 *On the Liturgical Year* does not admit Septuagesima and Sexagesima, in order to rebuke those who added Quinquagesima to Lent. A similar opposition exists between sermons 26 and 32. In the latter, only Sundays are exempted from the Lenten fast; in the former, Saturday also is exempted, according to the rite of the Church of Milan. Add that in sermon 26 the fast during Lent is prescribed only until the ninth hour. This contradicts Ambrose himself and the discipline of ancient times, when the Lenten fast could not be broken before evening.

LUDOVICO ANTONIO MURATORI,

on the sermons of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin.

*Anectoda*, volume 4, Padua, 1713

[Col. 0174B]

The manuscript codex from which I copied these sermons of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, is preserved in the Ambrosian Library, letter C, number 98. It breathes a venerable antiquity, for it seems to me to have been written about a thousand years ago. Its characters closely resemble Lombard script and are similar to those of the extremely ancient codex of Josephus, written on Egyptian papyrus and preserved in the same library as a notable monument of antiquity.

The distinguished scholar Jean Mabillon judged the age of this codex in the same way, in volume 1, page 2, of the *Museum Italicum*, in the preface to certain homilies of the same Saint Maximus that he himself first published and partly copied from this very codex. Everything that that most learned man noted there on this matter would certainly deserve to be repeated here. But I refer the reader to that work and shall briefly disclose here what belongs to my own task.

Maximus flourished in the fifth century of the Christian era. Not a few learned men think that he lived beyond the year 465, because he is found in that year attending the Roman synod under Pope Hilary. They do not place sufficient confidence in the manuscripts of Gennadius, where he is said to have died before the year 423.

Several homilies are read among the works of Saints Ambrose and Augustine which nevertheless had Saint Maximus as their author. The collectors of Saint Maximus’s works have not yet adequately distinguished them; both Mabillon’s aforementioned preface and our own undertaking will contribute substantially to that task. For we are not merely publishing many sermons that have not previously appeared; we also indicate which have already been published among the works of Saint Ambrose or of Saint Maximus himself.

I would by no means guarantee that every sermon found in the aforementioned Ambrosian codex should be assigned to Maximus of Turin. The codex is defective at its beginning, its end, and in other places; this may perhaps explain why clearer evidence concerning the author of these homilies is lacking. Moreover, certain sermons there are expressly attributed to Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, as will appear in the edition. This raises the suspicion that the others, whose author is not written there, may belong to different authors.

It is certainly well known to scholars that the ancients used to collect homilies by various writers into a single codex. Such a book was later called a *homiliary* and was available to less learned men, bishops, and sacred orators when sermons had to be delivered to the people, whether in explaining the Gospel or in presenting the praises of the saints. This plainly explains why, over the course of time, so many homilies were attributed to Saints Augustine, Ambrose, Chrysostom, and the other Fathers of the Church, although they had by no means all proceeded from those authors themselves.

Whatever the truth may be, I do not regret having brought all these materials into the public domain and having published them together under the name of Saint Maximus of Turin. I was moved both by the fact that some homilies found here do not bear Maximus’s name at their head and nevertheless unquestionably belong to him, and also by the fact that I seemed to detect throughout such similarity of style as properly indicates one and the same writer.

For the rest, sermon 1 *On Saint Alexander* has much in common and is very similar to another sermon on the same subject among the works of Saint Augustine in an ancient edition. Sermons 6, 7, 8, and 9, *On Saint Eusebius, Martyr of Vercelli*, had also previously appeared in a book entitled *Sermons and Letters of the Ancient Fathers Collected on Saint Eusebius, Bishop and Martyr of Vercelli*, commissioned by Giovanni Francesco Bonhomio, Bishop of Vercelli, and printed at Milan in 1581.

These sermons are said in our codex to have been delivered at Vercelli and therefore identify an author who lived in a church other than that of Vercelli. Yet, since I find three marginal notes attached to these same sermons:

“He shows himself to be from Vercelli”;

“Note that this man is the one from Vercelli”;

there is room for the conjecture that Saint Maximus—whose birthplace is unknown—was born at Vercelli, if he is indeed the author of those four sermons.

Nor should two sermons, numbers 32 and following, be dismissed without comment: *On Removing Idols from Private Estates*. They support the opinion of those who think that, under the first Christian emperors, pagans were called by the name “pagans” because, after their superstition had been driven from the cities and prohibited by imperial laws, it withdrew into villages and the uncultivated rural population, from which it had not yet been entirely eradicated even in Saint Maximus’s time.

There one could still see wooden altars, stone images, pallid turf, dead embers, sacrifices, and frenzied peasants secretly—so I think—making offerings of their own blood to false gods. See Baronius in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology* for 30 January, and Gothofredus in his notes on title 10 of book 16 of the *Theodosian Code*.

The same sermons mention *Domnedius*, which, in the corrupted speech of that age, was nothing other than *Dominus* (“Lord”). Saint Paulinus of Nola used this same word in more than one place, as I observed in dissertation 13, volume 1 of my *Anecdota*, to signify Saint Felix, his lord and patron.

We consider it unnecessary to compile a catalogue of the sermons of Saint Maximus edited by Muratori, since we shall indicate in their proper places what we owe to him.

LUDOVIC ELLIES DUPIN.

In the second part of volume 3 of the *Library of Ecclesiastical Writers*, Mont-Hannonia, 1691.

Maximus, Bishop of Turin, flourished during the reigns of Honorius and Theodosius. He lived until the year 465, since in that year he is found attending the Roman synod under Pope Hilary. Several of his homilies survive, the greater part of which are listed by Gennadius. Gennadius testifies that Maximus was well versed in the divine Scriptures and able to deliver extemporaneous sermons to the people with ease.

Some homilies concern the Nativity of the Lord, the Circumcision, the Epiphany, Easter, Pentecost, two Sundays of Advent, Ash Wednesday, Palm Sunday, and the Passion of the Lord. Others concern the saints: Saint Stephen; Saint John the Baptist; the holy apostles Peter and Paul; Saint Lawrence; Saint Cyprian; Saint Eusebius of Vercelli; Saint Michael the Archangel; and the holy martyrs of Turin.

There is one homily *On the Creed*, another *On Vigilance and Giving Thanks to God after Eating*, two *On Almsgiving*, one *On the Eclipse of the Moon*, and finally a sermon on the passage of Isaiah:

“Your tavern-keepers mix water with wine.”

There are seventy-three in all. Many are found among the sermons of Augustine and Ambrose, where they were wrongly attributed to those Fathers, although Saint Maximus is their author. For Gennadius mentions them, and they display one and the same style. It may be that some homilies published under the names of other Fathers will be restored to Saint Maximus.

His sermons are brief but dull; they lack ornament, elegance, and nobility. Maximus’s sermons were first published at Cologne in 1535, Antwerp in 1618, Rome in 1564 and 1572, Paris in 1614 and 1623 with the works of Saint Leo the Great, and in the *Libraries of the Fathers*. Mabillon published twelve homilies as previously unpublished, although three of them are found among Ambrose’s works.

EDMOND MARTÈNE AND URSIN DURAND,

in volume 9 of the *Collection of Ancient Writers and Monuments*, page 134, Paris, 1733. On the occasion of publishing six homilies of Saint Maximus, they preface them as follows:

In an extremely ancient codex of the monastery of Saint Gall among the Swiss, written in majuscule letters about a thousand years ago, Mabillon once discovered ninety-seven homilies of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, under the name of Saint Augustine. As he says:

“His eloquence and zeal for the Christian cause were so great that his published homilies deserve a clearer light.”

Although the Saint Gall codex bore Augustine’s name, that discerning scholar immediately detected the legitimate parentage of those homilies, both from their style and from Gennadius, who mentions many of them. He was aided especially by an extremely ancient Milanese codex in the Ambrosian Library, written in Lombard letters about a thousand years ago, in which the title “Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin” appears.

Of those homilies, the greater part had already seen the light, attributed either to Saint Ambrose, Saint Augustine, or their true author. Mabillon nevertheless found twenty-one unpublished homilies in the Saint Gall codex, of which he published twelve in volume 1 of the *Museum Italicum*. We found only six among the papers of that most learned man, and it seemed very appropriate to us to publish them here.

ANDREAS GALLANDIUS.

Volume 9 of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, etc., chapter 9, page 21, Venice, 1773.

After Gallandius has prefaced his work with what he considers useful for determining Maximus’s birthplace and origins, drawing especially from his sermons, he says the following about Maximus’s eloquence and excellence as a preacher in section 4:

That our holy bishop possessed great skill in speech is clearly established both by Gennadius’s testimony and by his own sermons, many of which the same priest of Marseilles expressly mentions. How highly his homilies were once valued is sufficiently suggested by the fact that some were attributed to Ambrose and others to Augustine, as we learn from the care and diligence of the distinguished Benedictines who, toward the end of the preceding century, published the works of Ambrose and Augustine.

But to return more closely to our present subject: besides the sermons of Saint Maximus which were published long ago as a collected group, and which were later restored to their author by the exactness [ἀκρίβεια] of learned men, the distinguished scholars Mabillon, Muratori, and Martène brought many others out of darkness. We present them together here, etc.

VINCENT OF BEAUVAIS, O.P.

In an unpublished work entitled *On Authorities*, among the other holy Fathers whose sayings the author uses in explaining various subjects, there is mention of Saint Maximus, from whom he drew several passages. The work is preserved in the Laurentian Library, codex 9, Pluteus 36, right-hand section; formerly in the library of the Conventual Friars Minor of Santa Croce. He flourished in the thirteenth century.

[Col. 0177]

SCHOENEMANN’S ACCOUNT OF SAINT MAXIMUS OF TURIN

(*Historical-Literary Library of the Latin Fathers*, volume 2.)

§ I. Life

[Col. 0177B]

If Maximus had been as distinguished by the greatness of his achievements as by his ability to preach, and if ancient memory had handed down as much about his life as he left material in his writings for reconstructing an image of his intellect and character, we would certainly not now have to complain of the poverty of our evidence, which makes it so difficult to determine accurately the period he spent in life.

This alone we know with certainty: Maximus, Bishop of Turin, signed in 451 the synodical letter of Eusebius, Bishop of Milan, to Leo the Great; and in 465 he attended the Roman council convened under Hilary, successor to Leo, signing its acts first after the Roman bishop and before the metropolitan bishops of Embrun and Milan. This should rightly be attributed not to the prerogative of his see but to the prerogative of his advanced age, since he had been ordained before the other bishops present at the synod.

From this established indication of his age, those who rely on whatever evidence they encounter in his sermons work backward to the earlier stages of his life. We shall not contest them if, from his eulogies of Saint Eusebius of Vercelli, they infer that Maximus was born and raised at Vercelli and was also ordained there, first exercising the office of preaching in that same city.

[Note: [Col. 0177D] See sermons 7, 8, and 9, *On Saint Eusebius*, and what Gallandius cites from them in the work mentioned below.]

But if, from what he says in the sermon *On the Holy Martyrs of Anaunia*, who were killed in the year 397, when commending their memory, they think it necessarily follows that he delivered that sermon either in the same year or shortly afterward, they will not have our agreement.

[Note: [Col. 0177D] Gallandius, in the Prolegomena to volume 9 of the *Library of the Fathers*, chapter 9, section 2, presses this point above all, as an argument he had recently discovered.]

Indeed, we do not even grant the second inference which they draw from the mention, in the second sermon on those same martyrs, of an imperial edict for the destruction of pagan shrines. They use it to reinforce their earlier conjecture, supposing that Maximus was referring to the constitution of Valentinian the Younger, issued on the third day before the Kalends of March, during the consulship of Tatianus and Symmachus—that is, in the year 391.

[Note: [Col. 0177D] The same, section 3. Brunus, in his *Life of Maximus* (page 138), observes in reply that Maximus might also have been referring to the law of Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian III, issued in the year 426, when the consuls were Theodosius XII and Valentinian IV.]

Those who accept this view want Maximus, when he delivered those two sermons, to have been marked by the rank of presbyter, so that his age may not be extended beyond reasonable limits if he is made a bishop as early as 397, while it is established that he was still alive in 465.

But I see no reason why he could not have referred to events mentioned in those passages as having occurred in his own time and recently, even after an interval of twenty or more years. Someone might likewise falsely infer, from the fact that in sermon 4, *On the Nativity*, he says:

“Our synodical assembly condemned the heresy of Jovinian with one voice,”

that he himself sat among the Fathers who condemned that heresy at the Council of Milan in 389.

Yet, even if we do not grant those arguments of learned men as much force as they themselves think they possess and wish others to recognize in them, we nevertheless do not deny that they contain some appearance of truth. Thus Maximus seems to have begun exercising ecclesiastical offices at the beginning of the fifth century or shortly afterward; he must therefore have been born toward the end of the fourth century and perhaps, at the age of eighty or ninety, died—as unknown as everything else about him—after completing his final day.

[Note: [Col. 0178D] Learned men long ago corrected Gennadius’s error on this point, or rather the carelessness of the copyists at that passage.]

§ II. Writings

Maximus, Bishop of the Church of Turin, says Gennadius,

“being sufficiently devoted to the divine Scriptures and capable of instructing the people extemporaneously, composed treatises in praise of the apostles, one on John the Baptist, and a general homily on all the martyrs. He also explained many passages from the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles with wisdom. He composed two treatises on the life of Saint Eusebius, Bishop and Confessor of Vercelli, and one on Saint Cyprian; he published a special book on the grace of baptism. He wrote on avarice; on hospitality; on the eclipse of the moon; on almsgiving; on what is written in Isaiah, ‘Your tavern-keepers mix water with wine’; on the Passion of the Lord; on the fasting of God’s servants; on the special fast of Lent and the prohibition of frivolity during it; on Judas the betrayer; on the Lord’s cross, his tomb, and his resurrection; on the Lord accused and condemned before Pilate; and on the Kalends of January. He also wrote homilies on the Nativity of the Lord; many homilies on the Theophany, Easter, and Pentecost; on not fearing carnal enemies and on giving thanks to God after eating; on the repentance of the Ninevites; and I have read many other homilies of his on various subjects, which I do not record [perhaps: which I do not mention].”

Trithemius gives the same information in almost the same order and with almost the same designations.

[Note: [Col. 0179D] Just as Gennadius calls some works treatises and others homilies, Trithemius divides them into books and homilies, but under both names he designates nearly the same works as Gennadius.]

Trithemius additionally mentions one book *On the Office of the Mass*, three homilies on Saint Lawrence, and one on Saint Stephen. After enumerating all these, he adds:

“He also wrote many other things—sermons and treatises, letters and homilies—which have not come to my attention.”

The ancient manuscript books plainly agree with this final assertion of both men. From them, through the repeated research of learned men, far more sermons than those explicitly praised by Gennadius and Trithemius have long since been recovered; more recently, their number has been increased by more than half in the Roman edition. Everything has been confirmed by the testimony of the oldest and best parchment manuscripts, so that no doubt can remain concerning the authenticity of the treatises here attributed to Maximus.

Let us now examine the index and arrangement of this latest edition. The editor established three classes or collections: homilies, sermons, and treatises. To these he added doubtful works or works that seemed plainly unworthy of Maximus, including two letters.

The homilies and sermons are divided and entitled in three ways: *On the Liturgical Year*, *On the Saints*, and *On Various Subjects*. These names generally designate discourses delivered on movable feast days; praises of saints, martyrs, and confessors delivered on the solemn day of their commemoration; and discourses intended to illuminate a particular passage of Sacred Scripture or delivered on certain solemn occasions.

This arrangement agrees with the earlier editions and is owed to the ancient lectionaries from which Maximus’s sermons first began to be selected. For what reasons the editor adopted it, however, he himself does not explain, nor can anyone else easily discover them. For the distinctions he adduces between homilies and sermons, drawing on Ducange, do not fit the Maximinian works and were not really required here.

[Note: [Col. 0180D] In the preface, section 28, page 37.]

The question was not so much what those words signify as by what right and on what evidence he assigned individual discourses to one collection or the other, especially since it is scarcely credible that the manuscript books served him as sufficiently consistent guides.

But here is the catalogue.

### On Various Subjects

[Col. 0181A]

LXXXIII. On the handing over of the Creed. LXXXIV. On the body of Christ. LXXXV. On what is written, “Who do you think,” etc. LXXXVI. On the tumult of war. LXXXVII. On enemies not to be feared. LXXXVIII–LXXXIX. On not fearing carnal enemies and giving thanks to God after a meal, I–II. XC. On the repentance and fasts of the Ninevites, I. XCI. On the Ninevites, II. XCII. On the barbarian not to be feared by one who fears God, and on Saint Elisha, I. XCIII. On the same Saint Elisha, II. XCIV. On the redistribution of the Milanese church, previously unpublished. [Col. 0181B] XCV–XCVI. On avarice, I–II. XCVII–XCVIII. On almsgiving and the Samaritan woman, I–II. XCIX. On hospitality. C–CI. On the eclipse of the moon, I–II. CII. The Roman editor infers from clear evidence that many of Maximus’s homilies and sermons have perished.

It was the conjecture of the Benedictines, who devoted themselves to the works of Ambrose, [Col. 0183D] that the books On the Sacraments, which commonly bear Ambrose’s name, may have had no other author than Maximus. This seemed to be supported by what Mabillon had observed shortly before: namely, that these books On the Sacraments, which are attributed to Ambrose in printed editions, are inserted without an author’s name among the sermons of Saint Maximus in the manuscript of Saint Gall, and are divided into seven sermons under the title, “Here begins the first day at Easter.” Thus each of the six books constitutes an individual sermon for as many days of the week; and the seventh begins from the final part of the sixth book with these words: “Although this may now be a little book of David’s Psalms,” etc. But the latest editor did not pay attention to this.

## § III. Editions

[Col. 0184A]

Homilies and sermons of the holy Fathers generally share this fate: either no reputation concerning their authors has reached us, or at least one that is obscure and uncertain, and the judgments of learned men have repeatedly been divided and have differed among themselves. The chief reason was that their authors did not take as much care with these meditations as they did with their other books, which we know they shared with their friends, frequently had copied, revised, and, when they reached a certain number, gathered together into one collection. Sermons, however, which they generally composed extemporaneously, were recorded only by their hearers and scarcely ever came again before the eyes of their authors.

From such collections, in which the works of perhaps more than one teacher were gathered, were subsequently made the breviaries or lectionaries of different churches. Selection was made according to what seemed most useful, either for individual Sundays, or for movable feast days and the feasts of the saints. Just as some collections were richer than others, so, as circumstances dictated, the names of the authors were sometimes supplied through the care—or negligence—of those who compiled them, and sometimes were lost. Elsewhere the name of the more important author—that is, the one whose homilies were most numerous or most distinguished—was placed at the head of the volume.

Sometimes, moreover, complete collections of the sermons of a notable preacher were compiled for the use either of churches or of private persons. But partly through fraud and partly through the carelessness of copyists, these collections were especially confused. [Col. 0184C] Above all, the homilies of Augustine, Ambrose, Maximus, and Caesarius were confused and repeatedly thrown together—not only because they were extremely numerous, but also because of a certain similarity observable even now in the style of one compared with another, such as that of Caesarius with Augustine and of Maximus with Ambrose. This is not merely a matter of opinion; as the Benedictine editors of Ambrose demonstrated concerning Maximus, it arose from imitation and a kind of rivalry.

The chief merit, therefore, of the present and the preceding century, especially at its close, was that these works were distinguished from one another and that each man was restored his true and genuine offspring. Stephen Baluzius accomplished this for Caesarius, the Benedictines for Augustine, and the same scholars for Ambrose; the brothers Ballerini for Zeno and Leo the Great; and finally, after the respectable efforts of others—which it is now my pleasure briefly to mention—Bruno Brunus for Maximus. [Col. 0184D]

Maximus’s homilies first began to be printed in the *Homiliarium doctorum*, which the deacon Paul, commonly called Alcuin, is believed once to have prepared at the command of Charlemagne. Its oldest edition appeared at Speyer in 1482 through Peter Drach; its latest, if I remember correctly, at Cologne from the press of Eucharius Cervicornus in 1530.

In the same city, in 1535, Johannes Gymnicus had seventy-four of Maximus’s homilies, which he had received from Damian Ascendiensis, abbot of Saint Pantaleon at Cologne, separately printed. They were subsequently reprinted many times in various workshops and different forms. In 1554 at Rome, in the *Chorus of Ecclesiastical Writers* edited by Peter Galesinius, they occupied the place immediately after Salvian; in 1579 they were reprinted at Cologne, with the sermons of Peter Chrysologus added; from 1613 onward, together with Leo the Great and other writers—whose collection was enlarged by Theophilus Raynaudus in 1633 and thereafter—they were printed very frequently at Paris and Lyons, and several times in the *Bibliothecae Patrum*.

Meanwhile, in 1684, the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur at Paris restored to Maximus, in volume V of the works of Saint Augustine, many sermons commonly attributed to Augustine. The most celebrated associate of that congregation, Jean Mabillon, then published in the *Museum Italicum* in 1687 twelve sermons of Maximus, almost all previously unpublished, recovered from excellent manuscripts found in Italy and Switzerland. Following the footsteps of their former colleague and taking account of other manuscripts, the editors of Ambrose enriched their edition in 1690 with a notable abundance of homilies belonging, as they thought, by right to Maximus and removed from Ambrose.

Their efforts were followed by Ludovico Antonio Muratori, who examined again the Ambrosian manuscript that Mabillon had first used and published from it a considerable number of previously unpublished texts in volume IV of the *Anecdota* in 1713. A few more were likewise extracted from Mabillon’s papers by his former associates Edmund Martène and Martin Durand, and brought out in their very extensive collection in 1733.

In 1741 and 1748 Maximus’s homilies were again printed at Venice together with the works of Leo the Great. In these two editions, perhaps the older collection was combined with these more recent additions. For in Galland’s *Bibliotheca Patrum* published at Venice in 1773, only what Mabillon, Muratori, and Martène had collected was presented.

Finally, Bruno Brunus of Rome, a cleric regular of the Pious Schools, once again brought forth from almost innumerable manuscripts all these materials and much else not previously seen, arranged them according to a new method, and furnished them with critical observations, arguments, introductory notices, and very extensive notes. This he did in the edition recently prepared at Rome in 1784 by command of Pius VI, Supreme Pontiff. Through the editor’s industry it attained as much distinction as, in appearance and splendor, it surpasses all the radiant editions of the Latin Fathers, worthy of the supreme pontiff and the king to whom it is dedicated. If you wish to know more about these matters, consult the following catalogue of the individual editions.

### 1535

Cologne, from the press of Johannes Gymnicus, octavo. A distinguished work of winter and summer homilies, both on the liturgical year and on the saints, by Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, who was truly “greatest” in delivering homilies to the people. Several highly learned and almost divine homilies of Saint John Chrysostom, previously unprinted, have been added. With an index.

The editor dedicated this little work to Damian of Ascanius, of the Order of Saint Benedict, at Saint Pantaleon in Cologne, to whom he credited the entire undertaking and whom he warmly congratulated and encouraged on this excellent opportunity of benefiting theological studies, urging him, if any remains of this author were in his possession, to see that they soon came to light.

Bruno Brunus reprinted Johannes Gymnicus’s entire letter to the religious and learned Damian in the Roman edition, [Col. 0186D] p. 158. Accordingly, I do not know how it happened that the same most learned and diligent man stated in the preface, p. 14, that Damian’s collection of Saint Maximus’s homilies was published at Cologne by Johannes Gymnicus in 1535 only because Damian, prevented by death, had been unable to bring it to light himself.

The following homilies are included in the winter section on the liturgical year: On the coming of the Lord, I–II. On the vigils of the Nativity of the Lord, I. On the Nativity of the Lord, I–VI. On the Circumcision of the Lord, or a rebuke concerning the calends of January, I. On the Epiphany of the Lord, I–VIII. On Ash Wednesday, I. On the fast of Lent, I–IV. On Palm Sunday, on the verse of the Psalm, “My God, my God, look upon me,” I. On the accusation of the Lord before Pilate, I–II. On Judas the traitor, I. On the passion, cross, and burial of the Lord, I–IV. On the holy thief, the apostle Peter, and the maidservant at the gate, I–IV.

The homilies of the summer section on the liturgical year are: On the Easter solemnity, I–V. On the litanies and the fasts of the Ninevites, I. On the solemnity of Pentecost, I–III.

The winter and summer homilies on the saints are: On the feast of Saint Stephen, I. On the feast of Saint Agnes, I. On the feast of Saint John the Baptist, I–III. On the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, I–V. On the feast of Saint Lawrence the martyr, I–III. On the feast of Saint Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, I–II. On the feast of Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr, I–II. On the feast day of Saint Michael, I. On the feast of the holy martyrs of Turin, I.

Finally, the homilies on various subjects are: On the exposition of the Creed, I. On not fearing carnal enemies and giving thanks after a meal, I–II. On avoiding avarice, I–II. On giving alms, I–II. On hospitality, I. On the eclipse of the moon, I. On that passage of Isaiah, “Your tavern-keepers mix water with wine,” I.

The total is seventy-four homilies, including twelve by Chrysostom and one additional homily by Origen. The index promised in the title is nothing other than the index of these same homilies, each identified by its opening words. The testimony of Gennadius is prefixed.

### 1555

Basel, through Hieronymus Froben and Nicolaus Episcopius, folio. Sermons of Saint Maximus of Turin, among those commonly called Ambrosian, in volume III of the works of Ambrose in the Erasmian–Costerian edition, pp. 225–323.

These sermons did not first appear in this edition of Ambrose; they also appear in the first Erasmian edition and had been printed in the earlier Basel editions. Anyone who wishes may count all of these among the editions of Maximus. But since it matters less to us to know everything printed here and there from Maximus’s meditations under the tacit name of the author or even under another’s name than to know what originally bore his name or was gradually restored to him, we mention this Costerian edition while passing over the others, since it was there that an author was first assigned to each individual sermon. It was Coster’s work, not Erasmus’s.

The latest editor, Bruno Brunus, should therefore be corrected. In the preface to the Roman edition (§ 4, p. 15), he praises Erasmus’s diligence in distinguishing Maximus’s works and comparing them with manuscript codices, relying evidently not on his own eyes but on Casimir Oudin, whose passage, however, he did not correctly understand when he quoted it in his own words. Erasmus stated nothing more than that these sermons were spurious and had nothing of the Ambrosian vein. Coster, however, attributed most of them to Maximus, both on the authority of manuscripts and on that of printed editions. Oudin confirms this in the passage cited, being wrong only in saying that Coster attributed all of them to Maximus. As for the extent to which Coster’s Cologne edition of Maximus’s sermons was useful, and how carefully he examined the manuscripts in this matter, others may judge.

### 1564

Rome, at the house of the Roman people, through Paolo Manuzio, son of Aldus, folio. Homilies of Maximus of Turin, together with Salvian’s eight books *On True Judgment and the Providence of God* and other works by Pacianus, Sulpicius Severus, Dorotheus, and Haymo of Halberstadt, edited by Peter Galesinius, pp. 85–181.

We mentioned this edition in the first volume of our work, in connection with Pacianus; nor did Maximus gain more from it than Pacianus did. No notes were added; the homilies were simply reprinted from Gymnicus’s edition, with the same index and testimony of Gennadius also prefixed.

Bruno Brunus informs us that two editions of this collection of the Fathers, published by Galesinius, exist in the same year, type, and format. He says that the first was available to him in preparing the latest collection from the library of the Florentine College of Saint John the Evangelist, while he found the other, much more perfect and complete, at Rome. He adds that he could not sufficiently marvel that Galesinius had passed it over in silence, nor less that he had entirely failed to mention Gymnicus’s edition. As for the latter point, however, one will not be so surprised after learning that Galesinius makes no mention at all of any earlier edition.

### [1579]

Notable winter and summer homilies alike of Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, together with sermons of Peter Chrysologus, here published for the first time in Germany. The index of sermons that had been added in the first edition is absent.

Muratori praises this edition in the preface to the sermons he himself published in the *Anecdota*, among which are those four, numbered VI, VII, VIII, and IX among the sermons on the saints. ### 1684

Paris, through François Muguet, folio. Several homilies of Maximus, separated from the Augustinian works and marked by the Maurist Fathers in the appendix of spurious sermons in volume V of Augustine’s works.

Namely, in the first class, sermons on passages of the Old and New Testament:

1. Sermon 80 on Matthew 27, concerning Judas the traitor, attributed to Maximus both in manuscript and printed copies; formerly *On the Liturgical Year* 128, and afterward Appendix 48.

2. Sermon 82 on the words of the Gospel of Luke 3: “They came,” etc., attributed to Maximus by the Louvain scholars; formerly *On the Words of the Lord* 19, afterward Appendix 3, and also among the Ambrosian sermons. The Benedictines nevertheless doubt whether Maximus was its author.

3. Sermon 100 on the words of Acts 4: “No one said that anything of what he possessed was his own”; formerly *On the Words of the Apostle* 25, and afterward Appendix 9. It was also published among the Ambrosian and Maximus sermons and is attributed to Maximus by Vindingus as well as by the Louvain scholars.

In the second class, sermons on the liturgical year:

4. Sermon 122 on the Nativity of the Lord, VI, attributed to Maximus in manuscripts as well as printed copies; formerly *On the Liturgical Year* 11, and afterward Appendix 23.

5. Sermon 134 on the Epiphany of the Lord, IV, attributed to Maximus by manuscripts and printed copies alike; formerly *On the Liturgical Year* 37, and afterward Appendix 29.

6. Sermon 145 on Lent, VI, formerly *On the Liturgical Year* 69. The Louvain scholars considered it doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus judged it spurious; the Benedictines were the first to place it in the appendix, although they testify that the Remigius manuscript bears Maximus’s name.

7. Sermon 152 on the Passion of the Lord, III, and on Susanna, attributed to Maximus in manuscripts and printed copies alike, and indeed placed among his homilies after the first sermon for Palm Sunday; formerly *On the Liturgical Year* 118, and afterward Appendix 44.

8. Sermon 185 on Pentecost, IV, formerly *On the Liturgical Year* 183, and afterward Appendix 60. In the Theodoric manuscript it is falsely attributed to Ambrose, but in the others it correctly bears Maximus’s name together with three other sermons.

In the third class, sermons on the saints:

9. Sermon 192 on the Chair of Saint Peter, III, formerly *On the Saints* 16. The Louvain scholars left it among the doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus regarded it as spurious; the Benedictines were the first to place it in the appendix. It was also printed among the sermons of Ambrose and Maximus, with only the beginning altered.

10. Sermon 202 on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, II, formerly *On the Saints* 27 and afterward Appendix 79. It also has a place in printed editions among the Ambrosian and Maximus sermons. In the manuscripts it is assigned partly to Augustine, partly to Ambrose, but most often to Maximus. The Benedictines note that it is also found under his name in the Roman Breviary on 5 July.

11. Sermon 207 on the feast of Saint Lawrence, II, formerly *On the Saints* 32. The Benedictines were the first to place it in the appendix, although only its latter portion, beginning with the words “It ought to be enough for us,” etc.

In the fourth class, sermons on various subjects:

12. Sermon 248 on the burial of the Lord, formerly *On the Liturgical Year* 133. The Louvain scholars left it among the doubtful; the Benedictines, however, following the judgments of Verlinus and Vindingus, placed it in the appendix. It is composed of the final part of Ambrose’s sermon 52, *On the Cross*, together with the whole of his sermon 53, *On the Burial of the Lord*. Both of these have also been published under Maximus’s name.

### 1687

Paris, through the widow of Edmund Martin, Jean Boudot, and Étienne Martin, quarto. Twelve homilies of Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, first recovered from manuscripts by Jean Mabillon. They are published in the second part of his *Museum Italicum*, pp. 1–31.

Their titles are:

I. On the barbarian not to be feared by one who fears God, and on Saint Elisha.

II. Likewise, the following—that is, on the same Saint Elisha.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] These two sermons on Saint Elisha were not, as Mabillon had persuaded himself, unpublished; they had long before been printed in the Roman edition of Ambrose, though in a place so inappropriate that they could easily have escaped even this most diligent man. The Benedictine editors of Ambrose first observed this in their notice to the appendix.]

III. Likewise, the following—that is, on enemies not to be feared.

IV. On the Ninevites.

V. [Col. 0191C] On the calends of January.

VI. On the eclipse of the moon.

VII. Before Christmas.

VIII. On the Nativity of the Lord.

IX. After the Nativity of the Lord.

X. On heretics who sell sins.

XI. That clerics ought not to engage in commerce.

XII. On the body of the Lord.

These were taken from three extremely ancient manuscript codices: one from the Ambrosian Library at Milan, the second from the Roman monastery of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, and the third from Switzerland, from the Abbey of Saint Gall.

“From these three codices,” Mabillon says, “however ancient they may be, no certain and established knowledge of all Saint Maximus’s homilies can be obtained, since the Saint Gall manuscript presents them under the false title of Augustine; the Santa Croce codex, with the true author’s name erased, gives Ambrose as the author; and the Ambrosian manuscript assigns some of them to Maximus, but only a few, as we shall see later.

“Yet from other indications, [Col. 0191D] especially from Gennadius, we understand that all, or nearly all, particularly those presented in the Saint Gall manuscript, must be attributed to Maximus. They are connected and linked together in such a way that, if the authorship of some is established, a judgment concerning the others follows. For the author frequently mentions the preceding homily in the subsequent one. Most of them, moreover, acknowledge Maximus as their legitimate parent, since they are the works especially identified by Gennadius. Anyone will easily be able to observe from the notes appended below that this is also true of those which we now bring to light [Col. 0192A] for the first time.”

He then examines each one and, with considerable acumen, draws out the signs that correspond to those whose subjects Gennadius described. Finally, he adds that not only are most of the sermons published under Maximus’s name in printed editions authored by Maximus, but that all those attributed to Ambrose among Ambrose’s works ought likewise to be restored to him. He thinks that only very few should be assigned to Ambrose, and far more to Maximus; he demonstrates through several clear examples that others can be attributed neither to Maximus nor to Ambrose, but belong to later authors.

### 1690

Paris, printed and financed by the widow of Jean-Baptiste Coignard and Jean-Baptiste Coignard the younger, folio. Sermons of Saint Maximus of Turin found among the Ambrosian works, in volume II of the works of Ambrose, Benedictine edition, appendix, from p. 391.

The greater part of these sermons, which bear the name of Ambrose in manuscript books and were printed with his works, and none of which the Benedictines judged to belong to Ambrose at all, acknowledges Maximus of Turin as its author. Most of them had also been printed elsewhere under the name of Maximus. Indeed, the Roman editors of Ambrose, whose work alone had habitually been copied for more than a hundred years, had taken no account whatsoever of these sermons, since they were more concerned to increase the number of Ambrose’s writings by whatever means than to perform the critic’s duty and tolerate its reduction through the identification of spurious works. This negligence caused the Benedictines to apply themselves all the more vigorously to the matter and, with a by no means hesitant sickle, to cut away everything alien. We have already said that they considered no sermons genuine apart from the four discourses presented in their proper places, namely, the sermon at the funeral of Valentinian, the sermon at the funeral of Theodosius, the sermon *On the Basilicas Not to Be Surrendered*, and the sermon *On the Relics of Saints Gervasius and Protasius*. Since some of those spurious works existed only in Ambrose, while others had also been published elsewhere, they retained only the former and presented them in the appendix, prefacing each sermon’s title briefly with the arguments that suggested it was not Ambrosian or indicated another author.

So that this alteration might not prove troublesome to anyone, provision was made by means of two indices. In the first, the omitted works are arranged in such a way that one can see at a glance not only what place each had previously occupied in the Ambrosian editions, but also in which of the Fathers it is found. In the second, the sermons that they retained are listed, so that a comparison may be made among the editions—namely, the old Roman edition and the newest one. Just as the first index shows that by far the greater number of the omitted works had already been published among those of Maximus, whom they reasonably demonstrate to be their author in a special note on the omitted sermons; so, among the sixty-three sermons to which they gave a place in the appendix, they showed that the greater part were owed to Maximus of Turin, although they had been printed only with Ambrose. More recently, the Roman editor of Maximus, Bruno Bruni, proceeded to claim for his Maximus almost all the sermons which the editors of Ambrose had either left uncertain or appeared at times to attribute to others, the testimony of the manuscript books outweighing the evidence.

The Benedictines judge that the reason why so large a portion of Maximus’s sermons was transcribed chiefly under Ambrose’s name—apart from the frauds of scribes, who used to inscribe illustrious names on books in order to make their copies more saleable—was that Maximus appears to have read Ambrose’s works carefully and to have inserted large excerpts from them verbatim, especially from the commentary on Luke, thereby giving careless scribes an opportunity to err. “From this,” they say, “one may perhaps likewise infer that no other author than the same Maximus should be sought for the books or sermons *On the Sacraments*, an inference to which both the place and the time lend support.”

## EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

### 1713

Padua, printed at the seminary, by Giovanni Manfrè, in quarto. *Sermons of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin* (73, partly published and partly unpublished), edited and prepared by Ludovico Antonio Muratori; in volume IV of the *Anecdota*, pp. 1–117.

From the same Ambrosian manuscript from which Mabillon had excerpted part of twelve unpublished homilies, Muratori not only extracted afresh a considerable number of new homilies which he believed truly to have Maximus as their author, but also took note of those already published either among the works of Ambrose or in Maximus’s own works, confirming them by his judgment. He followed style chiefly as his judge, but also gave no less weight to Gennadius and to other indications drawn from the homilies themselves.

### 1733

Paris, at Montalant’s, on the bank of the Augustinian Fathers, near the bridge of Saint Michael, in folio. Edmund Martene published six homilies of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, from Mabillon’s papers, in volume IX of the *Ample Collection of the Ancient Fathers and Monuments*, which he prepared in nine volumes together with Martin Durand, likewise a member and priest of the Congregation of Saint Maur; pp. 134–142.

Mabillon had selected them from the same Saint Gall manuscript from which he first published twelve homilies, reserving for another occasion others from among the ninety-seven that he included under Augustine’s name, although the greater part had already been written under the name of Augustine, Ambrose, or Maximus himself. Apart from these six, however, the present editor found nothing in Mabillon’s papers.

### 1741

Venice, by Augustino Savioli, in folio. *Works of Maximus of Turin*, appended to the works of Leo the Great published by the same bookseller.

This edition, like the following one, will be discussed in the annals of the editions of Leo. Neither was available to us. We therefore do not know whether only the seventy-four homilies customarily published at first with Leo were reproduced, or whether they were enriched from the collations of Mabillon, Muratori, and Edmund Martene.

### 1748

Venice, by Andrea Poletti, in folio. *Sermons and Homilies of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, Newly Corrected and Enlarged from Manuscript Books*, appended to the works of Leo the Great printed by the same publisher.

### 1749

Venice, by Carlo Pecora, in folio. *Various Sermons of Saint Maximus of Turin*, in the new edition of Combefis’s *Preaching Library*, chiefly in volumes I, II, V, and VI.

### 1773

[Col. 0194B]

Venice, from the printing house of Giovanni Battista Albritius, in folio. *Several Homilies of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, Which Were Missing from Earlier Editions, Published through the Care and Efforts of the Most Illustrious Mabillon, Muratori, and Martene, and Collected by Andrea Galland*, in volume IX of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers and Ancient Ecclesiastical Writers*, pp. 349–395. A new sermon from Combefis was also added. The editor appended several brief notes, variants, emendations, conjectures, and biblical passages which Maximus either explicitly quotes or merely alludes to. Finally, in the prolegomena, chapter 9, pp. 20–22, he discusses with refined judgment the affairs of Maximus and the editors of these homilies.

### 1784

[Col. 0194C]

Rome, from the press of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, in large folio. *The Works of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, Enlarged by Order of Pius VI, Supreme Pontiff, and Illustrated with Notes; Dedicated and Presented to Victor Amadeus, King of Sardinia.*

We have already given the series of both the homilies and the sermons contained in this edition. It is now appropriate first to explain how that feature was accomplished of which the edition may boast most proudly, so that it appears not merely enlarged but newly created.

As soon as the task of enhancing Maximus had been entrusted by the supreme pontiff to Bruno Bruni, he not only used his authority within Italy to ensure that wherever manuscript books containing any of Maximus’s works were concealed, they would be diligently sought out and compared with the printed editions, and that whatever results they yielded—whether new sermons or variant readings—together with statements of their format, script, and age, would be sent to Rome; he also arranged for the same thing to be done outside Italy through his legates. Finally, he ordered Bruni himself to visit the more distinguished libraries, especially those richest in manuscript books, such as Monte Cassino and Florence, and to discover by his own judgment how much profit he would derive from them.

At the same time, men everywhere distinguished by rank and learning, eager both to attest their duty toward the pontiff and to render service to Maximus, devoted exceptional effort to this undertaking for the editor. After surveying and investigating all the editions of Maximus that had hitherto been prepared, and then nourishing his understanding by reading the writings on Maximus of men distinguished for historical and critical expertise—among the earlier writers, Gennadius and Honorius of Autun; among the more recent, Trithemius, Erasmus, Sixtus of Siena, Latinius Latinius, Bellarmine, Baronius, Labbe, the editors of Augustine and Ambrose from the Congregation of Saint Maur, Natalis Alexander, Johann Albert Fabricius, Cave, Dupin, Oudinus, Tillemont, Ceillier, and the Ballerini brothers—and finally finding himself equipped with such a wealth of manuscript books, he followed a mixed procedure.

For the works already published, he partly followed the example of Gymnicus, who was the first to publish seventy-four homilies, shortly afterward reprinted by Galesinius, though in such a way that he either supplied or corrected some of Gymnicus’s readings and brought the whole into conformity with the evidence of the more reputable manuscripts. In part, he reproduced the models of the Paris editions of the works of Saint Ambrose from the years 1569 and 1690, Muratori’s *Anecdota* of 1713, and Mabillon’s *Museum Italicum* of 1724. As for the new and previously unpublished works, he admitted them into the number of Maximus’s writings only when several manuscripts of the highest quality agreed and his own judgment assented, applying this caution in evaluating manuscript books: he generally preferred the older to the more recent, the more correct to the less emended, and gave greater weight to those which he recognized as having been copied from the best exemplars.

“To distinguish this,” he says, “I obtained three rules as aids. The first was the agreement of numerous manuscripts, especially older and more correct ones; the second, the authority of ancient monuments and writers; the third, the consensus of historians and experts in critical scholarship. Fortified, therefore, by these supports, I rightly claimed a great many short works for Maximus, even though some people either denied or doubted that certain of them ought to be credited to him. And if at times one or almost all of these supports were lacking, I still could not bring myself to judge that works should be taken away from the holy bishop when the similarity of style and expression suggested that they had been written by him.

“Nor could I be deterred from assigning certain short works to Maximus merely because their expression was more humble than in the others. For I am not unaware that holy bishops, especially those of that age, were accustomed to use more elevated and elegant speech when they had audiences distinguished for eloquence and learning, but humbler speech when they were preaching to an uneducated crowd.—Yet although the loftiness and elegance of expression in some of Maximus’s short works does not appear wholly equal to that in many others, the sequence, arrangement, movement of the words, and manner of adducing passages of Sacred Scripture are nevertheless so similar that in both groups you can easily recognize Maximus as the author.

“But whenever I encountered short works written in language so ordinary, humble, base, or confused that they seemed wholly unworthy of Maximus, I unhesitatingly judged that they ought to be rejected among the spurious works, even though they were inscribed with the name of that same Maximus in certain manuscripts.”

Elsewhere the editor defends this position at greater length by the examples of the editors of Ambrose and Augustine from the Congregation of Saint Maur, of Leo the Great, and of the Ballerini brothers. [Col. 0196A]

These are his general directions concerning the method he followed in using the testimony of manuscript books. In the case of each individual discourse, however, he explains where it comes from, whether it is new or already published elsewhere, by what right it bears the name of Maximus, and by which manuscripts it is supported. He includes these matters together under the heading “Notices.”

Let us now turn to other features of this work which will appear exceptional to admirers of Saint Maximus—namely, the correction and elucidation of the text. As regards the former, there can scarcely be any doubt that this labor succeeded admirably for one who had so thoroughly absorbed the character and distinctive diction of Saint Maximus, as our editor had; nor can it readily be properly assessed except by someone equally practiced in reading this and other preachers. We affirm only this much: the variant readings were added with a generous hand and carefully recorded.

The elucidation is served both by the summaries prefixed to the sermons and homilies and by the notes, appended here and there—not to all of them, but chiefly to the longer pieces—which deal exclusively with the doctrines of the faith that Maximus happened to touch upon. On the same subjects he also commented separately, in systematic form, far more fully than anyone might have expected from such an author.

It remains now to describe the work as a whole and briefly explain how its individual parts follow one another in continuous order. The volume begins with a letter from Pius VI, Supreme Pontiff, to Victor Amadeus, King of Sardinia (dated at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, on 10 July 1784, in the tenth year of his pontificate). In it he praises both the services of Maximus to the people of Turin and the piety of the people of Turin and of the entire House of Savoy, especially its counts, dukes, and finally its kings; their zeal in preserving and propagating the doctrine of the Catholic faith; and their devotion to the Apostolic See. He supports each point with letters of his predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, and with the testimony of Guichenon, the historiographer of Savoy.

This is followed by the editor’s preface, divided into two parts. One explains from what assistance of writers and manuscripts, and in what order, the edition was completed; the other discusses Maximus’s doctrine at great length. Next comes an extremely lengthy commentary on the life of Saint Maximus, printed in double columns. Then follow the testimonies of ecclesiastical writers concerning the writings of Saint Maximus of Turin, together with a list of editions of his homilies and sermons. [Col. 0196D]

After this comes information about the manuscript books from which this fuller and richer edition of the works of Saint Maximus emerged, as well as a statement of the age of the manuscripts, specimens of which are displayed in engraved copper plates appended at the end. Finally, an index of the sermons and homilies is provided. All these sections together, in the order we have listed them, fill 200 pages.

The genuine sermons and homilies themselves then follow, printed in double columns; the doubtful and spurious works are added in an appendix and printed in broad lines. The work is crowned by two indices, one of passages of Sacred Scripture and the other of notable subjects and statements.

As for the remainder, we note that the printer’s skill did not fall below the editor’s artistry. The edition takes pleasure in exceptionally large, white, delicate paper; the variety, elegance, and brilliance of the type are outstanding; and the layout is as pleasing to the eye as it is convenient for use. Finally, typographical errors are exceedingly rare, so that anyone who values truth must acknowledge that neither care nor good judgment was lacking in the execution of this work undertaken at the will and by the plans of Pius VI.

## § IV. Manuscripts

Who could doubt that those ancient editions of homiliaries ought to be counted in place of manuscript books, in which the various sermons of Maximus, like those of so many other Fathers, were first printed with movable type? The celebrated editors of the works of Leo the Great would refute him by their own example and teach him that their readings, drawn as they were from manuscripts older than the ninth century, should not be lightly valued. All the more, then, do we wonder that the most recent editor of Maximus either forgot about them or entirely [Col. 0197B] disregarded them. But the immense abundance of manuscript books available to him was doubtless the reason why one or the other of these things occurred.

As far as I remember, no one has yet asked whether the collection of Maximus’s sermons which that Ascensian Damian gave to Johann Gymnicus to print was excerpted from printed or manuscript copies of such a Homiliary, or from other bundles of manuscripts.

Since the Roman editor also used Mabillon’s manuscripts—namely, the Ambrosian, Roman, and Saint Gall manuscripts—we shall have a more convenient opportunity to discuss them in what follows. We shall therefore now undertake to review the manuscript materials of Bruno Bruni, which were as extensive as those available to no previous editor of a writer of this kind, at least not one who had edited a work of only a few volumes. They were partly Italian and partly German; under the latter designation he also included certain Swiss and Belgian manuscripts. The entire series is as follows.

### A. MANUSCRIPTS ACQUIRED FROM ITALY

### I. Subalpine Manuscripts

#### 1. The Turin Manuscript

A parchment volume, in folio, certainly written in the eleventh century, and therefore more probably derived from the best exemplars. A later hand had added the inscription: “For the use of the greater church of Turin.” It contained 122 homilies and sermons of Maximus, partly homilies and partly sermons, many of which had not yet seen the light; their list, together with the titles and beginnings of each, is separately set out in the latest edition, pp. 167–172. It had, in particular, a distinctive continuous sequence and a sufficiently carefully executed arrangement of the homilies and their appended titles. The sermons and homilies had been distributed according to the seasons of the ecclesiastical year, so that they might serve the divine offices.

It is also clear from this manuscript that another collection older than it had existed, since its scribe repeatedly indicated items that were lacking from his own copy. From this the editor concludes that in ancient manuscripts there had once been many more homilies which Maximus had delivered and which had formerly been read than now survive. “This index,” he also says, “provided me with no slight basis for conjecture, enabling me to assign more securely to Maximus the homilies and sermons which I had gathered under his name from editions and manuscripts, arguing from the agreement of their titles and discourse that he was their author.”

Finally, he notes that in this manuscript, as in the three following ones, the forms of most of the letters had been wholly or largely erased, so that only [Col. 0198A] certain fragments remained; nevertheless, they can easily be understood, or read without great difficulty by an experienced reader.

#### 2. The Pedona Manuscript

Formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Dalmatius at Pedona; a parchment volume, in folio, indeed damaged in many places, but nevertheless such that from the numbers added one can determine that it contained 242 homilies and 20 sermons. It appears to have been compiled from the best exemplars.

It is said to agree almost entirely with the Turin manuscript in the titles of the homilies and sermons, but the verses appended at the end demonstrate that it is older and should be assigned to the eighth century. They state that it was written under Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Pedona, while Charles was reigning as king of the Lombards and Franks. The indications of the year have disappeared.

#### 3. The Second Pedona Manuscript

A parchment quarto, written in the eleventh century by Joseph the monk, at the time when Abbot Henry governed this monastery and King Henry held power in Italy, as is likewise declared in verses written at the end. It contains 170 homilies and 40 sermons, but arranged in an order different from that of the preceding manuscripts and mixed together with the sermons. On its front it bears, in large red initials, the name of Maximus.

Scipio Maffei judged it to be of the same age as the preceding manuscript, namely, of the eighth century.

[Col. 0198C]

#### 4. The Appiano Manuscript

That is, the manuscript of the monastery or priory of Appania, to which it formerly belonged; a small folio, incomplete both at the beginning and in the body, since many leaves have been torn out. It contained 31 sermons and 70 homilies [Note: [Col. 0197D] Thus in the preface; elsewhere 120 is written.], as can be gathered from the numbers of those remaining. From the form of the script it should be assigned to the ninth century, or at the latest the tenth [Note: [Col. 0197D] There appears to be an error in the information about the manuscripts, since it is assigned to the eleventh century [Col. 0198D].]; the subscription somewhat confirms this, since it mentions the emperor Lothair—uncertainly whether Lothair I, who gained the imperial power in 841, or Lothair II, who did so in 947.

Franciscus Meyranesius, theologian of the Turin Academy, had examined these four manuscripts long before Pius VI began his plan of publishing Maximus and had carefully compared them with the printed editions. Whatever he had recorded from them, together, as I conjecture, with an accurate description of them, he sent to Bruno Bruni at the urging of Giuseppe Vernazza. They were of great general use to him, both because of their antiquity and because of their remarkable agreement with one another; above all, however, they enabled him to claim for Maximus several previously unpublished works which bore his name in these manuscripts, including three treatises on Baptism.

### II. The Vercelli Manuscripts

That is, the manuscripts of the chapter of the church of Vercelli, which the editor counts among the Subalpine manuscripts in his preface.

#### 1.

A parchment manuscript, shelf-mark VII, in folio, of the eleventh century, written in two columns. It contains one homily *On the Kalends of January*, printed in all the editions.

#### 2.

A parchment manuscript, shelf-mark LXVII, in the largest folio, of the twelfth or thirteenth century, complete. It contains the already published sermon *On Miracles* and the four sermons *On Eusebius, Bishop and Martyr of Vercelli*, which Bruno rejected as spurious.

#### 3.

A parchment manuscript, shelf-mark LXXXI, in the largest folio, of the twelfth or thirteenth century, as noted [Note: [Col. 0199D] Thus in the information about the manuscripts; in the preface, however, he writes that it belongs to the eleventh century and contains 18 homilies, all already published.]. It presents 12 pieces, partly sermons and partly homilies.

The Ballerini brothers had already used the Vercelli manuscripts in the works of Saint Leo. For the use of the Roman editor, however, they were examined anew by Antonio Francesco Frisius, a canon of that church.

### III. The Novara Manuscripts

That is, the manuscripts of the library of the cathedral church of Novara.

#### 1.
