A parchment manuscript, shelf-mark X [Note: [Col. 0199D] In the preface it is called the seventh.], in folio, of the eleventh century, adorned with elegantly painted initials. It contains two homilies *On the Common of Holy Martyrs* [Note: [Col. 0199D] Thus in the preface. In the information about the manuscripts, however, he writes that a single sermon *On the Common of Martyrs* was found in it under the name of Saint Maximus, previously unpublished [Col. 0200D], and that it appears in the Roman edition, col. 631. But it is said there that this sermon is copied from manuscript CVIII of the library of Saint Mark at Venice. It therefore seems that the sheer number of manuscripts caused him to confuse these matters.].

#### 2.

A parchment manuscript, shelf-mark XI, in folio, of the twelfth century, likewise with colored initials. It contains one homily *On the Holy Martyrs*, found in this edition at col. 263.

#### 3.

A parchment manuscript, shelf-mark XXVII, in folio, of the eleventh century [Note: [Col. 0200D] In the preface it is said to belong to the ninth century or, at the latest, the tenth.], with colored initials and rubricated titles. It supplies 27 pieces, partly homilies and partly sermons, all already published.

#### 4.

A parchment manuscript, shelf-mark XLII, in folio, written, as is stated in the note attached to it, in the year 1234. It is ornamented like the others and contains 12 sermons already published and confirmed by other manuscripts.

The same Antonio Francesco Frisius had examined these Novara manuscripts for Bruni’s use. He writes that they supplied him with numerous and excellent variant readings, and from this he concludes that they were copied from complete archetypes. They often agree with the Vercelli manuscripts.

### IV. Roman Manuscripts

#### α. Vatican Manuscripts

The editor states that in the Vatican Library he found more than thirty homiliaries, the oldest of which appeared capable of being assigned to the beginning of the eighth century, since they were written in square Roman characters. Almost all were complete. Some had formerly belonged to Cardinal Sirleto, who had written certain notes in them in his own hand; part had belonged to Queen Christina of Sweden; others had come from the Ottobonian collection. Each contributed something to the formation of Saint Maximus’s collection.

He prefers three above the rest, because they display unmistakable signs of the eighth century. Among them is the celebrated manuscript containing Gennadius’s book *On Illustrious Men*. Two others, marked numbers 3835 and 3836, parchment manuscripts in small folio, written in clear, large letters, presented sermons and homilies for the whole year, divided into two parts. His catalogue of the remainder, arranged according to age, is as follows:

Vatican manuscript, small folio, no. 248, parchment, approximately eleventh century.

Vatican manuscript no. 1278 and Vatican Palatine manuscript no. 430, both parchment, in folio, approximately eleventh century.

Vatican manuscript no. 4222, written in Lombard script, in the largest folio, eleventh century (perhaps I meant to write eleventh if he truly maintained the chronological order).

Vatican manuscript no. 4951, eleventh or twelfth century, formerly Cardinal Sirleto’s, neatly and carefully written. From it several homilies on Epiphany, as well as homilies on Lent and Saint John the Baptist, were copied.

[Col. 0200B]

Vatican manuscript no. 1196, approximately of the same age, containing lives of saints and passions of martyrs. Four sermons on Saint John the Baptist were found in it.

Vatican manuscripts marked nos. 1267, 1269, 1270, 6450, 6451, 6452, etc., and Vatican manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden nos. 125, 128, and 539, all belonging to the twelfth century of the Christian era.

Vatican Reginensis manuscript no. 1025, parchment, in folio, thirteenth century.

Another manuscript, no. 19, in folio, of the same age.

Vatican manuscript no. 587, fourteenth century.

Vatican Palatine manuscripts nos. 183, 432, and 433, paper, fourteenth century.

Vatican Ottobonian manuscript no. 106, in folio, parchment, eleventh century.

Another Vatican Ottobonian manuscript, no. 773, in which the mysteries of human redemption are treated through the sayings and teachings of the Fathers, with many passages of Saint Maximus cited among them. It is an unpublished work, perhaps written without the author’s name, at the end of the fourteenth century.

Before examining these manuscripts himself, however, Bruni had received from Pietro Aloysio Galleti—then a monk of the Benedictine Congregation of Monte Cassino, later Bishop of Cyrene—various readings from the Vatican manuscripts and several sermons carefully copied from them. These gave him a much sharper stimulus to examine everything with his own eyes.

#### β. The Basilica of Saint Peter

Six manuscripts are listed:

#### 1.

Manuscript shelf-mark 106, C, parchment, in folio, twelfth century.

#### 2.

Another manuscript containing homilies and sermons divided into lessons.

#### 3.

Manuscript shelf-mark 210, containing a collection of sermons of Leo the Great, among which are some that in later times were assigned to Saint Maximus. It appears to be of the fourteenth century.

#### 4.

Manuscript shelf-mark 7, A. A lectionary and passionary; it contains part of Saint Maximus’s homily *On Miracles*.

#### 5.

Manuscript shelf-mark 40, A. A lectionary containing eight pieces, partly sermons and partly homilies of Saint Maximus.

#### 6.

Manuscript shelf-mark 9, A. A lectionary containing sermons on the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul and another on Saint Lawrence.

Bruni further testifies that the manuscripts of Saint Peter are more carefully corrected than the others. To both groups—namely, these and the Vatican manuscripts—he grants this distinction: they ought to be preferred to all the rest for the correctness of their text, the brilliance and elegance of their script, and their agreement with one another.

#### γ. Santa Croce in Gerusalemme

That is, the library of the Roman monastery of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, of the Cistercian order. Among these, by far the most distinguished was:

#### 1. The Nonantola Manuscript

That is, the manuscript which formerly belonged to the monastery of Nonantola in the region of Modena and was acquired by Abbot Anselm before the textually corrupt date given as “the eightieth year of Christ.” It is a parchment volume in folio, marked XC on its outer front, although inside, on page 1, it bears the number CXXXIV.

It surpasses all the manuscripts of that library both in antiquity and in the accuracy and age of its writing, and belongs to the seventh century or, at the latest, the eighth. The form of its letters is Roman, of what is called the second period, tending slightly toward Lombard script.

“From page 129 to page 160,” Bruni says in his preface, “it contains sixty pieces, partly homilies and partly sermons, all of which, in the judgment of Cardinal Besutius, acknowledge Saint Maximus as their author in the catalogue of that library.” In the information about the manuscripts, however, where he lists their titles individually, he counts sixty-three.

Mabillon, on the other hand, who had used it earlier, writes that it contains seventy-three homilies, most of which were also found in the Saint Gall copy. According to the same authority, the author’s name had been written at the front of the manuscript; after it had been erased, the name of Saint Ambrose was substituted. He nevertheless considers most of these homilies to belong to Maximus, although certain others of Jerome and Augustine had been inserted under their names.

#### 2. The Second Nonantola Manuscript

Marked XCIX (inside LXVII), a parchment quarto written approximately in the twelfth century in a rounded and elegant Roman script. At the beginning it contains exorcisms over the possessed, then two letters of Pope Maximus A. (Bruni supposes Alexander III), and finally, from pages 5 to 163, ninety-six homilies and sermons of Saint Maximus. Among them, forty-eight sermons differ in no way from those contained in manuscript XC. Hence Bruni, together with Besutius, considers Maximus to be their true author, with the barbarous verses written at their beginning and their title lending support to that judgment.

He also transcribed the individual titles of the sermons and homilies in this manuscript in his information about the manuscripts; but the number likewise differs from that in the preceding manuscript, and not ninety-six but ninety-two are presented.

#### 3.

A lectionary written approximately in the thirteenth century, marked no. 9 (inside 222), in large folio, parchment, written in square letters. It contained lessons *On the Temporal Cycle* and *On the Saints*, together with several homilies.

#### 4.

Another Cistercian lectionary, of the fourteenth century, likewise in large folio, parchment, written in a semi-Gothic script. It contained twelve homilies of Saint Maximus.

Bruni cites notices and variant readings as witnesses demonstrating how much benefit these manuscripts contributed to his edition.

#### δ. The Vallicellian Manuscripts

That is, the manuscripts of the Vallicellian Library of the Fathers of the Congregation of the Oratory of Saint Philip Neri, which abounds in highly distinguished lectionaries, as we were formerly taught by the Ballerini brothers in their edition of Leo the Great. Bruni examined seventeen of them, containing fifty sermons and homilies of Maximus, which he compared with the printed editions. They were as follows:

#### 1.

Manuscript II, parchment, in the largest folio, approximately eleventh century, containing nine sermons of Maximus.

#### 2.

Manuscript VI, parchment, in the largest folio, thirteenth century.

#### 3.

Manuscript VII, parchment, in the largest folio, fourteenth century.

#### 4.

Manuscript VIII, parchment, in the largest folio, thirteenth century. These contained only one or two sermons of Maximus.

#### 5.

Manuscript IX, of the same age and format as the preceding, containing three sermons.

#### 6.

Manuscript XV, of the same format and age, containing ten sermons inscribed to Maximus.

#### 7–9.

Manuscripts XIX, XX, and XXV. The first is parchment, in the largest folio, written in Lombard script, perhaps of the ninth century; the other two are of the same age and format, though not of the same script. Each contained only one sermon of Maximus.

#### 10.

Manuscript marked 4, presenting seven homilies throughout the annual cycle, among which were seven sermons of Maximus.

#### 11 and 12.

Manuscripts A 9 and A 10; both parchment, in the largest folio, thirteenth century. The former presents one sermon on the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul; the latter presents six.

#### 13–17.

Manuscripts A 16, B 5, H 2, H 7, and H 23, supplying one or two sermons or homilies.

#### ε. The Lateran Manuscripts

Bruni notes that it is clear from the numbers inscribed on the manuscripts that more formerly existed in the archives of this basilica than survive today. He nevertheless found four homiliaries. He judges that three of them, parchment manuscripts in the largest folio, neatly written in Roman script, were written in the eleventh century; the fourth was in smaller folio and of the thirteenth century.

Two of the larger manuscripts bore at the front of the volume the inscription: “Compiled by Secundinus, Bishop of Taormina, in the time of Saint Gregory the Pope.”

From the Lateran manuscripts he took certain previously unpublished works, namely, a sermon on Palm Sunday and one *On the Common of Many Martyrs*, and confirmed other works by their testimony. In every respect he subscribed to the judgment of the Ballerini brothers, who considered these manuscripts exceptionally well corrected.

#### ζ. The Casanatensian Manuscripts

The library of Cardinal Casanata, at the Dominican Fathers’ house at the Minerva, supplied two parchment homiliary manuscripts, in the largest folio, written in an elegant and clear Roman script in approximately the eleventh century. Bruni testifies, however, that he gathered only a few items from them for Maximus.

#### η. The Zeladian Manuscripts

That is, the manuscripts in the possession of Cardinal Francesco Saverio de Zelada, prefect of the Vatican Library. Among them the following stands out:

#### 1. The Orvieto Manuscript

A parchment volume in the largest folio, excellently written about eight hundred years ago, presented to him as a gift by the chapter of the cathedral church of Orvieto. Among numerous homilies of more celebrated Fathers, it contains several of Saint Maximus; some of these, although they lack the author’s name, nevertheless gain confirmation from other manuscripts.

The following were also placed at Bruni’s disposal from the same library:

#### 2.

A parchment manuscript in the largest folio, containing acts and passions of martyrs.

#### 3.

A lectionary containing four sermons of Maximus.

#### θ. The Chisian Manuscripts

In the Chisian Library, extraordinarily rich in manuscript books, he examined three homiliaries. Two of them were parchment folios of the twelfth century and had formerly belonged to the Church of Anagni. The third was a paper manuscript of the fifteenth century and contained several doubtful sermons of Maximus.

#### ι. The Carrarian Manuscript

That is, the manuscript of the prelate Francesco Carrara, secretary of the Sacred Congregation of the Council. It formerly belonged to the Church of Esztergom and contains its breviary.

It was written on bright parchment, in a neat and elegant script, near the beginning of the sixteenth century, and was adorned with splendid paintings by Giovanni Boccardino, a Florentine citizen outstanding in this branch of art. It presented seven homilies of Maximus, whose variant readings are set out in their proper places.

#### κ. The Manuscript of the Angelica Library of Saint Augustine

A parchment breviary of the fifteenth century, in folio, containing the same four sermons attributed to Saint Maximus as are contained in the breviary of the Church of Velletri.

Moreover, Brunus also examined the libraries of the Colonna, Barberini, and Albani families; but he declares that he found nothing in their codices that was not already familiar from the writings of earlier editors or otherwise widely known. When it was reported to the Supreme Pontiff how rich, beyond other libraries, the Casinensis Library was in manuscripts useful for Maximus, he ordered Brunus himself to go to Cassino and examine them. Brunus obeyed, and, with the assistance of several learned monks of that congregation, examined twenty codices. They were as follows:

**V. Casinensis Codices.** All were parchment manuscripts, written partly in Roman and partly in Lombard script, and, according to the judgment of the better critics, to be assigned to the tenth or eleventh century. They were designated by these numbers: 102 (formerly 1094); 203 (formerly 1075); 104 (formerly 2030); 106 (formerly 1072); 107 (formerly 1034); 126, 129, 123 (formerly 581); 131, 147 (formerly 1100); 144, 142 (formerly 1100); 193, 305 (formerly 1080). In them he found altogether sixty sermons, most of them rightly bearing the name of Saint Maximus. Nevertheless, he rejected a few of these into the appendix as spurious and unworthy of Maximus, despite the authority of the codices.

He considers it noteworthy that the homily *On the Evangelical Fishing* and the seventy-fourth sermon, *On the Nativity of Saint Lawrence*, although they could previously be attributed to Maximus only on the basis of the single inscription of a codex in the Laurentian Medicean Library, now seem to be assigned to him with an almost firmer assertion by the inscription of another codex in that same library. Although he writes that these codices greatly illuminate Maximus through their exceptionally rich supply of valuable variant readings, he nevertheless admits that they generally agree so closely with the Vatican manuscripts that scarcely anything different can be detected in them.

**VI. Farfense Codices.** Among the many manuscripts of the celebrated monastery of Farfa, books of the greatest antiquity and value, he particularly noted two parchment codices, in the largest folio format, lectionaries which, in the opinion of Cardinal Tamburini, were written in the eleventh century. A third codex, likewise parchment, in smaller folio format and dating from the tenth century, contained several homilies along with other treatises. In these he found twelve sermons of Saint Maximus already published (fourteen in the preface), and from them he extracted a larger number of variant readings.

**VII. Sublacensian Codices.** From the library of the very ancient monastery of Subiaco he collated three manuscripts with the printed editions. They were lectionaries of the fourteenth century, written on parchment in the largest folio format and in Gothic letters, containing three sermons of Saint Maximus.

**VIII. Beneventan Codices.** He reports that four codices are to be found in the library of the Beneventan Church, exceptionally well supplied with ancient manuscripts, which present ten sermons bearing the name of Saint Maximus. He states that they are parchment manuscripts, in the largest folio format, designated by the numbers I, II, III, and IV, and not later than the twelfth century, as may be inferred from their script and from the judgment of the Most Eminent Cardinal Stefano Borgia, who communicated excerpts from them to Brunus.

**IX. Veliternus Codex.** This is a Breviary of that church, preserved in the archive of the chapter of Velletri. It is a parchment manuscript in small folio format, dating from the fifteenth century, written in an excellent script and adorned with elegantly painted initials. It contains four sermons transferred into Brunus’s collection, two bearing the name of Saint Augustine and the other two that of Saint Maximus. The Most Eminent Stefano Borgia, then a cardinal of the Sacred Roman Church, had communicated it to Brunus.

**X. Bobian Codices.** The monastery of Bobbio is the monastery of Saint Columbanus in that district of the Duchy of Milan which now belongs to the King of Sardinia. Muratori praises its codices containing works of Saint Maximus in the catalogue of its library, published from a tenth-century source in *Antiquitates Italicae Medii Aevi*, volume III, page 819.

When the general abbot of the Casinensis monastery and of that congregation, Domenico Favilla, learned this, he wrote to the abbot of Bobbio and instructed him to investigate those codices and report back to him. The latter replied that he and his monks had searched for them in vain and did not know where they had been taken or to what place they had been transported, unless they had perished altogether. Among the codices that still remained in his monastery, however, eight sermons bearing the name of Saint Maximus had been found; he himself also arranged for them to be copied and sent to Brunus in Rome. Of these eight sermons, three were genuine and had already been published; the remaining five Brunus rejected into the appendix as spurious.

**XI. Neapolitan Codices**, which Angelus Maria Bandini examined and from which he communicated excerpts to Brunus:

**α. The Library of Monte Oliveto.** In his catalogue he lists two codices from this library, but three in his preface, containing several discourses of Maximus. They are all homiliaries, namely:

**1.** A parchment codex in the largest folio format, written in Roman script, dating, as Brunus says in the preface, from the eleventh century, but, according to his statement in the catalogue, no earlier than the fourteenth century and acquired at Florence in the fifteenth century. In this codex he discovered one genuine sermon of Saint Maximus, *On Saint Martin*, whose opening is: ““It has often been made known …” This sermon, according to the manuscript evidence, is joined to the sermon following it, under the title *On the General Fast*, among the other sermons on Lent.

**2.** Another codex very similar to the preceding one, as the preface says. In the catalogue, however, he says nothing at all about it.

**3.** A paper codex in small folio format, with initials ornamented in various colors, dating, as its script demonstrates, from the fifteenth century. In the catalogue he calls this the second codex. From it he also drew a genuine sermon of Maximus, formerly attributed to Ambrose, entitled *Before the Nativity of the Lord* and beginning: “I believe that I have said quite enough.”

He also placed two sermons from these same codices among the doubtful works, while he entirely rejected as unworthy of Maximus other sermons that those codices contained.

**β. The Library of the Augustinians of Saint John at Carbonara.** A parchment codex in folio format, written around the middle of the thirteenth century (in the catalogue, the fourteenth century). It supplied not unpublished material, but a very large number of variant readings.

**XII. Florentine Codices.** “Although,” says Brunus, “there is scarcely any library in Florence that is not adorned with some manuscript codices, nevertheless the Laurentian Library surpasses all the others in abundance and rarity, since the Medici princes spared no expense to enrich it. Their love of letters and their munificence were followed by Francis I, Emperor, and by his son Peter Leopold, Grand Dukes of Tuscany.”

He therefore judged that these codices should be consulted first—or rather, exclusively, since he says nothing about the others—and divides them into Laurentian and additional manuscripts.

**1. Among the Laurentian codices, which are Medicean, the following were available:**

Codex 1, Plut. XIV, parchment, largest folio format, twelfth century.

Codex 36, Plut. XVII, parchment, largest folio format, eleventh century.

Codex 37, same Pluteus, parchment, largest folio format, eleventh century.

Codex 38, same Pluteus, parchment, largest folio format, eleventh century.

Codex 39, same Pluteus, parchment, largest folio format, eleventh century.

Codex 42, same Pluteus, parchment, largest folio format, eleventh century.

Codex 41, Plut. XVI, parchment, largest folio format, eleventh century.

Codex 23, Plut. XVIII, parchment, largest folio format, eleventh century.

Codex 1, Plut. XIV, parchment, largest folio format, twelfth century.

Codex 10, same Pluteus, parchment, small folio format, fifteenth century.

Codex 9, Plut. XIX, parchment, small folio format, fourteenth century, containing the letters of Jerome.

**2. Among the additional manuscripts in the Laurentian Library in our own time:**

Codex 4, formerly of the Library of the Minor Holy Cross, Plut. XXXIII, left-hand section, parchment, small folio format, eleventh century.

Codex 1, same Pluteus, largest folio format, eleventh century.

Codex 4, Pluteus XIII, left-hand section, parchment, small folio format, eleventh century.

Codex 5, same Pluteus, parchment, folio format, eleventh century.

Codex 2, Plut. XXXIII, left-hand section, parchment, largest folio format, eleventh century.

Codex 117, parchment, largest folio format, eleventh century, formerly belonging to the library of the fabric-wardens of the major church of Florence.

Codices 172, 173, 174, and 169, parchment, largest folio format, eleventh century. The last formerly belonged to the library of the fabric-wardens of the major church of Florence.

He reports that among these five are especially important and carefully written codices, though the others are not of the same quality. They are:

1. The Sanctacrucian codex;

2. The codex that formerly belonged to the church of Meaux and now belongs to the Laurentian Library; but it is difficult to determine which of the codices listed above is meant;

3. Two codices formerly belonging to the Florentine church and now also in the Laurentian Library, prepared, in his judgment, for choral use;

4. A fourteenth-century codex in which the homilies are distributed in the same series and order as in Codex XCIX of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.

Nearly all these Laurentian codices are homiliaries. On this occasion the editor appropriately explains their character and their various types, so as to show how it could have happened that many, indeed most, of them are filled with errors and false attributions. He points out that homiliaries existed not only in cathedral churches but also in parish and monastic churches, and even belonged to individual priests, at least in certain regions. Hence it could scarcely have failed to happen that they sometimes fell into the hands of inexperienced scribes.

**XIII. Cistercian Codices of Monte Amiata**, that is, of the old Cistercian monastery of Saint Savior in the Sienese territory of the district of Chiusi. Two codices were found there, of which Brunus was informed; they contained several homilies and sermons of Maximus. Both were parchment manuscripts in the largest folio format, dating from the thirteenth century, and Brunus frequently mentions them in his notes.

**XIV. Lucchese Codices**, that is, those of the church of Saint Martin of Lucca. Among the many manuscript codices of this church, which gained renown through its celebrated archbishop Giovanni Domenico Mansi, there are three containing certain homilies and sermons of Saint Maximus. All are parchment manuscripts in folio format, written in Roman script in the twelfth or thirteenth century. They are:

**1.** Codex designated P. +, containing only one sermon *On Saint Lawrence the Martyr*, printed in the Roman edition, column 579.

**2.** Codex designated no. 89, containing one genuine homily printed in the Roman edition, column 285, and another spurious homily *On the Dedication of Saint Michael the Archangel*, rejected by Brunus.

**3.** Codex designated no. 85, containing eighteen homilies and sermons, all genuine works of Saint Maximus.

The editor of Maximus testifies that he derived no small benefit from the Lucchese manuscripts. But when he adds that he cannot remain silent in praising them because they contain nothing spurious or falsely attributed—and therefore considers them to have been drawn from the best exemplars—I confess that I do not know how this can be reconciled with what precedes.

**XV. Milanese Codices**

**α. The Library of the Ambrosian Basilica**

**1.** Codex designated by the letter C, no. 98, written in Lombard script around the eighth century. This is the very codex that Mabillon first examined and that Muratori afterward examined with no less diligence. Both extracted from it a considerable number of previously unpublished sermons and also noted several among the Ambrosian sermons already published at that time. Nevertheless, each confessed that his judgment concerning all of them was not sufficiently certain.

For the codex is mutilated not only at the beginning but also at the end and in many other places. Muratori rightly considers this to be the reason why clearer evidence concerning the author of these homilies is lacking. Moreover, some sermons in it are expressly attributed to Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin; hence, he thinks, the suspicion arises that the others, whose author is not recorded, may belong to different authors.

I consider it worthy of mention that Brunus learned about this codex only recently, when he inquired about it from Giovanni Battista Branca, deputy prefect of the Ambrosian Library. He discovered that it had once belonged to the monastery of Bobbio, had disappeared from there, and was acquired much later, at great expense, by Cardinal Frederick Borromeo and brought into the Ambrosian Library.

Since this codex had long been the only one known in Milan to contain certain writings of Maximus, only recently were others found both in Milan and in Monza, from which some unpublished sermons and many variant readings were sent to Brunus. They are as follows:

**2.** A homiliary codex written on parchment around the eleventh century. From it a homily bearing the name of Maximus, *On the Handing Over of the Creed*, was transmitted, together with many variant readings, from the preceding codex, no. 98.

**3.** A parchment codex in folio format, written in Lombard script in the ninth century.

**4.** Another parchment codex in folio format, dating from the eleventh century.

**5.** A codex of the same basilica, parchment, folio format, ninth century.

**6.** Another codex of the same period, which survives only in a copy written in 1514 by Canon Casola. From it the canon Frisius transmitted to Brunus several homilies bearing the name of Maximus, among them the important homily *On the Restoration of the Major Church of Milan*.

**β. The Library of the Metropolitan Church of Milan**

**1.** A parchment codex in small folio format, designated by the letter F, no. 56, thirteenth century.

**2.** A parchment codex in the largest folio format, designated no. 202.

**XVI. Monza Codices**, that is, those of the library of the chapter of Monza.

**1.** Codex designated III, parchment, folio format, eighth century, containing various sermons arranged as readings.

**2.** Codex designated B XI, parchment, folio format, twelfth century.

**3.** Codex designated B X, parchment, largest folio format, eleventh century.

**XVII. Venetian Codices.** As soon as the illustrious Republic of Venice heard of the plan, undertaken at the advice of Pius VI, to restore the memory and monuments of Maximus, it arranged for whatever might be useful to that undertaking to be collected from the manuscript codices of the libraries within its territories and, as an exceptional demonstration of its official devotion, presented to the Pontiff. They were:

**α. The Library of Saint Mark**

**1.** Codex designated no. CLIII, eleventh century. It is the first part of a homiliary divided into two immense parchment volumes in folio format, which formerly belonged to Cardinal Bessarion and were later given by him, together with his other books, to the Republic. It is written with sufficient correctness. From it two previously unpublished sermons on Lent were obtained: the first occupies a place among the homilies in column 109, and the second among the sermons in column 447 of the Roman edition.

**2.** Codex designated no. DVIII, likewise parchment, folio format, twelfth century. It is the second part of another homiliary, not written as carefully as books intended to be read publicly in church require. It had been found in Saint Mark’s church mixed in with a few volumes that Petrarch had donated to that church, and was subsequently transferred to the library. It contained three sermons bearing the name of Saint Maximus, published by Brunus in columns 631, 633, and 635.

**β.** A Paduan codex of the library of the canons, fifteenth century, from which two sermons were copied. One begins: “To present a sermon to your charity …”; the other: “Rightly and as duty requires …” The latter occupies a place among the genuine works in column 623; the former is among the doubtful works in the appendix, column 53.

**XVIII. Veronese Codices**, or the codices of the library of the chapter of Verona.

**1.** Codex designated no. 75, parchment, folio format, eighth century.

**2.** Codex designated no. 431, likewise parchment and of the same age and format. Each supplied several sermons, whose variant readings Brunus gives in the annotations.

**3.** Codex designated no. 49, of the same age, parchment, and format. From it come *Readings*, or *Expositions of the Gospels*, found nowhere else to date. Brunus considers these not different from the book entitled *On the Chapters of the Gospels*, which Gennadius, Honorius of Autun, and Trithemius list among the works of Maximus.

In addition, two treatises were copied from it, one *Against the Pagans*, the other *Against the Jews*. Although they do not bear the author’s name, this editor judged them worthy, because their language and ideas agree with other works of Maximus, to be attributed to him. Because of the codex’s antiquity, however, they suffer from several lacunae.

The bishop of that church, Giovanni Morosini, arranged for these Veronese codices to be collated for the benefit of the new edition.

**XIX. The Brescia Codex.** The chapter of the major church of Brescia preserves a parchment lectionary in folio format dating from the thirteenth century. Through the efforts of Giovanni Manni, bishop of Brescia, two sermons adorned with the name of Saint Maximus were extracted from it, namely *On the Body of Christ*, printed in the Roman edition, column 279, and *On Lent*, column 447, together with several variant readings.

This is what Brunus reports concerning the Italian codices. There were also:

## B. GERMANIC CODICES

Pius VI entrusted this province to Joseph Garampi, then apostolic nuncio at the imperial court in Vienna, so that if anything useful for enriching the works of Maximus could be extracted from the manuscript codices of German libraries, he should make it his concern and press the matter as far as he could.

Accordingly, after he had unsuccessfully examined the books of the Imperial Library through his own efforts and diligence, he turned to the monks of the Order of Saint Benedict and urged the abbots of the monasteries of Regensburg, Göttweig, Lambach, and Reichenau to order searches among the old exemplars of their libraries, in case anything useful to the collection of the works of Saint Maximus might be discovered.

They did not fail in this duty. Brunus writes that the monks eagerly undertook the work; that very full catalogues of the homilies and sermons of Maximus were completed; that variant readings of considerable importance were transcribed with the greatest care; and that the age and excellence of the codices in which works inscribed with the name of Saint Maximus were found were indicated. Finally, all this was sent to Rome by the aforementioned prelate.

The codices were as follows, some bearing a date and others lacking one:

**1.** Eight codices of the Abbey of Reichenau, designated by the numbers 12, 14, 15, 16, 19, 21, 29, and 39.

**2.** A codex of the library of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, parchment, folio format, designated by the letter E, no. 4, ninth century.

**3.** A codex of the library of Lambach, parchment, folio format, thirteenth century.

**4.** A codex of the library of Göttweig, paper, designated L 5, fourteenth or fifteenth century.

## C. BELGIAN CODICES

Two manuscript codices were found in the libraries of Belgium. Their care was undertaken, at the command of Ignatius Busca, apostolic nuncio to the Belgians, who in this matter obeyed the Pontiff’s order, by Canon Vandenvelder, prefect of the Louvain Library and professor of theology. They were:

**1.** A codex of the library of the canons regular of Saint Martin at Louvain, parchment, in the largest folio format, eleventh century. In two volumes it presents homilies *On the Temporal Cycle* and *On the Saints*, among which are thirty works, partly homilies and partly sermons, of Saint Maximus.

**2.** A codex of the library of the Cistercian abbey of Cambron, paper, octavo format, written in a clear script by Brother Jean de Waulx in 1620. It contains several sermons of Maximus, preceded by the title: “Sermons of Blessed Maximus, Bishop of Turin,” and so forth. The variants of these codices were appended to the Cologne edition of 1535.

## D. SWISS CODICES

No manuscript book is certainly more celebrated than:

**1. The Sangallensis Codex**, which Mabillon was the first to examine. How highly he valued it and what he extracted from it has been explained above. Hermann Schenkius, then prefect of the Sangallensis Library, lent Mabillon his assistance—a service that it would be wrong to pass over in silence.

More recently, the prefect of that library, Father Magnus Hungenblykerus, reported more carefully on the same codex to Brunus, on 5 January 1779:

“He states that he agrees with John Mabillon and with Martin Gerbert, prince and abbot of Saint Blaise, who say that the codex itself is a parchment manuscript in folio format, written in Lombard script, and not later than the eighth century. It falsely bears the name of Augustine. For it contains nothing among its homilies or sermons that should be attributed to Augustine.

This is established, in particular, by another ninth-century codex of the same library, which bears the following inscription: ‘A very ancient volume of the homilies of Bishop Maximus, on various feasts throughout the whole year.’ Since precisely the same homilies are contained in this codex and in that older one, this must certainly be a strong indication that the scribe was gravely mistaken in making Augustine the author of Maximus’s works.

In this matter he differs from Mabillon, because he himself counts no more than ninety homilies in both codices, whereas Mabillon counts ninety-seven. The reason is simply that Mabillon considered the seven books *On the Sacraments*, usually attributed to Ambrose, to be seven homilies of Maximus.”

**2.** Another codex, mentioned just above by Hungenblykerus, likewise written in Lombard script.

These are the observations made by the Roman editor concerning the codices that assisted in establishing this new collection. Among them, however, he himself gives first place to the three that Mabillon first examined: the Sangallensis, the Nonantulensis—now the codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem—and the Ambrosian codex of Milan.

A collation of the French manuscripts was also being prepared; but, although long awaited, it had not yet been brought to Rome, since he seemed unable to keep the expectations of those waiting in suspense any longer. Nevertheless, he promised that, as soon as it had been returned to him, he would not allow his diligence to be lacking in numbering, evaluating, and celebrating them.

Finally, I cannot pass over in silence the fact that, at the end of the Roman edition, four tables were added to provide a fuller illustration of this catalogue of codices. They are of the same size as the volume itself and engraved on copper; in them twenty-seven specimens of the scripts and formats of the more important codices are represented. The previously mentioned *Declaration of Age* refers to these specimens.

[Col. 0211]

# DECLARATION OF THE AGE OF THE MANUSCRIPT CODICES

## Codices of the First Plate

[Col. 0211A]

**[CLXXXVII] I.** Concerning the appearance of the script of the Vatican Codex no. 1, reproduced here, there is no single opinion among diplomatic scholars, as Mabillon explains in volume I of his treatise *On Diplomatics*, page 487. Some assign it to the eighth century; others consider it contemporary with the sixth century.

**II.** The judgment concerning the second type of script, represented by Codex no. 2 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, is subject to the same diversity of opinion, as Mabillon himself testifies, since it displays similar forms. See volume III, pages 40 and 41. His own opinion inclines toward assigning these forms to the seventh or eighth century.

**III.** The third type of script, that of Codex no. 3 of the chapter of Verona, appeared to the illustrious Marquis Scipione Maffei to be of the same age as the preceding codices—that is, to be placed between the seventh and eighth centuries.

**IV.** There can be no doubt about the age of Codex no. 4, formerly belonging to the chapter of Orvieto and now in the possession of the Most Eminent Cardinal de Zelada, since it records that the manuscript was copied during the pontificate of John IX. John held the Roman pontificate from 902 to 905.

## Codices of the Second Plate

**V.** Next comes specimen no. 5, showing the script of another Vatican codex, designated no. 248. Experts place its age no later than the tenth century, or at the beginning of the eleventh.

**VI.** The script of Codex no. 6 of the Library of Saint Mark in Venice is later. It displays a neat Roman form with few abbreviations. Nor does the date written at the end of the codex deceive us: it is dated 1138.

**VII.** The writing of the subsequent Codex no. 7 of the same Library of Saint Mark is not unlike that of the preceding codex; therefore we consider it contemporary with it.

**VIII.** There is a considerable difference between the script of Codex no. 8, formerly belonging to the Queen of Sweden and now in the Vatican Library, and that of the preceding codices of the Library of Saint Mark in Venice, since its letter-strokes appear more contracted. We therefore say that its age reaches into the thirteenth century.

**IX.** We place Codex no. 9 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem neither among the earlier nor among the later manuscripts, since the form of its script and its abbreviations display the writing style of the thirteenth century.

**X, XI, XII, XIII.** The four specimens of Lombard script that we present under numbers 10, 11, 12, and 13 are, if Mabillon is to be trusted—volume III, page 352, *On Diplomatics*—assigned to the ninth century. There is not enough variation among the scripts themselves for them to be referred to different periods.

## Codices of the Third Plate

[Col. 0212A]

**XIV, XV.** I need not trouble myself to investigate the age of the codices of the Vallicellian Library whose specimens are presented under numbers 14 and 15. The judgment of the most learned Joseph Blanchini has already preceded us: he affirmed that they belong to the eleventh or twelfth century.

**XVI.** The specimen of the script of Vatican Codex no. 19 appears to have been produced around the thirteenth century. Some may perhaps judge it slightly earlier.

**XVII.** Anyone who considered Codex no. 17 of the monastery of Saint Columbanus at Bobbio to be of a later period, namely the fourteenth century, would not depart from the truth, since no indications of an earlier period can be seen in it.

**XVIII.** I would call Codex no. 18 of the Library of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem much older, for the form of its letters indicates the twelfth century or the beginning of the thirteenth. The Most Eminent Cardinal Besutius held the same view; he had frequently had the manuscript codices of that library before him.

**XIX.** We do not depart from the same cardinal’s judgment when we must determine the age of Codex 99; he noted in his own hand that it should be assigned to the twelfth century.

**XX.** The script of Veronese Codex no. 20 approaches the older form of letters, namely that of the ninth century, and in this we follow the opinion of the highly praised Marquis Maffei. Certainly codices of this kind display a venerable antiquity.

## Codices of the Fourth Plate

[Col. 0212C]

**XXI.** I would not dare to assert that the codex of the Most Eminent de Zelada, whose specimen appears under no. 21, is earlier than the thirteenth century, since no traces of an older period can be observed in the form of its letter-strokes.

**XXII.** The codex of the chapter of Verona approaches the same period; its script is represented under no. 22. In both codices the Roman manner of writing appears to be that used between the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.

**XXIII.** We have also arranged for a specimen of the semi-Gothic writing of Codex no. 23, the lectionary of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, to be reproduced. More expert antiquaries assign it to the fourteenth century.

**XXIV.** Codex no. 24 of Subiaco should be considered contemporary with this one, or perhaps slightly earlier.

**XXV, XXVI, XXVII.** The three following forms of script—the first, no. 25, belonging to the Vatican Codex; the second, no. 26, to the codex of the church of Velletri; and the third, no. 27, to the codex of the Library of Saint Martin at Louvain—although dissimilar, must be assigned to the fifteenth century.

# SPECIMEN

of the manuscript codices from which most of the works of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, included in this collection were extracted.

[Col. 0221]

# HOMILIES OF SAINT MAXIMUS, BISHOP OF TURIN, DISTRIBUTED INTO FOUR CLASSES. (C, G, S)*

## FIRST CLASS: WINTER HOMILIES ON THE TEMPORAL CYCLE

### 1. HOMILY I. Before the Nativity of the Lord

### NOTICE

If one enumerates the codices distinguished by antiquity and by the recommendation of illustrious writers in which this homily bears the name of Saint Maximus, certainly no account need be taken of certain others—very few in number and written later—in which it is attributed to Saint Ambrose. Of those in which it is ascribed to Maximus, we shall first mention two Subalpine manuscripts, one from the major church of Turin and the other from the former abbey of Saint Dalmatius at Pedona; likewise two Vatican manuscripts, the former in the series, no. 433, p. 38, the latter in the Queen’s Library, no. 125, p. 41; then likewise two Reichenau manuscripts and Vallicellian no. 2; further, two Belgian manuscripts, the Martinian and the Cambron manuscript; then the Monza manuscript designated E 3, the Novara manuscript 27, Roman 99, that of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, that of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, and finally Florentine manuscript CLXIX, formerly of the library of the wardens of the metropolitan church. Nor is the situation otherwise in the collections of homilies: Alcuin, Venice, 1571, p. 16; Combefis, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, likewise Venice edition, 1749, vol. I, p. 3; Gymnicus, Cologne edition, 1535, p. 7; Galesini, Roman edition, 1564, p. 87; Theophilus Raynaud, *Heptad. Praes.*, Lyons edition, 1633, p. 195. The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur say that the same homily occurs under Maximus in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*; so in the index of omitted sermons in the Paris edition of Saint Ambrose, 1690. Now I do not remember ever having seen any manuscript codices in which it is attributed to Saint Ambrose except two Florentine manuscripts: one is in the Medicean Laurentian Library, no. X, Plut. XIV; the other is IV, Plut. XXXIII, of the library formerly of the Minor Conventual Holy Cross, now Laurentian. Yet how falsely this attribution is made is plainly demonstrated by Ambrose’s diction, than which nothing is more unlike the style of the author of this homily itself.

We think enough has been said concerning the author of the homily. Something must now be said about the variation of the title affixed by copyists of later times. The manuscript of the wardens of the metropolitan church of Florence has the title: *On the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord*; in Gymnicus and Galesini it is *On the Vigils of the Nativity of the Lord*. But the Roman editors of the works of Saint Ambrose report that it was delivered on the second Sunday of Advent, following the Sixtine edition of 1590. Codex 10 of Florence, mentioned above, differs from these; there it is entitled: *On the Devout Preparation to Be Made for Celebrating the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ*. We adopt none of these headings, but take the title *Before the Nativity of the Lord*, as it appears in the Turin codex, since the context shows that the homily could have been delivered neither on the day of the Lord’s Nativity nor on the preceding day, the vigil. “Therefore,” Saint Maximus says, “several days beforehand let us make our hearts chaste, cleanse our conscience, and purify our spirit, so that the birthday of him whose birth was accomplished through an immaculate Virgin may be prepared for by immaculate servants.” It was the custom of at least certain churches to anticipate the feast of the Nativity of the Lord over a longer period than is now done, with prayers and holier works. But in Maximus’s age that period was not designated by the name Advent. On this subject consult Mabillon, vol. I of *Museum Italicum*, p. 8, Paris edition, 1724, and the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, appendix to the works of Saint Ambrose, vol. IV, p. 488, Venice edition, 1751.

[Col. 0221A]

### ARGUMENT

Saint Maximus admonishes the faithful of Christ to meet the Nativity of the Lord, having cleansed themselves from the defilements of sins and clothed themselves in virtues; through that Nativity the most longed-for salvation shone upon the world.

How great the joy is, and how great the concourse, when the birthday of the emperor of this world is celebrated, you know well: how all his commanders and princes, and even the soldiers on active service, carefully dressed in silken garments, girded with elaborate belts gleaming with precious gold, customarily strive to appear before the king more splendidly adorned.

[Note: Novara Codex 27, p. 172, reads: “and even the soldiers.”]

For they believe that the emperor’s pleasure will be greater if he sees greater adornment in their appearance, and that he will be as much the happier as they themselves are devoted at his solemnity.

[Note: Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Vatican Codex 435 read: “at his festival.”]

Since the emperor, being human, does not see their hearts, they therefore prove their affection for him, or their loyalty, by observing their attire. Thus whoever loves the king more faithfully makes himself more splendidly prepared.

Moreover, because they know that on his birthday he will be generous and will distribute very many gifts either to his attendants or to those who are considered lowly and insignificant in his household, they first hasten to replenish his treasuries with a variety of riches, so that, to whatever extent he wishes to extend his generosity, an abundant gift may not be lacking, and the desire to give may fail before the means of giving do.

[Note: Vatican Codex 435 reads: “very many [gifts] to his attendants.”]

[Note: Codex X, Pluteus XIV of the Laurentian Library, reads: “To whatever extent he wishes to prolong it, to that extent let abundant prolongation not be lacking.” In Codex CLXXIV of the Library of the Aediles of the Major Church of Florence, p. 91 verso, the reading is: “To whatever extent he wishes to advance it, to that extent let abundant advancement not be lacking, and let the will to give fail before the substance for giving does.” The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem has: “To whatever extent he wishes to extend it, to that extent let abundant extension not be lacking, and let the will to give fail, etc.” Finally, Vatican Codices 433 and 435, and the Modoetian Codex 433, read: “To whatever extent he wishes it to be extended, to that extent let abundant extension not be lacking.”]

They do all this carefully because they hope that a greater reward will await them for this diligence. Therefore, brothers, if the people of this age receive the birthday of their earthly king with such display for the sake of the glory of present honor,

[Note: Vatican Reginensis Codex 125 reads: “receive [it] with such display that, etc.”]

[Note: The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “with what care ought we.”]

with what preparation ought we to receive the birthday of our eternal King, Jesus Christ? For in return for our devotion he will bestow on us not temporal glory but eternal glory; nor will he grant an administration of earthly honor, which ends with a successor, but the dignity of a heavenly kingdom, which has no successor.

[Note: Vatican Codex 435 reads “successors.”]

But what our reward will be,

[Note: The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “But what our reward will be, etc.”]

the prophet says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (Isaiah 64; 1 Corinthians 2).

With what garments ought we to adorn ourselves? By “ourselves” we mean our souls, because our King Christ seeks not so much the splendor of garments as the disposition of souls. He does not inspect bodily ornaments but considers the hearts’ merits.

[Note: The Camberon Codex reads “the merits of hearts.”]

He does not admire the elaborate work of a fragile belt encircling the loins, but admires far more the strength of chastity restraining lust toward purity. Let us therefore strive to be found approved before him in faith, adorned with mercy, and carefully ordered in our conduct.

[Note: Vatican Codex Reginensis 125 reads “content with mercy.”]

[Note: The Codex of the Aediles of the Florentine Church reads “adorned in conduct.”]

And whoever loves Christ more faithfully should make himself more splendid through observance of his commandments, so that he may truly see that we believe in him when we shine in this way at his solemnity, and may be the happier the purer he perceives us to be.

[Note: Vatican Codex Reginensis 125 omits “truly.”]

For this reason, several days beforehand, let us purify our hearts, cleanse our conscience, and purify our spirit; and, bright, spotless, and undefiled, let us receive the coming of the undefiled one.

[Note: Vatican Codex 435 reads: “Let us cleanse our bodies, purify our conscience, and, radiant and without stain, undefiled, let us receive the coming of the undefiled Lord.” The Codex of the Aediles, E, of Florence reads: “Therefore, beloved, let us adorn our souls with spiritual garments, and so that we may be able to remain watchful during the vigils of the approaching night, let us cleanse our consciences, etc.”]

[Note: The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem likewise reads “of the undefiled Lord.”]

Thus, since his birth was established through an undefiled virgin, let his birthday be prepared for by undefiled servants. For whoever is dirty and polluted on that day does not honor Christ’s birthday or his vow.

[Note: The same codex reads: “For whoever is dirty and polluted at the present festival, etc.”]

Though he may be bodily present at the Lord’s solemnity, in mind he is farther separated from the Savior.

The unclean and the holy, the greedy and the merciful, the corrupt and the virgin cannot share fellowship—except that the unworthy person incurs a greater offense by thrusting himself into it, since he does not recognize his own condition.

[Note: The same codex reads: “when he is not at all recognized; and while in mind he wishes to be dutiful.”]

For while he wishes to be dutiful, he proves injurious—like the man in the Gospel who, invited into the company of the holy, dared to come to the wedding without a wedding garment (Matthew 22; Luke 14). While one guest shone with righteousness, another gleamed with faith, and another sparkled with chastity, he alone, polluted by the foulness of his conscience, was filthy in hideous squalor amid all those who shone. And the more brightly the holiness of the blessed diners glowed together, the more clearly the wickedness of that sinner appeared—one who perhaps might have displeased less had he not given himself over to the company of the righteous.

Therefore he is seized, bound hand and foot, and driven into the outer darkness—not only because he was a sinner, but because, being a sinner, he claimed for himself the merit of holiness.

[Note: The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Martinenian Codex read: “Therefore he is seized, with his hands bound, etc.” The Vatican Codex reads: “Therefore he is seized, with hands and feet bound.”]

Accordingly, brothers, as we are about to celebrate the birthday of the Lord,

[Note: The minor conventual Codex IV of Santa Croce, Pluteus 33 in the Laurentian Library, agrees remarkably with the Galesinian text: “As we are about to celebrate the birthday of the Lord.”]

let us cleanse ourselves from every filth of sin and fill his treasuries with gifts of various offerings, so that on the holy day there may be something from which strangers may receive, widows may be refreshed, and the poor may be clothed.

[Note: The Florentine Codex of the Aediles’ Church reads: “so that on the holy day, which already hangs over us, there may be something from which, etc.”]

For what kind of thing would it be if, in one and the same household, among the servants of one master, one rejoiced in silk garments while another was consumed by rags; one burned with food while another endured hunger and cold; one belched up yesterday’s indigestion from overeating while another could not relieve yesterday’s hunger from fasting?

And what will be the effect of our prayer when we ask to be delivered from the enemy?

[Note: Vatican Codex 435 reads: “And what will be the effect of our prayer when we ask to be delivered from the enemy?”]

We ask to be delivered from the enemy, yet we are not generous toward our brothers. Let us be imitators of our Lord.

[Note: The Florentine Codex of the Aediles’ Church reads: “Therefore, brothers, let us be imitators of our Lord. If he wished the poor to be our companions in heavenly glory, etc.”]

For if he wished the poor to be our companions in heavenly grace, why should they not be our companions in earthly possessions?

[Note: The same codex reads “in glory” instead of “in grace.”]

Nor are those who are brothers by the sacraments strangers to material support.

[Note: The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Vatican Codex Reginensis 125 read: “Nor should those who are brothers by the sacraments be strangers to material support, etc.”]

Rather, through them we plead our own cause with God more rightly, so that we may nourish at our own expense those who may give thanks to him.

[Note: The Martinenian Codex omits “them.” The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads “thanks” (*gratias*).]

Whatever a poor person blesses the Lord for benefits the person through whose action he blesses the Lord.

[Note: The Codex of Santa Croce reads: “through whom the Lord is blessed.”]

And just as it is written concerning the one through whom the Lord’s name is blasphemed, “Woe to that man,” so it is also written concerning the one through whom the name of the Savior Lord is blessed: “Peace to that man.”

[Note: The same codex reads: “it is written concerning this man.”]

How great, moreover, is the merit of the giver: he alone works in the house—

[Note: The Florentine Codex of the Aediles’ Church reads: “so that someone alone may work in the house of God.”]

—and through many people the Lord is entreated in the Church?

[Note: The Codices of Santa Croce and Martinenian read: “and through many people the Lord is entreated in the Church.” Vatican Codex Reginensis 125 reads: “and through many churches the Lord is entreated.”]

What that man perhaps would not dare to ask from the Divinity, he may receive through the prayers of many who intercede, even what he had not hoped for.

[Note: The same Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “What the blessed Apostle says, recalling our assistance, etc.”]

In remembrance of this assistance of ours, the blessed Apostle says: “So that thanksgiving may be offered by many on our behalf” (2 Corinthians 1). And again: “So that our offering may be acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 15).

[Note: The Florentine Codex of the Aediles’ Church reads: “so that there may be equality, because the one who has much will not have an excess,” and the rest.]

## HOMILY II

On the Lord’s coming, and on what is written in Luke 17: “As lightning flashing from heaven, so will be the coming of the Son of Man”; and on the two in one bed, Matthew 24.

## ADMONITION

We are dealing with a great diversity of manuscript codices concerning the author, title, and beginning of this homily. The Florentine Codices I and X, Pluteus XIV of the Medicean Laurentian Library, certainly assign it to Saint Ambrose by their titles, as do all the older editors of that Father. But far more numerous and more authoritative witnesses agree in assigning it to Saint Maximus.

We shall first examine the very ancient Swiss Codex of Saint Gall, then Roman Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, the Ratisbon Codex of Saint Emmeram, Homily 1, p. 3; Lambach Codex 1, p. 1; Vatican Codex 1267; Vatican Palatine Codex 1276; Vallicellian Codex I; and the Modoetian Codex, siglum E III. Among the editors, Gymnicus agrees with these, Homily 1, p. 1; so do Galesinius, Homily 1, p. 35; and Theophilus Raynaudus, p. 193.

Having established the author of this homily, I shall say a little about its title. To begin with the Codex of Saint Gall, it bears this title:

“Here begins an exhortation to the people, and on what is written in the Gospel: ‘As lightning from beneath heaven, so will be the coming of the Son of Man’; and on the two in one bed.”

The old editions of Ambrose have the same title. But the Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur, in the index mentioned above, report that it appears under Maximus of Turin in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Homily 1, with the title: “On the coming of the Lord, on what is written, etc.” The same title appears in the Ratisbon Codex of Saint Emmeram.

The Lambach Codex, however, gives a different title, namely: “Sermon 1 of blessed Bishop Maximus, for the time of Advent.” We have preferred the title indicated by the Maurist Fathers and found in the Ratisbon Codex, so that we may conform to the other editors of Maximus. At the beginning of the homily also we follow them, placing the different openings found in some witnesses in the eleventh annotation.

## ARGUMENT

Since Saint Maximus treated in the preceding homily the first coming of Christ to earth and the outstanding preparation of soul with which he must be received, he now explains certain Gospel passages that foreshadow the Savior’s second coming.

Perhaps you are troubled, brothers, why the Lord, announcing his coming, indicated that he would appear at night, when surely his coming ought to be received by all with great daylight-brilliance, great splendor, and fear.

[Note: The Codices of Saint Emmeram, Lambach, and Modoetia prefix this beginning to the homily: “Therefore, since after a period we must refresh ourselves with spiritual feasts, let us see what the Gospel reading continues. For the Lord says, as we recently heard, concerning the time of his coming: ‘As lightning flashing from beneath heaven, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.’ And he adds afterward: ‘On that night there will be two in one bed; one will be taken and one will be left; two will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one will be left.’ Perhaps you are troubled, brothers, etc.”]

[Note: The Codices of Saint Gall and Santa Croce in Jerusalem attach the homily to the following preface:]

“For only a very few days I seem to have been absent from your gathering, detained by various occupations and summoned by the needs of another church, and thus not to have devoted my customary attention to you. Yet although I have been absent from you in body, I have not been absent from you in love; and, although I have been away in the intercourse of bodily members, I have not been a stranger to your spirit.

[Alternative reading: “Yet I have not been away in unity from your minds.”]

“Rather, I held you within me in longing, so that those whom sight withdrew from me, affection might present to me; or those whom I did not see with my eyes, I might embrace in my heart. For I was concerned each day about how eagerly you were coming daily to church. Although I was confident of your devotion, I was nevertheless anxious, because I did not see with my eyes what I knew to be present in you.

“This is the feeling of a father’s affection: concerning absent children, he rejoices not so much in confident hope as he despairs through anxious thought; and as soon as he ceases to see them, he learns to love them more. Thus we understand that love among those present is pleasing, but among those absent it is troublesome.

“I was therefore anxious, sorrowful, and afraid on your behalf, lest anyone should fall through negligence while I was absent, lest anyone should slip through the snares of the devil. For I remembered that the rage of wolves prevails more against shepherds who are absent. But thanks be to the Lord, who both kept you unharmed and restored my littleness safely.

“Therefore, since after a period we must refresh ourselves with spiritual feasts, let us see what the Gospel reading continues, etc.”]

We have frequently heard it proclaimed in the sacred Scriptures that, before the Lord Christ comes, Antichrist will reign. He will pour the darkness of his wickedness over the human race in such a way that scarcely anyone will look upon the light of truth. Covering human minds with his own gloom, he will display a kind of blindness to their spiritual eyes.

Nor is it surprising that the devil sends forth the darkness of wickedness, since he himself is the night of all sinners. Therefore Christ will come to dispel this dreadful darkness, like a kind of lightning. Just as night is overturned when day begins to shine, so Antichrist is put to flight when the Savior flashes forth; nor will he be able any longer to spread the darkness of his wickedness when the light of truth has shone out.

When he says, “On that night there will be two in one bed; one will be taken and one will be left” (Luke 17; Matthew 24), the merit of the resurrection is here already revealed: the grace of rising corresponds to the quality of one’s life, and the difference among individuals at the resurrection will be so great that even when two are sleeping together and resting in the same place, their being taken cannot be equal.

[Note: Vatican Palatine Codex 1276, in which the sermon is written in another hand under Ambrose’s name, reads: “Now the merit of the resurrection is revealed, namely, that it is not according to the quality of living,” etc.]

Although they occupy the same bed of companionship, one of them will nevertheless be snatched up to heaven according to his merits, while the other will be left on earth. Our common bed is the vast expanse of this earth, on which our bodies are laid down and rest in a most secure place. In this bed, whoever has conducted himself more harshly in life sleeps more softly.

We may also call our very limbs our own beds, in which our souls dwell most sweetly as upon a kind of couch.

[Note: The Florentine Codex of the Aediles’ Church and Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read: “as though in a certain couch, dwell most sweetly.”]

I believe that the holy prophet understood this when he says: “You have turned his entire bed in his sickness” (Psalm 40).

The man is blessed whose bed the Lord turns in his sickness, so that he who shortly before had been angry, adulterous, wanton, and full of the sicknesses of every crime may, as the Lord turns his body accustomed to evil, become chaste, humble, and temperate.

Concerning this bed the Lord said spiritually to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and walk” (Matthew 9; Luke 5).

[Note: Vatican Codex 1267 and Vallicellian Codex II read: “take up your pallet.”]

For there was not so much something astonishing in the paralytic’s carrying the wooden frame of a broken bed as in the fact that, with the limbs of his body loosened and broken by weakness, the paralytic himself carried, as it were, the necessary bed of his soul; and before the assembled Jews he walked away on his own feet, though he had been brought in on the hands of others.

Here, plainly, as I said, that prophetic sentence was fulfilled: “You have turned his bed in his sickness.” He carried in reverse the bed on which he had shortly before been carried, and his soul, which had previously been borne in the little vessel of the body, afterward carried its own body more usefully.

[Note: In Codex I, Pluteus XIV of the Laurentian Library, and in the Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem mentioned shortly before, the reading is: “so that in turn he might carry the bed.”]

It may also be understood in this way: “There will be two in one bed; one will be taken and one will be left”—the Christian people and the people of the Jews, who are held, as it were, in one bed, that is, under one law of commandments, and who boast as though in a similar form of resurrection.

Then the blessed people of the Christians will be taken up into glory, while the accursed assembly of the Jews will be left on earth.

[Note: The same Laurentian codex reads “but the accursed assembly of the Jews.” Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads “will be left in hell” instead of “will be left on earth.”]

## HOMILY III

On the same Gospel passage.

## ADMONITION

The evident connection and continuity of this homily with the preceding one sufficiently show that both flowed from the same source. The manuscript codices make us still more certain: the Codex of Saint Gall; the Lambach Codex; Codices 90 and 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem; Vallicellian Codex II; Vatican Codex 1267, p. 13; and Novara Codex 27, p. 18, which likewise display Saint Maximus’s name prefixed to them.

Nor does John Gillotius disagree. When he reprinted the works of Saint Ambrose at Paris in 1569 and placed this homily as Sermon 29, he noted in the margin: “The same is found in Maximus of Milan,” saying this in error, for he was Maximus of Turin.

The authority of these witnesses is further strengthened by the testimony of Alcuin, who in his *Homiliary*, Venice edition, Sermon 4, p. 8, transmits it under the name of Saint Maximus for the second Sunday of Advent. All the later editors follow him.

If it is attributed to Saint Ambrose in certain codices, those witnesses must certainly be considered inferior, since they cannot be compared with the others in either number or antiquity, which favor Maximus.

The reader should also be warned that we have added to this homily an as-yet unpublished fragment, which we transcribed from the Codex of Saint Gall, Florentine Codex I, Pluteus XIV of the Medicean Laurentian Library, and Codex 99 of the Library of Santa Croce in Jerusalem.

## ARGUMENT

The homily contains the same exposition of the Gospel, adorned with a fuller interpretation.

Last Sunday, while discussing the Gospel passage, we touched briefly upon one part of it; it remains for us to proceed through what follows. For we explained what the Lord meant when he said: “On that night there will be two in one bed,” etc. Now, therefore, let us see what remains. The divine utterance says:

[Note: Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem adds *eadem* (“same”).]

“There will be two women grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one will be left” (Luke 17).

First, then, we must consider how the work of grinding is constituted; second, who the two are who are said to grind; third, what the mill is and what the result of grinding may be.

No one doubts that grinding cannot be accomplished except with two prepared stones fitted to each other, so that the size of one is imposed upon the other. The stone that is laid down first is sluggish and slow and, so to speak, almost idle; unless it were adorned by the participation of the upper stone, it might perhaps seem unnecessary. Thus, while the one works, the other also proves useful.

The other—that is, the upper stone—

[Note: The Codex of Novara 27 reads: “But the same upper stone, etc.”]

—is carried around with the full speed of its operation, so that, deceiving the eyes by its very swiftness, it seems to stand still and is thought to be motionless while it runs.

[Note: The Codex of Saint Gall and Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem add “and with such speed.” Codex I of the Laurentian Library reads: “It is carried around with such speed of operation that, through its revolving motion…”]

The more violently it is driven, the more perfectly the work is completed. The other stone receives everything introduced, embraces everything that comes, and through certain little openings each of the two accomplishes its work. The function of the one who grinds is to break the hardness of the grains with unceasing care, draw out from their inner and hidden parts the fine flour and the kernel, and, removing the lightness of the husks, bring forth into the open whatever is pure. From this he makes the purest bread and gains his master’s favor.

These two millstones, therefore, seem to me to be the two Testaments, namely the law of Moses and the Gospel of the Lord. They are so arranged and prepared that each Testament fits the other, as the Savior says: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5).

In place of the millstones, one is first set upon the ground and the other placed above it: first, the law established for human beings, and then the Gospel perfected.

[Note: The Codex of Saint Gall reads: “and then confirmed unto the perfect Gospel.” Codices 90 and 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem have a similar reading, while Vallicellian Codex II reads: “and then unto the perfect Gospel.”]

This law, like the stone of the lower mill, was so slow, sluggish, and completely idle that it lost everything it had received by working. As the prophet says concerning the Jews: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Psalms 13 and 52).

Therefore, unless the Gospel had been placed above it, the law would still lie slow and heavy upon Jewish soil, confined within the narrow limits of one province. Unless, I say, the Gospel had been given, the law would have been entirely unnecessary.

Without the Gospel, the law accomplished what can be done with a single stone: it could break, but it could not benefit, as the blessed Apostle says: “The law produces wrath” (Romans 4:15); it does not provide grace.

While the law remained, the Gospel was given. Placed above the Old Testament, it adorns both Testaments and revolves around the whole world with such speed of its movement: that is, it visits the regions below, penetrates the heavenly places, and illuminates earthly things.

[Note: The Laurentian Codex mentioned above reads: “While the law remained, therefore…” Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem varies in what follows: “which, placed above the Old Testament, adorns both, and is carried around with such speed of operation that by its revolving motion it travels throughout the entire age.” Codices 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, Vatican Codex 1267, and Vallicellian Codex II agree with the present text.]

The Gospel, like the upper millstone, receives all who believe, welcomes everyone who comes, and sends them inward through certain openings of its commandments, so that there, with the harshness of paganism softened by the saving commands of the two Testaments on either side, it may bring forth whatever is pure.

[Note: In Codex 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, “there” is absent.]

I believe that the prophet Ezekiel touched upon this likeness of the Testaments when he says that one wheel was joined to another in the middle.

[Note: See Saint Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, Book 3, chapter 21.]

Through the operation of these millstones—that is, of the New and Old Testaments—the holy Church works with unceasing care to break through the hardness of sins, draw the kernel of a pure heart out of hidden thoughts, and, cleansed by heavenly commandments, bring forth spiritual nourishment from within.

The Apostle Paul speaks of these foods: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3). And again: “Solid food is for the mature” (Hebrews 5).

[Note: Codex 90 of the Vatican reads “on account of the habit.”]

The holy Church strives to purify our spirit of every human stain and to offer it to God like fine flour, as holy David says: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Psalm 51).

The Gospel is carried around with such speed that only the wise understand its course. Understanding this, the blessed Paul says: “So that the word of God may run and be glorified in you. Amen” (2 Thessalonians 3).

[Note: Codex 99 of Santa Croce reads “may run.” Codex 90 of the same collection adds “in us” and, omitting “Amen,” continues: “But in the eyes of the foolish, etc.”]

[Note: A fragment of the Codex of Saint Gall is also found without a break in Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem.]

In the eyes of the foolish, however, the Gospel appears to stand still. They think it stands still when they neglect its commandments and do not believe that what is written will come to pass.

The Synagogue also grinds, but it grinds uselessly, since it relies on working with one stone alone.

[Note: Codex I of the Laurentian Library, both Codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, and Vatican Codex 1267 read: “with one stone alone; that is, it relies on working with the Old Testament alone.”]

Therefore it does not so much grind as scatter and break apart. For this reason its work displeases him, and the prophet says to the Jews:

[Note: The same Laurentian codex reads: “its work displeases him.” In Vatican Codex 1267 a passage concerning the Samaritan woman is appended—“The water, therefore, of mercy, etc.”—which is entirely foreign to this homily. Codex 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem has the reading found in the Codex of Saint Gall.]

“Even if you bring fine flour, it is an abomination” (Isaiah 1:13).

[Note: Both Codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, after “even if you bring fine flour,” read “it is futile” instead of “it is an abomination.” This appears to have been taken from the Old Latin version, where the entire passage reads, according to Sabatier, vol. 3, p. 517, Rheims edition, 1743: “If you bring fine flour, it is futile; incense is an abomination to me.” The Vulgate reads: “Do not continue to offer sacrifice in vain; incense is an abomination to me” (Isaiah 1:13).]

The Lord himself, rejecting the function of its work, says: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Mark 8).

The Synagogue therefore attempts to grind while sustaining error. For since Moses had received two stone tablets of the Testament, it imagines that it is working with two necessary instruments, not knowing that the union of those tablets prefigured the coming of the two Testaments joined together.

For this reason the holy Church, which grinds the food of holiness for the Lord, is taken up into eternal glory, while the Synagogue is left at the bloody mills, destined always to suffer the turning of its own faithlessness.

*The homily ends.*

## ANNOTATIONS ON THE SECOND AND THIRD HOMILIES

### 1

Christ foretold his second coming into the world in Matthew 24:27: “For just as lightning comes out from the east and appears as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.” What Luke reported in the Gospel, chapter 17, verse 24, agrees with this: “For just as lightning flashing from beneath heaven shines upon the things beneath heaven, so will the Son of Man be in his day.”

Both Evangelists testify that other predictions followed these prophecies. Matthew says in verse 40: “Then two will be in the field; one will be taken and one will be left; two will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one will be left.” Luke includes the same material, writing in verse 34: “I tell you, on that night there will be two in one bed; one will be taken and the other will be left.”

Saint Maximus proposes to explain these passages in the second and third homilies. Following the second homily, which is entitled “On the Coming of the Lord,” and so forth, according to the better manuscripts, he undertakes to speak of Christ who will come at the end of the ages.

As anyone can see, Maximus did not take either Matthew’s or Luke’s entire passage for his purpose. Rather, he combined material from the two into one, in order to construct the subject of his discourse.

At the beginning of the second homily, therefore, the holy bishop says that Christ foretold that he would come at night. To reconcile this with the Gospel passages in which Christ is said to come with great brilliance and like lightning, he understands “night” as the corruption in which the world, seduced by Antichrist, will be enveloped.
