The darkness of this corruption must immediately be dispersed when Christ, the true sun of justice, the judge, reveals the devil’s fraud and the wickedness of Antichrist. Once Antichrist has been destroyed, the light of truth and the pursuit of virtue will shine forth again.

“To dispel this dreadful darkness,” Saint Maximus says, “Christ will come like a kind of lightning. And just as night is overturned as day increases, so Antichrist is put to flight when the Savior flashes forth; nor will he be able any longer to spread the darkness of his wickedness when the light of truth has shone out.”

Saint Ambrose had earlier explained this same Gospel passage in Book 8, chapter 7, of his *Commentary on Luke*: “He rightly said ‘night,’ because Antichrist is the hour of darkness, since he pours darkness over the hearts of human beings when he says that he is Christ, etc. For he, like flashing lightning, scatters throughout the whole world the globes of his light.”

Once this has been established, Maximus says nothing further about Antichrist or the Lord’s final coming. Following Ambrose, he proceeds to explain the meaning of the words concerning the two in one bed and the two women grinding. Here, he says, “the merit of the resurrection is revealed: the grace of rising corresponds to the quality of one’s life,” and the difference among individuals at the resurrection is so great “that even when two are sleeping together and resting in the same place, their being taken cannot be equal.”

By “resurrection” he does not here indicate the common restoration and revivification of human bodies that will take place at the end of the world, but the raising of the good to glory and the condemnation of the wicked to punishment.

In this matter Maximus agrees admirably with Saint Ambrose, whom he had set before himself as a model. Ambrose’s statement in the passage cited above is: “Is God unjust, that he should distinguish those equal in zeal, in their manner of life, and in the undifferentiated quality of their actions by a difference in the reward of their merits? It is not so; rather, the equality of reward corresponds to a person’s actions.”

From this it is entirely clear that both holy teachers are speaking here not of the eternal predestination of the saints, but of the execution of that same predestination, as it is called.

That Saint Maximus is speaking of the execution of predestination is also evident from the homily on Judas the betrayer. It says: “From the same clay of our body God reserves some, according to the merits of each, for punishment and others for glory.” It also says: “Although they occupy the same bed of companionship, one of them will nevertheless be snatched up to heaven according to his merits, while the other will be left on earth.”

These statements agree with the words of Ambrose in the same place: “The one who is taken is snatched up to meet Christ in the air; but the one who is left is rejected.”

### 2

In the third homily, Saint Maximus writes that the two millstones—one placed upon the other, grinding grain and producing flour—represent the two Testaments, namely the Old and the New.

“These two millstones, therefore, seem to me to be the two Testaments, namely the law of Moses and the Gospel of the Lord. They are so arranged and prepared that each Testament fits the other,” as the Savior says in Matthew 5: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it.”

From this he teaches that the law of the Gospel was placed above the Mosaic law, which was slower and less productive. Finally, he concludes: “Unless the Gospel had been given, the law would have been entirely unnecessary. Without the Gospel, the law accomplished what can be done with a single stone: it could break, but it could not benefit.”

These two points Maximus comprehends in these words. One concerns the old law, which he denies would have been necessary had the Gospel not been given; the other concerns the old law itself, which imposed such a burden that, without the Gospel, it could crush and break a person, but could not benefit him.

The first point relates to what the Apostle teaches in chapter 10 of the Epistle to the Romans, in chapter 10 of the Epistle to the Corinthians, and in chapter 4 of the Epistle to the Galatians: concerning the end of the law in Christ, Christ himself as the rock that followed, and the empty and beggarly elements of the Old Testament. The second requires us to understand that the law, while issuing commands, conferred no strength for their fulfillment; therefore, by itself and without the Gospel—that is, without the assistance of the Savior’s grace—it could, by its own weight, crush and break a person.

It is evident that some misuse this passage of Maximus and conclude from it that God, who required complete obedience to the law and flight from sins, abandoned humanity in its weakness. But they are gravely mistaken. So that they may not mislead others, we declare that Saint Maximus taught something quite different.

To establish this, we must inquire into his meaning when, under the figure of two millstones, he compares the two laws, the old and the new. He expressly states that the lower, stationary stone represents the Mosaic law, while the Gospel was foreshadowed by the stone placed above it.

The function of the two stones, then, is that the lower one contain the grains of wheat. Many commandments were indeed given to the Jewish people; and although they were good and holy, they were not sufficient in themselves for works of justice and holiness. They needed the impulse and movement of the superior agent, namely, the grace of the coming Savior. Saint Maximus indicated this grace by the upper stone, recalling the statement in Romans 8:14: “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.”

For this reason he also recalls that Christ said in Matthew 5: “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it”—that is, to provide the grace by which it might be fulfilled. In this sense the holy bishop affirmed that the two stones suited one another: through the Spirit of life that is in Christ Jesus, as the Apostle says somewhat earlier, the harshness of the grains—or commandments—was broken, so that, made sweeter and easier, they might produce fine flour and nourishment. This means bringing into the open what had lain hidden from the beginning of the world beneath figures and sacraments, and making manifest the most wise providence of the merciful God, who arranged that, even before Christ, his grace should work in human beings through faith in the Redeemer for their salvation.

Accordingly, Maximus added that the rolling of the upper stone—or the power of heavenly assistance—had passed through every age; that is, it had benefited those who lived under the law. But what does he mean when he says: “The law would not have been necessary had the Gospel not been given”? When was the old law ever necessary for observance except when it was given and while it remained in force? Thus, when the commandment was issued and required obedience, the aid of the grace of the coming Savior was also given, as Maximus testifies.

Maximus confirms this most strongly in his first homily on Easter, in which he discusses the saints of the Old Testament. Who, moreover, does not see that this resembles what Saint Leo, Maximus’s contemporary, set forth in sermon 22, his third on the Nativity of the Lord, chapter 4, p. 50 of the Roman edition of 1753, against those who complained that the divine Word had assumed human nature too late?

“Let those complaints cease,” says the holy pontiff, “who, protesting against the divine dispensations with impious murmuring, complain of the lateness of the Lord’s nativity, as though what took place in the final age of the world had not been bestowed in earlier times. The Incarnation of the Word, while still to be accomplished, conferred what it conferred once accomplished; and the mystery of human salvation never ceased in any antiquity . . . nor was what had always been believed fulfilled too late. The wisdom and goodness of God, through this delay in the saving work, made us more capable of his calling . . . But from the foundation of the world he established one and the same cause for all. For the grace of God, by which the whole company of the saints has always been justified, was increased when Christ was born, not begun; and long before the sacrament of great mercy with which the whole world is now filled, it was so powerful even in its signs that those who believed in the promise received no less than those who received the gift.”

Saint Thomas summarized the same doctrine more briefly in *Summa theologiae* I–II, question 98, article 2, reply to objection 4:

“Although the old law was not sufficient to save human beings, nevertheless another aid from God was present to them together with the law, by which they could be saved—namely, faith in the Mediator, through which the ancient fathers were justified . . . and thus God did not fail humanity, since he gave them the means of salvation.”

But why say more? This is the common doctrine of all the holy Fathers, drawn from the sources of Paul and the Gospels. No orthodox believer will suppose that Saint Maximus departed from it.

# HOMILY IV. A Discourse Beginning before the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 0233]

## NOTICE

13 From the most ancient and celebrated Saint Gall manuscript Mabillon extracted twelve homilies of Saint Maximus and transferred them to his *Musaeum Italicum*, as we have already stated in the preface. This homily, which is fourth in the series, had previously been attributed to Maximus on the authority of no other manuscript witness. We now confirm it for the first time through the authority of the manuscript of the major church at Turin. In that manuscript it appears as number 3, with the title: “Likewise, concerning that matter: homily III, and at the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.” It alludes to the title of Homily I, which begins: “How great is the joy, and how great the concourse,” etc.; that same title is also assigned to this homily.

[Col. 0233A] **SUMMARY.**—The very cycle of the days announces that a renewal of the world will shortly occur; and the signs that promise a better appearance and form of things on earth are signs of a spiritual restoration, which the faithful must strive with all their heart to attain.

Even if I were silent, brothers, the season itself reminds us that the nativity of the Lord Christ is near. For the final closing of the days anticipates my preaching. By its very confinement the world declares that something is imminent by which it will be restored to a better state, and in eager expectation it desires that the brightness of a more splendid sun illuminate its darkness. For, since it has deserved to complete its course within the short span of the hours, it indicates with a certain hope that its year will be renewed.

This expectation of creation therefore persuades us also to await the coming of the new sun, Christ, so that he may illuminate the darkness of our sins, and the sun of justice may, by the vigor of his nativity, scatter the long gloom of our transgressions within us. Let him not permit the course of our life to end in the darkness of life, but let the grace of his virtue enlarge it.

Therefore, since we recognize the Lord’s nativity even from the world’s own announcement, let us do what the world is accustomed to do. Just as on that day the world extends the spaces of its light, so let us extend our justice; and just as the brightness of that day is shared by poor and rich alike, so let our generosity be shared by strangers and the needy. Just as the world then cuts away the darkness of its nights, so let us cut off the darkness of our greed. And, after the manner of winter, just as in the fields the seeds are nourished when the frost is loosened by the sun’s warmth, so, when hardness has been softened in our breasts, let the seed of justice, warmed by the Savior’s ray, grow strong.

Therefore, brothers, as we prepare to receive the Lord’s nativity, let us adorn ourselves with pure and shining garments. I mean the garments of the soul, not of the flesh. The garment of the flesh is a cheap covering; the garment of the soul is a precious body. The former is woven by human hands; the latter was fashioned by the hands of God. For this reason it is a matter of greater concern to preserve God’s work without stain than to keep human works undefiled.

If an earthly garment becomes dirty, a fuller hired for the purpose can wash it; but if the garment of the soul is once polluted, it is scarcely washed except through one’s own diligent and continual works. The craftsman’s hand is of no use to it, nor the fuller’s labor. Water can wash the members of the conscience when they are polluted, but it cannot cleanse them.

These are the precious garments of the soul that the evangelist Mark praises highly in the Savior, saying: “And his garments became shining, exceedingly white, like snow, such as no fuller on earth can make” (chapter 9). Christ’s garment is therefore praised because it shone, not through weaving but through grace. The garment is praised not because it was made dense by the fineness of its threads, but because it was conceived in the integrity of the body. The garment is praised not because women’s hands wove it, but because Mary’s virginity produced it.

For this reason the grace of whiteness is magnified in it, because its spotless condition had not been provided by an artisan’s care. “Such as no fuller on earth can make,” he says. Clearly, no fuller can make Christ’s garment. A fuller can provide brightness, cleanliness, and purity, but cannot provide virginity, justice, or goodness. The former belongs to the craft of workmanship; the latter to the nature of virtue.

These garments of virtue the holy evangelist praises highly in Christ the Lord, and blessed David proclaimed them with the same meaning, saying: “Myrrh, and drops, and cassia from your precious garments” (Psalm 44). By these fragrances of spices the garments of holy virtues are signified.

Therefore, brothers, as we prepare to receive the Lord’s nativity, let us cleanse our conscience of every impurity. Let us adorn ourselves not with silken garments but with precious works. Shining clothes can cover the limbs, but they cannot cleanse the conscience. Indeed, it is a matter of greater shame to walk with shining limbs while one’s senses are polluted.

Let us therefore first adorn the disposition of the inner person, so that the clothing of the outer person may also be adorned.

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Gallandius’s edition should be corrected; it has *interiori* instead of *interioris*.]

Let us wash away spiritual stains, so that bodily garments may shine in us. It is of no benefit to shine in clothing and be filthy in wickedness. For where the conscience is dark, the whole body is darkened.

We have, however, with which to wash away the stains of the conscience. For it is written: “Give alms, and everything will be clean for you” (Luke 11:41). A good command concerning almsgiving, through which we work with our hands so that we may be cleansed in heart.

*End.*

# HOMILY V. On the Same Subject

[Col. 0235]

## NOTICE

Mabillon likewise had this homily copied and published from the same Saint Gall manuscript, just as he had the preceding one, in the first volume of his *Musaeum Italicum*. Gallandius received it from Mabillon and transferred it to volume IX of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Venice edition of 1773, retaining the title “It begins: On the Nativity of the Lord the Savior,” which Mabillon himself had taken from the Saint Gall manuscript.

The Turin manuscript provides very strong confirmation that this type of homily ought to be attributed to Maximus. It has the following inscription prefixed to the same homily: “Likewise, homily 35 on the Nativity of the Lord.” What if the style and the author’s treatment of the passage from Isaiah which he cites sufficiently prove that this homily should be attributed to the holy bishop himself, since this manner of adducing passages of Sacred Scripture was peculiar to that bishop—passages which he either translated himself from the Greek or borrowed, in one way or another, from some Latin version?

[Col. 0235B] **SUMMARY.**—The nativity of Christ, worthy of God, was to be displayed in every respect. The Virgin, overshadowed by the power of the Most High, gives birth while remaining incorrupt; the Son is born holy; and the heavenly beings, announcing peace and salvation to humanity, promise a new birth of the world.

Last Sunday, brothers, we reminded your love of the approach of this day, when we said that today we were receiving the Lord’s nativity, with the world itself bearing witness. For the world bears witness by being itself reborn when Christ is born. It is reborn when, as though by a birth, it is drawn out of the depths of the darkness of night into the light. It is reborn, I say, when its decline comes to an end and its brightness is restored.

Therefore, at Christ’s rising we ought rather to call it the rising of the world. On this day he rises to save all things. On this day light rises for the world, resurrection for the dead, and life for mortals. Thus today is not so much the nativity of the Savior as the nativity of salvation.

Christ, then, is born as the salvation of all, whom the prophets testify to be the king of the nations. He is born from a virgin, as Isaiah declares, saying: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us.”

The manner of the Lord’s birth therefore proves its truth. A virgin, ignorant of intercourse with a man, conceived. Her womb was filled without being touched by an embrace, and the chaste belly received the Holy Spirit; pure limbs preserved him, and an innocent body carried him.

Behold the miracle of the Lord’s mother. She is a virgin when she conceives, a virgin when she gives birth, and a virgin after giving birth. Glorious virginity and splendid fertility! The power of the world is born, and there is no groan of the woman in labor. The womb is emptied, the infant is received, and virginity is not violated.

For it was fitting that, when God was born, the merit of chastity should increase; that the integrity of the one who had come to heal what was corrupted should not be violated by his coming; and that bodily purity should not be harmed by him through whom the virginity of baptism is granted to the impure.

The child is therefore born, placed in a manger, and these are God’s first cradles. Nor does the ruler of heaven disdain this confinement, for a virgin’s womb was his dwelling place. Mary was entirely suitable as Christ’s dwelling, not because of her bodily appearance but because of her original grace.

Thus, relieved of her blessed burden, Mary joyfully recognizes herself as a mother, while she does not know herself as a wife; she is glorious because of her offspring, while she is ignorant of a husband. She marvels that she has borne a child, while she testifies that she received the Holy Spirit. And because she gave birth unmarried, she is not terrified, since she has the testimony both of virginity and of offspring.

The offspring indicates the Lord’s Father; virginity dispels the suspicion of those who are astonished. From one side, divinity bears witness to her virginity; from the other, the secret of nature does so.

I say that divinity bears witness to a virginal birth. In order that Christ might be conceived according to the Gospel’s foretelling, the grace of the Holy Spirit filled her, and the power of God the Father overshadowed her, as it was said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

At the Savior’s nativity, therefore, that divine statement was fulfilled which says: “Every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” Behold, the Word of God is born with the testimony of the Trinity. For when the Holy Spirit came upon Saint Mary in the womb, when the Most High overshadowed her, and when Christ was generated, a confession of faith was contained in him.

It was fitting that the Mother who was to bring forth salvation for the peoples should first confirm the mystery of the Trinity in her own womb, so that we might understand that, before the Savior’s birth, the sacrament of faith had already been confirmed.

Mary, as though in the sanctuary of her womb, carried the priest with the mystery. For whatever was destined to benefit the world—all of it came from her womb: God, priest, and victim; God of resurrection, priest of offering. We recognize all this in Christ. He is God insofar as he returned to the Father; high priest insofar as he offered himself; victim insofar as he was killed for us.

Therefore I should not call Mary’s womb a womb, but a temple. It is plainly a temple in which dwells everything holy that is in heaven—indeed, it should be considered above the heavens, since in a more secret tabernacle the mystery is arranged by the divinity, in such a way that many may ascend to heaven.

Mary’s womb should plainly be considered above the heavens, because it sent the glorious Son of God back to heaven more glorious than he had descended from heaven. From there he descended in order to suffer; from here he returned in order to reign. From there he descended, humbled, into humanity; from here he ascended, glorified, to the Father.

The temple of the body is plainly better than heaven. Christ is seated there: there he is terrible, here he is manifest; there invisible, here visible and tangible; there he avenges sins, here he forgives them; there he exercises the power of a judge, here he exhorts the brothers with love.

Therefore it is good for us to worship him when he invites us, so that we may not fear him when he judges.

*End.*

# HOMILY VI. On the Nativity of the Lord I

[Col. 0237]

## NOTICE

We transcribed this homily from a very ancient manuscript once belonging to the abbey of Saint Dalmatius, of which we have said enough in the notes, and we now publish it for the first time. The manuscript does indeed bear the name of Saint Maximus, and there is no reason why we should think it should not be assigned to the holy bishop.

[Col. 0237A] **SUMMARY.**—Although Christ is proclaimed as having been born in two ways, he must nevertheless be called one Son of God. For he is the same one who was begotten by the Father from eternity and who was born in time from the Virgin.

Brothers, as we celebrate with due honor the most solemn nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, let us exult and rejoice in the Lord that he who is the Son of the eternal God has at last come from heaven to earth as a human being, in order to redeem us from the devil’s slavery. He has descended from heaven—the inhabitant of heaven—in order to lead the inhabitants of earth into heaven.

Today, from a virgin who knew no intercourse with a man, a human being has appeared who is also God and human. Today one and the same person was born as God without any carnal conception, and became human without any begetter. God begot him from eternity, and in time the chaste Virgin received him through the working power of almighty God.

He was born from eternity without any beginning of created existence; he arose in time from an immaculate virgin. In the first nativity he was born as God; in the second he was born as a human being. In the first, as God, he made humanity; in the second, he released humanity from the bonds of sin by which it was held.

Exult, therefore, and rejoice, Zion, because you have been freed from every fear of the former transgression of the fathers. For the Lord has arisen in the city of David, which is called Bethlehem. He mercifully absolved our guilt—the guilt by which wretched humanity had been surrounded for so long through the devil’s deceits—and in his goodness shook the yoke of ancient slavery from our necks.

God, the Son of God, was born from a woman, wrapped in swaddling clothes, and placed in a manger. *(Here a leaf is missing; the text then continues.)*

Let us therefore approach this God, at once God and human, with humble heart, sincere mind, and chaste acts of devotion. Nor, because we are distressed by the clashing arms of foreigners, stirred up by the discord of opposing kings, should we therefore fail to celebrate the most sacred mysteries of this day with joy. Rather, let us venerate them with fitting rejoicing, beseeching God that in his mercy he may deem it right to free and preserve us from these dangers. *(Ten lines are missing here; they have faded from the manuscript.)*

Let us therefore offer ourselves to him, so that, freed by his mercy from the evils that threaten us, etc. *(The remainder is missing.)*

# HOMILY VII. On the Nativity of the Lord II

[Col. 0237]

## NOTICE

21 This homily too was taken from the same manuscript of the abbey of Saint Dalmatius, and we likewise now publish it for the first time. There is nothing to prevent its attribution to Saint Maximus, as it is also attributed to him in the Turin manuscript; and its manner of expression, certainly very similar to his, provides a strong additional argument for assigning this homily to him.

[Col. 0237C] **SUMMARY.**—Against the pagans who deny that God was born human from the Virgin, Saint Maximus proves that everything is possible for the divine Creator of all things. In his infinite wisdom and power, he accomplishes all things when and how he wills.

The holy and venerable mystery of the Lord’s nativity, which year after year we venerate with the deepest devotion, so excels in the greatness of its condescension that it confounds both the audacity of the pagans and the impudence of all heretics.

We, instructed by faith and with the simplicity of little children, steadfastly believe that the God whom we acknowledge could have been born from a woman. The Gentiles, on the other hand—to set aside the heretics for the moment—dulled by carnal arguments, still refuse to believe that he could have been born from a virgin, and they mock the priest of Christ who teaches this.

Although they themselves think and marvel that God performs wondrous deeds every day in other matters and has so often performed them in the past, they nevertheless contend that, in the holy and miraculous nativity of his Son, our Redeemer, he could neither have performed such a work nor ought to have done so.

But what is this foolish teaching of the wise men of this age—or rather, what should I call it but madness? They believe that God performed wonders at some time and still performs them now, yet they maintain that in the most sacred nativity of his Son, our Lord, from a virgin, he was in no way able to accomplish this.

For the one and the same God who at some time created heaven and the heavens of the heavens, together with all that is in them, from nothing by divine skill; who likewise fashioned the earth, the waters and seas, and all that they contain, from nothing by the omnipotent power of his Word—he is the one who gave a virgin childbirth and offspring.

If you believe that God was able to create heaven, the sun, and the stars from nothing; if you believe that he was able to create the earth, the seas, living creatures, and the entire adornment of this visible world; if, finally, you believe that he was able to form a human being from clay—*[the word “you admit” is missing]*—why do you insist that he could not give a child to an untouched virgin through the working power of that same God?

For what greater display of the omnipotence of God will there be: to have created from nothing all that he sees in heaven and in the world, or to create a human being in the womb of an undefiled virgin without any preceding carnal union?

If you marvel at the omnipotence of the Creator in those things that are seen, why will you deny it in the childbirth of an undefiled virgin? What will that foolish madness be—*[two lines are wholly missing here]*—to have done everything he wished in heaven and on earth, because his omnipotent power both willed and was able to do those things, yet that a virgin could give birth through the working power of God and truly bear a child—*[a leaf is missing here, and only a mutilated conclusion remains]*.

And so, brothers, as we celebrate the most sacred solemnities of so great a mystery, let us always venerate our God, who has done such great things for the undeserving. *(Here too ten lines are completely obliterated.)* . . . Let us therefore hasten to him with continual prayers, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

*End.*

# HOMILY VIII. On the Nativity of the Lord III

[Col. 0239]

## NOTICE

23 This third homily on the Lord’s nativity was supplied to us by a very ancient manuscript formerly belonging to the monastery of Appannis, commonly called Pagno, in the marquisate of Saluzzo, p. 16; like the preceding homily, it also enjoys the testimony of the Turin manuscript. For it is listed in its index as: “Likewise, a homily on the Nativity of the Lord, homily 19.” It greatly enhances the dignity and ornament of our edition that we present it complete in every respect.

[Col. 0239A] **SUMMARY.**—All the benefits that the day of the Lord’s nativity brought to the world are enumerated. Divine goodness and mercy provide us with great cause for joy through the coming of him who is God and human, whose gifts have enriched us.

[Col. 0239B] The most holy and venerable mystery of the Lord’s nativity, which the universal Church venerates today with exultant hearts, we too ought to celebrate with corresponding joy. Today that eternal Son of God, taking pity on human nature, descended from the royal dwelling places in order to restore us.

Today that new Adam, through his wondrous nativity, fashioned our nature anew, and what had been defiled and corrupted by the pitiable fall of the old Adam, through his precious nativity and tearful death, restored to life.

Today the Lord of heaven and earth deigned to visit our weaknesses. On this day Bethlehem—that city of the great God, which is called the city of bread—brought forth for us that heavenly bread and drink, by which those who are filled and made drunk will always taste eternal joys.

Hell is saddened that the one who is God and human has been born, for he closed its gates and transferred the inhabitants of earth to heaven. The heavens, however, rejoice that through his coming an entrance has at last been opened to the whole world, by which mortals themselves may ascend to the heights of heaven.

The heavenly inhabitants also rejoice that on this day hope has been given to all human beings of dwelling in those eternal abodes which God has prepared for those who love him; and they rejoice that they will one day become participants in that blessedness and companions in its joys.

Finally, the most blessed Virgin who has given birth herself rejoices that she bore the child whom, through the radiating power of the Holy Spirit from above, she conceived in her womb as both God and human, without any carnal union.

Let us therefore rejoice also, brothers, on this most sacred day on which the Lord was born for us, who is Christ Jesus in the city of David, and let us rejoice in the solemnity of so great a nativity.

For the one whom we now venerate as newly born, we believe to be not merely human but also God. He is human in the tenderness of his limbs, but God, proceeding from God, from the conception of his undefiled mother.

And truly, as you have heard from the different readings of the Gospel, the star itself that announced his rising to the Magi, and the angels who spoke with the shepherds, show that he was God and human. We must therefore believe entirely that he was both God and human.

*End.*

# HOMILY IX. On the Nativity of the Lord IV

[Col. 0239]

## NOTICE

We have spoken sufficiently about this homily in the notes on the life of Saint Maximus and in the preface. We think that nothing need be added except that it was taken from the same manuscript of Saint Dalmatius, number 9, “On the Nativity of the Lord”; in the Turin manuscript, however, it is homily 15. In both manuscripts it bears the title: “Likewise, on the Nativity of the Lord.”

[Col. 0239C] **SUMMARY.**—It recalls the condemnation of the heresy of Helvidius and Jovinian against the Virgin’s virginity and sets against it the Catholic doctrine.

Brothers, let us also celebrate with fitting joy this most holy day of the Lord’s nativity, which the whole rejoicing Church celebrates together with us.

Today that eternal Son of God descended from heaven to earth for us, in order to summon to heaven the whole world that he had created from the beginning. Today, at the end of time, he was born as a human being who, before all ages, proceeded as the only-begotten one from the Father.

He is a new human being in time, but God from eternity; a new Christ, but Lord of all ages.

Today that most blessed Virgin Mary gave birth to a human being whom she did not receive from a man, and she remained an inviolate virgin before giving birth.

Blind and foolish paganism laughs at the depth of so great a mystery. The impious blasphemy that in recent days presumed to diminish and corrupt the Virgin’s childbirth also mocks it, blaspheming that Christ our Lord could not be born from a virgin.

The holy Church of Milan shuddered at this blasphemy; our synodal assembly condemned it with one voice; and the pious imperial authority itself cursed it. For by daring to equate honorable marriage with virginity, it blasphemes Christ by saying that he could not be born from a virgin, while it does not dare deny that virgins can remain virgins after giving birth to human children from a woman.

But what is this shameless and reckless deceit: to say that Christ our Lord could not be born from a virgin, when these people believe that he could create a human being without a woman?

If he could bring a woman into the world without any union of the female and male sexes, why is it said that he could not generate a new human being without any carnal union? If you believe that, in the creation of the first Adam, the power of God alone was sufficient, why, brother, will you deny divine power in the coming of the second Adam, through whom eternal salvation descended upon us and through whom we were all restored?

But if, since God can do everything he wills in heaven and on earth, it is not contrary to nature for a virgin to conceive, why do you assert that it is contrary to nature for a virgin, through the working power of almighty God and with her virginity unharmed . . . For everything that God willed, he did in heaven and on earth.

He willed to form a human being from clay, and he did so. He willed heaven and earth—*[ten lines are missing because the writing has perished]*—and they came to be. He commanded the sun to stand still in its course at Gideon’s request, and it stood still. Finally, he willed that an untouched virgin should bear a child while her virginity remained intact, and she did bear one.

What, therefore, in this heavenly childbirth—*[a leaf is missing; the text later concludes as follows]*:

“Therefore, brothers, adhering with unconquerable faith and customary devotion to the priest’s repeated exhortations, and walking along the roads of religious conduct and the paths of truth which the universal Church follows, trample ever more forcefully the deviations and diabolical fictions of the heretics. For the faithful soul, which believes that God was able to do whatever he willed, ought not—*[two lines are missing]*—who will consume in eternal fires.”

*End.*

# HOMILY X. On the Nativity of the Lord V

[Col. 0241]

## NOTICE

Several manuscripts of the highest authority affirm this distinguished homily to belong to Maximus. In particular, we shall mention four Vatican manuscripts: 1267, p. 91; 4951, p. 6; Vatican Palatinus 433, p. 101; and Vatican Regina 125, p. 70. They are followed by the Turin manuscript, “On the Nativity of the Lord, homily I”; two Novara manuscripts, 27, p. 69, and marked l. O, number 11, p. 20; the Augia manuscript XVI; the Cassinese manuscript 106, p. 12; the Modoetian manuscript marked l. E III; and the Lambach manuscript, p. 95. All, bearing the name of Saint Maximus as the title of the homily, provide clear testimony.

Relying on these and similar witnesses, Gymnicus, p. 12; Galesinius, p. 88; Combefisius, volume I, p. 206; Cumdius, volume I, p. 169; Raynaudus, p. 195; and Margarinus, Lyon edition of 1677, volume VI, p. 1, published this as the first of Maximus’s homilies on the Nativity of the Lord.

[Col. 0241B] **SUMMARY.**—The divine Word, eternally begotten by the Father, when he deigned to be born as a human being on earth, was not conceived in the ordinary manner but assumed flesh from a virgin mother through the heavenly working power of the Most High. Such a birth was fitting for the Son of God among human beings.

Dearest brothers, today Christ was born and we were reborn. Today the Savior of the world received from his mother the time of birth, although from the Father he has no time of birth. Today, through a human being, the Son of God entered the world, although the world itself was made before humanity by his hand.

Today the inhabitant of heaven came to earth in order to summon the inhabitants of earth to heaven. “God is wonderful in his saints” (Psalm 67). If God is wonderful in his saints, how much more wonderful is he in himself?

If he is wonderful in John, whom he commanded to be born from an aged father and a barren mother, how much more wonderful is he in himself, since, in order to assume the flesh of our condition, he gave a virgin both a new conception and a new childbirth.

Saint Habakkuk the prophet says: “Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, and I was terrified” (chapter 3). Who would not be terrified and afraid at the depth of so great a mystery, since one and the same person was born as God without conception,

[Note: [Col. 0241D] In Vatican manuscript 1267, p. 90, the reading is: “He became human without a begetter.”]

An unpublished author of the fifteenth century, in the manuscript Ottobonianus Vaticanus 772, book I, chapter 5, *On the Mysteries of Human Redemption*, where he discusses the two generations of Christ, cites this passage of Maximus under his name.
] and without a creator was made man. We read, most beloved brothers, of two generations in Christ, but in both is the power of the incomprehensible divinity. There God begot him from himself; here the Virgin conceived him with God at work. There, without beginning; here, without precedent. There he was born to establish life; here he was made to abolish death. There he was born for the Father; here he was brought forth for human beings. By that birth he made man; by this generation he freed man. This one statement embraces both his generations, brothers, as incapable of being described: the one is before man, the other above man; the one inconceivable, the other marvelous.

When we are taught that Christ has two births, it is not asserted that the Son of God was born twice, but that in the one Son of God there is confirmed a twofold substance.

[Note: In the same Vatican codex, “He conceived through God’s cooperation.”]

[Note: This is taken from “twofold substance” in the fourth hymn of Saint Ambrose, volume IV of the Venetian edition of his works, 1751, p. 309. Pope Saint Celestine the Great praises this hymn in the sermon he delivered at the Roman council against the heresy of Nestorius. Compare volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, p. 1098, and Coustant’s Paris edition, 1721, p. 172. Maximus here recalls a twofold substance—that is, nature—in the person of the Word of God; this is the Catholic doctrine first defined by the Apostolic See and then by the Council of Ephesus against the heretical Nestorian doctrine. Saint Leo the Great’s teaching amounts to the same thing in Sermon 20, his first on the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, volume I of the Roman edition, 1753, p. 43: “He joined both natures by so great a bond that glorification did not consume the lower, nor assumption diminish the higher. Thus, with the distinct property of each substance preserved and humility received into majesty as the two came together in one person.”

What Maximus adds—that the Son of God is not asserted to have been born twice, nor God to have been born twice—may perhaps seem contrary to the opinion of theologians who say that it can rightly be stated that Christ was born twice. One should consult Saint Thomas, Part III, Question 35, Article 11, answer to the fourth objection, and III Sentences, distinction 14, question 1, article 2, answer to the fourth objection. But the matter is otherwise. Anyone who observes that Maximus is speaking of God, or of the Son of God, will understand that there is no contradiction. If someone says that he was born twice, he seems—as Maximus himself feared—to duplicate the person and to agree with the Nestorians. For whoever speaks of God, or of the Son of God, without introducing any mention of the human nature assumed by him, and says that he was born twice, seems to say that God, as God, was born twice.

Maximus, however, names two births in this way: “God was not born twice; rather, through two births—namely, God’s and man’s—the Father’s Only-Begotten willed to be himself one God and man.” Thomas, on the other hand, affirms that Christ may rightly be said to have been born twice. But whoever says “Christ” certainly means the one who is God and man, or the one in whom two natures come together in one person. Therefore, he says in the body of the article, “in Christ there are two natures, divine and human: one he received eternally from the Father, the other temporally from his mother. Hence it is necessary to attribute two births to Christ: one by which he was born eternally from the Father, the other by which he was born temporally from his mother.”

[Col. 0243A] There he was born as what he was; here he was made what he was not. Blessed John the Evangelist says of these things:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

And again:

> And the Word was made flesh.

Therefore God, who was with God, came forth from God; and God’s flesh, which was not in God, came forth from a woman. Thus the Word was made flesh—not so that God might be emptied into man, but so that man might be glorified into God.

[Note: Codex Casinensis 106: “Therefore God was born for us.”]

Thus God was not born twice; rather, through two births—namely, God’s and man’s—the Father’s Only-Begotten willed to be himself one God and man. “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53). Brothers, if Christ’s generation cannot be described, it can be believed. If the tongue fails, faith advances. Faith makes great progress when it conceives of its God as much as speech cannot bring forth.

Beware, beloved, lest unbelief ever disturb you concerning these things. For if a human being cannot explain what he perceives, God certainly can accomplish what he willed.

[Note: Codex 1267: “was able,” instead of “is able.”]

And it is utterly absurd, brothers, for us to measure the ineffable God by the feeblest speech of our frailty. It is madness to attempt to confine the works of boundless majesty within the narrow words of our corruptible mouth. For how can a created man comprehend the Unbegotten God, a mortal man the Eternal?

[Note: The Laurentian Codex and Vatican Codex 1267 add: “For how could a created, begotten man comprehend the Eternal God?”]

If you strive to investigate how God passed into man, or man into God, first investigate, if you can, how the world was made from nothing; from where the heavens shone forth; by what principle the fluidity of the waters and the solidity of the earth subsist; how, moreover, man came from earth, woman from man, and likewise man through woman; and what that is, finally, which brings forth light and darkness, which produces life and death.

If, then, O man, you cannot comprehend how or from where you yourself and the things made for your sake came into being, with what presumption or folly do you examine your own Creator and the Creator of all?

We confess, therefore, that God was born from God the Father and that the same one was made man from a virgin. But these things, beloved, are blind to reason and manifest to faith. We shall then be able to explore, in some measure, the immensity of his undefined majesty if we recognize that God’s greatness and nature cannot be known by us, as the Lord said to Moses:

> But you cannot see my face. (Exodus 33)

That is:

[Note: Codex Novatianus: “The bodily eye cannot.”]

The bodily eyes cannot behold my divinity as it is.

For blessed David, contemplating the power of his omnipotence, cried out:

> How marvelous are your works, O Lord, and my soul knows them exceedingly well. (Psalm 133)

The prophetic soul knew very well that God’s works surpass all meditation of the human mind. Therefore the wisest patriarch, confined within the narrow limits of mortal understanding, marveled at what he could not investigate.

Who, then, among human beings would dare examine or inquire into something so great that the prophet himself marvels at it?

> How marvelous are your works, and my soul knows them exceedingly well.

For the soul knew precisely this: that God is incomprehensible, while the flesh could not perceive it. Therefore anyone who wishes to scrutinize God’s works rather than believe them follows not the perception of the soul but error. And so, brothers, let us not examine how God was born from God; let us believe. Let us not investigate the Virgin’s childbirth; let us marvel, so that, confessing God’s Only-Begotten as God and man, we may hold firmly to the unbroken truth of heavenly faith.

# HOMILY XI  
## On the Nativity of the Lord VI

[Col. 0243]

## ADMONITION

Former editors attributed this homily to Saint Leo the Great. As the Ballerini brothers learnedly point out in their preface to his works, they acknowledge that it must be restored to Saint Maximus. Their judgment rests on five Vatican codices: 4951, folio 5 verso; 1267, folio 89 verso; 433, folio 99 verso; Regina 125, folio 69 verso; and Ottobonianus 773. These are supported by the Turin manuscript, Homily 13 on the Nativity of the Lord; Vercelli 81; two Novara manuscripts, 27, folio 68, and the manuscript marked l. O, no. 11, folio 18; the Modena manuscript E III; the Cistercian manuscript of Monte Amiata; and finally two Reichenau manuscripts, XII and XIII.

Alcuin likewise attributes it to Maximus on page 26 of the 1571 Venetian edition of the homilies; so do Gymnicus, p. 16; Combefisius, volume I, p. 207; Cumdius, volume I, p. 164; Galesinius, p. 90; and Raynaudus, p. 194. Margarinus, Bibliotheca Maxima, Lyons edition, 1677, volume VI, p. 5, confirms the same. Who could think otherwise, when there is such agreement among manuscripts and writers?

## ARGUMENT

Maximus abundantly sets forth the reasons for Christian rejoicing at the Lord’s Nativity and recounts the splendid benefits of redemption.

[Col. 0243D] Most rightly, brothers, on the feast of this present day the whole world everywhere rises into complete joy, because today the judge and redeemer promised through the ages has arisen for the whole world.

[Note: Vatican Palatine Codex: “of the whole world.”]

And it is necessary that all of us together who have received the saving faith in the coming judgment and promised resurrection should have fear of the judge, but joy in the redeemer. For every faithful soul is corrected by fear and rejoices in correction.

And in this, beloved, how great is the dispensation of the almighty Father toward the human race, and how great his kindness: the one whom he was preparing as judge for unbelievers, he sent beforehand as redeemer for believers, so that mercy preceding might forestall the severity of the approaching judge.

Today, therefore, Christ was born; but in his birth the life of us all has its birthday. For we who lost the privileges of the first birth, when Christ visited us, return to life through a holier birth.

Today Mary gave birth, but she brought forth her own creator. Today she gave the world a man whom she had not received from a man.

[Note: The same codex: “What is this?”]

What is this miracle, brothers? Flesh is born from flesh, yet it was not generated through flesh; and through a conception both mysterious and incomprehensible, a divine offspring proceeds from a mortal woman.

Nor is it surprising that there was a divine birth where there had been no human conception, or that childbirth did not violate that mother whom intercourse had not defiled.

Isaiah, once conscious of future things, opened to peoples and nations the sign of a new salvation:

[Note: Vatican Palatine Codex: “Opening the new sign of a new salvation: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive,’ etc.”]

> Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,

which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isaiah 7).

And so that we may recognize that the New and Old Testaments have one agreement and one purpose, blessed Luke, the distinguished narrator of the Lord’s generation, also says:

> The angel Gabriel was sent by God to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, and he said to her: Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Jesus. (Luke 1)

Jesus, beloved, is called “Savior” in the Latin language.

Behold how the divine testimonies confirm one another with mutually harmonious statements. Though the times of the proclaimers are different, the narrative is not different. The one foretold the Virgin’s childbirth; the other bears witness to it.

[Note: Vatican Palatine Codex 433: “Who, then, would hesitate concerning Christ’s birth, who …?”]

Who, then, would hesitate concerning Christ’s divinity or the redemption of all humanity, when Isaiah confesses him to be God and Gabriel announces him as Savior? Who would doubt that the womb of the untouched woman blossomed in childbirth, when evangelist, angel, and prophet proclaim it with almost one mouth and one spirit?

[Note: Vatican Codex 1267: “which they proclaim with almost one mouth.” Codex Ottobonianus Vaticanus 773: “which the evangelist proclaims with almost one mouth, in harmony of spirit,” etc.]

Where there are such great and such numerous witnesses, truth is not put to shame; rather, the unbelieving hearer is refuted.

But now let us see what injuries Christ endured, born for our sake, and by what virtues those injuries were again adorned. First of all, he permitted himself to be conceived in the female sex, although at the beginning of the world he had fashioned woman from man by his almighty hand.

[Note: The same Codex 1267: “Above all, he permitted himself to be conceived in the female sex.”]

Yet the integrity of the virginal mother exalts this humility of birth. Although Christ was born in the female sex and, as an infant, was nourished with milk, nevertheless, as the one possessing power over all things, he was nourished at a virgin’s breasts.

[Note: Vatican Palatine Codex 433: “Yet, as the one powerful over all things.” Codex Vaticanus 1267: “He is nourished at virgin breasts.”]

And when his mother’s womb first poured him into these storms of the world and the sewage of the tossing world, he was wrapped in the cheapest cloths.

[Note: The same Codex 1267: “wrapped in swaddling cloths.”]

He is clothed in swaddling cloths who, when he created all things, flooded the earth with light, adorned the heavens with stars, and clothed the sun with fiery brilliance. He is indeed wrapped in cloths, but these cloths are honored by the Magi through the shining of a new star and by exultant angels.

[Note: The same codex: “and honored by exultant angels.”]

And so that we may know that all these things are either done or spoken mystically, this one who is wrapped in cloths, proclaimed from the beginning from the Father’s bosom and the eternal bridal chamber as the bridegroom of the saving marriage, came from heaven, as venerable David says:

> He himself comes forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber. (Psalm 18)

Then, as we read, he is placed in a manger, because, as the evangelist says:

[Note: The same codex: “There was no place for him in the lodging-house.”]

> There was no place for them in the lodging-house. (Luke 2)

Let these things not disturb you, brothers, because all this lowliness in the Savior is the sacrament of our most precious salvation.

Consider with what wisdom Christ is said to be placed in a manger: by a twofold grace he was to become both food and shepherd for the human race. He is rightly placed in a manger so that the bleating of the heavenly Lamb might invite the flocks of spiritual sheep to the pastures of eternal life.

> There was no place for them in the lodging-house.

Were his dwelling’s quarters really so confined that they could not contain the limbs of a little child newly born?

[Col. 0246C] But for this reason it is reported in mystical language that he found no place in the lodging-house: because, on entering the world, Christ found no faith in which he could rest, as he himself says in the Gospel:

> The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. (Matthew 8)

From this we understand that the only-begotten Son of God rests not in spacious houses with gilded ceilings,

[Note: The same codex: “with gilded ceilings.”]

but in the faith of believers.

[Note: Ottobonianus Vaticanus Codex 673 has: “Behold Christ Jesus.” The entire passage is quoted by the author cited in chapter 72, On Praising the Lord after the Example of Angels.]

This Christ Jesus, then, sucking at the breast like newborn infants, crying in infant fashion, wrapped in cheap cloths, lying in a manger, is accompanied by angelic ministries, and the whole multitude of the heavenly army marvels, praising him with harmonious voice and saying:

> Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will. (Luke 2)

Glory indeed to God, who bestowed the gift of eternal salvation upon mortals who had despaired; and peace to people of good will, whom Christ, by his struggle and his battle, recalled from the devil’s captivity into his own kingdom.

And how fittingly the Gospel proclamation resounds when it says:

> Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people,

for the very Son of God is glorious in heaven among the angels and grants peace on earth to people of good will.

[Note: The same codex: “The angelic proclamation resounds.”]

Therefore, beloved, let us rejoice in such great salvation with fitting celebrations. Joining ourselves to the angelic voices, let us always praise Christ’s mysteries and virtues with the honor that is due.

[Note: The same codex adds: “He who, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God for ever and ever. Amen.”]

# HOMILY XII  
## On the Nativity of the Lord VII

[Col. 0247]

## ADMONITION

I would speak at greater length about the manuscripts in which this homily is read, if that were necessary. It will be sufficient to mention these very few, from which the others do not differ. The Turin M. E. manuscript contains it as Homily 22 on the Nativity of the Lord; likewise the Lucca manuscript 85, Vatican Palatine 433, folio 103; Vatican Regina 125, folio 71 verso; and finally two Belgian manuscripts, Martinensis and Camberonensis, in which it is Homily 7 on the Nativity of the Lord. All of them consistently announce Saint Maximus as its author.

These are supported by four other codices: Casinensis 106, Vercelli 81, Vallicella 125, and Reichenau XVI. The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, having found it among Saint Augustine’s sermons on the seasons, placed it in the appendix of sermons; relying also on the authority of manuscript and printed books, they assigned it to our Maximus. Compare volume V of Saint Augustine’s works, Antwerp edition, 1700, p. 155. Gymnicus, p. 22; Galesinius, p. 91; Combefisius, volume I, p. 108; Cumdius, p. 168; Raynaudus, p. 196; and Margarinus, Bibliotheca Maxima, volume VI, p. 6, likewise judged that it ought to be printed.

## ARGUMENT

The flesh of the divine Word, assumed from the Virgin and fitting the eternal divinity and majesty, was the work of heavenly power, which holds all things in its authority.

At the Lord’s coming, most beloved brothers, every fear of our father’s transgression was released—the fear into which mortal humanity, ensnared by the devil’s ancient deceits, had fallen.

[Note: Vatican Palatine 433 and Martinensis: “by the devil’s ancient deceits.”]

For the judge of heaven and earth is present among us; by canceling the record of sins, he mercifully absolved our guilt.

That Lord is present who, loosening the yoke of ancient captivity from our necks, makes the world’s sorrow rejoice in eternal freedom.

[Note: Vatican Codex 1267: “makes joyful.”]

The gentle king is present, who, walking across the whole expanse of the world with the steps of heavenly justice, crushed the tyranny of the raging enemy.

[Note: Vatican Palatine Codex: “who, traversing the whole extent”; Vatican Regina 125, Vatican Codices 1267 and 4651, Vercelli and Martinensis: “may he crush the tyranny of the raging enemy.”]

Today, as Mary gives birth, the Son of God was born for us, so that, produced through the true conception of our flesh, he might bestow upon the human being created by him both paternal compassion and fraternal affection.

And he was born from an untouched woman so that human childbirth might testify at once that he was man, while eternal virginity proved that he was God.

For just as flesh could be born only from flesh, so God’s flesh could proceed from a woman’s womb only without a begetter. Therefore the angel said to the most blessed Mary:

> The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and the holy thing that will be born from you will be called the Son of God. (Luke 1)

“The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you.” For this reason, brother, the angelic message protected you by the power of the Holy Spirit,

[Note: Vatican Regina Codex 1267, Martinensis, and Camberonensis: “by the power”; the Paris edition of Saint Ambrose, 1690: “covered over.”]

so that, dulled by the conjectures of fleshly argument, you would not fabricate a heavenly mystery through earthly reasoning.

[Note: Vatican Palatine 433: “confound.”]

Or do you not think that he could form a new child in a virgin’s womb who, when he first created man, sought neither a father’s seed nor a mother’s womb?

[Note: Martinensis: “Do you not?” Codex 4951: “Or do you not think”; Palatine Codex: “a new child for you.”]

Say, then, whoever you are, judge and examiner of the heavenly dispensation: which power seems greater to you—to give a virgin childbirth, or to create a perfect man from earth? For, as the Apostle says:

> The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. (1 Corinthians 15)

If you insist that it is contrary to nature that, in the mystery of our redemption, a girl is said to have conceived without a man, I ask: of what nature is it that, in the parent of our race, flesh was formed without flesh?

What sort of reasoning is this—or rather, what blind contention—that one should not believe God able to make man from a woman, when one believes that he made him from dust?

[Note: Ottobonianus Vaticanus 773 and Vaticanus 1267: “If, O man, you perceive the will of the Almighty in such a matter, why do you question his work?”]

If you perceive the will of the Almighty in such a matter, why do you question his work? For, as we read:

> The Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth. (Psalm 134)

And if you carefully investigate, you will discover that, besides this ordinary use of human conception, the Trinity brought about three exceedingly marvelous kinds of birth.

The first is that Adam was formed from clay;

[Note: Ottobonianus Vaticanus 773: “that Adam was formed from mud.”]

the second, that woman was formed from man;

[Note: The same codex: “from a man”; “the third, which was heavenly,” etc. The entire passage is quoted by the author cited, up to the words “what earthly birth had lost.”]

the third, which is also heavenly, is that Christ came forth from a virgin.

What is there among these that is not new? What is there that is not marvelous? What among them can human inquiry comprehend unless it follows faith?

The reason that God’s Son deigned to visit his world through this mystical conception was the necessity of our salvation—namely, that heavenly generation should at last restore what earthly birth had lost.

But perhaps you distrust that this one proclaimed as born from a woman is God, while he is wrapped in cheap cloths, content to lie in a manger, cries out in tearful wailing, and is nursed at his mother’s breasts?

Rather, brother, through these things recognize him: as man, he endured weakness for the weak; as God, he exercised heavenly power.

This one, then, who is wrapped in filthy cloths, is honored by the Chaldaeans with royal gifts (Matthew 21; Luke 11). This one who lies humbly in a manger shines from heaven with the light of a new star (John 6). This one who utters the cries of infancy is praised by the voices of the angelic host. This one who is nourished with a woman’s milk satisfied many thousands of people with a very small amount of bread.

What more shall I add? That he is God and truly the Son of God is proved by Lazarus rising from the dead (John 11), proclaimed by the blind man restored to the light,

[Note: Codices Regina Vatican 125 and Palatine 433: “the blind man restored to the light announces it.” Codex 4651 and Vercelli 81: “the blind man, receiving light, announces it.”]

attested by the water as it was trodden under his revered footsteps (Matthew 14), and—what surpasses all these things—confirmed by the Father’s voice resounding from heaven (Matthew 3).

Therefore, beloved, let us honor this great sacrament of the Lord’s Nativity with worthy voices. Let us love chastity above all, because, to show that chastity pleases him, Christ chose the purity of a virginal womb. Let us pursue mercy, because it is through compassion that we are saved. Let us carefully maintain justice, because for this reason the Only-Begotten Son of God deigned to become man: to proclaim the truth and cleanse the whole face of the world from condemned iniquity.

[Note: Palatine Codex 433: “to cleanse the whole face of the world, with iniquity condemned.” Codex 4951: “to renew the world, with iniquity condemned”; followed by: “to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.”]

# HOMILY XIII  
## On the Nativity of the Lord VII

[Col. 0249]

## ADMONITION

No writer, so far as we know, considers this homily not attributable to Saint Maximus. The authority of the manuscripts and printed editions agrees completely with the overwhelming consensus of the writers.

From the Vatican library we shall name four concordant codices: 4951, p. 21; 1267, p. 91; Regina 433, p. 98 verso; and another Regina 125, p. 72. It is entitled: “On the Nativity of the Lord, a sermon of blessed Bishop Maximus.”

The same title is found in three Reichenau codices, XII, XVI, and XXIX; in Martinensis; in Casinensis 106, p. 13; and finally in Modena E III, Sermon 23. The Laurentian codices lack it. It is found in the Turin codex under the title: “Likewise, Homily XIV on the Nativity of the Lord.”

All editors also include it among Maximus’s homilies on the Nativity: Gymnicus, p. 14; Galesinius, p. 92; Combefisius, volume I, p. 168; Cumdius, volume I, p. 65; Raynaudus, p. 197; and Margarinus, volume VI of the Bibliotheca Maxima Patrum, p. 6.

## ARGUMENT

It is not contrary to human reason that the Son of God, proceeding eternally from God, should in time have become a man like us. His twofold generation, proving a twofold nature in Christ and containing an ineffable mystery, is an argument for faith.

The sacrament of today’s mystery, most beloved brothers, is—as you have always believed and do believe—the restoration of human salvation, the birth of virtues, and the downfall of vices.

For today Christ Jesus, our Lord, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells, assuming the weakness of our flesh, was born as a new man.

Today that second Adam has shone forth—not an inhabitant but the lord of paradise, whom the beauty of the forbidden tree will not deceive, whom the serpent will not trick, and whom the woman will not seduce.

Today light has arisen in the darkness. Today the world unknowingly received what heaven and the heaven of heavens rejoiced to possess.

[Note: The Martinensis omits “heaven,” etc.]

For he did not suddenly emerge from a woman as something temporal, or as one who had not previously existed;

[Note: Vatican Codex 1267: “who had not previously existed.”]

rather, he who was always God with the Father and always reigned chose to appear to mortals through a new mystery by means of a virgin: a new man indeed, but the eternal Lord; a new Christ, but the king of all ages.

He is the one born from Mary at the end of time who, before all ages, proceeded from the Father as the Only-Begotten. He is the one foretold by the patriarchs, proclaimed by the prophets, announced by the angels, and confirmed by the apostles.

Of one and the same person you read:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was made flesh. (John 1)

Rejoice, then, and now exult toward your God at last, O Gentile world, turning yourself to him.

[Note: Vatican Codex 4951: “Rejoice, then, now, and exult at last toward God.” The Martinensis lacks “your.”]

You have received the gift that Abraham rejoiced to see in spirit. Through Christ you have attained what the once-elect nation of the Hebrews could not then attain.

For Israel, fearful and trembling, marveled, as we read, that Moses, the leader of the people, hidden in a cloud and alone on the summit of the highest mountain, spoke with the Lord (Exodus 19).

But Christ was born for you in such a way,

[Note: The same codex: “and granted us such condescension that he spoke to human beings.”]

and granted us such condescension that he spoke to everyone and was seen by everyone.

At that mountain, Sinai, whoever from the people approached was punished with immediate death.

[Note: Vatican Codices Regina 125 and Ottobonianus 115: “Whoever from the people present approached was punished.”]

But whoever does not approach this mountain—the one who was born today for the world—will die. Then one people was instructed in faith; now all nations are called to life.

Our venerable fathers saw innumerable and great wonders. Heaven rained down angelic food for them; the hardest stone supplied sweet drinks (Exodus 17 and 19); the Jordan turned back its perpetual course toward its source; the strongest walls of the enemies collapsed at the sound of trumpets; and the sun, lingering in the heavens, granted a longer day to the victorious people (Joshua 3, 6, and 10).

But no age before this was permitted to see that the Only-Begotten of the Most High,

whom the trembling powers of the archangels receive,

[Note: The same codex: “whom the powers look upon.”]

would present himself as man to human beings and transform the flesh he assumed from man into God.

[Note: The Martinensis: “which he assumed.” The editor explains: “That is, into the flesh of God. Because of the divine underlying subject uniting both natures, things belonging to man are predicated of God, and thus things belonging to God are attributed to the assumed man; this occurs through the communication of properties, as theologians call it.”]

Embrace, therefore, the condescension of eternal majesty, and do not scrutinize the hidden will of your God. Christ was indeed born for everyone, but he gives salvation to believers.

If, because of the frailty of your senses, it seems less worthy to you to believe that the Son of God was born from a woman, consider that a virgin gave birth.

If the cloths in which he was wrapped seem perhaps cheap to you,

[Note: Regina Codex: “in which he was wrapped.” Martinensis: “in which he was enveloped.”]

admire the angels praising him and the multitude of the heavenly army.

If you despise the manger in which the infant lay, raise your eyes for a little while and behold in heaven the new star proclaiming the Lord’s birth to the world.

[Note: The same codex: “If you do not believe the lowly things, believe the marvelous things.”]

If you believe the lowly things, believe the marvelous things. If you argue about what belongs to humility, revere what is lofty and heavenly.

For through the same witnesses and the same authors you have learned about the Lord and Savior both what is humble and what is glorious. The holy Gospels have handed down to you everything that pertained to the mystery of your salvation.

In them you have grounds both to believe that the Lord Jesus was born as a man and to be unable to doubt that he is God.

[Note: The same codex adds: “He who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God for ever and ever.” The text agrees perfectly with Casinensis 106.]

# HOMILY XIV  
## On the Nativity of the Lord IX

[Col. 0251]

## ADMONITION

The authority of the codices in the Vatican library deserves high esteem. They are of excellent quality, since they are both ancient and written with great accuracy. In three of them—1267, p. 92; 4951, p. 25; and Regina 125, p. 73—Saint Maximus is established as the author of this homily.

What if other distinguished monuments were added to these outstanding witnesses? Indeed, besides the Turin codex, in which it is Homily 20 on the Nativity of the Lord, we have two Reichenau codices, XVI and XXIX; Lucca 85; Casinensis 106, p. 13; and the Neapolitan manuscript of Saint John at Carbonara.

Moreover, it is attributed to Saint Maximus in the excellent Strigoniensis Breviary. The editors agree with the manuscripts: Gymnicus, p. 27; Galesinius, p. 93; Combefisius, volume I, p. 208; Cumdius, volume I, p. 107; Raynaudus, p. 197; and Margarinus, volume VI of the Bibliotheca Maxima, p. 6.

## ARGUMENT

The holy doctor rouses the faithful to contemplate the divine mysteries that shine forth in Christ’s Nativity, and to praise God, who has brought us forgiveness of sins and hope of eternal salvation.

The divine dispositions are beyond human comprehension, as the very grandeur of God’s works testifies. The more they exceed the capacity of mortal understanding by their magnitude, therefore, the more reverently we must contemplate Christ’s mysteries. And so, brothers, when it is proclaimed to us that the eternal Only-Begotten of God the Father, to whom all things are subject and through whom the universe was created, willed at the end of time to be born of a woman,

[Note: Vatican Codex 1267. Likewise Regina Codex 125: “to endure infancy, to enter into fellowship with our flesh.”]

to endure infancy and fellowship with our flesh, we must not scrutinize the grace of such condescension, but believe; not investigate, but marvel. For what is more fitting, or what more appropriate,

[Col. 0251C]

than that in divine matters we should follow God’s omnipotence rather than his wisdom?

[Note: Casinensis Codex 106: “Therefore, dearly beloved, this day is present to us, as …”]

Today, then, as we have learned from the Gospel reading that has been completed, Christ was born according to the flesh: he began to be what he was not, but did not cease to be what he was. For human birth could neither diminish nor divide the unity of his undivided majesty. That he proceeded as God from God the Father is the ineffable and abiding secret of his power; that he was born as man from a woman is the grace of our salvation. There is the glory of nature; here, the mystery of will.

Who, then, brothers, could estimate the depth of this heavenly plan: that the Lord of immortality and of incorruptible

[Note: Codex of Saint John at the Carbonaria reads “of incorruptible nature.”]

substance, in order that he might, in the condition of flesh, undergo death for mortals

[Note: The same codex reads “might undergo death for mortals.”]

be conceived from a woman’s womb without any law of bodily generation, and should will to emerge under human law—

[Note: Thus Regina Codex; others omit *voluit* (“willed”).]

and this in such a way that the blessed mother, who had conceived him while untouched, brought him forth without violation?

Moreover, he is wrapped in cloths and placed in a manger. This infant’s lowliness is God’s precious sacrament. For in the cloths he indicates that he has taken upon himself our weaknesses, our sins. But by allowing his limbs to be placed in a manger, where animals are fed, he shows that his body is to be eaten by mortals for eternal nourishment.

What shall I say of this: an angelic multitude descended to earth

[Col. 0252C]

and accompanied the whimpering child with glorious praise? Every creature is struck with wonder at so great a miracle: the one and the same being reigns as God in heaven and is nourished as man on earth.

The blessed David, announcing the novelty of this mystery, invites the entire human race to the harmony of a spiritual song, saying: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Psalm 95).

What is so new, dearly beloved, as that the almighty God, of immeasurable majesty, coeternal with the Father, and Lord of an everlasting kingdom, should stoop to bodily weakness and human humility?

[Note: Codex of Saint John at the Carbonaria: “What is so new, dearly beloved, as that, while a woman was conceiving, her inviolate virginity should remain untouched?” Regina Codex: “What is so new as that, while a woman was conceiving and giving birth, her inviolate virginity should remain untouched?”]

What is so new as that, while a woman conceives and gives birth, her inviolate virginity remains untouched? Truly, such an entrance befitted the Savior of the world, so that he who came to cleanse the sins of the human race might be born purer than all others.

The prophet also rightly added: “Sing to the Lord, all the earth.” To whom else should all the earth

[Col. 0254A]

sing

[Note: Codex of Saint John at the Carbonaria: “except to him who … throughout the whole world …”]

except to him who brought forgiveness of sins and the hope of eternal salvation to the entire world?

Let us therefore magnify the Lord and our God, let us sing psalms and songs to him; for it is right that he should be honored especially by the praises of those whom he saved through the suffering of his own body and the shedding of his blood.

# HOMILY XV. On the Nativity of the Lord X

[Col. 0253]

## Editorial Notice

41 Although, for attributing this homily to Saint Maximus, we are permitted to rely only on the support of two Vatican-library codices—namely, Codex 433, page 103, and Regina Codex 125, page 71—since none of the others mentions the same holy bishop, their place is nevertheless supplied by several others whose testimony we think should be admitted. These include the Augian codices XVI and XXIX, Casinensis 106, page 14, the Vallicellanus, volume VII, page 41, Lucensis 85, the Neapolitan codex of Saint John at the Carbonaria, and the Taurinensis, in which this is homily 22 on the Nativity of the Lord.

The editors likewise count it among the homilies of Saint Maximus. They are Gymnicus, page 30; Galesinius, page 94; Combefisius, volume I, page 209; Cumdius, volume I, page 166; Reynaudus, page 197; and Margarinus, *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VII, homily 6 on the Nativity of the Lord, page 7.

The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, who separated the genuine works of Saint Augustine from those falsely attributed to him, placed this homily in the appendix, sermon 122, and noted that in manuscript books and printed editions it is customarily attributed to Saint Maximus of Turin.

[Col. 0253B]

## Argument

Here Maximus treats the virginity of Mary, the mother of Christ, and celebrates God’s provident plan in preserving her integrity. At the same time, he urges us to rejoice because, through the birth of our Savior, we should all consider ourselves born to life.

At the Lord’s coming, dearly beloved brothers, whose due honor we render in the present festival, a multitude of heavenly mysteries is revealed through grace. Today—that is, at the end of time—he was brought forth whose eternity is contained by no span of the ages. Today the Lord of heaven and earth assumed the form of a servant for the freedom of servants. Today a virgin gave birth, a new glory of the female sex; and what the whole of creation marvels at with us has occurred: a man was born, not begotten by man.

Although it may seem new, it is not therefore incredible that Christ was conceived in Mary’s womb without a human begetter, since he proceeded from God the Father without conception. Insofar as he is God, he is the Only-Begotten of the Father alone; insofar as he is man, he is the son of his mother alone. Therefore we confess that he who is God from the Father and man from his mother—that is, both God and man—is one Lord.

All this happened so that God, through human flesh, might undertake the mystery of saving passion, and that man, through God’s power, might recover the dignity of his own eternity. Christ is therefore born from Mary,

[Col. 0253D]

so that the female sex might give birth to a man

[Col. 0254B]

and virginal integrity might reveal God.

Christ is born from a woman so that, just as Adam was unable to guard against the devil’s deception through Eve, so the devil would not recognize that God was present when he came through Mary.

[Note: The same codex of Saint John at the Carbonaria reads “the Lord.”]

Thus a woman gives birth to the salvation of the world, so that she who had been the tinder of iniquity might become the minister of righteousness, and through her, by whom death opened an entrance into this world, life might gain entrance to us.

And to show that the Creator of the human race cares for both sexes and wills to save both, a man is born and proceeds from a woman, so that we might understand that before God there is no distinction between man and woman in receiving salvation.

[Col. 0254C]

Why should we not believe with complete devotion that a saving child could be born from a virgin, when we believe that a complete man was formed from dust?

Let us therefore exult and rejoice, brothers, celebrating the birthday of our Lord Jesus Christ, because in his birth we all feel ourselves born to life. He became man not to live for himself—he who is the author of life—but so that by his death he might ransom the life of the dead.

For the enemy had bound the human race with such chains and weighed us down with so great a mass of monstrous sins that there was no return for us to salvation unless he were born who, by his own power, could return to life after death.

# HOMILY XVI. On the Kalends of January

[Col. 0253]

## Editorial Notice

43 Concerning the title of this homily and the time at which it was delivered, there is some disagreement among writers, and there is variation in manuscript codices and printed books.
