Gennadius, certainly older than all those whom we know to have mentioned the homilies of Saint Maximus, states that this homily bore the title *On the Kalends of January*. Vatican Codex 1222, page 285, confirms this.

The Taurinensis differs; I know it to be plainly older than the Vatican codex. It reads: “Also, a discourse delivered on the Kalends of January.” For “to say something on the Kalends of January” is not the same as “to say something about those Kalends.” Someone who does something on the Kalends of January is not bound by any rule to speak about those Kalends, since he remains free, if he wishes, to speak about any other matter. On the other hand, someone who discusses the Kalends of January is under no necessity to do so except on the very day of the January Kalends.

The first Vatican codex and the Taurinensis differ from Vatican Codex 4951, page 33; the Martinianus; Vatican Palatine Codex 434, page 67; Casinensis 106, page 20; and the Modoetianus E III. In the first of these the homily bears the heading “On the Circumcision of the Lord”; in the second and third, “On the Octave of the Lord. A sermon of Saint Maximus the bishop”; in the fifth, “On the Octave of the Lord, that is, on the Kalends of January. A sermon of Blessed Maximus the bishop concerning those Kalends.”

Among the editors, Gymnicus, page 32; Galesinius, page 85; Reynaudus, page 142; and Margarinus, *Bibliotheca Maxima of the Holy Fathers*, volume VI, page 8, have all approved this title: “On the Circumcision of the Lord, or a Rebuke concerning the Kalends of January.”

I cannot approve a homily being titled “On the Circumcision” when it contains not even the slightest mention of circumcision. Maximus’s entire argument in this homily is directed toward deterring the people entrusted to his care from the dishonorable and superstitious games that blind paganism had instituted in honor of Janus.

Gymnicus and the other editors whom I have just named perhaps thought that the title “On the Circumcision, etc.” should be used because they believed that the homily had been delivered on the Kalends of January, on which the celebration of the Lord’s circumcision falls. For Christ was circumcised on the eighth day after his birth, and that eighth day was formerly—and still is today—regarded as the first day of the month of January.

There is an important passage on this subject in Ivo of Chartres, *Sermon on the Circumcision of the Lord*, book II, chapter 8, no. 12:

“The octave and the circumcision agree in one sacrament.”

For this reason Louis Thomassin, in his work *On the Celebration of Feast Days*, says:

“All who have thought that the eighth day after the Nativity is commemorated on the Kalends of January interpret it as though they were speaking of the circumcision; and this is as true as it is that the eighth day is the proper day for carrying out the circumcision.”

In the ancient Martyrology commonly called the Hieronymian, the circumcision of the Lord is commemorated on January 1. The same is true in the book of Sacraments that bears the name of Saint Gelasius, Supreme Pontiff, in which there is a secret prayer concerning the circumcision of the Lord on the Kalends of January.

In canon 17 of the Second Council of Tours, held in the year 570, we read:

“Our fathers decreed that private litanies should be held on the Kalends of January, and that at the eighth hour on those Kalends, a Mass of the circumcision should, with God’s favor, be celebrated.”

Volume III of the Paris edition of the Councils, 1714, page 360.

I pass over the martyrologies of Bede, Rabanus, Usuard, Notker, and other more recent witnesses. For us, surely, the authority of the fathers of the Synod of Tours is sufficient: in the sixth century they testified that the circumcision was customarily commemorated on the Kalends of January by the institution of their ancestors. From this it is perfectly clear that this practice was much older than that same fifth century.

For this reason Alexander Politus, Clerk Regular of the Pious Schools, rightly censures the learned Isaac Casaubon, who claims that remembrance of Christ’s circumcision on the Kalends of January began only a few centuries ago.

I am not unaware that Casaubon appeals to chapter 2, *On Consecration*, distinction 3, “most especially by the stars.” But I am not concerned with what was promulgated in that chapter. First, it is not established who wrote it. “By the Council of Lyons,” Gratian says. Yet he himself neither indicates which Council of Lyons nor can we establish it by conjecture. Several councils of Lyons are counted, but in their acts not even a trace of this is found.

Nor should we attach authority or credibility to an irregular canon whose origin is unknown. But suppose that this canon rests on the decree of some Council of Lyons: what does it contain that conflicts with the antiquity of the feast of the circumcision? Is it because it commemorates the octave of the Lord rather than the circumcision? Nothing prevents the feast that is regarded as the eighth day after the Lord’s birth from also having been regarded as the feast of the circumcision.

Thus, in canon 20 of the statutes of Rheims, dated to the year 630, volume III of the Councils, page 570, “Circumcision” is put in place of “the octave of the Lord”:

“These are the feasts to be observed without any secular labor and celebrated with due reverence: the Nativity of the Lord, the Circumcision, and so forth.”

Again, in the statutes of Saint Boniface of Mainz, approximately 746, constitution 31, in the same volume of the Councils, page 1946:

“Let the priests be instructed to announce that Sundays throughout the year are to be kept as sabbaths, beginning as follows: on the Nativity of the Lord, four days before the Kalends of January; on the Circumcision of the Lord, one day on the Kalends of January; and so forth.”

What follows from this? That the feast called the circumcision here was not also called the octave of the Lord’s Nativity? Nothing could be less true.

There is therefore no reason to set chapter 2, *On Consecration*, distinction 3, against us, since we do not know to whom it should be attributed and since it is perhaps more recent than the statutes of Mainz and Rheims.

But let us grant that the institution of the feast of the circumcision is not so ancient that it can be traced to the third, fourth, or fifth century. Who, then, would think that in the time of Saint Augustine the day of the Kalends of January was not numbered among the sacred days?

Compare the holy doctor’s sermon 198, formerly 7 among the Sirmondian sermons, “On the Kalends of January,” page 631, volume V of the works, Antwerp edition, 1700.

Even if that day was sacred, nevertheless, so that Christians might be increasingly turned away from the superstitions and sacrilegious games of the pagans, ecclesiastical leaders in some places arranged that it should be passed in fasting. On this matter consult Caesarius of Arles, *Sermon on the Kalends of January*, sermon 129, no. 4, in the appendix to volume V of Saint Augustine’s works, page 165 of that edition; the Second Council of Tours, 567, canon 17, volume III of the Councils, Paris edition of 1714, page 360; and the Fourth Council of Toledo, 633, canon 11, in the same volume, page 583.

I return to Maximus’s homily. I deny that it ought to have been titled “On the Circumcision,” even if it had been delivered on the Kalends of January; rather, it should be titled “Delivered on the Circumcision.” For when one says “on the circumcision,” this indicates that the homily itself deals with the mystery of the circumcision, yet not a word about it appears in the homily.

Nevertheless, I also think that the editors should not have used the title “Delivered on the Circumcision.” For this homily was not delivered on the Kalends of January, but beforehand, since Maximus mentions the approaching Kalends in it:

“Although, dearly beloved brothers, I do not doubt that through fatherly concern and instruction in the divine word you have been taught wholly to avoid and abhor all the vanities of the approaching Kalends…”

We have therefore thought that the title mentioned by Gennadius and confirmed by the age of the codices should be restored to this homily.

[Col. 0255A]

## Argument

Maximus rebukes Christians because they continued to observe the superstitious festivals and games instituted long ago by the pagans in honor of Janus at the beginning of the turning year, and because they violated the holy law through an impious ritual.

[Note: Vatican Codex 4951 begins: “I do not doubt, dearly beloved brothers.”]

Although I do not doubt, dearly beloved brothers, that through fatherly concern and instruction in the divine word you have been taught wholly to avoid and abhor all the vanities of the approaching Kalends, nevertheless, as evidence of more complete correction,

[Note: From Codex I, Pluteus XIV of the Laurentian Library: “an increase of correction.”]

I was not reluctant to bring before your ears a discourse customary among you, just as the blessed Paul says: “Brothers, to write the same things to you is not burdensome for me, but necessary for you” (Philippians 3).

I regard it as necessary, dearly beloved, and not superfluous, that, as a holy reminder formerly given, the words of our predecessors be repeated to you.

[Note: Vatican Codex 4951: “that the words be repeated.”]

And indeed, what tedium or burden is there in often saying and frequently hearing things useful for progress in salvation and pleasing to God?

Therefore, dearly beloved, walking with your customary faith and devotion along the roads of the religious journey and the paths of truth, trample ever more firmly the byways of error and the devil’s fabrications.

For a faithful soul that longs for the fellowship of angels ought not to delight in the games of demons. Nor can there be any fellowship among God’s servants between light and darkness, truth and falsehood, disgrace and honor, as the teacher of the churches instructs us when he says: “What agreement is there between Christ and Belial? Or what accord does the temple of God have with idols?” (2 Corinthians 6).

Therefore, whoever among believers is either a temple of God or desires to be one must carefully beware lest, by pursuing dead and empty things, ceasing to be God’s temple, he become a dwelling place of darkness, a monument of the devil.

The most glorious prophet David says:

[Note: Vatican Codex 4951: “The most glorious of the prophets, David, says.” Martinianus has: “Hence he says.”]

“Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord,

[Note: The same Vatican codex: “whose hope is in him.”]

and who has not turned toward vanities and false insanities” (Psalm 33).

Therefore, whoever hopes in God,

[Note: The same Codex 4951: “who hopes in God.”]

and fixes the gaze of his lights with his whole heart upon his glory, ought not to turn his eyes, once consecrated, toward the thickest vanities.

[Col. 0257B]

For, as the Lord says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9).

Every plowman who looks back will either make his furrow crooked

[Note: Martinianus: “and instead of ‘or,’”]

or useless, or injure the tracks of his plowing oxen.

So also, whoever proceeds along the straight road, cutting through worldly vices with a spiritual plow toward the kingdom of God, if he turns his gaze toward impious and empty things, will wound his own fields—that is, his body and soul—and fall into the dangerous error of a good journey.

[Note: Vatican Codices 4222 and 4951, Casinensis 106, and Martinianus: “will fall into a very dangerous error.”]

“And he has not turned,” he says, “toward vanities and false insanities.”

How does blessed David call them “false insanities,” when those who cast aside the fear of God and turn toward the vanities of demons are truly insane? But the faithful man properly expressed the nature of impious falsity, because

[Note: Vatican Codex 4222: “because all things are insanity.”]

everything is insane that, through the devil’s deceitful lie, does not possess within itself the power of God.

[Col. 0257C]

Their sickness is more grievous and incurable who, deceived by the frenzy of superstitions and the pleasure of games, go mad under the appearance of health.

Are not all the things done by the ministers of demons on those days false and insane, when a man, weakening the vigor of his strength, completely breaks himself into a woman, and performs the whole business with such display and art as though he were ashamed to be what he is—a man?

Are not all things there false and insane when human beings, formed by God, transform themselves either into cattle, wild beasts, or monsters?

Does anything exceed insanity more than when they disfigure, with the grime of filth and adulterated ugliness, the beauty of the human face, specially fashioned by God’s hands in complete loveliness?

How is it not evident to the wise that there is no health in a place where people do and say impious, dishonorable, and utterly depraved things, without listening to blessed David crying daily in the Church and saying: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Psalm 4).

Their heart is indeed heavy and weighed down by every impiety: through sacrilegious jokes they mock the divine commands, love empty things, and pursue falsehoods.

[Note: Martinianus: “they follow them.”]

And finally, to complete their offense,

[Note: Laurentian Codex I, Pluteus XIV: “they call that very day the new year.”]

they call those very days the new year.

Although they do not improperly call the year new in their own way, since through their abominable festivals

[Note: Vatican Codex 4222 and the former Laurentian Codex of Santa Croce, 4, Pluteus 33: “through abominable festivals, with honor abandoned, false …” Martinianus has a different reading: “Since through abominable festivals dishonorable and false ugliness …”]

false ugliness is renewed in place of honor, and depravity is renewed.

[Note: Casinensis 106: “And they call it new, etc.”]

They call it the new year, as though heaven or earth then displayed anything new. They call the January Kalends the new year,

[Col. 0258B]

although they are always stained with ancient error and horror.

[Note: Codex of Santa Croce, etc.: “although they are always stained with ancient error.”]

They also say that they gather omens,

[Note: Laurentian Codices and Vatican Codex 4951: “For they say that they gather omens from very empty things.”]

and, judging the condition of their life by empty signs, they search out the future of the approaching year through uncertain signs from birds and wild beasts, although knowledge of the future belongs to God alone and the authority of the Law forbids this, saying: “Do not take omens; do not pay attention to auguries” (Deuteronomy 18).

But these wretched and pitiable people, seized by pagan errors and blinded by an imprudent heart,

[Note: Vatican Codex 4222: “by a heart lacking foresight.”]

go out from their houses in impiety and return in sacrilege.

Or how can someone think—or even say—that he is a Christian if, in such an observance, he sees himself sharing company with the faithless?

[Note: The Laurentian and Santa Croce codices: “he thinks he can be called one.” Thus Vatican Codices 4222 and 6450 and Casinensis 106.]

Thus, dearly beloved, I have learned that for a long time now you neither observe nor seek these things, as your open report makes clear.

[Col. 0258C]

Indeed, we must not investigate them at all, since we believe in almighty God, who, according to the quality of their merits or the testing of their faith, dispenses prosperity or adversity to all mortals by the power of his own judgment.

This is especially so since the Apostle accuses and rebukes such people, saying: “You observe days and months and seasons and years; I fear that I may have labored among you in vain” (Galatians 4).

See, dearly beloved, how they lost the apostolic labor bestowed upon them.

But you, as you have done up to now through fear of God,

[Note: The same Laurentian codex: “through love of God.”]

shun empty things, flee falsehoods, avoid impieties, so that you may always be able to come to the house of God with a confident heart.

[Note: The same Laurentian codex: “so that you may be able to come confidently to the house of God.”]

And may Paul, the teacher of the nations and judge, find in your faith the fruit of his teaching.

[Note: The same Laurentian codex adds: “May he who lives and reigns as God forever grant this. Amen.” Vatican Codex 4222: “May this please Christ the Lord, in whom Christ the Lord delights, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.”]

# HOMILY XVII. On the Epiphany of the Lord I

[Col. 0259]

## Editorial Notice

From the Taurinensis codex, which contributed much that is excellent to the honor and enrichment of this collection of Saint Maximus’s works, it can plainly be understood that the holy bishop delivered thirty-five sermons or homilies to the people on the Epiphany of the Lord. Some of these had already been published, some will now be published for the first time through my work, and the rest have perished.

In presenting the series of all those that survive, I shall begin with the unpublished ones. After discussing the meaning of the title, I shall explain why I thought this one should be placed first.

It is already established that the manifestation, appearance, or revelation of Christ the Savior is sometimes called *Theophany* and more often *Epiphany*, and that both are words transferred from Greek into Latin.

Alexander Politus, whom I mentioned in the preceding editorial notice, further teaches in his annotations on the Martyrology for January 6 that Gregory of Nazianzus seems to distinguish between *Theophany* and *Epiphany*: *Theophany* would indicate the birthday of our Savior, while *Epiphany* would indicate his baptism.

But Politus fears that Gregory may not have established this distinction with sufficient precision. For the Fathers use the word *Epiphany*, just as they use *Theophany*, to signify the day of the Lord’s birth. Whether appropriately or otherwise, he does not think it should be conceded without qualification.

However that may be, he says:

“Certainly, from the most ancient times Epiphany was not understood specifically and properly of the birthday of Christ, but of Christ’s baptism, on which Christ revealed his divinity to human beings through definite and manifest signs.”

But since on that same day the Church celebrates not only Christ’s baptism but also, with such solemnity, the worship offered to him by the Magi and the miracle of the water changed into wine, some therefore assert that this threefold manifestation of Christ was indicated by the plural name *Epiphanies*.

They express it in the plural, as do Jerome, book I on Ezekiel, chapter 1; Cassian, *Conferences* 10, chapter 2; and others whom Cotelerius names in his note on book V, chapter 13, of the *Apostolic Constitutions*; Du Cange in the *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin* under the word “EPIPHANIA”; Baronius in his note on January 6 in the Roman Martyrology; Jacobus Gothofredus on book V of the Theodosian Code, *On Spectacles*; Svidcerus in the *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus* under the word Ἐπιφάνεια (*Epiphaneia*); and six hundred others whom it would be tedious to list.

The Greeks call it ἡμέραν τῶν Φώτων, “the Day of Lights.” There exists a speech of Gregory of Nazianzus, his thirty-ninth, entitled Εἰς τὰ ἅγια φῶτα, “On the Holy Lights.”

Nazianzenus explains the reason for this designation in the same work, page 624:

“The holy Day of Lights, to which we have come and which today, by divine favor, we have celebrated, has as its beginning the baptism of my Christ—that is, of the true light that enlightens every human being coming into the world.”

His interpreter Nicetas comments on this passage:

“Baptism is called by the name of lights because it cleanses and illumines. Hence also it happens that at that time we light torches as a sign of joy.”

The beginning and cause of this feast, therefore, is the baptism of Christ.

I return to Maximus. Gennadius reports that Maximus delivered homilies on the Theophany. Galesinius retained such a title in the first edition of Saint Maximus’s works. We have thought that this and the following homilies should be entitled “On the Epiphany,” following the testimony of the manuscripts of Saint Dalmatius and of the Taurinensis, in which this homily is number 13. In this matter we agree admirably with Leo the Great, whose sermons are entitled “On the Solemnity of the Epiphany.”

We have arranged for this homily, drawn from the codex of Saint Dalmatius, to be published before the others because it is, as it were, an introduction to the rest. It indicates the time at which it was delivered and commemorates in order the mysteries whose memory is honored and celebrated on that day—something that I do not see being done so distinctly in the following homilies.

[Col. 0259A]

## Argument

In this sermon Saint Maximus recalls both mysteries: the manifestation of Christ the Lord and the miraculous conversion of water into wine. By the latter Christ is shown to be true God and true man; by the former the Savior is proved to be Lord of all nations.

Let us exult in the Lord, dearly beloved brothers, because new vows continually follow our vows, and joys are heaped upon joys. For scarcely have we celebrated with joy the solemn day of our most holy restoration when immediately we rejoice in the glorious manifestation of our Redeemer among the nations.

On this most festive day we celebrate the solemnity of that day on which he himself, born as an infant in a stable, willed to reveal himself to the world. So that the nations would not be unaware of his coming in the flesh—he who had descended from heaven to free the entire human race from the slavery of sin—he gave a star in the sky as a sign. From that time Judea, though unbelieving, could recognize it, but only the Gentiles who approached his cradle understood it.

Thus the Gentile world alone came to Bethlehem in the persons of the three Magi; Judea, however, remained in decline and, through the persons of those three men, paid its gifts to so great a king.

For, as you have heard, they offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh. In the gold they showed the beginnings of our redemption, which were already appearing in him; in the frankincense they signified that the worship of true religion would one day come and that the superstition of idols would cease;

[Col. 0260A]

in the myrrh they foretold that his resurrection and ours would one day take place from the dead.

[Ten lines are missing here; the text then continues.]

Therefore, brothers, let us who have come from the nations to the adorable light of faith exult and rejoice in this great solemnity of the manifestation of our Lord.

But we ought to rejoice no less because on this most sacred celebration of the day, as we are instructed by the tradition of our fathers, Christ our Lord himself was invited to a wedding on earth and came—not to enjoy that banquet, not to intoxicate himself with wine, but to show that he was the author of marriage and, by sanctifying it, to make his divine power known when he himself supplied the wine that had run out for the wedding guests.

Indeed, he supplied wine and provided drink—wine and drink capable of intoxicating those guests. He himself changed the water-filled jars into wine. The steward tasted the wine and judged it better than what had already been served.

Nor is this surprising. The wine they had drunk earlier had been produced from vines by human hands and made into wine. But this wine, from the water with which a hired servant had previously filled those jars, had been changed by divine power into precious wine through the transformation of the water’s entire nature—wine that intoxicated those wedding guests.

[Note: When Saint Maximus uses the verb *inebrior* (“to intoxicate”), it should not be understood as intemperate use of wine, but as its abundance, by which all the guests could be refreshed and satisfied.]

Seeing such a miracle, they believed, as the divine text says, in him—his disciples.

[Col. 0261A]

They no longer believed merely that he was human, but that he was the Son of God, as so great a miracle proved.

Let us too, brothers, believe this with our whole heart: that although he shares our nature, he is nevertheless equal in the divine substance of the Father.

Why, then, did only his disciples among the wedding guests believe in him after seeing so great a miracle? The others attended to the wine but did not notice his miracles. They knew that the wine had run out, but they did not know that water had been changed into wine.

As we have said elsewhere, it is clear that those people drank a harmful intoxication from those vessels, whereas these received eternal righteousness. Among the former, what they had drunk was earthly and passed away; among the latter, what they had received was heavenly and remained.

*End.*

# HOMILY XVIII. On the Epiphany of the Lord II

[Col. 0261]

## Editorial Notice

51 We now publish for the first time another homily on the Epiphany of the Lord, extracted from the same codex of Saint Dalmatius; but it is greatly defective because of the codex’s antiquity and the erosion of its characters. Wherever it was permissible, we supplemented it from the text of the Taurinensis codex. In that codex this homily is number 17 and bears the title: “Also, on the Epiphany of the Lord.”

From number 14 through number 17 in that codex, it is perfectly clear that two homilies, numbers 15 and 16, have been lost through the injury of time.

## Argument

Although our Church was first prefigured among the Israelite people, nevertheless, to show that it was to be gathered not from one nation but from all nations, God called the Gentiles to Christ through the Magi as soon as he was born, and in their recognition and worship he received the firstfruits of our faith.

The ineffable advent into this world of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, brothers, first began to become known to the Gentiles when the Magi came from the East, following the guidance of a new star, to adore him. For when he had come clothed in human flesh to free the whole world from the deadly captivity of the devil, [lacuna]. And indeed today’s festival declares to us the beginnings of our calling to the heavenly kingdoms, in which he wished to manifest himself more fully in the star. For in those men who came from Chaldaea to adore the newborn King in the stable, the whole Gentile world is included; and likewise, in the gifts that they then offered to the newborn King are contained those precious gifts which the Savior himself, reigning in heaven with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, received from the Gentiles.

Therefore the Magi were the first fruits of the Gentiles in the Christian faith. The faith of the Gentiles in Christ declared that its beginning came from those Magi.

[Note: [Col. 0261D] From the Turin manuscript.] *Although Christ our Lord wished his Church, and its most glorious leaders, to be Jews, the Church was indeed born from them, but it grew to full strength among the Gentiles. Thus, while the Jews still persist in their mournful blindness, the Church has been so clearly manifested among the Gentiles that it seems to have been formed from them alone; and even now the Hebrews are certainly no different from their predecessors.*

For when the Magi asked—and Herod himself inquired—whether and where the one whom they were seeking, the Redeemer of the ages, who had then been born, ought to be born, the Jews, from the volumes of the sacred Scriptures that they themselves read, not only said that he would be born in Bethlehem—

(Here some material is missing [Col. 0262B], to which the sentence was connected and joined.)

[Note: [Col. 0262D] From the same Turin manuscript.] *They displayed on this matter the prophecies of their prophets and asserted that the time of his birth had already arrived; yet they did not seek the newborn King. Truly pitiable was the blindness of the Jews. They were not ignorant that Christ would be born in Bethlehem. They possessed the oracles by which it was shown that Christ had already been born. They heard and saw the Chaldaeans asking about the place of his birth, yet they did not seek Christ.*

And so that prophetic saying was truly fulfilled: “Those to whom nothing was announced about him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand” (Isaiah 52; Romans 15). Nothing had been announced to the Chaldaean, yet he saw the star, believed, and understood that Christ was signified in the star. It had been told to the Hebrew that the Redeemer of the world would come. He possessed the prophets’ oracles concerning him. He knew that Christ had been born in Bethlehem. And although this had been foretold to him concerning Christ, he neither understood nor wished to see him after his birth, so that he might eventually crucify him.

Leaving them, then, to their blindness, rejoice and exult on this holy day, O Gentile world, turned toward God your Creator; and in those three Magi who came from the East to Bethlehem to venerate Christ, do not cease to venerate the beginnings of your faith. With exultant hearts, conceive hope of one day attaining those eternal dwellings, provided that you follow the faith you possess and the works that Christ commanded. And although even now the Jews regard our Redeemer, whimpering in his cradle and lying in a manger, as contemptible, let us nevertheless believe that Christ himself must be adored by all.

The end.

## HOMILY XIX. On the Epiphany of the Lord III

### ADMONITION

53. This discourse agrees with Maximus’s other homilies not only in its style, but also in the selection and arrangement of its thoughts. Therefore there is nothing preventing it from appearing attributable to Maximus himself. For this reason we do not doubt that experts in critical scholarship will plainly agree with us. This very discourse, or homily, was supplied to us by a most ancient manuscript formerly belonging to the monastery of Apannum; in that manuscript it is entitled: “Homily VIII, also on the Epiphany of the Lord.” The Turin manuscript is also relevant, in which this same homily is numbered 31 in the sequence of Maximus’s homilies on the Epiphany.

### ARGUMENT

The same star shone upon Jews and Gentiles. The former had been warned about it through prophetic prophecy; the latter, however, were not abandoned in the deep night of superstition. Illumination, therefore, was made available to all, because Christ had come to save everyone.

The venerable mystery of our redemption, brothers, by which the immortal God took pity on the human condition, shines with such majesty that no human mind can comprehend it. For who could explain why the only-begotten Son of God, whose divinity and omnipotence are one and the same with those of the Father and the Holy Spirit, and for whom willing and being able are one and the same, nevertheless wished to honor our nature so greatly that, assuming what he did not previously possess while not abandoning what was in himself, he inseparably joined the divine nature with the human, so that he was at once God and man?

[Note: [Col. 0263] At this point Maximus attacks the heresy of the Eutychians and sets against it the unshaken dogma of the Catholic Church.]

But if, in investigating these matters, all human understanding is disturbed and the entire philosophy of the Gentiles vanishes, nevertheless, in the mystery of today’s solemnity—by which the incomprehensible God wished to make his birth known to the Gentiles through the sign of a radiant star—

(Two lines are missing here.)

For today our Lord Christ wished to display his glory to all. And although, having been born according to the flesh among Hebrews from Hebrews, he may seem to have loved them more than others, nevertheless, when at his birth he caused a new star to shine in the heavens, the Gentile world itself also has something to rejoice over. That star appears to me to have been given especially to the Gentiles so that they too might recognize that the Redeemer had been born—the one whom Balaam, that priest of the Gentiles, had once prophesied would come into the world from the seed of Jacob.

And indeed the Jews possessed their sacred volumes, in which were contained both the praises of the patriarchs of that people and the prophecies of their prophets, declaring that Christ the Lord, the Redeemer of the world, would one day come. They knew from their own Scriptures that he would be born of a virgin, from the lineage of David according to the flesh. They also read in them the place of his birth, which had been foretold: Bethlehem, that city of David, was said to be destined to be honored by the birth of so great a divinity. The marvels that were to precede his birth were likewise announced. Only the pitiable Gentile world had until then remained in darkness.

Therefore, he who had come mercifully to restore everyone, lest the Gentile world too remain forever in its lamentable blindness, gave it a sign that even a Jew could see: the star that announced the rising of so great a King and revealed that the author of the redemption now present had come. In Chaldaea the Magi saw it gleaming with joyful, flashing rays. They recognized that it signified the birth of the new King. They followed the guidance of that light and truly found the one whom they approached from so great a distance to venerate. They offered him their gifts—gold, incense, and myrrh, as we read—precious gifts by which both the divinity of the newborn King and his united humanity were declared.

Then they returned to their own country by another route. Gentiles came to adore; Christians withdrew from him. Before the adoration they had served idols; after seeing the Savior of the world, they detested their idols. They returned to their own country.

Let us therefore, brothers, imitate the Magi. They saw the child in the stable and venerated him as God. We too see him reigning in heaven with the eyes of faith; let us therefore venerate him and always cling to him. For just as he freed those three men from the blindness of idols, so also he freed us from eternal death.

The end.

## HOMILY XX. On the Epiphany of the Lord IV

### ADMONITION

55. This homily is transcribed in a manuscript of the former abbey of Saint Dalmatius, where it bears the title: “Also on the Epiphany of the Lord and on the Magi.” It is read in the same way in the Turin manuscript. In the first of these manuscripts it is numbered 9; in the other, 30. From the latter it is clear that we lack five of Maximus’s homilies preceding this number. The title adds “and on the Magi” because in this discourse the holy bishop treats in a particular way of the arrival of those three men at the Lord’s cradle.

### ARGUMENT

Christ, scarcely born in Judaea, is presented to the Jews for recognition through the angels and the shepherds; to the Gentiles he is revealed through the star. Neither the Jews nor the Gentiles are deprived of the light appropriate to them. But the Jews, divinely warned, remain unbelieving, whereas the Gentiles go to adore the newborn Lord.

As we gather, brothers, for the venerable festivals of the Lord and the most sacred mysteries of our Savior, just as we rejoiced over his birth, so also we ought to rejoice over his manifestation. The only-begotten Son of God, coeternal with God the Father, having been born in time from an undefiled virgin, wished on this day, as the tradition handed down by our fathers teaches us, to manifest himself to the Gentiles.

[Col. 0264D] to stand.

[Note: [Col. 0265D] The Turin manuscript reads: “And therefore, while he whimpered in the cradle, while he was praised by the angels, and while the shepherds visited him, the new star was manifesting him in heaven to all the Gentiles. Thus, when the heavenly host, praising God and saying, ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace,’ had shown to the Jews—in whose land he had been born according to the flesh from the lineage of David—that he had appeared at the beginning of his birth, and when the Gentiles, to whom it had been promised through Balaam’s prophecy that the Redeemer of the world would come from the seed of Jacob, were ignorant of the marvels occurring in Judaea, he gave a new star as a sign, so that they might understand that what had once been prophesied by that soothsayer had then been fulfilled: that the star had arisen from Jacob and a man had come from Israel, and so forth.”]

While he himself whimpered in the cradle, while he was praised by the angels, and while the shepherds visited him, the new star manifested him from heaven to all the Gentiles. For to the Jews, in whose land and from whose royal seed of David he had been born according to the flesh, that multitude of the angelic army praising God and saying, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace” (Luke 2), had already made him sufficiently manifest at the beginning of his birth. But to the Gentiles, to whom it had been promised through Balaam’s prophecy that the Redeemer of the world would one day come from the seed of Jacob, while they were ignorant of the marvels then taking place in Judaea, he gave a new star as a sign, so that they might understand that what had once been prophesied by that soothsayer had been fulfilled: that the star had arisen from Jacob and a man had come from Israel.

And indeed, since he had come from heaven not merely to redeem the Jewish people, but all the Gentiles whom he had created from the beginning of the world together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he wished to give in the star a sign that Judaea could see and the whole world recognize. The Jew saw that sign, but did not understand it; the Gentiles marveled at it, but only three men from Chaldaea understood what it signified.

Through that visible sign he called everyone to himself and promised all the gifts of his grace. It announced that the author of the world had come, who would break the yoke of ancient slavery; finally, it promised eternal life to all. Yet that star shone only in the eyes of the Magi, while those who had the newborn Savior in their own land chose to remain ignorant of him; and the Gentile world hastened to venerate him.

The Magi therefore come from Chaldaea. They follow the course of the advancing star. They enter the royal city of the Hebrews, where the deranged Herod was reigning, and seek the newborn King of the Jews. Herod trembles and fears the arrival of the new King.

Why do you fear impiously and unhappily? The one who is going to give the heavenly kingdoms has not come to seize yours.

The Hebrews search the Scriptures, and then learn that the Lord would be born in Bethlehem; they say that he had already been born at that time. Then that prophetic saying was fulfilled: “Those to whom nothing was announced about him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand” (Isaiah 52:15; Romans 15:21). Nothing had been announced to the Chaldaean about Christ, and he had heard nothing; but when he saw the star, he understood from the star that Christ was present.

The Magi see the Redeemer of the world in the stable. They behold the child suckling at his mother’s breast. They adore him and offer him gifts. Wonderful faith: to adore as God a child lying at the breast of a nursing mother, surrounded by no royal majesty, and to present him gifts as King and as God!

Then, as the reading that has been completed bears witness, they returned to their own country by another route.

[Note: [Col. 0265] The Turin manuscript reads: “For those who came in unbelief to adore Christ’s cradle, illuminated by the rays of that eternal Sun whom they venerated, having laid aside superstition...”]

And those who had come in unbelief to adore Christ’s cradle, illuminated by the rays of that eternal Sun whom they had adored, returned to their own country by another route after laying aside superstition.

Therefore, brothers, since we too have come from the Gentiles to recognize the true light, let us imitate the Magi. After seeing the Lord, they venerated him as God; let us do the same, rejecting the false idols of the Gentiles, and let us venerate and serve him alone.

The star has not now led us to knowledge of him, but the preaching of the true faith, which by God’s grace has shone like a star in our hearts. Let us therefore exhort our brothers to lay aside that sacrilegious worship of idols and approach the new light of faith, which has also shone upon them.

The Magi offered their gifts to the newborn Lord; let us too offer him ours. Let us feed widows, support strangers, and show mercy to all, so that he in his great compassion may deign to free us from the present distress of those who come from foreign peoples. For he is powerful enough to do this. Let us entreat him with our whole heart, so that he may deign to grant it to us in his mercy.

The end.

## HOMILY XXI. On the Epiphany of the Lord V

[Col. 0265]

### ADMONITION

This homily of Maximus lay buried in the celebrated manuscript of Saint Gall until John Mabillon brought it to light and published it in the *Museo Italico* with other recently discovered works. The title that the editor transcribed from the manuscript is: “Here begins a discourse after the Nativity of the Lord.” Andreas Gallandius likewise transferred it, together with the homily, into his collection. The Turin manuscript has another title, namely: “Also, Homily X on the Epiphany of the Lord.” This title appears more suitable than the former, since immediately after the homilies on the Nativity of the Lord another follows on the Kalends of January, and this one is number 10 among those transcribed on the Epiphany. From the same Turin manuscript it is entirely clear that homilies 7, 8, and 9 on the Epiphany have likewise perished.

### ARGUMENT

The divine gifts that flowed upon humanity from Christ’s birth compel us, through purity of conduct, integrity of life, and devotion to piety, to earn for ourselves still greater and more excellent benefits. True joy belongs to the one whom righteousness makes pleasing and acceptable to God.

The joy of the Lord’s Nativity, brothers, still makes our hearts leap, and our continued rejoicing longs for the heavenly festival. Although the day of our vows has passed, the sanctification of those vows nevertheless remains with us. And just as the Savior’s birth grows from day to day after its rising, so too our devotion to his faith grows, and it provides evidence both of age and of salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0265D] “For the Lord grows in age for himself, but advances in holiness for us.” This does not mean that Christ’s holiness advances—for it is eternal and perfect—but he is said to advance when he causes an increase of faith in us. For after the Nativity Christ is indeed bodily a little child, yet he is God in majesty.

Such is Maximus’s view. But when he names Christ’s everlasting holiness—Christ who is God in majesty—in explaining the passage from chapter 2 of Luke concerning Christ’s advancing in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men, he does not name it exclusively in such a way as to deny that holiness and wisdom are present in Christ himself insofar as he is man. He did not agree with the Apollinarians, who thought that the divine Word occupied the place of the soul or mind in Christ’s human nature, since he strongly rejected the impious doctrine of Apollinaris. Nor did this man, utterly hostile to the Nestorian heresy, allow himself to be carried away to the point of thinking with Nestorius the heresiarch, with Leporius the monk, and with the Agnoetes, that wicked offspring of the Nestorians, either that Christ advanced day by day in an interior holiness and wisdom, or that ignorance belonged to Christ’s human mind.

On the error of Apollinaris, compare Saint Epiphanius, *Against the Heresies* 77, which is the second of the Dimoecritians, in the Paris edition of Petavius, p. 997; Saint Ambrose, whom Maximus was accustomed to follow especially, *Letter* 48 to Sabinus, no. 5, p. 1070, vol. III of the Venetian edition of 1751; the author of the letter to the monk Caesarius, vol. III of Chrysostom’s works, p. 746 of the Paris edition of 1721; Saint Augustine, *On Heresies to Quodvultdeus*, chapter 2, p. 14, vol. VIII of the Antwerp edition of 1700; and, if desired, the others named by Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, fourth century, chapter 3, article 14, p. 274, vol. IV of the Lucca edition of 1750.

On Nestorius, see the *Admonition of Saint Cyril* in the acts of the Council of Ephesus, part 1, chapter 12, p. 1319, vol. I of the Paris edition of the Councils of 1714. Leporius the monk had said that Christ, according to his humanity, was ignorant of something or other; but, repenting of what he had said, he not only abandoned the error that he had previously approved, after the rebuke, encouragement, and efforts of the Gallic and African bishops, especially Saint Augustine, but also anathematized it. See his *Book of Satisfaction*, vol. I of the Councils, p. 1268, and the *Letter of the Bishops of the African Church*, in the same place, p. 1261.

Who could persuade himself that Saint Maximus, who was most closely united with the Gallic and African bishops through fellowship in doctrine and communion in sacred things, would, not long after Leporius had publicly made satisfaction to the Church, have followed Leporius not in his repentance but in his former error, and publicly proclaimed that monstrous opinion which the agreement of so many orthodox and holy bishops had taken care to strike with an anathema?

Concerning the Agnoetes, descendants of the Nestorian faction, who sinned even more gravely in this matter than Leporius, consult Gregory the Great, *Letters* X.35 and X.39; and, omitting more recent authors, Petavius, *Theological Dogmatics*, book XI, treatise *On the Incarnation*, chapter 1, no. 15; and Cardinal Orsi, *Ecclesiastical History*, book XLV, no. 110.

For my part, when I consider the manner of writing used by Maximus and compare it with the views of the Fathers who opposed the Arians, Pelagians, Nestorians, and Agnoetes, I am certain that the holy bishop, although he expressed himself less clearly, nevertheless held this position: Christ, insofar as he is man, was not full of grace, wisdom, and truth by the power of human nature, but because of the hypostatic union with the eternal Word and divine Wisdom; Christ, I say, insofar as he is man, was by that union already full of grace, wisdom, and truth from the moment of his conception; and when he is said to have grown in grace and wisdom, this is said of him for us by manifestation—φανέρωσις (*phanerōsis*)—not for himself.

To this clearly pertains the statement of Augustine from book II of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 29, no. 48, p. 44, vol. X of his works: “I could in no way believe that there was such ignorance in that infant in whom the Word became flesh in order to dwell among us, nor could I suspect in the child Christ that weakness of mind which we see in little children.” And from *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 75, no. 2, p. 48, vol. VI: “If piety does not permit us to believe that the Lordly man first saw in part and afterward in full, although he is said to have advanced in wisdom, then the body in which he is understood to have advanced must be understood as the Church, whose members are taken as coheirs.”

And as it is written in the little book of Leporius—a book that is reported to have been accepted by Augustine by Saint Leo the Great and Theodoret: “It cannot be said that the Lord of the prophets was ignorant even according to his humanity.”

These statements agree with what Eulogius of Alexandria writes in Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 230; Eulogius’s doctrine was approved by Gregory the Great. Eulogius’s words are as follows: “For when he is joined in one hypostasis with the inaccessible and substantial Wisdom, he cannot be ignorant of anything, whether present or future. Nor can the statement, ‘Everything that the Father has is mine,’ be false, since it is a dangerous rashness to affirm that ignorance existed in him, either according to his divinity or according to his humanity.”

Saint Cyril of Alexandria had preceded him in book III *Against Nestorius*, vol. VI of his works, p. 87. Later, John of Damascus wrote in the third book of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 21: “Human nature, according to its essence, does not possess knowledge of future things. But the Lord’s soul, because of its union with God the Word and its hypostatic identity with him, was enriched, together with the other astonishing miracles of divinity, also with knowledge of future things.”

And in chapter 22: “Those who think that he had progress in wisdom and grace as though some addition had been made to them, rather than believing that the union of the flesh took place from the very beginning of his existence, or rather that the flesh existed in him from the beginning and had hypostatic identity with him, do not establish that hypostatic union; instead, following the utterly foolish Nestorius, they imagine that this joining was merely one of relationship and simple indwelling ... For if the flesh was truly joined to God the Word from the beginning of its existence, or rather existed in him, and had hypostatic identity with him, how could it fail to be perfectly enriched with all wisdom and grace?”

He indicates that Christ is said to have advanced not because his holiness and wisdom increased, but insofar as his wisdom and complete abundance of every good overflowed into the world like a fountain.

Gregory of Nazianzus indicates the same in Oration 20, which is in praise of Saint Basil, vol. I of his works, p. 343 of the Cologne edition of 1690: “He advanced in age, and likewise in wisdom and grace—not because these received an increase—for what could be more perfect than what was perfect from the beginning?—but because these things were gradually disclosed and manifested.”

Amphilochius, a contemporary of Nazianzenus, explains it somewhat differently, though his interpretation comes to exactly the same conclusion as that of our Maximus, even if Petavius approves of it less, vol. IV, part 2, *Theological Dogmatics*, *On the Incarnation*, book XI, chapter 2, no. 9, p. 72 of the Paris edition of 1765: “Amphilochius writes that Christ advanced in wisdom for the sake of those whom he made wise, and in grace through which we ourselves, delighted, advance, believing that those things which he proclaimed concerning our hope would be brought to completion. In this way he affirms that Christ advanced, not from worse to better, as fools think.”

But if this was Maximus’s opinion, why does he mention the wisdom and holiness of Christ, God in majesty, but not his wisdom and grace according to his humanity? Maximus did this because he understood the latter to follow from the former. For I do not see why Gregory was permitted to understand this, while Maximus was not.

Gregory, however, who wrote after the heresy of the Agnoetes arose, and who approved Eulogius’s doctrine concerning Christ as wise and holy according to his humanity so thoroughly that in the letters mentioned shortly before he professed it as his own, says: “The matter is very clear: whoever is not a Nestorian can in no way be an Agnoete. For whoever confesses that the Wisdom of God was incarnate, how can he possibly say that there is anything of which God’s Wisdom is ignorant?”

He then brings forward the passage from the first chapter of John’s Gospel: “All things were made through him,” and continues: “If all things, then certainly the day and hour of judgment. Who, therefore, would be so foolish as to dare say that the Father’s Word made something of which he is ignorant?”

What could be more similar to this and to Maximus’s passage? I am not unaware that Petavius finds this mode of reasoning less satisfactory. But it is enough for me if it has been shown that Gregory and Maximus considered this to follow from their premises. Whether this method of concluding the argument was sufficient to refute the Agnoetes, or not, is not my concern. My concern now is the doctrine, not the reasoning ability displayed by those holy teachers. Yet we have many arguments at hand by which it could be shown that their argument is not so weak as Petavius thinks. But bringing them forward does not belong to this place or time.]

For the Lord grows in age for himself, but advances in holiness for us. This does not mean that Christ’s holiness advances—for it is eternal and perfect—but he is said to advance when he causes an increase of faith in us. For after the Nativity Christ is indeed a little child in body, yet he is God in majesty.

59. The joys of the Lord’s festival therefore still shake our inward parts. They shake them because, in the midst of joy itself, they urge us to burst into speech, so that we too may say what the angels said at Christ’s birth: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2).

See what the angels said. They did not say “peace to people,” or “to any people,” but “to people of good will,” so that we might understand that the peace of Christ belongs not to human beings as such, but to their character. It is not birth that merits it, but will; not human wickedness, but Christian goodness. For it is not bestowed upon everyone indiscriminately, but offered to the approved; it is not given to be broadcast, but proposed to be chosen.

The peace of Christ belongs to the one who believes that Christ is its author. The peace of Christ belongs to the one who has no struggle with sins. The peace of Christ belongs to those whose will is not stained by the blood of idols. For it is fitting that the Savior whom undefiled virginity bore should be possessed by an incorrupt will; and just as Mary carried him in purity, so may our soul keep him undefiled.

Mary represented a certain type of our souls. For just as Christ sought virginity in his mother, so he also required integrity in our affection.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] Gallandius reads *requirit*, “requires,” instead of *requisivit*, “required.”]

A soul that is virgin from sins both conceives the Savior and gives birth to him when it preaches; it guards him when it follows his commandments. Faith retains what has been conceived; confession brings forth what has been born; vigilance guards what has come forth.

Let us therefore rejoice at this festival of his, whose birth is announced by the splendor of the angels, sought by the simplicity of the shepherds, and venerated by the religious devotion of the Magi. Angelic grace honors God in Christ; pastoral innocence honors the Lamb; Magian veneration honors the priest.

The veneration of the Magi plainly proves Christ to be a priest, for the whole mystery is confirmed by their gifts. They offered the Savior, insofar as they were able, what they thought most beautiful: gold, incense, and myrrh—gold as appropriate to reigning, incense as appropriate to making propitiation, and myrrh as appropriate to rising again. Gold shows power; myrrh signifies incorruptibility; incense manifests priesthood.

For it was not done without purpose that the Magi came to the Lord with their gifts.

[Note: [Col. 0270D] Gallandius likewise reads: “with these gifts.”]

When they found Christ, who would reign over all, through the curiosity of their superstition, they brought him the insignia of all the elements: gold, by which earthly things are conquered; incense, by which heavenly things are thought to be appeased; and myrrh, by which the things below are embalmed. In this way they showed that from Christ’s birth none of these things was any longer necessary, since through Christ there was established victory on earth, propitiation in heaven, and rest in the underworld.

The Magi therefore discovered through their own curiosity that after Christ’s birth they ought no longer to be curious; and their magical art benefited them in this respect: it taught them that it would no longer benefit them.

Finally, they did not continue to live in the same manner as before, but undertook another route both for returning and for living. Before seeing Christ, the star led the Magi, like superstitious people, to obedience; after they had seen the Lord and believed, faith led them back to their homeland as devoted people.

Therefore, brothers, let us who have come from the Gentiles imitate those Magi up to the point of knowing Christ. It would have been permissible not to have gone astray. But after receiving Christ, we must beware lest the credulity of our Gentile past lead us back by the same road by which we came.

For there are many Christians who, after receiving the faith, become entangled again in their former vanities. Although they have shared with us the joys of the Lord’s Nativity, they arrange drunken banquets with the Gentiles on the Kalends; although they have received with us the blessing of the Divinity, they observe every superstition with them.

It is plainly regrettable that the Magi abandoned auguries while Christians observe omens; that the former laid aside expertise in their art, while the latter refuse to abandon the indulgence of their conduct.

The end.

## HOMILY XXII. On the Epiphany of the Lord VI

[Col. 0269]

### ADMONITION

We likewise transcribed this homily from the Turin manuscript, as we noted in the preceding admonition. Its title there is: “Also, Homily IX on the Epiphany of the Lord.” It is written with such gravity of thought and such clarity, brilliance, and polish of expression that it rightly deserves to be counted among Maximus’s more excellent little works.

### ARGUMENT

Although the Jews possessed many washings, they had none that could wash away and erase original sin. This privilege was reserved for baptism, instituted by Christ the Lord.

[Col. 0269D] Recently, dearest brothers, we celebrated the sacrament of our redemption, by which God clothed himself with the weaknesses of humanity. Today, however, we celebrate that by which he revealed himself through divine powers in human form. For on this day—whether because a star in the heavens announced his rising, or because at a wedding feast in Cana of Galilee he changed water into wine, or because in the waters of the Jordan he consecrated the waters for the restoration of the human [Col. 0270C] race through his baptism—in each of these events the mysteries and joys of our salvation are contained.

He was born for us from a Virgin, as the star showed. For us the washing of baptism was granted, which he consecrated in the channel of the Jordan. He also demonstrated beforehand, through the miracle of his work, that we too are to be changed for the better, when he changed water into wine.

Therefore, brothers, let us celebrate Christ’s baptism while guarding our purity, because this regeneration of Christ is the confirmation of our faith. He intimated to us the baptism of his gift through the example of a second birth, and what he wished us to do, he first did himself.

We read that the Jews had various baptisms [Col. 0271A] under the Law, but none of them could provide a universal remedy against the evil of transgression. And therefore, for the absolution of the whole world, the water of regeneration needed to be sanctified from heaven. Since the sacrament of baptism was necessary for the human race throughout the whole world, he gave a blessing to all waters when, with unique and singular compassion, he descended into the channel of the Jordan. Then the stream did not so much wash Christ the Lord as itself was washed.

For you, therefore, Christ came by being born; for you he served by living; for you he contended by dying. The one whom you see dead for you, understand also to have been baptized for you. He was altogether such even before his baptism, and therefore his forerunner and baptizer addressed him in this way when he came to him to be baptized:

“Lord, I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me” (Matthew III).

What could be clearer concerning the purity of Christ before his baptism? What could be stronger? “I ought to be baptized by you”—that is, you who are the fountain of innocence, who, needing nothing, know how to give but do not know how to receive. “I,” he says, “ought to be baptized by you,” because with you and in you are the gifts of purity and the sacraments of baptism; and what I shall give through your generosity, you possess by nature.

[Note: [Col. 0271C] Christ is true God and true man. As God, he is good and almighty—not by receiving grace, but by the possession of his nature, says Augustine, *Book VI of the Unfinished Work against Julian*, chapter 16, p. 970, vol. X of the Antwerp edition of the works, 1700. But as man he was born just by grace; see Augustine, the same work, Book I, chapter 140, p. 713.]

By his touch the limbs are immersed, and the streams are enriched. The blessed water marvels that its own fountain descends into it, conceiving eternal remedies in a single moment and giving birth to God through the new fecundity of regeneration; returning what it had received and receiving what it did not possess.

Amid all this, it would be astonishing that the Lord subjected himself to the servant’s blessing, unless he had also subjected himself to the cross and to death. And indeed he taught beforehand that the human being was precious to him by the very dignity of the price paid for him, so that from this too we may understand how greatly our God esteems the causes of human crimes, for which he sent to earth not an angel, not an archangel, but God himself.

But the magi, who reached the revered cradle of that heavenly child by the sign of the star—what else did they express through those gifts except our faith? For in the fact that three gifts are offered, the Trinity is understood; but in the fact that there are three persons and each offers a single gift, unity in the Trinity is declared.

[Note: [Col. 0271C] Saint Leo, sermon 33, the fourth on Epiphany, p. 86, Roman edition, 1753: “A more radiant ray of truth instructed the hearts of the magi, so that … they understood that he had been marked out for them: in gold, royal honor; in incense, divine worship; in myrrh, an acknowledgment of mortality.” The passages he develops in sermons 30, p. 77, and 35, p. 92, point in the same direction. Theodoret agrees with this in his commentary on the *Song of Songs*, chapter 3, p. 1036, vol. I of the Paris edition of Sirmond; and in chapter 4, pp. 1044 and 1049. Juvencus the presbyter, an ancient Christian poet, in *Evangelical History*, Frankfurt edition, 1710:

“Gold, frankincense, and myrrh they bring
To the king, to God, and to man …”

[Col. 0272C] Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 38, p. 623, Cologne edition, 1690, vol. I, where he says: “When you see the star, run; with the magi offer gifts—gold, frankincense, and myrrh—to the king, to God, and to him who died for your sake.” An ancient author of the homily *On the Holy Birth of Christ*, among the works of Saint Basil, no. 2, vol. II, p. 602, Paris edition, 1722: “They offered gold to the king, myrrh to him who was to die, and frankincense to God.” Origen, Book I *Against Celsus*, no. 60, vol. I of the Paris edition of the works by P. de la Rue: “They offered gold to the king, myrrh to the one who was to die, and frankincense to God.” Irenaeus, Book III *Against Heresies*, chapter 9, no. 2, p. 184, Venetian edition, 1734, makes it entirely clear that this type of interpretation had passed down from the earliest centuries of the Church into the later period. The author of the sermon *On the Star and the Magi*, among the works of Saint Cyprian, appendix, p. 29, Oxford edition, 1682, writes that the priest is to be understood in the frankincense. The same is also read in ecclesiastical books [Col. 0272D]. But that too is referred to the honor of God.]

Through gold the king is shown; in frankincense God is recognized; through myrrh, which is suitable for preserving bodies, the burial of the man who was to be crucified is proclaimed.

Accordingly, dearest brothers, let us imitate the role of the magi through spiritual acts of service. Let us seek Christ continually, until we deserve to find him. Let the light of faith guide us like the star of heaven. Let it show him to us no longer crying in a manger, but reigning in the highest citadel of heaven; no longer to be worshiped in his mother’s lap, but on the throne of the Father; no longer to be judged in majesty, but coming to judgment with majesty.

Thus, as the perfect confession of the three gifts, let us believe in the one Godhead, distinct without division and without confusion: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

(Much is missing; a leaf is absent. Maximus continues:)

Thus the worship of God must be ordered in the hearts of the faithful so that neither division in unity nor confusion in the Trinity is admitted.

*The end, etc.*

# HOMILY XXIII. On the Epiphany of the Lord VII

[Col. 0271]

## NOTICE

65 There are so many indications of the sincerity and authenticity of this homily that, with the complete agreement of all editors, it has been attributed to Saint Maximus. It has been written both abundantly and elegantly, clearly demonstrating that it had no other author than that holy bishop; and this is confirmed by the testimony of nearly all the manuscripts. In these manuscripts, however, its title is not uniform. In Vatican 4951 and Vatican Palatine 176 it is entitled: “On the Epiphany of the Lord.” In another Vatican manuscript, 1269: “Likewise, the foregoing, on the Epiphany.” In Vatican Palatine 257: “Sermon of Saint Maximus on the octave of the Lord.” In Vatican Regina 125: “On the octave of the Epiphany.” But this is of little importance. The homily is certainly about the Epiphany. For this reason we have judged that it ought to be titled accordingly.

[Col. 0271C] **ARGUMENT.**—The three miracles of this celebration, transmitted to us by tradition, present an equal number of mysteries in which our faith rejoices. In the magi, all nations were called to recognition of the Savior. His humility in baptism bore witness to grace [Col. 0272C] and majesty. The changing of water into wine manifested divine power.

In this celebration, beloved, as we are instructed by the account handed down from our fathers, we ought to rejoice in a festival of many dimensions. For they say that today Christ our Lord was either worshiped by the Gentiles under the guidance of a star, or, invited to a wedding, changed water into wine, or, having received baptism from John, consecrated the waters of the Jordan and at the same time purified his own Baptist.

But let him who performed it know which of these events took place above all [Note: [Col. 0273C] Codex Laurentianus 2: “what in particular took place on this present day.” The same reading occurs in Vatican manuscripts 9451 and Casinensis 106: “but what in particular took place on this present day.”]; nevertheless, we must believe and not doubt that, whatever it was, it was done for our sake.

For the fact that the Chaldeans, stirred by the rays of the brighter star, worshiped him gave the Gentiles hope of worshiping the true God. The fact that the waters were changed into wine in a new manner was a foretaste of the sacrament of the new cup for us. But the fact that the Lamb of God was baptized consecrated for us the saving gift of regenerating baptism.

Therefore, brothers, in honor of our Savior, whose birth we recently celebrated with fitting rejoicing, we ought also to celebrate with complete devotion this birthday of his powers. And how rightly these three mysteries are proclaimed as having been enacted for us on a single day, since under the one name of God we confess the mystery of the ineffable Trinity.

Through these miracles, therefore, Christ the Lord, our Redeemer, [66] wished to reveal himself to mortal eyes, so that his invisible divinity, which lay concealed in the human being, would not remain concealed in his works; so that, while the tempter did not detect the Word of the almighty Father in the flesh, all everywhere who believed the Word and the flesh to be in the Son of God might be saved.

The devil saw an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes, but he did not know that this was the one who, removing the darkness at the beginning, clothed the world with light. He saw him suck the breasts of a mortal mother, but he did not know that this was the one who made the hungry Hebrew people grow fat on angelic bread, as though on heavenly milk. He saw a little child resting in a narrow cradle, but he could not see that this was the one whom the world cannot contain.

How greatly, then, did the enemy waver in bewilderment, distracted by uncertainty at Christ’s humility, when he saw a new infant, through the Chaldeans—surely the foremost ministers of his tyranny—honored with royal gifts as the king of a new empire?

[Note: [Col. 0273C] Vatican manuscript 257: “Or how could he not be disturbed with amazement when he beheld [him] by the magi?” [The variant is syntactically incomplete.]]

Or how could he not be astonished when, in confusion, he saw his own magi worshiping a child whom he himself did not know? In what anguish did he writhe when he simultaneously despised his cradle on earth and marveled at the star in heaven?

The Only-Begotten of the Most High entered the world so humbly that he nevertheless displayed unmistakable signs of his divinity [Note: [Col. 0273C] Vatican manuscript 257: “that he would defer the signs of his divinity.”]. He was born of a woman, but born of a virgin [Note: [Col. 0273C] Vatican manuscripts 4951 and 257: “he was concealed in the present moment.”]. He lay in a manger, but shone in a star, so that both his earthly mother and the heavenly sign might show that he was man and God.

With what rays, and with how great a light, do we believe that the Lord’s star then shone among the ancient stars? How far did it surpass them in brilliance, since it went so far before them in its mission? Like the eye of the whole world, it renewed the ancient sight of the darkened world.

[Note: [Col. 0273D] “Behold, brothers, a single star led the Chaldeans to seek the King of kings,” etc. Concerning the time when that new star appeared to the magi, Graveson, in dissertation 8 *On the Mysteries and Years of Christ*, and Monilia, in dissertation 1 *On the Year of Christ*, have written with great learning, each in support of his own opinion. It is not necessary here to investigate whether the magi were Arabs or Chaldeans, since the same authors have fully answered that question. We note only that our Maximus always calls the magi Chaldeans and never Arabs. A third question is whether the worship which the magi offered to the child Jesus was merely civil or religious. On this subject, my colleague Liberatus Fassonius published a very extensive dissertation at Rome in 1756. Drawing decisive arguments from the New Testament and the Fathers, he proves that the magi venerated Christ as God in a pious and holy manner. In this work Grotius, Basnagius, and Simonius are refuted, since they attempted to present the magi’s worship as merely civil.]

Behold, brothers, a single star drew the Chaldeans onward to seek the King of kings [Note: [Col. 0274C] The same Vatican manuscripts: “to inquire after him.”]; but not even the fiery pillar of old could turn the Jewish people to obedience to their God.

Nor should anyone be disturbed by this great faithlessness of the Jews, because neither the brilliance of the new star nor the pregnant virgin compelled them to embrace faith in Christ [Note: [Col. 0274C] Vatican manuscript 257: “nor did the pregnant virgin join them to him.”]. For they did not believe in their God even then, when, with God himself accompanying them, heaven fed them as they passed through parched deserts and the rock gave them drink.

But let us now come to that principal miracle of Christ by which, as proof of his divinity, he changed water into wine.

Accordingly, as we read, the Lord went to a wedding when he was invited [Note: [Col. 0274C] Vatican manuscript 4951: “Therefore, when he was invited, the Lord …”]. But why the son of the Virgin deigned to do this is a matter for our instruction: so that, taught by this example, we would not deny him to be the author of lawful marriages.

The Son of God therefore goes to a wedding in order to sanctify by the blessing of his presence those marriages which long before he had established by his power [Note: [Col. 0274C] Codex Laurentianus: “which he now sanctifies by his presence.”]. He goes to a wedding of the ancient institution, intending to make for himself, from the way of life of the nations, a new bride of perpetual virginity. He goes to a wedding, although marriage did not create him. He goes to a wedding, certainly not to take pleasure in the banquet, but to make himself known through a miracle [Note: [Col. 0274C] Codex Laurentianus and Vatican manuscript 4951: “to make himself known through miracles.”]. He goes to a wedding, not to receive cups but to give them.

For when the wine had failed the wedding guests, the most blessed Mary said to him: “They have no wine.”

To her Jesus replied, as though expressing displeasure [Note: [Col. 0274C] The same Vatican manuscript: “the Lord replied.”]:

[Note: [Col. 0274D] “What is there between me and you, woman?” Who could doubt that these words express displeasure? But, I think, the reason was that his mother was suggesting to him so rashly that the supply of bodily wine had failed, although he had come to offer the nations of the whole world the new cup of eternal salvation. The adverb *temere* (“rashly,” “without due occasion”), which Maximus uses here, if the entire sequence and structure of the discourse are considered, has the same force as *non ex re* or *neque ex tempore*, that is, “not appropriately” or “not at the proper time.” This meaning was often assigned to the adverb by ancient writers of purer Latin, especially Terence in *Phormio*, act 5, scene 8, line 9, and elsewhere. I say this so that no one may either despise Maximus, as though he had understood the word in a sense different from that given it by the ancients, or think that we have invented the interpretation at our discretion in order to excuse the holy bishop. That Maximus understood it in this way is perfectly clear from what he adds immediately afterward. He observes that Christ addressed his mother in this manner not because she had asked anything improperly, but because she had asked before the hour of Christ himself had come—the hour in which he promised the wine of our redemption, which would benefit human life. … Nevertheless, the most gracious Lord was not unwilling, while great things were approaching, to perform lesser ones. “And therefore,” he says, “venerable Mary, and truly as the mother of the Lord, foreseeing future things in spirit,” etc. For this reason I could wish Petavius had been more exact and much more cautious in judging passages in the Fathers than he was. He claims that our Maximus appears to have thought the Mother of God at fault and therefore deserving of the mark of rashness, Book XIV *On the Incarnation*, chapter 1, §6. For it is the sign of an intemperate person to seize by caviling upon the worse interpretation of words which can and ought rightly to be interpreted kindly.]

“What is there between me and you, woman?” Who could doubt that these words express displeasure? But, I think, the reason was that his mother was suggesting to him so rashly that the supply of bodily wine had failed [Note: [Col. 0275D] Vatican manuscript 4951: “the failure of the bodily wine.”], although he had come to offer the nations of the whole world the new cup of eternal salvation [Note: [Col. 0275D] The same Vatican manuscript: “the cup of eternal salvation to the nations of the whole world,” etc.].

For when he says, “My hour has not yet come,” he was surely promising that most glorious hour of his passion [Note: [Col. 0275D] Laurentian manuscripts, Vatican manuscript 257, and Casinensis 106: “and that hour.”], or the wine of our redemption which would benefit the life of all. For what Mary was requesting was temporal grace; what Christ was preparing was everlasting joy.

Nevertheless, the most gracious Lord was not unwilling, while great things were approaching, to perform lesser ones. Therefore venerable Mary, truly as the mother of the Lord, foreseeing future things in spirit [Note: [Col. 0275D] Vatican manuscript 257: “foreseeing what was to come.”], and perceiving the Lord’s will beforehand, carefully instructed the servants, saying: “Whatever he tells you, do it.”

[Col. 0275B] The holy mother certainly knew that the rebuke of that Lord and Son of hers who was not angry was not an offense, but bore the mystery of compassion [Note: [Col. 0275D] The same Laurentian manuscript: “but bore the mystery of compassion.”].

Then the Lord, relieving the shame of his rebuked mother [*Alias*: “revealing the shame”], and now disclosing his majesty, said to the waiting servants: “Fill the jars with water.”

Without delay, the obedient servant performed his service. And suddenly those waters began miraculously to gain strength, assume color, give off fragrance, acquire taste, and altogether change their nature. This transformation of the waters from their own nature into an alien creature [Note: [Col. 0275D] The same Laurentian manuscript: “from one creature into another”; Vatican manuscript 4951: “from one nature into another.”] bore witness to the power of the Creator present there.

[Note: [Col. 0275D] The same Vatican manuscript 4951: “For no one at all,” etc.; Vatican manuscript 257 is almost identical throughout.]

No one could change water for other uses except the one who made it from nothing. The astonished servant therefore marveled: he had poured in water and was receiving wine. He rejoiced exceedingly that he had carried those streams in their proper measure, through which the glory of God had been revealed [Note: [Col. 0275D] Both of the manuscripts mentioned above: “and he rejoiced exceedingly.”].

[Note: [Col. 0276D] The same Vatican manuscript 4951: “For no one at all”; Vatican manuscript 1267: “Nor had anything been put into the jars except water; nothing had been added, no art had been employed,” etc.]

For no one said anything at the time; [Col. 0276A] nothing but water had been put into the jars; no art had been employed; and so great a miracle, amid the fearful silence of those standing around, was accomplished solely by the will of the silent Lord.

Nor should we doubt, dearest brothers, that it was he who changed the waters into wine who, in the beginning, condensed them into snow, hardened them into ice, changed them into blood for the Egyptians, and commanded them to flow from the dry rock for the thirsty Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0276D] In Vatican manuscript 257 the word “dry” is absent.]. That stream nourished an innumerable multitude of peoples by the trickling of a new spring, in place of a mother’s breasts.

What should you first be astonished at, [70] what should you marvel at—the wine from water, or the water from the rock?
