But let no unbelief trouble you, whoever you are who hesitate among these things, because there is no doubt that the elements of creation depend upon the command of the Creator [Note: [Col. 0276D] Vatican manuscript 257: “that the elements obey.”]. Or why should we not believe that, by the Lord’s power, wine could be made from water, when, through God’s action, water rises from the earth’s womb by means of rain and the service of the vineyards and becomes wine?

“This,” he says, “Jesus did as the beginning of signs in Cana of Galilee, and manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him” (John II).

The disciples believed—not merely in what they saw taking place, but in what carnal sight could not see. They believed [Note: [Col. 0276D] Vatican Palatine manuscript 257: “The disciples believed not,” etc.] not that Christ Jesus was the son of a virgin, which was known, but that this same person was the Only-Begotten of the Most High, which was proved by his work.

Therefore let us too, brothers, believe with all our heart that he is the Son of God whom we confess as the son of man. Let us believe him both a sharer in our nature and equal to the Father in substance, since he attended a wedding as a human being and changed water into wine as God; so that, in accordance with the merit of this faith, our Lord may graciously deign to give us also to drink of that sober wine of his grace [Col. 0276C] [Note: [Col. 0276D] Vatican manuscripts: “to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong power and dominion throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”].

# HOMILY XXIV. On the Epiphany of the Lord VIII

[Col. 0275]

## NOTICE

What the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur observed in the appendix to the works of Saint Ambrose—concerning sermon 9, which is the second sermon on the Epiphany of the Lord in the Venetian edition of 1751, p. 499—that this homily ought to be attributed to some other writer, perhaps Saint Maximus, we now believe can safely be stated. For anyone who compares it with the preceding homily will clearly discover that the same author treats the same subject in both. This is confirmed, so far as Maximus is concerned, by the Turin manuscript, in which the preceding homily is third among the homilies on the Epiphany and this one is fourth. It is also attributed to Maximus himself in the manuscript numbered 99 of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, where it is number 16.

Nor, because in many manuscripts it does not bear Maximus’s name, should there be doubt whether it ought to be assigned to him. For in order that this homily also—which is certainly the genuine companion of the preceding one—be regarded as having Maximus as its author, it will be sufficient if it is clear, on the authority of nearly all writers and manuscripts alike, that the preceding homily was assigned to Maximus.

**ARGUMENT.**—The authority of Scripture teaches us what the apostles received through ocular observation. When they saw the portentous transformation of water into wine, they rose to a great faith in Christ; instructed by the sacred Scriptures, we too should assume the same firmness of belief and be ready to profess it.

Your Holiness remembers, brothers, our preceding preaching, in which we described how the blessed apostles, upon seeing one miracle—that is, the water changed into wine by the Savior—immediately believed in him [Note: [Col. 0277D] Manuscript 99 of Santa Croce: “that his disciples believed in him.”].

For the Evangelist says of the Lord: “And he manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him” (John II). This event was written down not only so that the glory of the faith of those who were present when it occurred might be displayed, but also for our sake, since by the same example of devotion we are summoned to the glory of belief [Note: [Col. 0277D] The same manuscript of Santa Croce: “we are summoned to the glory of faith.”].

For what Christ performed, he performed not only for those who were present with him then, but also for us who would follow afterward, so that although our forebears preceded us in time, they would not precede us in the glory of miracles [Note: [Col. 0277D] Codex Laurentianus X: “the grace of miracles.”]. The power that was displayed in the actual presence of miraculous events has been preserved for us in the treasury of written texts, so that the page might provide us with what history enacted for them. Indeed, whatever is presented to us is enacted in us [Note: [Col. 0277D] Manuscripts Santa Croce 99 and Laurentianus: “whatever would be dictated to us as the mirror of the Scriptures suggested to us.”]; whatever is conveyed to us, so that through the mirror of the Scriptures it might be spoken, enables us to see by spiritual light the power of the Lord which they beheld with bodily eyes.

“And they believed in him, and he manifested his glory to his disciples” (ibid.). How fittingly the servants’ devotion follows the Lord’s power, and how the disciples inscribe in their hearts what the Master teaches through his works.

Behold to whom the power of the worker is revealed, and the manifest faith of the believers is proclaimed [Note: [Col. 0277D] Codex Laurentianus: “For behold, the power is revealed.”]. The faith of the apostles must surely be proclaimed: having seen one sign, they believed in the Savior’s omnipotence.

While the apostles marveled that water had been changed into wine, they themselves were similarly changed from all the dregs of sins. In imitation of the miracle, they were transferred from the vile superstition of the Gentiles into the precious devotion of believers. And just as water changed into wine acquires savor, redness, and color, so what was insipid in them received the savor of knowledge; what was pale took on the color of grace; what was cold grew warm with the ardor of immortality.

The faith of the apostles must therefore be magnified. It was described in the Gospel’s language so that it might bring them praise and benefit us as an example.

But what is worse is that their praise endures, while their example does not move us. For the later we are in time, the lower we are in merit. They believed in the Lord immediately upon seeing one sign, while we hesitate even after receiving so many marvelous benefits.

We hesitate, I say, because we love present things while we do not believe in future ones; we love riches in this world while we hesitate to receive them from Christ. We are raised up excessively by anger because we do not fear the judgment of retribution.

But whoever knows that it is written, “With what judgment you judge, you shall be judged” (Matthew VII), is undoubtedly gentle, moderate, and mild; he compels more by goodness than by severity, is a friend of indulgence and familiar with forgiveness, [72] [Note: [Col. 0278D] Manuscripts Santa Croce 99 and Laurentianus: “so that, while he frequently grants it, he may always receive it from the Lord.”] so that, by frequently granting it, he may always receive it from the Lord.

For it is the mark of a prudent ruler to conduct himself toward earthly honors in such a way as to acquire the honor of heavenly dignity.

And although bodily weakness sometimes dulls the vigor of our speech, we are nevertheless strengthened by your devotion. For the more attentively you listen, the more willingly we preach; and the power of speaking is increased in us when you lend your ears to understanding.

Who would not try to sow the seed of the heavenly word there where the fertile soil of a pure heart receives it [Note: [Col. 0278D] Paris edition of Ambrose: “receives it”]? Who, I say, would not wish to place the Savior’s word there where it is not choked by worldly anxiety but nourished by the power of spiritual disciplines?

Therefore, brothers, because we have rejoiced in the holy Epiphany as we behold the Savior’s miracles, we ought to do what the disciples of that time did then. As for what I said—that we now see what was accomplished long ago—we plainly see it, and we see it every day.

For Christ’s miracles are such that they do not pass away through wickedness but grow strong through grace [Note: [Col. 0278D] Manuscript 99 of Santa Croce and the Paris edition: “miracles.”]; they are not buried in forgetfulness but renewed through miraculous works.

For in God’s power nothing has been abolished, nothing is past; rather, because of his greatness, everything is present to him. All time is “today” for him. Hence the holy prophet also says: “A thousand years in your sight are like a single day” (Psalm LXXXIX).

And if all the time of the world is a single day for the Lord [Note: [Col. 0278D] Manuscripts Santa Croce and Laurentianus: “on that same day on which the Savior performed miracles for our fathers,” etc.], then on the same day on which the Savior performed miracles for our fathers, he also performed them for us.

We too, therefore, have seen the Lord’s miracles, like our forebears, receiving them with equal astonishment. We too have tasted from the very jars, for they drank wine from them, whereas we have received the cup of salvation.

Therefore, having seen the Lord’s sign, we ought to do what our predecessors did. For if the same grace of the Godhead has shone upon us, then the same devotion of faith ought also to be found among us.

The Evangelist says of the Lord, after this miracle had been performed: “And he manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him” (John II). We ought therefore to believe as the apostles believed then.

Another also says: “We too are Christians, and we believe in God the Savior.” But belief must be expressed in action, not in speech; by the heart, not by the tongue, lest it also be said to us: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah XXIX, 13; Matthew XV, 8; Mark VII, 6).

# HOMILY XXV. On the Epiphany of the Lord IX

[Col. 0279]

## NOTICE

73 That this homily too is a genuine work of Saint Maximus is demonstrated not only by the similarity and consistency of its style, but also by the complete agreement of the manuscripts and learned men who either published it or mentioned it. One manuscript of Casinensis, no. 103, p. 128, attributes it to Saint Augustine; but this is contrary to the truth. For it differs from Augustine’s sermons as greatly as Augustine’s manner of writing differs from that used by Maximus.

**ARGUMENT.**—Saint Maximus sharply reproaches the Jews for their hardness and blindness: struck by the brilliance of the unusual star and by the offerings of the magi, they nevertheless disdained to seek the Savior who had been born.

[Col. 0279B] You have heard, brothers, the Gospel reading recounting the saving mysteries of the present day. You have heard how Christ the Lord, who came into this world secretly [Note: [Col. 0279D] Cod. Vat. 4222: “who came secretly.”], gradually deigned to disclose his majesty to mortals; although, dearest ones, heavenly light could not remain hidden amid the darkness of the world. Indeed, while the earth did not yet recognize his visitation, heaven, to the amazement of the Chaldeans, silently proclaimed its joys and the gladness of the whole world through a quiet star. And while unbelieving Judaea could not yet see who and how great he was, the Gentiles, already aroused by signs from heaven, perceived his glory [Note: [Col. 0279D] Cod. Vat. 1267 and 4951, and Laur. I, Plut. XIV: “aroused by heavenly signs.”]. For a new star revealed that a new man had arrived—and truly new, since, although he was the Son of God, he assumed flesh without carnal generation and, as man, had a time of birth, while as God he had no beginning of birth. It was surely new that the tiny manger of a very small shelter should suffice for the Only-Begotten of the Most High, whom heaven cannot contain. It was new that he who reigned in heaven with God the Father, content with an earthly mother, should utter the cries of infancy in swaddling clothes [Note: [Col. 0279D] The Cassinese manuscripts: “he who.”]. Let us therefore rejoice, brothers, and exult with every joy, because Christ was born for us from a woman, for us he lay in a manger, for us he whimpered in a cradle, and for us he smiled upon us from the star. For everything that the Savior did as a human being for human beings benefited us [Note: [Col. 0279D] Cod. Vat. 1267 and 4222: “everything that the Savior of humanity did as a human being.”].

The Gospel narrative says: “Behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East, and we have come to worship him’” (Matt. II). How long, most obstinate Jew, will you persist—with deafened ear, closed eyes, and faithless heart? Behold, after the proclamations of the patriarchs and the prophecies of the prophets, Christ is now also proclaimed by the Gentiles. If you refuse to believe your fathers, who from the beginning of the world sang with countless sacred voices of the coming of the eternal King [Col. 0280A], believe at last those who testify that he is not still to be born after the passage of ages, but has already been born among you and for you. What aversion of deadly obstinacy is so great in your heart that you alone do not hear what everyone is saying, you alone reject what the whole world believes, and you alone disdain to see what shines from heaven? Among you a virgin conceived, and a stranger recognizes the birth of your virgin; angelic voices cannot persuade you of your salvation, yet a single star led the Chaldeans to your Christ.

“Where is he,” the Magi say, “who has been born king of the Jews? We saw his star in the East, and we have come to worship him” (ibid.). [Note: [Col. 0279D] The Laurentian manuscripts, Vatican 4951, and Casinensis: “It was foretold: ‘Those to whom he was not announced will see him, and those who have not heard will understand. For behold, the Chaldean…’” Codex Vaticanus 4222: “In these things was fulfilled what the prophetic word foretold: ‘Those to whom he was not announced will see him, and those who have not heard will understand. For behold, the Chaldean…’”]

In these things was fulfilled what was foretold by the prophetic word (Isa. V): behold, the Chaldean, to whom Christ had neither been announced nor of whom he had heard, saw the star of Christ and understood from the star that he was present. The Magi therefore worship the Lord and offer gifts, so that what the foremost of the prophets, David, said might be fulfilled: “Bring to the Lord, families of the nations; bring to the Lord glory and honor” (Ps. XXVIII). By saying “to the Lord” and again “to the Lord,” he mystically declares that Christ is Lord according to Godhead and Lord according to humanity; for as God he is the creator of the world [Note: [Col. 0280D] So read Vatican manuscripts 1267, 4222, and 4951, and two Cassinese manuscripts.]. As man, he is the redeemer of the world. How, then, is Christ not Lord of all by the privilege of both substances, since he has subjected all things to himself either by creation or by redemption?

“Bring,” he says, “to the Lord glory and honor” (ibid.). What the Gentiles offer is therefore honor, dearest ones; what they do in worship is glory: the Chaldeans offer gifts and worship. One is presented to him as king, the other as God. Thus, after worshiping Christ and offering their gifts, they returned to their own country by another way, as has been read. [Col. 0280D] Most rightly did they return by another way, lest bloodthirsty Herod, who was plotting the infant’s death, should be able to reach Christ by the route of the Magi; for those who had come to worship the Lord could not become the Lord’s betrayers. How fittingly, brothers, are they said to have returned by another way! For those who had come to Judaea under the guidance of the star returned to their homeland illumined by the rays of the eternal Sun. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0281D] Cod. Vat. 4951: “with all reverence.”] let us celebrate this day with all reverence [Col. 0282A], surpassing the service of the Magi with our devotion; for if they found Christ lying in swaddling clothes [Note: [Col. 0281D] The Cassinese manuscripts read “nursing” instead of “lying”], we have him reigning in heaven.

# HOMILY XXVI. On the Tenth Epiphany of the Lord

[Col. 0281]

## ADMONITION

I see that the same conclusion must be established concerning the following homily as concerning the preceding one. For not only do all the editors, but also all the manuscripts mentioned in the preceding admonitions, demonstrate that it ought to be attributed to Saint Maximus. Its title is nearly the same in the various manuscripts: “On the Epiphany of the Lord,” or “The Blessed Maximus on the Day of the Epiphany”; in the Taurinese manuscript it is numbered twentieth, from which notation it can plainly be understood that the ninth and tenth homilies are missing.

## ARGUMENT

The humility in which the Word made flesh appeared to the world was irradiated by such great portents and splendors that, while in the former he showed himself to be a true man, in the latter he wished to be recognized as true God.

Although, dearest brothers, Christ, the Lord of our salvation, the Son of the almighty Father, coeternal with him, covered with the veil of flesh and humbly deigning to visit mortals, nevertheless gave so many and such great signs of his majesty that the human mind might perceive both that a new man had been born and that God had come from heaven. For when our Lord himself, subject to the law of human birth, whimpered as a little child and infant among the Jews in a cradle and lay hidden in swaddling clothes [Note: [Col. 0281D] Cod. Vat. Reg. 125 reads “was nursed in swaddling clothes.”], a wondrous star from on high nevertheless proclaimed his magnificence to the whole world.

Who could doubt that the star itself flashed with more joyful light and more brilliant rays, since it brought the light of heaven and earth before human eyes? It was necessary that this star, which announced Christ—whose birth differed from that of all mortals—should stand apart from the other heavenly bodies by the greater brilliance of its light; and indeed, heaven then shone with a new star, but the world shone forth even more with a new light.

Who could investigate the glory of this miracle: that, for the remedy of our salvation, at one and the same moment a creature shone in heaven while the Creator shone upon earth? [Note: [Col. 0281D] Cod. Reginae: “a creature shone in heaven.”] Nor is it astonishing, dearest ones, that a heavenly testimony accompanies the Lord of heaven [Note: [Col. 0281D] Cod. Vat. 4951: “if heavenly attendance accompanies the Lord of heaven.”]; or why should it seem incredible to us if obedient creation bears witness to its creator? The earth indeed wondered that it saw a new star in heaven [Note: [Col. 0281D] Cod. Laurent. I, with which readings Vatican manuscripts 1267 and 4951, Vall. A 10, and the Cassinese manuscripts agree: “but heaven wondered more”;]; but heaven wondered that it saw a new Sun upon earth.

How profound are the Lord’s thoughts, and how unsearchable are his ways! [Note: [Col. 0281D] Cod. Vat. 4951: “and how unsearchable, etc.”] He gave from on high a most brilliant sign, lest human unbelief should attack the Virgin’s child [Note: [Col. 0281D] The text is corrected from the Laurentian and Vatican manuscripts; the printed text mistakenly reads *quae*.], a sign that neither the Gentiles could reject nor Judaea conceal.

[Col. 0282A] Thus, as has been read, the Chaldeans come from the East, following the star that goes before them—not recognized by magical art, but wondrous through its novelty. The Magi seek the king born especially among Israel because that diviner Balaam, once a priest of the nations, whose ass is said to have spoken [Note: [Col. 0281D] The same Regin. manuscript: “is said to have spoken.”], had prophesied that a star would arise from Jacob [Note: [Col. 0281D] The same Cod. Vat. 1267: “a star that would arise from Jacob.”] and that a man would come from Israel. For among other things he said, as we read: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise from Israel” (Num. XXIV).

Let no one therefore now wonder that the Chaldeans recognized the Lord’s birth. If God’s revelation could enable him to foretell it, a Gentile could recognize it. For this was, as far as can be judged, the decision of divine providence: amid the most sacred voices of the prophets, the coming of him who was to come for the redemption of believers and unbelievers alike should also be foretold by an unbelieving man [Note: [Col. 0282D] The Cassinese manuscript 106: “his coming; and the priest of idols prophesied the Redeemer of souls, so that, if the Jews’ preachers concerning Christ’s coming…”; it omits the intervening words.]. And the priest of idols prophesied for this reason: so that, if the Gentiles should perhaps refuse to believe the Jewish preachers announcing Christ’s coming, they might at least follow the testimony of their own authorities.

Nor should we doubt that the almighty and most benevolent God could have granted that foreigner Balaam a prophetic utterance [Note: [Col. 0282D] Vatican manuscripts 1267 and 4951, and the Laurentian manuscript: “who could loosen the tongue of that very ass”; but manuscript 4951 reads *relaxare* instead of *laxare*.], when he was able to loosen the tongue of his own ass for human speech.

The ass of the diviner’s rider was therefore speaking—an animal inclined downward and naturally looking toward the earth [Note: [Col. 0282D] Cod. Reg.: “looking toward the earth.”]—so that it might clearly signify that the whole Gentile world, devoted to altars and always weighed down by the burden of its unbelief toward the earth, despising the worship of almighty God, was silent and mute. But at the coming of the star from Jacob and the man from Israel, it would lift its eyes to heaven and speak of the glory of the eternal God in daily confessions [Note: [Col. 0282D] Cod. Regin.: “even for the glory of God, etc.”; Vatican codex 4941: “the eternal glory of God, etc.”].

Thus, brothers, the Gentiles come from the East, illumined, while Judaea, blinded by the unbelief of its most hardened heart [Note: [Col. 0282D] The same Regin. and Vallicell. A 10 manuscripts: “most hardened.”], remains in the West. How could all the defiance of the Jews not truly waste away in the West and in darkness, since, rejecting the presence of the tireless Sun, they lost the everlasting day?

And rightly, dearest ones, three Magi came together on one journey to worship [Note: [Col. 0283C] Cod. Vat. 4951: “three Magi came together on one journey to worship.”], because in the one Christ Jesus, who is the way of all believers, the inseparable Trinity was to be worshiped by them. They also bring gifts [Note: [Col. 0283C] Cod. Regin. reads: “They also bring gifts, which were proved to be mysteries.”], which were proved to be not so much gifts as mysteries [Note: [Col. 0283D] Cod. Laurent.: “In gold, brothers, is shown the precious redemption of our captivity. In incense is proclaimed both the superstition of demons, which is to cease, and the worship of true religion, which is to come. In myrrh, since bodies are customarily preserved after death, the restoration of our flesh and the resurrection of the dead is prefigured.]. They offer him gold, frankincense, and myrrh. In gold, brothers, is shown the precious redemption of our captivity; in frankincense, the superstition of demons, which is to cease, and the worship of true religion, which is to come, is revealed; in myrrh, with which lifeless bodies are customarily preserved, the restoration of our flesh and the resurrection of the dead are prefigured.

That such sacred gifts should be offered to Christ was chosen not by the Magi’s judgment, but by the inspiration of the Almighty. For, considered materially, these gifts seem altogether unworthy of his majesty, insofar as they concern Christ’s glory [Note: [Col. 0283D] Cod. Vat. 1267: “for insofar as it concerns Christ’s glory, these gifts…”]. For what use or attraction does gold—which belongs to and is prized by mortals—have for the immortal Lord? [Note: [Col. 0283D] Cod. Vall. A 10: “How can frankincense be offered to almighty God, to whom even images are worshiped by the Gentiles through its fragrance?”] What use has frankincense for almighty God, whose fragrance even causes idols to be honored by the Gentiles? Or what use has myrrh, the seasoning of stinking bodies, for him over whose flesh no corruption of death was to have dominion [Note: [Col. 0283D] Cod. Laurent.: “for whose flesh…”]?

All these things, dearest ones, would appear superfluous and empty in the Son of God unless we believe that the mysteries of our life were symbolically shadowed forth in them [Note: [Col. 0283D] Cod. Vall. A 10: “all these things, dearest ones, in the Son of God…”; the Cassinese manuscripts: “in the Son of God, etc.”]. Therefore, brothers, let us hope in the Lord, and let our heart be strengthened, so that in us also the star of faith may shine forth, leading us by a straight and unerring path to Christ. Let us too offer the small gifts of our actions and devotion, which Christ may receive—not now lying on earth in a cradle [Col. 0284B], but seated at the right hand of the Father and embracing them in heaven [Note: [Col. 0283D] Cod. Vat. 4951: “in heaven, with whom he lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever. Amen.”].

# HOMILY XXVII. On the Eleventh Epiphany of the Lord

[Col. 0283]

## ADMONITION

What we have taught elsewhere—that whatever is presented by us in this collection has been drawn from better sources—will become even clearer from what is to be said about this homily. We first mention three Vatican manuscripts: namely, 4222, folio 86 onward; 4951, folio 44; and 1267. These are followed by the three Vallicellian manuscripts A 10, folio 4; A 16, folio 89; and XX, folio 75, as well as by two other Cassinese manuscripts, 103, folio 123, and 106, folio 234. The following agree with them: the manuscripts of Lambach, Cistercianus of Monte Amiata, Augiensis XVI, Lucensis 85, Novariensis 27, Modoetiensis E III, Laurentianus I, Plut. XIV, folio 10, Vercellensis 81, and Taurinensis under the number of homily 21. All of these acknowledge Saint Maximus as its author. The editors likewise confirm this testimony: Gymnicus, page 50; Galesinius, page 101; Combefisius, volume II, page 78; Cumdius, volume I, page 507; Raynaudus, cited page 201; and Margarinus in *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, page 10.

## ARGUMENT

Jesus Christ, lying in a cradle, draws human beings to himself by a portentous manifestation; heaven bears witness to him; and the kings of the earth approach to worship him.

The foremost of the prophets, Isaiah, says, dearest brothers: “Shine, shine, Jerusalem; for your light has come, and the majesty of the Lord has risen upon you” [Note: [Col. 0284C] Vatican manuscript 1267 and Vall. A 10: “has arisen.”] (Isa. L). It is clear that Jerusalem is the city of the faithful. Therefore we, brothers, who have begun to enter the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0284C] Vall. manuscript marked XX: “we desire to enter.”], illumined by saving mysteries, must exult with new joy in the sight of our God, because today a new star has revealed a new man to the world.

On this day Christ Jesus, coming from the Father, born God and man from a woman, consecrated the faith of the nations under the appearance of the Chaldeans who came to worship him. Although he veiled his divinity beneath the shadow of our body [Note: [Col. 0284C] Cod. Vat. 4222: “yet heaven revealed him to be God”; Vall. A 16: “yet heaven came forth revealing him to be God.”], heaven nevertheless revealed him to be God [Col. 0284B], and earth recognized him. He came humble, yet wondrous, so that in him alike the truth of the flesh he assumed and the ineffable nature of the Godhead might shine.

And although earthly cradles received him at his birth [Note: [Col. 0284D] The same codex 4222: “received him.”], a heavenly sign nevertheless testified that he was not earthly [Note: [Col. 0284D] Vatican codices 4222 and 4951, Vallicellian manuscripts A 10 and A 16, and the Cassinese manuscripts: “a sign.”] [Col. 0284C]. He lay in a cradle, but shone in heaven [Note: [Col. 0284D] The same Vatican manuscripts 4222 and 4951: “from heaven.”]; he whimpered among the Jews, but reigned among the Gentiles; he was nursed by his mother in Bethlehem, and worshiped by the Magi in Chaldaea.

For the most blessed evangelist Matthew says: “Behold, Magi came from the East, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?’” (Matt. II) [Note: [Col. 0284D] Vatican manuscripts 1267 and 4222 and the Cassinese manuscripts omit the word “for.”]. How fittingly are they said to hasten from the East [Note: [Col. 0284D] The same codex 4222: “they are recognized as coming”; Cod. Vallic. XX: “how fittingly are they recognized as coming prophetically from the East.”]! They come to worship the eternal Orient, of whom it was said: “The Orient from on high has visited us, to enlighten those who sit in darkness” [Note: [Col. 0284D] The same codex 4222: “those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death”; Vall. XX: “and in the shadow of death.” Likewise Laurent. I, Plut. XIV, and the Cassinese and Modoetian manuscripts] (Luke I).

Then the Chaldeans add: “We saw his star, and we have come to worship him” [Note: [Col. 0284D] Cod. Vallic. XX and the Cassinese manuscripts: “to worship the Lord.”]. “We saw his star,” they say. Properly “his,” because although all stars, created by the same one, belong to him [Note: [Col. 0285D] Vatican manuscript: “belong to him.”], this one was Christ’s in a particular way, since it specifically announced his coming. The other stars were made to distinguish the times and courses of this world; but this one was commanded to appear in order to show that the Lord of the world himself was present, and that the time of the heavenly kingdom had arrived.

Thus the Magi say: “We saw his star, and we have come to worship him.” Behold, those who do not possess Christ want to possess him, and strive to find him. The Jew flees his God [Note: [Col. 0285D] Cod. Novariensis 27: “whom the pagan seeks.”], while the pagan seeks him; what a neighbor does not recognize, a stranger understands. The Gentile sees the star and comes; the Jew sees Christ and envies him, as it has been read: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John I).

Truly, most obstinate Judaea, blinded by its own unbelief, did not see what the star was shining, nor could it hear what the angels were proclaiming aloud. Therefore, when the Magi were seeking and saying, “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?” “Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.” [Note: [Col. 0285D] Cod. Vat. 1267: “Herod was troubled.”]

The king is troubled by the kingdom, I suppose, fearing for his own, unaware that Christ had not come to seize his kingdom but to save it; and that he who is the life of all would bring death to no one [Note: [Col. 0285D] Vatican manuscripts 4222, Laurentianus, and Novariensis 27: “who is the life of all.”].

And as the Magi traveled about, the star that they had seen in the East went before them, as has been read, until it came and stood above the place where the child was [Note: [Col. 0285D] Vatican manuscripts 4222 and 4951: “where the child was. ‘It came,’ he says, ‘and stood above where the child was. Surely…’”]. Did it not seem to speak and cry aloud: “This is the child whom I testified from heaven had been born” [Note: [Col. 0285D] The same Cod. Vat. 4222: “This is the child whom the star testified from heaven had been born”; Cod. Novariensis: “the child whose birth the star testified from heaven.”]? This is that great king who has come to join an earthly kingdom to a heavenly empire.

Truly, this star was the servant of the Lord’s birth [Note: [Col. 0285D] Vatican manuscript 1267 and Vall. A 10 add: “this was.”], so obediently did it serve the Chaldeans [Col. 0285C] [Note: [Col. 0285D] The same Vatican codex 4122: “so that they might seek Christ”; the Cassinese codex: “in seeking Christ.”], that in their search for Christ it not only warned them from heaven but also provided them guidance on earth.

After worshiping the Lord and offering their gifts, the Magi passed by Herod and returned to their own country by another way [Col. 0286A]. Nor could they return through Herod—that is, by the way of death [Note: [Col. 0286D] The same Cod. Vat. 4222: “through Herod, the way of death.”]—since, after worshiping the Son of God, they were carrying back to their homeland the gifts of heavenly life [Note: [Col. 0286D] Vall. A 10: “For they could not, etc.”].

Thus Herod, deceived and scorned by the Magi, became exceedingly angry, as the evangelist says (Matt. II), and sent and killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem, “from two years old and under,” he says [Note: [Col. 0286D] The same Vatican codex: “‘from two years old,’ he says, and so forth; and let the cruelty be made known.” Cod. 4951: “‘from two years old,’ I say, etc.”]. The age of those killed is recorded so that the cruelty of the killer might be made known. O perverse anger and unconsidered indignation of a raging man! He is angry with the Chaldeans and kills the innocent; and, while he directs his attack against the death of the immaculate infant, he destroys crowds of nursing children—so that the most unjust king, who sought blood to which he had no right, might be enveloped in the manifold guilt of the fallen multitude. Nor could the madness of the raging man perceive that he who was coming to give life to the dead could not be compelled to die against his will [Note: [Col. 0286D] Vatican manuscripts 1267 and 4951: “could not be compelled against his will.”].

[Note: [Col. 0286D] The same Cod. Vat. 4222: “And the devil did all these things, dearest ones, through Herod.”] And the devil did all these things, dearest ones, through Herod, so that by serving his will he might either kill Christ or, through the slaughter of the little ones [Note: [Col. 0286D] Cod. Vat. 1267: “most choice.”], darken the most joyful beginning of Christ’s coming.

[Note: [Col. 0286D] The same Cod. Vat. 4222: “But among the faithful there should be no…”] But among the faithful there should be no grief over the death of the innocent, because Christ, the most just giver of reward, made those who suffered for his sake participants in his passion and patiently allowed those for whom he was willingly preparing eternal life to be killed.

Therefore, dearest ones, as we come from the nations, for whom the saving light of the Lord’s star shone from heaven, among whom the Virgin’s faithful childbirth is honored, and for whom Christ is God both in the cradle and in heaven [Note: [Col. 0286D] The same Cod. Vat. 4222: “and in the cradle, and in heaven God is, and of devotion…”], let us bring the gifts of our devotion and faith; let us avoid Herod’s unbelief; and, sanctifying body and spirit and loving mercy [Note: [Col. 0286D] The same Cod. Vat. 4222: “loving mercy with body and spirit sanctified.”], let us always honor the Lord’s most sacred coming. Thus, just as we rejoice in his illumination, so may we rejoice in our reward, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0286D] Cod. Vat. 4951 adds: “who lives and reigns, God, forever and ever. Amen.”].

# HOMILY XXVIII. On the Twelfth Epiphany of the Lord

[Col. 0285]

## ADMONITION

This homily proves no less clearly than many others that the Roman editors, in reviewing the works of Saint Ambrose, consulted neither the ancient manuscript codices nor the earlier editions of the Fathers, since they included this homily among the sermons of that same holy teacher. Nor did they err only in identifying its author; they also erred in its title. Both points must be demonstrated.

As regards the first, we produce twelve repeatedly commended manuscripts that attribute this homily to Saint Maximus. Four of them are Vatican: namely, 4951, 4222, Palat. 433, folio 236, and Reginae 125, folio 120; the others are from different libraries. Laurentianus I, Plut. XIX, folio 70, explicitly reads: “Sermon of Saint Maximus, bishop, as above.” Likewise there are Casinensis 106, folio 30 onward; Novariensis 27, folio 135; Vercellensis 81; Lucensis 85; Augiensis XVI; Modoetiensis E III; and finally Taurinensis, homily 25, “On the Epiphany of the Lord.”

Gymnicus, who preceded the Roman edition of Ambrose by twenty-five years, placed it among the homilies of Maximus as number 5, page 55. Galesinius followed Gymnicus, homily 5, “On the Epiphany,” page 102; as did Combefisius, volume II, page 79; Cumdius, volume I, page 508; Margarinus in *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, page 12; and Raynaudus, page 202.

The title, however, is entirely unrelated to the homily. For in the Roman Sixtine edition this homily is entitled “On the Baptism of Christ,” although the author says not a word about it, and from beginning to end praises the Magi who sought the Christ who had been born and vehemently rebukes the unbelieving Jews.

## ARGUMENT

Saint Maximus explains why the Lord had to be manifested to human beings through an unusual star. He demonstrates that King Herod and the unbelief of the Jews are without excuse.

It is salutary and fitting for us, brothers, as we gather for the Lord’s festivals and the mysteries of our Savior, whose birth made us rejoice, to rejoice in his manifestation as well [Note: [Col. 0287D] Laurentianus I, Plut. XIV: “let us rejoice in his manifestation.”]. For just as the Son of God is glorious in being born, so he is wondrous in appearing.

It is truly wondrous that Christ came forth from a virgin; and no less magnificent that he was revealed from heaven. It is exceedingly wondrous that the earth received a new man; and likewise astonishing that a new star from heaven disclosed this new man.

Among the Jews Christ whimpered in a manger; in Chaldaea he sparkled among the stars before the eyes of the Magi. Among the Jews he lay in lowliness in swaddling clothes; among the Gentiles he shone in glory. And indeed it was necessary that a heavenly testimony precede the Lord of heaven, and that the sign of light reveal the author of light [Note: [Col. 0287D] Cod. Vat. 4951: “the sign of light.”].

A great and fearful mystery this is, when one and the same person is proclaimed God from the Father and man from his mother; one and the same is the son of a woman and the Son of Majesty; one and the same is a participant in humanity and Lord of the angels.

For who could estimate how great a mystery and how great a glory it is that he who feeds all should suck milk, and that he who grants from heaven the substance of life to every living creature should, for the salvation of earthly beings, be nourished with earthly milk?

Let no one therefore doubt, let no one hesitate, that Christ, while dwelling on earth, shone in heaven, because he came to the earth in such a way [Col. 0287C] [Note: The same Vatican codex: “that he might not leave heaven.”] that he did not leave heaven.

For this reason the angels praise this virginal child, the shepherds marvel, heaven bears witness, and the Magi venerate him, because his mystical birth filled both earth and heaven with everlasting joy.

This king, therefore, ruler of heavenly and earthly beings, coming under the mystery of flesh, is shaken by envious Herod, while unbelieving Judaea denies him. Herod trembles at the infant’s royal dignity because he does not know the goodness of the one being born. Judaea denies the Christ whom it proclaims, because, fearing the just Judge on account of its impieties, it flees his justice. Blinded by the darkness of its crimes, it alone cannot see what shines from heaven for everyone.

And although the teaching of all the patriarchs and the words of the holy prophets [Col. 0288A] could not bend Jewish hearts toward recognition of the Son of God, the ray of a single star aroused the faith of the Gentiles.

What great reversal is this, brothers, and what transformation? Among the Jews the prophet speaks, and he is not heard; among the Gentiles the star is silent, and it persuades. Truly, as it is written: “Those to whom he was not announced will see him, and those who have not heard will understand” (Isa. LII; Rom. XV).

For behold, the Chaldeans, to whom nothing had ever been proclaimed about mysteries of this kind [Note: [Col. 0287D] Cod. Casin. 106: “understood.”], understood the birth of Christ. Earnestly seeking Christ himself [Note: [Col. 0287D] Vatican codices 4951 and Palat. 433: “earnestly seeking him, with heaven showing the way.”], they deserved to find him under the guidance of the star displayed by heaven [Note: [Col. 0287D] The same Cod. Casin.: “they found him, with heaven’s star showing the way.”].

Nor were these things understood or seen by just any lowly, obscure, and despised people, but by Chaldeans—that is, among whom the error of superstitions reigned [Note: [Col. 0287D] Cod. Novariensis: “superstitious.”].

Among these Christ, entering the world, found the first fruits of saving faith; and there arose between Jews and Gentiles a kind of contest between unbelief and faith. When Christ was born, Chaldaea rejoiced, while all Jerusalem with its rulers was tormented. The Jew persecuted, the Magus worshiped [Note: [Col. 0288D] Vatican manuscript 4951 and the Cassinese manuscripts: “worshiped. Herod sharpened the sword.”]; Herod sharpened the sword, while the Chaldean prepared gifts.

But why be surprised if that Jewish multitude did not receive Christ’s infancy [Note: [Col. 0288D] Cod. Vat. 4951: “who even raised the dead, etc.”], when it stubbornly and contemptuously rejected him even when he raised the dead? Why be surprised if the Jews scorned Christ lying in a cradle, when, as he gave the blind new light or restored what they had lost, and healed various illnesses by his saving word [Note: [Col. 0288D] The same codex: “healed” instead of “treated.”], they accused the Lord who redeemed them, ungrateful for all his benefits, with the slanders of a lying tongue [Col. 0288C]?

Why be surprised if they disregarded the signs of the shining star at his birth, when at his passion they rejoiced even while the sun itself mourned? Why be surprised if, when the Chaldeans came, they refused to believe—those whom even the gathering of angels could not lead to faith in the truth [Note: [Col. 0288D] Cod. Novariensis 27: “they did not wish to return, etc.”]?

Let us therefore rejoice, brothers, and exult in the Lord, celebrating with every joy the festival of the everlasting mystery: we do not deny the Lord’s birth through carnal conjectures, but confess it with simple faith; we learned of the Savior’s coming not from announcing Magi, but from the Father bearing witness from above; and we do not now seek Christ the Lord whimpering among the cradles, but venerate Jesus Christ the Lord reigning in heaven [Note: [Col. 0288D] Cod. Vat. 4951 adds: “with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”].

# HOMILY XXIX. On the Baptism of Christ I

[Col. 0287]

## ADMONITION

Although the Cassinese and Vallicellian manuscripts lack this homily, many others take their place, offering certain testimony concerning Saint Maximus. The Vatican Library supplies four manuscript witnesses, namely 1267, folio 185; Palat. 433, folio 237; 4951, folio 42; and 189, in which the homily is attributed to Saint Maximus the bishop.

The same attribution is found in Laurentianus I, Plut. XIV, folio 71. To these we add Augiensis XII and XVI, Lucensis 85, Novariensis 27, folio 136, and the Taurinese manuscript. In this codex the title is: “First Homily on the Epiphany and on the Baptism of Christ.” Quite appropriately so, since the holy bishop first treats the manifestation of Christ made to the Magi and the portentous conversion of water into wine at the banquet in Cana of Galilee, and then Christ’s baptism.

But since he touches upon the first two miracles only lightly and discusses the third at greater length, we have followed the editors in entitling the homily “On the Baptism of Christ.” Gymnicus indeed has this title on page 38, as do Galesinius, page 103; Combefisius, volume II, page 80; Cumdius, volume I, page 509; Raynaudus, page 203; and Margarinus in *Bibliotheca Maxima*, page 12—all writing “On the Baptism of Christ.”

Here we must also note that Saint Augustine and Saint Leo the Great—the former having six sermons on the Epiphany and the latter eight—treat only the manifestation of Christ through the unusual star shown to the Magi, and in them discuss the calling of the Gentiles to faith; but concerning the other two miracles, which the Church celebrates on the same solemnity, they maintain a profound silence.

Our Saint Maximus therefore deserves particular commendation for having discussed the threefold mystery elegantly and learnedly, and for having made the hidden teaching of the sacred Scriptures manifest, with the richness and ease of his speech, less in this homily than in those that follow.

In this he seems to have followed the Greek Fathers, namely the two Gregorys, Gregory of Nyssa and Gregory of Nazianzus, who recalled Christ’s threefold manifestation in their orations and called the sixth day of the month of January the day of the Epiphany.

Whether, however, on the same day on which the Magi, guided by the star, came to worship the Lord who had been born, Christ, having become about thirty years old, wished to be baptized by John, and on that same day attended the banquet in Cana of Galilee and changed water into wine, writers disagree among themselves, some following the affirmative opinion and others the negative. The Church has defined nothing concerning this matter; it has merely combined the celebration of those three miracles into a single day.

Saint Maximus explicitly defends the affirmative view in the fifth homily on the Baptism of Christ. “Even if,” he says, “some believe that only one or another of these events took place, nevertheless I believe that all of them occurred on that day, and that one is contained in the other.”

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0289A] The holy teacher briefly gathers together what he had treated in the preceding homilies concerning the Epiphany of the Lord. Nearly the whole of this discourse is about the baptism of Christ, through which his divinity shone forth more clearly.

Many and diverse mysteries of the saving rites are multiplied for us, brothers, by the solemnity of the present day. For, as antiquity faithfully handed down to posterity, today the Savior of the human race, manifested by heavenly signs [Note: Codex Vaticanus 189: “manifested by heavenly signs”], was worshiped by the Chaldaeans (Matt. 2). Today Christ, through the ministry of blessed John, consecrated the waters of the Jordan by the blessing of his own baptism (ibid. 3). Today also, invited to a wedding, manifesting the power of his divinity, he changed water into wine—water, I say, into wine, that is, the water which he sanctified in baptism he ennobled at the wedding (John 2). These three mysteries, brothers, belong to one faith [Note: The same codex: “the mysteries of one day”], yet they were accomplished by the one Lord through the gracious condescension of the Trinity. For the unity that belongs to the divine nature can never be absent from the working of miracles, nor can that which is undivided in divinity ever be separated from itself. Finally, when the Savior was baptized, the Father revealed by his voice that he was not absent from the Only-Begotten, and the Spirit revealed himself in the form of a dove. Therefore, brothers, let us not wonder that, for those whose faith is in the Trinity [Note: The same codex: “for those in whom there is faith in the Trinity”], three mysteries have consecrated one day for us.

Today, then, as we have said, the magus discovered through the star what the Jew refused to believe through the prophets. Today the Gentile world, taught from heaven about the Redeemer of the world, seeks him as king, presents gifts to him as the mighty one, and worships him as God. And how fittingly, dearest ones, as a testimony to the new birth, a new star shone upon the earth [Note: The same codex omits “upon the earth”], whose ray the treacherous Jewish people could neither conceal, nor could they hide its truth; nor could the darkness of malicious interpretation any longer have a place through them, where heaven itself was shining before the eyes of all with the light of the stars, proclaiming what was to be believed. And how marvelous it is that a small ray of a star moved the astonished hearts of foreigners, when neither the fiery pillar itself, flashing from heaven, could turn that Jewish people for whom the sea had been divided and manna had been provided from the clouds!

But let us now hasten to Christ’s baptism. “Jesus came,” it says, “to the Jordan, to be baptized by John.” John said to him: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matt. 3). I ought indeed to be baptized by you, because corruption is mine through ancestral transgression, whereas you share in the majesty of the Father [Note: Codex Laurentianus, cited above: “and you share in paternal necessity”]. I was brought forth into this world by a fleshly parent; you came here as the Only-Begotten from the unbegotten Father. The natural union of man and woman generated me; but you were given to us by venerable virginity, overshadowed by the power of the Most High [Note: The same Laurentian codex: “venerable virginity brought you forth for us”]. I am an earthly animal; you are the Lamb of God. I am mortal under the law of sin [Col. 0290B], but you, coming against sins, do not know subjection to sin. And, above all, I was made one who must be redeemed by you, whereas you were born in order to redeem.

Jesus graciously replied to him: “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (ibid.). That is: Everything you mention is true; but this is the reason for my coming: since I have been made under the law, the lawful order must be completed. For I have come not to live for myself—for I possess eternal life with the Father—but to remove the condition of your death [Note: Codex Novariensis 27: “to take away”]. And this is most just: since I have assumed the whole human being, I must pass through every rite belonging to humanity.

And truly, brothers, how could Christ fail to come to baptism for our sake, when for our sake he did not avoid even the indignity of bodily circumcision? Hence John, recognizing the saving mystery [Col. 0290C], no longer sanctifies the Son of God as a baptizer, but, as a devoted minister, obeys the commands given from heaven. For the servant could not fail to obey his master, the herald his judge, the soldier his king, or the forerunner his author.

And so that the prophet might recognize more fully and perfectly that all these things were being accomplished by the Divinity, the Holy Spirit allowed himself to be seen in the form of a dove, and the Father to be heard in the sound of a voice. For he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3).

See and consider, brothers, how great a grace mortal humanity receives from the divine condescension. For, so that the most sacred mysteries of our redemption might be confirmed and the eternal Trinity might be revealed to us more clearly [Note: Codex Vaticanus 189: “might be revealed”], the Son is baptized in the Jordan. The Spirit sanctifies the mystery; the Father discloses the truth.

It remains now that the reason for this third act of devotion become clear to your charity. Today also, as the Fathers report, the Lord Jesus made wine from water in Cana of Galilee [Note: The same Vatican codex: “made wine from water”] (John 2). Brothers, you should not hesitate in the face of such wonders concerning the Creator. For he who at the beginning of the world gave water its existence [Note: The same Vatican codex: “caused water to exist”], at the end of the world likewise made from water whatever he wished [Col. 0291B]. It is plainly a greater manifestation of majesty to create things that did not exist than to transform things that have been created [Note: The same Vatican codex: “to create what did not exist”].

And what is so astonishing if, at the command of its Lord, water became wine, when by his will the grape, the mother of wine, itself is nourished by the life-giving moisture of the rains [Note: Codex Laurentianus: “by whose will, through the nourishment of the rains, the grape…”; likewise the Vatican codex; but Codex Novariensis reads: “by whose will, through the nourishment of the salutary rains, he changed the waters into wine for the sake of humanity. He who, in order to create humanity, transformed the earth…”]? What is so astonishing if the Lord of all, for humanity’s sake, changed water into wine, when, in order to create humanity, he transformed earth into flesh [Col. 0292A]? What is so astonishing if, at his command, water advances into a better flavor, when by his action, though it was bitter, it was sweetened at Marah by a healing wood for peoples who were to drink [Note: The same Laurentian codex: “in the sea, for peoples who were to drink”]? And by his command it also sprang forth, driven out from the rock, so that it would not be lacking for the thirsty in the wilderness [Note: The same Vatican codex: “it sprang forth and leapt from the rock”]?

There water proceeds from the rock [Note: The same Laurentian codex: “And there, since water proceeds through Moses from the rock”], where the spiritual figure of the cup still exists; here, through Christ, it becomes wine, where the true salvation of those who drink is now present.

What, then, brothers, is more joyful than this day, what more sacred than this solemnity? On this day a star of greater brightness shone forth to the nations and revealed the virgin’s offspring, who lay hidden in a cradle [Note: The same Vatican codex: “revealed him to the nations”]; on this day the wave of the Jordan received the Only-Begotten of God for its own sanctification; humanity saw the Holy Spirit, and the world heard the Father; on this day also Christ showed that he had visited the mortal race, drunk with sins, with that sober and wondrous cup of wine [Note: The same Vatican codex: “with that sober, wondrous wine, the remedy for sin,” and so forth].

Therefore, dearest ones, let us lay aside the slippery pleasures of the flesh in spiritual gifts and rejoice spiritually, so that the light of the heavenly star may illuminate the darkness of our hearts, the blessing of the Father’s voice may enlighten us, and the saving wine, offered by Christ, may make us glad.

# HOMILY XXX. On the Baptism of Christ II

[Col. 0291]

## ADMONITION

It is perfectly clear from the Taurinensis codex that Saint Maximus composed thirty homilies on the baptism of Christ. Very few of them survive, and because of their antiquity their integrity has not been sufficiently preserved. The homily which we now publish was copied from a codex of the abbey of Saint Dalmatius; in that codex it is the fifth homily, *On the Baptism of Christ*, whereas in the Taurinensis codex it is numbered eighth and entitled *On the Same Epiphany and the Baptism of Christ*. The consistent style, the uniformity of the sentences, and the manner of adducing passages of Holy Scripture provide grounds for referring it to Maximus alone.

## ARGUMENT

Christ, who came not so much as Savior as teacher of holiness, established salvation in baptism and preceded those who would believe in him by his example, so that they might be cleansed from sins by the bath of regeneration and obtain the grace of justification.

From the Gospel, brothers, we recently heard that our Lord Jesus Christ came to the sacred waters of the Jordan for the sake of baptism and wished to be consecrated in that same river by heavenly mysteries. We should not, however, wonder why he himself did this. He wished first to carry out what he commanded others to do, so that, like a good teacher, he might insinuate his teaching not so much by words as by practicing it himself in deeds.

It is clear that all these things took place on this day, and we can gather this even from the reasoning of the matter itself. Reason requires that, after the day of the Lord’s Nativity—even if years intervened—this solemnity should follow at the same season; and I think that it too ought to be called a nativity. For then he was born for humanity; today he was reborn through the mysteries. Then he was brought forth through the Virgin; today he was regenerated through the mystery. In this way the Lord arranged everything in his infinite wisdom, so that human prayers would not be far removed from one another; indeed, at one and the same season, the one whom people rejoiced had been born on earth might be celebrated as sanctified in heaven. Thus those who already possessed the Virgin’s offspring, announced by angels, might retain him as the Son of God, attested by heaven, and might be certain that the one whom the Virgin had borne was truly the Son of God; for Divinity itself recognized him as God.

New births deserve new acts of devotion. There, when he is born according to humanity, Mary his mother embraces him in her lap; here, when he is begotten according to the mystery, God the Father embraces him with his voice. For he says: “This is my Son, in whom I have been well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 2). Thus the mother gently caresses him in her lap at his birth, while the Father speaks to him in baptism through a loving testimony. The mother presents him as one more worthy of worship; the Father reveals him to the nations as one to be honored.

The Lord therefore comes today to baptism and wishes his body to be washed by water. Someone might perhaps say: If he is holy, why did he wish to be baptized? Listen, then: Christ is baptized not so that he may be sanctified by the waters, but so that he himself may sanctify the waters and purify by his cleansing the streams that he touches. For Christ’s consecration is the consecration of the element in a higher sense. When our Savior is washed, all water is already cleansed for our baptism, and the font is purified, so that the grace of the bath may afterward be supplied to the peoples who follow.

He therefore goes ahead through baptism, so that Christian peoples may confidently follow him. Thus the pillar of fire went before through the Red Sea, so that the children of Israel might fearlessly follow the route it showed; it first passed through the waters, so that it might prepare a path for those coming after it. As the Apostle says, this was the mystery of baptism (1 Cor. 10). Indeed, in a certain sense it was baptism, where the cloud covered the people and the water carried them [Col. 0294A].

The Lord Christ accomplished all these things—the same one who does so now. Just as then he went before the children of Israel through the Red Sea in a pillar of fire (Exod. 13), so now through baptism he goes before Christian peoples in the pillar of his body. He, I say, is that pillar which then supplied light to the eyes of those who followed, but now provides illumination to the eyes of believers; then he made a firm path through the flowing waters, while now in the bath of baptism he strengthens the footsteps of our faith. Whoever walks fearlessly by that faith will not fear the Egyptian persecutor and will reach the heavenly kingdoms, if he confirms the faith he holds by good works.

*Explicit.*

# HOMILY XXXI. On the Baptism of Christ III

[Col. 0293]

## ADMONITION

The observations we made concerning the attribution of the preceding homily to Maximus apply quite suitably to this one as well. Therefore I do not doubt that this homily too had the same author, the bishop of the people of Turin. We received it from two codices of the abbey of Saint Dalmatius and from the Taurinensis. Both Saint Dalmatius codices transmit its title in this form: *Likewise, the third homily on the Baptism of Christ*. The Taurinensis, however, has: *Likewise, the thirtieth homily on the Epiphany and the Baptism of Christ*.

## ARGUMENT

When John the Baptist sees Christ approaching him to be baptized, he proclaims to the crowds that Christ is the author of justification, since he is the Lamb of God, sent for the purpose of taking away the sins of the world.

A few days ago, brothers, we explained that our Lord Jesus Christ was baptized not for his own sake but for ours, since he himself had committed no sins. Nevertheless, he came to the waters of the Jordan for this reason; he mingled with that crowd of sinners who had approached John’s baptism, both to sanctify the waters of the Jordan and to invite us to the bath of baptism—and especially you catechumens, who cannot attain the joys of paradise without baptism.

That blessed Baptist of Christ, John, also understood this. For when he saw Christ coming toward him, he turned to that crowd of sinners who had come to him to be baptized and said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world. Behold, indeed, the one who never committed sin. Behold the Lamb of God. Behold, he takes away the sins of the world. Run, therefore, to him. Receive baptism from him. For he is able to cleanse your sins. And I too desire to be baptized by him.”

John truly desired this, and therefore he said to Christ: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” That is: You who are God, do you descend to your creature? You who are king and Lord of lords, do you come to your servant? You who are holy, do you descend to a sinner so that you may be baptized by him? [Note: Codex Taurinensis: “And John would have refused the ministry of this holy office unless Christ himself had commanded him to perform it,” and so forth.]

John himself would have refused to perform so great a ministry for Christ unless Christ had commanded him to do so. “Let it be so for now,” says the divine utterance that was read earlier; “for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness. I ought to be baptized by you” (Matt. 3).

Jesus is therefore baptized by John—not for himself, but for us. God is baptized by a creature, the Lord by a servant, so that he himself might fulfill all righteousness. If, then, the one who committed no sin was baptized, why should we, who are sinners, not be baptized? If Christ, who was purity itself, sobriety, and innocence, wished to be immersed in the baptism of his servant, why should we, whose burden of sins is excessive, not be cleansed for salvation?

Let us therefore do what that venerable Baptist of Christ desired to have done to himself but did not obtain. He desired Christ’s baptism; he wanted to be baptized by Christ, and yet he did not deserve to obtain it. Baptism is freely offered to us; let us therefore be baptized. For our Savior himself, in order to fulfill all the commandments of the Law that he had given, wished to be baptized, just as he himself said elsewhere: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5).

*Explicit.*

# HOMILY XXXII. On the Baptism of Christ IV

[Col. 0293]

## ADMONITION

Only this small portion of the homily could be copied from the codices of Saint Dalmatius and the Taurinensis. The remaining portions are missing, I do not know through whose fault: someone removed two leaves from those same codices. In the Dalmatius codex it is entitled: *Likewise, the ninth homily on the Baptism*; in the Taurinensis: *Likewise, the fourteenth homily on the same Epiphany and on the Baptism of Christ*.

## ARGUMENT

From these few passages it is understood that in this homily Saint Maximus treated the manifestation of Christ’s divinity at the banquet in Cana of Galilee and his baptism.

The omnipotent power of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ is clearly gathered from the reading we have just heard. Although his omnipotence—by which at the beginning of creation he created heaven and earth from nothing together with the Father and the Holy Spirit—seemed hidden in the human being whom he had assumed for our redemption, it was clearly manifested to his disciples.

For when he came to a wedding of the ancient institution at Cana of Galilee, and suddenly the wine failed for those dining, he, who had not disdained to be present at that wedding, also wished to confirm that wedding by a miracle, and changed water into wine.

[Two leaves are missing from the original; it then concludes as follows:]

So that, freed from every pollution of this world, we may be able to reach the heavenly kingdoms, with the help of him who reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY XXXIII. On the Baptism of Christ V

[Col. 0295]

## ADMONITION

It is established from the Taurinensis codex and that of the abbey of Saint Dalmatius that this homily too was attributed to Maximus. Its style, the structure of its sentences, and its continuity demonstrate that Maximus was its author. In the Taurinensis codex it is the twenty-ninth of the homilies: *On the Epiphany and on the Baptism of Christ*; in the Saint Dalmatius codex, the fifth: *On the Baptism of Christ*. This title seemed to us more appropriate.

## ARGUMENT

After first recalling the threefold mystery of the Epiphany, Saint Maximus begins a special discourse on Christ’s baptism and eloquently explains the great gifts of grace that flow from it.

I believe, brothers—and especially you catechumens—that you understood my preaching on the holy day of the Epiphany. In it I said that, according to the claims of some, our Lord Jesus Christ was worshiped by the Magi who came from the East under the guidance of a star; according to others, that he changed water into wine at that time; and according to still others, that he was baptized by John in the Jordan on that day. Yet in all these accounts he is believed to be the Son of God, and in all of them our true festival is present.

Although some believe that one or another of these events took place, I nevertheless believe that they all occurred on that day, and that one is contained in the other. For when Christ our Lord came into this world to restore human nature, he certainly first called the Jews—of whose stock he had been born according to the flesh—to life. Yet, as we have often impressed upon your holiness, he did not abandon the people of the nations in their blind unbelief.

For he who wished, by his wondrous incarnation and grievous death, to free everyone from eternal death also called everyone to the venerable light of his faith. Thus angels reveal the newborn Redeemer to shepherds, while a new star invites the nations to his sacred and venerable cradle. Shepherds come to Bethlehem, and the Magi hurry to his cradle with gifts. Shepherds venerate him, and the Magi also worship him. At his birth, mad Herod trembles and the proud Synagogue is terrified; the Gentile world, however, exults and rejoices that its Savior has at last come.

And indeed, while the Jews were left in their unbelief, the Church grew from the nations. On this day, in fact, the Church of the nations was born, because through that most brilliant star the Gentile world was called, in the persons of those three Magi, to the recognition of the true light [Col. 0295D]. It grew because on this day the sacrament of the saving bath was also instituted by Christ the Lord.

Today, as the venerable tradition of the ancients teaches us, our Savior came to the waters of the Jordan. Today the one who was without sin came to the Jordan among crowds of sinners in order to be baptized. Finally, today our Redeemer wished to be baptized in the Jordan and in turn to sanctify his own Baptist.

Christ is therefore baptized in the Jordan, and on this day he sanctified the waters of the Jordan by his baptism. But why do I say “of the Jordan”? For he sanctified the entire substance of the waters, wherever they are, by his baptism.

See, then, how on this most holy day the Church from the nations was gathered through the calling of the Magi, and how it was spiritually reborn—and is reborn each day—through Christ’s baptism. For each day the Church passes into the life of regeneration whenever it receives catechumens for baptism.

Before the bath, the catechumen is weak [Note: Why Saint Maximus said here that catechumens lack knowledge of the most holy Trinity, and that this knowledge is imparted to them when they have been baptized, I shall explain in the note to the first treatise on Baptism]; but after receiving baptism, he acquires knowledge of the Trinity and becomes steadfast and faithful. He is no longer like the water which, on this day, Christ the Lord, invited to the wedding, changed into wine—pale and without flavor. After receiving baptism, the faithful person becomes changed into wine.

For the grace of the Holy Spirit is signified in wine, just as our Savior himself affirmed when he said that new wine must be put into new wineskins (Matt. 9) [Note: The Taurinensis codex reads: “Therefore on this most sacred day, through the flashing of the new star, the Gentile world was converted to faith in those three Magi. Our Redeemer instituted the saving bath of regeneration for all and changed the substance of the waters into wine. He bestowed such great grace upon his baptism that he both sanctified his own Baptist and promised eternal life to all who received it and observed the commandments he gave.”].

See, then, how on this most sacred day the Gentile world was converted to faith through the flashing of the new star. Our Redeemer instituted the saving bath of regeneration for all; and why, on that same day, he changed the substance of the waters into wine.

Christ our Lord bestowed such great grace upon his baptism that he not only sanctified his own Baptist, but the river Jordan itself was turned backward.

*Explicit.*

# HOMILY XXXIV. On the Baptism of Christ VI

[Col. 0295]

## ADMONITION

This distinguished homily has been attributed to Maximus by the unanimous agreement of all editors. The manuscript codices agree: two Vatican codices; two Belgian codices, the Martinensis and the Camberonensis; and two Casinenses. Four Subalpine codices, namely the Taurinensis, that of Saint Dalmatius, the Vercellensis, and the Novariensis, also agree. To these may be added the Augiensis, Lucensis, Vallicellanus, Florentinus, and Amiatensis.

When the Benedictine monks of the congregation of Saint Maur removed it from the series of Saint Augustine’s sermons and transferred it to the appendix as number 134, they nevertheless freely admitted that it is attributed to Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, not only in the published collections of his works but also in manuscript copies. The codex of Saint Dalmatius contains much in this homily that does not agree with the texts already published. We have relegated it to the notes on pages 93 and following, so that readers may conveniently compare it with the commonly published versions.

## ARGUMENT

The difference between Christ’s baptism and John’s baptism is established. John’s bath could not remove sins except through the merit of faith and repentance, whereas the Redeemer’s baptism washes away faults of itself and bestows righteousness.

Although, beloved brothers, there is a different tradition among the ancients concerning the solemnity of this day, there is nevertheless one faith of holy devotion. And although some today believe that our Lord Jesus Christ was worshiped by Magi coming from the East under the guidance of a star, while others assert that he changed water into wine, and still others maintain that he was baptized by John, in all these accounts he is believed to be the Son of God, and in all of them our festival is present [Alternative: “our true festival”].

The fact that the Magi, clearly Gentiles, were permitted both to worship the Lord and to offer gifts signifies beforehand the calling of the nations [Note: Codex Vaticanus 1267: “The transformation of water into wine signifies the hidden mystery of our religion; but the fact that…”]. The fact, however, that Christ is baptized in the streams of the Jordan signifies that the waters are consecrated for our baptism.

It is therefore fitting, dearest ones, that we now say something about baptism itself to your holiness, as the Lord grants, so that you may recognize both the humility of our Savior and the glory of the mysteries.

John preached in the desert a baptism of repentance to a sinful people [Alternative: “to the people for the remission of sins”]. Not one that erased crimes already committed, but one that corrected those who had gone astray. For the remission of sins was reserved for the grace of Christ.

A very great multitude of various people therefore flocked to John out of desire for the bath [Note: The same Laurentian codex: “Therefore a multitude flocked to the Jordan out of desire…”; Codex Vaticanus 1267: “whose life was so ruined by such criminal acts that he…”]. Their deeds were so wicked and their life so ruined that the venerable Baptist compared them to a brood of vipers.

Among such people the Lord of heavenly powers, he who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble, Christ Jesus, does not disdain, humble and tranquil, to hurry to the baptism of his little servant. But what is surprising about the Savior’s gentleness, if he bent himself to the hands of the prophet, when he allowed himself to be crucified by his enemies?

As he hurried toward the river, John burst forth in these words before the surrounding crowds: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). This is to say: Stop now, stop coming to my baptism, in which repentance is received. Behold the Baptist through whom crimes are forgiven. No longer desire to be baptized by your fellow servant. The Lord of us all is present, the one who baptizes unto life. Follow him; believe in him; with your whole mind, as suppliants, ask from him the bath of salvation. I myself, your Baptist, desire to be baptized by him.

Jesus did not reject the testimony of this voice. Yet because he wished to fulfill everything in due order, he nevertheless requested to be baptized by John. Then the devoted Baptist, terrified by the power of the one who was to be baptized, said: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matt. 3). That is: I am a creature, but you are the Creator; I am a servant, but you are the Lord; I am a figure, but you are the reality.

But Jesus said: “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (ibid.). That is: Why do you mention these things now? The purpose of the humility I have undertaken must be fulfilled.

Then the one who was afraid to presume obeyed the command of the one giving orders without delay. Jesus is therefore baptized not for himself but for us; he is baptized not to be purified by the waters, but to sanctify the waters himself; the new man is baptized in order to establish the sacrament of the new baptism.

“The heavens were opened,” he says. I think that in the heavenly realms there was a miracle concerning what was taking place on earth, as it says: “Into which angels long to look” (1 Pet. 1). For how could the powers of heaven, the dominions, cherubim, and seraphim fail to marvel when they saw the Lord of Hosts being baptized by a human being in the river?

And so that John’s testimony might also be confirmed by heavenly testimony, he saw the Holy Spirit in bodily form, descending like a dove and remaining over Jesus (John 1). He also heard the Father saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I have been well pleased” (Matt. 3).

Pay attention, beloved brothers, to how great a grace has been disclosed to us in the baptism of our Lord Jesus [Note: The same Laurentian codex: “how great a grace has been disclosed to us in the baptism of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth], and by what subtle mystery the Trinity revealed itself to humanity today. The Father is heard in the voice, the Son is manifested in the human being, and the Holy Spirit is recognized in the dove.

By what wondrous mystery, moreover, does our Lord Jesus Christ, whether by the touch of his body or by the passage of his glory, sanctify, vivify, and illumine every creature in an instant? He consecrates the waters when he is baptized; he sanctifies the earth when he is buried; he raises the dead when he rises again; he glorifies the heavenly things when he ascends into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father [Note: The same Vatican codex adds: “with whom he lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.” The same words occur in Codex Casinensis no. 106.].

## THE SAME HOMILY FROM THE CODEX ONCE OF SAINT DALMATIUS

[Col. 0297]

Although, brothers, the ancient Fathers have handed down various and diverse traditions concerning the venerable solemnity of the present day, there is nevertheless one sincere faith among them all. Although some believe that our Lord Jesus Christ was worshiped today by Magi coming from the East, while others assert that he was baptized by John on this day, and still others think that today he changed water into wine, all alike nevertheless believe him to be the same Son of God, and therefore our festival is true in every respect.

When the Magi are permitted to worship God and offer him their gifts, the future calling of all the nations is already foreshadowed. When the waters are changed into noble wine, the sanctification and transformation of our souls through the most holy bath of baptism is shown. When Christ is baptized by John in the Jordan, the entire substance of the waters is consecrated for our baptism.

Today Christ is indeed baptized by John, and through that baptism the humility of our Savior and the glory of the mysteries are then revealed most clearly. John preached in the desert a baptism of repentance to a sinful people—not one that already erased sins committed, for the remission of sins was reserved for the grace of Christ, but one that brought those who had gone astray back onto the way of salvation.

An innumerable crowd of sinners flocked to him out of desire for the bath. Among such people, whose deeds were so wicked and whose life was so utterly ruined that the divine Baptist compared them to a brood of vipers, the Lord Christ did not disdain to mingle, nor did he blush to bow himself to the hands of his little servant.

As he hurried toward the river, the astonished John burst forth before the surrounding crowds: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). This is to say: Stop now coming to my baptism, in which repentance has begun. Behold the Baptist through whom crimes are forgiven. No longer desire the bath for repentance from your fellow servant. Behold the one who baptizes unto life; follow him, then, cling to him. Believe what he says; do whatever he commands; finally, as suppliants, ask from him the saving bath. For I, your Baptist, also desire to be baptized by him.

But Jesus did not disregard such a testimony of the voice. Rather, because he wished everything to be fulfilled in due order, he requested to be baptized by his John. For Jesus said to him: “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3). That is: Why do you mention these things now? The purpose of the humility I have undertaken must be fulfilled. Then the one who was afraid to presume quickly obeyed the command of the one giving orders.
