Jesus is therefore baptized by John not for himself but for us. He is baptized not to be purified by the waters, but to sanctify the waters himself. Then the heavens were opened: all the powers of heaven marveled at the Lord of Hosts in the river. John then saw the Holy Spirit in bodily form, descending like a dove and remaining over him; he also heard the Father saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I have been well pleased” (ibid.).

See, then, brothers, how great a grace has now been disclosed to us in the baptism of our Lord, and by what subtle mystery the whole Trinity manifested itself to humanity. The Father is heard in the voice; the Son is manifested in the human being; the Holy Spirit is recognized in the dove.

By what wondrous mystery, therefore, does the Lord, through the touch of his body and through the passage of his glory, sanctify every creature in a moment and illumine it with life-giving light? For he consecrated all the waters in his baptism.

*Explicit.*

# HOMILY XXXV. On the Baptism of Christ VII

[Col. 0299]

## ADMONITION

In the published editions this homily is entitled *On the Grace of Christ*, contrary to what nearly all the manuscript codices require and to what the work itself indicates. For Maximus discusses Christ’s baptism extensively in it, not grace; and of all the codices we have seen, only the Martinensis has the title *On the Grace of Christ*. We have therefore entitled it *On the Baptism of Christ*, following the Taurinensis codex.

Codices Vaticanus 1267 and 4991, Vaticanus Regius 125, Casinensis 106, Florence, Laurentian Library II, Plut. XIV, Lucensis 85, Lambacensis, Modoetiensis E III, and Novariensis 27 bear the title *On the Epiphany* or *On the Epiphany*, because the homily was delivered on the same day of the Epiphany on which the solemnity of Christ’s baptism is celebrated.

Some made Saint Ambrose the author of this homily. They were mistaken. Nothing is more distant from Ambrose’s style. It must certainly be attributed to Maximus, whose style it possesses, as well as the same manner—at least in our judgment—of citing passages of Holy Scripture and weaving sentences together.

## ARGUMENT

Maximus touches on the circumcision to which the Lord submitted in order to show himself a true human being and an observer of the Mosaic Law. He again begins a discourse on Christ’s baptism and, from his admirable abasement, accumulates illustrious arguments for the worship of his divinity.

The eternal author of our redemption, the almighty Lord, the only-begotten Son of the living God, [Note: Codex Vaticanus 190: “the only-begotten Son of the living God.”] remaining always inseparably with the Father, deigned for our sake to assume a perfect human being; and, though he was God, he so emptied himself that he might pass through all the sacramental observances of the Law. For as soon as he came forth from the holy womb of his blessed Mother, he was consecrated by the sign of circumcision—either to demonstrate the undeniable reality of his flesh, or lest the Jewish people, nurtured by circumcision, reject him as a foreigner. [Note: Codices Vaticanus 190, Laurentianus Reginae 125, and Casinensis: “lest they reject him as a foreigner.”]

100 [Col. 0299D] Then, because the precepts of the Law handed down through Moses could not be passed over, an offering for his purification was presented (Exod. XIII, 2; Luke II, 23); and for him, brothers, an offering for purification was presented, although he had come to purify the uncleanness of all human beings. [Note: In Codex Casinensis the word “purification” is omitted.]

But when John, sent ahead before his face, was correcting the crowds flocking to him by his preaching and consecrating them through the baptism of repentance, he himself hurried to John amid the undistinguished and lowly crowds, as though he were one of the people. In such immeasurable goodness he humbled himself that that most sacred head, dreadful to the powers and venerable to the angels, inclined itself to receive baptism at the hands of its little servant. [Note: Codex Reginensis: “of his servant.”] [Note: Likewise the Vatican Codex: “he humbled himself,” etc.]

When John saw him coming to his baptism and recognized in him the marks of the Lord’s glory, [Note: Codex Vaticanus 3951 and Codex Reginensis 125: “the marks of the Lord’s glory in him.”] he said to him: “I ought to be baptized by you” (Matt. III). That is: the earthly by the heavenly, the mortal by the eternal, the fragile by the powerful. “And you are coming to me?” The judge to the forerunner, the Creator to the creature, the king to his minister? [Note: Likewise Codex Vaticanus 4951: “and you humble yourself in what is insignificant, although I am not worthy to carry your sandals,” etc. Codex Martinensis likewise has: “although I am not worthy to carry your sandals,” etc.]

And will you humble yourself to me, an insignificant man, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry? You come to baptism among sinners, although no deceit was found in your mouth (Isa. LIII, 9; 1 Peter II, 22), and through whom the sins of the whole world are taken away. You so subject yourself to your own creatures that you might seem to forget that you are God. Indeed, I see a human being, but I recognize my Lord; [Note: Codex Reginensis Vaticanus: “but I recognize my God.”] I behold a human body in you, but I understand a heavenly mystery. Nor does this appearance of assumed flesh draw me away from faith in the truth: you are the Lord—you are he himself who sent me for these things. But how could I now fail to recognize him standing here and present, whom not long ago, while he was still established in the virginal womb and within his mother’s entrails, before he himself had yet been born, I recognized?

To him Christ said: “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. III, 15). [Note: Codex Reginensis: “for thus it is fitting for us.”] “Let it be so for now,” says the Lord—that is: “What you mention is indeed true, and I do not reject it; but I have come to fulfill the ministry of service, [Note: Codex Vaticanus 4951: “to fulfill the ministry of humility.”] so that I may recall to my freedom those whom sin has subjected to slavery. [Note: Codex Laurentianus: “so that I may recall to my freedom those whom sin has subjected to slavery.”]

Nor should you marvel, John, if I incline myself to your hands; for since I was content to be born, content to be circumcised, and even content to be wrapped in swaddling clothes, 102 how could I not willingly be content to enter this Jordan? [Note: Codices Vaticani 1267 and 4951, and Codex Casinensis: “I am content to be born.”] Do not think that this baptism seems insulting or unworthy to me. Other insults await me; there are other indignities which I have resolved to endure for the salvation of the human race. [Note: Codex Vaticanus 4951: “for the salvation of those who are born.”]

After this, blessed John devoutly received the one whom fear had restrained him from receiving. He did not fail to know that the Lord, the foremost of the prophets, was to be baptized by him; but he did not wish to complete his ministry without confession. Thus faith confessed the Lord, and obedience fulfilled its service.

[Note: The same Vatican and Regina codices: “When the Lord had therefore been baptized.”] When the Lord had therefore been baptized, the Holy Spirit was present, and a voice from heaven was heard, speaking with the majesty of the Father: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17). [Note: Codex Martinensis adds “my.”]

That this event benefited our faith is clear, brothers: through it the presence of the Holy Spirit, the authority of the Father’s voice among the whole human race, John’s testimony, the truth of the Son, and the sacrament of baptism were confirmed. [Note: Codex Laurentianus: “so that the presence of the Holy Spirit [might be confirmed].” Codex Vaticanus 4951 and Codex Casinensis: “so that the presence of the Holy Spirit and the authority of the Father’s voice [might be confirmed].”] Through it we magnify and glorify God the almighty Father, through our Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: This agrees with Codex Vaticanus 4951.]

## HOMILY XXXVI. On Ash Wednesday

[Col. 0301]

### ADMONITION

103 There is no controversy concerning the author of this homily, since the manuscripts and editors remarkably agree in attributing it to Maximus. The only disagreement concerns the title attached to it. Codex Vaticanus 1278, p. 14, has: “Sermon of Saint Maximus on the day of Lent.” Two Vatican Palatine codices, 432, p. 120, and 435, p. 147, differ from each other. In the first one reads: “Homily III on Lent”; in the other: “Sermon of Saint Maximus during Lent.” In Augiensis XIV it is: “Homily V on Lent.” Two Casinensis codices, 103, p. 221, and 106, p. 373, together with Vallicellanus, vol. II, p. 219, Lambacensis, Laurentianus I, Plut. XIV, p. 141, and Saint John ad Carbonariam, have: “Homily on Lent.” The Taurinensis, however, gives the following for the second sermon on Lent: “Likewise, Sermon II on the fast of Lent.”

The title of Codex Lucensis 85 is distinctive: “Sermon at the beginning of the fast.” This recalls the ancient designation used by that Church for the day, namely: “Wednesday at the beginning of the fast.” That this usage was current is shown by the Council of Agde, held in the year 506, through the canon cited by Burchard in chapter 26 of book XIX of the Decretum: “At the beginning of Lent all penitents,” etc. Here one may incidentally observe how ancient was the custom in the Church of beginning the fast on the Wednesday before the Sunday called the first Sunday of Lent.

Nor do we wish to pass over in silence the fact that, among so many codices which we ourselves have examined or whose extracts we have received from others, only two Belgian codices, Martinensis and Camberonensis, bear the title: “On Ash Wednesday.” Yet it seems probable that the same inscription is found in other ancient manuscript witnesses, since Damian of Ascend, a celebrated Benedictine monk, whose collection of the homilies of Saint Maximus was published at Cologne by Gymnicus in 1535—and we know of no earlier edition—placed this as the first homily on Lent and assigned it the title: “On Ash Wednesday.”

The other editors subsequently followed him: Galesinius, p. 107; Combefisius, vol. II, p. 49; Cumdius, vol. II, p. 42; Raynaudus, p. 205; and Margarinus, Bibliotheca Maxima, vol. VI. All entitle this homily “On Ash Wednesday.” Remigius Ceillerius rightly observes, in vol. XIV of his Ecclesiastical History, that it may be learned from this homily that in the time of Saint Maximus it was customary for the same Gospel from chapter VI of Saint Matthew to be read in the Church on Ash Wednesday; and we see that this practice has been preserved to the present day.

For this reason Francesco Gaetano Incontri, archbishop of Florence, highly distinguished for piety and learning, wrote in his excellent work published at Florence in 1762, Explicatio de celeb. dierum festorum, p. 56, when citing the beginning of this homily of Maximus, that in all the most ancient codices that Gospel is found assigned to the Wednesday before the first Sunday of Lent; from this, he says, it can plainly be understood that on that day the faithful generally took up the beginning of the Lenten fast.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0301C] According to the Gospel, hypocrisy, or the display of repentance, is condemned. Fasting ought to be holy; and it can become all the more pleasing and acceptable to God the more brightly it is adorned with virtues.

Because it is the custom of some, dearly beloved, to anticipate the coming days of Lent with more devoted fasting, [Note: Codex Laurentianus I, Plut. XIV: “more devoted to fasting.”] the present Gospel reading has necessarily been expounded. In it our Lord, the bestower of spiritual virtues, gave us a holy and perfect rule for fasting, saying: “When you fast, do not become like the hypocrites, who are gloomy; for they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to fast” (Matt. VI).

For whoever seeks human glory by displaying his fasting does not fast for God but for human beings. They disfigure their faces who, through feigned sorrow, falsely present a devout expression to the eyes of the people. The teacher of heavenly discipline does not wish that what is commanded to be done for religion should be performed irreligiously; nor does he permit the labor of those who call upon him, for whom he prepares an eternal reward, to perish through the fault of fruitless ostentation.

“Do not become,” he says, “like the hypocrites, who are gloomy.” For if you are truly sad and sorrowful because you are fasting, you will reserve no grace for yourself with God, ungrateful as you are: although you perform a good work, you nevertheless unwillingly commit the perversity of a degenerate mind. But if, for the sake of some appearance of holiness, you pretend to be sad, you lose, by displaying your obedience, the entire fruit of the divine promise.

And if you offer your service to God, why, as one pursuing empty glory, do you display it to human beings who live under the same condition as you? Following this very judgment, the apostle Paul said: “Do not become desirous of empty glory” (Gal. VI). For whatever lacks the solidity of weight and virtue is empty and vain. Empty is whatever, fading away with the passing world, does not pass into eternal life; for whatever labor is expended for bodily honor slips away with corruptible flesh, as the prophet says: “All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass; the grass withered, and the flower fell; but the word of God remains forever” (Isa. XL).

Nor can we, dearly beloved, seek both the praise of a flattering world for one and the same work and acquire the reward of heavenly life. “But anoint,” he says, “your head when you fast, and wash your face.”

Every devout person truly anoints his head, whose religious fasting grows rich through the abundance of holy almsgiving. And if we think of something deeper, you anoint your head, which is Christ, if, joining better works to good works, you gladden him with simple devotion.

You will doubtless also wash your face and wipe it clean with every serenity of joy, if it does not become soiled by any affectation while you practice a more joyful worship of God. [Note: The same Laurentianus: “if it does not become soiled by any affectation of vanity.” Codices Casinensis and Martinensis: “but the word of the Lord.”]

Their face is unwashed who purchase worldly praise by the false sorrow of their eyes. [Note: Codex Vaticanus 1278: “For their countenance is exposed,” etc.; the Casinensis codices agree.] The Apostle marks them with his judgment, saying: “They consider godliness to be a source of gain” (1 Tim. VI). [Note: The same Vatican codex: “as the Apostle [says].” Codex Casinensis: “by affectation.”]

Yet although these things are so, the Lord does not reject those who mourn either their sins or the world. He said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V). [Note: So Codex Vaticanus 1278.]

The person is not reproved who, having previously strayed from the path of salvation with a wayward heart and slipping steps, tries to restore himself to God through the satisfaction of sorrowful repentance, as is read in the fiftieth psalm: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.” 106 God certainly does not despise holy sorrow; but he does not wish a servant of his to carry about sorrow that is artfully and deceitfully feigned. [Note: From Codex Laurentianus and the Vatican codices, Galesinius’s text is corrected, where it has “of one who serves.” An even better reading is found in Codex Martinensis: “artfully fashioned for himself as a servant,” etc.]

Of such people Christ says to his disciples: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI). What hope of faith, then, or what expectation of future recompense can there be for those who consume the entire reward of their works in the present age through ambition for the transient breeze of popular favor?

Therefore, brothers, preserve in all things an unoffending measure pleasing to God. Let there be among you pure fasting, simple mercy, and every sincere devotion, so that the reward of our God may accompany your holy life, perfected according to evangelical instruction.

## HOMILY XXXVII. On the Fast of Lent I

[Col. 0303]

### ADMONITION

It is sufficiently clear that this homily was delivered on the first Sunday of Lent, from the Gospel of Matthew, chapter IV, which Saint Maximus illustrates with exceptionally eloquent exposition. Nevertheless, none of the manuscript codices that attribute it to the holy bishop assigns it to that day; nearly all append the simple title: “On Lent.”

Among these are two codices: Vaticanus 1268, p. 57, and Vaticanus Palatinus 432, p. 76, which have: “Sermon of Saint Maximus, bishop, on Lent.” The same heading is used by Vallicellanus, vol. XI, p. 175; Novatiensis 27, p. 204; Laurentianus I, Plut. XIV, p. 109; Lucensis 85; Augiensis XIV; and Taurinensis, no. 17, Sermons on Lent.

Two Belgian codices differ from these, Martinensis and Camberonensis, which entitle the same homily: “On the Fast of Lent.” All the editors, accepting this title in preference to the others, gave it the first place among the homilies on Lent: Gymnicus, p. 72; Galesinius, p. 108; Combefisius, vol. II, p. 526; Cumdius, vol. I, p. 136; Raynaudus, p. 205; and Margarinus in Bibliotheca Maxima, vol. VI, p. 14.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0303B] After completing a forty-day fast, the devil attacked Christ in three ways, and the Lord won a threefold triumph over the evil enemy. By this example he admonished us concerning the weapons with which we ought to resist our hostile adversary.

You have heard, dearly beloved, as the evangelical trumpet has proclaimed, that our Lord and Redeemer resisted the devil’s temptations—resisting in words, but fighting in spirit. He engages in combat through speech, but completes the victory through majesty. [Note: The author cited above, On the Mystery of the Redemption of the Human Race, who treats in chapter 3 of the cause and origin of Christ’s temptation, uses this passage of Saint Maximus; he has: “Therefore, let us not think that this was without a great mystery.”]

Nor should we think that this conflict occurred without a great mystery, in which either the enraged devil bursts into words, [Note: Codex Laurentianus I, Plut. XIV: “bursts forth into words.”] or the Lord nevertheless deigns to answer his tempter with words. In all these things there is a plan for our salvation. The Savior hungers for us; he speaks for us. [Note: In the cited chapter 3 of On the Mystery, it reads: “he fought for us by speaking.”] We conquer in him because we are the reason for his struggle.

For who could doubt that the only-begotten Son of the Father, against whom no creature could prevail, entered into combat on behalf of those whose flesh he put on? The form of a human body therefore induced the most cunning enemy to come forth to battle, and the true Son of God confounded him with the answer of a true human being.

For this reason the wandering and uncertain tempter examines subtle and hesitant temptations. Although he contemplated in Christ the appearance of a fleshly man, he was nevertheless stirred by the presence of Christ’s divinity and suspected that he was more than a human being. The female birth encouraged him to undertake the encounter, but the virginity of the mother frightened him. For although Mary, certainly a daughter of Eve, had given birth to Christ, she had not conceived him from Adam.

When the enemy therefore saw the Son of God brought forth through such great miracles, he turned the matter over in himself and, as I suppose, said in astonishment: “Who is this who, without my knowing it, has entered this world? I know indeed that he was born from a woman, but I do not know from where he was conceived. Here stands his mother, but I cannot investigate his father. I see the birth, but I do not recognize the one being born. [Note: Codex Martinensis: “but I do not recognize him.”] And what adds to my astonishment is that, contrary to the customary law of giving birth, even after the Son of God has been delivered the mother rejoices as a virgin. [Note: Codex Vaticanus 1268: “after the Son of God has been delivered.”]

“Behold, a little child lies in a cradle; he drenches his face with tears and reveals himself to be like mortals through his cries. [Note: Codices Vaticanus and Martinensis: “and reveals himself to be like [mortals].”] And although he lacks nothing of infancy, there is nevertheless in him none of the corruption proper to an infant. Covered with rags, he appears filthy; yet heaven smiles upon him with the ray of a brighter star. Angels who minister to him hasten among the stars and the earth in his honor, and rejoicing they announce a novelty that I do not understand.

“What miracle is this? I see what I cannot comprehend; I hear what I cannot endure: a man born is honored as God. Never through the ages has this happened to me, that anyone should be born a human being and possess nothing of human fault. What is this birth, so new and powerful? Born among sinners and impious people, proceeding even from a mortal mother, he appears purer than all who are born and purer to me than heaven itself.

“No root of greed rises in him; no envy beats in his heart. His tongue knows no falsehood; his eyes admit no lust; no pleasure of the ears softens him. Luxury, through which I have subjected the human race to myself, certainly cannot penetrate his breast. There is no boastfulness in him, no [Note: The same Vatican codex and Codex Martinensis: “no softness.”] wickedness. And what more? I find nothing in him that delights me; he empties all my efforts. What shall I do? Where shall I turn?

“I sense that he is stronger. I think he wishes to reign in my kingdom—unless perhaps this is God, whom no offense can stain. But if he were God, how could he endure the indignities of a female birth? How could he be content with a cradle and swaddling clothes? Who could believe that the cries of infancy exist in God? Who would not find it ridiculous, if he did not hear it, that God is nourished by a woman’s milk?

“After all this, behold, he is hungry, although no reason at all would persuade us that God can be hungry.” [Note: The same Vatican codex: “persuades.”]

The devil was evidently unaware that Christ’s acceptance of the nourishment of infancy, and his hunger as a human being, were not signs of bodily weakness but a sacrament of heavenly grace. For the Son of God, whose eternity with the eternal Father is timeless, who reigns naturally with his begetter in an incorruptible dominion and is impassible, enacted in our flesh the saving mystery. For this reason he underwent the common suffering of mortals, so that by a human struggle he might triumph over the enemy of the human race.

Hence that presumptuous being, blinded by his own fury, said to the Lord: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matt. IV). His attempt was utterly foolish and empty: he wishes to tempt with bread the one who is bread, supposing that the one who voluntarily endured hunger was suffering from lack of food. [Note: The same codex: “For he wishes to tempt him through bread.”]

The Lord answered him: “It is written: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God’” (Deut. VIII). This means: “In vain, devil, are you again trying to trip me up through food. Let it be enough for you that by your persuasion Adam was deceived in paradise into eating forbidden foods. [Note: Codex Martinensis: “forbidden foods.”] Hunger does not conquer me, nor do I yield to your persuasions. [Note: Another reading: “I believe.”] The will of God is my food; the word of God is my perfect refreshment.” [Note: Codex Camberonensis: “is my [perfect refreshment].”]

Struck back by this reply, the devil again, as I suppose, said: “What is this? I see him hungry, yet I find no necessity of eating in him. [Note: Codex Camberonensis: “and I find no necessity in him [to eat].”] He suffers everything as a man and conquers everything as God. That Adam, certainly made by the hands of God, once yielded to my snares; this man, born from a woman, is swayed neither by his own necessities nor by my counsels. I overcame the former through the serpent’s mouth; this one despises even me while I am speaking.”

Again, when the Lord was standing on the pinnacle of the temple, he said to him: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (Matt. IV). [Note: The same codex adds: “he said.”] [Note: The same codex: “How disturbed he is when he says this, thinking that he can persuade him to plunge headlong.”]

How disturbed he is when he says this, thinking that he can persuade the one to plunge headlong from whom he could obtain nothing concerning the loaves. Christ answered him: “It is written: ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God’” (Deut. VIII). That is: “What you are proposing, devil, is the presumption of temptation, not a counsel of salvation; it is empty boastfulness, not an example of virtue. [Note: Another reading: “a counsel of holiness.”] For every miracle that does not produce a benefit for human salvation is vain. [Note: Another reading: “of holiness.”]

“After this answer of the Lord had frustrated him, he showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their honors, saying: ‘All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me’” (Matt. IV). He is again answered: “It is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’” (Deut. VIII).

That is: whoever worships you, demon, deserves not kingdoms but the infernal regions. For to worship the true God and serve him is the privilege of reigning. [Note: The same codex: “But you,” he says, “the honors of the world.”] But you, who promise the honors of the world in exchange for a sought-after transgression, should know that you cannot bestow a kingdom.

Behold, tempter: after three questions you have already accomplished nothing. Uncertain he came, more uncertain he departed; he attacked in order to test, and he left rejected.

Therefore now, dearly beloved brothers, since in recalling the victories of the fasting Lord we have recognized the triumph of our salvation, let us sanctify our fasts with devout observances. What else is it to sanctify a fast than to desire a holy purpose for fasting, to do what is just, and to avoid what is wicked?

That person sanctifies his fast whose heart is not turned from the straight path by the flattery of the powerful, by the favor of friends and relatives, or by the small and great gifts of clients. [Note: The same codex: “do not turn from the straight path.”] That person sanctifies his fast whose justice is not cheapened in his heart. [Note: The same codex: “whose justice is not cheapened by a price.”]

That person sanctifies the fast who extinguishes the flames of raging anger through the gentleness of a peaceful mind. That person sanctifies the fast who turns lustful eyes away from shameful sights with the reins of chastity. That person sanctifies the fast who scatters the darts of insults after repelling them with the shield of patience.

That person sanctifies the fast who restrains the tumult of quarrelsome people by the peaceful health of speech and the skill of a wiser tongue. That person sanctifies the fast who, like a cultivator of his own breast, cuts out the thorns of vain thoughts rising within him, plowing them with the evangelical plowshare.

That person sanctifies the fast who consoles the poverty of the needy, according to the measure of his means, through the humanity of a compassionate hand. Above all, that person sanctifies the fast who, attentive to the precepts of the divine law, rejects the devil’s temptations from his heart.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, if we wish to offer fasts pleasing to God, let us be strong in heart, [Note: The same codex: “let us be strong in faith.”] just in judgment, faithful in friendship, patient under injuries, moderate in disputes, avoiding foul speech, steadfast against wickedness, sober at banquets, simple in charity, cautious among the deceitful, compassionate toward the sorrowful, resistant to the defiant, sparing in suspicion, silent among slanderers, and equal among the humble.

If we wish to sanctify our fasts with virtues of this kind, then, by the Lord’s favor, we shall come to the festival of paschal grace and to the joys of heavenly promises with unwavering confidence and a more joyful conscience.

## HOMILY XXXVIII. On Lent II

[Col. 0307]

### ADMONITION

Here we depart from the customary order of the editors in order to place this homily among the earlier homilies on Lent. We are moved not so much by the authority of certain codices as by the internal character of the homily itself. For Saint Maximus discusses the fulfillment of the precept of the Lenten fast.

Indeed, the title of Codex Vaticanus 1278, p. 9, is as follows: “Sermon of Saint Maximus, bishop, on the first Sunday of Lent.” Another Vatican codex, 6452, p. 3, has: “Sermon of Saint Maximus, bishop, on the Sunday of Lent.”

As many other codices as there are, so many different inscriptions are found. Vaticanus 1268, p. 56, bears: “On the Fast of Lent.” Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme has: “Homily 39 on Holy Lent.” Two Modoetian codices have: “Sermon of blessed Maximus, bishop, during Lent.” Likewise Codex Bobiensis L + and Lucensis 85 have: “On the Sunday during Lent.” Vallicellanus, vol. II, p. 171, has: “Sermon of Saint Maximus on Lent.” Laurentianus I, Plut. XIV, p. 108 verso, has: “Sermon of Saint Maximus, as above”; and it precedes the homily on Ash Wednesday.

Codex CLIII of the Library of Saint Mark in Venice, p. 200, has: “Likewise, Sermon of Saint Maximus, bishop, on Lent.” Finally, the Taurinensis has: “Likewise, Sermon III on Lent.”

If the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur had not overlooked so many and such weighty manuscript authorities, they would certainly have pronounced a more assured judgment concerning this homily. Since, however, only three codices were available to them—one Remigianus and two German codices, which bore the name of Saint Maximus—they expressed their judgment about it hesitantly. See the edition of the works of Saint Ambrose, Paris, 1690, vol. II, p. 429, in the preface to sermon 28.

Accordingly, the title should be corrected in the older editions of the works of Saint Ambrose: Paris, 1569 and 1603, and Rome, 1590.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0307C] Maximus recounts the spiritual fruits of observing Lent: through it sins are forgiven, more vigorous devotion and firmer justice grow up, precisely as the earth, once bound by winter’s cold and frost, bursts forth more energetically into grasses and flowers when spring blows upon it and the snows have melted.

[Note: [Col. 0307D] Codex Bobiensis: “A few days ago.”] A few days ago, when preaching the devotion of the holy Quadragesima, we brought forward examples from the sacred writings by which we might prove that this number of forty [Note: [Col. 0307D] Codex Laurentianus I, Plut. XIV, mentioned above: “not instituted by human beings.” Codices Vaticanus 1278 and 99: “begun.” Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Codex Bobiensis [Col. 0308D] Vaticanus 1268: “appointed.”] was not established by human beings but consecrated by God; nor invented by earthly reasoning but commanded by heavenly majesty. And therefore the person who exceeds the appointed number by eating on a single day is accused not [Note: [Col. 0308D] In the same Codex 99 and in the Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, *ut* (“as”) is lacking.] as a violator of one day, but is charged as a transgressor of the whole Quadragesima. Hence [Col. 0308C] it is good for a person [Note: [Col. 0308D] Codex Laurentianus: “and also the day without labor,” etc. The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Vallicellanus I: “so as to reach the day.” Codex Bobiensis: “so as to complete the appointed number by the day.”] to fast the prescribed number without difficulty and likewise to attain the holiness of the whole Quadragesima. [111] These things, however, are not so much the commands of priests as of God. And therefore the person who despises them does not despise a priest but Christ, who speaks through his [Note: [Col. 0308D] The same codex: “who has spoken through his priest.”] priest.

Let us therefore see at what season the Lord imposed this observance upon us, if he did not perhaps wish all the elements to prosper through this devotion. For behold, [Note: [Col. 0308D] Codex Parisinus: “For behold, just as in the saying.”] with the Quadragesima imposed, the earth, bound by winter’s frost, is loosened, and the streams of the waters recover their channels when the ice has melted; so also at this same time the sins of our bodies, contracted through transgressions, are released, and the purer course of our life, when the devil’s rigidity has melted, recognizes its former channel. The earth, I say, when the Quadragesima is imposed, lays aside winter’s harshness, [Note: [Col. 0309C] Codex Vaticanus 1268: “but the body, when the Quadragesima is imposed, casts off the harshness of sins.” Codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “I cast off the harshness of sins.” Codex Bobiensis reads likewise.] and I, when the Quadragesima is imposed, abandon the harshness of my sins. That earth is split by ploughs so that it may be suitable for worldly crops; my earth is furrowed by fasts so that it may be fit for heavenly seeds. For just as the person who works a field by repeatedly troubling it receives a richer yield, [Note: [Col. 0309C] Codex Bobiensis: “so also he receives a greater [yield].”] so the person who works the field of his body by fasting more frequently receives greater grace.

For behold, during the season of abstinence the grass [Note: [Col. 0309C] Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “of the grain.”] of the crops revives into a harvest, the shoot of the tree strives toward becoming a shrub, and the vine-shoot of the vineyard matures into a bud; and everything rises from lower things to higher ones. So at this same time the hope of human beings, which had almost died, revives for the future, lost faith is restored to glory, temporal life advances toward eternal life, and the whole human race [Col. 0309B] rising toward heavenly things ascends from the lowest to the higher.

Now the farmer, carrying iron, prunes the vine-shoots. So now, too, the bishop, handling the Gospel, cuts away the filth of the peoples; and throughout this forty-day course all creatures are doing this, so that, after laying aside what is superfluous, they may proceed adorned and embellished at Easter. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Codex Bobiensis: “may go forth.”] Now everything is in labor, so that then [Note: [Col. 0309D] Codex Vaticanus Palatinus: “so that then they may be received into,” etc.] it may be found in fruit. Then, contrary to nature’s pattern, the thorn produces a rose; [Note: [Col. 0309D] Codex Bobiensis: “the reed gives off fragrance, the lily exhales sweetness, dry shrubs put forth [flowers], and thus everything [is adorned] with blossoms.”] the reed perfumes the lily, and dry shrubs bring forth sweetness. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Codex Laurentianus, and likewise Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “and thus everything [is adorned] with blossoms.”] Thus all things are adorned with flowers, [112] so that creation itself may be thought to celebrate the festival of the great day by its own splendor. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Codex Bobiensis: “of the great God, for the great day.”] [Note: [Col. 0309D] Codex Vaticanus Palatinus: “So let us also.”]

Therefore let us also, during this same season of fasts, bring forth roses from our thorns—that is, justice from sins, mercy from severity, [Col. 0309C] generosity from avarice. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Codices 90 and 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “These.”] For the thorns of our body are those things that choke the soul, concerning which Scripture says: “It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3). My earth produces thorns for me if it pricks me with the distress [Note: [Col. 0310C] Codex Bobiensis: “with the titillation” instead of “with the distress.”] of bodily lust. It produces thistles for me when it torments me with desire for worldly riches. For avarice is the root of its own thorn in a Christian; ambition for honor is a thorn in a good man. Such things appear pleasing in form to their own people, but they cause injury.

Unless we keep watch and fast, therefore, we cannot rid ourselves of these things; indeed, through abstinence the thorns themselves will be turned [Note: [Col. 0310C] Codex Vaticanus and Codex Bobiensis: “into roses.”] into roses. For through fasting lust produces chastity, pride produces humility, and sobriety produces moderation. These are the flowers of our life: they give off a sweet fragrance to Christ and breathe a good odor toward God. Hence the Apostle says: “For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (1 Cor. 2).

The Lord has therefore granted us this Quadragesima so that during this period, after the manner of all creation, we may now conceive the shoots of virtues, [Note: [Col. 0310C] Codex Bobiensis: “desire.”] in order that on Easter day we may bring forth the fruit of justice. In this number of forty days [Note: [Col. 0310C] Codex 99 adds “Christ.” Codex 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “the Lord Christ himself exercised himself.” Codex Bobiensis: “the Lord Christ himself exercised himself.”] the Lord himself exercised himself, not so that he might gain progress, but so that he might show us the progress of salvation. [Col. 0310B] For there was no thorn of sin in him to be turned into a flower; he himself was the flower born not from a thorn but from a branch, as the prophet says: “A branch shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11). [Note: [Col. 0310D] Codex Vaticanus Palatinus: “A branch shall arise.”] For Mary was the branch—bright, delicate, and virgin—who brought forth Christ as a flower through the integrity of her body.

After forty continuous days [Note: [Col. 0310D] The Vatican, Laurentian, and Vallicellanus codices add “and nights.”] the Lord arranged these fasts, not because he was hungry; yet the evangelist says that he became hungry afterward (Matt. 4). How, then, can it be that one who did not feel hunger or thirst for so many days afterward became hungry? He was plainly hungry, and we cannot deny that he was hungry; for he hungered not for human food but for salvation. Nor did he desire the feasts of worldly foods, but he desired the heavenly holiness of souls. [113] The food of Christ is the redemption of peoples; the food of Christ is the accomplishment of the Father’s will, as he himself says: “My food is to do the will of the Father who sent me” (John 4). Therefore let us also [114] hunger for food—not food prepared for earthly banquets, but food gathered by reading the divine Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 0310D] Codex 432 Vaticanus Palatinus: “For that.”] The former nourishes the body for a time, [Note: [Col. 0310D] In the codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Bobiensis: “but this.”] but the latter refreshes the soul forever. [Note: [Col. 0310D] Codex Vaticanus Palatinus adds: “through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”] Explicit.

**Homily XXXIX. Also on the Quadragesima III**

[Col. 0309]

**ADMONITION**

The three following homilies were published by the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur among the Ambrosian sermons, Paris, 1690, nos. 19, 20, and 21. From their remarks we gather two principal points: first, that they greatly doubted whether these homilies should be attributed to Saint Ambrose; second, that they said all three had flowed from the same source. They display a uniform style, and the same theme proposed in the first homily is embellished by fuller exposition in the two remaining ones. They are so interconnected that the second homily refers to the first, and the third to the second.

But by what evidence shall we prove Saint Maximus to be the author? We admit that we found only three codices that attribute this first homily to our holy bishop: Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, *Homily 17, On the Holy Quadragesima*; Codex Laurentianus X, Plut. XIV, p. 244; and the Taurinensis, with the title: “Also a sermon on the Quadragesima XX.” Among so many and such extensive Vatican codices, this homily occurred to us only in Codex 1268, p. 36 verso, in which the copyist, expressing doubt, wrote the title: “On the same fast, as is thought, of Ambrose.” And rightly was he doubtful, since codices are exceedingly rare that contain this homily and the two following ones, so that even the Benedictine editors themselves make no mention of any manuscript codex.

Alongside the testimonies supporting Maximus, weighty conjectures may be added. One is the similarity of style to the preceding homily; another is the deliberate connection among the homilies themselves, which is characteristic of Maximus, as Remigius Ceillier observed; a third is that several codices confirm the final of these homilies. We publish these three homilies as they appear in the Paris edition of the works of Saint Ambrose, 1569.

**ARGUMENT.—** [Col. 0311A] The reason is given to the faithful of Christ who are about to undertake the quadragesimal fast why the command to fast was imposed for this number of days; from this the origin of ecclesiastical law and the observance handed down by the forefathers may be recognized.

We have frequently set forth the meaning of the holy Quadragesima, whose beginning we celebrate today, and we have often taught [Note: [Col. 0311C] Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “why [we fast] for the number of so many days.”] why we fast for this number of days. For we have said that the Lord Jesus Christ consecrated this same number of fasting and, taking no food for continuous days and nights, made one single body of fasting; that is, although the succession of day was interrupted by the arrival of night, the succession of the fast was nevertheless not interrupted.

Thus there were many periods of time with him, but one day of abstinence, showing us that we ought to fast this number in its entirety. Since we cannot complete the whole Quadragesima in one solid and single fast, we should celebrate it through daily fasts without interruption, so that if anyone lets one day pass without abstaining, he may violate the whole Quadragesima and, because of food taken for a brief time, lose the fruit of great labor. [Note: [Col. 0311C] Codex Vaticanus 1268: “so that if anyone omits one day.”]

But someone may say: “We have heard the meaning of the Quadragesima on several occasions, and we have frequently heard that it was consecrated by the Lord; but we eagerly wish to hear why this same Quadragesima has forty [Note: [Col. 0311C] Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem adds *et* (“and”).] two days.”

We read in the Old Testament (Deut. 48) that when holy Moses rescued the children of Israel from the yoke of Egyptian captivity in order to lead them into the promised land, he reached that land by encampments over forty-two days, [Col. 0311C] and possessed the promises for as many periods of time as we rejoice to enjoy the promises made to us by the Savior. In the same number, I say, Moses reached rest through his encampments, just as we hasten toward heaven through fasts.

For our fasts are certain encampments through which, traveling spiritually, we walk by means of the virtues of the soul and by daily progress become nearer to the land promised to us, [Col. 0312A] so that the more devoutly one fasts, the more quickly [115] one arrives. Faith and fasting are swift feet of the soul; they quickly climb from lowly things to higher ones and quickly travel from earthly things to heavenly things. Concerning these feet the Apostle says: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim good things” (Rom. 10). The Lord commanded that these feet be washed, as the Apostle says concerning the widow: “If she has washed the feet of the saints” (1 Tim. 5). Worthy of honor are the feet of those who proclaim peace; spiritual and clean, they walk over the hearts of human beings with their teaching.

The people of Israel also reached the streams of the Jordan in the number of forty-two days. [Note: [Col. 0311D] Codex 99 reads: “in the course of those same days.” The Vaticanus reads: “in that same cycle of days.”] In the same cycle of days the Christian people reach the waters of baptism. And as the prophet says: “The Jordan turned back” (Ps. 113), [Note: [Col. 0311D] In the same Codex 99: “There, when the Israelite people entered the river’s waters, the wave withdrew beneath them; now, when …”] there, when the Israelite enters the river’s water, the wave flows on; here, when the Christian descends [Col. 0312B] into the font, the sins of his crimes flee away.

And it is wonderful: there the river, turned backward, returns to its source; [Note: [Col. 0312C] Codex Vaticanus: “is turned back.”] here the human being, recalled to his origin, is restored to the infancy of his beginning. There the wave seeks the spring from which it had emerged; [Note: [Col. 0312C] Codex Vaticanus: “from which the wave had gone forth.”] here innocence recognizes the human being from whom it had departed. There the riverbed is emptied of its waves; here hearts are emptied of crimes, so that there muddy water does not wet God’s servants, while here a filthy conscience does not defile God’s servants. [Note: [Col. 0312C] The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “so that there muddy water does not wet God’s servants, while here an earthly conscience does not defile Christ’s servants.” The same appears in Codex Vaticanus 1268.]

The Jordan is, in a certain sense, the font of the washing, through which the person who crosses, leaving behind his filth, enters the promised paradise.

In this number of forty-two, therefore, the people of Israel, leaving Egypt, crossed the waters of the Red Sea; and we too, in this same number, leaving the Egypt of the world, cross the pools of burning Gehenna. [116] [Note: [Col. 0312D] The same is read in Codex 99: “The wave supports them in the waters; the flame does not burn us in the fires; for them it becomes solid,” etc. The same also appears in Vaticanus 1268.] For them the water becomes solid; for us the fire is cooled. And, contrary to nature’s order, the sea is dried up by heat, while through the font of baptism Gehenna is made mild.

In this mystical number, I say, when the children of Israel came to Marah, they could not drink the water because of its bitterness. The spring had water but no sweetness; it was pleasing to the sight but not pure in taste. When Moses cast wood into it, [Note: [Col. 0313C] Codices 99 and Vaticanus 1268: “They drank sweet water with delight; for the sacramental meaning of the wood removed the harshness that the harmful water carried.”] they drank its sweetness with delight. The sacramental meaning of the wood removed the harshness carried by the harmful water.

I think this was done as a figure. I think that the bitter water in Marah signifies the law of the Old Testament, which, before it was tempered by the Lord’s cross, was harsh. For it commanded that an eye be given for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, and, being austere, offered no refreshment of mercy. But when it was tempered by the wood of the evangelical Passion, it immediately exchanged its bitterness for sweetness and showed itself sweet for all to drink, as the prophet says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118)!

Sweet are the words that command: “If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also; if anyone takes away your tunic, leave him your cloak as well” (Matt. 5; Luke 6). This, then, is the bitterness that was exchanged for sweetness: the harshness of the law was tempered by the grace of the Gospel. For the letter of the law without the mystery of the cross is bitter; concerning it the Apostle says: “The letter kills” (1 Cor. 3). [Note: [Col. 0313C] Codices Vaticanus and 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “But when the mysteries of the Passion are joined to it.”] But when the mysteries of the Passion are joined to it, all its bitterness is spiritually seasoned; and concerning it the Apostle says: “But the Spirit gives life” (ibid.).

**Homily XL. Also on the Quadragesima IV**

[Col. 0313]

**ADMONITION**

[117] I understand that this homily is attributed to no author in certain codices, such as Vaticanus 6452, Basilica of Saint Peter, shelfmark G, and the Urbevetanus; but in others it is inscribed to Saint Ambrose. Yet in more numerous manuscripts I see that it was copied under the same title as the preceding homily and bears the name of Saint Maximus. In the Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem it is announced under this title: “Homily XXXII on the fasts at the beginning of the Quadragesima”; in the Sangallensis: “Also the following, namely LVIII, on the Quadragesima”; in the Taurinensis: “Also a sermon on the Quadragesima XX”; in Santa Croce in Jerusalem 99, Homily 19; and in Laurentianus X, Plut. XIV, it is likewise entitled “On the Quadragesima.” It is published third by the monks of Saint-Maur among the sermons of Ambrose, but by us, who have followed the old editions and manuscript codices, second.

**ARGUMENT.—** [Col. 0313B] After speaking at length about the benefits of abstinence, Saint Maximus urges his hearers to observe the quadragesimal fast carefully.

I believe that you have understood, brothers, why I compared these fasts of ours to those encampments in which the people of Israel, as though stationed in a military camp, overcame King Pharaoh by daily labor and defended themselves from their enemies as though from certain camps of encampments, so that whoever [Note: [Col. 0313D] Codices 6452, Vaticanus, and Urbevetanus: “did not complete the number of daily stations from that company.” Codex Saint Peter 105 C: “did not complete the distances of the daily station from that company.”] failed to complete the distances of the daily station from that company of travelers was either seized by Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 0313D] Codex Urbevetanus: “was occupied by him, or was overtaken by solitude.”] or overtaken by solitude.

So we too ought to complete with every effort the journey of forty days set before us and fortify ourselves, as with certain camps, by devotion to fasting. For our fasts are camps, [Col. 0313C] which defend us from the devil’s assault. Indeed, they are called “stations” because, standing and remaining in them, [Note: [Col. 0313D] Codex Laurentianus X: “we repel the ambushes of enemies in them.” Codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, Vaticanus, and Saint Peter: “for they are camps.”] we repel enemies lying in ambush.

Fasts are plainly camps for Christians. If anyone strays from them, he is attacked by the spiritual Pharaoh or devoured by the solitude of sins. The solitude of sins is suffered by the person who is abandoned by the fellowship of the saints.

Fasting is therefore a kind of wall for a Christian—unassailable by the devil and impossible for the enemy to cross. For who among Christians has ever fasted and [118] been captured? Who has remained sober [Note: [Col. 0314C] Codices 99, Vaticanus, and the cited Saint Peter codex: “and been defeated.”] and been defeated? The devil attacks the drunken; the enemy assaults the lustful. [Note: [Col. 0314C] Codex Laurentianus: “But when he sees fasting, he flees, fears, and is terrified; he is frightened by its pallor, weakened by hunger, and struck down by weakness. ‘Struck down,’ etc. The same also appears in Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, Vaticanus, and Saint Peter, though the latter reads *viderit* (“has seen”) instead of *videt* (“sees”).] But when he sees fasting, he is struck down by hunger and weakness. He is struck down, I say, by weakness, because Christian weakness is strength. Hence the Apostle says: “When I am weak, then I am stronger” (2 Cor. 12).

But someone asks how weakness can be strong. Weakness is strong when the flesh wastes away through fasts and the soul grows rich through purity. For as much nourishment is withdrawn from the flesh, so much is the power of justice increased in the soul. Then the human being is indeed weak [Note: [Col. 0314D] Vaticanus 6454, Saint Peter, and Urbevetanus: “for worldly works, but strong for divine works. Then he thinks more of God, then he fears judgment, then he conquers the enemy.”] for worldly matters, but strong for divine works. Then he thinks more of God, fears judgment, and conquers the enemy.

For the Savior says concerning the devil: “This kind is not driven out except by fasting and prayers” (Matt. 17). He says, of course, that a person possessed by the devil can be cleansed only through fasts.

See, therefore, what power fasting has: what grace it grants to the person who practices it, since it provides so great a remedy for another; how it sanctifies its own practitioner, since it thus purifies another. It is a marvelous thing: one person fasts, and the benefit of the one who fasts helps another.

Therefore, brothers, let us not lay down the weapons of abstinence, but let us carefully complete the fasts of forty days without interruption. For this is the perfect number for conquering. After the Lord had fasted forty days, he conquered the devil, [119] [Note: [Col. 0315C] Codex Vaticanus 6452: “not because he could not conquer him even before the fasts,” etc.] not because he could not have conquered him even before the fasts, but so that he might show us that we can then be conquerors of the devil when, by fasting for forty days, we have become conquerors of carnal desires; [Note: [Col. 0315C] The same codex: “while the person who violates this number.”] whereas the person who violated this consecrated number through gluttonous excess could easily be overcome by the enemy as weak and wretched.

For how can a person conquer the devil’s wickedness in another who does not conquer gluttonous excess in himself? [Note: [Col. 0315D] Codex 99: “first” instead of “earlier.”] Let a person therefore first be victor over himself, so that he may be able to be victor over another. For there are within you enemies of your own, who attack you daily. Behold, avarice surrounds you with ambition for riches, lust captivates you with the sweetness of banquets, and heresy [Col. 0315B] perverts you through the falsity [Note: [Col. 0315D] Codices Laurentianus, 99 of Santa Croce, Vaticanus 6452, Saint Peter, and Urbevetanus: “heresy perverts through the falsity of knowledge,” etc.] of knowledge. Conquer your own enemies, therefore, so that you may be able to conquer those of another.

For it is no slight sin, brothers, not to fast during the Quadragesima imposed by the Lord upon the faithful and to dissolve the consecrated fasts through the voracity of the belly. It is written: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought to walk just as he walked” (1 John 2). If you wish to be a Christian, you must do what Christ did. He who had no sin fasted the Quadragesima; you, who sin, do not wish to fast the Quadragesima. He, I say, had no sin, but fasted for our sins.

What sort of Christian are you, then, in your conscience, when Christ is hungry for you and you dine? When the Savior fasts for you, [Note: [Col. 0316C] The same Vaticanus and Saint Peter codices: “you refresh yourself.”] you refresh yourself? Therefore, as I said, it is no slight sin to violate the fast imposed.

To demonstrate this briefly by examples, we read in the Books [Note: [Col. 0316C] Codices Saint Peter and the cited Vaticanus: “of Kings” instead of “of the Kings.”] of Kings that when Saul, king of Israel, was waging war against the Philistines, he imposed a fast upon his entire army; and while all were abstaining, he began to fight against his adversaries (1 Sam. 14:24 ff.). A good king indeed, who conquered his enemies not so much by arms as by devotion, and fought more by religion [120] than by weapons.

When Saul had imposed the day’s abstinence upon all his men, his son Jonathan, unaware of the command, moved victoriously through the midst of the enemy lines and tasted a honeycomb with the tip of his scepter dipped into it. Such indignation was suddenly aroused that both victory was delayed and the Divinity was offended. In the end, neither was the battle brought to completion nor was a prophetic response given to the king.

From this we understand that Saul overcame his enemies not so much by the soldiers’ valor as by the soldiers’ abstinence. Indeed, because of one person’s fault, cowardice was attributed to all, and because of one person’s offense, weakness arose in everyone. For strength fails in an army when fasting fails in its observance. When Saul recognized this sin through the very offense against the Divinity, he immediately [Col. 0316B] told Jonathan that he should not be spared, but that the sin committed should be expiated by the shedding of his blood.

See how great the religious observance of King Saul was: he even wished to appease the offended God by parricide; and see how serious is the guilt of a broken fast, which is punished only by the shedding of blood. Although Jonathan, unaware that his father had imposed the fast, was condemned to death because he broke it, what does the person deserve who knowingly breaks the fast imposed by Christ?

Therefore, brothers, let us guard the fast established for us with every observance, so that we may conquer our spiritual and bodily enemies. For, as you know, we have bodily enemies. Let us fast, then, so that our army and Saul may overcome and [Note: [Col. 0316D] Codex Laurentianus: “may obtain; and, being placed in abstinence, let us not turn aside toward the honeycomb. The same appears in the Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, to which the Vatican codex agrees, except for the word *obtineat*; it reads *obtinet* (“obtains”).] obtain victory over them. For the honeycomb is, in a certain sense, the pleasure—or the vices—of the world, which, as it is written, fatten the throat for a time, but their end is more bitter than gall (Prov. 5). [Note: [Col. 0316D] From Codex Vaticanus 6452.]

Let us therefore pray that, while we fast, the Lord may grant us that spiritual honeycomb which, in eternal blessedness, becomes sweet upon the palate of the soul’s throat. With his help, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

**Homily XLI. Also on the Quadragesima V**

[Col. 0315]

**ADMONITION**

[121] Although this homily is closely connected with the two preceding homilies, the scribes of the codices nevertheless disagree among themselves. Some, as in Vaticanus 4652, inscribe the name of Saint Leo the Great; others, as in Laurentianus I, Plut. XIV, p. 112 verso, that of Saint Ambrose; but more numerous manuscripts, such as the Sangallensis, Homily 59, “On the Quadragesima,” Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, and the Taurinensis, Sermon 21, assign it to Saint Maximus.

It is not counted among Saint Leo’s sermons by the Ballerini, who most diligently prepared the latest edition of his works, nor is it attributed without hesitation to Saint Ambrose by the monks of Saint-Maur. Therefore we shall never assert that it is not Maximus’s unless, on the authority of ancient codices and documentary evidence, it is shown that Leo, Ambrose, or someone else was the author of this homily.

We wish to inform our readers that the sermon dealing with the bitter water that Moses made sweet is included by the Benedictine monks of Saint-Maur in the appendix to the works of Saint Augustine under no. 25, because it is read in Origen’s *Homily 7 on Exodus* in almost the same words. Yet you will find nothing similar in this homily of Saint Maximus if you attend to Augustine’s words, which we reproduce on the following page.

**ARGUMENT.—** [Col. 0317A] Saint Maximus again teaches that the Quadragesima was prefigured by the forty-two encampments of the people of Israel in the wilderness, who advanced not only with bodily steps but also through religious actions.

Your memories still retain, brothers, that we preached last Sunday [Note: [Col. 0317C] Codex Vaticanus 6450: “previously.”] that the forty-two encampments were a figure of our Quadragesima, through which the people of Israel, departing from Egypt, entered the promised land by daily progress and, as though by certain steps of salvation, ascended to the kingdom after the yoke of slavery (Num. 33:3 ff.).

Those encampments, I say, were a figure of our fasts not only in the quantity of their number but also in the observance of virtues. For the children of Israel did not walk through the wilderness on bodily steps as much as they advanced on the Lord’s way through religious actions. They plainly walked on the Lord’s way, which gave them drink from the waters and fed them from heaven. [Note: [Col. 0317C] Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “which both carried them through the waters and fed them,” etc.]

For when they were hungry in the wilderness, manna was not lacking; when they were in danger at sea, the land did not flee from them. There the sea [Note: [Col. 0317C] Codex 99 reads: “on the path.”] was spread out as a path; here heaven was provided as food. For the sake of the grace granted to God’s servants, the Jordan holds back its streams. It changes its water into myrrh. [Note: [Col. 0317C] Codex Vaticanus 6450: “Marah.”] There, the wave that had been following, when turned backward, goes before; here, the stream that had been trickling bitterness, tempered for the better, becomes sweet. [Note: [Col. 0317C] Codex Vaticanus 6450: “the stream that was dripping bitter poison becomes sweet.”] And, wonderfully, [122] the river lost its course, while the spring lost its taste.

But since we said that the children of Israel, coming to Marah, suffered from the bitterness of the water and could drink it only after wood had been cast into it, let us also see that a figure of the Old Testament was present in it, to which the people themselves, proceeding thenceforth, came [Note: [Col. 0318C] Codex Vaticanus 6450: “at Marah.”]. [Note: [Col. 0317C] In the Vulgate, Exodus 15 reads: “Moses led Israel from the Red Sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur. They traveled for three days through the wilderness and found no water. And they came to Marah, but they could not drink the waters of Marah because they were bitter … But he cried to the Lord, who showed him a piece of wood; and when he had cast it into the waters, they were changed into sweetness,” etc.

Saint Augustine, *Book II of Questions on Exodus*, has: “They came, but they could not drink from Merra, for it was bitter.”

Then, explaining the words “And the Lord showed him a piece of wood,” etc., he says: “Was it a kind of wood possessing this power? Or could God, who performed such great wonders, do this with any wood? Yet this seems to signify what is said: He showed it to him, as though it were already a sign by which this could be done—unless perhaps it was a place where no wood at all could be found, so that the very fact that the Lord showed him wood where none existed was itself a sign of divine assistance; and through the wood he made the waters sweet, prefiguring the glory and grace of the cross. But even in such a nature of the wood, who but the Creator and the one who showed it should be praised?

Dionysius Carthusianus, in his *Commentary on Exodus*, article 32, calls that river Marath and notes that in the bitterness of its waters were figured the temptations and illnesses by which the just are tested by God; these nevertheless become sweet not so much through meditation as through the power of Christ’s Passion and cross. He also cites Augustine interpreting this passage in this way.”]

He came to a place called [Note: [Col. 0318C] Vatican Codex 6450: Elim], where there were twelve exceedingly pure springs and a multitude of seventy flourishing palm trees. See the mystery of God: how, after the bitterness of the Law, the streams of evangelical mercy overflow. There one single spring is harsh for drinking; here there are many, all sweet for drinking. There, after weariness, there is no refreshment; here, after labor, there are relief and victory. For springs are provided for the thirsty, and palms are offered to the victorious. Palms, I say, are offered to the victorious, because to have reached the grace of the Gospel after the harshness of the Law is to have conquered. For it is a kind of victor’s prize to moisten the mouth at a living spring and to arm the right hand with a triumphant palm. Through the spring, the tongue of confession is purified; through the palm, the martyr’s right hand is honored. The former, because it exalted the glory of Christ; the latter, because it refused the altar of sacrilege. The palm of martyrdom is a kind of prize, for it grants sweet fruit to the confessing tongue and provides glorious adornment for the victorious right hand. The palm is plainly sweet food for martyrs, shady rest, honorable triumph, ever green, ever clothed with leaves, ever ready for victory; and therefore the palm does not wither, because the glory of martyrs does not wither.

[Note: [Col. 0318C] Likewise in the Vatican manuscript: “Finally, the palms are offered by the apostles to the Lord, seated upon the ass and coming to the Temple. For when the apostles, etc.”]

Finally, the palms are offered by the people to the Lord, seated upon the ass and coming to the Temple. When the disciples spread their garments and fortified Christ’s path with their clothing [Note: [Col. 0318C] Codices 99 and Vatican 6450: “with the garments of Christ”], devotion of the people had no greater offering for him than palms. This signified that, with garments spread along the road, the way in the world was undefiled, and that, with palms offered, he himself was the victor of the world. He, I say, is the victor of whom Scripture says: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. 5); he is plainly the victor who destroyed the devil’s death and illumined eternal life. Therefore palms are raised up for Christ as he comes. It is written: “The righteous shall flourish like the palm” (Ps. 91). Rightly, then, the banners of righteousness are raised for the righteous one who comes, and the titles of their triumphs render homage to their author.

Before the palms are taken up, however, the Lord’s path as far as the Temple is covered with the disciples’ garments; and, so that the Savior’s path may be undefiled, it is fortified with the apostles’ clothing. Consider that this was done as a mystery. For Christ’s way, which leads to the Temple, is his faith and teaching. Therefore the disciples, so that we might walk this way without stumbling, stripped off the garments of their own bodies and spread them out through their martyrdom, so that amid the crowds of the various nations they might lay down the garments of their limbs upon the path of righteousness, cover the muddy mire [Note: [Col. 0319D] Another reading: “pit”] of the world, and display the Savior’s undefiled way.

After the myrrh, therefore, the people of Israel came to the twelve springs [Note: [Col. 0319D] Vatican Codex 6450: “Merra”]. We read in the prophet: “Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel” (Ps. 67). The Lord is Christ, who is learned only through the mouths of the apostles and the teaching of the disciples. The apostles are to be called springs, because, like exceedingly pure springs [Note: [Col. 0319D] Codex 99: “all exceedingly pure springs”], they overflow with the grace of preaching, and after the bitterness of the Law the abundant wisdom of their channels lets fall the sweet draughts of the mystery. Nor is it surprising that the drink of the springs is sweet, when in their bosom the food of the palms is sweeter.

The apostles, therefore, are the springs that watered the face of the whole earth with the river of their teaching and offered the drink of the divine mystery to peoples wearied by their labors. The seventy palms generated beside the apostolic springs—I would say that they signify those seventy disciples who, second in rank after the apostles, are sent by the Lord for the salvation of humanity. The evangelist Luke (chapter 10), describing them, says that they were sent two by two. These, truly like palms, return with rejoicing after their labors for humanity and glory in the presence of the Lord that even the demons are subject to them. Rightly, therefore, they are compared with palms: by the prize of palms they became victors over the devil.

## HOMILY XLII. Also, On Lent VI

[Col. 0319]

### NOTICE

I return to the series of the homilies of Saint Maximus published in print. This homily is found in six manuscripts with the following inscription: “Sermon of Saint Maximus on Lent.” It appears in two Vatican manuscripts—that is, 1268, folio 81 verso, and Palatine 433, folio 390—in Laurentian I, Pluteus XIV, folio 110 verso, in the Turin manuscript, sermon 16, in the Aunensis XIV, and in Lucensis 85. For this reason it is counted among the homilies of Saint Maximus by Gymnicus, page 79; Galesinius, page 110; Combefisius, volume II, page 528; Cumdius, volume II, page 137; Raynaudus, page 206; and Margarini, in *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, page 15. What more? Is it not sufficiently clear from the very manner of composition that Saint Maximus is its author?

### SUMMARY

The devil is introduced testing, by his evil stratagems, whether Christ is truly God. With Christ’s help we can conquer the devil. We must fast from vices in order properly to celebrate the days of Lent.

That remarkable conflict which, as the reading from the holy Gospel just completed has testified to your ears, took place between the King of heaven and the tyrant of the heavenly kingdom, resounds to us as the triumphant mystery of the Lord’s incarnation. For the almighty Lord, moved by an ineffable affection of mercy and pitying the human race in its captivity, while also wishing to remove the devil’s power from the world [Note: [Col. 0320D] Laurentian Codex: “to remove it now by his own [power], etc.”], sent his only-begotten Son—not degenerate in divinity, not unlike in power, not discordant in will. Taking our flesh upon himself, and rejecting the old condition of birth, he was born as a new Son from a woman by a new law of incorrupt bodily birth, so that, even if the devil should presume to tempt this saving man, taken up into fellowship with divinity, he would be unable to overcome him.

And so, when that savage lion saw the Lamb of God hungry after a very long and continuous fast of forty days and nights, and did not believe that the hungry one was God, he attacked him by the art of a most cunning temptation, saying: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matt. 4). The craftsman of so great a deceit was, I suppose, thinking and saying to himself: “If this is the one at whose command manna flowed from heaven for the people hungry in the desert (Exod. 16); if he is the one whom I know to have brought forth streams from the rock (Exod. 17), he will now be able to transform stones into bread, even if not at my request, nevertheless from his own need, since he is hungry. If he does so, I shall prove him to be God; if he is unable, I shall detect him as a man.”

The devil was therefore waiting for bread, which he was trying not so much to obtain for himself as to take away from the world. But the Lord of all things, who could also make bread from a stone, and who did not wish the mystery of human salvation to become clear to the one testing him, so regulated his reply in his holy mouth that neither he, who was the truth, would speak falsehood, nor would the one who was a liar from the beginning be able to recognize the truth that he would not believe. The Lord therefore said: “It is written: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God’” (Deut. 8).

The tempter received an answer from the Law that he could not contradict; he did not receive the bread that he had requested, not from the custom of eating but through the fraud of deception. For why would the Son of God need human bread, when every substance was his own in divinity? Or by what reasoning would Christ make earthly bread from a stone (John 6), when he himself, as we read (Matt. 21), was both spiritual bread and a stone?

Thus mocked and derided, the tempter undertakes another engine of temptation. For when the Lord was standing secretly, according to his hidden plan, upon the pinnacle of the Temple [Note: [Col. 0319D] Maximus is silent about Christ’s being transported above the Temple pinnacle, which the evangelists mention. He presupposes this and explains only the devil’s crafty request, as he had proposed, while highly praising Christ’s reply, full of divine wisdom], the devil said to him: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” How foolish and exceedingly perverse was this persuasion, that he should say to the Son of God, “Throw yourself down”! Would he not have spoken more appropriately by saying, “If you are the Son of God, ascend into heaven” [Note: [Col. 0321D] Vatican Codex 1268: “ascend to heaven”]? If the Lord had done that, he would truly have proved him to be the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0321D] “and would have proved him truly to be the Son of God,” in the same manuscript].

But the enemy of heaven, even while tempting, does not wish to suggest a heavenly ascent; he urges downward and toward the depths, because he desires everyone to fall, having realized that he himself fell before all others. Blind, he does not understand that he is trying to persuade the one to fall who not only cannot fall but came to restore the ruins of those who had fallen. For the Lord, as it is written, “raises up those who are bowed down; the Lord loosens those who are bound” (Ps. 145).

He therefore came not to be deceived but to save those who had been deceived. He nullifies the tester’s art by a response of such carefully measured wisdom that the dark enemy not only cannot see the mystery set forth for our sake, but, more and more ensnared by the Lord’s answers, is bewildered by an even darker uncertainty. For the invincible warrior of the spiritual battle said to him: “It is written: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test’” (Ps. 145).

How simple is the wisdom in this answer, and how watchful the simplicity, by which the truth is neither concealed nor can the reprobate test what is true. Truly, as it is written: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1). The devil hears that God must not be tested, yet he does not recognize that the one whom he is testing is both God and man. He sees Christ at once answering in the manner of a man and being able to do what belongs to God.

But these things are not enough for his wickedness; he weaves the snares of a third temptation. “He led him,” it says, “onto a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their honors, saying: ‘All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.’” Pay close attention, brothers, because everything the enemy persuades one to do is a falling. Truly everyone who worships the devil falls; and truly he falls who, with the enemy promising, pursues the powers and honors of the world by sacrilegious arts.

But our Lord and Savior confounded him with his customary reply, saying: “Go away, Satan; for it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’” The testimonies of the holy Scriptures are brought against him, not to instruct one who cannot be converted, but to refute one who is shameless.

[Note: [Col. 0321D] Vatican Codex 433 and Regius add: “Christ commands him to depart behind him, so that the most stubborn enemy, now deprived of the freedom to speak, may feel the power of one whose will he cannot recognize.”]

Christ orders him, who would give the kingdoms of the world, to go behind him, so that he might submit unwillingly to the authority of the Son of God, to whom he would not yield voluntarily, and so that he might acknowledge that the one whom he wickedly demanded should worship him deserved to be worshiped by all. And what more, dearest ones? While the tempter spoke abominable things and presumptuously demanded what was not permitted, he fell silent as though defeated by a man and departed as though commanded by God.

It was necessary that he withdraw from the temptation of the one against whom he had moved with his whole mass and exerted all his strength, yet could not find even a trace of his own will. He was astonished and amazed, after so many ages, to have found a man without human desires, born in the flesh yet possessing absolutely nothing of carnal corruption.

When the devil had therefore withdrawn, the angels came and ministered to him, as we read. The angels’ service teaches us how great was the glory of this triumph. Nor is it surprising that his angels came to meet him in their ministries [Note: [Col. 0322D] Laurentian manuscript: “the angels came to meet him in their ministries,” because they marveled at his victory], since they marveled at his victory.

Therefore, brothers, if we do not wish to be overcome by the devil, let us cling to the one who triumphed over the devil. To cling to Christ is to believe both that he possesses the nature of the Father’s divinity and that he truly possesses the body of his mother. Anyone, with the Lord’s help, will be able to conquer the devil if, longing for God’s saving commandments, he diligently works to bend the pride of his arrogant mind, hated by all; restrains avarice, the root of all evils; curbs lust, the enemy of good virtues; moderates envy, the foe of holy charity; avoids the useless and often dangerous conversations of slanderers [Note: [Col. 0322D] Laurentian manuscript: “and also those of usurers”; Vatican, Regius 433: “and often circuitous conversations of slanderers, and also the destructive [or “pernicious”] profits of usury”]; does not love the destructive profits of usury; does not burden justice, the guardian of peace, with gifts; dreads the harmful schemes of factions; avoids the inglorious and sometimes bloody pursuit of undeserved honor; restrains the insults and curses of a contentious tongue, the sparks of discord; drives from a Christian mouth the lies that stain life, wound the soul, and scatter friendships; and flees, through love of the true God, from every superstition and sacrilege of demons and idols, by which the goodness of the Almighty is especially offended.

If, then, we fast from these and all similar crimes and vices, the days of this holy Lent will be properly celebrated, and we shall pass through all the feasts of our solemnities rejoicing, with the confidence of a happier conscience and the tranquility of peaceful times, with the assistance of our Lord Jesus Christ.

## HOMILY XLIII. On Lent VII

[Col. 0321]

### NOTICE

The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur rejected this homily to the appendix of the sermons of Saint Augustine, uncertain to which author it ought to be attributed.
