But not only do the editors Gymnicus, Galesinius, Cumdius, Combefisius, Margarinus, and Raynaudus judge that it must be assigned entirely to Maximus; the authority of the old manuscripts also demands this: Laurentian I, Pluteus XIV, Vallicellana II, page 203, Lucensis 85, Augiensis, Martinensis, and Turin. This is supported as well by the remarkable similarity of style and by the manner of using testimonies from Sacred Scripture, which Maximus habitually employed. We thought it should be printed before the following homily, not only because most manuscripts present it in that position, but also because it appears to belong with the preceding homily.

### SUMMARY

Everything that Christ endured is an incentive for us to imitate him. He allowed himself to be tempted by the devil for no other reason than to teach us with what weapons we ought to repel him.

The contest with the tempter undertaken by our Lord Jesus Christ, as we have read, benefits our security and salvation [Note: [Col. 0323D] Vallicellana II and Martinensis: “has benefited”], dearest brothers, because those whom the ancestral transgression, through the serpent’s persuasion, once cast down into death in paradise, the Lord’s triumph has now raised up to life [Note: [Col. 0323D] Vallicellana II and Martinensis: “He conquered for us”]. He conquered for us, since he deigned to hunger for us.

The devil therefore attacks Christ and anxiously investigates whether he might discover him to be the Son of God, in whom he sees no trace of his own corruption [Note: [Col. 0323D] Laurentian I and Vatican 6452: “in whom he saw no trace of his corruption”; Martinensis: “he saw”]. He is simultaneously amazed and disturbed that a man of this kind has come into this world [Note: [Col. 0323D] The same Vatican manuscript: “into this age”], one who was indeed born of a woman but was not begotten by a man.

He suspects him to be the Son of God, whom he sees completing an uninterrupted fast of forty days; but he again doubts that the one whom he sees hungry, apparently weak among other human beings, possesses a divine nature [Note: [Col. 0323D] Laurentian I: “that a divine nature was not present in him”]. He is stunned and astonished at this novelty: that he does not possess human sin yet endures the necessity of sinful humanity.

But Christ our Lord and Redeemer, in order to recall fallen and weakened humanity to God, took upon himself hunger, weariness, sorrow, and all the weaknesses of the human body. Amid these things, therefore, the doubtful and uncertain devil engages the hungry Lord in conversation: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matt. 4).

Foolish and audacious was he to suppose that the Son of God would act according to the devil’s will merely from the necessity of eating—as though it were impossible to change stones into bread for the one who once brought forth abundant streams of water from a dry rock for peoples thirsty in the desert (Exod. 17) [Note: [Col. 0323D] Vatican 6452 and Laurentian I: “as though it were truly impossible”]; or as though he could not provide food for himself while hungry after a fast of forty days, at whose command, so that an innumerable army of Hebrews might be fed, heavenly nourishment flowed from the clouds (Exod. 16) [Note: [Col. 0323D] Vatican manuscript: “the elements flowed”].

But the almighty Only-Begotten, who hungered rather for our salvation [Note: [Col. 0323D] Laurentian I: “who hungered rather for our salvation”], confounded his tempter with this reply: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Deut. 18).

By this answer, dearest ones, the Lord of immeasurable wisdom made the investigator, who had come uncertain, still more uncertain. He neither denied that hunger was present in him nor admitted that he was subject to the necessity of eating: “Man,” he said, “does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.” That is: “Even if I am hungry” [Note: [Col. 0324D] Martinensis: “I hunger”], “nevertheless, devil, bread is not necessary for me; but the word of God produces for all the faithful the sustenance of eternal salvation.” [Note: [Col. 0324D] Laurentian I: “For me nevertheless, devil, [you] knowing whether bread, which comes down through your counsel and will, is necessary [reading uncertain]. Bodily bread indeed refreshes hunger; the word of God [provides] for all the faithful sustenance, etc.” Vallicellana II likewise reads: “but the word of God.”]

But the enemy, incapable of learning, again says to the Lord standing upon the pinnacle of the Temple: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down; for it is written that he has commanded his angels concerning you, that they should take you up in their hands, lest you ever strike your foot against a stone” (Matt. 4).

“Throw yourself down,” he says. It is characteristic of the devil, dearest brothers, to persuade one toward a precipice; but he could not obey him who did not know how to fall. The deceiver obtains nothing from the Lord, because his words are not religious but fraudulent [Note: [Col. 0324D] Vallicellana II and Martinensis: “but fraudulent”]. The Redeemer of the human race again strikes him with the weapon of a heavenly sentence, saying: “It is written: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”

By this reply, so that the author of falsehood might hear nothing contrary to manifest truth, the Lord, ruler of words and meanings, neither disclosed that he could throw himself down from on high nor falsely claimed that he could not [Note: [Col. 0324D] Laurentian I, Vallicellana, and Martinensis: “neither disclosed that he could give himself from on high”]; but he said: “It is written: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” That is, he tests God who, through the fault of his own boastfulness, wishes to display a superfluous and useless power.

For what benefit is there, what advantage does it provide, if I descend unharmed from here by a headlong fall onto the level ground [Note: [Col. 0324D] Martinensis: “if I descend from here headlong without injury”]? Or why do you persuade me to do this by the temptations of your flattery, when it is your work to cast one falling from the heights down to the depths [Note: [Col. 0324D] Laurentian and Vallicellana II: “why do you persuade me to do this by the temptations of your flattery”]?

After this, as the reading just completed testifies: “He led him onto a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world, saying: ‘All these I will give you if, falling down, you worship me.’” The deceitful deceiver offers what he does not possess; and, truly blind, he promises the kingdoms of the earth to the Lord of heaven: “All these,” he says, “I will give you if, falling down, you worship me.”

Truly he falls and collapses who acquires the dignities of the world not by God’s generosity but at the devil’s command [Note: [Col. 0324D] Laurentian Codex I: “Truly he will fall and collapse…”]. The Lord answered him: “Go away, Satan; for it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”

By tempting, he reached the point of demanding that he himself be worshiped by the Son of God, thinking that Christ, who could not be deceived by the theft of praise, might expose himself to the investigator through anger at the insult inflicted. But the strongest defender, who was waging a new war against his tyrant for our life and freedom, is neither broken by soft flattery nor moved by the harshest insults. He answered every temptation of the enemy in such a way that the enemy could not discover, in the one and the same God and man, the mystery of the heavenly sacrament.

Therefore, brothers, following the example of the Lord’s contest and victory, and guarding against the devil’s ambushes, let us celebrate these forty days in a fast acceptable to our God. We shall then be able to overcome the adversary’s deceits if, through continual prayers, we either restrain the vices of the body by chaste fasts or cleanse our heart from every vanity and ambition, as the Savior himself says: “This kind is driven out only by fasting and prayer” (Matt. 17).

He fasts well who satisfies his hunger with the fullness of a restored poor person; he fasts well who, mindful of the divine fast, restrains himself and abstains from every pleasure of seduction [Note: [Col. 0325D] Laurentian, Martinensis, and Vatican manuscripts: “abstains from every pleasure of seductions”]; he fasts well who chastises his flesh, which produces the shoots of vices, through meditation upon holy virtues and love of sobriety [Note: [Col. 0325D] Vatican Codex: “through the correction of holy virtues”]; he fasts well who forgives his brothers’ injuries with the gentleness of a peaceful heart.

He offers a fast most pleasing to God who guards his mind from evil thoughts, his eyes from covetousness, and his tongue and hands from quarrels. And afterward, brother, you will be blessed, and you will hunger properly for bread and thirst for drink, if with the disposition of a Christian mind you begin to hunger and thirst for righteousness, as the Lord himself said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

Therefore, dearest ones, if we wish to overcome the devil with Christ; if we desire, after passing from this world, to reign with God; if we wish to celebrate the most sacred day of the Lord’s resurrection with joyful minds, let us abstain from food and drink as far as our strength permits, but let us fast from vices with all our strength.

## HOMILY XLIV. On Lent VIII

[Col. 0325]

### NOTICE

In the Venice edition of the works of Saint Peter Chrysologus, published in 1750, page 20, this homily is attributed as though it had been written by that holy archbishop of Ravenna. The editor of the Augsburg edition noticed the error and therefore did not think it should be given a place among Chrysologus’s sermons in 1758. The authority of the ancient manuscripts, which are of the very best quality, must nevertheless be added, and the homily must certainly be assigned to Maximus. Vatican manuscripts 6450 and 6452 have: “Sermon of Saint Maximus on the Lenten fast.” The Laurentian I, Pluteus XIV, Vallicellana II, Novarien 27, Lucensis 85, and Augiensis manuscripts do not differ; in them the inscription reads: “On Lent.” In the distinguished manuscript of the Cistercian monastery of Monte Amiata, it bears this heading: “Sermon of Blessed Maximus, bishop, for the First Sunday of Lent.” The agreement of the editors Gymnicus, Galesinius, Combefisius, Cumdius, Margarinus, Raynaudus, and others concerning Maximus as the author of the homily is complete.

### SUMMARY

On the fast of Christ and of Moses. As Christ is believed to be God through his divine powers, so he is recognized as man through human weaknesses. We chastise our limbs with fasts so that we may nourish our souls with virtues.

Pay attention, dearest brothers, to how many lessons for the spiritual life grow before us, although we are urged toward our purpose of holiness by magnificent examples: we are told that blessed Moses and the Son of God fasted for forty days [Note: [Col. 0325D] Laurentian I, Pluteus XIV: “and by how magnificent [examples]”]. Observe this carefully: just as far as a servant is from his master, so far must their fasts differ. Moses is the promulgator of the old Law; Christ is the founder of the New Testament.

Moses fasts in order to instruct one people in the discipline of legal commands; Christ fasts in order to redeem all the nations of the whole world [Note: [Col. 0325D] Laurentian I, Vatican 6450, and Vallicellana II: “in order to redeem all the nations of the whole world”]. Moses fasts in order to receive the commandments of the present life; Christ also fasts in order to establish the mysteries of eternal salvation. Moses fasts in order to see God; Jesus also fasts in order to show, while triumphing over the devil, that he is one with God [Note: [Col. 0325D] The same Laurentian I, Vatican 6350, and Vallicellana II manuscripts: “Moses fasted in order to see God; Christ also fasted…”].

After his fast, Moses broke the tablets written by the finger of God because of the people’s transgression; Christ, through his fast, preserved the Gospel, which would remain throughout the ages [Note: [Col. 0325D] Novara manuscript: “which would remain throughout the ages in the whole Church”].

But what does it mean that, although both fasted for forty days [Note: [Col. 0326D] Vatican 6450: “although both fasted for forty days”], Moses is not said to have been hungry after his fast, whereas Christ was? Moses did not hunger, so that divinity operating in a frail human being might be demonstrated; the Son of God hungered, so that by assuming our flesh he might reveal that he had taken upon himself frail humanity [Note: [Col. 0326D] Laurentian I, Vallicellana II, and Vatican 6450: “that he had assumed frail humanity”]. Moses’ not hungering is an example of heavenly ability; Christ’s hungering is the mystery of our redemption [Note: [Col. 0326D] Vallicellana: “Moses did not hunger”].

The Lord performed this mystery in his own flesh, so that, just as he is believed to be God through divine powers, he might also be recognized as man through human weaknesses [Note: [Col. 0326D] Laurentian I: “For the Lord performed this kind of mystery…”]. Hence Christ hungers as man and feeds the hungry as God; hence he grows weary on a journey and grants the lame the power to walk; hence he loosens his eyes into tears [Note: [Col. 0326D] Laurentian and Vallicellana manuscripts: “he loosens his eyes into tears”] and wonderfully restores sight to the blind; hence he is saddened as death approaches and raises the dead Lazarus from the tomb.

Our Creator and Redeemer does all these things, brothers, as God and man [Note: [Col. 0326D] Vatican and Vallicellana manuscripts: “Our Redeemer acts as God and man”]—not because there was such a necessity for him to be born, but because he wished such a mystery to reign in heaven and on earth.

How great also is the wonder in Christ that he answered all the tempter’s questions in such a way that he neither revealed the truth of his kingdom to the tyrant nor allowed the investigator to recognize the mystery of the flesh he had assumed. Finally, he surrounded his speech with such subtlety that the enemy, the craftsman of every deceit, deceived by the error of his own rage, did not see God in the man while he was tempting Christ as a man.

But we, brothers, to whom the invincible defender has dedicated this venerable Lent, must reject carnal desires and chastise our limbs with fasts so that we may nourish our souls with virtues. Let harmful luxury fast within us; let every iniquity fast; let hateful contention fast. Let us abstain from banquets, but let us abstain still more from vices. Let us restrain ourselves; let us be so sober from wine that no drunkenness of pleasures may rule us.

For what benefit is there in observing the period of forty days appointed for fasting while failing to keep the law of the fast [Note: [Col. 0327C] Vallicellana II: “What benefit is there for us…”]? What benefit is there in abstaining from banquets while spending the day in quarrels? What benefit is there in not eating one’s own bread while plundering the food of the miserable?

The fast of a Christian ought to be the nourishment of the needy; the fast of a Christian ought to foster peace, not quarrels.

What kind of fast is it when you do not eat meat, yet from your mouth there proceeds a curse dirtier than any food? [Note: [Col. 0327C] “What kind of fast is it, when you do not eat meat, yet from your mouth there proceeds a curse dirtier than any food?”—On the precept of abstaining from meat during the Lenten fast, John Baptist Cotelerius dealt so extensively and learnedly in volume II, book III, against Dallaeus, that we consider ecclesiastical discipline sufficiently defended against the complaints of a heretical author. It is nevertheless not superfluous to observe that Saint Maximus here and elsewhere assumes, as a settled matter, that the use of meat is forbidden during Lent, and that he must therefore be counted among the Fathers who taught the discipline of fasting according to the mind of the Church.]

What kind of fast is it when the belly is sanctified by fasting but the tongue is polluted by lies? It is right, brother, that you frequent the church, if that greedy usury does not entangle and ensnare your steps in deadly traps. You will rightly pray to your Lord if the envy of your heart does not oppose your prayers. You will rightly beat your breast with your hands if you have shaken out from it all the fury of an evil will [Note: [Col. 0328C] Vatican Codex 6450, which nevertheless reads *excesseris* for *excusseris*]. You will also give a coin justly to a poor person if you have not taken it away from another poor person.

This, then, dearest ones, is religious hunger; this is the nourishment of the souls of the faithful: that chastity sanctify our fast, patience adorn it, kindness nurture it, mercy gladden it, and humility commend it. Let us follow Christ’s Lent, as far as we can, through these virtues, so that by a kind of twofold fast of body and soul we may always commend ourselves to divine grace.

## HOMILY XLV. On Palm Sunday, on the words of Psalm 21: “My God, my God, look upon me”

[Col. 0327]

### NOTICE
The title of this homily recalls for us the question that arose among scholars concerning the antiquity of the rite of blessing palm branches in the Church. Edmund Martène, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur and especially skilled in such matters, denies in chapter 20, section 2, of his work entitled *On the Ancient Discipline of the Church in the Celebration of Divine Offices* that any trace of this blessing is found in liturgical books before the eighth century of the Christian era. For he observed that, in the Roman calendar published by Fronto, mention is made of the solemnity of the Sunday preceding Easter, but not likewise of the blessing of palms.

Others, on the contrary, believe that the beginnings of this blessing must be placed earlier. Among them are Benedict XIV—distinguished not only by his rank but especially by his reputation for learning and scholarship—and Meratus, part 2, volume I, page 1004. In their support is an older Roman calendar, which they judge to have been written in the fourth century, or at least at the beginning of the fifth, and which they report to have been found in two manuscript codices: one belonging to the monastery of Saint Andrew of Avignon, the other to the monks of Grasse in Septimania. The editors of that same calendar report, on pages 63 and 64, that the latter had been given to the monastery by Charlemagne. In it the station is announced as follows:

> On Sunday amid the palms, at Saint John in the Lateran.

The same argument appeals to the Sacramentary commonly called the Gelasian, in which the Sunday before Easter is called *Sunday amid the palms, concerning the Passion of the Lord*. From this, they say, it can readily be concluded that the Sunday acquired the name “of the Palms” because people had become accustomed to bless palms on that day.

It is certainly not for me to determine which of these opinions is the stronger. I say only this: if the inscription of this homily is as ancient as the homily itself, it must be admitted that the rite of blessing palms was already established in the fifth century. Three Vatican codices—385, 1268, and 1269—give this title prefixed to the same homily: “On Palm Sunday.” In the Saint Gall codex its inscription is: “On Psalm XXI, amid the branches of palms.” In two Novara codices, 27 and 24: “A sermon of blessed Maximus, bishop, on Sunday amid the palms.” In the Cistercian codex of Monte Amiata: “A sermon of blessed Maximus, bishop, on Sunday amid the palms, on Psalm XXI.” In the codex of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg: “A sermon of Saint Maximus on the Sunday amid the branches of palms.” In the Augia codex: “A sermon of Saint Maximus amid the palms.”

I admit that in two codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, 90 and 99, in the Laurentian codex I, Plut. XIV, and in the Turin codex, mention of the palms is omitted. From this it can plainly be understood:

1. That this homily must be attributed to Maximus, since none of the ancient codices attributes it to anyone else, while most of them bear the name of Saint Maximus; this is also freely conceded by the editors Gymnicus, Galesinius, Raynaudus, and Margarinus, and the character of its style agrees with Maximus’s genuine homilies, while its opinions are in the highest degree consistent with those in his other homilies.

2. That we have rightly preferred the inscription “Amid the branches of palms” to the other inscriptions, because the greater number of codices bear either this title or one similar to it.

## 137. ARGUMENT

[Col. 0327C] Saint Maximus explains David’s prophetic psalm and demonstrates that its prophecy had its true significance in Christ.

Before carefully proceeding through the sequence of the twenty-first psalm that has been read, we must first attend closely to what is contained in its superscription, so that, once its origin has been recognized, we may more easily grasp its meaning and, once its head has been disclosed, distribute its members more correctly. [Col. 0328C] For it is inscribed as follows: [Col. 0329A] “For the end, concerning the morning reception, a psalm of David himself.”

Unless I am mistaken, the morning reception always precedes the rising of the sun. [Note: [Col. 0329C] See the note for what is further contained in both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem.] Before the bright radiance illuminates the circle of the earth, it sets a morning boundary to the darkness of night; and, as the blindness of the shadows is gradually dissolved, a kind of appearance and light is poured over all things. [Note: [Col. 0329C] Vatican Codex 1268: “is poured back.”] When the world, as though under a single substance of darkness, has lain in confusion, the coming of morning distinguishes it by the varied diversity of its forms. That is, when everything has been blind, everyone’s eyes are restored.

Night, in a certain sense, takes the eyes away from the world; dawn restores them. Thus we first enjoy the morning reception, so that afterward we may partake more gloriously of the sun’s radiance. But since, as the Apostle says, “the law is spiritual, and spiritual things must be compared with spiritual things” (Romans 7; 1 Corinthians 2), I think that the sun here signifies the Sun of righteousness, that is, Christ the Lord. To us, submerged in the darkness of ignorance and the blindness of sins, he poured out the light of his heavenly teaching; and he implanted in us eyes of the heart, which we did not possess. [Note: [Col. 0329C] Laurentian Codex I, Plut. XIV: “and the eyes which we had not possessed.”] He sent his apostles like rays, so that they might free us from the most dreadful night of wrongdoing [Note: [Col. 0329C] Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “from death”; in the margin is noted: “otherwise, from night.”] and, as the darkness of sins was gradually dissolved within us, accustom us to the morning reception. [Note: [Col. 0329C] In Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, “us” is omitted.] Thus we might more easily endure the sun’s heat in perfection: that is, they would first instruct us in simpler commandments, so as to make us more capable of heavenly mysteries.

By the morning of this Sun of righteousness, therefore, the whole darkness of sins is destroyed, as the prophet himself says in the person of the Lord: [Col. 0329C]

> “In the mornings I destroyed all the sinners of the earth” (Psalm 100).

That is: when the Sun of righteousness rises within us, who are the Lord’s dwelling place, every evil thought is overthrown. [Note: [Col. 0330C] Vatican Codex 1278: “we are God’s dwelling place.”]

[Note: [Col. 0329D] In both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, after these words the following is read: “The blessed Solomon also mentions this sun in the person of those sinners who reflect and say to themselves: ‘The sun has not risen for us, and the light of righteousness has not shone for us.’ We may also assign this morning reception in the holy Gospel to Mary Magdalene. Keeping vigil early and at dawn at the tomb of the Savior, she was the first to receive the Lord’s resurrection; and, as the sun of the world grew bright, she alone before all others recognized the rising of the Sun of righteousness. She rejoiced in the morning reception because the day had been restored, but rejoiced even more because Christ had been raised from the dead. In her the prophecy was fulfilled: ‘In the evening there shall be weeping, but in the morning gladness.’”]

*(Here ends the preface of the homily.)*

The whole of this psalm, however, is arranged as spoken in the person of the Lord and Savior, since many passages concerning him have been set forth in the New Testament.

[Note: [Col. 0329D] Thus he says: “My God, my God, look upon me,” and so forth. Why does he plead the cause of the assumed man, so that he seems in a certain way to ask, saying: “God of all, who are my God, why have you forsaken me?” and so forth?

Saint Ambrose had preceded our author in explaining this passage of Psalm XXI. In Book X of his commentary on Luke he says: “The man cried out, about to die through the separation of divinity.” Saint Hilary, in his *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 3, says: “That cry is the voice of the body to God, testifying to the separation of the Word of God from it.” And Saint Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 69: “Seeing that the divinity was already on the point of abandoning the holy body, he uttered that cry.” Our Maximus, however, said that Christ uttered that cry to show that he had been forsaken on our account, because he bore our sins, and so forth. But as to what should be understood by that abandonment of divinity in Christ, theologians diverge into several opinions; we refer readers to them.]

Thus he says:

> “My God, my God, look upon me,”

and what follows. Why does he plead the cause of the assumed man, so that he seems in a certain way to ask, saying: “God of all, who are my God, why have you forsaken me?” For I am conscious of no fault. According to the prophet, he did not know sin, and there was no deceit in his mouth. He says this to show that he was forsaken on our account, since he bore our sins, and so that, when we saw this, we might learn to die for that Holy and Just One, since he too died for sinners. [Note: [Col. 0330C] In both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “and he seems in a certain way to ask, saying.”] [Note: [Col. 0330C] Codex 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “since he died for sin.”]

Finally, he used this voice during the Passion, as we read in the Gospel:

> “Eli, Eli, lamma sabacthani?”

That is:

> “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27).

I say that he used this voice so that the outcome of events might confirm what prophecy had announced. And since what follows is almost entirely clear, let us examine the verse in which he says:

> “But I am a worm and not a man” (Psalm 21).

Why did the Lord of all creation wish to compare himself to a little worm? We may first attribute this to humility, which is the greatest of the virtues of the saints. Thus holy Moses professes before God that he is an irrational creature, and David often calls himself a flea. [Note: [Col. 0330C] Vatican Codex 1278 reads: “David, a gnat.”]

But I think the passage should be understood more particularly in this way: since a worm is produced without any external admixture of another body, from earth alone and pure earth, he was compared to the Lord because the Savior too was born from Mary alone and pure. [Note: [Col. 0330C] In both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “and from pure earth.”]

I have also read in the books of Moses that worms were produced from manna (Exodus 16): a wholly fitting and appropriate comparison. For if a worm is born from manna, and the Lord Christ is born from the Virgin, then—better still—I should call Mary herself manna, because she is delicate, radiant, sweet, and a virgin. As though coming from heaven, she poured forth upon all the peoples of the churches food sweeter than honey. Whoever neglects to eat and partake of it cannot have life in himself, as the Lord himself says:

> “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in himself” (John 6).

Rather, that food will be turned into judgment, as the Apostle says:

> “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11).

This was subtly prophesied to the children of Israel in the Testament. When they handled manna contrary to the divine commandments, it became worms for them—that is, avengers and judges of their obstinacy.

This likeness points to Christ the Lord. Whoever neglects to receive him as sweet food and pleasant drink will experience him as judge, as he himself says:

> “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).

As for what he says:

> “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots” (Psalm 21; John 19),

we find that this happened in the Gospel. The four soldiers who crucified the Savior divided his garments among themselves into four parts; but his garment, which was not sewn together but woven from the top, they received by lot.

Let us therefore see what these garments are, who the soldiers were, and what the garment signifies. [Note: [Col. 0331D] In both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “what they may be.”]

[Col. 0331B] I think the garments are the prophecies, or the readings of the heavenly Scriptures, in which the mystery of Christ the Lord was announced. The opponents of the Savior—that is, perverse heretics—divide these prophecies, though they sing one thing and proclaim one message throughout, according to their own will; like soldiers, they daily lay impious hands upon him. [Note: [Col. 0331D] Vatican Codex 1278 reads “laid hands upon” (*inierunt*) instead of “thrust upon” (*ingerunt*).] [Note: [Col. 0331D] Vatican Codex 1278 reads “laid hands upon” (*inierunt*) instead of “thrust upon” (*ingerunt*).]

They divide this garment among themselves according to their own will, [Note: [Col. 0331D] Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “and one garment of the body.”] and distribute the garments of one body among its various members; and, after stripping the Lord, they clothe him in their false doctrines.

His garment, however, which was not sewn together, may be understood as his heavenly wisdom, [Note: [Col. 0331D] In both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “because he says, ‘but woven from above.’”] because it was woven from above.

Our wisdom—that is, human wisdom—is sewn together. [Note: [Col. 0331D] In both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, “for” (*enim*) is added.] It is stitched on when we send children to grammarians for study, hand them over to philosophers, and educate them so that wisdom, which was not previously in them, may be acquired. The Lord’s wisdom, however, was not stitched on or sought out. He did not learn it from a teacher, as the Jews themselves say:

> “How does this man know letters, since he has not learned?”

and as he himself says:

> “My teaching is not of this world, but is of him who sent me” (John 7). [Note: [Col. 0332D] In both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “but my teaching.”] [Note: [Col. 0332D] The Laurentian codex reads: “It is not mine, but …,” and so forth.]

This is what is meant by “woven from above.” In this garment—or, rather, in all these garments—the Catholic Church is always clothed, as the prophet says:

> “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold” (Psalm 44).

## HOMILY XLVI. On the Lord Accused and Judged before Pilate

[Col. 0331]

### ADMONITION

[141] There is great variation in both the printed books and the manuscripts concerning the author of this homily. It bears the name of Saint Ambrose in Vatican Codex 1270, page 27, and in Laurentian Codex I, Plut. XIV, page 290. In certain others, it bears that of Saint Augustine. Joannes Gillotius published it in the Paris edition of the works of Saint Ambrose in 1569, among the sermons, as number 49. The editors of the Sixtine edition of the same works of Saint Ambrose followed Gillotius in assigning it to that archbishop.

Yet it is clear that Gillotius fell into error, as is shown by the distinguished testimony of Gennadius, an ancient and careful writer, who also counts this homily among the works of Saint Maximus and reports that it was entitled *On the Lord Accused and Condemned before Pilate*. The authority of four very ancient manuscript codices is added. For in the Saint Gall codex, in the two codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, 90 and 99, and in the Turin codex, this same homily is entered by number among Saint Maximus’s sermons after the preceding one.

Their inscriptions nevertheless differ somewhat. In Santa Croce 90 it reads: “Here begins a homily on the Lord accused before Pilate, and on Susanna.” In 99: “On the Lord accused before Pilate.” In the Turin codex: “Likewise, on the Lord accused and judged.” In the Saint Gall codex, as in Santa Croce 99, this very homily immediately follows the preceding one.

The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, in the appendix to the fifth volume of the works of Saint Augustine, sermon 152, note that it should be attributed to Saint Maximus, relying on the testimony of the Louvain editors; they entitle it *On the Passion of the Lord and Susanna*. The editors of Maximus’s homilies—Gymnicus, Galesinius, Cumdius, Raynaudus, and Margarinus—agree with the Louvain editors, with the sole exception of Combefisius, who omitted it. There is no reason, however, why I should dissent from them.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0331C] Christ, accused before Pilate, remains silent—not to confirm his accusation by silence, but because he needs no defense in order to conquer; in the same way Susanna remained silent before her enemies and conquered.

It may perhaps seem strange to you, brothers, that the Lord is accused before the governor Pilate by the chief priests and remains silent, and does not refute their wickedness by his answer, since ordinarily a defense follows only in order to rebut an accusation that has been brought. Strange, I say, that the Savior should be accused and remain silent; for silence is sometimes regarded as consent. Indeed, he seems to confirm what is alleged when he does not wish to answer what is asked.

Does the Lord therefore confirm his accusation by remaining silent? [Col. 0331D] He certainly does not confirm his accusation by remaining silent, but despises it by not refuting it; for he rightly remains silent who has no need of defense. Let the one who fears defeat seek defense. Let the one who fears being conquered hasten to speak.

Christ, however, when he is condemned, also conquers; when he is judged, also triumphs, as the prophet says:

> “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Psalm 50). [Note: [Col. 0332D] Santa Croce Codex 99 reads: “when you are judged.”]

What need, then, was there for him to speak before the judgment, when the judgment itself was his complete victory?

[142] Christ conquers when he is judged because he is thereby proved innocent. Hence Pilate says:

> “I am innocent of the blood of this just man” (Matthew 27).

The cause that is not defended yet is proved is therefore the better cause; the justice that is not established by words but supported by truth is the fuller justice. The tongue must necessarily be silent where equity itself is present; it must be silent in a good case, since it is accustomed to prevail even in bad cases. [Note: [Col. 0332D] Laurentian Codex I, Plut. XIV, Santa Croce codices 99 and 90, and Vatican Codex 1270 read: “must necessarily be silent where …”] [Col. 0332D]

I do not want justice to be defended in the way in which wickedness is usually excused. [Col. 0333A] Christ’s victory is not a victory of eloquence but of power. The Savior, who is wisdom, knows how to conquer by remaining silent and how to overcome without answering; he prefers to prove his case rather than speak it. What, indeed, would compel him to speak, when silence was sufficient for victory?

But perhaps fear would have compelled him, lest he lose his life—except that this itself was the whole cause of his victory. He lost his own life in order to gain the salvation of all; he preferred to be defeated in himself so that he might be victorious in all.

But why should I speak of Christ? The woman Susanna remained silent before her enemies and conquered (Daniel 13). [Note: [Col. 0333C] Thus, on the authority of Laurentian Codex I: “before her enemies,” and so forth.] She did not defend herself before Daniel the judge by a verbal argument; [Note: [Col. 0333C] Laurentian Codex I and Santa Croce codices 99 and 90: “by a verbal argument.”] she did not protect herself with the language of advocacy. [Note: [Col. 0333C] Codex 99 likewise reads: “was kept safe.”] Rather, in the holy woman, while her tongue was silent, chastity spoke on her behalf.

[Col. 0331B] Susanna’s chastity was present at the judgment: it defended her both in paradise and there—in paradise it guarded her modesty, here her salvation; there, so that her chastity would not be stained, here, so that her innocence would not be condemned.

[143] Susanna’s chastity therefore convicted both the priests and the impure men in paradise, [Note: [Col. 0333C] Laurentian Codex I and Santa Croce codices 99 and 90 read: “and the impure priests,” and so forth.] and in the judgment overcame the false accusers; and, victorious twice over, it made them guilty of the testimony by which they had made themselves guilty of adultery. [Note: [Col. 0333D] From the Laurentian codex I, the reading of Galesinius and others is corrected; they have: “And at last the judge …”]

But what sort of judge does chastity deserve? Daniel, a younger boy not yet of pubescent age. Purity therefore obtains much from God when it wins a virgin as judge. Chastity is secure of victory when virginity is its judge.

The case of purity ought to be heard only by a pure man. Chastity deserves such an arbiter, one before whom modesty will not be endangered.

When Daniel had learned of Susanna’s affair, and the ignorant crowd wished to condemn her on false accusations, he said:

> “I am innocent of the blood of this woman” (Daniel 13:46).

By these words he recalled the sinful people from their error.

Daniel therefore uses this declaration concerning Susanna which Pilate used concerning the Lord. Pilate said:

> “I am innocent of the blood of this just man” (Matthew 27:24).

[144] Purity is therefore released by the same judgment by which justice was acquitted.

Daniel acted better than Pilate: he did not condemn innocent blood but liberated it; whereas Pilate both acknowledged the just blood and handed it over. What benefit was there in bearing witness to innocence and yet sentencing him as though he were guilty, except that it is a graver sin both to pronounce him just and to hand him over [Note: [Col. 0334B] In the Maurist edition of the cited passage from Saint Augustine, section 3, it reads: “and to hand him over to criminals.” From Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, we judge that the word *as though* should be restored, since it seems appropriate; it is absent from the editions of Gymnicus and the two editions of Galesinius.] as though he were a criminal?

He himself is a witness to his wickedness, since he acquits with his mouth and condemns with his heart. Although Pilate washed his hands, he did not wash away his deeds; and although he thought he could wipe the just man’s blood from his limbs, his mind nevertheless remained stained by that blood. [Note: [Col. 0334C] The Laurentian codex and Santa Croce 90 read: “nevertheless, by that same blood.”]

For he himself killed Christ who handed him over to be killed. A steadfast and good judge, so as not to condemn innocent blood, ought not to have yielded either to envy or to fear. Daniel therefore acted better than Pilate: he recalled the sinful people from their error, whereas Pilate confirmed the sacrilege of the raging synagogue.

## HOMILY XLVII. On the Same Judgment II

[Col. 0333]

### ADMONITION

There is no lack here of arguments by which it may be established that this homily should be attributed to Saint Maximus. There are chiefly three.

The first is drawn from its connection and continuity with the preceding homily, in which he had discussed the matters that he continues to discuss at the beginning of this one. The second argument comes from the Saint Gall, Turin, Santa Croce in Jerusalem, and Laurentian codices, in which this same homily follows the preceding one and bears the name of Saint Maximus. The final argument is supplied by the agreement of the editors Gymnicus, Galesinius, Raynaudus, Combefisius, and Margarinus.

The connection of its style and the arrangement of its arguments are the same here as in the preceding homilies. Those who noted that it should be attributed to Saint Ambrose were therefore mistaken; and the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur deserve praise because they removed it from the number of the works of that same holy archbishop.

### ARGUMENT

On the similarity between the judgment instituted against Susanna and that instituted against Christ, and on the same punishment by which Judas and heretics are punished.

A few days ago [Note: [Col. 0334C] The Laurentian codex reads: “A few days earlier.”] we showed that the judgment against holy Susanna was very similar to the judgment against the Savior, and that the chastity of the woman mentioned had been assailed by the same accusations by which Christ’s integrity had been assailed.

For purity suffered persecution in Susanna in the same way. While she convicted the priests of adultery, she herself was detained as an adulteress; [Note: [Col. 0334D] The Laurentian codex reads: “convicted.”] while Christ reproved the Pharisees for sacrilege, he himself was accused as a sacrilegious man. [Note: [Col. 0334C] Vatican Codex 1270 reads: “while he reproved the sacrilegious men.”] [Note: [Col. 0334D] The Laurentian codex reads: “he himself, a sacrilegious man, …”] [Col. 0334C] That sacrilege in the Pharisees may rightly be called a greater adultery; for it is more serious to be an adulterer against religion than against the body, and it is a greater offense to injure the integrity of divinity than to violate the integrity of a human being.

Susanna is therefore condemned, and the Lord is condemned as well: she because she was protecting the chastity of her body, he because he was defending the sanctity of religion.

The cause of judgment was therefore similar in both cases, except that Susanna had a better judge than the Lord. The governor judges him; the prophet judges her. A man who was frightened by the seditions of the Pharisees hears him; a boy filled with the Holy Spirit hears her. The former declares firmly what he thinks but does not defend it. The judge of Susanna acquits and liberates her; Pilate, who recognizes the Lord’s innocence, condemns and hands him over. Thus the judgment of Susanna and of the Lord was similar in almost every respect.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] In both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “He firmly declares what he thinks; the one who declares it does not defend it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0335D] Two codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Vatican Codex 1270 supply the following.]

Indeed, the accusation in the two cases was not dissimilar. The elders bring charges against Susanna; Judas accuses the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0335D] Vatican Codex 1270 reads: “the Apostle accuses.”] Her accusers are her teachers; his own disciple denounces him.*

Susanna, I say, is accused by false priests; the Savior is betrayed by a pseudo-bishop. Judas too was a bishop, as the prophet says of him:

> “Let his days be few, and let another take his office” (Psalm 108).

Nor does the place in the two cases appear dissimilar, brother. Susanna is surrounded by her accusers in a garden paradise; [Note: [Col. 0335D] The Laurentian codex and the Santa Croce codices read: “in her husband’s garden-paradise.”] the Lord is surrounded by his betrayers in the paradise of a little garden. There she suffers the ambush of plotters; here he endures a betrayer.

Let us also examine the outcome of the two judgments. Susanna’s accusers are struck down by the prophetic sentence as false witnesses, and are punished as guilty of the very crime by which they were eager to condemn innocent blood.

But I do not find that the Lord’s betrayer was condemned by a judge. Pilate does not condemn him, nor does the people. Rather, what is more serious, he condemns himself; [Note: [Col. 0335D] The Laurentian codex, Vatican Codex 1270, and Santa Croce codices 90 and 99 read: “and, the judge’s sentence being absent, he is judged by his own sentence.”] with justice absent, he is judged by his own sentence.

For the one judged by another can in some way be excusable; but the one condemned by the judgment of his own conscience is guilty without excuse. The one judged by another may at some point hope for mercy from his judge; but the one who judges himself—from whom will he seek mercy?

Judas, returning the price of the Lord’s blood, said to the Jews:

> “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Matthew 27).

The testimony to the Lord’s innocence is therefore great, since his accuser both confesses his crime and is guilty because of the payment. In his misery, when he returned the price of the sale, he thought that he could dissolve the contract of his crime; but he is not acquitted. Since the author of the sale is himself guilty, it is clear that these men entered into a criminal contract with the sacrilegious man. Judas the betrayer is therefore condemned by his own sentence.

It may perhaps seem strange to you that the people did not judge him and that the governor did not condemn him. But this is the judgment characteristic of a sacrilegious person: while remembering his impiety, he himself punishes it; while recognizing his crime, he himself avenges it. For he surpasses all judgments who is condemned by his own conscience and by his own sentence.

[Note: [Col. 0336D] The Laurentian codex and Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read: “This, I say, is the judgment characteristic of a sacrilegious person: when he himself casts himself out of the Catholic Church and proceeds from the assembly of the saints, though no one expels him,” and so forth.]

This, I say, is the judgment characteristic of a sacrilegious person: conscious of his deed, he condemns himself, as the Apostle Paul says concerning a heretic:

> “Avoid a heretical person after one and a second admonition, knowing that such a person is subverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (Titus 3).

The heretic condemns himself when he himself casts himself out of the Church and proceeds from the assembly of the saints, though no one compels him. He himself shows what he deserves from all, since by his own judgment he is separated from all.

The heretic, I say, condemns himself. For while all criminals are expelled from the Christian fellowship by the sentence of a bishop, the heretic, anticipating everyone’s decision, is cast out by the sentence of his own will. [Note: [Col. 0336D] Laurentian Codex X and Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read: “the heretic, anticipating everyone’s wishes.”]

The heretic is therefore condemned by the same punishment as Judas: he is both guilty of his own crime and judge of his own punishment. The heretic is condemned by the same punishment as Judas—and not undeservedly, because the Lord whom Judas sold, this man blasphemes; the one whom Judas handed over to persecutors, this man persecutes daily.

For the heretic persecutes the Lord when he detracts from his divinity and asserts that he is a creature.

## HOMILY XLVIII. On Judas the Betrayer

[Col. 0335]

### ADMONITION

[147] This homily is so closely connected with the preceding one that, once the author of one is known, the author of both is known. Yet there is great variation concerning its author in the manuscripts, and among writers there has been considerable dispute over the attribution.

In Vatican Codex 1268 it is attributed to Saint Ambrose. In another Vatican codex, number 6452, and in the Florentine codex of Santa Croce Minor, now Laurentian IV, Plut. XXXIII, it is attributed—perhaps, rather, ascribed—to Saint John, bishop of Constantinople. The author’s name is absent from Vatican Codex 4951 and likewise from the Urbevetan codex.

There may also be some codices in which it is attributed to Saint Augustine. For several editors would not have attributed it to that same Saint Augustine, as in fact they do, unless his name appeared in at least one codex.

But the doubt is removed by Gennadius, especially an ancient and careful author, together with Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, the Turin codex, Laurentian Codex X, Plut. XIV, and the Saint Gall codex.

Accordingly, the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur say in the appendix to Saint Augustine’s sermons, sermon 80, page 102 of the Antwerp edition of 1700:

> Long ago it was restored to its proper author, Maximus, bishop of Turin, whose name it bears in manuscripts and printed books.

I am not concerned about the title. I have used the title used by Gymnicus and the other editors, although I am not unaware that, among the monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, this same homily is entitled:

> “On Matthew, chapter 33, on Judas the betrayer, and on the field purchased for the burial of foreigners with the price of Christ’s sale.”

### ARGUMENT

Saint Maximus explains the history of Judas’s betrayal allegorically.

[The supplied source ends here.]

Your love remembers [Note: MSS Vatican 1268 and formerly Santa Croce Minor Conventual IV: “Your holiness, brothers, retains that we already preached this to you,” etc.] that last Sunday we preached to you [Col. 0336D] that Judas Iscariot, condemned by his own judgment, returned to the Pharisees the price of the Lord’s blood and, in an act of repentance, repaid the price of the sale and hanged himself with a noose [Col. 0337A], so that he who had punished himself with money might also punish himself with his life. For, understanding what a great crime he had committed, it was not enough for him to be deprived of the reward of his sacrilege unless he were also deprived of salvation; [Note: Cod. Vatican 1268; 4951: “for he judged himself worthy of death.”] for he judged himself worthy of death because he had betrayed Christ, the life [Note: Cod. Laurentian X: “the life of human beings.”] of all. [Note: MSS Santa Croce Minor and 99 Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “Therefore Judas was exceedingly savage.”] Therefore Judas, the most severe judge of himself, confesses even in punishing the one whom he had denied in betraying.

He therefore returned the money to the Pharisees; but the Pharisees too did not willingly accept it, for they said [Note: Cod. 99 Santa Croce and Urbevetanus: “it is forbidden.”] that they had been prohibited from keeping it in their treasuries. [Note: Three Vatican MSS: “Observe, then.”] Observe, then, how great is the power of the Lord’s money: [Note: Laurentian MSS, and Vatican 1268 and 4951: “which Judas rejects from the Jews; here the Pharisees do not shut it away in their purses,” etc.] Judas rejects it from them, while the Pharisees do not put it into their purses. For iniquity fears to possess the price of righteous blood. Nevertheless, the Pharisees take counsel that with it a potter’s field should be purchased, [Col. 0337B] in which the bodies of foreigners might be placed.

I think this was done by providence [Note: Santa Croce Minor Conventual, three Vatican MSS, and Urbevetanus: “by the providence of God”], so that the price of the Savior might provide no benefit taken by sinners, but might supply rest for foreigners; it might not serve sacrilegious persons for [Note: Laurentian MSS, Santa Croce Minor, Santa Croce in Jerusalem, three Vatican MSS, and Urbevetanus: “for luxury.”] dissipation, but might serve the dead as a tomb; so that from then on Christ might [Note: Cod. Vatican 4951: “redeem the living through the blood of his passion and receive the dead in a precious possession.” Cod. Urbevetanus: “and, living, redeem through the blood of his passion, and, dead, receive in a precious possession.”] redeem the living through the blood of his passion and receive the dead through his precious passion.

Therefore, with the price [Note: MSS Santa Croce Minor, both Santa Croce in Jerusalem, Vatican 1268, and Urbevetanus: “with the price of the Lord’s blood.”] of the Lord’s blood, the potter’s field is purchased. We read in the Scriptures that the salvation of the whole human race has been redeemed by the Savior’s blood, as the apostle Peter says: “For you were not redeemed with perishable gold or silver, but with the precious blood of the spotless and immaculate Lamb, Jesus Christ” (1 Peter I). Therefore, if the blood of the Lord is the price of our life, [Note: Cod. Vatican 1268: “see, then, that by it not so much…”] see that it is not so much the frail earthly [Col. 0337C] portion of the field that has been redeemed as the everlasting safety of the whole world. For the Evangelist says: “Christ did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him” (John XIII). [Note: Cod. Vatican 1268: “See, I say, that that money was not so much used to purchase a field.”]

See, I say, that that money is not so much the purchase of a small portion of land as the rich possession of the whole world, as the prophet David says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm III). Therefore this field is the whole world, in which we, scattered and sown, bring forth the fruit of good works for the Lord.

But perhaps you may ask me: If the field is the world, who is the potter who can possess dominion over the world? Unless I am mistaken, he is the potter who made the little vessels of our body from clay; of him Scripture says: “And God made man from the clay of the earth” (Genesis II). He is the potter who gave life to the muddy clay of our flesh by the breath of his spirit and baked the fluid, earthly material [Note: Vatican MSS 6452 and 4951: “with fiery heat.”] with fiery heat.

He, I say, is the potter who fashioned us with his hands for life and refashioned us through his Christ for glory, as the Apostle says: “We are refashioned into the same image, from glory to glory” (2 Corinthians III); that is, so that we who fell from our first creation through our own sins might be restored in a second birth through the mercy of this potter. This means that, having fallen into death through Adam’s transgression, [Note: Cod. Vatican 4951: “we fell into death.”] we might rise again through the grace of the Savior.

He plainly is the potter of whom the blessed Apostle says: “Will the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me thus?’” And again: “Does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans IX). [Note: Three Vatican MSS, Urbevetanus, and Laurentian, Santa Croce Minor, and 99 Santa Croce in Jerusalem MSS: “For from the same clay of our body God, according to the merits of each, preserves some for punishment and others for glory.”] For from the same clay of our body God, according to the merits of each, reserves some for punishment and others for glory.

The field of this potter, then, was bought with Christ’s blood for foreigners. Foreigners, I say, who were without a home, without a country, and were driven about as exiles throughout the whole world: rest is provided by Christ’s blood for those who have no possession in the world, so that in Christ they may have a tomb.

But whom do we call these foreigners, except the most devoted Christians, who renounce the world and possess nothing in the world, and rest in Christ’s blood? For the Christian who does not possess the world possesses the whole Savior. For this reason burial in Christ is promised to foreigners, [Note: Cod. Vatican 6452 omits the particle “so that.”] so that whoever guards himself from carnal vices as a foreigner and stranger may deserve Christ’s rest.

For what else is Christ’s burial than the Christian’s rest? We, then, are foreigners in this world, and live in this light as guests, as the Apostle says: “For while we are in this body, we are foreigners from the Lord” (1 Corinthians V). We are foreigners, I say, and a burial purchased at the price of the Savior’s blood has been provided for us.

“For we have been buried with him,” as the Apostle says, “through baptism into death” (Galatians II). Therefore Christ’s baptism is our burial, in which we die to sins, are buried with respect to crimes, and, with the consciousness of the old person dissolved, are restored in a second birth to renewed infancy. Baptism, I say, of the Savior is our burial, because there we lose what we previously lived, [Note: Vatican 4951 and Urbevetanus: “and there we lost what we had barely lived before.”] and there again receive it so that we may live.

Great, therefore, is the grace of this burial, in which a useful death is inflicted upon us and a more useful life is granted; great, I say, is the grace of this burial, which both purifies the sinner and gives life to the dying.

## HOMILY XLIX. On the Passion and Cross of the Lord I

[Col. 0339]

### ADMONITION

Those who first undertook the edition of the works of Saint Ambrose thought that this homily ought to be attributed to that holy teacher. Gennadius contradicts them, for he counts it among the writings of Saint Maximus and says that it was entitled *On the Cross of the Lord*. On this matter, compare the preface of the monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur to the omitted sermons of Ambrose, where they say that this same homily was included by the editors of the Sixtine edition among the 514 sermons of Saint Ambrose and urge that, following Gennadius’s judgment, it be restored to Maximus.

Although in Vatican 1270 and in the manuscript formerly belonging to Santa Croce Minor Conventual, now Laurentian Library IV, Plut. XXXIII, it is inscribed under the name of the bishop of Milan, it is nevertheless numbered among the homilies of Maximus in two manuscripts of distinguished authority, 90 and 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, and in Laurentian X, Plut. XIV. In the latter its title is: “Here begins [the homily] on Holy Easter Day and on the Cross of the Lord”; in the Taurinensis it is stated more briefly: “Likewise, on the Cross of the Lord.”

The editors of Maximus’s works—Gymnicus, Galesinius, Cumdius, Raynaudus, and Margarinus—agree, and in their editions the homily bears this heading: “First Homily on the Passion and Cross of the Lord.”

[Col. 0339B] **ARGUMENT.**—Taking up the story told about Ulysses, he discusses Christ’s saving cross, teaching that in the Church it is the mast of the ship.

The fables of the age tell of that Ulysses who, tossed about for ten years by wanderings at sea, could not reach his homeland. When the course of his voyage brought him to a certain place where the cruel song of the Sirens resounded with sweet variety, [Note: In both Santa Croce in Jerusalem MSS the reading is “sweet song, cruel”; in Cod. 90 the word “sweetness” is found instead of “variety.”] they charmed those who approached with such seductive melody that they experienced not so much a spectacle of pleasure as a shipwreck of salvation.

Such was the delight of their song that whoever heard the sound of their voices, as though captured by a certain enticement, no longer made for the harbor he desired but proceeded toward destruction, [Note: Cod. Vatican 1270: “toward what he did not desire.”] which he did not desire.

Therefore, when Ulysses had encountered this sweet shipwreck and wished to avoid the danger of that sweetness, he is said to have stopped the ears of his companions with wax and tied himself to the ship’s mast. In this way they would be deprived of the perilous enticement of hearing, and the course of the voyage would carry him away from danger.

If, then, the fable tells of that Ulysses that the binding to the mast rescued him from danger, how much more must we proclaim what truly happened: namely, that today the tree of the cross has rescued the whole human race from the danger of death?

For from the moment Christ the Lord was fastened to the cross, we pass through the seductive dangers of the world as though with closed ears; we are neither held by the perilous hearing of the age nor do we turn the course of the better life toward the rocks of pleasure.

For the tree of the cross not only restores to his homeland the person bound to it, but also protects by the shadow of its power the companions placed around it. That the cross brings us back to our homeland after many wanderings, the Lord declares when he says to the thief hanging on the cross: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII).

That thief, who had long wandered and suffered shipwreck, could not otherwise return to the homeland of paradise, from which the first human being had departed, unless he had been tied to the tree. For the cross is a kind of tree on the ship of the Church, which alone remains unharmed amid all the world’s alluring and destructive shipwrecks.

In this ship, therefore, whoever either binds himself to the tree of the cross or closes his ears with the divine Scriptures will not fear the sweet storm of sensuality. For the figure of the Sirens is a certain image of the soft lust [Note: Both Santa Croce in Jerusalem MSS: “of pleasures.”] of pleasure, which by harmful blandishments weakens the steadfastness of the captured mind.

Therefore the Lord Christ hung upon the cross so that he might free the whole human race from the shipwreck of the world.

But, leaving aside the fable of Ulysses, which was invented rather than enacted, let us see whether we can find in the divine Scriptures a similar example which the Lord would later fulfill in person and which he had previously announced through his prophets. [Note: Both Santa Croce in Jerusalem MSS: “had previously set forth.”]

We read in the Old Testament (Numbers XXI) that when the holy Moses had led the children of Israel out of Egyptian captivity, and that same people was suffering under a severe attack by serpents in the desert, with no defense of weapons able to protect them, then the holy Moses, filled with the divine Spirit, raised up a bronze serpent fixed to wood among the crowds of the dying and commanded the people to place their hope of healing in that sign.

Through this there arose such a remedy against the bite of the asps that whoever had been wounded and either looked upon or placed his hope in that serpent-cross immediately received the remedy of salvation. The Lord also recalls this deed in the Gospel, saying: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so the Son of Man must be lifted up” (John III).

Therefore, if the serpent fastened to wood brought healing to the children of Israel, [Note: Cod. Santa Croce Minor: “brought such healing,” etc.] how much more does the Lord, crucified on the gallows, bestow salvation upon the peoples? [Col. 0340D] And if the figure accomplished so much, how much do we believe the reality accomplishes?

Therefore the serpent is crucified first—entirely fittingly, since the devil had first sinned against God, and should first be struck by the sentence of the cross. [Note: Cod. 90 Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “Christ is crucified on the wood.”] He is crucified on the wood. It was reasonably done so that, because the human being had been deceived in paradise through the tree of desire, the same human being might now be saved through the tree of wood, and the same material that had been the cause of death might now become the remedy of healing.

Then, after the serpent, the human being himself is crucified in the Savior, so that after the author the crime too might be punished. For by the first cross vengeance was taken upon the serpent; by the second, upon the serpent’s poison. That is: first the author himself is punished, and then his malignity is condemned.

For the venom which, through his persuasion, he had poured into the human being is now expelled and now healed. When the human being is given over to suffering, he is not handed over to death; rather, the crime of death in him is corrected. This is what the Lord accomplishes through the human nature he assumed: while the innocent one suffers, the disobedience of that diabolical transgression is corrected [Note: Cod. Vatican 1270: “is shattered”] in him, and thereafter he becomes free from guilt [Col. 0342A] and free from death.

Therefore, since we have the Lord Jesus, who freed us through his passion, let us always look upon him [Note: MSS Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Laurentian: “and let us place our hope in the sign of his wood.”] and hope for healing of our wounds through his sign.

That is, if perhaps the poison of avarice spreads through us, let us look upon him, and he heals us; if the lust of the scorpion pricks us, let us ask him, and he cures us; if the bites of earthly thoughts tear us, let us pray to that same one, and we live.

For these are the spiritual serpents of our souls, to trample which underfoot the Lord was crucified. Of them he himself says: “You will walk upon serpents and scorpions, and they will harm you in nothing” (Luke X).

[Note: Maximus used the fable of the Sirens to explain the mystery of the cross. Everyone knows that Homer was its inventor; through this splendid image he greatly commended Ulysses’ prudence, shrewdness, and firmness in eluding the allurements and dangers of pleasures. In the twelfth book of the *Odyssey* it is read from verses 47 to 54, and below more fully at verse 177. All commentators on Homer discuss it; among Latin authors, see Diodorus Siculus, Book III; Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book VII; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book XIV; Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, Book IV, meter 3; and Saint Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 17. Saint Maximus, in order to explain the mystery of the cross, set forth Ulysses’ ingenious device. For, tied to the mast and with his companions’ ears stopped, he escaped the Sirens’ snares and reached safely the place toward which he was heading. Christ, fastened to the cross and having completed the work of redemption, overcame the devil’s frauds and brought salvation to all. Maximus then passes from the fable to the truth of Scripture, preserving the character of the sacred writer and illuminating the mystery of the cross prefigured in the serpent.]

## HOMILY L. On the Cross of the Lord II

[Col. 0341]

### ADMONITION

The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, following Gennadius, judged that Maximus, not Ambrose, was also the author of this homily. Nor should the testimony of this most weighty writer be rejected merely because in three manuscripts of the twelfth century—the Vatican 1270, p. 27; 6451, p. 18; and IV Plut. XXXIII, formerly of Santa Croce Minor Conventual and now in the Laurentian Library—the name of Saint Ambrose is found.

For five excellent and ancient manuscripts are available to us in which we see the name of our holy Maximus written: the Sangallensis; 90 Santa Croce in Jerusalem, homily 36; 99 Santa Croce in Jerusalem, homily 59; Laurentian X, Plut. XIV, p. 298, “Likewise, on the Cross and Resurrection of the Lord”; and the Taurinensis, “Likewise, on the same [Cross] and the Burial of the Lord.”

The general agreement of the editors—Gymnicus, Galesinius, Cumdius, Raynaudus, and Margarinus—also supports this attribution. But Margarinus differs from the others concerning the heading. In their editions it reads: “On the Cross and Passion of the Lord.” In Margarinus: “Second Homily on the Cross and Burial of the Lord.”

Finally, I wish to warn readers that in our edition this same homily ends with these words: “He caused to spring forth all whom he held among the dead.” This is because the remaining material found in earlier editions belongs to the homily *On the Body of Christ*, as will be demonstrated in its proper place.

[Col. 0341B] **ARGUMENT.**—He again discusses the sign of the saving cross, by which, he says, the sea is cleft, the earth is cultivated, heaven is governed, and human beings are preserved.

Yesterday we said that the Lord’s cross brought salvation to the human race; and it is true. His passion is our redemption, his death is our life. He therefore endured all these evils so that we might experience every good; he therefore allowed cruelty to be exercised against himself so that he might bestow mercy upon us. He wished to be so good toward us that he had first been harsh toward himself.

For, taking away through the cross the injuries of the human race, he consumed them all in his passion, so that thereafter there might be nothing that could harm the human being. [Note: Cod. Vatican 6451: “anything that could harm a human being.”]

Great, therefore, is the mystery of the cross. And if we understand it, the world itself is also saved through this sign. For when the sea is cleft by sailors, a tree is first raised by them and a sail is spread, so that, when the Lord’s cross has been formed, the streams of the waters may be parted. By this secure sign of the Lord [Note: Both Santa Croce in Jerusalem MSS: “and by a secure sign.”] they seek the harbor of salvation and escape the danger of death.

For the suspended sail on the tree is a kind of figure of the mystery, as though Christ had been exalted upon the cross. Therefore, drawing confidence from the mystery, people disregard the storms of the winds and undertake the vows of their journey.

Just as the Church cannot stand without the cross, so the ship is weak without the tree. For immediately [Note: The Vatican manuscript: “immediately the devil also disturbs this.”] the devil troubles it, and the wind strikes it. But when the sign of the cross is raised, the devil’s iniquity is immediately driven back and the storm of the winds is stilled.

The good farmer also, when he prepares to turn the soil and seek nourishment for life, attempts to do so only through the sign of the cross. For when he fits the *dentale* (plough-beam) to the plough, fastens the *aures* (“ears”), and inserts the *stiva* (plough-handle), he imitates the form of the cross. [Note: Cod. 90 Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “the arrangement”; Cod. Vatican 1270: “the comparison.”] For the very joining together is a certain likeness of the Lord’s passion.

Heaven itself has also been arranged in the figure of this sign. For when it is divided into four parts—that is, east, west, south, and north—it is contained by what are, as it were, the four angles of the cross. [Note: Cod. Vatican: “it is contained. For the movement of the human being,” etc.]

The very movement of a human being, when he raises his hands, depicts a cross. Therefore we are commanded to pray with raised hands, so that by the gesture of our limbs also we may confess the Lord’s passion. For our prayer is heard more quickly when the body too imitates Christ, whom the mind proclaims.

The holy Moses also, by this example, when he was waging war against Amalek, overcame him not with weapons or iron but with hands raised to God. For thus it is written: “When Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed, but when he lowered his hands, Amalek grew strong” (Exodus XVII). [Note: Cod. Vatican 6451: “but whenever he lowered his hands slightly, Amalek grew strong.”]

By this sign of the Lord, then, the sea is cleft, the earth is cultivated, heaven is governed, and human beings are preserved. By this sign of the Lord, I say, the underworld too is unlocked. For from the moment that the human Lord Jesus, who carried that very cross, was buried in the earth, the earth, as though split open and plowed by him, [Note: Both Santa Croce in Jerusalem MSS: “and the earth plowed open.”] caused to spring forth all whom it held among the dead. [Note: Here the sermon ends in Cod. Vatican 6451; what follows belongs to the homily *On the Body of Christ*.]

## HOMILY LI. On the Holy Thief I

[Col. 0343]

### ADMONITION

There is great disagreement among writers concerning the author, the title, and the beginning of this homily. The scribes who inserted it into the Vallicellian II and Vatican 6452 manuscripts thought it should be attributed to Saint Leo the Great. But the Ballerini brothers, in their celebrated edition of that holy pontiff’s works, judged these manuscripts worthless.

In Vatican Palatine 4951 the author’s name is omitted. Gillotius, the Parisian editor of the Ambrosian works, placed it among the sermons of Ambrose, and the editors of the Roman Sixtine edition followed him.

We, however, maintain that it should be attributed to Maximus. There are certainly many reasons for this judgment. The connection with the preceding homily is sufficiently clear; the style is plainly Maximian; the method of citing passages of sacred Scripture is certainly peculiar to Maximus; and the more distinguished manuscript witnesses—the Sangallensis, 99 Santa Croce in Jerusalem, the Taurinensis, and Laurentian X, Plut. XIV—have led us to this conclusion.

We have been confirmed in it all the more because the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur advise, in their collection of the sermons of Saint Ambrose, that this homily should be sought among the works of Maximus. Gymnicus, Galesinius, Cumdius, Raynaudus, and Margarinus likewise attribute it to Maximus.

So much for the author of this homily. Now for the title. In the Sangallensis and Taurinensis manuscripts, and in Gymnicus, Galesinius, Raynaudus, Cumdius, and Margarinus, it is: “On the Holy Thief.” In Laurentian X: “On the Holy Passion.” In 99 Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “On Holy Easter Day.” In Vatican Palatine 4951: “On the Faith of the Holy Thief, who Confessed the Lord on the Cross.”

We thought that the title in common circulation should be adopted, which, as we have observed, is “On the Holy Thief.”

The place concerning the beginning of the homily remains. In Vatican 6452 and Vallicellian II it is as follows: “Your love hears at the present time, brothers, what it is that this thief, with the Lord fixed upon the cross, not only obtains forgiveness of his sins but is also granted the delights of paradise,” etc.

In the Sixtine edition of the works of Saint Ambrose: “Since today’s Gospel reading has mentioned the thief, let us see,” etc.

We have followed neither of these readings. We approved the one that is found in the more distinguished manuscripts and is supported by the agreement of the editors.

[Col. 0343B] **ARGUMENT.**—The reasons are discussed why the repentant thief, crucified with Christ, so quickly merited paradise from him.

Because yesterday we mentioned the thief, let us see who this thief is who, while the Lord was fixed upon the cross, not only obtained forgiveness of his sins but was also granted the delights of paradise: so that he who had been condemned to punishment on account of his crimes might, on account of his faith, be transferred [Note: Codex Vat. 4951 reads “into glory.”] to glory, and the cross which he endured might be for him not so much a condemnation to punishment as an opportunity for salvation.

[Note: For while he was placed upon the cross, he believed our Lord Christ to be crucified, and therefore he who shares in the fellowship of the Passion is granted a share in paradise.—Maximus must be vindicated from the injurious criticism of Remigius Cellier, who, in volume XIV of his *Sacred History*, while reporting the substance of this homily, maligns our holy bishop as though he had taught that the thief hanging upon the cross was justified by faith alone. Maximus clearly had another intention when he adduces several reasons by which the thief obtained from Christ forgiveness of sins and the glory of paradise. “Great,” he says, “brothers, and manifold is the reason.” First he brings forward the devotion of faith, that is, the perfect assent of mind and heart by which the thief believed Christ, suffering with him, to be God wholly free from every fault, and to have willed to undergo punishment and death for human beings in order to procure their salvation. The thief did not think about his present punishment, but about avoiding the future one. Accordingly, although he saw Christ afflicted by the same punishment, he directed his prayers and vows toward him; and, beyond faith in his majesty and power, he showed himself lifted up by great hope that he would be saved by Christ. “He begins to desire more,” Maximus says, “what he hopes for than to feel what he suffers.” Truly, Christ’s cross, which appeared to others a scandal, the thief regarded as the power by which, once guilt had been erased, the kingdom of God was to be restored. Therefore, suffused with these illuminations, the thief made that noble confession by which, as Saint Leo the Great says, he deserved to hear, not so much from the wood of the cross as from the throne of mercy, that he would become a participant in Christ’s glory. “Today you will be with me in paradise.” But the thief’s faith and hope did not procure this judgment of divine mercy for him so much as did the love with which, amid his sufferings, he burned toward the Lord: “For he understood,” Maximus continues, “that he was receiving these blows for the sins of others and enduring these wounds for the crimes of others . . . and therefore he began to love more after he recognized his own wounds in Christ’s body.” Again: “Thus, while placed upon the cross and seeing his bruising, the thief loves God more”; and below: “A wondrous thing: the thief loves Christ more upon the cross than Judas loved him at the supper.” Saint Maximus then also teaches that the thief recognized that the whole Passion of the Lord took place by Christ’s own will; this knowledge inflamed him all the more to love Christ. Since, therefore, Maximus commends not faith alone but also the thief’s hope and love, we consider it injurious to him whenever he is said to have taught that the thief was justified by the excellence of faith rather than by faith working together with love.]

For while placed upon the cross [Col. 0345A] he believed our Lord Christ [Note: The words “our Lord” are absent from Vatican Codex 6452] to be crucified; 157 and therefore he who partakes in the fellowship of the Passion is granted a share in paradise. For the blessed thief, while undergoing punishment, obtains the heavenly kingdom. Behold, he is called guilty, [Note: Vatican Codex 6452 reads: “Behold, he is called guilty, for whom it was advantageous to be condemned at that time; for he would not have reached glory unless he had been handed over to punishment.” The same reading occurs in Vatican Codex 4951 and Codex 90 of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.] just as it was advantageous for him to be condemned for a time. [Note: The same Codex of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads: “It was advantageous for him at that time.
