For he would not have reached glory if he had not been handed over to punishment.”] For he would not have reached glory if he had not been handed over to punishment.

Let us see, I say, why one guilty of so many crimes deserved paradise from the Savior so quickly, when others, with many years of tears and frequent fasts, scarcely obtain forgiveness of their sins. Great, brothers, and manifold is the reason: first, because this thief was so suddenly transformed by the devotion of faith that he despised his present punishment and begged forgiveness for the future, and believed that it was more useful for him to ask concerning the eternal judgment than [Note: Vatican Codex 6452 reads: “than to ask concerning such a punishment”; Vatican Palatine Codex 4951 reads: “for, recalling his crimes and repenting, he begins to desire more . . .”] to ask concerning temporal punishment [Col. 0345B]; for, remembering his crimes and repenting, he begins to desire more [Note: All the Latin editors correct the text to *dolere* (“to grieve”); but it is not grief, rather love, that is aroused by what is hoped for.] what he hopes for than to feel what he suffers. [Note: Vatican Palatine Codex 4951 reads: “For he could have begged more earnestly to be spared his present punishment, unless he had thought more about future punishments—he who had once believed in Christ. Next . . .”] For he who had once believed in Christ could have begged more earnestly to be spared his present punishment, unless he had thought more about future punishments. [Note: Vatican Codex 6452 reads: “Next, another point contributing to his greater merit before grace is that he believed Christ, placed upon the cross, to be Lord, and the Passion . . .”]

Next, this contributes to the greater merit of his grace: he believed Christ, placed upon the cross, to be Lord; and the Passion, which became a scandal to others [Note: Codex of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads “causes scandal,”] became an advance in faith for him. For the Passion of the cross was a scandal to many, as the Apostle says: “But we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews indeed a scandal, and to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. I). Rightly, therefore, he deserves paradise who did not think Christ’s cross a scandal but a power; [Note: Vatican Codex 6452 reads: “For the Apostle says this, calling Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. Quite rightly.”] for the same Apostle says: “But to the Jews who are called, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (ibid.). [Col. 0345C]

Quite rightly, then, the Lord grants this man paradise, because the one whom Judas Iscariot had sold in the garden of paradise, this man confesses upon the gallows of the cross. [Note: Vatican Palatine Codex 4951 reads: “A wondrous thing: the thief confesses and honors the suffering one whom Judas destroyed by kissing; from the one, kisses are given for destruction, from the other, the wounds of the cross are proclaimed; for he says: ‘Remember . . .’”]

A wondrous thing: the thief confesses him whom the disciple denied; a wondrous thing, I say: [Col. 0346A] the thief honors the suffering one whom Judas betrayed with a kiss: 158 from the one, the caresses of peace are sold; from the other, the wounds of the cross are proclaimed. For he says: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII).

[Note: Codex of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads: “This is the full devotion of true faith, and so forth: when the blood flowing from the Lord’s wounds is seen, forgiveness is then sought from his power, and so forth”; Palatine Codex 4951 and Vatican Codex 6452 read: “This, then, is full devotion, and so forth.”]

This is the full devotion of faith: when the blood pouring from the Lord’s wounds is seen, forgiveness is then sought from his power; when his humility is seen, his divinity is then held in greater reverence; when he is thought to have been delivered over to death, the honor due to that king is then paid him. [Note: “For this faithful thief did not believe him to be about to die whom he announces as about to reign,” and so forth.—Maximus is entirely occupied here with proclaiming the converted thief’s faith: he confessed Christ, suffering with him, to be God, and asked him for forgiveness of sins and paradise. Among the other things by which he commended him, Saint Maximus said that the thief did not believe Christ was going to die. This must be understood of the necessity of dying, from which Christ as God was free; unless he had willed it, he would not have died. For the thief knew, as the holy teacher says below, that the whole Passion of God took place by Christ’s own will: he pitied the fallen race of Adam, and its salvation was the reason why he suffered. Therefore, believing in him, the thief asks to be washed in his blood and to become a participant in so great a benefit.]

For this faithful thief did not believe him to be about to die whom he announces as about to reign; he does not think him subject to the underworld whom he confesses to rule in [Note: The same Vatican codex reads “in heaven.”] heaven; he does not suppose him to be held in Tartarus from whom he also asks to be set free. Let him behold, if he will, Christ’s gaping wounds; let him gaze upon his blood flowing forth [Col. 0346B]; yet he believes him to be God whom he knows not to be guilty; he confesses him to be just whom he does not remember as a sinner. For he says to the other thief who was reproaching him: “We indeed receive what is just and deserved for our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong” (ibid.).

[Note: Vatican Codex 6452 reads: “He would endure them. He knew also that these were not his wounds but . . .”]

For he understood that Christ was receiving these blows for the sins of others and enduring these wounds for the crimes of others; and he knew that those wounds in Christ’s body were not Christ’s wounds but the thief’s. Therefore he began to love more after he recognized his own wounds in Christ’s body. The prophet says: “For he himself bears our weaknesses and suffers for us; but we thought him to be in pain; by his bruising we were healed” (Isa. LIII).

[Note: Codex of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads “his bruises.”] Therefore, while placed upon the cross and seeing his bruising, the thief loves God more. [Note: Vatican Codices 6452 and Vallicellianus read: “The thief loved the Lord.”] A wondrous thing: the thief loves Christ more upon the cross [Col. 0346C] than Judas loved him at the supper. The one, through food, ensnares the Master; this man believed in the Lord through suffering, as the prophet says: “The one who ate my bread has magnified his treachery against me” [Note: Vatican Palatine Codex 4951 reads “has amplified.”] (Ps. XL).

This thief therefore recognized that the whole Passion of the Lord took place by Christ’s own will, and that it lay within his power either to hand over his soul to death 159 [Note: Vatican Palatine Codex 4951 reads “or into death”] or to return again to life, as the Lord himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power 160 to take it up again” (John X). Indeed, he judged him so free from the laws of hell that he even asked to be freed from them himself.

## HOMILY LII. On the Same Holy Thief II

[Col. 0347]

### NOTICE

161 At first glance everyone will recognize that this homily is related to the preceding one, since the faith of the same thief is commended and his excellence is illustrated by new arguments. The preceding homily, therefore, having been vindicated for Saint Maximus by the unquestionable support of manuscripts and editors, takes this one as its companion. Nor would it be necessary for us to assemble particular proofs to demonstrate this, unless we were striving to establish a stronger foundation for the truth.

We therefore cite four codices: Santa Croce in Gerusalemme 99, homily 48; the Sangallensis, homily 65; Laurentianus X, Plut. XIV, p. 285, with the title “The following likewise”; and the Taurinensis, with the title “Likewise, on the same subject, on blessed Peter and the maidservant.” The editors mentioned above assigned this homily a similar heading. Gymnicus, p. 129, has: “On the same thief, and on the apostle Peter and the doorkeeper maidservant, homily 2.” Galesinius likewise, p. 126; Raynaudus, p. 215; Cumdius, vol. II, p. 1335; and Margarinus in *Bibliotheca Maxima*, vol. VI, p. 23.

Armed with these supports, we can easily accuse the Parisian editor and the Roman editors of falsely attributing it, since, like their predecessors, they reprinted it under the name of Ambrose; as did Vatican Codex 6452 and Vallicellianus II, which bear the same name. The title of this homily in the Sixtine edition, however, is peculiar: “The Collect, which the Church read today, dearest brothers, is as follows: ‘O God, from whom Judas also received the punishment of his guilt,’” and so forth.

[Col. 0347B]

### ARGUMENT

First, the excellence of faith is discussed in general; then the faith of the holy thief, who was justified because, confident in Christ’s divinity and will, he asked that he himself be set free; finally, the apostles’ fear during Christ’s Passion and the doorkeeper maidservant.

You remember, brothers, that I explained why this thief, hardened by the wickedness of so many crimes and condemned by the confession of his offenses, was able to deserve paradise upon the very gallows of punishment, and was saved with such speed that grace anticipated his sins before punishment, and that he began to glory in his evils before he could be punished; for he does not suffer punishment while he deserves paradise.

Christ says to Peter: “You cannot follow me now; you will follow afterward” (John XIII). But to this man he says: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII).

[Note: Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads: “As that one, being overly hasty, is delayed, and this one . . .”; Vatican Codex 6452 reads “hasty.”]

[Note: “As that one is loved as a disciple, and this one is invited as a companion; that one is still reserved for the reward, while this one is loved even for companionship.”—Maximus refers to Peter’s present condition: he was to be tested in the ministry of the Church entrusted to him, and to the thief’s confession, full of faith and love. For he had said: “We indeed receive what is just, for we receive what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong.” Then, turning to Jesus, he begged him to grant forgiveness and salvation: “Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII). Since the thief had thus given so splendid a testimony concerning the Savior’s divinity and had burned with love for him, he deserved to be invited to the reward and to be made by Christ a companion of heavenly glory: “Today you will be with me in paradise.” Peter’s crown, however, was delayed because he was to found the Church and undergo the struggle of martyrdom.]

That one is delayed as a disciple, while this one is invited as a companion; that one is still reserved for the reward, [Note: The same Codex of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme and Vatican Codex 6452 read: “while this one is loved even for companionship.”] while this one is loved even for companionship.

“You cannot,” he says, “follow me now.” It is impossible for Peter to follow the Lord; yet it is easy [Note: The same Vatican codex reads: “It is also easy for this man to be with the Lord. ‘Today,’ he says, ‘he will be with me in paradise. He is not delayed to another time, nor reserved for another day; at the very hour when paradise received the Lord . . .’”] for this thief to be with the Lord. “Today you will be with me in paradise.” [Col. 0348B] He is not delayed to another time, nor reserved for another day; at the very hour when paradise receives [Note: The editors have “at the very hour when paradise received God”; we have followed the better reading of Vatican Codex 6452.] the Lord, it also receives the thief: one suffered for the salvation of all, and the gate of immortality is opened equally to two.

[Note: Codices of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, Vaticanus, and Vallicellianus XI read “such great.”]

But faith bestowed all this glory upon the thief. For faith is what covers sins, conquers crimes, and makes the guilty innocent. Although the guilt of wrongdoers is great, the grace of faith is greater: it is more significant to have believed Christ than to have sinned against the world; and it is more meritorious to have hoped for forgiveness from the Lord than to have contracted guilt from the world. For just as unbelief makes one criminal, so faith makes one innocent.

Finally, after Judas lost faith, he lost the innocence of his apostleship: he became guilty of every crime after he denied the Lord of all virtues. Therefore, just as it is sufficient for this man’s guilt that he abandoned Christ, so for that man’s innocence it is sufficient that he believed in the Lord. Thus faith makes thieves innocent, and [Note: Vatican Codex 6451 reads: “unbelief makes an apostle criminal. Truly great and marvelous is the faith which believed Christ crucified more than it punished him. For here is the whole pattern of salvation: it recognizes the Savior as the Lord of majesty precisely when his humility is seen.”] unbelief makes apostles criminal.

Great, therefore, and perfect was the faith in that thief, [Note: Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads: “Truly great and marvelous is the faith which believed Christ crucified to be glorified more than punished,” and so forth.] a great and marvelous faith which believed Christ crucified to be glorified rather than punished. 163 For in this lies the whole pattern of salvation: it recognizes the Savior as the Lord of majesty [Note: Codex of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads “recognized.”] when he is seen to be suffering in the endurance of humility. Hence the Apostle says: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. II).

This, I say, is perfect faith: to believe Christ upon the cross not guilty. [Note: The same Codex of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads: “to believe Christ upon the cross to be God, not guilty.”]

Therefore that thief was justified, because, while the Savior stood upon the gallows and the Jews mocked him, [Note: The same Codex of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads: “and were saying as though he were a criminal,” and so forth.] saying, “Save yourself, if you can” (Matt. XXVII), he, confident in Christ’s divinity and secure concerning his will, asked rather to be set free.

Great, I say, was the faith in that thief [Note: Codex of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads “was.”] and comparable to that of the holy apostles—except that perhaps he even preceded them. For he who preceded them in devotion also preceded them in reward: the thief reached paradise before the apostles. Finally, Peter follows the Lord, while this man accompanies him. But the Lord grants both the service of reward and the reward itself according to faith and merit.

For all the disciples, as we read (Matt. XXVI), trembled during the Savior’s Passion; they all [Col. 0350A] 164 almost abandoned him when he was betrayed. It happened as it was written: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zech. XIII). [Note: See Augustine, *On the Soul and Its Origin*, book I, chapter 9, where the thief’s outstanding faith and confession are compared with the apostles’ fear and flight.]

Finally, even after being warned, Peter could not keep the faith: he fell as many times as he had been warned not to fall; and unless the Lord had set a limit to his denial at the third time, perhaps, if questioned more often, he would have denied him more often. For the Savior’s Passion brought such fear upon the disciples that what Christ had foretold to the apostle was undone by a maidservant, and the doorkeeper prevailed more strongly toward unbelief than the apostle toward caution.

She was not a good doorkeeper, who shut Peter inside the high priest’s house in order to shut him out from faith in the Savior. Eve brought Adam in badly; the maidservant brought Peter in badly. The former shut Adam out from paradise, the latter shut Peter out from Christ. The former deceived her husband by her persuasion, the latter ensnared the apostle by her question. The former drove Adam to transgress, the latter drove Peter [Note: Codex of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads: “this one compelled Peter to deny.”] to deny. And the same sex, serving in the office of doorkeeper in both cases, either excludes from life or shuts in for death.

## HOMILY LIII. On Peter’s Repentance and the Doorkeeper Maidservant

[Col. 0349]

### NOTICE

165 We read that this homily is ascribed to Saint Maximus in eight codices. The oldest is the Sangallensis, homily 66; next comes the Ratisponensis of Saint Emmeram, p. 23; the Martinensis, homily 54; Laurentianus X, Plut. XIV, p. 76; and the Taurinensis, with the title “Likewise, on Peter’s repentance and on the maidservant”; the others have “The following likewise.”

Codex Casinensis CXI, p. 11 verso, and Augiensis XV do not agree in their inscriptions. In the first one reads “On Peter’s repentance”; in the other, “On the holy day of Easter.” It is also found in the Ambrosian Codex H 146, written more than eight hundred years ago, which we name in eighth place.

Therefore Vatican Codex 1270, the only one in which it is dedicated to Saint Ambrose, and the Parisian and Roman editors, who attribute this homily to the same holy teacher, do not possess enough authority to overturn the agreement of the many manuscripts; especially since Gymnicus himself, p. 133; Galesinius, p. 127; Raynaudus, p. 216; Cumdius, vol. II, p. 1336; and Margarinus in *Bibliotheca Maxima*, vol. VI, p. 23, contradict them.

Following these witnesses, we have accepted the title of the homily: “On Peter’s repentance and the doorkeeper maidservant.” The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, in the frequently cited preface to Saint Ambrose’s sermons, observe that everything loudly proclaims Maximus to be the author of this homily, and they declare that they hold the same opinion concerning the other homilies collected with it.

[Col. 0349C]

### ARGUMENT

On the customary use of the female sex for deception; on Adam deceived by Eve and Peter by the doorkeeper; on the repentance of both; and on the excellence of tears. Let us cure our sins by Peter’s example: after his tears he was appointed shepherd and received others to govern.

We have said, brothers, that, after the likeness of Eve, a woman—the doorkeeper—also deceived Peter; and just as a woman ensnared Adam, so a woman also overcame the apostle. For the female sex is accustomed to deception: the devil recognizes in the doorkeeper the little vessel of his fraud, [Note: In the Ambrosian codex, *quia* (“because”) is absent; it is also absent from the cited codices of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, the Martinensis, and Vatican Codex 1270, fol. 28 verso, which reads: “he recognized that faithful men are attacked only through . . .”] because he is accustomed to attack faithful men only through a woman.

There the devil drives Adam away through Eve (Gen. III); here he conquers Peter through the doorkeeper. For, as we read, the devil was in the paradise of delights; nor was he absent, as we understand, in the praetorium of the Jews. There Satan, the serpent, threatened; here Judas, the snake, pressed forward.

Thus the same likeness of deception exists in Peter as existed in Adam, because the likeness of the commandment is also the same. For each received a commandment from the Lord: Adam was not to touch, [Note: In the Martinensis, the conjunction “and” is absent.] and the apostle was not to deny. The former was not to presume upon the tree of knowledge; the latter was not to pass by the cross of wisdom. But, transgressing the commandment, both sin in like manner: the one tastes what is forbidden; the other says what is unbecoming. Yet Peter’s denial is easier [Note: The Martinensis adds “is.”] than Adam’s transgression; for help comes more quickly to the apostle than to the first-created man.

God seeks out the former, Adam, wandering at evening; the Lord seeks out the latter, Peter, denying at the crowing of the rooster. Adam, guilty of his deed, was ashamed in his nakedness [Col. 0351A]; Peter, conscious of his words, groaned when reproved. The one, as though detected, hastens into hiding; the other, as though corrected, bursts forth into tears.

As though he were hiding and concealing himself from the Divinity, Adam hears: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. III). This does not mean that Adam could escape the Lord’s sight, but that, for a sinful conscience, there is no safe or secure place while it fears discovery.

The Lord looked upon Peter and corrected his error by opening his eyes (Luke XXII). Rightly does he correct him through his eyes, because it is written: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are attentive to their prayers” (Ps. XXXIII).

Therefore Peter burst forth [Note: The Martinensis reads “into tears.”] into tears, praying nothing with his voice. [Note: “For I find that he wept; I do not find what he said. I read his tears, but I do not read his satisfaction.”—Maximus took this from Ambrose, book X. Some people appear to misuse this passage of Ambrose in attacking the precept of auricular confession in the sacrament of penance. No one is unaware that they have been refuted by the monks of Saint Maur: they have taught that Ambrose is not speaking here of sacramental confession but of private repentance, which ought to begin with tears and then proceed to the accusation of one’s guilt and the request for forgiveness. “I find,” Ambrose says, “why Peter remained silent: lest a request for forgiveness so quickly should offend more; first one must weep, then pray.” See the commentary on book X of Luke’s Gospel, Paris edition, 1790, p. 1523. Maximus spoke in the same spirit, and the same doctrine is defended against the criticism of the heterodox.]

For I find that he wept; I do not find what he said. I read his tears; I do not read his satisfaction. Peter rightly both wept and remained silent, because what is customarily mourned is not customarily excused, and what cannot be defended can be washed clean. For a tear washes away the offense [Col. 0351B] which shame forbids one to confess aloud. Tears therefore serve modesty and salvation alike; they are not ashamed when asking, and they obtain [Note: The Lambacensis reads “by watering.”] what they request when pleading.

Tears, I say, are in a certain way silent prayers: they do not ask forgiveness, yet they deserve it; they do not state the case, yet they obtain mercy. Indeed, the prayers of tears are more useful than those of words, because speech may sometimes deceive in prayer, [Note: The Codex of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads: “tears deceive in nothing.”] whereas a tear never deceives at all. Speech sometimes does not reveal the whole matter; a tear always discloses the whole feeling.

Therefore Peter no longer uses the speech [Note: The Martinensis adds: “with which he had lied when he sinned.”] by which he had lied, by which he had sinned, by which he had lost faith; lest, through the very means he had used to deny, he should not be believed when confessing. [Note: His denial was external, not an expression of the feeling of his soul, which burned when he said to his Lord: “I will lay down my life for you.”] Hence he prefers to weep his case rather than speak it, and to confess with tears what he had denied with his voice. [Note: The Ambrosian codex reads: “and confess with tears him whom he had denied with his voice.”]

I also find another reason why Peter remained silent: lest a request for forgiveness should so quickly, through shamelessness, offend more than it obtained. For the person who asks more modestly is accustomed to deserve indulgence more quickly. 168 In every fault, therefore, one must first weep, and then pray.

We already know from this example how we should cure our sins. [Note: The Martinensis reads: “In this example, behold, nothing that the apostle denied harmed us.”] Behold: nothing harmed us that the apostle denied, and what he corrected profited us greatly.

Finally, let us imitate him when he says elsewhere: when the Lord asked him for the third time, “Simon, do you love me?” he answered [Note: The Martinensis omits “for the third time.”] for the third time: “Lord, you know that I love you.” The Lord said: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI).

And this happened for the third time, as a compensation for his earlier [Note: The Ambrosian, Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, and Vatican Codex 1270 read: “it profited as a compensation for his earlier error,” and so forth.] error. He who had denied the Lord three times confesses him three times; and as often as he had contracted guilt by sinning, so often he obtains grace by loving.

See, therefore, how much weeping profited Peter: before he wept, he fell; after he wept, he was chosen. He who before his tears had been a transgressor was appointed shepherd after his tears, and received others to govern [Note: The Lambacensis reads “whom he did not correct”; Vatican Codex 1270: “who had not governed himself.”] although previously he had not governed himself.

## HOMILY LIV. On the Same Apostle Peter

[Col. 0351]

### NOTICE

I judge that this homily, which clearly establishes Peter’s primacy, should not be ascribed to Saint Ambrose, as it is read in two codices—Vatican Codex 1277, p. 62, and the Urbevetanus—and in certain editions, but rather to Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin.

This may be inferred from its connection with the preceding homily, from its similar style of composition, from the accumulation of antitheses characteristic of Maximus, and from the number of codices in which his name is written. These codices are: the Sangallensis, homily 67; Santa Croce in Gerusalemme 99, homily 50; the Taurinensis; Laurentianus X, Plut. XIV, p. 288; and IV, Plut. XXXIII, formerly in the library of Santa Croce Minore Convent, now in the Laurentian Library.

The Vatican Codex 1277 mentioned above has the following inscription: “Sermon on the feast of Saint Peter proper”; another Vatican codex, 6451, has: “Sermon on the chains of Saint Peter.” Neither title can be correct. The first cannot be correct because the feast day of saints ordinarily means the day of their passage into glory; the second cannot be correct because nothing concerning the festival of Peter’s chains is read in this homily.

The Taurinensis has: “Likewise, on the same Saint Peter”; the others have “The following,” namely, the same homily which concerns Peter’s repentance. Alcuin, p. 336 of the Venice edition of 1537, placed the same homily under Maximus’s name among the sermons for the feast of Saints Peter and Paul.

Gymnicus, p. 136; Galesinius, p. 128; Raynaudus, p. 216; Cumdius, vol. II, p. 1237; and Margarinus in *Bibliotheca Maxima*, vol. VI, p. 24, ascribed it to Saint Maximus under the designated title “On the Same Apostle Peter.” We preserve both the title and the same beginning of the homily—which others altered at will—as we read them in the Maurist appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine, no. 192, p. 226, Antwerp edition, 1700, and in Vatican Codex 6451.

[Col. 0353A] 169

### ARGUMENT

Peter is the shepherd of the flock and the rock of the Churches, containing the framework and mass of the whole Christian work, in fellowship with Christ in that work. On the faith and love of Peter walking upon the sea.

[Note: [Col. 0353D] Vatican Codex 6451 and the Urbevetan manuscript begin the homily thus: “You heard, dearest brothers, that the most blessed Peter, during the Savior’s Passion, etc.”]

We established on the preceding Sunday that St. Peter had advanced through his errors during the Savior’s Passion and that, after he denied the Lord [Note: Codices Vatican 1277 and 6451, as well as the Urbevetan manuscript, omit “God.”], he had become better. For he became more faithful after he had wept that he had lost his faith; and therefore he found greater grace than he had lost. For, as a good shepherd, he received the flock to guard, so that he who had previously been weak for himself might become a support for all [Note: The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads “for all human beings” instead of “for all.”]; and he who himself had faltered under the temptation of questioning [Note: The Urbevetan Codex reads: “and he who himself had denied in the interrogation”] might establish the others through the steadfastness of faith.

Finally, because of the firmness of his devotion, he is called the “rock” of the Churches, as the Lord says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16). For he is called “rock” because he first laid the foundations of faith among the nations and, like an immovable stone, contains the structure and mass of the whole Christian work. “Rock” [Note: The Codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Urbevetan manuscript read *ergo* (“therefore”) instead of *autem* (“but”).] is said of Peter because of his devotion, while “rock” is applied to the Lord because of his power, as the Apostle says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10). Rightly does he share the name who shares the work; for in the same house Peter laid the foundation, Peter plants, and the Lord gives the increase; the Lord supplies the irrigation (Matthew 4). For Peter advances through his temptations, rejoices through his tears, and grows through his dangers.

Thus, in the sea, while the rash traveler walks upon the waves, he falters in his step but grows stronger in his devotion; he is endangered in body, but does not fall in devotion; he sinks with his feet, but is sustained by Christ’s right hand [Note: The Minor Codex of Santa Croce reads *sustentabat* (“sustained”), while the Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, Vatican 6451, and the Urbevetan manuscript read *sustinebat* (“was sustaining”).]. Faith sustains him whom the wave was engulfing; and the love of the Savior strengthens him whom the storm of the waves was troubling. [Note: The Urbevetan manuscript reads “He was walking.”]

For Peter walked upon the sea more through love than through his feet. He did not see where to place the imprint of his feet, but he saw where to fix the imprint of charity. Set upon the sea, he gazes upon the Lord; and, led by love of him, he descends into the sea. He does not consider the slipping waters or the flowing currents; and while he looks upon Christ, he does not look upon the element. Through faith he believes that even amid the waves he will find solid footing [Col. 0354A]. Although the sea is tossed by the waves and the deep by the winds, Peter’s path, which leads to the Lord, is nevertheless confirmed and not disturbed [Note: The Minor Codex of Santa Croce, the Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, and Vatican 1277 read “is not disturbed.”]. Peter therefore walks upon the waters, and beneath his feet the yielding wave does not give way.

We read in the Old Testament (Exodus 14) that the children of Israel walked through the Red Sea by dry paths, and that, for the safety of those walking, lest the wave should slip beneath them, it was changed into a kind of solidity. [Note: The same Minor Codex of Santa Croce, the Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, and Vatican 6451 read: “How much better here, where, while Peter walks…”] How much better here, where, while Peter walks, the wave is neither changed, nor slips away, nor is the water solidified, nor does it retreat. Better, I say, is that condition in which the same wave both surges and sustains, in which the same whirlpool both engulfs and serves. There, so that the people of Israel might be carried across the sea, nature had lost its course; here, Peter is carried upon the waters, but the current does not lose its course [Note: Vatican 1277 reads “and its course”; Vatican 6451 reads “and the current did not lose its course.”].

The apostle, therefore, a rash traveler, takes the road of a new journey. At one moment he climbs the mass of the curving whirlpool; at another, as the hollow subsides, the wave descends; and amid the sea’s waves, neither ascent nor descent is lacking from that journey [Note: The Minor Codex of Santa Croce reads “the ascent of that journey.”]. But when, troubled by the winds and driven by storms, he begins to fear what he had believed [Note: The Laurentian Codex reads “he who believed begins to fear”], immediately the whirlpool is withdrawn from him and the wave is drawn away; for as soon as faith grows weary, the path begins to gape open [Note: The two Laurentian codices, the Minor Codex of Santa Croce, and the Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read “for as soon as faith grows weary.”]. Then, crying out, he begs the Lord Jesus to save him. The Savior takes him by the hand [Note: The Urbevetan Codex reads “whom the Savior frees after taking him by the hand”], delivers him, and rebukes him, saying: “Man of little faith, why did you doubt?” [The printed text has *dubistati*, evidently an OCR or typographical error for *dubitasti*.]

That is: Why are you of such little faith that, having begun to walk upon the sea by believing [Note: The Codices Vatican 1277 and 6451, and the Urbevetan manuscript, read “upon the sea”], you did not cross it by persevering? For it is written: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10). But while you hesitate and doubt, you have lost the road upon which you had entered [Col. 0354C]. Why, I ask, are you of such little faith that you do not reach your destination with the faith by which you began to come?

Understand, therefore, that in the sea faith was carrying you, while faithlessness was drowning you. Thus, brothers, while St. Peter is tossed, while he is submerged, while he is endangered, he reaches the Lord. He shows us that we hasten to Christ only through dangers; for there are many diabolical waves in this world and many shipwrecks of temptations. We can be delivered from them only if the Savior stretches out his hand to us when we cry aloud. Let us therefore not cease to cry out to the Lord; he will not refuse his customary help [Note: The Codices Vatican 6451 and the Urbevetan manuscript add: “Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever.”]

[Note: What Maximus has gathered together in this homily concerning Peter’s primacy in the Church should be weighed in a brief consideration. First, he asserts that Peter wept over his guilt so deeply that he received greater grace than he had lost, and that he who was the first to deny was also the first to confess. Second, he praises in the apostle the firmness of devotion—namely, his intimate and steadfast love toward the Lord—by which he deserved to be constituted the rock of the Church, or the foundation of the new spiritual building, and to rejoice in the similarity and propriety of his name with that of Christ himself. Third, he teaches that Peter first laid the foundations of faith among the nations and that upon him, as upon an immovable rock, the entire Christian work was raised and sustained. Fourth, he asserts that what Peter plants in the Church—that is, what he sows through the teaching of the word of God—grows through heavenly irrigations and reaches maturity. Thus the supreme power, preeminence, truth of teaching, and universal governance of the mystical body entrusted by Christ to Peter are confirmed.]

## CLASS TWO. SUMMER HOMILIES FOR THE LITURGICAL YEAR

## HOMILY 55. On the Feast of Easter I

### ADMONITION

It may perhaps seem strange that this homily, so elegant and composed with such great learning, has come down to us in only seven manuscripts, of which three agree in attributing it to Maximus, while the others differ among themselves. For the two Vatican codices, 1270 and 1240, do contain it, but lack the author’s name. In a third Vatican codex, 4951, page 100, the following inscription appears on the reverse: “Sermon of St. Faustinus, bishop”; and in another hand there is written in the margin: “The author should be sought.”

It is known to learned men that the distinguished Edmund Martène and Ursin Durand, in volume 5 of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, Lyon edition of 1717, published this homily under the same name of St. Faustinus, bishop. They acknowledge that they copied it from a manuscript codex of Saint-Allyre at Clermont; but they maintain that neither of the two Faustini whom they name was the author of this discourse, and consequently demonstrate that the attribution is plainly spurious.

It also exists in Codex II, page 21, of the library formerly belonging to the Minor Santa Croce and now in the Laurentian Library, where it is attributed to St. Augustine; nevertheless, the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of St. Maur do not number it among Augustine’s sermons. Accordingly, since three codices of unquestionable authority agree in attributing the homily to Maximus—namely the Turin codex, where it bears the title “Also, Sermon V on Easter,” the Casinensis CXI, page 4, and the Ambrosian codex—we assign it to St. Maximus.

All the editors—Gymnicus, page 140; Galesinius, page 130; Combefisius, volume 5, page 478; Cumdius, volume 1, page 1443; Raynaudus, page 217; and Margarinus in *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume 6, page 24—give it the title “The First [Homily] on the Feast of Easter” and place it among the homilies of that same holy bishop.

### ARGUMENT

St. Maximus carefully gathers together and explains all the figures of the Old Testament by which the Passion and Resurrection of Christ the Lord were prefigured. He urges his hearers to perceive how much they are worth and how much they ought to be worth.

Although the benefits of our God are great and wondrous, they are nevertheless shown to be neither new nor sudden; rather, from the beginning of the world they were both foretold by oracles and prefigured in mysteries. For the Old Testament’s responses proclaimed the Lord’s sacred Passion from the very beginnings of the world as it came into being. Therefore we openly affirm from their own books and volumes that Christ the Lord was preached and announced [Note: The same Minor Codex of Santa Croce reads “announced to the Jews.”].

Beyond doubt, he rests upon powerful privileges who defends his cause by the documents of his adversaries. It is a splendid victory to entangle the opposing party in its own writings as though in its own snares, to refute it by the voices of its own testimonies, and to defeat one’s rival with his own weapons, so that the arguments of your opponent may be shown to serve your own purposes.

Thus, in the person of our Lord, while Eve, the mother of all living, is produced from the rib of Adam, the first man (Genesis 2), the Church, the mother of all the faithful, is shown to be restored from his sacred side and life-giving wound [Note: The Ambrosian Codex reads “from his sacred side and the wound of the Savior.”]

In his type, righteous Abel is slain (ibid., 4), and the innocent man is sacrificed by fraternal—so to speak, Judaic—impiety. This same Lord, at the final age of the aging world, is offered in the figure of the long-lived father, blessed Abraham. At that moment, while the devout killer rises against the throat of his only son in a new sacrifice, a ram suddenly appeared before his eyes, as the divine word says: “And Abraham saw a ram caught by its horns among the thorns” (Genesis 22).

“Among the thorns,” it says. Let us inquire what this novelty signifies. “Among the thorns,” that is, amid the multitude of surrounding sinners; “caught by its horns,” that is, hanging upon the horns of the cross, fastened by nails, as we read elsewhere: “He has horns in his hands” (Habakkuk 3:4; cited in the printed text as Matthew 3). This is because the arms of the gibbet received his venerable hands [Note: The Codices Vatican 248 and 1270, and the Minor Codex of Santa Croce, read “because his venerable hands.”]. He was counted among thorns when the author of innocence and justice was mocked with a crown of thorns.

But we must look more deeply into what is signified when Isaac is brought by his father to the altar [Note: The Minor Codex of Santa Croce reads “Isaac is removed from the altar by his father”; Vatican 248 reads “is brought near”], and suddenly a ram is substituted for him—not with the offering changed, but doubled. Here the twofold substance of the Redeemer is shown for our adoration. For God’s Only-Begotten is offered, and the Virgin’s firstborn is sacrificed.

This too prefigured the marks of the Lord’s Passion [Note: The Ambrosian Codex and Codices Vatican 248 and 1270 read “This too prefigured the distinguished signs of the Lord’s Passion”: namely, the event]—that we read how blessed Elisha, after his burial, raised a dead body by the touch of his sacred body when a corpse thrown by robbers into his tomb touched it (2 Kings 13). [Note: The Minor Codex of Santa Croce and three Vatican codices read: “Who else was prefigured here?”]

Who else is prefigured here except our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: The Ambrosian and Casinensis codices read “except our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.”], who grants resurrection from death and, though buried, brings about life? Recognize the guilty world in the robber, and Christ the Lord in the prophet’s powers.

Again, throughout the holy Scriptures, the Passion and Resurrection of Christ are most abundantly prefigured in the labors and sufferings of the prophet Jonah. Jonah is prescribed as having borne the type of the Lord—a matter which we do not suppose to be unknown to your faith—for the Lord himself says: “For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matthew 12).

This Jonah, I say, is sent by the Lord’s command to preach to the Ninevites the offense of heavenly wrath (Jonah 2). But, foreknowing that the grim prophecy would be nullified by the people’s conversion, he flees and boards a ship bound for Tarshish. When the sailors are troubled by the storm that has arisen, he is given to the waves by lot and is swallowed in the mouth of the sea-monster. But when the fish vomits him forth unharmed, the man deposited there is restored to the earth on the third day. [Note: From the Minor Codex of Santa Croce, the Casinensis, the Vatican codices, and the Ambrosian Codex.]

See how the Lord, in the form of a servant, appears wondrously even in the Old Testament. See how in ages long past he revealed that he would come beneath the humility of a servant’s form. Jonah is sent to the great city of Nineveh to proclaim the Lord’s wrath, saying: “Forty days, and Nineveh will be overthrown” [Note: Vatican 248 reads “Yet forty days”]. Christ is sent to the city of the world to announce the day of salvation and the appointed time of judgment.

Jonah seeks a ship; Christ seeks the Church. Jonah is driven by the waves; Christ is tested by the storms of the world. Unless Jonah is cast down, the ship’s danger is not calmed [Note: The Minor Codex of Santa Croce reads: “Unless Jonah is given up, the danger of the shipwrecked vessel is not calmed”; the Ambrosian, Vatican 1270, and Vatican 4951 codices agree in substance]. So also the Church is not delivered unless it is saved by Christ’s death.

The sailors, although they are about to cast Jonah out, nevertheless fear and say: “Lord, do not charge innocent blood against us” (John 1). [Note: The same Vatican codices read “Does it not seem to you?”] Does not the sailors’ rebuke seem to you to be Pilate’s confession? He hands Christ over, yet washes his hands and says: “I am innocent of the blood of this just man” (Matthew 27). [Note: The Ambrosian Codex reads: “How fittingly, through the person of a gentile, the faith of the nations is proclaimed.” The Codices of Santa Croce and Vatican 248 read: “How fittingly, through the person of a gentile, the faith of the nations is proclaimed.”]

How fittingly the faith of the nations is proclaimed through the person of a Gentile.

Jonah says in his prayer: “Take my soul, therefore, Lord, because death is better for me than life.” Let our Lord Jesus Christ say this more truly: “Death is better for me than life”—that is, “While alive I could not save one Jewish nation; let me die, and the whole world may be saved by one death.”

The sea-monster received Jonah after he had been submerged, but did not touch him as one devoured. The malice of human beings had destroyed him, but a hungry beast guarded him. With its entrails full, it suffers hunger, and it is astonished that it has no power over the prey it swallowed. Who is this who can be taken into ravening jaws but cannot be consumed? He is food, but not corruption; he is handed over to the depths of destruction and preserved through the service of death.

Who is this who enters safely into the vast recesses of danger, and, enclosed beneath an immense and deadly height, is nourished by vital air; who, sent down into a foreign order of things, lives together with life in the exile of life, and, surviving death, announces the salvation of the world to come? This is our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: Vatican 4951 reads “for this is our Lord”], whom savage death, an incomprehensible beast, snatched as its food, and whom, though it had captured its prey, it trembled to possess.

It trembled, I say. For although it knew him crucified, it could not hold as condemned the one whom it did not remember as guilty, because punishment does not create guilt; the cause does. It swallowed the human being lost in the world’s beginning as though he were its customary food, but when it was suffocated, it recognized the great dignity of that food. Therefore the divine word records: “And the Lord commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto the dry land” (Jonah 2).

He therefore commanded the beast; he commanded death, always hungry; he commanded the abysses and hell, to restore the Savior to the world [Note: The same Vatican codex reads “that they should restore.”]. That it vomited him forth, however, we must understand in this way: victorious life returned from the innermost entrails of death, and destruction, embittered in the deepest recesses of hell, gave him back.

Thus we see most clearly prefigured in the prophet’s afflictions both the death and the resurrection of Christ [Note: The same Vatican codex reads “both the death of Christ and the resurrection.”]. Therefore, when you see what was fulfilled in the servant, do not hesitate to believe it of the Lord.

Since these things are so, consider, O human being, how much you are worth, and weigh how much you ought to be worth. Consider how much you are worth, so that at last you may cease to be worthless in your own eyes; so that, at least for this reason, you may blush and disdain to be subject to vices [Note: The Minor Codex of Santa Croce reads “so that, blushing at this, you may disdain to be subject to vices”; from this reading Galesinius’ text, which has “may you deign,” is corrected]. Measure your nobility by the dignity of your Creator and Redeemer.

There are reasons by which a human being may rightly be ashamed of himself: why should one whose eternal glory is promised submit, with a conquered heart, to unworthy masters? If once you seemed honored through participation in the divine image, by a twofold privilege you are now made precious also by the nobility of the exchange [Note: Vatican 4951 reads “that the human being may himself be confounded.”] [Col. 0359A]. Hence, as a strong person, you may be able to stand against your enemy. Examine your condition: the Lord has granted you free power to battle the prince of this world in your members and to overcome spiritual wickedness [Note: Vatican 4951 reads: “See how strong you may be against your enemy, since the Lord has placed in your hands the prince of this world to be fought”; the Ambrosian, Minor Codex of Santa Croce, and Vatican 248 read “to be conquered in your members, the prince of this world.”]. Thus do not think it impossible that you may be transferred into angelic blessedness, since in this world you have conquered angelic powers.

Therefore let not a life make you degenerate and despised when either your creation has proved itself illustrious in bringing you forth or grace has done so. Rather, let the faithful of Christ raise their course confidently toward heavenly things; for those who see that they have been redeemed at a heavenly price should not doubt that they have been prepared for heavenly things [Note: The Ambrosian Codex reads “those who see themselves redeemed at a heavenly price.”]

## HOMILY 56. On Mary Magdalene and the Resurrection of the Lord II

### ADMONITION

Although we can produce only two codices in support of regarding this as a homily of St. Maximus—namely the Turin codex, with the title “Also on the same subject, and Mary Magdalene,” and Santa Croce in Jerusalem 99, homily 61, whose inscription is “Here begins [the homily] on Mary Magdalene”—we nevertheless have no doubt that no one will think us deserving of criticism for considering him its author, once they understand that the most learned Maurists share the same judgment. Anyone who wishes may consult them in the appendix to the sermons of St. Augustine, number 153, and in the preface to the Ambrosian sermons.

It should be noted that in Codex 172, page 6, of the library formerly belonging to the aediles of the metropolitan church of Florence and now Laurentian, the title of this homily is: “Sermon of St. Augustine, bishop, for Tuesday in Easter week.” In Vatican Codex 1270, page 38, on the reverse, only these words are read: “Whence above,” whose preceding sermon is “On the Resurrection of the Lord,” attributed to Pope St. Gregory. In the Urbevetan codex, page 123, on the reverse, it appears without a name: “On the Resurrection of the Lord, Thursday.”

Since Maximus speaks chiefly about the Resurrection of the Lord, we prefer the title found in the manuscript codices to the title given by the editors, “On the Burial of the Lord and Mary Magdalene.” Thus Gymnicus, page 122; Galesinius, page 124; Combefisius, volume 5, page 585; Cumdius, volume 2, page 1585; Raynaudus, page 214; and Margarinus in *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume 6, page 21, attribute it to St. Maximus.

### ARGUMENT

Christ rebukes Mary Magdalene because, when she sought him in the tomb after the Resurrection, she wished to touch him. If we wish to find and touch the Savior, we must not seek him on the earth, nor according to the flesh, but according to the glory of divine majesty.

Brothers, there still clings to our minds what we proclaimed only a few days ago: that Mary Magdalene was not lightly rebuked because, after the Resurrection, she sought the Lord in the tomb; and because, not remembering his words in which he had said that he would rise from the dead on the third day, she thought that he was being held by the laws of hell.

For she is not lightly charged with failing to remember the promise of the Resurrection and searching instead for the evidence of death [Note: The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads “failing to remember.”] Humble and ignorant faith seeks what it does not know and forgets what it is taught. It is indeed quick to serve, but not perfect in believing; it is anxious over the injury done to the Lord’s flesh, but uncertain about the glory of the Resurrection; it weeps out of love for Christ, but grieves in despair because his body is not found. She thinks that the one whom she knew already to be reigning has perished; she searches for him in the tomb whom she ought rather to invoke from heaven [Note: The Laurentian Codex and Santa Croce in Jerusalem 99 read “for she searches for him.”]

St. Mary is therefore rebuked as slow to believe; and when, late though it is, she recognizes the Lord, the Savior says to her: “Do not touch me, because I have not yet ascended to the Father” (John 20).

“Do not touch me” is a word of rebuke. That is: “Do not touch me with your hands, because through forgetfulness of mind you do not retain my Resurrection.” [Note: From Laurentian Codex CLXXII.] That is: “Do not touch me with your hands, because you do not touch me with the perfection of faith.” You cannot hold me in bodily embraces, because she who has lost her hearing is forbidden to touch [Note: The Minor Codex of Santa Croce reads “what has lost its hearing is prohibited by touch.”]. “Do not touch me,” he says, “because I have not yet ascended to the Father” (John 20).

Let us see how Christ has not yet ascended to the Father, when he himself says: “Because the Father is in me, and I am in the Father” (John 14), from whom he has never been separated by the undivided substance of divinity. For while one remains in one, he always signifies that the Father and the Son are together. Or does the Son say that he is to ascend to a place where he dwells before he ascends? For the same Lord said: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3). If, therefore, when the Savior descends he is in heaven, much more is he in heaven before he ascends [Note: The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads “before he ascended.”]

But see whether this saying perhaps pertains to Mary’s rebuke. A little earlier, when she was seeking the Lord among the tombs, she was told: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” Now let this be added: “Do not touch me, because I have not yet ascended to the Father.” That is: “Why do you wish to touch me, since, while seeking me among the tombs, you still do not believe that I have ascended to the Father; since, while searching for me among the depths below, you doubt that I have returned to heavenly things; since, while seeking me among the dead, you do not hope that I live with God my Father?”

“I have not yet ascended to the Father,” he says—that is, “For you I have not yet ascended to the Father, because in your faith I am still being held in the tomb. As far as you are concerned, I still dwell among humble things; I still cling to earthly things, because your faith has not yet raised me to heaven.”

Why then do you hasten to touch me as the Son of God, when you do not follow me in the devotion of your mind as I return to the Father? Whoever, therefore, wishes to touch the Lord Savior must first set him by faith at the right hand of the Divinity and place him through the belief of the heart in heavenly things, rather than seek him among the dead.

The Lord has ascended to the Father for those who believe that he is always in the Father. He has ascended to the Father for the blessed apostles, to whom he said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14). He has ascended to the Father for John the Evangelist, who sought him with the Father and found him; therefore he says: “And the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1).

He has also ascended to the blessed Paul, who, not content merely to know what he knew [Note: The codices Santa Croce in Jerusalem 99 read “not content merely with knowing himself,” etc.], taught us also how to seek the Savior in heavenly places [Note: The same Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads “how we should seek the Savior in heavenly places, saying”]: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3).

And to remove us completely from Mary’s humble or earthly search, he adds: “Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth.” Therefore, we must no longer seek the Savior upon the earth, nor in the earth, nor according to the flesh, if we wish to find and touch him, but according to the glory of divine majesty, so that we may say with the Apostle Paul: “Now we know Christ no longer according to the flesh” (2 Corinthians 5).

Thus blessed Stephen, by his faith, did not seek Christ upon the earth, but recognized him standing at God’s right hand. He found him where he sought him with the devotion of his mind. Stephen not only sees Christ in heaven, but also touches him through his martyrdom. For he touches the Lord when, praying for his enemies and holding him by faith, he says: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7).

Understand, therefore, how great is the glory of devotion. Mary, standing beside the Lord, does not deserve to touch him; Stephen, placed on earth, touches Christ in heaven. She, though present among the angels, does not see the Savior; Stephen, within the heavens, beholds the Lord who is absent.

## HOMILY 57. On the Same Solemnity of Easter III

### ADMONITION

The number of manuscript codices that affirm this most elegant homily to belong to St. Maximus is indeed remarkable and almost unparalleled. We shall first commend the two Vatican codices, 4951, page 99, and 6451, page 4; likewise the two of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, 90, homily 48, and 99, homily 55; likewise the two Casinenses, CXI, page 3, and 123, page 139; also the two Belgian codices, the Martinensis and the Camberonensis; the Cistercian codex of Monte Amiata; and finally the Laurentian Codex X, Pluteus XIV, page 293, on the reverse.

The editors agree remarkably with these codices: Gymnicus, page 146, with the title “On the Same Solemnity”; Galesinius likewise, page 133; Cumdius, volume 2, page 1444; Raynaudus, page 218; and Margarinus in *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume 6, page 25. Therefore, moved by such agreement among the manuscripts and printed books, the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of St. Maur established Maximus as the author of this discourse, not Ambrose, as a few codices report.

### ARGUMENT

The miracles that took place at Christ’s Resurrection are eloquently reviewed by Maximus.

Not without good reason, brothers, is this psalm read today (Psalm 13), in which the prophet commands us to exult and rejoice. For holy David invites all creatures to the celebration of this day. On this day, through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, Tartarus is opened [Codex Casinensis 123: “of our Lord Jesus Christ”; Codex X, Plut. XIV reads *tartarum*, as also later]; through the neophytes of the Church the earth is renewed; through the Holy Spirit heaven is opened. For opened hell gives back the dead; renewed earth makes the risen spring forth; opened heaven receives those ascending. Finally, the thief ascends into paradise; the bodies of the saints enter the holy city; the dead return to the living; and, as it were by a certain progress in Christ’s resurrection, all the elements raise themselves to higher things. Hell returns to the world above those whom it holds; earth sends to heaven those whom it buries; heaven presents to the Lord those whom it receives. In one and the same operation of the Savior, the Passion raises some from the depths, awakens others from earthly things, and places others in the heights.

For Christ’s resurrection is life for the dead, forgiveness for sinners, and glory for the saints [Codex Vaticanus 4951: “life for the deceased,” and so forth]. Holy David therefore invites every creature to the celebration of Christ’s resurrection. For he says that on this day, which the Lord has made, we should exult and rejoice.

But someone may say: “If this day is a day for rejoicing, then surely those things should rejoice which the day itself embraces. Heaven and hell, however, have been established outside the day of this world. How, then, can those elements be called to the celebration of this day, since they are not contained within its bounds?” [Codex Martinianus: “which are not contained within the compass of this day”]

But this day, which the Lord has made, penetrates everything and contains the universe; it embraces heaven, earth, and hell [Codex Martinianus omits “heaven”]. For Christ the Light [Laurentian and Vatican codices, like those of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem and the Martinianus, read *Christi* (“of Christ”) for *Christus* (“Christ”)] is not confined by walls, divided by the elements, or darkened by shadows. The Light of Christ, I say, is a day without night, a day without end: it shines everywhere, radiates everywhere, and nowhere fails.

That this day is Christ, the Apostle declares: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Romans 13). “The night has passed,” he says; “it does not follow” [both codices of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem: “does not follow”]—so that you may understand that, when Christ’s light arrives, the darkness of the devil is driven away; the obscurities of sins do not follow; former gloom is dispelled by perpetual brightness; and stealthily arising offenses are prevented [Codex Vaticanus: *subripientiaque* (“and those that steal upon [us]”); Martinianus and Laurentianus: *subripientia* (“those that steal upon [us]”); codices 99 of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem and 90: *subrepentia* (“those that creep in”)].

For Scripture testifies that this day, Christ, illumines heaven, earth, and hell. That it shines upon the earth, John says: “He was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1). That it shines in hell, the prophet says: “Upon those who were sitting in the region and shadow of death, light has arisen” [Codices Belgici: “light has arisen for them”] (Isaiah 9).

That this day remains in heaven [Codex Laurentianus, and likewise the Casinensis and Vaticanus codices: “That this day remains in heaven”]; David likewise reports, saying: “I will establish his seed forever, and his throne like the days of heaven” [Codex 99 of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem: “his seat, and his seed like the days of heaven”] (Psalm 88). And what is the day of heaven except Christ the Lord?—to which reading the codices of the Holy Cross and the Casinensis agree. Of him it is said through the prophet: “Day unto day pours forth the Word” (Psalm 18). For he is the Day, the Son, to whom the Father, the Day of his divinity, pours forth the mystery.

He, I say, is the Day who says through Solomon: “I caused an unfailing day to rise in heaven” (Sirach 24) [both codices of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem and the Casinensis read “light” instead of “day”]. Therefore, just as night does not at all follow the day of heaven, so the darkness of sins does not follow Christ’s righteousness. The day of heaven always shines, gleams, and glows, and no obscurity can enclose it. In the same way Christ’s light always flashes [Codex Vaticanus: “sparkles”], radiates, and sparkles [Codex Laurentianus: “radiates and flashes”], and no darkness of sins can seize it. Hence the evangelist John says: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1).

At Christ’s resurrection [Codex Martinianus: “At Christ’s own resurrection”], therefore, all the elements rejoice. For I think that even the sun itself is brighter than usual on this day. It is necessary that the sun rejoice at the resurrection of the one whose Passion it grieved over [Codex Casinensis 123: “of whose death”]; and that it receive the life of the one whose death it followed in a kind of mournful darkness with the splendor of a brighter light.

Like a good servant, just as it was then darkened for the rites of the burial, so now let it flash forth in service of the resurrection. For during Christ’s Passion it surrounded itself with the night of darkness, and, with the world as witness, groaned over the crime of the Jews. There is a kind of judgment of grief in the sun: by withholding the service of its light from so great a crime, and by a kind of vengeance pouring darkness into the eyes of the Jews, it ensured that the blindness which had invaded their minds [both codices: “their minds”] should occupy their eyes also. The light of the world did not shine for those by whom the light of salvation had been extinguished.

A kind of condemnation is therefore inflicted upon the Pharisees, so that they may already suffer in the world above the darkness promised to sinners on the day of judgment [Codex Casinensis: “they are condemned”].

Thus darkness lingers in the world above while Christ is crucified [codices Vaticanus, Holy Cross at Jerusalem, Casinensis, and Martinianus: “Thus, while Christ is crucified, darkness lingers in the world above”]. Is it surprising that there is darkness in the world above when the Light has descended to the realms below?

Therefore, brothers, we must all exult on this holy day. Let no one withdraw from the common rejoicing because of consciousness of sin; let no burden of offenses hold anyone back from the public vows [Codex Martinianus omits “Although”].

Although he is a sinner, no one on this day ought to despair of forgiveness. For the privilege is by no means small. If the thief merited paradise, why should a Christian not merit forgiveness? And if the Lord has mercy on that man while he is being crucified [Codex Martinianus: “on that man”], much more will he have mercy on this one when he rises [the same codex: “when he rises”]. If the humility of the Passion bestowed so much upon the one who confessed, how much will the glory of the resurrection grant to the one who entreats? [Codex 4951 and the Martinianus: “will grant”]

For, as you yourselves know, joyful victory is usually more generous in giving than captivity under submission.

# HOMILY LVIII. On the Same Solemnity of Easter IV

## Notice

The number of manuscript codices in which Saint Maximus is identified as the author of this homily is no smaller than that just described. Out of respect, we first commend two Vatican codices, 4951, page 100, and 6451, page 17; then two codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, 90, homily 52, and 99, homily 56, bearing the title “The following also concerning holy Easter”; the Turin codex, where sermon 29 is entitled “Likewise, also, concerning Easter”; the Laurentian codex X, Plut. XIV, page 195; Vercelli 85; Augia XV; the Ambrosian codex; the Cistercian codex of Monte Amiata; and the Martinian codex, homily 59. All of these call it a homily on Easter or on the Paschal feast.

The editors likewise agree, under the title “On the Same Solemnity,” namely of Easter: Gymnicus, page 157; Galesinius, page 135; Cumdius, volume III, page 1447; Combefisius, volume III, page 85; Raynaudus, page 220; and Margarinus in the *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, page 27.

We omit here the third homily in the printed books and shall place it first among the sermons on Easter. Since, therefore, this homily is supported by such numerous and authoritative testimonies, we dissent from the Sixtine edition of Saint Ambrose, which placed it under number 55 among the sermons of that holy teacher.

## Argument

The true resurrection of Christians is a change of life. Easter is called a passage; therefore Christians should pass from sins to repentance, from vices to virtue, and from languor in piety to devotion to religion, so that they may rise with Christ to immortality.

A great and wonderful gift [Codex Martinianus: “an admirable gift”], brothers, God has granted us: this saving day of Easter, on which the Lord, rising again [Codex Ambrosianus: “Christ rising again”], bestowed resurrection upon all and, ascending from the depths to higher things, raised us also in his body from lower things to what is above.

For, according to the Apostle, all we Christians are the body and members of Christ (1 Corinthians 12). Since Christ rose, therefore, all his members necessarily rose with him. While he passed from the realms below to those above, he caused us also to pass from death to life.

For Easter in Hebrew is called *passage*, or *advance*, namely because through this mystery one passes from worse things to better [Laurentian codex X and Ambrosian codex: “because through this mystery, when Christ rose from…”]. A good passage is to pass from sins to righteousness, from vices to virtues, and from old age to infancy. I mean infancy not of age but of simplicity. For merits too have their ages. Previously we had been established in the setting of the West, in the old age of sins. When Christ rose, we were renewed in the innocence of little children.

Christian simplicity also has its infancy. For just as an infant does not know how to become angry, does not know how to defraud, and does not dare to strike back, so Christian infancy does not become angry with those who injure it, does not resist those who despoil it, and does not fight back against those who beat it.

Finally, as the Lord commanded, it also prays for its enemies; it leaves its tunic to those who take it, and its cloak; it offers the other cheek to those who strike it [the same codex of the Holy Cross: “to pray, to leave the tunic and cloak to the one taking them, and to offer the cheek to the one striking it”; the Martinianus reads “to leave the tunic and cloak, and to offer the cheek to the one striking”].

Yet in this Christ’s infancy is better than nature’s: nature’s infancy does not know how to sin, whereas Christ’s despises sin. The former is innocent through weakness; the latter is innocent through virtue. Therefore it is more deserving of praise to be unwilling to do evil than not to be able to do it [Codex Laurentianus: “not so much not to be able to do evil, etc.”].

As we have said, then, there are certain ages of merits. For the old age of character is found in children, and the innocence of infants is found in the elderly. That there is a kind of old age of goodness in the young, the prophet says: “For old age is honorable” [Codex Martinianus adds “is”], “not measured by length of time or counted by number of years” [Codex Casinensis: “is not computed by the number of years”]; “for the understanding of human beings is gray hair” (Wisdom 4).

To the apostles, who were already older and advanced in years, the Lord says: “Unless you turn and become like this child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16) [Codex 99 of the Holy Cross: “you will not enter”]. He therefore recalls them to the fountain of their origin [the Martinianus omits “their”] and compels them to return backward to infancy, so that those who had grown old in frail bodies might be reborn in the habits of innocence, as the Savior says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of God” (John 3) [both codices of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem: “the kingdom of heaven”].

The apostles are therefore told: “Unless you turn and become like this child.” He does not say “like these children,” but “like this child”: he chooses one and sets forth one [Codex 99 of the Holy Cross: “he chooses one and sets one before them”].

Let us see, then, who this great one is who is offered to the disciples as an example for imitation [the Martinianus adds “of him”]. I do not think that this child is from the common people, from the public, or from the multitude of others—especially since through the apostles he bestowed an example of holiness upon the whole world [the same codex of the Holy Cross: “through the apostles throughout the whole world, etc.”]. No, I say, I do not think that this child is from the public, but from heaven.

For he is the child from heaven of whom the prophet Isaiah says: “A child is born to us; a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9) [the Martinianus: “to him, a son”]. Clearly he is the child who, like an innocent person, did not curse in return when cursed [the same codex: “did not curse in return”], did not strike back when struck; indeed, in the very Passion he prayed for his enemies, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 24).

Thus the Lord, by the goodness of his mercy, enlarged the simplicity that nature grants to infants. This, then, is the child who is set before little ones for imitation and following; for he himself says: “Take up your cross and follow me” (Matthew 16).

# HOMILY LIX. On the Same Solemnity of Easter V

## Notice

Unless the complete connection of this homily with the preceding one were evident, its authorship might be considered doubtful, since it is supported by very few manuscript testimonies. From this, however, one may judge that the collection of works of this kind was assembled fortuitously by copyists, since they omitted several works of the same author which greater diligence would have recovered.

I therefore cite only four codices that transmitted this homily to posterity under Maximus’s name: two of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, 90, homily 53, and 99, homily 57, bearing the title “The following also”; the third, Laurentian X, Plut. XIV, page 296, with the same heading; and the fourth, the Turin codex, whose title is “Likewise, also, sermon XXXII on Easter.”

The Benedictine monks of the congregation of Saint Maur nevertheless make the homily more securely Maximus’s. They removed it from the sermons of Augustine, to whom it had formerly been attributed, and transferred it to the appendix as a work of Saint Maximus. The editors Gymnicus, page 159; Galesinius, page 135; Cumdius, volume II, page 1447; Raynaudus, page 220; and Margarinus in the *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, page 27, adopted the same view.

It is therefore sufficiently clear that those who attributed it to Saint Ambrose, as well as those who attributed it to Saint Leo the Great, were mistaken.

This homily has one distinctive feature: it presents the discipline of the Church at that time, namely the solemn administration of baptism to adults on Holy Saturday. The holy bishop of Turin therefore preached to those regenerated for grace and, reminding them who they had been and what they had become through the gift of regeneration, lovingly exhorted them to show themselves new people through the newness of a holier life.

## Argument

Maximus exhorts the neophytes to be renewed through the righteousness they received in the washing of regeneration. Like eagles laying aside the cast-off garments of age, they have put on new garments of holiness.

Your Holiness remembers, brothers, that I recently preached that a human being is restored to a younger age through righteousness and, although exhausted by old age, is reborn once more as a child in the habits of innocence, so that, through the intervention of the mystery, we may see old men become infants again.

For it is a kind of renewal to cease to be what you were and to assume what previously you were not. It is renewal, I say, and for this reason they are called neophytes: because by a certain newness they have cast away the stains of age and assumed the grace of simplicity, as the Apostle says: “Putting off the old person with his own deeds” [the same codices of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem and the Laurentianus read *cum actibus ejus*, “with his deeds,” for *cum actibus suis*], “put on the new person, who has been created according to God” (Colossians 3).

Hence holy David says: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Psalm 102). He understands that, through the grace of baptism, the declining portions of our life can come back to life, and that what had collapsed within us through the oldness of sins can be renewed by a kind of youth.

To make you understand that the prophet is speaking of the grace of baptism, he compared this renewal to that of an eagle [Codex 99 of the Holy Cross: “he compares it”]. This bird is said to prolong its life through the continual changing of its appearance and, when its old feathers are already decaying, to grow young again through the succession of new feathers. Thus, having laid aside the cast-off garments of age, it clothes itself in a reborn form of its plumage. From this we understand that the eagle’s limbs do not experience old age, but its feathers.

It therefore clothes itself anew, and, as its feathers sprout, the old mother is renewed once more into a young bird. It must be compared with young birds [both codices of the Holy Cross: “then it must be compared”] when, with its feathers shining, it is compelled again to practice unskilled flight and to restrain within the nest, like a fledgling bird, the oarage of wings long trained in exercise. Although by habit it possesses knowledge of flight, it lacks confidence because its feathers are sparse.

The holy Psalmist therefore prophesied this concerning the grace of baptism. Our neophytes, newly baptized, have indeed, like eagles laying aside the cast-off garments of age, put on new garments of holiness. As their old stains decay like light feathers, they are adorned with the reborn grace of immortality. Thus the sins of old age have grown old and died in them, but life has not grown old; they have been recalled from old age to infancy, like an eagle becoming a young bird [Codex of the Holy Cross: “renewed into infancy”].

They possess knowledge of the world from their former way of life, but through restoration they now possess the security of righteousness.

Let us examine more carefully what holy David says. He does not say, “The youth of eagles will be renewed,” but “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.” He therefore asserts that the youth of one eagle is to be renewed in us. That one and only eagle I may rightly call Christ the Lord, whose youth was renewed when he rose from the dead.

For, having laid aside the cast-off garments of mortal corruption [Codex 99 of the Holy Cross: “the cast-off garments of the corruption of the body”; Codex 90: “the cast-off garments of bodily corruption”], he blossomed again by taking up his flesh anew, as he himself says through the prophet: “My flesh blossomed again, and by my will I will confess to him” (Psalm 72).

“My flesh blossomed again,” he says. Observe the word he used. He does not say “blossomed,” but “blossomed again”; for only what had blossomed before blossoms again.

The Lord’s flesh blossomed when it first came forth from the undefiled womb of the Virgin Mary, as Isaiah says: “A shoot will come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root” (Isaiah 11).

It blossomed again when, after the flower of his body had been cut down by the Jews, it sprang from the tomb in the glory of resurrection, blooming anew, and breathed upon all human beings, like a flower, both the fragrance and the radiance of immortality: carrying the sweetness of good works as its fragrance, and displaying the incorruptibility of perpetual divinity as its radiance.

# HOMILY LX. On the Ascension of the Lord

## Notice

After the homilies on Christ’s resurrection have been completed, the editors list one to which they attached the title “On the Litanies and Fasts of the Ninevites.” Since Saint Maximus also delivered another sermon on the Ninevites, I decided to join the two and then discuss the prayers called litanies.

Nor do I follow them in the order and title of this homily. I have observed that the author says nothing about the mystery of Pentecost, but immediately celebrates the wondrous ascension of Christ the Lord by recalling his glorious resurrection. I have therefore entitled it “On the Ascension of the Lord” and assigned it a place before the homilies on Pentecost, with Latinius also supporting my judgment.

The clear connection with the preceding homily likewise compelled me to do this, since this one appears to have been delivered after the preceding one.

Six highly esteemed codices support my attribution of it to Saint Maximus: two of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, 90, homily 54, and 99, homily 66; Ambrosian C 98; Saint Emmeram of Regensburg, page 19; Laurentian X, Plut. XIV, page 307; and the Turin codex, whose title is “Likewise, also, the eighth homily on Pentecost.”
