The others have “The Following” as their title, while counting this homily among those on Pentecost.

Two codices disagree with them. One is II, formerly of the library of the Minor Convent of the Holy Cross, page 57, now Laurentian, which attributes it to Saint Leo the Great; the other is Vatican 1270, page 79, which attributes it to Saint Ambrose. In both cases, however, the copyist’s error was detected both by the Ballerini brothers and by the monks of Saint Maur.

The former did not admit this homily among the genuine works of the holy pontiff. The Benedictines, however, in the preface to the sermons of Saint Ambrose and in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine, number 185, declared Saint Maximus its author.

I therefore set aside the Paris edition of Saint Ambrose by Gillotius, where it is sermon 62 under the title “Likewise, on Pentecost,” and the Sixtine edition, where it appears as sermon 61 under the title “On the Meaning of the Pentecost Celebration.” This is all the more appropriate because other editors more correctly count it among the homilies of Maximus: Gymnicus, page 170; Galesinius, page 139; Raynaudus, page 222; and Margarinus in the *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, page 27.

In the Roman Breviary, part of this homily is also read under Saint Maximus’s name on the Tuesday within the octave of the Ascension.

## Argument

The first part of the homily concerns Christ’s resurrection; the second concerns his ascension into heaven. Saint Maximus describes Christ’s triumph together with the prophet David. Finally, he teaches that Christ sits at the Father’s right hand not because he is greater than the Father, but so that he may not be believed to be lesser.

Not inappropriately, brothers, as you remember, our preaching proceeded several days ago. In it we described how the Lord’s flesh blossomed from the tomb, revived as though in the brightness of a flower [Codex 90 of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem: “as though it were sprouting from the tomb with the renewed radiance of a flower”; Codex II of the Minor Holy Cross, now Laurentian, and Saint Emmeram of Regensburg: “with the renewed radiance of a flower”]. The evangelist testified that the tomb was situated in a garden (John 19); and we followed this line of thought not without reason.

For it was fitting that the more precious flower should be born in a garden, and that the seed commended to the soil for a good harvest should sprout for the salvation of all within domestic yet verdant enclosures [Codex of the Minor Holy Cross, codex 90 of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem, the Ambrosianus, and Saint Emmeram of Regensburg: “pleasant verdure”]. Christ’s resurrection is the redemption of all peoples.

Therefore in the garden the Savior assumes his revived body. Among flowering trees and shining lilies, his flesh, already dead, blossoms again, and he springs from the tomb in such a way that he finds all things springing and shining.

Thus, after the cold burial, as it were, of winter’s rigor, all the elements hastened to sprout, so that when the Lord rose, they too might rise. For through Christ’s resurrection the air is healthier, the sun brighter, and the earth more fertile [Codex II of the Minor Holy Cross and the codex of Saint Emmeram: “the earth more fertile, the sun warmer”; both codices of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem: “the sun warmer, the earth more fertile”]. From it a shoot grows into a shrub, grass grows into a field of grain, and the vine grows to maturity into a branch.

If, then, when Christ’s flesh blossoms again, all things are clothed with flowers, it is necessary that, when he bears fruit, all things should also bear fruit, as the same Lord says: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the ground, dies, it remains alone; but when it has died, it bears much fruit” (John 12).

The Lord therefore blossomed again when he rose from the tomb; he bears fruit when he ascends into heaven [Codex II: “He bore fruit when he ascended into heaven, carrying the fruit of the flesh”]. He is a flower when he is born from the lower regions of the earth; he is fruit when he is stored in the highest place.

He is a grain, as he himself says, when he alone suffers the cross; he is fruit when he is surrounded by the faith of many apostles. For during those forty days after the resurrection, while he lived with the disciples, he taught them with the complete maturity of wisdom [Codex Ambrosianus: “with the entire maturity of wisdom”] and turned them toward good fruit through the fertility of every kind of instruction.

Then he ascended into heaven, to the Father, carrying the fruit of the flesh [codices 90 of the Holy Cross and Saint Emmeram: “carrying before him the fruit of the flesh”] and leaving in the disciples the seeds of righteousness.

The Lord therefore ascended to the Father. Your Holiness remembers that I compared the Savior with that eagle from the Psalter whose renewed youth we read about. The resemblance is considerable. Just as an eagle abandons lowly things, seeks what is high, and ascends near the heavens, so the Savior abandoned the lowly regions of hell, sought the heights of paradise, and penetrated the summits of heaven [the two codices of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem preserve the marked passage: “ascends near the heavens: so the Savior abandoned the lowly regions of hell and sought the heights of paradise”].

And just as an eagle, leaving behind earthly filth and flying aloft [Codex II: “flying aloft”], enjoys the healthfulness of purer air, so the Lord, abandoning the dregs of earthly things, rejoices in his saints, flying about in the simplicity of a purer life.

The comparison with the eagle therefore suits the Savior in every respect. But what shall we do about the fact that an eagle frequently snatches prey and often takes what belongs to another? Even in this the Savior is not unlike it. For he carried off prey, so to speak, when he took the human being whom he had assumed, snatched him from the jaws of hell, and carried him to heaven. Having torn from captivity the servant of another dominion—that is, of the devil’s power—he led him upward as a captive, as it is written in the prophet: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Psalm 67; Ephesians 4).

This statement is understood as follows: the Lord rescued the human being whom the devil had taken captive and, by rescuing him, made that captivity his own captive; then, as the text says, he carried the captured captivity itself to the heights of heaven [codices Ambrosianus and II of the Minor Holy Cross: “the captivity made captive”].

Both captivities are therefore called by one word, but they are not equal [Codex II: “but there is no equality in the two”]. The devil’s captivity subjects one to slavery; Christ’s captivity restores one to freedom [Codex of Saint Emmeram: “freedom”].

“Ascending on high,” he says, “he led captivity captive.” How well the prophet describes the Lord’s triumph! They say that the chariot of a triumphant king was customarily preceded by a procession of captives. But behold: as the Lord goes to heaven, the glorious captivity does not precede him but accompanies him. It is not led before the chariot; it itself carries the Savior upward.

For in a certain mystery, while the Son of God lifted the son of man to heaven [Codex II: “lifted the son of man to heaven”], the captivity itself is both carried and carries. When he says, “He gave gifts to human beings,” this is the insignia of the victor. For after a triumph the victor always distributes gifts, and, seated in his own kingdom, rewards the joy of his servants.

Thus Christ the Lord, victor over the devil, sitting at the Father’s right hand, bestowed gifts upon the disciples today [Codex 90: “Christ the Lord, victor over the devil, sitting…”]—not talents of gold or masses of silver, but the heavenly gifts of the Holy Spirit. Among other graces, he enabled the apostles to speak in various tongues.

That is, a man of the Hebrew nation might proclaim the glory of Christ with the eloquence of Roman speech, and foreign ears, unable to understand the redemption of the human race when preached in the language of Judea [Codex of Saint Emmeram offers: “because they could not comprehend it when preached in the language of Judea”; or “because they could not comprehend the preaching when delivered in the language of Judea”], might recognize it in their own speech.

Every tongue is released in the preaching of Christ, so that every language may confess his majesty, as holy David says: “There are no tongues or speeches whose voices are not heard” (Psalm 18). [Codex Ambrosianus: “Do not wonder, however…”]

Do not be surprised, however, that we have said that the Son sits at the Father’s right hand. He sits at the right hand not because he is greater than the Father, but so that he may not be believed to be lesser [Codex II and the codex of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem: “but so that he may not be believed lesser than the Father”], as heretics customarily blaspheme. For just as divinity knows no rank of honor, so Holy Scripture knows how to oppose blasphemies [Codices II and 90: “knows how to oppose blasphemers”].

# HOMILY LXI. On the Solemnity of Holy Pentecost I

## Notice

This homily is famously cited under the name of Ambrose by Gratian, Distinction 77, chapter 8: “Throughout these fifty days we have an unbroken and continuous celebration, so that during all this time we neither prescribe fasting nor fall upon our knees to entreat God.”

I shall first discuss the custom of not fasting and not kneeling in prayer from the solemnity of Easter to Pentecost, and then the author of the homily.

Some infer that this practice derived from the apostles, because the testimony of Tertullian, who flourished in the second century, appears to be clear on this matter. “On Sunday,” he says, “we consider it unlawful to fast or to adore on our knees. From Easter Day until Pentecost we rejoice in the same freedom.”

They add the authority of Saint Epiphanius, who says in *On the Exposition of the Faith*, number 22: “During the fifty days of Pentecost, neither are the knees bent nor is fasting prescribed.”

I pass over Saint Irenaeus, bishop and martyr, whom Pseudo-Justin mentions. Critics have serious doubts about that author, as may be seen in Massuetus, *Dissertation 2 on the Books of Irenaeus*, article 3, section 60, page 105.

The monks of Saint Maur entirely reject that Pseudo-Justin, not only because they do not believe him to be older than the fifth century, but also because he plainly reveals himself to be infected with Pelagianism. See the Paris edition of Justin, 1742, especially Prudentius Mairanus’s notice, page 434.

The reason for this custom is said to have been accepted not so much from joy at Christ’s resurrection as from remembrance of the benefit bestowed upon us through him, since Christ, rising again, conquered death and guilt in order to free us from both.

It is also relevant that the Hebrews were commanded in the Law of Moses to keep those fifty days from Easter to Pentecost as festive and solemn, and to recall their freedom from Egyptian slavery. From the earliest times, therefore, the Christian people appeared to have an even greater reason to multiply joy upon joy, having been freed from the captivity of the devil.

Fully agreeing with this holy exultation, Maximus preached this homily on the same joy to his people and explained why during those fifty days they prayed standing and were free from fasting.

This homily, however, must be assigned not to Ambrose, to whom it was formerly attributed, but to our Maximus, since six ancient codices bear the name of Saint Maximus. They are the two very old codices of Saint Gall and 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, homily 41; the Regensburg codex of Saint Emmeram; the Turin codex, homily 15; another codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, 99, homily 65; and Laurentian X, Plut. XIV, page 35 verso. The title in all of them is “On Pentecost.”

Gennadius should not be passed over either, for he wrote that Maximus of Turin composed many homilies on Easter and Pentecost.

When the Benedictine monks of the congregation of Saint Maur discovered that this homily had been included among the sermons of Ambrose by earlier editors, they noted that it should be sought among the works of Maximus in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

Carlo Sebastiano Berardi reached a similar judgment in his commentary on Gratian’s canons, part 3, chapter 12, volume IV, page 124, Turin edition, 1757. He says that the canons on the Pentecost fast, as reviewed by Gratian, are of uncertain authority, and observes that the passages belong not to Ambrose but to Maximus, as is clear from volume VI of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

Relying, therefore, on the number of codices and on the judgments of the most learned men, I shall depart from Vatican codex 6451 and from codex II of the Minor Convent of the Holy Cross, now Laurentian, as well as from the Roman and Parisian editors of 1569, who attribute the homily to Saint Ambrose.

I am preceded by Gymnicus, page 174; Galesinius, page 134; Cumdius, volume III, page 202; Raynaudus, page 223; and Margarinus in the *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, page 23. They called this the third homily on the same solemnity, that is, on Pentecost. I shall call it the first, since I have just given the second under the title “On the Ascension of the Lord,” and the homily that they place first follows this one.

[Col. 0371A] **ARGUMENT.**—Maximus asks why, during those fifty days from the Resurrection to Pentecost, the faithful neither fast nor pray kneeling, but upright; and he replies that they do this for the sake of joy, to show their gladness that the risen Christ dwelt among human beings throughout that period and afterward went up to heaven, intending to send the Holy Spirit upon the apostles.

Your Holiness ought to know, brothers, for what reason we observe this holy day of Pentecost, and why these fifty [192] days are for us a continuous and uninterrupted festival, so that [Note: [Col. 0371B] Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read: “throughout this whole period.” Manuscript Laurentianus X, Pluteus XIV: “nor do we indicate that fasts are to be observed.”] throughout the entire period we neither proclaim fasts to be observed nor [Note: [Col. 0371B] The same manuscript mentioned above, manuscript II of Santa Croce in Florence: “nor do we fall upon our knees to entreat God, but, standing and keeping holiday, we celebrate the Lord’s Resurrection.”] kneel to entreat God; rather, as we customarily do on Sunday, standing and keeping holiday, we celebrate the Lord’s Resurrection.

Sunday [Note: [Col. 0371C] Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “For Sunday is likewise venerable to us,” etc.] is therefore venerable and solemn for us because on it the Savior, like the rising sun, having dispelled the darkness of the underworld, [Col. 0371B] shone forth with the light of the Resurrection; and for this reason that day is called by worldly people [Note: [Col. 0371C] The same manuscript of Santa Croce Minor: “that day itself has been called by all ages ‘the day of the sun,’ because on it the sun of righteousness, Christ, rises and gives light.”] “the day of the sun,” because on it Christ, the sun of righteousness, rises and gives light.

[Note: [Col. 0372B] Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “Therefore, in the likeness of Sunday,” etc.] Therefore, in the likeness of Sunday, the whole course of the fifty days is celebrated, and [193] all these days are reckoned as Sundays. For the Resurrection is the Lord’s; on Sunday the risen Savior returned to human beings, and after the Resurrection he dwelt among them throughout the entire Pentecost. It was therefore necessary that the festival of those whose holiness was equal should likewise be equal.

For the Lord arranged it so that, just as [Note: [Col. 0372B] Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “just as we were saddened by his Passion through the fasts of Lent, so …”] we were saddened by his Passion through the fasts of Lent, so we might rejoice in his Resurrection through the festal days of Pentecost. We therefore do not fast during Pentecost, because during those days the Lord dwells among us. I repeat: [Note: [Col. 0372B] The same manuscript: “let us not fast.”] we do not fast while the Lord is present, because he himself says: “Can the children of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Luke 5).

Why should the body abstain from food [Note: [Col. 0372C] The same manuscript: “For why should the body abstain from food …”] when the soul is nourished by the Lord’s presence? Someone who is refreshed by the Savior’s grace cannot be fasting. For Christ’s fellowship is, in a certain sense, the Christian’s food. We are therefore refreshed during Pentecost while the Lord dwells among us.

But when, after these days, he ascended to heaven, we fast again [Note: [Col. 0372C] Manuscript Laurentianus: “let us fast again.”], just as the same Savior says: “But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them; then they will fast in those days” (ibid.). For when Christ ascended to heaven, he was taken from our eyes; we suffer hunger—not of the body, but of love—and we struggle not so much with hunger for food as with longing.

Our eyes endure certain longings [Note: [Col. 0372C] Manuscript 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “For a certain longing …”] while they do not see the one they seek, as the prophet says: “My eyes have failed while I hope in my God” (Psalm 68). [Col. 0373A] The prophet’s eyes failed because he did not yet see the one whom he hoped he would see. So also the apostles’ eyes failed when they were unable to gaze upon the Lord as he went up to heaven, according to what Luke says: “While they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” (Acts 1).

The blessed apostles stood suspended in their whole bodies and followed with their eyes the Lord ascending to heaven, because [Note: [Col. 0373C] Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read: “because their eyes could not follow his progress,” and omit “of his feet.”] they could not follow his progress with their feet. And although human sight failed in accompanying the Savior, the devotion of faith did not fail. For their eyes escorted Christ as far as the cloud [Note: [Col. 0373C] The same manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “their eyes escort him as far as the cloud.”]; by the devotion of faith they accompany Christ as far as heaven. Hence the Apostle says, knowing that our faith is in heaven with the Lord: [194] [Col. 0373B] “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3). Therefore a cloud received the Savior from the apostles’ eyes.

Let us see, then, what sort of cloud this was—how splendid, how glorious—that it should be worthy to receive Christ, the light of the world. For it could not have been obscure, foul, or dark, because it is written: “And the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1). Darkness could not carry the light.

That cloud which received Christ as he ascended had also borne witness to Christ on the mountain, of which the evangelist says: “A voice was heard from the cloud” [Note: [Col. 0374C] The same manuscript Laurentianus and the manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “A voice was heard from the cloud.”], saying: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” (Matthew 17).

It was therefore not a cloud that received Christ, but God the Father received the Son, and in a certain encounter of loving-kindness [Col. 0374A] embraced him as he ascended in a gentler bosom. For this reason the Father is said to receive the Son beneath the shelter of a cloud, so that he might be shown to cherish the wounds of his Passion with a kind of refreshment.

After the cross, after the insults, after the underworld, Christ had no greater refreshment [Note: [Col. 0374C] The same manuscript Laurentianus and that of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “unless he were overshadowed by the power of his divinity.”] than to be overshadowed by the power of divinity, just as at his birth it is said to Mary: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1).

The Most High Father, therefore, who at Christ’s birth overshadowed Mary by his power, received him in a cloud as he ascended. For God always protects with the shelter of a cloud those whom, after their sufferings, he brings to rest. Thus the pillar of cloud protected the children of Israel after they had been delivered from Egypt; and, in order to lead them into the promised land after their long labor, he cherished them beneath the shelter of refreshment, as the prophet says: “He spread out a cloud for their protection” (Exodus 13; Psalm 104). He spread out a cloud [Col. 0374B] [Note: [Col. 0374C] The same manuscript Laurentianus and that of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “so that they would not be wearied in the aridity of the desert …”] so that they would not be worn out by the dryness of the desert and even by the sun’s heat.

Let us therefore rejoice on this holy day, just as we rejoiced at Easter. For the solemnity is similar and the same on both days. At Easter all nations are customarily baptized; at Pentecost, however, the apostles were baptized, as the Lord said to his disciples when he was about to ascend to heaven: “John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you will receive not many days from now” (Acts 1).

And therefore Luke says: “When the days of Pentecost were completed, suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as of a mighty wind approaching, and it sat upon each of them; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2).

# HOMILY LXII. On the Solemnity of Holy Pentecost II

[Col. 0373]

## ADMONITION

[Col. 0373B] [195] This homily compels me to undertake a considerable discussion, since it appears to conflict with the preceding one. In this homily the author teaches that one ought to fast on the vigil of Pentecost; in the preceding homily, on the contrary, he says that, for the sake of joy, one ought not to fast throughout the entire fifty days from Easter to the coming of the Holy Paraclete.

Neither the style, which is not plainly similar, nor the manuscript codices, nor the editors—who attribute both homilies to Saint Maximus—allows us to escape by declaring this homily spurious and considering it much later than the holy bishop of Turin. What path of reconciliation, then, should be followed?

I begin by observing that the discipline—that is, the observance of rites—has not been identical in all Churches, but that, according to the tradition of the ancestors, different customs have been in use. At one time people were accustomed to baptize by a single pouring or sprinkling; at other times, by a threefold immersion. Among the Greeks, the consecration of Christ’s body in leavened bread became customary; among the Latins, in unleavened bread—to omit many other examples.

Nor has the Church always retained the same discipline. In the earliest times the sacraments of baptism, confirmation, and the Eucharist were conferred upon children together; later they were administered separately and to those regenerated at a more mature age. Formerly fasting was observed on three days of the week; afterward fasting was established only on Friday and Saturday.

To come, then, to the question of the apparent contradiction: I admit that before Saint Leo the Great no trace is found among the Fathers of a fast preceding the solemnity of Pentecost. Indeed, Tertullian in *On the Crown*, chapter 3, Ambrose, Augustine, Cassian, Leo the Great, and Maximus himself all declare that the Saturday of the vigil of Pentecost was free from fasting.

The whole controversy therefore concerns whether, while Leo was still seated in the chair of Peter, the fast of the Saturday preceding Pentecost was introduced. The solution of this question depends upon the author of the Sacramentary, or Book of Sacraments, which the most learned Blanchini first published from a very ancient manuscript of Verona in volume IV of Anastasius the Librarian, in 1735.

In it, number 26 contains the following prayer for the Mass of the vigil of Pentecost:

“Grant us, we ask, O Lord, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, the new discipline of spiritual observance of your Paraclete, so that our minds, purified by sacred fasting, may be made more ready for all his gifts. Through the Lord, etc.”

This manuscript of the sacraments was attributed to Saint Pope Leo by its editor Blanchini, who maintained that Saint Leo himself was its author, or compiler. This opinion was approved by not a few scholars, including Cajetan Cennius in his dissertation *On the Roman See*, volume IV of Anastasius the Librarian, sections 11 and 12, page 152, and by the editors of the Paris Missal of 1739.

Ballerini, however, in volume II of the works of Saint Leo, preface, pages 3 and following, Venetian edition of 1756, opposed Blanchini and his followers. They admit that the Roman Sacramentary is the most ancient of all those published thus far; they also concede that it contains many passages belonging to Leo and perfectly corresponding to his manner of writing. Nevertheless, they deny that the work was composed by Leo. They hold its author to be uncertain, though they regard the work as ancient and older than Pope Gelasius I.

[Col. 0375] It is therefore not impossible that, in the days of Maximus—who in the year 465 attended the Roman council under Hilary—the fast of the Saturday before Pentecost began to be observed in the Church of Turin and in certain others.

For just as Saint Mamertus, who was appointed bishop of the Church of Vienne in the year 474, instituted the Rogation observances and perhaps the fast before the Lord’s Ascension, which Leo III later extended as public prayers to the universal Church, so the Church of Turin, while Maximus still governed it, could have preceded the solemnity of Pentecost with a fast.

The defenders of Leo’s Sacramentary, in order to show that Leo—who in three sermons on Pentecost, namely the first, second, and fourth, had said that fasting was suspended for the fifty days from Easter to Pentecost—did not write contradictory statements, say that, when the discipline of not fasting was prevailing in the Roman Church, Leo spoke in that manner; but afterward, when the fast had been introduced by him, it began to be mentioned in the liturgy.

If I say that Maximus acted in precisely the same way, since he lived for a long time as bishop of Turin, I shall seem to have alleged nothing incongruous: namely, that at one time he commended the custom of the Church not to fast from Easter to Pentecost, while at another he urged fasting.

The authorship of this homily is asserted above all by the scribes of two manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem. The first, number 90, homily 38, bears the title: “Here begins [the homily] on Pentecost”; the second, number 99, homily 68, is entitled: “Here begins [the homily] on Pentecost and on the psalm: ‘The Lord said to my Lord.’”

It is also asserted by the scribes of the manuscript of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, page 18, whose title is “On the Solemnity of Pentecost”; by Ambrosian manuscript C 98; and by the Turin manuscript, with the heading: “Likewise, on Pentecost,” homily 7.

Three manuscripts differ from these and name three different authors. The Vatican manuscript 172, page 39, attributes it to Saint Augustine; another Vatican manuscript, 6451, page 55, attributes it to Saint Ambrose; and finally manuscript II, formerly of the Minor Convent of Santa Croce and now Laurentian, attributes it to Saint Leo.

We nevertheless think the case sufficiently defended by the excellent critics, the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, who assigned it neither to Ambrose nor to Augustine, and by the Ballerini, who judged that it should not be counted among the works of Saint Leo.

All the editors hold the same view: Gymnicus, page 166; Galesinius, page 138; Combefisius, volume V, page 261; Cumdius, volume III, page 226; Raynaudus, page 222; and Margarinus in *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, page 28.

[Col. 0375A] [197] **ARGUMENT.**—The descent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles proves that Christ became a sharer in the same power and glory as the Father. The words of Psalm 109 are expounded: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand.’”

I believe, brothers, that you know why we have taken care to celebrate this venerable day of Pentecost with no less joy than we celebrated holy Easter, and why we pursue the observance of this solemnity with the same devotion with which we fulfilled the offices of that festival. [Note: Manuscripts II of Santa Croce Minor and 174 of the Florentine ecclesiastical library read: “we have taken care to celebrate holy Easter.”]

For then, just as we have just done, we fast on Saturday, have kept vigils, and have persisted through the night in prayers; and therefore a similar observance must be followed by similar joy. [Note: Manuscript 174 reads: “as we have done now.” Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read “we fasted,” rather than “we fast.”]

The joy is indeed alike: then we received the Savior rising from the underworld; now we await the Holy Spirit from heaven. Then, anxious or troubled, we proclaimed Christ’s coming; now, trembling, or fasting, we long for the coming of the Paraclete. [Note: Manuscripts II of Santa Croce Minor and 90 and 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read: “or troubled, we prayed for Christ’s coming.” Manuscript 90 reads “and” for “or.”]

For in all things God has provided for human salvation. Then the Savior opened the underworld for us so that we might rise again; now the Paraclete has opened heaven for us so that we may reign. By certain steps, as it were, of advancement, we then learned to return from death to life; now we meditate upon ascending from earth to heaven. [Note: The manuscript of Santa Croce Minor reads “has provided.” Manuscript II of Santa Croce Minor reads: “and by certain steps, as it were, of advancement.”]

All these things Christ the Lord works in us. Before he returned to heaven, he promised his disciples, saying: “When I have ascended, I shall ask my Father, and he will send you another Paraclete, that he may be with you for ever, the Spirit of truth” (John 14).

We must therefore believe that Christ has reached the Father when we see the Paraclete descend upon the apostles. We must believe, I say, that, as David says of the Savior, he sits at God’s right hand, because we see the Holy Spirit rejoice in the disciples, as the Lord promised. Thus the prophet of the psalms says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 109). [Note: Manuscript 174 reads “the Paraclete Spirit descended.” The Ambrosian manuscript reads “thus the prophetic [writer] of the psalms says”; the manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads “thus the prophetic psalm says.” Manuscript 90 reads “Sit at my right hand.”]

According to our [198] custom, a seat is offered to one who arrives after completing some work and deserves, as a mark of honour, to sit down. So too the man Jesus Christ, having overcome the devil by his Passion and opened the underworld by his Resurrection, arrives victoriously in heaven as one whose work is completed, and hears from God the Father: “Sit at my right hand.” [Note: The manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads “arriving as victor.”]

Nor is it surprising that the Father offers the Son a share in one seat, since he is of one substance and nature with the Father. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript and manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read: “since he is of one substance and nature with the Father.”]

But perhaps someone may wonder why the Son is believed to be at the right hand. Although there can be no rank of dignity where there is the fullness of divinity, the Son sits at the right hand not in order that he may be preferred to the Father, but lest he be believed inferior. [Note: The manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads “why the Son is said to be.”]

And therefore the Son is at the right hand, because, according to the Evangelist (Matthew 25), the sheep will be placed at the right hand and the goats at the left. It is necessary, therefore, that the first Lamb should occupy the sheep’s portion, and that the spotless leader should secure beforehand a place for the spotless flock which follows, as John says in the Apocalypse (chapter 14): “These are they who follow the Lamb wherever he goes, who have not defiled themselves with women.” [Note: The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read “according to the Gospel.” The manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads “wherever he goes.”]

David the prophet therefore relates: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.” That is, the Lord Father offers to the Lord God Christ the Son an exalted share in his throne, and, as a mark of honour, establishes him at his own right hand in an eternal seat. [Note: The manuscripts of Santa Croce Minor, Florence, Ambrosian, and Santa Croce in Jerusalem read “at his own right hand.”]

In the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 1), moreover, we read the blessed Stephen saying, when he was being stoned by the Jews: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Lord Jesus standing at the right hand of God.” Let us therefore consider why the same Lord is foretold by David as sitting, but proclaimed by Stephen as standing. [Note: The manuscript of Santa Croce reads: “is foretold by David as sitting.”]

First of all, how can God, who is incorporeal and invisible—for he is spirit, as the Lord says, “God is spirit” (John 4)—sit or stand? Further, on what sort of seat does God sit, who is infinite and immeasurable, and who rather contains the whole creation within himself? [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “but rather himself contains all created things.”]

I think that these things were said concerning the Lord by holy men not because they contradict one another, but so that at one time his [199] omnipotence and at another his mercy might be described. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “so that at one time his power and at another his mercy may be described”; the manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “at one time his power, at another mercy.”]

For he is said to sit in respect of the authority of a king, and is represented as standing in respect of the kindness of an intercessor. For the blessed Apostle says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ” (1 John 2). Thus Christ is judge when he sits; he is advocate when he rises. He is indeed judge to the Jews and advocate to Christians. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “He is indeed judge to the Jews, advocate to Christians.”]

For here, standing [200] before the Father, he pleads the causes of Christians, though sinners; there, sitting with the Father, he condemns the sins of the persecuting Pharisees. Against the former he takes vehement vengeance in anger; for the latter, intervening, he has gentle mercy. Here he stands to receive the spirit of Stephen the martyr; there he sits to condemn the crime of Judas the traitor.

# HOMILY LXIII. On the Solemnity of Holy Pentecost III

[Col. 0377]

## ADMONITION

This homily was formerly falsely attributed by some to Saint Augustine; the monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur rightly rejected it into the appendix of that doctor’s sermons. It was no less falsely attributed to Saint Ambrose, both by certain others and by the person who transferred it into the Theodorician manuscript. Yet it contains certain passages plainly similar to those which Saint Maximus included in his homilies when treating the same mystery. I therefore judge that Maximus is likewise its author. I am all the more confirmed in this opinion when I read that it is attributed to Maximus himself in the two oldest manuscripts of Saint Dalmatius and in the Turin manuscript.

[Col. 0377B] **ARGUMENT.**—The holy bishop proves the wondrous return of Christ to heaven from the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, for this shows that his promise was fulfilled.

Your Holiness, beloved, ought already to be familiar with the festival through your devotional observances. For from the celebration itself we learn what we observe and for what reason we observe it.

For when a solemnity already passed is repeated in its appointed course, we become more learned as we celebrate it more often.

Let us therefore celebrate Pentecost today—that is, the fiftieth day from the Lord’s Resurrection—not because on this day, as most people think, the Savior ascended to heaven. For after the Resurrection he remained with the apostles and on the fortieth day returned to the right hand of God the Father, as the evangelist Luke says: “To whom also he presented himself alive after his Passion, appearing to them for forty days” (Acts 1).

For a period of forty days the Savior therefore displayed his fellowship to his disciples, so that we might rejoice in the grace of his Resurrection for as many days as we had mourned the injuries of his Passion, and so that we might be refreshed by his presence for the same span of days during which we fast in his absence.

Christ therefore did not ascend to heaven today; rather, Christ’s Spirit descended from heaven, as the Lord himself promised: “When I have ascended to the Father, I will send you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, and he will teach you all things” (John 16 and 14).

A great grace indeed, and a twofold joy: we do not lose Christ as he departs, and we possess the Spirit as he comes. We retain the former through the merit of faith; we receive the latter through the advance of sanctification.

“When I have gone,” he says, “to the Father, I will send you the Paraclete” (John 16). We believe that the Son has reached the Father when we see the Paraclete descend to the apostles.

For we believe that he reigns in heaven whom we see bestowing holy gifts on earth, as it is written through the prophet: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Psalm 60).

The victor is rightly rewarded; the victor bestows gifts. Hence the Savior, victorious over the devil after his triumph, enriched with blessing the disciples whom he had freed from captivity.

He freed us when, in order to rise again, he closed the underworld by himself; he enriched us when, in order to reign, he opened heaven to us through the Paraclete.

By certain steps, as it were, of advancement, we then learned to return from death to life; now we are taught to ascend from earth to heaven, as it is written: “He himself will teach you all things” (John 14:26).

What does the Holy Spirit teach? Surely he knows how to teach only what is holy. What does the Paraclete teach us? He teaches what the Savior says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all things” (John 16:12).

The Paraclete is therefore a good teacher, because he teaches what Christ reserved for teaching. For the Holy Spirit teaches what the Lord says he has to teach. He is plainly a good teacher, the executor of the Savior’s commands.

[Note: [Col. 0378D] The older manuscript of Piedimonte reads: “Therefore it is necessary that he be of one substance and nature with Christ, since we see that he has the same teaching as Christ.”]

It is therefore necessary that he have one substance and nature with Christ, since we see that he has one teaching with Christ. [201] And therefore, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of the flesh, so that we may be worthy to receive the Holy Spirit.

If we leave this world, we shall receive, like the apostles, the Paraclete—that is, the Spirit of truth, whom the Father will send—because there is no partiality with God the Father. The promises already made to the apostles benefit us if we perform the works, desires, [202] and actions that the apostles performed.

But if, by fulfilling the Lord’s immaculate law, which converts souls, we complete his commandments, we entrust ourselves, with Christ’s grace, as heirs of the Lord and co-heirs with Christ to an eternal inheritance and to dwelling with the angels. May he himself deign to grant this, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

# CLASS THREE: HOMILIES ON THE SAINTS

[Col. 0379]

# HOMILY LXIV. On the Feast of Saint Stephen, Levite and Protomartyr

## ADMONITION

This homily is preceded by a great and splendid apparatus of manuscript witnesses, which, in admirable agreement, have joined together in declaring Saint Maximus its author. From the Vatican Library we examined four manuscripts: 4951, page 23; 480, page 167; Vatican Palatine 435, page 146; and Vatican Regina 25, page 84. We also inspected three Cassinese manuscripts, 206, page 162; 110; and 462; likewise two Vallicellian manuscripts, B 5, page 64, and A 16, page 48; and manuscript XII of Santa Croce in Jerusalem.

To these we add the Lambach manuscript, page 120; two Augian manuscripts, XII and XXXIX; the Modena manuscript E III; two Belgian manuscripts, the Martinian and the Camberonian; the Novara manuscript 42, page 24; and the Vercelli manuscript 81.

The Turin manuscript lacks this material, since it contains only homilies and sermons for the liturgical year. In its place we cite Alcuin, who attributes the homily to Saint Maximus, as is clear from his *Homiliary*, page 31, Venetian edition of 1571.

The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur transferred into the appendix of Saint Augustine’s sermons, number 210, a sermon on the feast of Saint Stephen formerly attributed to Saint Augustine and containing this homily; they declared it to have been composed from passages of Caesarius.

But since we possess the agreement of so many and such important manuscripts, and the same reading in all of them, would it not be more reasonable to judge that Maximus’s homily was appropriated and that whatever is found to be extraneous was attached to it by a later hand?

The editors followed the authority of the manuscripts: Gymnicus, page 179; Galesinius, homily 1 on the Saints, page 142; Combefisius, volume I, page 398; Cumdius, volume I, page 348; Raynaudus, page 234; and Margarinus in *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, page 30.

As a final testimony, there is the Strigoniensis Breviary, which, on the eighth day of the feast of Saint Stephen, assigns this homily to Saint Maximus the bishop as the readings for the second nocturn.

[Col. 0379B] **ARGUMENT.**—Maximus explains why Saint Stephen the Levite, when he was about to die, said of Christ that he saw the Son of Man in heaven and not the Son of God. Stephen was the first of all to bear witness to the truth with his blood, and the first to imitate divine love in loving his enemies.

The reading from the Acts of the Apostles that has been read to us today, dearly beloved brothers, although it contains a great deal that is astonishing in its outward form, nevertheless contains no less of dignity in its mystery: “Behold,” blessed Stephen says, “I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God” (Acts 7). [Note: The Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads, “standing at the right hand of God.”]

Consider more attentively, dearly beloved brothers: when the blessed martyr had seen our Lord Jesus Christ seated at the right hand of God the Father, [Note: Codices I, Pluteus XIV, the Laurentian, and the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read, “standing.”] why did he testify that he saw the Son of Man, and not rather the Son of God, since he would plainly seem to be attributing greater honor to the Lord if he had said that he saw the Son of God rather than the Son of Man? But a definite reason required that this should be shown in heaven in this manner and proclaimed in the world. [Note: The same Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads, “that this should thus be shown to him in heaven and proclaimed,” etc.] For the whole scandal of the Jews consisted in this: why was our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to the flesh is the Son of Man, [Note: The same Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads *erat* (“was”) for *est* (“is”).] also said to be the Son of God? Therefore divine Scripture fittingly remembered that the Son of Man was standing at the right hand of God the Father, so that, to confound the unbelief of the Jews, he might be shown in heaven to that martyr who was denied by the faithless in the world; and that heavenly truth might bear witness to him from whom earthly impiety had withdrawn its faith. [Note: The Laurentian manuscript reads, “to whom through faith” (a fragmentary variant).] [Note: The Codex of Laurentiana and the edition in the appendix to St. Augustine read, “to confute.”] [Note: The same Laurentian and Vatican 4951 manuscripts read, “he was shown in heaven to that martyr.”]

Hence, although according to the psalm that was read, “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115), [Note: Vatican 4951 reads, “Precious in the sight of the Lord,” etc.] nevertheless, if there can be any distinction among martyrs, the one who is first seems to be foremost. For when St. Stephen had been ordained deacon by the apostles, [Note: Vatican 4951 reads, “had been ordained deacon by the apostles.”] he preceded the apostles themselves in a blessed and triumphant death. Thus, he who was lower in rank became first in suffering; and he who was a disciple in status began to be a teacher through martyrdom. He fulfilled what the blessed prophet said in the psalm: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Psalm 115). [Note: The same Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and the cited edition read, “in the psalm that was read, he said,” etc.]

For Stephen the martyr first wished to render to the Lord [Note: The same Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads, “beforehand.”] what he had received from the Lord together with the whole human race. [Note: Vatican 4951 reads, “what he had received from the Lord together with the human race.”] The death that the Savior deigned to suffer for all, he first returned to the Savior.

After this, Holy Scripture added and said: “Having knelt down, he cried out, saying: Do not hold this sin against them.” [Note: The same Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and Casinensis 190 read, “Lord, do not hold,” etc.] Observe, dearly beloved brothers, the feeling of this blessed man; observe his great and admirable love. He was under persecution, yet he was praying for his persecutors; and amid that shower of stones, when another might have forgotten even his dearest friends, he was commending his enemies to the Lord. [Note: Casinensis 100 reads, “his enemies.”]

What was he saying as he was being stoned? “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Thus he grieved more over their sins than over his own wounds, more over their impiety than over his own death—and rightly so. For in their wickedness there were many things that ought to be mourned, [Note: The same Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads, “which ought to be mourned.”] whereas in his death there was nothing that ought to cause grief. Eternal death followed upon their impiety, but everlasting life followed upon his death.

Let us therefore imitate in some measure, dearly beloved brothers, the faith of so great a teacher and the love of so illustrious a martyr. Let us love our brothers in the Church with the same disposition with which he then loved his enemies. But what is worse, at times we not only fail to love our enemies, but do not even preserve perfect fidelity toward our friends. [Note: The edition and Casinensis 100 read, “but do not even preserve fidelity toward friends.”]

But someone says: “I cannot love my enemy, whom I suffer daily as though he were a most cruel foe.” O whoever you are, you pay attention to what a human being has done to you and do not consider what you have done to God. Since you have committed far more serious sins against God, [Note: The edition reads, “much more serious.”] why do you not forgive a small matter to a human being, [Note: Vatican 4951 reads, “a small thing to a human being.”] so that God may deign to forgive you much? [Note: The edition reads, “Recall what.”]

Recall what Truth itself promised you in the Gospel, and what sort of security, so to speak, it gave you, or what agreement it entered into with you. “For,” he says, “if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive your debts” (Matthew 6). [Note: Vatican 4951 reads, “and your Father will forgive you your sins.”] [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “neither will your Father forgive you your sins.”]

You see, brothers, that by God’s grace it has been placed in our power how we shall be judged by the Lord. “If,” he says, “you forgive, you will be forgiven.” [Note: The edition reads, “For often.”]

I have often said this, brothers, and I must say it frequently: let no one deceive himself, let no one mislead himself. [Note: The same Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads, “for whoever hates even one person in this world,” etc.] Whoever hates even one person in this world loses everything that he may have offered to God in good works, [Note: The same Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads, “whatever he has offered, he will lose it all.”] because the apostle Paul does not lie when he says: “If I give all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I deliver my body so that I may burn,” [Note: The edition reads, “so that I may burn.”] “but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13). Blessed John also confirms this when he says: “Everyone who does not love his brother remains in death.” [Note: The same Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads, “Everyone who hates his brother remains in death.” The edition has, “For everyone who does not love,” etc.] And again: “He who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3).

Here “brother” must be understood as every human being; we are all brothers in Christ. Therefore let no one presume upon virginity without love; no one upon almsgiving; no one upon fasting; no one upon prayers. [Note: The same Laurentian and Holy Cross manuscripts read, “no one upon fasting, no one upon prayers.”] Whoever keeps enmity in his heart will not be able to make the Lord favorable to him either by these works or by any others. [Note: Vatican 4951 reads, “or by any other good works.”]

But if he wishes to have God favorable to him, let him not disdain to hear good counsel. [Note: The Laurentian manuscript reads, “my counsel.”] Let him hear, not me, but his own Lord. “If,” he says, “you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5).

But we have quarrels within us [Note: The edition reads, “having [quarrels].”] and carry deceit in our hearts; [Note: The Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Vatican, and edition read, “as though those who have a good conscience.”] as though we had a good conscience, we presume to approach the altar. We do not fear what is written: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11). [Note: In the Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, “and drinks” is absent.] “But,” someone says, “it is a great labor to love one’s enemies and to pray for one’s persecutors.” [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “to pray for sinners.”]

We do not deny it, brothers: it is indeed no small labor in this world, but the reward will be great in the future. Through the love of one enemy you will become a friend of God; indeed, not only a friend but also a son, as the Lord himself says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Luke 6). [Note: Vatican 4951 and the edition read, “you will become a friend of God.”]

If some rich person in this world wished to adopt you as a son, how would you serve him? What humiliations even from his servants, what harsh and sometimes shameful services would you endure in order to attain his fleeting and fragile inheritance? [Note: The edition adds, “insults.”] What another would endure for earthly possessions, endure for eternal life. For we are convicted by the clearest reasoning that we can endure injuries for God’s sake, but do not wish to.

Finally, if some powerful person injures us, [Note: The edition reads, “does [us an injury].”] even if he curses us to our face, we do not dare to answer anything harsh—let alone repay him in kind. [Note: Vatican 4951 reads, “even if he curses us to our face.”] Why? So that we may not suffer still greater things from that powerful person than those we have already endured. [Note: The edition reads, “Why is this so?”] What fear of a human being extorts from us, the love of Christ ought to have demanded from us. [Note: The Laurentian manuscript reads, “ought to demand from us,” etc.; the cited Codex 12 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads, “ought to have demanded from us,” etc.]

If, then, a powerful person rages against us, we remain silent and dare say nothing; but if an equal, or perhaps an inferior, inflicts even a slight insult upon us, [Note: The Maurist edition omits the particle “or.”] we rise up like a wild beast, without any patience and without any consideration of God; either we avenge our injury on the spot, or at least prepare our mind to repay it with something greater. [Note: The Laurentian manuscript reads, “at once, as if we were wild beasts.”]

What is this? When a powerful person has inflicted an injury upon us, we accept it patiently; when an inferior has done so, we are inflamed with excessive fury. [Note: The Laurentian, Codex 12 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, and the edition read, “What is this, that when,” etc.] There we feared a human being; here we do not wish to fear God. [Note: Codex 12 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads, “we accept it.”]

Therefore, brothers, let us prepare our heart for patience as much as we can, with God’s help, [Note: The Laurentian, Vatican 4951, and the edition read, “Therefore, I ask you, dearly beloved brothers, let us prepare our heart as much as we can,” etc.] and strive to act as physicians toward all evil people. Let us hate not the people themselves, but their wickedness. [Note: The same Codex 12 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and the Maurist edition read, “their wickedness.”] Let us pray for the good, that they may always advance toward better things; for the wicked, that they may quickly turn to reform their lives through the tears of repentance. [Note: The edition reads, “that they may flee for refuge through patience.”] May he deign to grant this to us when we pray, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY LXV. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist I

[Col. 0383]

## ADMONITION

No disagreement presses upon us here, either among the manuscript codices or among the editors, since they all present St. Maximus as the author of this homily under essentially the same title. Their enumeration will be lengthy, and from it confidence in them will be all the greater. The Vatican Library supplied us with four codices: 6451, p. 136; 1146, p. 209; 1269, p. 39 verso; and 1277, p. 42 verso. We also collated three other codices with our manuscript in the Casinensian archive: 12, p. 321; 104, p. 166 verso; and CXI, p. 70. We also saw two codices in the Vallicellana Library: 7 A and XV, p. 153 verso; and in the Cistercian monastery of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Codex XII, a lectionary, p. 63.

These are followed by confirmations from the two Augian codices XV and XVI, Novariensis 42, p. 76, the Ratisbon manuscript of St. Emmeram, the Martinian manuscript, the Ambrosian manuscript marked C 98, the Veronese manuscript 431, and finally the Breviary of the Church of Strigonia. Among the editors, Alcuin comes first, p. 317. For those already mentioned are much later: Gymnicus, p. 193; Galesinius, p. 247; Cumdius, vol. IV, p. 393; Combefisius, vol. VI, p. 122; Raynaudus, p. 317; and Margarinus in the *Bibliotheca Maxima*, vol. VI, p. 32. The title of all of them is: “On the day of the Nativity of St. John the Baptist,” which we too have adopted.

[Col. 0383B] **ARGUMENT.**—The holy martyrs, bravely enduring torments and a bloody death for Christ, bestow honor upon the Lord. John the Baptist was granted the glory of glorifying the Lord through the fullness of prevenient grace and of preparing the way for the Redeemer.

[Note: Vatican 6451, both Ambrosian codices, the manuscript of St. Emmeram at Ratisbon, the Veronese manuscript, three Casinensian manuscripts, and the Martinian manuscript read, “The solemnity of various martyrs has consecrated for us.”]

The passing away of the present life and the suffering they accepted for Christ’s name have consecrated for us the solemnity of various martyrs, dearly beloved brothers. For we have learned from many accounts of the ancients that some martyrs, struck down by the sword, others burned by fire, many torn apart by the teeth of wild beasts, and countless others subjected even to various tortures, gave testimony to the Christian faith while despising the death of their bodies. But blessed John the Baptist, whose feast we joyfully celebrate today, born today from a barren womb, brought heavenly joys into the world. [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “he introduced them.”]

Those martyrs confessed, with unquestionable glory, the Son of God already reigning; but John, through the illumination of the prophetic spirit, foresaw the Lord who was to be born and, through the privilege of singular grace, revealed him when he had been born. [Note: The same Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and the Vallicellana manuscript read, “So singular was the election that shone forth in blessed John,” etc.]

So singular was the election that shone forth in him that he deserved to announce the Lord before he had received either the beginning of birth or a tongue with which he could proclaim him. [Note: The manuscript of St. Emmeram reads, “a tongue with which he could proclaim”; the Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, “which could announce”; and Vatican 1269, “with which he could announce him.”]

Finally, that old woman and new mother Elizabeth, who before her own delivery rejoiced in the ministry of her future son, said to blessed Mary when she came to her, at the very meeting of the greeting: “Behold, as soon as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb” (Luke 1). [Note: The Vatican, Veronese, two Vallicellana, and several Casinensian codices read, “as soon as it came to be.”] [Note: The Martinian manuscript omits “for joy.”]

What kind of miracle is this, brothers? What unprecedented greatness of joys, that Elizabeth testified that she had an infant in her womb who, while not yet perceiving himself, already perceived the Lord’s arrival? Truly, he was the most blessed of all infants, who, still enclosed within his mother’s womb, revealed through prophetic joy that the Savior of the world was present, since at that time he could not do so by speech.

No one is unaware, dearly beloved, that every infant emerging from the mother’s womb begins the very dawn of life with mournful cries. Only the Lord’s Baptist, contrary to the law of those being born, anticipated his birth with a joyful exultation.

And how fitting it was, brothers, that he should be born of a barren mother, who revealed the fruitfulness of a virgin, so that, born miraculously, he might display a miraculous birth.

How astonishing and magnificent also was this: Zacharias the priest, the future prophet’s father, because he did not believe what was happening when the angel spoke, lost the use of speech, [Note: The manuscripts of St. Emmeram, the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, and Vatican 1269 read, “lost the use of speaking.”] until, once the promise had been fulfilled, the birth of the new man, the herald, loosened the bonds of his father’s tongue. The mouth that the angel had closed was opened by the son whom the angel had promised.

When the relatives and neighbors were deliberating anxiously about the child’s name, the mute father suddenly recovered his former power of speech and declared the proper name that he had learned at the angel’s command. [Note: The manuscript of St. Emmeram reads, “which he had learned from the announcing angel”; the Veronese, “which he had learned from the angel dictating it,” etc.] [Note: The Codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and Verona read, “having suddenly recovered his former power of speech.”] Thus, as he had silently awaited the child’s birth in obedience to the heavenly command, he spoke the name of the one who had been born; and the anxious old man recognized that through him he had been restored to himself, although he had not believed that the child would be born from him. Nor could he doubt thereafter that the child had either been promised or born from heaven, since because of him he had proved both the loss and the recovery of speech.

What is more glorious than this piety, brothers? What more distinguished than this faith? In it, the barren woman conceives, the mute man speaks, and, in the secret recesses of the mother’s womb, the infant anticipates the future joys of the whole world. For mortal nature could not preserve its customary order under the old law, when, through the new grace of the Divinity, a new mystery of salvation for all was being prepared. [Note: The Martinian manuscript omits “future.”]

This, then, is John, of whom Isaiah prophesied, saying: “A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Isaiah 40). “A voice,” he says, “crying”; how fittingly he is called a voice, who with joyful mouth cried out about the Only-Begotten Son of God, coming from heaven in human flesh. Rightly he is called a voice, at whose resounding proclamation deaf humanity, long unhearing, began to hear the mystery of human redemption.

For just as the venerable Baptist opened the tongue of his mute father, so he renewed the hearing of human ears with saving grace. [Note: The Martinian manuscript reads, “so he renewed human ears.”] [Note: The Vatican and Veronese codices read, “he renewed their hearing.”] [Note: Vatican 10 reads, “But he cried out.”] [Note: The Casinensian manuscript reads, “But he cried out.”]

He cries out in the wilderness, where neither the insolent crowd would drown out his preaching nor an unbelieving hearer mock it, but only those could hear who, with concern for divine worship alone, sought to hear the word of salvation being preached and recognized that he spoke truth about Christ. [Note: Vatican 10 reads, “where the unusual crowd would not disturb his preaching.”] [Note: The Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads, “could hear”; the Casinensian manuscript, “may be able to hear.”]

For in defense of justice he rebuked Herod’s unlawful marriage, neither fearing to offend the king, nor avoiding the squalor of prison, nor fleeing death by the tyrant’s sword. [Note: The Ambrosian, Holy Cross, and Veronese codices read, “in defense of justice.”] [Note: The Martinian manuscript omits “so that.”]

Let us listen a little longer, brothers, to what the Savior’s messenger preached for the benefit of us all: [Note: The Ambrosian and Holy Cross codices read, “Prepare,” he says, “the way of the Lord.”]

“Prepare,” he says, “the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.” Truly blessed John was worthy to have a prophetic birth, since he was born by God’s gift to parents whose posterity had been despaired of. For with such authority and such weight of teaching he broke forth into the voice of holy preaching, proclaimed the Lord’s imminent arrival, and directed the crookedness of those living wickedly into straight paths. [Note: The Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads *ut* (“so that”) instead of *et* (“and”); the Veronese reads, “so that he might also earnestly announce the Lord’s arrival.”]

For what is “Prepare the way of the Lord” except to prepare, for the Judge coming from heaven, a dwelling place in a pure heart, cleansed of vices? [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads, “What is ‘prepare the way for the Lord’?”; Codex 12 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads, “What is it to prepare the way for the Lord, unless, when the Judge comes from heaven, having purified,” etc.]

What is “Make straight the paths of our God” except to build such roads for yourself through your actions that the Lord, coming favorably to you, may delight to walk along them? [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads, “What is ‘make straight the paths of God’?”]

He prepares a way for his Lord who, rejecting the pleasures of his luxuriant flesh, suspended in his whole mental spirit toward God, girds himself with the strength of chastity. [Note: The Ambrosian and Veronese codices read, “rejecting the desire of his luxuriant flesh.”]

He prepares an excellent way for the Lord who restrains his thoughts, seething with the waves of avarice, through the calm of a serene conscience. He prepares a way for the Lord who, trampling upon the empty images of idols and all the fabrications of superstitions, seeks the worship of the one living God and faith in the truth. [Note: Vatican 1269 reads, “the profane images of idols.”] [Note: Vatican 1196 reads, “all the superstitious fabrications.”]

But whoever languishes in the sensual allurements of this world, rages in the fever of burning avarice, and blazes in the jaws of deadly envy against his brothers, and, to the insult of almighty God, walks as a wandering traveler along the winding paths of demons, [Note: The Casinensian and Veronese codices read, “along the winding paths.”] does not prepare a way for the Lord, but opens within himself a ruinous entrance for his wretched enemy. [Note: The Veronese reads, “opens it up.”]

These habits and this kind of life open broad roads and spacious ways for barbarian nations into the exile of the common salvation. These habits deliver the people of God to enemy nations under the yoke of miserable captivity. These habits scatter armed peoples and destroy fortified cities.

What more need be said, dearly beloved? Whatever power and strength we see in our enemies is nourished by the corruption of our life and by our unbelief. This is why we ask nothing of God in poured-out supplication: because, clinging incessantly to impious and wicked desires, we do not prepare the way for our Lord according to the prophetic admonitions. [Note: The Veronese reads, “we do not prepare it.”]

Therefore, returning to the commands of the most blessed John, let us prepare the way for the Lord; let us make straight the paths of our God, so that the Lord, seeing in us the roads of good will, may meanwhile, as a most kind shepherd, seek his little sheep, already wearied by many dangers. Thus, just as today we rejoice in the birth of the Lord’s Baptist, so may we rejoice in the reconciliation of our God, to whom be honor and glory. [Note: Codex 12 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and the Casinensian manuscripts read, “so that, just as we rejoice today in the birth of the most blessed Lord’s Baptist, so may we rejoice in the reconciliation of our God, to whom is honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.”] [Note: Codex 12 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and the Casinensian manuscripts read, “so that, just as we rejoice today in the birth of the most blessed Lord’s Baptist, so may we rejoice in the reconciliation of our God, to whom is honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.”]

# HOMILY LXVI. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist II

[Col. 0387]

## ADMONITION

It must surely be regarded as a clear testimony to the truth that many writers, at different times and from different places, have come together in one judgment. This homily enjoys that singular support, which we are now about to present.

We shall first list four Vatican codices: 6451, p. 136; 1196, p. 209; 1269, p. 1269 verso; and 1277, p. 42 verso. Next come three Casinensian codices: 12, p. 521; 104, p. 166 verso; and CXI, p. 70. Corresponding to these are two Vallicellana codices, XV, p. 153 verso, and 7 A; two Augian codices, XV and XVI; Codex XII of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, p. 63; Vercellensis 81; Veronensis 431; the Subiaco manuscript; Novariensis 42, p. 79; the Ratisbon manuscript of St. Emmeram; the Martinian manuscript in Belgium; the Ambrosian manuscript C 98; and the Breviary of the Church of Strigonia.

Alcuin preceded the editors, and has this same homily under Maximus’s name on p. 517 of the Venetian edition of 1571, with the title “On the Nativity of St. John the Baptist.” This title was later adopted by Gymnicus, p. 193; Galesinius, p. 147; Cumdius, vol. IV, p. 393; Combefisius, vol. VI, p. 122; Raynaudus, p. 226; and finally Margarinus in the *Bibliotheca Maxima*, vol. VI, p. 32. This homily and the preceding one are absent from the Laurentian codices.

[Col. 0387B] 211 **ARGUMENT.**—The Spirit of God entrusted to the holy prophets was always a great glory for them. But John surpassed them all in glory, since they foretold the Redeemer who was to come, whereas he announced him as present.

The venerable memory of all the prophets is indeed fitting, dearly beloved brothers. [Note: The Ambrosian, Veronese, Camberon, Martinian, and another Veronese manuscript read, “But blessed John,” etc.] Blessed John the Baptist, whose genuine nativity is honored today, surpassed the glory of all those prophets to such an extent that, by the truth of his present testimony, he revealed that our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior was not only going to come, but had already come and was dwelling among human beings. [Note: The Codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Verona, and the Casinensian manuscripts read, “by a certain singular merit.”] When he saw him hurrying among the mixed crowds toward his baptism, he pointed him out, as though with a finger, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads in full, “Behold him who takes away the sin of the world.” The Casinensian and Veronese codices read, “How innocent was his life, or with what devotion can we repay his merits?”]

How innocent was his life—or with what devotion can we repay the merits of him who was the first to recognize the coming of the heavenly Lamb and the only one to point him out? [Note: The same codices read, “How venerable is his proclamation for all.”] How venerable for all was his proclamation, from whose mouth the world first heard its absolution! [Note: The Ambrosian and Veronese codices read, “from whose mouth the world first heard.”]

This is he, dearly beloved, of whom it was foretold by prophetic announcement: “A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Isaiah 40; Luke 3). [Note: Vatican 1269 and 1196, as well as three Casinensian codices, read, “the way of the Lord.”] He was going to cry out, as he did cry out, so that, while the herald of salvation was proclaiming, heavenly preaching might open the ears of mortals, long stopped up. [Note: The Martinian manuscript reads *et* (“and”) instead of *ut* (“so that”).]

Who, then, would not receive such a prophet with complete admiration, recognizing that he obtained so much from God that his merits were praised before his birth had taken shape? [Col. 0388B] 212

This John, then, was promised by the providence of almighty God, through an angel, to the most just priest Zacharias, when he was advanced in years and had despaired, because of the barrenness of his very old wife, of the succession of the desired offspring. And fittingly a new son was given to very old parents, who would show the Only-Begotten Son of God to the aging and declining world as the hope of future youth. [Note: The Martinian manuscript reads, “of future life.”]

What could be more astonishing, and with what great wonder should it be regarded, than that Zacharias himself, while believing somewhat too slowly that the Forerunner of the saving Word was to be conceived in an aged womb, [Note: The Ambrosian, Holy Cross, and Casinensian codices read, “while believing somewhat too slowly”; the Martinian, “believed.”] became mute through the sudden silence imposed upon him, and did not recover his former use of speech until the child’s name, by which he was to be called, loosened the bonds of his closed mouth?

Thus it came about that the priestly mouth, which the trembling of doubt had bound, was freed by the merit of the child who was being born, [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads, “the name of the son who was being born rightly freed it.”] and that the father’s restored tongue testified to the infant’s glory.

What shall I say about the virtue of his continence, or about his love of justice, whose manner of life, as we read, was inimitable, and for whom truth was more precious than light itself? [Note: Vatican 1196 reads, “inimitable sustenance, and truth more precious than light.”] Living in the wilderness, wearing a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist, he ate locusts and wild honey (Matthew 3; Mark 1), so that, when rebuking the evils of human beings, he would have no pleasure at all either in clothing or in food. [Note: The Veronese and three Casinensian codices read, “Living in the wilderness, wearing a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist.”]

Finally, such zeal for divine law possessed his mind that he rebuked the wickedness of a faithless generation with prophetic vigor [Note: The Martinian manuscript reads, “with prophetic rigor.”] and, with the authority of the Holy Spirit burning within him, fearlessly rebuked the king in his error. The most blessed man preferred to succumb to the sword under the denunciation of justice in its fury rather than to keep silent about the truth, since he had come to reveal its author. [Note: The Veronese reads, “he had come to reveal the author of truth.”] [Note: The Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem adds: “The author, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”]

Amen.

# HOMILY LXVII. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist III

[Col. 0389]

## ADMONITION

213 Several more manuscript codices also attribute this third homily, *On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist*, to St. Maximus. The foremost place is held by three Vatican codices: 1277, p. 42; 1269; and 1196, p. 24 verso. Next come three Casinensian codices: 12, p. 322 verso; 104, p. 167 verso; and CXI, p. 71 verso.

The following fully agree with them: Codex XII of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, p. 71; Novariensis 42, p. 80; Augiensis XV; the Ratisbon manuscript of St. Emmeram, p. 33; Veronensis 431; the Martinian manuscript; and the Ambrosian manuscript. All of these, bearing Maximus’s name in their title, proclaim him the author.

There is no question concerning the editors, since all who included the preceding two homilies likewise attributed this one to St. Maximus: Gymnicus, namely, p. 201; Galesinius, p. 149; Cumdius, vol. IV, p. 394; Combefisius, vol. VI, p. 123; Raynaudus, p. 328; and Margarinus in the *Bibliotheca Maxima*, vol. VI, p. 35. It must not be omitted, however, that until now no one has denied these three homilies to our Maximus.

[Col. 0389A] 214 **ARGUMENT.**—All the prophets’ proclamations were confirmed through John the Baptist. For he alone deserved to see our Lord Jesus Christ with his own eyes and announce him as present. He was called more than a prophet, the voice crying in the wilderness, and greater than those born of women.

[Col. 0389B] The genuine birth of the most revered John the Baptist has consecrated the festival of the present day, dearest brothers—he who was sent into this world by a heavenly dispensation so that not only he himself might be exalted by prophetic glory, but also that through him the proclamations of all the prophets might be confirmed. [Note: Vatican manuscript 1196 and the Martinian manuscript omit “also.”] [Note: The same Ambrosian manuscript reads “his genuine festival consecrated”; Vatican manuscript 1196 reads “the nativity of the one born.”] Nor is it without reason that we now venerate him with particular honor [Note: The same Vatican and Casinensian manuscripts read “with particular honor now.”], since, by a special grace, he was the last to prophesy the Redeemer of the world for this very purpose: that he might be the first to point him out. [Note: Vatican manuscripts 1269 and 1196 read “so that he might be the first to show him.”]

For he alone among the prophets deserved to see with his own eyes and proclaim as present our Lord Jesus Christ, whom the others knew beforehand as destined to come only after a long passage of time. [Note: Three Casinensian manuscripts read “deserved to see with his own eyes.”] For, as the most sacred Gospel relates, when the Lord came to his baptism, John burst forth in these words: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away” [Col. 0389C] [Note: The same Ambrosian manuscript, all the Vatican manuscripts, and the Casinensian manuscripts read “behold him who takes away the sin of the world.”] “the sins of the world” (John 1).

For this reason the Savior himself was saying of him to the crowds: [Note: The Martinian manuscript omits “of him.”] “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? I tell you, and more than a prophet” (Matthew 11). [Note: The Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscript reads: “Blessed John the Baptist is greater than…” [Col. 0390C].]

He truly is more than a prophet, since all the others were still heralds of Christ who was to come, whereas this most approved one came as the attesting witness of the Lord who was already present. He is more than a prophet, in whose hands the Son of God humbled himself to be baptized—an honor granted to no other prophet. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “in whose hands.”] [Note: The Martinian manuscript reads “in being baptized.”]

He is more than a prophet, whose merits possess such a great prerogative that, at one and the same moment, he immersed in the Jordan the arbiter of heaven and earth submerged beneath the waters, saw the Holy Spirit coming in the form of a dove, and heard from heaven the voice of the Father bearing witness (Matthew 3). [Note: The Vatican manuscripts 1277 and 1196, as well as the Casinensian manuscripts, read “whose prerogative is so great.”] [Note: The same Ambrosian manuscript and the Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscript read “the arbiter of heaven and earth.”]

This is the one whom Isaiah, foreknowing through the inspiration of God, announces when he says: [Col. 0390B] “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way” [Note: The same Ambrosian manuscript reads “Prepare the way of the Lord.”] “of the Lord” (Isaiah 40).

How appropriately, dearest brothers [Note: The Martinian manuscript omits “dearest.”], was blessed John proclaimed a voice, since he was sent both as herald and witness of the heavenly Word. This is the one whose birth, name, and merit were foretold through the angel Gabriel. [Note: The Casinensian and Martinian manuscripts omit “and.” The Martinian manuscript adds after “voice”: “he who…”]
