This is also the one who, by the judgment of a heavenly decree, is placed before all mortals, for the Lord says: “Among those born of women there has not risen a greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11). How beautifully it is said that among those born of women there is none greater than John, because the one born of a virgin was greater in every respect. [Note: Casinensian manuscript 12 reads “who was born.”]

This is also the one who preferred to be struck down by a king rather than fail to rebuke a king who was sinning. Considering these things, beloved, observe how much reverence [Note: Vatican manuscripts 1269 and 1277 read “how much reverence, how much devotion…”] and devotion we ought to offer to him who, so that he might be honored, was prophesied by the Holy Spirit, promised by an angel, praised by the Lord, and consecrated by the perpetual glory of a holy death. [Note: The Martinian manuscript reads “crowned” instead of “consecrated.”]

For it was fitting that a wondrous life should follow his mystical birth, and that death, devoted to God, should bring his holy and perfect life to its conclusion. [Note: The Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscript reads “Therefore.”]

For this reason, brothers, throughout the whole world today the Church of Christ celebrates together, in a most joyful festival, the beginning of his birth—he who revealed to a world struck with wonder that eternal joys were coming to mortals, as their most faithful witness.

## HOMILY LXVIII. On the birthday of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul I

[Col. 0391]

### NOTICE

That Saint Maximus delivered distinguished panegyrical discourses concerning Peter and Paul, the princes of the apostles, is clear both from manuscript codices and from printed editions. The first testimony was given by Gennadius, who says that the holy bishop of Turin wrote treatises in praise of the apostles. By this general commendation he embraced all the homilies and sermons that Maximus himself delivered for the celebration of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

Two Vatican manuscripts bearing the name of Saint Maximus for this homily are Vatican manuscripts 1273, folio 54 verso, and 1277, folio 54 verso; and three Casinensian manuscripts, 102, folio 153 verso, 109, folio 88 verso, and 305, folio 171. We include among these the very ancient Ambrosian manuscript, highly praised by Mabillon and Muratori, and its contemporary manuscript from Saint Gall; then Augiensis XV, the manuscript of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, page 34, Veronensis 431, the two Belgian manuscripts Martinian and Camberonian, and Vallicellian manuscript 9; and finally manuscript 99 of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, which bears the same title, “On the birthday of the saints Peter and Paul.”

We do not deny that certain copyists attributed this homily to Saint Leo the Great, as occurs in Vatican manuscript 1269, page 52 verso, in manuscript 9 A of the Basilica of Saint Peter, page 400 verso, and in manuscript II, formerly of the library of the Minor Holy Cross, page 226, now Laurentian. But every suspicion has been removed by the Ballerini brothers, since they did not receive it among the Leonine sermons.

And although the following homilies are found inserted in ancient collections of Saint Leo, this one was certainly always assigned to Saint Maximus. This should be noted for the stronger confirmation of its authorship. Corresponding to the manuscripts that support Maximus are the editors: Gymnicus, page 205, whose title is “On the birthday of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul”; Galesinius, page 150; Combefisius, volume VI, page 204; Cumdius, volume IV, page 444; Raynaudus, page 228; and Margarini, in the *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, page 34, who adopted Gymnicus’s same title.

We omit a list of the authors who used Saint Maximus’s words to prove Peter’s primacy in the Church and the full power of judgment conferred upon him by Christ through the keys, since these matters are so well known that they cannot be made better known.

[Col. 0391A] **ARGUMENT.**—The princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, are exalted by Saint Maximus with wondrous and entirely truthful praises, especially Peter, from whose confession of Christ’s divinity it is plainly understood that the primacy of the universal Church was entrusted to him.

As we honor with annual solemnities [Note: The Casinensian manuscript reads “festivals.”] the most glorious princes of the Christian faith, dearest brothers, we venerate with due religious devotion the Lord and God himself, who is the author of this faith. For the apostles are called *missi* in Latin, “those who have been sent.” Therefore, it is evident that those who honor the ones sent honor the one who sent them; for the dignity shown to ministers is undoubtedly shown to the one whose ministers they are. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “it is evident that they honor the sender”; the Martinian and Casinensian manuscripts omit “them.”] Thus the Savior himself says [Note: The Basilica of Saint Peter manuscript reads “to his disciples”] to his disciples: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever receives you receives me” (Luke 10; Matthew 10). [Note: Manuscript II, formerly of the Minor Holy Cross convent, and the Martinian manuscript read: “and whoever despises you despises me, and whoever receives you…”] [Note: The Martinian manuscript reads: “Truly blessed are the merits of the apostles…”] Truly blessed are the merits of the apostles, in whom Christ proclaims that he is both received [Col. 0391B] [Note: The Basilica of Saint Peter manuscript omits “and”] and heard.

Blessed likewise are those whose devotion, offered to the apostles, returns to Christ. [Note: The same Saint Peter manuscript reads “whose confession, offered to the apostles, returns to Christ.”] Therefore, holding fast, brothers, to the faith of so great a promise, let us rejoice with faithful joy over the sufferings endured by our fathers for the confession of Christ; for whoever rejoices in the death of martyrs [Note: Vatican manuscript 1277 reads “rejoice”] does not doubt that the martyrs reign with Christ after death. [Note: The same manuscript reads “do not doubt.”]

Let us honor with the most devout zeal the most revered fathers of all the Churches [Note: The cited Saint Peter manuscript reads “the most revered.”]—Peter, I mean, and Paul—to whom, by the grace of Christ, death has become a birthday today: for them the end of life gave a beginning to living; for them, as the apostle Paul says (Philippians 1), “to live was Christ” [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript lacks “was.”] “and to die gain.”

Christ was indeed life for them, since life was not life for them without Christ. Christ was life for them because everything that they lived benefited the Churches of Christ. And to die was gain for them, because by such a death they purchased eternal life. [Note: The same Jerusalem Holy Cross, Ambrosian, and Veronese manuscripts read “because by this kind of death.”] To die was gain for them, since incorruption succeeded their corruption, and the losses of present times were followed by eternal gains.

But now, dearest brothers, I think it necessary that we speak of their particular and distinctive virtues, insofar as the dryness of our tongue and the weakness of our intellect permit—or rather, insofar as merciful God grants his assent.

This, then, is that Peter who, by confessing that Christ the Lord is the Son of the living God, established for us the strongest and unconquerable foundations of belief. For when the Lord asked who people said he was, he replied: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16). [Note: The Casinensian manuscript reads “For when he asked…”]

That is: “You, Lord, made from the flesh of a virgin, are Christ, who are the eternal Son of the living God. You, Lord, born among human beings, are human, while in your unthinkable majesty you are God with God.” [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads: “You, Lord, are the eternal Son of the living God; you, Lord, born to human beings, are human.”] You are Christ, who, coming to suffer for our redemption, remain impassible with the Father.”

Who, then, could ever have raised the gaze of human understanding to so great a mystery of the incomprehensible Godhead, unless the truth of this saving faith had shone forth from Peter’s mouth? [Note: The cited Saint Peter manuscript omits “human.”]

Who could match, even with great eloquence, the glory of his merits, from whom faith in the divinity that must be adored both began for us and endures? [Note: The Casinensian manuscript reads “who is so much more glorious.”] What is more glorious than a man who, by speaking, revealed faith in an inscrutable secret, taught it by living, and confirmed it by suffering?

But to show how great was the magnitude of this confession, the Savior also said: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” [Note: Vatican manuscript 1277 reads “because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you…”] “but my Father, who is in heaven; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:17, 19). [Note: The Saint Peter manuscript reads, “How great was the magnitude of blessed Peter’s confession.”] [Note: Vatican manuscript 1277 reads “because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you…”] [Note: The Saint Peter 40 F and Casinensian manuscripts read “who is in heaven.”]

Who, then, could have perceived that Christ, born in the flesh and through the flesh, was the Son of the almighty Father, unless the Father himself, in his favor, had revealed this to us from heaven through Peter? [Note: Saint Peter manuscript 9 A reads “this also the Father himself.”]

This confession granted him that he should receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven before he entered through the gates of heaven. [Note: The Holy Cross and Saint Peter manuscripts read “This confession granted him…”] [Note: The Ambrosian, Veronese, Casinensian, and Saint Peter 40 F manuscripts read “of the heavenly kingdom.”]

But do not let an earthly thought about the keys of the kingdom entrusted to Peter disturb you, brothers, as though they were keys like our own. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads, “But let no earthly thought about the keys entrusted to you, brothers, disturb you”; Saint Peter manuscript 9 A reads, “about the keys entrusted to Peter”; the Veronese manuscript reads, “But let not an earthly thought about the keys entrusted…”] For the key of heaven is Peter’s tongue, because, judging the merits of individuals, the apostle either closes or opens the kingdom of heaven to each one. [Note: The same Holy Cross manuscript reads “Peter’s tongue, by which he judges the merits of each person…”]

This key, therefore, was not fashioned by the hand of a mortal craftsman; it is the power of judgment given by Christ. Finally, he says to them: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven, and whose you retain are retained” (John 10). [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “Finally, he says to him.”] [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “and whose you retain, they are retained.” The Saint Peter 9 A, Casinensian, and Vatican 1269 and 1277 manuscripts read “they will be retained.”]

This is Peter, whom the seas placed beneath his feet and proved to be Christ’s most confident servant. For when he asked his Lord that new steps be given him upon the waves, he obtained them as a faithful servant had asked and as a beloved disciple deserved. [Note: Saint Peter manuscript 9 A reads “and as the beloved deserved.”]

He seemed to tremble for this one reason: so that human frailty might recognize how great is the distance between Lord and servant, while flesh weighed down by sins sinks, and an immaculate foot does not know how to sink. [Note: Vatican manuscript 1277 reads “seemed to have trembled.”] [Note: Saint Peter 40 F reads “and the immaculate foot does not know how to remain.” Vatican manuscript 1277 reads “the foot does not know how to sink.”]

Likewise, this also occurred so that, if Peter had reached Christ walking upon the waters with an unafraid foot, he might perhaps have been considered equal to the powers of his Lord. [Note: Vatican manuscripts 1269 and 1277, the Casinensian manuscript, and Saint Peter 9 A read “Likewise, this too.”] [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “he might be equated with the powers.”]

But why do we say that he trembled so greatly, when his faulty trembling contributed to a greater faith? [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads “when his pious trembling advanced him to a greater faith.” Saint Peter 40 F reads “with his pious trembling…” The Belgian manuscripts, Martinian and Camberonian, read “slight.”]

For just as Peter believed, at his Lord’s command, that he could be sustained from the waves, so likewise, while he was sinking, he believed that he would be saved by the power of that same Lord. [Note: The Martinian manuscript omits “Peter”; the Ambrosian lacks “himself from the waves.” The second Minor Holy Cross manuscript reads “while he is sinking, he believed in that same Lord.” The Veronese and Vatican 1277 manuscripts read “he could be sustained from the waves; so nevertheless he sinks, while he believes that he will be saved by the power of that same Lord.”]

Truly, the faith of blessed Peter is wondrous even when he trembles, because not even fear amid pressing danger could disturb it. For while he was sinking he cried out, “Lord, save me”; he distrusted himself, not the Lord. [Note: The same Holy Cross manuscripts, Saint Peter 9 A, Vatican 1277, and the Casinensian manuscripts read “It is truly the faith of blessed Peter; and while he trembles, his faith is wondrous, since not even fear of pressing danger…”]

Therefore, let no one count this fear of the most glorious Peter as a fault. For although this fear disturbed his faith at first, it adorned in him the confidence of a belief restored. [Note: Saint Peter 9 A reads “although it first disturbed his faith.”]

This is Peter, to whom Christ the Lord willingly granted a share in his own name. For just as the apostle Paul teaches (1 Corinthians 10), “the rock was Christ,” so through Christ Peter became a rock, as the Lord said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16). [Note: The Martinian manuscript reads “but the rock…”]

For just as in the desert, at the Lord’s command, water flowed from the rock for the thirsty people (Exodus 17), so from Peter’s mouth a fountain of saving confession arose for the whole world, exhausted by the dryness of unbelief. [Note: The Saint Peter manuscript reads: “For just as in the desert, at the Lord’s command, water flowed from the rock for the thirsty people, so from Peter’s mouth, for the whole world wearied by the dryness of unbelief…” The Martinian manuscript reads “for the weary”; the Camberonian reads “for the world wearied.”] [Note: The Minor Holy Cross manuscript preserved in the Laurentian, the Veronese, Vatican manuscripts 1269 and 1277, and the Casinensian manuscripts read “for the whole world wearied by the dryness of unbelief.”]

This is Peter, to whom Christ, about to ascend to the Father, entrusted his little sheep and lambs to feed (John 21), so that those whom Christ had redeemed through merciful compassion might be preserved by Peter’s power of faith. [Note: Saint Peter 9 A reads “his little lambs and sheep.”]

And rightly did the Son of God, the judge of hidden things, entrust sheep to be fed and guarded to the one whom he knew lacked neither diligence nor faith in nourishing the Lord’s flock. [Note: The Casinensian manuscript reads “his sheep.”]

This is Peter, who, when he was being led to the cross as a disciple of the Crucified One, requested that he be crucified with his body turned around. He did not fear the passion but avoided equality with the Lord’s cross, so that he might show to all that, even amid torments, he had preserved the virtue of admirable humility and the discipline of a new mystery. [Note: Saint Peter 40 F reads “even amid torments.”]

How confidently Peter went to the cross, dearest brothers, who, having driven away the fear of death, sought such a bitter passion as the manner of dying! [Note: Vatican manuscript 1269 omits “in.”]

What, moreover, shall I say of the most glorious Paul, in whom the Lord chose the faith in his own name while Paul himself was persecuting that faith? [Note: The Vatican and Casinensian manuscripts read “while he was persecuting it.”] While he was devastating the Christian Church as an exceedingly fierce persecutor, Christ found in his still-hostile breast a heart that could become his friend. While Paul was handing Christians over to temporal punishments, he himself, seized for eternal grace, suddenly became a shepherd from a wolf, a guardian from a robber, and a defender from an enemy. Thus it became clear both that Paul had not persecuted the Lord’s people from a purpose of malicious intent, and that Christ had not failed to know whom he should choose in Paul. [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads “that he should choose in Paul.” The Casinensian and Saint Peter 9 A manuscripts read “what he should choose in Paul.”]

This is Paul, who, summoned from heaven by the voice of Christ, did not lose the power of sight when the eyes of Jewish unbelief in him were blinded; rather, he changed it. He lost his eyes and received them again. Thus, at one and the same time, the punishment of blindness advanced against the persecutor, while the grace of God calling him illuminated the chosen man. For the Lord said to him from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9). [Note: The Camberonian manuscript reads “and against the persecutor.” The cited Saint Peter manuscript reads “called by the grace of God.”]

That is: “Why are you persecuting me, Saul? What injustice of mine has stirred up your hatred against me? Is it because I have given sight to the blind, healed the sick, driven out demons, and fed hungry peoples with five loaves? Or because I have raised the dead from their tombs?” [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “raised the dead.”] “Or perhaps especially because I promised my faithful ones the heavenly kingdom? But if you doubt that I can grant what I promise, look—if you can—at the source and the kind of one by whom I address you.

“But why are you persecuting me, Saul? Or what will you accomplish by persecuting me? Will your persecution have any effect against the one who reigns in heaven? Will you be able to harm me at all, whom you cannot see? For I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting, the one who has changed earth into heaven, the cross into a kingdom, and death into perpetuity. That you should have no uncertainty about any of these things, the sight now taken from you and restored a little later will persuade you.”

But blessed Paul, restrained by sudden blindness, nevertheless understood the majesty of the one speaking from heaven. Immediately he became faithful, ceased his persecution, and acquired new eyes with which to behold Christ.

This is Paul, who, as a reward for his virtues, was caught up beyond human merit into the third heaven and learned heavenly secrets (1 Corinthians 12), so that, destined to be a teacher of the Churches, he might learn among angels what he would preach among human beings.

Or who would henceforth not believe him with impunity, since he speaks not only of the Lord’s mysteries as things heard, but also bears witness to them as things seen? [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “who would not believe henceforth with impunity.”] What great grace of our God was this, brothers: that he who was called to the apostolate from heavenly places should have his apostolate consecrated in heaven.

And after all this, this is Paul, who submitted the necks that he had proudly raised against the name of Christ to be cut down by the sword of unbelievers, humbling himself for the honor of Christ. [Note: Vatican 1277, Saint Peter 9 A, Vallicellian 25, A 9, and the Casinensian manuscripts read “who submitted his neck, which…”] Nor did he hesitate to die for the one whom he had often proved to live and reign after death. [Note: Vatican manuscript 1269 omits “often”; manuscript 1277 reads “whom he had proved to live and reign after death.”]

And so it came about that Rome received the most glorious Paul in triumph as the conqueror of the world—Paul who, fighting for the faith of Christ among various peoples with immense struggle, had waged countless battles. [Note: The Martinian manuscript reads “many struggles.”]

These, then, are the most blessed Peter and Paul, who, preaching with one spirit the mystery of the heavenly kingdom, consecrated their teaching with devoted blood and most courageous death on the same day. [Note: The number “222” appears in the edition at this point.] They also, having been made princes of all the Churches by heavenly dispensation, went to Rome and placed their most sacred bodies in the citadel of that city, [Note: The Veronese manuscript writes “most sacred” in larger characters.] which had held the primacy of the whole world; so that Christ, displaying the power of his might, might place the princes of his kingdom where the world possessed the seat of empire. [Note: The Saint Peter 9 A manuscript reads “who obtained the primacy of the whole world.”] [Note: The same manuscript adds: “He who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”]

## HOMILY LXIX. On the same birthday of the holy apostles Peter and Paul II

[Col. 0395]

### NOTICE

Following the most learned Ballerini brothers, we judge that no one other than Maximus, bishop of Turin, is the author of this homily. When they found it, together with the two that follow, in the first collection of sermons of Saint Leo the Great—said to have been compiled by Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino and later Pope Victor III—they testified, in the preface to the sermons of Saint Leo, page 72 of the Venetian edition of 1753, that it was not Leo’s work but unquestionably Maximus’s.

For this reason we do not agree with the scribes of manuscripts 210 D and 40 F of the Basilica of Saint Peter, Vatican manuscript 1269, page 59 verso, Laurentian manuscript 33, Pluteus XIV, page 155, and perhaps others who attributed such homilies to Saint Leo. For in this matter one must proceed by the antiquity of the manuscripts rather than by their number.

The first place in antiquity belongs to the Ambrosian and Veronese manuscripts 431, not later than the eighth century. These are followed by Vercellensis 81; three Vatican manuscripts, 6451, page 142, 1273, page 57, and 1277, page 56 verso; Casinensis CXI, page 82; the manuscript of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, page 36; two Vallicellian manuscripts, XV, page 61, and A 9; Holy Cross in Jerusalem XI, page 66; manuscript II, formerly of the library of the Minor Holy Cross, now Laurentian, page 128; another Ambrosian manuscript, 146; Farfensis B; Martinian; Camberonian; Augiensis XV; and finally the Cistercian manuscript of Monte Amiata. All of these call the homily the work of Saint Maximus, bishop, with a similar inscription.

To these manuscripts, distinguished by antiquity and by universal esteem, is added the testimony of Alcuin, who records it as attributed to Maximus in his *Homiliary*, with the title “On the nativity of the holy apostles Peter and Paul,” page 321 of the Venetian edition of 1571.

To avoid excessive length, we omit a list of the editors, since all of them, beginning with Gymnicus on page 211, published this homily and the following ones in repeated editions. One point remains to be mentioned: in Vatican manuscript Ottobonianus 106 and in the manuscript of Orvieto, the author’s name is absent.

[Col. 0397A] **ARGUMENT.**—Saint Maximus celebrates the privileges, gifts of grace, and prerogatives of excellence belonging to both apostles.

At the joy of the apostles’ birthday, dearest brothers—the birthday of Peter and Paul, whose blessed passions give us joy today—the Church of Christ rejoices more joyfully throughout the whole world. Although she is certainly to be adorned by the martyrdom of all the saints, nevertheless she is more gloriously illumined by the victory of these men, since she sees the fathers and teachers of the faith themselves triumphing over this world. [Note: The Farfensis manuscript reads: “although she is certainly to be adorned by the martyrdom of all the saints; nevertheless she is more gloriously illumined by their victory; since indeed…” The Holy Cross in Jerusalem manuscript reads: “nevertheless she is more gloriously illumined by their victory, since she sees, etc.”]

For what is more distinguished than Peter, who, while still in the flesh and having passed beyond the measure of flesh, truly confesses Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God? [Note: Vatican manuscript 1277 reads “confesses Christ Jesus, the Son of the living God.”] What had previously been hidden from the breast of every mortal was first confessed by Peter’s tongue in a new utterance.

What, my brothers, is more magnificent than Peter, who, by the merit of so great a confession, while he was still in a corruptible body and had not yet himself ascended into heaven, was permitted both to close and to open the heavenly kingdom?

What is more exalted than the faith of one who, while the Lord walked upon the waters, forgetting human condition, both asked and deserved that a path be given him upon the waves? [Note: The Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscript 12 reads “obtained”; Saint Peter 40 F reads “both asks and deserved.”]

Such was the confidence of his mind that he believed he could accomplish through faith what he knew was impossible for a human being by nature. Since he was afterward sinking, it was, as I think, necessary that the frailty of flesh—perhaps made equal to Christ by the greatness of so sublime a miracle—should not become proud to its own destruction.

Let it certainly have been bodily weakness that he feared a little later. [Note: Manuscript 11 cited above and Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscript 12 read “It was”; the Martinian reads “It had certainly been.”] Yet who could doubt that what enabled him to descend from the boat was a faith beyond imitation, when the trembling yet unwavering wave of the sea sustained him on human feet? [Note: The Martinian manuscript reads “who, however, would doubt…”] [Note: Saint Peter 40 F, manuscript 210 D, and Vallicellian 7 A read “forbidden” or “unallowed” instead of “unwavering.”]

But now let us come to the most blessed Paul, whose fullness of faith was no less great, so that the Savior, who foresaw all things, chose him in a certain special way as his own leader for illuminating the hearts of the nations. [Note: The Martinian manuscript reads “chose him.”]

For he was so outstanding in teaching, so powerful in strength of spirit, and so holy in innocence and integrity that, at one and the same time, on the one side the priests and rulers of the Jews, through zeal for the ancient law and with authority granted to persecute Christians, sent him forth, while on the other Christ called him from heaven for the consolation of the Church and the support of all believers. [Note: The Camberonian manuscript omits “support.”]

For this reason the Lord immediately blinded his eyes, so that, once he had received the grace of truth, they might shine with heavenly sight and a brighter light. [Note: Vatican manuscript 1277 reads “whose eyes were immediately blinded for this reason”; Saint Peter 40 F reads “whose eyes were blinded by the Lord for this reason, so that they might shine…” The Farfensis manuscript reads “so that they might shine with a brighter, true heavenly light.”]

At the same time, this was done so that all might understand that Christ, whom the future prince of the Christian name had been persecuting, possessed the power both to blind and to illuminate.

But, to pass over the other things that make him wondrous to the whole world, who could estimate how great is the glory of this one fact, sufficient for all his praises: that while he lived among human beings, by a certain special grace of the Godhead, paradise was accessible to him and heaven open? [Note: Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscript 12 reads “the things that make blessed Paul wondrous to the whole world.”] [Note: The same manuscript reads “while he dwelt among human beings”; Vatican manuscript 1277 reads “while he lived among human beings.”]

What, then, brothers, is more perfect than this teacher, who learned in heaven what he would teach on earth? [Note: Four Casinensian manuscripts and Vatican manuscript 1277 read “what he would teach on earth.”] What witness is more truthful than this one, who, with eyes raised toward heaven, was granted to see and approve what he would afterward promise to those who believed? [Note: Manuscript II reads “to whom, with his eyes raised above the heavens…”]

These, then, are the astonishing merits of the apostles Peter and Paul. Advancing through these miracles, they consecrated their apostolate to our Lord and God by the outpouring of their devoted blood. [Note: Manuscript II reads “and through these things advancing…”]

## HOMILY LXX. On the same birthday of the holy apostles Peter and Paul III

[Col. 0397]

### NOTICE

The Ballerini brothers likewise assigned this homily to our Saint Maximus after carefully considering both the Vatican manuscripts and those of the Basilica of Saint Peter, some of which inscribe it to Saint Leo the Great.

The manuscripts that support the same bishop of Turin are far superior in number and excellence. Besides Vatican manuscripts 1273, page 56, and 1277, page 56, and the two Vallicellian manuscripts XV, page 71, and A 7, page 197, the following explicitly give his name: manuscript XII of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, page 77; manuscript II of the Minor Holy Cross, in the Laurentian, page 128; Farfensis B; Augiensis XV; Martinian; Veronensis 437; and finally two Ambrosian manuscripts, namely the very ancient C 98 and H 146.

To these manuscript books, distinguished by antiquity and by universal esteem, is added the testimony of Alcuin, who attributes this homily to Saint Maximus in his *Homiliary*, on page 71 of the edition mentioned above.

And so that we may not repeat the names of the editors already listed, it will be enough to note that none is found who disagrees with Gymnicus on page 113, where this is the third homily on the festival of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0397D] **ARGUMENT.**—The two apostles are compared with one another: one is praised for his faith, the other for his teaching. Peter became more eminent than the other apostles through faith; Paul, illumined by heavenly lights, was appointed teacher and instructor of the nations.

The inseparable faith and kindred passion of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, brothers, we must celebrate with every devotion, because their praiseworthy life led them to a most glorious end, and their wondrous death transmitted them to everlasting life. And although faith shines forth in Peter and doctrine excels in Paul, [Note: Codex Vat. 539 and S. Pet. 40 F omit the conjunction “and.”] Paul’s teaching, nevertheless, is the fullness of faith, and Peter’s belief is the foundation of doctrine. Such was the dignity of their heavenly election [Note: Three Casinenses add: “raised them up.”] that one became a teacher from a fisherman, the other a defender from a persecutor.

But in this the majesty of almighty God must be exalted: by a marvelous inspiration he granted the grace of teaching to an unlearned man; he made an enemy love what he had hated and defend the faith he had attacked. He did not take away the former man’s fishing, but changed it. He blinded the latter’s eyes so that, once a purer light had been received, he might be able, with the sharpness of a most brilliant mind, to see beyond human sight. [Note: Codices II of Santa Croce Minor and 12 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read: “might be able.”] [Note: The same codex II of Santa Croce Minor reads: “How great, therefore, etc.”]

How great, then, was Peter’s merit before his God, that after the rowing of a little boat the helm of the whole Church should be entrusted to him? [Note: Codices 17, Plut. XIV of the Laurentian Library, Farfensis, Veronensis, S. Pet. 40 F, 210 D, and Vat. 1277 read: “before the Lord.”] [Note: Codex S. Pet. 210 D reads: “But how greatly.”] Or how greatly do we believe that Paul pleased Christ in the ministry of his apostleship, since a persecutor could please him so greatly? He pleased him because he was not fighting out of the zeal of an iniquitous heart, but was erring through the heedless devotion of simple ignorance. Finally, as soon as the Spirit of truth had been poured into his understanding, he immediately showed that he had not raged against Christ out of hatred, but had innocently gone astray through love of the ancestral law. [Note: Codex Vat. 1277 reads: “as though innocently.”]

What, then, should I say about him above all, since he himself is the most faithful witness to himself? For although he does not wish to boast of his own praises, [Note: Codex Reg. 539 reads: “who wished to boast, etc.” Codex Vat. 1277 reads: “who does not wish to boast of his own praises, etc.” Three Casinenses agree with it.] and desired to proclaim the majesty of Christ, [Note: Codex Vat. 1269 adds: “and desired to proclaim the majesty of Christ.”] he confesses with greater modesty what was done in him. For, as though speaking of someone else, he says:

“I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—such a one was caught up. And I know such a man—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—that he was caught up into paradise and heard secret words, which it is not permitted to a human being to speak” (2 Corinthians 12).

What is more magnificent than this apostle, who, while placed in the midst of mortals, was granted to ascend above the heavens and permitted to return to earth? [Note: Codex S. Pet. 40 F reads: “But what is more blessed than this, etc.”] What is more blessed than a man who, among the secrets of paradise, [Note: Codex Martinensis reads: “to learn.”] was worthy to learn what neither the tongue of a human being could speak nor anyone could be worthy to hear? [Note: Codex Martinensis has: “And if those things are of such greatness, etc.”]

And since what he taught is of such sublimity that the human mind cannot comprehend it, how great a glory do we think that to be which he declares himself forbidden to reveal? What, moreover, shall I say about Peter, whose righteousness was so greatly approved by God, [Note: Codex Veronensis reads: “and how great a power of judging was granted to him.” Codices Vat. Reg. 539, S. Petri 40 F, and the Casinenses read: “and to whom such power was granted, etc.”] and to whom such power of judging was granted, that heavenly judgment was placed in his discretion? [Col. 0399B]

Observe, therefore, and consider with what honor the apostle Peter must be revered by us, since the justice of the eternal Judge does not reject the sentence he pronounces on earth. [Note: Codex S. Pet. 40 F reads: “does not repel it.”] Therefore attend carefully to the greatness of his glory, to whom, when the keys [Note: Codex Veronensis reads: “the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”] of the eternal kingdom were entrusted, permission was given to close and open heaven. [Note: Codex Reg. Vat. 539 reads: “even heaven was entrusted to him, etc.”]

Accordingly, dearest brothers, the venerable passion of these men is celebrated today throughout the world. Today Rome honors their martyrdom with the most joyful gathering; and although once an impious people persecuted their blood, now she glories in their special and devoted patronage. [Note: Codex Vat. Reg. 539 adds: “with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”]

## HOMILY LXXI  
### On the same feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, IV

[Col. 0399]

### NOTICE

To remove every suspicion of interpolation from this homily of Maximus, since divergent manuscripts are found, it will be worthwhile to list them and to acknowledge what those more experienced in the critical art have judged concerning them. We should not hesitate to mention once again the manuscripts frequently cited above: namely, the Veronensis 431; Vaticanus 1277, p. 77; Ambrosianus 146; Santa Croce in Jerusalem XII, p. 60; Augiensis XV; n of Santa Croce Minor, p. 129, now Laurentianus; Vallicellanus XV, p. 72; Ratisponensis of St. Emmeram, p. 35; Martinensis; Farfensis B; and Casinensis CXI, p. 83 verso. All these, in their series of homilies on the holy apostles Peter and Paul, which they unanimously attribute to Saint Maximus, also include this one.

There are, however, five codices that attribute the homily to Saint Leo the Great: namely, Laurentianus 39, Plut. XIV, p. 135; two of the Basilica of Saint Peter, 40 F and 210 D; and likewise two Casinenses, 115, p. 161, and 104, p. 171. Another Casinensis, 126, p. 148, gives the name of the Venerable Bede. In the Ottobonianus 106, however, the homily is attributed to no author.

We do not think the question is settled merely by the greater number of manuscripts that affirm Maximus’s authorship, but also by the Ballerini, who taught in their preface to the sermons of Saint Leo that it should be restored to Saint Maximus. All the editors mentioned above agree with them.

### ARGUMENT

Christ chose Peter the fisherman and Paul the persecutor to establish the Church. The election of both is admirable and displays the divine work of raising up the Church: Peter was appointed to acquire human beings for God, while Paul was appointed to enlighten them through doctrine. They were called the pillars of the Churches.

The passion of the most blessed apostles, brothers, whose feast we solemnly celebrate today, must be honored by all believers. Because of the fullness of their righteousness and devotion, the Savior of the world gave them to the human race both as fathers and as judges. How great their integrity and devotion were may be seen above all from this: the one who does not deceive in his election chose them to correct the corrupt age and to carry out his will.

For he called Peter, poor in possessions and a fisherman by occupation. Separated from popular society and from the fellowship of cities, he led an innocent life amid the waves and sought his livelihood through simplicity. Yet I would call him poor only in such a way that he lacked no adequate means of support: the rich wave of the bountiful sea sustained him, as one who had deserved well from God.

He was therefore chosen [Note: Codex Martinensis omits “was.”] for the preaching of the word of salvation, so that, with the exchange of his former role through the heavenly mystery of the sacrament, [Note: Codex Martinensis reads: “with life changed.”] [Note: Codex Vat. 1277 reads: “through the ministry of the heavenly sacrament.”] the man who had been fed by the catch of fish might feed others by the salvation of human beings.

Christ also called the most glorious Paul from heaven to faith in his name. [Note: Codex II of Santa Croce Minor reads: “who seemed to be persecuting.”] Although he appeared to persecute the Church, he did not rage through the impiety of an irreligious spirit; rather, beneath a cloud of ignorance, he failed to perceive the new grace and went astray through love of his ancient devotion. Therefore the darkness of the old shadow was removed from his eyes, so that he might acquire for himself and reveal to all that true light which flashed from the heavens. [Note: Codex Farfensis reads: “which flashed from the heavenly realms.”]

He was blinded and then enlightened, by no other dispensation than this: that, with his bodily eyes closed, spiritual sight might be formed in him to contemplate the glory of God.

The most faithful Peter also received these eyes, [Note: Codex Vat. 1269 omits “these.”] [Note: Codex Martinensis reads: “with which he saw Christ.”] and, illuminated by the ray of the Holy Spirit, recognized our Lord Christ, placed in the flesh and concealing his divinity under the appearance of the assumed man, as the Son of the living God. [Note: Codex Martinensis reads: “saw.”] For when the Lord asked whom people supposed him to be, he replied: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16).

Who would not marvel that a fisherman uttered the fullness of this response, which he disclosed in the briefest summary of confession, declaring both what the Lord had from the Father and what he had assumed from human birth? For “Christ” and “Son of the living God” together contain the undivided mystery of both natures, which all must truly receive; and they reveal the wondrous fisherman who, while searching the depths of the sea, reached the most profound secret of eternal majesty.

These, then, are the pillars of the Churches: Peter and Paul. Their most holy life led them to a venerable death, and their glorious end made them everlasting. We honor them not only as martyrs, but also venerate them as teachers and fathers of martyrs, for they founded the Church of God both through the doctrine of heavenly preaching and through the shedding of their devout blood. [Note: This agrees perfectly with all the Casinenses.]

## HOMILY LXXII  
### On the same feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, V

[Col. 0401]

### NOTICE

This homily is frequently mentioned by ecclesiastical writers because it gives clear testimony concerning Simon’s sudden fall from the air to the earth. Almost all of these writers assign it to Saint Maximus, although scribes copied it under various names.

In particular, the manuscripts of the Vatican Library assigned it to Ambrose: Vaticanus 1277, p. 43; 1269, p. 53 verso; Vaticanus Reginensis 539, p. 129 verso; Laurentianus X, Plut. XIV, p. 18; and IV, Plut. XXXIII, left-hand part, formerly in the library of Santa Croce Minor, p. 161 verso, now in the Laurentian Library.

Others thought it the work of Augustine, as is clear from Vatican codices 1195, p. 310 verso, and 3835, p. 200 verso; also from two Casinenses, 102 and 305; and from the Urbevetanus, p. 157, which bears this title: “Here begin the sermons of Saint Augustine on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul.”

But the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, who examined the sermons of both Ambrose and Augustine with the greatest care, assigned it to neither; rather, they wrote that Maximus should be regarded as its author. Thus it appears in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine, third class, sermon 210.

Some did attribute it to Leo the Great, as did codex F 40 of the Basilica of Saint Peter, Vallicellanus A 7, Vaticanus Ottobonianus 106, and a few others. The Ballerini, however, regarded these as worthless, as they did the ancient editions of Leo, as was stated in the preceding notices.

The manuscripts whose inscriptions announce Saint Maximus as author deserve precedence in number and antiquity. First we present three codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: namely, the most ancient 90, which contains the first of the sermons under this title, “Here begins the sermon on the feast of Saints Peter and Paul”; codex 99, homily 70, with the same heading; and codex XII, p. 67 verso.

We then add the Martinensis; the Ratisponensis of Saint Emmeram, homily 5 on the same feast; Augiensis XV; Vallicellanus XV, p. 62; Farfensis B; Cisterciensis of Monte Amiata, II Plut. XXXIII, formerly of the library of Santa Croce Minor, now Laurentianus, p. 129; Ambrosianus 146; and finally Modoetiensis B XI, whose title is: “The Nativity of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, on the third day before the Kalends of July. Sermon of blessed Maximus the bishop.”

Alcuin, whose testimony is older than that of many of these codices, assigned the homily to Saint Maximus, as is clear from his Homiliary, p. 326 of the Venetian edition of 1571. The editors Gymnicus, p. 218; Galesinius, p. 155; Combefisius, vol. VI, p. 230; Cumdius, vol. IV, p. 447; Raynaudus, homily 5, *On the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul*, p. 231; and Margarinus in the *Bibliotheca Maxima*, vol. VI, p. 36, agree with him. After so many and such weighty witnesses, who would refuse to assign this homily to Saint Maximus?

### ARGUMENT

Saint Maximus had taught that Peter and Paul should be preferred to the other apostles; here he explains the basis of this rank and honor. He says that Peter was given the keys of the heavenly kingdom, to bind and loose on earth, while Paul received the key of knowledge, whose power of heavenly doctrine would penetrate the hearts of all peoples and lead them from error to truth.

[Note: Since all the most blessed apostles possess an equal grace of holiness, etc., some once thought that our Maximus had divided the unity of the Church’s head when, in this homily, he divided the keys signifying supreme authority, granting one to Peter and the other to Paul. But this interpretation must be regarded as wholly foreign to Maximus’s mind. For Maximus, who had acted as an orator and had just now praised Peter’s marvelous confession of Christ’s divinity, now his election to found and raise up the Church, and elsewhere his courage in undergoing the punishment of the cross, and who had also discussed Paul at length—especially how he had become a teacher of the Church from a persecutor, and by what illuminations he had been enlightened—took up from the twofold key a new argument of expression.

Maximus first states that all the apostles had obtained an equal grace of holiness before the Lord, since all had been chosen and called to the same work of spreading the truth. Nevertheless, he proclaims Peter and Paul more eminent than the others because Christ endowed them with greater gifts and privileges.

To prove what he had proposed, Maximus conceived the double key as signifying two different things: one, the supreme power of governing; the other, the knowledge of teaching heavenly truths. “For to Peter,” says Maximus, “as to a good steward, he gave the key of the kingdom of heaven; to Paul, as to a suitable teacher, he entrusted the teaching of ecclesiastical instruction: so that those whom the one has instructed for salvation, the other may receive into rest; and that the souls of those whose hearts Paul opened by the doctrine of his words Peter may receive into the kingdoms of heaven.”

But Maximus was so far from wishing to divide the primacy of governing the Church between Peter and Paul that he rather professed to teach the unity of the head and Peter’s preeminence. Since it is certain that access to God is obtained through faith alone, and that faith is produced by hearing, knowledge is the first preparation and, as it were, the key that unlocks the hearts of unbelievers and sinners and suffuses them with the light and power of grace. Whenever people have been conformed to the teaching and law of God, then the key of authority is present for them, by which they are absolved from sins and made capable of the eternal inheritance. The ministry of the divine word must precede every path to salvation.

The first duty of knowledge, therefore, is to provide the light by which the things to be believed are seen; but the granting of forgiveness for crimes is the office of the higher authority handed down by God. The former prepares souls; the latter, once the faithful have been disposed and prepared, opens the heavenly kingdom to them.

That this, and no other, was Maximus’s doctrine is also clear from the fact that he requires the foundation of inward faith and promises possession of the enjoyment of God to those who persevere in it faithfully. “Both,” says Maximus, “received keys from the Lord: this one of knowledge, that one of power. The latter distributes the riches of immortality; the former bestows the treasures of knowledge.” For there are treasures of knowledge, as it is written (Colossians 2): “In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.”

Maximus also calls this task of unlocking the truth not simply a key, but a key “in a certain sense,” so that it may be understood that he is speaking allegorically and that he is far from making the Church of Christ two-headed—something which certain later writers unjustly attributed to him.

They have plainly overlooked another passage of Saint Maximus, namely sermon 44 on the same apostles, where he says: “To Peter he gave the keys of his kingdom; to Paul, wisdom.” The holy bishop of Turin therefore knew that Peter’s personal prerogative of primacy was expressed in the keys handed to him by Christ, and he did not make it common to Paul. To Paul he said that the dispensation of the wisdom and mysteries of God had been entrusted—a dispensation to which the other apostles were also called—but Paul excelled them in doctrine and in heavenly illumination.

See the tenth observation of the Ballerini in Quesnel’s sixth dissertation, and the specimen of the work of the most learned Cardinal Gerdil, p. 75. We add nothing here concerning Peter’s primacy in the Church, since we have already dealt with it sufficiently in other notes and in the dissertation on the doctrines of Saint Maximus. The most learned Steph. Borgia, secretary of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, recently incorporated this homily into his discussion of the Velitraean Cross, p. 94, and adorned it with various notes.]

Since all the most blessed apostles possess an equal grace [Note: Codex Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “of blessedness.”] of holiness before the Lord, [Note: Codex Vat. 3835 reads: “obtain.”] I do not know by what manner Peter and Paul nevertheless appear to excel the others by a certain particular power of faith. [Note: Codex Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “to excel the others by a certain particular prerogative in the power of the Savior’s faith.”] We can confirm this from the judgment of the Lord himself.

For to Peter, as to a good steward, he gave the key of the heavenly kingdom; [Note: Three Vallicellan codices, the Urbevetanus, and a Casinensis read: “the keys.”] but to Paul, as to a suitable teacher, he entrusted the teaching of ecclesiastical instruction; [Note: Codices S. Pet. 40 F, Vat. 1195, and 3835 read: “but to Paul, as to …”] so that those whom the former has instructed for salvation, the latter may receive into rest; [Note: Codices 12 and 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Vallicellanus 25 read: “whom he might instruct.”] so that the souls of those whose hearts Paul opened by the doctrine of his words [Note: Codex Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “shall have opened”; codices Farfensis, two Vallicellani, Vat. 539 and 1277, read: “might open”; Modoetensis reads: “might open.”] Peter may open the kingdoms of heaven to their souls. [Note: Codex S. Pet. 40 F reads: “Peter may lead their souls to the kingdom of heaven.” Codex Vall. 25 omits “their.” Codex 174 of the former Florentine civic library, now Laurentianus, and codex 37, Plut. XVII of the Laurentian Library, read: “Peter may receive their souls into the kingdoms of heaven.”]

Paul also received from Christ, in a certain sense, the key of knowledge. For it must be called a key by which the hard hearts of sinners are unlocked for faith, the secrets of minds are disclosed, and whatever is held shut within is brought into the open through rational manifestation. “A key,” I say, [Note: The Ambrosianus and Martinensis read: “A key, I say, is that which, etc.” Codex 174 of the Florentine civic church library reads: “The key, I say, is the doctrine of the apostle Paul, which also, etc.” Codex S. Petri 40 F and the Urbevetanus and Modoetianus support this reading.] which opens the conscience to confession of sin and encloses grace within the eternity of the mystery of salvation. [Note: The Urbevetanus reads: “and encloses the grace of the eternity of the mystery of salvation.”]

Both, therefore, received keys from the Lord: this one of knowledge, that one of power. The latter distributes the riches of immortality; the former bestows the treasures of knowledge. For there are treasures of knowledge, as it is written: “In whom are hidden [Note: Codex Martinensis omits “all.”] all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2).

Therefore blessed Peter and Paul stand out among all the apostles and excel by a particular prerogative. [Note: Codex Farfensis reads *percellunt* (“surpass”).] But which of the two should be placed before the other is uncertain. For I think that they are equal in merits, because they are equal in passion; and we see that they lived with a similar devotion to the faith, since together they reached the glory of martyrdom. [Note: Codex Vat. 1277 reads: “whom we see brought by a similar path to the glory of martyrdom.” The Casinenses read: “with a similar [faith].”] Let us not think that it happened without reason that they endured the sentence of one tyrant on one day and in one place. [Note: Codex S. Pet. 40 F reads: “endured the sentence. On one day, etc.”]

They suffered on one day so that they might reach Christ together; in one place, so that Rome might not be lacking in either; under one persecutor, so that equal cruelty might bind both. Thus the day, I think, was decreed according to merit; the place, according to glory; the persecutor, according to virtue. [Note: In three Santa Croce codices, in the Farfensis, S. Petri, Urbevetanus, and Casinenses, “I think” is absent.] [Note: In several manuscripts “but” is used instead of “and.”]

But in what place, finally, did they suffer martyrdom? In the city of Rome, which holds the primacy and is the head of the nations; namely, so that where the head of superstition had been, there the head of holiness might rest; and where the leaders of the Gentiles had dwelt, there the leaders of the Churches might die. [Note: Codex S. Pet. 40 F reads: “namely, so that where the leaders of the Gentiles dwelt, there memorials of the blessed apostles might be erected. But whose merits, etc.” Codex Vallicellanus A 9 reads: “namely, so that where the head of holiness might rest, where the leaders of the Gentiles dwelt, there the leaders of the Churches might remain.” This codex first reads *morerentur* (“might die”), but the letter *e* was evidently erased and changed into *a*. The Urbevetanus reads: “and where the leaders of the Gentiles dwelt, there apostolic dignity might reside. But by what merits the most blessed Peter and Paul, etc.” These words are written in the margin of the codex in an old, though different, hand. The Santa Croce codices and two Casinenses read: “might dwell.”]

From this we can understand how great the merit of the most blessed Peter and Paul was: although the Lord illuminated the region of the East by his own passion, he graciously chose, so that nothing might be lacking, to illuminate the region of the West through the blood of his apostles. And although his passion is sufficient for our salvation, [Note: Three codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem add “also” here; they likewise add “he bestowed upon us,” as do the Farfenses, four Vaticani, and S. Petri: “nevertheless he also bestowed their martyrdom upon us as an example, etc.”] nevertheless their martyrdom was given to us as an example.

Therefore, on this day the blessed apostles poured out their blood. [Note: Vaticanus Ottobonianus 106 reads: “shed their blood for Christ.” The Farfenses read: “drenched [the earth] with their blood.”] But let us examine why they endured these things. [Note: Vat. 539 reads: “why they suffered these things”; codices 1297, Vat. Ottobonianus 106, and Casinensis 142 likewise read: “why they endured these things.”] It was because, among their other miracles, they also struck down that magician Simon by their prayers, throwing him headlong from the empty air. [Note: Codices 12 and 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, likewise the Farfensis, three Vaticani with Vall. 7 A, and Vat. 1277 read: “had struck him down.” Vat. Ottobonianus 106, [Col. 0406C] and all the Casinenses have: “had prostrated him. For when that same Simon …”]

When that same Simon said that he was Christ and claimed that, as a son ascending to his father, he could rise by flying, and when, puffed up, he suddenly began to fly by magical arts, Peter, [Note: Codex Martinensis reads: “with knees bent.”] kneeling, prayed to the Lord, [Note: The former codices of the Florentine civic church library, 12 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, the Urbevetanus, Casinenses 102 and 305, read: “and holy prayer conquered magical levitation; for prayer ascended first, etc.” Codex Vaticanus reads: “and holy prayer.”] and holy prayer overcame magical levitation. Prayer ascended to the Lord before the flight, and a just petition arrived before an unjust presumption. [Note: At least eleven codices read “a just petition”; trusting their authority, we have likewise judged that this is what should be written.] While still on earth, Peter obtained what he was asking before Simon reached the heavens toward which he was striving. [Note: Codex 174 of the former Florentine civic church library reads: “before Simon reached the heavens toward which he was striving”; codices 12 and Vat. 1277 read: “the heavenly places”; others read: “heaven.”]

Then Peter, as though bringing him down in chains from the lofty air, shattered his legs by throwing him headlong against a rock. [Note: In the Ambrosianus “as though” is absent.] [Note: Three Roman codices, Ottobonian codices, and Casinenses read: “striking him against a rock.”] And this was to the disgrace of his deed, so that the man who a little earlier had attempted to fly might suddenly be unable to walk, and he who had assumed wings might lose the use of his feet. [Note: Codex 174 of the Florentine civic church library adds: “and to the disgrace of that deed.” Codices 12 and 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, four Vaticani, one S. Petri, and two Vallicellani read: “to the disgrace.”]

But lest it seem strange that this magician flew through the air for a time in the presence of the apostle, [Note: Codices S. Pet. 40 F and Vat. Ottobonianus 106 read: “through the air.”] Peter’s patience caused this. [Note: The Ambrosianus and Farfenses read: “that he flew.”] He permitted him to ascend higher so that he might fall farther. He wished him to be raised aloft before the eyes of everyone [Note: The Ambrosianus reads: “to be raised aloft before the sight of everyone.”] so that all eyes might see him falling from on high. [Note: Vat. 1269 reads: “so that they might also see him falling, etc.” Codex Martinensis reads: “so that they might see him falling from on high.”]

This, then, is the exaltation of iniquity: to carry oneself high and raise oneself aloft. But holy prayer humbles every pride and casts down every vanity. [Note: Codices Vat. 539, 1195, and Vat. Ottobonianus 106 add: “and every form of it.”] [Note: Codex Vat. 539 adds: “with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns, etc.”]

## HOMILY LXXIII  
### On the same feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, VI

[Col. 0405]

### NOTICE

Everyone can see how much ornament and value the unpublished writings of Saint Maximus that we have presented thus far, and the many others still to be presented, will bring to our collection. Among these, this homily claims a place of particular importance. It was recovered from a very ancient codex formerly belonging to the monastery of Apannis, and appears to be an abridgment, or summary, of the preceding homilies on the holy apostles Peter and Paul, briefly embracing their illustrious merits.

From the title found in the codex—“Homily I on Saint Peter”—it may be inferred that Saint Maximus composed several other homilies in honor of the holy apostles. We have supplied this homily with the same heading as the others, since it celebrates the distinguished deeds of Peter and Paul together.

### ARGUMENT

Maximus demonstrates that Saint Peter was appointed chiefly as the apostle to the Jews, while Paul was given as teacher to the Gentiles. Although each labored for the propagation of the faith unto the crown, both reached it by pouring out their blood equally for Christ.

Let us rejoice in the Lord, brothers, because today is the feast of the most blessed Peter and Paul, and let us exult with spiritual joy over the great solemnity of this day.

Today, indeed, that most blessed Peter, to whom the Lord entrusted, on account of the merit of his faith, the power of binding and loosing on earth, entered through the punishment of the cross into the calm heavens. Today Paul, that chosen vessel and teacher of the Gentiles, having given his most glorious head, obtained an immortal crown.

It is necessary that the merits of these most illustrious apostles have been equal, since their glorious confession for Christ was equal in the unity of the true faith. For if Peter is said to have been chosen to preach Christ’s grace to the Jews, Paul appears to have been appointed above the other apostles to instruct the Gentiles.

Peter preaches the Gospel in Judea, where the seeds of faith had already been planted by our Lord himself. Paul presents to the Gentiles the glory of the despised cross, which seemed to them a disgrace, as something worthy of veneration.

Peter led the Jews, who had gone astray from the womb, back to the path of true salvation. Paul illumines with heavenly wisdom the Gentiles who did not know God. Peter softens the hardest neck of his brothers. Paul disperses the blind ignorance of the nations.

Let the most blessed apostles therefore travel throughout the whole world and preach to the Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel the faith they received from Christ the Lord, confirming it by miracles. They were truly the salt of the earth, by which the souls of all believers are seasoned and guarded unharmed from eternal corruption.

Throughout the whole earth, these spiritual stewards of eternal salvation distribute the price of salvation and pour out the treasures of holiness, entirely equal in the merits of their works. For although Peter lived on earth with Christ, Christ nevertheless called Paul from heaven while Paul, a frenzied persecutor, was raging against those who believed in him.

Peter received the Gospel from that same Christ while Christ was on earth. But while the blessed Lord sat in heaven at the right hand of the Father, Paul received from him the grace of preaching. Indeed, having been raised even to heaven, Paul learned not only the Gospel that he had not heard, but also heard secret words that it is not permitted to a human being to speak.

Peter, uncertain lest he be drowned, trod the unstable waves of the sea. Paul, however, was in the depths of the sea night and day, and he did not shrink from the burden tossed about by the marine waves; rather, as though unwilling to violate a sacred deposit, the sea returned him alive, because the wave, serving him and guarding him unharmed, was preserving him still for the peoples.

The most blessed Peter and Paul were therefore equal in merits and virtues. What wonder, then, if on one day, in the same place, they endured the impious sentence of death imposed by one tyrant?

They suffered on one and the same day so that both might reach Christ together; in one place, so that neither might lack Rome as spectator of his triumph; and finally under one and the same persecutor, so that similar cruelty might bind them both. Thus, since their preaching of the faith had always been one and the same, the cause and occasion of their death should also be the same; and those who had received the same faith from Christ should likewise merit the palm of martyrdom for that same faith.

[Ten lines are missing, the writing having been obliterated; only the conclusion remains.]

Therefore, if we honor the martyrs, we also venerate Christ in the martyrs. But if we despise the saints, we mock Christ, who is in the saints, as the divine Truth itself says: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

*Explicit.*

## HOMILY LXXIV  
### On the feast of Saint Lawrence, deacon and martyr, I

[Col. 0407]

### NOTICE
### 237

From the manuscript witnesses, once they have been arranged in sequence, it will become clear which writers have established the author of this homily. Four Vatican codices—namely, 1273, p. 85; 1297, p. 95; 1269, p. 84; and the Vatican Ottobonianus 106, p. 208—unanimously assign the name of Saint Maximus. Three Casinensian codices likewise bear a similar inscription: 104, p. 153; 109, fol. 234 verso; and CXI, p. 104. We can further cite four from the Laurentian Library: 39 Plut. XVII, p. 170; 122, p. 153; and 174, p. 246, formerly belonging to the library of the aediles of the major church of Florence; and II of Santa Croce, Minor. Plut. XXXIII. These are followed by two Vallicellian codices, 7 A and XV; Vercellensis 81; the Ratisponensis of Saint Emmeram; Augiensis XV; Martinensis; Santa Croce in Jerusalem XII; and Farfensis B. Among the sermons of Maximus, Alcuin has the same homily, p. 331; and the Ballerini brothers judged it attributable to Maximus in the preface mentioned above, p. 387, although formerly they had found it inscribed as a homily of Saint Leo the Great. This attribution is supported by the codices listed above and by the editions of Gymnicus, p. 221; Galesinius, p. 156; Combefisius, vol. VI, p. 626; Cumdius, vol. IV, p. 481; Raynaudus, p. 231; and Margarini, *Bibliotheca Maxima Patrum*, vol. VI, p. 37. Once these witnesses have been examined, no one can doubt that this homily should be attributed to Maximus.

### 238. Argument

Maximus commends the holy Levite for his moral innocence, the exalted character of his ministry, and his generosity toward the poor. He adorns with elegant praise the prophecy of Saint Sixtus, bishop and martyr, concerning the imminent martyrdom of his Levite, as a pledge of the glory soon to be his.

It is holy and pleasing to God, brothers, that we should venerate with exceptional devotion the feast of blessed Lawrence, whose radiant flames have made the victorious Church of Christ shine throughout the whole world on this day as well. While he was carrying out the office of deacon in the see of the most glorious patriarch Peter, he joined himself to apostolic fellowship through the purity of an innocent life and the triumph of a most courageous death.

[Note: Vatican codex 1269 reads: “the archdeaconate of the most glorious Peter.”]

[Note: The Martinensis codex reads: “on this day also the Church throughout the whole world shines brilliantly.”]

Nor do we proclaim him the equal of the apostles without reason. The chastity of his soul bestowed upon him the ministry of a Levite, and the fullness of his faith conferred upon him the dignity of martyrdom. When the venerable Sixtus, bishop of the city of Rome, was overcoming the impiety of the raging world through torments and was already near the heavenly kingdoms, he saw Lawrence grieving most bitterly over his father’s death. He is said to have addressed him thus, in the spirit of foreknowledge:

“Do not be sad, my son. After three days you will follow me.”

[Note: Vatican codex 1277 reads: “the bishop of the city of Rome.”]

From this it is clear, dearest brothers, that blessed Lawrence was not saddened by the victory of the supreme priest, but grieved because he himself was not at that moment overcoming the world together with his priest.

[Note: The Casinensian codices and Vatican Ottobonianus 106 read: “because he himself also was not.”]

“Do not be sad, my son. After three days you will follow me.” That is: Do not be sad as though you had been abandoned in this world; for neither your faith nor your life will deprive you of such a death. Let no anxiety disturb you over my departure, at which I rejoice, since you too will soon have cause to rejoice in your own passion.

Truly singular was the glory of blessed Lawrence, who received from his God such an abundance of grace that a martyr prophesied martyrdom to him, and who was made glad by the privilege of his merits before the battle could terrify him. Therefore, when he learned from the mouth of the priest and martyr that he too would certainly be taken up, he distributed the Church’s wealth among crowds of needy people with devout generosity.

How profound was the spiritual man’s counsel, and how heavenly: both to provide for the needy and, when the multitude had consumed what he had given, to ensure that nothing would remain for the persecutor to seize.

[Note: The Casinensian codices omit “and.” Codex 12 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “might be found.”] He followed, of course, the saying:

“He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever” (Psalm 111).

[Note: Vatican codex 1277 reads: “forever and ever.”]

It was an act of mercy that he gave nourishment to the poor; but it was an act of justice that, as a most prudent man, he took care that the sacrilegious persecutor should not seize the substance of the saints with greedy hands.

“His righteousness,” he says, “endures forever.”

[Note: Codex 12 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “How could this righteousness of his not endure forever, since he both completed it in the holy man…” The same reading is found in Vatican codex 1277; the Martinensis also has: “since he.”]

How could this righteousness not endure forever, since he completed it in a holy work and consecrated it through a most glorious martyrdom?

Inflamed by this grief, the pagan fury immediately prepared a red-hot gridiron, upon which he would tear Lawrence apart limb by limb, so that he might avenge the flames of his anger with impious fires.

[Note: Vatican codex 177 reads: “inflamed by the counsel of the devil, he prepared a gridiron on which he might tear Lawrence apart limb by limb.” The Martinensis reads: “might stretch him out limb by limb.”]

### 239

The most courageous martyr was plainly burning with all his entrails and being consumed; but, contemplating with faithful mind the kingdom of heaven and God’s promises, he exulted in the refreshment of his victorious conscience. He was not bent by the punitive fire, because the unconquerable flame of the Holy Spirit burned within his breast.

[Note: Codices 109, 126, and the Casinensian codices read: “he was burning entirely.” Vatican codex 1269 has: “was burning. He did not yield to the momentary burning of the body, whose faith would extinguish the heat of eternal Gehenna. Thus, conquering the flames through the promises…”]

Could he have yielded to the momentary burning of the body whose faith extinguished the eternal heat of Gehenna?

### 240

When the ministers of the flames had been overcome, the whole fire of worldly madness cooled; and the devil’s purpose advanced only so far that the faithful man ascended gloriously to his God, while the cruelty of his persecutors, together with its fires, grew confused and languished.

## HOMILY LXXV. On the Same Feast, II

### Admonition

Almost all the manuscript codices by which we established that the preceding homily belongs to Saint Maximus also show that this one was written by the same author. In the Vatican Library we examined four manuscripts bearing the name of Saint Maximus: nos. 1273, p. 84; 1269, p. 85; 1277, p. 54; and Vatican Ottobonianus 106, p. 209.

We also found no less agreement among the codices at Florence, in the Laurentian Library: codex 39 Plut. XVII, fol. 170 verso; codex II Plut. XXXIII, left part, p. 144, formerly Minor. Convent. Santa Croce 172; and 174, the same page 154, formerly belonging to the library of the aediles of the major church of Florence, recently added to the Laurentian manuscripts.

Two Casinensian codices bear a similar inscription: 109, p. 235, and CXI, p. 105; as do Ambrosianus C. 98; Vallicellanus 7, p. 9; Augiensis XV; Martinensis, Homily 2 on the Nativity of Saint Lawrence; Santa Croce in Jerusalem XII, p. 100 verso; Ratisponensis of Saint Emmeram, p. 37; and finally Vercellensis 82, a very ancient codex, with the title: “On the feast of Saint Lawrence.”

Nothing more authoritative could be produced than the agreement of so many manuscripts. We therefore omit a detailed account of the editors and add only this: the Ballerini brothers stated that this homily, which had been numbered among the sermons of Saint Leo in ancient collections, should be restored to Maximus.

### Argument

Maximus vividly displays the savagery and cruelty of Saint Lawrence’s martyrdom and represents his steadfast courage and unconquered heart amid every torment, even the burning of his body, not merely in verbal ornament but almost as though in a visual image.

As we have learned, dearest brothers, from the reliable report of our fathers, when the venerable Sixtus was exercising the priesthood of the apostolic see and the Roman Church was flourishing through the ministry of the most holy archdeacon Lawrence, the envy of the devil blazed forth, and the flame of a most severe persecution against the name and faith of Christ began to burn.

[Note: The Martinensis codex reads: “of the most holy.”]

And so that the insatiable rage of the savage beast might tear the Lord’s flock apart with still greater destruction, the enemy, skilled in causing harm, first contrived to tear away the vigilant guardianship of the shepherd.

[Note: Vatican codex 1277 reads: “might devour.” Another codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, no. 12, reads: “first seeks to seize the vigilant guardianship of the shepherd.”]

For this reason pagan fury first attacked Sixtus, the supreme priest of the Lord, so that, once the ecclesiastical members had been beheaded and the protection of heavenly defense removed, the bloodstained persecutor might invade them.

[Note: The same codex 12 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem has: “with the head cut off.”]

But that great Sixtus, who had been a shepherd on earth for the sheep entrusted to him by God, was present as their protector from heaven.

[Note: The Casinensian codex reads: “who had been a shepherd of the sheep entrusted to him by God.”]

Finally, the pagan hand sought out Saint Lawrence, as though he had already been deprived of the assistance of his bishop, in order to subject him to punishment. But the remarkable Sixtus armed him against every evil of the raging world with the prophecy of prophetic speech.

For when Lawrence, like a most dutiful son, was lamenting his father’s passion with inconsolable grief, Sixtus, taught by the foreknowledge of the Holy Spirit and discerning what was to come, said to him:

“Lay aside all sadness over my death, my son; for my absence will not grieve you long. After three days you will follow me.”

When his devout mind had received this answer and had accepted as unquestionable the truth given by the excellent bishop and martyr of Christ, he cared above all that the persecutor’s greed—which had been grieved by the death of the saints—should not rejoice in plundering the Church.

[Note: Vatican codex 1277 reads: “which was grieved by the death.”]

The most prudent man found a way to torment his torturer more severely. He therefore distributed all the wealth of the Church and all the sacred vessels used in its ministry among crowds of needy people in a charitable act, so that the future martyr might be enriched in the heavenly recompense both by the reward of his blood and by the prize of such generosity. He did not doubt that in his own person he would preserve both faith in his Christ and the Church’s riches in the poor.

### 241

For this reason the man, innocent in his simplicity and most courageous in virtue, was immediately dragged before the tribunal of the impious. He brought nothing before the judge except the steadfastness of a living mind and the purity of an uninjured conscience. He offered his soul devoted to God and surrendered his most chaste body to the persecutor for punishment, observing the Gospel saying:

“Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10).

[Note: The same codices 12 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Vatican 1277 read: “the victorious steadfastness of the mind.”]

A savage torture was therefore devised for Lawrence, so that he who was unmoved by fear of death might be broken by the severity of punishment. But the multitude of his virtues strengthened him, and the magnitude of the tortures could not conquer him.

A gridiron blazing with fire was prepared, one that would weary the soul of the triumphant martyr and burn his body. But the ignorant crowd of persecutors, blinded by demonic darkness, did not see that the burning of those limbs was the eternal purification of the faithful soul, and that the body which the present life would abandon to destructive flames was passing through a death imposed upon it into incorruptible life.

Truly incomparable is the mystery of this saving faith, through which blessedness is sought by torments and refreshment is prepared by flames, as the patriarch David says in the words of the martyrs:

“We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Psalm 65).

[Note: The same codex 12 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “and you led us out.”]

Blessed Lawrence passed through fire and water: on the one side the deadly flame of the world scorched him, while on the other the heavenly, life-giving stream of refreshment poured over him.

[Note: The Martinensis reads: “the wave of heavenly refreshment.”] He passed through fire and water when the mercy of the divine fountain moderated the force of the raging blaze.

Lawrence was therefore burning, but he was overcome by the fire of which the Savior says:

“I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it should burn?” (Luke 12).

[Note: The same codex 12, as well as Vatican codex 1277 and Vallicellanus 7 and Vatican Ottobonianus, reads: “and what do I desire except that it should burn?” The Belgian codices, the Martinensis, and Camberonensis read: “and what do I desire it to burn?”]

O new and wondrous thing! In one and the same man, his body was burned by flames, while his mind, kindled by the heat of ardent faith, was glowing. This was as the evangelical men said to one another:

“Was not our heart burning within us on the way?” (Luke 24).

[Note: Vatican codex 1277 and the Casinensian codices read: “those men said to one another: ‘Was not our heart burning within us on the way?’” Codex 12 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem omits “within us.”]

Where the heart burns, the limbs do not feel the flame. Where the fire of Christ is at work, the fire of the devil must be conquered; and where the Spirit of God is fervent, the flame of mortals becomes cold.

[Note: Vatican codex 1277 reads: “And from this it follows.”]

This is why, dearest brothers, the whole world everywhere celebrates the triumph of blessed Lawrence today with unanimous devotion. This is why rejoicing Rome marvels at his inseparable faith: he was kindled by the rays of the eternal sun, endured the world’s fire patiently, and escaped it confidently, and so forth.

[Note: Codex 12 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “this is why it marvels at his unconquerable faith.”]

## HOMILY LXXVI. On the Same Feast, III

### Admonition

Three Vatican codices bear this title for the homily we call the seventy-sixth: “On the Nativity of Saint Lawrence”—namely, 1273, p. 84; 1177, p. 55; and Ottobonianus 106, p. 210. The same title appears in three Laurentian codices, 39 Plut.
