XVII, p. 171, and in two codices formerly belonging to the library of the aediles of the metropolitan church of Florence, 172 and 174, both p. 246; as well as in Augiensis XIX; Ratisponensis of Saint Emmeram, p. 37; Martinensis; Beneventanus; and finally Farfensis, marked B, whose title is: “Sermon within the octave of Saint Lawrence, sermon of blessed Maximus, bishop.” In each of these we read that its author was Maximus, bishop of Turin. Alcuin clearly confirms the same in his *Homiliary*, p. 337, as do the editors of the works of Saint Maximus.

### Argument

Just as blessed Lawrence, inflamed by perfect charity, did not yield to the raging fires, so the fire of various tribulations and the flame of worldly evils must not move us away from fellowship with Christ.

The annual and ever-new feast of the most blessed Lawrence, dearest brothers, continually kindles the Church of God with spiritual joy, admonishing the whole community of believers that, just as he did not yield to raging fires through the ardor of perfect devotion, so the fire of various tribulations and the flame of worldly evils should not move us away from fellowship with Christ.

[Note: In the cited codex 12, the words “annual and ever-new” are absent; it reads “of perfect love” for “of perfect devotion.”]

As the most glorious Paul, that teacher of heavenly mysteries and example of every virtue, says:

“Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Romans 8).

[Note: In codex 12 the words “or persecution” are absent.]

And indeed, no danger of present persecutions can bend one who has once received, with steadfast faith and an unshaken mind, the promises of almighty God and the eternal rewards of the most generous Redeemer.

[Note: Codex 12 reads: “But not even by any”; the Casinensian codex reads: “And truly no one,” etc.]

For a weak mind and a lame faith cannot climb that lofty and arduous road of immortal goods. Therefore neither the torments inflicted upon the most courageous martyr nor the flame of the fiercest persecutor could overcome him, because his mind burned far more intensely, kindled by the rays of truth. Hence that bodily fire, administered by mortal hands, could not drive from his tireless breast the warmth infused by God.

[Note: Codex 12 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “nor could it.”]

Of this mighty soldier of Christ we must believe that the prophet spoke when he foretold it many thousands of years earlier:

“And if you pass through fire, the flame will not burn you” (Isaiah 43).

For behold, blessed Lawrence passed through fire. He was not terrified by the fire that did not burn him, but shone forth illuminated by it.

[Note: The Ottobonian Vatican codices 106 and the Casinensian codex read: “he passed through.”]

He passed through momentary earthly fire, but escaped the flame of Gehenna, which burns forever.

[Note: The Martinensis reads: “of burning Gehenna.”]

What could be more blessed than a man who, through the grace of the merciful God’s dispensation, burned so that he might not burn, and was burned so that he might not be consumed?

[Note: Codices 1277, Vatican Ottobonianus 106, and two Casinensian codices add: “and so that he might not be burned.”]

If he had been handed over to no fires or punishments, there would indeed have been the security of freedom, but no glory of one who had fought.

[Note: The Casinensian codex reads: “no victory instead of glory.”]

For Christ trains us by examples and teachings in his Church not so that we may suffer no evil in the world, but so that we may conquer the world through manifold suffering.

The illustrious patriarch and prophet David, once constrained by various tribulations, sang:

“My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire will blaze” (Psalm 38).

This saying plainly applies also to the venerable Lawrence. His heart burned with such greatness of spirit in the faith of Christ that, scorning the torments of his own body, he joyfully mocked his mad torturer after conquering his fires. Truly, in his meditation an unconquerable fire blazed: kindled by hatred of falsehood and love of truth, it either did not feel the flame placed upon him from outside or overcame it.

[Note: The Casinensian codex reads: “which, kindled not by hatred of falsehood but by love of truth…”]

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us exult and rejoice in the Lord, without doubting that the martyr’s persecutor will endure, in return for the fires he kindled, the fires prepared for the impious, while the most blessed martyr himself will shine before almighty God with the illumination of incorruptible light, in return for the flame he endured.

## HOMILY LXXVII. On the Feast of Saint Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli, I

### Admonition

Gennadius, discussing the writings of Saint Maximus, states that Maximus composed two treatises on the life of Saint Eusebius of Vercelli. We have observed elsewhere that what were once called treatises were accustomed to be called homilies and sermons. Someone may perhaps wonder whether those two treatises mentioned by Gennadius are these two homilies of ours, or two of the five sermons published by Muratorius in volume IV of the *Anecdota*.

But if we consider the witnesses, those that assign the name of Maximus to these two homilies are far superior in both number and antiquity to those that assign it to the five sermons of Muratorius. Among these witnesses are three Vatican codices, 1268, 1273, and 1277; and three Casinensian codices, 12, 109, and CXI. To these may be added the Sangallensis, Vercellensis 66, the Martinensis, and the Ratisponensis of Saint Emmeram.

These are supported by the examples of Gennadius’s catalogue and by all editions of Maximus’s works. They are certainly corroborated by the style, the sublimity of the doctrine, and the method of adducing testimonies from Scripture, all of which anyone can plainly see to be wholly characteristic of Maximus.

Moreover, if Gennadius testifies that Maximus wrote two treatises on the life of Saint Eusebius, and if these two homilies speak at length about Eusebius, whereas the sermons concern the Maccabees and monks rather than Eusebius, and are composed so ineptly, confusedly, and inelegantly that they appear to have been patched together from the little works of some unskilled and crude writer rather than from Maximus—what conclusion can be drawn? We shall say much more about these matters in the preface to the appendix of the sermons.

The title of the homily we now publish varies in the codices. In the Sangallensis, Vatican 1273, Ratisponensis, Augiensis, and Martinensis it appears as follows: “On the Feast of Saint Eusebius of Vercelli.” Two Vatican codices, 1766 and 1277, and likewise two Casinensian codices, have: “On the Feast of Confessors,” plainly contrary to what the subject requires. The Vercellensis finally has: “On the Solemnity of Blessed Eusebius of Vercelli, sermon of Saint Maximus, bishop.” We have followed the title found in the codices first mentioned.

### 245. Argument

Following the solidity of the rock upon which the Church was built, Saint Eusebius confounded and triumphed over the Arians. Saint Maximus refutes their wicked heresy with great learning and fullness.

As we honor the memories of the holy Fathers in religious assemblies, dearest brothers, we marvel both at their personal merits and at the divine gifts bestowed upon them. They are venerable to us because, despising the light of the present life and disregarding the suffering of their bodies, they conquered the raging world through the love of God.

[Note: The Martinensis reads “effort” for “suffering,” and Vatican codices 1277 and 1269, together with the Martinensis, read “for honor” for “through love.”]

So did this most blessed Father of ours. Rising with fervent spirit in defense of the indisputable deity, he opposed the impieties of the Arians. He restored to tranquility of serene faith the Churches of God that had been disturbed by the storms and whirlwinds of threatening heretics, and through manifold suffering he won eternal rewards for himself.

He followed, of course, the firm and unshaken footsteps of the one to whom the Lord said:

[Note: The same Vatican codex reads: “following the footsteps.”]

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16).

[Note: The Vatican codices and the Martinensis read: “will not prevail against it.”]

Truly, and deservedly, he must be honored by all future generations: he followed the solidity of the firmest rock, confounded the enemies of Christ by the authority of the heavenly Spirit, and triumphed through the strength of tireless patience.

Nor did the gate of hell, as it was said, prevail against him who, confessing the King of glory, opened for himself the entrance of the eternal gate. Or how could that life-giving gate fail to open to him who, instructed by the fullness of the Gospel reading, asserted in the Father and his Son the mystery of their one inscrutable majesty, teaching and demonstrating both the nature of the flesh assumed in the one and the same Son of God and the privilege of his natural deity?

[Note: The same Vatican codex omits “his.”]

He certainly knew that the Savior had said:

“I and the Father are one”; and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 12 and 14).

This confession made him honorable on earth and glorious in heaven.

But I now think it necessary that, on the occasion of this blessed Father of ours—whom the faith of the Catholic Churches, steadfastly preserved by him, raised to such glory—we too, with the Lord’s gracious favor, should be instructed by the saving testimonies of the Lord’s teaching.

### 246

The Lord therefore says:

“I and the Father are one.”

The one who says “we are” is not solitary; and the one who says “we are one” cannot be separated from the one with whom he is one.

Why, heretic, do you now try to establish diversity between the Father and his Son, when the Son, teaching us the truth of his substance, said: “I and the Father are one”?

[Note: The same Vatican codex reads: “between the Father and the Son.”]

By saying both “one” and “we are,” he is divided neither by separation nor confused by union. He who is one with the Father differs from the Father neither in eternity nor in power. Although he is one with the Father, he is nevertheless asserted to have been born from the Father, so that, as the impious Arius blasphemes, he may not be thought either a creature or unequal to the Father.

You hear, then, O man, that God was born from God. But in this unfathomable depth you have something to believe by faith; you do not have something to investigate by arguments.

[Note: Vatican codex 1269 reads: “in this great depth.”]

You hear that the Son was born from the Father. But, lest you seek to examine some bodily sex in the Godhead, the Son himself is called both Word and light. He is also called the power of God and the wisdom of God, so that you may understand that the Father did not bring him forth bodily, as though through the contours of reproductive organs, but that through the ineffable secrecy of majesty Power proceeded from Power and Light flowed from Light.

Again, lest you think that the Word itself is not the substance of truth but merely a spoken utterance proceeding from the speaking God, he is called the Son, so that you might learn that in him there are both the harmony and the affection of the one who is Father.

[Note: The same Vatican codex omits “itself” and reads *prolativum* (“uttered”) for *prolatitium* (“spoken forth”).]

Again, because he is called light, lest you think that he shines with a borrowed radiance like a ray of the sun or the brightness of a lamp, blessed John the Evangelist—who was permitted both to see and to reveal God’s mystery—says of him:

[Note: Vatican codex 1269 reads: “shine with radiance.”]

“He was the true light” (John 1).

[Note: Vatican codex 1277 reads: “The true light is…”]

He says “true light,” so that you may know that he is not the radiance of some created and passing light, but that what is light is truth from the true Light.

He is so truly light that he not only has no need to be illuminated but possesses the power to illuminate. For, as it is written, he illuminates every person coming into this world (ibid.).

Christ therefore says, as was stated:

“Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14).

“Whoever sees me,” he says, “sees the Father.”

How can the two not also be one, when one is seen in the other and seeing one is knowledge of both?

And truly, brothers, just as seeing the Son is seeing the Father, so, when the Father is understood, the Son is understood. For whoever believes and confesses that the Father is eternal must necessarily believe that the Son is coeternal.

But let us now see what kind of vision in the Son it is by which the Father is likewise said to be seen. Without doubt, the one who believes that the Son was ineffably born from the Father according to the inconceivable nature of the Godhead sees the Father in the Son. He understands that the one who was born cannot be other than the one who begot him.

He sees the Father in Christ who believes that Christ’s works belong not to an alien power but to the Father’s power.

[Note: The Martinensis reads: “He saw.”]

He sees the Father in the Son who recognizes that, under the shared name of Father, Christ changed water into wine, changed the natures of created things, not through ingenious craftsmanship but by the simple authority of a command. By the abundance of his blessing he also made bread consumed by the hungry fruitful again. For, multiplying food in the mouths of those who chewed it and reforming loaves from crumbs, he made it almost unsurprising that manna had flowed from heaven.

[Note: The Martinensis reads: “forming loaves.” Vatican codex 1169 reads: “he made it not seem remarkable.”]

Who would not perceive in Christ the work of the Father’s equality when he sees him, with the authority of one who rules, terrifying demons, driving away sicknesses, and giving eyes, not yet formed in him, to a man?

A sick woman secretly approached and touched the fringe of his garment, as though stealing health from him. But, since he was the true God from whom no secret of human hearts could be hidden, he immediately revealed the healing that had gone forth from him and made known to the surrounding crowds the merit of the believing woman.

[Note: Vatican codex 1269 reads: “no secret could be hidden from him; the healing that had gone forth from him…”]

He sees the Father’s majesty in the Son who beholds Christ raising the dead from their beds or tombs, not by the favor of one making a request but by the command of one who orders, with the assent of the Father’s will.

[Note: Vatican codex 1277 reads: “not by the favor of one seeking, but…”]

If creating a human being and giving him life is a divine work, how could restoring health to the dead not be a divine work?

“Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14).

How, brothers, could there be one undivided vision in the Father and his Son unless there were one undivided substance?

[Note: The Martinensis omits “brothers.”]

Christ, therefore, is God by nature and human by nature, true in both and perfect in both: for he truly received humanity from his mother, and naturally possesses deity from the Father.

### 247

Whoever sees the Son in this way also sees the Father, because when we confess Christ as the same God and Lord, we necessarily attribute human sufferings to the man and miracles to God, so that the Only-Begotten of God may be understood to be neither unlike the Father’s majesty nor unlike his mother’s flesh.

[Note: The cited Vatican codex reads: “the sufferings of the man.”]

Through this faith, dearest brothers, the Arian unbelief was refuted by our fathers. Arius, contradicting the Gospel of blessed John, denied that the Word of God was God and that he was with God. Blinded by the darkness of his own faithlessness, he could see neither the Father nor the Son. While he insisted that the maker of all things was a creature and tried to ascribe temporal things to the timeless God, he was confounded by the madness of his presumption and lost the saving mystery of both natures in Christ.

[Note: The cited Casinensian codex reads: “while he denies that the Word of God is God.” The Martinensis reads: “blinded by the misery of his own…” Vatican codex 1269 reads: “while he insists that this maker of all things…”]

But this venerable Father had read that the Lord said:

“I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (ibid.).

Knowing that this teaching distinguishes the persons but not the natures, he firmly maintained and taught the inseparable unity of the Father and his Son, who are not one person but one substance. He likewise asserted that in Christ the Lord there are both passible flesh and impassible deity.

[Note: Vatican codex 1269 and two Casinensian codices read: “of the Father and his Son, who are not one but are one…” The Martinensis omits “and taught.” Casinensian and Martinensis codices read: “in our Lord.” The same ending is found in Vatican codex 1277 and in the Augiensis and Monte Amiata codices, as well as in the Casinensian codices.]

## HOMILY LXXVIII. On the Same Saint Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli, II

### Admonition

### 249

Not only the testimony of Gennadius but also the authority of many codices proves that this homily was written by Saint Maximus. Among the codices are two Vatican manuscripts, 1177 and 6451, p. 203; two of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, 99 no. 73 and 12, p. 81; Mediolanensis F 56 of the library of the metropolitan church, p. 149; Ratisponensis of Saint Emmeram, p. 39; Martinensis; Cisterciensis of Monte Amiata; Laurentianus 47 Plut. XVII; and Gotwicensis.

The homily also appears in the Urbevetanus, though no author is identified there. In two breviaries, Roman and Strigonian, it is plainly attributed to Saint Maximus.

As great as the agreement of the codices is in commending the name of Maximus, so great is their disagreement in the title itself. Some, such as the Ratisponensis and Martinensis, title it “On the Same Feast.” Vatican codex 4951 and the Gotwicensis have “On the Feast of the Confessor.” Another Vatican codex and the Laurentianus have “On the Feast of Saint Eusebius.” Two other codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, no. 99, agree with the latter and read: “On the Feast of Saint Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli.” The codex of the metropolitan church of Milan has: “On the Feast of Saint Eusebius.”

The Cistercian monks of Monte Amiata divided the homily into eight lessons, assigning it the title: “On the Nativity of Bernard, abbot.” In the codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem another title was attached: “On the Translation of Saint Benedict.” In the breviaries the lessons belong to the second nocturn of the common of a bishop-confessor and seem to have been adapted for choral use in later times.

The editors also give it another heading: “Second homily from the foregoing,” as do Gymnicus, p. 236; Galesinius, p. 161; Raynaudus, p. 234; Margarini in *Bibliotheca Maxima Patrum*, vol. VI, p. 38; and Cumdius, vol. IV, p. 1137. Whether the ancient editors of the works of Ambrose rightly or wrongly attributed this homily to him, each reader may judge for himself.

Finally, we note that a fragment of this homily reached us from the Gotwicensis, but it was so disfigured by corruptions that we thought it should be omitted as spurious. Fortune, however, favored our wishes: while we were consulting the Vatican manuscripts, codex 4951 supplied the same fragment in an entirely different form, composed with considerable elegance and striking imagery, as readers can see.

### 250. Argument

Saint Maximus urges that the memories of the saints be celebrated, and all the more because their merits are more illustrious. Who, then, was more outstanding than Eusebius, who endured so many labors and so many hardships for the Catholic truth, for the glory of God, and for his pastoral office, even to the end of his life?

To add anything to the praises of this holy and most blessed Father of ours, whose feast we celebrate today, is to detract from them. For the grace of his virtues must not be set forth in words but demonstrated by deeds. [Col. 0418C] Since Scripture says, “A wise son is the glory of his father” (Prov. 10), how great is the glory of this man, who rejoices in the wisdom and devotion of so many sons? For in Christ Jesus he himself begot us through the Gospel (1 Cor. 14). Whatever virtue and grace there may be in this holy congregation, the purity of all its streams flowed from him as from a certain most limpid fountain. [Note: Codex 1277: “from a certain fountain.”] [Note: Codex Urbevetanus: “this purity.”]

For because he was powerful in the strength of chastity, because he gloried in the rigors of abstinence, because he was endowed with the charm of gentleness, he stirred the affection of all his fellow citizens toward God; and because he shone through the administration of the episcopate, he left behind many disciples as successors to his priesthood. Well and appropriately on this day—which the passage of this blessed Father of ours to paradise makes joyful for us—we sang the verse of the present psalm: “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Ps. 111). For he rightly enters the remembrance of human beings [Note: Codex Vaticanus 4951: “of angels, who, already glorified by the grace of Christ, did not seek the glory of the world, taking care of that, etc.” Codex Urbevetanus: “because he passed to the joys of the angels, because, already glorified, he found the grace of Christ, taking care, etc.” Codex 37, Plut. XVII: “who, already glorified, found the grace of Christ, because he did not seek the glory of the world, taking care of that which the divine utterance says.” The Breviary of the Church of Velletri has the same wording.], since he passed into the joy of the angels.

The divine utterance says: “Do not praise a man during his life” (Eccl. 11), as though it were saying: praise him after life; magnify him after his completion. For it is more advantageous, for two reasons, to give praise to people after their death rather than during their life: so that you may exalt the merits of holiness especially at the time when neither flattery moves the one who praises nor exaltation tempts the one who is praised. Praise him after the danger; proclaim him secure. Praise not the happiness of one still sailing, but of one who has reached the harbor. Praise the courage of the commander, but only after he has been led to triumph. [Note: Codex Vaticanus 4951: “after he has been led.”]

Who, while alive, could safely and without trembling be praised, when he remembers that he has something to regret in the past and sees that something remains in the future for him to fear? [Note: The Breviary of Velletri: “Who, placed in this little body, should claim anything for himself from merits whose journey through life is beset by the hidden assaults of demons, etc.” The same codex: “from merits whose journey through life is again beset by the hidden assault of demons.”]

But those who are placed in this little body—what can they claim for themselves from merits, when a multitude of demons, like robbers, again besets them, and hateful subverters stretch snares for souls along every road, snares to be feared because of their countless devices? [Note: Codex Vaticanus 1277: “to whom all”; Codex Vaticanus 4951: “for whom, along all the roads.”] [Note: The same Laurentian codex: “to be feared because of the conduct of innumerable beings.”]

For as we sail across this great and spacious sea, in which there are creeping things without number, small and great animals—that is, various kinds of enemies [Col. 0419C]—they struggle against us in a contest measured according to the extent of our strength. [Note: The same Laurentian codex: “who, according to the measure of our strength.”]

In the sea of this world, therefore, we must fear greatly lest either the storm of the tempest carry away our ship, or the waves swallow it, or a cruel pirate drag it away as eternal booty. [Note: Here the sermon ends in the Breviary of Velletri.]

Against these manifold evils of the age, then, let us resist with disciplined and chaste conduct. [Note: Codex Vaticanus 1277: “with chastened actions”; Codex Martinianus: “let us resist with chastity.”] Let us now confidently magnify the merits of our blessed Father, which have been placed in safety [Note: Codex Martinianus: “having been placed [in safety].”]. Firmly holding the rudder of faith, he has already set the anchor of hope in a tranquil harbor and placed his ship, full of heavenly riches and eternal cargo, on the desired shore. [Note: The Laurentian and Vatican 1277 codices: “the author of faith, or of hope.”] Against all adversaries he held the shield of the fear of God tirelessly until he reached victory. [Note: Codex Martinianus: “the shield of faith and of the fear of God.”]

For what was the whole course of his life except a single struggle with a vigilant enemy? [Note: Codex 4951: “For what indeed?” It continues: “You had in him a physician fallen from heaven, with whom the author of healing entered your borders in the hope of healings. How many, etc.” Codex Urbevetanus likewise supplies this passage.] How many blind men wandering from the way of truth, already hanging from the highest cliff over the abyss, did he restore to sight, repairing that vision by which Christ might be seen? [Note: Codex Urbevetanus: “by which he might be seen.”]

To how many deaf ears, condemned by the hardening of unbelief, did he pour precious hearing, so that they might receive the voice of the heavenly commandments and answer God’s call to mercy through obedience? [Note: The same codex: “condemned by the hardening [of unbelief].”]

How many wounded inwardly did he heal from infirmity by the art of an angelic mouth and by prayers? [Note: Codex Vaticanus 1277: “How many wounded inwardly did he heal by the art of an angelic mouth and by the steadfastness of prayers?” The same wording is found in Codex 4951. The Urbevetanus, Martinianus, and Laurentianus codices omit “from infirmity.”] How many, dissolved through long neglect by the stain of sin and covered with a kind of leprous contagion, did he cleanse by purifying them with chastisements and exhortations, while God worked within him?

How many souls living in the body but already dead, weighed down and buried beneath the mass of their sins, did he resurrect by calling them to amendment as to the light? [Note: Codex Vaticanus 4951: “God calling, he resurrected them.” The codices of Santa Croce 12 and Vatican 1277 add: “so that, as an admirable imitator of his Lord, he might, in the opposite sense, mortify to God souls already dead, etc.”] And, as an admirable imitator of his Lord, he in turn mortified those souls, already dead to God, to sin with a life-giving death. [Note: Codex Martinianus: “he mortified [them].”]

[Note: Codex Vaticanus 4951: “Assenting to no evil through others’ enticements, with condemnation of mind” [the reading is corrupt]. “Then, in another respect, he beneficially closed what he had opened. In what order did he do this? He closed them, of course, by teaching them not to see another’s evil, lest another’s possession appear desirable to them, lest an external fault transmit [a stain] that would infect the soul with the poison of sin, lest darkness enter the heart by the way of light, etc.” Codex Urbevetanus: “He assented to no evil of men through enticements, with corruption of mind. Then, in another respect, he healthfully closed what he had opened. In what order did he do this? He closed them, of course, by teaching them not to see another’s evil, lest another’s possession appear desirable to them; lest an alien wife be beautiful to them unto the poison of sin and penetrate the soul through affection; lest an external fault transmit a stain to the inner person.”]

Then, in another respect, he beneficially closed what he had opened, so that no alien possession might appear desirable to them; so that an external fault might not transmit a stain to the inner person; so that darkness might not enter the heart by way of the paths of light; so that the prophetic threat might not be fulfilled in each one: “Death has entered through your windows,” he says (Jer. 9). [Note: The Laurentian codex continues: “In what order did he do this? He closed them, of course, by teaching them not to see another’s evil.” Codex 12 reads “people” for “them.”]

For the ministries of the ears and eyes are shown to be the windows of souls. When, through deeds, our hearing is exposed to those who speak evil and wicked things, who slander damnably and urge what is contrary to God, death enters through our windows; the horror of deadly night breaks in through those openings through which the sun of righteousness ought to have entered. When these windows of sin are open, the gate of salvation and life, and the doors of paradise, are closed.

This blessed man blocked these windows with many bolts of divine fear. From how many hearts, possessed by shameful iniquity and impiety [Note: The Laurentian and Vatican 4951 codices: “From how many hearts he drove out…”], did he drive luxury, cast down anger, and extinguish envy? And, as though an ancient house had been disturbed by barbarian guests, he brought faith, chastity, justice, and mercy back into it and introduced these peaceful inhabitants, through whom Christ, the head of these virtues, might enter the dwelling of the mind. [Note: Codex Martinianus does not have “of these.”] Applying the remedies of repentance, he awakened them, like one who had lain four days and stank, with the sound of reproof. [Note: The Laurentian codex, Santa Croce 12, the Jerusalem codex, Vatican 4951, and Vatican 1277: “he awakened them with the roar.”] Once amendment had been received, he rescued them from the very jaws of death and restored them to life through a temporary resurrection.

Doing these and many other things [Note: The Laurentian, Vatican 4951, and Urbevetanus codices read: “doing many more such things, which you yourselves remember more fully, and which, since it is right for us to bring them forth and explain them, etc.” The cited codices 12 and 1277 read: “he did these things, and those which it is [right] for us to bring forth and [explain], etc.”], which our poor little speech cannot adequately set forth and explain through our words, your own affection will tell you better. For he was a man devoted to and vigilant over souls with the utmost zeal: cutting away desires, restraining anger, and uprooting evil. [Note: Codices 4911 and Martinianus: “This man was even more [necessary] for these times, etc.”]

This man was especially necessary in these times, when such great iniquity, daily taking up strength as justice declines, grows powerful. And indeed, although in this pilgrimage he was present in body alone, in thought and desire he lived in that eternal homeland. [Note: The Laurentian codex reads: “he lived there; crucified and dead to this world, whatever he labored for in this life he transferred to that life, and, like a good accountant, etc.” The Vatican 4951 codex has the same.] Like a good accountant, as though always reaching out for a hundredfold, he transferred from the left hand to the right and stored his labors in heaven; for although his works are visible here, the merits of his works have passed there.

Let us follow his footsteps as far as we can. By them he showed us how we should follow him as he hastened by that exceedingly narrow way toward the spaciousness of heaven.

## Fragment from Codex Vaticanus 4951

For the Lord placed him here on our earth so that we might be formed for good action by his example and, looking toward him as toward a mirror, might compose the faces of our souls and cultivate within ourselves, like good sons, the likeness of our father.

Just as a great householder, desiring to paint his house most splendidly, seeks out every kind of form and image to place before the eyes of an industrious painter, who eagerly seizes upon the work of another and, with a hand already trained, transfers onto the face of the walls the dignity of living persons, so that true householder, God, appears to have brought forward and displayed, for painting his house—that is, for adorning our souls in his Church—certain models of living, as it were, or examples for painting: the deeds and merits of this man, presenting them to the inner eyes of our souls.

Accordingly, let each of us apply to the faces of our souls, as though precious colors, the virtues of this man. Let one seize from him the grace of compunction, another the purity of chastity; one, the strength of abstinence; another, modesty; one, ardent faith in the things of God; another, the gentleness of patience.

In this way, having in this man’s life an example of right living, let us adorn our house with diverse virtues—that is, let us paint the whole Church of God. And when he sees us thinking either about the fear of eternal judgment or about future blessedness, may this patron of ours be able to take up that evangelical saying of Christ: “Father, I ask that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17). When we eventually depart from this age, may he, like Abraham, receive us as his own into his seat and bosom; and on that day may he recognize us, safe and sound, as sheep, like a joyful shepherd—with the help of him who lives and reigns, God, forever and ever. Amen.

# Homily LXXIX: On the Feast of Saint Cyprian, Bishop and Martyr I

[Col. 0421]

## Notice

Saint Maximus is testified by Gennadius to have been the author of this homily as well. The codices of St. Gall, Santa Croce in Jerusalem 90 and 99, Ambrosianus C 97, Veronensis 75, Vaticanus 1269, Augiensis XIX, Ratisponensis of Saint Emmeram, Laurentianus X Plut. XIV, and the metropolitan library of Milan, shelfmark F 53, agree with him.

In some of these, the homily bears the title “On the Feast of Saint Cyprian”; in others, “On the Nativity of Saint Cyprian.” The sole exception is Codex 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, which reads: “Here begins [the sermon] on the feast of Saint Cyprian.” Several other discourses by the same Saint Maximus on Saint Cyprian are to be published among the sermons.

But here we have reserved a special mention for the codex of the archive of the imperial basilica of Milan, since we can never adequately express our thanks to Canon Antonio Francesco Frisius for having supplied us not only with testimonies from the Milanese codices, but also for having recovered and communicated to us a distinguished fragment of this homily from the aforesaid very ancient codex, which bears notes from the ninth century. Nor should we fail to mention that the beginning of such a fragment is also found in Vaticanus 1269 and Santa Croce in Jerusalem 99.

Gymnicus published the same homily on page 241 under the title “First Homily on the Feast of the Divine Cyprian, Bishop and Martyr”; Galesinius published it on page 162, Cumdius in volume IV, page 774, Raynaudus on page 285, and Margarinus in the *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, page 39. Therefore it must be judged that it was rashly included among the works of Saint Ambrose in the Paris edition of 1569 and the Roman edition of 1570.

[Col. 0423A] **Argument.** Saint Maximus teaches that the Lord’s cup, of which Scripture speaks, was a figure of the sufferings of the martyrs; and since Christ gave everyone outstanding examples of patience, the martyrs are more praiseworthy the more they showed themselves imitators of the divine Teacher.

We celebrate today, as everyone knows, the feast of Saint Cyprian; and, with the vintage of his martyrdom approaching, as they say, we observe the anniversary of his martyrdom. [Note: Both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem lack the word “anniversary.”] Our vows therefore coincide with those of the world. The world rejoices in the abundance of its vintages; we rejoice in the passion of the saints. That passion is indeed comparable to the vintage: just as wine is poured out through the pressing of grapes, so blood is poured out in place of wine through the martyrdom of the saints—except that [Note: Codex Vaticanus 1269: “except that the vineyard…”] the grape provides temporal fruits, whereas passion provides eternal ones.

Martyrdom is therefore rightly compared with the vintage. It has its intoxication and its cup, concerning which the prophet David says: “Your cup that inebriates, how splendid it is!” (Ps. 23). And the Lord himself, standing at the end of his passion, said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26). Again the prophet says: “I will receive the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115).

I say that the cup is rightly compared with martyrdom, because just as, when the cup is drunk, every harmful liquid is boiled away by the heat of the wine, so, when the cup of martyrdom is drained, all the dregs of the sinner [Note: Codex Veronensis: “all the dregs of the sinner”; both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “of sinners.”] are tempered by the glory of the passion.

Martyrdom is therefore a kind of saving wine, which grants joy to the heart, warmth to faith, and purity to the soul. It is plainly the wine of that spiritual grape which hung upon the tree for the salvation of all. For just as a cluster destined to produce wine is first suspended in a vineyard by a certain work of nature, so Christ, destined to produce the spiritual wine of martyrdom on the cross, is prepared by a certain providence of the Godhead. [Note: Both codices cited above and the Veronensis read: “so Christ, destined to produce the spiritual wine…”]

He is plainly the cluster which those two explorers—namely, Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh [Note: Codex 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads “Jephonias.”]—carried on a pole upon their own shoulders to the children of Israel (Num. 13). This action already foreshadowed the coming of the Lord Savior. For the cluster suspended on the pole represents Christ hanging upon the cross; and the two men carrying the grape on the pole represented two peoples: the Christian and the Jewish. And just as is customary among bearers, one going ahead and the other following, so the Jewish people are signified as first and the Christian people as second.

And just as the one who goes ahead, carrying what he bears, does not see it and, keeping it behind him, despises it with a turning of his back, while the one who follows always sees it with his eyes, always guards it with his gaze, and always possesses it in bodily proximity [Note: Codex 90 cited above: “and, always going away”]—so it is with the Jewish and Christian peoples. The Jewish people are first: they carry Christ in the Law without knowing him, and, placing him behind them, despise him with a turning of their back. Hence the prophet says: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see; and bend their back continually” (Ps. 68).

The Christian people, however, following behind, always behold Christ with their eyes, always guard him with their gaze, and embrace him with the closeness of their steps. [Note: Both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Veronensis: “with the closeness of their steps.”] And to the degree that that people leaves him behind on a crooked road, this people hastens to reach him along a straight course. [Note: The Veronensis ends the homily here.]

## Fragment drawn from the Codex of the Archive of the Imperial Basilica of Saint Ambrose of Milan

Therefore, brothers, let us follow the footsteps of this most blessed martyr Cyprian, who followed Christ by a straight path and reached the palm of martyrdom when the grapes were ripening. The time of the vintage was also approaching. Since he suffered at this season of the vintage, it is as though we have gathered sweet and varied fruits from his passion, as from a vintage.

For he has fattened us and refreshes us with the must of his martyrdom. It is must that refreshes and intoxicates the Christian; but that intoxication makes him more sober. For whoever is intoxicated with heavenly grace is sobered of the burden of sins.

Filled with this must, the holy apostles, as Scripture says (Acts 2), spoke of the mighty works of God in foreign tongues. In this event they appeared at once intoxicated and sober. They were thought intoxicated because another, unnatural speech resounded from them; they were sober because, according to custom, they praised the Lord with the devotion of their minds. This did not happen through any arrogance or lack of self-control, as though holy men were speaking in an alien tongue; it happened by the providence of the Godhead, so that, since one language was insufficient to magnify God, the devotion of the mind might be expressed through many languages.

We have therefore been gladdened, because we have received the fruit of refreshment from the vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth. The vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth, as the prophet says (Isa. 5:7), is Israel; and we are that house. For according to faith, we are Israelites. Hence the Apostle says: “Those who are of faith are sons of Abraham” (Gal. 3). Since, therefore, we are Israel, we are the vineyard of the Lord.

Let us carefully see to it that from the branch of our work there grows not a sweet grape but one of gall, and that it not be said to us what was said to the Jews through the prophet: “I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns” (Isa. 5). What a harsh condition—that the possession which ought to have brought its master fruits of sweetness should prick him with the sharpness of thorns! This is what happened when the Jews, though they ought to have received the Savior with the whole devotion of faith, crowned him with the passion of thorns.

That crown was as great an insult of injuries to the Jews as it was a crown of virtues to the Lord. The Jews therefore prick the Lord while they crown him; they prick him while they crucify him. Hence Holy Scripture says: “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12:10; John 19:37).

Therefore, brothers, see to it that it not also be said to you: “I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns.” That is, let us not add by wicked thoughts the thorns which the Jews placed upon the Lord with bloodstained hands, nor pierce him by the harshness of our dispositions, but by the depravity of our deeds.

The Savior recalls these things in the Gospel when he says that the seed which was sown fell among thorns, grew up, and choked what had been born (Luke 8). He himself goes on to explain what the thorns are. He says that they are worldly anxieties, which, when they grow in the human heart, choke the Savior’s commandments within it.

For who could ever be anxious about the world and at the same time be properly anxious about Christ? Who, while providing for the profits of his household, could provide for the welfare of the Church? Hence the Apostle says: “The unmarried man is anxious about the things of God, how he may please God; but the married man is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (1 Cor. 7).

Therefore, brothers, see to it that your vineyard produce not grapes but thorns, and that your vineyard bring forth not wine but vinegar. Whoever gathers in a vintage and does not give to the poor gathers vinegar, not wine. Whoever stores up his harvest and does not distribute it to the needy has stored up not the fruit of nourishment but thistles of greed.

For this reason Scripture says concerning our earth: “It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:18). Therefore, brothers, if you want your crop to produce for you not thorns and thistles but the abundant fruits you desire, refresh with all the exertion of your mind the hunger of the needy from the fruits of your harvest. And so that your vintage may bring you not vinegar but the most excellent wine, extinguish the burning thirst of the poor with the liquid of wine, so that you may not suffer, with the wicked rich man of the Gospel placed in torment, the tortures of hunger and thirst, but may deserve to rejoice with Lazarus the beggar and blessed Tobias, the giver of alms, in everlasting happiness—through the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# Homily LXXX: On the Same Feast II

[Col. 0425]

## Notice

This homily, attributed to Saint Maximus, follows the preceding one in five manuscript codices: those of St. Gall, Vaticanus 1273, Veronensis 75, Ratisponensis, and Augiensis 19. Certainly no one has reason to deny them authority and credibility, especially since, as anyone who reads it will readily see, this homily of ours is so similar to the other homilies of Maximus in style that nothing more similar could be imagined.

I therefore pay no attention to the codices in which this homily of ours is omitted. In the Vatican codex it bears the title “On the Feast of Saint Cyprian.” In some of the others, “On the Same Feast.” In the Veronensis, “Likewise, as Above.” No editor has thought that this very homily should be omitted. Gymnicus printed it on page 243 under the title “Second Homily, as Above”; Galesinius on page 163, Cumdius in volume IV, page 774, Raynaudus on page 235, and Margarinus in the *Bibliotheca Maxima*, page 40, under the heading “On the Same Feast.”

[Col. 0425C] **Argument.** It is right and proper that the whole Christian world should rejoice in the glory of Saint Cyprian, whom holiness consecrated as a priest, learning as a teacher, and faith as a martyr.

In the martyrdom of the most blessed Cyprian, the whole Church of Christ rejoices with us. He instructed her in every kind of joy through the teaching of heavenly discourse and adorned her with the gift of triumphant blood. For, as we know, in him there was both a fullness of spiritual wisdom against the errors of the devil and tireless steadfastness of a Christian heart against the persecutions of the world.

Who could celebrate such a man with praises proportionate to his worth? His eloquence, inspired by God, both taught the churches and refuted the world. Truly he was remarkable and worthy everywhere of the devotion of all: holiness consecrated him as a priest, learning as a teacher, and faith as a martyr.

“Precious,” David says, “in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 116). See, beloved, to what prophetic praise the venerable Cyprian also attained: in the sight of the Lord not only his death but also his life was precious. By dying he gave his own blood to Christ; by living, nevertheless, through his most courageous exhortation, he acquired countless martyrs for heaven.

What could be more glorious than this priest, whose heavenly way of life shone among the throngs of human beings, and who by his own death became one of the angelic choirs and was conspicuous there through the death of others? Most justly did he sing with the patriarch David to his Lord God, saying: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Ps. 84).

His heart rejoiced in the living God when, despising the vanity of the world as it dies and is dying, he devoted his whole self to divine service. His flesh also rejoiced in God: it departed from this world consecrated not by the miserable corruption of illness but by pious sufferings endured for religion.

This is that evangelical householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old (Matt. 13). Proclaiming the one and same mystery of the Old and New Testaments, he enriched the churches with a most abundant exposition. His treasure is incorruptible and indefatigable even today: lending the money of his master at interest to the money-changers, he daily gathers in the hearts of the faithful the holy interest of heavenly riches (Matt. 25).

What, then, brothers, is more splendid than this man, whose rule and measure of speech are such that, amid the various circumstances and differing emotions of human beings, he consoles the humble sometimes with a father’s affection, restrains the proud with a teacher’s authority, reproves the negligent, and rebukes the unbelieving? And finally, this most faithful man adorned his priesthood and his life with such dignity that he confirmed his teaching by subsequent deeds, holding to that saying of the Lord: “Whoever teaches and does them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

How great and how eminent in the kingdom of heaven is this man, whom prophetic utterance, a remarkable life, and a death devoted to God exalt to every glory? Nor is it without reason, brothers, that the memory of his name is celebrated with such honor throughout the widest expanses of the world, because across the whole earth both his passion and his teaching have advanced the strengthening of our faith. [Note: Collated with the Veronensis, it agrees perfectly.]

# Homily LXXXI: On the Feast of the Holy Martyrs of Turin, Octavius, Adventius, and Solutor

[Col. 0427]

## Notice

Among the many codices that we ourselves have examined, and the many that others have read, very few have been found that contain this homily and agree concerning its author. The homiliary codex of the Lateran, page 91, attributes it to Saint Ambrose. The Casinensis CXI, page 180, attributes it to Saint Augustine; the Urbevetanus to no one.

But older codices—such as Ambrosianus, the St. Gall homiliary 10, Santa Croce in Jerusalem 90, homily 10, and the same Santa Croce 99, homily 81, as well as Vallicellanus XIX, page 47—provide clear testimony for Saint Maximus. The authority of these manuscripts is so great that the homily must be reclaimed from the old Parisian and Sixtine editions, in which it was published under Ambrose’s name, and restored to Saint Maximus.

We do not wish to pass over the distinctive title of the homily supplied by both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem: “Here begins [the homily] on the passion or feast of the holy martyrs Octavius, Adventius, and Solutor.” From this title it may be inferred that Maximus had delivered several discourses on these same holy martyrs of Turin.

The St. Gall codex bears the title “On the Holy Octavius, Solutor, and Adventius.” I see no reason why anyone should doubt that this homily, which contains the praise of these same saints, was delivered at Turin. Those who judged that it should be attributed to Ambrose or Augustine were therefore mistaken.

Whom else should we suppose to have delivered it but Maximus, the bishop of that city, since both the elegance of the discourse and the manner of adducing passages from Sacred Scripture are plainly characteristic of Maximus? Added to this is the agreement of the editors Gymnicus, Galesinius, Raynaudus, and Margarinus, and of those who have written about the holy martyrs of Turin.

In the editions of Gymnicus and Raynaudus, the same homily is entitled “On the Feast of the Holy Tauric Martyrs [Tauricorum], Octavius, Adventius, and Solutor”; in those of Galesinius and Margarinus, “On the Feast of the Holy Martyrs of Turin [Taurinensium], Octavius, Adventius, and Solutor.” We have followed the latter.

[Col. 0427B] **Argument.** The saints, defenders of the faith, are to be honored throughout the whole Church; yet they claim a particular love and special veneration wherever they shed their blood. Maximus therefore urges the people of Turin to honor those whose relics they possess and by whose protection they are aided.

When, brothers, we ought to celebrate the feast of all the holy martyrs with the utmost devotion, then especially we must honor with complete veneration the solemnity of those who shed their own blood in our dwellings. For although all the saints are everywhere and benefit everyone, nevertheless those intercede for us who endured punishments for our sake. For when a martyr suffers, he suffers not only for himself but also for his fellow citizens: he suffers for himself unto reward, for his fellow citizens unto example; he suffers for himself unto rest, for his fellow citizens unto salvation. For by their example we have learned to believe in Christ; we have learned to seek eternal life through insults; we have learned not to fear death. See, therefore, what we owe to the martyrs: one was tortured so that another might be saved; one endured the executioner so that another might acknowledge Christ; one was handed over to death so that another might obtain eternal life; and, finally, a holy man was killed so that a sinner might escape.

[Col. 0428B] Therefore the blessed martyrs neither lived for themselves nor died for themselves; they left us an example by living well, by their manner of life, and by enduring their passion bravely. For this reason the Lord wished martyrs to suffer in different places throughout the world, so that, as trustworthy witnesses, they might urge us onward by a present example of faith in their confession; so that human frailty—which scarcely believes the Lord’s preaching even after prolonged hearing—might not delay to believe through the visible testimony of the blessed martyrs.

[Col. 0428C] All martyrs, therefore, must be honored with the utmost devotion, but especially those whose relics we possess must be venerated by us. They help us by their prayers; these also help us by their suffering. We have a special familiarity with them, for they are always with us and dwell with us: that is, while we are living in the body, they protect us, and when we depart from the body, they receive us—here, lest the stain of sins seize us; there, lest the horror of hell overwhelm us.

For this reason our forebears made provision that we should join our bodies to the bones of the saints: so that, while Tartarus fears them, punishment might not touch us; while Christ illumines them, the darkness of shadows might flee from us.

[Col. 0428D] Let us therefore, resting with the holy martyrs, escape the darkness of the underworld, through their own merits and yet as companions in holiness. For the Lord says to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16).

[Col. 0429A] If, then, the gate of hell does not prevail against the apostle and martyr Peter, whoever is joined to a martyr is not held by Tartarus. For the gate of hell does not possess the martyrs, since the kingdoms of paradise receive them.

[Col. 0429C] We see, indeed, that they already reign here. For we behold people possessed by the most unclean demons being freed by them, so that, through heavenly medicine, both the captive soul is snatched from the devil’s snares and the devil himself, bound with fiery chains, is brought forth from his captivity as a captive; so that he who had seized the prey shortly before is himself subjected to punishment as prey.

It is known to everyone that these and other, greater miracles are performed through the saints. Therefore, brothers, let us venerate in this age those whom we may have as defenders in the age to come; and just as we are joined to the bones of our parents, so let us also be joined to them by imitation of their faith. For we can in no respect be separated from them if we are joined to them as much by religious devotion as by bodily association [the text is uncertain here; the manuscripts continue with a formula equivalent to “may he himself deign to grant this, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen”].

# HOMILY LXXXII. On the Holy Martyrs

[Col. 0429]

## ADMONITION

I remember having said at some time that the titles of homilies and sermons were occasionally composed at the discretion of copyists. This can be confirmed to a very considerable degree by those manuscript codices through whose assistance this homily of Maximus has been preserved for us. For the person who transferred it into Vatican Codex 1629 prefixed this title: “On the feast of many martyrs.” The person who entered it into the other Vatican codex, 1273, gave it the title: “On the feast of one martyr.” The Ratisbon codex of Saint Emmeram has: “On the holy martyrs.” The two Casinensis codices, 109 and 111, have: “On the nativity of the holy martyrs.” Finally, the Martinian codex has: “On the feast of the holy martyrs of Turin, Octavius, Aventius, and Solutor.”

In the old Strigonian Breviary the same homily bears this inscription: “For the common feast of many martyrs: a homily of Saint Maximus the bishop.” Nor is there any less variety among the editors in recording the title. In Gymnicus, Galesinius, and Raynaudus it reads: “The same author, on the martyrs”; but in Cumdius and Margarini: “On the holy martyrs.” We have followed these last two, supported by the Casinensis codices. For there is nothing in this homily of Maximus so specific to the holy martyrs of Turin that it could not appropriately apply to many other martyrs.

Moreover, since there is remarkable consistency among the manuscripts and editors in establishing Maximus as the author, and since nothing in the homily departs from the course of expression characteristic of that same holy bishop, the authority of the editors of the first Paris and Roman editions of the works of Saint Ambrose—who ascribe it to that same Saint Ambrose—must surely be regarded as worthless.

[Col. 0429B] ARGUMENT.—Since martyrdom is the perfection and crown of one’s entire preceding life, the martyr must have shown himself a lover and perfect keeper of the whole Christian law. Accordingly, the holy teacher commends the martyrs for the holiness by which they deserved the palm of victory. He then inveighs against avarice, a vice from which very few wise people defend themselves.

The examples of the holy martyrs ought to be sufficient for our progress in salvation: they subjected themselves to every command of the Lord in order to obtain the heavenly crown, and so bound themselves to all the laws of the Savior that, because of their preceding life, they deserved to arrive at this glory of martyrdom.

For they did not fulfill the Lord’s command only at the time when they endured the punishment of confession; rather, they must first have lived according to the Gospel of Christ in order to obtain a share in Christ’s sufferings. For it is necessary that the beginnings of those whose end was to be so excellent should have been good; and that they were not martyrs only when they suffered, but that they were martyrs of Christ also while they lived.

For in Latin “martyr” means “witness”; and whenever we fulfill Christ’s command through good works, we bear witness to Christ. Hence the Lord’s cross is called not only that which is constructed by fastening someone to wood at the time of the Passion, but also that which is formed throughout the course of the whole life by the virtues of every discipline. Concerning this, the Savior seems to say to me: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me” (Luke 9).

Were all the martyrs who followed the Lord crucified? Were all the virgins who, according to the Apocalypse (chapter 14), follow the Lamb of God crucified in order to follow him? Had the apostle Paul been crucified when he said: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14)?

He says this so that you may understand that the cross is not the gallows of wood, but the purpose of life and virtue. The whole life of a Christian, if he lives according to the Gospel, is therefore a cross and martyrdom.

But this is what is difficult to find in us: that all our actions should be directed according to the Gospel. And therefore, whenever we wallow in pleasures, we lose the Savior’s cross. For Christ is chastity, peace, truth, and gentleness. How, then, can a corrupt person bear witness to chastity? Or how can someone whose soul is always engaged in conflict preach peace? In what way, too, will an unstable person preserve truth or gentleness?

How, I ask, can we attain the glory of martyrdom when the Lord says: “Do not possess gold” (Matt. 10)? He says this to those who have gold. If, then, he forbids those who have gold to possess it, what punishment does he impose upon the desire of those who do not have it? And if those who retain their own possessions are ordered to give them up, how severely are those struck who seize what belongs to others?

For there are many, brothers, who, although they were born in a humble station and received no wealth from their parents, are so driven by the desire for avarice that they think themselves born for no reason unless they possess gold by some means or other. Thinking, as the prophet says (Wisdom 15), that human life has been ordered toward profit, they do not hesitate to acquire wealth from anywhere, even from evil; and thus such people, while seeking the profit of gold, find the loss of salvation.

Let us ask, brothers: how many people are there who have not been imbued with this? Very few wise people defend themselves from this plague.

If you consider the merchant, he is first in guilt because of avarice. [Note: The Martinian codex reads: “If you consider soldiers, then avarice is their cause.”] If you look only at military service, desire is entirely the reason for military service. If you examine each office individually, you will find that people are not led to service by honor, but are enticed to it as though to a business by the prospect of plunder.

Almost everyone, therefore, pursues profits and business; and when they rise at dawn, they think of nothing except how to obtain something from somewhere. If either honesty has convicted them or the authority of the judge has restrained them, when they seize the property of others they complain that they have suffered a loss.

“We serve as soldiers for no reason,” they say; “we labor for no reason. Today I was unable to bring anything home; the injustice of the judge did not allow me to do wrong.”

Avarice therefore drives almost all people and allows none of them to be at peace. Those who have nothing are tormented by desire; those who possess riches are tortured by anxiety. Nor is it well with those who lie upon their hoarded gold—indeed, it is worse for them. They are always anxious, sad, and worried that a servant may take it away or a thief dig it up. Therefore, pushing it back into darkness, they conceal it so that it may escape everyone’s knowledge, bringing nothing of it forth for use lest the opening of its hiding place become the cause of its discovery.

They preserve it but do not use it—preserve it, I say. I should therefore call such people guardians, not masters: they carefully watch over what belongs to another, rather than appropriately spending what belongs to them.

What, then, brothers, do you think? Is possessing gold the same as having riches? I would say that greater riches consist in not having gold. For the mind that despises gold is more precious than the mind that seeks gold. Clearly, greater riches consist not in having gold, but in excelling those who have gold.

For whoever abounds in his own goods does not seek the treasures of the world. One’s own goods are honor, sobriety, mercy, and chastity; all these goods are more precious than gold. Thus you may know how inferior metals are to them: talents of gold can be purchased; vessels of silver can be acquired. Honor, however, is not bought but acquired, because it is not established by a price but by virtue.

You, therefore, who possess gold, if you please, let us compare our goods with one another. When you travel abroad, your treasures necessarily remain at home. With them far away from you, you are always trembling and always uncertain lest, when you return home, you no longer have what you had. Thus, while you are always fearing their loss, in your conscience you are naked and poor.

But wherever I go, my riches follow me, and my goods cannot be separated from me, because they are kept not in an earthly cavern but in the treasure of the heart.

When you depart from the world, leaving it behind, you have lost your riches; but when it happens that I depart from this world, I carry my riches with me to paradise. After your death, fire and darkness will follow your riches, like those of that purple-clad rich man; but my riches, like those of Lazarus, will be received by the bosom of Abraham and by blessedness.

# CLASS FOUR. HOMILIES ON VARIOUS SUBJECTS

[Col. 0431]

# HOMILY LXXXIII. On the Giving of the Creed

## ADMONITION

We have already said that Saint Maximus has deserved exceptionally well of the Church because he published and propagated the purer and holier doctrines of the Christian religion not only by his voice but also through his writings. Among the many matters with which his homilies and sermons abound, the exposition of the Creed that the holy bishop wisely and elegantly provided in this homily is especially worthy of commendation.

After first listing the manuscript codices that attest to Maximus, we shall present the varying forms of the title. Three Vatican codices bear the name of Saint Maximus: namely, Vatican 1278, p. 126; Vatican 6452, p. 78; and Vatican Palatinus 432, p. 320. In addition, the name appears in Novariensis 27, p. 240; Brixiensis, p. 210; Augiensis XIV; Ratisbonensis of Saint Emmeram, p. 42; and finally Laurentianus I, Plut. XIV, p. 143.

No other manuscript book or codex has come to our attention that attributes this homily to another name. Yet I see great variation in the titles found in the codices.

In the Ratisbon codex it is designated by these words: “Homily of Saint Maximus on the giving of the Creed, concerning its exposition.” The same title appears in the Laurentian codex. The Augiensis codex has a shorter title: “Homily of Saint Maximus on the giving of the Creed”; and the Vatican Palatinus and Novariensis codices bear a similar one.

The other Vatican codex, 6452, has: “On the exposition of the Creed: a sermon of Saint Maximus the bishop.”

More elaborate is the title of Vatican Codex 1278, namely: “On the Saturday before Palm Sunday, on the giving of the Creed: a sermon of Saint Maximus the bishop concerning its exposition.” A similar inscription appears in the Brixiensis codex: “On the giving of the Creed: a sermon of the blessed Maximus the bishop before Palm Sunday.”

These inscriptions contain several points. First, the time at which the homily was delivered by the holy bishop is indicated: namely, on the Saturday before Palm Sunday, when, according to the Church’s then-current discipline, the catechumens who had been instructed and approved were to be admitted to the bath of regeneration on Holy Saturday.

Second, it is shown that throughout the period of instruction those preparing for baptism were accustomed to be given only the first documents of the faith, and were admitted to the knowledge of the more sublime and hidden mysteries once they had provided evidence of Christian perseverance.

Third, the excellent institution of the Church becomes apparent: to give the neophytes the rule of faith eight days before baptism, so that they might commit it to memory and profess it before the Church when they were initiated through baptism.

Fourth, the ecclesiastical canon of solemnly administering baptism on Holy Saturday is recalled. This custom is also observed at the vigil of Pentecost, as Saint Leo the Great wrote to the bishops of Sicily, warning them not to confer baptism at another time in a solemn rite contrary to apostolic tradition. Thus he wrote in Epistle 16, volume I, p. 715 of the Venetian edition of 1753.

Fifth, it is recognized as the duty of bishops first to form new believers through instruction, and then to wash them with the saving waters.

The distinguished Trombellius, who rendered excellent service to theological studies, teaches that this Creed, which Saint Maximus explains, is the very Creed used by the Church in that period in the administration of baptism, and that it agrees with the rule of faith transmitted by Augustine in his book On Faith and the Creed. See his Dissertation 6, On Baptism, chapter 1.

We shall not linger over listing the editors. In all of them it is the first homily of the section On Various Subjects and is attributed to Saint Maximus. Nor do we wish to press the Roman collectors, who published it among the sermons of Saint Ambrose as number 20.

[Col. 0433A] 269 ARGUMENT.—The Creed was handed down by the apostles so that the future diversity of believers—that is, the faithful—might be distinguished from the faithless. After explaining it, Maximus says that through the truth of the Creed each believer becomes a Christian, the living are sanctified, and the dead are restored to life.

When, among our fathers, as the Book of Judges relates, certain Israelite tribes were fighting one another in civil war, and because of the identical appearance of the single people no distinction could be made among the combatants, that tribe whose cause for fighting was more just, and which rightly presumed victory through God’s assistance, established for itself a certain sign in speech, so that those whom the common appearance of their arms confused might be distinguished by the sacramental sign of a more secret word [Note: [Col. 0433C] The Laurentian and Brixian codices read, “and which deservedly through God [incomplete reading].” Likewise, Vatican codices 6452 and 1278 read, “and because [it did so] deservedly through God’s assistance.” The Vallicellian codex reads, “and because [it did so] deservedly for God’s assistance.”]. Following this example, as I think, the blessed apostles handed down the mystery of the symbol to the Church of God [Note: [Col. 0433C] The Brixian codex omits “of God.”], which they had armed against the warfare of the devil’s fury [Note: [Col. 0433C] The Brixian codex reads, “which they had armed for the warfare of the devil’s fury.”], so that, since among believers there was to be a diversity under the one name of Christ, the sign of the symbol might distinguish the faithful from the faithless, and one alien to the faith and hostile to the Church might be exposed—either as one who, though baptized, had not known it, or as one who, though a heretic, had corrupted it [Note: [Col. 0433C] The Vatican codex 1278 reads, “who either as one who …,” and so forth.].

“You believe,” he says [Note: [Col. 0433C] The Laurentian codex reads, “You believe,” he says, “in God.”], “in God, the almighty Father.” Without doubt God, the almighty Father, is to be believed [Note: [Col. 0433C] The Brixian codex reads, “Without doubt the almighty Father is to be believed.”]—he whose power is perceived in such a way that his magnitude and quality remain unknown. For we attain knowledge of his being and his power not by investigation, but by believing. Our Redeemer’s authority teaches us whom we ought to believe when he says: “Whoever believes in me and in him who sent me has eternal life” (John 5); and elsewhere: “You believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14) [Note: [Col. 0433C] The Vatican codices 1278 and Vallicella read, “Believe in God,” and so forth.].

What we contemplate with the eyes of faith, brothers, is greater than what bodily sense can see. “You believe,” he says [Note: [Col. 0434C] The same codices read, “You believe,” he says, “in God.”], “in God, the almighty Father.” In God, the unbegotten nature; in the Father, the truth of the Only-Begotten; in the Almighty, the fullness of power, is revealed [Note: [Col. 0434C] The Brixian codex reads, “Therefore, the unbegotten nature.”]. For he is almighty through his innate divinity, and Father through his omnipotence; nor should one inquire how he is Father, since how God is, or how he is almighty, cannot be comprehended [Note: [Col. 0434C] The second Vallicellian codex reads, “that God is Father, because how God is almighty God cannot comprehend.”].

“And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.” That Christ was made, although he was the Son, belongs to the dispensation of human redemption; that he is Lord belongs to the propriety of his nature. He is proclaimed and believed to be unique, or the Only-Begotten, because he alone was begotten in this way and has no companion in his birth [Note: [Col. 0434C] The second Vallicellian codex, omitting *ita*, reads, “because he alone is begotten.”]. When you hear “Son,” do not suppose that he was brought forth by any sexual process; rather, believe that in incomprehensible majesty God proceeded from God, as he himself says: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world” (John 16).

“Who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.” You hear “Holy Spirit” so that you may recognize that birth as at once wondrous and blameless. For what the Spirit effects is heavenly, and what the Holy One accomplishes is inviolate [Note: [Col. 0434C] The Laurentian and Vatican 1278 codices read, “For what the Spirit effects is heavenly.”]. Since the necessity of our redemption demanded that God’s Only-Begotten become man, he introduced into his birth this privilege of his own divinity: that he should be born of a virgin. For he who came to restore the nature of human beings, grown old through sins, willed to have a new law of birth [Note: [Col. 0434C] The Vatican codices 6152 and Brixian read, “to renew nature.”]. Thus God’s Only-Begotten became the son of man, so that he who was the Creator of the world might also become its Redeemer.

“Who was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate.” Let there be no shame for us in Christ’s cross [Note: [Col. 0434C] The Vatican codices 1278, 6452, Laurentian, and the second Vallicellian read *sit* instead of *fit*.], because we have victory through his passion [Note: [Col. 0434C] The Vatican codex 6552 reads “who” instead of “because”]. For just as the eternal Son of God was born not for himself but for us, so the spotless Lamb of God suffered not for himself but for us.

Who would not recognize this as a wondrous mystery, in which the very man who is God is proclaimed, and the same Lord who is affirmed to have been crucified? Nor was what happened to him, when he was slain, unconsidered or unforeseen: by the counsel of his divinity he assumed humanity for this very reason, so that he could be killed for humanity. He chose the punishment of the cross so that a more exalted victory might be produced by a more degrading penalty; and he who suffered for the good of the universe [Note: [Col. 0435C] The Brixian codex reads, “and he who suffered for the good of the whole world.”] might, as though in the sight of the world, be lifted up on high and die [Note: [Col. 0435C] The Vatican codices 6452 and Brixian read, “lifted up, might die.”], so that those who saw the crucified man might at the same time behold the wonders of the one crucified. The sudden darkness of the sun, the trembling of the earth, the splitting of the rocks, and the resurrection of the dead sufficiently and abundantly display the glory of the one who suffered.

And how great a testimony is it that the thief, crucified alongside him, asked his fellow-sufferer that remembrance of him be made in the heavenly kingdom? Therefore, dearest ones, although Christ endured mockeries and insults, we do not lament his cross and death with sighs; rather, we celebrate them with continual praises.

“He was buried,” because it followed that he who had died should receive burial. The Lord was buried so that the earth too might receive, for the consolation of the buried, the blessing of his body. He was buried so that he who was seen to have truly died might be believed truly to have returned from the dead.

“On the third day he rose from the dead.” If you have believed concerning Christ what belongs to dishonor, believe what belongs to glory; if you have believed what belongs to death, believe what belongs to life. For just as in his passion there is the mystery of piety, so in his resurrection there is the operation of power [Note: [Col. 0435C] The Vatican codex 6452 reads, “there is the operation of power.”], as he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10). How, then, could life fail him after death, for whom dying was not a condition but a power?

It is certainly no great thing to say, “Christ was able to rise,” since it would have been impossible for the author of life not to return to life; or how could he be held by the laws of hell who died for this very reason, that death might lose its power? Let us therefore no longer be ashamed of anything concerning his sufferings, nor tremble at anything concerning his death—he who possessed both the power to rise and the nature of living.

What madness, then, is it not to believe that he rose, at whose command the buried man emerged from the tomb?

“He ascended into heaven.” It was fitting, brothers, that such glory should belong to the man who was born of a virgin; nor was it impossible for him to ascend into heaven, for whom it was possible to triumph over the underworld. And it was necessary that he who had come from the kingdom to death should return after death to the kingdom.

In this, dearest ones, there was a saving and incomprehensible communion between heaven and earth: just as the earth rejoiced that it had received the Son of God, so heaven rejoiced that it had received the Son of Man, as was sung through the prophet: “Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult” (Psalm 95). For just as it is clear that the earth exults because of God, so there is no doubt that heaven rejoices because of man.

“He sits at the right hand of the Father.” That Christ sits is the gift of victory [Note: [Col. 0435C] The same Vatican codices 6452, the second Vallicellian, and the Brixian read, “is the gift of victory.”]; that he sits at the right hand of the Father is the privilege of divinity and a sharing in undivided love [Col. 0436B]. And rightly is he proclaimed to sit at the Father’s right hand, in whom the devil, who is wholly left-handed, found nothing of his own will [Note: [Col. 0436C] The same Vatican codex reads, “nothing of pleasure.”].

“From there he will come to judge the living and the dead” [Note: [Col. 0436C] The same Vatican codex 6452 reads, “From there he will come to judge.”]. It is necessary, brothers, that he who created the human race should examine it, and that he who redeemed it should himself judge it. It is just that the almighty Lord should distinguish his mortals—whom he formed by the power of his divinity and saved by the Father’s mercy—by the examination of a judge. For what could be more equitable before God than that those whose lives in this world were different should, after this world, have their merits distinguished?

“The living and the dead” are mentioned as those to be judged, so that it may be believed that God cares for all human beings [Note: [Col. 0436C] Vatican codex 1278 reads, “But from there the living and the dead are referred to be judged.”].

“And in the Holy Spirit.” This is, dearest ones, the unimpaired rule of truth [Note: [Col. 0436C] Vatican codex 1278 reads, “This is, dearest ones, the unimpaired rule, the truth, that …”]: since they have one name, their confession should not be different, and those who in heaven are one in themselves should not be separated by us on earth.
