For just as nothing created can be made equal to divinity, so the nature of divinity excludes every division and inequality [Note: [Col. 0436C] Vatican codex 1278 reads, “excluded.”].

[Note: [Col. 0435D] According to evangelical truth, just as the Son came forth from the Father, so also the Spirit proceeds from the Father; and just as the Only-Begotten is the Son of God, so also the Holy Spirit is of God. And just as the Father reveals to whomever he wills, so the Spirit too is read to inspire as he wills and to distribute the gifts of heavenly graces as he wills.

Before I begin the exposition of the article concerning the Holy Spirit, I think it best to point out that Maximus is explaining in this homily the apostles’ creed, which all Christ’s faithful are bound to know as the rule of faith; and he calls it the sign by which Christians are distinguished from unbelievers. In the Apostles’ Creed, therefore, and in the Nicene Creed, it is simply said: “I believe in the Holy Spirit.” Maximus’s sole aim was to demonstrate that the divinity of the Holy Spirit must be believed, and he establishes this by three arguments.

First, he derives it from origin, by which the Spirit is equal to the Son; therefore he says: “Just as the Son came forth from the Father, so the Spirit proceeds from the Father.” Since the Son came forth from the Father from eternity, the procession of the Spirit from the Father is likewise eternal. And just as, in the Son of God, the eternity of his existence demonstrates identity of nature with the Father, and the generation of the Son from the Father himself implies that he was begotten from the Father’s substance, so, if the Spirit proceeded from the Father from eternity, he could not have proceeded from him without possessing the same nature and substance.

In second place Maximus says: “And just as the Only-Begotten is the Son of God, so also the Holy Spirit is of God.” By this he wished to signify that, just as the Only-Begotten of God the Father cannot be, by virtue of generation, anything other than God—for, as Saint Basil teaches, the Father, by understanding himself, produces the Word, and the Son is the terminus of the paternal intellection, of the same nature and substance—so likewise the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from love and is the terminus of divine love, is the Spirit of God and possesses everything that belongs to God.

Maximus confirms this truth all the more strongly by arguing it, third, from the equality of power operating similarly in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. “And just as the Father has mercy on whom he wills, and the Son reveals the Father to whom he wills, so also the Spirit is read both to inspire as he wills and to distribute the gifts of heavenly graces as he wills.”

Whenever, therefore, we confess in the Holy Spirit the complete power to bestow his gifts—gifts of grace and sanctification—no less than the revelation of divine mysteries is attributed to the Son, and the inexhaustible fountain of mercy is said to flow from the Father, it is clear that the Holy Spirit is God, as the Son is God and the Father is God—not, however, three gods, but one God.

No one will be surprised that Maximus said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and did not add that he also proceeds from the Son. In this he acted together with the other Fathers who opposed those heretics who made the Holy Spirit inferior to the Son; for Eunomius taught that the Spirit proceeds at the Father’s command, through the Son’s operation and power. At that time, therefore, Catholic teaching was chiefly concerned with the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father, and the Church did not require an explicit confession that he also proceeds from the Son; it was enough for her that all should believe and worship the Holy Spirit as true God.

Later, however, when from the ashes of Macedonius and Nestorius the Greeks revived the error by which they denied that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, the Church judged it necessary to condemn the heresy that had arisen, and to confess his procession from both the Father and the Son. This confession was first accepted in Spain, where several councils were held for this reason and the phrase *Filioque* was added to the creed. Three further synods—the Council of Gentilly, the Council of Friuli, and the Council of Aachen—approved it while condemning the heresy of the Greeks.

The definition and addition of these councils were confirmed, after the ecumenical Council of Lyons, with greater solemnity and with a larger attendance of Fathers, both Latin and Greek, by the ecumenical Council of Florence under Pope Eugene IV. At that council, in the presence of the emperor John Palaeologus, John of Montenegro, Andrew of Rhodes, John of Torquemada of the Dominican order, and Julian Cesarini, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, argued from the authority of Scripture and the tradition of the Fathers concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son with such force of eloquence that they not only dissolved but completely crushed the sophisms of Mark of Ephesus.

There is no need for me here to collect the testimonies by which this orthodox dogma can be demonstrated and proved. Nicephorus Blemmidas, John Beccus, George the Protosyncellus, George of Trebizond, John Ploussiadenus, and others had already discharged this task with distinction; Leo Allatius gathered their works in his *Orthodox Greece*. Emmanuel Calecas of the Order of Preachers, Bessarion, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and, in more recent times, Dionysius Petavius in Book VII of *On the Trinity*, Leo Allatius in the treatise he wrote in the vernacular Greek on the Procession of the Holy Spirit, and in his *Vindications of the Council of Ephesus and of Cyril*, and Michael Le Quien of the Order of Preachers in his *Panoplia* against Nectarius, patriarch of Jerusalem, also treated this subject with distinction. To pass over the others, Louis Vallaeus, prefect of the library of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris, treated it in a very learned dissertation which he composed and published at Paris in 1722.

I shall now discuss, as briefly as I can, the teaching of Saint Maximus on this dogma. He mentions the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father, but does not explicitly mention it from the Son. Nor was it necessary for him to make an explicit mention of this when transmitting the creed, since at that time no controversy had been raised by innovators against the Catholic dogma, and especially in the West there was one common teaching among all concerning the Holy Spirit’s procession from the Son as well.

Indeed, if Saint Augustine, apart from the treatise *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 8, no. 19 and following, volume VI of the Antwerp edition of his works, 1700, page 117 and following; and *Sermon 1 on the Tradition of the Creed*, no. 1, volume V, page 652; and *Sermon 3*, no. 6, page 655; and *Sermon 3*, no. 10, page 660—where he speaks exactly as Maximus does, mentioning the Spirit proceeding from the Father while omitting an explicit mention of that same Spirit’s procession from the Son—if, I say, apart from those treatises he had written no others concerning the Trinity, and someone had therefore concluded that Augustine did not grant the Spirit’s procession from the Son, that conclusion would have been gravely mistaken. For although he does not mention that procession from the Son in the works just cited, he nevertheless actually believed that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son, as is clear from Book II against Maximinus, chapter 14, page 498, volume VIII, and from Book XV of his *On the Trinity*, chapter 27, no. 48, in the same edition. Therefore, if Maximus had published a treatise on the Trinity and had encountered this question in it, I do not doubt that he would have affirmed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Moreover, what Maximus writes in this homily about one name, one confession, and the equality of the divine persons, when speaking of the Holy Spirit, is so arranged that it seems to be a kind of epitome of the Ambrosian books on the Holy Spirit. See Ambrose, Book I, chapter 13 and following; Book II, chapter 2 and following; and Book III, chapter 4 and following. If he passed over the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, what was silent in words is expressed in faith, as Ambrose likewise observes in another connection, in the same work, Book I, chapter 3, no. 43, page 13, volume IV of his works, Venetian edition, 1751. Otherwise, it would also remain to charge the Fathers of the First Ecumenical Council of Constantinople with denying the procession from the Son because, when they mentioned the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father in the creed, they omitted *τὴν* [“the”] procession from the Son (compare volume I of the Councils, under the year 381, page 814, Paris edition, 1714). What could be more unjust than that?]

According to evangelical truth, just as the Son came forth from the Father, so also the Spirit proceeds from the Father [Note: [Col. 0437B] Vatican codices 1278 and 6452, and the Laurentian codex, read, “and just as the Only-Begotten is the Son of God.”]; and just as the Only-Begotten is the Son of God, so also the Holy Spirit is of God; and just as the Father has mercy on whom he wills, and the Son reveals the Father to whom he wills, so also the Spirit is read both to inspire as he wills and to distribute the gifts of heavenly graces as he wills. How, then, should the Spirit not be believed to be one with the Father and the Son, when the power to do what he wills belongs to him equally?

“The holy Church.” The Church must truly be confessed as holy, through which sanctification has been given to mortals, and, as the number of believers grows, the world, made holier in almost every tongue, exults in the praises of God. Holy is the Church which, having cleansed away the contagion of sins through the sacrament of baptism, transfers the inhabitants of the earth to heaven.

“The forgiveness of sins.” Above all, brothers, the forgiveness of sins must be believed, because this alone is the remedy that releases the human race from the sentence of perpetual death. Therefore the Only-Begotten of the Most High deigned to assume flesh [Note: [Col. 0437B] Vatican codex 1278 reads, “he embraced the cross.”], he embraced the cross, so that you, who could not escape your crimes and sins, might be made innocent by pardon. Therefore the spotless Lamb was slain, so that by his blood the stain of the human race might be wiped away.

See, brothers, the depth of the mystery; see the height of the sacrament: here death restored life, and the filth of sinners was washed away by the blood of the innocent. This forgiveness does not nourish you toward sin; rather, it admonishes you now to fear sin, since you understand that you could not have been saved without pardon [Note: [Col. 0437B] The Brixian codex reads, “could not be saved without pardon.”]. For the goodness of God, through the gift of his indulgence [Note: [Col. 0438B] The Vatican codex 6452 omits “of God.”], does not arm us for guilt, but washes us clean for glory [Note: [Col. 0438B] The Vatican, second Vallicellian, and Brixian codices read, “but absolves us for glory.”].

“The resurrection of the flesh.” This is the end of our religion; this is the sum of belief. And indeed, who could believe in God and doubt the resurrection, since it is evident that this alone was Christ’s reason for being born? For what other reason or benefit was there for the Eternal One to deign to assume flesh, unless it was to grant perpetuity to flesh [Note: [Col. 0439A] Vatican codex 1278 reads, “so that he might grant perpetuity to flesh.”]? What glory would there be in the Son of God not refusing the cross, seeking death, and enduring burial, unless by his resurrection he bestowed life upon mortals? The divinity makes faith in this possible, for to it everything it wills is possible.

Finally, to take examples of resurrection beyond doubt, the world itself, losing and recovering the form of its beauty, both dies and rises again. We receive a proof of the future resurrection when the grain entrusted to the furrows returns to its stalk, and when the woods stripped by frost revive with renewed leaves; everything also that the earth produces is multiplied and restored either by seed [Note: [Col. 0439A] Vatican codex 6452 reads, “either in seed,”] or by root. What hardness of heart, then, is it not to believe that man can be restored, when the things that were made are restored [Note: [Col. 0439A] Vatican codices 1278 and the second Vallicellian read, “when all things that were made …”]?

This, dearest ones, is the symbol, whose truth makes each believer a Christian; this is the symbol whose sign, as was said at the beginning, distinguishes the faithful from unbelievers [Note: [Col. 0439A] The Laurentian codex reads, “This is, dearest ones, the symbol by whose sign …” [Col. 0440A] The Vatican codices 1178 and the second Vallicellian also supply “truly at the beginning.”]. This is the symbol which sanctifies the living and restores the dead to life.

# HOMILY LXXXIV

Begins the preface concerning the body of Christ.

[Col. 0439]

## ADMONITION

Before the preface of this homily was brought forth from the Saint Gall manuscript and published by Mabillon, it had already been published by Gymnicus and by later editors together with the homily entitled *On the Cross and Burial of the Lord*—that portion which begins with the words, “Let us examine this very body of the Lord,” and ends with these others: “This has speedily raised up the salvation of all.” Gymnicus himself and other collectors then constituted another homily, distinguished by a different title, *On the Passion and Burial of the Lord*, whose beginning is: “Perhaps someone may say concerning the preaching of the preceding Sunday,” and whose ending is: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?”

But we have discovered from four manuscripts of the highest quality—that is, Vatican 6452, the Lateran manuscript, and two Casinensian manuscripts—that all the scribes and editors were mistaken: these manuscripts make one homily out of the two portions just mentioned. We have been confirmed still more in this judgment by the same homily to which the other portion is attached, since the whole of it concerns the Lord’s cross, while the fragment added to it is plainly extraneous. If, however, the beginning of the homily *On the Passion and Burial of the Lord* is removed, up to the words “The womb brought forth,” we obtain a clear connection with the preceding homily, in which the comparison was begun between the Virgin’s womb and the tomb that received the body of the Lord Christ.

Nor is it something new, as we have already said elsewhere, that the ancient monks, who preserved the precious writings of the Fathers from the wreck of antiquity, made two or three readings out of a single homily or sermon, adding certain material for their own use.

Once these matters have been brought to light, it must be investigated whether the first part of this homily, which is presented under the following title in the Saint Gall manuscript—“Begins the preface concerning the body of Christ”—belongs with it and is, as it were, its head. We therefore say that this opening seems to have been taken by Maximus from the circumstances of place and time, and that it suits an address delivered in an assembly of bishops, whom the presiding bishop had previously addressed, as was customary.

Maximus himself, after first commending the speech of the presiding bishop and mentioning its subject, begins to organize his own discourse on the burial of Christ’s body: “Let us therefore examine what happens to the Lord’s body after it is taken down from the cross.”

Mabillon brought to light only the preface and the portion of the homily beginning “Let us examine” [Col. 0441A] and ending “This has speedily raised up the salvation of all,” although the other portion of the Saint Gall manuscript—“Perhaps someone may say,” and so forth—which in his own work appears under the title *On the Tomb of Christ*, was known in all editions.

We publish the homily in full. We consider it highly probable that Maximus delivered it at the Council of Milan under Saint Eusebius. Having vindicated the integrity of this homily, we undertake to vindicate the holy bishop of Turin from the manuscripts that attributed it to Saints Ambrose, Augustine, and Gregory the Great.

Three manuscripts have come before us that attribute the same homily to Ambrose: Vatican 6452, Laurentian X Plut. XIV, and manuscript 1 of the left-hand section, formerly of Santa Croce Minor and now in the Laurentian Library. But since the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, in their preface to the sermons of Saint Ambrose, volume II, Paris edition, 1690, citing the testimony of Gennadius, by which it is established that Maximus wrote on the tomb of Christ, judged the homily dealing with that subject to be Maximian, these manuscripts cause us no difficulty.

The Benedictine monks themselves, when they transferred the same homily to the appendix of Saint Augustine’s sermons, no. 248, page 288, Antwerp edition, 1700, and declared that opinion about it had varied, said that they were more inclined to attribute it to Maximus than to the other Fathers. We therefore think that the authority of the opposing manuscripts, in which Augustine’s name is read, has been overturned.

That it is attributed to Saint Gregory the Great in Vatican codex 1270, folio 31 verso, is plainly a scribe’s error: in no manuscripts, nor in any printed books, has anyone else imagined Gregory the Great to be the author of this homily.

But lest we seem to be playing with conjectures in a matter of such importance, four highly authoritative manuscripts are available to us, whose testimony converges on Maximus.

The first is the Turin manuscript, which divides the homily into two discourses: it makes the first the one beginning “Perhaps someone may say,” and begins the second with the words “Yesterday, [there was] enough joy,” and so forth, with the title *On the Tomb of the Lord* in the first and *Likewise, on the same subject* in the second—this order having been reversed through the scribe’s negligence.

The second manuscript is the Saint Gall manuscript, homily 68, bearing the title “Preface concerning the body of Christ.”

The third is manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, no. 51, which has the first part of the homily under the title *On the Body of Christ*, and the second under the title *On the Tomb of the Lord Savior*.

Finally, the fourth is the Lateran manuscript, page 212, which, under the heading *On the Body of Christ*, adds: “A sermon of Saint Maximus, bishop,” and begins: “Let us examine the Lord’s body,” and so forth.

Since, therefore, this homily rests upon these principal testimonies, and since Mabillon, Ceillier in volume XIV of his *History*, and the Benedictine monks in their editions of the works of Ambrose and Augustine have given judgment in its favor, we have acted justly in vindicating it for Saint Maximus.

[Col. 0441A] 279 **ARGUMENT.**—Saint Maximus praises most highly Joseph of Arimathea, who prepared a tomb for Christ, and explains several mystical statements concerning that same tomb; finally, he discusses Mary Magdalene, who anxiously sought the Lord in the tomb.

I believe, dearest brothers, that yesterday you received ample joy from the discourses of the present bishop, our lord and brother, who discussed divine matters with such eloquence that his preaching was full of priestly grace, an orator’s eloquence, and a teacher’s instruction. [Note: Codex S. Crucis in Jerusalem corrects Gallandius’s text, which reads “our Father.” Since this homily was delivered at the Council of Milan to bishops, the bishop ought to have been addressed as “brother,” as we noted in the preface.] It is no wonder that he who holds primacy of honor in the episcopate should also possess primacy of eloquence in preaching, commending the virtues of God, which he draws forth from the hidden treasury of his holy heart, through the discourse of fluent speech.

And therefore I know that my own humble offering will please your ears less than usual. [Col. 0441B] For who is content to drink from a stream when he can draw water from springs? [Note: Codex S. Crucis in Jerusalem here gives a more correct form of Gallandius’s passage, which reads: “For who would be content to drink from a stream when he could draw from springs?”] The earth does not receive even a light dew of water after a copious rainstorm has drenched it. So, then, your affection, inundated by the eloquence of the holy priest, will not endure the cheap tedium of my discourse. For however learned or eloquent an orator may be, he will appear speechless if he begins to speak in the presence of someone better.

Nevertheless, this confusion has its consolation. There is no shame in a lesser priest displeasing in comparison with a supreme priest, especially [Col. 0442A] since the distinguished company of the blessed can help me. For if David openly declares that, through the company of one saint, another can become holy, saying, “With the holy you will be holy” (Ps. XVII), [Note: From Codex S. Crucis in Jerusalem, Gallandius’s text appears incomplete, where it reads: “Why, then, cannot I, although inexperienced and sinful, become a preacher by the power of the Lord?”] who, then, would not think that I, although inexperienced and sinful, could become a preacher through the power of the Lord, in the company of so many—280—teachers?

Since, therefore, our most blessed brother has praised the holy apostles with great eloquence, we too ought to preach the Lord’s burial, so that, because we appear to be members of one body cared for by similar services, the whole body may likewise be adorned by similar preaching.

Let us therefore see what was done with the Lord’s body after it was taken down from the cross. [Note: Codices Casinenses 47 and 108: “after it had been laid down, what happened?” “He received it,” and so forth.] Joseph of Arimathea, a just man, received it, as the Evangelist says, and buried it in his own new tomb, in which no one had yet been placed. [Note: Codex Lateranensis: “and buried it.”] [Note: Vatican, Casinensis, and Lateranensis codices: “had been,” instead of “was.”]

Blessed, therefore, is the body of the Lord Christ: when it is born, it is brought forth from a virgin’s womb; when it departs, it is entrusted to the tomb of a just man. [Note: Codex Lateranensis: “and when it departs.”] Blessed indeed is the body that virginity bore and justice guarded. [Note: Codex S. Crucis in Jerusalem corrects an error in Gallandius’s printed edition, which reads: “the body that virginity found.”] Joseph’s tomb preserved it incorrupt, just as Mary’s womb kept it undefiled. [Note: Vatican Codex 6452 has “for it” instead of “it”; the Lateranensis has: “For he guarded it, just as she preserved it”; Vatican Codex 6452: “For just as it is not touched by pollution, so it is not affected by the corruption of death,” and so forth.] Here it is not touched by the pollution of a man; there it is not harmed by the corruption of death. [Note: Codex Lateranensis omits the word “man.”] A new womb conceived it. [Note: Codices S. Crucis in Jerusalem, Vatican 6452, 1270, and Casinensis.] Thus both the Lord’s birth and his burial are virginal; indeed, I should call the burial itself a womb, for the likeness is considerable. For just as the Lord came forth alive from his mother’s womb, so he rose alive from Joseph’s burial place. And just as then he was born from the womb to preach, so now he was reborn from the tomb to proclaim the Gospel.

Except that this birth is more glorious than that one. The former brought forth a mortal body; this one produced an immortal body. After the former birth, he descended to the underworld; after this one, he returned to heaven. [Note: Codex Casinensis 108: “He descended to the underworld; after this one he returned to heaven.”] This birth is plainly more sacred than that one. The former kept the Lord of the whole world enclosed in the womb for nine months; this one guarded him in the bosom of the tomb for only three days. [Note: Codices Casinensis 108 and Vatican 1270: “for three days.”] The former brought forth the hope of all more slowly; this one raised the salvation of all more quickly.

[Note: In all the editors, this homily bears the title “On the Passion and Burial of the Lord,” and begins as follows: “Perhaps someone might say this concerning the preaching of the preceding Sunday, in which we proclaimed that the glory was no less in the fact that Joseph’s tomb raised the Lord than in the fact that holy Mary’s womb brought him forth.”]

What comparison can there be between a womb and a tomb, when the former brought forth a son from the innermost parts of the body, while the latter merely provided a place for burial? [Note: “But I say that Joseph’s affection was no less than Mary’s,” and so forth. Here Maximus undertakes to adorn Joseph of Arimathea’s love for the Lord Christ and seems to compare it with the love of the Virgin Mary. Yet, if what he praises in Joseph is carefully considered, Maximus’s intention becomes clear: he praises Joseph for the final services he performed for Jesus, providing a worthy burial for him after his death and laying him in his own new tomb. Similar things are said to have been provided by Mary for the Son of God at his birth in human form. She gave the Savior blood, life, and bodily members in her most pure womb, and nourished and cared for his infancy. Thus the beginning of love and its end are similar in both, but the intention and extent of the love are not equal. For the love of God is more perfect in proportion as the soul is purer and holier; and when hearts are kindled by that fire from God himself, the flame is more intense in proportion as the disposition to receive it is greater. Joseph, therefore, is praiseworthy because he omitted nothing in order to show honor and reverence to the Redeemer; but Mary is more venerable because she brought the Savior into the world and had no equal in loving him.]

But I say that Joseph’s affection was no less than Mary’s. For she conceived the Lord in her womb, while he conceived him in his heart. [Note: Vatican Codex 1270 and Casinensis have “conceived.”] She provided the Savior with the hidden place of her limbs, while he did not refuse the hidden place of his own body. She wrapped the Lord in cloths when he was born; he wrapped him in linen when he departed. She anointed the blessed body with oil; he honored it with spices.

Their services, therefore, correspond, and their affection corresponds; hence their merit must also correspond—except that an angel admonished Mary to perform her service, whereas justice alone persuaded Joseph. Joseph placed the Lord in his own tomb.

We read in the prophet: “Their throat is an open tomb” (Ps. V). If, then, the throat of human beings is an open tomb, see whether, according to this likeness, Joseph placed the Lord not so much in an earthly burial place as in the monument of his own heart, and received him to be guarded not by the fragile memory of the elements but by the holy memory of virtues. [Note: Codices S. Crucis in Jerusalem and S. Crucis Minor in the Laurentian Library: “For this is the faithful memory of virtues.”]

This is the faithful memory of virtues: containing Christ within itself, it does not allow him to be harmed by the corruption of heretics. Concerning this memory the Lord says in the sacred writings: “Whenever you do this, you will do it in memory of me, until I come” (Luke XXII). For whenever we speak of Christ, we commend him to the memory of the sacred mouth. [Note: Codex Lateranensis: “to the memory.”]

“ Their throat is an open tomb.” [Note: Codices 90 of S. Crucis in Jerusalem and Lateranensis: “the throat of human beings.” “Which he rightly and plainly says,” and so forth.] The prophet rightly and plainly says this. For the tomb of Christ is the blessed open throat of the Evangelists, through which they placed him in the eternal treasury of the written word.

The tomb is called open because whoever wishes to reach the mystery of Christ does not enter it except through the hidden meaning of the Gospel Scripture. [Note: Codex Lateranensis: “except through the secrets of the evangelical Scriptures.”] For the Lord must be entrusted to the sacred writings as though to a kind of new vessel. [Note: Codex 1270 of the Vatican: “For in the mystery of the sacred writings”; Codex 90 of S. Crucis in Jerusalem: “For in the treasury of the writings.” Codices S. Crucis Minor and S. Crucis in Jerusalem: “The Lord was entrusted to a new vessel.”] Whoever, therefore, desires to see him finds there the sacrament of his Passion and recognizes the glory of his Resurrection. [Note: Codex S. Crucis Minor: “will find the sacrament there and recognize the glory of the Resurrection.”]

The throat of the saints is open; hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians” (1 Cor. VI), inviting them to enter through the ever-open door of his preaching into the secret mysteries of Christ. [Note: Codex Casinensis: “into the mysteries of Christ.”]

Joseph therefore places the Lord in this memory of the heart, [Note: Codex S. Crucis Minor: “so that the seat of justice may rest there.”] so that he may rest in the seat of justice and the Son of Man may have somewhere to lay his head.

Let us therefore see why the Savior is placed in another’s burial place and does not have one of his own. He is placed in another’s burial place because he was dying for the salvation of others. For this death was not inflicted upon him but transferred to us; this death did not befall him but benefits us. [Note: Codex S. Crucis Minor: “Death did not happen to him; it was rather sleep. For death was inflicted upon him, but transferred to us”; Codex 99 of S. Crucis in Jerusalem: “For this death was not inflicted upon him but transferred to us”; Codex Casinensis 108: “but offered to us.”]

Why, then, should he have a burial place of his own, who did not have a death of his own? Why should he have a tomb on earth whose dwelling remained in heaven? Why should he have a burial, who, for only three days, did not so much lie dead in the tomb as rest there like one sleeping on a bed? [Note: Codex Lateranensis: “who, for only three days, resting not so much dead in the tomb as lying in a bed, rested.”] The brevity of the time itself shows that it was sleep rather than death. [Note: Vatican Codex 6452: “rather sleep.”]

A tomb is the necessary dwelling place of death. Therefore Christ, who is life, did not need the dwelling place of death, nor did he, who is always living, need the dwelling place of the dead. Yet rightly did we place this life in our tomb, so that, when he makes our death alive, we might rise from the dead together with him. [Note: Codex S. Crucis in Jerusalem: “so that, when he makes our death alive, we might rise from the dead together with him.”]

Hence that Mary Magdalene, who was seeking the Lord among the other dead in the tomb, is rebuked and told: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” (Luke XXIV). That is: why do you seek among the dead one whom it is already certain has returned to the living? [Note: Codex II of S. Crucis Minor: “That is: why do you seek in the tomb the one whom you ought to adore in heaven? Why do you seek among the dead,” and so forth.] She, still not understanding or recognizing him, replied: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him.” [Note: Codex Lateranensis: “since she still did not understand or recognize this.”]

For she thought, as Scripture says, that he was the gardener. Thus the holy and simple woman was seeking Christ from Christ; and, by the devotion of her mind, she prophesied without knowing it. For she says to the Lord concerning himself: “If you have taken him away, tell me.” [Note: Codex Lateranensis: “and she does not know it.” After this, the homily does not proceed further in the Lateran Homiliary; a note in the margin states: “A portion of the sermon is missing.”] [Note: Vatican Codex 1270 and Casinensis have “taken him up” instead of “taken him away.”]

She asks correctly: “If you have taken him away.” For he himself took up his body, who raised it; he himself took up the body who brought it forth from the tomb; he himself took up the body who gathered it, lying and sleeping, by his own breath; he himself took up the body who, carrying it by the power of his divinity, bears it to heaven. [Note: Vatican Codex 1270 and Casinensis: “who carried it.”]

And therefore the woman wisely asks and inquires: “If you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him.” That is: if, taking him from the tomb, you have transferred him to paradise. For she had heard him say to the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII).

Or certainly, you have placed him from the lower regions at the Father’s right hand, as the Apostle says: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is at the right hand of God” (Col. III). [Note: Codex Casinensis 108: “sitting at the right hand of God.”]

Blessed, therefore, is the person who seeks the Lord Christ in such a way as to believe that he has been established both in paradise and in the heavenly places. For whoever seeks him either among the dead or in tombs is told: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?”

## HOMILY LXXXV. On the text written: “Who do you think is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” (Matt. XVIII)

[Col. 0445]

### NOTICE

There is no need to refute those who have judged that this homily should be taken away from St. Maximus and attributed to St. Ambrose. Their opinion is refuted and overthrown both by the authority and abundance of ancient manuscript codices and by considerations of style. The title attached to this homily in the printed books does, however, call for investigation; it runs as follows: “On the feast of the holy archangel Michael, on the text written,” and so forth. First, the older codices must be reviewed. They entirely lack any mention of that feast, and prefix to the homily the passage from Matthew, chapter XVIII, though not in identical words. The codices of S. Crucis in Jerusalem, no. 90, homily 47, and no. 99, sermon 10, read: “Begins: on the text written: ‘Who do you think is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?’” The St Gall codex, homily 44: “On the text written: ‘Who do you think is greatest,’” and so forth. The Vercelli codex 81: “Homily of blessed Maximus, bishop, on the Gospel of Matthew: ‘The disciples came to Jesus, saying: Who do you think is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?’” Vatican codices 6490, p. 190, and Palatine 477, p. 187, as well as Vallicellianus XV, p. 113, have similar headings: “On the Gospel of Matthew: ‘Who do you think is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?’ Sermon of blessed Maximus, bishop.” The Casanatensian codex of homilies, part 1, agrees with these; codex XII of S. Crucis in Jerusalem differs little, adding: “A sermon on ferial days of St. Maximus, bishop of Turin, on that passage of the Gospel of Matthew: ‘At that time the disciples came to Jesus, saying: Who do you think is greatest?’” and so forth. Many other codices, however, copied in a later age, contain a commemoration of the feast or dedication of the holy archangel Michael. Among them are codex Lucensis 89: “At the dedication of St. Michael the archangel, a homily of St. Maximus, bishop”; Casinensis 102, p. 136 verso; Ratisbon, St. Emmeram; and two Laurentian codices, 36 and 43, Plut. XVII: “On the feast of the holy archangel Michael: on the text written, ‘Who do you think is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?’” and so forth. Codex Augiensis XV also differs in its title, having only “On the feast of the holy angel,” as does the Cistercian codex of Monte Amiata, at the head of which is read: “On the feast of St. Michael the archangel. In the Gospel: ‘The disciples came to Jesus, saying,’ and so forth: ‘Who do you think is greatest?’ and so forth. Homily of the same blessed Maximus, bishop.” Since the apparition of St. Michael the archangel on Mount Gargano occurred in the time of St. Gelasius I, Roman pontiff from 492 to 496, and since the dedication of his first basilica at Rome in the Circus Maximus by Boniface II was even later than the death of St. Maximus, it is entirely clear that this homily could not have been delivered by the holy bishop of Turin on the feast of St. Michael the archangel, when that feast had not yet been instituted in the Church. Unskilled copyists attached that title to Maximus’s homily because of the Gospel of Matthew read on that day. Leaving aside the editors who did not guard against so manifest an error, we have more correctly transferred it among the homilies on miscellaneous subjects.

[Col. 0455C] 284 **SUBJECT.**—St. Maximus writes much that is distinguished about the virtue of humility and the sin of causing scandal; by “little ones” he means not children in age, but suitable clerics, devout monks, or laypeople.

If you have listened attentively to the Gospel reading, you can understand what reverence is due to the ministers and priests of God, and also how clerics themselves ought to anticipate one another in humble attentiveness. [Note: Vatican Codex 6450: “because to the ministers.” Both codices of S. Crucis in Jerusalem: “ought to anticipate one another in humility. For he says.”] For when the disciples asked which of them would be greater in the kingdom of heaven, the Lord set a little child before them all and said: “Whoever humbles himself like this child will be greater in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII). From this we understand that one reaches the kingdom by humility and enters heaven by simplicity. [Note: Codex Casinensis reads “heaven,” omitting “one enters … the kingdom,” and so forth.] Whoever, therefore, wishes to attain the heights of the Godhead should pursue the lowliness of humility. Whoever wishes to outstrip a brother in reigning should first outstrip him in serving, as the Apostle says: “Anticipating one another in honor” (Rom. XII). Let him overcome him in services, that he may be able to overcome him in holiness.

For if your brother has not injured you, he deserves your service, so that you may love him; but if he has perhaps injured you, he deserves service all the more, so that you may overcome him. [Note: Vatican Codex 6450: “If a brother’s service has not injured you, he deserves that you should overcome. Both codices of S. Crucis in Jerusalem read: ‘he deserves that you should love’; if he has perhaps injured you, he deserves service all the more, that you may overcome.” Vallicellianus 15 has the same reading, and then “For this is,” and so forth.] For this is the sum of our Christianity: to return affection to those who love us, and patience to those who injure us. [Note: Vatican Codex 6450: “weigh out.”] Whoever, then, is more patient under injury will be made more powerful in the kingdom. One does not reach the dominion of heaven by pride, riches, or office, but by humility, poverty, and gentleness.

For narrow and strait is the way that leads to the kingdom (Matt. VII). [Note: Both codices read: “But narrow.” Codex Vallicellianus 15: “to life” instead of “to the kingdom.”] Whoever is puffed up by honors and enlarged by treasures of gold will be unable to pass through the narrow path of the kingdom, like a beast weighed down and impeded. Indeed, when he thinks he has arrived, since the narrow gate cannot contain his burden, he will be driven back from the threshold and compelled to go away again. [Note: Both codices of S. Crucis in Jerusalem read: “driven back from the threshold, he is compelled to return.” Vatican Codex 6450 reads: “checked at the threshold.”] For the gate of heaven is as narrow to a rich man as the tiny eye of a needle is to a camel. Hence the Lord says: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX). Just as a camel, a crooked and misshapen animal, is not permitted to pass through a tiny opening, [Note: Codex 99 of S. Crucis in Jerusalem: “the tiny cavity of a needle.”] so the narrow gate of heaven does not at all permit an avaricious and deceitful rich man to enter.

For this reason we are born naked into the world, we also approach the font naked, [Note: The cited codex of S. Crucis in Jerusalem reads: “that naked … we may hasten.”] and naked and unencumbered we hasten to heaven’s gate. How incongruous and absurd it is that one whom his mother bore naked, whom the Church receives naked, should wish to enter heaven rich! Therefore the Savior says in the Gospel to that rich young man: [Note: Vatican Codex 6150: “to the rich young man.” Both codices of S. Crucis in Jerusalem have: “it is said to him, who seemed to himself righteous and holy and to have fulfilled all the commandments of the Law.”] “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor.” [Note: Vallicellianus 15: “Go, sell,” and so forth. The same codices of S. Crucis in Jerusalem add: “and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.”] So wholly fitted for heaven is virtue stripped bare that, however righteous and holy one may be, if one possesses gold or riches, one cannot be perfect.

For the Lord wished that young man to return to paradise such as Adam had been when he was cast down from paradise’s height. Adam, indeed, was a naked inhabitant of paradise; finally, after sin, perceiving his nakedness, he covered his shame with a leaf. [Note: Vatican Codex 6450: “foreseeing his nakedness.” Vallicellianus: “his private parts with leaves.”] Before he sinned, he was clothed in the brightness of honor; thus it was not nature that made nakedness shameful, but the guilt of sin that discovered it. Are the holy angels, too, who are established in the most splendid attire, clothed with tunics and cloaks? Yet, though the naked substance of their own nature is in them, they appear clothed because they are holy. Thus Adam also, preserving the dignity of angelic honor, was naked indeed of worldly garments, but clothed in the splendor of immortality.

His eyes then looked upon nothing evil; his heart conceived nothing shameful; among honorable minds nakedness itself was clothed. [Note: Both cited codices: “Nothing evil then.”] For just as, among wicked people, a shameful thought is not kept from lust by clothing, so, among holy persons, honorable simplicity is not drawn by nakedness into lust. But as all things are naked for corruption to the vicious, so all things are covered for chastity to the devout.

But what does the Gospel reading say? “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it is expedient for him that a millstone turned by an ass be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matt. XVIII). [Note: Vallicellianus 15 and Casinensis 102: “and be submerged.”] By “little ones” he means here not children in age, but those little in malice, as the Apostle says: “Be little children in malice, but be perfect in understanding” (1 Cor. XIV, 20). [Note: After these words of Scripture the Vallicellian codex ends.] Who are these but suitable clerics, devout monks, or laypeople? Whoever, then, proves irreverent or insulting toward them will be punished by this beastly penalty: with a shapeless stone tied to his neck, he will be hurled into the sea.

But let us see why this penalty was decreed for those who cause Christians to stumble, [Note: Codex Casinensis: “those causing Christians to stumble,” and so forth.] or what this sentence itself means; for I think it contains some mystery. [Note: Both aforementioned codices: “for I think that it.”] As if it were not enough, in drowning a man in the sea, to tie around him any stone, not large or enormous, but a millstone turned by an ass is tied around his neck, so that with the perishing man an object necessary for use may perish. Yet I think this is rather the point: in the Scriptures an ass figuratively denotes the people of the Gentiles, who, with closed eyes, are drawn around the millstone of ignorance by the circular course of their error and, without any direction in their course, repeatedly returning unwillingly upon their own tracks, labor for another’s use.

Does it not seem to you that the Gentile people turn an ass-mill so long as they remain occupied in the labor of their ignorance? [Note: Vatican Codex 6450: “in the labor of their inexperience.”] Bound by the chains of nature, they grind the word of God and seek the Lord of heaven; but, enveloped in the blindness of a veiled mind, they cannot raise the countenance of their soul to God or lift the eyes of their heart to heaven. [Note: Codex 90 of S. Crucis in Jerusalem reads: “nor can [they lift] the eyes of the heart to heaven.”] But since an ass-mill is admittedly a stone, [Note: Codex Casinensis: “is also admittedly a stone.”] let us see whether the millstone of the pagans is such as this. It certainly is. The pagans’ Jupiter is a stone millstone, and Hercules likewise is made of stone, around whom they circle in frequent error with blinded eyes. [Note: The same Vatican codex: “blind eyes.”] I call blind the eyes of those who think they see what they do not see; for, looking at a stone, they trust that they see God.

Nevertheless, one who turns a mill has at some time an end to complete his work and holds the hope of leaving off his labor. But one to whose neck a true ass-mill is hung bears the stone, whereas he ought to have borne Christ’s yoke. Therefore the ass is at the mill, the blind man at the stone, and the Gentile at the rock: he worships what he neither sees nor recognizes. For God does not dwell in things made by hands and is not known in metal or stone. Thus, when this Gentile people has inflicted persecution upon a Christian, it is punished by being drowned, together with its sacrilegious millstone, in the waves of the judgment to come.

## HOMILY LXXXVI. On the tumult of war

[Col. 0449]

### NOTICE

Muratori was the first of all to restore to St. Maximus of Turin this homily, which had been appropriated among the sermons of St. Ambrose. He found it in Ambrosian codex 98, which we have often mentioned, and published it, together with many others drawn from the same manuscripts, in volume IV of his *Anecdota*. Down to the present, it has appeared thus adorned with this testimony in subsequent editions of Maximus’s works. We illustrate it from the authority of codex 99 of S. Crucis in Jerusalem, where it occurs on p. 160 as sermon 93; nor do we hesitate to assign it to the holy bishop of Turin, since both its manner of speaking and its subject suit him.

[Col. 0449B] **SUBJECT.**—St. Maximus delivered this discourse to the citizens of Turin, who were alarmed by the irruption of barbarians into the neighboring provinces and were preparing the protection and defense of the city. He accordingly endeavors to raise their minds to hope in divine assistance, warning them to correct their evil ways, to beware of provoking God’s vengeance further, and to strive to appease it by pious and holy works.

Perhaps you are troubled, brothers, because we constantly hear that there are tumults of wars and incursions of battles; and perhaps your love is troubled still more as to why these things happen in our times. But this is the reason: the nearer we are to the destruction of the world, the nearer we are to the kingdom of the Savior. For the Lord himself says that in the last days “nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom” (Mark XXXI); and elsewhere: “When you see wars, earthquakes, and famines, know that the kingdom of God is near” (Matt. XXIV). Therefore this nearness of wars shows that Christ is nearer to us. Accordingly, I ought not to fear the enemy when he comes, because by these signs I understand that the Savior is coming instead. Although the one inspires temporal fear, the other brings everlasting salvation. The same Lord is able both to drive hostile fear away from us and to grant us his presence.

Through these tumults of war, then, a kind of destruction of the world is signified; for this unrest precedes the future judgment of God. It is a kind of judgment of God’s commotion to see what you may fear. For while we are made cautious by what we see, we become more cautious concerning what we await. A wise person is instructed by these earthly events how he ought to escape the judgment of the age to come. [Note: Codex S. Crucis in Jerusalem: “how he ought to escape the judgment of the age to come.”] For while he sees leading men preparing defenses upon the walls amid this common upheaval, [Note: The same codex: “protections on the walls.”] he is admonished how, in the future overthrow of the world, he should prepare a defense for souls. [Note: The same codex: “prepare.”]

We see the gates of the city armed; we too ought first to arm within ourselves the gates of righteousness, of which the holy prophet said: “Open to me the gates of righteousness” (Ps. CXVII). The gate of the city can then be fortified if the gates of righteousness are first fortified within us. For it does no good to strengthen walls with ramparts and to provoke God by sins. The one is constructed with iron, stones, and stakes; the other is armed with mercy, innocence, and chastity. The one is guarded by a multitude of weapons; the other is defended by frequent prayers. And, for the complete protection of cities, the standards of princes are customarily borne before the gates; let the sign of the Savior go before the gates of our souls.

Therefore, brothers, let us arm ourselves with heavenly weapons for the coming judgment; let us gird ourselves with the breastplate of faith, let us be protected by the helmet of salvation, and let us be defended by the spiritual sword, the word of God. Whoever is equipped with these weapons neither fears the present upheaval nor dreads the future judgment. Thus holy David, protected by this devotion, though himself unarmed killed that very mighty armed Goliath and, by the power of faith alone, overthrew a warrior surrounded on every side by fortifications. Although St. David was not covered by a helmet, was not girded with a sword, [Note: The same codex of S. Crucis in Jerusalem: “with a shield.”] and did not use a spear, he killed him not with an iron weapon but with a spiritual sword. Although he appeared unarmed to human eyes, he was sufficiently armed with the grace of the Godhead.

Yet that spiritual sword was not a sword; for Goliath did not fall stricken by a sword, but by a stone. In the Scriptures we read that Christ is figuratively denoted by the name of a stone, as the prophet says: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. CXVII). Therefore, when Goliath is struck with a stone, he is overthrown by Christ’s power. And in what part of his body is he finally struck down? In the forehead, certainly. He is a Gentile, a sacrilegious man: he is struck by Christ where Christ was absent; and there the destruction of death is inflicted upon him, where the sign of salvation is not found. Though Goliath was fortified on every side by the protection of arms, his forehead nevertheless lay open to death because he did not bear the seal of the Savior. Therefore he is struck where he is found naked of God’s grace.

No one fails to know that these things were done figuratively. [Note: The same codex of S. Crucis in Jerusalem: “as a figure.”] David had first girded himself with the equipment of arms; but since he was weighed down and hindered in it so that he could scarcely walk, he cast it aside without delay, signifying that those weapons were vain and luxurious works of such a kind that whoever wished to entangle himself in them would be weighed down and would not have a free course to run toward heaven. At the same time, he taught us also that victory is not to be hoped for in arms alone, but sought in the name of the Savior.

## HOMILY LXXXVII. On not fearing enemies

[Col. 0451]

### NOTICE

Mabillon likewise published this homily, taken from a St Gall codex, in the *Museum Italicum*, after the two preceding homilies, as Gallandius is known to have done from volume IX of the *Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*, p. 351. Its title in those editions is *Sequentia*, as it is found in the manuscripts. We have entitled it “On not fearing enemies,” since here St. Maximus exhorts Christians to perform works of virtue so that they may be delivered from their enemies. We illustrate the St Gall manuscript by the testimony of no other codex, since all entirely lack it; but who could doubt that Maximus should likewise be judged the author of this discourse, when, scarcely having begun, it embraces the substance of the preceding one?

[Col. 0451B] 291 **SUBJECT.**—Prayer, fasting, and almsgiving are an impregnable bulwark for resisting enemies. Those who try to build a fortification for themselves without God’s grace seem, like foxes, to prepare a hole as a hiding place for themselves.

Your affection remembers that last Sunday we preached that we should open for ourselves the gates of righteousness by good works and continual prayers, and fortify ourselves with frequent almsgiving as with a rampart of mercy. For resisting the adversary, almsgiving is a kind of impregnable wall; fasting is a form of combat. Although the enemy’s weapons are strong, these weapons of the Savior are stronger. Whoever is clothed in them, even if he appears unarmed to human eyes, is nevertheless sufficiently armed, because the supreme Divinity guards him. It is therefore good in tribulation to pray, fast, sing psalms, and show mercy. With these weapons, as we have presented David’s example against Goliath, Christians customarily defeat their adversaries; with these arms they guard the walls of the city.

For the holy prophet says: “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Psalm 126). In vain, then, does the man keep watch who thinks he is arming the city when he himself has no weapons of faith. Entirely in vain does he labor who thinks he can prepare protection for another while he himself is deprived of God’s grace. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4). This example should be applied as follows: first, you, O man, take care of your own salvation, so that you may be able to provide for the salvation of many.

But when I see that you are weak and infirm, deprived of the help of the Divinity, I not only have no confidence in the protection of the city prepared through you; I fear that your despair may disturb the city. The city is fortified, then, when God himself guards it most fully. God guards it when, as it is written, all who inhabit it are temperate, serious, Christian, and catholic. For God must preserve a city in which he finds something from his commandments that he may preserve. But where there are luxury, faithlessness, and blasphemy, the Lord does not preserve that city, lest it be not so much the city as the sins within it that are preserved.

Therefore, whoever provides the city with a fortification in the name of the Lord truly prepares security for its citizens. For whoever attempts to build a fortification for a city without God’s grace seems, after the manner of foxes, to be preparing a hiding place for himself in a den. Is such a man not like a fox in that den, continually digging into the earth and never looking toward heaven?

For the Lord says, as we recently heard read: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of the air nests where they may rest; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8). Let us carefully consider what meaning this statement has. The Lord was not speaking specifically about that animal, but about those people who, always crafty and cunning, continually strive to imitate foxes in their behavior. While they deceitfully seize what belongs to others, they dig out a den for their own destruction. Therefore Christ’s head, which is God, cannot find a dwelling among those who live in excavated places.

There is no doubt that heretics in particular are compared with foxes. For, like foxes, they are deceitful, troublesome, and cowardly. Wherever they sense security, there they exercise the rage of their fickleness; wherever they encounter vigilance, from there they flee by deceitful trickery. For just as that animal is always deceptive, always uncertain, and can never change its cunning ways, so every heretic is always deceptive and always uncertain. Even when he appears to speak simply with you, he changes his words but not his character: he promises moderation in speech but reveals rage in his heart.

The fox deceives with its tail; the heretic ensnares with his tongue. The fox pretends gentleness toward animals in order to capture them; the heretic promises moderation to people in order to harm them. The former first plays with its prey so that it may slaughter it; the latter first flatters so that he may despoil it.

It is characteristic of the fox always to lie in wait for the hen and her chicks, so that if one of them strays farther from its mother, it may be caught as prey. So too the heretic always lies in wait for Mother Church and her children, so that, if he happens to find someone more careless, he may encircle him with his own fury.

That the Church is rightly compared with a hen we read in the Gospel, where the Lord says to Jerusalem: “Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings” (Luke 13). The Church is rightly compared with a hen. For just as she nourishes not only her own children but also receives those who come from elsewhere, so the hen not only feeds those whom she herself has hatched but also raises other chicks placed with her.

Therefore, brothers, let us arm ourselves throughout this week with fasting, prayers, and vigils, so that, with the mercy of God intervening, we may both repel the savagery of the barbarians and blunt the snares of the heretics.

*The end.*

# HOMILY LXXXVIII  
## On Not Fearing Carnal Enemies and on Giving Thanks to God after Food I

[Col. 0453]

## Editorial Notice

It may perhaps be questioned whether this homily should be assigned to Saint Maximus, since it was formerly confused with the Ambrosian sermons, as the Paris edition of 1569 indicates, and since only one or two manuscripts are found to support its attribution. Such are manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, no. 46, and Vatican manuscript 1268, p. 144. It also appears in Laurentian manuscript X, Plut. XIV, p. 281, where it lacks the author’s name.

But Gennadius decisively establishes its authenticity, for he records its title with its principal characteristics as follows: *On Not Fearing Carnal Enemies and on Giving Thanks to God after Food*. The three manuscripts mentioned above present an almost identical title. The manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem has: *On Fearing Spiritual Enemies More than Carnal Ones, and on Returning Thanks to God after Food*. The other two, the Vatican and Laurentian manuscripts, agree in reading: *On Fearing Spiritual Enemies More than Carnal Ones, and on Giving Thanks to God after Food*, omitting only the phrase “than carnal ones.”

The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur seem to have attached great importance to Gennadius’s authority. Accordingly, they removed this homily from the collection of Saint Ambrose’s sermons and asserted it to belong to Saint Maximus, noting that older editions of Ambrose had the title: *Sermon on the Seventh Chapter of Job*, and so forth. Later editors, however—Gymnicus, p. 267; Galesinius, p. 171; Raynaudus, p. 240; and Margarinus in the *Bibliotheca Maxima*, vol. VI, p. 43—retained the same title recorded by Gennadius.

[Col. 0453B] **ARGUMENT.**—For the wise, enduring adversity is an exercise of virtue; for the foolish, it is an occasion of transgression. The proper repayment for divine benefits is that, when refreshed, we give thanks to God.

I have frequently admonished you, brothers, that, while it is permitted, [Note: [Col. 0453C] The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Laurentian add: “while time remains available, [provide] for your salvation by every means, etc.”] while there is time, you should provide for your salvation in every way, and in this short life should provide yourselves with eternal life. For every wise person understands that this human life has been given not for rest but for labor: that one may labor here and rest hereafter.

[Note: [Col. 0453C] But here there is no rest; this life is so full of evils that, by comparison with it, death is considered a remedy rather than a punishment. For this reason God made it brief: its troubles, since they could not be ended by prosperity, might be ended by the shortness of time.—Maximus had earlier reminded the faithful of the brevity of life, in which all must labor, so that eternal blessedness may be acquired through the contest of virtues. He then teaches that death ought willingly to be undergone, since through it all earthly calamities and troubles, which the pleasures of this world can neither soften nor remove, come to an end. Death, therefore, although it is the punishment of sin, is not the greatest of all evils, as the pagan philosophers called it, but a salutary remedy by which human beings are wholly freed from adversities and afflictions. Saint Ambrose teaches the same doctrine in his book *On Faith in the Resurrection*, or Book II of *On the Death of His Brother Satyrus*, no. 46, vol. IV of the works, Venice edition of 1751, where he proves by many arguments that death is to be borne with a resolute spirit. First, he sets before us the example of Christ, who could have avoided death had he wished: “But he neither judged that death was to be avoided as cowardly, nor could he have saved us better than by dying. Therefore his death is the life of all [lacuna]; his death is victory; his death is sacrament. Death, therefore, is not to be mourned—a death which the Son of God neither disdained nor fled; nor is the order of nature to be dissolved.” He further adds that this is the common condition of all human beings, from which none escapes free; and, since death is unavoidable, the mind that fears death is afflicted by frivolity and makes a mournful grief of it. Third, Ambrose confirms this truth: death was indeed not in nature, but it has been turned into nature. For God did not institute death in the beginning, when he made the first parents immortal and established them as inhabitants of paradise; but after their transgression had been condemned to daily labor and intolerable groaning, human life began to be miserable. An end to evils had to be given, since even premature death produces eternal salvation. Thus of the righteous person we read in Wisdom, chapter 4: “He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding.” For, freed from carnal enticements and those of the world, the person whom God has brought out of an earthly prison and transferred into his kingdom lives for God. Human nature is not destroyed by death; rather, as the Savior’s grace breathes upon it, it receives again the immortality in which it was created, and the image and likeness of the Creator, impressed upon the human being at creation, rises more perfect and more beautiful.]

But here there is no rest; this life is so full of evils that, by comparison with it, death is considered a remedy, not a punishment. [Note: [Col. 0453C] Manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Vatican manuscript 1268 read: “by comparison with it, death is considered to be a remedy, not a punishment.”] For this reason God made it brief: its troubles, since they could not be ended by prosperity, might be ended by the shortness of time.

Finally, holy Job says: “Piracy is the life of man upon earth” (Job 7); that is, either because human beings experience every kind of evil in this life—for *piraterium* can in Latin be called “experience”—or certainly because in this life the devil rages around human beings like a pirate; for *piraterium* is the dwelling-place of pirates. Therefore we are in piracy as long as, placed in this flesh, we are subject to the temptations of spiritual robbers. Yet even in this very life we do not lack carnal pirates, namely barbarians; but I fear them less, for although they take away estates, they cannot take away righteousness. If they take gold, they certainly cannot take Christ; if they plunder silver, they cannot plunder the Savior. Who, then, does not hasten [Note: [Col. 0454C] The same manuscripts, 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Vatican, read: “Who, then, does not hasten?”] to possess Christ, whom neither a robber can despoil, nor an enemy take away, nor captivity separate from him? For one who possesses Christ does not fear a human enemy. What can he do to a wise person? Will he drive off his livestock? Pestilential disease is accustomed to do this as well. Will he plunder his herds? By enduring it, he has already learned to bear that loss from cattle-stealers. Perhaps he kills him; [Note: [Col. 0455C] Vatican manuscript reads: “Perhaps he kills him; this does not …”] this does not bring him troubles, but removes them. For he has inflicted on him what fever would have brought with greater distress, especially since the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10).

Those spiritual pirates, then, are more to be feared: they customarily despoil not only human bodies but also souls; they strive to take away not so much the gold of the world as the gold of faith, and to plunder not so much worldly substance as Christ’s wisdom. For these spiritual enemies themselves send upon us these carnal enemies, so that, placed in tribulation, we may be tested as to how confident we are in God, and may seek a remedy from him alone. For there are some who, placed in tribulation, say that enemies are to be conquered by evil arts and ought to be overcome by the same arts; despairing of God, they demand victory from demons. Wretched people! They do not know what they are doing or saying. While they fear for their possessions, they have forgotten religion and faith; perhaps they do not lose their possessions, [Note: [Col. 0455C] Vatican manuscript reads: “do not lose.”] but, what is more serious, they have lost their souls.

Holy Job says: “If we receive good things [Note: [Col. 0455C] The same Vatican manuscript reads: “have received.”] from the hand of the Lord, why shall we not endure evil things?” (Job 2). That is, if we rejoice when good things come upon us, why are we not strengthened when adversities befall us? For the wise, enduring adversity is an exercise of virtue; for the foolish, it is an occasion of transgression.

I have often said that in this short life you should provide yourselves with eternal life; and I grieve that you disdain to do this. For when we say that you must fast, apart from a few, no one fasts; when almsgiving must be done, greater greed constrains you. But I suppose that most of you do not know what it is to pray and give thanks to God: when you rise at first light, you think of nothing but breakfast; when you have breakfasted, you give yourselves to sleep, never returning thanks to the Divinity, who gave you both breakfast for refreshment and sleep for rest. Certainly, Christian, if you are worthy, you ought to remember whose bread you eat and give him praise. Tell me: if you give something of your own to anyone, do you expect him to thank you, and finally to bless the person from whom kindness was bestowed upon him? If he should not thank you, how do you mark him as ungrateful? Thus God, who feeds us, also expects from us that for the food furnished by him [Note: [Col. 0455C] The same manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Vatican read: “we should return thanks to him.”] we should return thanks and, filled with his gifts, speak his praises. For this is the repayment for divine benefits: when we have been refreshed, we should duly acknowledge what we have received. But if, when receiving divine gifts, we are silent and forgetful, we shall, as ungrateful and unworthy persons, be deprived of their provision; so that, when evils press upon us, we may seek the God whom we did not recognize in his benefits, and may be driven by adversities to pray [Note: [Col. 0455C] The same manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Vatican read: “who in prosperity, etc.”]—the God to enjoy whose prosperity we did not give thanks. Thus it now happens [Note: [Col. 0456C] Vatican manuscript reads: “conceives.”] that we who were sluggish in peace to return praise are now fearful in tribulation to lament dangers.

# HOMILY LXXXIX
## On the Same Subject II

[Col. 0455]

## Editorial Notice

I believe that last Sunday I said enough, and more than enough, to correct those who enjoy divine gifts but do not give thanks to the Creator; who make use of heavenly benefits but, as ungrateful and unworthy beneficiaries, do not repay their benefactor. I mean those ungrateful people who neither fear God as servants fear their lord nor honor him as children honor their father. God says through the prophet: “If I am Lord, where is my fear? If I am Father, where is my love?” (Malachi 1). That is: if you are a servant, render the obedience of fear to your Lord; if you are a son, show affection to the father of the household. But when you do not give thanks, you neither love nor fear God; therefore you are either a rebellious servant or an arrogant son.

[Note: Vatican manuscript 1268 reads: “What, then, is a useful Christian?”]

What kind of person, then, is a useful Christian? He should always give praise to his Father and Lord and do everything for his glory, as the blessed Apostle says: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10).

[Note: Laurentian manuscript 10 reads: “If you do anything else.”]

[Note: [Col. 0456C] Vatican manuscript reads: “See what sort of banquet the Apostle wished Christian men to have.”]

See what sort of banquet the Apostle wished Christian men to have: that the faith of Christ should be eaten more than the fullness of the meal, and that the frequent invocation of the Lord’s name should refresh a person more than the varied and abundant presentation of dishes; that religious devotion should nourish the hungry better than bodily fullness.

“Do everything,” he says, “for the glory of God.” Therefore all our actions should be completed with Christ as our companion or witness [Note: [Col. 0457D] The Laurentian manuscript reads: “He wishes Christ to be the companion of all our actions.”], specifically so that we do good with him as its author and avoid evil because of his fellowship.

[Col. 0457A] For the person who knows that Christ is his companion is ashamed to do evil. Christ is our helper in good actions and our protector in evil ones.

Therefore, when we rise at dawn, before leaving our room we ought to give thanks to the Savior and, before all worldly activities, perform acts of piety, since he guarded us while we rested and slept in our beds. For who but God guards a sleeping person? When a person is so dissolved in sleep and deprived of human strength that he becomes alienated from himself, he does not know what he is or where he is staying, and cannot even be present to himself.

God is therefore necessarily present to those who sleep, because those who sleep cannot be present to themselves. He alone guards the human race from nocturnal ambushes, since at that time no one else remains awake as a watchman. [Note: [Col. 0457D] The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, Laurentian 10, and the Vatican read: “since at that time no one else keeps watch to guard [them].”] I ought therefore to give thanks to him who keeps watch so that I may sleep safely.

God himself receives us when we go to bed as though into a quiet embrace; he stores us away in the treasury of peace and protects us for the light by a kind of defense formed from darkness. Thus the malice of hostile people is held back by the darkness, since it cannot be dispelled by kindness; and the darkness grants peace to the weary, which human goodwill did not grant. For when a person does not know where to pursue his adversary, he provides, unwillingly, the peace that he refused willingly to provide.

We ought therefore, when we rise, to give thanks to God [Note: [Col. 0457D] The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Vatican read: “to give thanks to Christ.”] and perform every work of the day under the sign of the Savior.

Do you not remember that, when you were still a pagan, you used to search for omens and, after careful investigation, determine which signs were favorable for which matters? Now I do not want you to be mistaken about the number: know that, in the one sign of Christ, the prosperity of all things is secure. Whoever begins to sow under this sign will obtain the fruit of eternal life; whoever sets out on a journey under this sign will reach heaven.

All our actions must therefore be directed in this name, and every movement of our life must be referred to him, because, as the Apostle says: “In him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28).

When evening closes the day, we ought to sing praise to him through the psalter and join in celebrating his glory with measured sweetness, so that, when the contest of our labors has been completed, we may acquire rest like victors, and the oblivion of sleep may be a kind of palm of victory for our labor.

[Note: Vatican manuscript 1268 and Galesinius read: “So that, like victors, we may deserve to acquire rest.”]

Brothers, we are taught to do this not only by reason but also admonished by examples.

[Note: Vatican manuscript reads: “Do we not indeed see?”]

Do we not see even the tiniest birds, when dawn brings on the coming day, singing with varied sweetness in certain chambers of their nests? Before they go out, they diligently perform this act so that, since they cannot do so by speech, they may charm their Creator with sweetness; and since each cannot offer confession, it reveals its obedience through melody. The one that sings more sweetly seems to give thanks more devoutly. They do the same thing after the course of the day has been completed.

What, then, is the meaning of this song arranged for fixed times and this continual attentiveness, unless it is a kind of boundless confession of thanks? The harmless bird cannot flatter its shepherd by speech, so it does so by sweetness. Birds too have their shepherd, as the Lord says: “Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matthew 6). [Note: [Col. 0458D] The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Vatican omit “nor do they sow.”]

And with what foods are the birds fed? With very cheap and earthly ones, of course. The birds therefore give thanks for cheap food, while you are fed with the most precious dishes and remain ungrateful.

Who, then, possessing human understanding, would not be ashamed to close the day without the celebration of psalms, when the birds themselves leap into song with the sweetness of the psalter in order to give thanks? Why should he not make resound, with the sweetness of verses, the glory of the one whose praise the birds proclaim in measured song?

Imitate, then, brother, the tiniest birds by giving thanks to the Creator morning and evening. If you are more devout, imitate the nightingale: since a single day is not enough for it to sing praises, it passes through the hours of night in sleepless song. You too, surpassing the day with your praises, add to your work the courses that run through the night, and console the wakeful diligence of your undertaken labor with the sequence of the psalter.

Since I have mentioned birds that keep watch at night, I do not want you to imitate the owl. Although it is awake through the night, during the day it is sluggish or blind. With its large eyes it loves the darkness of shadows and dreads the brilliance of the sun. In a remarkable way, it is illumined by darkness and blinded by light.

This animal represents heretics and pagans, who embrace the darkness of the devil and dread the light of the Savior. With the large eyes of their disputations they see empty things but do not look upon eternal realities. Of them the Lord says: “They have eyes, and do not see; they walk in darkness” (Psalm 113). They are sharp in superstitious matters but dull in divine ones; and while they think that they soar aloft through their subtle arguments—

[Note: Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Galesinius read: “While they think that they soar aloft through subtle arguments …”]

[Col. 0458D]—like owls, they are bewildered by the splendor of the true light.

# HOMILY XC  
## On the Repentance and Fasts of the Ninevites I

[Col. 0457]

## Editorial Notice

If the only question here concerned the author of the homily, the matter could quickly be settled from the manuscripts that assign it to Saint Maximus. But because the title varies greatly, we are compelled to undertake a longer discussion.

Some manuscripts give the homily the simple title *On the Fasts of the Ninevites*. These are the very old Sangallensis, Homily 71; Vallicellianus A 7, p. 41; and manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, Homily 43.

The Belgian manuscripts, Martinensis and Camberonensis, as well as the manuscript of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, p. 27, have the title: *On the Litanies and the Fasts of the Ninevites*.

These differ from Ambrosian manuscript II 164, which calls the homily one concerning the Rogations: “Here begins the sermon on the Rogations”; and from Casinensis CXI, p. 26, which has: *Sermon of Saint Maximus, Bishop, on the Greater Litany*.

In Laurentian manuscripts 37, Plut. XVII, and 137, formerly belonging to the metropolitan church of Florence, the title is absent, and the author is indicated only by the customary words “As above,” since the preceding homily is adorned with the name of Saint Maximus.

Here we should also inform our readers that in two Vatican manuscripts, 1268 and 645, the author’s name appears to have been erased and Saint Ambrose substituted in its place. Two other manuscripts, Vaticanus Palatinus 435, p. 281, and Urbevetanus, p. 130, are anonymous.

How, then, can such a variety of titles be reconciled? Gennadius, who was the first to review the original titles of Maximus’s homilies, called this one *On the Repentance of the Ninevites*. Those who called it *On the Fasts of the Ninevites* therefore followed Gennadius, since the Ninevites’ repentance, according to Jonah’s preaching, was carried out through a universal fast.

Those who added to the old title *On the Litanies* or *On the Rogations* followed a rite introduced into the Church many years ago, according to which fasting and public supplications were held for three days before the Lord’s Ascension.

“Litany” certainly means the same as “supplication,” and there are two kinds. The more solemn one is held on the feast of Saint Mark, and its institution is considered extremely ancient, since Saint Gregory the Great mentions it in Book II of his *Letters*.
