Some attribute the same institution to Saint Lazarus, Bishop of Milan and predecessor of Saint Eusebius.

The other litanies are less solemn. They are also called the Rogations of the Ascension and are said to have been instituted by Saint Mamertus, Bishop of Vienne in Gaul. Later the Roman Church, in the time of Pope Leo III, and other churches adopted a similar rite. See Archbishop Incontrius of Florence, *Explanation of the Feasts*, p. 221.

The fast of the Rogations is now retained only by the Church of Milan. On those days it supplements the Lenten fast, whose beginning in that church does not occur until the first Sunday of Lent.

In arranging this homily, we have departed from the order followed by the other editors, who placed it after the Easter homilies: Gymnicus, p. 162; Galesinius, p. 138; Raynaudus, p. 221; and Margarinus, *Bibliotheca Maxima*, vol. VI, p. 27. We have instead placed it among the homilies on various subjects, because Maximus’s sermon contains nothing concerning Rogations or litanies. Since the following homily refers to it and is the second homily on the Ninevites, we thought it best to publish both together so that their connection might be apparent, omitting the addition to the title, “On the Litanies.”

[Col. 0459A] **ARGUMENT.**—The whole city of the Ninevites fasted in tribulation. We too, enduring the difficulties of our times, ought all alike to fast and implore God’s mercy through the abstinence of everyone.

We read in the prophets (Jonah 3) [Note: [Col. 0459B] The Casinensis manuscript reads: “for when Nineveh,” etc.] that, when destruction from God threatened the city of Nineveh and, in accordance with God’s sentence, the time for its overthrow was approaching, those who lived there had no other defense than, after setting aside their gluttonous banquets [Note: [Col. 0459B] Three Ambrosian manuscripts, the Vatican manuscript, and the manuscript of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme read: “after the abundant feasts.”], to undertake continual fasts and, laying aside their ambition for wealth [Note: [Col. 0459C] The Vatican manuscript reads: “having laid aside.”], to clothe themselves in the humility of poverty. They were to receive a remedy from the very source whence their destruction was coming: that is, by abstaining they were to soften the anger of the Divinity which they had provoked by their indulgence, and humility was to mitigate the offense which pride had incurred against them.

For it is said [Col. 0459B] 302 that in that tribulation the king himself, having laid aside his imperial purple and removed his royal magnificence, girded his limbs with sackcloth and rolled himself in sackcloth [Note: [Col. 0459C] Five manuscripts read: “rolled himself in sackcloth and ashes,” etc.] day and night. He was therefore a wise king, who knew how he ought to overcome adversity [Note: [Col. 0459C] The Urbevetanus manuscript omits “for himself.”]; for he overcame enemies by courage, but conquered God by humility. Clearly a wise king, who understood what weapons to use according to the circumstances of the time: when men lay in wait for him [Note: [Col. 0459C] The Vatican manuscript 1270 reads: “were plotting against him.”], he seized weapons of war; when God was angry with him [Note: [Col. 0459C] The Vatican manuscripts 1270 and 6451 read: “when God was angry with him, he snatches up,” etc.], he took up the weapons of righteousness.

A wise king, I say, who, for the salvation of his citizens, confessed himself a sinner more readily than a king. He forgets that he is king when he fears God, the King of all; nor does he remember his own power when he acknowledges the power of the Divinity. He therefore forgets that he is king while he casts off his purple, while he lays down his diadem, while he clothes himself in sackcloth and a haircloth garment, while he persists in fasting and lingers in prayers [Note: [Col. 0459C] The Vatican Palatine manuscript 435 has the following: “he persists, and thus deserved to obtain the Lord’s mercy together with those subject to him, as Scripture bears witness, saying: ‘God saw their works, that they had turned from their evil way, and the Lord had compassion concerning the evil which he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.’ At this point this homily ends in the cited Vatican Palatine manuscript.”].

A wondrous thing: while he does not remember that he is king of men [Note: [Col. 0460B] The Vatican manuscripts 1270 and Casinensis omit “to be.”], he begins to be king of righteousness. Thus the devout ruler did not lose his authority, but changed it. Previously he held the authority of military discipline; now he holds the authority of heavenly disciplines. No, I say, he did not lose his authority, because whether by the sword or by righteousness, he is the first to keep watch for the salvation of his citizens. He is plainly the first to keep watch, because, so that the whole city might fast, the king first imposed hunger upon himself [Note: [Col. 0460C] The Vatican manuscripts 1270 and Casinensis read: “and for the sake of everyone’s salvation he was the first to begin suffering hunger.”], and for the sake of all alone [Col. 0460B] he began to hunger before the soldier. For it was necessary that he who had been more powerful than the others should become more devoted than all.

By his own example [Note: [Col. 0460C] The Ambrosian, Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, and Vatican manuscripts read: “he had ordered an army of devotion.” The Vatican 6451, Casinensis, and Urbevetanus manuscripts read: “he prepares an army of devotion.”] he prepares an army for religious observance, armed not with weapons but with devotion alone [Note: [Col. 0460C] The Vatican manuscript reads: “to be fortified by devotion alone.”]. He orders every sex [Note: [Col. 0460C] The Urbevetanus, Vatican 6451, and Casinensis manuscripts read: “and every age.”], every age, to abstain from daily feasts. The number of the devout army is increased when even infancy is compelled to serve in such devotion. For in such a case it is considered an act of piety to deny even little children their necessary food [Note: [Col. 0460C] The Urbevetanus and Casinensis manuscripts read: “For in such a case it is believed to be an act of piety to deny little children their necessary food.”]. The satisfaction of sinners was not sufficient to placate God [Note: [Col. 0460C] The Vatican 6451 manuscript reads: “the sin of the sinners.”], unless the innocence of the children also mourned the sins of their elders, and youth washed away its own offenses through the tears of others [Col. 0461A].

Now, brothers, there is no one who does not know that all these things were done as a warning to us [Note: [Col. 0461C] The Vatican 1270 and Casinensis manuscripts read: “Who does not know that these things were done as a warning to us?” The Vatican 6451 reads: “No one can fail to know that these things were done as a warning to us.”], so that whenever we are hard pressed by tribulations, we may hasten to these defenses. For example, an adversary threatens, an enemy is at hand: let us fast and conquer [Note: [Col. 0461D] Three Vatican manuscripts and the manuscript of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme read: “and we conquer.”].

Some people, whenever they suffer an especially difficult crisis, ordinarily send envoys to neighboring peoples to seek assistance [Note: [Col. 0461D] The Vatican 1270 manuscript reads: “Some people indeed, whenever…”]. We, which is better, should send an embassy to God through fasting; let us implore assistance from him [Note: [Col. 0461D] The Vatican 1270, 6451, and Casinensis manuscripts have the singular: “assistance.”], let us turn to him with heart and prayers. For they did not ask assistance from elsewhere, but by fasting they drew it forth from their own innermost being. Why then should one ask another for what he can find within himself?

For the nearer we are to God, the farther our adversaries will be driven from us [Note: [Col. 0461D] The Vatican 1270, 6451, and Casinensis manuscripts read: “are driven away.”]. We must therefore draw near to God, since the prophet says: “Behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish” (Psalm 12) [Note: [Col. 0461D] The Casinensis manuscript reads: “from you, Lord, they will perish.”]. And if those who are far from God will perish, surely those who are near will be saved. We therefore cannot be near to God in any other way than by approaching him through fasting, prayers, and almsgiving.

For God himself is merciful, fasting, and holy; and therefore whoever wishes to be near to God must imitate that which God is [Note: [Col. 0461D] The Vatican 1270 manuscript reads: “must fast and imitate this—that is, must be what God is,” etc.]. Thus the entire city of the Ninevites fasted in its tribulation [Col. 0462A]. It was well said that the whole city did so; for not only the old, the young, and the infants, but even the beasts [Note: [Col. 0462C] The Vatican 1270 and Urbevetanus manuscripts read: “cattle” instead of “beasts.”], as we read, fasted.

A wondrous thing: a creature not bound by the condition of sin fasts for the city’s sin. Therefore we too, dearest brothers, enduring the distresses of our times, must all fast together and implore God’s mercy through the abstinence of everyone. [Note: [Col. 0462D] The Casinensis and Urbevetanus manuscripts read: “For what is it? Is it not the case that a Christian fails to do for his own salvation what beasts did for the salvation of human beings?”] For how can it be that a Christian does not do for his own salvation what beasts did for the salvation of human beings? Unless he is more stupid than a beast, the person who does not fast when a priest has imposed a fast for his sake [Note: [Col. 0462D] The Urbevetanus manuscript reads “more foolish” instead of “more stupid.”]. Is he not a beast who does not understand what threatens and presses upon him? A beast, indeed, seeing a pit, avoids it and guards against precipices. But you do not wish, by fasting, to avoid the danger that you see?

For it is a kind of despair to eat when you ought to abstain, to rejoice when you ought to mourn [Note: [Col. 0462D] The Urbevetanus manuscript does not have the words “then you eat when.” The Vatican manuscript reads: “when you ought to weep.”]. Concerning this despair the Apostle says—may God turn it away from us: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Corinthians 15).

Let us therefore fast, brothers, without interruption, so that with the help of our Lord we may overcome our enemies through prayers and abstinence [Note: [Col. 0462D] The Vatican manuscript adds: “through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”], through him who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XCI. On the Ninevites II

[Col. 0461]

### ADMONITION

When Augusta Taurinorum was trembling and its citizens were preparing to flee because of the imminent invasion of the barbarians—namely, the army of Attila—it appears that Saint Maximus delivered this homily and the preceding one. As in the first homily, Maximus urged the people of Turin, by the example of the Ninevites, who turned God toward pardon and mercy through repentance, to deserve preservation from so great a danger through holy works; so in this repeated discourse, attacking the more fearful not so much with new admonitions as with stronger counsel, he warns them not to abandon their homeland and encourages them to turn all their hope of salvation toward God.

Both homilies are so characteristic of our holy bishop, when the circumstances of the time are considered, that neither can belong to another. From the Sangallensis manuscript, where it is copied as Homily 72, Mabillon first published it in volume I, part 2, of the *Museum Italicum*, and Gallandius followed him. Its authenticity is confirmed by the testimony of manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, where Homily 90 occurs with the title “Likewise, what follows,” which is also read in the Sangallensis manuscript. We add nothing concerning its style; it is certainly such as to display Saint Maximus’s eloquence.

[Col. 0461C] ARGUMENT.—Again concerning the repentant Ninevites, who by humility and fasting turned God’s anger away from the destruction of their city. By these and similar works Saint Maximus the bishop admonishes his people to entreat divine assistance for themselves when great calamity threatens, and to take care not to abandon their homeland.

We said on the preceding Sunday that the Ninevites, placed in tribulation, had merited the mercy of the Divinity through abstinence and had freed their city from danger by fasting. They possessed such wisdom that they did not defend themselves by foreign resources but saved themselves through their own devotion. For they did not immediately despair of their salvation, because they had heard from the prophet that they were to be overthrown together with the walls of their city [Col. 0462C]. But the nearer the destruction was announced to be, the more they armed themselves with religious acts. Nor did they abandon their city to be overthrown; rather, they remained in it, wisely judging that the city which was afflicted by the sins of its citizens might be saved by the prayers of its citizens, and that the religious devotion which had brought salvation to the city whose evil conduct had brought destruction upon it.

For it was just that those whom the city had endured as sinners should become its own defenders. A city is destroyed only because of the sin of its citizens. Cease therefore to sin, and the city will not perish. Why do you flee your homeland? If you wish to be safe, flee your own sins instead. [Col. 0463A] If you cease to sin, the enemy is defeated. Scripture tells Abraham that a homeland can be saved by ten righteous persons. Therefore, if it is the righteous who save a homeland, those who abandon it are certainly unrighteous; and if the former obtain grace through their presence, the latter must deserve desolation because of their flight.

A son is plainly unjust and impious who abandons his mother when she is in danger. For a homeland is in a certain sense a dear mother: she gave you birth, nourished you, and made you wealthy so that you might be able to flee. If you did not possess abundant resources for expenses, you would have no means of flight. Thus, led by greed, while you fear losing your wealth, you do not hesitate to be impious toward your mother. Hence we understand that you care more for your money than for your salvation.

Tell me, good citizen, why do you plan to flee? Why do you abandon your homeland? Perhaps you fear captivity; do you not understand that you are granting pardon? [Note: [Col. 0463C] The manuscript of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme corrects Gallandius’s edition, which reads: “you do not understand how to grant pardon.”] Do you not know that the first captivity is not to see one’s homeland, and that—more grievous than every evil—to endure exile in a hostile foreign land? Someone who has committed a crime is customarily condemned to this sort of punishment: he is driven from his homeland and banished to unknown regions.

You are therefore providing for yourself, by your own choice, the evil which a person condemned as punishment ordinarily undergoes. But let us suppose that you are courageous and can endure the hardship of exile with equanimity. Tell me, with what freedom will you live among strangers? Will they not say to you as soon as you begin to speak, “Where is this man exiled from? From where has this fugitive come?” “He is also trying to oppress our city, just as he oppressed his own homeland.” [Note: [Col. 0463C] Manuscript 10 of the Laurentian collection, which agrees elsewhere, reads: “Thus you will be perplexed.”]

You will be so perplexed and disturbed that, fearing for your freedom, you will be afraid that there you will not find anyone to defend your status as a freeborn man. Believe me: in a foreign homeland you will hear as much as you have often said to others in your own homeland.

I do not even wish to mention that, however wealthy you may be in your homeland and however much you may enjoy your resources, as soon as you leave your house you become a beggar and a poor man. God therefore says to Abraham that a city can be saved through ten righteous persons. You therefore think badly of yourself, Christian people, if you do not believe that in our great assembly there are ten righteous persons capable of saving the city [Col. 0464A] 307. For when you abandon your homeland, you declare that there are not in it people worthy, by their merits, to deliver it.

But I fear that, after leaving all the righteous in it, you alone—the one who abandons it—may be found unrighteous. Yet I do not want you to be troubled by the number ten. We read that, when Sodom was destroyed [Col. 0464B] 308, Lot alone, by his merits, delivered the city; that the favor of one person was more powerful for salvation than the sins of many were for destruction. As he was leaving Sodom, the little city of Zoar was granted to him as a place of refuge. If a city is granted to a righteous guest, how much more is a homeland granted to a righteous inhabitant?

*Explicit.*

## HOMILY XCII. On not fearing the barbarians when one fears God, and on Saint Elisha I

[Col. 0463]

### ADMONITION

Mabillon, who found this homily and the following one in the celebrated Sangallensis manuscript, said that the former had already been published among the sermons of Ambrose; he published the latter in volume I, part 2, of the *Museum Italicum*, as the first of twelve previously unpublished homilies of Saint Maximus. In his preface, however, he warns that, if Maximus had been taken up to heaven in the year 420, as Gennadius reports, barbarians invading Italy would not have been found at that time, since that calamity occurred much later. Therefore either Gennadius’s testimony concerning Saint Maximus’s death has collapsed, or another author of the homily must be sought.

We believe that we have met this difficulty in our commentary on the Life of Saint Maximus, where, through a long series of homilies and sermons, we demonstrated that the period of the holy bishop of Turin should be placed around the middle of the fifth century, so that what is handed down about him in reliable documents may remain secure. Mabillon himself lists the same evidence: namely, two councils, the Milanese and the Roman, at which it is certain that Saint Maximus was present.

Therefore, so that we do not linger any longer over the established period of Saint Maximus, we acknowledge that this homily must be granted to him, persuaded less by the circumstances of that age than by three manuscripts of the highest authority: the Ambrosian, the Sangallensis (Homily 73), and manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme (Homily 21). The title in the latter two manuscripts is the same, though incomplete—for something is missing—and reads as follows: “On not fearing barbarians by those who fear God, and on Saint Elisha.” Two manuscripts attributing the homily to Ambrose oppose us: one is Vatican manuscript 1277, page 60; the other is Laurentian X, Plut. XIV, page 341. But we believe the matter has been sufficiently answered in the preceding admonition. The subject treated by the homily does not fit Ambrose’s age, since under the emperors Theodosius the Elder and Valentinian Italy rested in peace. Moreover, the diction is characteristic of Maximus, and among all critics the Ambrosian and Sangallensis manuscripts, by reason of their antiquity and esteem, claim greater confidence.

We have designated the title according to the Ambrosian manuscript. Gallandius followed Mabillon’s reading, or that of the Sangallensis manuscript, which we have supplemented according to the better manuscripts.

[Col. 0463C] ARGUMENT.—The holy bishop exhorts his people not to fear the approaching barbarians, if they fight with prayer, mercy, and fasting, which are the weapons of Christians. He gives the example of Elisha, who, when sought by the king of Syria for death, did not fear his ambushes because he was certain of divine assistance.

I remember often saying that we ought by no means to fear these warlike disturbances or to dread any multitude of enemies, however great; for, as the Lord says [Note: [Col. 0464C] Gallandius’s edition reads: “as the Apostle says.”], “Greater is he who is in us than he who is in this world” (1 John 4). That is, Christ is more powerful in protecting his servants than the devil is in inciting enemies.

For although that same devil gathers crowds to himself and arms them with cruel madness, they are nevertheless easily destroyed, because the Savior surrounds his people with better defenses. The prophet says: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will deliver them” (Psalm 33). If the angel of the Lord delivers those who fear him from dangers, the person who fears the Savior cannot fear a barbarian, nor can the one who keeps Christ’s commandments dread an enemy’s attack.

For Christ’s commandments are weapons for Christians, and divine fear drives hostile terror from us. These are our weapons with which the Savior has equipped us: prayer, mercy, and fasting. Fasting protects better than a wall; mercy frees more readily than plunder; prayer wounds from farther away than an arrow.

An arrow strikes only an adversary seen nearby; prayer, however, wounds an enemy positioned at a greater distance. Thus Saint Elisha the prophet, when the king of Syria wanted to capture him and bring him under his power, and had surrounded him with a great force of armed men, was neither terrified nor disturbed. Instead, he said to the boy who was reporting this: “Do not fear, for there are more with us than with them” (2 Kings 6:16). [Note: [Col. 0465C] The Vatican 1277, Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, Laurentian, and Ambrosian manuscripts read this way.]

O faith of the holy prophet! He does not fear the adversaries whom he sees [Note: [Col. 0465C] The same edition reads: “whom he beholds.”], because he knows that angels whom he believes are with him; he does not fear earthly ambushes, because he knows that heavenly assistance is present to him. “There are more with us than with them.”

A wondrous thing! Holiness deserves more defenders from heaven than wickedness has brought attackers on earth. “There are more with us than with them.” [Note: [Col. 0465C] The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, Vatican 1277, Ambrosian, and Laurentian 4 agree in this variant.]

Observe the merit of blessedness. The prophet announces even the number, while the boy is still uncertain about his safety. How much more do spiritual eyes see than bodily eyes! One sees the number of armed men; the other does not see the sign of protection.

How great is the divine mercy! A benefit is conferred upon human beings, yet it is not seen; those in danger receive assistance, yet they do not know it. For this is the Savior’s compassion: to intervene for salvation [Note: [Col. 0465D] Some, such as Gallandius, read “for affection,” and others “for appearance.” The Laurentian 4 and Ambrosian manuscripts read: “and not reveal himself to sight.”], without displaying himself to the eyes; to be felt through his benefits, but not seen by human vision.

Hence the person who thinks that, when he has accomplished something successfully, he has overcome by his own strength is mistaken. He must know that adversaries are conquered more by merits than by strength, and overcome not so much by power as by holiness—just as Saint Elisha overcame his enemies not with weapons but by prayer.

For when he told his servant that more defenders were present in order to drive away his fear [Note: [Col. 0465D] Vatican 1277 reads: “and could not remove fear from him.”], and was unable to take away his fear, he then prayed to the Lord, saying: “Lord, open his eyes so that he may see.” And his eyes were opened, and he saw; and behold, the whole mountain was full of cavalry [Note: [Col. 0465D] The manuscript of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads this way; Gallandius has “horsemen.”] (2 Kings 6:17), and so forth.

The prophet’s prayer therefore opened the boy’s eyes. It is not surprising that prayer opened his eyes so that he might see the army, since it opened heaven so that the army might come. It is not surprising, I say, that he experienced new eyes [Note: [Col. 0465D] The Laurentian 4 and Ambrosian manuscripts read: “if he inserts new eyes.”] who had earned new assistance.

Or why would the one who drew up the ranks of angels not extend the line of his sight? [Note: [Col. 0465D] The Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, Laurentian, and Ambrosian manuscripts read: “Or why would he not extend the line of his sight?”] Why, I say, would he not dispel the dullness of the pupils with his prayer [Note: [Col. 0466C] The Ambrosian and Vatican 1277 manuscripts read: “would dispel the dullness of the pupils, who by his merits penetrated the darkness of the clouds.”], when by his merits he penetrated the obscurity of the clouds?

Saint Elisha therefore necessarily granted security through this deed to the fearful servant, to whom he had already restored brightness; he removed the fear from his heart from whom he had removed blindness of sight. Rewarding him with a double benefit, he freed him from fear and freed his vision. He began to fear less after he had merited to see more; indeed, he merited peace and sight alike [Note: [Col. 0466C] The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, Laurentian 4, Ambrosian, and Vatican 1277 supply this text and agree in the supplement.].

Armed men are therefore seen on the mountains. It is evident that those whose arrival is first found on the mountains truly descended from heaven. The very proximity of the places demonstrates this: descending from heaven, they could have trodden only the nearby ridges of the hills.

Then Elisha prayed and struck the entire hostile army with blindness. It is not surprising that he inflicted blindness on his adversaries, since he had bestowed brightness upon his servant; nor is it surprising that he took sight from the enemies, since he had granted vision to the servant [Note: [Col. 0466D] The Laurentian 4, Ambrosian, and Santa Croce in Gerusalemme 99 manuscripts read: “and if he takes sight from the enemies, who grants vision to the servant.”].

Where are those who say that weapons can accomplish more than the prayers of holy men? Behold, one prayer of Elisha wounded an entire army, and through the merits of one prophet the entire number of the enemies was taken captive [Note: [Col. 0466D] The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme and Vatican 1277 read: “the entire number,” etc.]. What bands of kings, what crowds of soldiers achieved such a victory, that they struck down their enemies in such a way that no one among them was killed?

This is the true and bloodless victory [Note: [Col. 0466D] The Laurentian manuscript reads: “This is the true and bloodless victory.”], in which the adversary is conquered without any of the victors being harmed.

*Explicit.*

## HOMILY XCIII. On the same Saint Elisha II

[Col. 0465]

### ADMONITION

What we said in the preceding admonition should be consulted. It demonstrates that this homily too ought to be attributed to Maximus. It is read in the same manuscripts: the Sangallensis, Homily 74; the Ambrosian; and manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, Homily 71. The title of the first two is “What follows”; the inscription of the last is “Likewise, what follows.”

After Mabillon, Andreas Gallandius furnished this homily with a new edition in volume XI of the Venetian edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. We believe that we have sufficiently answered the writers of the Vatican 1277 manuscript, page 61, and Laurentian X, Plut. XIV, page 343, who assert that Saint Ambrose is also the author of this homily, in the preceding admonition.

[Col. 0467A] ARGUMENT.—Maximus again treats of Saint Elisha and narrates the wonders performed by God through him. Finally, he explains the truth of those things which then occurred figuratively.

It may perhaps seem surprising [Note: [Col. 0467D] The manuscript of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads “may seem” instead of “seems.”] that, when describing Saint Elisha’s grace a few days ago, we said that heavenly assistance descended in his defense, that armed horsemen or chariots had been divinely provided for him, and that a fiery chariot had also stood around him.

It was indeed a great thing, but it is not astonishing in a holy man. For what is surprising if he merits assistance from heaven [Note: [Col. 0467D] Laurentian manuscript 10, page 343, and Vatican 1277 read: “if he merits assistance from heaven, whose spirit is in heaven?”] whose mind is always in heaven? As the Apostle Paul says: “Our way of life is in heaven” (Philippians 2).

Therefore, if our way of life is in heaven, the way of life of heavenly beings can also be with us [Note: [Col. 0467D] The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme 99 and Laurentian read: “can be with us.”]—that is, those who live the life of angels rightly deserve their fellowship.

There is indeed among those who live holily a certain kinship, union, and fellowship. It makes no difference whether they remain in heaven or on earth, whether their manner of life is angelic or human, provided that the same life or holiness is in them. Their manner of life joins together those whom the elements separate; and although they are divided by different bodies [Note: [Col. 0467D] The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme read: “although they are divided by different bodies.”], they are nevertheless united by the same actions.

And so it comes about that the saints, bound together by a kind of fellowship, do not depart from one another. At one time angels come to earth; at another, human beings are transferred to heaven. Through a greater advancement, those whose life is shared begin to have the elements of their existence shared as well.

But someone may say: We have often heard of angels descending to human beings; we also wish to hear how human beings have migrated to heavenly places [Note: [Col. 0467D] The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme and Vatican 1277 read: “might migrate.”]. The matter is clear and readily available. Was not Elijah, the teacher of Elisha, carried up to heaven under the guidance of angels and, placed upon a fiery chariot, carried upward in triumph like a victor?

For he had been victorious—not over barbarian nations, but over worldly pleasures. Indeed, evil habits are more dangerous enemies than hostile foes; and in the present age we more easily understand that the wickedness of enemies can be conquered than that of character.

Thus the angels carry Elijah to heaven; they guard Elisha on earth. What is surprising if the angels who had carried his teacher now protect his disciple, and offer the son the new services which they had offered the father? [Note: [Col. 0467D] An old edition reads: “certain new services.”] For Elisha himself is the heir of his holiness.

Elisha is therefore rightly called the spiritual son of Elijah, because, when he ascended to heaven, he left him a double portion of his spirit. For when Elisha had been given the opportunity to ask for whatever he wished, before Elijah was taken away from him he asked that Elijah’s spirit might become double in him. Then Elijah said: “You have asked for a hard thing, but it shall be done for you” (2 Kings 2:10). [Note: [Col. 0467D] The manuscript of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme in Gallandius’s text reads: “You have asked a hard thing,” etc.]

O precious inheritance! In it more is left to the heir than is possessed; more is received by the one who accepts than was possessed by the one who gives [Note: [Col. 0468D] Vatican 1277 reads: “than was possessed by the one who gives,” etc.]. A truly precious inheritance, which, when transferred from father to son, is doubled by a kind of interest on merit.

Thus, while Elijah himself possessed a single spirit of holiness, he left Elisha a double one [Note: [Col. 0468D] The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme 99 and Ambrosian read “a simple spirit,” not “a symbol,” as elsewhere.]. A wondrous thing indeed! Elijah left more grace on earth than he carried with him to heaven. Although he was lifted to higher places and transferred there whole in body, he nevertheless remained with his son in greater holiness [Note: [Col. 0468D] The same manuscript of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme and Vatican 1277 read more correctly than Mabillon and Gallandius, who have: “yet he remains with his son in holiness.”].

What shall we say of Elisha’s merits? His first praise is that he wished to surpass his father in grace, asking that more be given to him than he knew was possessed by the one who owned it. He is indeed greedy in asking, but worthy in obtaining.

For when he demanded more from his father than he had, he caused him by his own merits to provide more than he could. When that same Elisha, after his teacher’s ascent, came to Jericho, and the citizens asked him to remain in the city, they said to him: “The situation of the town is good, but the water is bad and barren” (2 Kings 2:19).

Then he ordered an earthen vessel to be given to him [Note: [Col. 0468D] Mabillon’s reading is: “and, having put salt into it.”]. Having put salt into it, he went to the source of the waters and threw it into the waters, saying: “Thus says the Lord: I have healed these waters; from them there shall no longer be death or barrenness.” And the waters were healed to this day [Col. 0468C] (ibid.).

See, then, how great were Elisha’s merits: his first hospitality in the city became a great fruitfulness for its children. While he removed barrenness from the waters, he bestowed a succession of heirs.

For by this deed Elisha did not heal merely one person or provide medicine for one household; he restored the people of the entire city. If he had done this later, with barrenness intervening and everyone growing old, the city would have remained without an inhabitant [Note: [Col. 0468D] Two manuscripts of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme correct the text, where it reads: “had remained.”].

Thus, while Elisha healed the waters, he also healed the people; while he blessed the spring of the waters, he bestowed a certain fountain of souls [Note: [Col. 0468D] The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “he blesses the spring of the waters; he bestowed a certain fountain of souls.”].

For just as, through his sanctification, healthy water emerged from the hidden veins of the earth, so healthy offspring proceeded from the hidden interior of the womb. Elisha did not bless only the streams that were already held in the bosom of the springs [Col. 0468D] 314, but also those which, mingled with the moist soil of the earth, were gradually destined to flow forth in the future [Note: [Col. 0468D] Both Mabillon’s and Gallandius’s texts are made clearer by the manuscripts of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme and Vatican 1277.].

Hence Scripture says that Elisha blessed the sources of the waters, so that the sanctification [Note: [Col. 0469D] The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “so that the sanctification of the prophet might receive it.”] might receive the trickling water before the basin of the spring enclosed it.

Therefore, since the holy Apostle Paul says: “These things happened to them figuratively” (1 Corinthians 10), let us see what truth this very figure contains. That is, let us ask what city this was that suffered from barrenness, what the earthen vessel signifies, and how the scattered salt brings sweetness.

We read that the same Apostle said concerning the Church: “Rejoice, barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not give birth” (Galatians 6) [Note: [Col. 0469D] These words are added in the three aforementioned manuscripts, completing the sense.]. Therefore the Church is that barren city which, before Christ’s coming, endured barrenness because of defective waters—that is, because of the sacrilege of the pagan peoples—and was unable to produce children for God.

But when Christ came, taking on a human body like an earthen vessel, he healed the defects of the waters—that is, he cut away the sacrileges of the peoples. Immediately the Church, which had been barren, began to be fruitful. Hence the Apostle also says: “Rejoice, barren one.”

For the Church that had been barren produced more children from him than the Synagogue, which had been fruitful, received. Now, as for the scattered salt—what it is and what healing it brought, we shall readily understand. The Lord says to the apostles: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13). Therefore, if the apostles are compared with salt, the figure is rightly completed: just as then the salt poured from the vessel seasoned the waters, so now the apostles sent by the Savior season all peoples, so that, once the barrenness of vices has been removed, they may begin to bring forth the offspring of virtues.

*Explicit.*

## HOMILY XCIV. On the restoration of the Milanese church

[Col. 0469]

### ADMONITION

As we have already said in the preface to this collection of the works of Saint Maximus, we owe the valuable acquisition of this homily to the diligence and scholarly dedication of the most learned canon Francesco Antonio Frisi. He recovered it from two very ancient manuscripts of the imperial basilica of Milan and courteously made it available to us, together with several variant readings drawn from an older manuscript.

Tristanus Chalcus had offered a specimen of this discourse under the name of Saint Maximus in his *History of Milan*; but it now appears in full for the first time, and contributes greatly to establishing that Saint Maximus flourished in the fifth century.

[Col. 0469B] 315 ARGUMENT.—Although God sometimes permits his servants to be afflicted by hardships and calamities in order to correct them and recall those who have gone astray to himself, he nevertheless deals with them more generously whenever they seek him humbly and obediently and pursue him with love.

There are many clear and manifest examples of divine severity and compassion, dearest brothers, by which we can plainly perceive that our God, in his ineffable and righteous governance, chastises the obstinacy of the proud and is present to the sorrows of his suppliants. For as Creator of his creatures, and as Lord of his servants, he chastises sins, just as a father consoles the grief of his children. We are his creatures by the law of nature; we are his servants because he redeemed us at the price of his blood; we are his children because he has bestowed upon us the sacraments of heavenly birth [Col. 0469C]. Thus we are creatures so that we may reverence him, servants so that we may fear him, and children so that we may love him.

Finally, just as the almighty Lord brought upon this Church the anger of a desolation that had to be mourned [Note: [Col. 0469D] The Codex of the Basilica of Milan, namely, of this Church.], so, as the most merciful Father, he brings about the effect of its desired restoration. To show that in the times to come he would restore the appearance of this city as though restoring a body after death, he restored its Church first—since it is, of course, the city’s head—by rebuilding it as though it had risen again. Therefore, he who was present at the restoration of the fallen head will grant, if we deserve it, that the limbs of that head, which now lie prostrate, may rise again.

Or why should it be doubted that God can restore their earthly dwellings when he promises that, if they believe rightly and live rightly, he will give them in heaven blessed and secure [Col. 0469D] abodes? Therefore [Col. 0470B] let us not lose confidence [Note: [Col. 0470D] The same codex reads, “let us not despair.”] that God will restore what belongs to us, if we restore within ourselves what belongs to God.

For long ago, when the Lord deigned to call his wandering people [Note: [Col. 0470D] The same codex omits “his.”] back to himself, he said to them through his prophet: “Return to me, and I will return to you” (Malachi 3:7). That is: “Restore your faith in me, and I will restore my grace to you. Give back what you owe, and demand what I promise. Hear what I command, and I will do what you ask. Remove the causes of offense, and I will take away punishment.”

Yet, dearest brothers, even amid our tribulations—which, under God’s governance, we endured as best we could—some rather inexperienced interpreters have said: “This city has perished; the Church has collapsed; there is no longer any reason to live.” On the contrary, there is reason to live more justly 316 and more holily [Col. 0470C], because almighty God, who orders all these things with great compassion, delivered into the hands of the enemy the city—not the city that is in you, but the city’s dwellings [Note: [Col. 0470D] The same codex reads, “not the city, which is in you.”]. Nor did he command his Church, which is truly the Church, to be consumed by fire; rather, for our correction, he allowed the Church’s buildings to be burned.

For no wise or faithful person is unaware that the city consists in its people, and the Church in its congregation. Therefore, dearest brothers, it is not beams and rafters that you present to our God as a living Church, but yourselves. You constitute the whole city, and for that reason, in this chastisement of his household, God in his mercy deigned so to temper everything that our iniquity might not be excessive, and that he might grant his suppliant servants a season of salutary conduct.

For by his merciful favor, after that immense and grievous destruction, behold: his high priest stands unharmed, the clergy remains intact, and the people themselves, although still living under daily fear and in mourning, nevertheless continue in freedom. It is not, then, the Church that has now been restored—for, under God’s protection, it did not perish—but these walls and roofs that have received you, who are God’s Church. For you are, as the Apostle says, “the temple of the living God” (II Corinthians 3).

Understand therefore, brothers, that although our sins justly demanded vengeance against us, the kindness of the merciful Judge ensured that it was not we ourselves but the things that seemed to belong to us that either the plunderer carried away or that perished, consumed by fire and sword.

Thus, sometimes, for our terror, while God is angered against us and heaven resounds with dreadful voices, sacred buildings and private houses, flocks of cattle and various four-footed animals, fruitful [Col. 0471B] and barren trees, rocks and the lofty peaks of mountains are struck down by flashes of lightning. So that our minds may be turned toward God and our life may be saved, those things are struck for us which either lack perception or do not know how to live. How gentle this vengeance is, and how fatherly in the compassion from which it descends! We sin, and heaven rages against cattle; we deserve the flames, and a tree is burned; we commit sins that ought to be punished, and rocks undergo punishment in our place.

Sometimes, indeed, certain people, whom God distinguishes in this way, are tested under a shadowy likeness, as human beings. First, so that sinners may not continually feel secure in their impunity [Note: [Col. 0471D] The Codex of the Basilica of Milan reads, “so that there may not be continual security for sinners.”]—and second, so that he may correct the multitude of sinners through the punishment of a few.

Who would not marvel at such a great dispensation of heavenly anger and grace? For when the walls had been breached, the unarmed population fled from armed and plundering enemies, as the swiftest horsemen flee from slow and heavily burdened wagons trembling beneath their own weight. Indeed, some among the clergy or the people lacked either the opportunity or the will to escape. The account of their life and death must be left to divine judgment.

Let us therefore console ourselves, brothers, and let us not sigh so deeply [Note: [Col. 0471D] The same codex reads, “let us not suspect that the houses have collapsed because of God.”] over the fallen houses, since we see that the restoration of houses has been reserved for their masters.

That command of the Lord concerning his servant Job appears to have been fulfilled also in us, when, while the devil was acting against him, he set a limit to the devil’s persecution. For he said to him, as we read: “All that he has I give into your hands; only do not touch him” (Job 1). And again: “Behold, I deliver him to you; only keep yourself from his soul” [Note: [Col. 0471D] The same codex omits “you.”].

When the enemy had received this order, he immediately destroyed all Job’s possessions and covered his body with ulcers, but restrained himself from harming his soul alone. See, beloved, how sparingly the Lord tempered his vengeance toward us, in consideration of our weakness: cities were devastated, fields laid waste, and possessions diminished, yet neither our souls nor our bodies were harmed [Col. 0472A].

The body of that great Job, corrupted by the decay of worms, was made to shudder for this reason: that strong man was being tested for glory, whereas we, as weak people, were being preserved for grace. Therefore, let us not doubt that God can restore what we and our descendants have lost, when we see that, after the devil had been conquered, the wealth of faithful Job was doubled, his children restored, and the savage wound of his body healed with marvelous health.

And so, with greater appropriateness and necessity, this most blessed man and high priest of the supreme God, Eusebius, can sing with us and on our behalf that Davidic verse addressed to God, saying: “I have declared my life to you; you have placed my tears in your sight” (Psalm 55). 318 That is: “Lord, I confessed my sins to you, and you did not deny me your mercy. I have experienced the strictness of the Judge; I acknowledge the grace of him who spares. In exile I wept over my sorrows and the grief of your people, but I rejoice that you have not despised my tears” [Note: [Col. 0472D] The same codex reads, “my tears to you.”].

For, as the prophet says, “You have turned my mourning into joy for me” (Psalm 30). You expelled me in anger and brought me back in mercy. Or, to speak more truly, you expelled me in mercy, so that, remaining rashly in that place, I would not suffer the misery of captivity. [Note: [Col. 0472D] The same codex reads, “I acknowledged what I did not deserve; I obtained what I did not deserve.”] I obtained what I deserved.

Therefore I render due thanks to your eternal glory, because you deigned, through me your servant, to restore this holy house of yours, which barbarian fury had leveled because of our merits; and, although your people’s congregation had been scattered, you have now restored it to my eyes. In your name we dedicate new things from old, and, under a certain likeness of resurrection, the image of this temple's roof has been raised to its former summit.

Thus once, after Jerusalem had been burned and the temple overturned, the Israelite people were led captive into the region of Babylon; after a fixed period, they were recalled to their homeland and rebuilt both their soil and their city and their temple.

Preserve now, Lord, what you have accomplished in us. Show mercy, Lord; spare, Lord; save your people and bless your inheritance. Do not, while you conceal yourself, allow the nations to laugh any longer over the destruction of your flock, saying—as they said before—“Where is their God?” (Psalm 79). Rather, just as vengeance in your anger against us was not absent, so may your compassion in showing mercy to us endure [Col. 0472D]. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XCV. On Greed, and on What Is Written in Acts, Chapter 4: “Everything Was Common to Them.” I

[Col. 0471]

### ADMONITION

319 Gennadius testifies that Saint Maximus wrote on greed, and the two sermons that follow concern this subject. The copyists, who do not disagree with Gennadius in identifying the author, give the homily a different title.

The very ancient Ambrosian codex entitles it “Homily on the Unity of Charity,” as does Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, homily 62, and Laurentian Codex IV, Plut. XX, p. 252 verso, which attributes it to Saint Ambrose. Three other codices that identify Maximus as the author—namely, the Sangallensis, homily 15; Santa Croce in Jerusalem 90, homily 15; and Laurentian X, Plut. XIV, p. 302—read as follows: “Here begins [the homily] on what is written: ‘Everything was common to them.’” Codex 90 of Santa Croce adds, “and on Cain and Ananias.”

The title prefixed to the sermon numbered C in the appendix of Saint Augustine’s sermons is different from all these: “On the Words of Acts 4: ‘No one called anything of what he possessed his own.’” The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, excellent critics, write that this sermon was formerly published among the Augustinian sermons as number 15, “On Time,” but acknowledge that it was falsely attributed to the holy Doctor. Since they found it attributed both to Ambrose and to Maximus, they noted at the beginning of the sermon that Vindingus, following the Louvain editors, judged it should be assigned to Maximus.

Their judgment is certainly based on Gennadius’s authority and on the testimony of three older codices, which Muratori and Mabillon value highly: the Ambrosian, the Sangallensis, and Santa Croce in Jerusalem 90. Thus Gillotius is shown to have been plainly mistaken when he published this sermon as number 9 among the sermons of Saint Ambrose.

We have used the common heading found among the editors, which appears to have been taken from the better codices. Gymnicus, p. 276; Galesinius, p. 173; Raynaudus, p. 244; and Margarinus, *Bibliotheca Maxima*, vol. IX, p. 45, use this heading.

### ARGUMENT

Saint Maximus compares the Christians of the Church’s beginnings with the faithful of his own time. The former were poor in spirit and in material possessions: they owned nothing privately but held everything in common. The latter are reproved for excessive concern with increasing their wealth and are urged to show mercy toward the needy.

We read in the book entitled *The Acts of the Apostles* that, among the people living under the aforementioned men, such devotion prevailed and the beginnings of the Christian people flourished so greatly that, after receiving the faith, no one claimed his own house [Note: [Col. 0473C] Both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Vatican Codex 1270 read, “would defend your own.”], and no one asserted anything as his own; rather, by the law of brotherhood, everything was common to them.

The point was that those who were bound together by the same fellowship of religion should also enjoy the same fellowship in life: those who had one faith should also have one substance, and those who had Christ in common should also have their resources in common.

For these devout men considered it wrong not to admit into partnership in their possessions one who was a partner in grace. Therefore, through the charity of brotherhood [Note: [Col. 0473C] Both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, Vatican Codex 1270, and Laurentian Codex 4 read, “through the brotherhood of charity.”], they used everything in common—except that the brotherhood of Christ was greater than brotherhood by blood. Blood-brotherhood reflects only bodily resemblance; the brotherhood of Christ demonstrates unity of heart [Note: [Col. 0473C] From both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem]. As it is written: “The heart and soul of the believers were one” (Acts 4).

Truly, then, he is a brother who is related not so much by body as by unity of mind. I repeat: he is a true brother whose spirit [Note: [Col. 0473C] The same Codex 10 reads, “whose spirit and will are the same in his brother.”] and will are one with his brother. Therefore, as I said, the brotherhood of Christ is better than brotherhood by blood [Note: [Col. 0473C] Codex 90 of Santa Croce reads this passage as follows: “Therefore, as I said, the brotherhood of Christ is better than brotherhood of the flesh. That carnal brotherhood is sometimes hostile to itself,” etc.].

Blood-brotherhood is sometimes hostile to itself, but the brotherhood of Christ is unfailingly peaceful. The former divides what its members hold in common through rivalry; the latter shares even what is privately owned with rejoicing. The former often despises its own kinsman within the partnership; the latter frequently takes in a stranger.

Such, then, as I said, was the devotion of the Christian people at that time: no one called his house his own, and no one claimed anything as private. As Saint Luke says: “No one said that anything of what he possessed was his own” [Note: [Col. 0473D] Both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Laurentian Codex 4 read, “was his own property.”]; “everything was common to them” (ibid.). For, I repeat, no one among them was in need [Col. 0474A].

Blessed, therefore, was that people which, while possessing many rich people in Christ, had no needy person in the world; and which, while contemplating eternal riches, drove temporal poverty away from its brothers. For, as Scripture says, “they sold their estates and houses” (ibid.) and carried the proceeds of what they sold to the apostles’ feet, so that they might be distributed according to each person’s need.

Observe the faith of those holy men: see how, for Christ’s sake, they stripped themselves of their entire patrimony [Note: [Col. 0474C] The codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Laurentian Codex 10 read, “they stripped themselves entirely of their patrimony.”], leaving nothing for themselves. They were not afraid that they themselves would hunger while they feared that someone else might take away [Note: [Col. 0474C] The codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Vatican Codex 1270 read, “might hunger,” instead of “might take away.”].

Such was the devotion of the people under the apostles. What comparable thing do we find today? Christ is indeed the same in us, but our spirit is not the same; the faith among the people is the same, but generosity itself is not found among the people [Col. 0474B]. Thus one person gives no thought to another’s poverty, so that what the Apostle says comes to pass: “One is hungry, while another is drunk” (I Corinthians 11).

For many Christians not only fail to distribute what is their own, but even seize what belongs to others. I repeat: they not only do not carry their money to the apostles’ feet, but they even drag away their brothers, who take refuge at the priests’ feet [Note: [Col. 0474C] The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads, “they drag them away.”].

This is the time described by the blessed Apostle, who says: “In the last days the iniquity of many will abound, and charity will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12). For now the iniquity of greed abounds [Note: [Col. 0474C] The Codex of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads, “the greed and iniquity.”], whereas previously it was held back by the goodness of generosity; and the charity of brotherhood grows cold, though previously it burned with love of Christ.

For the love of brotherhood under the apostles was so great that need did not arise in their gathering [Note: [Col. 0474C] Laurentian Codex 4 and the three codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read, “then, because of such great…” instead of “for such great…”; the same is also found in Codex 1270: “so that then in the gathering…”]. But now there is such a difference in Christian conduct [Note: [Col. 0474D] Both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Vatican codex read, “such dissimulation”] that in our assembly you can scarcely find a wealthy person. And when I say that it is difficult to find a wealthy person, I mean wealthy not in possessions but in works. The Apostle says: “Let them be rich in good works” (I Timothy 6).

He intended that person to be understood as wealthy in the Church who is rich in Christ. For when he says that under the apostles no one was needy, he plainly shows that they were endowed with such abundant grace of faith that all overflowed with the generosity of heavenly riches [Col. 0475A].

Rarely, therefore, do we find a wealthy person in the Christian people of this time. Although many are rich in gold in their houses, they are beggars in justice within the Church. For while they do not act toward the poor according to their ability, neither what they offer is pleasing nor what they keep is sufficient.

The Lord says to Cain when he was offering gifts: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Genesis 4). So too you, Christian: you do not divide rightly, because from all your considerable gold you reserve a greater portion for Mammon than you give to the Lord.

Thus Ananias in the Acts of the Apostles, while thinking that he was offering rightly but not dividing rightly, lost both the money he offered and what he had kept at home. I mean, he lost both his money [Col. 0476A] and his salvation. For when he withheld part of what he had promised, he was condemned both for sacrilege and for fraud: for sacrilege, because he deceived God in his promise; for fraud, because he thought that some portion of an entire gift could be withheld [Note: [Col. 0475C] Laurentian Codex 10 reads: “for sacrilege, because he deceived the Lord by his promise; for fraud, because he thought that some portion of the complete gift ought to be withheld.”].

The Apostle Peter says: “You have not lied to human beings, but to God” (Acts 5). If, then, brothers, Ananias is condemned because he did not give all that he himself had promised from his own possessions, what do we think about someone who is unwilling to return what another person promised [Note: [Col. 0475C] Both Laurentian codices read, “what he promised to others.”]?

Consider therefore yourselves, brothers, what you promised to God when you first received the grace of faith. Behold, our city is full of guests and travelers: do what you promised, lest what was said to Ananias also be said to you: “You have not lied to human beings, but to God.”

## HOMILY XCVI. On the Same Subject II

[Col. 0475]

### ADMONITION

The subject treated in this homily, Gennadius’s authority, the testimony of the most distinguished codices, and its title all confirm that it should be assigned to Saint Maximus. Gennadius handed down the memory that Maximus had written against the vice of greed, but he did not state whether he completed this task in one sermon or in two.

It is nevertheless clear from the codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, the Sangallensis, the Ambrosian, and Vatican Codex 1270 that both sermons were attributed to Saint Maximus. The inscription also shows that this homily is genuinely the continuation of the preceding one. Thus Codex 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “Here begins the continuation”; and Codex 99: “The continuation on greed and Ananias.”

The Sangallensis has a shorter title, namely, “The Continuation”; but Laurentian Codex X reads: “The continuation on greed and Ananias.” Since this is so, the collectors of homilies mentioned above published them in this order, with the title prefixed: “The second homily on the subject treated above.” The Roman editors, in reprinting the Ambrosian sermons, likewise titled it among the sermons of Saint Alexius the Confessor, number 13.

### ARGUMENT

Again, by presenting the example of Ananias, Maximus treats of greed and shows that it is a great evil—indeed, the origin of all evils.

Your affection remembers, brothers, that a few days ago, when we were praising the unity and generosity of the people who lived under the blessed apostles, we reached the greed of Ananias. At that time, amid the purest life of the whole human race, he alone was found like a diseased sheep.

For he was so infected with the plague of greed that Saint Peter wished not so much to correct him as to condemn him. He had read: “Cast the pestilent man out of the assembly, and all strife will depart with him” (Proverbs 22). He alone, then, was pestilent in the holy assembly: while everyone else, scorning money, sought the profit of life, he alone purchased the profit of money rather than of salvation; and while he hoped for gain from the price, he found the loss of his soul.

Ananias was therefore found greedy even among the apostles; our own weakness is already excused. For it is less surprising that this vice should abound among us, since it began to sprout even under the apostles [Note: [Col. 0475D] Codex 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem has “these vices.” The Ambrosian reads: “that these vices should abound among us, since they began to sprout under the apostles.”]. And if the authority of the apostles could not correct this vice in Ananias, what blame will attach to us if we cannot correct the same vice in many of our brothers [Col. 0476B] [Note: [Col. 0475D] The Ambrosian codex reads, “if we are unable”?]?

If Peter could have corrected greed in Ananias, he would not have punished him. But in punishing him, he corrected others: he wanted the punishment to reach one person, but fear to reach many. An example was therefore set before all greedy people in Ananias, so that whoever was guilty of the same crime might be struck by the sentence of the same punishment on the day of judgment.

Greed, then, is a great evil; indeed, it is the origin of all evils, as the Apostle says: “Greed is the root of all evils; by desiring it, some have wandered from the faith” (I Timothy 6). You see, therefore, that the person who desires money loses faith, and the person who gathers gold squanders grace.

For greed is blindness and brings about religious error [Note: [Col. 0476C] The Ambrosian codex reads: “For greed introduces religious error. Greed, I say, is blind, but, made watchful by various kinds of fraud, it is concealed.”]. Greed, I say, is blind; yet, though given sight by various devices of fraud, it does not see what belongs to divinity but considers what belongs to desire [Col. 0476C]. Although he is rich, the greedy person is always thinking how to acquire something from anywhere, even through evil [Note: [Col. 0476C] Both codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Vatican Codex 1270 read: “for, although he is rich, he is always thinking how or from what evil he may acquire.”]. He regards his whole life as a business [Note: [Col. 0476C] The Ambrosian codex reads, “he regards his whole life as his business.”]; suppressing every profit, he imposes interest on his empty service [Note: [Col. 0476D] Both the Ambrosian and Santa Croce codices, Laurentian Codex 10, and the Vatican codex read “greater,” not “empty.”]. He is ashamed of the name “usury,” but he is not ashamed of usurious profit.

The greedy person therefore always uses what belongs to another; he feeds himself on another’s loss [Note: [Col. 0476D] “Loss” is absent from the Ambrosian codex]. Another person’s poverty is his booty; another person’s tears are his joy, as we have always seen happen.

How many people mourn what they have lost, while many rejoice over what they have seized [Note: [Col. 0477D] Vatican Codex 1720 reads, “How many mourn what they have lost, over which many rejoice when it has been seized”?]?

Behold, an aged father mourns his captured son, while you boast over him as though he were already your little slave. An innocent farmer groans over his lost young ox, while you plan to cultivate your land with it and think you can harvest fruits through another’s groans.

Behold, a devout widow grieves that her house has been stripped of all its household goods [Note: [Col. 0477D] The Vatican codex reads, “all her furnishings.”], while you boast that your house has been adorned with those same goods [Note: [Col. 0477D] The same codex reads, “with the same furnishings.”].

Tell me, Christian: do you not feel pierced, do you not feel troubled, when you see another’s tears in your lodging?

Scripture says to the children of Israel: “You shall not touch an animal seized by a wild beast; for whatever the bloodthirsty beast has touched is polluted and defiled” (Exodus 22:22). And for this reason, whoever takes what the beast has left behind is worse than the beast.

Tell me, then, Christian: why did you presume to take the booty left by plunderers? Why did you bring into your houses what had been torn apart and contaminated, as you yourself suppose? Why did you, a fiercer beast, devour what the hostile beast had spared?

Many say that wolves customarily follow in the tracks of lions and do not stray far from their hunts, so that they may satisfy their own rage with another’s prey, and that what remains after the lions are satisfied may be consumed by the wolves’ rapacity [Note: [Col. 0477D] The codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Vatican read, “may be consumed.”].

So too these wolves of greed followed the tracks of the plunderers, so that what had escaped their rapacity might fall to the ferocity of the wolves.

But perhaps you say that you purchased the goods, and that therefore you escape the charge of greed. A purchase and sale does not ordinarily stand in this way: it is good to buy what is sold willingly and in peace, not what is taken in plunder.

Examine the origin of the transaction, the seller, and the amount of the price, 325 and you will understand that you are more a partner in the booty than a purchaser in a sale [Note: [Col. 0477D] Both the codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Ambrosian read, “and you understand that you are more a partner in booty than a purchaser in a sale,” etc. The Vatican and Laurentian codices likewise read, “and you will understand that you are…”].

Where did the barbarian get necklaces of gold and gems? Where did the wearer of skins get silken garments? Where, I ask, did you obtain Roman slaves [Note: [Col. 0478D] The cited codices omit “you obtain”?]? We know that they belong to our provincial neighbors or to our fellow citizens. Therefore, he acts as a Christian and a citizen who bought in order to return it.

## HOMILY XCVII. On Almsgiving and on the Samaritan Woman I

[Col. 0477]

### ADMONITION

Gennadius, who first compiled a summary of Saint Maximus’s works, stated that Maximus discussed almsgiving; the copyists of the codices used that title, with a few additions.

Codex 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, where the homily is numbered 20, gives the following inscription: “Here begins [the homily] on almsgiving, and on the place where the Lord Christ sat beside the well of Samaria.” Codex 99 of the same library, where it is numbered homily 34, bears this title: “On almsgiving and the Samaritan woman.” The same title is found in Laurentian Codex X, Plut. XIV, p. 267.

The Sangallensis, however, retained Gennadius’s old heading, entitling homily 20 simply “On almsgiving.” The same title is used by the editors Gymnicus, p. 280; Galesinius, p. 176; Raynaudus, p. 143; and Margarinus, *Bibliotheca Maxima*, vol. VI, p. 43; it is not different in Cumdius, vol. II, p. 554.

But that author, Gillotius, and the Roman editors of the works of Saint Ambrose also numbered this homily among the homilies of that holy Doctor. We have used the title found in Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and in the Laurentian codex.

### ARGUMENT

By presenting many testimonies from the Sacred Scriptures, Saint Maximus commends the merit of almsgiving and tells those for whom greed had been the fire of death that mercy is the fountain of salvation.

Divine Scripture says: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Sirach 3:33). This is plainly a great and universally desirable statement, promising an almost revived benefit to people already dead and dried out by the fire [Note: [Col. 0478D] Codex 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads “by the sores” instead of “by the fire.”] of their sins: when almsgiving intervenes, refreshment is poured into those who are parched, just as water supplies moisture to things nearly dead.

That is, miserable people who had dried up in sins [Note: [Col. 0478D] Codex 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Laurentian Codex 10 read, “who had withered in sins unto death”; Codex 99 reads, “who had withered in death through sins,” etc.] may be restored to life through almsgiving; and mercy may be a fountain of salvation for those for whom greed had been the fire of death. Thus they may extinguish by generosity the flames they had kindled for themselves by sinning.

By a more profitable exchange, the person who once gave money to commit adultery may now spend money so that he may cease to be an adulterer; and the person who once bought sin for himself may in a certain sense buy innocence for himself.

For the Lord says to his disciples: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11). Therefore, although you are polluted and surrounded by many crimes, if you give alms you have begun to become innocent. Almsgiving wipes away what greed had polluted; and the stain you acquired by seizing another’s possessions you cleanse by distributing your own.

See, then, what grace belongs to mercy: it is the one and only virtue that redeems all sins. Let us examine the interpretation of the divine statement itself, so that we may understand what almsgiving is compared with. It says: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.”

Water, therefore, is compared with mercy. But I find water proceeding from the fountain of mercy [Note: [Col. 0478D] Laurentian Codex 10 reads, “proceeding from the fountain of mercy.”]; I must seek the fountain of mercy. Plainly, I find the fountain of mercy: the fountain of which the prophet says, “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 36). It is that fountain, I say, which, as we recently heard read, asks the Samaritan woman for water in the Gospel, but forgives sins; rejects the water of the well, but grants the fountain of everlasting life [Note: [Col. 0478D] The codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Laurentian Codex 10 read, “for he himself is the fountain of mercy, of which the prophet says,” etc.].

For he says: “Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks from the water that I shall give him will never thirst” (John 4).

The Savior therefore asks the woman for water and pretends to be thirsty, so that he may grant eternal grace to those who thirst. For the fountain could not thirst; nor could he in whom there is living water draw up a stream of earthly dregs.

Was Christ thirsty? Certainly he was thirsty—not for human drink, but for salvation; he thirsted not for the water of the world, but for the redemption of the human race.

In a wondrous manner, then, the fountain, sitting beside the well, pours forth streams of mercy there, and the wave of its living channel purifies a woman who was fornicating with a sixth man, who was no longer her husband but her adulterer. In a new kind of marvel, the woman who had come to the well of Samaria as a prostitute returns chaste from Christ’s fountain [Col. 0479B]. She had come to ask for water but carried away chastity.

Immediately, when the Lord disclosed her sins, she recognized them, confessed Christ, and announced the Savior. Leaving behind her water jar, she did not carry a jar back to the city but brought back grace. She appears to return empty in the burden she carries, but she returns full of holiness.

Full, I say, she returns: she who had come as a sinner returns as a preacher [Col. 0480A]. She who had left behind the jar carried back the fullness of Christ, causing no loss to her city. For although she did not bring water to her fellow citizens, she brought in the fountain of salvation [Col. 0477D]. Thus, sanctified through faith in Christ, the woman returned home.

It is about her, I think, that the prophet said: “Such is the way of an adulterous woman” (Proverbs 30): “When she has washed herself, she says that she has done nothing wrong.” This was plainly said about her. After she had been washed in the Savior’s fountain, she no longer remembered the vices of her sins; she assumed the power of preaching. Having wiped away her stains with living water, she was drawn to evangelize not by a conscience holding her back because of sin, but by the warmth of faith compelling her.

She says that she has done nothing wicked while she becomes a messenger of truth; in the forgetfulness of her former shame she denies her immodesty, while in devotion she preaches chastity.

For this is the virtue of Christ the Lord: although a person is a sinner, if he washes himself in Christ’s water, he is restored anew as a virgin, remembers nothing of what he did before, and, through a rebirth that revives him, displays the innocence of infancy and does not acknowledge the crimes of youth. Thus, through faith in Christ, the person who was an adulterer through the corruption of sin becomes a virgin.

## HOMILY XCVIII. On Almsgiving and on the Same Samaritan Woman II

[Col. 0479]

### ADMONITION

As Gennadius testifies, as we said in the preceding admonition, that the holy bishop Maximus of Turin discussed almsgiving, and since several codices also bear the name of Maximus at the beginning of this homily, it is extremely probable that no one other than Maximus was its author.

Such codices are the Sangallensis, number 78; Codex 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, number 21; and Laurentian Codex X, Plut. XIV. In these the homily is entitled “On almsgiving and the Samaritan woman.” The very old Ambrosian codex also attributes it to him, with the title “On the same subject.”

Gymnicus, p. 287; Galesinius, p. 177; Raynaudus, p. 144; and Margarinus, *Bibliotheca Maxima*, vol. VI, p. 46, title it “The second homily on the subject treated above.”

### ARGUMENT

From the conversion of the Samaritan woman, Saint Maximus, the holy Doctor, argues for the clemency of divine mercy in forgiving human crimes. Flowing from Christ as from a fountain, this mercy, especially through the power of baptism, brings about the grace of regeneration.

Your Reverence remembers that, a few days ago, when we were preaching to you about almsgiving, we first wished to seek the origin of mercies;

[Note: Manuscripts 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and X of the Laurentian Library omit “a few.”] and, having discovered their source among the virtues, we showed that the filth of the Samaritan woman had been better washed away by Christ’s water than cleansed by the water of Samaria, and that mercy had wiped away sins more thoroughly than the well. Mercy plainly removes stains more thoroughly than a well, because the water of a well washes only the skin of the body, whereas the goodness of mercy purifies the inner parts of the soul.

We also demonstrated that this evangelical woman corresponded to that prophetic prostitute who, after washing herself with living water, rejoices in the brightness of purity, having been possessed by forgetfulness of her wickedness. For the prophet would not speak such a judgment about a prostitute of this world, whose pollution is not only not washed away by water but even pollutes whatever she touches, as the Apostle says: “He who joins himself to a prostitute is one body” (1 Cor. 6:16). If by her touch she makes one body and pours her disgrace into the members joined to her, how can she herself purify anyone, when she pollutes? Let us therefore investigate more carefully who this prostitute is, who this Samaritan woman is, whose adulterous filth the fountain of Christ has washed away.

[Note: Cardinal Baronius writes in the *Apparatus to the Ecclesiastical Annals*, no. 118, that from the earliest times the Church was accustomed, in calculating the years from the creation of the world to Christ, to follow the Septuagint version rather than the Hebrew text. Hence the early Fathers—Justin, Irenaeus, Eusebius, and Epiphanius—did not depart from this reckoning. Why then should it be surprising if Maximus likewise placed the end of idolatry and abominations in the sixth thousandth year? For through Christ the light of truth shone upon the world, and he came to wash away the stains of all. Even now, in the Roman Martyrology, the year of Christ’s birth is announced according to the ancient custom, because at the time when it was published the Roman Church was using the Septuagint version; and, as Baronius says, it is established that both the Western and Eastern Churches followed it. Thus the Martyrology reads: “In the five thousand ninety-ninth year from the creation of the world, when in the beginning God created heaven and earth,” and so forth. Nevertheless, as Natalis Alexander rightly observes in his second dissertation, section 1, this discrepancy does not harm religion, since the Church is not particularly concerned with how many years before Christ the world was actually created. Yet among the many divergent opinions of chronologists concerning the year in which Christ was born, the Usserian epoch, which places the Lord’s birth toward the end of the four-thousandth year from the creation of the world, is preferred by many writers. See Mamachi, *On the Origin and Antiquity of Christianity*, book II, chapter 4, §2. It remains to explain why Maximus said that the Gentiles were subject to fornications in the sixth thousandth year, as though idolatry, together with all vices, had not reigned long before. For we learn from Scripture that in the time of Moses the Hebrews sacrificed to a calf cast from gold; moreover, we read that Isaac commanded Jacob not to take a wife from the daughters of Canaan, because they served false gods, and that Rachel had stolen the idols of her father Laban. It must indeed be admitted that superstitious worship had dominated all peoples long before Christ; but when the Romans had extended their empire throughout the earth and had everywhere endeavored to introduce their false religion, Christ’s birth is assigned to the sixth thousandth year of the world, that is, about the year 749 from the founding of Rome. Therefore Saint Maximus said that the Church, gathered from the Gentiles, consisted of those who had been unhappily lost in the crimes and blindness of idolatry. In truth, besides all pagan writers, Saint Luke also bears witness that the whole world obeyed the rule of Caesar Augustus, in chapter 2, where he mentions the edict of that Caesar commanding a census of the entire world: “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered.” Indeed, the Evangelist also mentions another census, previously conducted by the governor Cyrinus, or, as others prefer, Quirinius; and they find this distinction between the one census and the other: in the first, the number of subject peoples was recorded to gratify the ambitious prince who boasted of possessing dominion over all nations; in the second, all households are said to have been registered, and a tax was imposed upon them. Monilia, *On the Year of Christ*, dissertation 1, should be consulted; he concludes the matter as follows: “We consider it more probable that the census mentioned by Saint Luke was carried out in the year 749 from the founding of Rome, when Roman affairs were everywhere peaceful among the nations and the gates of Janus were closed.”]

I think that this woman is the Church gathered from the Gentiles.
