After five thousand years had passed, when in the sixth thousandth year she was subject to the fornications of idols, she washed away all her disgrace when the fountain of Christ arrived, wiped away by faith in the Savior the stains she had contracted through adulterous sacrileges, and, abandoning her former ancestral course like an empty water jar,

[Note: The two manuscripts cited read “her former worship of the fathers.”]

announced the Lord’s coming to the whole world. This, I say, is that prostitute who, after being washed, says that she did nothing wicked. For after the Church had been cleansed by the splendor of baptism, she does not remember the impiety of the devil; she rejoices in the religion of truth, and, having been made a virgin from a prostitute, she does not remember her former crimes,

[Note: Both manuscripts read “she does not remember her former crimes.”]

but glories in her integrity.

The prophet therefore says: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.”

We often see this happen, when poured-out water quenches blazing fires. But conversely, we sometimes see immense masses of fire consume streams of water, and, as though receiving fuel from the water, grow stronger with renewed flames, so that the water seems not to have extinguished the fires but to have increased them. What is that water which consumes flames without itself being consumed?

[Note: Manuscript 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem supplies the missing wording; manuscript X of the Laurentian Library agrees with it.]

I think it is the water that flows from Christ’s fountain in the bath of baptism: it is not consumed by sinners but consumes the fires of Gehenna. When it is poured into human beings through baptism, it extinguishes both the heat in them and the burning of Tartarus. It plainly lives in human beings, as the Lord says: “The water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up” (John 4:14), and so forth.

[Note: Thus manuscript 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem; the Laurentian manuscript agrees exactly. Galesinius reads: “Christ, the water, wonderfully,” and so forth.]

It is therefore marvelous how the water of Christ, through one and the same operation, both gives life and extinguishes: it gives life to souls and extinguishes sins; it restores these through the refreshment of its bath, while it consumes those through the flood of its torrent. And, for the greater grace of baptism, the mystery is celebrated among those above, while Gehenna is extinguished among those below:

[Note: The Laurentian manuscript reads “he celebrated the ministry among those above.”]

here the waters flow, and there the fire grows cool; here a human being is immersed in the fountain, and there he is freed from Tartarus.

Nor is it surprising that in the sacrament of baptism hell is opened, since heaven too is then unlocked. For these elements are opened so that freedom and grace may come together at Christ’s bath. Freedom is granted to those who will rise again; grace to those who will reign. The former are rescued from punishment; the latter are taken up into glory. Those who were slaves of sin become free for righteousness; those who were held by the distress of the world receive the delights of paradise. In Christ’s baptism, therefore, the heavens are opened, and Tartarus is opened as well: the Holy Spirit may come from there, and the Savior’s mercy may descend there; life may be brought down from heaven, and death destroyed in Tartarus.

Thus almsgiving extinguishes sins, just as the water of baptism extinguishes the fire of Gehenna:

[Note: Manuscript 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads “extinguishes.”]

therefore almsgiving is, in a certain sense, another bath for souls, so that if someone should sin after baptism through human weakness, he may still have the means to be cleansed again through almsgiving, as the Lord says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41). I say this without prejudice to faith: almsgiving is more lenient than the bath. The bath is given once and promises forgiveness once; but whenever you give alms, you earn forgiveness.

These, then, are the two fountains of mercies: they grant life and forgive sins. Whoever preserves both will be enriched with the honor of the heavenly kingdom; but whoever, after staining the living fountain, has recourse to the streams of mercy will himself obtain mercy.

# HOMILY XCIX. On Hospitality

[Col. 0481]

## ADMONITION

Gennadius also testified that this homily, *On Hospitality*, was by Saint Maximus; and the scribes of the manuscripts agree with him: Sangallensis manuscript 32; manuscript 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, homily 18; and manuscript 99 of the same library, homily 35. In the Sangallensis manuscript and in manuscript 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, only *On Hospitality* is read; but in the older manuscript 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “Here begins [the homily] on hospitality in the Gospel.” To these we add manuscript X, Pluteus XIV, page 268, of the Laurentian Library, which, omitting the word “Here begins,” has the same title as manuscript 90 of the Holy Cross.

[Col. 0483]

The shorter title of manuscript 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, *On Hospitality*, pleased the editors Gymnicus, page 291; Galesinius, page 178; Raynaudus, page 244; and Margarine, *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, page 47, and we too have placed it at the head of the homily. Gillotius therefore rashly included this homily as number 32 among the sermons of Saint Ambrose.

[Col. 0483A] **ARGUMENT.**—After Maximus has explained the Gospel’s teaching about choosing earthly hospitality, he passes from the literal sense to the spiritual one. He discloses this by saying that “the Church” is to be understood by the lodging that must never be changed, and “the Savior” by the guest.

Your Holiness has noticed, brothers, how the Gospel reading prescribed the obligations of hospitality among the other virtues the Lord commanded his disciples to practice. For he says: “Into whatever city you enter, ask who in it is worthy; and remain there until you depart” (Matthew 10:11), and so forth. This is plainly a holy and divine saying, which first granted the disciples the option of choosing, yet entirely removed fickleness. For he provided a rule, lest a holy man be hasty in judging or fickle in changing his host. Just as he permitted you the choice,

[Note: Besides the two manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, the Laurentian manuscript X also reads “to us” instead of “to you,” and likewise “he wished us to remain.”]

so he also wished you to maintain constancy.

For how reprehensible it is that a man who announces the Gospel and teaches that one must not go astray should himself begin to wander through various places, abandoning the house to which he had spoken peace and grieving the host upon whom he had bestowed a blessing! Great indeed is the grace of hospitality, and it must not easily be violated. It is open to all and ready for all; it gladly receives the holy and patiently tolerates sinners.

But let us repeat that holy and divine saying itself. If it pleases in the literal sense, perhaps it will please even more in its mystery. He says, then, that when we enter a city, we should ask which guest or which house in it is worthy or suitable, and remain there until the day of departure arrives (Matthew 10:11). This saying grants us a higher understanding. For it does not seem to me that he commanded us to inquire about a guest or house of this world, nor to search so carefully, but rather about one who can preserve us as unoffending and unharmed guests until the day of our departure.

For we quickly harm and offend the host of this world; sometimes we displease him even after three days. We have therefore been commanded to seek a faithful house and a worthy host. What house is more faithful than the Church? What host is more worthy than the Savior? He receives strangers as sons; she refreshes those received by her as infants. This host, as we have experienced, desires to wash the feet of his guests; she hastens to prepare a table. For those whom the Savior refreshes with living water, the Church restores with heavenly food.

The evangelist therefore commanded us to seek this host and ordered us to dwell with him until the day of our departure, lest through some fickleness we perhaps move elsewhere in the meantime. That is: having once believed in Christ, let us not return again like transgressors to idols. For it is written: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24); while he desires to please one, he finds the other angered.

We must not therefore abandon Christ our host, just as the Apostle Peter, when others like him were abandoning the Lord, did not leave him. Rather, let us say to the Savior what he said: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we believe” (John 6:68–69). Behold the executor of heavenly commands: because he did not change Christ’s lodging, he deserved to share with Christ in the heavenly kingdom.

# HOMILY C. On the Eclipse of the Moon I

[Col. 0483]

## ADMONITION

There would be room for doubt about the true author of this homily, since some copies are inscribed with the name of Ambrose and others with that of Augustine, had not the testimony of Gennadius shone like a torch in the darkness. In clear and unambiguous words, he records that Saint Maximus composed, among the works he wrote, a treatise *On the Eclipse of the Moon*. Accordingly, either following Gennadius or some other ancient authority, the scribes of the most distinguished manuscripts—Sangallensis, homily 28; Ambrosianus C 98; and manuscripts 90 and 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem—agree in assigning it to Maximus, all bearing the uniform title *On the Eclipse of the Moon*.

Nothing therefore undermines their agreement: neither Vatican manuscript 4951, page 213, which attributes the homily to Saint Augustine under the title “To those who try to aid the eclipse of the moon with their shouting”; nor Laurentian manuscript X, Pluteus XIV, page 337, which, on the reverse side of this sermon, assigns the praise to Ambrose. Nor can the Paris edition of Ambrose, published in 1569, prevail, in which Gillotius placed this homily among his sermons as number 83. Against him stand Gymnicus, page 293; Galesinius, page 179; Raynaudus, page 245; and Margarine, page 47 of *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, in whose works the title of the homily is *On the Defect of the Moon*.

[Col. 0483C] **ARGUMENT.**—The holy bishop complains that his faithful receive Christian instruction from him without profit, since he does not see them advancing in piety and virtue. He then rebukes their foolishness because, during the eclipse of the moon, they uttered shouts, struck by a vain fear of its obscurity lest it be completely extinguished.

You yourselves also see, brothers, that my humility does not cease laboring with every concern for you and turning you with all haste toward good fruit. Yet the more I labor with you, the more I am confounded by you. For when I see that you make no progress from all my admonitions, my labor is now a cause not of rejoicing but of shame.

The Apostle says: “Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who feeds a flock and does not partake of the milk of the flock?” (1 Corinthians 9:7). Behold, I feed Christ’s flock, yet I cannot obtain the flock’s fruit; I feed the Lord’s flock, yet I receive no nourishment of religious devotion from it.

[Note: The manuscript of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads “the nourishment of religious milk.”]

No sweetness of its faith makes me glad; whatever flows from it is harsh

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “is harsh or bitter.”]

and bitter. For the shepherd of a Christian flock is nourished by its milk when he rejoices in the brightness of its good works.

Who among you, brothers,

[Note: Vatican manuscript 4951 omits “not.”]

would not take it gravely—though I am not speaking of everyone, for there are some among you whom you ought to hold up as examples of religious devotion—

[Note: Vatican manuscript 4951 reads “as an example.”]

who, I ask, would not be distressed that you are so forgetful of your salvation that you sin even with heaven as your witness?

For when a few days ago I reproached you concerning your greed for avarice, on that very day, toward evening, such a great shouting arose from the people that its irreligion penetrated to heaven.

[Note: Vatican manuscript 4951 reads “reached heaven.”]

When I asked what this shouting meant, they told me that your uproar was helping the suffering moon and assisting its eclipse with your cries. I laughed, indeed, and marveled at your foolishness: as though devout Christians, you were bringing aid to God.

[Note: Vatican manuscript 4951 reads “to the moon instead of to God.”]

You were shouting lest, if you remained silent, the element should perish:

[Note: Vatican manuscript 4951 reads “lest God should lose, and so forth.”]

as though he were weak and feeble and, unless supported by your voices, unable to protect the heavenly bodies he had created. You do well, then, to offer assistance to the Divinity, so that, with your help, he may be able to govern the heavens.

But if you wish to do this more fully, you ought to keep watch throughout every night. For how often, while you are sleeping, do you suppose that the moon has suffered violence—and yet has not fallen from the sky? Or does it always suffer an eclipse toward evening?

[Note: Vatican manuscript 4951 reads: “Does it also sometimes suffer it toward dawn?”]

Does it never suffer one around dawn? But among you it is accustomed to suffer only in the evening hours, when the belly is distended by a lavish dinner and the head is shaken by larger cups. The moon therefore suffers among you when wine suffers as well; the moon’s sphere, I say, is disturbed by your songs when your eyes are also disturbed by your cups.

How then, drunkard, can you see what is happening in heaven around the moon, when around you you do not see what is happening on earth?

[Note: Vatican manuscript 4951 reads: “How can you, drunkards, see what is happening in heaven around the moon, when you do not see what is happening on earth around you?”]

This is precisely what Solomon says: “The fool is changed like the moon” (Ecclesiasticus 27:11).

[Note: Vatican manuscript 4951 reads: “You are changed like the moon, having become foolish and senseless at its movement—you who were Christians are truly foolish and truly sacrilegious. For you commit sacrilege against the Creator when you attribute weakness to the Creator. You are therefore changed like the moon: having shone a little earlier with the devotion of faith, afterward you decline through weakness of faith.”]

You are changed like the moon when, though you had been a Christian, you begin, foolish and senseless at its movement, to become sacrilegious. Sacrilege is committed against the Creator when weakness is attributed to the creature.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “against the Creator.”]

You are changed like the moon: though a little earlier you shone with devotion to the faith, afterward you decline through the weakness of unbelief. You are changed like the moon when your brain is so emptied of wisdom

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “as the sphere of the moon is emptied of nocturnal brightness. A small obscurity of clouds covers it; but you are overtaken by the most dreadful darkness of death,” and so forth.]

that you are darkened like the moon.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “as the sphere of the moon is emptied of light; a small obscurity of clouds covers it, but you are overtaken by the most dreadful darkness,” and so forth.]

But would that, foolish man, you were changed like the moon!

[Note: The same Ambrosian manuscript reads: “O foolish man, would that you were now changed like the moon!”]

For it quickly returns to its fullness; may you, even if late, return to wisdom. It swiftly gathers again the light it had lost; may you, even if not quickly, receive again the faith you denied. Your change, therefore, is more serious than the moon’s: the moon suffers a loss of light, but you suffer a loss of salvation.

How well it is written concerning the wise man:

[Note: The manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Vatican manuscript 4951, and the Laurentian manuscript read: “How well it is written: ‘The fool is changed like the moon,’ because it is written concerning the wise man: ‘And he will remain with the sun,’ and so forth.”]

“And he will remain with the sun” (Psalm 71:5).

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript omits “And.”]

For the wise man remains with the sun; through steadfastness of faith he remains with the Savior.

But someone may say: “Then does the moon not suffer?” It certainly suffers; we cannot deny it. But it suffers together with the other creatures, as the Apostle says: “Every creature groans and labors in childbirth until now” (Romans 8:22), and below: “The creature itself will also be set free from the slavery of corruption,” and so forth.

“It will be set free,” he says, “from slavery.” You see, then, that the moon does not suffer because of songs but because of service; it does not suffer through dangers but through duties; it does not suffer in order to perish but in order to serve. “For the creature was subjected to vanity, not willingly” (ibid.), and so forth.

Therefore the moon is changed from its state unwillingly, whereas you willingly change from your understanding. It is led into its diminution by the condition of its nature; you are dragged into your ruin by your will.

I do not want you, brother, to be like the moon when it wanes; be as it is when it is full and perfect. For it is written concerning the righteous: “He shall endure like the moon forever, and as a faithful witness in heaven” (Psalm 88:38).

# HOMILY CI. On the Same Subject II

[Col. 0485]

## ADMONITION

Once the authorship of the homily just published had been recognized as Saint Maximus’s, anyone who pays attention can see from the similar manner of writing and the connection of the subject matter that this homily too was composed by the same author. The same manuscripts support this attribution—namely, Sangallensis manuscript 29, the Ambrosian manuscript, and manuscript 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, page 277—which transmitted the earlier homily to posterity under Saint Maximus’s name.

We have already said that Mabillon first extracted this homily from the Sangallensis manuscript and published it as number 6 in the *Museo Italico*. In its preface we noted that this homily, like the preceding one, rests on the testimony of Gennadius, who said that Maximus had written *On the Eclipse of the Moon*. Gallandius also transferred it into his collection, as he did the other works of the *Museo Italico*, but without consulting the Ambrosian manuscript, from which we obtained several variant readings and added them to Mabillon’s text.

[Col. 0487A] **ARGUMENT.**—Maximus writes that he had urged the brothers to abandon pagan error and understand that the moon’s rising and eclipse persist by reason rather than by weakness. He teaches that the moon contains a great mystery, since Christ and his Church are compared to it.

A few days ago, brothers, we spoke against those who thought that the moon could be drawn down from heaven by the songs of magicians. We also refuted the foolishness of those who suffer no less an eclipse of mind than that heavenly body suffers an eclipse of light.

We urged them to abandon pagan error and return to wisdom as quickly as the moon returns to its fullness;

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “it turns back,” and so forth.]

and, just as it quickly gathers the light it had lost, so let them hasten to receive the faith they had denied.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “so that” instead of “and.”]

Having laid aside the cloud of folly, let them begin to judge light not by the eye of the body but by that of the mind, and understand that its rising and eclipse persist by reason rather than by weakness.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has “its risings and eclipses” in the plural.]

This change would never be so great in all things unless this reason had been assigned to it by the Creator.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “which would never bring about such a great change in all things unless this reason had been bestowed upon them by the Creator.”]

Behold the element of the sea: when the moon wanes, it withdraws; when the moon increases, it swells, so that at its motion either the waves retreat into themselves or the streams cannot contain themselves.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “or the waters do not contain themselves.”]

Thus, whenever the moon changes in light, the seas change in their waves.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “the sea changes in its waves.”]

Finally, the swimming creatures of the sea are said to be fuller in their flesh when the moon is full, and exhausted and diminished when it wanes. Great, then, is the moon’s rational principle, and great its excellence: by its power it diminishes the elements and then fills them again; it fills them in such a way that they are diminished once more.

Clearly, the alternation is pleasing through its varied cycles, as restoration reaches completion. Everyone knows how much increase it gives to the earth, and how much dew it bestows upon the forests, which the sun’s heat has scorched during the day.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “while it restores the groves with nocturnal dew.”]

With a kind of wonder, it supplies moisture in clear weather to things burning with heat.

[Note: The same Ambrosian manuscript reads “to things burning.”]

By a new kind of process, the moon’s illumination causes clear weather to make the earth moist.

Great, then, is the moon’s rational principle—indeed, a great mystery. It empties itself of light so that it may restore the whole universe with moisture and rain.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript omits “and rain.”]

So too Christ the Lord emptied himself of divinity so that he might fill human beings with immortality.

Hence the blessed Apostle says: “Although he was established in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7).

Christ therefore emptied himself so that he might bestow life upon human beings; he emptied himself so that he might bring increase to the elements.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “The moon empties itself so that it may provide increase to the elements.”]

But we read concerning the Savior that he himself is rather the sun of righteousness. How, then, do we compare him with the movements of the moon? These luminaries are not far apart; they correspond to one another.

For the moon, through a kind of fraternal fellowship, receives light from the sun, and, struck by the rays of its light, receives the splendor of its own brightness. Therefore, if Christ the Lord is more properly compared with the sun,

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “What else but the Church shall we compare with the moon?”]

we shall compare the moon only with the Church. For, like the moon, so that it may shine among the nations, the Church borrows light from the sun of righteousness and from Christ’s rays—that is, reflected by the preaching of the apostles, it acquires from him the splendor of immortality.

The Church shines not by its own light but by the Savior’s, and radiates not with its own brilliance but with that of the Father, as the Apostle says: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20); and again: “So that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29).

The Church is rightly compared with the moon, because it too drenches us with the dew of the bath and gives life to the earth of our body through the dew of baptism.

The Church is rightly compared with the moon because it too gains increase and suffers eclipse.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “because it too has its risings and suffers its eclipses. It is diminished,” and so forth.]

It is often diminished and frequently enlarged: it is diminished by persecutions and expanded by preaching.

[Note: The same Ambrosian manuscript reads: “It decreases when it is bereaved of children.”]

It decreases when it loses children; it grows when it is crowned with martyrs. The very cause that brings it diminution also supplies its increase. For often those whom it mourns as persecutors it receives as confessors.

How often do you suppose that it, like the moon, has suffered from the songs of magicians?

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “How often do you suppose that they tried it, like the moon, with the songs of magicians? How often did evil arts wish to draw it down from the heavenly kingdom,” and so forth.]

How often have evil arts wished to draw it down from the kingdom of heaven?

For first the magicians Jannes and Jambres, when they resisted Moses with signs and wonders, were seeking to overthrow the Church; but the song of the sorcerers could not harm it amid sacred utterances. Incantations have no power where Christ’s song is sung.

Then, when Simon Magus attacked the Apostle Paul before Sergius Paulinus, the proconsul,

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript and manuscript 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read “Paul,” not “Paulinus.” This reading agrees with the text of Acts 13:7.]

he was attempting to shake the vessel of the Church and wished to assail him with magical arts. But he was convicted by Paul with such power that Paul not only exposed the weakness of his art but also blinded him by taking away his sight; thus he deprived him at once of both his incantation and his vision. He did not deserve to have bodily eyes who had no eyes of the mind.

What, moreover, shall we say about the Apostle Peter? When Simon again disturbed the foundations of the Church in the city of Rome, Peter struck him down by the solidity of his prayers. For when Simon, lifted up by magical arts, had even flown through the air,

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “He cast him down by the power of his faith, so that he fell all the farther the higher he had flown.”]

Peter cast him down by his power, so that he fell all the farther the higher he had flown.

For Peter, truly a rock as solid as stone,

[Note: The same Ambrosian manuscript reads: “For Peter, like a solid rock of stone,” and so forth.]

crushed him by the impact of his fall, so that the man who promised himself the heavenly kingdoms perished through the harshness of earthly death.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “perished through the harshness of earthly death.”]

*The end.*

# HOMILY CII. On the Words Written in Isaiah, Chapter I: “Your Tavern-Keepers Mix Water with Wine”

## ADMONITION

This same title is found in Gennadius’s catalogue of the works of Saint Maximus. If nothing more could be brought forward in support of its authenticity, that alone would be sufficient. But the testimony of three outstanding manuscripts also agrees with Gennadius: Sangallensis, homily 82; and both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, in whose older manuscript 90 it is homily 26, and in manuscript 99 homily 82. All bear the corresponding title: “Here begins [the homily] on what the prophet says to the children of Israel: ‘Your tavern-keepers mix water with wine.’”

All other manuscripts lack this homily. Gillotius reprinted it in his edition of Ambrose as sermon number 78. The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, however, in their preface to the sermons of the same Saint, Bishop of Milan, declared that nothing else should be thought concerning the homily on the first chapter of Isaiah than what Gennadius wrote. The same opinion was held by Gymnicus, page 297; Galesinius, page 180; Raynaudus, page 246; and Margarine in *Bibliotheca Maxima*, volume VI, page 48, all of whom concluded their collection of Saint Maximus’s homilies with this one.

[Col. 0489B] **ARGUMENT.**—Teaching that Isaiah’s words must be explained mystically, Maximus says that the prophet is speaking of tavern-keepers who preside over churches, not over taverns. He accuses them of mixing the appearance of water into wine when they take delight in worldly pleasures and insert base things into sacred matters. He also demonstrates in what manner the priests of the Jews mixed water with wine.

Not long ago [Note: Both Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscripts omit “a few.”] we explained that this priestly office retains a certain character of business and that the clerical office is no small commercial enterprise. It is plainly no small profit when the gain acquired is not money but souls; it is a great transaction when the redemption of a human being is secured not by counting out a price [Note: Both Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscripts read: “not by reckoning the price, but by reckoning the commandment.”] but by proclaiming a commandment. For Christ’s commandment is a precious talent [Col. 0489C], by which salvation is purchased and life redeemed; and redemption is great when a price is given although no money is seen. The Savior’s commandment is therefore a great talent, which, entrusted to capable people, can yield profit, but in the hands of the negligent can be lost. To some it is returned with multiplied grace; from others it is demanded with interest in punishments.

For Christ must require the talent that he entrusts, and must return grace to the one who repays it, and subject the one who does not repay to injuries. He does indeed subject him to injuries according to the custom of the world: just as a debtor who cannot satisfy the debt by restoring his property satisfies it at least by the punishment of his body. This talent, brothers, we entrust by our preaching to your hearts, so that we may designate to the Lord some profit from your salvation. We shall have to give an account of how our preaching advances and how your obedience bears fruit. For the Gospel is not proclaimed without reason, nor does the Apostle cry out, nor do priests speak: whoever hears the holy voice will either be blessed through devotion or found guilty through the testimony brought against him. We speak of blessedness to believers; we bear witness to judgment against criminals.

The administration of priests is therefore a commercial enterprise. Hence the prophet says to the children of Israel: “Your tavern-keepers mix water with wine” (Isaiah 1). Isaiah the holy prophet is not speaking of those tavern-keepers who, serving in public establishments, adulterate the appearance of pure wine with a fraudulent mixture of water [341]—for this could not have concerned the blessed man in the manner of a judge of the world, asking why, with the vessels of taverns corrupted, the people should drink a less intoxicating beverage—but he is certainly speaking of those tavern-keepers who preside over churches, not taverns; who offer thirsty peoples not the cup of desire but the cup of virtue; who serve not the drink of drunkenness but the cup of the Savior.

The prophet therefore censures and rebukes these tavern-keepers, and complains that they mix water with wine. He reproves them because, although they were leaders of divine offices, they became followers of human affairs, just as the prophet himself says: “Let each of you pursue his own house” (Haggai 1). Any priest who, having abandoned the duty of the episcopate, delights in the pleasures of the world mixes water with wine—that is, he inserts cheap and cold things into holy and fervent things.

We may also understand the passage in this way: the same priests of the Jews mixed water with wine when they did not receive the Lord Savior as God [Note: Both Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscripts read: “they did not receive him as God, but judged him as a human being.”] but judged him as a human being, and wished to introduce something turbid and filthy into his sincere and pure divinity, saying to him: “Although you are a human being, you make yourself God” (John 10); and again: “We were not born of prostitution” (ibid. 6). While they excuse themselves from the adultery of prostitution, they attempt to adulterate him in the divinity of his birth.

But let us examine more carefully what he means by saying: “They mix water with wine” (Luke 5). We read that wine is especially abundant in the Church, as it is said in the Gospel (Matthew 2; Luke 5): “New wine must be put into new wineskins”—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit must be bestowed upon new people, the newly baptized. If, then, the precious and spiritual grace of wine abounds in the Church, to what else should the cheap and foul water be referred except to the Synagogue? For the water of the Synagogue is foul: by its baptism it does not wash away sins but acquires them; it does not purify a person by its own washing but pollutes him.

Finally, just as the Church is honored in wineskins, so the Synagogue is cast out with a skin of water. [Col. 0491A] For that Hagar who bore the type of the Synagogue, concerning whom it is said to Abraham, “Cast out the slave woman and her son” (Genesis 21), was cast out from the tents not with wine but with a skin of water. Certainly Abraham’s household was rich, prosperous, and abundant. Yet she received neither wine, nor oil, nor bread, which are the strongest nourishments of life; and the Synagogue did not receive the nourishment of upright life because it does not know the life that is Christ. The sick person is dragged along by water alone, and the weakened person is sustained by it. For it was fitting that she who was not worthy to receive the nourishment of the living should at least receive the solace of one who is dying.

The priests of the Jews are therefore rebuked when they wished to mix the rejected and already disapproved water of the Synagogue with the precious ecclesiastical wine. Water is not ordinarily mixed in the Church but changed, just as the Lord, invited to a wedding, did not mix the jars full of water with wine but changed the water into wine. For, lest anything of Jewish cheapness remain in the holy banquet, he preferred to change its nature rather than adulterate its substance.

## HOMILY 103. On the Calends of the Pagans

[Col. 0491]

### ADMONITION

The proper and fitting title of this homily is not the one copied from the Sangallensis manuscript by Mabillon, its first editor in *Museo Italico*, part 2, no. 5—namely, “On the January Calends,” a title later followed by Gallandius. It should instead have been copied from the Ambrosian manuscript, where it reads: “On the Calends of the Pagans.” For in this homily Saint Maximus attacks the Saturnalian games, whose beginning, according to the ancient Roman custom, was on December 17 and which were celebrated for three or five days, depending on the differing opinions of writers.

The entire homily “On the January Calends” contains a vehement denunciation of that day’s obscenities and of masked men transformed into beasts. In the present homily, however, he condemns the intemperance and disgracefulness of the banquets to which the pagans devoted themselves during the Saturnalian games, and he disapproves the greed of the wealthy, who received New Year’s gifts and presents from slaves and clients.

The principal argument of this homily—and one that clearly proves that Saint Maximus preached it before the Nativity of the Lord—is drawn from its opening. He commends God’s providence because he arranged for Christ the Lord to arise in the midst of pagan festivals, to disperse their dark superstitions by the light of his divinity, and by his coming to bring true joy and happiness to the world. Such pagan festivals had therefore been established in the months of December and January and were conducted with the greatest display—not so much of noise as of vice. Christians, filled with more joyful rejoicing and holier gifts, ought to shrink from them.

Having restored the homily’s true title, I shall add, for its particular commendation, that other Fathers—Ambrose, Augustine, Leo the Great, and Peter Chrysologus—delivered sermons against the superstition of the January Calends; but only Maximus preached learnedly and vehemently in order to turn the faithful away from the Saturnalian games.

[Col. 0491B] **ARGUMENT.**—Saint Maximus severely reproaches the superstitious observance of the Saturnalia and the Calends, which still prevailed among Christian peoples, and writes that it ought especially to be condemned and avoided by those who honor the mystery of the Lord’s Nativity.

It was, in a certain sense, wisely arranged by God’s providence that Christ the Lord should arise in the midst of pagan festivals and that, amid the very darkness of superstitious errors, the splendor of the true light should shine forth. Thus, perceiving that the righteousness of the pure Divinity had appeared amid their various superstitions, people might forget their past sacrileges and refrain from honoring those of the future.

For what wise person who honors the mystery of the Lord’s Nativity would not condemn the drunkenness of the Saturnalia and avoid the wantonness of the Calends? And, desiring to have a share with Christ, who would not refuse to share with the world? This is the rule of divine worship: whoever has entered into fellowship with pagan vanity cannot have union with the truth of the saints. The blessed Apostle says: “What partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?” (2 Corinthians 6). [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “That is, a Christian cannot at the same time practice the luxury of iniquity and have the God of righteousness pleased with him.”]

Yet there are many who, carrying over the custom of an ancient superstition of vanity, arrange for the day of the Calends as though it were the greatest festival. They wish to have such joy that it becomes rather a source of sorrow. [Col. 0492B] They behave so wantonly and gorge themselves so on wine and banquets that the person who has been chaste and temperate throughout the year is drunken and polluted on that day. Unless he acts in this way, he thinks he has lost the festival [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “through such festivals he has lost his salvation.”] because he does not understand that through such festivals he has lost his salvation.

What shall we say about the custom by which people rise early and go out in public, each one with a little gift—that is, with New Year’s presents—and, intending to greet their friends, greet them with a reward before a kiss? They offer lips to lips and join hand to hand, not to return affection but to pay homage to avarice; by one and the same service they embrace a friend and defraud him.

Judge for yourselves what sort of kiss this is when it is for sale. The more dearly it is purchased, the more cheaply it is valued. How many people will be judged unworthy of a kiss before the gold of the wealthy? Once gold has shone in the right hand, it makes them worthy through plunder, not through favor.

And what is more unjust amid this very injustice than that the inferior is expected to give to the superior, and that a poor man is compelled to give generously to a rich man when perhaps he borrows what he is to give? They even call this generosity “New Year’s gifts,” although the surviving text continues incompletely, “although what is more onerous …” [lacuna]. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript says: “They call them New Year’s gifts, although there is no New Year’s gift. He is compelled, I say, to give what he does not have and to offer a present for which he leaves his children liable.”]. [Col. 0492C] He is compelled, I say, poor man, to give what he does not have and to offer a gift for which he leaves his children liable.

The rich, too, are generous with this generosity; yet they themselves do not seem free from sin. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “For the rich man gives a solidus to anyone who is wealthy, while he disdains to give a denarius to a beggar; and on the Calends he hastens to his friend’s house laden with gold…”] For the rich man gives to anyone who is wealthy, while he disdains to give a denarius to a beggar. On the Calends he hastens to his friend’s house laden with gold, although on the Lord’s Nativity he comes empty and destitute to the church.

You see, therefore, that among most people present flattery counts for more than future reward. They prefer the kiss of a superior to the glory of the Savior. That kiss ought not to be called a kiss, because it is for sale. Judas Iscariot also kissed the Lord with such a kiss, but by this means he was attempting to hand him over [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript conveys this sense: “He kissed him here, and sold him there.”].

What shall we say about the custom by which, after the intervening day, people go out of the city with such an empty beginning, as though they were beginning to live, in order to gather omens and investigate everything, and thereafter measure out for themselves either the prosperity [Col. 0494A] or the sorrow of the entire coming year? Although these practices are foolish and ridiculous, they are also useless or harmful to the very people who perform them. They do not possess prosperity, since they are deceived by auguries; they always possess sorrow, since they are anxious, through remembering everything, lest those things come to pass.

They add this to their evils: as though returning home after taking auspices, they carry little branches in their hands, evidently as an omen, so that they may return to their lodging laden with something. The wretches do not understand that they indeed return laden—not with a burden of gifts but with a heap of sins.

*The end.*

## HOMILY 104. It Begins: On Heretics Who Sell Sins

[Col. 0493]

### ADMONITION

Mabillon found a homily bearing this title in the Sangallensis manuscript, no. 80, without the author’s name. But since it appeared to that distinguished man to be inserted among the other homilies of Maximus and its style was entirely consistent with them, he decided that it should be attributed to Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, rather than to another author. He was the first to publish it, together with the other newly discovered homilies, as no. 9; Gallandius followed him.

We have likewise followed their examples, while noting what we mentioned in the preface concerning this homily: namely, that the heretics against whose audacity and impiety Maximus directed his attack should be regarded as a kind of offspring of the Manichaeans who were spreading through Italy.

[Col. 0493B] **ARGUMENT.**—First the holy bishop warns Christians not to devote their anxiety to acquiring temporal goods. Then he earnestly exhorts them to seek faith, justice, and charity. Finally he attacks those heretics who, after receiving money, used to forgive sins.

We must always remember and keep before our eyes, dearly beloved brothers, that the Lord Jesus Christ descended to earth from heaven for this reason: to bestow eternal life upon us. Although he was the Son of God, he chose to become the son of a human being so that he might make us, who were human beings, children of God.

He did not work so great a mystery for the sake of this present life, which is brief, fleeting, and mortal, but for the sake of that life which is perpetual and eternal. For God was not going to grant us a long duration of this life, which is full of hardships, labors, and poverty, lest he provide not so much a lengthening of life as a perpetuity of labor. Its only apparent remedy is that it is brief. Hence the Apostle says: “If in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are more pitiable than all human beings” (1 Corinthians 15).

We must not therefore hope in Christ only in this life, in which evil people can accomplish more than good people; in which those who are worse are more fortunate and those who live more criminally prosper more. For what good does this life possess? Honors, riches, and health—things which, although fleeting, do not come in accordance with merit but occur by chance.

How many do we see whom not uprightness but power has made honored? How many have acquired riches not left to them by their parents but seized through bloodshed? How many possess bodily health but are not governed by God’s mercy, instead growing fat on the blood of beasts? These things, therefore, because they are temporal and worthless, are bestowed indiscriminately upon anyone without merit or judgment; for they were given not as a reward but as a temptation.

We, then, to whom eternal life is promised, must always possess and seek eternal goods—that is, faith, justice, and charity. These goods have their adversaries; and although such gifts cannot be bestowed by human beings, they are frequently taken away by wicked people.

For this reason we must be concerned and watchful about the good of faith, and always be armed for its protection by devotion of mind, not quickly believing deceptive flatteries. The enemy is accustomed to creep in under the pretext of peace: that is, under the name of Christian, a heretic enters secretly. To deceive simple people, he carries Christ on his lips but bears the devil in his heart; he confesses him with his tongue but blasphemes him in his mind.

We must therefore avoid him completely and join him in no association. For if he is an enemy of the Lord, how can he be a friend of his servants?

We should not be surprised that heretics of this kind have begun to stray into our region. The wolf that lies in wait always follows a flock of sheep; the deceiving devil always attacks the Christian assembly. This happens beneficially, so that, through more watchful guardianship, neither the sheep may leave the flock nor the Christian abandon the Church.

Hence the Apostle says: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Corinthians 11)—as though he were saying: Christians must have a struggle over the faith so that those who are approved may have a certain victory.

But, leaving their blasphemies aside for the moment, let us disclose what their rules of life are. Their leaders, whom they call presbyters, are said to have this sort of command: if one of the laity confesses that he has committed a crime, the presbyter should not say to him, “Do penance; lament your deeds; mourn your sins,” but should say, “Give me this much for your crime, and you will be forgiven.”

Clearly vain and foolish is the presbyter who, when he himself receives the spoils, thinks that Christ forgives the sin. Does he not know that the Savior is accustomed to forgive sins and to seek precious tears, not counted-out money, in payment for wrongdoing? Hence he himself says: “You receive freely; give freely” (Malachi 10). [Note: Gallandius’s edition reads: “You have received freely.”]

Finally, when Peter sinned by denying the Lord three times, he obtained pardon not through gifts but through tears. The Evangelist says of him: “He wept most bitterly” (Luke 22:62; Matthew [Col. 0496A] 26:75). You see, I say, that with Christ the measure lies in tears, not in gifts. As gravely as he wept for his fault, so quickly did he obtain forgiveness.

The presbyter therefore receives gifts and, by a certain agreement, promises indulgence from the Savior. What a foolish bargain, in which it is said that the person who has given more to the priest has offended the Lord less! With such teachers, the rich are always innocent and the poor always criminal. How can a poor person make satisfaction for an offense when he does not have what he can offer for his sin?

## HOMILY 105. It Begins: That Clerics Ought Not to Engage in Business

[Col. 0495]

### ADMONITION

Mabillon thought that this homily was connected with the one we published above as no. 102, “On What Is Written in Isaiah, Chapter 1: ‘Your tavern-keepers mix water with wine,’” in which Saint Maximus discusses the ministry of the altar and teaches that the priesthood is a commercial enterprise not of riches but of souls.

Since the same subject is taken up here and secular business dealings by clerics are likewise rejected, no one can doubt that this homily should be assigned to the same Maximus. In addition to the authority of the Sangallensis manuscript and the judgments of Mabillon and Gallandius, who published it again, there is the testimony of manuscript 90 of the Jerusalem Holy Cross, where it is homily 23. We collated Gallandius’s text with it and corrected it in several places.

In the aforementioned Holy Cross manuscript the title is: “Likewise, the following on the same subject.” It follows a homily entitled: “On What Is Written: ‘Render to God the Things That Are God’s,’ and On Soldiers.”

[Col. 0495B] **ARGUMENT.**—Priests distribute worldly money in order to acquire eternal riches. The Christian office is a kind of commercial enterprise, and the ministry of priests is a precious business transaction.

Recently we censured clerics who practice business and chastised them, in a certain sense, with a just judgment. But if we consider the matter correctly, our office truly is a business; and the exercise of the priestly ministry is a kind of spiritual commercial enterprise. For this reason we expend earthly things in order to attain heavenly things; we distribute worldly money in order to acquire eternal riches; we feed others with our own hunger so that our own nourishment may not perish but increase.

For what is the meaning of our feeding the poor, protecting the naked, and visiting prisoners, unless the expense that is distributed among them is not spent but increased, and the business transaction of silver is preserved with a certain interest of profit? [Col. 0495C] For a hungry poor person is a kind of treasure to the rich. He does not consume the alms that have been given but preserves them.

Even if the flesh is dissolved and the human being is reduced to dust, the holy work nevertheless lives and endures in him. It will be for you on the day of judgment a reliable witness—the person who was useless as an agent for his own nourishment—so that your works may quickly be believed because his own deeds are not believed. See, then, whether almsgiving is not a commercial enterprise.

Whatever you give to a friend is lost to you; only what you give to a beggar is not lost to you. On the day of judgment the poor will benefit you, while friends and sons will benefit you nothing. The poor will plead your case; the others will not even be able to defend their own.

[Col. 0495D] The Christian office is therefore a kind of commercial enterprise and a precious business transaction, the ministry of priests. [Col. 0496B] For we have received the Lord’s money—that is, the Savior’s words—to distribute to the peoples. Concerning these words the Lord says in the Gospel to the tenacious and unskilled merchant of the priesthood: “Wicked servant, you ought to have given my money to the money-changers, and when I came I would have collected it with interest” (Matthew 25).

He is condemned because he kept silent about the divine commandments entrusted to him, although he ought to have multiplied them by preaching. He will be condemned, I say, because he did not sow by distributing what he could have reaped by gathering, as the Apostle says: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians 6).

For the Lord says: “When I came I would have collected it with interest.” Understand, then, that there is a commercial transaction wherever interest is demanded as though for a loan. But this is not the interest by which the minds of the greedy are nourished through the profitable repayment of money, in which the debt is paid to the creditor while the debt itself is not canceled [349] [Note: Here the holy teacher gives a concise and clear definition of interest.]; rather, it is the interest demanded where not the accounting of denarii but the conduct of morals is reckoned; where the principal of the loan is not at issue but the principal of salvation is investigated.

We are debtors and are held liable for a debt, not by a written bond but by the bond of sins. Hence the Apostle says of the Lord: “Erasing the bond that stood against us” (Colossians 2), and so forth.

We are commanded to pay the interest on this debt. For the Lord remembers this debtor in the Gospel, saying that he must be handed over to the exactor, sent into prison, and not released until he pays the last penny (Matthew 5). [350]

We too, brothers, owe interest on these utterances, because “interest” derives from *utendo*, “using”; we shall have to give an account of how we use these utterances.

For the Gospel does not preach in vain, the Apostle does not cry out for nothing, and priests do not speak without cause. Whoever hears the holy voice will either be blessed because of devotion or found guilty because of the testimony brought against him.

*The end.*

## HOMILY 106. On the Fear of God and the Correction of Tongues

[Col. 0497]

### ADMONITION

We have acknowledged that we owe a great deal, in the preface, to the most learned man Giovanni Battista Branca, deputy director of the Ambrosian Library, who was the first to make this homily available to us. He also informed us that he had copied it from an eleventh-century manuscript formerly belonging to the provost church of Biasca in the diocese of Milan, recently acquired by the Ambrosian Library; he found it printed nowhere except in a very old Breviary for the use of the Church of Milan, from the year 1490.

While we were searching in Florence among the Laurentian manuscripts, and here in Rome among the celebrated manuscripts of the Jerusalem Holy Cross, for the hidden riches of Saint Maximus, we obtained the testimony of two excellent manuscripts, by which the reliability of the Ambrosian manuscript is strengthened and clarified. They are manuscript 172, formerly belonging to the cathedral church of Florence, now in the Laurentian Library, on page 69 verso, and manuscript IX of the Jerusalem Holy Cross, page 31.

Yet as many manuscripts, so many titles—entirely different—for this homily. The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “On Saturday, at the handing over of the Creed: A homily of Maximus. Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord.” The title in the Milanese Breviary is the same.

The manuscript of the cathedral church of Florence first supplies the passage from Luke’s Gospel, chapter 6: “Jesus said to his disciples: Be merciful, as your Father is merciful,” and so forth. “A sermon of Saint Maximus the bishop, from the same place as above.”

Finally, the Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscript is entitled: “A sermon of Saint Maximus the bishop on the fear of God and the correction of speech.”

We do not consider the first or second title acceptable, since the homily contains nothing at all about what they announce. Since the third title indicates the subject that the preacher pursues throughout the sermon, we have placed it before the homily and judged that it should be called “On the Fear of God and the Correction of Speech.”

We have already said enough in the first homily of this class about the handing over of the Creed, which was delivered on the Saturday before Palm Sunday to catechumens who were to be baptized on the approaching Holy Saturday. Thus nothing remains for us to add here except to make Maximus’s very manner of expression clear.

[Col. 0497B] **ARGUMENT.**—In treating of the fear of God, Maximus presents rules for disciplined speech from the royal prophet and, in eloquent discourse, explains how many evils are perpetrated through wicked words.

The most glorious of the prophets, and likewise the king of the Lord’s people, the blessed David, who by a general exhortation compels all people to gather in order to hear the precepts that purify life, says: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Psalm 33).

Truly this venerable patriarch was supremely skilled in teaching. In order to impress the fear of God upon human minds through the precepts of prophetic authority, he first offers the tenderness of paternal affection. He calls those subject to his rule “children,” so that he may recall them from sins not so much through the terror of royal power as through the affection of one who cares, implanting in the hearts of all a ready desire to live well.

Often those whom the harshness of a more severe rebuke does not correct are reformed by the fullness of gentler speech: “I will teach you,” he says, “the fear of the Lord.” The holy man teaches us religious fear, so that we may put love of earthly judgment second. He teaches the fear of the Lord, which is always salutary, because fear of human beings often nourishes offense against God.

Let us now see what steps the excellent teacher establishes for divine fear and what rule of holier discipline he sets forth. [Note: The Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscript reads: “Restrain your tongue,” and so forth.]

“Keep your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit.” The perfect teacher of religious life restrains the tongue above all from fault, for it was the first thing to sin at God’s paradise in the serpent from the beginning of the world.

It was the work of an evil tongue to persuade Adam, to the destruction of his race, to pluck the fruit of the forbidden tree. Nor would envy have driven him into an eternal fall [Note: The same Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscript reads: “the devilish envy would have driven him into an eternal fall.”] if Eve, with wiser counsel, had wished to restrain her tongue from evil.

An evil tongue is therefore the devil’s servant and the handmaid of every depravity. An evil tongue, serving in place of a very sharp sword [Note: The same Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscript reads: “by its voice.”], wounds not only the body but also the innocent soul. An evil and thoughtless tongue strikes a brother’s heart with insults [Note: The same Jerusalem Holy Cross manuscript reads: “strikes it.”] and joins a destructive quarrel to hearts that had been at peace with one another.

An evil tongue assumes the appearance of truth and discolors truth with lies. Entrusted to the ears of enemies, an evil tongue betrays the secrets of friends. Those whom it fears to address openly, it tries to defile by secret slander. Through deception it lays snares for the simple; it seeks the blood of good men, inflames the minds of the powerful, and disturbs the hearts of the humble.

As though it were not enough for it to confuse human beings, it strikes heaven itself with blasphemies and most unworthy insults, as the prophetic utterance testifies concerning the impious: “They set their mouths against heaven, and their tongue traversed the earth” (Psalm 72). [Col. 0498C]

And after all this, dearly beloved, although there is a remedy for every other sin, through an evil and uncontrolled tongue a sin is committed that is forgiven a human being neither in this present age, as the Lord says: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Luke 12).

And what more shall I say, brothers? Whatever iniquity the devil entices in the human heart is accomplished with the evil tongue serving him. But for its destruction and judgment the Lord is invoked, as the prophet cries out: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue” (Psalm 11). And elsewhere: “You will destroy those who speak lies.”

To warn and turn us away from these evils, the blessed David says to each one of us: “Restrain your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit” (Psalm 33). And shortly afterward he adds: “Seek peace, and pursue it.”

Once your tongue has been corrected and cleansed of every stain of evil speech, you will both find and follow true and eternal peace—that is, Christ the Lord. Let no one deceive himself: unless someone restrains his wandering and wanton tongue with the reins of a disciplined heart, he will be able to find neither human peace nor Christ’s peace.

Therefore the venerable prophet, knowing on what slippery ground the human tongue stands and how great a danger an uncontrolled tongue can bring upon our soul and life, prayed to his God, saying: “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth” (Psalm 140:3); and elsewhere: “O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise” (Psalm 50:17).

The supremely faithful man asks the Lord to guard his mouth and open his lips, lest the devil, that teacher of lies and craftsman of every deceit, ever insert into him the falsities of his impiety. Truly, the person who desires both to speak and to remain silent under God’s dispensation will be able to restrain his tongue from every evil.

Therefore, brothers, considering how severe a sentence awaits deceitful lips and how great a grace follows a simple tongue, let us too pray with the prophet to the Lord and almighty God that he guard our mouth and himself always deign to open our lips for words pleasing to him.

## HOMILY 107. On What Is Written in Psalm 118: “Teach Me Goodness, Discipline, and Knowledge”

[Col. 0499]

### ADMONITION

In the same manuscripts of the Laurentian Library and the Jerusalem Holy Cross mentioned above, we found that the writer and originator of this homily—which the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine, no. 55, page 70 of the Antwerp edition, called the work of an uncertain but not unlearned author—was Saint Maximus of Turin.

Both manuscripts—that is, manuscript 172, formerly belonging to the cathedral church of Florence, page 70, and manuscript IX of the Jerusalem Holy Cross, page 32—place it immediately after the preceding homily. The first has the customary heading: “By the same author as above,” explicitly identifying the same Maximus, who was named in the preceding homily.

The second manuscript supplies both a title and the name of Saint Maximus: “A sermon of Saint Maximus the bishop on goodness, discipline, and knowledge.”

We have retained the title assigned to the homily by the Benedictine editors, since the entire homily is in fact a lucid exposition of that passage of the Psalmist and contains excellent lessons in moral discipline.

We also encountered this same homily in manuscript Vatican Regina 83, although no author’s name is inscribed there. The text we present was taken from the Laurentian manuscript, and we have added the variant readings of the other manuscripts.

[Col. 0499B] **ARGUMENT.**—Maximus explains at length the brief prayer for addressing God handed down by David and urges us, following David’s example, to pray that the Lord teach us the paths of a holier life.

Among the other remedies by which blessed David heals the weaknesses of our souls, as a most skilled teacher he instructs us to hold fast to a pattern of prayer under a certain rule of trinity, saying: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0499D] In the Maurist edition, “Lord” has been added.].

Therefore, brothers, attend more carefully to which virtues the prophetic king chiefly begs to be granted to him. “Teach me,” he says, “goodness, discipline, and knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0499D] In the edition mentioned above, “Lord.”]. He knows how to live rightly who knows how to pray rightly. For he did not ask for treasures of worldly riches, neighboring kingdoms, or a longer span of life; rather, he asked that he himself be taught goodness and discipline. Goodness makes discipline lovable, and discipline makes goodness blameless.

Nor, I think, should anyone be unaware that goodness without discipline is the mother of sins, while discipline without goodness is a certain bitter sadness of life. He likewise implores that knowledge be granted to him, so that he may know how to distinguish intelligently and wisely the limits of goodness and what measure discipline ought to have, lest goodness be defiled by the fault of excessive laxity [Note: [Col. 0499D] The Maurist appendix and Codex Vat. Reg. 83 read: “lest unconsidered goodness be defiled.”], or discipline, by its own excessive austerity, be ashamed of itself.

Do you wish, brother, to be good toward a sinner? You are acting kindly indeed; but, if you wish truly to be good, apply to him the severity of discipline [Note: [Col. 0499D] Codex Vat. Reg. reads: “apply firmness.”], so that your goodness may benefit him unto salvation [Note: [Col. 0499D] The Maurist edition and Codex Vat. Reg. 33 read: “so that your goodness may benefit him unto salvation; for if you do not terrify him by any rebuke of corrective judgment…”]. For if you do not terrify him by any rebuke of corrective judgment [Col. 0499D], this goodness of yours will be harmful to him, because [Col. 0500B] you permit the sinner to perish, although you could have saved him once corrected.

Again, if through excessive severity of discipline you offer no medicine of healing goodness, then, while the sinner flees your terror, you will not cure the sinner’s sickness. And what manner of life, what justice, will there be if either a too-relaxed gentleness offers connivance to the sinner, or immoderate severity does not recall the offender from his fall?

But so that we may learn more fully and perfectly that this mastery of goodness and discipline existed among our forebears, let us recount at least a few examples from the many venerable Fathers [Note: [Col. 0500D] The Maurist edition omits “or.”] [Note: [Col. 0500D] The Maurist edition and Codex Vat. Reg. 83 add: “Without doubt blessed Peter fulfilled the pattern of this goodness and discipline, since, as one truly good, he is said to have healed the sick who were brought to him, and, as a lover of heavenly discipline, is reported to have punished liars with just retribution. Certainly the grace of his goodness is attested by that weak Aeneas, who, lame, etc.”].

Beyond doubt, most blessed Peter fulfilled the work of goodness and discipline, since, as a truly good physician, he healed the sick brought to him, and, as the founder of heavenly discipline, punished liars with just retribution [Col. 0500C]. That he possessed the grace of goodness was demonstrated by the weak Aeneas (Acts 3), who, lame from infancy and sitting at the gate of the temple begging, received his former health in the name of Jesus Christ at the command of the apostle who healed him.

Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5) likewise demonstrated the severity of his discipline. They sold a field which no one had compelled them to sell, but, while lying to the apostle about the amount of the price, purchased death for themselves by their falsehood. By this deed glorious Peter taught that goodness and discipline were present in him: he both supplied a remedy to the sick and exacted a fitting punishment from liars. That he had acted rightly and holily is shown by the agreement of heavenly judgment.

Who could doubt the perfection of his knowledge, since, when the Father revealed it to him from heaven, he recognized Christ the Lord as the Son of the living God [Col. 0500D]? [Col. 0501A] [Note: [Col. 0501C] “And because he did not lack goodness, discipline, or knowledge, the Lord entrusted his little sheep to him for feeding.” Firmly established in Maximus is the doctrine of Peter’s primacy, and we have already demonstrated above that he was chosen, by a calling unlike that of the other apostles, to found the Church. Here, however, when he again begins to speak about Peter and Paul, although he acknowledges that both were of the greatest service to the Church, he nevertheless describes the ministry of one as so distinct from that of the other that he does not make Paul share the characteristic of office or rank that appears to be properly attributed to Peter. For he declares Peter to have possessed such great goodness and knowledge that the Lord entrusted his little sheep to him for feeding—as though he had said, in Homily 40: “Because Peter, as a good shepherd, received the flock to guard and became a support for all, he who had previously been weak, and because he himself had faltered under the test of questioning, he was to establish the others by the stability of faith”; or, in the first homily on the holy apostles Peter and Paul: “This is Peter, who established for us the strongest and unconquerable foundations of belief”; or, in Homily 41: “Peter proved to have such great merit before God that, after the rowing of a little boat, the governance of the whole Church was entrusted to him.”]

And because goodness was not lacking to him for discipline and knowledge, the Lord entrusted his little sheep to him for feeding [Note: [Col. 0501C] The Maurist edition reads: “And because he did not lack goodness, discipline, and knowledge.”].

Glorious Paul possessed goodness and discipline. As his writings testify, he displayed both the rod of correction and the spirit of gentleness; consequently, goodness made him lovable to all, while discipline made him fearsome [Note: [Col. 0501C] The Maurist edition incorrectly reads: “At the very beginnings of the world.”]. For, at the very beginnings of the faith, in order to teach Christ’s Churches goodness and discipline, he both ordered that the sinner be removed from communion with the saints and received him again when he repented.

What shall we say of his knowledge, when everyone knows that he learned in heaven what he was to teach on earth, where he remembered having been taught things that it would not be lawful for him to utter to mortals [Note: [Col. 0501C] Codex Maurin. reads: “There he remembered having been taught such things.”]?

That lordly witness and Baptist, John, likewise possessed goodness and discipline [Col. 0501B]. With the affection of prophetic compassion he washed people who repented of their sins in the baptism of repentance; and, as an unchanging guardian of the precepts of the Law, he accused King Herod of his unlawful wife and charged all who came to him with the precepts of a purer life.

Whoever can be ignorant of the fullness of his knowledge, since he was the first to reveal to humankind that Christ had come from heaven for the salvation of humanity [Note: [Col. 0501C] Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, the Maurist edition, and Codex Vat. Reg. read: “See, therefore, brothers, by what brief form of prayer…”]?

You see, therefore, brothers, by what brief form of prayer, and with what small number of words, the venerable prophet sought the perfection of life [Col. 0502A]. In the briefest speech he gathered together everything contained in the multitude of spiritual virtues.

If, then, that foremost of prophets prayed so earnestly that the Lord would teach him these paths of holier life, what must we do [Note: [Col. 0501C] Codex Vat. Reg. reads: “What, I say, must we do, who are both sluggish through weakness of understanding and corrupted by the habit of a harmful laxity of life…”]—indeed, how much more ought we to pray—saying: “Teach us goodness, discipline, and knowledge, Lord,” so that goodness may conquer evil [Note: [Col. 0502C] The Maurist edition and Codex Vat. Reg. 83 read: “so that goodness may conquer malice, discipline may restrain vices and pleasures, and knowledge of the truth may illumine the blindness of ignorance…”], and discipline may chastise vices and the desires of the will.

For if, knowing the almighty Lord to be the Father, and his Son to be of one substance with him, you believe also that the Holy Spirit reigns with equal eternity, no empty persuasion of the pagans or faithless impiety of the Arians will ever disturb you. If knowledge of the future judgment fills your heart and mind [Note: [Col. 0502C] Codex Vat. Reg. and the Maurist edition read: “has filled you”], you will possess discipline in your conduct [Col. 0502B]. Again, if you observe the measures and rules of discipline itself, you will maintain suitable goodness in everything, because goodness is the moderation of discipline, and discipline is the seasoning of goodness.

Beware, therefore, brother, lest you wish to appear good in such a way that you cast aside discipline; and pursue discipline in such a way that you remove goodness [Note: [Col. 0502C] Codex Vat. Reg. and the Maurist edition read: “or pursue discipline so rigorous that you remove goodness, etc.”]. Blessed David asks that knowledge be added to these things so that, through the direct judgment of our mind, we may know how both stricter goodness and gentler discipline ought to exist in us [Note: [Col. 0502C] The Maurist edition reads: “how it may exist.”].

# HOMILY 108

On the passage of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 6: “Jesus got into a boat and crossed over.”

[Col. 0501]

## ADMONITION

In the Roman Breviary, part of this homily is read on the eighteenth Sunday after Pentecost under the name of Saint Peter Chrysologus. The distinguished Sebastian Pauli, Cleric Regular of the Mother of God, assigned it to the same author in his Venetian edition of the works of that archbishop of Ravenna, published in 1750, as had Combefis much earlier in volume 7, page 397, and others.

These considerations seem to me sufficiently weighty that I do not dare challenge the opinion generally received; nevertheless, I think I may report the judgment of ancient writers. In the Vatican Library we found Codex 6451, which, on page 19, names Saint John Osavreus, or Chrysostom, as the author of the homily. In the Cassinese archive, Codex 102, page 253, attributes it to Saint Severian, bishop.

We attest, however, that two other codices of no inferior authority agree in assigning it to Saint Maximus of Turin: namely, Vatican Codex 4222, page 341, and Laurentian Codex 36, Plut. XVII, page 251; for immediately after the Gospel passage they explicitly read: “Homily of Saint Maximus, bishop.”

Such testimony can be confirmed by similarity of style. Yet although our opinion may perhaps deceive us, we believe that we have nevertheless done something pleasing for fair-minded readers by appending to this homily the many variants collected from Vatican Codex 6451.

### 357 ARGUMENT

“Christ does not need the boat,” says Maximus, “but the boat needs Christ; for without heavenly guidance the boat of the Church cannot reach the heavenly harbor.” He then continues the sequence of the Gospel narrative.

Today’s reading has shown that Christ carried out divine mysteries in human actions and performed invisible works through visible things [Col. 0503A]. “He got into a boat,” it says, “and crossed over, and came to his own city.”

Is he not the one who, having driven back the waves of the sea, laid bare the depths so that the Israelite people might pass on dry ground through the astonished waters, or through the hollows of the mountains (Exod. 14)? Is he not the one who bent the sea’s summits beneath Peter’s feet, so that the liquid path might offer solid service to human steps (Matt. 14)? And what does it mean that he so denies the sea’s service to himself that he crossed a very short stretch of lake by paying a sailor’s fare [Note: [Col. 0503C] The Cassinese Codex reads: “that he himself…”]?

“He got into a boat,” it says, “and crossed over.” And what is surprising in this, brothers? Christ came to take upon himself our weaknesses [Note: [Col. 0503C] The Cassinese Codex reads: “to confer health.” Vatican Codex 6451 omits “and to confer on us his remedies of health,” through “for the physician who does not bear…”], and to confer his virtues upon us; to seek human things and provide divine things [Col. 0503B]; to receive insults and return honors; to endure weariness and bring back health. For a physician who does not bear infirmities does not know how to cure infirmities, and one who has not become weak with the weak cannot confer health upon the weak.

Therefore, if Christ had remained in his own powers, he would have had nothing in common with human beings; and unless he had fulfilled the order of the flesh, his assumption of flesh in him would have been purposeless. He therefore endured these necessities so that, as a true human being, he might be proved by human necessities.

“He got into a boat,” it says. Christ got into the boat of his Church, always intending to calm the waves of the world [Note: [Col. 0503C] Vatican Codex 6451 reads: “Christ got into the boat, the boat of the Church, in order always to calm the waves of the world. He got in so that believers…”], so that he might lead those who believe in him to the heavenly homeland by peaceful sailing and make citizens of his own city those whom he had made sharers in his humanity.

Therefore Christ does not need the boat, but the boat needs Christ [Col. 0503C], because without heavenly guidance the boat of the Church cannot reach the heavenly harbor through the worldly sea amid such great and perilous danger [Note: [Col. 0503C] The same Vatican Codex reads: “through such and so great dangers.”].

We have said this, brothers, insofar as spiritual understanding is concerned [358]; but now let us pursue the order of the narrative itself.

“He got into a boat,” it says, “and crossed over, and came to his own city” [Col. 0504A]. The Lord, Creator of the world and of all things, after narrowing himself for our sake in the flesh, began to have a human homeland [Note: [Col. 0503C] The same Vatican Codex reads: “He began to be a citizen of the Jewish city, began to have parents, himself the parent of all parents.”]. Himself the parent of all parents, he did so in order that love might invite, charity attract, affection overcome, and humanity persuade those whom domination had driven away and fear had scattered [Note: [Col. 0503C] The same Vatican Codex reads: “and the force of power had made outcasts, etc.”].

“He came to his own city,” [Note: [Col. 0504C] The Vatican and Cassinese codices read: “and behold, they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed, and Jesus, seeing him, said…”] and behold, they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed. “And when Jesus saw,” he says, “their faith, he said to the paralytic: Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.”

He hears forgiveness and the paralytic remains silent, giving no thanks [Note: [Col. 0504C] The same Vatican Codex reads: “and he gave no thanks”], because he was more concerned with the cure of the body than of the soul. He lamented the temporal punishments of his weakened body in such a way that he did not lament the eternal punishments of the soul’s dissolution, judging the present life more desirable for himself than the future [Note: [Col. 0504C] Vatican Codex 6451 reads: “than the future life.” Cassinese Codex reads: “he judges the present life more desirable for himself than the future.”].

Christ rightly looks not at the faith of those who brought him the sick man, but at the senselessness of the one lying there, so that, through the support of another’s faith, the paralytic’s soul might be healed before his body.

“He saw,” it says, “their faith.” You see in this passage, brothers, that God does not seek the wishes of the foolish, does not regard the faith of the ignorant, and does not examine the foolish desires of the sick, but comes to the aid of another’s faith [Note: [Col. 0504C] The same Vatican Codex reads: “but comes to the aid of another’s faith; and truly, brothers…”], granting through grace alone whatever he granted, since he did not refuse anything that belonged to the divine will.
