And truly, brothers, when does a physician of the sick either seek or heed their wishes, since the sick person always desires and asks for what is contrary to health? Hence he now applies iron, now fire, now bitter drinks, and places them upon unwilling patients, so that they may experience the cure which, while sick, they could not perceive.

And if a human being disregards insults, despises curses, and willingly confers life and health upon those wounded by disease, how much more does Christ the physician, by divine goodness, draw even the unwilling and reluctant to salvation—those wounded by the diseases of sins and suffering from the madness of crimes?

O that we might wish, brothers—O that we might wish—to perceive all the paralysis of our mind! We would see our soul, deprived of virtues, lying on the beds of vices; and it would become clear to us how Christ daily regards our harmful desires and draws and urges us, unwilling as we are, toward saving remedies [Note: [Col. 0503D] “O that we might wish, brothers—O that we might wish—to perceive all the paralysis of our mind, we would see our soul, deprived of virtues, lying on the beds of vices; it would become clear to us how Christ daily regards our harmful desires and draws and urges us, unwilling as we are, toward saving remedies.—What does this mean: ‘He draws and urges us, unwilling as we are, toward saving remedies’? It refers, of course, to the prayer of the Church in which the priest, when about to celebrate the divine service on the fourth Sunday after Pentecost, asks God mercifully to compel our rebellious wills toward himself. This does not mean that God, by the support of his grace, imposes necessity upon those whom he wishes to convert to himself, since both the Church and Maximus teach and proclaim freedom of choice; rather, it means that, in his supreme mercy, God works certain things in us without us, as Saint Augustine observes, by which we are stimulated and urged, as it were, to act rightly.

“By these stimuli, which are forms of assistance—such as illuminations of the mind, threats and terrors of punishment, and so forth—we sometimes feel ourselves, unwillingly at first, or without desire, moved and drawn toward repentance. For we resist and struggle against them. But who would resist and oppose something whose influence upon him he felt, not unwillingly but willingly? From the word ‘unwilling,’ Saint Maximus’s preface plainly shows that he understands not a person compelled by necessity, but a free person who nevertheless acts without desire; we have placed that preface in the annotation at column 364.

“Even if at first we resist these aids, God nevertheless, by the effective help that proceeds from them, so softens us—whom he wishes effectively to pity—when hardened, quiets us when resisting, and attracts us when we bear things heavily, that, without violating our freedom, he determines us wonderfully and grants us the strength by which we determine ourselves together with him to obtain saving remedies, and, led by love, strive toward the fountain of justice and devote ourselves diligently and faithfully to keeping his divine law.

“Moreover, what is it, when we resist and struggle against illumination and other helps by which God urges us toward the good as though with goads, except to be rebellious toward the light and, unwilling or without desire, to be stimulated toward saving things? Again, to resist those helps and oppose them belongs to a human being who is not compelled by necessity but is free. When at last, moved by effective assistance, you repent spontaneously and, willingly and gladly, are led—and lead yourself—to embrace virtue, conscious that you could resist if you wished, you clearly recognize that you are stimulated, urged, and drawn to embrace and cultivate virtue in such a way that you exercise your freedom in embracing and cultivating it.

“This is Saint Maximus’s doctrine, if his works are read carefully. If anyone thinks otherwise, let him beware lest he accuse not only Augustine, who affirms that God possesses an all-powerful authority to incline human hearts, but also the apostle Paul, who wrote: ‘God has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens’; and: ‘It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish’; and: ‘It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy’; and: ‘Who resists his will?’ ‘O man, who are you to answer back to God?’ ‘Does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?’ Who, unless impious, would dare accuse Augustine and Paul of having harmed or abolished freedom?

“What, then, is the reason that anyone should say that Maximus did not believe a human being could be urged freely toward saving remedies, since Maximus followed Augustine and Paul, as is plainly evident from his homilies?—The words ‘from his homilies’ are repeated in the source: ‘as is plainly evident from his homilies, plainly from his homilies.’”]

O that we might wish, brothers—O that we might wish—to perceive all the paralysis of our mind! We would see our soul, deprived of virtues, lying on the beds of vices; and it would become clear to us how Christ daily regards our harmful desires [Col. 0505A] and draws and urges us, unwilling as we are, toward saving remedies [359].

“Son,” he says, “your sins are forgiven you.” In saying this, he wished to make himself understood as the one who was still hidden from human eyes by means of a human being. For in virtues and signs he was compared with the prophets, who had themselves performed miracles through him; but since the power to forgive sins does not belong to a human being [Note: [Col. 0505B] Vatican Codex 6451 reads: “But since the power to forgive sins does not belong to human beings, and is the distinctive mark of divinity, etc.”], and since it is the distinctive mark of divinity, he was impressing God upon human hearts.

The envy of the Pharisee proves this. For when he had said, “Your sins are forgiven you,” the Pharisees answered: “He blasphemes. For who can forgive sins except God alone?” Pharisee, who by knowing do not know, by confessing deny, and by bearing witness attack: if it is God who forgives sins, why is Christ not God for you, since he is proved, by the one gift of his forgiveness [Note: [Col. 0505B] The Cassinese Codex reads: “who by one…”], to have taken away the sins of the whole world?

“Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

But so that you may grasp greater signs of his divinity, hear that he penetrated the secret places of your breast [Col. 0506A]; see that he reached the hiding places of your thoughts; understand that he lays bare the silent counsels of your heart [360].

“And when Jesus had seen,” he says, “their thoughts, he said” [Note: [Col. 0505B] Vatican Codex 6451 and the Cassinese Codex read: “he said to them: Why are you thinking…”]: “Why are you thinking evil things in your hearts? For which is easier to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’?” [Note: [Col. 0506B] Codex Vall. 6451 reads: “or to say…”]

“But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins,” he said to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house”; and he rose and went to his house [Note: [Col. 0506B] The same Vatican Codex reads: “Rise, take it up…”].

The Searcher of souls anticipated the evil designs of their minds and displayed the power of his divinity by the testimony of his work: he restores the scattered members of the body, tightens the sinews, joins the bones, completes the inner organs, strengthens the limbs, and raises to walking feet that had already been buried in a living corpse [Note: [Col. 0506B] Vatican Codex reads: “in a living corpse already.”].

“Take up your bed”; that is, carry the one who carried you [Col. 0506B] [Note: [Col. 0506B] The Vatican Codex reads: “Change the role of the burden, so that what was a testimony of weakness…”]. Change all the roles, so that what is a testimony of weakness may be proof of health; so that your bed of pain may be a clear indication of healing; so that the greatness of the weight may assert the greatness of the strength you have recovered.

“Go,” he says, “to your house”: now that you have been healed by Christian faith, do not die again on the roads of Jewish faithlessness.

# HOMILY 109

On the Mustard Seed I

[Col. 0505]

## ADMONITION

We have encountered a kind of conflict among the manuscript codices and editions concerning the author of this homily [361]. That it was formerly attributed to Augustine is clear from its inclusion in the appendix to his sermons; the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, judging it a spurious work, placed it there under number 87.

Gillotius believed it to be an Ambrosian sermon and placed it second in his Paris edition, which we have often mentioned, under the title “On the Mustard Seed.” Codex Laurentianus X, Plut. XIV, agrees with him and bears a similar inscription.

We, however, judge it more proper to assign the homily to Saint Maximus, since the most ancient codices bear witness to this. First among these we cite the Sangallensis and the Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem 90, which Mabillon said breathed venerable antiquity. We then mention Vallicellianus A 9, Vaticanus 6451, the Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem 95, Laurentianus 39, Plut. XVII, page 172 verso, and Codex 176, formerly belonging to the aedile of the metropolitan church of Florence, page 248 verso in the Laurentian Library.

Concerning the last two codices, this should be noted: after the title “On the Mustard Seed,” I read the addition “and on Saint Lawrence,” because Saint Maximus has some material at the end of the sermon concerning the holy deacon and martyr; perhaps he delivered the homily on the day of his feast.

There is, however, another not insignificant disagreement concerning the beginning of this homily. Some, after the Gospel passage cited above, begin with these words: “Perhaps your understanding is troubled…” These are the Sangallensis and Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem; they title the homily “On the Mustard Seed.”

Others begin from the Gospel, adding: “The Lord says in the Gospel,” as in the Laurentian codices; the same reading of the homily is found in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine.

Others follow a different course. Retaining the same title, “On the Mustard Seed,” they place before the Gospel a certain preface, as in Codex 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, the Vallicellian and Urbevetan codices, and Gillotius and the other editors of Ambrose.

Since we judge that preface to have been added in later times, we place it among the variants and publish the homily in the form in which the older codices present it.

[Col. 0507]

### ARGUMENT

Saint Maximus wonderfully draws out the meaning of the holy Gospel hidden in the likeness of a mustard seed, explaining how the kingdom of heaven is compared with a seed so very small. He says much about Christian faith and hope and compares the holy martyr Lawrence with a mustard seed.

[Note: [Col. 0507D] Codex Vallicellianus A 9 begins here.]

The Lord says in the holy Gospel, as the reading just given testifies: “To what is the kingdom of God like, and to what shall I compare it? It is like a mustard seed, which a man took and put in his garden; and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the sky rested in its branches” (Luke 13).

[Note: [Col. 0507D] Codex X, Plut. XIV, page 221 verso of the Laurentian Library likewise reads this.]

Perhaps your understanding is troubled as to why the kingdom of God, so glorious and so magnificent, is compared with a tiny mustard seed, and why so great a consolation of our hope is said to be like something so insignificant [Note: [Col. 0507D] The Urbevetan Codex reads: “is said to be like, let us say.”], especially since elsewhere the same Lord says to his disciples: “If you have faith like a mustard seed, say to this mountain: ‘Move from here and throw yourself into the sea,’ and it will happen” (Matt. 17) [Col. 0507B].

Therefore, if faith is wonderful—faith which can move the foundations of mountains from their very seats—then necessarily the mustard seed is also great, in whose likeness we are compelled to have faith [Note: [Col. 0507D] Codices 172 and 10 of the Laurentian Library read: “if faith is so great.” Codices Vat. 6411 and Vallicellianus A 9 read: “if faith is so great.”].

I would call it great, not in appearance but in power [Note: [Col. 0507D] The Urbevetan Codex reads: “I would call it great, not in appearance but in power and faith; not to be compared in the quality of a vegetable, but to be compared and equated in the force of its sharpness.”], and not to be compared with faith in the quality of a vegetable, but to be equated with it in the force of its pungency [Note: [Col. 0508C] Vatican Codex 6451 reads: “and of faith; not comparable in the quality of a vegetable, but equal in the strength of its pungency.”].

For, if we attend carefully, we find that the Lord made this comparison rightly [Note: [Col. 0508C] Codices 172 Florentinus, Vat. 7451, and Urbevetanus read: “we shall find.”]. Just as a mustard seed, at first sight and in its outward appearance, is small, common, despised, offering neither flavor nor fragrance and giving no indication of sweetness [Note: [Col. 0508C] Vatican Codex 6451 reads: “in its appearance”], yet, once it begins to be crushed, immediately displays its fragrance and pungency [Col. 0507C] [Note: [Col. 0508C] Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Codex 172, and the others read: “immediately pours out its fragrance and displays its pungency.”], emits food of fiery taste, and is kindled with such a heat of ardor that it is astonishing that so great a fire was enclosed in such insignificant seeds—of this seed, too, people especially in winter season partake as food with great relish [Col. 0508A], so that they may repel the cold, expel bodily fluids, and warm the inner parts of the organs; often they also apply it as a medicine to the head, so that whatever is weak or diseased may be cured by the fire of mustard [Note: [Col. 0508C] Codices Vallicellianus A 9 and Urbevetanus read: “as food.”]—

so Christian faith, at first sight, seems small, common, and slight; it does not display its power, offer arrogance, or supply grace. But once it begins to be crushed by various temptations, it immediately reveals its strength, displays its pungency, breathes forth the warmth of belief in the Lord, and is driven by such a burning of divine fire that it itself burns and compels those who share in it to burn also [Note: [Col. 0508C] Codices 172, Vaticanus, and Urbevetanus read: “those who share in it.”].

As the disciples of Emmaus and Cleopas said in the holy Gospel when the Lord was speaking with them after the Passion: “Was not our heart burning within us on the way, while the Lord Jesus opened the Scriptures?” (Luke 24) [Note: [Col. 0508C] Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read “Emmaus.” The Vatican Codex 6451 omits the names of the disciples. The Urbevetan Codex reads: “two of the disciples said.”] [Note: [Col. 0508D] Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, the Vatican and Urbevetan codices, read: “while the Lord Jesus opened the Scriptures to us.” Both Laurentian codices read: “while he opened the Scriptures to us.”].

Thus the mustard seed warms the inner parts of the limbs, while the strength of faith burns away the sins of the heart [Col. 0508B] [Note: [Col. 0508D] Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and the others add: “and that [mustard] removes the harsh chill of the cold.”]; the former removes the harsh chill of cold, while the latter expels the devilish cold of sins. Mustard, I say, cooks away unhealthy fluids from bodies, while faith consumes the streams of lust [Note: [Col. 0508D] The four codices mentioned read: “Mustard, I say, etc.”]. Through the former, medicine is prepared for the head [Note: [Col. 0508D] Codex Vallicellianus A 9 reads: “medicine for the head.”]; through faith, our spiritual head, which is Christ the Lord, is very often refreshed.

Moreover, in keeping with the comparison with mustard, we enjoy the holy fragrance of faith, as the blessed Apostle says: “For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (1 Cor. 2).

Therefore, we may compare the holy martyr Lawrence with a mustard seed. Having been crushed by various sufferings, he earned that the grace of his martyrdom should be fragrant throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0508D] The Vatican and Urbevetan codices read: “by his grace he deserved to blaze with the fragrance of martyrdom.”]. Previously established in the body [Col. 0508C], he was humble, unknown, and insignificant; but after he had been tormented, mangled, and burned [Note: [Col. 0508D] The Vatican Codex omits “was”], he poured the fragrance of his nobility into all the Churches throughout the entire world [Note: [Col. 0508D] The Urbevetan Codex reads: “he infused.”].

Rightly, therefore, this comparison is attached to him [Note: [Col. 0508D] Codex Vallicellianus A 9 reads: “this comparison.”]. For, just as a mustard seed is kindled when it is crushed, Lawrence is inflamed when he suffers; the former vomits forth the heat of its crushing [Note: [Col. 0509C] Codex 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and Laurentianus 172 read: “moves.” The Vatican Codex reads: “moves its heat by its crushing.”], while the latter breathes out fire amid his many torments.

Mustard, I say, is cooked in a vessel heated by warm vapor; Lawrence is roasted on a gridiron by the fire of flames [Note: [Col. 0509C] The Urbevetan Codex reads: “is tormented. And although the wicked king…” It omits the intervening material.]. Blessed Lawrence was therefore burning outwardly in the fires of the raging tyrant, but inwardly a greater flame of Christ’s love was roasting him [Note: [Col. 0509C] Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read: “was tormenting him.”].

Although the wicked king added wood and heaped greater fires upon him [Note: [Col. 0509C] The Vallicellian Codex reads: “so that he might heap greater fires upon him”], Saint Lawrence did not feel these flames because of the warmth of faith; while he considered Christ’s commandments, everything he suffered was cold to him.

For he could not feel the torments in his inner organs caused by the fires, since in his senses he already possessed the refreshment of paradise [Note: [Col. 0509D] The codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Vaticanus, and Vallicellanus read: “he could not.”].

Let burned flesh and an insensible body lie before the tyrant’s feet [Col. 0510A] [Note: [Col. 0509D] The Vatican Codex reads: “which nevertheless suffers no…” The Urbevetan Codex reads: “which nevertheless suffers no…” The Vallicellian Codex reads: “which nevertheless suffers no harm.”]; no harm, however, is suffered on earth by the one whose spirit dwells in heaven.

He is therefore stretched out over the glowing balls of flame and turned repeatedly onto his sides [Note: [Col. 0509D] Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, and the Urbevetan and Vallicellian codices, read: “is tormented.”]. Yet the more punishment he suffers, the more devotedly he fears Christ the Lord. In a new kind of marvel, one person tortures him, while the torments of the raging man benefit another [Note: [Col. 0509D] The codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and the Vatican read: “The harsher the sufferings, the more devoted they made Lawrence to the Savior.” Codex 172 Laurentianus reads: “to the Savior’s.”]: harsher punishments made Lawrence more devoted.

# HOMILY 110

Also on the Mustard Seed II

[Col. 0509]

## NOTICE
[Col. 0509]

365 It has been demonstrated from the most reliable evidence that the preceding homily is to be attributed to no one other than St. Maximus of Turin. Since this homily clearly refers back to it and mentions it, it is sufficiently proved that it was composed and committed to writing by the same author. All hesitation is then removed by the two codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem mentioned above, in which it appears under the title, “Continuation concerning the mustard seed,” and by the Codex Sangallensis, which indicate Maximus as the author. We should nevertheless note that the monks of St. Maur included part of this sermon in the appendix to the sermons of St. Augustine, first class, no. 88; there they stated that it had been published among the works of St. Ambrose, though they subsequently judged it more prudent to remove it from the list of that holy Doctor’s works. For, in addition to the two codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Codex Vaticanus 6451 also supports its attribution to Maximus. It is also found in the Codex Urbevetanus, p. 169, where, after the words “Therefore, above,” it begins: “To what is the kingdom of heaven like, and to what shall I compare it?” says the Lord. It likewise begins in Codex Vallicellianus A 9.

ARGUMENT.—St. Maximus shows again that the Christian faith is the kingdom of God and possesses the same force that the nature of mustard draws forth. He also teaches how Christ is the grain that grew into a tree; what the garden was into which that grain was cast; and who are the branches of this tree.

In our discussion on the preceding Sunday of the Lord’s parable in which he says, “To what is the kingdom of heaven like, and to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed,” and so forth, we touched on many points [Codex Vallicellianus: “we sketched many things”] by which we proved that the kingdom of God is not improperly compared with a grain of mustard seed, and that the difference lies solely in the estimated meaning of the words, not in the comparison of their qualities [Codex Vallicellianus A 9: “not in the consolation of the virtues”]. For the Christian faith is the kingdom of God [Codex Vallicellianus: “It possesses the same power which, etc.”] and possesses the same force that the nature of mustard draws forth.

For just as, when we take mustard juice, we are compelled to shed tears, our faces are saddened, our brows contracted and moved, and we receive the very healthfulness of our bodies together with a kind of weeping born of austerity. On the one hand, its bitterness irritates us and its pungency penetrates us; on the other, the heat of its fiery flavor kindles us [Codex Urbevetanus: “is kindled, and, with the whole body disturbed”], and, though disturbed throughout our bodies, we become all the healthier when we lament more deeply.

So also, when we receive the commandments of the Christian faith, we are saddened in spirit, afflicted in body, moved to tears [Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “we are deeply moved”], and attain our very salvation with a kind of weeping and sorrow. Hence our fasts also irritate us; there the consciousness of sins torments us, here the loss of property troubles us; and, saddened in our whole condition, we attain salvation more fully if we weep more deeply, according to what the Lord says: “You will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice” (John 16).

Just as, when the head must be treated with mustard, we are ordered to remove the shaved hair and lay aside every obstruction of the skin, so that the medicine may reach the bare body more effectively, so also, when the soul is to be healed through faith, we are commanded to remove from ourselves the substance of the world and lay aside the impediments of gold and silver, so that spiritual medicine may reach the soul, bare and alone, more suitably [Codex Laurentianus X: “so that it may thereby reach the soul alone”; Codices Vallicellianus and Urbevetanus: “may be applied”]. For whoever is wrapped in worldly possessions and the riches of the age will not benefit from the medicine of faith.

Therefore, what mustard juice effects in the body, let Christian faith effect in the soul. But since the same Sunday saying records that the kingdom of heaven is compared with a grain of mustard seed which a man took and cast into his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds rested in its branches [From Codex Sangallensis; both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Laurentianus X, and Urbevetanus lack these words], let us inquire more carefully who it is to whom all these things apply.

Above, we said that the nature of mustard could fittingly be applied to the holy martyrs, who have been worn down by various sufferings. But since Scripture says, “It grew and became a tree, and the birds rested in its branches,” I think this is more properly compared with Christ the Lord himself: by being born as a human being, he was humbled like a grain; by ascending into heaven, he was exalted like a tree. Christ is plainly a grain while he suffers, but a tree when he rises again. He is a grain, I say, when, hungry, he endures hunger [Codex Vallicellianus reads “was enduring.”] He is a tree when, with five loaves, he satisfies five thousand men. There he suffers the barrenness of human condition; here, by his own divinity, he bestows fullness.

I would call the Lord a grain when he is struck, despised, and rebuked [Codex Urbevetanus: “a mustard grain, etc.”]; but a tree when he gives sight to the blind, raises the dead, and forgives sins [Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “but a tree.” Codex 99 reads: “but he is a tree.”]

That he is a grain, he himself says in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the ground, dies, it remains alone” (John 2). The words “it remains alone” are absent from both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and likewise from Laurentianus X.

Therefore, the Jews, unable to endure the pungency and bitterness of this grain—that is, of the Lord and Savior—despised it and refused to receive the juice of heavenly teaching, saying to the man whose sight had been restored, “You be his disciple; we are disciples of Moses” (John 9).

Yet they themselves utterly failed to understand the commandments of Moses, who ordered them to eat this bitterness. When he established the rites for celebrating Passover, he said, “You shall eat it with bitterness; for it is the Lord’s Passover” (Exodus 12). For he did not, as they suppose, command the sharpest juices of lowly herbs to be eaten with the roasted flesh of the lamb; rather, he commanded that the usefully bitter words of Christ’s commandments be swallowed together with the very sacrament of the Lord’s Passion.

Do not the Lord’s words seem bitter when he says, “If you wish to be perfect, leave all that is yours, and come, follow me” (Matthew 19)? And when he says that one should possess neither two tunics, nor a bag, nor sandals, this bitterness of his words is medicine for souls [Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, and Laurentianus X of the Bible, attest this reading].

But when the Gospel says, “Which a man took and cast into his garden” (Matthew 10), who do we think this man was, who took the grain and sowed it in his little garden like a mustard seed? I think he was the man of whom the evangelist reports: “And behold, Joseph, who was a councillor from Arimathea, went to Pilate and asked that he might bury the body of the Lord after it had been taken down” (Luke 23). Having received it, he committed it to burial in a tomb that had been prepared in a garden; and therefore Scripture says, “Which a man took and cast into his garden.”

Joseph’s garden, then, was a garden of little flowers, filled with various blossoms, but as yet he had not planted in it such a shoot. The particular garden of his soul did indeed give off the fragrance of varied virtue with a pleasant sweetness [Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “spiritual”], but he had not yet placed Christ with spices in the secret place of his heart. Thus, when he buried the Savior in the tomb of his little garden, he placed him even more deeply in the innermost part of his soul.

If you seek the branches of this tree, you will find that Peter is a branch, Paul is a branch, and all the apostles or martyrs are branches [Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “the martyrs of the Savior”]. Whoever wishes to hold fast to them with strength will not be submerged by the floods of the world; rather, hiding beneath their shade, he will not suffer the heat of Gehenna, secure from the storm of the devil [Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem add: “and from the fire of the consuming judgment.”]

HOMILY CXI. That the kingdom of God is like leaven.

[Col. 0511]

ADMONITION.

[Col. 0511B] We admit that the homily transcribed here is found among the sermons of St. Ambrose, no. 5 of the Paris edition, and is likewise attributed to that holy Doctor by Codex Laurentianus X, frequently mentioned above. Nevertheless, since both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, namely 90 and 99, assert that it is by Maximus, relying on their testimony we judge that it should be assigned to the holy bishop of Turin, and we hope that it will be useful to readers to have this homily, corrected from the variant readings, published. The similarity of style also supports this attribution, as does the same ingenious facility in explaining the Gospel.

[Col. 0511C] ARGUMENT.—St. Maximus writes that he has been a father to most of his hearers by exhorting them, but to some a stern teacher by rebuking them; then he discusses the mystical meaning of leaven splendidly and at length.

And you yourselves know, brothers, that from the day on which I began to be with you, I have not ceased to admonish you all concerning the Lord’s commandments, and, partly by exhorting you and partly by rebuking you, to impress divine precepts upon you [Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem]. Thus I have been more a father to most [Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “a brother”], while to some I have proved a stern teacher.

Whoever gladly embraced my sermon rejoiced to have me as his father; but whoever grieved that his conscience had been struck by my preaching felt me to be a stern teacher—provided that, whether through kindness or correction, Christ is proclaimed in you [Codex Laurentianus X: “is proclaimed among us”]. Indeed, correction itself is kindness, for it is applied to more negligent children so that through fear they may learn what they neglected through love.

For it is not that a father does not love all his children equally, but that it is a father’s indulgence to display paternal affection according to differences of character [Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and Codex Laurentianus 10: “Not that”; both codices of the Holy Cross: “of kindness”; Codex Laurentianus 10: “But that it is a father’s negligence, according to differences of character, to display the affection of kindness”], so that he may draw the gentle child forward by encouragement but confront the stubborn one with severity. Yet he remains confident of the correction of both: he strikes one out of love and chastises the other with severity. As the Apostle says: “All discipline, for the present, seems not to be joyful but sorrowful; afterward, however, it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12) [Codex Laurentianus X: “returns”].

Therefore, since I believe that you have made progress through so many of my discourses, I wish to discuss certain matters from the divine writings, so that I may understand [Three codices cited above read “so that you may grasp what I shall say”] that you receive what I say with the vitality of faith.

The Lord says in the holy Gospel: “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in flour until the whole was leavened” (Luke 13).

There is no doubt that the power and efficacy of leaven are known to everyone. For although it is small in size, simple in appearance, and ordinary by nature, it carries such strength within that, once it has been put away, its juice makes the whole mass become what it is [Codex Laurentianus 10: “juice, so that it makes this whole thing be, as the thing itself is”]; and thus it continually spreads its power throughout the entire bulk of the mixture [Codex 90 cited above: “continually throughout the whole mass”], so that it makes the whole quantity of meal into leaven. In this way the substance itself, by its strength, acquires a mass corresponding to its own power.

Women do this so that they may carefully provide their husbands with healthier bread and useful food. But since the law is spiritual, and the Gospel exists spiritually through the form of parables [Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “especially spiritually”], let us see what the leaven is, who the woman is, and what the flour is.

We read in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the ground, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12). Therefore, if the Lord is wheat, and the Lord is leaven—for leaven is ordinarily made only from wheat—Christ is rightly compared with leaven [Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “therefore leaven is rightly compared with the Lord.”]

Although he was a human being in appearance, small through humility and cast down through weakness, he possessed such great power of wisdom within that the world itself could scarcely contain his teaching. When he began to spread throughout the whole world by the power of his divinity, he immediately drew the entire human race into his substance by his own power [Codex Laurentianus X: “he immediately drew the whole human race into his substance by his power”], so that he might pour the yoke of his Holy Spirit upon all [Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “the juice”]—that is, make all Christians become what Christ is.

For when the Lord Jesus, as a human being, was alone in the world, hidden like leaven in the mass, he caused all human beings to become what he himself is. Therefore, whoever clings to that leaven, Christ, becomes leaven himself, both useful to himself and beneficial to everyone, confident of his own salvation and secure in the acquisition of others [Codex 90 omits “that”].

Just as leaven, when it is to be mixed into a mass of flour, is broken, crushed, scattered, and itself wholly dissolved, so that by its power it may bind that scattered multitude of flour into one [Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “bind it into one by its power”] and restore to a solid body what had languished in the form of dust through its very reduction, making by its union a useful mass out of what seemed useless through its own dissolution—

so also the Lord Jesus Christ, when he was the leaven of the whole world, was broken, torn, and dissolved through various sufferings, and his juice, which is his precious blood, was poured out for our salvation, so that by being mixed with it he might solidify the whole human race, which previously lay dispersed and dissolved in different directions.

371 Thus, like a certain leaven, we who seemed to be flour from the nations clung to him. We, I say, who lay scattered and utterly diminished throughout the whole world, were transformed by the power of Christ’s Passion into his body, as the blessed Apostle says: “For we are the body of Christ and members” (Ephesians 5).

We, therefore, who were scattered like dust from the nations, are gathered into the solidity of his mass by the sprinkling of the Lord’s blood.

But who is that woman who is said to hide leaven in the flour, if not the holy Church, which daily strives to hide Christ’s teaching in our hearts? She, I say, is the woman who is also said elsewhere to grind, as the Lord says: “There will be two women grinding; one will be taken, and one will be left” (Matthew 24).

The holy Church grinds through the law, through the apostles, and through the prophets, when she makes catechumens and breaks apart and pulverizes the harshness of paganism, so that, once ground into the form of flour, she may make them fit to cling to the Lord’s blood [Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and Laurentianus XIV, Bible, read this].

For one may call the whole Passion of the Lord the leaven of faith. The leaven of our salvation is the very symbol [Both of the three cited codices agree], which is handed down; without this leaven or symbol no one can obtain the substance of eternal life.

And since the Gospel describes two women grinding, and we have said that one Church grinds beneficially, whom must we understand the other to be except the Synagogue? For it too grinds through Moses and the prophets, but uselessly, as the Apostle says concerning the Jews: “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.”

Uselessly, I say, the Synagogue grinds, because it does not temper its mass with the teaching of Christ. Therefore the Lord commands that the leaven of the Synagogue be avoided, saying: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matthew 10).

For it has been tempered with the blood and cruelty of the Jews who said concerning the Lord, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” [Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “his blood”].

Hence the Gospel says: “There will be two women grinding; one will be taken, and one will be left.” The holy Church will be taken into eternal rest, for she grinds food of holiness for the Lord; the faithless Synagogue will be left at the mills [Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “the bloody Synagogue”], forever suffering the turning of its own faithlessness.

HOMILY CXII. A rebuke to the people concerning their absence from church.

[Col. 0515]

ADMONITION.

Although the Maurists write that they found no trace of St. Ambrose in this homily, they nevertheless place it among his sermons, no. 43 of the Paris edition of 1690; we attribute it to St. Maximus on the authority of Codex Sangallensis no. 21 and Codex 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, no. 88, with the title “A rebuke to the people.” We follow the reading of the cited edition of the works of St. Ambrose.

[Col. 0515A] ARGUMENT.—St. Maximus compares priests to bees; he grieves that his frequent preaching does not correct the brothers through any progress in salvation, and that, in his absence, few come to church.

Brothers, after these many days I ought to preach something more abundant and, returning from so great a swarm of priests, refresh us with a pleasing discourse. I rightly spoke of a swarm of priests, because, just as bees make sweet honey from the little flowers of the divine Scriptures and skillfully prepare whatever pertains to the medicine of souls through their mouths, priests are rightly compared with bees. For just as bees prefer bodily chastity, provide the food of heavenly life, and exercise the sting of the law, they are pure for sanctification, sweet for refreshment, and severe for punishment.

Those who are contained, as it were, in a hive of the grace of Mother Church are plainly comparable to bees. In that hive they arrange the cells of different merits through the sweetest preaching, and from the one swarm of the Savior they produce many swarms of Christians.

Although I have never ceased to correct you with paternal kindness, I am amazed that you have made no progress through my admonitions, and I grieve that my frequent preaching does not correct you with any advancement in salvation, but binds you with a certain punishment of accusation.

For the preaching of a priest is correction for the people who are to be saved, and a solemn warning for those who are to be judged. For before judgment we bear witness to them concerning what awaits them in the judgment itself, so that then, when every excuse has been removed, they may be both guilty concerning their sins and liable concerning their contempt.

Therefore I sometimes wish, out of consideration for you, to remain silent; but I would rather have you give an account of stubbornness than have myself bear the judgment of negligence.

For I have discovered, brothers, that in my absence you come to church so rarely and proceed in such small numbers, as though, when I departed, you had departed along with me, and as though, when I am dragged away by necessities, necessity itself had dragged you away with me.

We are alike absent from the house of God; but the difference is that necessity makes me absent, whereas your absence is caused by your will.

Do you not know that, even if I am absent from the church, Christ, who is everywhere, is not absent from his Church? You come, brother, to church and do not find there the Bishop of bishops, the Savior? For the Christian who comes to church only when the bishop is present seems to have come not so much for God’s sake as for a human being’s; nor does he seem to have fulfilled the duty of a fearful Christian, but rather the service of an obsequious friend.

Why, then, do I rebuke you, when you can convict me with a single word? I am convicted because in this matter I see that the clergy are more negligent than you. For how can I correct children when I cannot correct brothers? Or with what confidence can I be angry with the laity when, out of shame before my fellow ministers, I am silent?

But, brothers, I am not speaking about everyone. There are certainly some who are devoted, and there are others who are negligent. I name no one; let each person’s conscience confront him.

HOMILY CXIII. An address after the rebuke.

[Col. 0515]

ADMONITION.

We likewise believe that this homily should be attributed to Maximus, bishop of Turin, and not to Ambrose, bishop of Milan, because it bears the name of the former both in the Ambrosian codex and in Codex 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem; moreover, in the place indicated in the preceding admonition, the Maurists deny that it has a style of composition like that used by Ambrose. The same homily is read in Codex Vaticanus 1277, p. 61, under the heading “Likewise, by the same author, on the same subject”; in the codex of the Holy Cross it bears the title “An address after the rebuke”; and in Laurentianus XIV, under Ambrose’s name, “An address after the rebuke.”

[Col. 0515C] ARGUMENT.—Maximus rejoices, knowing that the disciple’s sadness is the teacher’s joy. He explains Matthew 16: “But whom do you say that I am?”

My preaching may perhaps have been more bitter, brothers, on the preceding Sunday, because I dealt more sharply with many of you through my teachings and truth, and pursued matters that offered no flattery but caused sadness [Codices Laurentianus and 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “did not bring flatteries”; Codex Vaticanus 1277: “brought”; Ambrosian Codex: “through your harsh teachings and truths”; Laurentianus X: “through the severity of teaching”]. But this makes no difference to me; for I rejoice, knowing that the disciple’s sadness is the teacher’s joy.

The hearer makes progress when the preacher announces sterner things [Codex 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “pronounces them”]; salvation is produced in him when the sadness of correction is imposed. For the blessed Apostle says: “The sadness that is according to God produces repentance leading to lasting salvation” (2 Corinthians 7) [The Ambrosian Codex omits “in.”]

Therefore I rightly rejoice, because when I rebuke I work salvation [Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “I”]. Although the son may grieve at the harshness of my speech [Codex Vaticanus and Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “Although the son may grieve”; Codex Ambrosianus: “who would make progress,” etc.], I understand that he is making progress through grief.

The holy Apostle says: “What son is there whom the father does not beat?” (Hebrews 12). A father does not always kiss his son; sometimes he also chastises him.

Therefore, when the one who is loved is chastised, kindness is being exercised toward him. Love too has its wounds, and they are sweeter when they are inflicted more bitterly; religious chastisement is sweeter than indulgent leniency. Hence the prophet says: “The wounds of a friend are sweeter than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27).

Therefore, brothers, since I believe that after the useful words of my many rebukes you have made progress through the kindness of your understanding [Codex Ambrosianus: “useful blows”], let us discuss some matters from the sacred Scriptures [Codex Vaticanus 1277: “let us pursue”].

Just as a spring that does not flow with its customary moisture is stirred with rods and is then found to be more abundant, and turbid water first flows from it so that purer water may follow, so also your holiness had indeed been irritated by the austerity of my speech, but has become more devoted through the sweetness of kindness.

Your minds perhaps retained something turbulent, but now everything pure flows forth from your conduct.

Let us see, then, what the Lord says to his disciples: “But whom do you say that I am?” (Matthew 16) [Codex Ambrosianus omits “then”; the same codex omits “to be”].

The Lord therefore did not ask, as though ignorant, what the people and the disciples thought about him. Rather, as one who knew, he wished the minds of all to reveal the faith of each, so that they might declare with their mouths what they believed in their hearts concerning the Lord [We have appropriately added these words from Codices Vaticanus 1277 and Ambrosianus].

Some believed the Lord to be Elijah, others Jeremiah, and others John the Baptist. Peter alone confesses him to be Christ, the Son of God.

There are degrees of faith, and whoever believes more devotedly makes a more religious confession. For this devotion it is said to Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

When he was called Simon, he was therefore given the name Peter because of this devotion.

We read, when the Apostle speaks of the Lord himself: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10). Since Christ is rightly the rock, Simon was therefore named Peter, so that he who shared the faith with the Lord might also share with the Lord the unity of the Lord’s name: just as a Christian is named from Christ, so the apostle Peter was named from the Rock, Christ.

Nor can we reject the opinion of the people, who considered the Lord to be one of the prophets. For some perhaps thought the Savior to be Elijah because Elijah ascended into heaven as the Savior did [The Ambrosian Codex: “ascended”].

But Christ is not like Elijah. Elijah is carried up into heaven, whereas Christ returns; Elijah, as a weak man, is carried up in a fiery chariot, whereas Christ, as God, is borne by his own power; Elijah is led like a human being, whereas Christ ascends like the Savior; Elijah follows the angels who lead him, whereas Christ goes before the angels who accompany him [The Ambrosian Codex: “he follows, with an angel leading him”].

Finally, those same angels, returning to earth, said to the apostles on behalf of the Lord Savior: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 11).

HOMILY CXIV. Concerning what is written in Matthew, chapter 22: “Render to God the things that are God’s,” and concerning soldiers.

[Col. 0517]

ADMONITION.

We do not hesitate to assert that St. Maximus is the author of this homily, although others hold a different opinion. We rely especially on two codices, the Sangallensis and Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. In the former it appears under no. 24, and in the latter under no. 23.

Their testimony is plainly confirmed by three other codices: first, Codex Casinensis 12, p. 337, which at the beginning of the homily reads, “Concerning what is written: ‘Render to God the things that are God’s,’ and concerning soldiers, a sermon of St. Maximus, bishop”; second, Codex 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, where the same title appears under no. 7; and third, Codex Beneventanus 1, p. 337, which agrees entirely with the preceding manuscripts both in its inscription and in naming Maximus.

We know that in older editions this homily was attributed to Ambrose and also to Augustine; but we know equally well that the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of St. Maur judged that it should be left among the spurious works. In the preface to Ambrose’s sermons they passed over it in silence and transferred it to the appendix of the sermons of St. Augustine, no. 82.

But someone may object that these same critics seemed to disagree less with those who assigned the homily to Augustine than with those who assigned it to Maximus. For they noted that it certainly did not belong to Augustine, but perhaps did not belong to Maximus either.

What, then, should be concluded? The Benedictine editors had doubts about Maximus, but did not absolutely deny the attribution. For if the codices we have praised, which explicitly bear the name of the holy bishop of Turin, had been known to them, they would not have hesitated to acknowledge this homily as Maximian.

Perhaps the style seems unlike that which Maximus generally uses. But no one is unaware that in moral sermons Ambrose, Augustine, and other Fathers likewise conveyed lessons concerning eternal life in plainer language.

[Col. 0517C] ARGUMENT.—St. Maximus teaches, while expounding the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures, that a rule of life is prescribed for every duty and that, for every Christian, military service ought to be the foremost honorable service.

Some, brothers, who are either held by the military belt or occupied in public office, when they commit serious sins, commonly excuse themselves aloud from the penalty of their sin [Col. 0518C] by saying that they are soldiers; [Note: [Col. 0518C] Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “They are wont first to excuse themselves aloud for their sins by saying that they serve as soldiers.” Codex 99 reads: “They are wont first to excuse themselves aloud for their sins.” Codex 10 Laurentianus likewise reads: “They are wont first to excuse themselves aloud for their sins.”] and, to avoid ever doing good, they complain that they are occupied with evil actions—as though the fault lay in human military service, not in the will. Thus they attribute to their offices what they themselves do.

For it is not a crime to serve as a soldier, but it is a sin to serve as a soldier for plunder. Nor is administering public affairs criminal; but to administer public affairs in order rather to increase one’s private fortune appears damnable. [Col. 0519A] For this reason pay has been established for soldiers: so that, while seeking expenses, they may not resort to plunder.

But what of this? When, because of some error, they are rebuked by their superiors, [Note: [Col. 0519D] Codex 10 Laurentianus reads *aliqui* (“some people”) for *aliquem* (“some error”).] and some of them are asked why they were drunk, why they seized another’s property, or why, in their disorder, they committed murder, they immediately reply: “What was I to do, a secular man [Col. 0519D] and a soldier? Surely I have not professed to be a monk or a cleric.” [Note: Three cited manuscripts have *aut* (“or”) instead of *et* (“and”).] [Note: Codex 10 Laurentianus reads: “Surely I have not professed to be a monk or a cleric?”] As though everyone who is not a cleric or monk might do what is forbidden.

Therefore a rule of life is prescribed for every office [Note: The Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “Sacred Scripture prescribes a rule of life,” and so do the Cassinese manuscripts, adding words absent from the printed text.]; every sex, age, and rank is summoned to do good. Let no one, then, excuse himself on account of public duties; let no one complain about the occupation of military service. For every Christian, the first military service ought to be the service of uprightness. [Note: This agrees with Codex 10 Laurentianus and with both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.]

To confirm what we say by evangelical authority, let us consider the reading that has just been recited. The Gospel says:

“Tax collectors also came to John to be baptized by him, and they said to him, ‘Teacher, what shall we do?’ But he said to them, ‘Exact nothing more than what has been appointed for you’” (Luke 3).

A thoroughly honorable question from the tax collectors, and a just answer from the holy prophet. They ask anxiously so that, either through ignorance by exacting more they may not fall into sin, or by ceasing to act they may not defraud the public office. He commands them moderately, so that injustice may have no place and the appointed tax may be collected. For he did not say, “Exact nothing,” but “Exact nothing more.” From this we understand that before God it is not exaction as such, but unjust exaction, that is condemned. [Note: Codex 10 Laurentianus reads: “It is not so much exaction as unjust exaction that is condemned.”]

The Lord himself says: “Render to God the things that are God’s, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Matthew 22). Therefore what Caesar commands must be borne; what the emperor imposes must be endured. But it becomes intolerable when plunder adds to the exaction.

What, however, are we to make of this: that the very men who administer such necessities double their sins by their sins? They call their frauds and robberies “profit,” although the plunder itself is turned into profit. They add this to their crimes: that they persecute those whom they see to be defenseless, and think that they have failed to deceive the public necessities unless they have deceived the houses of orphans. [Note: [Col. 0519D] Both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem have this reading.] Thus the children of one who perhaps two days earlier had been their friend, colleague, or brother, once death has intervened, are treated as though they were strangers, worthless, and wretched. [Col. 0519D]

If there is a widow, she is harassed by injuries until she marries; or, if she wishes to remain in her resolve of chastity, she scarcely remains in possession of her property while giving away her gifts. [Note: Both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read “is stirred up” instead of “is harassed.”] [Note: This reading is found in the manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Laurentianus 10, and the Cassinese manuscript.]

When they have filled their purses with these frauds, you will see them hastening cheerfully and carefully to church and giving thanks to God, as though this money had been bestowed on them by him. They commit the further sin of wishing God to share in their robberies. [Note: Codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads *videas* (“you may see”); the Laurentian manuscript reads *videbas* (“you used to see”).]

The holy Gospel says:

“The soldiers also asked him, ‘And what shall we do?’ John said to them, ‘Do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your pay’” (Luke 3).

Here every soldier ought to recognize himself. Scripture is not speaking only of those soldiers who are engaged in armed service; anyone who uses the belt of an office is reckoned a soldier of his rank. [Col. 0520B] Therefore this statement may be applied, for example, to soldiers, protectors, all governors, and anyone who receives pay publicly assigned to him. If he seeks more, he is condemned by John’s sentence as a slanderer and extortioner. [Note: Both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem have this reading.]

This evil has become so deeply rooted that now, as though by custom, laws are sold, rights corrupted, and the judgment itself put up for sale; no case can any longer exist without a “cause.”

This divine sentence, however, which addresses soldiers, can also be turned upon clerics. For although they may not appear to serve the world as soldiers, we nevertheless serve the Lord God, as the Apostle says: “No one serving God entangles himself in worldly affairs” (2 Timothy 2). [Note: Codex 99 reads: “We therefore seem no longer to serve with loosened and flowing tunics, but we have the belt of our service, with which we bind the inner parts of chastity.” Codex 10 Laurentianus reads: “We seem, I say, not to serve with loosened and flowing tunics, but let us have the belt of our service, with which we bind the inner parts of chastity, and receive pay and a gift from him.”]

We seem, I say, not to serve with loosened and flowing tunics, but we have the belt of our service, [Col. 0520C] with which the inner parts of chastity are bound. Concerning this belt the Lord says to his Apostles: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12).

We are therefore soldiers of Christ, and receive pay and a gift from him, as the blessed Apostle says: “He has given us the pledge of the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 1); by this he has enriched us with the reward of the Holy Spirit. If, therefore, any Christian is not content with this gift and seeks something more, he begins to lack precisely what he has earned. [Note: Both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Cassinese 12, and Laurentianus 10 add the following.]

This happens especially to the Arian heretics: while they seek I know not what more, they found the spirit of error and lost the grace of the Holy Spirit. [Note: Codex 10 Laurentianus reads: “They betrayed the Spirit of the grace of Christ, having found the spirit of error.”]

The Catholic cleric, too, is restrained by this sentence. For if he is not content with the pay that, by the Lord’s command, he receives from the altar, [Note: [Col. 0520D] Both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read *de altario* (“from the altar”).] but conducts business, sells intercessions, and gladly accepts the gifts of widows, [Col. 0521A] he can be seen more as a businessman than as a cleric. [Note: Codex 10 Laurentianus adds: “For we can say, ‘No one accuses us of seizure; no one charges us with violence,’ and so forth.”]

Nor can we say, “No one accuses us of seizure; no one charges us with violence,” as though sometimes greedy flatteries did not extract greater plunder [Note: Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “as though greedy flatteries did not sometimes extract greater plunder”] from widows than tortures; for before God it makes no difference whether one seizes another’s property by force or by deception, provided that one possesses what belongs to another by whatever means.

*Here ends the homily.*

# HOMILY CXV  
## On what the Lord says in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 8: “Foxes have dens”

[Col. 0521]

## NOTICE

Four manuscripts of distinguished authority agree that Saint Maximus is the author of this homily: namely, three of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and the manuscript of Saint Gall. The older manuscript of the Holy Cross, numbered 90 among the homilies of Saint Maximus, contains it as number 36 with the title: “On what is written: ‘Foxes have dens,’ etc.” The second manuscript, number 99, has it as number 83: “On what was said, the Lord saying: ‘Foxes have dens,’ etc.” The third manuscript of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem is a lectionary. After the Gospel passage has been cited, as in manuscript 90, it reads: “Homily of blessed Maximus, bishop.” Finally, the Saint Gall manuscript, homily 30, fully agrees with the title of manuscript 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.

Supported by these clear testimonies, we easily refute the Laurentianus X manuscript mentioned above in the notice, as well as the editors of the works of Ambrose, who circulated this homily among the sermons of Saint Ambrose. We add a fragment recovered from the Saint Gall manuscript, by which the homily, hitherto mutilated, is restored to completeness.

[Col. 0521B] **ARGUMENT.**—God is not a respecter of persons. We must cry out to him not so much with the mouth as with the heart. Cunning and insolent people are compared with foxes, as are many Christians who confess the Lord with their mouths but not in their conduct, and especially heretics, whose pestilential plots we must avoid.

If your devotion carefully considered the Gospel chapter that was read, that very chapter could have penetrated your understanding of why the Lord, as Scripture relates, when one man approached him and asked to follow him wherever he went for the sake of religious service, said instead to another, “Follow me,” and, rejecting and disregarding the first, chose another who was silent and unsuspecting. [Note: [Col. 0521D] Manuscripts 90 and 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.]

Since willing service is ordinarily more acceptable than forced service, and service is more pleasing when offered freely than when exacted by command, why then is this man rejected, or even deemed unworthy? The Lord says to him: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8).

First, therefore, we must consider that the Lord is not a respecter of persons. He is an impartial and just judge; but according to the quality of their conduct he returns the affection of love, [Note: [Col. 0522D] Codex 10 Laurentianus reads *pro qualitate morum* (“according to the quality of their conduct”).] and chooses not the one who is ready with words but sluggish in devotion, but the one who is silent with his tongue and devoted in mind. Of such a one the Prophet says: “If you make yourself silent, you will appear wise” (Proverbs 17). Of the one who speaks insolently Scripture says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father” (Matthew 7).

From this we learn that we must cry out to the Lord not so much with the mouth as with the heart. Our Savior, therefore, who sees the thoughts and intentions of human beings, [Note: [Col. 0522D] Codex 10 Laurentianus and the manuscript of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read *pervidebat* (“saw through”).] hearing the obedience of the voice but recognizing the craftiness of the mind, compares this man to an animal that indicates one thing by its voice but does another in its conduct. The fox imitates the dog’s bark, but by deceit practices the robbery of fraud.

He therefore takes the silent and unsuspecting man. His tongue was silent, but [Col. 0522B] he spoke in spirit. We understand how devoted he was: as he himself declared, he had left his father dead in order to find the Lord of life. For he says: “Permit me first to go and bury my father” (Luke 9). He had left him dead so that, on returning, he might bury him. Pain had not held him back, nor had death delayed him, because he was hastening toward life.

He had not yet closed the eyes of the dying man, nor yet buried his stiffening limbs. As soon as he learned that the Lord had arrived, he forgot the affection of filial devotion and, moved by a greater devotion, believed that he loved Christ more than his parent. Perhaps he had read the prophetic passage that says: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 14). [Note: Both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem have this reading.] Therefore he forgot his father while remembering the Savior.

He had also heard the Lord’s Gospel: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10). Thus the reason why Tobias is justified, and why he left his meal for the sake of burial (Tobit 1), is proved here: for Christ’s sake this man left his father’s burial. Tobias did not fear that, because of an earthly meal, he would miss the banquet; this man feared that, because of delay, he would lose the nourishment of heavenly bread.

Therefore, although we owe burial to everyone, in contemplation of Christ this man, out of love for Christ, abandoned his father’s burial. Let us first examine his interpretation and the response of the Lord and Savior. He says to him: “I will follow you wherever you go” (Luke 9). It is a ready but arrogant declaration. The Lord was going to his passion, descending to the underworld, and ascending to heaven. Can human frailty follow him in all these things? This presumption is foolish rather than a religious confession.

The Lord says the same to the Apostle Peter when Peter thought that he would follow the Savior in everything: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now” (John 13). And when Peter obstinately declared that he would not be separated from him even by death, he was condemned as a boaster and told that he would deny the Lord three times. [Note: [Col. 0522D] Codex 10 Laurentianus.] Thus the man who promised that he would not be separated from the confession of Christ even by death was separated from Christ’s company by the question of a servant girl; and unless, as though setting a limit, he had been told that he would deny him three times, perhaps, questioned more often, he would have denied him repeatedly.

What, then, is said to this insolent man? “Foxes have dens, and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8). Observe the matter to which he is subtly compared. The fox is a deceitful animal, always intent upon plunder, [Col. 0523D] practicing robbery by fraud; [Note: [Col. 0523D] Manuscripts 90 and 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read *rapinam fraudis exercens* (“practicing robbery by fraud”).] it allows nothing to be safe, nothing undisturbed, nothing secure, and seeks prey even among human dwellings.

I think this comparison was written not only on account of that man, but also on account of many Christians who confess the Lord with their mouths but conduct themselves with fox-like deceit. Every Christian who wishes to conceal his sins is spiritually a fox. Just as the fox remains in hiding because of its deceit, so the sinner, silent because of the burden of his conscience, hides in dens. [Note: The manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, cited repeatedly, and Laurentianus 10 supply this wording.] And just as the fox does not dare display the deceitfulness of its ways amid crowds of people, so the sinner is ashamed to confess the wickedness of his conduct in the midst of the church.

I would plainly call every Christian a fox who lies in wait for his neighbor, who daily strives to gnaw away another’s boundaries, seize his fruits, and devour his animals; and, as is common in our time, who steals not chicks in the manner of foxes but pigs in the manner of wolves—one who, although he could live by his own labor, hunts another’s property with the savagery of wild beasts.

I also think that all heretics should be compared with foxes. Since they cannot dwell in the house of the Lord, they prepare for themselves certain dark meeting places like dens, in which they stubbornly hide and plot against the Church, so that, if some innocent soul should venture forth, they may swallow it like a chick of the mother hen.

The foxes, I say, lie in wait for the Church—that is, for that evangelical hen of whom the Lord says: “How often I have desired to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings” (Matthew 23). [Note: Both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem end the homily here, as does the Paris edition from which the text was extracted and corrected from manuscript copies; the Saint Gall manuscript, however, supplied what follows.]

Therefore, brothers, let us avoid—let us avoid—the pestilential plots of the lurking foxes; let us avoid the deadly traps of the most wicked creatures, lest, like those foxes that the exceedingly strong Samson once armed with torches and sent into the field of the Philistines (Judges 15), which burned up in flames everything their tracks touched, the foxes of perverse doctrines or seize the fruits of our fields through the deception of their plots or consume them by the burning of their flames.

Let us therefore be, as we read, both simple as doves and shrewd as serpents, so that the shrewdness of serpents may protect the simplicity of doves, and so that we may not know how to do evil while nevertheless being able to avoid it; through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory, etc.

# HOMILY CXVI  
## Where the Lord healed the withered hand on the Sabbath (Luke, chapter 6)

[Col. 0523]

## NOTICE

The reading of the homily itself makes clear to anyone familiar with the eloquence of Maximus who its author is. The authority of four manuscripts also supports its attribution to Saint Maximus: three of the Holy Cross and a fourth, that of Saint Gall.

In manuscript 90 of the Holy Cross it appears as number 38; in manuscript 99 as number 8; and in manuscript 9 as number 2, with this uniform title: “Where the Lord healed the withered hand on the Sabbath.” The Saint Gall manuscript has the same title as number 41. The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, neither in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine nor in the preface to the sermons of Saint Ambrose in the Paris edition of 1690, contain anything contrary to our view.

[Col. 0523C] **ARGUMENT.**—Saint Maximus explains the Gospel passage in which we read that Christ the Lord healed a certain man who had a withered hand, and offers several interpretations suited to understanding Scripture.

I believe, brothers, that you listened attentively to the Gospel reading that was recently read: the passage in which the Lord Jesus Christ entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and healed by spiritual medicine a man who had a withered hand—not by applying the juices of herbs or binding on medicinal ointments, but by commanding with a word and, in anger, restoring health to the body.

Anger, I say, as the Evangelist relates, restored strength to the right hand. From this we understand what sort of healing belongs to the Lord’s kindness, whose medicine is such indignation; or how he benefits when pacified, who shows such mercy when angry. By a word, therefore, he commands that the juice of the veins be poured into the withered right hand. [Note: This is the reading of manuscripts 90 and 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and Laurentianus 10: “that the juice of the veins be poured in.”]

It is not surprising that the one who restored the withered hand is he who created the entire body from withered dust, and restored by the command of his word what at the beginning he had established through the work of creation. [Note: [Col. 0524D] The three manuscripts just cited read *opportune* (“appropriately”).] As the body recognized its creator, it obeyed even in the small part to which, as a whole, it owed itself. [Note: [Col. 0524D] Both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.]

But let us see what the withered hand in the synagogue signifies, which is of no benefit to its own body; let us inquire when it became withered through its works, and when it first began to be dry. For the Savior’s action is not concerned with one man alone, nor is the weakness of one man being treated, but the infirmity of the entire human race is healed. [Note: The manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and Laurentianus 10 read “is healed.”]

No one doubts that the right hand, or the more distinguished part of the whole body, has the function of supplying daily nourishment to its body and, with a certain providence, feeding and sustaining the other limbs so that they may enjoy life.

I would say, then, that this right hand in the Jewish people signifies the scribes or teachers. They were established by the Lord as the more distinguished part in the body of the Pharisees, but neglected to nourish the other members—[Note: [Col. 0525D] This is from Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.][Col. 0525A] that is, they did not wish to offer Christ to their body, according to the prophecies, as food for eternal life. Therefore their teaching withered like a weak hand, because it did not seek the fountain of everlasting wisdom. [Note: Both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem have this reading.]

For this reason it finally happened that, like a contracted hand, it could not hold the key of knowledge, as the Lord says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who have hidden the key of knowledge” (Luke 11), and so forth. This key is Christ the Lord, through whom the hidden places of our hearts are opened to the faith of belief. [Note: [Col. 0525D] The same manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.] The Pharisees lose this key; the Apostles find it, as the Lord says to Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” [Note: This sentence is supplied from both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.]

Therefore the hand of the synagogue withered when it abandoned Christ; [Note: [Col. 0525D] This is the reading of Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.] the right hand of the synagogue consequently became worse in the leaders of the Jews. For whoever abandons Christ, the fountain, is immediately weakened, indeed found weaker in all his members. [Note: Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem has this reading.]

Yet I find that this hand was once better than the other members. For holy Moses, leader of the Jewish people, was like the brighter right hand of his body when he was deemed worthy to receive from the Divinity the Law that was to be handed on. Moses was the right hand, I say, who nourished the children of Israel with heavenly manna like a provident hand.

This is plainly the right hand that defeated the magicians Jannes and Jambres by the brightness of its snowy splendor. For thus it is written: [Note: Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem supplies the following.] “When Moses brought his hand out from his bosom, it shone with the light of brilliant whiteness.” [Col. 0525C] Therefore the darkness of the magicians was destroyed, because the shining right hand gleamed through Moses’ merits.

But let us see when this hand first began to wither or die. I affirm that it first withered in Adam, when he plucked the fruits of the forbidden tree against the Lord’s prohibition, [Note: [Col. 0526D] Codex 10 Laurentianus reads *pomum* (“fruit”) instead of *poma* (“fruits”).] and then lost the juice of immortality. It was dried up, so to speak, when it caused the human being made in the image of God to be dissolved into dust by his sin.

Would that only the hand had been held accountable for the sin! What is more serious is that the entire body was condemned to death when the right hand first sinned. Nor should you be surprised that the right-hand member did not remain whole in Adam: the vigor of eternity dried up within it. For just as the right hand of Moses, guarding the Lord’s commands, shone with snowy brilliance, so Adam’s right hand, transgressing God’s commands, was contracted by deadly pallor. [Note: Both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem have this reading.]

The Savior heals this hand of Adam in the synagogue—that is, he hastens to heal the weakness of the entire human race. [Note: This is the reading of Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.] Hence the medicine is universal.

He says also to the man who contracted it by sacrificing to idols: “Stretch out your hand.” He says, “Stretch out your hand,” whose right hand withered through taking interest. He says, “Stretch out your hand,” who by means of it eagerly seeks to seize the property of orphans [Note: Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and Codex X Laurentianus read: “who by means of it have been accustomed to seize the property of orphans and widows.”] and widows.

But you also, who think that you have a sound hand, beware lest avarice contract it. Rather, frequently stretch it out in mercy toward the poor; often stretch it out in hospitality toward the stranger. Always stretch it out to the Lord for your sins. Be merciful; be generous. Observe what the prophet says: “Do not let your hand be extended to receive and contracted when it is time to distribute” (Ecclesiasticus 4).

Thus your hand can be sound [Col. 0526C] if it is restrained from evil deeds but extended toward good works. [Note: Both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem add this sentence.]

# HOMILY CXVII  
## On the camel

[Col. 0525]

## NOTICE

This homily has a longer title in manuscript X, Pluteus XIV, of the Laurentian Library, in these words: “On avarice, which is to be detested above all, signified by the camel.” The name of the author is absent. Some attributed it to Saint Ambrose, as did the older Paris editors of his works. The Maurists assigned it to Maximus. They were more correct, since the frequently cited manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem number this homily among the sermons of Maximus.

In manuscript 90 it bears this title: “Here begins the homily on what was said in the Gospel, the Lord saying: ‘It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven’; and it is number 30.” Manuscript 99 records it as number 4 with the title: “On the camel.”

**ARGUMENT.**—Saint Maximus, who often preached against the vice of avarice, here again warns the rich, with the clear teachings of Christ the Lord, to beware lest through excessive devotion to earthly riches they lose the treasures of heaven.

The Lord Jesus Christ says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19). I fear that this saying may perhaps apply to you, who either possess or seek the riches of this world.

For just as the animal camel, which is crooked and misshapen, is prevented by the very distortion of its body from passing through the narrowest opening of a needle, so the deformity of life does not permit the rich, burdened with avarice and defiled by greed, to enter by the narrow way of the kingdom. [Col. 0526C] For the same Lord says: “Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life” (Matthew 7).

Thus in the camel the shape of its limbs makes entry difficult. In the rich man, however, the magnitude of his sins creates the impediment. It is a kind of hump of the soul to think or do something shameful; it is a kind of crooked deformity of the mind always to attend to unclean things and to be drawn away from the Church’s holy threshold by worldly cares.

Therefore it seems to me that the prophet, speaking spiritually of this bodily deformity, indicated rather the foulness of conduct when he says: “Let not the hunchback glory as the straight.” As though he were saying: “Let not the sinner, distorted by the crookedness of his vices, glory as the righteous man, made upright by the simplicity of a good conscience.”

Even if you rejoice, sinner, in the height of your body, even if you take pleasure in the equality of your shoulders, your soul is nevertheless deformed by the crookedness of your conduct. The rich man is therefore rightly compared with a camel. The bulk of the camel’s body keeps it from passing through the needle’s opening; the concern for his possessions keeps the rich man from entering the Church. The small opening cannot contain the camel burdened by the mass of its limbs, and the holy entrance cannot receive the rich man weighed down by a heap of sins.

Each has its own burden: the camel is loaded with flesh, the rich man with sins. Just as the camel is unsuited to the narrowest opening of the needle, so the rich man is unfit for the blessed kingdom of God—except that nature makes the camel physically misshapen, whereas the will makes the rich man morally crooked. [Note: Both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem supply this sentence.]
