I say this, brothers, about those who, so as not to attend the most joyful feast of the holy Epiphany in the Church, are held fast by the fetters of their possessions and bound by a kind of earthly chain, so that they cannot come to the house of the Lord. It is not that anything external holds them back, but that they are so entangled in their own actions that they have now lost control over their manner of life. While they display concern for their property, they seek no remedy at all for their souls.

“What difficulty of the moment are you putting before me, rich man? What sudden necessity are you introducing?” If you have a heart, understand that the necessity of salvation is greater than every other necessity, and that it is more beneficial to care first for life than to repair losses to one’s property, lest, while seeking an increase in our possessions, we experience the loss of our soul.

Perhaps you fear the judge whom you left in his tribunal. Believe me: you ought much more to fear God the judge, who will judge that very judge. You fear the man who will soon receive a successor, but do not fear the Lord, whom no one ever succeeds.

Consider, then, the approaching day of judgment, the unquenchable flames of Gehenna, the dreadful gnashing of teeth, and the final torment of darkness. And if you can, leave the Church and entangle yourself in worldly cares. I fear that, while you seek the riches of the world, you may instead find the riches of sin; and that, having discovered the treasures of this age, you may lose the treasures of heaven.

*Here ends the homily.*

# HOMILY CXVII  
## On the pearl

[Col. 0527]

## NOTICE

The style, entirely similar, shows that this homily is genuinely connected with the preceding one, and two manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, 90 and 99, confirm it. In the first manuscript the title appears as number 3: “Here begins the homily on the Gospel pearl”; in the second, as number 6: “Sermon of blessed Maximus, bishop, on the pearl.”

Someone might oppose our view with Vatican Codex 1277, folio 59 verso, which attributes the homily to Ambrose under this title: “Sermon of blessed Ambrose, bishop, in which he laments the neglected solemnity of the Apostles Peter and Paul.” We nevertheless say that this testimony does not hinder us, first because it is only one witness; second because the title is demonstrably carelessly assigned and belongs to a later age, since, with most of the homily silently omitted, the text is copied from its conclusion; and third because the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur did not say a single word about this sermon when reprinting the works of Ambrose.

[Col. 0527C] 389 **ARGUMENT.**—Maximus laments with his people that they neglect to hear the word of God and rarely attend church. He proves that those who do not devote themselves to divine matters at the proper time inflict an injury upon God and bring many losses upon themselves.

I think, beloved brothers, that what I did on the previous Sunday ought to suffice for your correction: I was about to depart without bestowing upon you any spiritual gifts from the sacred Scriptures, but merely rebuked and accused you for your sin and dismissed you without any consolation of preaching. For I wanted you to understand precisely how gravely you had sinned, since you had proved entirely unworthy to hear the divine utterances. For this is the priests’ severe and abundant punishment: not to entrust the sacraments of the heavenly Scriptures to those who are unworthy, nor, as the Lord says, to give what is holy to dogs or throw pearls before swine to be trampled underfoot (Matt. 7). Whoever tries to place the heavenly pearl around the foulest sinner destroys its grace. [Note: The Vatican codex reads “crush” (*contundere*).] For a jewel, as you yourselves know, is suitable only for gold, and a pearl is fitted only to precious necklaces. [Col. 0528C] Be excellent gold, then; be a precious necklace, so that the spiritual pearl may be enclosed in you.

For Christ the Lord is the pearl which that rich merchant in the Gospel hastened to purchase after selling all his possessions; he preferred to lose all the jewels of the world that he possessed, provided only that he might buy Christ’s one pearl. [Note: The same Vatican codex omits “of the world.”] Therefore I too, brothers, because of the magnitude of the offense you had committed, did not wish to open for you the words of evangelical nourishment. Rather, I preferred to inflict upon you the injury of spirited indignation, and first to correct you with spiritual blows, and then to enrich you with the pearl’s gifts. I preferred, I say, to rebuke your sin sharply by accusing it rather than gently to nourish it by pretending not to notice it. For whoever does not rebuke a sinning brother in some way encourages him.

But do not think that I do not do this out of love when I so often strike you. [Col. 0528D] [Note: Thus the Vatican codex.] For the son [Note: The same codex.] who is worthy of correction is loved more, as Holy Scripture says: “For whom the Lord loves, he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3). Tell me: was it not grievous that you were then so forgetful of your salvation that you failed to render due honor to the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, although you know them to be teachers of the nations, founders of martyrs, and leaders of priests? You were unwilling to celebrate their most festive birthday feast with us or to attend that heavenly banquet at which the Lord himself supplied us with the sustenance of life amid such great joy for the martyrs. [Col. 0529A] [Note: The Vatican codex reads “for his martyrs.”]

[Note: “Do you wish to know of how many good things you were deprived? Ask, brothers, those who were present there with me, how refreshed they departed from the Lord’s table, or what spiritual riches they carried home with them.” This passage of Saint Maximus seemed to me not to be passed over, since much may be drawn from it for understanding the discipline of the Church’s ancient times. First, it presents the institution of the feast of the birthday day, or glorious passion, of the holy chief apostles Peter and Paul, for whose celebration the faithful people assembled in church with the bishop. Second, it mentions the heavenly banquet, or the sacrifice of the Mass, which was solemnly celebrated on feast days and which Christians ought to attend. Third, it provides a clear testimony to the sacrament of the Eucharist, in which the true body of Jesus Christ and his true blood are contained. Fourth, Saint Maximus teaches the customary practice of bishops—of which Tertullian likewise speaks in his book *On the Soldier’s Crown*—of offering the faithful, in the celebration of Mass, the most holy Eucharist, namely the consecrated species of bread. Fifth, he recalls the wonderful effect of this sacrament: in those who receive it, it bestows spiritual riches, that is, a fuller abundance of graces. Long ago Saint Ambrose taught, in his exposition of Psalm 118, that Christians ought to approach to receive the sacrament of the Eucharist fasting, even if the sacrifice of the Mass were prolonged into the evening hours, as in Lent. Maximus says nothing here about fasting to be observed by communicants; but since the Church of Turin was included in the province of Milan, it must be acknowledged that the same discipline in administering the sacraments prevailed there.]

Do you wish to know of how many good things you were deprived? Ask, brothers, those who were present there with me, how refreshed they departed from the Lord’s table, or what spiritual riches they carried home with them. I know one thing: if some honored or wealthy person had invited you to dinner as far as ten miles away on the occasion of his son’s birthday, you would undoubtedly have gone for the sake of the carefully prepared dishes and generous portions. [Note: The Vatican codex reads “on the occasion of his birthday.”]

Therefore, brothers, whenever we celebrate the memory of the martyrs, we must set aside all worldly affairs and hasten together without any delay or hesitation, rendering honor [Note: The same Vatican codex reads “without any delay.”] to those who obtained salvation for you by the outpouring of their blood, who were offered to the Lord like a consecrated victim for our reconciliation—especially since almighty God says to his saints: “Whoever honors you honors me; and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10). Whoever, therefore, honors the martyrs also honors Christ; and whoever despises the saints also despises the Lord.

[SERMONS]

[Col. 0529]

SERMONS OF SAINT MAXIMUS, BISHOP OF TURIN, DIVIDED INTO THREE CLASSES

FIRST CLASS: SERMONS ON THE LITURGICAL YEAR

[Col. 0529]

SERMON ONE. Before the Nativity of the Lord

ADMONITION

393 Having completed the collection of the homilies of Saint Maximus, I now undertake the sermons. I have already said that “homily” and “sermon” mean the same thing, namely, a discourse on sacred subjects addressed to the people; but editors and scribes use such terms indiscriminately. Two matters, however, must be investigated: first, who is the author of this sermon; second, what its title is.

The first is established by the agreement of many manuscripts. For, together with the older Sangallensis and Taurinensis codices, the following manuscripts assign it to Saint Maximus: codex 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Casinensis 103, the Neapolitan manuscript of the library of Monte Oliveto, the Ambrosian manuscript of the Imperial Basilica Archive, and two Beneventan manuscripts, to omit the others. Although the monks of Saint Maur published this sermon among the Ambrosian works, they nevertheless stated that it should more properly be attributed to Saint Maximus, in volume II of the Paris edition of 1690, p. 392—both because Erasmus held the same opinion and because its style has more the flavor of Maximus than of Ambrose.

As for the title, I observe that the older manuscripts clearly indicate that the sermon was delivered before the Nativity of the Lord, in preparation for it. Thus the Sangallensis, no. 32, reads: “To be delivered before the Nativity of the Lord.” In the Taurinensis codex, since this sermon follows the first homily, which begins, “How great the joy, how great the gathering,” and whose title is “Here begins the discourse before the Nativity of the Lord,” the words “Likewise, concerning that one” are prefixed to this sermon. Another title is given by codex 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, no. 26, and by the Beneventan manuscripts, to which the aforementioned Paris edition conforms: “On the coming Nativity of the Lord.” Finally, manuscripts copied after the tenth century, such as Casinensis, Mediolanensis 146, and Neapolitanus, have: “On the Third Sunday of Advent,” or “On Advent.”

The distinguished Benedictine monks mentioned above rightly observe that, since some manuscripts read “The sequel concerning the Nativity of the Lord,” one should infer that it was a very ancient custom of the Church to urge the faithful to anticipate the Lord’s natal solemnity through holy works and devout dispositions. We have already said that this is clear both from this sermon and from Saint Maximus’s first homily. We have adopted the heading “Before the Nativity of the Lord” from the Sangallensis and Taurinensis manuscripts, which we regard as possessing greater authority.

[Col. 0531A] ARGUMENT.—The sermon’s entire purpose is to urge Christ’s faithful to prepare themselves to celebrate his Nativity through worthy deeds; to compel the Lord through almsgiving and tears; and to wash away their spiritual stains, so that their bodily garments may shine.

I believe that in the previous Sunday’s sermon [Note: The codices of the Basilica of Milan and Monte Oliveto read “in the previous discourse.”] I said fully and sufficiently how we ought to receive the Nativity of the Lord, adorned and cleansed, and how, when his feast arrives, we ought to retain it with eager devotion. [Note: The codices of the Basilica of Milan and Monte Oliveto read: “in which, even if the day of his solemnity passes, its sanctification and blessedness nevertheless remain among us; in the future it passes to those predestined, and in the past it remains for the devout.” The Urbevetanus and Casinensis 103 codices read: “so that in the future it may pass to the predestined, and in the future pass to the devout.”]

To retain it, I say, so that even if the day of its solemnity passes, the blessedness of its sanctification may nevertheless remain among us. For this is the grace of the Nativity of the Lord and Savior: that it may pass into the future for those who have been predestined, while it remains in the past for the devout. Therefore we ought to be pure in holiness, clean in chastity, and bright in uprightness, so that the nearer we see the festive day approaching, the more carefully we may conduct ourselves.

[Col. 0531B] For if women commonly wash away the stains from their clothing with water when they are preparing to observe some festival, why should we, who are about to receive the Nativity of the Lord, not wash away the stains from our souls? If their garments are so deeply stained and darkened by dirt that water does not cleanse them, they add the softness of oil and also the sharpness of soap. So we too, if we bear so grave a sin that it cannot be washed away by tears alone, should add the oil of mercy and the sharpness of fasting. [Note: The Casinensis 103 and Monte Oliveto codices read “and its sharpness.”]

For no offense is so grave that abstinence cannot cleanse it and almsgiving extinguish it. For the holy prophet says: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3). Great, then, is almsgiving, which cools the blazing masses of crimes with the spring of its goodwill and, as though by a channel of generosity, overwhelms the fires of sins, so that, although God is offended and provoked by crimes, he is compelled by almsgiving to set free the one whom he had resolved to punish for his sins. [Note: The Urbevetanus and Basilica of Milan codices read “and although.”]

For in some way he is compelled by us, since he is pressed by our deeds to change his sentence; [Note: The Basilica of Milan codex reads: “Yet he is compelled by us, just as he is forced,” etc.] and in one and the same person he is now moved with the severity of a judge, now caressed by a father’s compassion. God is our Father when we act well; he is our judge when we sin. [Note: The Urbevetanus codex omits “is.”] The Lord is therefore compelled by our works to bestow his mercy upon us. Hence he himself says in the Holy Gospel: “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence” (Matt. 11). [Note: The Urbevetanus codex reads “suffers violence.”] Let us see what meaning this statement has.

The kingdom of heaven is none other than Christ the Lord, who reigns in heaven. [Note: The Urbevetanus and Basilica of Milan codices read: “The kingdom of heaven is none other than Christ the Lord.”] The word “compelled” is ordinarily used when something relatively sparse is made dense through continuous activity. From the time, therefore, that John the Baptist announced the Savior’s coming, [Note: The Monte Oliveto codex reads “announced the Savior’s advent.”] the kingdom of heaven—which previously lay fluid and relaxed in John—began [Note: The Monte Oliveto codex reads “which was previously fluid.”] to be made dense by the constant activity of believing peoples; and all that scarcity of the kingdom was consolidated by the frequent proclamation of preaching. [Note: Codex 99 reads “all”; the Cologne edition reads “all things.”]

It was so sparse among the Jews that it passed to the nations; so fluid that it remained among the peoples. But it is compelled by such a density of believers that it remains solid without end, as Scripture says: “And of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1). [Note: The Basilica of Milan and Casinensis codices read: “Let us contemplate the kingdom of heaven and in some way do violence to it.”]

For we compel the kingdom of heaven and in some way do violence to it, as the Gospel reading says: “And those who do violence seize it” (Matt. 11). We do violence, I say, to the Lord—not by compelling him, but by weeping; not by provoking him with injuries, but by imploring him with tears; not by blaspheming through pride, but by grieving through humility. [Note: From “by compelling him,” the Urbevetanus codex omits what follows and joins the words to those found below: “but we must first reign over ourselves, so that we may be able,” etc.; the Basilica of Milan codex has the same omission and continues from “the Gospel says.”]

O blessed violence, which is not struck down by indignation but pardoned through mercy! Blessed, I say, is the violence that draws goodness from the one who suffers violence and grants benefit to the one who inflicts it. An evil deed is admitted, and no one complains of the injury; violence is admitted, and religion is spread. For whoever is more violent toward Christ will be regarded by Christ as more religious. [Note: The Cologne edition reads “will be considered.”]

Let us therefore attack the Lord on the road, since he himself is the way (John 14:6), and, like robbers, let us strive to strip him of his garments. [Note: The Urbevetanus codex reads “let us strive to strip him of his goods.”] We desire to take away his kingdom, his treasures, and his life; but he is so rich and generous that he does not refuse or resist. Even after giving everything, he nevertheless possesses everything himself. [Note: The Cologne edition reads “will possess.”]

We attack him, I say, not with sword, club, or stone, but with gentleness, good works, and chastity. These are truly the weapons of our faith, with which we fight in the encounter.

But if we are to use these weapons in doing violence, let us first in some way do violence to our own bodies and conquer the vices of our members, so that we may attain the rewards of virtues. For we must first reign over ourselves, so that we may be able to seize the Savior’s kingdom.

The Gospel says: “And those who do violence seize it.” [Note: The Cologne edition reads “seize it”; the Casinensis and Urbevetanus codices read “were seizing it.”] We are therefore robbers; but robbers seize only what belongs to another. [Note: The Cologne edition reads “seize what belongs to another.”]

I recognize that the statement is true: the Church seized Christ from the Synagogue and, by doing violence, took possession of the kingdom of another people. For the Savior, sent under the Law, born under the Law, and brought up according to the Law (Gal. 4), was neglected by the Jews and seized by the Gentiles (Acts 13). When he was rejected by the priests, [Note: The Urbevetanus, Basilica of Milan, and Monte Oliveto codices read “rejected.”] he was found by sinners, as he himself says: “Tax collectors and sinners will go before you into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 21). [Note: The Cologne edition and the Monte Oliveto codex read: “Tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of heaven.”]

[Note: In the Urbevetanus and Basilica of Milan codices, after the words “into the kingdom of heaven,” everything is omitted up to: “Therefore, brothers, as we are about to receive the Nativity of the Lord…”]

We are therefore robbers. It is not surprising, since we descend from such an ancestor. For it is written of our patriarch Benjamin: “A ravenous wolf” (Gen. 49); for he seizes what is not his own. Thus we too, like sons of a ravenous wolf, seize the shepherd of alien sheep through our intention, as he himself says: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 13).

Christ is therefore seized when he is abandoned by the Jews and proclaimed by others. Christ is seized when he is killed by the Jews and buried by us. Christ is seized by disciples who keep watch, but is lost by Pharisees who sleep. For they themselves confessed this falsely when they placed guards at the tomb and, after the Lord’s resurrection, said: “His disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping” (Matt. 28).

From this we understand spiritually that all who sleep lose Christ, while those who keep watch find him. Therefore the Apostle says: “Rise, you who sleep, and Christ will illumine you” (Eph. 5). You see, then, that the one who sleeps in such a way that he does not guard the Savior is dead; and therefore those Pharisees, like dead men, could not preserve the living one.

For this reason, brothers, let us not sleep but keep watch around the Lord our Savior, so that, with guards continually posted, no one may take him away from the tomb of our heart: “They came and, while we were sleeping, stole him.” For we have enemies who, if we fall asleep, strive to take Christ away from our hearts. Therefore let us guard him with vigilant care in the tomb of our souls; there let him rest, there let him sleep, and there, whenever he wishes, let him rise again.

[Note: The Cologne edition reads “let him rest there.”]

[Note: Here the sermon ends in the Casinensis codex.]

Therefore, brothers, as we are about to receive the Nativity of the Lord, let us cleanse our consciences from every impurity; let us adorn ourselves not with silken garments but with precious works. Bright clothing can cover the limbs, but it cannot adorn the conscience—except that it is a matter of even greater shame to walk with shining limbs while one’s thoughts are polluted.

Let us therefore first adorn the disposition of the inner person, so that the clothing of the outer person may also be adorned. Let us wash away spiritual stains, so that bodily garments may shine in us. [Note: The Urbevetanus codex adds: “But it is of no benefit to shine in clothing and be foul with crimes.” The same wording appears in the imperial Basilica codex of Milan, in the Maurist edition of Ambrose, and in the Monte Oliveto codex.]

For where the conscience is dark, the whole body is somewhat dark. [Note: The same Monte Oliveto codex reads “is dark.”] We have, however, with what to wash away the stains of conscience, as it is written: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11). A good command concerning almsgiving, through which we work with our hands and are cleansed in heart—through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

SERMON II. On the Two in One Bed (Matt. 24)

[Col. 0533]

ADMONITION

To conform the sequence of the sermons to the order we established in arranging the homilies, this sermon should be placed before the discourses on the Nativity of the Lord. That its author is Saint Maximus cannot be doubted, as we read in Vatican codex 1267, p. 13, from which it was copied, since the holy bishop of Turin treated the same Gospel parable in the second homily of this collection.

We rejected the title “On the Advent of the Lord,” which that codex gives it, because we stated there, following Mabillon and Muratori, that this title was introduced into the Church much later, in the fifth and sixth centuries. The sermon exists in three other codices: Vatican Regina 125, Vatican Palatine 1276, and Vallicellana II, where it is attributed to Augustine, as also in the Modoetian codex E III. But the Benedictine monks of the congregation of Saint Maur did not include it among Augustine’s sermons, nor did they mention it in the appendix.

[Col. 0533D] ARGUMENT.—Saint Maximus writes that there are three classes of Christians: some live in leisure, others are occupied with the affairs of the world, and others minister to God. From these three classes, one person is taken and one is left: those who remain are taken, and those who fall are left. Noah, Daniel, and Job belong to the three classes that are taken.

Who are the two in one bed during that night, the two women grinding together, and the two in the field, of all of whom one of each pair will be taken and one of each pair will be left? Three classes of people seem to be signified here.

One class consists of those who choose [Note: Vallicellana II reads “choose.”] leisure and quiet, occupied neither with secular business nor with ecclesiastical affairs. Their rest is signified by the name “bed.” The second consists of those established among the congregations of the people and governed by teachers, engaged in the affairs of this world. He signified them by the name of women because it is advantageous for them to be guided, as I have said, by the counsels of the experienced. He said that they were grinding because of the temporary cycle and circulation of affairs. Yet he said that they were grinding together because, from those very possessions and occupations of theirs, they provide for the needs of the Church.

The third consists of those who labor in the ministry of the Church, as in God’s field; the Apostle speaks of this cultivation of the field.

In these three occupations there are again [Note: The Vatican Palatine codex omits “again.”] two classes of people in each, distinguished according to the strength of their abilities. For although all may seem to belong to the members of the Church, when the trial of tribulation arrives, some in the Church remain and some fall—both among those who live in leisure, those engaged in worldly affairs, and those who minister to God. Those who remain are taken; those who fall are left. Therefore one will be taken and one will be left.

This is not said of two people, but of two kinds of disposition within each of the three classes. [Note: Vatican Regina 125 reads “within each class of occupations.” The Vatican Palatine and Vallicellana II read “within each class of the three occupations.”]

When he says “during that night,” he means during that tribulation. I think that the three names of the holy men whom the prophet Ezekiel declares alone to be deliverable also belong to the three classes that are taken: Noah, Daniel, and Job.

Noah appears to belong to those through whom the Church is governed, just as the ark, which bore the figure of the Church, was guided through the waters by him. Daniel, because he chose a celibate life—that is, because he despised earthly marriage—in order to live without anxiety, as the Apostle says, thinking about the things of God, signifies the class of those who live in leisure, yet are very strong amid storms [Note: Vallicellana II reads “in trials.”], so that they may be taken.

Job, because he had a wife, children, and abundant resources in earthly possessions, belongs to the class to which the mill was assigned; yet they too must be very strong amid storms, as he was. Otherwise they cannot be taken.

Nor do I think that there are other classes of people from which the Church is constituted than these three, each possessing two distinctions because of being taken and being left, although within each class many differences of pursuits and desires may be found, converging toward harmony and unity. [Note: The Vatican Palatine codex reads “from which the Church is constituted.”]

SERMON III. On the Nativity of the Lord I

[Col. 0535]

ADMONITION

Although this third sermon may seem to the learned Maurist editors, in the Paris edition of the works of Saint Ambrose, vol. I, p. 394, 1690, to have been compiled from sermons of various Fathers, especially Augustine, we nevertheless believe that it can confidently be defended as the work of Saint Maximus alone, on the basis of the number of ancient manuscripts.

The following manuscripts bear the inscription “Sermon of Saint Maximus the bishop, from above”:  Vaticanus 4222, p. 34; Holy Cross in Jerusalem 99, sermon 12; Vallicellanus VI, p. 56; Casinensis 106, p. 122 verso; Lucensis 81; and the Neapolitan manuscript of Saint John at Carbonara.

What then? Was it not permissible for Saint Maximus to follow and expound Augustine’s opinions? This may indeed be said of Maximus, who lived later than Augustine; but it cannot be said of Ambrose, whom Augustine heard. Nevertheless, the same sermon is found placed among the sermons of Saint Ambrose as number 4.

[Col. 0535C] ARGUMENT.—Maximus adorns with various explanations the words of John the Baptist concerning Christ: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” He demonstrates that these words were perfectly fulfilled in the Nativity of Christ the Lord.

It is true what Saint John the Baptist said concerning the Lord and Savior: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). For this is first confirmed by the very seasons themselves. [Note: The Vatican 4222 and Vallicellana codices read “is confirmed.”] Behold: at the Nativity of Christ the day increases, while at John’s nativity it decreases. When Christ rises, the light advances; when John is born, it diminishes.

For the seasons themselves, in a certain way serving their respective parts, suffer loss when a servant is born; but when the Lord is born, they gain increase. The days plainly advance when the Savior of the world arises, and suffer decline when the last prophet is born. For it is written: “The Law and the Prophets lasted until John” (Luke 16).

Therefore it was necessary for observance of the Law to grow dim where the calling forth of the Gospel’s grace shone brightly, [Note: The Vallicellana codex omits the words “where the calling forth.”] and for the prophecy of the Old Testament to cease when the glory of the New Testament succeeded it.

[Col. 0536C] Thus the day advances at the Nativity of the Lord. It is not surprising that the day advances on which the new Sun of righteousness flashes forth. It is not surprising that the day advances which the most splendid light of truth illumines. [Note: Codex 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem supplies this wording; Vatican 4222, Casinensis, and Vallicellana agree.]

For the evangelist says of Christ the Lord: “He was the true light which enlightens every human being” (John 1). Therefore, if he was the true light that enlightens every human being, [Note: The same codex and all the preceding manuscripts supply the following.] why would he not enlighten the world?

And so the day that brought forth the light for the human race first itself shone with that same splendor of light; and, having already enclosed its appointed spaces in the darkness of night, it dispersed them by the brilliance of the Lord’s light. For the length of night would have occupied the whole day had not the advent of him who by his rising dispels the darkness of the human race’s sins shone forth in the very shortness of the day. [Note: Vatican 1267 and Casinensis 106 read: “had not the advent of Christ shone forth, who by his rising…”]

Thus, on the day of his Nativity, he cut away the darkness of gloom and by one and the same rising brought light equally to human beings and to the days. Hence it is not surprising that the day increases, since it is clothed in a twofold splendor of brightness. [Note: The codex of Saint John at Carbonara reads “clothed in a twofold splendor of brightness.”]

But let us see further how the Lord and Savior increases and John the Baptist decreases. [Note: The Casinensis codex adds “If.”] We said above that John represented the figure of the Law and the Prophets. It was therefore necessary for the Law to decline while the Gospel flashed forth, and for the Jewish people to diminish while the Christian people arose.

Who could doubt that, after the Nativity of the Lord, the Synagogue’s meeting places were emptied, the Church’s congregations multiplied, and, in a wondrous manner, Christ daily increased through his Christians while John diminished through the Jews? We shine with the splendor of the Lord’s day, while they labor in the darkness of night.

For a greater night, in a certain sense, settled upon the Jews from the time when they said concerning the Savior’s death: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). They were plainly darkened by greater darknesses of night from the time when they attempted to kill the day of truth.

But so that we may establish what we are saying more convincingly, let us briefly explain the nativity of each. Behold: when Christ is born, angels rejoice, shepherds keep watch through the night, the Magi arrive, the star goes before them, and all the most beautiful things in heaven and on earth are offered to the Lord himself.

To him are offered glory through the angels, brightness through the star, worship through the Magi, and simplicity through the shepherds. And because all these things were destined to belong to him alone, everything serves him at his birth.

But when John is conceived, Zechariah becomes mute, the solemn priest falls silent, and Elizabeth his mother conceals herself. [Note: The codex of Saint John at Carbonara reads “Elizabeth his mother conceals herself.” This signifies, after Christ’s birth, the silence of the Law, the loss of the priesthood, and the concealment of the Synagogue.]

There is no doubt [Note: The Casinensis and Vallicellana codices read “that John.”] that when John was born he took the righteousness of the Law away from the Pharisees, just as, when he was conceived, he took from his father the service of speech. [Note: Vatican 1267 and Vallicellana read “when he was conceived.”]

The Lord therefore always increases, while John the Baptist decreases. He does not decrease because anything is taken away from his merits, but because, as the Savior’s glory is daily increased, John’s grace appears to become less. [Note: The Vallicellana codex reads: “but because the Savior’s glory is daily increased, his grace appears to become less.” The codex of Saint John at Carbonara has the same wording; the others agree with the text.]

Finally, John is called a lamp, as the Lord says: “He was the burning lamp” (John 5). The lamp’s light is therefore obscured when the sun’s ray shines forth, and it suffers a kind of decline when it is surpassed by the splendor of a brighter light. For what wise person would seek a lamp in the sun?

It is not extinguished, but it is no longer necessary. That is: who would come to John’s baptism of repentance when he can be saved by the Savior’s baptism? The former is not condemned, but the latter appears more useful and necessary, because remission of sins is granted in it. [Note: Codex 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads “is judged.” The Casinensis and Vallicellana codices likewise read “is judged,” and the sermon ends there in them. The codex of Saint John at Carbonara also has “is judged.”]

SERMON IV. On the Same Nativity II

[Col. 0537]

ADMONITION

403 What the monks of Saint Maur conjectured concerning this sermon—that it proceeded from Maximus rather than Ambrose—we confirm on the authority of three outstanding manuscripts and by the similarity of its diction.

The first manuscript is the Taurinensis, with the inscription: “Likewise, on the Nativity of the Lord, homily III.” The second and third are codices 90 and 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “On the Nativity of Our Lord and Savior.”

The same Benedictine editors rightly said, in sermon 6 of the sermons of Saint Ambrose, p. 397 of the Paris edition of 1690, that this sermon is chiefly concerned with the fact that the day of the Lord’s Nativity was called the new sun—that is, the new year—since in former times the year began on that day.

The distinguished Alexander Politius writes in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for the Kalends of January that the most ancient of all Martyrologies, bearing the name of Jerome the presbyter, begins the year on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, and that the Martyrology of Ado begins it on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. From this it can be understood that in certain Churches the new year began on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, since, as our Maximus says, when the Savior rises, not only the salvation of the human race but also the brightness of the sun itself is renewed.

[Col. 0537C] ARGUMENT.—Why the day of the Lord’s Nativity is called the new sun. It is both new and old. The difference between the sun of the world and Christ the Sun.

Appropriately, in a sense, the common people call this holy day of the Lord’s nativity the “new sun,” and they confirm this with such authority of their own that Jews and gentiles alike agree in the expression. We should gladly embrace this, because, when the Savior rises, not only is the salvation of the human race renewed, but the brightness of the sun itself is renewed as well. As the Apostle says: “That through him he might restore all things, both those in heaven and those on earth” (Ephesians 1). For if the sun is darkened when Christ suffers, it must necessarily shine more brilliantly than usual when he is born. And if it poured out darkness upon the Jews who were bringing about his death [Note: [Col. 0538D] The Cologne edition reads *offundit tenebras*, “pours out darkness.”], why should it not display its brightness to Mary in childbirth? Or do we not believe that, when Christ was born, the sun came forth brighter in his service, since a brighter star went before the Magi as a sign? And if a star performed the service of daylight at an unusual time, why should we not believe that the sun also shortened the nocturnal hours somewhat by arriving earlier than usual? I think that this is why the night grew shorter: the sun, hastening in service of the Lord’s nativity, brought light to the world before the night had completed the course of its allotted time.

Indeed, I would not say that it was night at all, nor that there was any darkness in which the shepherds kept watch, the angels rejoiced, and the stars served. Nor should we be surprised that everything was made new at Christ’s birth, since this itself was new: that a virgin gave birth. But if the nativity occurred beyond the ordinary, and extraordinary services were rendered, then, as the Lord rose, the shepherds kept watch, the angels rejoiced, the sun served, and the star ministered. Angels and shepherds, of course, expressed their joy with their voices and words; [Col. 0538D] these elements, however, because they could not speak, proclaimed their joy through their service.

Thus the sun [Col. 0539A] shone forth earlier than usual at this festival; and no wonder. For if, at the prayer of Joshua son of Nun, it stood still during the day, why should it not hasten forward into the night at the nativity of Jesus Christ? The common people therefore call this day the “new sun,” and by saying “new” they clearly show that there is also an old one.

By the old sun I mean the sun of this world, which suffers eclipse, is shut out by walls, and is obscured by clouds. I mean the old sun that is subject to vanity, fears correction, and dreads judgment. For it is written: “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood” (Joel 2:31; Acts 2:20). I mean, I say, the old sun that is present at human crimes, does not shrink from adultery, does not avoid murder, and, although the whole human race wishes that he not be a witness, whenever some crime is committed, he alone stands present at every wrongdoing [Note: [Col. 0539D] The Eadwine edition reads *stat*, “stands.”].

Therefore, since it is clear that this is the old sun, whom but Christ the Lord do we find to be the new one? Of him it is written: “The sun of righteousness shall rise for you” (Malachi 4:2). Of him the prophet also says in the person of sinners: “The sun has not risen for us, and the light of righteousness has not shone upon us” (Wisdom 5:6). For when the whole world was oppressed by the darkness of the devil, and the age, filled with crimes, was held by gloom, this sun deigned, at the final time—that is, when night was already approaching—to pour forth the rising of his nativity.

First, before the light—that is, before the Sun of righteousness shone—he sent, as it were, a kind of prophetic dawn-oracle: “I was sending my prophets before the light” (Jeremiah 7). Afterwards he himself shone forth with his rays—that is, with the radiance of the apostles [Col. 0539C]—and scattered so great a darkness of the world with the light of truth that no one would stumble into the darkness of the devil.

This, then, is the new sun who penetrates locked chambers, opens the underworld, and searches hearts. This is the new sun who by his spirit gives life to the dead, restores what has decayed, and raises those already dead; or who by his heat cleanses what is filthy, burns up what is fluid, and boils away what is diseased. He, I say, is the one who sees all our works in all our deeds, and who does not so much condemn crimes as correct them.

This is plainly the just and wise sun who, unlike the sun of this world, is not carried indiscriminately around the good and the wicked [Note: [Col. 0539D] The Eadwine edition reads *justus mundi sol*, “the just sun of the world,” but incorrectly; the manuscripts read *istius*, “of this [world].”], but who, shining with the judgment of truth, sets for the sinner.

The difference between the two suns is this: the one is the minister of corruption, while the other is the Lord of eternity; the one is situated around the earth, while the other is its Creator. Nevertheless, before this worldly sun rises, a lamp customarily precedes it before dawn for the necessary uses of human beings.

Christ the sun also has his own lamp, which preceded his coming, as the Prophet says: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Psalm 138). The Lord shows us what this lamp is when he says of John the Baptist: “He was a burning lamp” (John 5). John himself, as the small light preceding the lamp, says: “Behold, there comes after me one whose sandal-thong I am not worthy to untie; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (John 3).

At the same time, understanding that his own light would be overshadowed by the sun’s rays, he foretells this beforehand: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (ibid.). For just as the brightness of a lamp is destroyed by the arrival of the sun, so John’s baptism of repentance was rendered void when Christ’s grace arrived.

Let us see, then, from what source our new sun is born. As is true, it rises with God as author. [Note: [Col. 0539D] Here the holy teacher used an abstract noun for a concrete one, *Deo* for *Deus*, as if he had said: “Therefore he is the Son of God,” just as below he says: “The Father God is plainly a craftsman,” with reference to eternal generation. In the Psalter we find the following prophecy concerning Christ: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2), a passage which Saint Maximus most learnedly expounded in Sermon 21.] Therefore he is the Son of divinity—of incorruptible, complete, undefiled divinity, I say.

I plainly understand the mystery. The fruitful nativity therefore took place through the immaculate Mary because the earlier one had remained undefiled through divinity: he whose first nativity was glorious would not have a second that was dishonorable. That is, just as divinity had brought him forth as a virgin, so Mary too would give birth as a virgin.

He is also said to have a father among human beings, as we read when the Pharisees say in the Gospel: “Is this not the son of Joseph the carpenter, and is not his mother Mary?” (Matthew 13). Here too observe the mystery. Christ’s father is called a carpenter. And plainly the Father God is a carpenter, who fashioned the works of the whole world; plainly he is a carpenter, but one who determined to construct Noah’s ark during the Flood [Note: [Col. 0540D] Codex 99 of Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “constructed the ark.”].

He is a carpenter, I say, who ordered Moses to build the tabernacle, established the ark of the covenant, and raised Solomon’s temple. I would call him a carpenter who smooths rigid minds, cuts back proud thoughts, and raises humble deeds.

This carpenter also uses a curved tool around trees, as we read in the Gospel, where John says: “Now the axe is laid at the root of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3; Luke 3) so that in the future he may arrange trees useful for the heavenly structure, while uprooting the fruitless and consuming them at the burning of the flames.

*Here ends the text.*

## SERMON V. On the same nativity, III

[Col. 0539]

### ADMONITION

That Saint Maximus had many more sermons on the nativity of the Lord than are contained in the Turin manuscript is established by the fact that the number 35 is noted in that same manuscript. We have published some of them among the homilies; we have transferred another part into this class; the rest have been scattered or consumed by antiquity.

This sermon is found in the same Turin manuscript as number 4, under the title: “Also, a homily on the nativity of the Lord, IV.” It is confirmed as Maximus’s by the testimony of manuscript 99 of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, number 13, whose title is: “On the nativity of the Lord our Savior,” and also by the Bobbio manuscript.

The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, in the Paris edition of the works of Saint Ambrose, published in 1690, placed this sermon before the preceding one, observing that part of it was taken from Ambrose’s *Commentary on Luke*, book 2, number 50. But since they recognized that the form or character of the diction of both works agreed more with Maximus than with Ambrose, they therefore acknowledged that it could be assigned to the holy bishop of Turin.

Nothing, however, detracts from the authenticity of their attribution because Saint Maximus interpreted the sacred Scriptures according to the thought of Ambrose or Augustine; we have already said that later Fathers received many things from their predecessors.

[Col. 0541A] **ARGUMENT.**—The song of the angels at Christ’s nativity both renders honor to God in heaven and presents peace to human beings on earth. It was shown that the flock represents the people, the night the age, and the shepherds the priests. Mary is rightly compared with a fleece.

By what grace or with what praises we should proclaim this day of the Lord’s nativity, I truly do not know. For at so great a festival human speech is insufficient to magnify God. If, when Christ was being born, he was praised by the voice of angels, with what human voice should he now be praised when he reigns? Our solemnity surpasses the festival of that time, since then they merely marveled at the Lord who was being born, whereas we receive him as one who is being born, rising again, and reigning.

Therefore the praise of this time ought to be all the more fruitful insofar as its miracles are greater. [Col. 0541B] But since human frailty cannot offer praise worthy of him, let us turn to the proclamations of the angels. And because we cannot rightly equal them, let us accompany them in devotion. That is, in this festival let us leap for joy with the same joy as they, and with the same declaration, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2).

Plainly this is a worthy and just declaration, which at Christ’s nativity both renders honor to God in heaven and presents peace to human beings on earth. Before the Savior’s rising, heavenly things did not abandon reverence, nor did earthly things possess rest.

But observe what the declaration itself says: “Peace to people of good will.” Not to just any people, but to people of good will, so that you may understand that Christ’s peace is not a matter of obligation but of merit; [Col. 0541C] for it is not condition but will that merits it. [Note: [Col. 0541D] Codex 99 of Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “Therefore with this voice the angels leaped for joy on that night, and the shepherds, watching their flock and keeping vigil over the newborn Lord, learned it before all others.” The cited Vatican manuscript reads: “Therefore with this voice the angels leaped for joy on that night when the shepherds,” and so forth.]

The shepherds heard this first of all on that night when, as the Lord was being born, they were keeping watch over their flock. They learned of the Savior’s birth before all other human beings, with the angels announcing it [Note: [Col. 0541D] The same codex 99 of Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “announcing it.”]. [Note: [Col. 0541D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “For they first learned of the Savior’s birth before all other human beings, with the angels announcing it. Hence it is not surprising that the shepherds of the world deserved to know the world’s redemption before its rulers. For the angels announced it not to kings, not to judges, but to rustic people. Therefore it is no longer surprising if innocence deserved to know Christ’s grace before power,” and so forth.]

For the angels announced the world’s redemption first not to kings or judges, but to rustic people. Nor is it surprising if innocence knew Christ’s grace before power, or if simple rusticity recognized the truth before proud distinction. What the shepherds knew, the rulers could not know. Hence the blessed Apostle says: “None of the rulers of this age knew it” (1 Corinthians 2), and so forth.

[Col. 0541D] Therefore at the Lord’s nativity the angels rejoiced together with the shepherds, proclaiming glory to God in the highest. For they proclaimed God’s glory in choirs that were, as it were, neighboring and joined. Hence I believe that these same angels, at this same Lord’s festival, rejoice together with us in a similar joy by virtue of their nearness [Note: [Col. 0542D] The Vallicellan manuscript reads: “At the same festival they rejoice with us in a similar joy.”].

For those who customarily addressed the shepherds because of Christ’s birth cannot fail, because of the joy of that same Christ, to seek out the priests. Indeed, what they said then to those who were keeping watch over their flock at dead of night signified the mystery of the present time. For by that event it was certainly shown that the flock represented the people, the night the age, and the shepherds the priests, who, keeping constant watch over the people out of concern for Christ, are not abandoned by the angels.

Today, therefore, the Lord was born according to the flesh so secretly and silently that the age knew nothing of his birth. The age did not know, because he was conceived outside the awareness of his father and born outside the order of nature [Note: [Col. 0542D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “because he was conceived outside the order of nature. For Joseph received as his son one whom he did not beget.”].

For Joseph received as his son the child whom he did not beget; Mary gave birth to the child whom, according to the usual condition of her sex, she did not conceive. Thus the Lord was born so that no one anticipated his birth, no one believed it, and no one perceived it. How could they believe that this would happen when, after it had happened, they scarcely believe that it did happen?

For David the prophet had already testified that the Savior would descend into the Virgin so secretly and quietly, saying: “He will descend like rain upon fleece” (Psalm 71). What happens more silently and without disturbance than when rain is poured into a fleece of wool? It strikes no one’s ears with sound, nor does it sprinkle anyone’s body with the moisture of impact [Note: [Col. 0542D] Codex 99 of Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “with the moisture of dew striking it.”]; but without disturbing anyone it draws all the rain poured out through its many parts into its entire body. It knows nothing of a tear in a single opening, while in its solid softness it offers many openings; and what appears closed because of its density is open because of its fineness.

Mary is therefore rightly compared with a fleece [Note: [Col. 0542D] Codices 99 of Holy Cross in Jerusalem and the Vatican read: “We compare Mary with a fleece.”]. She conceived the Lord in such a way that she absorbed him with her whole body and suffered no tearing of her body [Note: [Col. 0542D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “nor suffered a tearing of that same body.”], but was soft in obedience and firm in sanctity.

I say again, Mary is rightly compared with a fleece, from whose fruit garments of salvation are woven for the peoples. Mary is plainly a fleece, since from the softness of her womb came forth the Lamb, who himself, bearing his mother’s wool—that is, the flesh [Note: [Col. 0542D] Vatican manuscript 1267 reads: “that is, bearing the flesh.”]—covers all the wounds of sinners with soft wool [Col. 0543A]. For every wound of sin is drenched with Christ’s wool, warmed by Christ’s blood, and clothed in Christ’s garment so that it may regain health.

## SERMON VI. On the Kalends of January

[Col. 0543]

### ADMONITION

We have seen elsewhere that Saint Maximus delivered a homily on the Kalends of January, and we investigated what the title “On the Kalends” or “On the Kalends of January” signifies. The same subject is proposed in this sermon by the holy bishop of Turin, and he vigorously attacks superstitious people who spend that day, like the gentiles, in impious amusements. He threatens that they will have no part with God, since they associate with worshipers of idols—that is, of the devil—and with people devoted to intemperance and vanity.

On the basis of three manuscripts of great authority, we judge that this sermon should be assigned to Saint Maximus. The first is the Turin manuscript, where it follows the homilies on the nativity of the Lord under the title: “Also, a sermon delivered on the Kalends of January.” The other two are manuscripts 90 and 98 of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, both of which bear the title: “Here begins [the sermon] on the Kalends of January.”

The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur included it among the Ambrosian sermons as number 7, as they knew had formerly been done; but they wisely warned that it should not readily be granted to Ambrose, since in the sermons that are certainly admitted as belonging to the holy teacher, he nowhere inveighed against the superstitions and depraved practices of the January Kalends. From this it could be argued that these practices had already been eliminated at Milan.

Nothing, therefore, prevents us from assigning this sermon to Saint Maximus. Indeed, its evident stylistic similarity shows that it had wrongly been attributed to others.

[Col. 0543B] **ARGUMENT.**—Saint Maximus gravely complains that most of the faithful have devoted themselves to the festivals of the gentiles, rendering divine service to Janus, the man from whom the January Kalends are named. He says that not only the company of gentiles must be avoided, but also that of the Jews, whose conversation itself is a great defilement.

I have a considerable complaint against most of you, brothers. I am speaking of those who, while celebrating the Lord’s nativity with us, devoted themselves to the festivals of the gentiles and, after that heavenly banquet, prepared for themselves a meal of superstition, so that those who had previously been gladdened by holiness might afterwards be intoxicated by vanity. They do not understand that one who wishes to reign with Christ cannot rejoice with the world, and that one who wishes to find righteousness must avoid luxury.

The way of eternal life is one thing; the despair of temporal wantonness is another. [Col. 0543C] To the former one ascends through virtue; into the latter one descends through destruction. Therefore anyone who wishes to share in divine things must not be a companion of idols.

It is part of an idol to intoxicate the mind with wine, distend the belly with food, torture the limbs with dances, and become so occupied with wicked actions that one is forced to forget that God exists. Hence the holy Apostle, foreseeing these things, says: “What partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what portion has the faithful with the unbeliever? And what agreement has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Corinthians 6).

Therefore, if we are the temple of God, why is a festival of idols celebrated in God’s temple? Why, where Christ dwells—Christ who is abstinence, moderation, and chastity—are feasting, drunkenness, and wantonness introduced? The Savior says: “No one can serve two masters, that is, God and Mammon” (Matthew 6).

How, then, can you devoutly observe the Epiphany of the Lord, when, as far as lies within you, you celebrate the Kalends of Janus with the greatest devotion? [Note: [Col. 0543D] Maximus took this passage from book 8 of Virgil’s *Aeneid*, line 355, where Virgil makes Janus the founder of a city on the hill across the Tiber, now called the Janiculum, just as he attributes the construction of another city, in the opposite location—namely, on the Capitoline—before Rome was founded, to Saturn:

“Here you see two towns, their walls thrown down,  
Remnants and monuments of men of old;  
Father Janus founded this one, Saturn that city;  
The name of this was Janiculum, of that, Saturnia.”

Pliny, book 3, chapter 5, calls Janus’s city “Antipolis,” because it faced Saturnia on the opposite side. “Saturnia,” he says, “where Rome now is; Antipolis, which is now the Janiculum, in the part of Rome.” See Pitis, volume 1, *Lexicon of Roman Antiquities*, and Nardini, *Ancient Rome*, book 7, chapter 11.]

For Janus was a human being, the founder of a single city called the Janiculum; in his honor the gentiles named the January Kalends. Therefore whoever celebrates the January Kalends sins, because he renders divine service to a dead man.

Hence the Apostle says: “You observe days and months and seasons and years; I fear that I may have labored over you in vain” (Galatians 4). Anyone who on those days either did not fast or did not go to church observed the day and the month. He observed the day who yesterday did not go to church but went to the field.

Therefore, brothers, let us avoid with every effort the festival and holidays of the gentiles, so that when they feast and rejoice, we may now be sober and fasting, in order that they may understand that their joy is condemned by our abstinence.

But we must avoid not only the company of gentiles, but also that of Jews, whose conversation itself is a great defilement. For they insinuate themselves into people by a certain art, enter houses, go into governors’ residences, and trouble the ears of judges and public officials. For this reason they prevail all the more because they are all the more shameless.

This is not a recent characteristic among them, but an old and original evil. For long ago they persecuted the Lord and Savior within the governor’s residence and condemned him by the judgment of the governor. Thus in the governor’s residence innocence is oppressed by the Jews, secrecy is betrayed, and religion is condemned. For when Christ is killed, all truth and righteousness are condemned in him, since he is innocence, religion, holiness, and mystery. Amen.

*Here ends the text.*

## SERMON VII. On the Day of the Holy Epiphany

[Col. 0543]

### ADMONITION

Whether because he did not consult manuscript copies or because he devoted too little attention to distinguishing the works of Saint Maximus, Joannes Dominicus Valarsius placed this sermon of the holy bishop of Turin—without even mentioning Maximus—among the spurious works of Jerome, volume 2, page 304, of the works of Saint Jerome, Verona edition, 1742.

It is therefore our task to bring this learned and cultivated sermon out of obscurity and publish it adorned with the proper name of its author. This is shown by three excellent manuscripts: two of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, numbers 90 and 99, and Laurentian manuscript I, Pluteus XIV, where after the title one plainly reads: “On the Holy Epiphany, a sermon of Saint Maximus the bishop.”

In the manuscripts of Holy Cross in Jerusalem the sermon is entitled “On the Day of the Holy Epiphany,” and we have adopted that title. Consult especially what Saint Maximus writes in his homily on the Cross; from it you will easily perceive that this sermon too must be assigned to the same author.

[Col. 0545A] **ARGUMENT.**—The holy teacher explains the mystery of the day of the Holy Epiphany and declares at length that it benefits us, not Christ. His humility is our exaltation; his cross is our victory; his gallows is our triumph.

Today the true sun has risen upon the world; today light has come forth in the darkness of the age. God became human so that the human being might become God; the Lord assumed the form of a servant so that the servant might be changed into the Lord. The inhabitant and creator of the heavens dwelt on earth so that the human tenant of the earth might migrate to heaven.

O day brighter than every sun! O time desired by all ages [Note: [Col. 0545D] Laurentian manuscript I, Pluteus XIV, reads: “desired by all ages and awaited.” The Vatican manuscript reads: “more eagerly awaited.”]! What the angels awaited, what the cherubim and seraphim and the mysteries of heaven did not know [Note: [Col. 0545D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “and the heavenly ministers did not know.”], has been revealed in our time.

What they saw through a mirror and in an image, we see in reality. He who spoke to the people of Israel through Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets now speaks to us through the Son.

Observe what difference there is between the Old Testament and the New [Note: [Col. 0545D] The manuscripts of Holy Cross in Jerusalem and the Vatican read: “Observe what difference there is between the Old …,” and so forth.]. In the former he spoke through a cloud; to us he speaks through clear skies. There God was seen in a bush; here God is born from a virgin. There fire consumed the sins of the people; here a human being forgives the sins of the people—indeed, God forgives his servants. For no one can forgive sins except God alone.

Whether the Lord Jesus was born today or baptized today—for different opinions circulate in the world, and because of differing traditions our judgment varies—this is utterly certain: whether he was born today from the Virgin or reborn in baptism, his nativity in both flesh and spirit benefits us. [Col. 0545C] [Col. 0546A]

Both mysteries are mine; both benefits are mine [Note: [Col. 0545D] The same Laurentian manuscript reads: “Both his humiliations are mine,” and so forth.]. The Son of God did not need to be born or baptized; he had committed no sin that needed to be forgiven in baptism. But his humility is our exaltation. His cross is our victory; his gallows is our triumph.

Let us joyfully raise this sign upon our shoulders; let us carry the banners of victory; let us carry the immortal *labarum* upon our foreheads [Note: [Col. 0545D] Codex 90 of Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “the immortal standard.”]. When the devil sees this sign on doorposts, he will tremble. Those who do not fear gilded Capitols fear the cross; those who despise royal scepters, the purple robes of Caesars, and sumptuous banquets fear the filth and fasts of Christ [Note: [Col. 0545D] The manuscript of Holy Cross in Jerusalem and the Laurentian manuscript read: “the filth and fasts of Christians.”].

Finally, in the prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel 9), when the angel who had been sent had killed everyone and the slaughter had begun from the holy places, only those were preserved whom the letter Tau—that is, the figure of the cross—had marked [Note: [Col. 0545D] Vatican manuscript 1267 reads *signaverat*, “had marked”; it continues: “Therefore, dearest brothers, receive also a few words concerning the sacrament of baptism. The Lord is baptized by a servant, and the Son is called by God. What is more exalted than this humility? What is nobler than this lowliness? He comes to the bath among tax collectors, prostitutes, and sinners, yet he is holier than his baptizer. He is washed by John in the flesh, but he washes John in the spirit. The waters that were accustomed to cleanse other things were themselves cleansed when our Lord washed. The river Jordan, which at that time, when the leader of the people of Israel had been summoned to the promised land, had wished, if it could have gathered all its waves together in one place, did so in order to touch the Lord’s body.” Afterwards the codex has, in red letters, the words “from the same sermon.”].

Therefore let us rejoice, dearest brothers, and, in the likeness of the cross, raise our holy hands toward heaven. When the demons see us armed in this way, they will be crushed. When Moses (Exodus 17) held his hands raised, Amalek was defeated; if they drooped even slightly [Note: [Col. 0546D] The Laurentian manuscript reads: “if they considered them for a little while.”], he grew strong again.

The masts of ships and the horns of sails move about in the shape of our cross. Birds too, when they rise to higher places and hang in the air with outstretched wings, imitate the cross. Moreover, trophies and triumphal victories are adorned with the cross, which we ought to have not only on our foreheads but also in our souls, so that, armed in this way, we may trample upon the serpent and the basilisk in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. The Same, on the Holy Epiphany, II

[Col. 0545]

### ADMONITION

The Turin manuscript, which numbers this sermon seventh among the homilies of Maximus, is not alone in agreement with it: manuscript 99 of Holy Cross in Jerusalem also agrees, as does Combefis, who published the same sermon under Maximus’s name in volume 2, page 142.

Their titles nevertheless differ. The Turin manuscript has: “Also, on the same Epiphany and on Christ’s baptism”; the manuscript of Holy Cross has: “On the Holy Epiphany,” as does Combefis.

Some manuscript copies may regard the Turin title as more precise, since in this sermon Saint Maximus truly writes several things about Christ’s manifestation and his baptism. But since that twofold mystery is expressed under the single name of Epiphany and is celebrated on the same day, the title “On the Holy Epiphany” should not be rejected.

In Vatican manuscript 1276, folio 105 verso, the same sermon is found under a title written in another hand: “A sermon of Saint Ambrose on the octave of the Epiphany.” But I do not see why, merely because of the title of a single manuscript written in another hand, the sermon should now be attributed to Ambrose, since both its style and the other manuscript copies show that Maximus was its author.

[Col. 0547A] **ARGUMENT.**—Christ, as a good teacher, conveyed his teaching not so much through words as by putting it into practice. Born for human beings, he was reborn through the sacraments. Christ’s bosom is wherever virtue has its dwelling.

The Gospel Scripture reports, as we recently heard read, that the Lord came to the Jordan for the sake of baptism and wished to be consecrated in that same river through heavenly mysteries.

We should not be surprised that the Lord and teacher himself underwent this baptism, since he says: “Whoever does and teaches will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). He therefore wished first to do what he commanded all to do, so that, as a good teacher, he might convey his teaching not so much through words as by putting it into practice, and might confirm us equally by his action and his meaning.

It is clear that all this took place today. We can gather that this is true from reason itself. Reason demands that after the day of the Lord’s nativity, even though years intervened, this festival should follow at the same season; and I think that it too should be called a nativity festival.

Then he was born for human beings; today he was reborn through the sacraments. Then he was brought forth through a virgin; today he was generated through a mystery. The Lord arranged this so that human hopes would not be far removed from one another, but so that at one time people would rejoice that the one whom they celebrated as born on earth had been sanctified in heaven.

Thus those who, when angels announced it, possessed the Son of God in the Virgin’s birth, would retain him with heaven bearing witness, and people would be certain that he was the Son of God whom the virgin had borne and the Divinity acknowledged.

For new births deserve new services. [Col. 0547B] There, when he is born according to humanity, his mother Mary embraces him in her bosom. Here, when he is begotten according to the mystery, God the Father embraces him with his voice. For he says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3) [Note: [Col. 0547D] The Vatican manuscript omits *enim*, “for.”].

Thus the mother tenderly caresses the child in her gentle lap, while the Father serves the Son with loving testimony. The mother, I say, presents him as one who should rather be worshiped; the Father reveals him to the nations as one who should be honored.

He is therefore held in his mother’s bosom when he is born, but the Father continually supplies him with the warmth of his own bosom. For we read that he rests without interruption in the Father’s bosom, as the Evangelist says: “No one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1).

The Lord gladly rests in the bosom of the saints [Note: [Col. 0547D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “The Lord gladly rests in the bosom of the holy.”]. Hence he gladly chose the bosom of John the Evangelist, in order to recline there.

The bosom in which Christ rests is not prepared in the lap of the body, nor arranged by the display of garments; it is gathered from heavenly virtues. For Christ’s bosom in John the Evangelist was faith; in God the Father, divinity; in Mary his mother, virginity.

Christ’s bosom is wherever virtue has its dwelling. There he reclines his head where he finds a dwelling for the heavenly commandments. For this reason he says to sinners and unbelievers: “Foxes have dens, and birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9) [Note: [Col. 0547D] Vatican manuscript 1276 reads: “where he may lay his head.”].

Therefore the Lord Jesus comes today to baptism and wishes his holy body to be washed in water. Someone may perhaps say: “If he is holy, why did he wish to be baptized?” Listen, then: Christ is baptized not so that he may be sanctified by the waters, but so that he himself may sanctify the waters and, by his purification, purify the streams that he touches.

For Christ’s consecration is a consecration greater than that of the element. When the Savior is washed, all water is already cleansed for our baptism, and the spring is purified so that the grace of the bath may afterwards be supplied to the peoples who follow.

Christ therefore goes before through baptism so that Christian peoples may follow him confidently.

Understand the mystery, then. In the same way, the pillar of fire went before through the Red Sea so that the children of Israel might follow an unafraid path; and it first went through the waters [Note: [Col. 0547D] Codex 99 of Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “and it first came out.”], so that it might prepare a path for those coming after it [Note: [Col. 0547D] Laurentian codex 10 reads: “so that it might provide light for the eyes of those following.”].

As the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 10), this event was a mystery of baptism: the cloud covered the people, and the water carried them.

But all these things were accomplished by Christ the Lord, the same one who acts now. Just as he then went before the children of Israel through the sea in a pillar of fire, so he already went before Christian peoples through baptism in the pillar of his body.

It is that same pillar, I say, which then provided light to the eyes of those following and now supplies light to the hearts of believers. Then in the streams of water it made a solid path [Note: [Col. 0548D] Codices 99 of Holy Cross in Jerusalem and 10 of Laurentian read: “in the waves”; Vatican manuscript 1276 reads: “Then from the waves of water he made a solid path; in our bath …”]; now in the bath it strengthens the footprints of faith. Through this faith, whoever walks without fear, like the children of Israel, will not fear the Egyptian persecutor.

## SERMON IX. On the Holy Epiphany, III

[Col. 0547]

### ADMONITION
Erasmus judged that this sermon, attributed to Ambrose by its earliest editors, ought to be assigned to St. Maximus. Later, however, when the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of St. Maur had arranged for it to be republished in the appendix to the works of St. Ambrose, no. 8, under this title, “On the Holy Epiphany I,” they observed that it was much more likely to be attributed to Maximus than to anyone else. And if consideration is to be given to the style and to the ancient manuscripts—and certainly the greatest consideration must be given to them—it will have to be admitted that the sermon must unquestionably be restored to our bishop of Turin himself. There is no reason for me to argue about the style, since it can be obvious to anyone who takes the trouble to compare this sermon with the genuine sermons of Maximus. Nor do I think there is any need to discuss the manuscripts at length. I shall therefore proceed briefly.

In Vatican Library manuscript 1267 this sermon is found, preceded by the following inscription: “The same as above” [Col. 0549]. The person referred to as “the same as above” is Maximus, to whom the preceding sermons are attributed. In Vatican Palatine manuscript 1257 the same sermon is found with this heading: “A sermon on the Epiphany by St. Maximus, bishop.” The manuscripts of Turin, the Abbey of St. Dalmatius, Lambach, and the ninety-ninth manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem agree with this. Accordingly, Ceillier, in volume fourteen of his *General History of Authors*, etc., asserts that it is sufficiently established that this very sermon was written by Maximus.

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0549A] *Epiphany* is Greek; in Latin, “appearance.” At that time Christ God first shone into the hearts of believers through signs, appearing not so much to human eyes as for salvation. The changing of water into wine was plainly a great sign, sufficient for belief in God’s majesty and containing the mystery of the resurrection.

We ought to rejoice, dearest brothers, because our prayers are followed by prayers and joys are heaped upon joys. For behold, while our hearts are still celebrating the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity [Col. 0549D: Manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads, “our hearts are still leaping with joy, and so forth”], we are already rejoicing in the festival of the Holy Epiphany. We must therefore give thanks to the Lord, who frequently visits us, often gladdens us, and visits us more abundantly so that he may bless us more plentifully.

Although the pagan rejoices—albeit vainly—in numerous solemnities because of the diversity of his gods, one visitation of a single Lord provides us with more festivals than their superstitious presumption concerning many demons [Col. 0549D: Laurentian manuscript 10 reads, “one visitation of the one Lord provides more festivals than their superstitious presumption concerning many demons”]. For just as we surpass them in the truth of religion, so we surpass them in the number of our celebrations. Today, therefore, we are arranging the joys of the Epiphany.

Someone may ask what this word means, namely why *Epiphany* is called in Latin “appearance” [Col. 0549D: Vatican manuscripts 1267 and Palatine 1257 read, “to appear”]. It is therefore because the Savior first appeared in the world at that time [Col. 0549D: Vatican manuscript reads, “the Savior of the world”] that the day itself was called Epiphany by that name. Let us inquire, however, in what way he appeared—not because he had not previously been in the world, since the world was made through him, but because it was then that Christ God first shone into the hearts of believers through signs and miracles, and the splendor of faith entered the darkened consciences of human beings [Col. 0549D: Vatican Palatine manuscript reads, “the faith of splendor”].

Although God is everywhere and possesses all things, he is said to have appeared as though he had not previously been seen. He appeared not so much to human eyes as for salvation. For even though he had previously been born of a Virgin and could be seen with bodily eyes, he did not appear, because the eye of faith did not yet recognize his power [Col. 0549D: Vatican Palatine manuscript reads, “because”]. Hence it is said to the Jews through the prophet: “Seeing, you shall see, and you shall not see” (Isaiah VI). That is, they would behold the Savior with bodily eyes but would not see him by spiritual illumination.

After he had manifested his humanity through wonders [Col. 0549D: Laurentian manuscript 10 and manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read, “his divinity”], appearing to human minds as something new and unexpected, he poured into them certain eyes of the heart, so that the understanding might recognize him whom the outward gaze had not recognized. Thus it comes about that we contemplate Christ the Lord through faith, although we have never seen him, while the Jews, who looked upon him with their eyes and touched him with their hands, do not see him even today.

Let us therefore inquire what sign he performed in order to manifest his divinity to the peoples. It is said that he first performed this miracle: he changed water into wine. Plainly, this was a great sign and sufficient for belief in God’s majesty. For who would not marvel that the elements were transformed into something other than what they had been? No one can change nature except the Lord of nature.

From this, then, we must believe that mortal human beings can be changed into immortality, since a lowly substance was changed into a precious substance. I do not want you, hearer, merely to look at the names “wine” and “water”; but if you wish to establish the power involved, look at the force of the realities themselves. For something far greater is being demonstrated here.

When the Lord changed water into wine, he did not merely act so that the drinkers would not lack drunkenness [Col. 0549D: St. Maximus used the word *ebrietas*—“drunkenness”—for satiety, following the Gospel of John II, where it is said of the guests, “when they have become drunk,” that is, satisfied], but so that eternity might abound for believers [Col. 0550D: Manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads, “so that eternity may abound”]. For this reason Christ came into the world: not to supply the storerooms of banqueters, but to provide for the salvation of human beings; not to fill jars with a substance of good odor, but to water souls with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, when the guest wished to taste the flavor of excellent wine from that lowly water [Col. 0550D: Laurentian manuscripts 10 and Vatican 1267 read, “when he wished the guests to taste it”], he wished believers all the more to taste from this lowly flesh the wisdom of the heavenly resurrection. For this sign unquestionably contains the entire mystery of the resurrection [Col. 0550D: The cited manuscripts read, “For this sign certainly contains the whole mystery of the resurrection”].
