Water is lowly, pale [Col. 0550D: Manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads, “pallid”], and cold; when it is changed into wine—that is, something precious—red [Col. 0550D: The same manuscript reads, “red”] or fiery, it signifies that the substance of the human being, lowly by its condition, pallid through weakness, and cold in death [Col. 0550D: Vatican Palatine manuscript reads, “growing cold”], is to be changed into the glory of the resurrection: precious through eternity, colored by grace, and set ablaze by the spirit of immortality.

This, then, is worthy of belief: the Lord wished to perform this act so that through this earthly sign the heavenly mystery that was to come might already then be perceived by the wise. For if it is marvelous to supply the banquets with wine when it had run out, how much more marvelous is it to restore to human beings the life that had been exhausted? And if it is glorious to change water into wine, how much more glorious is it to change sins into righteousness, and to regulate moral character rather than cups?

I dare to say that those jars supplied that precious substance not merely to that banquet but to the whole world—except that they supply it to us more perfectly [Col. 0551A]. Those people drank drunkenness from those very vessels; we drink righteousness. They received a cup of wine; we receive the cup of salvation [Col. 0552A]. And, if it is lawful to say so, what they drank passed away, whereas what we have received remains in us [Col. 0551D: Vatican Palatine manuscript adds, “through the provision of our Lord Jesus Christ, and so forth”].

## SERMON X. On the Holy Epiphany IV

[Col. 0551]

## ADMONITION

[421] In some manuscript books this sermon is also read as attributed to Augustine, and in others to Ambrose; the Maurists transferred it to the appendix of the sermons of St. Augustine under no. 137. We attribute it to St. Maximus, together with the scribes of manuscripts 90 and 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem; after the judgment of the illustrious Cardinal Besutius, no one can doubt the reliability of those manuscripts.

In the very old manuscript 90 the sermon is numbered 41; in the other, manuscript 99, it is sermon 31, whose title is as follows: “On the Day of the Epiphanies, and on the Gospel in which the Lord was baptized, and on Psalm XXVIII.” In the manuscript of St. Gall: “On the Day of the Epiphanies.” If anyone compares this sermon with St. Maximus’s homilies dealing with the same mystery of the Epiphany, he will find the same kind of arguments and the same manner of expression.

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0551B] Christ the Savior is recognized at the time when he is baptized by John in the Jordan and is called Son by God. In Psalm XXVIII Christ’s baptism was foretold.

The Day of the Epiphanies is so called by a Greek name. What we call “appearance” or “manifestation,” the Greeks call *Epiphany* [Col. 0551D: The cited manuscripts read *hoc* (“this”) for *id* (“that”)]. We say this [Col. 0551D: The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Vatican manuscript omit “we say” (*dicimus*)] because today our Lord and Savior appeared in the flesh on earth [Col. 0551D: The words “in the flesh” are absent from both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and from the Vatican manuscript].

Although he had been born long ago from Mary and had completed the age of thirty years [Col. 0551D: Vatican manuscript reads, “and had already completed thirty years”], he was nevertheless unknown to the world. He became known at the time when he came to John the Baptist to be baptized in the Jordan, and the voice of the Father thundering from heaven was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew III) [Col. 0551D: “well” is absent from the manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem].

The one whom the Father had pointed out from heaven by his voice, the true Holy Spirit wished to indicate, as though in the form of a dove and by settling upon his head through actual contact [Col. 0551D: The cited manuscripts read, “and by that very contact he wished,” etc.], so that no one might suppose that someone else from the people was the Son of God.

What is more sublime than this humility? What is nobler than this lowliness? He is baptized by a servant and is called Son by God. He comes to the washing among tax collectors, prostitutes, and sinners, and he is holier than his baptizer [Col. 0551D: Manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads, “He is washed by John”]. He is baptized by John in the flesh, but he himself washes John in the spirit.

The waters, which had been accustomed to cleanse other things, were cleansed when our Lord washed. The Jordan River, which at the time when Jesus son of Nave led the people of Israel and brought them into the promised land had been dried up [Col. 0551D: Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Vatican 1267 read, “when Jesus son of Nave led the people and brought them into the promised land, had been dried up”], now wished, if it had been able, to gather all its waters together so that it might touch the Lord’s body [Col. 0552D: Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read, “had wished”; Vatican manuscript 1267 reads, “would have wished”]. “The Jordan,” he says, “turned back” (Psalm CXIII) [Col. 0551D]. See, brothers, how what was read in the Gospel had previously been foretold in Psalm XXVIII: “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters” (Psalm XXVIII).

For the Son of God said to John: “Let it be so now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew III). It follows: “The Lord of majesty thundered” [Col. 0552D: Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem add “God”], when the Father bore witness to the Son, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

“The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars” (Psalm XXVIII). For Christ was baptized, and the demons, previously upright and exalted, fell. The Lord cut them down like the cedars of Lebanon and shattered them like calves (ibid.), scattering fragments of trees and dispersing the roots in different directions with his kicks [Col. 0552D: Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Vatican manuscript read, “But, on the contrary”].

What, on the contrary, is said of the Savior? “And my beloved is like the son of unicorns” (ibid.). Our beloved Lord and Savior, the Son of God, is the son of unicorns, the son of the cross, concerning whom it is said in the song of Habakkuk: “He has horns in his hands; there he concealed his strength” (Habakkuk III).

After this beloved one had been crucified, what follows in the psalm was fulfilled: “The voice of the Lord dividing the flame of fire” (Psalm XXVIII). For when he was baptized and the whole world was cleansed by Christ’s washing, the fire of Gehenna was extinguished.

“The voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness” (ibid.). The Church was a wilderness because previously she had no children. At Christ’s preaching this wilderness was shaken, gave birth, and a whole people was born in one day [Col. 0552D: Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem read, “the whole people together: on that day which had formerly been called the wilderness of Kadesh,” etc.].

That place which had previously been called the wilderness of Kadesh—that is, a wilderness, since it had possessed no holiness—began to give birth to stags and to send forth the flocks of its saints. They kill serpents on earth and despise poisons. As they run throughout the world and preach the Gospel of Christ, everyone in his temple will say, “Glory to God” (ibid.).

It follows: “The Lord makes the flood to dwell.” Let us consider the whole world; let us look upon the barbarian nations; let us survey the Roman Empire as well [Col. 0552D: Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Vatican 1267 read, “Let us survey the Roman Empire with our minds: everywhere they believe in Christ”]. Everywhere they are baptized in our Lord [Col. 0553A]. Thus it comes about that there is not one body of water but, in a certain sense, a flood of baptisms.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since the tabernacle has been completed—for this is indicated beforehand in the title of this psalm—and since the Church has been built with living stones [Col. 0553C: Manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads, “has been constructed”], let us bring to the Lord sons of God; let us bring sons of rams, apostles and saints [Col. 0554A]. Let us imitate our Savior, who is himself called both Shepherd and Ram and Lamb [Col. 0553C: The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Vatican read, “who himself is called both Shepherd and Ram and Lamb”]; who is sacrificed for us in Egypt; who, for Isaac’s sake, is held by the horns in the thickets; and let us say:

“The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. In a place of pasture, there he has placed me; beside the water of refreshment he has brought me up” (Psalm XXII).

To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XI. On the Baptism of Christ I

[Col. 0553]

## ADMONITION

I shall transfer this sermon, published among the works of St. Ambrose, to the sermons of Maximus, moved not only by the authority of the manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and Turin, but also by that of the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of St. Maur, who seem to hold the following opinion in their preface to sermon 10 of the appendix to the works of St. Ambrose.

They say that what the same St. Ambrose teaches near the end of Book II on Luke concerning Christ’s baptism and the manifestation of the testimony of the Father and the Holy Spirit ought to be compared. Since Ambrose’s exposition differs from what is transmitted in this sermon, whereas Maximus is found elsewhere expressing not merely similar ideas but almost the very same words, they sufficiently establish that not Ambrose but Maximus should be judged the author of this sermon.

I do not deny that Maximus had that commentary of Ambrose on Luke before his eyes, since he writes several similar things; but our holy bishop forges his own path and renews the discourse with his own arguments.

To return to the manuscript codices: the Turin manuscript presents the sermon under this title: “Also on the same Epiphany and on the Baptism of Christ, homily IX.” The inscription of manuscript 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, no. 42, reads as follows: “Here begins the treatise on the Epiphany”; in the other manuscript, 99: “Here begins [the sermon] on the Epiphany.” Manuscript 40 F of the Basilica of St. Peter contains this same sermon, omitting the author’s name.

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0553B] St. Maximus brings to light, for the instruction of his faithful, the heavenly mysteries contained in Christ’s baptism. He also explains several testimonies of Holy Scripture, especially those concerning the dove and the Jordan turned back.

Most people, on this holy day of the Epiphany, commemorate the miracles previously performed by the Lord: when, invited to a wedding, he changed the substance of water into the appearance of wine and transferred the liquid of the springs to a better use by his blessing [Col. 0553C: Manuscript of St. Peter reads, “to its own use”]. The servants drew water from wells and found wine in the jars, and at a more useful expense lost what had been lacking [Col. 0553D: The same manuscript reads, “the servants draw water from wells, find wine in the jars,” etc.]. It was then, they say, that he first manifested the power of his divinity through this wondrous sign.

Others testify that on this holy day he was baptized by John in the Jordan [Col. 0553C], and that God the Father was present at his washing, speaking, while the Holy Spirit descended [Col. 0553D: The same manuscript reads, “and that God the Father was present at his washing, speaking, and that the Holy Spirit descended. Nor is it surprising if, in the Lord’s washing,” etc.].

Nor is it surprising that the mystery of the Trinity was present in the Lord’s washing, since it completes the sacrament of our washing. For the Lord could not fail first to display in himself what he was later to command the human race, since he accomplished everything not for his own benefit but for the grace of our salvation.

Or did he perhaps wish to be baptized for his own sake, although he had no sin, as the prophet says: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isaiah XIII; 1 Peter II)? Rather, he was baptized for us, who, burdened with the sins of many crimes, needed to be cleansed in Christ’s baptism [Col. 0553D: Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and St. Peter’s read, “in Christ’s baptism,” rather than “for baptism”].

And therefore the Lord came to the washing, not to be himself purified by the waters [Col. 0553D: Manuscript 90 omits “himself”], but to purify the streams of water for us [Col. 0553D: Manuscript of St. Peter reads, “From the moment he plunged himself into the waters, he washed away the sins of all. It was necessary that he wash away the sins of all, since he bore the sins of all,” etc.]. For from the moment he plunged himself into the waters, he wiped away the sins of all believers.

It was necessary that he wipe away the sins of all, since he took upon himself the sins of all, as the evangelist says: “This is the Lamb of God; this is he who takes away the sin of the world” (John I) [Col. 0554C: Manuscript 90 omits “of God”; both cited manuscripts and St. Peter’s manuscript read “sins”].

It is therefore wondrous indeed: one is plunged beneath the waters, and the salvation of all is restored.

God the Father is present when the Lord is baptized; the Holy Spirit is present as well [Col. 0554C: Manuscript of St. Peter reads, “See the Savior’s graciousness, for he alone,” etc.]. See the Savior’s graciousness: in his Passion he alone submitted to insults; in the washing he alone did not seek grace, but he wishes others to share in glory [Col. 0554C].

The Father is present, as I said, and the Holy Spirit is present. And because God cannot be seen, the Spirit descends in a dove and the Father in a voice; and, since this alone was necessary to establish faith, he presents the Savior [Col. 0554D: Manuscript of St. Peter reads, “to instruct human beings in faith, and what was necessary was presented by the Savior. For our faith consists only through hearing and sight”]. For our faith consists through hearing and sight. Therefore the Spirit submits himself to the eyes in the form of a dove, and the Father offers himself to the ears in a voice.

For unless these things had needed to occur for the sake of our belief, the Father and the Holy Spirit, as the invisible God, could have descended invisibly to the Word, the invisible Son [Col. 0554D: Manuscript of St. Peter reads, “For unless this had needed to happen for the sake of our belief, the Father and the Holy Spirit, as the invisible God, could have descended by an invisible movement to the Word”].

Thus, for the sake of our faith, when heaven had been opened [Col. 0554D: The same manuscript reads, “when heaven had been opened”], the Spirit descended to Christ, the Father to the Son, and the voice to the Word.

For Christ is the Word, of whom it is written: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I) [Col. 0555D: Manuscript of St. Peter reads, “of whom it is written”]. As I have said, the Father is rightly called “voice” and the Son “Word,” because the word proceeds only from the voice. Thus voice and word correspond to each other and provide for human salvation through their shared mystery.

Let us consider, then, by what reasoning the Holy Spirit descended to Christ in the form of a dove—whether there is some resemblance between the dove and the Lord, just as there is between voice and word [Col. 0555D: St. Peter’s manuscript omits “there is”]. There certainly is. For I would even call the Lord himself a dove, since he is lively, gentle, and simple. He is a dove because he commands his saints to be like doves, saying: “Be simple as doves.”

That Christ is a dove, the prophet says in his person, describing his return to heaven after the Passion: “Who will give me wings, and I shall fly and rest?” (Psalm LIV).

When Christ the Lord was inaugurating the sacraments of the Church, a dove came from heaven [Col. 0555D: St. Peter’s manuscript reads, “a dove came from heaven to announce the sacrament to the Church”; Laurentian manuscript X Plut. XIV reads, “a dove came from heaven,” etc.]. I understand the mystery; I recognize the sacrament as well.

For it is the same dove that now comes to Christ’s Church in baptism, which once hastened to Noah’s ark during the Flood, then announcing safety to it by an olive branch (Genesis VIII), now conferring eternity upon this Church through the indication of divinity [Col. 0555D: St. Peter’s manuscript reads, “through the judgment of divinity”]. Then it carried a sign of peace in its beak; now it pours forth peace itself—Christ—through its substance [Col. 0555D: The same manuscript reads, “the substance of Christ himself”].

The Lord, therefore, was baptized in the Jordan [Col. 0555D: The same manuscript reads, “Thus, then, the Lord is baptized in the Jordan”]. Scripture often recounts that many wonders were performed in this river. Among them is this: “The Jordan turned back” (Psalm CXIII) [Col. 0556D: St. Peter’s manuscript omits “turned back”]. I think that what happened there when the Lord Jesus was present is more wondrous.

Previously, the waters had turned back; now sins have turned back. And just as then the force of the river lost the channel of its course [Col. 0556D: St. Peter’s manuscript reads, “And just as then the riverbed lost the force of its course, so also,” etc.], so now the force of sins has lost the dominion of its error [Col. 0556D: Manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads, “so now the force of the sins of human beings has lost its course”].

I think that this had already happened at the time of the prophet Elijah. For just as Elijah made a division in the waters, so the Spirit of the Lord effected a separation of sins in that same Jordan [Col. 0556D: Both manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem and the Laurentian manuscript read, “so also Christ the Lord effected a separation of sins in that same Jordan. Elijah commanded the waters to stand; Christ commanded crimes to stand; and just as under Elijah,” etc.]. Elijah commanded the waters to stand; Christ commanded crimes to stand.

And just as under Elijah the waves sought the beginnings of the springs from which they had flowed, so under Christ the Lord human beings returned to the infancy of their origin, from which they had arisen.

[Col. 0556D: Here the sermon ends in the manuscript of St. Peter.]

## SERMON XII. On the Baptism of Christ II

[Col. 0555]

## ADMONITION

[427] Martenius and Durandus, Benedictine monks of the Congregation of St. Maur, deserve the highest praise for publishing this sermon and five others found among Mabillon’s papers, as stated above. To this is added the testimony of St. Gall manuscript 87, which attributes it to Maximus, and of Turin manuscript 43. For this reason we too attribute such a sermon to the same holy bishop. Its connection with the preceding sermon also supports this attribution.

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0555C] Christ is baptized not for himself but for us. In him there was the fullness of divinity and the eternal possession of righteousness. In order to transmit to us the gifts of his holiness and grace, he instituted baptism and sanctified all waters by his contact.

Your Holiness remembers, brothers, what we said on the most festive day of the Epiphany: that the Lord was baptized in the Jordan, and that we explained how he wished to be consecrated by this mystery more for our sake than for his own.

He accomplished all these things plainly for our sake. For what benefit required consecration for him who is himself the sacrament? What use could the solemnity of the mystery have for him in whom the fullness of the mystery exists?

For in him there is fullness, as the Apostle says: “For in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians II, 9). And again the evangelist says: “From his fullness we have all received” (John I).

Therefore, since the fullness of divinity was in him, he did not need to be filled by the mysteries of the sacraments. But he wished to fulfill the mystery not so that he himself might gain benefit, but so that the fullness of the mystery might benefit us [Col. 0556C].

Finally, when John the Baptist resisted and said, “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” the Lord said to him: “Allow it now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew III).

“To fulfill,” he says, “all righteousness.” Why, then, is the Lord baptized? Righteousness does not justify Christ; rather, righteousness itself is sanctified by Christ, and partial virtue is completed by him in whom the fullness of virtues resides.

John therefore says: “I ought to be baptized by you.” He thus bears witness that the Lord was not baptized for his own sake, since before John baptized him, John was rather asking to be baptized by him. By saying this, he demonstrates that greater grace exists in the Lord’s mystery than in the minister of the mystery.

For what consecration could he have imparted to the one from whom he himself desired to receive sanctification? Was the minister inferior in merits to the disciple in holiness? In comparison with Christ, the minister is unskilled, righteousness is incomplete, and the water is turbid [Col. 0556D].

But when the Lord is baptized, through his blessing the minister advances, righteousness is completed, and the water is cleansed. The water was cleansed: although it had been lowly and cold, it was enriched by the warmth of the Lord’s blessing, so that what previously scarcely washed away the stains of earthly things now purifies the spiritual stains of souls.

Do not be surprised that we say water—that is, a bodily substance—can reach the purification of the soul. It certainly does reach it; it penetrates every hidden place of the conscience. Although water itself is subtle and thin, through Christ’s blessing it is made subtler still and, through the hidden causes of life, passes like spiritual dew into the soul’s crimes. For the flow of blessings is subtler than the passage of waters.

Hence we also said that in the Savior’s baptism the blessing, which flowed down like a special river, permeated the courses of all waters and the veins of every spring.

For it is wondrous, I say, that when Christ was present in the Jordan, the rivers of water were washed. But streams of blessing were also flowing; from there the riverbed’s current was carried along more turbidly. From here the Savior’s most pure spring cleansed. And, in a certain wondrous manner, the consecration of baptism ascended downward toward the source of the Jordan, while the river of blessing flowed against the current of the waters.

Hence I think that holy David said: “The Jordan turned back” (Psalm CXIII). In Christ’s baptism the Jordan did not turn back in its waters but in its sacraments, and it returned to its source by the blessing rather than by its physical substance.

For while the grace of consecration is carried through it to all springs, it seems to have recalled its proper course to the beginning of the veins.

*The end.*

## SERMON XIII. On the Grace of Baptism

[Col. 0557]

## ADMONITION

[429] The title “On the Grace of Baptism” properly belongs to this sermon; as stated above, the editors wrongly assigned it to Homily 5 on Baptism. St. Maximus urges the catechumens not to delay receiving the washing of regeneration, lest they be deprived of the benefit of its grace.

Since a title should provide a sample of the subject of a discourse, and since this entire sermon concerns the remission of sins and the infusion of righteousness acquired through baptism, no other inscription can suit the sermon than “On the Grace of Baptism.”

This title is indeed borne by the six manuscripts that attribute the sermon to St. Maximus: St. Gall manuscript 11; Vatican manuscript 1267, page 158; the Turin manuscript, in which it is homily 13; manuscript 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, no. 11, with the title “Here begins [the sermon] on the grace of baptism”; manuscript 99 of the same Santa Croce, no. 44; and Laurentian manuscript X Plut. XIV.

If these testimonies, expressed in such clear words, had been available to the Benedictine monks who edited St. Ambrose, they would have pronounced a more certain judgment concerning this sermon.

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0557B] Maximus urges the catechumens to receive the grace of baptism with all haste, so that they may become what Christ is; and he teaches clearly and at length what difference exists between John’s baptism and Christ’s baptism.

Since it is established—as we explained a few days ago—that Jesus Christ was baptized not for his own sake but for ours,

[Note: Vatican Manuscript 1267 reads, “a few days ago.”]

dearest brothers—I am speaking to you catechumens—we must receive the grace of his baptism with all haste, draw from the Jordan’s stream, which he blessed, the blessing of consecration, and plunge our sins into that flood into which his holiness immersed himself. Thus the same water that surrounded the Lord may cleanse his servants all around, so that the holy wave from Christ’s venerable bath may benefit us

[Note: The same Vatican manuscript reads, “from Christ’s venerable bath.”]

and, by the same traces and mysteries through which it received its blessing from the Savior, purify us with a more blessed refreshment and pour upon Christians the grace it received from Christ.

Therefore, brothers, we must be immersed in the same font in which Christ was baptized, so that we may become what Christ is. For—let me say this without compromising the faith—although both baptisms belong to the Lord, I consider that baptism by which we are washed more gracious than that by which the Savior is baptized.

[Note: Both the Saint-Crucis-in-Jerusalem manuscript and the Vatican manuscript read, “is baptized.”]

The former is celebrated through Christ; the latter was celebrated through John. In the latter the Master excuses himself; in the former the Savior invites us. In the latter there is a partial righteousness; in the former the Trinity is perfect. To the latter the Holy One came and the Holy One emerged; to the former the sinner comes and the holy person departs. In the latter, a blessing is conferred upon the mysteries; in the former, sins are forgiven through the mysteries.

[Note 1: This is clearly a theological distinction between grace arising from the sacrament itself and grace arising from the acting minister: the former is attributed to the sacrament’s efficacy and power, which is why Maximus says of baptism, “in this baptism sins are forgiven through the mysteries”; the latter to the sanctification conferred upon the elements through blessing, “in the former a blessing is conferred upon the mysteries.”]

[Note: Both the Saint-Crucis-in-Jerusalem manuscript and the Vatican manuscript read, “through the mystery.” Laurentian Manuscript X reads, “in the former, through the mystery he forgave sins.”]

Therefore, brothers, we must be baptized in the same flood as the Savior. But in order to be immersed in the same font, we do not need to seek the eastern region or a river of the Jewish land. For wherever Christ is, there too is the Jordan.

[Note: Manuscript 90 reads, “everywhere there is the Jordan”; likewise the Laurentian manuscript, “for wherever Christ is, everywhere there is the Jordan.”]

The same consecration that blessed the rivers of the East sanctifies the streams of the West. Hence, even if the river perhaps bears another worldly name, the mystery of the Jordan is nevertheless present in it. Indeed, the same sacramental action is performed as was then performed, except with fuller grace.

Then we saw the Trinity with bodily eyes; now we contemplate the same Trinity with the eyes of faith. Then scarcely a human face looked upon Christ; now the human mind embraces that same Christ. Then the Holy Spirit enveloped a human being in the likeness of a dove; now he pours himself into a person’s inmost being by the very power of his divinity.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “by the very power of divinity,” and so forth.]

Then the Father came to the Lord because of the Son, through the extended hearing of a voice; now the Father himself descends to us with the Son. Grace, therefore, is fuller where God descends to human beings—not after assuming an outward form, but in his own substance.

[Note: Manuscript 99 of Saint-Crucis-in-Jerusalem reads, “but deigns to come to his children in his own substance.” Manuscript 90 reads, “but in his own substance deigns to come to his children,” and so forth.]

There, as though addressing unbelievers, he wished to persuade them of faith through bodily signs; here, as though addressing believers, he bestows grace through spiritual power. It is therefore a fuller grace to see God as God is than to see him in such a way that one must still seek him. Here the Trinity is perfect; there the divinity is still to be investigated. It is therefore a fuller grace to know God by his own power than to conjecture him in an assumed form.

[Note: The sermon ends here in the Vatican manuscript.]

Let us therefore do for ourselves what we see God has done for us; let us do toward ourselves what John wished to be done toward him.

[Note: Manuscript 90 of Saint-Crucis-in-Jerusalem supplies the following.]

[Note: Manuscript 99 of Saint-Crucis-in-Jerusalem also has this passage; but because it is written in a smaller and more vivid hand, the addition seems to have been made at a later time.]

If he, who was a prophet, teacher, and holy man, desired the Savior’s baptism, how much more ought we sinners—humble and ignorant as we are—to seek this grace. To see the Savior’s mercy: this is freely offered to us, which the prophet, though he asked for it, was not worthy to receive.

But we must consider why John asked for Christ’s baptism and did not receive it. For the Lord said to him when he made his request: “Let it be so for now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3).

We know, moreover, that John the Baptist bore the figure of the Law. It was therefore right that he should baptize the Lord: namely, so that just as the Savior was born from the Jews according to the flesh, so the Gospel might be born from the Law according to the spirit; and that from the source from which he derived his ancestral origin he might also receive the tradition of consecration. This, then, is what he says: “For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” It was right that he himself should fulfill the commands of the Law that he himself had established, just as he says elsewhere: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (the same passage).

## SERMON XIV. On the General Fast

### ADMONITION

This sermon was first recovered by the distinguished man Joan. Dominico Maria Mansio, a cleric regular of the Mother of God, later the most deserving archbishop of his native city, from Manuscript 85 of the chapter church of Lucca. It was published in the appendix to the works of Stefano Baluzius, volume II, page 452, bearing the name of Saint Maximus.

Moved by the testimony of four other manuscripts, we declare Saint Maximus its author: two from the Laurentian Library, I Plut. XIV, page 120 verso, and the second, 174, formerly belonging to the cathedral chapter of Florence; the third from the library of the Congregation of Monte Oliveto at Naples, page 100; and finally the fourth, from Turin.

All identify Saint Maximus as the author of the sermon, but they do not all bear the same title. In the Lucchese manuscript the sermon is entitled “On the General Fast”; in the others, “On Lent.” We adopt not the title preferred by the other manuscripts, “On Lent,” but that of the Lucchese manuscript, because in this address Saint Maximus does not speak specifically about the Lenten fast, but generally about the virtue and merit of fasting, although what he says can also apply to Lenten abstinence.

### ARGUMENT

On the fall of Adam, who desired to know good and evil. If he sinned by tasting, why should I not please God by fasting? Established in the paradise of the Church, we have received the command to preserve the law of fasting.

It has often been impressed upon your ears, both from the divine Scriptures and from our preaching, that the first cause of Adam’s sin was an enticement of the mind and that the cause of his offense was a desire for food.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “an enticement of the belly” in place of “of the mind.”]

For, although surrounded by so many precious foods in paradise, he refused to observe the fast of abstinence from a single tree, and lost the enjoyment of all delights; he forfeited what had been granted because he desired what was forbidden.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “he refused to observe the fast from one little tree.”]

[Note: Another reading: “pleasure.”]

If he had endured abstinence from a single food, he would not have been deprived of so many blessings through fasting.

[Note: Another reading: “he would not have become deprived.”]

Therefore, brothers, recognizing in our forefather the cause of the offense, let us cut away from ourselves the occasion of sin. Let us keep within the limits of the command the desire that he extended beyond the line of the commandment.

[Note: The Neapolitan manuscript reads, “the desire that he extended beyond the line of the commandment.”]

Let us not, because of fasts imposed for the briefest period, allow ourselves to lose the sweetness of our whole life. If he sinned by tasting, why should I not please God by fasting? If food became a means of death for him, why should abstinence not benefit me for salvation? He is plainly foolish who is instructed neither by commands nor by examples.

Consider, then, whether a command like Adam’s was not given to us when we are reborn, as that command was given to Adam when he was created. For we are told, as people established in a paradise of delights and resting amid the pleasantness of the Lord’s fountains,

[Note: The Neapolitan manuscript reads, “amid the pleasantness of the Lord’s fountain.”]

to take food from the fruits of every virtue, but not to taste from the single tree of knowing good and evil.

Who would be content with such a law, which requires abstinence from only one thing so that he may enjoy everything else?

[Note: The Neapolitan manuscript reads, “I mean, we are commanded to abstain from the little tree of knowing good and evil.”]

We are commanded, I say, to abstain from the tree of knowing good and evil; we must understand what that tree is. For if the holy are nourished by the fruits of discipline, what tree is forbidden to the righteous except worldly indiscipline?

Whoever, after receiving grace, tastes of worldly wantonness comes to know the distinction between good and evil. For he begins to know both what holiness he has lost and into what ruin he has fallen. It is not that tasting the tree itself supplies human beings with this knowledge, but that the conscience was innocent; after it has been polluted, it mourns the good things it has lost and laments the evils it has committed.

An undefiled life, however, does not possess this knowledge; for what is always holy or simple considers that the only thing in a human being is what is pure. But wantonness makes one highly expert in evil through experience of sins.

It is therefore better for a Christian to possess holy simplicity than criminal knowledge.

[Note: The Neapolitan manuscript reads, “I mean the little tree in which good and evil are to be known: I do not want such knowledge.”]

The tree in which good and evil are to be known—I do not want such knowledge.

For what benefit is there in knowing what is not beneficial to know, what one will regret having learned?

The Lord therefore established for human beings in the tabernacle of the Church the same kind of law that he commanded in the possession of paradise. Paradise is the Church, sheltered by the pleasantness of diverse virtues—or trees—from whose womb Christ proceeds like a most brilliant spring, and from there flows forth, like a paradise, into the four rivers of the evangelists.

The blessed apostles and evangelists are to be compared with rivers, because by the spirit of their teaching the face of the entire people is watered. There is no Christian soul that does not draw water from the holy fountain of the evangelists.

The Gospel is plainly like a river, of which Saint David also says: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Psalm 45). The city of Christ is made glad when, through the course of evangelical teaching, a purified people is brought into it and its court is filled by a certain rush of preaching with the commerce of holiness.

I say, the rush of evangelical speech makes God’s city glad: it brings some things into it and purifies others.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “the rush of the evangelical river,” and so forth.]

It brings in the pearls of righteousness; it cleanses away the filth of wickedness.

Therefore, brothers, established as we are in the paradise of the Church, we have received the command to preserve the law of fasting. Let us not violate the consecrated number of forty days even by a slight taste, because the Lord is not offended by satiety but by transgression of the law. Indeed, as soon as Adam tasted against the prohibition, he fell from the grace of immortality.

## SERMON XV. On Lent I—On the Lord’s Fast in the Desert, and That Man Does Not Live by Bread Alone (Matthew 4)

### ADMONITION

This sermon appears in the appendix to the works of Saint Ambrose, volume IV, page 529; it is now numbered twenty-seven and is the eleventh on Lent. In their preface to the same sermon, the monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur say that it is credible that both this sermon and the one immediately following it should be attributed to one Maximus. This sermon concerns Christ’s first temptation, while the other concerns the second. The third sermon, which concerned the third temptation, is missing; on this matter I refer the reader to those same monks.

In the two ancient manuscripts of Saint-Crucis-in-Jerusalem, 90 and 99, both surviving sermons bear the name of Maximus, as they also do in the Turin manuscript.

### ARGUMENT

On the Savior’s being tempted by the devil’s cunning, when he said: “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.” Seeing him hungry, the devil thinks he is a human being and doubts that he is the Savior. We must not accept the bread the devil offers, but the bread Christ distributes.

Your charity should remember that last Sunday I preached this to you and explained why the Lord fasted for forty days, or why he spent those fasts in the desert. We said that he observed all these things not for the sake of his own justification—for he was a virgin in every respect—but for the sake of our salvation: so that the generation whose sin had arisen through intemperance might be healed through abstinence.

Let us therefore see what happened at that time, in that very solitude. The evangelist says that the devil was present there and that the Savior was tempted by his cunning. For the sacred Reading says that the Lord was hungry, and that the devil said to him: “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread” (Matthew 4).

Observe the Lord’s strategy, by which he outmaneuvers his adversary.

[Note: “By what strategy he outmaneuvers his adversary”; thus Manuscript 90 of Saint-Crucis-in-Jerusalem. The others read, “not by deception.”]

After many fasts he pretends to be hungry, so that by becoming hungry he may again provoke the devil, whom he had already conquered by fasting.

[Note: Maximus openly confessed elsewhere, in Homily 6 on Lent and in other passages, that Christ truly became hungry as a human being. Here, however, he says that Christ simulated hunger because he became hungry willingly and voluntarily, not from necessity, as other human beings ordinarily do when deprived of food. We must attend to Maximus’s meaning when he speaks of Christ as the divine person who had assumed for us a human nature subject to weaknesses. Just as, had he not wished to suffer or die, he would neither have suffered nor died—as Saint Augustine says—so after fasting in the desert he became hungry because he willed it.]

He thus grants the devil, in a sense, hope of engaging him on account of the weakness of hunger; and while the devil attacks one who appears weak, he is defeated all the more gloriously.

For this is the true victory: since the devil had overthrown Adam when he was immortal, glorious, and feasting, he is now conquered by a mortal, humble, and hungry human being.

Seeing the Lord hungry, the devil thinks he is a human being and doubts that he is the Savior. Therefore he says: “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread” (Matthew 4).

O wretched and final encounter of Satan! In the desert of temptation the devil found no solid weapons.

[Note: Manuscripts 90 of Saint-Crucis-in-Jerusalem and Vaticanus 1068 read, “solid weapons.”]

The pleasantness of the trees of paradise is absent; Eve, his counselor, is absent; the beautiful deception of the fruits is absent. And because he could not find food to offer to the hungry man,

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “to offer.”]

he asks that rocks be changed into food.

Excluded and frustrated on every side, he resorts to the pavement. He plainly shows that the wilderness has left him in desolation, since he supposes that, because of the scarcity of things, even the elements can be transformed.

He therefore asks that stones be changed into bread. Cunning and clever, he knows what he is asking; he knows that what he says has happened before. For he remembers that, in the Old Testament, water flowed from a stone for those who were thirsty; here too he wishes to provide food from a stone for one who is hungry.

He also retains the hardness of the rock dissolved into the liquid of springs.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “He also retains there the hardness of the rock.”]

Here too he desires the roughness of the stone to be transformed into the sweetness of bread. For he suspected that this was Christ, who might be accustomed to perform such things from the nature of stones, just as the apostle Paul says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10).

He suspected, I say, that he was Christ when he asked him to make bread from a stone; but when he saw him hungry, he thought him merely a human being.

The Savior, however, condemns his cunning with a wondrous answer. He does not do what the devil says, lest he appear to display the glory of his power at his adversary’s discretion. Yet he did not answer that it could not be done, since he could not deny what he had often already done.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “because” in place of “who.”]

Thus he neither yields to the petitioner nor denies the tester; in this way he both reserves the power of his strength to his own discretion and refutes the adversary’s cunning with divine speech.

He therefore answered him: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matthew 4).

[Note: Both manuscripts of Saint-Crucis-in-Jerusalem supply the following, in agreement with Vaticanus 1268.]

That is: not by earthly bread, not by material food—the food with which you deceived Adam, the first human being—but by the word of God, in which are the nourishment of heavenly life.

The Word of God is the Lord Christ, as the evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1). Whoever is nourished by Christ’s word does not seek earthly food. For one who is refreshed by the Savior’s bread cannot desire the world’s bread.

The Lord has his own bread; indeed, the Savior himself is bread, as he taught when he said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6). Of this bread the prophet says: “And bread strengthens the human heart” (Psalm 103).

Why, then, should I want the bread the devil offers, when I have the bread Christ distributes? Why should I want food by which I remember that the first-created human being was cast down? I have seen Esau deprived of his birthright and Judas Iscariot branded by the crime of betrayal.

Adam lost paradise through food; Esau lost the honor of primacy through lentils; Judas laid down the exalted dignity of apostleship through a morsel. For from the moment he took the morsel, he began to be no longer an apostle but a betrayer.

For you have it written, when the Lord says: “The one to whom I shall give the dipped bread is the one who will betray me.” And immediately after the morsel, Satan entered into him (John 13).

Not good is the food after which the Lord is denied, after which the enemy enters; not good is the food after which Christ is rejected and Antichrist is devoured. Not good is the food that lacks blessing and is filled with a curse.

That food, therefore, is necessary for us which grants life, which nourishes the soul, after which Christ follows and the enemy is excluded. We must receive the food that the Savior, not the devil, follows—food whose reception makes one a confessor, not a betrayer.

How appropriately, moreover, during the time of fasting he said that the word of God is what nourishes, so that he might show that our fasts ought not to be occupied with the activities of the world but exercised through the sacred Scriptures.

The person who attends to the nourishment of reading disregards bodily hunger; nor can one who acquires the food of the heavenly word be concerned with the belly. For this is the refreshment that satisfies the soul and makes the inward parts flourish, when we acquire from the divine Scriptures the nourishment of everlasting speech.

[Note: Manuscript 99 of Saint-Crucis-in-Jerusalem reads, “when we receive it.”]

This is the food that grants eternal life and excludes from us the snares of the devil’s temptation. That the reading of the sacred Scriptures is life, the Lord himself testifies when he says: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6).

## SERMON XVI. On Lent II

### ADMONITION

In the preceding admonition we stated, following the judgment of the Benedictine monks of Saint Maur, what should be thought about this sermon. They themselves confirmed the same conclusion in the preface to this sermon, number 22 and number 6 on Lent in the same Paris edition, saying that it suits Maximus rather than Ambrose.

So that I may omit nothing relevant to clarifying the truth, I shall add two excellent manuscripts: the Sangallensis, where it is sermon 60, and Manuscript 99 of Saint-Crucis-in-Jerusalem, number 20, both supporting Saint Maximus. While consulting the Casinensian manuscripts, I encountered this same sermon in a very old manuscript, number 117, page 219, whose title is “Homiliary with Lives of the Saints,” many of which are not commonly published; it bears no author’s name, as likewise in the Urbevetanus manuscript.

### ARGUMENT

On the Savior being tempted again by the devil. What it means to stand above the pinnacle of the temple, and what it means to be thrown down from the pinnacle. God forgets no one; but we make him forget us when we sin.

We ought not to be so deeply saddened, brothers, that the temptation of tribulation has come upon us during these days of Lent, since we see that our Savior too was tempted because of Lent itself.

[Note: The Casinensian manuscript reads, “when it finds us.”]

We, then, who are servants, should grieve less, since we have the Lord’s example.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “be wearied” in place of “grieve.”]

For where there is devotion like Christ’s, there is also temptation like Christ’s. The condition of fasting imposes upon us the condition of enduring.

We believe, moreover, that just as our Savior overcame the devil when he was tempted, so we too can conquer our enemies when we are afflicted. Christ’s fasts can indeed be tested; they cannot be overcome. They contain hardships in their observance, but they bestow prosperity

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “for salvation.”]

and salvation.

Let us therefore see by what device the Lord is wearied amid the other temptations. When the Savior was standing above the pinnacle of the temple, the devil said: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (Matthew 4), and so forth.

Truly, the cunning of diabolical fraud employs the argument of its customary practice. It always tries to cast religious people down from higher things to lower ones, and hastens to draw them away from holy and venerable actions toward earthly and muddy things, so that one who stands at the summit of the temple in purity of mind may throw himself into the depth of hell through the contagion of sin.

For when it tries to cast the Lord down from the pinnacle of the temple, it is certainly trying to remove him from perfect religious worship. The pinnacle of the holy place is the heavenly perfection of the sacrament.

The Lord is rightly said to stand above the pinnacle of the temple, because it is written of him: “He walks upon the wings of the winds” (Psalm 103). The Lord in a certain sense walks upon the wings of the winds when he moves joyfully in flight above the eager conduct of our lives.

[Note: The Casinensian manuscript reads, “when he proceeds joyfully above the active conduct of our lives.”]

Our good morals are wings, for they lift us from the lowliness of earth to the heights of heaven, and by a kind of flight of the mind lead us out of the dark abyss and bring us to the pleasantness of paradise.

Desiring to possess the wings of such morals, the prophet says: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I shall fly and rest?” (Psalm 54).

The Savior is therefore said to stand above this pinnacle of the temple—that is, to stand as though in a kind of temple of our faith. Hence the Apostle says: “You are the temple of the living God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (2 Corinthians 6).

Standing in this temple, then, and not departing from it, the Lord rebukes the devil, saying: “It is written, ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God’” (Deuteronomy 6). That is: you shall not tempt the one whom you think must be driven down as though he were a human being; rather, you must recognize and adore him as God and Lord.

During these days of fasting we are tempted in imitation of the Savior. In the same way our enemies try to disturb us from the pinnacle of the temple—that is, from the observance of Lent.

[Note: The same manuscript adds, “They try to disturb us. For when…”]

While they instill terrors and prepare snares, they desire to lead us away from the stronghold of religion.

But the Lord says to them: “You shall not tempt holy men and servants of God. Those whom you think you can trample down as humble, you will find worthy of honor as strong.”

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “The Lord says to them: ‘You shall not tempt holy men,’ and so forth; ‘you will think them as…,’ and so forth.”]

For, as I have said, there are many brothers whom our enemies lead away from the perfection of religion. When they fear present evil, they think that God has forgotten our salvation, not knowing that God forgets no one; but we make him forget us when we sin.

When we do evil things, he turns his face away; when we speak abominable things, he closes his ear. Therefore God does not so much withdraw his goodness himself as our sins reject him.

The same Lord says through the prophet to those who were placed in tribulations: “Is my hand not strong enough to rescue you?” (Isaiah 50), and so forth.

You see, then, that sins separate God and the human being. Remove sin from your midst, and you yourself have made God near to you.

[Note: The same manuscript omits “to you.”]

For how can God forget us, brothers, when in the Gospel he says that even the hairs of our head are numbered before him (Matthew 10)? If he remembers our hairs, how much more does he remember our souls?

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “he remembers our souls.”]

Through numbering we recognize his care and solicitude toward us; for no one counts except what he wishes to guard more carefully. No one counts except one who fears that something counted may be lost without his knowing it.

A shepherd counts his flock frequently so that he may keep it safe.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “he counts it.”]

Indeed, when one little sheep had strayed from a hundred sheep, the Lord, who is the good shepherd, returned to the number and carried it back to the flock on his own shoulders (Matthew 18).

So greatly is what is counted held under protection that, when it strays, it is carried on the shepherd’s own shoulders, lest anything be diminished from the number.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “So great is the love for the one that is held in the number that, when it strays, it is carried on the shepherd’s own shoulders.”]

Do not think, therefore, brothers, that God forgets even the least person.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “that God forgets anyone.” “He remembers everyone,” and so forth.]

God remembers everyone and calls everyone to mind—provided only that, through our intervening sins, forgetfulness is not imposed upon him.

## SERMON XVII. On Lent III

### ADMONITION

Fortune has smiled upon our labors in a manner not unwelcome. After first examining the manuscripts of the Laurentian Library, from which we gathered one or another sermon of Saint Maximus, while inspecting Manuscript 169 of the library formerly belonging to the cathedral church of Florence, we encountered this new sermon, adorned with the name of Saint Maximus.

Freed, therefore, from every dispute, since it is found neither among the sermons of Ambrose nor among those of Augustine, we gladly brought it into the light for use—especially since it is read in Vatican Manuscript 4222, page 144, and in Manuscript IV Plut. XXXIII, page 70 verso, formerly belonging to the Minor Convent of Saint-Crucis and now Laurentian, both of which bear the name of Saint Maximus as their inscription. The text is taken from the Vatican manuscript.

### ARGUMENT

The Lenten fast was instituted as a remedy for sin. The first man, Adam, fell away from the righteousness in which he had been created by violating the command not to eat from the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. His guilt is therefore repaired through the virtue of abstinence and obedience to the commandment. It is explained with great learning why God, although good and merciful, did not wish to relax the punishment of death inflicted because of original sin.

Your Holiness remembers that a few days ago we explained that, through this care of holy Lent, a kind of restoration of the human race is being carried out, so that through this most sacred season the frailty of our condition may be renewed.

[Note: Manuscript 169, formerly belonging to the Florentine cathedral chapter, reads, “the condition of our frailty is renewed.”]

Christ, by his indulgence, restored the grace of immortality that Adam had lost through sinning, and by fasting according to the commandment justified the one who had sinned by eating against the prohibition.

For this is the entire cause of Christianity and faith: that what had perished may be saved, what had gone astray may be recalled, and what had already died may be reborn.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “may be reborn. Reborn, I say, anew, not merely born.”]

The offense of the first generation became the occasion of the second birth; and from the guilt of that transgression arose the grace of this justification.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “from the guilt of that transgression.”]

There would have been no need for a human being to be born again if what had existed had not perished.

But someone may say: God could have forgiven the sins contracted through Adam in such a way that it would not have been necessary for a human being to be born again.

Listen, then, and understand the reason. God, as we know, is truthful and just and can never lie. When he had fashioned Adam and established for him in paradise a law of this kind—that he should absolutely not taste from the tree of knowing good and evil, and that on the day he tasted it he would die—then, while the human being was bound by such a command, he passed over the command, fell under the law, and through transgression sought the death that God had foretold.

Therefore, as we have said, because it is impossible for the decrees of the divinity to be overturned, and because the human being had fallen into the snare of the law, he could not be forgiven without a second birth. The order of the commandments could not be dissolved, but God willed the human being to be reborn and in a certain sense to become another person.

Since the judgment of the law could not be changed, the person subject to the law would be changed: in one and the same human being, one condition would bind one person while grace would free another; the old person would satisfy severity, while the new would increase in goodness. Thus the commandment would retain its force in the human being, while another status would rescue the human being.

The one who is reborn fulfills the condition of the first generation and takes his origin from the second birth. The one, I say, who is reborn has ceased to be what he was and begins to be what he was not; he has died to the old things and has been renewed for things to come.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “the old person has died, and, having been renewed, now belongs to the future.”]

How good, then, is our Lord: he established the law in such a way that he did not omit mercy; he showed mercy in such a way that he did not violate the ordinances of the law. As just, he carried out the sentence; as merciful, he granted pardon.

For the fact that we die is the decree established by the earlier judgment; the fact that we rise again is the gift bestowed by the later one.

Therefore, brothers—I am speaking to you catechumens—hasten to the grace of the second birth, so that Adam may come to an end in you and Christ may begin; let death be emptied, life take its place, the sentence of severity be abolished, and the grace of renewal follow.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “and the grace of the second birth follow.”]

For the severity of the judge is abolished when, with renewal intervening, God does not recognize the sentence against the one who has returned in newness.

[Note: The same manuscript adds: “For the severity of the judge is abolished when, with renewal intervening, he does not recognize the sentence against the one who has returned in newness. Otherwise, unless our old person has been changed and follows the new person, he will be able to avoid neither the punishment of sin nor the condition of death—he who has not fled to the authority of the author of his condition. For he says,” and so forth.]

Otherwise, unless our old person has been changed and follows the new person, whoever has not fled to the authority of the author of his condition will be unable to avoid either the punishment of sin or the condition of death.

For Christ the Lord says: “Unless you believe that I am, you will die in your sins” (John 8).

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “But if we believe in Christ, if we faithfully put on his grace, what he says is true: ‘Unless someone…,’” and so forth.]

Let us therefore believe in Christ, and let us faithfully put on his grace, so that what he says may be true: “Unless someone is born again of water” (John 3), and so forth.

Let us therefore put on the Lord both in grace and in commandments. Death will not retain those in whom it sees Adam living with Christ, who is life.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “when it sees Adam living with Christ, who is life. Let us preserve his commandments above all, and especially the days of the Lenten fast.”]

Let us preserve his commandments, he says, above all, and especially those concerning the fasts of Lent.

For just as many people, when this most sacred period of fasting is imposed upon them, violate the divinely established time by eating during the intervening weeks, not understanding that by tasting against the prohibition they are guilty of no lesser transgression than Adam, who ate against the command,

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “but Christ’s Passion redeemed that transgression.”]

Christ’s Passion redeemed Adam’s transgression. Who will redeem these people, who are transgressors after the Lord’s Passion?

## SERMON XVIII. On Lent IV

### ADMONITION

[The supplied source ends here.]

In the Turin manuscript this sermon is found as number 28, *On Lent*, while the following sermon, found in the two manuscripts soon to be cited, is referred to this same sermon. We have therefore attributed both to our Saint Maximus. We do not fail to inform readers that the eminent editors of Saint Augustine’s works, the monks of Saint-Maur, placed this same sermon in the appendix of sermons under number 143, *On Lent IV*, column 189 of the Antwerp edition of 1700; there, after reviewing the judgments of Verlinus and Vindingius, they said that it should not be rejected. The Louvain editors doubted whether it ought to be ascribed to Saint Augustine—and rightly and properly so, since the Maximian manner of expression shines through more clearly than that of the bishop of Hippo. In the Turin manuscript it is noted that sermon 27, *On Lent*, is missing.

**ARGUMENT.**—We ought rightly to observe by fasting the number forty days, which we read was consecrated through the examples of Moses, Elijah, and Christ the Savior. We who abstain from meat and fast from foods should first of all flee sins, fast from vices, and serve good works.

We ought to regard the whole period of our life as a kind of arena of virtues and strive with our whole mind toward the heavenly prize. But this must be fulfilled especially during the days of Lent [Note: Maurist edition: “must be fulfilled.”], which, devoted to abstinence and fasts, contribute as much to the virtue of the soul as they drive pleasure away from the body [Col. 0568C] [Note: Same edition: “they tear away.”]. That number of fasting is a lawful one, and one celebrated in holy examples [Col. 0568D] [Note: Same edition: “which is celebrated in these holy examples,” etc.]. Moses, about to receive the Law from God, spent forty days and nights without food or drink, and prepared himself by fasting to receive the Lord’s will. After forty days of fasting, Elijah was transferred from this world to the heights of heaven in a chariot of fire. Our Lord and Savior himself, fasting for forty days, triumphed over the temptations of the devil, so that he might approach the preaching of the Gospel already victorious [Col. 0569A]. Rightly, therefore, we too ought to observe by fasting this number of days, which we read was consecrated through such examples.

Let us therefore celebrate these days with every readiness of mind and joy, and prefer them to all banquets and bodily pleasures. For during these days above all, let us be inflamed to fulfill the Lord’s will, when the pleasure of the flesh is most extinguished through abstinence. The mind then hastens more purely toward the Lord and toward his future promises, when it is not made gross by any gluttony or by satiety of food and drink. Hence the Savior also said in the Gospel: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your bodies be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness and worldly cares, and that day come upon you suddenly [Col. 0569D] [Note: Same edition: “that sudden day”; “for like a snare it will come,” etc.]. For it will come upon the whole world like a snare, and no one will escape” (Luke XXI) [Col. 0569B].

There is also this great advantage during the days of Lent: while we abstain even from things that are permitted, we are more and more admonished to avoid what is forbidden. We who abstain from meat, which it is permitted to eat on other days; we who abstain from wine, which it is permitted to use moderately [Note: The same edition omits: “we who abstain from wine, which it is permitted to use moderately.”]—we who therefore avoid these things, which are sometimes permitted, should first of all flee sins, which are altogether [Note: Same edition: “never permitted.”] forbidden.

Therefore, if we wish to fast from foods, let us first of all fast from vices. For what does it profit to turn livid through hatred and envy [Col. 0570D] [Note: Same edition: “to grow pale from fasting.”]? What does it profit not to drink wine and to become drunk on the poison of anger? What does it profit to abstain from meats created for eating and to tear the members of our brothers apart with malicious slanders [Col. 0570A]? What does it profit if we abstain from things that are sometimes permitted and do things that are never permitted? For God honors and loves those who flee what is forbidden.

Thus, as I have said, let us fast from foods, so that we may fast much more from vices, so that we may be filled with the abundance of holy conduct [Note: Same edition: “of holy works.”], and so that in the future we may deserve to be satisfied by the recompense of those works, as we read in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew V).

We ought to choose that recompense more willingly: that the foods from which we abstain should be distributed by us to the poor and the weak, according to what is written: “Blessed are those who are content to hunger so that others may be refreshed.” A gift is very acceptable to God when the needy person is fed, when the naked person is clothed, when anger is not carried through and no occasion for anger is reserved, when evil is not repaid with evil [Col. 0570B].

Our fasts are then pleasing to God, if those who fast from necessity are refreshed by us. Then we shall deserve to hear that saying of the Lord: “Amen, I say to you, as long as you did it for one of these least ones, you did it for me” (Matthew XXV). O most kindly Lord, who, to tame human greed, says that what is given to even the least poor person is given to him!

May the Lord’s mercy grant you, brothers [Note: Same edition: “that you may serve him through fasting and almsgiving in good works,” etc.], to serve through fasting and almsgiving and good works, and may he himself bring you to true eternal life, he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XIX. On Lent V

[Col. 0569]

**ADMONITION**

The monks of Saint-Maur taught that this sermon belongs to the author of the preceding sermon, in the appendix of Saint Augustine’s sermons, page 182 of the Antwerp edition of 1700. They admit that it was attributed to Ambrose by earlier editors and that it contains some sayings of that Father; nevertheless, they assign it neither to him nor to Augustine, because they find the style of neither in it. Since, however, besides the similarity of expression, a connection with the preceding sermon is apparent, and the testimony of the Turin manuscript is added—in which it is entitled “Likewise, sermon VI on Lent”—as well as that of Laurentian manuscript X, Plut. XIV, page 275, the reason is sufficiently established why we too ascribe this sermon to Saint Maximus.

[Col. 0569C] **ARGUMENT.**—Saint Maximus considers the reason why Christ ordained fasting to have been that the glory of immortality, which the first Adam lost through intemperance, might be restored by the second Adam, Christ, through abstinence. He brings forward much concerning Adam, Christ, Eve, the Virgin Mary, and the desert.

If your affection remembers well, dearest brothers, on the preceding Sunday we preached that the Lord himself had consecrated holy Lent by abstaining, and that by taking no food at all throughout the course of so many days and nights he had made one solid body of fasting, which it is sacrilegious not to observe in its entirety [Note: Another copy: “the period.”] [Note: Laurentian manuscript X: “It is sacrilege not to observe it in its entirety.”]; to violate it in part is a sin. He did this for the sake of our salvation, so that he might teach a useful thing not only by words but also by examples, and so that we who run toward faith might advance toward abstinence [Col. 0570C].

But let us see what the reason was that the Savior imposed fasts and first fasted for himself, as a good physician of the human race. A good physician first tastes the potion that he is about to give to the sick person, so that he may demonstrate beforehand his mastery of his art [Note: The same Laurentian manuscript: “may demonstrate it in you himself.”], and so that the sick person, receiving the test of it, may be confident about the potion and still more confident about his recovery.

Next, let us consider in what place he arranged this period of fasting. The evangelist says that the Lord abstained for forty days and nights in the desert. I therefore judge that this is the reason for fasting: because the first Adam, placed in paradise, had lost the glory of immortality through the intemperance of his appetite, the second Adam, Christ, restored that same immortality through abstinence.

And because, by tasting in opposition to God’s command from the forbidden tree, he had fallen into the sin of death, now, by fasting in accordance with the Lord’s command, he would merit the righteousness of life. The Savior did this so that sins might be cleansed by the same paths through which they had been committed—that is, because the human being had sinned by eating, he should correct the fault by abstaining; or because, by feasting, he had known the woman, he should now despise her by fasting [Col. 0571A].

Adam knew Eve only when intemperance had brought it about [Note: Maximus means by this that Adam and Eve had intercourse after the sin, or after eating the forbidden fruit. On this matter compare Saint Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book IX, chapters 3 and 4, and Saint Thomas, *Summa theologiae* I, question 97, article 2, replies to objections 2 and 3.]. As long as unviolated moderation remained in them, unpolluted virginity also remained; and as long as they fasted from forbidden banquets, they likewise fasted from shameful sins. Hunger is the friend of virginity and the enemy of lust. Satiety, however, squanders chastity and nourishes enticement [Col. 0571C].

Therefore, as I have said, the Lord acts so that human beings may be freed from the very prejudices by which they had become subject to sin. For this reason, in every respect, according to the likeness of Adam, he would dissolve all human sins [Col. 0571B].

Adam was born from virgin earth, and Christ was born from the Virgin Mary. The maternal soil of the former had not yet been split by ploughshares; the maternal secret of the latter had never been violated by desire. Adam was formed by God’s hands from clay; Christ was formed in the womb by God’s Spirit. Both therefore arise from God the Father; both are born from a virgin mother; both, as the evangelist says, are sons of God. But Adam is God’s creature, whereas Christ is his substance.

The Lord therefore acts, as the second Adam, so that what the first human being lost by eating, the other may recover by fasting, and so that he may observe in the desert the law given in paradise through abstinence. For he knew that God’s command was not the law of one place but of the world.

It makes no difference to the divine command whether you observe it at home or in the field, since he who commanded is everywhere. In the desert, therefore, the Savior fulfills God’s command and saves Adam in the very place where Adam had been cast from possession of paradise [Col. 0571C].

Adam, expelled from paradise, endured the deserts of the uncultivated world. In the desert, therefore, salvation is first restored to the human race: where there are no banquets, where luxuries are absent, where—what is the cause of all evils—the woman is absent [Col. 0572A]. Adam could have remained steadfast amid those undisturbed delights of paradise if Eve had not been there with her devilish allurements [Note: Antwerp edition: “ambushes.”].

The desert is therefore suited to salvation, where Eve is not present to persuade and no woman is present to flatter. Behold a wondrous thing: in paradise the devil contends with Adam; in the desert the devil fights with Christ. Everywhere he lies in wait for humanity; everywhere he engages in combat. But where he finds a woman, he conquers; where he does not find a woman, he departs defeated.

God therefore gave us a pattern in this event: during the time of fasting, let us live as though in a desert, abstaining from banquets, pleasure, and woman, lest Eve be joined to us and overturn us from our chaste observance through seductive persuasion. For during Lent the fasting and chaste person is, in a certain sense, seen to live in the desert [Col. 0572B].

Indeed, the Christian’s body itself is a kind of desert when it is not filled with foods and not watered with drinks, but is neglected in the dryness and roughness of hunger. Our body, I say, is a desert when through abstinence its warmth withers, pallor is spread over it by thirst, and through contempt of worldly things the appearance of the whole person becomes neglected and squalid.

Then Christ the Lord dwells in the desert of our breast, when he finds our land squalid and dry with thirst, according to what the prophet David says: “As in a desert land, pathless and waterless, so I have appeared to you in the sanctuary” (Psalm LXII). We cannot otherwise appear to him as in a sanctuary [Note: Laurentian manuscript: “as in the Holy Spirit.”], unless the land of our body has become a desert of worldly pleasures [Note: The same manuscript: “of worldly sins”], pathless through devilish desires, and waterless through lustful enticements [Col. 0572C].

Then, dwelling in this desert of our body, the Savior overcomes all the devil’s intrigues there and makes it his secluded and secure dwelling, free from worldly thoughts, so that thereafter, established within ourselves as though in a wilderness, we may look only toward heaven and earth—that is, think of no one other than the Lord of the heavenly kingdom and the author of the earthly resurrection.

## SERMON XX. On Lent VI

[Col. 0571]

**ADMONITION**

I see that many manuscripts ascribe this sermon to Saint Maximus: namely, the three Vatican manuscripts 1268, 4951, and 6452; Casinensis 117, page 209 verso; Laurentianus 167, page 157 verso, formerly in the municipal library of the Florentine church; Vallicellanus XIX; the lectionary of the Church of Brescia, page 298; and manuscript CLIII, page 166, in the library of Saint Mark at Venice. The Remigian manuscript may be added to these; the monks of Saint-Maur, in the appendix of Saint Augustine’s sermons, page 180 of the Antwerp edition of 1700, mention it while remaining uncertain about the sermon’s author. Since, therefore, several other manuscripts of excellent reliability agree with the Turin manuscript, which asserts this sermon for Saint Maximus under number 29 with the title “Likewise, on Lent,” it ought rightly to be assigned to him. If anyone wishes to examine its manner of expression, he will find nothing inconsistent with Maximus; indeed, he will admire his genius in the excellent use of the sacred Scriptures. It exists in the Perugian manuscript without the author’s name.

[Col. 0573A] **ARGUMENT.**—The course of Lent is holy and salutary: through it the judge is brought to mercy, the sinner to repentance, and the righteous person to rest. The number forty has a mystical meaning.

We ought to receive these days of holy Lent, dearest brothers [Note: Vatican manuscript 2268: “dearest brothers, you ought,” etc.], with every reverence and not grow weary of the extended duration of this season. For the more numerous the days of fasting, the greater the occasion for healing [Note: Venetian manuscript 113, cited above, Perugianus, and Casinensis: “the more numerous the days are,” etc.; Vatican manuscript 4951: “the more numerous the days of fasting, the greater the occasions for healing.”]; the longer the course of abstinence [Note: Vatican manuscript 1268: “the more prolonged it is”], the more abundant the salvation of redemption [Note: Vatican manuscript 4951: “the more abundant is the salvation of redemption”]; the more severe the treatment of wounds, the more healthful the medicine for sins [Note: These words are absent from the cited Venetian manuscript.].

For God, who is the physician of our souls, established an appropriate period: one sufficient both for the righteous to pray and for sinners to plead [Note: The same Venetian manuscript reads, “sufficient for them to pray”; Vatican manuscripts 1268 and 6452, together with Casinensis 117, also add *sit* (“may be”).]—so that the former might seek rest and the latter implore forgiveness [Note: Vatican manuscripts 1268 and 6452, Vallicellanus XIX, Casinensis, and Perugianus II: “the former seeking rest, the latter beseeching pardon.”]. Lent is an appropriate period, for it is neither too short for entreating nor too long for earning favor [Note: Vatican manuscript 1268: “because it is neither short,” etc.]. Through forty days of fasting, any iniquity of the sinner can be entreated away [Note: Vatican manuscript 1268: “every iniquity of the sinner is erased, and however great the severity of judgment is mitigated.” Vatican manuscript 4951 omits “any.” Perugianus II: “every iniquity can be entreated away for sinners.”], and however great the severity of the judge can be softened [Col. 0573B].

The period may perhaps seem long and wearisome to the person who neither prays concerning his guilt nor hopes for pardon. For despair knows neither how to confess a crime nor how to hope for indulgence from the judge [Col. 0573D].

The course of Lent, therefore, is holy and salutary: through it the judge is brought to mercy, the sinner to repentance, and the righteous person to rest [Note: The Venetian manuscript omits “the judge” and reads: “through which the sinner is brought to mercy through repentance, and the righteous person to rest”; so also Vatican manuscript 4951 and Perugianus II. Vatican manuscript 6452 and Casinensis 117 read: “through which the sinner is brought to pardon through repentance,” etc.].

During these days the Godhead shows more mercy than usual, the offender makes entreaty [Note: The Navarrese manuscript: “and diligence pleads.” The Remigian manuscript: “and the righteous person’s prayer earns rest.” The same Venetian manuscript reads: “and the Godhead shows more mercy than usual to those who offend, and the righteous person’s prayer earns rest. For everything is open: heaven for pardon, the sinner for forgiveness, and the tongue for asking.” Vatican manuscript 1268 and Perugianus: “and heaven for pardon.” Vatican manuscript 6452: “and heaven for pardon, sin for confession, and tongues for asking”; Vatican manuscript 4951 and Casinensis 117 agree with this.], and righteousness earns its reward. Everything is open: heaven for granting pardon, the sinner for confessing, and the tongue for asking [Col. 0573C].

The number forty, I say, is salutary and mystical.
