For when human iniquity first possessed the face of the world [Note: Urbevetan manuscript: “when iniquity possessed the structure of the world”], God, over the course of that many days, covered the whole earth with a flood by rains poured down from heaven [Col. 0574A]. You see, therefore, that even at that time the mystery was arranged in a figure. For just as then, so now he shows mercy for forty days to purify the human being [Note: The Venetian manuscript: “For just as it then rained for forty days to cleanse the world, so now he shows mercy for forty days to purify the human being,” etc.].

Although that flood of the earlier time must also be called an act of mercy, by which iniquity was overwhelmed and righteousness preserved. It was done out of mercy so that the righteous might escape and the unjust might no longer sin [Note: The Venetian manuscript; Vatican manuscripts 4951 and 6452: “so that the righteous might escape and the unjust might no longer,” etc.].

Clearly, out of mercy we see that flood as having taken place through which, as through a kind of baptism [Note: Vatican manuscript 4951: “formerly, as through a certain…”], the face of the whole world was renewed: so that what had been sullied by the crime of ruined humanity might flourish in grace through the dwelling of blessed Noah; and what had then been a brothel of iniquity [Note: Two manuscripts read this; the printed editions have “a purgatory.” The Remigian, Laurentian, Venetian, and nearly all the other manuscripts cited up to this point read *pyraterium*, apparently “a pirate’s den” or “a place of piracy.”] might now become a dwelling place of holiness [Note: Venetian manuscript: “of piety” instead of “of holiness.”] [Col. 0574B].

That flood, I say, was a likeness of our baptism. For what happened then is now taking place: as the fountains of the waters overflow, vices are imperiled and righteousness alone reigns; sins are submerged in the depths, while holiness is carried near to heaven [Col. 0574C]. Then, as I have said, what is now taking place in the Church of Christ was taking place.

For just as Noah was borne by the water, with all the vices of sins submerged—the following transmitted word, *adulta*, is materially uncertain—so the Church is borne near heaven by the font of baptism, and when all the superstitions of idols have been erased, faith reigns on earth, proceeding from the Savior’s ark [Note: Venetian manuscript: “For just as Noah’s ark, after all the vices of sinners had been submerged, so…” Vatican manuscript 1268: “For just as Noah is saved in the ark after all the vices of sins have been submerged, so the Church, carried near to heaven in the font of baptism,” etc. Vatican manuscript 4951: “Therefore, just as Noah’s ark, so, after all the vices of sins have been submerged, the Church is carried near to heaven in the font of baptism, and after all the superstitions of idols have been erased,” etc. Vatican manuscript 6452: “Now, as I have said, this is what is taking place in the Church of Christ. Just as Noah’s ark, after all the vices of sins had been submerged, so the Church is carried near to heaven in the font of baptism,” etc.].

Holy, therefore, and consecrated is the season of Lent, which from its very beginning began to distinguish the righteous from the unrighteous and, as though by a judgment, to separate the good from the evil. We see the same thing taking place in this observance of our Lent. For during these forty days the evil are separated from the good: the lewd from the chaste, the intemperate who eats from the person who fasts [Note: In the Remigian manuscript: “the one who lunches”], the pagan from the Christian. The evil, I say, is separated from the good: the sinner from the righteous, the devil from the holy person, the heretic from the faithful [Col. 0575A].

When all these have been left behind, the Church alone, like that ark, is raised aloft with her virtues, as though in the shipwreck of the world. We too, although sinners, following the example of holy Noah, announce to you that the world’s destruction is to come; and we say that only those will escape the danger whom the threefold ark has enclosed within the bosom of religion [Note: Perugianus II: “will escape the dangers.”].

For the Church is a threefold ark, because it contains the mystery of the Trinity. When Scripture says that it was two-chambered and three-chambered, it clearly demonstrates that it is distinguished by the threefold grace of the Godhead.

Therefore, like Noah, we announce that the world’s shipwreck is to come and admonish all people to flee to this house. And just as Noah received his sons into the ark, so we too desire to receive our sons into this ark. Whoever wishes to dwell with us in this house is our son.

But someone may say that Noah’s preaching voice is nowhere described in the Scriptures. Listen, then: although Noah was silent in voice, he spoke through his work; his tongue was silent, but his construction cried out. For when he was undertaking a new work, one previously known to no one, he was warning everyone that new shelters were being prepared for new dangers. He therefore spoke through his work [Note: Urbevetan manuscript: “He therefore spoke through the work of the Lord, who said: ‘If you do not believe me, believe the works.’” The sermon ends here in the Urbevetan and Venetian manuscripts.], and he uttered that evangelical saying of the Lord: “If you do not believe me, believe the works” (John X). By believing, you will be able to escape the danger, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXI. On Lent VII

[Col. 0575]

**ADMONITION**

This sermon follows the preceding one in the Turin manuscript, where it is entitled “Likewise, sermon XXIX on Lent.” It is also noted in that manuscript that sermons 30, 31, 32, 33, and 34 have been lost.

The sermon we now present was relegated by the Benedictine monks of the congregation of Saint-Maur to the appendix to volume V of Saint Augustine’s works, under number 144. They judge that it should be attributed neither to Ambrose, nor to Jerome, nor to Augustine; nor do they indicate to whom it should ultimately be assigned. What moves us to ascribe it to Maximus is the authority of the Turin manuscript, which we mentioned shortly before. Moreover, it appears to have been composed by the same author by whom the fourth sermon *On Lent* was written. We have shown that the fourth sermon *On Lent* published by us ought to be assigned to Maximus.

[Col. 0575B] **ARGUMENT.**—By proposing examples of holy men, Saint Maximus urges the brothers to fast; but, he says, if fasts are to be complete, they must be nourished by the richness of mercy.

The venerable [Note: Maurist edition: “and medicinal”] and healing season of Lent is here with us, dearest ones, during which we ought to cure the wounds of our sins by fasting. Let us discuss, with examples added, how great a good fasting is and how much grace it confers [Note: Same edition: “Let us discuss briefly, adding examples, how great a good fasting is and how much grace it confers.”].

When Moses first fasted for forty days and nights, he deserved to receive the Lord’s law [Note: Same edition: “he deserved to receive it, by which he might rule the peoples.” “They obtained it,” i.e. the fasts obtained it.]. For the fasting of one man obtained what the satiety of the whole people had despaired of. Let us therefore consider how great the difference is between fasting and satiety [Note: Same edition adds: “between an empty belly and lungs burning with banquets. Moses, therefore, who…”].

Moses, who fasted, saw the Lord. The people, who ate and drank, fashioned idols (Exodus XXIV) [Col. 0575C].

But why should I speak of Moses and the Israelite multitude? Adam, that prince of the human race (Genesis III), remained in paradise as long as he fasted, keeping the Lord’s command [Note: Same edition omits “of the Lord.”]. But when he ate, he was expelled from paradise; and he who had been a virgin in God’s paradise, once expelled from paradise, knew his wife. For luxury is always joined to satiety [Note: Same edition: “lust.”].

Food expelled us from paradise; hunger, fasting, should lead us back. We have said what Saint Moses merited by fasting; next, let us consider everyone else [Note: Same edition: “We have said, therefore, etc.”]. The elements themselves served Saint Elijah while he was fasting. Indeed, for three years and six months he shut the heavens [Note: Same edition reads “closed them”: “at whose word,” etc.] (4 Kings I) [Col. 0576B]. At his voice even fire descended from above.

When Queen Jezebel wished to kill him and he, exhausted, was lying beneath a leafy tree in the desert, an angel was sent to him and said: “Take a little bread and water” (3 Kings XIX). See, dearest ones, how great God’s clemency is toward those who fast. It was not enough that the Lord had sent an angel to the fasting man to order him to take food [Note: Same edition: “to admonish him”]; he also commanded him to flee farther from his pursuer.

He said, therefore: “Take a little bread and water.” For he was about to continue for forty days through the desert as far as Mount Sinai. Could the Lord, who made heaven and earth and whose is every creature, not have sent a meal through an angel in the wilderness, just as he sent one to Daniel in the lions’ den through Habakkuk [Col. 0576C]? But God knew that his prophet could not otherwise overcome the devil who was tempting him unless, trained by fasting, he repelled the temptations of the enemy lying in wait.

That Daniel also (Daniel XIV), who knew future events, who was aware of the Lord’s coming, and who was a most explicit herald of Jerusalem’s destruction, was called “a man of desires” because he did not eat the bread of desire or drink the drink of longing, because he desired Christ more than banquets.

John too, the Lord’s forerunner [Col. 0577A], was nourished in the desert on locusts and wild honey; he was not fed on the flesh of animals or the delicacies of birds. He could certainly, living beside the Jordan, have procured for himself the delicacies of fish, but because he was going to preach repentance, he ought to have taught the strictness of fasting more through his example and deeds than through his voice [Note: Maurist edition: “but, since he was going to preach repentance, he ought to have taught the doctrine of strictness and fasting more by his example than by his voice.”].

In the Gospel also (Matthew XVII), when a man possessed by a demon had been brought before the Lord, whom the apostles had been unable to cure, they heard the Lord answer their question that this kind cannot be driven out except by prayers and fasts [Col. 0577B].

See, brothers, how great the power of fasting is, since fasts can do what the apostles could not. I omit the rest; but let each person consider how great the difference is between fasting and satiety, between an empty and a stuffed belly, between a flushed face and pale cheeks, between a fasting mouth and lips relaxed by gluttony, between the person oppressed by banquets and the person kept watchful by the thinness of hunger [Col. 0578A].

I do not mean weeks of fasting, nor doubled or multiplied fasts; let us merely pass even single days without excess in foods [Note: Maurist edition: “without the luxury of foods.”]. Let baths, wine, and meats cease—not because we judge God’s creation to be condemned—but because, although we have lived for ourselves throughout the entire year, we should at least live for the Lord for a few days [Col. 0577D].

But let our fasts, if they are to be complete and well supported [Note: Same edition: “complete and fortified”], be nourished by the richness of mercy. Let us give our bread to the hungry. Let us not suppose [Note: Same edition: “Do not suppose”] that fasts alone suffice to heal the wounds of sins unless they are restored by the medicine of almsgiving [Note: Same edition omits “in.”].

Let your fasting chastise you, but let it gladden another; and your hardships will be fruitful if they provide another with relief. Fast in such a way that, when another is eating, you may rejoice as though you had dined [Note: Same edition: “that you rejoice that you have dined.”]. For God loves a cheerful giver (1 Corinthians IX).

When the poor person eats from your goods, Christ dines, for he testifies that he hungers in the poor person.

**The end.**

## SERMON XXII. On Lent VIII

[Col. 0577]

**ADMONITION**

It is certainly regrettable that, because of the age of the manuscript from the monastery formerly called Appianum, the greater part of this sermon cannot in any way be read. We are therefore compelled to publish it diminished in many places and in many of its parts, exactly as we received it. There it is entitled: “Likewise, sermon VII on Lent.”

[Col. 0577B] **ARGUMENT.**—From what this incomplete sermon preserves, we know that Saint Maximus praised the fasts of Moses and Elijah, as well as that of Jesus Christ, in order to kindle the faithful to fasting.

Although, brothers, we ought to strive toward our heavenly homeland throughout the whole period of our life, nevertheless during these holy days of Lent, with all the strength we can [lacuna], we must make a special effort. This number of forty days, as we have often made known to your holiness, is mystical and consecrated in the sacred Scriptures. For you know, as we have often said, that Saint Moses, in order to deserve to receive from God the tablets written by his finger, abstained from every food and drink for the number of forty days and nights.

We also added that blessed Elijah, after forty days of uninterrupted fasting, was carried into heaven in a chariot of fire. Nor did we demonstrate this only through these examples, but also through others from the Old Law. Indeed, we added the example of our Lord and Savior himself [Col. 0578B], who, in order to prepare himself for the preaching of his Gospel, abstained from all food and drink for the number of forty days and nights; hence, concerning the devil’s temptations [Two folios are missing from the original; the following fragment then continues].

But what does it profit a person if the body fasts from food while the mind does not fast? What if you abstain from foods but do what is forbidden? If you persecute an orphan, if you persecute a widow, if [lacuna]

Then your fasts will be pleasing and acceptable to God, if you return what you hold that belongs to another; if you forgive the brother who has offended you; if you abstain from another man’s wife; if you give alms to the poor from what belongs to you [Fifteen lines are missing from the original]. May divine mercy therefore grant you this, so that through fasts, almsgiving, and holy works you may deserve to attain eternal life.

**The end.**

## SERMON XXIII. On Lent IX

[Col. 0577]

**ADMONITION**

Another sermon has come before us in which, as we have often said, traces of the antiquity of the manuscript formerly belonging to the abbey of Saint Dalmatius are recognizable. It is afflicted by very many lacunae. In the original its title is: “Likewise, sermon XII on Lent.”

[Col. 0577D] **ARGUMENT.**—The author discusses Moses’ fast and urges us to keep him before our eyes. For if he, righteous and holy, spent forty days fasting, much more must we sinners observe the same number of days in the Lenten fast.

The days of Holy Lent, whose beginning we are observing today, how our Lord and Redeemer consecrated them, and in what manner Moses and Elijah likewise sanctified them under the Old Testament, brothers, we have already told you many times. Indeed, we have previously explained to your holiness that, during those forty days in which Moses and Elijah kept holy fasts under the old law, they fasted, as it were, a Lent, and thereby prefigured, as a type, the holy fast that we begin today. [lacuna] For if Moses, the leader and savior of the Israelite people, who lived his life so blamelessly that he deserved to speak with the Lord face to face, as a friend ordinarily speaks with his friend, we, who are weighed down by the burden of innumerable sins and reduced to straits, not observe the holy fasts? If he, who was righteous and holy, fasted, why do we, who are unjust and sinners, refuse to do so? If he who was humble, gentle, and chaste … [lacuna] why do we, who are proud, angry, and incontinent, neglect to do so? Finally, if he who … [lacuna] God in all things and above all things with the whole devotion of his mind … [lacuna] why do we, who are always earthly-minded, toward the same [things] with the whole devotion of our mind … [lacuna] always think about these things, but never about God, during these holy days of Lent, through fasting … [lacuna] Yet … [lacuna] why did Moses observe the holy fast of forty days? “So that,” says the divine discourse, “he might deserve to receive the law of God.” (The original is missing three folios here; its conclusion is as follows.)

Therefore, by believing and steadfastly clinging to good works, we shall be able to overcome the danger that we see, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ. Explicit.

## SERMON XXIV. On Lent X

### NOTICE

These relics of a sermon of Saint Maximus have been drawn from the aforementioned monastery codex of Appiano; its title is: “Likewise, Sermon XII on Lent.”

### SUMMARY

Saint Maximus exhorts the faithful that, when they impose fasts upon themselves, they should first renounce their vices and fulfill the duties of holy compassion.

Since, brothers, today we are observing the beginning of the most sacred Lent, [we speak] about the Lenten fast with your holiness … [lacuna] (All this has entirely perished in the original; moreover, a complete folio is missing, and nothing remains except the following fragment.)

… therefore, the mind in particular must fast from evils. For whoever devoutly imposes holy fasts upon his body first renounces the vices to which he had previously and unhappily clung; he suppresses the fuel of wicked desire, breaks the attacks of Satan upon the mind, conquers blind lust, extinguishes the torches of greed, extends the power of love more widely through good works, and distributes the resources of his own patrimony as nourishment for the poor. And then he will certainly be able to obtain what he ardently desires, if everyone proceeds with a chaste body and a devout spirit through careful observance of holiness. These, brothers, are the means by which a person, even when regularly refreshed by food, obtains what he desires, while fasting he attains greater rewards of holiness.

Such fasting pleases Christ. He is not inflamed by the vain desire to obtain temporal glory or to amass a great patrimony; rather, he is always driven by a sincere religious devotion, and by a devout … [lacuna] When this has been accompanied by duties of complete piety, to the extent that one possesses the capacity, to that extent one will advance; and by acting in this way one will always and immediately have the Lord present and favorable. Fulfill, therefore, the duties of holy compassion, and you have sanctified your fasts. Clothe the naked; strive to receive the stranger in hospitality. (Ten lines are missing here.) Explicit.

## SERMON XXV. On Lent XI

### NOTICE

From Gennadius we learn that Saint Maximus preached a sermon “On the special fast of Lent, and that one must not jest during it.” We find not the same title, but one close to it, in two highly celebrated codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, 90 and 99; it is prefixed to the sermon that we are now about to publish. They read: “The following also: and one must not indulge in luxury during the time of fasting.” In the older codex, 90, it is Sermon 38; in the other, 99, Sermon 36. No one is unaware that the verb *luxuriare* expresses the same thing as “to devote oneself to delicacies and amusements.” The Turin codex, whose testimony we cite in confirmation, uses this inscription: “Likewise, Sermon X on Lent.” The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur included this sermon in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine, no. 146, Antwerp edition, 1700, p. 181. They remarked that it is attributed to Ambrose in a certain Remigian codex and in the editions, and that it seemed to them to have the character of Caesarius, since he wrote more vigorously against hunters. Yet although we have often professed our great respect for the judgment of very learned critics, the agreement of the outstanding codices and of Gennadius seems preferable to us in this matter. We are not, however, concerned by what they say about Caesarius, since it is sufficiently known and established that several writers dealt with the same subject.

### SUMMARY

Saint Maximus teaches that a fast is useless if it does not free the soul from perdition. He especially rebukes those who spend the whole day hunting, who beat their servants with whips and punish them, and who take greater care of their dogs than of their servants. He says that fasting is salutary and perfect if the soul is restrained from vices and if we distribute our meals among our brothers and the poor.

Last Sunday we said that the first duty of our faith is that, throughout the course of these forty days, we should fast with the greatest devotion, and that our salvation depends upon devoting ourselves to abstinence during this period. Therefore, dearest brothers, we must examine what the form of this fast is, so that we may recognize how great its usefulness is. For sometimes fasting is useless and empty: although it drains the stomach and all the inward parts of the nourishment of satiety, it is nevertheless not acceptable to God, because it does not at all empty the mind and its inmost feelings of the bond of iniquity.

What benefit is there in fasting from food and indulging in hunting; abstaining from nourishment and wandering into sins; chastising the body with hunger, refusing to drink strong wine, and yet proceeding drunk with thoughts of wickedness? Except that the well-fed or drunken person has an easier case than the person who is at once wicked and fasting. The former sometimes ceases to sin because sometimes, when drunk, he falls asleep; the latter does not cease to go astray, but, trained in evil, remains constantly alert even during his fasts. Hence such fasting is useless and empty: it weakens the limbs through hunger but does not free the soul from perdition. Concerning this fast the holy prophet speaks in the person of the Lord: “Why do you fast for me? I have not chosen such a fast, says the Lord.” (Isaiah 58.)

Do you think, brothers, that the person is fasting who, at first light, does not keep vigil at church, does not seek out the holy places of the blessed martyrs, but rises, gathers his little servants, arranges his nets, brings out the dogs, and scours the thickets and forests? He drags the little servants along with him—perhaps they would prefer to come to church—and through his pleasures he heaps up the sins of others, unaware that he will be held guilty both for his own offense and for the destruction of his servants. Thus he spends the whole day hunting, now raising an excessive outcry, now secretly ordering silence; happy if he has caught something, angry if he has lost what he did not possess. He pursues it with such zeal as though the fast had been imposed for the purpose of hunting.

In these indulgences, brothers, tell me: what worship of God can there be, what devotion of mind can belong to one who fasts for this reason—not to devote himself to God and to prayers, or to spend the whole day free and at leisure, but to practice his own pleasures? Even if you are such a person, brother, and return home in the evening, even if you eat when the sun is already declining, you may appear to have eaten late, but you have not therefore fasted for the Lord. Nor can you be seen, while pursuing your pleasure, to have done the will of the Lord. [Note: Maurin edition: “will.”]

For this is the will of the Lord: that we fast both from foods and from sins. We impose abstinence upon the body so that we may be more able to make the soul abstain from vices. An exhausted body is, as it were, a bridle for the luxuriant soul. Whoever fasts and sins appears to have gained the profit of food, not of salvation; by sparing his provisions he has filled his storeroom, not nourished his mind with virtues.

Some people, forgetful of the commandments, exercise their power of domination over their servants and subjects so harshly that during these days they do not hesitate to beat them with whips, afflict them with punishments, and impede them with fetters. If, when the time for eating comes, a servant has arrived somewhat late, they immediately strike him with blows and first satisfy themselves with the servant’s blood rather than with the pleasure of the banquet.

Such is the fasting of these people: they fast not to move the mercy of the Divinity, but to provoke the cries of a groaning household. Whoever wishes to earn mercy from God must himself be merciful first. For it is written: “With the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.” (Luke 6.)

And what is more grievous, a Christian master does not spare a Christian servant during these days, giving no consideration to the fact that, although the servant is one by social condition, by grace he is nevertheless a brother. For he likewise represents Christ and shares in the same sacraments; he uses the same God as Father that you do. Why should he not use you as a brother?

There are some who, returning from hunting, take greater care of their dogs than of their servants. They make the dogs recline or sleep beside them, supplying them with their daily food by their own presence, while they do not know whether their servants are dying of hunger. Worse still, unless food has been carefully prepared for the dogs, the servant is punished in the dog’s place.

You see sleek and fat dogs running about in the houses of certain people, while human beings walk about pale and stumbling. Will such people ever have pity on the poor, when they show no pity to their own household servants?

We must therefore know, brothers, that this fast is acceptable to God if we chastise our bodies not by abstinence alone, but also clothe our souls with humility. Let us be gentle toward our little servants, gracious toward strangers, merciful toward the poor. Let us rise at first light and hasten to church; let us give thanks to God; let us ask forgiveness for our sins, requesting pardon for past offenses and caution concerning future ones. Let either prayer or reading be our constant occupation throughout the day. Whoever does not know letters should seek out a holy man and feed upon his conversation.

Let no worldly activity hinder the activity of the Divinity. Let no game of tables distract the mind; let no pleasure in dogs obscure the senses; let no advantage in business corrupt the soul through greed. Whatever you do contrary to the commandment of God, even if you abstain from food, you are not fasting.

For this is salutary fasting: just as the body abstains from banquets, so the soul must be restrained from vices. This also, brothers, must not be omitted when speaking of the perfection of fasting: those who abstain and do not take a meal during this period should distribute their meals in advance among their brothers and the poor. [Note: Another edition: “let us distribute.”]

For this is true justice: if, while you are hungry, the poor person is filled with your food; and if, while fasting, you pray to the Lord for your sins, while he, having been filled on your behalf, intercedes for you. Both things will benefit you—your hunger and the beggars’ fullness.

But whoever abstains in such a way that he gives nothing from his meals to the poor appears to have made fasting his own profit and to have conducted a business by his thrift. He abstained for this purpose—not to please God, but so that he would not have to distribute more. And therefore a good deed of almsgiving together with fasting is, as it were, not a kind of business transaction, so that he may live so sparingly that his abstinence surpasses that of monks and clergy. The only difference is that they do this for profit, whereas we do it for salvation: they mortify their souls for the sake of monetary gain, while we chastise our bodies for the sake of the soul’s gain. Explicit.

## SERMON XXVI. On Lent XII

### NOTICE

Gennadius gives this sermon the title “On the general fast of the servants of God.” In the codices that assign it to the same Saint Maximus, it is entitled “On Fasting and on Lent.” These codices are the Sangallensis, no. 61; Holy Cross in Jerusalem 90, Sermon 47; likewise Holy Cross 99, Sermon 37; and the Turin codex, Sermon I, “On Lent.” Here Maximus discusses the proper manner and season of fasting, and commends not the fast that some choose for themselves according to their own judgment, but the fast that true believers—that is, the servants of God—perfectly carry out as instituted in the Church. This is the substance of the sermon.

Those, therefore, who entitled it “On Fasts and on Lent” agree with Gennadius. During Lent, those who fast do not indulge their own vanity but obey God, who commands through the Church, and, like servants, imitate Christ as their leader and teacher. The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur published it among the Ambrosian sermons as no. 23 in the cited Paris edition of 1690. They discussed a great deal about it, especially the designation *Quinquagesima*, “the fiftieth-day [fast],” which was not used before the ninth century. Trusting the testimony of Gennadius and of the manuscript copyists, we too have ascribed this sermon to the holy bishop of Turin.

### SUMMARY

Having rejected the Quinquagesimal fast, Saint Maximus writes that anyone who abolishes the divinely given law of the Lenten fast is guilty of obstinacy. He also rejects the fast of those who eat for seven days during Lent and fast for seven days. Hence he explains the origin of the number forty in the fast.

Some Christians, brothers, imagining that they are observing the commandments of the Divinity more religiously, neglecting the devotion of Lent, whose beginning we are observing today, falsely claim to keep the *Quinquagesima*, although this is commanded neither by the divine Scriptures nor handed down by the authority of our ancestors. They do this solely through presumption of mind, and, while they think they are acting more devoutly, they conduct themselves more superstitiously. Someone claims to observe the Quinquagesima who perhaps can scarcely complete the Quadragesima.

It is indeed good to fast at all times, but it is better to fast the Quadragesima with Christ. For the Lord consecrated this Lent for us by his fast. I said “fast,” not “fasts,” for the Lord’s fast was one: for forty continuous days and nights he took no food at all.

Therefore, whatever Christian does not complete the Lent consecrated by fasting will be held guilty of transgression and obstinacy, because by eating he himself abolishes the law divinely given for his salvation. You abolish the law when you do not keep the example of the Lord’s fast. What sort of Christian are you, when the Lord is fasting and you eat? [Note: The words “What sort of Christian … you eat?” are absent from the Vallicellian and Lyons codices.] What sort of Christian are you, when Christ is hungry and you refresh yourself? He endures hunger for your salvation, and you are afraid to fast for your sins?

Tell me, I ask you, those of you who eat during Lent: if you are not guilty in your consciences, why, while the whole people abstains, do you alone devour food contrary to the Lord’s command? Are you not ashamed when you go out in public, lest you encounter someone who is fasting? Or, when you go to church, do you not consider how you will offer the bishop the kiss of peace, lest the very spirit of your kiss condemn you?

If you do not consider these things, perhaps you are seriously mistaken. You must know that, during the days of Lent, when someone who has eaten encounters one who is fasting, the one who is fasting does not judge him favorably.

I say this because I hear that many faithful—more grievously still—abstain during alternate weeks of Lent and violate that consecrated number of days through gluttonous excess: that is, they eat throughout a seven-day period and fast for seven days.

To them I say: why do they defraud themselves by fasting during those seven days as well, when such fasting does them no good? For although someone abstains on specified days, although he does not eat the sweeter kinds of food, the fast of Lent is not credited to him if he does not fast for forty days.

It is shameful to say: old men and old women keep Lent; young men and young women do not. Let us therefore celebrate this most sacred season with every care. Let no day pass us without fasting; let not a single week pass without vigils. For the person who fasts and keeps vigil ascends to Easter and truly keeps Lent.

Just as fasting during the rest of the year is a reward, so not fasting during Lent is a sin. The former fasts are voluntary, the latter necessary; we are invited to the former, compelled to the latter; the former arise from personal choice, the latter from law.

But let us see where this most sacred number of forty days first originated. We read first in the Old Testament, in the time of Noah, when sinful iniquity had seized the entire human race, that, with the floodgates of heaven opened, rains poured down for that number of days, and that, through a certain mystery, when the world was flooded by the Quadragesima, what occurred was not so much a deluge as a baptism. It was plainly a baptism, through which iniquity was removed from sinners and Noah’s righteousness preserved.

So now also the Lord has given us Lent in the likeness of that time, so that, with the appointed number of days, the heavens being opened, the rain of heavenly mercy may shower upon us, and, when the flood has come, the rain of saving baptismal washing may enlighten us; and just as it happened then through the waves of water, so now the iniquity of sins may be extinguished in us and the righteousness of virtues preserved. The same pattern that operated under Noah is at work now: baptism is a deluge for the sinner and a consecration for the faithful.

Through the Lord’s washing, righteousness is saved and unrighteousness destroyed. We see this accomplished in one and the same apostle, Paul, who, before he was washed by spiritual commandments, was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and Saul. But when the rain of heavenly washing flowed over him, the blasphemer was destroyed, the persecutor was destroyed, and Saul too was destroyed; the apostle was brought to life, the righteous man was brought to life, and Paul was brought to life.

So completely did he lose his former self together with his deeds [Note: The cited codex 90 omits “his”] that, when his character changed, his name changed as well. Therefore, whoever in this devotion of Lent observes the Lord’s commandments will have the devil’s impiety destroyed in him, while apostolic grace will be preserved; and, in a sense succeeding himself, he dies insofar as he is a sinner [Note: The cited codex 90 reads “will be brought to life”], and is brought to life insofar as he is righteous.

Let us also see whether we can find this mystical number of Lent elsewhere in the Scriptures. We read that holy Moses (Exodus 16), in the wilderness, nourished the children of Israel with heavenly manna for a period of forty years. It is therefore a good number, one that always opens heaven; a good number, I say, through which Noah’s righteousness is saved and the children of Israel are nourished.

Let us therefore observe this number as well, so that the heavens may be opened to us, the rain of heavenly grace may shower upon us, and the manna of spiritual sacraments may refresh us. In imitation of our fathers, through this observance of Lent we are both justified and fed: we are justified by the washing and fed by the sacraments.

Someone may say that, when the children of Israel were filled with manna in the wilderness, they were certainly not fasting. I reply that at that time they did nothing but practice abstinence, and therefore deserved the grace of heavenly nourishment.

First, because the whole wilderness is a fast: the distress of solitude repels the desire for food. Then, in the wilderness, where could carefully prepared banquets come from? Where could precious wines come from? Where, during a period of forty years, could any kind of abundance come from?

We understand, therefore, that the children of Israel fasted, because we know that they lacked an abundance of food and took nourishment only when the Lord, who supplied it, was pleased. Indeed, the person fasts sufficiently who refreshes himself in accordance with Christ’s will.

The abstinence of the children of Israel in the wilderness pleased the Savior so greatly that even the intemperance of certain individuals among them was censured. Whoever, being more greedy, had gathered a double portion of food in the morning was struck by this punishment: he was found to have stored up not so much food for himself as worms. Since he had desired more than a moderate refreshment, he was driven, as though by certain goads of conscience, in the manner of worms. [Note: The Holy Cross codex 90 in Jerusalem reads “was reproved.”]

Therefore, brothers, let us too observe daily and moderate fasts during Lent. As though established in the wilderness, let us think of none of the world’s luxuries; let no sweetness of bodily desires trouble us. Let us be sober and chaste. Though our way of life is in the cities, let us possess the wilderness in our minds. If we live in abstinence in this way, we shall be refreshed by the nourishment of heavenly manna and shall not be pierced by the goads of any worms.

## SERMON XXVII. On Lent XIII

### NOTICE

The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, in the appendix to the final volume of the works of Saint Ambrose, sermon 33—which is sermon 17, “On the Fasts of Lent”—say that it is probable that this sermon belongs to Maximus, whose style, and in the Remigian codex even whose name, provide evidence of this. The Turin codex agrees with the Remigian codex praised by them; in it the following title is prefixed to the same sermon: “Likewise, Sermon XIII on Lent.” They suppose that it may have been delivered on Palm Sunday. For, as those monks conjecture, on that day in most churches it was customary to hand over the Creed to the candidates for baptism.

### SUMMARY

By observing fasts like Elijah and adding appropriate prayers, we should open the closed heaven and take up Peter’s key—that is, faith.

With the Divinity favorable, behold, we have now almost completed the prescribed fasts of Lent and fulfilled Christ the Lord’s commands through devout abstinence. It remains now that, just as his servants Moses and Elijah earned grace by observing this most sacred number, so we too may deserve it by keeping this same period, and that there may be a similar reward in the reception of the prize for those whose labor in observing the fast is similar.

When heaven had been closed because of human iniquities, and no abundance of rain fell from above upon earthly things, while everything languished under the squalor of a long drought and there was great famine for the entire human race—for since heaven gave no rain, the earth produced no food—holy Elijah opened heaven by his fasts and made the earth fruitful by his prayers. (2 Kings 18.) The former’s drought he turned into rain; the latter’s barrenness he transformed into fruitfulness. So great an abundance of rain watered the world through his prayers that dry things grew green again, the dead rose again, and the sick were healed.

Thus a kind of network of springs was infused into all things, so that, when purification had been effected by the rain, the vices of all creatures might be washed away, and through the benefit of that inundation the appearance of the whole world might rise renewed. [Note: The Lyons and Vallicellian codices read “of all”; all editions read “all the vices of creatures.”]

Therefore, by observing the same fasts as Elijah, let us also, with prayers, open for our candidates the heaven that is closed to them, so that the rain of saving baptism may enlighten them. [Note: The Vallicellian codex reads “may cleanse them—the rain.”]

For heaven is closed to them as long as the Holy Spirit has not yet come from heaven to give life to their hearts. They suffer a kind of drought because they have not yet been watered by the grace of baptism. They also labor under great hunger because, like starving people, they desire the heavenly sacraments.

Let us therefore open heaven for them, so that, when the spiritual rain comes from above, their earth may be filled by the irrigation of the washing, and, casting off the barrenness of sins, they may begin to produce the fruits of virtues. For the heavenly rain washes away the vices of sins, opens the way for the growth of righteousness, shakes off the dry dust of desire, gladdens the beneficial purity of chastity, buries the filthy dregs of greed, and nourishes the eternal generosity of mercy.

Just as, when Elijah’s rain came, the earth produced every kind of food, so, when Christ’s washing comes, the soul produces every kind of righteousness. And just as there the springs of rain watered the world so that the seeds of plants, already dead, might be brought to life, so the fountain of baptism waters the human race so that it may give life to hearts of souls that have been put to death.

The merit of those who observe these fasts is that, through their prayers, the world may be renewed or their brothers may be born again.

Heaven must therefore be opened for our candidates for baptism, since it is still closed to them. Heaven is closed to them because they do not yet perceive the mystery of the Trinity. With heaven closed to them, they do not know what takes place above heaven; nor can they know what the substance of the Son and the Father is unless they first transcend the elements of the world.

A person will then be able to behold the divine mysteries of the Trinity when, by his own power, he has had the heavens opened to him, just as blessed Stephen the martyr opened the heavens for himself through his martyrdom and saw the Savior standing at God’s right hand, as he himself said: “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.” (Acts 7.)

Therefore, whoever has the heavens closed must act so that they may be opened to him, in order that he may be able to behold Christ above the heavens. For as long as the heavens are closed to a person, he cannot see Christ reigning.

We must inquire, then, how the closed heavens are to be opened. I think that they cannot be opened in any other way unless we take up the keys of the apostle Peter, which he received by the Lord’s gift, as he himself said: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” (Matthew 16.)

Indeed, let us ask Peter himself, so that, like a good doorkeeper, he may open the royal heaven for us. Let us investigate more carefully what this key is. I would say that Peter’s key is Peter’s faith, through which he opened the heavens, entered the underworld securely, and walked upon the seas without fear.

Such is the power of apostolic faith that all the elements lie open to it: that is, the angelic gates are not closed to it, the gates of Tartarus cannot prevail against it, and the streams of the waters do not subside before it.

Let us see how this key itself, which we call faith, is constituted and how it has been solidified. I believe that it was forged through the work of twelve craftsmen. For holy faith was conceived in the Creed of the twelve apostles, who, like skilled artisans, came together and forged the key through their counsel.

I would call the Creed itself a certain key, through which the darknesses of the devil are unlocked so that the light of Christ may come; the sins closed within consciences are opened so that the manifest works of righteousness may shine forth.

Therefore, this key must be shown to our brothers, so that they too, like Peter’s disciples, may learn to unlock the underworld for themselves and open the heavens.

## SERMON XXVIII. On Lent XIV

### NOTICE

The Benedictine monks of Saint Maur observed, both from the style and from the Sangallensis codex, where Sermon 61 bears the name of the same Saint Maximus, that no one other than Maximus, bishop of Turin, was the author of this sermon. We add the codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, 90 no. 33 and 99 no. 22, and the Laurentianus X, Plut. XIV, p. 250, in which the title is: “On Fasts.”

### SUMMARY

Saint Maximus proves that fasting is, as it were, a second baptism. For just as the stains of sins are cleansed through spiritual washing and those who receive it are reborn to a new life, so abstinence wipes the conscience clean of the filth of sins and bestows an abundance of heavenly grace.

The holy Apostle bears witness concerning the prophets, saying: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you”; and he himself continues: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (1 Cor. 6). Therefore I also testify to you that these are the days of redemption—that is, a time in some sense of heavenly medicine—during which we shall be able to heal the stain of all our vices and all the wounds of our sins, if we faithfully entreat the physician of our souls [Col. 0587D] and by no means despise his precepts, as suitable recipients of what we have received.

For then the sick person finds a remedy for his illness if he observes the physician’s instructions with every care; but if he does one thing when another has been commanded, then, as the disease increases, it is not the physician but the transgressor who is at fault. Our physician, however, is the Lord Jesus Christ, who says: “I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deut. 32). For the Lord in a certain sense kills before he gives life. Through baptism he first kills in us murders, adulteries, crimes, and thefts, and thus gives us life as new men through the immortality of eternity. [Col. 0588C]

We therefore die to sins—that is, through the laver—but are regenerated to life through the Spirit, as the Apostle says: “For you have died to your offenses, and your life is hidden [Note: [Col. 0587D] Cod. 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem adds: “with Christ in the Lord.”] with Christ” (Col. 3). “For you have been buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. 6). We are killed, in a sense, when we cease to be what we were. For through a new kind of piety, death and life operate in one and the same person. We die to the desire for sins, while the order of virtues is given life. [Note: [Col. 0587D] Cod. 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “the desire for holy things is given life.” [Col. 0588D]] In one [Note: [Col. 0588D] Cod. 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem omits “for.”] and the same person the impious man and the adulterer are killed, so that the merciful and chaste man may be born again. Idolatry is destroyed, so that religion may be propagated. The fornicator and the drunkard are extinguished, so that the self-controlled and sober man may be brought forth. Thus the Lord mortifies in order to make alive; thus he kills in order to benefit; thus he strikes in order to correct. [Col. 0588D]

This, then, is all his severity toward his own people: that sins may be punished in them, while the soul is preserved; that detestable vices may be removed, while the best virtues are nourished. To such an extent do we see many people transformed by this godly killing of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0588D] Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read “occasion.”], advancing so greatly toward what is better, and becoming so completely the best instead of the worst, that when you see them you believe they have become different people, although you do not see their persons changed. For what we formerly were is so utterly killed, removed, and extinguished in us that we believe what we subsequently become has been born anew. Hence this second birth signifies that the end of the former life has already occurred. [Col. 0589A]

When he says, “I will strike and I will heal” (Acts 9), the Lord plainly strikes sinners with his precepts in order to heal them; he scourges them with commandments in order to correct them; he commands fasts, enjoins continence, threatens judgment, and applies medicine by instilling the grim fear of Gehenna [Note: [Col. 0589D] Cod. 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “by instilling it.”], so that, while we dread the future, we may correct the present.

Thus he made the Apostle Paul healthy by striking him. For when he was an impious persecutor and blasphemer, and indeed was hastening to Damascus to devastate the Churches, suddenly he struck him with the terror of heavenly brilliance, so that he might suffuse him with the light of evangelical splendor. He changed the blindness of his bodily eyes in order to illuminate the sight of his spiritual eyes. He terrified him with bodily weakness in order to save him through the devotion of faith [Note: [Col. 0589D] The same Cod. 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “to heal him.”].

When Paul therefore rose from the ground, [Col. 0589B] with his outward eyes he did not see men or the air, but with the eyes of his mind he saw Christ [Note: [Col. 0589D] The same Cod. 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem adds: “Thus he saw heaven from heaven.”] from heaven. Finally, the Lord’s striking benefited him so greatly that from a Jew he became a Christian, from a blasphemer an apostle, and from Saul he became Paul; and he so changed the old man together with his ways that he even changed his name. [Note: [Col. 0589D] The same codex adds “to him.”]

Since, then, we have such a physician, who heals by striking and gives life by mortifying, let us submit to him with complete patience for treatment, so that [Note: [Col. 0589D] This is found in the two cited codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.] whatever he perceives in us to be shameful, whatever is soiled by sins, whatever is foul with ulcers, he may cut into, amputate, and excise, so that, after all the wounds of the devil have been repaired, he may cause only what belongs to God to remain in us.

His first commandment is that during these forty days we devote ourselves to fasts, prayers, and vigils. Through fasts the wantonness of the body is chastised; through prayers the devout soul is nourished; through vigils the devil’s snares are driven away. Then, when this period has been completed through observance of these commandments, the soul, purified and wearied by so many observances, comes to baptism and is refreshed by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit; and whatever the heat of various illnesses had dried up within it is drenched with the dew of heavenly grace. [Col. 0589D] [Note: Cod. 10, Laurentian Plut. XIV: “so that, laying aside the corruption of the old man…”]

Thus, laying aside the corruption of the old man, it acquires the vigor of new youth. And, wondrously, in one and the same person holiness succeeds sins, righteousness succeeds iniquity, and infancy succeeds old age; and through this new kind of birth, the one who is reborn is another person, although he is the very one who sinned.

Thus Elijah, by continuing in a fast for forty days and nights, merited both to quench the long and excessive drought of the whole world with the dew of rain and to drench the thirsty earth with the abundance of heavenly rain [Note: [Col. 0590D] These words are supplied by the cited codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.] (3 Kings 9). We recognize that this was done as a figure of our own experience, so that we too, through the cycle of these forty days [Note: [Col. 0590D] The two cited codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “through the cycle,”] might merit the spiritual rain of baptism; so that the heavenly shower from above might pour upon the earth, long dry in our brothers throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0590D] The cited codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem add these words,] and the long drought of the Gentiles might be watered by the flood of the saving laver [Note: [Col. 0590D] Cod. 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem: “salutarily.”].

For whoever is not moistened by the grace of baptism suffers the drought and burning of his soul. Through the fast of these days and nights, holy Moses also merited to speak with God, to stand and remain in his presence, and to receive the precepts of the Law from his hand. Although the human condition kept him from the sight of God, the grace of fasting nevertheless brought him close to fellowship with the Divinity.

For this is God’s share in the virtues within us: that we fast frequently, since God himself always fasts. Whoever, therefore, he sees to possess more of his works is more familiar, intimate, and dear to him, as Scripture says: “And Moses spoke with God face to face, as one speaks with his friend” (Exod. 33).

Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ, who was about to receive the glory of the resurrection, dedicated his powers to a fast of forty days and nights, to show that the life of human beings is not bread, [Col. 0590C] [Note: The codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem add these words: “but the commandments.”] but the commandments. Through these forty days of fasting, therefore, God is reconciled, the heavens are opened, and the underworld is unlocked.

Let us too, therefore, dearest brothers, fast continually and devoutly during this period of time, so that the Lord may be propitiated toward us, the heavens may be opened for us, and the underworld may not [Note: [Col. 0590D] Cod. 10 Laurentianus: “may not prevail against us.”] prevail against us.

Explicit.

## SERMON XXIX. On the First Solemnity of Easter.

[Col. 0589]

### ADMONITION

There is great agreement among manuscripts and printed editions in recognizing Maximus as the author of this sermon. We shall give first place to the Taurinensis manuscript, in which it bears the following heading: “Also, Sermon I on Easter.” Two Casinenses, 104 and CXI, and the Ambrosianus agree, prefacing it with this inscription: “Monday of Easter. Sermon of blessed Maximus, bishop.” The Cistercian manuscript of Monte Amiata confirms the same with the title: “On the Sunday within the Octave of Easter,” and begins with these words: “Let us rejoice, dearest brothers, on the day of Christ’s resurrection,” etc. To these we add Cod. II of the Holy Cross Minor in the Laurentian Library, Vallicellian XIX, the Ratisponensis of St. Emmeram, and two Vatican codices, 1270 and 6451. All the editors also agree with Alcuin, p. 197: namely, Cumdius, vol. II, p. 1445; Combefisius, vol. V, p. 475; Gymnicus; Galesinius, Homily III on Easter; and Muratorius, vol. IV of the Anecdota. We have followed the reading of Galesinius.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0589D] The holy Doctor begins his sermon with the portents and wondrous signs that occurred at the Lord’s resurrection, which demonstrate it to have been a divine work shining forth with the greatest glory. He then gathers many arguments by which he shows that the day of Christ’s resurrection is to be celebrated with the greatest rejoicing.

We must rejoice, brothers, with continuous gladness on this day which the Lord has made, and at its festival we must give thanks with unceasing glory. [Note: [Col. 0591C] Cod. Vallicellian XIX has “continually” instead of “with unceasing.”] Nor, because night intervenes in the solemnity, has it cut short our joys; [Note: [Col. 0591C] The Ambrosianus reads: “For neither, because night intervenes in the solemnity, has it cut short our joys.”] [Note: [Col. 0591C] The Vatican codices 1270 and 6451 and the two Casinenses read: “nor, because darkness has divided the evening hours,” etc.] nor, because night has divided the evening hours, has the light of the resurrection abandoned our eternal hopes.

For yesterday and today there is for us one day—the very same day—[Note: [Col. 0591C] The Ambrosianus likewise has: “there is one and the same day.”] because, as the blessed Apostle says concerning the Savior, [Note: [Col. 0591D] The edition of Galesinius omits “he says.”] “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today” (Heb. 13). Therefore, if Jesus [Note: In the Ambrosianus, “Christ” is absent.] Christ is the same yesterday and today, he is always for us the same and one day, [Note: [Col. 0591D] Cod. Vallicellian XIX reads: “for if we live in him, we shall live in him and die in him.”] because “in him we live, and move” (Acts 17), and in him we do not die. We do not die, I say, because just as no darkness of sin has invaded the light of Christ, so no old age of time consumes those who live [Note: [Col. 0591D] The Ambrosianus, Cod. II of the Holy Cross Minor, and Vat. 6451 read: “so no old age of time consumes those who live in it,” etc.] in it.

Let us therefore rejoice in the day of Christ’s resurrection [Note: [Col. 0591D] The Ambrosianus reads, “Let us therefore rejoice in Christ.” Cod. II of the Holy Cross Minor reads, “Let us therefore rejoice in Christ. The day of resurrection is our common joy,” etc.]; for our joy is the common joy of all. The joy is plainly common, because when he rose, we all rose with him. [Col. 0591B] For he who was handed over to suffering for the sins of all came back to life for the salvation of all.

Our Savior, therefore, rose from the dead. The event is new and wondrous, but this assertion has truth in it. For, to say nothing of the prophets’ oracles, the ministry of the angels, the opened recesses of the tomb, and the Lord himself speaking, living, and eating with his disciples after the resurrection, and also Thomas touching the wounds of the nails even with his finger (John 20)—to pass over all these things nevertheless the impiety of the Jews confirms our faith. Their excessively cautious [Note: [Col. 0591D] The Vatican codices 1270 and 6451 have “cruelty” instead of “credulity.”] credulity is sufficient for our belief.

For the more carefully they guarded the tomb, the more clearly it is established that he rose [Note: [Col. 0591D] Vatican 1270 and the Casinenses: “that he rose.”]; and the more guards they stationed, the more witnesses they left [Note: [Col. 0591D] The Ambrosianus, Cod. II of the Holy Cross Minor, the two Vallicellian codices XIX and A 9, and Vat. 6451.]. For divine providence arranged this, so that not only angels and disciples, but also—and this is more significant—enemies might bear witness to the resurrection.

We therefore more willingly accept as witnesses those who observed him more carefully [Note: [Col. 0591D] Casin. 104 and Vallicellian XIX: “We therefore more willingly accept as witnesses those who guarded him more carefully.” Other codices, Casin. CXI and Vallicellian XIX: “guarded him.”]. For we believe that, with so many guards, he could come forth more quickly than perish [Note: [Col. 0592C] The Ambrosianus reads: “that the Lord could come forth from the tomb.”], and proceed lawfully from the tomb as Lord rather than be carried away through the fraud of the disciples. For impiety blocked the sepulcher with such care that no human hand could destroy it; only the power of the resurrection could open it.

Finally, the holy evangelist says (Matt. 20) [Note: [Col. 0592C] Cod. II of the Holy Cross Minor reads: “Finally the holy Evangelist says: Before the angel descended, there was a great …,” etc.] [Col. 0592A] that, as the angel descended, the earth was shaken by a great earthquake, the foundations of the tomb were moved, and the guards who had come to guard the dead man were struck with fear and became like dead men. Like dead men, I say: a perfectly fitting judgment, if, when the just man rises, the sinner dies; when the innocent comes back to life, his enemy is killed [Note: [Col. 0592C] The Ambrosianus and Vat. 6451: “his enemy is destroyed.”]. For this reason they could not even see the Lord as he came forth, [Note: [Col. 0592D] Cod. II of the Holy Cross Minor: “while their criminal minds…”] because terror had overwhelmed their criminal minds, and they were unable to endure the radiance of the brilliant resurrection.

The Pharisees therefore guarded the Lord more anxiously when he was dead than they had persecuted him when he was alive, since a greater concern pressed upon them. They understood that it would be easier for him to be scorned among those above than to be despised when returning from the underworld [Note: [Col. 0592D] Vatican 6451, Vallicellian A 9 and XIX, and the two Casinenses: “than for him, returning from the underworld, to be scorned.”]; and that, whereas he could then easily be killed while preaching, now, rising again, he could no longer be killed, as the Apostle says: “But, having risen, he no longer dies; death no longer rules over him” (Rom. 6).

They therefore guarded him anxiously in the tomb, especially because he had said that he would rise on the third day [Note: [Col. 0592D] Cod. Casinensis reads, “They therefore guarded him,” etc.; Vat. 1270 reads, “They guarded him.”]. They guarded him anxiously in the tomb because they had to fear him no longer as teacher but as judge—a judge, I say, not only of themselves but also of the cruel sentence by which they condemned their children and descendants to their crimes [Note: [Col. 0592D] The Ambrosianus: “by which they subjected their descendants to their crimes.” Thus Cod. II of the Holy Cross Minor, Vat. 1270, and Vallicellian A 9 have “by which”; the others agree with the Ambrosianus. The two Casinenses and Vat. 6451 read: “by which they condemned their descendants, their children,” etc.], saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

Cruel was the plight of the Jews under such a sentence: by their crime it condemns not only their children already alive, but also kills those not yet born. For how many did they summon by this utterance to consciousness of the crime who were not held by knowledge of the offense? Cruel, I say, was their impiety, because it called their descendants to guilt before it brought them [Note: [Col. 0592D] The Ambrosianus: “before it brought them forth into the light,” etc.] into the light, so that they would first come to sin before they came to life. Truly bloodstained were those parents who became murderers before they became parents, and who took as partners in their crimes those whom they did not know whether they could have as sharers in their blood.

It is therefore not surprising that they were so cruel toward the Savior, since they proved so cruel toward their own descendants.

Not without reason did holy David command that on this day there should be universal rejoicing and gladness, on which the joys of the whole world are celebrated. For everyone must rejoice, [Note: [Col. 0593D] Vatican 1270, 6451, and the two Casinenses, with which Vallicellian XIX agrees, though it has *quod* (“which”) instead of *quia* (“because”).] because it benefits everyone; all must exult, because it is saving for all. Therefore the joy must not be flattering or counterfeit.

Whoever rejoices in Christ’s resurrection should rejoice rather because he himself has risen in Christ. For in him our portion and our condition both underwent death and came back to life. And although [Note: [Col. 0593D] Cod. II of the Holy Cross Minor, Vat. 6351, and the two Casinenses: “And although our bodily dissolution still awaits us…”] the dissolution of our little body still awaits us, at that time we began already to live eternal life in Christ. Hence, although the approach of untimely death hastens our frailty, in the Savior we have learned to rise before we perish [Note: [Col. 0593D] The same codices, Cod. II of the Holy Cross Minor and Vallicellian A 9, read: “in the Savior, however, we learned,” etc. Vatican 6451 and the two Casinenses have “then.”]. For the human being who was destined to be rose in Christ before he received life in this world.

The Lord did not grant the grace of resurrection only to that generation in whose time he rose; he also provided this for the peoples who would follow, so that we might first be secure concerning the resurrection before being anxious about death, and might live with God in heaven before living among human beings on earth.

In the Savior we all rose, we all came back to life, and we all migrated to heavenly things. For in that human being, Christ, there is a portion of each of us—our flesh and blood [Note: [Col. 0593D] The same codices, Cod. II of the Holy Cross Minor, Vat. 1270, Vat. 6451, and the two Casinenses: “flesh, blood, and portion.”]. Therefore, where my portion reigns, I believe that I reign; where my blood rules, I feel that I rule; where my flesh is glorified, I recognize that I am glorious.

Although the sinner should not despair of this communion of grace [Note: [Col. 0593D] Cod. II of the Holy Cross Minor: “Although, therefore, the sinner…” Vatican and the Casinenses omit “nevertheless.”], because, even if sins forbid us, substance calls for us; even if our individual offenses exclude us, the communion of nature does not reject us [Col. 0593C], for [Note: [Col. 0593D] Thus Vat. 1270.] on account of the goodness of the Divinity, the Savior owes us a particular affection—namely, because just as our God is in him, so our blood is in him.

The Divinity therefore owes me mercy; relationship by kinship ought to display it. For the Lord is not so harsh [Col. 0594A] that he would forget the human being and not remember the one whom he himself bears: [Note: [Col. 0593D] The same Cod. II of the Holy Cross Minor reads: “so that, since he received the one whom he took up for my sake, he might seek me—not, I say,” etc. Thus Vatican 1270 and 6451 have: “so that, since he received the one whom he took up for my sake, he might seek me, not for the sake of the one whom he received.”] so that, having assumed [humanity] for my sake, he may seek me, not, I say, on account of the one whom he assumed. No, I say, the Lord is not so harsh that he would not love his own flesh, his own members, his own entrails.

The holy Apostle says: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church” (Eph. 5). Let us therefore despair of nothing concerning forgiveness, brothers, and fear nothing concerning hatred. We have the privilege of our own blood [Note: [Col. 0594D] Cod. Vallicellian: “We have the privilege of our own blood’s substance in Christ,” etc.]; for in Christ our flesh loves us, since we are his members and flesh, as the same blessed Apostle says: “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: this is a great mystery, but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Gen. 2; Eph. 5).

Let us therefore exult, brothers, as Scripture says, on this day of the Lord. Let us rejoice fully, because when we give thanks to the Lord with our vows, we are caring more for our own vows [Col. 0594B]. [Note: [Col. 0594D] Cod. II of the Holy Cross Minor: “What is this that the prophet says? ‘This is the day which…’” Cod. Casin. 104: “to the Lord.”]

For what does the prophet say? [Note: [Col. 0594D] The Vatican codices and the Casinenses have the masculine form: “This is the day which…”] “This is the day which the Lord has made.”

A good day indeed, which brought light to all—but not the light of this world [Note: [Col. 0594D] Vat. 1270: “the light of his resurrection,” etc. The same Cod. of the Holy Cross Minor adds “of his eternal [resurrection],” etc.; it then continues: “Let us therefore rejoice, brothers, as Scripture says, on this day of the Lord. For the light…” Vallicellian has: “but it shows the true light of eternal resurrection. For this light…”], but of eternal resurrection. For this light did not bring the darkness of night; it cut away the shadows of death.

A good day, I say, and better than that day on which the world first shone forth. The former was created for human beings to labor in; this one was made for rest. The former incurred death; this one escaped the fear of death. The former is shared by the good and the wicked; this one belongs to the righteous. The light of that day is buried in darkness [Note: [Col. 0594D] Vallicellian XIX reads “is driven away” instead of “is buried.”]; the splendor of this day illuminates even the graves. Finally, the dead do not see the light of that day, whereas the light of this day has shone even upon the dead [Col. 0594C], as the prophet says: “Light has dawned upon those who sat in the region and shadow of death” [Note: [Col. 0594D] Vatican 1270, the two Casinenses, and Vallicellian XIX have “upon them” instead of “upon those.”] (John 9).

Let us therefore rejoice on this day, which surrounds the living with light, gives life to the dead, and illuminates those who are to come, as the blessed Evangelist says: “The true light was present, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1).

## SERMON XXX. On the Second Solemnity of Easter.

[Col. 0593]

### ADMONITION

This sermon, placed by the Maurists in the appendix of the sermons of St. Augustine, no. 164, is read in Cod. Novariensis 2 under the name of St. Maximus. Anyone can clearly recognize from its style, phrases, and sentences that it must be attributed entirely to him. It is also found in the Taurinensis with the title: “Also, Sermon VI on Easter.” When we compared its text with the Maurist edition mentioned above, we found it to be especially similar to that edition.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0593C] When Christ the Lord, whom all the figures of the old covenant had promised, rose again, all creation applauds [Col. 0593D] and in a certain sense rouses us [Col. 0594C] to give thanks to our King and to enjoy his glory through the attainment of an innocent life.

[Col. 0594D] How the legal lamb, by whose immolation the ancient Hebrew [Col. 0595A] people cast off the yoke of Egyptian slavery, contained in its own figure, through manifold sacraments, the truer victim of the holy Church, was demonstrated most fully by the reality of events when Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed. He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth (Isa. 53; 1 Cor. 5).

This is the Lamb who, offered on the altar of the cross as a living sacrifice to God the Father for us, as a pleasing fragrance, opened for us the passage from the region and shadow of death to the promised land. This one, I say, who was both victim and priest, clearly revealing all the shadow of the ancient priesthood and sacrifice, brought the figures and riddles to an end. He inaugurated a new priesthood and a new sacrifice for the Church’s new people, so that new wine might be put into new wineskins. [Col. 0595B]

And if the grain of wheat, falling into the ground and dying, renewed all things so wondrously (Matt. 9; John 12), then how much more did he, rising again in himself with multiplied fruit, make all things fruitful, granting at this time a richer yield not only to the rational earth through spiritual growth but also to earthly seeds themselves.

Hence now, when the earth bursts into shoots, its whole face is more cheerful, and, adorned with varied fruits [Note: [Col. 0595D] The Maurist edition: “with the varied adornment of its fruits.”], it raises together with its risen Lord the whole of nature, which until now had seemed dead. Here the pleasing beauty of trees and grasses, through the diverse gift of shoots but with an equal gesture of joy, hastens to meet this singular solemnity.

What shall I say of the sky, whose face until now had been in a certain sense sorrowful, but at last is joyful? For a dense gloom of clouds had for some time covered it and troubled the whole expanse of this air. And behold, suddenly, as if justice were looking from heaven upon the earth, wondrous serenity smiles upon the world, and the hopes of heaven and earth converge in a single joy, so that with shared exultation they may receive Christ, God and human being, who came to bring the common peace of both and, destroying the dividing wall of the barrier, made the two one (Eph. 2).

Here, too, the source of all the stars—the solar splendor—wrinkles its face greatly and now at last cleanses it; and, like a conspicuous king wearing his crown on the day of his wedding and on the day of the joy of his heart, it bestows richer gifts of its light, with the other stars as its companions. The moon, which from the day of its rising has always been placed in a certain state of waning [Col. 0595D], prepares itself with full light for the joys of Easter.

And, to touch everything briefly, just as everything that subsists in the universe serves human rule by divine dispensation, so all things together bear one rejoicing over human salvation. Since, then, all creation displays its joy for humanity through such signs, it follows that the testimony of such joy must not cease among human beings themselves.

Christ’s resurrection was prefigured in the first-formed man, Adam. For just as Adam, rising after sleep, recognized Eve fashioned from his side (Gen. 9), so Christ, rising from death, built the Church from the wound in his side.

Noah also, a man of the soil, planted a vineyard, became drunk with wine, and lay uncovered in his tent. When he awoke from sleep and imposed a curse of perpetual servitude upon his son, who had not concealed his father’s shame, he signified Christ: he who made the Church a vineyard [Note: [Col. 0596D] The Maurist edition: “his own vineyard.”], became drunk through love of it from the cup of his passion, was stripped of the covering of the flesh he had assumed, and rose from the dead, as he himself says in the Song of Songs: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” (Song 5).

Jonah’s own expression of the Lord’s death and resurrection is also plainly declared by the Gospel narrative.

Since, therefore, brothers, all creation rejoices in our salvation through a certain service of love (Matt. 12), it is our task to draw from this something useful for our manner of life, lest the common joy of all lose its rightful claim in us, upon whom the whole matter is focused in its head.

First, then, like the sheep of the Lord’s pasture, roasted by the fire of love upon the altar of the heart, let us offer ourselves as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God (Rom. 12). Having already put to death, by the unleavened bread of continence, our members that are upon the earth—that is, fornication, impurity, and the other prisons of vice—let us shun them and establish for ourselves a place in the station of the virtues. Renouncing dead works, let us offer the best fruit as good soil, and, following the example of a good tree, let us bear fruit in every goodness and righteousness (Col. 3).

And so that the sun’s brightness may not be absent from our conduct, let our light shine before human beings, so that they may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5).

If we act in this way and the final day finds us so living, then the resurrection of our bodies itself will one day be our reward. When Christ, our life, appears, then we too shall appear with him in glory (Col. 3)—he who lives and reigns, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Explicit.

## SERMON XXXI. On the Third Solemnity of Easter.

[Col. 0595]

### ADMONITION

This sermon is inscribed under the name of St. Maximus in three very ancient codices. The first belongs to the abbey of St. Dalmatius, the second is from Appanni, and the third is the Taurinensis. I see no reason why I should think it necessary to depart from their testimony. The same sermon was miserably interpolated by some unknown Semi-Pelagian writer, whom the Benedictine monks rightly refute in their note on sermon 211 of the appendix to volume V of the works of St. Augustine. Some suspect that this writer was Faustus of Riez; whether rightly or otherwise, I do not concern myself with that question.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0595D] St. Maximus urges the brothers to exult because Christ, having pursued death all the way to the underworld, raised up his sacrificial victims. He showed his own flesh and bones so that no one might any longer doubt that he had risen [Col. 0596D]. Thomas, by touching him, confirmed the faith of all.

Let us exult in the Lord, brothers, at this present solemnity which the Lord has made: on it our Lord Jesus Christ, rich in the spoils of the underworld and triumphant over death, was restored to the world from the darkness of the tomb that Jewish impiety had sealed.

For when he pursued death all the way to the underworld, he deigned to call back to the eternal joys of paradise the human being whom he had created and redeemed. He pursued death all the way to the underworld, made that same death captive more gloriously in its own kingdom, and triumphed over it.

Then those dark recesses of the underworld were opened. Eternal night marveled at the heavenly light which it had never seen. [Note: [Col. 0597C] From the Taurinensis: “Thus he could say together with the prophet: ‘O death…’”]

Thus he himself could say together with the prophet: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O underworld” (Hos. 13). For the one whom it had supposed to be dead, it was compelled to release, and in those whom it already held it experienced the liberator. [Col. 0597B] Moreover, at this most sacred festival of the resurrection, when the Lord raised himself, many bodies of the saints were raised and came back to life, and they entered the holy city [Note: [Col. 0597C] The same Taurinensis adds: “Thus, on this most sacred festival of Christ’s resurrection…”].

For when the Savior rose today, he raised up his sacrificial victims; and whenever the festival of the resurrection is celebrated, we believe that the saints rise as well.

Our Savior therefore rose, in the mortal flesh that he had assumed from his virgin Mother [Note: [Col. 0598C] The same codex: “and which, for our salvation, had hung upon the wood, he restored from the tomb to new life.”], and which had hung upon the wood for our salvation. He restored to new life from the tomb that body which had been laid in the tomb.

The same body entered to his disciples through closed doors. You therefore have nothing further, Gentile: you see that Christ was crucified, yet have nothing by which to allege that he feared to die. Behold: the one whom you say feared to die, whom you see was crucified, came forth alive from the tomb by his own power—the tomb that impiety had wanted guarded.

Behold, he has the same flesh and the same bones. Hear him saying to his disciples: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24). He showed his flesh and bones so that no one might any longer doubt that the same one who died nailed to the wood had come forth alive from the tomb.

“Touch,” he was saying, “and see.” Touch my body with your hand, and see me and my wounds. Touch with your hand and see with faith, because there is in me both the reality of that body which hung upon the cross and was laid dead in the tomb, and the proper nature of divinity [Col. 0598B], by which I raised myself after being dead and laid in the tomb.
