And truly, when Thomas examined the wounds of the Lord’s body and touched the flesh, he recognized the true body in Christ. The blessed Apostle therefore saw and touched; what he then did benefited everyone. For when he directed his attention to Christ’s body, he confirmed the faith of all.

The same body, which was nailed to the wood for all, now reigns at the right hand of his Father in heaven. And truly it was fitting that the true substance of body and soul should exult eternally with Christ in heaven: it had trampled these earthly impediments underfoot and served him alone on earth [Col. 0598C].

Explicit.

## SERMON XXXII. On the Fourth Solemnity of Easter.

[Col. 0597]

### ADMONITION
481 From the Gospel of John, chapter 20, it is perfectly clear that Christ, risen from the dead, appeared a second time to the apostles and rebuked Thomas’s unbelief: “Do not be unbelieving, he said, but believing. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” Maximus must nevertheless be reconciled with this passage, since in this sermon he commends Thomas’s faith and devotion to Christ and says that he touched Christ’s wounds, not so that he himself might believe, but so that he might remove from everyone any doubt about Christ’s return to life. Yet if the Gospel narrative is carefully considered, Christ presented himself to Thomas as glorious and risen, making himself recognizable in two ways: first, when he stood before the apostles with the doors shut and announced peace to them; second, when he brought Thomas’s hand to his side and displayed his wounds for touching. Thus, as soon as Thomas saw Christ standing resurrected among the apostles, he believed him to be a living man; and, although he had no doubt about Christ’s divinity, he was given the testimony of his faith by the Savior himself, who said: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed.” Afterwards he touched and felt Christ’s limbs, and, adoring him, exclaimed: “My Lord and my God.”

Christ’s first appearance had already made Thomas faithful, and Maximus commends the readiness of his faith. But because he also touched the Redeemer’s wounds and burst forth with the words, “My Lord and my God,” Maximus says, Christ acted for our sake “so that he might touch what he saw; so that, if perhaps someone unbelieving should say that his eyes had then been deceived at the sight of Christ, he could not nevertheless say that his hands had been deceived when they touched him.” Gregory the Great has similar remarks about the doubting Thomas in Homily 26 on the Gospels:

> “This did not happen by chance, but by divine dispensation. For heavenly mercy acted wonderfully, so that, while that doubting disciple felt the wounds of the flesh in his master, he might heal in us the wounds of unbelief.”

Augustine likewise teaches in Tractate 121 that Thomas saw a man in Christ risen again and touched a man; but, his doubt concerning Christ’s bodily resurrection having been removed, he uttered the confession that he already held concerning Christ’s divinity:

> “Thomas was seeing and touching a man, yet he was confessing God, whom he neither saw nor touched; but through what he saw and touched, he already believed that without any doubt. Hence what follows: ‘Thomas answered and said to him: My Lord and my God.’”

To attribute this sermon to Saint Maximus, we are moved by three Subalpine codices: namely, those of Turin, Saint Dalmatius, and the monastery formerly at Appannia. In the Turin codex it is entitled: “Likewise, a sermon on Easter and on blessed Thomas, sermon VII.” The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur placed this sermon in the appendix of the sermons of Saint Augustine, second class, no. 161. When the text we had transcribed from the codex of Saint Dalmatius—where it appears under the title “Likewise, sermon X on Easter and on blessed Thomas”—is compared with the text printed in the said appendix of Saint Augustine’s sermons, no. 162, p. 203 of the Antwerp edition of 1700, its variation will become evident.

**ARGUMENT.**—[Col. 0597C] Thomas earnestly sought Christ by touch within Christ himself, not because he doubted his resurrection, but so that he might remove every suspicion from unbelievers. Our entire faith must be placed in the glory of the resurrection.

[Col. 0598C] Last Sunday we said that blessed Thomas, in order to strengthen the faith of all believers by his example, touched the limbs of the Lord’s body after the resurrection; and that, in order to dispel everyone’s uncertainty concerning the resurrection of Christ the Lord, he wished to examine the scars of his wounds. Yet the blessed apostle did not do this solely for his own sake; rather, what he examined with such exceptional care then benefited everyone. For when he exercised his concern in examining Christ’s entire body, he confirmed the faith of all. Who, indeed, could still doubt that the Savior had returned from the dead, when Thomas not only saw him but also touched his limbs and examined each of his wounds?

[Note: [Col. 0599D] Turin Codex: “Therefore, even if he is a man of only moderate faith, although a Christian of weak understanding.”]

Although, therefore, he may be a person of moderate faith, although he may be a Christian of weak understanding, no one will ever be able to compare his concern with Thomas’s inquiry. Indeed, after knowledge and conversion, no one would have dared to ask or inquire that he might examine Christ even more thoroughly by touch within Christ himself; nor would anyone have sought more curiously, in the very man whom he saw, the human body, or have proved by the indignity of his passion that resurrection which Christ himself had undergone for us.

Therefore blessed Thomas, being holy, faithful, and just, earnestly examined all these things—not because he doubted Christ’s resurrection, but so that he might remove every suspicion from everyone. For the sight of that body, which he had already known, was sufficient for the confirmation of his own faith. But Christ acted for our sake “so that he might touch what he saw; so that, if perhaps someone unbelieving should say that his eyes had then been deceived at the sight of Christ, he could not nevertheless say that his hands had been deceived when they touched him.” For in the manifestation of the resurrection someone may indeed doubt sight, but he cannot doubt touch. The truth itself is established by the testimony of touch: the Savior had returned from the dead.

If, therefore, Christ has risen, he who is our hope, who, brothers, would not believe that he too will rise? If we believe that he returned from the dead, why should we doubt that we too will rise, since the blessed Apostle says: “For if the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen” (1 Corinthians 15)? Since Christ has therefore risen, the dead too will be raised; since the Lord has risen, his servants will also live again. For he himself, as the same Apostle says, “is the firstborn from the dead.” He is indeed the firstborn from the dead because he alone first rose from the underworld; and with him we too trust that one day we shall rise.

[Note: [Col. 0600D] Turin Codex: “For we must place our entire faith in the glory of the resurrection that is to come and hope in the Lord more in the age to come. For the same blessed Apostle says: ‘If our hope is only in this life, we are more pitiable than all human beings.’ Explicit.”]

We must place our entire faith in the glory of the resurrection that is to come and hope in the Lord more in the life to come. The blessed Apostle therefore rightly said: “The hope that is seen is not hope” (Romans 8). Let us therefore hope in eternal life. *(A leaf is missing here.)*

The reader will find there the sermon as it appears in the appendix to volume 5 of the works of Saint Augustine.

Your Holiness remembers, brothers, the preceding treatise, in which we wrote that the apostle Saint Thomas, in order to confirm everyone’s faith, touched the limbs of the Lord’s body after the resurrection and, to dispel everyone’s uncertainty, wished to examine the scars of his wounds. For the blessed apostle did not do this solely for his own sake; rather, what he did for himself benefited everyone. When he exercised this concern, he confirmed the faith of all. Who could doubt from this that the Savior had returned from the dead, when the eye recognized his presence after the underworld, the hand touched him, and the finger examined him?

Although, therefore, a person may be of moderate faith, although a Christian may be of weak understanding, he could never have equaled his concern with Thomas’s inquiry. For after recognition, conversation, and speech, no one would ever have dared to ask to examine Christ by touch within Christ, and, in the very man whom he saw, to investigate the human body, and to believe his resurrection not so much through the glory of miracles as to prove it through the dishonor of his passion.

Thomas, therefore, being holy, faithful, and just, earnestly examined all these things—not because he himself doubted anything, but so that he might exclude every suspicion of unbelief. For, to establish his own faith, it had been enough for him to see the one whom he knew. But he acted for our sake, so that he might touch the one whom he saw; so that, if perhaps we should say that his eyes had been deceived, we could not say that his hands had been frustrated. For in the manifestation of the resurrection one may doubt sight, but touch cannot be doubted. It is established by the testimony of the truth itself that the Savior returned from the dead.

Who would not place his hope in Christ? Who would not place his faith in the Lord, so that he too may rise from the dead? The blessed Apostle says: “For if the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen” (1 Corinthians 15). Since Christ has risen, therefore the dead also will be raised; since the Lord has risen, his servants will also live again. For he himself is, as the Apostle says, “the firstborn from the dead.” Just as among those above he is the firstborn among many brothers, so also from the underworld he is the firstborn from the dead.

Someone is called firstborn because he is born first before the others who will follow. He brought forth a birth from the darkness of the underworld into the light of the resurrection. It must be called a birth when, through a certain transformation, the soul dies to the laws of Tartarus so that it may be reborn for the renewed use of the body. For the birth of the resurrection in the world above is a kind of death of the underworld. Hence death itself, in a certain sense, suffers death, when the multitude of the dead is taken away from it into life. For, as the blessed Apostle says: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (ibid.). And again: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (ibid.).

When death is swallowed up in victory, it is destroyed by a kind of self-annihilation through its own defeat. It suffers defeat when its power is emptied of all who rise. Let us consider what it means that he says death has been consumed in victory. Death was plainly consumed in its own victory when, by subjecting Christ to the laws of the underworld, it overwhelmed itself as it conquered him. For in possessing the one whom it thought it had overcome, it was itself defeated by him when he rose.

We must therefore place our entire faith in the glory of the resurrection and hope in the life to come in the Lord. For the blessed Apostle says: “The hope that is seen is not hope” (Romans 8). Let us therefore hope in the Lord for the life to come, which is solid and everlasting, so that we may be not more pitiable than all human beings but better than they, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIII. On the Same Solemnity of Easter V

[Col. 0599]

### NOTICE

This sermon, not previously published, has now been printed for the first time from the codex of the priory formerly at Appannia. In that codex it is entitled: “Likewise, sermon XII on Easter.” Its extreme brevity, though its statements are weighty, together with the antiquity and authority of the codex, and also its style, clearly demonstrates and establishes that it was written by Maximus.

485 **ARGUMENT.**—[Col. 0601A] Christ, risen again from the dead, presented himself as an image of our resurrection and renewal, which takes place in baptism. Let us rejoice so that we may rejoice with him when he reigns, provided that our life also does not depart from faith in him.

Today’s solemnity of Easter, consecrated to so great a mystery of our God, announces the power of the Lord’s resurrection through the angels, manifests it through the apostles, and multiplies everlasting blessings throughout the hearts of all believers. This, then, is the day that the Lord has made, as you have heard: higher than all others, brighter than everything, the day on which our Lord rose from the underworld after conquering death; the day on which he acquired for himself, as you see, a new people through the holy spirit of regeneration; the day on which he fills the minds of individuals with joy and exultation.

[Col. 0601B] This, then, is the day of Christ’s resurrection, which grants eternal life to the dead, the desired forgiveness to sinners, and unfading glory to the saints. Through the working of his power he raises us from earthly things, to which we cling, and always places us on high, where we ought to strive; he establishes the just in his mercy, strengthens those who are uncertain on the way of salvation, and condemns all unbelievers.

For this reason Christ the Lord rose today from the dead, so that he might provide an image of the future resurrection. And therefore, today, through the life-giving bath, the faithful people gladden the Church with the whiteness of their splendor, like the brightness of the resurrection to come.

[Col. 0602A] We ought therefore to give thanks to our Lord, since, while we celebrate the most glorious solemnity of holy Easter, we already behold an image of the resurrection that is to come. For when, at the future completion of this age, the whole human race must rise, it already rises now in baptism from sins to life. Then the people of God will be raised after sleep; then they will be raised after unbelief; then they will be freed from mortal condition, while now they are released from the blindness of ignorance in which they were held; then they will be reborn to eternity, while now they are born to salvation.

Let us therefore rejoice, brothers, and exult on this day, on which our rising Lord brought peace to all and bestowed the salvation desired by everyone. Let us rejoice because we see that he who had died for all has now risen. Let us exult because we believe that he now sits at the right hand of the Father. Let us therefore exult and rejoice at the Lord’s resurrection, so that we may rejoice with him when he reigns.

The merciful Lord himself will grant this, provided that true faith not only fortify our life, but that our life also not depart from faith in him. Let us therefore strive to show everyone an example of good conduct. Explicit.

## SERMON XXXIV. On the Same Solemnity of Easter VI

[Col. 0601]

### NOTICE

We have already seen that the sermons of Saint Maximus found in the Subalpine codices were transcribed from excellent archetypes; this can be recognized more fully from the sermon that we have published here as no. 34. In the codices mentioned above, it appears in the Appannian collection as *On Easter*, no. 6, and in the Turin collection as no. 7. Compare it with the sermon published by the Maurists in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine, no. 165, *On Easter* 7; if you wish to learn its variants, read that version at the end of this sermon.

**ARGUMENT.**—[Col. 0601C] The holy bishop proves that the glorious resurrection of Christ the Lord was prefigured in various figures of the Old Testament; “Let us,” he says, “be made like Christ in all things, so that we too may appear with him in glory.”

That notable and greatest sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection, which divine providence also willed to be prefigured in the venerable books of the Jews by various figures of events and by the divine oracles of the holy prophets, we celebrate today with devoted hearts. Why, from the very beginning of the world’s coming into being, and repeatedly elsewhere in the old law, did God wish this to be prefigured? For no other reason than to show that, throughout the successive ages of the passing world, the hope of all the saints continually tended toward that one who is the expectation of all nations.

[Col. 0601D] Although we have at other times made this known to Your Holiness from the books of the Hebrews, we are pleased to declare it to you again now. At the very beginning of the world’s creation, when Eve, that mother of all living beings, was brought forth from the rib of the sleeping Adam, the Church, mother of all believers, is shown as destined to be born from the side of Christ dying on the cross.

487 [Col. 0602C] In the act of Adam’s awakening, the resurrection of our Lord from the dead was prefigured. In Noah, however, who in the work of the ark and even in his own name signifies rest among the saints—for he was a farmer and had planted a vineyard, and, having become drunk from a cup of wine, was found naked in his dwelling—the figure of our Redeemer is represented. He was so intoxicated by the blood of his tearful passion that for a time he was stripped in the garment of his own body; but, awakening in his resurrection, he blessed those who, like Noah, venerate his passion as a mystery, while he gave a curse to those who mocked him.

That rod of Moses, too, which, when thrown upon the ground, was turned into a serpent but, when held by the tail, became a rod again, signified the power of divine majesty descending from heaven, which willed to become mortal for us; but, after the dispensation of the assumed flesh had been completed, it returned to the rod and withdrew to the right hand of the Father’s majesty.

Finally, concerning Jonah, whom the fish vomited out unharmed after swallowing him, we have the Lord’s own clear statement: “Just as he was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12).

These, brothers, are the holy Easter joys of this day. These are the solemn celebrations desired and proclaimed throughout the ages, which we ought always to venerate and imitate with our whole heart, as that most blessed apostle John says: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk just as he walked” (1 John 2:6).

Christ was crucified for us for a time; we ought daily both to take up the cross and to follow him. He tasted death for an hour; we must always put to death our members that are upon the earth. He rose from the dead; we must rise from vices, as the Apostle says: “Rise, you who sleep, and Christ will illumine you” (Ephesians 5).

[Col. 0603B] Let us therefore be made like him in all things, so that, when Christ our life appears, we too may appear with him in glory, and so forth. Explicit.

### From the Appendix to the Sermons of Saint Augustine

The sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection divine providence willed to be prefigured on several occasions through various figures of events and the oracles of the prophets, so that throughout all the ages of the passing world the hope of all the saints might tend toward that one alone who is the expectation of all nations.

Hence the fact that, at the very beginning of the world’s creation, Eve, the mother of all living beings, was brought forth from the rib of a sleeping man, shows that the Church, mother of believers, arose from the side of Christ dying on the cross; just as the act of the awakening Adam is a figure of the Lord rising from the dead. Therefore the Apostle says: “The first man was made into a living soul; the second man into a life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15).

Noah, who in the work of the ark and in his very name signifies God’s rest among the saints, represents the figure of our Redeemer especially in this respect: being a farmer, he planted a vineyard, and, made drunk by a cup of wine, was stripped in his tent. This event properly concerns the one who became so drunk from the cup of his passion that he was temporarily stripped of the covering of his body, and, immediately awakening in the resurrection, gave a blessing to those who venerate his passion as a mystery, but a fitting curse to those who mocked him.

Concerning this cup the Psalmist says: “How splendid is my intoxicating cup!” (Psalm 22); and in the Gospel the Lord says: “Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?” (John 18).

The rod of Moses, too, thrown upon the ground and changed into a serpent, returned again to a rod when it was held by the tail, because the power of divine majesty, descending from heaven to earth, willed to become mortal for us; but, after the dispensation of the assumed flesh had been completed, it withdrew to the seat at the Father’s right hand.

Concerning Jonah, whom the fish vomited out unharmed upon dry land after swallowing him, we have the Lord’s own clear statement: “Just as he was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12).

There are also very many other holy proclamations concerning this solemnity of solemnities. The very course of the seasons confirms all of them: it assigned the Easter term to the spring equinox, with only the full moon of the following first month awaited. Thus, just as the sun, advancing from the lower regions toward the heights, now first equals the nights in length, and the moon also appears completely full through its daily increase, so the sun of justice, rising from the underworld, would illuminate with its light the Church that had until then been established in darkness.

These are the holy Easter joys of this day, these are the solemn celebrations desired and proclaimed throughout all ages. It is right for us always to venerate them in our hearts and always to imitate them in action according to our ability, as the apostle John says: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk just as he walked.”

He was indeed crucified for us for a time; we ought daily to take up the cross and follow him. He tasted death for an hour; we must always put to death our members that are upon the earth—sexual immorality, impurity, and so forth. He rose from the dead; we are commanded to rise from vices, as the Apostle says: “Rise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will illumine you” (Ephesians 5).

If, then, we now crucify our flesh with its vices and desires, and, being planted together in the likeness of his death, are joined to him through the mortification of vices, when Christ our life appears, we too will appear with him in glory—he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXV. On the Same Solemnity of Easter VII

[Col. 0603]

### NOTICE

489 In the same codices indicated immediately above, this sermon 35 follows the preceding one *immediately* (*ἀμέσως*), under the title: “Likewise, sermon XIX on Easter.” But in the Appannian codex from which it was copied, a large part of it was lost when a leaf was removed. Those who know the method of writing used by Maximus will certainly judge that this sermon too must be attributed to him.

**ARGUMENT.**—On this day that the Lord has made, writes Saint Maximus, we ought to rejoice because, although through Adam’s transgression we had been vessels of wrath, on account of Christ’s resurrection we have become citizens of the saints.

Therefore, brothers, no mean price for our redemption was paid by the Lord our God. Therefore he who, for the salvation of mortal human beings whom he had created, hung nailed to the wood, who endured death, and who rested in the tomb, rose again from the underworld, returned to life.

Rejoice, therefore, and be glad, Zion, on this most holy celebration of so great a day. For while Christ our Lord returned from the underworld to the realms above, he caused us to pass from death to life. We who, because of the primordial fault of our origin, had long been condemned to death, have now been recalled to our former innocence through his death. We who had deserved the punishments of the underworld because of our sins have been recalled to the joys of eternal blessedness through his most precious death. We who had been vessels of wrath through Adam’s transgression have now, because of his resurrection, become citizens of the saints.

[Col. 0604D] Truly wonderful is the love of our Savior, who, in order to raise up the weak and call the fallen back to life, chose death for them. Who, then, would not exult in the great joy of this day? Who would not rejoice with continuous joy on this day that the Lord has made?

Heaven rejoices; the whole earth is glad, while it looks upon its Creator and Redeemer returning from the underworld after conquering death. The entire multitude of angels rejoices, because by the death of its eternal King all the wickedness of the devil’s deceit has been overcome. The sun itself also rejoices, and on this day shines with brighter rays upon those mournful shadows with which, when the Lord and Creator had died, it had covered the whole world.

Let us therefore rejoice, brothers, and be glad on this day that the Lord has made. Although we had been far away, we have been brought near; and in his resurrection we hope that the future resurrection of our own flesh will also one day take place.

We shall rightly rejoice, brothers … *(A leaf is missing; the sermon then concludes as follows:)*

Therefore, brothers, since we have been freed without any preceding merits from the fire of Tartarus and from the punishments of eternal death, let us order our life in such a way that we may be able to reach that eternal homeland which our Savior opened for us today, with his assistance, and so forth.

## SERMON XXXVI. On the Same Solemnity of Easter VIII

[Col. 0605]

### NOTICE

This sermon 36 was first brought out from the hiding place of a very ancient Ambrosian codex by the distinguished Muratori, who published it together with many others in volume 4 of the *Anecdota*. In the frequently mentioned Turin codex, the same sermon is attributed to Saint Maximus and is the first sermon on Easter.

Although in the Laurentian codices, 39 Plut. XVII and IV Plut. XXXIII, formerly belonging to the Minor Convent, it bears the name of Augustine, the Maurists placed it neither among Augustine’s sermons nor in the appendix. In Vatican Codex 1270, p. 10, it is assigned to Saint Ambrose. It is anonymous, however, in the Urbevetan codices, p. 121; the Vallicellian codex XXV, p. 8; codex A 9, p. 17; and codex 174, formerly belonging to the civic church of the Florentine metropolitan church, now in the Laurentian Library.

The fragment that we are publishing is found not only in the Laurentian codices but also in the aforementioned Vatican, Urbevetan, and Vallicellian codices. Yet the fragment contains no connection among the matters that are read in the sermon.

491

**ARGUMENT.**—[Col. 0605B] Our Maximus explains and wonderfully illuminates those passages of Scripture: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today”; “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” From these passages he proves Christ’s divinity, eternity, and unfailing light of heavenly glory. The Lord’s resurrection has made human beings participants in this light, and this is for us the cause of the greatest joy.

We ought to rejoice no less now, brothers, than we rejoiced yesterday. For although a dark night of the past has intervened between our joys, the same day of holiness remains. Although evening darkness has divided the times,

[Note: [Col. 0605C] Codices 2 and 4 of Plut. XXXIII, formerly of the Minor Saint-Crucian Library, etc.: “Nevertheless, it shines with perpetual light … he himself has enveloped us.” Codex 172, formerly belonging to the civic church of Florence, and Codex 39 Plut. XVII of the Laurentian Library read similarly. Vatican Codex 1270, however, reads: “Nevertheless, the blessedness will shine with perpetual light,” and so forth.]

nevertheless the Lord’s blessedness shines with perpetual light. For Christ, who illuminated us yesterday, also today himself surrounds us with warmth. As the blessed Apostle says: “Jesus Christ is himself yesterday and today”

[Note: [Col. 0605D] Vatican Codex 1270: “the same himself forever.”]

( Hebrews 13). He himself has become our day.

He himself has been begotten for us today, according to what David says in the person of God the Father: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2). “Today,” he says, “I have begotten you”—that is, not that he begot the Son on a particular day, but that he begot that Son as day and light.

Therefore, when Christ the only-begotten is begotten today,

[Note: [Col. 0605D] All the codices cited above agree: “Therefore, when Christ is begotten, he is generated today, so that you may understand that in the nativity of the Savior,” and so forth.]

it is understood that in the Savior’s birth not so much a human being was born as a light that shines for all and illuminates everyone.

Today is said because, like a present and unfailing light, he holds all the ages of the world in perpetual light and, because of the perpetuity of his radiance, seems to be one day.

[Note: [Col. 0605D] The same codex: “a light that embraces all the ages with continual and perpetual brightness.” The Urbevetan Codex: “continues.” Vatican Codex 1270: “continues.” Ambrosian Codex, in Muratori’s *Anecdota*, volume 4, p. 7: “a light that holds all the ages in perpetual light,” and so forth.]

Hence the holy prophet says: “A thousand years in your sight are like one day” (Psalm 89). Christ is plainly one day, because the eternity of divinity is one in him.

He is called “today” because neither things of ancient antiquity escape him nor things yet to come pass him by in ignorance.

[Note: [Col. 0605D] Codex 2 of the Minor Saint-Crucian Library: “nor do they escape the ancient antiquity.”]

Rather, like the most powerful light, he contains everything, knows everything, and, possessing all things as though they were present, holds them, because with him neither past things slip away nor future things remain hidden.

[Note: [Col. 0605D] Elsewhere Saint Maximus used this Psalmist’s passage to prove the eternal generation of the Word, or to show that Christ the Lord, even insofar as he is man, is the Son of God.]

At what time, then, was it said to the Son, “Today I have begotten you”? We must know that it was not when he was born from the Virgin Mary according to the flesh, nor when he proceeded according to his divinity from the mouth of God the Father, but at the time when he rose from the dead. For the Apostle Paul says: “Raising the Lord Jesus Christ, as it is written in the Psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Acts 13:32).

[Note: [Col. 0606D] Vallicellian Codex A 9 and the Urbevetan Codex: “Therefore he is rightly called ‘today’ when, from the foul night of the underworld, he shone forth to the realms above like a splendid light. He is rightly called ‘day,’ whose truth the dark faction of the Jews could not obscure,” and so forth. In the Vatican, Urbevetan, and Vallicellian codices, *fraus* (“deceit”) is read instead of *factio* (“faction”).]

Therefore he is rightly called “today” when, from the foul night of the underworld, he shone forth to the realms above like a splendid light. He is rightly called “day,” whose truth the dark activity of the Jews could not obscure.

[Note: [Col. 0606D] All the cited codices, together with the Ambrosian codex in Muratori: “unless it should receive the name.” The Ambrosian codex, in the same place: “unless today should receive the name,” and it restored both day and salvation. Vatican Codex 1270: “unless it should receive the name today.”]

Nor could anyone have received the light better than the one who gives both day and salvation to all the dead,

[Note: [Col. 0605D] Codex 39 cited above, and Codices 2 and 4 of the Minor Saint-Crucian Library: “who, having been released from the old age of humanity through death, [restores them] to the life of today,” and so forth. The Ambrosian Codex in Muratori: “who restored human beings, released from old age through death, to the life of today,” and so forth.]

who raised human beings, released by death from old age, into the presence of today’s life.

Let us therefore rejoice and exult on this day, on which the Lord brought us light, brought us salvation, and brought us peace. I say, peace: Christ, rising again, brought us peace, because, even when he was about to suffer, he did not deny peace to the betraying disciple,

[Col. 0607A]

or how does he embrace those who confess him, when he thus kissed the one who denied him?

[Note: [Col. 0607D] Ambrosian Codex in Muratori: “to the betraying disciple.”]

Do not suppose that the Lord gave that kiss to Judas Iscariot for any reason other than love,

[Note: [Col. 0607D] Thus the Ambrosian Codex; Muratori reports the variant reading: “given out of love, given out of affection”; and certainly he already knew that man.]

for he already knew that he would be a betrayer. He plainly knew that it was a pledge of love, and therefore he did not refuse it. For it is an act of compassion not to deny a final kiss to those who are perishing, and to offer a last consolation to those whom we have loved.

At the same time, through this very act of affection, he wished to correct him, so that, admonished by kindness, he would not abandon the one who loved him or betray the one who kissed him. Therefore that kiss was given, as it were, for Judas’s judgment: if he amended his ways, it would be a bond of peace for the disciple; if he betrayed him, it would be testimony of crime against the betrayer.

And so the Lord says: “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22).

Where is the subtlety of conspiracies? Where are the hidden deceits? Behold, every secret of wickedness is exposed, and the betrayer is denounced before he betrays: “With a kiss,” he says, “are you betraying the Son of Man?” That is: you inflict a wound by the pledge of love; through an act of affection you shed blood; you bring death by a sign of peace? What kind of love is this, I ask? You offer a kiss and threaten? These are not kisses, but poisons, through which a servant betrays his lord, a disciple his teacher, and the chosen one his author.

### Fragment from the Laurentian Codex
Let us therefore rejoice and exult on this day, dearest brothers, which we venerate with annual devotion. Just as it promises us life and glory in the future, so also from it arise, in the past, the causes and occasions of our salvation [Note: [Col. 0607D] Manuscripts 2 and 4 of Santa Croce Minor: “in the future … in the past, causes and occasions of our salvation arise.”]. And thus he who is worshiped so that he may have mercy has already shown mercy. Since we have been made and restored by him, let us now rejoice more fervently in his benefits, because the days on which we are freed are better than those on which, by being born, we are brought into the dangers of this life [Note: [Col. 0607D] Manuscript 174: “we are brought forth.”]. And therefore we read: “For your mercy is better than lives” (Psalm 62) [Note: [Col. 0607D] All the cited manuscripts agree.]. The days on which we are reborn to eternal life are therefore better than those on which we are brought forth into this temporal existence [Note: [Col. 0607D] Manuscript of Orvieto: “into these times.”]. For the gifts of grace are greater than those of nature. In this twofold work of our God, the former contains the reality of power, the latter that of gift. There power is contained; here, mercy [Col. 0607D]. By our first birth we enter earthly things [Col. 0608A]; by the second we are prepared for heavenly things [Note: [Col. 0607D] Manuscript 2 of Santa Croce Minor: “By our first earthly birth we enter [the world]; by the second we are prepared for heavenly things.”].

Just as the feasts of the present time admonish us, so also he who fought for the salvation of the world [Note: [Col. 0607D] The same manuscript 2 of Santa Croce Minor: “fought.”], as we read of the mighty Samson, killed more of his enemies when dead than he had slain when alive [Note: [Col. 0607D] The same manuscript 2 of Santa Croce Minor: “he killed more when dying.”]. Secular literary tradition also reports and relates that a certain man, throughout the practice and experience of combat [Note: [Col. 0607D] Manuscript 2 of Santa Croce Minor: “in the exercise and practice …,” etc.], possessed this kind of strength and power: whenever, through the assault of an adversary, he touched the earth, the friend and nourisher of his strength, he rose from the ground and prevailed ever more strongly against his opponent; thus the overthrow of the fallen became the occasion of triumph. For weakness somehow gave him strength, a fall the palm of victory, and ruin triumph.

I think that all this can be applied even more appropriately to that heavenly athlete who is said to have wrestled with Jacob [Note: [Col. 0607D] In Vatican manuscript 1270, the word “this” appears to have been erased.]; I judge that these things truly fit his person [Col. 0608B]. For when, in the arena of the world, he fought with the public enemy, he acted for this purpose, that he might rise more gloriously [Note: [Col. 0608D] Vatican manuscript 1270: “yielded for this purpose.”]; he fell so that he might lift everyone up. He overwhelmed the adversary when poured out, struck him down when prostrate, and, cast down, raised up fallen humanity [Col. 0608D] [Note: [Col. 0608D] The same manuscript 1270: “dug out” instead of “poured out.”]. When he submitted, he struck death [Note: [Col. 0608D] Thus manuscript 174, formerly belonging to the cathedral of Florence; manuscript 2 of Santa Croce Minor has instead: “and, while he succumbed, he struck his death.”]; when he rose again, he raised the dead.

This is that angel who wrestled with Jacob at night, as we have it in Genesis: “And behold, a man wrestled with him until morning. And when Jacob had prevailed, the angel said to him: ‘Let me go, for dawn has already risen.’ Jacob answered: ‘I will not let you go unless you bless me.’” Thus the angel blessed him and said to him: “If you were strong against God, how much more will you prevail against human beings”; and the angel touched the breadth of his thigh [Note: [Col. 0608D] Vatican manuscript 1270 has: “his.”], while he himself limped in his foot (Genesis 32) [Note: [Col. 0608D] Vatican manuscript 1270 adds: “The one who is defeated blesses, and the one who thought he had conquered limps. In Jacob, therefore …”].

What does this mean [Col. 0608C]? The one who is defeated blesses, and the one who thought he had conquered limps. In Jacob the Jewish people are recognized; in the angel, Christ. And so that we may know that the Lord was in that angel [Note: [Col. 0608D] Vatican manuscript 1270: “that God was in him.”], blessed Jacob himself says: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” (ibid. 31).

Jacob therefore prevailed as the angel yielded. [Note: [Col. 0608D] In the Orvieto manuscript, what follows is omitted up to the words “when they killed.”] The Jews prevailed for a time, and in Christ’s Passion [Note: [Col. 0608D] Manuscript 174 of the metropolitan church of Florence: “the Jews, raging.”], fleeing the day into the night [Note: [Col. 0608D] Vatican manuscript 1270: “fleeing the day into that night.”] and raging against him with every form of impiety [Note: [Col. 0608D] Thus manuscript 2 of Santa Croce Minor: “raging against him with impiety.”], they prevailed when they crucified him [Note: [Col. 0608D] Vatican manuscript 1270 has: “when they crucified him. Therefore, when Jacob had conquered …”]; they prevailed when they killed him.

Yet, although Jacob had conquered, he recognized that he could still be blessed by the victor, saying: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” [Col. 0608D].

What a mystery in this struggle! He is judged the weaker, yet he is found capable of bestowing a blessing [Col. 0609A]. Christ openly blessed his adversaries when he also prayed for those who were killing him, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23). The defeated one blessed: he who liberates the afflicted, intercedes for the guilty, and acquits the condemned [Note: [Col. 0609D] Manuscript of Valliscelliana: “The defeated one blesses: he who liberates the afflicted, intercedes for the guilty, and acquits the condemned; for even to his adversaries, if they repent, he grants redemption, though slain.”], for even if his adversaries repent, he grants them redemption by being slain [Note: [Col. 0609D] The Orvieto manuscript agrees with the text except in these words: “for even to his adversaries, if they repent,” etc.].

What, moreover, does it mean that after that struggle Jacob received a blessing and walked lame? For Scripture says: “And the angel touched the breadth of his thigh, and he limped in his foot.” The breadth of the thigh is the multitude of the Jewish race [Col. 0610A]. What, I ask, does it mean that he limped on one foot [Note: [Col. 0609D] Vatican manuscript 1270 reads: “What does it mean that he limps in his foot? This is what it means: from Jacob—that is, from the Jewish people—when Christ rose again, one part believed, another remained in unbelief, and limped away from the paths of righteousness”; the Orvieto manuscript agrees, but adds: “from the paths of righteousness and life.”]? It means that, when Christ rose again, some of Jacob—that is, of the Jewish people—believed, while others remained in unbelief and limped away from the paths of righteousness and life.

But when the angel himself says: “Let me go, for dawn has already risen,” this indicated that he could be conquered by death but could not be held by it [Note: [Col. 0610D] Manuscript 174 of the metropolitan church of Florence: “could be conquered by love.”]. After the night of the Passion had been driven away by light [Note: [Col. 0610D] Vatican manuscript 1270 and the Orvieto manuscript: “After that flight, he promises that the light of the Passion will immediately be restored by the dawn of the Resurrection,” etc.], he immediately promised that the dawn of the Resurrection would be restored.

He who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVII. On the same solemnity of Easter IX

[Col. 0609]

### NOTICE

This sermon first appeared in Muratorius’s *Anecdota*; until now it had been attributed to Saint Maximus only on the authority of a single Ambrosian manuscript. Besides the Turin manuscript, in which sermon 9 appears with the title “Also, on Easter,” we now produce two Casinensian manuscripts, namely 302, page 7 verso, and 305, page 71. They bear both the name of the holy bishop of Turin and the inscription “On Easter.” Although such testimony is sufficient for Saint Maximus to be regarded as its author, anyone who still doubts should attend to its diction and to similar passages written elsewhere by the same author. It is nowhere attributed either to Ambrose or to Augustine.

### SUMMARY

[Col. 0609B] Maximus shows from Christ’s resurrection that he possessed a twofold nature and a twofold operation. For Christ suffered and died as man; he rose again as God. In the flesh he assumed, the whole divinity shone forth, and with his divinity the flesh joined its own weakness.

The venerable Passion of our Saviour and his wondrous return from the lower world attest that he possessed both a divine and a human substance. For who can doubt that he is ineffably both the Son of God and the son of man, since he was able both to suffer death and, death having been conquered, to raise himself from the tomb? For, having assumed flesh from a virgin, lest we should suffer any cloudiness in the faith of our confession, throughout the whole time of his preaching he revealed himself as true God and showed himself also perfect man. He wept, grieving with our sorrow; yet, powerful by his own strength and moved with pity at the blindness of the blind, he made eyes for one whose eyes had not yet been formed and restored lost eyes to another. Sailing with his disciples, he slept in the stern with the sleep of a man; yet by the command of his conscious majesty he immediately restrained the swelling masses of waves and the threatening winds in calm tranquillity [Col. 0609C]. As a man of temporal life he very often declared that he would die; but as eternal God, by sending the life-giving spirit back into bodies, he commanded the dead to return to the light. Insults of blasphemers were hurled at him as Son of Man; but, so that ignorant mortality might learn the manifest truth that it ought to believe, the Father addressed him from heaven as though he were his only Son. If, then, O man, you believe the indignities which Christ endured, why do you not all the more believe the wonders which he performed? Thus flesh is incomprehensibly in God, and God in flesh [Col. 0609D]: neither does the Passion separate God from man, nor does God, through man, become subject to human sufferings [Col. 0610B].

That the Son of God, who is proclaimed, was born of a virgin ought not to make human weakness waver amid so great a miracle, because we confess that God, for whom every work is possible, is the author of this astonishing novelty. For blessed David, with the Holy Spirit revealing it, sings the omnipotence of God: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 134). He, therefore, who did what he willed, caused a virgin to conceive; he who did all that he willed did what would aid us [Note: [Col. 0610D] Casinensian manuscript 305: “aid all of us.”].

“God did,” he says, “all that he willed.” Did he will to form the world from nothing? The accomplishment of so great a work was in the Word. Did he will to fashion man from dust? Power did not fail so great a will. Did he will, amid the very beginnings of heaven and earth, to bring forth woman from the body of a man? At once Eve, the mother of the human race, came forth from Adam’s side [Col. 0610C]. Did he will that human beings of both sexes should be born from man and woman? The fertility he commanded filled the world by the law of his will. Did he will, as has been said, that a virgin should give birth? Then Christ came forth from Mary under the overshadowing of his majesty, with no injury to virgin modesty.

This is why the philosophers of the nations and the wise of the world, who want everything to rest upon their own disputation, fail to attain the fullness of truth: while they examine divine things with an earthly mind, they become foolish in their wisdom. They labour to maintain the doctrine that, puffed up with proud spirit because they cannot discern it, God either does not will rightly or cannot act. As the Apostle says, “Claiming to be wise, they became foolish”; and again, “they became vain in their thoughts” (Romans 1) [Col. 0610D]. For who is so mad as to seek human seed in that virginal conception, where a heavenly mystery is being enacted [Col. 0611A]? What folly is it to object the common condition of mortal birth to that manner of birth, when through the work of the Almighty a saving offspring flowered forth for the life of those who perish?

But perhaps the faithless man comes forward and says: “No one was ever born in this way.” Truly, no one was, because no flesh but this was united with God [Note: [Col. 0611D] Casinensian manuscript 305: “but this one.”]. Why do you doubt in vain? He who alone granted human beings to be born through marriage alone willed to come forth from a virgin. Christ was wondrously born, and in faithless obstinacy you do not believe God? What would you do if he had been conceived by the common law? Thus it is empty and foolish argument to say that none was born in this way: the sacrament of the fruitful virgin, which is the unique work of God, could have no example before it and left none after it. Therefore you too, brother, if you wisely inquire into things beyond comprehension, believe to be divine what you perceive to be unique.

Finally, when the Saviour asked his disciples who he was and whom people believed him to be, the most blessed Peter then answered in consecrated speech: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16). Behold, brothers: the tongue of a man speaks what the heart of a man did not know. The Apostle speaks what he learned not by reflection but knew by revelation. For how could an earthly and mortal man know the secret of an incomprehensible generation unless the Father himself, whose true Son he was, had revealed it from heaven [Col. 0611B]? As the Lord says to him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed it to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid.). In calling the Redeemer of all the Son of the living God, the chief of the Apostles confesses in him the substance of paternal divinity; in pronouncing him the Christ, he asserts that the reality of maternal flesh is present in him. Thus the most blessed Peter truly embraced both natures in Christ under a single designation: tasting the sacrament of the ineffable mystery in the briefest utterance, he neither divided what was twofold nor confused what was united.

So that we might more fully perceive that in the Saviour neither man is to be separated from God nor God from man, Paul the Apostle, the glorious teacher of faith, says: “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Galatians 3). Certainly the Son of God was not made in order to be sent; rather, for that to which he was sent, he was made Son of Man. For, with the divine property of his nature preserved, he assumed human nature into himself—not by a confusion, but by a perfect union. “God sent his Son,” he says: he sent one not subject to the condition of a creature, but in harmony with him by natural love. For the Lord himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). Those, therefore, who are one cannot be separated from one another by unequal power [Col. 0611D]. The Father sent his own Son, not one departing from him, but one coming to us for our salvation [Col. 0612A]. The Son of God came, moreover, not merely to execute the command of the Father who sent him, but to accomplish their common will. The Son of God came not by passing from place to place, but by fulfilling, in the place where he willed, the office of his purpose. Indeed, though God is always everywhere and embraces all things in the bosom of his majesty, he is nevertheless believed to go or come there where he deigns to reveal himself. Unless you follow this, brother, by faith, you will grasp it by no reasoning of worldly sense. For mortal intelligence is as far from understanding God’s works as mortality can be distant from eternity. But the best reasoning for a human being is, in matters which the mind cannot comprehend, to yield to the author of the mind [Col. 0612B].

Therefore, dearest brothers, we must know that it was not his condition but his will that gave us the Lord’s birth and Passion. The necessity of our case required that Christ the Lord should not decline the modesty of a woman’s womb, should endure the infancy made filthy by swaddling-clothes, should await childhood’s growth by gradual delays, should pass through youth’s strengthening with time, and should bear, with every patience, the injuries and slaughter of Jewish fury. Nor was it a superfluous or empty act of will that the Son of God should die on earth, in the human condition, through the shameful material of so many sufferings—he who lived with paternal divinity in the heavenly kingdom—unless the necessity of our remedy had required him to be born [Col. 0612B]. What has God to do with flesh? What has the immaculate one to do with the cross? What has the eternal one to do with death? For words and wounds, and all the reproaches inflicted by the Passion, would indeed have to be counted against the Son of God [Col. 0612C], unless the resurrection which immediately followed had healed all that he suffered. Who, then, is so foolish as to presume by criticism to disparage the fact that Christ was crucified, he who was made more wonderful by his Passion through so many powers and such great miracles? Who would dare reproach him with a three-day burial, whose eternity abiding with the eternal Father is proclaimed [Col. 0612C–D]? Rather, who would not marvel with complete astonishment that he deigned to descend to the lower world, he who by his own power was able to return to life after death and did not hesitate to ascend to heaven after the lower world [Note: [Col. 0612D] Casinensian manuscript: “there is no doubt that he ascended.”]? Therefore, brothers, this one thing is salutary for us: measuring ourselves, and restraining the narrowness of our heart when it overreaches itself, let us follow in all things the will of the true God, whose power we acknowledge, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVIII. On the same solemnity of Easter X

[Col. 0611]

### NOTICE

This sermon, also published by Muratorius, is preserved in three old manuscripts: the Turin manuscript, with the title “Also, on Easter, sermon X”; Casinensian 305, page 13; and the manuscript of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg. In the latter two manuscripts the name of Saint Maximus is explicitly given, but in Vatican manuscript 6451, page 21, the same sermon is copied without the author’s name.

### SUMMARY

[Col. 0611D] In Christ’s resurrection, says Saint Maximus, one and the same joy was produced for the heavenly and earthly realms. The Lord gave every day, but he made this day especially Paschal: shining perpetually with light, it admits no alternation of darkness. Let us hold fast to the mysteries through the faith of true belief.

At the Paschal feast, dearest brothers, when we exult that our Lord has returned from the lower world [Col. 0613A], we share a common joy with heaven. The angels rejoice because the enemy of their Lord and the tyrant of the heavenly realm has been destroyed by the power of the lawful and eternal King [Note: [Col. 0613D] Vatican manuscript: “cast down.”]. We mortals and weak human beings also glory in the gift of the Lord’s Passion, because, having at last laid aside the devil’s servitude, we have been restored to the freedom of life and to the right bestowed by the Father’s mercy.

This is surely what the blessed David says: “Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult” (Psalm 15). One and the same joy has indeed been produced for the heavenly and earthly realms [Note: [Col. 0613D] The same Vatican manuscript adds: “because one and the same is he who conquered on earth and reigns in heaven. ‘This is the day,’ he says, ‘that the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.’ Thus he says, ‘This is the day that the Lord has made,’ as though there were some day that the Lord had not made.”], because one and the same Lord conquered on earth and reigns in heaven. Again the same prophet says: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.” Does he say, “This is the day that the Lord has made,” as though there were some day that God had not made [Col. 0613B]?

The Lord indeed gave every day, but he made this day especially: shining perpetually with light, it admits no alternation of darkness. This is the day that, dispersing the cloud of sins, shines with the light of eternity upon the eyes of mortals darkened by blindness. This is the day on which the Lord of life, by the new and unexpected brilliance of his majesty, terrified hell, raging with death and dreadful with the horror of grim death [Note: [Col. 0613D] The same Vatican manuscript: “raging with death and dreadful with the horror of grim death.”].

“Let us exult,” says the prophetic word, “and rejoice in it.” It would not have been enough to say “Let us exult” unless he had added “and let us rejoice.” Prophetic foreknowledge therefore repeats for us the words of spiritual joy [Col. 0614A], so that, once the sorrow of most bitter death has been wiped away [Note: [Col. 0613D] The same Vatican manuscript: “so that, once every horror of death has been wiped away,” etc.], it may proclaim both the joy of the present life and that of the future. Let us therefore exult now as the redeemed, so that afterward we may be able to rejoice as the saved. Let us exult while the Lord rises again, so that we may rejoice when he reigns.

And rightly shall we rejoice, brothers, if the gifts of true faith [Note: [Col. 0614D] Casinensian manuscript: “if the gifts of true faith.”], the redemption already bestowed, and the Resurrection promised make us glad. Why, dearest brothers, should we doubt the benefits of the Almighty? Was he made man from a woman without purpose, who was incomprehensibly born God from God? Did he wish to wail in a cradle for no reason, who makes earth and heaven tremble with the terrifying thunder of his voice? Did he weep uselessly, who from birth endowed a blind man with new eyes through the power of his spittle? Was he served vinegar and fed gall without purpose, who could provide streams from the rock for the thirsty in the wilderness and manna from heaven for the hungry [Col. 0614B]? Was his Passion vain, when in the hiddenness of his unfathomable will [Note: [Col. 0614D] Vatican and Casinensian manuscripts: “in the secret of his inscrutable will”] he descended from heaven to the cross?

Therefore, since we cannot comprehend the mysteries of his Passion with the dullness of our carnal understanding [Col. 0614B–0615A], let us hold fast through the faith of true belief to what it has bestowed. We shall hold and receive the gifts of his glory if faith fortifies our life and life does not depart from faith. And just as he wished to please us by dying, so let us eagerly strive not to displease him by living; by his favor, he who lives with the Father, etc.

## SERMON XXXIX. On the same solemnity of Easter XI

[Col. 0613]

### NOTICE

We confidently assign the authorship of this sermon, which the copyist of Vatican manuscript 6451, page 21, did not know, supported by the authority of three manuscripts. These are the Ambrosian manuscript, from which Muratorius drew and published it in volume 4 of the *Anecdota*, sermon 6; the Turin manuscript, with the heading “Also, on Easter, sermon XI”; and Casinensian 105, page 13. Before Muratorius’s edition, Cumdius had already published it in volume 1 of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, page 164.

### SUMMARY

[Col. 0613C] We above all should rejoice when Christ rises again: through the sacrament of the new mystery, sins are removed, heaven is given, and paradise is restored. The faith of the thief hanging on the cross benefited the entire human race. Christ’s prayer for those who killed him is explained.

Most justly, brothers, the world exults today in universal joy, since, when Christ returns from the dead, the hope of resurrection has arisen for all mortals everywhere. It is necessary that, when the Lord of creatures triumphs, the creature enlightened by him should rejoice.

Heaven therefore rejoices because it sees the earth, long stained by sins, cleansed by the blood of its Lord. The multitude of the heavenly host rejoices because, through the conflict of its King, the entire army of the hostile prince has been defeated. The sun also rejoices because the mournful darkness it had endured at the Lord’s death it restrains with brighter rays and perpetual rejoicing [Note: [Col. 0614D] Vatican manuscript: “repays.”].

Amid all this, dearest brothers, it is especially fitting that we should exult [Col. 0614C], since for our sake the Only-Begotten of God, himself God, put on human flesh, so that through human flesh he might come to the cross, through the cross undergo death, and through death strip hell of its spoils.

Should we not rejoice, since through the sacrament of the new mystery [Note: [Col. 0614D] Vatican and Casinensian manuscripts: “through the sacrament of the new mystery”] sins are taken away, heaven is given, and paradise is restored? Finally, to the thief hanging then on the cross, whose faith was shaken neither by his own punishment nor by Christ’s, the Lord himself said: “Amen, I say to you: Today you will be with me in paradise.” For the thief had said: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23) [Note: [Col. 0614D] Vatican and Casinensian manuscripts: “when you come.”].

How marvelous this faith is, brothers! The thief, who did not deserve to possess the present life, amid his torments took up the hope of eternity and believed that it could be granted to him by the Crucified One [Note: [Col. 0614D] Vatican manuscript: “when the Crucified One was with him.”]. And how justly the faithful thief received the gift of so great a promise! He confessed Christ’s kingdom when even the apostles were troubled [Note: [Col. 0614D] The same Vatican manuscript omits “also.”]. Thus one confession’s merit absolved all the thief’s former crimes, and whatever he had committed over a long lifetime he wiped away in a very brief utterance [Col. 0615A].

Nor did the blood of his own robbery condemn him before God [Note: [Col. 0615D] The same Vatican manuscript: “Nor did the blood of his robbery condemn him before God …”], because he believed Christ’s blood to be a kingdom, not a punishment. There can be no doubt, dearest brothers, that this deed benefited the entire human race [Note: [Col. 0615D] The same Vatican manuscript: “the entire human race.”]. For who would despair of God’s grace, once the thief had been acquitted, provided that the prayers of those who plead are accompanied by the thief’s faith?

We also have another magnificent example of the Lord’s mercy [Note: [Col. 0615D] The same Vatican manuscript: “We have another most magnificent example of the Lord’s mercy …”], by which, laying aside every fear of deadly despair, we may trust in the ineffable indulgence of our Redeemer. When Christ, condemned by the impious, hung upon the cross [Note: [Col. 0615D] The same Vatican manuscript: “When Christ, condemned by the impious, hung upon the cross”], and Jewish fury mocked the Crucified One, the merciful advocate prayed to the Almighty Father for those who were killing him, even amid his wounds [Col. 0615B], saying: “Father, forgive them; they do not know what they are doing” (ibid.) [Note: [Col. 0615D] The same Vatican manuscript: “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing; and although judgment was in his hand,” etc.]. Although judgment over the living and the dead was in his hands, he nevertheless asked pardon for sinners [Note: [Col. 0616D] Vatican manuscript: “nevertheless prayed pardon for sinners”; but, as I judge, for this reason: that he might unmistakably show both that he forgave them their most heinous offense and that they would not be condemned by his Father, whom he himself spared. The Casinensian manuscript agrees.]. In my view, he did this so that he might unmistakably show both that he forgave them their most heinous offense and that they would not be condemned by his Father, whom he himself spared, provided that, rejecting their unbelief, they should come to the name of Christ. The Casinensian manuscript agrees throughout.

For who could truly doubt the effectiveness of a petition when a good man asks a good God for a remedy for the wretched? “They do not know,” he says, “what they are doing.” The Jews knew that they were shedding the blood of an innocent man, but they did not know that the sins of all were being wiped away by that blood. They knew that they were punishing Christ with the most bitter punishment of the cross, but they did not know that the Son of God was triumphing through the cross. They knew [Note: [Col. 0616D] Casinensian manuscript: “For they knew”] that he would die, but they did not know that he would return from the dead.

Thus the Lord rightly said: “They do not know what they are doing.” The Jews certainly did not know how great a ministry of mercy their impiety was serving [Note: [Col. 0616D] Vatican manuscript omits “their.”]. But the Lord, conscious of his own power and compassionate toward human error, knowing fully what joys would follow those punishments and how great they would be, mercifully absolved the crime of those who crucified him even amid his torments. He willed that his death should become the life of those who were killed, and that the condemnation should become that of those who killed him [Col. 0616B].

When he returned from the lower world, he sought out his apostles in such a way as to show that he possessed both the power of divinity and the reality of flesh. Therefore, dearest brothers, let us rejoice as Christ rises from the dead, and let us believe that he recalled his flesh from the lower world, so that we may be found worthy to share in apostolic grace and the desirable fellowship of the Lord’s Resurrection [Note: [Col. 0616D] The same Vatican manuscript: “He who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”].

## SERMON XL. On the same solemnity of Easter XII

[Col. 0615]

### NOTICE

As is known, Muratorius was the first to bring this very elegant sermon on Easter to light from the Ambrosian manuscript, together with the other sermons of Saint Maximus. The testimony of the Turin manuscript strengthens the authority of that manuscript and editor; there it is inscribed: “Also, on Easter, sermon XII.” The very sequence of the sermons shows that this one proceeds from the same source.

### SUMMARY

[Col. 0615C] Saint Maximus explains how the Son of God must always be believed to be new; then he discusses the mystery of his humility, the cross, the name, and the Resurrection.

The annual feast of the Lord’s Resurrection returns for us, dearest brothers, but wherever the truth of religion is present, the sacrament is always new for the faithful, as the blessed Paul says: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5). And rightly the Son of God must always be believed to be new, since he experiences none of the old age of passing time. He is new, brothers, in whom there is no change of age and who has never known himself to be anything other than what he was born. For God proceeding from God, just as his birth has no temporal beginning, so his life cannot have an end, as the glorious patriarch David says to him: “But you are always the same, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 101) [Col. 0615D].

Nor is only Christ the man, who has been made one with God, always new; he is also always seen to renew the failing old age of the human race through the refreshing of spiritual waters and the nourishment of heavenly faith [Col. 0616C], as the blessed David says: “Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 103). The face of the human earth is indeed renewed when, laying aside the ancient captivity of the devil, it puts on the new freedom of the new King. For the Lord himself says: “If the Son makes you free, you will truly be free” (John 7). And rightly, dearest brothers, only the Son of God frees sinners, because he alone is free from sin, as he himself deigned to testify concerning himself through the prophet, saying: “I became a man without help, free among the dead” (Psalm 87) [Col. 0616D].

He appears to have become “without help” when Jewish fury was given power to rage against him. Yet he was free among the dead because, among all mortals, he alone had no cause for dying. Therefore death, conquered by him, could not hold him when he rose again.

Consider, dearest brothers, how great is the mystery in Christ’s humility: although he is eternal from eternity and Lord of the universe, he nevertheless completes the freedom of his servants. He rejoices in insults, exults in reproaches [Col. 0617A], and all his triumph is in the cross. By an astonishing kind of remedy, he overcomes the devil by suffering and gives life to humanity by dying.

The Only-Begotten of God undertook all these things for us in mercy, endured them in power, and completed them in humility. The prophet Isaiah speaks of this humility: “As a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth in his humility” (Isaiah 53).

How beautiful, brothers, and how fitting to the truth is this comparison! For just as a lamb, when it is shorn, does not know how to protest against its shearer, so Christ, when he was crucified, did not resist the one wounding him. The lamb is stripped and silent; Christ is killed and silent. The silence of the lamb, once its woolly fleece has been shorn, clothes humanity. Christ’s silence spreads the garments of eternal salvation over all believers.

“He did not open his mouth in his humility”—that is, Christ’s silence amid insults and curses [Col. 0617B] was not misery but strength. With this purpose the Son of God came to redeem the world: to triumph over the proud by humility, the insolent by gentleness, and those who cursed by silence. Thus it is also written: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2).

Nor should we doubt this, brothers, because he knew how to answer cursing with true blessing. He could not be shaken by earthly curses, since he had come to bestow blessings from heaven. And rightly Christ, the Wisdom of God, returned no curses to those who cursed him, because every curse repelled by patience returns to its author.

Christ therefore humbled himself, as the Apostle says, “becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2) [Col. 0617C]. He humbled himself to the death of the cross so that the heavenly sacrifice would not succumb to some cheap and ordinary death [Col. 0618A], but, as mediator between God and humanity, would accomplish the mystery of the death he had assumed in the space between heaven and earth [Col. 0618A].

The author of life therefore died under the condition of our nature, so that we might live through the privilege of his. The Son of God was crucified, not so that the cross would defile Christ, but so that, through the mystery of Christ, the cross would become the emblem of our victory. Finally, all of us who rejoice in confessing Christ glory in the sign of the cross. No one can be counted among the Christian soldiery unless, with faithful hand, he has raised the standard of the Crucified One.

Because of this death on the cross, as it is written, the Almighty exalted his Christ and gave him the name above every name. He gave him the name above every name when he handed over the heavenly realms to his rule and power and subjected the world and the lower regions to him, as the Saviour himself says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 11) [Col. 0618B].

Does he not appear to hold dominion over all things? Does he not possess the highest authority, before whom, as it is written, every creature bends the knee, trembles, and looks up at him as he commands?

Finally, some nations, although they disagree among themselves because of differences in manner of life and variety of languages, nevertheless agree with one voice in confessing Christ. Even though some of them, through a most evil persuasion, differ from us concerning his divinity, they nevertheless confess with us both that he suffered and that he returned from the dead.

Therefore, dearest brothers, believing in Christ’s Resurrection and kingdom, let us rejoice with pure minds and holy devotion, so that by faith and works we too may show that we do not disbelieve what the whole world believes [Col. 0618C].

## SERMON XLI. On the same solemnity of Easter XIII

[Col. 0617]

### NOTICE

Muratorius, an excellent master of textual criticism, relying on the testimony of a single Ambrosian manuscript, rescued this sermon from obscurity, attributed it to Saint Maximus, and published it with the other sermons of the same author. It is likewise found in the Turin manuscript, inscribed: “On Easter, sermon XIII.”

## Argument

—[Col. 0617C] After presenting and explaining at length testimonies first from Isaiah and then from David, Saint Maximus says that we too should offer religious joys to our God and celebrate Easter in the unleavened bread of sincerity and chastity.

The foremost of the prophets, the most blessed Isaiah, who proclaimed aloud the mysteries of the Lord’s nativity and resurrection, says among other things: “Rejoice, heaven, and let earth exult; let the mountains break forth in gladness, and the hills in righteousness, because God has had mercy on his people and has comforted the lowly of his people” (Ps. XCV). From the sequence of the reading itself, brothers, and from what follows, we understand most clearly that this proclamation belongs to these days and foretells the Easter festival. Heaven is rightly now summoned to complete gladness, when the Only-Begotten of the Most High, having shattered the gates of hell and cast down the devil, has brought the joys of blessed perpetuity to the most sorrowful mortals.

How, then, could heaven not rejoice when it saw its Lord, after completing the battle for our salvation, sitting victorious at the seat of his majesty and at the right hand of the Father? Heaven rejoices because its Lord, having fulfilled the purpose of the Father’s will and by the merit of his triumph, [Col. 0618C] received dominion over the universe. “Rejoice,” he says, “heaven, and let earth exult.” The earth of the human race certainly exults: sprinkled with the blood of the heavenly Lamb, it is not only restored to paradise but is summoned to heaven to reign with the Lord.

Let our flesh also exult, for it truly is earth, since, glorified through Christ, it has merited fellowship with the Divinity. “Let the mountains break forth,” he says, “in gladness, and the hills in righteousness.” We may appropriately understand these mountains and hills, which are summoned to joy, as the patriarchs, just as we read in holy David: “You who wondrously illumine from the everlasting mountains” (Ps. LXXV); and elsewhere: “The mountains leapt like rams, and the hills like lambs of the sheep” (Ps. CXIII). Nor is it without reason that all the righteous are called mountains and hills: leaving behind the lowliness of earthly conduct, they have raised the summit of their faith toward the higher things of heavenly life.

Most justly, therefore, the venerable patriarchs are urged by the prophetic word to take up gladness. Their offspring—that is, Christ the Lord—through the mystery of his death and resurrection restored the life that had been lost even to the Fathers of the age that preceded us. The patriarchs rejoice in every way: the Son of God, born from their stock, has cleansed with the new blood of his immaculate body the whole face of the world, previously defiled by diabolical impieties.

And therefore, brothers, because we know that heaven rejoices, earth exults, and mountains and hills are glad, let us too offer religious joys to our God. Let us celebrate the Lord’s Passover, as the Apostle says: “Not in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity [Note: [Col. 0619D] The Vulgate reads “and truth.”] and chastity” (1 Cor. V).

You will celebrate Easter in the unleavened bread of sincerity and chastity, brother, if your senses, fragrant with the Lord’s bread, do not grow together through any leaven of vice or any sprinkling of the devil. You will celebrate Easter and shine with the splendor of its brightness if no darkness of adulterous thought obscures the light of so great a sacrament in your heart. You will celebrate [Col. 0619B] Easter in the unleavened bread of truth if you come to the Church of God chaste, [Col. 0620A] sober, just, peaceable, and full of brotherly love.

For no one can live an unreformed life, remain unrepentant in heart, and maintain fellowship in crimes with the devil while celebrating the mystery of holiness with Christ. Let us therefore put away every leaven of iniquity, so that we may truly share in this joy to which the mountains and hills are summoned by the Holy Spirit’s prophetic voice, and to which heaven and earth are also invited. Who is so dull in understanding, who is so blinded in a darkened mind with eyes sunk toward the earth, that he would not celebrate with complete exultation these longings of the whole world, in which the forgiveness of sins, the grace of regeneration, the mystery of redemption, the glory of resurrection, and the hope of eternity [Col. 0620B] smile upon us?

## Sermon XLII. On the Same Solemnity of Easter XIV

[Col. 0619]

### Notice

So that we do not weary our readers by writing the same things again, we wish to remind them that this sermon and the following Sermon 43 were copied from the Ambrosian codex and published by Muratori in volume IV of the *Anecdota*. They also exist in the aforementioned Taurinensis codex, no. 20, where it is noted that Sermons 21, 22, 23, 24, and 25 are lacking.

## Argument

—[Col. 0619B] The audacity of human wisdom probing divine mysteries is refuted, and whatever the pagans brought forward against Christ’s birth, manner of life, and shameful death is decisively rebutted.

The mystery of our redemption, dearest brothers, which, coming from heaven, works our salvation on earth, manifests itself with such majesty and such condescension that its power and truth are hidden from the faithless [Col. 0619C] but manifest to believers. For just as what is holy becomes known to the faithful, so unbelief cannot see the matter of faith. In examining heavenly realities, all human wisdom is made foolish and every mortal heart grows numb, as the most glorious teacher, the Apostle Paul, says: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. V).

Our Lord and Savior himself, rejecting the wisdom of this world, also said: “I give you thanks, Father, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants” (Matt. XI). Learn from this, brothers, that the mysteries of our life are not to be attained through philosophical teachings but believed with the simplicity of infants, because by that profound and great judgment of our God, what is concealed from the wise is revealed to the infant.

An infant is so called not because his age is immature, but because he does not know how to oppose the divine mysteries. And rightly is he called an infant who offers no arguments against the will of his God, but faith. The matter is therefore hidden from the wise man, lest he see what is manifest, because, swollen with pride and folly, he contends that he can know more than God.

And therefore, rejecting the questions of worldly wisdom, let us hold fast the faith revealed to infants, believing without hesitation that, by heavenly operation, a virgin conceived and remained a virgin after giving birth to her son. Nor should we doubt that he was born of a virgin whom virginity alone could worthily bring forth.

And this, dearest ones, is where we differ from the wise men of this world: they, in their excessive disputations, despise in Christ the lowliness of a woman’s childbirth; but we, enlightened by faith, revere the mystery of the virginal womb.
