For Christ, our God and Lord, so bound together in himself, by an ineffable union, what he had from the Father and what he assumed from his mother, that the depth of his incarnation might be contemplated by the simplicity of infants, while the prudence of the wise was driven far away.

Finally, to come to what follows, the nations laugh that Christ was crucified, failing to consider that through his cross the world trembled, daylight was shut off, and—a thing that had never happened in any previous age—the inhabitants of hell saw the Lord of heaven. They add this, saying: “How do you worship your Christ as God, when he was afraid to die?”

If, then, you know that Christ was afraid to die, why do you not understand that what he feared arose not from cowardice but from mystery? Christ certainly feared, but he assumed that fear from the weakness of our body, so that he might either will or be able to fear. For he feared from the same source from which he hungered, from which he was sad, from which he slept, from which he suffered, and from which he wept.

What of this? You see Christ fearing to die, yet do not behold him stripping away, with triumphal hand, the spoils of captive death? You see that he feared death, yet refuse to see that he raised the dead? After traversing the realms below, he restored life to himself after the tomb.

Do not therefore despise him dead who glorifies his burial by his resurrection. From his mother he took what enabled him to undergo death; from the Father he brought what would raise the dead. Rising from the dead, to show that the reality of the body he had raised was present in him, he said to his disciples: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke XXIV).

He showed his bones and flesh, so that no one would doubt that the one who had been pierced by nails on the wood had returned from the tomb. “Touch,” he says, “and see”—that is, touch with your hand, see with faith—because both the reality of my body and the distinctness of my divinity are present in me. “A spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.” That is: it is not the nature of a spirit to be able to have either bones or flesh; but by my mystery and by the power of my Father and me it has come about that my flesh in the spirit and the spirit in the flesh should always remain inseparably joined to me.

“See, see, for I am the very one who, pierced by nails and lance, did not fear death while fearing it; who healed my wounds not through the skill of medical art but by dying; who preserved in my body the marks of the nails, not for myself but for your faith. For I wished not to erase in myself the memory of that saving Passion, so that the truth of my resurrection might remain in your hearts.”

And therefore, brothers, let us honor the mystery of the dying Lord, so that we may receive the glory of the risen Lord. Let us venerate the crucified one, so that we may be worthy to see him reigning. For he chose to die not so that hell might claim him, but so that he might free the dead from the dead.

## Sermon XLIII. On the Same Solemnity of Easter XV

[Col. 0621]

## Argument

511 —[Col. 0621A] Christ’s humility was illumined by wondrous and certain manifestations of divinity. Each nature performed what was proper to it in him, so that the human condition might serve the divine dispensation, and the form of divinity might show the Son of Man—namely, Christ—to be equal to God.

The depths of the heavenly will and disposition, dearest brothers, disturb human understanding unless we follow them in faith; and amid the greatness of divine works, unless we are awed by the judgment of almighty God, the reasoning of mortal intelligence, as though weak, collapses. Therefore the things God does are not to be scrutinized with words but believed with devotion.

For in Christ our Lord the mysteries of God and humanity converge in such a way that, under the single office of a twofold action, humility shines in his majesty and majesty reigns in humility. Christ himself, through the mysteries of our redemption, was, in the unity of a diverse substance, a powerful man and a humble God. But according to the purpose of his glory, the humility of God is man, and the power of man is God.

God is rightly called humble when, lowering the prerogative of his own divinity, he allowed his body to be fastened to the cross while the world itself mourned. And man is powerful in his God when, at the command of his word, illnesses depart, health returns to the sick, unclean spirits flee, and angels serve.

Since this new man possesses such great power, we must understand that all that humility of God is the merciful condescension of kindness, not the destruction of power. Through this most sacred mystery of the incarnation, flesh and the Word came together in one Lord and one person, so that God might be thought to have been born from a woman and man believed to have come from heaven, according to what the Savior says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III).

I ask, then, how Christ, before his Passion, when he had not yet hastened glorified to the Father, could say that he was in heaven and that he had ascended or descended from heaven. How, brothers, unless he was the son of man who was the Son of God? We cannot confess separately either man without God or God without man.

Does it not seem that man transcended heaven when he was united to the Word of God in the virgin’s womb? And that he descended from heaven when, claiming nothing for himself from his innate majesty, he delivered his manhood to penal suffering? Thus Christ was in heaven when he performed wondrous things with heavenly power; yet he was also on earth when, gentle and humble, he endured earthly injuries at the hands of the wicked.

This also explains why, while differing opinions about the Lord of the peoples raged among disputing Jews, one despised him as a man while another marveled at him as God; why some crucified him while others worshiped him. So too, of the two thieves crucified with him, one, treating him as a companion in punishment, rebuked him as an unbeliever, while the other, recognizing him as God, prayed to him.

And therefore, brothers, at that time there existed together in Christ both the dominion of the reigning one and the service of the servant. For although he was in the form of God, as the Apostle teaches, he assumed the form of a servant.

Christ was truly in the form of God when, turning water into wine, he revealed himself to be Lord of created things. He was in the form of God when, at his command, demons crying out from possessed bodies and ancient dwelling places were driven away. He was in the form of God when, amid the waves, the water was made solid and yet, not without fear, served his venerable footsteps.

But he was in the form of a servant when, wearied by the fatigue of travel, he sat as though resting beside the mouth of a well. He acted in the form of a servant when the wicked, insulting him, cast the spittle of their filthy mouths upon him. He had assumed the form of a servant when he did not turn away his face—which believers feared to behold—from the palms and blows of those who mocked him; and when he inclined even his shoulders, with which he had come to bear our sins, to the hands of those who scourged him—a thing most disgraceful for those who are truly servants to endure.

He was plainly like a servant when a crown of thorns woven by the hands of his enemies disfigured his saving head. Thus, brothers, when the one and same Son of God performed wondrous deeds and endured things worthy of lamentation, he was at once servant and lord. He could do everything as lord, and endured everything as servant.

But now let us see by what particular virtues and stages he who was a servant confirmed to his disciples that he was God. First of all, when the indispensable servant of the most faithful centurion was being afflicted with a deadly illness, Christ, asked by his master, healed the absent man while himself absent, as God truly does, by sending health; and he visited with the eye of his divinity the sick man whom he did not see bodily, lying some distance away.

Finally, when the only son of a pitiable widow was already being carried on a bier to the tomb for burial, Christ, by the command of his life-giving authority, raised him and restored him at once both to life and to his mother, amid the crowds and with death itself as witness.

After this, when the ruler of the priests pleaded for the health of his daughter, he who had given life to the girl at her birth restored the soul of the dead girl to its own body. And lest any suspicion of collusion concerning miracles involving a recent death remain among the wicked, and lest they suppose that those raised so quickly had not truly been dead, he proceeded to the burial of blessed Lazarus. Lazarus, four days dead and stinking, moreover bound with wrappings as was customary, leapt forth at Christ’s command and immediately became a participant in conversation with his Lord and a fellow guest at the table.

All these things happened, dearest ones, so that no one at all might dispute his return from the dead, since he was shown to have raised the dead with such glory. Therefore let us believe in our Lord God, who performs such astonishing wonders. Let us love him, who bestows such great benefits upon us and raises the dead. Let us venerate him rising from the dead; let us honor and worship him also seated at the right hand of the Father; and with complete devotion let us serve the Judge who is to come of the living and the dead, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.

## Sermon XLIV. On the Ascension of the Lord I

[Col. 0623]

### Notice

The fact that Maximus is the author of this sermon is demonstrated not only by its style but also by the authority of the manuscripts. Muratori readily concedes this, relying solely on the testimony of the Ambrosian codex. Examining the ancient monuments, we found that the Taurinensis codex agrees with the Ambrosian: in it the same sermon appears among the Maximian sermons as “Sermon XI on the Ascension of the Lord,” and it is also found in Casinensis 102, p. 70.

## Argument

—[Col. 0623B] The elevation of Christ into heaven, by which he led captivity captive—that is, the righteous whom he freed from the power of Tartarus—and made them his fellow heirs of the heavenly kingdom, should fill us with great delight, as we behold the Lord returning to eternal glory and are commanded to hope confidently for a share in it.

With deeply religious joy and devoted gladness, dearest brothers, we must celebrate the festival of today’s mystery, because Christ our Lord, to whom the tempter said at the beginning of his contest: “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread” (Matt. IV), today, entering heaven, confirms every believer with the protection of the living stone and gives life through the nourishment of heavenly bread.

And when the author of every deceit tested him, saying: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down,” he did not merely avoid falling downward, but, taking up the wings of eternal glory, flew victoriously over his enemy to heaven: “For he ascended,” as it is written, “upon the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. XVII).

And to the one to whom the devil then promised the kingdoms and powers of the world if he would be worshiped by him, Christ, rejecting the tempter’s vanity, received dominion over the world and the everlasting sovereignty of heaven, as he himself says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father in heaven and on earth” (Matt. XI). Nor was he undeservedly rewarded with the most blessed kingdom, since, possessing the mind of a lawful king, he rejected tyrannical promises.

Thus, with great and incomprehensible miracles approved, Christ’s mysteries and powers grow for us. For the one whom his mother’s womb brought forth for the use of this present human life by gradual growth, joined in innate union with the Father, sat down at his right hand as everlasting ruler; and the one whom the impious voice of his persecutors on earth blasphemed [Note: [Col. 0623D] The Casinensis codex reads “blasphemed against.”] is now ceaselessly praised in the song of the attending angels, as it is written: “His praise remains for ever and ever” (Ps. CXX).

Let us therefore rejoice, brothers, and exult in the Lord, because today Christ, transcending the heights of heaven, ascended to the unimaginable majesty of the Father’s throne [Col. 0624B]. The man whom the envy of the malignant enemy had driven from that first habitation of paradise and cast out, making him a stranger amid this world's ruin [Note: [Col. 0623D] The same Casinensis codex reads “cast out and expelled”], he placed in the angelic homeland and made a citizen of the heavenly beings, though he had been an exile from paradise.

For this reason, dearest ones, we must rejoice with immense gladness, because the Savior raised those whom the tempter had struck down, and the grace of Christ freed those whom the devil’s sin had bound, as the most blessed Apostle Paul says: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. V).

Truly an overflowing grace, which for ruined man transformed death into life and changed punishment into reward. For what reward could truly be greater for the sinner than that, for his sake, the Only-Begotten of God assumed flesh, endured the cross, deigned to undergo burial, did not shrink from the realms below, and, after the author of sin himself had been condemned, carried the man he had assumed into heaven?

Pay attention, therefore, beloved [Note: [Col. 0623D] These words are written emphatically and point toward what the Church sings on Holy Saturday: “O happy fault,” etc. In enumerating the splendid benefits that Christ’s resurrection brought to humanity and by which he completed the work of redemption, Maximus wished to show that the loss inflicted upon us by original sin was restored through the more abundant supply of gifts. Saint Ambrose wrote something similar when speaking of Emperor Theodosius in Letter 40, where he said: “O blessed falsehood, by which one acquires the absolution of others for one’s own sake!”], because guilt benefited man more than it harmed him. For the one who, humbled under the law of transgression, had subjected his neck to the devil’s yoke, escaped all the bonds of tyrannical captivity by being taken captive by the Son of God.

As venerable David says of the Lord our Redeemer: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” [Note: [Col. 0624D] Ps. LXVII: “You ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts among men.”]

What, then, does it profit us if the Lord led our captivity captive upward and did not allow what had been captured by the devil to remain captive? It profits us in every way, dearest ones; it profits us immeasurably, because in the devil’s captivity slavery is harsh, while in Christ’s captivity freedom is blessed.

There is no doubt that everyone captured by the devil and handed over to the darkness of hell remains always in mourning, whereas Christ’s captive exults in the light of the heavenly kingdom. Blessed David says, then: “He led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.”

See and understand how advantageous it is for us to be Christ’s captives: to his captives he grants not only eternal freedom [Col. 0625A] but also bestows the ineffable gifts of heavenly blessings. Therefore, elsewhere the patriarch sings: “Restore our captivity, O Lord, like a stream in the south” (Ps. CXXV).

“Restore,” he says, not “turn away”—that is, “Grant, Lord, that we who were long ago captured by the devil may at last be worthy to be your captives.” For we know that being subject to the devil is a bitter and unending condition, [Note: [Col. 0625D] The Casinensis codex reads: “To serve you, Christ, is joy.”] while serving you, Lord, is joy.

This is not ambiguous, brothers, because the Lord himself says: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. XI). Therefore, breaking the bonds of unbelief and casting the devil’s yoke from our necks, let us submit our necks with complete devotion to the Lord’s authority, because the yoke of the Gospel and captivity to Christ bring great sweetness to believers.

He who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, etc.

## Sermon XLV. On the Same Ascension of the Lord II

[Col. 0625]

### Notice

This sermon is placed before the preceding one in the Taurinensis codex, where it is the tenth among those entitled “On the Ascension.” We preferred to follow Muratori’s sequence, since it corresponds exactly to the Ambrosian codex, from which this same sermon was copied.

## Argument

—[Col. 0625A] Just as we must believe that the Redeemer came from heaven, so the same faith persuades us that he returned to heaven. The Lord’s return to the seat of glory must be held in high esteem; and the happiness he obtained greatly consoles us, because Christ has enrolled humanity among the inhabitants of heaven.

The mystery of the Lord’s Ascension established for us the festival of this day, dearest brothers, so that we might rejoice that the Only-Begotten of God, whom we are glad came to earth for the redemption of all, entered heaven for our eternity. For this is the truth of saving faith: if we believe in his Passion, we must not deny his glory.

It is certainly no great miracle that the one who came from heaven returns to heaven; the greater miracle is that he carried to the Father the man whom he assumed from the earth. The most blessed David says: “Let the heavens rejoice and the earth exult” (Ps. XCV). There is no doubt that he sang this concerning the mystery of Christ: the earth exults because it sees its Redeemer reigning in the heavens; heaven rejoices because it has not lost the God whom it possessed and has received the man whom it did not possess.

The earth rejoices that the Son of God descended from heaven, but heaven exults no less that the Son of Man ascended from earth. “He sat,” it says, “at the right hand of the Father.” How necessary it was, dearest ones, that the flesh of man, which had long been held captive under the domination of sin, should receive there [Col. 0626A] the freedom to live [Col. 0626B], where guilt cannot pass!

The Savior therefore ascended to the Father so that he himself might obtain the dominion due to him and the hope of the promised eternity might remain intact for us.

Nor should we doubt this ascent of the Lord whom we proclaim. If Elijah, once the servant of God, was lifted up to heaven in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses because of the merits of his chastity and faith, why should we not believe with complete devotion that our Christ was able to rise above the heavens, since he is both the Word and the will of the eternal Father?

[Note: [Col. 0625D] What Paul said in 1 Cor. I, 24—“Christ the power [Greek: Χριστὸν Θεοῦ δύναμιν, καὶ Θεοῦ σοφίαν], that is, Christ the power or might of God, and the wisdom of God”—Maximus understood in such a way that he wrote that Christ is the Father’s will and word. Since God’s will is almighty, he expressed the Father’s power or might by the term “will.” Saint Thomas says in his commentary on the passage of the Apostle indicated immediately above that Christ is called the power and wisdom of God by a certain appropriation. He is power insofar as the Father accomplishes all things through him: “All things were made through him” (John I); and he is wisdom insofar as the Word itself, which is the Son, is nothing other than begotten or conceived wisdom: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High,” etc. (Ecclus. XXIV).]

Of this, certainly, it was said through the Holy Spirit: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing praises to the Lord, who ascends above the heavens of heavens toward the east” (Ps. CII); and again: “The Lord prepared his throne in heaven, and his kingdom shall rule over all” (Ps. CII, 19); and elsewhere: “The Lord ascended above the heavens, and he thunders.”

Or how could he not be received into heaven, who was calling the human race to heaven? Let us therefore exult, beloved, and rejoice, because we know that our Redeemer is there, from where he can both behold and govern all things; and because there he has placed the man rescued from hell, where no tree of the knowledge of good and evil displays deadly fruits, but where the fullness of healthful and simple goodness dwells.

## Sermon XLVI. On the Same Ascension of the Lord III

[Col. 0625]

### Notice

Both the character of the style and the authority of the ancient manuscripts—especially the Taurinensis—led us, in agreement with Muratori, to judge that this sermon too should be attributed to Saint Maximus, the bishop. It is found in the same Taurinensis codex among Saint Maximus’s sermons as “Sermon XIII on the Ascension.” Muratori likewise transferred it, copied from the Ambrosian codex, into volume IV of the *Anecdota*.

## Argument

—[Col. 0625D] The Lord’s glorious Ascension supplies a new reason for joy. David prophesied that Christ would be received among the heavenly powers. The prophetic words and other passages of Scripture are illuminated by learned commentaries.

The greatness of the ineffable mysteries of almighty God, which is immense and unfathomable in his works, declares how great and how inscrutable the Only-Begotten is [Col. 0626D]. Having undertaken battle against the ruler of the world, he fought in man and conquered through man, making him the inhabitant and lord of heaven and earth.

He also subjected that body of our humiliation, which he had assumed from fragile woman, to the various injuries of his persecutors and even allowed it to be fastened to the cross. Today, raising the everlasting gates with him and in himself, he carried it up to the Father [Col. 0627A].

Finally, instructed by blessed David, we learn that these things were foretold to mortals while the powers of heaven conversed among themselves. For he says: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. XXIII).

Rightly, dearest ones, the everlasting gates were lifted up, because a wondrous entrance into the heights was being prepared for the most glorious King and Lord of eternity. Through the patriarch and prophet, therefore, the lifting up of the everlasting gates is announced, so that we may understand that, with Christ going before us there, heaven is now open to mortals.

Those gates, beloved, which the Savior opened by going before us to the Father after conquering death and triumphing over the devil, will be open to the faithful—and will remain open forever.

When they marveled and asked who this King of glory was, the immediate answer was given: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII). He is mighty, therefore, because he is strong. And truly that power must be proclaimed which, supported not by the virtues of others but by its own power in every respect, stands by itself. It was not arrogantly assumed by the Lord and our Redeemer, nor purchased through an exchange of gifts, nor sought through any flattery; it was possessed through perfect and unadorned virtue.

For because he was obedient to the Father even unto death on a cross, as the Apostle says: “He gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II).

Here, when he says “the Lord strong and mighty,” he does not praise a twofold power of Christ from the Father, but the unconquered strength of the new man. Nor was it a great thing to call him strong through whom all things were created and who, almighty, proceeded from the Almighty.

Therefore the Lord is strong and mighty in battle 519 [Col. 0628A]. Strong, not because he killed his enemies powerfully, but because he was killed patiently for us. Mighty, because amid the insults and punishments of his Passion he was conscious of possessing such great power that he might fulfill the ministry of redemption, yet did not wish to display his power.

“For although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II).

Thus he is strong, mighty, and glorious. Strong when he is not conquered by the devil in the struggle. Mighty when, intending to subjugate death, he shattered the barriers of hell. Glorious when, having erased with his immaculate blood the bond written against us by the law, he ascended to the seat of the Father’s glory, to be adored by all the powers of heaven.

What, then, is the depth of this mystery? What an inscrutable secret of divine operation: that the one who proceeded from the Father before the ages and the one who came forth from a woman at the end of time became one God? 520 [Col. 0628B]

[Note: [Col. 0627D] How these words of Maximus should be understood can readily be learned both from other passages of this holy bishop and from Saint Thomas, *Summa theologica*, Part III, Question 16, Articles 6 and 7.]

And this occurred so that, while the Only-Begotten remained undivided from the Father, man might share in the paternal immortality through the Only-Begotten of God.

Therefore, brothers, let us confess that the Lord ascended into heaven in such a way that we do not believe ourselves to have been left without him, because at the moment of his Ascension he said to the apostles: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

For the one who descended from the Father in such a way as to remain inseparable from the Father likewise ascended from earth to heaven in such a way as not to leave the world. This is the omnipotence of our God; such and so boundless is his power that, by reason of his immensity, every creature has him present everywhere.

To him be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## Sermon XLVII. On the Same Ascension of the Lord IV

[Col. 0627]

### Notice

This sermon now appears for the first time. We copied it from a very ancient codex of the monastery of Appannis. It is so similar in expression and style to the other sermons of Maximus that nothing more similar could be desired.

## Argument

—[Col. 0627C] In the triumph of Christ as he ascends into heaven, we should contemplate not so much the eternal possession of the heavenly kingdom by his humanity as the inheritance of that same blessedness obtained for us. Here lies the end of the entire divine dispensation, toward which all our efforts must be directed.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, about to depart from this region of the shadow of death, in order to console his apostles, whom he had previously instructed in the faith as most beloved, concerning the necessity of his absence—[lacuna] the Holy Spirit, who with him and the Father has one and the same will. (The original lacks fifteen lines, the letters having been worn away.)

Hell grieves over its plundering together with its prince, while the entire heavenly army rejoices over the restoration of its loss. Today the flesh which, through the operative power of the Holy Spirit, he had assumed from the Virgin Mother on earth has been placed at the Father’s right hand, and the natures of all the heavenly spirits have bowed before it. Today that new way of which the Apostle once spoke has been opened for us, because through that most blessed flesh of Christ the eternal entrance into heaven—through which no flesh had previously passed—has been opened for us. Today the book which no one but the Lamb could open has been unsealed, since in his death the mysteries of that book were revealed; and those things which are found written about him in the Law and the Prophets have been completed on this day, when the dispensation of his majesty reached its fulfillment.

Christ first descended so that he might become a sharer in our nature; now he has ascended so that he might make us sharers in his glory. Descending, he rejoiced the little ones by visible miracles through his wondrous way of life. Ascending, he gave gifts to human beings, so that, instructed in faith and raised to manly strength, they would no longer desire his temporal presence, but would strive with all the devotion of their hearts to follow him where he had gone before them.

Therefore, since we have been deprived of his temporal presence, let us hasten with complete devotion toward the vision of him for eternity, and let us say to him with the Psalmist: “My heart has said to you, ‘I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I shall seek’; do not turn your face away from me” (Psalm 26:8). For the entire most holy dispensation of Christ’s humanity intends and demands nothing else than to direct us toward heavenly things, so that, when the period of our mortality has been completed, he may lead us to the vision of himself in manifestation and satisfy us with the eternal glory of his face. The Apostle bears witness: “Then we shall see him as he is” (1 Corinthians 13); and, as the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Psalm 16). We shall enjoy forever those blessings “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2).

Those blessings holy David contemplated with admiration, insofar as they could be seen in an enigma, when he said: “What is there for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Psalm 72). For he was unable either to express by speaking the greatness of heavenly glory or to comprehend it sufficiently by thought.

Let us therefore hunger and thirst not merely for these things, since for this purpose the supreme Priest, our forerunner, has ascended on our behalf into the Holy of Holies and sits at the right hand of his Father: to confirm our hope by the example of his members, so that the lowliness of the entire flock might one day follow to the place where it believes its shepherd has gone before it. For the Lord himself also promised this to his apostles, saying: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matthew 14). He calls holy eagles those who desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ. For the nature of eagles is said to be such that, when they sense carcasses beyond the waves of the sea by their smell, they swiftly fly there to satisfy their hunger.

The hunger of these eagles signifies the desire of holy souls. Sensing by the nostrils of faith that their Head has already been established in the highest tranquility beyond the storms of the world, they would wish, on the wings of their sweetest hope, to stand in the presence of their Creator and rejoice in the satisfaction of his face.

Let us believe that he reigns at the right hand of his Father, and let us always strive toward him as though with twin wings of virtue, love and hope. But so that we too may be able to reign with him in eternal life, let us— (The original lacks five lines.) Let us merit to become, cleansed from every vice, a dwelling place of God, who may always remain in us.

Here ends the sermon.

## SERMON XLVIII. On Pentecost I

[Col. 0629]

### Editorial Notice

Eight sermons on Pentecost follow. Muratori transcribed and published the first six from the Ambrosian manuscript; we publish the seventh and eighth, hitherto unedited, transcribed from a manuscript formerly belonging to the abbey of Saint-Dalmas. All bear the name of Saint Maximus in the manuscripts mentioned, and anyone may recognize both his fluency of expression and his style. This first sermon is also found in the Turin manuscript as the eighteenth sermon on Pentecost.

### Argument

[Col. 0609B] Saint Maximus undertakes especially to prove the divinity of the Holy Spirit. To open a way for himself toward this end, he recalls that the Spirit was present with his heavenly gifts in all the mysteries of our restoration. Since it is certain that all divine things proceed from one source, where the gifts are shared, the nature also must be shared, and consequently the will and beneficence. Nor do different kinds of grace introduce disagreement or inequality, since God, the giver of all things, is one and the same.

How great is almighty God’s concern for the salvation of mortals is declared by the very frequent sacraments of our solemn celebrations. First of all, so that human nature might be able to pass into heavenly glory, the divine substance assumed the body of mortal humanity. Then, so that the grace of the mystical washing might prepare us for so great a blessedness, the Lord consecrated all the world’s waters by his baptism, and the blessing of his sacred body granted every water everywhere the power to regenerate.

Finally, so that the just Lord might triumph over the devil himself—the enemy of our salvation and of his will—in a just contest, he permitted himself to be crucified by him, by his own will and that of his Father, so that the Passion of the immaculate one might become the condemnation of his persecutors. By dying, Christ also made himself equal to mortals, so that, having overcome death, he might restore the life of mortals. Nevertheless, he ascended to the heights of heaven so that he might confirm by the example of his wondrous ascension the hope of believers, which he had nourished by a gracious promise.

But because all these things seemed in some way to have been specially bestowed upon us through the gifts of God’s Only-Begotten Son, the Holy Spirit also—whose saving coming we celebrate today—showed that he possessed the same will and divinity as the Son of God. By the power of his majesty he filled those redeemed by Christ’s blood. He who had formed in the womb of blessed Mary the body of the new human being while preserving her virginity likewise strengthened the hearts of Christ’s apostles with heavenly vigor and endowed their tongues with a new utterance, so that the same Spirit who had wondrously brought Christ forth from a woman’s womb for the redemption of all might, by granting a diversity of languages, have him proclaimed through the apostles to all nations.

Who would not perceive, beloved, the concordant will of God’s Only-Begotten Son and the Holy Spirit, since those whom Christ chose on earth were visited by the Spirit from heaven? Therefore, since we see one grace in the apostles, we must believe that there is also one power in the divinity. Thus the Paraclete filled the breasts of the apostles so that Christ’s presence would not be lacking; for where the gifts are undivided, the divinity is certainly inseparable.

When the Spirit enters those in whom Christ dwells, he does not increase the divinity in them, but advances their faith in unity. The Son of God, who created the faculty of speech, could indeed have given his disciples a diversity of languages; but the power was reserved so that through it the Spirit might be proved to be truly God.

For this, as we believe, is the incomprehensible dispensation of the Trinity: although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit work inseparably and together in all things through the effect of the same divinity, certain things are nevertheless bestowed specially by each individual Person. For the Father granted us the Son as the remedy of our life; the Son bestowed the grace of regeneration; the Spirit supplied the power, as the teaching of the patriarch who sang announces when he says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 32).

How necessarily the Spirit gave the apostles knowledge of the languages of the nations, so that all the Gentiles might hear the truth of saving faith through them! But what the Spirit bestows, the Father also bestows, for the Spirit possesses everything together with the Father and proceeds wholly from the Father. And what the Spirit bestows together with the Father, the Son also bestows, since the Son was born from the same Father, from whom the Spirit also proceeds.

For Christ says: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16). If everything the Father has belongs to the Son, then what the Spirit has is also common to the Father and the Son. Therefore, since there is no division in their name, we must believe that in every work their will and power are one.

Thus the heavenly Trinity performs its mysteries in its faithful, so that, although its operation appears distinct, its authority may nevertheless be proved undivided. The Son and the Holy Spirit therefore have one divinity with the Father. Just as one could not be born from God without being God, so there is no doubt that the one who proceeds from God is God.

How the Son, who already existed, was born from the one and same Father, while the Spirit, who was not born, proceeds from him, is known only to the Divinity itself, which, being alone, knows itself. For no one knows the Father, as it is written, except the Son (Luke 10). Therefore what the Son knows, the Spirit also knows, since with the Son and the Father he has one name and one divinity. He, as the Apostle Paul says, “searches the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2).

The Spirit is said to search the depths of God, not as though he were examining in another something hidden and inaccessible to himself, but so that you may understand that what belongs to God is inscrutable to you. Consider, therefore, brother, that no one can know the depths of the Father except the Son, who is from him, and the Spirit, who is from him. Do not attempt to penetrate what no one has been granted to see. It is right to believe what he is; it has not been permitted to investigate how he is what he is.

The apostles therefore received through the Holy Spirit a diversity of languages, but they proclaimed one God. For this reason they began with a variety of languages, so that the diversity of nations might learn, through many kinds of speech, the unity of faith. Finally, as it is written, when blessed Peter was speaking, three thousand people believed (Acts 4).

This should not seem incredible to us, because the same Spirit both instructed the tongues of the apostles so that they might speak what was to be believed and prepared the hearts of their hearers to believe when the apostles preached. He who gave understanding to those speaking supplied comprehension to those hearing, so that there can be no doubt that one power was present in the mouths of the speakers and in the hearts of the believers.

In these events, beloved, the work was visible, but the worker invisible; the effect of the power was manifest, but the majesty of the one producing it concealed. The Spirit therefore most rightly announces the victory and faith of Christ: he had promised his coming through the prophets; he was present with Christ in the Virgin’s womb; and at Christ’s baptism he was present in a dove, together with the testimony of the Father’s voice.

Let us therefore believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have always one will, and, united also by the bond of their work in Christian peace, let us direct the paths of our life according to the divine commandments, so that we may merit the fullness of God’s grace and the visitation of the Holy Spirit through the soundness of our faith and the conduct of our deeds, etc.

## SERMON XLIX. On Pentecost II

[Col. 0631]

### Editorial Notice

525 In the Turin manuscript this sermon is numbered among the homilies of Saint Maximus as number 20. It was published from the Ambrosian manuscript by Mabillon and Muratori in the places indicated above.

### Argument

[Col. 0613C] Maximus again proves the divinity of the holy Paraclete, because he himself came as witness and announcer to human beings of Christ’s glory with the Father. For no one, says the holy bishop, could disclose the divine secret unless one who shared in the Divinity had descended from heaven. He then teaches that the Holy Spirit remains in the hearts of those who love peace and concord.

After the celebration of the Lord’s Ascension, beloved brothers, today we celebrate the holy mysteries of Pentecost, so that, just as we rejoiced that a human being had ascended into heaven for us, so now we may exult that the Holy Spirit has descended from heaven for our sake.

Christ went to the Father; the Paraclete came from the Father, so that we may not doubt that all the gifts of eternal salvation are conferred upon us by the disposition and will of almighty God the Father, from whom the Spirit comes and to whom the Son goes.

The new human being therefore ascended into heaven, so that through his grace the Spirit might deign to come to earth. The Holy Spirit came from heaven so that he might announce to mortals that Christ reigns with the Father. For who else could disclose the divine secret to those dwelling on earth unless one who shared in the Divinity had come from heaven?

It is therefore written, as you have heard: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, they were all together in one place with one accord” (Acts 2). And shortly afterward it says: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in various languages, as the Spirit gave them utterance.”

The apostles were therefore of one accord, and they were filled with the Holy Spirit. [Note: In Muratori, “unanimous.”] The Spirit came to those of one accord, visited those who were harmonious, bestowed gifts upon those who were peaceful, and gladly filled the hearts of the venerable apostles, whose breasts Christ, their author and teacher, already inhabited. And, as we heard, “the Holy Spirit sat upon each one of them” (Acts 2).

Pay attention, beloved: the breast of those who are peaceful is the seat of God, as blessed David says: “His place has been established in peace.” Nor should it be doubted that the apostles preserved among themselves the grace of unanimity, since Christ, as he was passing over to the Father, had foretold to them: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13). And again: “I give you my peace; my peace I leave you.”

It is therefore no wonder that mutual love and the peace of Christ delighted the Holy Spirit in the breasts of the apostles. We also read in the Gospel that the Savior said to his disciples: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14). And again he said: “For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you.”

Who, then, could safely refuse to believe either that the Holy Spirit is God, since he came as foretold through the Son of God, or that Christ is Lord, whose saving promise the eternal Father fulfilled?

This is a great and incomprehensible mystery, brothers: a human being goes from earth to heaven, while sending God to us from heaven to earth. Truly, this is the peace and harmony of the Divinity: Christ was born with the Spirit announcing him, and the Spirit descended with Christ promising him.

[Note: [Col. 0633D] Saint Maximus, who in the preceding sermon demonstrated by invincible arguments that the work of our redemption must be referred to all three Persons, here again confirms the same truth, deriving his argument from the unity of will, since that will is the same in all three for the salvation of the world. But when the subject concerns actions internal to the Godhead, as the theologians say, Saint Thomas teaches in the first part, question 43, article 8, that in divine matters the Person who sends and the Person who is sent must be distinguished. The Father is not sent, because he is unbegotten; the Son is sent by the Father, because he is begotten by him; and the Holy Spirit is also sent, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son. “Not every Person sends,” says Saint Thomas, “but only the one to whom it belongs to be the principle of that Person”; thus the Son is sent only by the Father, and the Holy Spirit by the Father and the Son. [Col. 0634D] Since Maximus here is wholly engaged in commending the mystery of our restoration, in which all three divine Persons have acted, he said: “They send one another, they obey one another, because in them there is neither a different will nor a different power,” etc.]

They speak to one another, they send one another, they obey one another, because in them there is neither a different will nor a different power, and together with the Father they always accomplish one mystery for the eternity of mortals.

“It is advantageous for you,” he says, “that I go away” (John 16). What a marvelous gift of our salvation this is: just as it is advantageous for Christ to come from heaven, so it was also advantageous for him to return. It was advantageous for him to come, so that he might give his blood for us; nevertheless, it was advantageous for him to return, so that he might bestow his Spirit upon us.

They were therefore filled, as it is written, with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in various languages, as the Spirit gave them utterance (Acts 2). This variety of languages announces the unity of the Divinity. Different and manifold speech proceeded from each individual, but one person spoke in all of them.

528 The Hebrew speaks a language he had not previously learned, so that the Gentile may hear the faith he did not know. Nor is it surprising, beloved, that Christ gave his apostles knowledge of languages through the Holy Spirit, since he was able to restore walking to the lame, sight to the blind, and speech to the mute.

Therefore, brothers, let us not doubt these things, but let us believe with complete devotion, because all things are possible for God, and it was necessary that a new faith be confirmed by new miracles of speech.

## SERMON L. On Pentecost III

[Col. 0633]

### Editorial Notice

This sermon exists not only in the Ambrosian manuscript but also in the Turin manuscript, where it is numbered homily 21.

### Argument

[Col. 0633B] Maximus rightly extols the mercy of the eternal Father: it had seemed too little to him to have given human beings the Son as redeemer, unless he also poured his Spirit into their hearts and heaped heavenly gifts upon them. He treats the gift of languages given to the apostles, heralds of the new law, in elegant discourse.

It is manifest, brothers, and clear to everyone, how great is almighty God the Father’s concern for all mortals. It was too little for him to have handed over his only Son to death for us unless he had also poured the fullness of his gifts into the hearts of his faithful, as the Lord said through the Prophet: “In the last days I shall pour out my Spirit upon my servants and maidservants, and I shall give wonders in heaven above and signs on earth below. The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood” (Joel 2).

The Lord surely gives wonders in heaven when, at Christ’s birth, a new star shines before the eyes of the Chaldaeans, and when, during his Passion, the midday sun is darkened by sudden obscurity and sets. He gives signs on earth when the earth itself trembles with unaccustomed movements, when rocks split apart after being torn asunder, and when even the tombs give the bodies of the dead back to the light.

“The sun,” he says, “shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood.” What else does it mean, beloved, if we contemplate spiritual realities, for the sun to be turned into darkness, except that Christ passes into death? Or for the moon to be turned into blood, except that the holy Church is bloodied by various sufferings on behalf of the confession of her Christ?

Christ is handed over to death, not to remain in the corruption of the grave, but so that, after the darkness of the underworld, he might shine forth more brilliantly. The Church is afflicted by the hands of the bloodthirsty, not so that she might fail amid torments and punishments, but so that through the many titles of her victories she might be adorned in complete beauty by the blood of her triumphant martyrs.

All these things are acted and accomplished by the one and same grace of Christ and the Spirit in harmony. Christ kindles the breasts of his servants with the desire to endure all things, through hope of perpetual reward. The Spirit, likewise, confirms the hearts of believers, by the strength of divine power, in contempt for death.

Therefore, after the Lord returned victorious to the Father and entered again into his kingdom, the Father’s grace bestowing it with him, he gave his apostles the Paraclete whom he had promised, so that the Spirit, coming from above, might preserve the faith that Christ himself had planted in them.

The Spirit descended upon the apostles with Christ’s promise, so that it might be evident that their will was one and indissoluble in all things. How fittingly the Divinity itself inserts itself into human perception by mutual testimony, when Christ foretells that the Spirit will come from heaven and the Spirit attests that Christ reigns in heaven! Who, then, would doubt that the voice is most true, both of the one who goes to heaven and of the one who comes from heaven?

The apostles, therefore, were filled today, as it is written, with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in various languages, as the Spirit gave them utterance (Acts 2). The Spirit filled those whose hearts the blood and teaching of Christ had cleansed for his coming.

This was the first benefit of the Spirit’s coming: that these men, who had been appointed for the salvation of all nations, should speak in the language of them all. So great was the Paraclete’s grace that it filled both the apostles’ tongue and breast, so that neither power was lacking in their words nor words in their power.

Indeed, in divine and human affairs there is nothing that makes a person glorious in the same way as perfection of holy speech and fullness of heavenly strength. The apostles therefore spoke in various languages through one Spirit, so that the diversity of the nations might come together in the one faith of Christ.

Hence there is no doubt that this Holy Spirit must be confessed as God with the Father and the Son. For who else could have accomplished these things, so that a Roman, a Parthian, a Mede, a Phrygian, and every barbarian might hear his own language while abroad in Judaea, and a Galilean man might speak the mysteries of heaven to barbarian ears not only in the elegance of Greek and Roman speech but also in harsh murmuring and groaning effort?

Long ago, when human presumption was striving to go to heaven and was building a tower for itself, its rebellious effort did not achieve its purpose. The fellowship of one language was suddenly divided by the introduction of a variety of languages, so that, when one person no longer understood another speaking, that entire structure of impiety immediately collapsed.

But now, when God prepares an ascent to heaven for humanity, the heralds of so great a grace are given knowledge of all languages, so that the great promise of God might not remain hidden from a person of any nation, as was said long ago in prophetic speech: “There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard” (Psalm 18).

Thus it is evident, beloved, that the Son of almighty God, who willed the mystery of eternal salvation to be preached through the truth of every language, came as redeemer not merely of the one Jewish people but of all human beings.

Therefore, brothers, since Christ’s goodness desires no mortal to perish, let us cleanse ourselves from every impurity and iniquity, so that the most merciful Spirit of God may also deign to illuminate our hearts for the assistance of our life, etc.

## SERMON LI. On Pentecost IV

[Col. 0635]

### Editorial Notice

This fourth sermon on Pentecost, as well as the fifth that follows, is found not only in the Ambrosian manuscript but also in the Turin manuscript, where they are read as homilies XVIII and XXIII on Pentecost.

### Argument

[Col. 0635B] Although we see that the benefits of God’s Only-Begotten Son and of the Holy Spirit are distinct, nevertheless their will, purpose, and plan are one: Christ promises the Spirit to humanity, the Spirit announces Christ, and the Paraclete himself enlightens those whom the Savior chose. Let us therefore venerate this Spirit with divine worship.

How great is God’s concern for the salvation of mortals, beloved brothers, and with what feeling of gracious condescension, pitying human dangers, he has emptied the devil’s power, we can assess fully and without doubt from this: he both drew us to faith in the truth by the blood of his Son and strengthened the hearts of believers by granting the visitation of the Holy Spirit.

Christ redeemed us for life and raises us to virtue, so that we may preserve, with the Spirit guarding it, the grace we received through the Son’s gift. We see, beloved, that the benefits of God’s Only-Begotten Son and of the Holy Spirit are distinct in the dispensation of the mystery, but we perceive in both the same will and one sacrament of devotion.

Christ was born from a woman for our salvation, but the Spirit cooperated in forming that human being in the Virgin, as was said to blessed Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1).

The Son of God was also baptized for us in the Jordan, but the Holy Spirit was present from heaven in the form of a dove to glorify his baptism. Their purpose and plan are so entirely one that Christ promises the Spirit to humanity, while the Spirit announces Christ, as the Lord says: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from my Father—he will testify about me” (John 15).

They proclaim one another by alternating testimonies, knowing that they reign with undivided majesty. Finally, so that we may recognize more clearly that they are not separated at all by any division, the Paraclete himself visits and enlightens those whom the Savior chose and made fit for his mysteries.

The Lord Jesus was hung upon the cross for the whole human race, but his Gospel would not have shone upon everyone unless, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, who granted the apostles knowledge of various languages, the Lord’s Passion had reached the knowledge of all nations.

Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and the other nations, as it is written, hear in their own languages in Judaea the great works of God and the remedies for their life being preached. Who but truly almighty God could have accomplished these things, so that savage minds might learn religious holiness and barbarian speech might receive heavenly teaching?

Therefore, brothers, let us venerate this Spirit with divine worship. To him belong the fullness of the power to regenerate and the authority to forgive sins, as the Lord instructs his disciples, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 18); and elsewhere: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose you retain, they are retained” (John 20).

Who, then, could be so insane as to doubt that he is God, since with the Father and the Son he possesses inseparable glory and an undivided name, and by their common authority both punishes the pride of the sinner and absolves the humility of the one who confesses, etc.

## SERMON LII. On Pentecost V

[Col. 0637]

### Argument

[Col. 0637A] The Paraclete Spirit, who promised that the Son of God would come for the redemption of the world, was himself announced by the Redeemer as being sent by the Father to his disciples. The majesty of the Persons is undivided, but their individual properties are distinct. Who, unless perhaps an impious heretic or faithless Jew, could doubt that the Holy Spirit is God?

From the beginning of the ages, beloved brothers, the Holy Spirit promised us through patriarchs and prophets that the Son of God would come for the redemption of the world. He prophesied that the Son would be born from a Virgin, having assumed the flesh of a new human being; that he would suffer insults, reproaches, and the cross from the impious; and, many thousands of years beforehand, he also prophesied his resurrection from the underworld.

When this had been fulfilled through our Lord Jesus Christ and the mystery had been completed, the Spirit enlightened the hearts of Christ’s apostles by the wondrous coming of his majesty, so that he who had earlier sung of Christ’s humility and Passion might now proclaim the eternal glory of his kingdom, after the devil had been triumphed over and death defeated.

Yet our Redeemer himself announced to his disciples, not many days beforehand, that this Paraclete would come from heaven and be sent by the Father. Thus, while the Spirit prophesies Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, and while Christ promises the Spirit who will come from the Father, they mutually foretell one another and are believed to be one, to will one thing, and always to be able to do one thing.

This is the Holy Spirit, beloved, who through the operation of the more hidden mystery endowed the Virgin’s womb with heavenly fruitfulness. This is the Spirit who visited the baptism of Christ our Lord in the form of a dove—seen by John, but silent—and did not consider his own voice necessary when the Father himself spoke from heaven, saying: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 17).

We are taught these things by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures so that the undivided majesty but distinct property of the Persons may be revealed to us. For as far as the unity of the Divinity is concerned, in the Father’s Word there is the Spirit’s agreement, and in the Spirit’s speech there is the Father’s will.

Who could doubt that the Holy Spirit is God, unless perhaps an impious heretic or faithless Jew, since without him neither is the sacrament of baptism completed nor is forgiveness of sins granted? Who could be so mad as to deny that he is God, when to blaspheme against him is so impious and deadly that no pardon follows the sin of the blasphemer, as our Savior declared, saying: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matthew 12)?

This Holy Spirit, I say, proceeding from the Father and promised by the Son, deigned to pour out the gifts of his glory upon Christ’s apostles, so that they might speak of his Passion and kingdom in the language of every nation. Through this gracious condescension, since the entire human race was being called to life, the whole world everywhere might hear the dispensation of God’s mysteries.

What a great miracle it was, brothers, that a Hebrew man, suddenly breaking into words that were not his own, instructed a Greek about God’s great works, taught a Roman, addressed an Egyptian, and instructed all the barbarian nations in their own languages for faith!

Therefore, beloved, let us implore the mercies of almighty God, so that we may be able to announce worthy things about God, and so that you may be able to hear and understand what is said with the reverence that is due, etc.

## SERMON LIII. On Pentecost VI

[Col. 0637]

### Editorial Notice

This is the last sermon in the Turin manuscript: homily XXVII on Pentecost. It is noted there that homilies 24, 25, and 26 are missing. It was especially pleasing to us that as many of Saint Maximus’s sermons as Muratori drew from and published from the Ambrosian manuscript have, with the authority of other manuscripts as well, been assigned by us to that same holy bishop of Turin.

### Argument

On the grace of goodness that God grants us either by creating or by regenerating us; on the conception and birth of Christ; on the Virgin Mother Mary and her husband Joseph; and on the Holy Spirit. Saint Maximus clearly and at length demonstrates that the Spirit is God and that the will of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one.

The grace of immeasurable goodness, dearest brothers, is what the almighty God has powerfully bestowed upon us either by creating us, [Col. 0637D] or mercifully granted by regenerating us. By creating us, he provided that, through a wondrous act, dust might be brought to life in man and that we—all who previously did not exist—might exist; by regenerating us, he conferred what our first nature had not given us, so that a second birth might bestow it. This second birth, through the sacraments of baptism, begets servants as sons and promises heaven to the faithful.

That first creation of human beings was indeed noble; but this subsequent one is not only nobler in the purity of its mysteries, but also heavenly through the consecration of the blessed Spirit. The former [Col. 0638C] birth receives sins; this one lays them aside. There we die by being born; here we live by dying.

Finally, so that Christ might bestow this nobility upon the human race, he accepted for our sake the indignity of a servile birth, and, although his conception was different, the manner of his birth was nevertheless similar. In that conception, although the eternal Father was present, neither was the law of giving birth changed for the Mother, nor was the newborn child deprived of the crying of infancy. The Father evidently maintained in the Son, by his own power, the strength of a twofold substance, so that, by the majesty of his power, the venerable Mother in childbirth might both conceive him as God and bear him as man.

Is it not apparent that the Son of God was conceived where, the agency of a bodily seed having ceased, a man is believed to have been formed in a virginal womb, and the one who was born is without doubt God? Miraculous was the birth of an untouched Mother, but far more miraculous was that her virginity remained after childbirth. For, strange as it may be to say, flesh born from inviolate flesh preserved [Col. 0639A] the barriers of modesty [the transmitted reading “napudoris” is uncertain; the sense appears to concern the preservation of the barriers of modesty].

These things, so holy and so magnificent, were accomplished by that God to whom all the works of heaven and earth respond according to the will of his power, and for whom doing incomprehensible things consists not in labor or activity, but in command. When he wished to give the Virgin a novel birth, he acted by the power through which he made all things from nothing. For the angel Gabriel, sent to Mary, revealed that the virginal fruitfulness that had shone upon this world was the work of God, saying to her:

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

And through a heavenly dispensation, blessed Mary, while preserving uncorrupted the inviolate seals of her undefiled womb for the venerable Joseph—always a spouse, and never a husband—gave birth not to a son but to the Lord. The angel said to Joseph:

“What is conceived in Mary is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1).

And [Col. 0639B] for this reason the angel’s voice of testimony resounded in the patriarch’s ears, lest the mind of the young man, astonished at so great a miracle, should be wounded by the stain of an evil suspicion, and lest he should suppose a woman’s fault where a saving mystery for us was being born. For, brothers, that innocent and anxious spouse could not otherwise have believed in the novelty of a fruitful womb unless an advocate sent from above had proclaimed the virginal chastity of the bride who was to give birth.

Thus, as we read, the Holy Spirit united human flesh to the Father’s Only-Begotten in the Virgin’s womb. He united it not by the skill of an artisan shaping a figure, but by the majesty of one who forms. The power and truth [535] of this new work testify that the Spirit is truly God. For how could that same Spirit be proclaimed the author of the construction of our salvation—of Christ’s conception, in which the Father was not absent, in which the Son was present, and in which our flesh was joined to divine fellowship—unless he possessed with the Father and the Son the same power in nature and communion in will? [Col. 0639C]

You see, therefore, brothers, that God’s co-worker could not be anything other than God. For the Holy Spirit, as he is, was both undivided from the Father and inseparable from the Son. With them, as the faithful statement of sacred Scripture teaches us, there is no difference in power, but a distinction in operation. For Christ said of him to his disciples:

“When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from my Father—he will testify about me” (John 15).

The Savior also said of himself:

“I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14).

“I am,” he says, “the truth.” If, then, the Son, who is truth, asserts that the Spirit is the Spirit of truth, who could deny that he is God except one who does not believe that truth comes from truth?

Therefore the true Spirit is God, whom Christ testifies, in the same confession, both to proceed from the Father and to be sent by himself. The Son of God sends the Spirit of his Father; he sends him not as one obedient to a command, but as one in agreement with the mystery. And for this reason the Spirit who proceeds from the Father is read as being sent by the Son, lest anyone should believe that he is other than the Father, or that he wills anything [536] different from what the Son wills. [Col. 0640A]

For this reason, brothers, it becomes clear without hesitation that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one will. For the Son sends what belongs to the Father, and the Father imparts what is his own, so that it may be directed by the Son.

This Spirit, therefore, performing with the Father and the Son the one sacrament of redemption, announces the majesty of Christ the sender in the languages of all nations—not rendering service to one who is superior, but indicating the authority of one who reigns together with him. For this reason he gave the apostles a variety of languages, so that through them the saving teaching of the faith might penetrate the hearing of all peoples.

Indeed, the Paraclete himself was manifold in speech, almighty in power, diverse in languages, and one in all. Every hearer marvels that the mouth of a foreign people utters a speech that is not foreign. The speaker himself is astonished that words not his own proceed from his mouth. Thus it came about that, while varied speech proclaimed one faith through many people, discordant nations were brought together into the fellowship of one faith. [Col. 0640C]

And therefore, brothers, turning away from the vanities of the world and trampling underfoot the pleasures of this exceedingly brief life, let us continually hold him in our minds and always speak of him, who has granted mortals to savor heavenly things and earthly people to speak divine things. To him be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LIV. On Pentecost VII

[Col. 0639]

### Argument

[Col. 0639C] Saint Maximus treats the same subject in both sermons: namely, that we must believe that the Son truly reached the Father, since we see the Paraclete descend upon the holy apostles. The Holy Spirit certainly descended upon them, in accordance with Christ’s promise, to teach them all truth.

It is known to you all, brothers, how great is the venerable solemnity of this day and with what rejoicing so great a festival is to be celebrated by all. For today was fulfilled that promise of our Savior in which he had said that, as he ascended into heaven, he would send the Holy Spirit upon the apostles. For he had promised:

“But when I have ascended to the Father, I will send you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, and he himself will teach you everything” (John 16).

We believe that the Son truly reached the Father when we see the Paraclete descend upon the holy apostles. We do not doubt that he reigns in heaven when we see him bestowing the most sacred gifts of the Holy Spirit on earth. Certainly the Victor now sits at the Father’s right hand, while, as Victor, he bestows gifts. Thus the Savior, victor over the devil, after his triumph enriched the disciples whom he had freed from the devil’s captivity with the blessing of the Holy Spirit.

He freed us when, by rising again himself, he closed Tartarus to us; he enriched us when, through the Paraclete, he opened heaven to us so that we might reign. Then we learned to return from death to life; now we are taught to ascend from earth to heaven, as it is written:

“He will teach you everything” (John 16).

But what does that Holy Spirit teach? Certainly he knows how to teach only what is holy. What does the Paraclete disclose to us? Precisely what the Savior says:

“I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When that Spirit of truth comes, he himself will teach you everything” (John 16).

The Paraclete is therefore a good teacher, because he teaches what Christ reserved to be said. For the Holy Spirit teaches what the Lord says he has to teach. He is plainly the best teacher, since he is the executor of the Savior’s instructions.

It is therefore necessary that the one whose teaching we see to be one with Christ’s teaching should have a nature of one substance with Christ. And therefore, dearest brothers, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of the flesh, so that we too may deserve to receive the Holy Spirit. If we now leave the world with its pleasures and desires, we shall likewise have the Paraclete, like the apostles—the Spirit of truth, whom the Father will send to us, since with God there is no partiality.

Therefore, if we strive to fulfill the law of the Lord, which is spotless and converts souls, and to carry out his commandments, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, we shall reach that eternal homeland which God himself has prepared for us. May he deign to grant this. Explicit.

## SERMON LV. On Pentecost VIII

[Col. 0641]

Today, brothers, we celebrate that most joyful solemnity on which our Lord Jesus Christ, having returned in greater glory to the Father after conquering death, granted the apostles the Holy Spirit whom he had previously promised them, with the Father’s grace bestowing this gift, so that the faith he had preached while he was previously present on earth might be strengthened and fortified by him.

On this day, therefore, that divine Paraclete descended upon the apostles, when, as was read earlier, the days of Pentecost were fulfilled and they were all united in one place with one mind. The apostles were together, then, when the Holy Spirit descended upon each of them. That divine Spirit came upon those who were of one mind; he descended upon those who were in harmony; and, as was read, the apostles were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various languages, as the Spirit granted them utterance (Acts 1).

That Spirit who filled the hearts and minds of the disciples completely cleansed them of earthly allurements. That heavenly fire consumed every evil remnant of former desire. Those tongues with which the apostles spoke when filled with the Holy Spirit signified the future Church among the nations.

“And they began to speak in various languages, as the Spirit granted them utterance.”

The apostles therefore spoke in various languages, as that Holy Spirit himself granted them utterance, so that the whole of all nations might be united in one and the same faith. For Parthians, Medes, and Elamites, and the remaining nations, as was read, hear the apostles speaking in their own languages of the mighty works of God.

[In the original, fifteen lines are missing, the text having been completely erased.]

Even if they too gather together as one on this most holy day; even if they too hear what we say, nevertheless they hear it for judgment unless they repent. For what benefit will it be to them to hear with attentive ears what they reject in their hearts, and to celebrate with us the day of that same Holy Spirit whose light they turn away from?

But you, brothers, members of Christ’s body, living and genuine shoots of unity, celebrate this day always [lacuna]. For even now what was foreshadowed in those days, when the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles, is fulfilled in you. For just as then whoever received that Spirit descending upon him could speak in the languages of all, even if he were one solitary person, so now throughout all nations the truth itself speaks in the languages of all. Explicit.

## SECOND CLASS. SERMONS ON THE SAINTS

[Col. 0641]

## SERMON LVI. On the feast of Saint Agnes

### Admonition

[Col. 0641]

537 Tillemont believes that this panegyric should be taken away from our Maximus, and he brings together several arguments for his opinion. First, he appeals to the silence of Baronius and the Bollandists, who, when discussing the martyrdom of Saint Agnes, did not mention this sermon. Next, he uses the testimony of the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, who report that they found this sermon attributed to Saint Ambrose in three manuscript codices and published it under his name as an unpublished work. Third, he says that its style differs from Maximian purity and elegance. Finally, he complains of the barbarous character of certain words, for which he blames the author of the discourse; he therefore concludes that the little work was more probably composed in later centuries.

I answer these points briefly. Regarding the first, I say that, according to the canons of criticism, a negative argument proves nothing. Baronius, who began writing the Annals of the Church only around the year 1560, may have been unaware of this sermon of Maximus, published at Cologne in 1535 together with the others; just as the Benedictine monks who edited Saint Ambrose, much later than Baronius, were unaware of that edition. The same Cologne printing escaped the Bollandists, although they had devoted themselves to this field; consequently it is not surprising that they remained silent about Saint Maximus among the Fathers who discussed Agnes’s martyrdom.

As for the three codices on which the Benedictine monks relied when attributing this sermon to Ambrose, I say this: six codices support me—namely, Vat. 1025, p. 132; 169, p. 115; and 174, p. 139, of the former library of the magistrates of the metropolitan church of Florence; IV Plut. 33, left-hand part, of the former library of the Minor Conventuals, now in the Laurentiana; and, in addition, codex Lucensis 85 and Casinensis 144, p. 283. All of these explicitly inscribe Saint Maximus as the author.

Moreover, all collectors of homilies and sermons up to the present have assigned this discourse to our holy bishop. Ruinartus, in his admonition to the Acts of the Martyrdom of Saint Agnes, p. 402 of the Verona edition of 1731, says this about Maximus’s homily in praise of Saint Agnes:

“Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, also sets forth her martyrdom at greater length in the homily he wrote in her praise.”

Tillemont’s second objection therefore falls entirely. Nor is the third any stronger. For, in our judgment, the difference of style that Tillemont says he observed does not exist. The discourse is adorned and resplendent with the same qualities that anyone may frequently observe in the other works. As for the barbarous words that Tillemont brings forward last, I shall say only this: Maximus used only the word *subarro*, which Jerome had already used. In all other respects he used pure Latin. Therefore, if no one will accuse Jerome of writing barbarously because he occasionally used words that were less purely Latin, Saint Maximus should not be charged with the same fault. Once Tillemont’s arguments have been examined, I believe there is no reason why this sermon should be taken away from Maximus.

### Argument

[Col. 0643A] Saint Maximus extols the blessed Agnes wonderfully in praise because, following the footsteps of the Virgin Mother, she reached the heavenly bridal chamber by despising the riches of the world, abhorring the desires of the flesh, and loving the beauty of Christ alone.

Since throughout the whole world Mary’s virginal flower weaves unfading crowns and preserves, with stainless devotion, the scepter-bearing court of chastity, integrity persevered all the way to victory, so that among girls she seized the trophy of holiness and, following the footsteps of the Virgin Mother, reached the heavenly bridal chamber.

Hence Agnes declares that she has been betrothed with the ring of faith, and cries out [Note: [Col. 0643C] Cod. Vat. 1267, under the name of Ambrose, “that she has been inscribed for the love of Christ.” Galesinius reads, “bound by love of the bridegroom.”] that she is bound by love.

O virgin worthy of imitation by virgins, to whom you have given an example of love! [Note: [Col. 0643C] Galesinius likewise reads, “You gave them the example of your love.” [Col. 0643D] Cod. Vat., “You gave them the example of your love.”] O what a holy answer you gave to virginal hearts by despising the riches of the world, abhorring the desires of the flesh, [Col. 0643B] and loving Christ’s beauty alone!

Come to the girl, girls, and learn, in the years of childhood, 538 what flames she kindled in her heart for the love of Christ [Note: [Col. 0643D] Galesinius likewise reads, “kindled flames.”]. She says that she preserves fidelity for her lover and desires the body only of the one who, for the love [Note: [Col. 0643D] Galesinius: “of all human beings.”] of all, did not refuse death’s destruction.

Learn, virgins of Christ, of the love burning in this girl, and of her rejection of all the riches of the world as though they were dung. For this reason the examples of the saints are handed down in writing, so that each person, according to sex and [Note: [Col. 0643D] Cod. Vat. 174, “according to the suitability of one’s years,” etc.] age, may maintain the proper measure of his or her vocation; and so that, just as virgins through a virgin, married women through married women may strive, for the love of Christ, to overcome the world, rejecting by their resistance of spirit the world’s sweetness and not rejecting its austerities, and may attain everlasting pleasures [Col. 0643C] and eternal joys.

In saying this, we do not disparage the chaste relations of married couples, but adorn the perseverance of virgins. Virginity is not to be placed above evil things, but is to be preferred to the best things. For what is purer than the pure and holier than the holy does not need to be praised by condemning evil things.

Let holy marriages therefore follow the wives of the patriarchs, established in religion and instructed by the divine [539] Scriptures, and let wives imitate Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Hannah, Susanna, and Zipporah. But let the virgins of Christ follow the Virgin Mother alone [Note: [Col. 0643D] Galesinius omits “of the Virgin”] of the virginal Light.

Agnes, her blessed attendant, raised up in herself a great example of chastity: she preferred virginity to life, expelled every earthly love through heavenly love, seized the trophy of Christ’s cross, and fought and conquered, armed more with faith than with iron, against lust as well as every form of torture.

Finally, she looks upon the one who flatters her and refuses him; upon the one who threatens her and despises him; she watches the fire and laughs.
