[Note: [Col. 0643D] Galesinius: “she kindles the fire and looks upon it.” Cod. 4 of the Minor Convent of the Holy Cross: “she attends to the fire and smiles.”] She does not know how to love anything that passes away. And because she loves virginity exceedingly, she fears neither mockery, nor flames, nor punishments, nor executioners; finally, she did not even fear the sword [Col. 0644B] [Note: [Col. 0643D] Thus also cod. 4 of the Minor Holy Cross.]

of the raging persecutor.

The virgin is compelled to receive bodily adornments, but she refuses, because she had already received the adornments of the mind; [Note: [Col. 0644C] Codices 174 and Vat. likewise read, “and because she did not strive to please men by the elegance of the human body,” etc.] and because she did not strive to please men through the elegance of the human body, fearing to displease the Lord through the ugliness of her soul, she gave inwardly, through faith, brightness to her mind and beauty to her soul, which she cultivated. And insofar as she knew that this made her soul beautiful, [Note: [Col. 0644C] Galesinius likewise reads, “so much did she blush in her body” [Col. 0644D] “that she was beautiful.” Cod. Vat. likewise reads, “so much did she blush in her face.”] so much did she blush at being beautiful in the flesh; and she strove to displease carnal people in the sight of the flesh to the same extent that she devoted herself to pleasing Christ [Note: [Col. 0644D] Cod. Vat., “to which Christ instructed her”] and his angels.

The young man, rejected by the girl, is thrown into confusion. Believing that he could win her favor with gifts, he brings gold, doubled heaps of gems, garments, and costly estates. [Note: [Col. 0644D] Galesinius reads, “precious rewards, not estates.”] But because the love of Christ has no price in money, [Col. 0644C] the most sacred virgin remained steadfast in her station even to the shedding of blood, since Christ had betrothed her with his own blood.

The wealth therefore returns to the lustful man, while the unshaken virginity once offered to Christ endures. Learn, virgins of Christ, the examples of a girl’s proper conduct; reject with your whole attention the little gifts offered by men under the guise of piety, and refuse them with every joy, as though from the bite of a rabid dog.

[Note: [Col. 0644D] Galesinius: “From the one from whom you receive, fear God; do not accept what would make you love the world. The readings of codices 174 and 4 of the Minor Holy Cross, however, are: “From the one from whom you have not received what makes you fear God, do not accept what would make you love the world.”]

From one from whom you have not [540] received what makes you fear God, do not accept what would make you love the world. Take it, [Col. 0645A] take it, virgin—but take what advances eternal love. Whenever you have received wealth from a man, receive it in such a way that you recognize yourself as Christ’s bride. [Note: [Col. 0645C] In Galesinius and in the cited codices, “take it” is not repeated.] He sees inwardly in your mind what you are doing and observes how eagerly you accompany his virgins. [Note: [Col. 0645C] The two codices cited immediately above: “Receive it in such a way that you recognize yourself as Christ’s bride.”]

See, therefore, how Agnes follows Mary through reproaches. She could fear no punishment at all, for even the brothel of disgrace became for her a place of prayer. Where the devil had prepared for her the shame of corruption, there the Lord caused her to receive the crown and palm of her virginity. But this is to conquer enemies in their own dwelling: the virgin was led captive into the inner chambers of the king of lust, yet she bound the very king who had taken her captive and emerged victorious with the triumph of virginity. [Note: [Col. 0645C] Cod. Vat.: “to the innermost chambers of the king of lust, to conquer the very king who had taken her captive, and to emerge with the example of virginity after his defeat. For…” [Col. 0645D]]

For the one who had held her was himself held; the one who had dragged her was himself dragged; the one who had thought he would kill her was himself killed.

Finally, to prove that the devil was then defeated by the virgin, let us recall what happened to the young man whom the enemy had armed against Agnes’s childhood, so that he would have her dragged naked [Note: [Col. 0645D] Cod. 4 of the Minor Holy Cross: “have her dragged naked through the streets to the brothel,” etc.] through the crowd to the brothel, while, at the herald’s proclamation, the leader invited the people to lust.

No one can doubt that this leader was the devil’s agent; and once the leader was defeated, it is known that the people were overcome as well. Once the people and their leader had been overcome, it is clear to all that the tyrant himself was held captive. It is established that the devil was defeated whenever he took up arms against the virgin. [Note: [Col. 0645D] Cod. Vat.: “whenever he seized them.”]

The virgin was stripped, but covered by her hair; and, naked before evil men, [Note: [Col. 0645D] Cod. 4 of the Minor Holy Cross and Galesinius: “was clothed.”] she was clothed by good angels. Condemned to a brothel of disgrace, she appeared in the embrace of chastity.

A place that had belonged to lost souls became an oratory of angels; and where chastity had always suffered shipwreck, there virginity was crowned. Finally, the crowds whom the herald had invited to lust, the virgin won over to chastity. Those whom the devil brought to her defiled, she sent away cleansed. For they entered one by one, each supporting [541] the other’s entrance, and, when they believed that the one who emerged was not clean, he showed himself to be unclean. [Note: [Col. 0645D] Cod. Vat. likewise reads, “while they believed the one who emerged to be unclean, he showed himself clean.”]

Yet the one who had entered for lust was held there by the virgin’s merits so that he might adore the Lord; and he left as God’s servant, though he had entered as the devil’s servant. As many became worshipers of Christ as the devil had thought he would find corruptors of the virgin.

The young man therefore remained [Note: [Col. 0645D] Cod. Vat. likewise: “who had been the author of this test.”] who had initiated this trial. He had thought that he would overcome the virgin’s defender; but when he challenged the splendor [Note: [Col. 0645D] Cod. 174: “when he boldly challenged him.”] to combat, he lost the life he seemed to possess and found the death he had sought. [The transmitted reading “ad uxum” is uncertain; the context appears to concern a challenge to combat.] Laughter was followed by tears, and lamentations brought an end to insults. [Note: [Col. 0646C] Cod. 174: “lamentation puts an end to it.”]

The virgin looked upon the grieving judge and heard him, now pleading, whom she had previously despised when he threatened her. Immediately, when she began to pray for the dead man, she raised from the dead the one who had been sentenced to death, restoring him alive; and she summoned to joy the one who had been plunged into mourning.

For the one who had died incestuous rose chaste; and the one who had been a persecutor of chastity became its preacher.

At this, the sacrilegious were thrown into confusion in the temples. Not fearing Christ who performed these miracles, [Note: [Col. 0646D] Galesinius: “they tremble at him performing these miracles; they stir up a sedition,” etc.] they stirred up a revolt of the ignoble mob, so that reason—which urged an end to the sedition—might, driven out by shouting, find no place in people’s minds.

The father of the resurrected son departed in grief and, as it is read, abandoned him amid the raging crowds.

Thus shrill flames were prepared for the virgin’s body, [Note: [Col. 0646D] Cod. 4 of the Minor Holy Cross: “they prepared.”] but the body that had overcome the fires of lust found refreshment [542] amid the flames. She who had entered the fires so as to burn began, through holy virginity, to grow cold, [Col. 0646B] so that virginity might learn that flames and fires could in no way master it. [Note: [Col. 0646D] The same codex 4 of the Minor Holy Cross: “so that virginity might learn that flames and fires could in no way…”]

Do not suppose that those whom the fire consumed for the name of Christ perished. For when you read that Elijah was carried away by fire, and that the three boys were not consumed in the midst of the fires, [Note: [Col. 0646D] Galesinius reads, “in the midst of the flames.”] or when you recall that Lawrence was consumed on the gridiron [Col. 0646C] [Note: [Col. 0646D] Cod. 4 of the Minor Holy Cross: “or when you recall that Lawrence, placed upon the gridiron, was consumed.” Galesinius instead: “or when you recall Lawrence being roasted on the gridiron.”], and recognize that Agnes, like Thecla, escaped the globes of flame, do not suspect in these cases that there was any difference of faith. For one faith exercised God’s saints in their passion and made both victorious through different kinds of glory.

The martyr who was consumed rejoices, and the victor who escaped rejoices. God made Isaiah, who was cut apart, a martyr; and he displayed Daniel, who despised the fury and bites of lions, as a most proven confessor. [Note: [Col. 0646D] Galesinius: “And Isaiah, being cut apart, made himself a martyr, and Daniel… despising [lacuna], presented the most proven confessor of God. Our text, however, agrees with both cod. 174 and cod. 4 of the Minor Holy Cross, as well as with Cod. Vat. 1267.] By this he showed that both were victors over the devil: one dies and triumphs; the other escapes and reigns.

[Col. 0647A] Come now, virgin, to the bridal chamber you sought, and for love of the bridegroom receive the sword of the executioner, so that spotless virginity may prove you Christ’s bride and approved confession may mark you as a martyr.

[Note: [Col. 0647D] Cod. Vat. 1267: “Happy is the company of virgins whose desire is to follow the crown of your confession in heaven. Those who overcome the enemy in the world together with you…”]

Happy is the company of virgins whose desire is to follow the path of your confession. [Col. 0648A] For those who overcome the enemy in the world together with you will have a crown in heaven. For just as eternal reward appeared to you when you followed Mary’s footsteps, [Note: [Col. 0647D] Galesinius reads, “so we believe that eternal joys must not be denied to those who imitate you.”] so we believe that eternal joys must not be denied to those who imitate you.

[Note: [Col. 0647D] Cod. 4 of the Minor Holy Cross and Galesinius: “Therefore, O radiant one for Christ, beautiful to the Son of God and pleasing to all angels and archangels, we beseech you with whatever prayers we can, that you deign to remember us; that he may grant us forgiveness of sins who gave you the palm of all your labors, he who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit. For to him belong honor, praise, glory, and power for ever and ever. Amen.” [Col. 0648D]]

[Note: [Col. 0647D] We have followed not the edition of Galesinius but the Paris edition of the Maurists, which we know to be more accurate, having collated the Laurentian codices mentioned above, from which we extracted certain variants.]

## SERMON LVII. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist I

[Col. 0647]

### Admonition

[Col. 0647]

543 Learned writers infer that the institution in the Church of a feast in honor of the nativity of Saint John the Baptist is extremely ancient from Augustine’s Sermon 292, delivered on the feast of the same holy Forerunner, where he says that he received it from the tradition of his ancestors. From this passage of Augustine it may be inferred that the feast of Saint John’s nativity began to be celebrated long before the Council of Agde, held at the beginning of the sixth century, as Thomassinus judged in book V, *On the Celebration of Festivals*, chapter 5.

That this day was regarded by the Church among the principal celebrations is attested by Saint Bernard in Letter 174:

“Although she indicates and proclaims the death, not the birth, of the other saints to be precious, by a singular exception she grants this day the joys of a festival and venerates his nativity, concerning which it is uniquely read, when announced by an angel: ‘Many will rejoice at his birth.’”

Muratorius first transcribed and published this sermon from an Ambrosian codex.

### Argument

[Col. 0647B] Saint Maximus writes that we should rejoice at the nativity of John the Baptist because he came, predestined by God, to proclaim the joy of the human race and the gladness of heaven. He adds several things about John’s parents, Zechariah and Elizabeth.

The character of our religion and devotion requires, brothers, that today we rejoice over the nativity of blessed John the Baptist, who, predestined by God to proclaim the joy of the human race and the gladness of heaven, came into the world. This is the one from whose mouth the world heard, in a new voice, that our Redeemer was present, that the Lamb of God was present. He was sent through an angel to be born to parents who had despaired of offspring, as both a witness and an unmistakable messenger of so great a mystery.

Who would not more wisely believe that he announced divine mysteries, when one sees that heavenly care was at work in his conception? Although he was not yet a son and was still being formed in the womb, the privilege of the grace granted to him nevertheless filled his mother’s womb with eternal joy; and the blessed mother recognized the happiness of her long-sterile womb before his birth.

For, as it is written, Elizabeth said to Mary:

“Behold, as the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy. And how has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1).

It is not surprising, beloved, that this old woman was endowed with the gift of foreknowledge, since she was to bear the herald of the Most High God. Her sterility [544] [Col. 0648B] made her more glorious: while her fruitfulness was delayed, through the gift of one child she obtained the honor of an entire posterity.

While she had groaned as though fruitless before her husband into extreme old age, she suddenly gave birth not merely to a son for herself but to a messenger of eternal salvation for the whole world—and to such a messenger that, before he emerged from the womb, by the privilege of his future ministry, he already imparted a prophetic spirit to his mother’s tongue and, through the power of the name foretold by the angel, opened the mouth of his father Zechariah, which unbelief had closed.

Zechariah had fallen silent, not so that he would remain mute, but so that, when the use of speech was divinely restored to him, he might offer heavenly testimony to the infant through prophecy. The priest who spoke to the whole people therefore became mute so that, since the priest’s silence was public, [Col. 0648C] the mystery of the sacred birth might come to the knowledge of the entire people and no one would dare not to believe it.

The father, who had already doubted that he would be born, suffered the penalty of his silence. For the Evangelist says of him:

“He was not himself the light, but came to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him” (John 1).

He was not the light, indeed, but he was wholly in the light, since he deserved to bear witness to the true light. And therefore, brothers, let us celebrate the day of his nativity in honor of blessed John with every exultation. He recognized the eternal light of heaven, which came to dispel the world’s darkness, before everyone else, and he was the first to reveal it.

## SERMON LVIII. On the Same Saint John the Baptist II

[Col. 0647]

### Admonition

[Col. 0647]

545 Taken from an Ambrosian codex and published by Muratorius in volume IV of the *Anecdota*.

### Argument

[Col. 0647D] John, sent by God as the messenger of Christ’s coming and of his saving restoration, was to be consecrated to every mystery from the moment of his birth. Saint Maximus discusses Zechariah’s silence and the power of John before his birth.

[Col. 0648D] By many great virtues, dearest brothers, our God and Lord confirms the faith and hearts of the peoples who flock to him. He has made not only the life of his chosen ones worthy of praise but also their birth wondrous, as we have learned from the Gospel reading concerning blessed John the Baptist. Such a privilege was granted to him at birth that, before he was born, his coming was foretold by prophetic and Gospel voices. For how could he fail to be consecrated by every mystery, when he came to reveal the Lord of the sacraments for the redemption of a failing world?

He was conceived, as you heard, by a most righteous aged man and a barren woman, so that, through the manifold hopelessness surrounding the child’s birth, both the glory of the one born and the power of the working God might appear all the more magnificent. This is the one of whom we read that it was foretold through the Prophet: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Isaiah 40; Luke 3). And therefore the priest Zechariah fell silent under the sentence of the rebuking angel, because, troubled by the greatness of the promise, he did not believe that he would become the father of the announced voice.

We clearly perceive that this happened through a great dispensation of God, so that the whole Jewish people, while asking about the cause of such silence, might learn the truth of the child’s generation, and that the silence of the high priest might make public the secret of the holy conception. Silence was therefore imposed upon the father, so that the herald of the heavenly Word might be born through silence, although deeper mysteries are disclosed in this event. For in that silence of the priest, as the grace of Christ was approaching, the severity of the ancient Law also fell silent, and every rite of carnal sacrifices ceased to speak. Yet, so that nothing in blessed John might be without wonder, the child who was born released the father’s tongue, which had been bound when he was conceived. Thus the most blessed old man, who had lost the use of speech amid the observances of ancient traditions, proclaimed new mysteries with a voice renewed through his son.

[Col. 0650A] Nor is it surprising that such astounding miracles occurred through the merits of the one whom so great a grace of God accompanied that, while still within his mother’s womb, he rejoiced at the coming of Christ, surpassing the measure of human conception. For Elizabeth said to Mary, as we heard: “Behold, when the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy” (Luke 1). Even while he was being formed, such power was already at work in him that, as a sign of the heavenly mystery which he sensed he would proclaim to the human race, he anticipated his own birth by prophetic indications.

Why, then, do we wonder that John recognized the approaching Christ without any hesitation when Christ came to his baptism, if, before he himself had yet emerged into the light, he perceived him present in the Virgin’s womb? What joy had stirred him within his mother’s womb he later attested with the clearest voice, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). For the sake of this voice, dearest brothers, all those sacraments that you heard about were set forth beforehand in John; for this reason his glorious conception and his praiseworthy life were prepared, so that the world might hear from so holy a mouth the voice of its absolution.

How beautifully he named Christ our Lord by the title “Lamb,” by whose blood alone God was to be appeased and the whole of mortal humanity redeemed! It is therefore fitting, brothers, that we should always rejoice with the most devout celebrations in honor of so great a man, who by one united testimony both disclosed the presence of the Lord and prophesied the remedies of his approaching coming.

## SERMON LIX. On the Same Birth of Saint John the Baptist III

[Col. 0649]

### ADMONITION

[Col. 0649]

547 This sermon has been published here for the first time from an old manuscript of the library of Saint Emmeram.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0649C] On the meeting and greeting of blessed Mary the Virgin and Elizabeth; on John, who was called by Isaiah “the voice of one crying in the wilderness.” What it means to prepare the way of the Lord and make his paths straight.

The venerable feast of blessed John the Baptist is celebrated today by the faithful throughout the whole world. By prophetic dignity he merited that the posterity of the faithful should not be silent concerning his praises, since his very birth is said to be of God. Such a special election shone forth in him that, born of most righteous parents, he was found worthy to announce the coming of the Lord, the Savior of this world, before he had even begun to be born.

Finally, when holy Elizabeth, an aged woman who had despaired of having a son because of her barrenness and because her husband was already old, conceived after the angel’s announcement, the most chaste virgin Mary visited her. Mary too had conceived the Savior in her womb from the Holy Spirit, at the angel’s command. At the very meeting of their greeting Elizabeth said: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. For behold, when the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy” (Luke 1).

O how worthy and blessed was the meeting of these holy women! O how holy was the greeting, when the Virgin mother of the Lord and Savior visited the mother of the Forerunner! O how blessed were the mothers and most holy nurses of the most blessed children! O glorious office of the herald, who, while still enclosed within his mother’s womb, revealed in prophetic spirit the future Savior of the world, whom he could not yet reveal in speech. Nature under the old Law could not preserve its order among mortals, when, through the new grace of divinity, a new mystery for human salvation was being prepared.

[Col. 0650D] This is the John who was called by the prophet Isaiah “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Isaiah 40). He is rightly called a voice, because, when the herald’s proclamation thundered, mortal humanity—which had long been deaf to every good sound—began to hear the mysteries of human redemption.

Let us therefore, dearest brothers, hear what the Savior’s messenger proclaimed for the benefit of us all: “Prepare,” he says, “the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Luke 3). Truly blessed John was worthy to direct the crookedness of those living wickedly into straight paths. For what is it to prepare the way of the Lord except to prepare, for the Judge coming from heaven, a dwelling of a simple heart, with the breast cleansed from vices through confession and repentance? What is it to make straight the paths of our God except to fortify for ourselves such ways through our actions that the merciful Lord, coming to us, may delight to walk along them?

He prepares the way of his Lord who, rejecting the desires of his luxuriant flesh, clings solely to the Lord’s commands with the strength of his mind and girds himself with chastity and self-restraint. He prepares an excellent way for God who, resisting evil thoughts, continually strives to walk before God with a pure heart and chaste body.

Therefore, brothers, as long as we remain attached to the desires of the flesh and earthly cravings, we do not prepare the way of the Lord according to the prophetic admonitions. For this reason, returning to John’s command of baptism, let us prepare within ourselves a way worthy of the Lord through fitting repentance, the most truthful confession of the evils we have committed, almsgiving, diligent care for the poor, and the other works of justice and piety. Then, seeing in us the paths of good will, may the Lord deign to lead his little sheep—already worn out by many labors and tribulations—from the distressing life of this age with him into eternal joys. Thus, just as we rejoice today in the birth of the Lord’s Forerunner, may we also rejoice in our reconciliation with God the Father, through the working and granting of this grace by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the coeternal Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LX. Also on the Birth of Saint John the Baptist IV

[Col. 0651]

### ADMONITION

[Col. 0651]

549 This sermon too is attributed to Saint Maximus in the aforementioned manuscript of Saint Emmeram; it is also found in Laurentianus 39, Pluteus XVII, in the quarto manuscript of the library formerly belonging to Holy Cross Minor, and in manuscript 174 of the library formerly belonging to the officials of the major church of Florence, folio 224 verso.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0651B] On John the Baptist, greater than the other prophets, born of aged parents; on the priest Zechariah, who fell silent while serving in the division of Abijah; on John’s austerity of life, his baptism, and his martyrdom; and on how the Forerunner’s solemn feast should fittingly be celebrated.

The holy birth of the Lord’s Forerunner, John the Baptist, which the holy universal Church celebrates today, had previously been foretold in many ways by the holy prophets of the Lord, dearest brothers. We must understand that this was accomplished by the providence of divine mercy, so that the one who was to be greater than the other prophets might also be honored with a greater prophetic spirit than they:

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Manuscript 39 cited above: “might be adorned.”]

For the office of a prophet is to announce what is to come, but not also to point it out. John, therefore, was greater than the other prophets because he both announced that the Lord and Savior would come and showed that he was already present.

For this reason, just as the Lord’s coming had previously been prophesied, so too had the birth of his Forerunner been foretold. The one who had come to announce new things and preach repentance was thus not to be rejected by anyone’s disbelief as a proclamation unheard of through the ages; rather, the office of his preaching was to become more credible to all who heard it.

[Note: [Col. 0651D] The same manuscript 39: “For it was worthy that …”]

For it was fitting that the one who had come not only to announce but also to point out the King of all kings and Lord of lords should be born by a mode of generation unlike that of the others. No one doubts that in the aged the desire of the flesh had by then grown cold:

[Note: [Col. 0651D] The same manuscript 39: “There is no doubt that in the aged the desire of the flesh had by then grown cold.”]

Nor could children be generated beyond the sixtieth year of age. He was born of aged parents already freed from every wantonness of the flesh, as the sacred Gospel text proves:

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Manuscript 174: “Nor can children be begotten beyond the sixtieth year of age. John, however, was born beyond the measure of nature from aged parents already free from every impulse of the flesh. For Abijah was high priest in the time of King David. [Col. 0652D] For when David, etc., the construction of the Temple, etc.”] “There was,” it says, “in the days of Herod, king of Judea”—that is, as the time of Christ’s birth was approaching—“a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah” (Luke 1).

But first we must speak of Abijah, and afterward follow the order we have begun. When David was dealing with and arranging the construction of the Temple and its service, he divided the entire lineage of Aaron’s sons into twenty-four divisions, and from each division he selected one chief priest, so that they might minister in turn according to their order in the sanctuary of the Temple.

[Note: [Col. 0652D] The same manuscript 174: “might minister in the sacrifice of the Temple; with this provision, however, that if any of the chief priests died, they would choose the best successor to the priesthood from that division.” The reading of manuscript 39 Laurentianus conforms to this.]

In that division this Abijah, from whose division and lineage Zechariah descended, was found placed eighth. Zechariah’s wife was from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. “They were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without blame. And they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and they were both advanced in years.”

It happened that Zechariah entered the sanctuary according to the order of his division to offer incense, and suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared to him, saying: “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.”

[Note: [Col. 0652D] Manuscript 39 reads: “It happened that, when Zechariah had entered the sanctuary in the order of his division to offer incense, suddenly an angel appeared to him.”]

When Zechariah heard this, he trembled. Since he was already old and his wife was ninety years old, he did not believe, because of their age, that what the angel had truthfully promised could happen. Because he did not believe, he remained mute until the eighth day after John’s birth.

Here it must plainly be understood that John was brought into being by his father’s entreaty, not by his mother’s desire: against the impossibility of the body and the barrenness of the womb, Elizabeth’s womb swelled through Zechariah’s prayers, and she conceived—not by nature but by grace.

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Manuscripts 174 and 39: “and she conceives—not by nature but by grace was he born, so that what the body’s members could not offer, the grace of the Savior might grant. In …”]

[Note: [Col. 0653] That is, not through the customary powers of nature but through the effect of heavenly blessing.]

John’s conception in his mother’s womb occurred in the seventh month, at the autumnal equinox. The conception of the Lord and Savior in the womb of the Virgin mother occurred in the first month of the following year, at the vernal equinox.

O herald of the Lord and Savior—how wondrously born, how born even of righteous parents! What the body’s members could not offer, the grace of the Savior had granted. He who made the barren mother fertile also loosened the tongue of the mute father, and he immediately burst forth in praise of the Savior.

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Manuscripts 174 and 39: “so that he might immediately break forth in praise of the Savior.”]

Born of righteous parents, he also demonstrated the practice of righteousness in himself. He who had come to prepare the way of the Lord in the hearts of the faithful rightly preached that sinners should also practice repentance. The austerity of life that he preached to others he demonstrated in his own conduct: “His garments were of camel’s hair, and a leather belt was around his loins; his food was locusts and wild honey. He did not drink wine or strong drink, and he ate nothing unclean all the days of his life” (Mark 1).

In the thirtieth year after his birth he began to baptize those who came to him and to preach to the people the baptism of repentance, so that through repentance and confession of sins they might become worthy to receive the remission of sins. Although he could not grant this through his own baptism, he nevertheless preached that Christ the Lord and Savior was soon to come to us. Of him John himself, all who believe in him, and those baptized in his name were to receive not only remission of sins but also eternal life.

Why, then, did John baptize, when he could not grant remission? It was so that he might preserve the order of Christ’s foretelling. Just as he preceded the Lord and Savior in birth and in the office of preaching, so too he would precede Christ’s baptism with his own baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Manuscripts 174 and 39: “the order of his foretelling, and so forth.”]

Through his preaching many were converted to the Lord, repenting of their sins and believing that, if Christ should ever come—the one John proclaimed as destined to come—they would receive remission of sins and eternal life.

[Col. 0653D] And therefore many who came to John’s baptism came to hear the word of salvation.

[Col. 0654A] Many also came to be healed of their illnesses, because John performed many signs and healed the sick; and so, when he performed so many signs, many believed that he was the Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0653D] Manuscripts 39 and 174: “many were also healed of their illnesses, because John performed many signs and healed the sick; and so, when he performed so many signs, many …”]

To these, however, he said: “I am not the Christ, but I am the Forerunner of Christ.”

Likewise, in the thirtieth year of Christ’s birth, Christ and John both came to the Jordan, and Christ was baptized by John—not because he himself needed baptism for any sin, but so that John might baptize him, and so that Christ, through his own baptism, might both sanctify water for us and give everyone an example of baptism, without which no one can be saved. It was also so that no one, however rich or powerful, might be too proud to be baptized by a servant, when he heard that Christ had been baptized by his servant John.

When Jesus had been baptized, as soon as he rose from the water, the heavens were opened to him, and the Holy Spirit came and remained upon him in the form of a dove. The Father’s voice was heard from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Luke 3).

When Saint John saw and heard this, he immediately pointed out the Lord with his finger to the crowd that was present, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

[Note: [Col. 0654D] Manuscripts 174 and 39: “immediately pointed out the Lord with his finger to the crowd that was present.”]

“Behold the one whom all the prophets foretold as coming; behold the one I promised to you, through whom you may receive not only remission of sins but also eternal life and immortality, and likewise eternal joy and blessedness, if you believe in him.”

[Note: [Col. 0654D] The same manuscript 29: “Therefore, through such deeds …”]

While blessed John was shining forth through such deeds, the aforementioned King Herod took the wife of his brother Philip and joined her to himself in marriage. When blessed John rebuked him for this, Herod had John beheaded, and he happily completed his martyrdom.

Therefore, dearest brothers, if we wish worthily to celebrate the solemn feast of so holy a Forerunner of the Lord, we must adorn ourselves with the merits of holy good works: with fasting and chastity, self-restraint, humility of life, gentleness and sobriety, vigils and prayers, generosity in almsgiving,

[Note: [Col. 0654D] Manuscripts 174 and 39: “in repentance.”]

patience and confession of crimes, and every diligent good work.

[Note: [Col. 0654D] The same manuscripts: “let us mortify.”]

We must mortify the desires of the flesh and become worthy to save our souls in eternal life, with blessed John assisting us by his holy prayers and our Lord Jesus Christ helping us toward every good endeavor. He, with the coeternal Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXI. Also on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist V

[Col. 0653]

### ADMONITION

[Col. 0653]

553 This excellent sermon, indeed, is ascribed to Saint Maximus in the three manuscripts we have seen: manuscript 174, formerly of the library of the officials of the metropolitan church of Florence; Laurentianus 39, Pluteus XVII; and Vatican manuscript 1060, page 42.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0655A] Anyone meditating on the birth of John the Baptist immediately encounters the birth of Christ. John did not require circumcision in order to escape original sin. How is John the Baptist not surpassed by anyone born of woman? Further praise of John concerning Elijah and Elisha, from the mouth of the highest Truth.

Today’s feast, beloved, conspicuous throughout the whole world, illumines our minds with the brighter radiance of a certain new light, inviting us to recall both the beginning of our redemption and the arising of the true light. For who, while meditating on John’s birth, does not immediately encounter Christ’s birth? Especially since there was no other reason why John should be born of an aged father and a barren mother except that, wondrously born, he should precede the one born uniquely:

the friend should precede the Bridegroom, the servant the Lord, the voice the Word, the lamp the Sun, the herald the Judge, and the one saved the Savior.

John himself also bears witness that this was the reason for his coming—not that he should come simply, but that he should precede the Lord as a sign of his manifestation. “After me,” he says, “comes a man who was made before me, because he was before me, and I did not know him. But so that he might be manifested in Israel, for this reason I came baptizing with water” (John 1).

He preceded Christ in being born, preaching, baptizing, dying, and finally descending into the underworld. Thus he preceded the Lord, and he preceded himself.

Before he was conceived in the womb, disbelief closed his father’s mouth; before he could speak, he wondrously opened it through the expression of his name. Clearly, although he could not yet bring forth words for human beings, he could announce through his leaping the hidden King of heaven in the Virgin’s maternal womb. For the Holy Spirit, who animated him before he drew the breath of life, also filled the dwelling of maternal modesty in which he lived.

Hence Elizabeth said: “Behold, when the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy” (Luke 1).

Here it must be asked how the Holy Spirit could pour his gifts into him when, according to the order of human condition, he still existed conceived in iniquities and had not yet dissolved the bond of original sin by receiving the circumcision prescribed by the Law. For the divine voice says through Moses: “The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised—that soul shall perish from his people,”

[Note: [Col. 0655D] The Vatican manuscript adds: “because he has broken my covenant.”]

“because he has broken my covenant” (Genesis VII).

But it must be noted that the grace of the Holy Spirit is not constrained by the Law or held by the bond of necessity. Rather, just as he breathes where he wills, so he freely distributes his gifts to whomever he wills. He also inspired the centurion Cornelius before he received the washing of baptism; and upon certain Gentiles, while Peter was speaking, the Spirit not only fell, as Scripture testifies (Acts 10), but also instructed them to speak in tongues.

What, then, is surprising if the Holy Spirit filled blessed John before any remedy prescribed by the Law, when divine providence established him as a kind of boundary of the Law and the prophets and of the whole Old Testament—and, so to speak, an impassable limit? For, as the Truth says, “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke 16).

This John received circumcision in his flesh together with the Lord, but by receiving it he brought it to its conclusion. Therefore, although he shone forth as the herald and magnificent announcer of the new grace, he did not need circumcision in order to escape original sin; divine election raised him above the Law and above the order of human condition.

He was also granted the glory of so great an honor that the very Mother of God was present at his birth, and the Creator of the world dedicated the beginning of his hidden life in the womb by his presence. The evangelist Luke bears witness to this when he says: “Mary remained with her”—that is, with Elizabeth—“about three months, and she returned to her own home” (Luke 1).

From the conception of the Lord to the birth of blessed John there are three months. Mary therefore did not wish to depart until she had faithfully attended the aged woman in childbirth and she, who bore the King in the palace of her body, might see the herald go before him.

Blessed is the birth received by that light which illuminates every person coming into this world.

But as we speak of these things, a question suddenly arises that may not without reason seem to introduce doubt. The Lord testifies: “Among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist” (Luke 7). He excluded one who was greater; he did not deny one who was equal.

This is why the angel said to Zechariah: “He will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1). John therefore appears equal to Elijah, in whose spirit and power he is said to come. Especially since the Truth itself says elsewhere: “Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but they did to him whatever they wished; and if you wish to know, he is John” (Matthew 17).

But, on the other hand, it occurs to us that Elisha received a double portion of Elijah’s spirit according to the measure of his request: “I ask that your spirit be double in me” (2 Kings 2). If Elisha also excels twofold, how could he not surpass John, who is said to be equal to Elijah, since no one greater than John has arisen among those born of women?

Yet, to resolve the question, the meaning must be weighed, so that a soberly thinking discernment may understand that what sounds harsh in the outward words proceeds from devout intention. It is indeed difficult that Elisha should have asked for a double spirit from his teacher, since a disciple is not above his teacher. But this request proceeded from a pure mind, because he sought not something earthly but a spiritual grace.

Thus Elijah, as though displeased, rebuked the disciple’s careless words, saying: “You have asked for a difficult thing.” Yet, looking upon the simplicity of his devout intention, he immediately added: “Nevertheless, if you see me when I am taken from you, you shall have what you asked” (2 Kings 2).

It was not, then, the double portion which careless speech had uttered, but the gift of the Spirit which his humble and sincere mind had sought in its intention.

[Note: [Col. 0656D] The Vatican manuscript omits “his own.”]

In this way Elisha does not surpass John, just as he is not greater than Elijah. Nevertheless, if we examine carefully the course of sacred history, we find that Elisha was more abundant—or more illustrious—than Elijah in the power of miracles.

The one, while alive, restored a dead boy to life; the other, after his death, raised a dead man. While the former was prophesying, the jar of flour and the vessel of oil did not fail; the latter, though dead, immediately crushed the incredible forces of the enemy camps for a besieged and afflicted city.

To conclude everything briefly: Elijah shone forth with twelve miraculous signs, while Elisha, as the truth of Scripture reports, shone forth with twenty-four. Since we wish to avoid tediousness, we postpone enumerating them here.

How, then, shall I escape the knot of this question, so that the Truth’s statement about John’s greatness does not waver—the statement that “among those born of women there is no one greater than John the Baptist”? For if Elisha is greater than Elijah, then he is also greater than John—which is impossible.

But it must be observed that doing something great through miraculous signs is one thing, while being great through excellence of merits is another. If miracles are under discussion, John is found in the pages of Scripture to have performed no miracle. But will he therefore be altogether the least among the saints because he is not recorded as having performed signs of power?

Elisha, then, is greater than Elijah in the display of signs, yet he does not at all surpass him in the accumulation of merits. So too John is indeed equal to Elijah, because just as Elijah was the herald of the future Judge, so John became the Forerunner of the Redeemer; yet he is greater than Elijah because he not only pointed out the one whom Elijah announced but also baptized him.

In that sacrament of baptism, the water of the Jordan was more washed than it washed; and from it, moreover, every water throughout the world received the power of sanctification. There blessed John heard the Father’s voice, saw the Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove, and immersed in the waters with his own hands the Son of God, dreadful to the angels, who had bowed himself before him.

For he showed in deeds the foundation and origin of baptism, which the Truth later taught the disciples to administer in words full of power: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28).

There, the reality was manifest and there were no words; here, there are words and the true reality, but it is hidden.

John, therefore, is the boundary of human merits. However greatly the authority of the apostolic senate may excel; however much the faith of the patriarchs may advance in the knowledge of God; however strongly the prophetic oracles may prevail in disclosing hidden mysteries; however greatly the glory of the triumphant martyrs may be heaped up; however richly the fresh chastity of virgins may bloom; or however much the tongue of teachers may exercise itself in the words of life—everything is confined this side of John’s boundary. No human virtue, no religion, no perfection advances beyond it.

The course of his incomparable life was not composed by some historian after his death. Rather, that chief archangel, before he was conceived in the womb, narrated the wondrous works of John, just as he narrated those of the Lord.

We learned John’s praise not from the assertion of some truthful human being, but from the mouth of Truth itself. The one who asserts and praises John is the one praised and blessed by all heavenly and earthly creatures.

The praises of John were drawn from that Word through whom the dry land was founded, the stars move, and the elements were created. Indeed, how great is the magnificence of meriting glory of praise from him, in whose sight the highest happiness is to be approved in any degree!

[Note: [Col. 0657] The Vatican manuscript: “is to obtain the pardon of mercy? And to be preferred by him over human beings, by whom it is glorious to be approved in any degree?”]

He says: “What did you go out to see? A prophet? I tell you, and more than a prophet” (Matthew 11).

But since a prophet is distinguished and eminent among other human beings, and since one who has no equal in the common human order is even placed above the prophets, it remains that John should now be called not a man but an angel. Hence he adds: “For this is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel, who will prepare the way before your face” (Mark 1).

Blessed John is also more clearly shown to be preferred to other human beings in the statement that follows, where the Lord says of him: “But the one who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” (Luke 7). For our Redeemer, who is less than John on earth through the succession of his growing age, is greater in heaven through the privilege of eternal majesty.

O blessed humiliation, when a human being is placed below God, when the creature is preceded by the Creator, when the small is surpassed by the glory of the immeasurable! Christ is said to be greater than John in heaven, where he is adored by all the powers of angelic dignity; before him the cherubim and seraphim humbly fall; his dominions and powers tremble at his command. Indeed, although the angels desire to behold his face, he shows himself superior to John in heavenly dignity.

Before him all nations are like a drop in a bucket and, according to the prophecy of Isaiah (40:17), are regarded as nothing and emptiness. He does not disdain to place himself above the blessed man by comparison, so that a human being may be found to have, before God, a place of comparison according to the excellence of his merits.

The author of exaltation himself became the teacher of humility. To him be glory and dominion, now and forever, throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXII. Also on the Birth of Saint John the Baptist VI

[Col. 0657]

### ADMONITION

[Col. 0657]

We have read this sermon, edited by Muratori from an Ambrosian manuscript, also in Casinensis 105, page 159, adorned with the name of Saint Maximus.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0657D] John the Baptist’s conception and birth teach that the Lord’s birth is not to be denied. John is truly greater among those born of women, because as prophet he proclaims the Son of God beforehand, as Forerunner he precedes him, as baptizer he receives him, and as witness he points him out.

The conception and birth of the venerable John the Baptist, which has now been recounted in the Gospel reading, testifies that the Lord’s birth—whose mystery the human mind cannot comprehend—is credible, and the fruit of an aged womb teaches that the fruitfulness of a virgin’s womb must not be denied. For who, in truth, would refuse to believe in the birth of the Christ who was being born, when an unexpected offspring proceeds from aged parents? There, from old people, a prophetic child is brought forth; here, from a virgin, the Lord of the prophets is born. There, the question concerns the old age of two people; here, the miracle concerns the virginity of one young woman. Nor, indeed, is it strange that the barren woman and the virgin conceived [Note: Codex Casinensis omits *indeed*], since there the messenger of the mystery of salvation was born, while here the very mystery of our life was being born. There, a temporal lamp shone forth; here, the sun of eternity illuminated the world.

From there John is read to have been born a prophet and more than a prophet; from here the new man, and more than man, Christ, the salvation of all, came. John is certainly more than a prophet: he enters the world as the light of this world, foretold by other prophets, and he prophesies Christ the Lord while still in his mother’s womb; then, when Christ’s baptism had been celebrated, he not only proclaims him with his mouth but, to complete his testimony, marks him out for the people standing by as though pointing with his finger, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

Christ, however, is more than man, because the Word and flesh are one Lord, one and the same, both eternal and new: eternal from God, new from a woman. There he was incomprehensibly begotten from the Unbegotten; here he was wondrously born from a virgin. There he was brought forth in the majesty of the Father; here he was formed through the operation of the Spirit. There the nature is simple in the Begetter; here the substance is twofold in the Redeemer. 559 There he is wholly God, incapable of suffering, from his Father; here he proceeded from his mother in such a way that he also could not suffer. For the flesh born from flesh could suffer, just as it did suffer, while God born in the flesh could not suffer. For God brought forth flesh for us through the virgin’s womb, and flesh brought forth God.

Nor should we doubt, brothers, that he who did everything he willed could become whatever he willed. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “He did everything that he willed.”] Nor should we hesitate to believe that the Son of God could join to himself a passible human being whom he could crown with the glory of impassibility through the triumph of suffering. If it was something new that God was born on earth, it is much more new that man reigns in heaven.

When these matters have been considered, we recognize the perfect blessedness of the most glorious John the Baptist, whom heavenly condescension raised to such sublimity that he deserved to prophesy, while still unborn, and to reveal, once born, the mystery of our salvation, wondrous to earth and heaven. For John was then, by divine dispensation, immature for birth but mature for grace. He who did not yet seem fit for his own birth was made fit to be the preacher of the Lord’s birth. While, according to the law of nature, the maternal womb still enclosed the whole human being, the joyful tongue of his mother was already bringing forth the spirit of the son who was to be born. For Elizabeth said, as we have read, to blessed Mary: “Since the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb” (Luke 1). [Note: Another manuscript reads: “the voice of your greeting … in joy.”]

Consider, brothers, how great were the gifts bestowed upon those blessed mothers, and with what miracles women about to give birth were adorned. “The infant,” she says, “leaped in his mother’s womb”; he leaped so that he might at once reveal both his own merit and the glory of the virgin womb. For, as God inspired her, that aged womb perceived that the Lord’s womb had arrived, and with a new joy announced to mortals how great a gladness the Christ who was to be born would bring to the world.

Who would not be astonished, brothers, that amid the mysteries of human redemption, while the mothers marvel, an unborn infancy rejoices? In the midst of these events John is born and precedes Christ in birth, so that he might offer dutiful service to his Lord, whom he celebrated with joy within his mother’s womb. 560

This, then, is the John of whom the prophet said: “A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way for the Lord” (Isaiah 40). He cried in the solitude so that he might cultivate with the richness of prophetic speech the hearts of mortals, deserted by the barrenness of unbelief.

This is the angel sent before the face of Christ, who carefully prepared the hearts of the peoples for the Savior’s coming, furnishing them through admonitions with a holier way of life.

This is that Baptist who deserved to baptize his Lord for this reason: that he might feel himself more fully cleansed by the power of the one he had baptized.

This is the herald of the eternal kingdom who cried, with his own tongue but with God speaking through him, that the Lamb of God was present on earth and that he himself was taking away the sin of the world.

This is the one whom the Lord declared to be greater than those born of women—and truly greater, because he foretells the Son of God as prophet, goes before him as precursor, receives him as Baptist, and reveals him as witness.

And after all this, this is the man whom no softness of pleasing garments clothed: a harsher tunic, woven from camel hair, covered him. No sweeter pleasure of food, nor temptation of a gluttonous appetite, captured him; rather, as though he were truly the censor of his own throat and the master of his fasting belly, as he walked through the arid deserts he was sustained by a locust. He is also read to have eaten wild honey, so that we may understand that he lived not on food prepared through human care but on simple nourishment, unworked and barely processed.

And this, I think, brothers, was so that neither a more splendid garment might draw the champion of justice away from proclaiming the truth, nor the pleasure of foods corrupt him. From this great courage surely came the fact that, while he confidently reproved King Herod for intercourse with his brother’s wife, he neither feared to undergo a glorious death nor shrank from the light of this world. Nor did he leave this life sorrowfully, because, always preserving prophetic rigor, he had never been thoroughly softened by the sweetness of the deceitful age.

Therefore, with the greatest patience, he is beheaded in prison at the command of an unjust king; for he knew that the King of the heavenly realm, rewarding him with the prize of a most courageous death, would restore to him both his head and his salvation.

## SERMON LXIII. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist VII

[Col. 0661]

### Editorial Notice

In the frequently cited codex of Saint Dalmatius, this sermon bears the name of Saint Maximus together with its title. The same is true of the third homily on Saint John the Baptist.

### Argument

Saint John the Baptist was illustrious in descent, miraculous in birth, and most glorious in life and death; more than a prophet, he was the voice crying in the wilderness—a voice that even now proclaims to all what must be done and what must be avoided.

As we celebrate today, dearest brothers, the birthday of Saint John the Baptist, let us rejoice and be glad in the Lord: he was born under the old law, a man illustrious in descent, miraculous in birth, and most glorious in life and death. For he is that precursor John who, although the Savior of the world was still hidden in his mother’s womb, greeted him with exultation while enclosed within his mother’s bosom and announced his presence by his leaps. Once born, and gloriously dwelling amid the darkness of the wilderness, he proclaimed him openly; to the peoples coming to him he preached without fear and pointed him out with confidence.

This is that illustrious Baptist of Christ who so vigorously rebuked the crowds of people coming to him that he refused to spare either the arrogance of the Pharisees, the scribes’ ignorance of the law of the Lord, or any of the vices with which that faithless people … [lacuna] …; nor did he refuse to expose them. Neither the threats of impious kings, nor the many pleasures of a luxurious court, nor the pride of priestly birth could prevent him from speaking the truth.

Therefore Christ the Lord truly said that he was more than a prophet. For he was born beyond the common manner of human birth: holy prayer brought him forth, not pleasure. When the aged organs of his mother’s womb had grown cold, and her weary limbs no longer promised any grace of fertility, against the impossibility of an aged body and the barrenness of her womb, through the prayers of Zechariah Elizabeth’s belly swelled. John was conceived in a most aged womb, and a child was granted to a father who had never before possessed one. Elizabeth’s womb, previously empty, was filled, and she rejoiced to find herself a mother.

Zechariah exulted with joy. When there was a dispute among their neighbors concerning the child’s name, the father set his stylus to the tablets in order to write down the name of the child according to his own decision. Since he could not express it in speech, his tongue was suddenly released into voice; he anticipated the letters with speech and, although he intended to write “John” with the stylus, testified to it by speaking.

What wonder, then, if Christ proclaims him more than a prophet? For which of the prophets, by being born, restored both a voice and a priest to the people? Therefore it is no wonder that he later said of himself: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Luke 3). That is, not merely a voice able to penetrate the ears of those who hear, but the voice of one crying out, which shakes the hearts of those who hear and leads them onto the way of salvation.

This voice even now proclaims to all. It also continually announces to you, brothers, through our humility, what must be done and what must be avoided: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (ibid.).

Therefore we are commanded to prepare the way for the Lord by the purity of our faith: not only by opposing the empty and superstitious inventions of idols, but also by detesting and correcting them among our brothers. We are commanded to prepare it by the chastity of the mind, through which we pity our brothers, restore to everyone what belongs to them, oppose no one, correct those who err, and finally do good to each person as far as lies within our power.

Therefore, in accordance with the admonitions of the venerable Baptist, let us always live while continually entreating God to grant us perseverance in good works and preserve it for us.

*Explicit.*

## SERMON LXIV. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist VIII

[Col. 0661]

### Editorial Notice

563 We have taken care to transcribe this fragment of a sermon from the same codex of Saint Dalmatius.

Today, brothers, we celebrate with the most devout festivities the birthday of the most blessed John the Baptist. Not only was his life praiseworthy, but his birth itself was also miraculous. For he was born from a barren woman, proceeding from an aged womb. He is John the Baptist of Christ, concerning whom it is written: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Luke 3).

John certainly cried in the wilderness [Col. 0662C], so that he might stir the hardest hearts of the unbelieving people to repentance. He cried so that he might [lacuna] from his most wicked unbelief … [lacuna] …; he cried and said: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Luke 3).

*(A folio is missing.)*

Therefore, for a time let us dwell with him in this world, so that we may be able to be with him forever.

*Explicit.*

## SERMON LXV. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist IX

[Col. 0661]

### Editorial Notice

Since this sermon too is attributed to Saint Maximus in the codex of Saint Dalmatius, but is placed by the Maurist monks in the appendix of Augustine’s sermons, no. 197, we have judged that it should be attributed to Saint Maximus rather than to Augustine, as in the Roman Breviary for 24 June.

### Argument

The nativity of one John is celebrated. He was a figure of the Old Testament, the voice crying in the wilderness—that is, in this world—promised before Christ and sanctified in his likeness.

After that most sacred day of the Lord’s nativity, we read of no human birth being celebrated except that of John, Christ’s Baptist. Among other holy and chosen servants of God, the day is honored on which this present life brings them, after the completion of so many labors and the conquest of the world, into everlasting eternity. In others, the achievements completed on the final day are celebrated.

But in John, Christ’s most holy Baptist, even the first day and the beginnings of the man himself are celebrated, because through him the Lord wished his coming to be attested, so that people would not fail to recognize it as something suddenly and unexpectedly appearing.

John was a figure of the Old Testament and bore in himself the form of the law. Therefore John foretold the Savior, just as the law ran ahead of grace. But the fact that, while not yet born, he prophesied from the hidden place of his mother’s womb, and, still deprived of light, was already a witness to the truth, signified that the law, lying hidden beneath the veil of the letter, proclaimed in spirit the Redeemer who had already come, and proclaimed our Lord to us from something resembling the womb of the law.

Therefore, because the Jews went astray from the womb—that is, from the law, which was pregnant with Christ—“they went astray from the womb; they spoke falsehoods” (Psalm 57). For this reason John came as a witness, “to bear witness concerning the light” (John 1).

But when John, placed in the painful confinement of prison, sends his disciples to Christ, the law sends the world onward to the Gospel. That law, in accordance with the type represented by John, lay as though shut in a prison of ignorance, in darkness and concealment; and, through Jewish blindness, the understanding remained enclosed within the letter.

Therefore the blessed Evangelist speaks of him in these words: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (ibid.). He was kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit so that, while the world was occupied by the night of ignorance, he might display the light of salvation and, as though amid the thickest darknesses of sins, reveal the most brilliant sun of righteousness by the ray of his light.

For he said of himself: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Luke 3). John certainly cried in the wilderness—that is, among a gentile and unteachable people. Hearts empty of the fear of God and lacking the Holy Spirit are compared with the desolate wilderness of a wasteland.

This world was deserted by every cultivation of faith and fear of God, covered with the thorns of sins, and lay desolate like an untilled field, bringing no pleasure whatsoever from good works and receiving no light of spiritual grace.

John was therefore sent to announce repentance by prophetic and apostolic preaching, to break up, fertilize, and cultivate the uncultivated field, and to prepare it for mature fruit—that is, for the grace of regeneration.

Now consider how great a glory it is that a son was promised to the aged priest Zechariah and the barren Elizabeth by Gabriel—the angel by whom the birth of the Lord was announced to the most blessed Mary. A son was sent beforehand, as it were, from a barren woman, in some likeness to the Lord, before the Son of the Virgin; and this reveals something like an even greater miracle in the very nativity. Barrenness is endowed with unexpected offspring because virginity was to be enriched by a new birth.

John is promised before Christ because the Old Testament precedes the New, as “day unto day utters the word.” A lamp is therefore sent before the sun; a servant before the Lord; a friend before the bridegroom; a herald before the judge; a voice before the Word.

For this reason the blessed John says of himself: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.” He says that he is a voice because he was the announcer and preacher of the Word.

While still in his mother’s womb he was filled with the Holy Spirit and, by prophesying, preceded Christ’s birth. He was sanctified in the likeness of the Lord before he was born, leaping within his mother’s womb and, through his mother’s mouth, bearing witness to the Savior’s coming.

He truly was a burning lamp, in whom so singular a grace of divine condescension shone forth that he was already announcing through the voice of his holy mother that the Redeemer was immediately to appear; and through her, as through some kind of truth … [Note: The editor remarks: “Here some word seems to be missing that would complete the sense of ‘truth.’”] though not yet brought forth into the light, he was showing Christ as present.

He was indeed a suitable mediator between the Old and New Testaments and a worthy revealer of the glorious Lamb, having merited at one and the same time to announce and to see his Lord.

Therefore, brothers, as we celebrate the solemnity of so great a day … [lacuna: fifteen lines have been obliterated] … by lamenting our sins and redeeming them through fasts and many almsgivings.

*Explicit.*

## SERMON LXVI. On the Nativity of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul I

[Col. 0663]

### Editorial Notice

This sixty-sixth sermon, together with the following sermons 67, 68, and 69, was copied from the noted Ambrosian codex and was first published by Muratori in volume IV of the *Anecdota*.

### Argument

We should rejoice that Peter and Paul, the leaders of the churches and our most glorious fathers, died for Christ. In them the Church’s twofold form is represented: simplicity is commended in Peter, doctrine in Paul, so that we may understand that in the Church of God knowledge is necessary and simplicity is beloved.

Of necessity, dearest brothers, we rejoice each year in the solemn celebration of the sufferings and death of the venerable apostles, our fathers, because in the confidence of Christian faith we believe that through their torments they obtained glory and that by the end of their lives they sought an everlasting life.

Who could doubt that those who followed his footsteps and conquered death by dying now reign with the Lord? Or how could it not be evident that victory exists amid torments before that king whose triumph is on the cross?

The leaders of the churches therefore chose patiently to die for the honor of the faith. The author of life, by setting before them the example of his own death, taught them not to fear death.

Let us therefore rejoice and exult that our most glorious fathers died for Christ, because the one who first, for the sake of the Eternal One himself, earned eternal life by the price of his blood deserved it.

A transaction for eternity is carried out where not the amount of money but faithful blood is the price, where death takes away life in such a way that immortal life follows upon the death inflicted.

And therefore, brothers, whoever hates the world because of his love for Christ does not lose the world unwillingly, as the most blessed Paul said: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1). How beautifully he says, “to die is gain”! For whoever lives for Christ, if he dies for Christ’s honor, acquires for himself the kingdom of heaven at the cost of the present light. To die for Christ is to reign with Christ.

Whoever counts a religious death as gain for himself shows that through his death he advances rather than perishes. For our Lord and Savior also says: “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 10).

What does this mean, dearest ones? How can a person find again a soul once lost? He can, brothers; he can—not by reasoning, but by faith. He certainly can, because, when the body has been restored through the benefit of the resurrection, the preserved soul will be returned to it.

What is possible for God is not impossible for a human being to conceive, as the apostle Paul, who knew the future, says: “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2).

Therefore, by saying, “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it,” the Lord revealed that at the glory of his coming, when every person will receive again the condition and life of his substance, the fellowship of soul and body will be formed. [Note: The corrected Ambrosian codex reads *consortium* (“fellowship”); the transmitted reading requires correction.] A human being consists of soul and body. One separated from the other is a nature divided and scattered. If the body is removed, the soul suffers loss.

When it is said, “Whoever loses his life will find it” (Matthew 10), it is revealed to us that, when the world is renewed according to the faithful promise of our God, the soul must be restored to the body and the body to the soul.

Therefore the Savior also said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna” (ibid.). The power to destroy the soul thus reveals in Christ the power to restore the human being.

Nor should we be astonished, dearest ones, if Paul condemned the faithlessness of the savage age with the sword and Peter with the cross. Their Lord had terrified the very prince of the world with wonders, rebuked him with denunciations, and triumphed over him through sufferings. [Note: The corrected Ambrosian codex reads: “He rebuked [him] with denunciations; he terrified [him] with wonders.”]

The devil found in them something he could kill, but he did not find anything he could hold captive. And what wonder if the servant of the One who was killed is killed by the sword? What wonder if the disciple of the Crucified is lifted up on the cross? Those who followed the example of the suffering one obtained the authority of the reigning one.

Christ therefore took Peter and Paul to himself: one fishing, the other persecuting. To Peter he gave the keys of his kingdom; to Paul, the wisdom of the word.

This is not incredible, since the one who brought forth water from the rock founded the Church upon Peter, and the one who compelled a magician to worship taught a persecutor to preach.

In these two, dearest ones, insofar as it is lawful to perceive such things in what is small, the Church’s twofold form and the diversity of the human race are represented. Simplicity commends Peter; doctrine elevates Paul, so that we may understand that in the Church of God knowledge is necessary and simplicity is beloved.

By simplicity I mean not that which grows sluggish through the stupor of laziness, but that which, burning with vigilance, knows how to benefit others and cannot itself cause harm, so that in one and the same person there may be cautious simplicity and kindly prudence, according to what is said: “Therefore be shrewd as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew 10). [Note: The Vulgate reads: “Therefore be prudent as serpents,” and so forth.]

For Peter’s simplicity was armed by the vigor of a most lively mind and fortified by the foresight of spiritual counsels. Peter had a simple yet prudent heart when he confessed the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation not by investigating but by believing, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16).

By this confession, dearest ones, he benefited everyone in his simplicity, and as a shrewd man he rejected the opinions of those who did not believe rightly.

Thus Paul enters heaven through the grace of doctrine, while Peter receives, through the merit of simplicity, the power of opening heaven. This is why I have said these things, dearest ones: so that we may understand that from faith in our God neither the learned are rejected nor the simple condemned.

As far as the truth of the faith is concerned, it is evident to all that Paul possessed Peter’s simplicity and that Peter was not lacking Paul’s prudence. For the same Spirit taught both.

For this reason, dearest ones, Paul too is Christ’s rock, and Peter too is a chosen vessel. Each, like a heavenly stone, supplies strength to the weak; each, a chosen vessel, pours forth for those thirsting for the faith of Christ the streams of a life-giving drink from the eternal fountain.

And therefore, because they had one faith, one glory, and one day of victorious suffering, one devotion of all peoples venerates them both with a full confession.

## SERMON LXVII. On the Same Nativity of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul II

[Col. 0665]

### Editorial Notice

569 Although in Vatican Codex 1269, folio 77 verso, this sermon is attributed to Saint Leo the Great, the Ballerini brothers, highly learned men, judged that it should not be counted among the sermons of that holy teacher. Therefore, following the Ambrosian codex, we too attribute it to Saint Maximus, as did the distinguished Muratori.

### Argument

The Church grew strong through the paternal blood of the apostles. The kingdom of the Christian faith dominates worldly empires. Peter, firmer than every rock, suffered as a shepherd for the sheep entrusted to him. We must beware of claiming anything for our own virtue and prudence. Why did Paul defend himself by the privilege of citizenship?

Let us exult, brothers, and glory in the Lord our God, because the apostles’ birthday is nourishment for the Church. Just as every infant is nourished by the milk of its mother’s breast, so the infancy of the rising Church then grew strong through the abundance of paternal blood.

For from the moment sterile earth received the blessing of fruitful blood, an innumerable multitude of believers sprang up throughout the whole world.

Who would be so insane as to deny that the Christian faith contains truth—a faith which sorrows do not exhaust, punishments do not disturb, and no terror of bodily death bends? For even the torments of persecutors contribute to its everlasting joy, and its kingdom, through eternal and unconquerable power, dominates worldly empires.

To understand more fully how great is the difference between the heavenly kingdom and the earthly, let us take instruction from present examples.

Behold, the kings of this passing age preserve their soldiers’ devotion toward them only through honors and gifts in this life, possessing absolutely nothing that they could bestow upon their own men or upon themselves after death.

Christ, however, the king of all ages, sends his chosen ones to be afflicted by labor, nakedness, hunger, tortures, and even death, because he has the power to raise the dead, to clothe the one stripped of the present life with the light of his kingdom, and, removing the law of death, to give immortality to the mortal. [Note: The corrected Ambrosian codex reads: “Why? Because he has the power,” and so forth.]

The fact that faithful men sometimes reject the rewards of kings, that all the dignities of this age are hateful to them, and that they reject as worthless whatever this world offers them as precious, is wholly produced by that hope: through the grace of Christ, faith presumes that better things will one day be granted to them.

Who is not astonished that this wondrous mystery lies in Christ’s will? He promises his saints their rewards in such a way that he sends them torments beforehand; he proclaims the love of the future life in such a way that he teaches them not to love the present.

Here is the truth of religion: here sorrow produces joy; here needy nakedness conceals garments of incorruption; here glory is disfigured—or perhaps, *where disfigurement is glory*; here being burned is refreshment; here being killed is triumph.

This is death, dearest ones, if only the authority of the Holy Spirit may raise up and strengthen our faith—a death which children do not reject, young men do not avoid, the mature choose, old men desire, and women have not feared. In the passion of martyrdom, wherever faith reigns more firmly in a person, neither age withdraws nor sex excuses itself, as has often already happened.

There, brothers, there is bodily weakness displayed where faith has no strength.

Therefore the most glorious Peter, firmer than every rock through the stability of his faith, conquered his own cross while preaching Christ’s cross. He did not fear crucifixion because he feared and loved the Crucified One.

Peter therefore suffered as the best servant for his Lord, as the faithful disciple for his teacher, and as the chosen shepherd for the sheep entrusted to him. He followed to death the footsteps of the one whose path he followed to life. Because he underwent a passion like that of his king, he received the key of the heavenly kingdom and assumed the likeness of the reigning one.

How could he fear the end of his own life, since he had learned that his Christ reigned after death? How could he flee the cross, since he had recognized the signs of the blessed cross in the body of his Lord returning from the dead? How could he refuse the wounds of the crucifiers, since he knew that the Redeemer of the world had carried the traces of the nails with him to the Father?

Could he fear death for his Lord when the author of life himself had foretold both death and its manner by the mouth of his foreknowledge, saying: “When you were younger, you girded yourself and went where you wished; but when you grow old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish” (John 21)?

This means: “When you were younger, Peter, your own hands girded you for service, and in everything you followed your own will. But when you grow old, an unfamiliar hand will gird you and lead you where you do not wish, and you will exchange the freedom of your youth for the service of old age.”

“Another will lead you where you do not wish.” Peter was never unwilling to suffer for his Lord, to whom he had already said: “I will lay down my life for you” (John 13). He certainly wished to die as a devoted servant; but because he thrust himself forward willingly into death, he seemed to possess a kind of presumptuous boldness.
