For one who, in weakness, does not wish to die, but, once strengthened by God, does not shrink from suffering, displays within himself both the feeling of trembling flesh and the duty of a faithful spirit.

Thus, when the apostle offered himself to death voluntarily, he feared to die; but when he was led unwillingly to the cross, he did not fear crucifixion. There human weakness was wearied; here the strength of the heavenly Spirit conquered.

All our devotion, if it trusts as though in its own strength, immediately grows weary as weakness overtakes it. But if someone entrusts the fulfillment of his good purpose to divine grace through humble prayer, no adversity of this age can compel him to waver.

Therefore we must beware, brothers, of claiming for our own virtue and prudence anything we rightly accomplish. The Lord taught his apostles, saying: “For without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

By this warning we are reminded that everything must be hoped for from him. Everything that comes successfully must also be reckoned among his gifts, without whom, as he himself says, we can have no success at all in any of our desires.

Finally, how did Peter presume to say to the Lord, “I lay down my life for you” (John 13)? Not long afterward, troubled by a girl’s question, he replied that he did not know the man. For this reason he wept most bitterly; and when Christ said that Peter would be led where he did not wish, it was there that he obtained the victory of triumphant suffering. [Note: The Ambrosian codex continues: “Afterward, when Peter presumed to say to the Lord, ‘I will lay down my life for you,’ he was troubled not long afterward by a girl’s question,” and so forth.]

The apostle should not therefore be reproved because, for Christ’s honor, he eagerly desired to die. For that presumption, which arose from the fervor of faith, even if it does not appear praiseworthy, nevertheless possesses great confidence before the Lord because of the devotion of his own conscience.

Yet, for the caution of his faithful ones and as a refuge for our weakness, the Savior said to his disciples: “If they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matthew 10).

This means: “Avoid suffering, lest you perhaps be overcome through torments; but once captured, do not yield to the persecutor. For I wish my servants neither to await death nor to fear it, so that a foolish persecutor may recognize that wisdom is present in you and faith is not absent. To fail to avoid death when you can is the fault of recklessness; not to yield to the one who seeks to destroy you is the courage of a believer.”

Reason and the strength of our faith require this: in confessing the Christian name, we should neither desire death nor fear being killed.

Thus Paul, that chosen vessel, most glorious, lest he be scourged by the gentiles, proclaimed that he was a Roman citizen and removed the injury to his body by the protection of secular laws. He rejoiced in writing that he had been rescued from dangers and deaths.

If, as a curious inquirer, you ask why the apostle defended himself by the privilege of citizenship, know that this belonged to apostolic strategy: he wished to refute those who had no reverence for our God by terrifying them with their own laws, and he did not wish to exercise against them the power given to him by the Lord, since he knew that he had been sent for the salvation of his persecutors.

For the magician who was blinded perceived what the apostle’s power could accomplish, and the expelled fortune-telling woman named Python proved it. Yet when the time of his passion arrived by the Lord’s dispensation, he confidently submitted his faithful neck to the gentile sword; and he who earlier rejected scourging did not flee the sword.

This is the holy and perfect measure of belief; this is the soundness of irreproachable devotion in the struggle of faith: both not to wish to die and patiently to die, because our God does not seek our death but the mind that death cannot conquer.

## SERMON LXVIII. On the Same Nativity of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul III

[Col. 0669]

### Editorial Notice

573 This sermon is anonymous in Vatican Codices 539, 1269, and 4951, and in Regina Codex 535. It is attributed to Saint Ambrose in Gillotius, no. 67. We wish to attribute it to Saint Maximus, since it is not only adorned with his name in the distinguished Ambrosian codex, but is also attributed to him in two ancient and outstanding codices of Santa Croce in Jerusalem—codex 90, sermon 2, and codex 99, sermon 31—and in the codex formerly belonging to the Minor Convent, now in the Laurentian Library, Pluteus XVII, where the title reads as follows: “A sermon of Saint Maximus, bishop, on the holy apostles Peter and Paul.”

### Argument

On the vision of a vessel full of four-footed animals and birds presented to Saint Peter, by which the gathering of peoples of different nations into one Church is signified.

Today, as we celebrate the feast of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, dearest brothers, we ought to refresh ourselves with varied fare and celebrate so great a festival with great joy. [Note: In both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, all the words placed between asterisks are absent. They are also absent in Vatican 1269.] *For who would not celebrate the solemnity of such men with great joy? Who, at the solemnity of such men, would not prepare great provisions for himself, so that the more he spent, the more he might show that he loved the apostles?* Nevertheless, no private expense is needed for our refreshment. For on his feast day Saint Peter himself refreshes us: his vessel, which was brought down to him from heaven [Col. 0669C] while he was hungry, is filled with every provision. Therefore, whoever hungers like Peter is himself refreshed with Peter.

Why, then, should we prepare our own meal when we are nourished by an apostolic dish? Why should we seek earthly foods when we possess heavenly provisions? Saint Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles (chapters X, XI, and elsewhere) that, after Peter had prayed and was hungry around the sixth hour, a certain splendid vessel, like a linen cloth, was brought down through the opened heaven. In it were all the four-footed animals of the earth and the birds of heaven. [Note: Vatican Palatine 495 reads: “four-footed animals and creeping things and birds of heaven.” Vatican 539 has *reptilia* (“creeping things”) instead of *repentia* (“creeping things”).] The Lord said to him: “Peter, rise, sacrifice, and eat” (Acts X). [Note: The same Vatican manuscript, 539, reads: “Rise, Peter; slaughter and eat.”]

Behold Peter, who elsewhere says, “I have neither gold nor silver” (Acts III); now the vessel of his banquet is more splendid than silver, so that he who had rejected the appearance of silver for Christ’s sake [Note: Vatican manuscripts 1269 and 539 read “rejected.”] might, through Christ, be enriched with the gleam of silver. [Note: The manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Vatican 1269, and Regina 539 read “is enriched.”]

As Peter is about to dine, there are no cooks’ preparations and no services of attendants; but what is better, the divine ministries are not lacking. Through a more advantageous exchange [Note: Vatican 1269 reads “communion.”], what is lacking for the holy man on earth abounds in heaven. [Note: “But what is much better.” So read manuscripts 539 and 495, though the latter reads *mysteria* (“mysteries”) instead of *ministeria* (“ministries”).] For Peter to be refreshed, the storeroom is not carefully unlocked; heaven itself is immediately opened. [Note: Vatican 4951, after “is opened,” reads “After the prayer, therefore,” and omits the intervening material.]

We read in the Scriptures (1 Kings XVII) that holy Elijah was fed in the wilderness by ravens serving him. How much better for Peter, to whom not a small portion of earthly food is offered by a bird [Note: Vatican manuscripts 1269, 539, and 1277 read *tetra* (“black”) instead of *terrena* (“earthly”).], but a whole banquet is supplied by a multitude of angels!

After his prayer, therefore, Peter is hungry. It is surprising that hunger follows prayer in the holy man, since hunger is usually driven away by prayer, and the hungry soul is nourished only by spiritual observances. [Note: Vatican 495 reads: “Not with food, but with supplication, to be nourished.”] But I think that after prayer Peter was hungry not for human food but for salvation; he was afflicted not by bodily want but by the scarcity of believers.

For when the faithless and ungrateful Jewish people did not believe in Christ while Peter preached, Peter in some sense suffered the hunger belonging to his office. He suffers hunger who does not attain the fruit of his labor. [Note: Vatican 4951 presents this passage as follows: “He therefore hastens up from prayer into the upper room, because every holy person, when he prays, leaves lowly earthly things and is lifted high in mind; suspended on high, he is carried away, so that through holy thought he may become nearer to heaven. And there, to him who was hungry—that is, in the more elevated place of his heart—as though a divine voice were saying: ‘You hunger only for the Jews,’ and so forth.”]

He therefore hastens up into the upper room for prayer. It is rightly said that Peter went up into the upper room for prayer, because every holy person, when he prays, leaves lowly or earthly things and is lifted high in mind, and, suspended on high, is carried away [Note: Manuscript 4 of the Holy Cross Minor and others add: “so that through holy thought he may become nearer to heaven.”] and through holy thought becomes near to heaven.

There, to him who was hungry—that is, to him who was thinking, in the more elevated place of his heart, about the salvation of the Jewish people—a vessel filled with animals of various kinds is offered, [Note: The same Holy Cross Minor manuscript and others add: “as though a divine voice were saying to him: ‘You alone hunger for the Jews; behold, hunger … is refreshed.’” Vatican 1277 and Regina 539 read: “as though a divine voice were saying to him: ‘You alone hunger for the Jews,’ and so forth.] as though the Divinity were saying to him:

“You alone hunger for the Jews; yet behold, I refresh your faith with the diversity of all nations.”

For indeed the various animals gathered into one vessel demonstrate the gathering of diverse nations into one Church. [Note: Vatican 1269 and Regina 539 read “through diverse [things],” and so forth.] That Church shines in the splendor of that bright vessel, since it has neither spot nor wrinkle, and gleams with the brightness of linen. [Note: Vatican 1269 reads: “That Church, while it has neither spot nor wrinkle, shines in the bright appearance of that vessel.” Vatican 4951 reads: “That Church shines in the splendid form of that vessel, having neither spot nor wrinkle, in the brightness of linen. In it, first …”]

In it, first, the centurion Cornelius, an animal from the nations, is sacrificed to God.

From this vessel, then, Peter refreshes us today. For when we see crowds of Gentiles hastening to the Christian faith, we rejoice together with the apostles. Those whose feast we celebrate today are not dead, but, having been reborn, they live fully, because they have become participants in Christ, who is the life of all. [Note: Vatican 4951 reads “whose feast we celebrate.” The cited manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read “but reborn.” They continue: “They live fully, because they are participants in Christ.” Vatican 1269 likewise reads “but reborn,” and omits the words “who is the life of all.” Vatican 4951 reads: “but reborn. They live fully, and so forth. Although their bodies have ceased through suffering, the vigor of life has not been interrupted. For continually, and thanks be to God, and so forth.”]

Although their bodies have been struck down by suffering, the order of their living has nevertheless not been interrupted. [Note: The manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read: “The order of living has not been interrupted. For continually, and thanks be to God, and so forth.” The same reading is found in the four cited manuscripts of the Holy Cross Minor, Vatican 1269, Vatican 1277, and Regina Vatican 529.] They continually give thanks to God and return praises to the Savior; except that, once the burden of their limbs has been dissolved, they cling more closely to Christ. [Note: Vatican 4951 reads: “They cling more closely to Christ, and so forth: ‘To depart and be with Christ is much better,’ and so forth.] As the apostle Paul says: “To depart and be with Christ—how much better!” (Philippians I).

Therefore, death should not be called that by which we escape the persecutor and are joined to Christ. Death should certainly not be called that which, by joining the dead person to Christ, makes the dying person’s gain, as the blessed Apostle says: “For me, to live is Christ and to die is gain” (ibid.).

But that is the true death which binds even a living person with the death of sins. For although he seems to live, by his crimes he appears devoted to death, as the Apostle says of that pleasure-loving widow: “But she who lives in pleasure is dead” (1 Timothy V). [Note: Here the sermon ends in Vatican 4951 and Regina Vatican 539. Vatican 1269 reads: “That is true death.”]

## SERMON LXIX. On the same feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul IV

### NOTICE

What was said above about the benefit we have obtained from comparing many manuscript copies, by which we can distinguish writings assigned by the ignorance of copyists to different authors, will become clearer here. Two Vatican manuscripts, 1269 and 1277, attribute this sermon to Saint Ambrose; another Vatican manuscript, 4951, attributes it to Saint Augustine, with the heading: “A sermon of Saint Augustine to be delivered on the feast of the holy Peter and Paul.” The Vallicellian manuscript A 9 names Saint Leo the Great as its author.

Our judgment in this diversity would therefore be uncertain if we did not have the agreement of many manuscripts in favor of Maximus. For four witnesses join the Ambrosian manuscript: namely, the two manuscripts 90 and 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, and the two Cassinese manuscripts 102 and 305, which support Saint Maximus. Since neither Ballerini nor Cacciari included this sermon in their editions of the works of Saint Leo the Great, and since the monks of Saint Maur did not place it among the genuine sermons of Saint Augustine but transferred it to the appendix under number 201, there should be no question of its belonging to those Fathers.

The same Benedictine monks, in that appendix, wondered whether it might perhaps be attributed to Ambrose. Yet since they omitted it from their edition of 1690, they seem to have abandoned that opinion. This sermon should therefore rightly be ascribed to Saint Maximus, contrary to the Paris edition of the works of Saint Ambrose of 1569, where it was placed among the sermons under number 68.

**ARGUMENT.**—[Col. 0671C] Peter’s power has spread throughout the whole earth, and the words of Paul’s Epistles have penetrated to the ends of the world. The lame man healed by Peter; Paul, the vessel of election; and the martyrdom of both apostles.

It is known to all of you, brothers, and most widely known throughout the world, that today is the feast of the most blessed Peter and Paul. [Note: Vatican 1269 reads: “that today is their feast day.”] No part of the world can be unaware of so great a devotion. [Note: Vatican 6451 reads *potuit* (“was able”) instead of *potest* (“can”).] For when the prophet David says of them, “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm XVIII), the wondrous power of Peter has spread throughout all the earth, and the words of Paul’s Epistles have penetrated to the ends of the world. [Note: Both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read: “The power of Peter’s miracles is wondrous, and to the ends …” The same reading is found in Vatican 1269, 1277, 4951, and 6451. Vallicellian A 9 reads: “The wondrous power of Peter has been heard.”]

For who has not heard that the blessed apostle Peter first restored the strength of the feet to the lame man sitting at the Beautiful Gate of the temple? [Note: The words “the blessed apostle” are omitted in the manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.] He had long been disabled from his mother’s womb. [Note: Vatican 6451 and 4951 read: “and restored the strength of his feet, which had long been disabled from his mother’s womb.”] Thus what nature had bestowed insufficiently, apostolic grace restored. [Note: A Cassinese manuscript reads: “and what was lacking from birth,” and so forth.]

When that lame man, asking for alms, thought that he would receive some money from the apostles, the apostle Peter said to him: “I have neither silver nor gold; but what I have, I give you: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk” (Acts III). [Note: In the manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and in Vatican 1269, the word “apostle” is absent.]

Blessed indeed is the generosity which did not give the petitioner silver but gave him health! Blessed is the generosity which did not bring forth gold from its treasures [Note: Some Vatican manuscripts read “gold,” others “silver”; in the rest they agree.] but brought forth medicine! [Note: The manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem omit “brought forth” and read “but gave medicine.”] Blessed is that lame man who, while seeking a monetary gift, received the riches of health. For he deserved to receive from the apostles what he could not have purchased from any physician with all his treasures.

Peter therefore performed the first of his miracles by restoring the traces of feet to the lame man. [Note: The Holy Cross Minor manuscript in the Laurentian Library has this passage differently: “We say that the first sign of miracles which the blessed apostle performed was restoring the imprint of feet to the lame man.” Vatican 4951 likewise reads “we have said” instead of “we say.”]

We have often said that Peter was named “rock” by the Lord, as he says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI). If, then, Peter is the rock upon which the Church is built, he rightly heals the feet first, so that, just as he contains the foundation of faith in the Church, he may also strengthen the foundations of the limbs in a human being. Rightly, I say, he first heals the feet in the Christian, so that he may be able to stand upon the rock of the Church no longer trembling or weak, but walk robust and strong. [Note: Vatican 4951 reads: “the rock upon which the Church is built,” and so forth.]

Where are Paul’s words not read? What place does not inscribe them in its writings, retain them in its heart, and preserve them in its way of life? Paul was named by the Lord a vessel of election. A good vessel, in which the precious commandments of Christ are stored; a good vessel, from whose fullness the substance of life is continually dispensed to the peoples—and it is full.

Excellent are the names of the apostles: rock and vessel, necessary to the house of the Savior. [Note: The manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and four Holy Cross Minor manuscripts in the Laurentian Library read: “For the house is founded upon the strength of the rock and adorned by usefulness,” while Vatican 6451, 4951, and 1277 read: “For the house is founded by the strength of the rock.”] The house is built by the strength of stones and adorned by the usefulness of a vessel. The rock supports the peoples for stability, lest they fall; the vessel covers the Christians for protection, lest they be tempted.

No one is unaware how blessed their departure from this world was. [Note: Vatican 1277 reads: “No one is unaware how blessed their entrance was,” and so forth.] For this is their first blessedness: both are known to have suffered on the same day, so that those whom one faith had bound together in service might be crowned by one day in martyrdom. [Note: Holy Cross Minor in the Laurentian Library reads: “For this is their first blessedness, that …”]

Then, although their passion was different in each case, how richly it was filled with the holiness of grace! [Note: Vallicellian A 9 reads: “Although the passion itself was different in each, nevertheless it was made equal by the holiness of grace.” A Cassinese manuscript reads: “Although the passion itself was different in each, nevertheless it was filled with an equal grace of holiness.” Vatican 6451 reads “so great” instead of “how great.”]

Peter underwent the death of the cross, like the Savior, and was not separated from him in death by the likeness of his devotion—so that he who imitated Christ in faith might imitate him also in suffering. [Note: Vatican 6451 reads: “underwent the death of the cross.” The same manuscript and Cassinese manuscripts read: “nor was he separated from him by death.” Vatican 4951 reads: “nor was he deceived by death.” Vatican 1277 reads: “nor was he torn apart by death.”]

From Paul’s neck, however, when the persecutor struck it with a sword, there is said to have flowed a stream of milk rather than blood; and, astonishingly, the holy Apostle appeared in that very slaughter radiant rather than bloody.

This is not surprising in Saint Paul. For what wonder is it if the nourisher of the Church abounds in milk, as he himself says to the Corinthians: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians III)? [Note: Four Holy Cross Minor manuscripts in the Laurentian Library read: “What wonder is it if the Church is abundantly nourished with milk, just as he himself …”]

This is that land full of promise which God promised to our fathers, saying: “I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus III). [Note: The same Holy Cross Minor manuscript in the Laurentian Library reads: “I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey.”]

For he was not speaking of this earth, which, with its flowing waters, contains and mixes mud, but of that land of Paul and of men like Paul, which continually distills what is pure and sweet. Which of Paul’s letters is not sweeter than honey and whiter than milk? [Note: Vatican 1269 reads: “For Paul’s letters are sweeter than honey and whiter than milk.”] Which letters, like excellent breasts, nourish the peoples of the Churches unto salvation? [Note: Cassinese manuscripts and Vatican 6451 read “excellent breasts.”]

From the Apostle’s neck, therefore, milk flowed in place of blood. [Note: Vallicellian A 9 and Cassinese 102 read “from the neck of the apostle Paul.”] We read in his own Epistle that “flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians V). Paul therefore already possesses the kingdom, since he lacks blood, which is said to hinder those who will reign. [Note: Vatican 1277 reads “who lacks flesh and blood.” The manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read “who will reign”; the same reading is found in Vatican 6451, 4951, and Vallicellian A 9.] Therefore, while still placed on earth, Paul is already transformed into the substance of the heavenly kingdom. [Note: The manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, ten Laurentian manuscripts, and others read “already” instead of “even.”]

Therefore, dearest brothers, whenever we celebrate the memorials of the martyrs, setting aside all the activities of the world, we must hasten without delay to the house of God and render honor to those who procured salvation for us through the shedding of their blood, who offered themselves to the Lord as a sacred victim for our propitiation. [Note: Vatican 4951 adds: “We must hasten together; we must render them honor, who procured salvation for us through the shedding of their blood, who were offered to God like a sacred victim for our propitiation; especially …”] This is especially so since almighty God says to his saints: “Whoever honors you honors me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X). [Note: Vatican 1269 reads “through the shedding of their blood,” and so forth.]

Whoever, therefore, honors the martyrs honors Christ also; and whoever despises the saints despises our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so forth. [Note: The sermon ends here in both manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem; the remainder is absent from them.]

## SERMON LXX. On the feast of Saint Laurence, deacon and martyr I

### NOTICE

We find this sermon attributed to Saints Ambrose and Augustine in old editions of the works of these Fathers; in Cassinese manuscript CXI, folio 205 verso, to Saint Leo; and in the Urbevetan manuscript and the two Vatican manuscripts 1269 and 1272, to no one. Yet not only in the distinguished Ambrosian manuscript and in Holy Cross in Jerusalem 90 and 99, but also in two Laurentian manuscripts—39, Plut. XVII, and 174, formerly belonging to the library of the cathedral chapter of Florence—and, in addition, in Vatican 6451, Vercelli 66, the Imperial Library of Milan, Basilica of Saint Ambrose, page 214, Chisian manuscript 16, page 8, the Farfense manuscript, Cassinese 122, page 108, and the Lucensian Passionary, page +, we read that it is attributed to Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin.

We have therefore judged that it should be inscribed to him, and we have appended to the published text a fragment not previously edited, transcribed from the Laurentian manuscripts mentioned above.

**ARGUMENT.**—[Col. 0675A] Saint Laurence illuminated the whole world through his passion. Tortured by a long and varied punishment, he is to be preferred in glory to no lesser degree than the three boys shut up in the furnace of fire. Let us think about imitating the martyrs. [Col. 0675B]

I believe that you know the passion of the most blessed martyr Laurence, whose feast we celebrate today, and I do not doubt that your devotion is able to know how much he endured in persecution. [Note: The Farfense manuscript reads: “I believe that you know.”] So great was the glory of his martyrdom that through his passion he illuminated the whole world. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “So great was the glory of his martyrdom that Laurence plainly illuminated the world.”]

Laurence plainly illuminated the world with the light by which he himself was kindled, [Note: Vatican 1269 reads: “So great was the glory of his martyrdom that Laurence plainly illuminated the world with the light by which he himself was kindled, and with the flames which he endured,” and so forth.] and with the flames which he himself endured he warmed the hearts of all Christians.

Who, following this example, would not wish to burn for Christ with Laurence, so that he might be crowned by Christ with Laurence? [Note: The same manuscript reads: “Who, following this example, would not wish to burn for Christ and be crowned with Laurence?”] Who would not wish to endure for a time Laurence’s fire, so as not to suffer the eternal burning of Gehenna? [Note: The Holy Cross Minor manuscript in the Laurentian Library reads: “to be burned for a time by Laurence’s fire.” The Farfense manuscript reads: “Who would not wish to be burned by Laurence’s fire, so that he might not suffer the eternal …”]

By the example of blessed Laurence, therefore, we are summoned to martyrdom, enflamed toward faith, and made fervent toward devotion. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “We are summoned by the example of blessed Laurence. We are summoned to martyrdom,” and so forth.] Although we lack the persecutor’s flame, we do not lack the flame of faith. [Note: The same manuscript adds: “and in us the flame of persecution is not absent: we do not burn bodily for Christ, but we burn in affection.”] We do not burn bodily for Christ, but we burn in affection. The persecutor does not impose fire upon me, [Note: Vatican 102 reads: “Now we burn.”] but the desire for the Savior supplies me with fire. [Note: Manuscript 174 of the cathedral library of Florence, together with the Farfense and Urbevetan manuscripts, reads: “but the desire for the Savior is sufficient for me.”]

We read in the Gospel that this fire belongs to the Savior, when the same Lord says: “Do you not know that I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII, 49). [Note: The manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Vatican 1269, Cassinese, and Urbevetan manuscripts add “upon the earth.”]

Kindled by this fire, the two disciples of Emmaus and Cleopas said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV, 32). [Note: The Holy Cross Minor manuscript in the Laurentian Library reads: “The two disciples of Emmaus, kindled by him …” The Farfense and Vatican 1269 read: “When those two disciples were kindled by the fire, they said: ‘Was not our heart …’” Vatican 1269 reads: “Was not our heart burning within us on the road, when he opened the Scriptures to us?” Manuscript 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “and opened to us the Scriptures of Christ.”]

Kindled by this fire, blessed Laurence does not feel the burning of the flames; [Note: Ten Laurentian manuscripts, the Farfense, and Vatican 1269 read: “he did not feel the fire.”] and while the desire for Christ burns within him, he does not burn from the persecutor’s flame. [Note: The Urbevetan manuscript reads: “and while the desire for Christ burns within him, he does not feel the persecutor’s flame.” The Holy Cross Minor manuscript in the Laurentian Library and the cited manuscripts 174, Farfense, and Vatican read: “he does not feel the persecutor’s punishment.”]

To the degree that the ardor of faith burns fervently within him, to that degree the flame of punishment grows cold. Blessed Laurence was suffering in a bodily fire. [Note: The Farfense manuscript reads: “As great as the ardor of faith was in him.” The manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, ten Laurentian manuscripts, Vatican, and Cassinese manuscripts read “was suffering.”] On one side he is enkindled by love of Christ; on the other he is tortured by the persecutor’s flame. But the divine ardor of the Savior extinguishes the tyrant’s material fire. [Note: The Holy Cross Minor manuscript in the Laurentian Library reads: “extinguished the tyrant’s ardor”; manuscript 174 reads “extinguished it.”]

Although his limbs are dissolved into ash, the strength of faith is not dissolved. [Note: The manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read: “He suffers bodily loss.” Manuscript 174 has the same reading, confirmed by the Farfense, Vatican, and Cassinese manuscripts.] The body suffers loss, but gains salvation. [Note: Cassinese 102 reads: “the gain of eternal salvation.”]

For blessed Laurence is not destroyed by a brief or ordinary punishment. [Note: The Farfense manuscript reads: “For, brothers, blessed Laurence is not destroyed by a brief or simple punishment.” Vatican 4951 and the Urbevetan manuscript read: “is not oppressed by a brief or simple passion.”] Whoever is struck by the sword dies once; whoever is plunged into a furnace of flames is freed in a single assault. But he is tortured by a long and varied punishment: death is not absent from his torment, but it is absent from its conclusion. [Note: Manuscript 174 reads: “so that death may not be absent from the punishment, but may be absent from faith.” The Farfense manuscript reads: “and death is not absent from the punishment,” and so forth.]

The savage persecutor is said to have appointed this continuous punishment for him: he was stretched upon a mass of burning coals and fastened upon an iron grate, so that a slow flame might consume him. [Note: Manuscripts 174 and Farfense read: “this punishment was appointed for him.” Manuscript 174 adds: “and he was stretched upon an iron grate.”] The intention was not to kill the man quickly by setting him aflame, but to torture him for as long as the burning continued. Thus, when the persecutor saw that one side had been burned, he exposed the other side to the flames to be burned. [Note: The ten Laurentian manuscripts agree in substance.]

We read that Ananias, Azariah, and Misael, most blessed young men, shut up by the king in a furnace of fire, walked amid the flames of their punishments and trampled fiery balls beneath their feet (Daniel III). Therefore blessed Laurence is to be preferred to them in no lesser glory. [Note: The Urbevetan manuscript reads: “in no lesser joy and glory.”] For while they walked amid the flames of their punishments, he reclines in the very fire of his punishment; they trampled the fires beneath the soles of their feet, while he extinguishes them by spreading out his sides. [Note: The Farfense and Cassinese manuscripts read: “Just as they walked amid the flames of their punishments, so he reclines in the fire of his punishment; they trampled the fires with the soles of their feet, while he restrains them by spreading out his sides.” The ten Laurentian manuscripts and the two cited manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem read “trample the fires.”]

Those three, I say, standing amid their punishments, prayed to the Lord with their hands raised. [Note: The manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Vatican 1269 and 1277, and the Cassinese manuscript read: “Those three, I say, standing amid their punishments, worshiped the Lord with their hands raised.”] But he, lying prostrate in his punishment with his whole body, pleaded with the Lord. [Note: Two manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and the Holy Cross Minor manuscript read “begged the Lord.”]

Again blessed Laurence is turned onto his back, and his loins are burned by the flames, so that the prophecy of the psalm might be fulfilled, which speaks in Laurence’s person: “Test me, Lord, and try me; burn my loins and my heart” (Psalm XXV). [Note: The Farfense manuscript reads: “Burn, he says, my loins and my heart,” omitting the first part.] He asks, therefore, to be burned by a double fire. [Note: Vatican 4951 reads: “He asks to be burned by a twofold fire.”] For if he were speaking of one and only one fire of the world, it would have been enough to offer only his loins to be burned by the flames.

But the heart is burned only by the flame of Christ. [Note: Cassinese manuscripts 102 and 109 read: “unless it is burned by a spiritual [fire].” Two manuscripts of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, together with Vatican 1269 and a Cassinese manuscript, repeat the words cited above: “As Emmaus and Cleopas said: ‘Was not our heart burning on the road, when the Lord opened the Scriptures to us?’ And therefore …”]

Therefore, to demonstrate his devotion, he asks for a double fire, so that, after the struggle, he might show that the love of Christ can accomplish more in him than the tyrant’s punishment. [Note: Ten Laurentian manuscripts and four Holy Cross Minor manuscripts in the Laurentian Library read: “so that, by the appearance of the struggle, he might show that the love of Christ can accomplish more in him than …” The same reading is found in Vatican 1277 and 4951, Cassinese, and Vallicellian A 9.]

Let us therefore honor blessed Laurence, who, by conquering the persecutor’s flames through his faith, showed us through fire how to overcome the fires of Gehenna and not fear the day of judgment. [Note: The Farfense manuscript omits the words beginning “who, by conquering …” The Farfense manuscript reads: “Let us therefore pray to blessed Laurence.” The Urbevetan manuscript reads: “Let us therefore pray to blessed Laurence, who, when the persecutor’s flame did not conquer his faith, may show us through …”]

But we, dearest brothers, if we wish to reach fellowship with the holy martyrs, should think about imitating the martyrs. [Note: The sermon ends here in Laurentian manuscript 10 and Vatican 1277. The following fragment was extracted from the Laurentian manuscripts. The same fragment is found in the Farfense manuscript, Vatican 1269, two Vallicellian manuscripts, XXV and A 9, Cassinese 109 and 111, and the Urbevetan manuscript.]

For they ought in us [lacuna] to recognize something of their virtues, so that they may deign to pray to the Lord for us. If we cannot endure the torments which the holy martyrs endured, then, with their intercession, let us fight against evil desires. [Note: The Urbevetan manuscript reads “let us struggle.”] And because daily sins are not lacking, daily remedies are not lacking either. [Note: The Holy Cross Minor manuscript in the Laurentian Library reads: “Let daily remedies also not be lacking.”]

Let no one suppose that he possesses any happiness or any true joy in this world. [Note: The Farfense manuscript reads: “Let no one suppose that he possesses any happiness or any true joys.”] Here he can prepare blessedness; he cannot possess it. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “Blessedness can be prepared here; it cannot be possessed.”]

Two periods follow one another in their proper order: a time for weeping and a time for laughter. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “When two periods follow one another in order.”] Let no one deceive himself, brothers: there is no time for laughter in this world.

We know that every person desires to rejoice, but not all seek joy where it ought to be sought. [Note: The Farfense manuscript reads: “But not all seek joy there,” and so forth; the Urbevetan manuscript continues: “where it ought to be sought.”] True joy was not, is not, and cannot be in this world. For the Lord himself, in the Gospel, warns his disciples, saying: “In the world you will have tribulation” (John XVI). And again: “The world will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful; yet your sorrow will be turned into your joy” (ibid.).

Therefore, in this life, with labor and sorrow, let us do what is good with the Lord’s help, so that in the world to come we may gather the fruits of good things with joy and exultation, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen. [Note: The same fragment extends this far in the Laurentian manuscripts; the Farfense manuscript adds the continuation.]

## SERMON LXXI. On the same feast of Saint Laurence, deacon and martyr II

### NOTICE

This sermon, not previously edited, is found attributed to Saint Maximus in four manuscripts of the Laurentian Library: 39, Plut. XVII, page 171; 173 and 174, formerly belonging to the library of the cathedral chapter of Florence; and IV Minor. Convent., Plut. XVII. It is also found in Cassinese manuscript 100, page 136, with the following heading: “On the nativity of Saint Laurence the martyr, a sermon of Saint Maximus, bishop.”

Strengthened by these clear testimonies, we do not hesitate to bring it to light.

**ARGUMENT.**—[Col. 0679A] Saint Laurence is called by Saint Maximus the nurturer of the Roman Church, a native martyr, and archdeacon of the apostolic see. His mercy toward the poor, his courage, and his martyrdom are elegantly described.

Although, dearest brothers, the whole world is amazed with us at the passion that on this present day triumphed over the world’s faithlessness, nevertheless the Roman Church marvels with especial joy at the virtue of her foster son. For she ought to rejoice above all others, since, ennobled by so noble a blood, she possesses, in a certain sense, the peculiar dignity of a native martyr. Thus, while he was carrying out the office of archdeacon at the Apostolic See, and a greedy persecutor was pressing him to surrender the vessels dedicated to heavenly mysteries, the most faithful man mercifully distributed among the assembled multitude of the needy what the sacrilegious persecutor was attempting to seize as plunder. The exceptional man preferred to endure the assaults and attacks of the authorities [Col. 0679B] [Note: The Casinensis manuscript reads “to receive”] rather than have the venerable ministries exposed by him to impious eyes.

As soon as this most religious deed had been performed, the fury of the pagans blazed up with unrestrained cruelty; he immediately seized him and ordered him to be placed upon a gridiron [Col. 0679D] [Note: The same manuscript reads: “He orders him to be placed above the fires,”] over the flames, so that the strength of his devoted mind might be demonstrated by the burning of his body. For a most faithful heart does not know how to yield to mortal fire when the ardor of the spirit had already kindled it for every courage against the world [Note: The same manuscript omits “already”].

Why, perhaps, pagan, are you raging so savagely? What empty things are you plotting? Your fire is not Lawrence’s punishment, but his light. Your flame, by which you think he is being tortured, is a testing of the truth, not a cause for pitying the Christian. For the fact that divine power permits its servants to suffer such things, dearest brothers, 586 is a secret of eternal majesty and a hidden plan [Col. 0679C], so that every form of unbelief may recognize [Col. 0680A] that our faith is supported by complete truth. Its possession is so secure that it laughs at the raging world and glories in the very punishments inflicted upon its body [Note: The same manuscript reads “and from”]. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “Therefore Lawrence is burned…”]

Lawrence is burned in defense of the true God; and while he endures the flames of this world, he extinguishes for himself the everlasting fire of Gehenna. O torment desirable to all the faithful, by which all the punishment of that fearful judgment is dissolved! O desirable fire, by which eternal refreshment is obtained for devout minds! The flesh of Lawrence is indeed discolored by the flames, but the martyr’s soul is adorned; the body is weakened, but the spirit grows strong; and the corruption of his limbs sends his rejoicing soul to God, so that the body which did not yield to torments for the truth might be restored more gloriously through the privilege of its victorious soul.

But let us now see with what patient faith Saint Lawrence endured [Col. 0680B] the torments of the flames. Thus, when he was being tormented by the multiplied fire and the burning of glowing iron, and when, driven by the savage punishment, he was already thought to be failing, he suddenly burst into the voice of one who was indignant and laughing: “Turn me over,” he said; “King, eat; it is cooked now.” With what shame, I ask, was that most cruel torturer confounded, when, amid the torments of a man who stood firm, he was not only honored by no entreaty, but rebuked by the reproach of one who mocked him! And how greatly did Lawrence consign him to ridicule, when, having deprived him of food at a rich meal, he offered him the flesh of his own roasted body as food!

These, then, brothers, are Lawrence’s merits; this is the glory of his martyrdom. He enriched the poor, he did not betray the sacraments [Note: The same manuscript reads “did not surrender them”], he mocked the fires, and, as a victor leaving the world behind, he condemned the madness of his persecutor with a triumphant voice.

## SERMON LXXII. On the same feast of Saint Lawrence the deacon and martyr III

[Col. 0679]

### NOTICE

[Col. 0679]

587 I understand that this sermon too had not yet been published in print. I transcribed it from Vatican Ottobonian manuscript 106, because it alone, among the other three attributed to Saint Maximus, bore his name.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0679C] In the holy martyrs there shines more brightly the love by which God and one’s neighbor are loved. Lawrence displayed wondrous courage, conceived from the love of Christ. Jerusalem was glorified by Stephen, Rome by Lawrence.

Since the whole sum of virtue and the fullness of all righteousness arise from that love by which God and one’s neighbor are loved, this love is certainly found nowhere to excel more sublimely or shine more brightly [Col. 0679D] than in the blessed martyrs. They closely imitated the Lord Jesus Christ, who died for all human beings, both in the ardor of charity and in the deed of suffering.

For although no kindness of anyone can be equal to that love by which the Lord redeemed us—for it is one thing for a human being, destined to die by necessity, to die for a righteous person, and another to die for the ungodly, being free from the debt of death—nevertheless the martyrs also conferred much upon all human beings. By their courage the Lord, its giver, made use of them in such a way that he wished the punishment of death and the cruelty of the cross to be terrifying to all, but made them imitable by many.

If, then, no good person is good for himself alone, and wisdom is not friendly only to the wise person himself, and if this is the nature of true virtues—that the one who is bright with their light draws many away from dark error—then, for the instruction of God’s people, no model is more useful than the unconquered patience of the martyrs. The argument is easy for exhortation and effective for persuasion. Yet examples are stronger than words, and teaching by deed is greater than teaching by speech.

In this most excellent kind of instruction, blessed Lawrence, whose passion makes this day illustrious, possessed such glorious dignity that even his persecutors were able to recognize it. What wondrous strength of spirit he displayed, conceived principally from the love of Christ! It not only did not yield, but also strengthened others by the example of his endurance.

When pagan fury raged against every noblest member of Christ, and especially attacked those 588 who belonged to the priestly order, the impious persecutor boiled with rage against the deacon Lawrence [Col. 0681A], who excelled not only in the ministry of the sacraments but also in the administration of the Church’s resources. He proposed to himself a double spoil from one man: if he could make him a betrayer of sacred money, he would also make him an outsider to the true religion. Thus the man greedy for money and hostile to truth armed himself with a double torch: greed, to seize gold; impiety, to take away Christ.

He demanded from the spotless holy prelate the Church’s wealth, which he eagerly coveted. The most chaste deacon showed him where it had been deposited and presented him with very numerous flocks of holy poor people, in whose food and clothing he had stored imperishable riches. These resources were all the safer because they were proved to have been spent more holily.

The plunderer, frustrated, raged; and, burning with hatred of the religion that had established such a use of wealth, he attacked the seizure of the more precious treasure, in which he found no store of coins. He ordered Lawrence to disclose that deposit which was richer because it was more sacred, and prepared to force that most solid courage of the deacon’s spirit with dreadful torments. When the first failed to achieve their purpose, more severe ones followed: he ordered his mangled limbs, cut by many strokes of the whip, to be roasted over a fire laid beneath him, so that, upon the iron grate, which had already acquired from constant heat the power to burn, the alternating turning of his limbs might make the torture more severe and the punishment more prolonged [Col. 0682A].

You achieve nothing; you accomplish nothing, savage cruelty. While Lawrence is lifted up into heaven, you are consumed by your own flames. The flame of Christ’s love could not be overcome, and the fire that burned outwardly was weaker than the one that had been kindled within.

You raged against the martyr, persecutor, and increased his palm of victory while piling on punishment. For what did your ingenuity fail to discover for the victor’s glory, when even the instruments of punishment passed over into the honor of triumph?

Let us therefore rejoice, dearest brothers, with spiritual joy at the most fortunate end of this illustrious man. Let us glory in the Lord, who is wondrous in his saints, in whom he has established for us both protection and example. Thus 589 he glorified his glory throughout the whole world, so that from the rising of the sun to its setting [Col. 0682B] the lights of the deacons’ lamps might flash forth; and as Jerusalem was glorified by Stephen, so Rome became illustrious through Lawrence.

By his prayer and patronage we 590 confidently trust that we shall be helped without ceasing, so that, because—as the Apostle says—all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution, we may be strengthened by the spirit of charity and fortified by steadfastness of constant faith to overcome every temptation.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and with the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXIII. On the same feast of Saint Lawrence the deacon and martyr IV

[Col. 0681]

### NOTICE

[Col. 0681]

In Vatican manuscripts 6451, page 155, and 6454, page 353, and in Casinensis manuscripts 100, 102, and 109, folio 87, this brief sermon is also adorned with the name of Saint Maximus. From the very manner of its composition, however, we think it can plainly be recognized as having no other author than Maximus.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0681C] The most faithful martyr Lawrence, kindled by divine fire, patiently endured mortal flames and bravely conquered them, tortured by a certain doubled punishment of fire and iron.

Although pagan impiety had often been conquered by the virtues of countless martyrs, and, after exhausting every kind of punishment, saw that the people of God could not only not be overcome but were made stronger by its punishments, it attacked the most blessed Lawrence, kindled by the flames of its own fury.

But in him the most savage persecutor found a fire that no mortal flame could conquer. For that fire had kindled the breast of the most faithful martyr, concerning which the Lord said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12).

So patiently did that most courageous man endure and so bravely did he conquer those flames [Col. 0681D] that, while the executioner raged and his limbs were entirely burned, he neither denied Christ nor betrayed the vessels consecrated to heavenly mysteries. Who could estimate the confidence of his mind and the strength of spirit he displayed in this matter [Col. 0682C]? In the midst of such bitter punishment, he neither exposed the secret of the holy Church to impious eyes nor was compelled to deny the name of his Redeemer.

Consider, moreover, into what execrable savagery of a cruel mind the persecutor burst. As though a single flame, blazing from the fires laid beneath, were insufficient for the burning of a human body and for torturing the servant of God more violently; and under the appearance of a single torment, by a kind of doubled punishment, he tortured the most blessed martyr with both fire and iron.

But earthly fire completely melts away wherever the heavenly spirit grows hot with the fervor of the Holy Spirit. He is not overcome by glowing iron who invokes the Creator of iron to aid his struggle. Thus it happened that from unheard-of torments a new victory was born for the Christian soldier.

Nor should it disturb us, brothers, that pagans are permitted such power against God’s saints; this power is granted to them for the very reason that, while they rage more cruelly, they may be more gloriously conquered in the martyrs.

## SERMON LXXIV. On Saint Cyprian I

[Col. 0682]

### NOTICE

The first sermon on Saint Cyprian, as well as the second and third, was transcribed before anyone else by the distinguished Muratorius from the celebrated Ambrosian manuscript and published in volume IV of the *Anecdota*. We were unable to find any of them in another manuscript. Accordingly, we have followed the final Paduan edition of Muratorius’s *Anecdota*. We merely note that Saint Maximus wrote something distinctive about Saint Cyprian, as Gennadius testifies; this can be said equally of the two homilies published on pages 255 and following of this volume and of these sermons.

### ARGUMENT

591 [Col. 0683A] The Church honors the memory of Saint Cyprian, whose doctrine no less than whose blood is her glory. Cyprian taught many of the faithful not to fear death. This alone suffices for the complete praise of Saint Cornelius: he adorned the Apostolic See with his own blood.

Not undeservedly, dearest brothers, do you offer special observances to the blessed martyr Cyprian with a particular celebration and a most frequent gathering. The distinction of his earlier life raised him to the summit of the high priesthood, and his faithful service in the episcopate lifted him to the palm of martyrdom.

It is truly just and fitting that the Church should honor the memory of his confession with more devoted reverence toward Christ, since she glories no less in his doctrine than in his blood. For what is holier among ecclesiastical men than a martyr? What is clearer than a teacher? What is more exalted than a priest? “Precious,” says blessed David, “in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115).

How greatly, then, brothers, should he be honored by the faithful, whose end was not only precious in the sight of the Lord, but whose life was rich in faith and whose speech was most abundant? Rightly, I think, his life is proclaimed rich, 592 since his holy conduct rejoiced in an abundance of good morals and in the treasure of ever-varied virtues [Col. 0684A]. Nor is it unfittingly called most rich and splendid speech, since his eloquence shone forth with such great light that amid the threats of the wicked and the terrors of persecutors it raised up the faithful, strengthened the doubtful, and refuted unbelievers.

For no fear could divert him from teaching that faith for which, secure in Christ’s promise, he did not fear to be killed. What confidence in faith and virtue was his! What constancy! He not only armed himself against the assault of the world with the strength of a noble mind, but also, by establishing the hope of future blessedness, taught many of the faithful not to fear death.

From this it is clear, dearest brothers, with what glory he now shines among the angelic choirs: wondrous in his own passion and glorious in the confessions of others. Such were the ornaments of his spiritual words, and so forceful was the judgment of his heavenly teachings, that his exhortation moved the minds of believers more than the sword of the raging enemy.

What should I say about blessed Cornelius? This alone suffices for his complete praise: he adorned the Apostolic See, which he rightly obtained, with the gift of his reverend blood.

## SERMON LXXV. On the same Saint Cyprian

[Col. 0683]

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0683B] In the books of Saint Cyprian one observes how great was the purity of his chastity, the holiness of his goodness, and the greatness of his faith. His sound went out into all the earth. Truly he was a spiritual teacher and physician, whom the perfection of his mind and speech made illustrious in the world and glorious in heaven.

How great was the merit of blessed Cyprian, and how great his glory and venerable martyrdom were, his doctrine, known to everyone, bears witness, dearest brothers. He does not need praise from outsiders, whom the magnificence of his own speech makes illustrious among all people.

Finally, admirable eloquence produced monuments of his teaching so that he might reach even our own age; for while, as a skilled teacher, he instructed the peoples entrusted to him in the observance of heavenly commandments, he transmitted his life and faith to posterity.

Every diligent reader acknowledges that this is so, because in his books one observes how great was the purity of his chastity, the holiness of his goodness, and the greatness of his faith. For while he chastises the vices of sinners with severe rebuke and pursues the merits of the saints with worthy praise, he reveals that heavenly discipline dwells in his heart.

Without doubt, therefore, he is one of those brothers of whom it was said through the prophet: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18). The sound of the most blessed Cyprian has indeed gone out into all the earth, because under the whole heaven the glory of his passion became known and the trumpet of his most illustrious tongue resounded.

Truly the blast of his speech sounded forth when he kindled the Church of God, contending in spiritual warfare against the threats and terrors of the pagans, with the sound of heavenly eloquence. And lest he seem to arm God’s people against contempt of the present life by eloquence rather than courage, he trampled underfoot the death which by his preaching he had taught not to be feared, by undertaking the passion suffered for Christ’s name. Thus it came about that he urged every believer to undergo torments for religion not only by the exhortation of holy words but also by the most courageous example of his blood.

Truly he is to be honored by all and throughout the whole world, for with the full perfection of divine virtue he both asserted and fulfilled the work [Col. 0684C].

593 Here we append a fragment of another sermon of Saint Maximus on Saint Cyprian, published by Muratorius after Sermon 3 on Saint Lawrence, *Anecdota*, volume IV, page 65:

[lacuna] preserved, he urged peace by his words, preserved peace in his heart, and rejected every vice with his holy mouth, condemning it with a holier mind. Thus he cut away the thorns of various crimes as they sprouted, with the sharpest edge of his tongue, so that he might cut them down even more by the integrity of his blameless life.

He was also, as a truly spiritual teacher, harsh toward vices and gentle toward virtues; and he seasoned the tranquility of the sinner with the medicine of a harsher remedy, so that those whom the mercy of his goodness did not restrain might be frightened by the judgment of his rebuking tongue [Col. 0684D]. Thus he softened his severity with the sweetness of mingled gentleness, just as hotter water is often tempered by drops of cold water.

Indeed, he wounded some who were harder in spirit with the salutary arrows of his armed mouth, so that spiritual wounds might help those whom peaceful treatment could not benefit. He acted in the manner of a most skilled physician: when he found deadly ulcers deeply settled in a human body, 594 although he was good and exceedingly kind, he attacked the putrefaction of the dead flesh with iron, as though he had assumed cruelty, cutting away what was harmful. He did not spare the highest art of healing, in order to spare the patient; he grew angry in order to help, and for the sake of his sick person he displayed severity in order to heal.

For the wisest Solomon also says: “The wounds of a friend are sweeter than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27).

[Note: The Vulgate reads: “The wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates.”]

This life and this spirit advanced the most blessed Cyprian both to the priesthood and to martyrdom. This perfection of mind and speech made him illustrious in the world and glorious in heaven. “Precious,” he says, “in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115).

Rightly, brothers, the death of venerable Cyprian became precious, since he purchased it for himself from the Lord his God at the price of his manifold virtues [Col. 0686A]. Truly precious was his death, by whose exchange he bought for himself the inheritance of heaven and the eternal kingdom.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us celebrate this most magnificent martyrdom with complete devotion and reverence, because a rich life, a most eloquent tongue, and a precious death exalt him in Christ Jesus our Lord, who, with …, etc.

## SERMON LXXVI. On the same Saint Cyprian III

[Col. 0685]

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0685A] After presenting and explaining several testimonies from the Sacred Scriptures, Saint Maximus again praises Saint Cyprian aptly and at length.

We ought to learn above all from this how great is the magnitude and confidence of Christian faith: amid the wondrous gifts of heavenly promises, a desired joy arises for us from the death of the saints. For it is not the reasoning of nature but of religion that the death of a human being, when God is the cause of dying, saddens the minds of unbelievers but gladdens Christian hearts.

Therefore the deaths of martyred persons are celebrated in the Church of God as a genuine birthday, because through a new order of birth they are born, with death giving birth to them, for a new life in heaven.

In such a death, which comes for the truth of saving faith because the living and true God is believed in, and because carnal affection has been driven far away by hope of a better age, the father does not mourn, the mother does not cry out, the son consoles his sighing, the brother drives away sorrow, the husband rejects grief, and the wife tramples underfoot her affection for her beloved spouse.

For the warmth of earthly love yields—indeed, it yields—where the divine flame of charity has kindled the Christian’s mind. Set ablaze by this fire, the most ardent Cyprian despised his priesthood and his life in his passion, so that his passion might now make him a more glorious priest of Christ.

What could be more magnificent in a man whose death is no less admirable than his life? His confession was faithful in speech, and his martyrdom was wondrous in confession. In him there was a simple agreement and undivided fellowship of heart and tongue; for whatever the spirit of his own heart had brought to his lips, his holy tongue dictated to all who heard him, as the Savior says: “The good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart” (Matthew 12).

And who can possess a good treasure in a mortal heart except one whose breast Christ inhabits, as the most glorious Paul taught, saying: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power may be God’s and not from us” (2 Corinthians 4).

This, brothers, is the treasure of a good heart, which makes the mouth of God’s servants good and their tongue rich. This is the treasure by whose price every believer purchases for himself a blessed dwelling in paradise and an eternal kingdom.

With this treasure venerable 595 Cyprian enriched every believer through the abundant generosity of his tongue, while, though he is read by all, he himself felt no poverty in his riches [Col. 0686A]. For so great is the abundance of this treasure that the one who receives obtains the whole, while the one who gives loses nothing—like a burning lamp, which supplies its flame to lamps brought near it and nevertheless remains undiminished, without loss of the light it has transmitted [Col. 0686B].

I know, brothers, I know: it is a marvelous thing to possess what one can give and, by giving it, not lose it; to pour out the whole and feel no lack.

For this reason the most blessed Cyprian is to be celebrated by the devotion of all the faithful. By giving to the peoples what he possessed and retaining what he had given, he both exalted his admirable life with the clearest speech and consecrated it with his most precious blood, so that the courage of the one suffering might display the follower’s faith to the whole world.

Most rightly is that saying of David applied to him: “His mouth shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment, and the law of his God is in his heart” (Psalm 36).

In the perfection of his priesthood Cyprian’s heart was holy and his mouth wise. His tongue was truly terrifying: it impressed upon sinners both the integrity of his heart and the dreadful judgments of almighty God. He poured himself so completely into holy speech that he left nothing hidden in the secrecy of his heart.

596 Everyone who is skilled remains hidden within himself—remains hidden—unless a tongue trained in speech reveals the wisdom of his heart. What was not exceptional in that man? What was not wondrous, in whose mouth there was wisdom, in whose tongue judgment, and in whose heart the law of God, the mother of justice, remained?

Nor is it without purpose, dearest brothers, that the following order of the psalm adds: “And his steps shall not be overturned” (Psalm 36). Cyprian’s footsteps were truly not overturned, because the law of God lived in his heart. He who meditates upon heavenly wisdom and divine judgment with his mouth and tongue cannot have his steps stumble [Col. 0686D].

What moment of sin, or what instant of diabolical stealth, could ever be found in that man whose mouth and tongue throughout the whole span of night and day both know and speak the will of God, according to what was said by the prophet: “And he shall meditate on his law day and night” (Psalm 27)?

Believe, brothers, that the feet of him whose breast does not depart from the path of true faith will never be moved amid the adversities of this world. And because the most blessed Cyprian possessed every kind of virtue—as priest, as righteous man, and as wise man—he stood with an unwavering foot and could not be shaken in his passion.

Thus it is that from this one man we possess both an unoffending rule for living rightly and the strongest example of martyrdom. For he taught us to live for God and to die for God not only by his speech but also confirmed it by his deed [Col. 0688A].

## SERMON LXXVII. On the same Saint Cyprian IV

[Col. 0687]

### NOTICE

We read this sermon in the manuscripts of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, 90, no. 8, and 99, no. 77, as well as in Laurentian X Plut. XIV, page 320, with the name of Saint Maximus noted. In the latter manuscript we found that this same sermon occurs after the sermon beginning, “The feast of Saint Cyprian” (which we, following the editors, numbered among the homilies), with the following inscription: “Likewise the following, a continuation by Maximus.”

For this reason we do not agree with Gillotius, who attributes this very sermon to Saint Ambrose, Paris edition of 1569, works of Saint Ambrose, no. 73.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0687A] Since Saint Cyprian suffered at the time of the grape harvest, Maximus says, he fattened and refreshed us with the new wine of his martyrdom. On the new wine that refreshes and intoxicates the Christian; with this wine the apostles were filled, drunk and sober. Some observations on the grape and on thorns.

A few days ago, when we were celebrating the birthday of the most blessed martyr Cyprian, we were most sweetly gladdened at his feast, because, since he suffered at the time of the grape harvest, we too gathered sweet and varied fruits from his passion, as though from the vintage [Note: Manuscript 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads “we gather”].

For he fattened and refreshed us with the new wine of his martyrdom. There is a new wine that refreshes and intoxicates the Christian, but that intoxication makes him more sober: for whoever is intoxicated with heavenly grace is sobered from the burden of sins.

Filled with this new wine, the holy apostles, as Scripture says (Acts 2), spoke of the mighty works of God in foreign tongues. In this event they seemed at once to be drunk and sober: 597 they were thought drunk because speech that was beyond nature resounded loudly in them; they were sober because, in accordance with the custom of the mind, they praised God with devotion [Col. 0687C].

This did not happen through any arrogance or shamelessness, as though holy men had chosen to speak in an alien language; it happened through divine providence. Since one language is insufficient to magnify God, the devotion of the mind was poured forth through many tongues.

We have been gladdened because we have received the fruit of refreshment from the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth. For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth, as the prophet says (Isaiah 5), is the house of Israel; and that house is us. In faith we are Israelites, which is why the Apostle says: “Those who are of faith are sons of Abraham” (Galatians 3).

Since, therefore, we are Israel, we are the Lord’s vineyard. Let us carefully see to it that from the shoot of our work there be born not a sweet grape but gall, lest it be said to us as it was said to the Jews: “I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns; not justice, but a cry” (Isaiah 5).

What a harsh condition: that the possession which ought to have brought its lord the fruit of sweetness should have pierced him with the roughness of thorns [Note: Manuscript 90 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem explains: “that is, when the Jews ought to have received the Savior with devotion, they crowned him with thorns in his passion.” Manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Jerusalem reads: “that is, when the Jews ought to have received the Savior with complete faith and devotion, they crowned him with thorns in his passion. That crown, insofar as it came from the Jews, was an insult of injuries; insofar as it was upon the Lord, it was a crown of virtues. The Jews pierce the Lord when they crown him; they pierce him when they crucify him. Hence Scripture says, etc.”], that is, instead of receiving him, they crowned him with thorns in his passion.

That crown, insofar as it came from the Jews, was a crown of virtues. Hence Holy Scripture says: “They saw the one whom they pierced” (John 19). Therefore, brothers, see to it that it is not said to you also: “I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns.”

598 The thorns which the Jews placed upon the Lord with bloodstained hands, let us not place upon him with wicked thoughts, piercing him not with the sharpness of thorns but with the perversity of our deeds.

For there are thorns of the heart which also habitually wound the word of God. The Savior mentions them in the Gospel (Matthew 13), saying that the seed of the sower fell among thorns, that the thorns grew up, and that they choked what had been sown.

He himself goes on to explain what these thorns are: worldly anxieties, which, when they grow in a person’s heart, choke the Savior’s commandments within him. For who has ever been anxious about the world and been able to be anxious about Christ? Who, while providing for the profits of his household, has been able to provide for the needs of the Church?

Hence the Apostle says: “The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please God; but the married man is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (1 Corinthians 7).

Therefore, brothers, see to it that your vineyard does not produce thorns rather than grapes, and that your vintage does not bring forth vinegar rather than wine. Whoever gathers a vintage and does not distribute it to the poor gathers vinegar, not wine. Whoever stores up harvests and does not minister to the needy has stored up not the fruit of nourishment but the thistles of greed. For this reason Scripture says concerning our earth: “It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Genesis 3).

## SERMON LXXVIII. On the feast of the saints, especially Saint Cyprian

[Col. 0687]

### NOTICE

This sermon too exists in an Ambrosian manuscript inscribed with the name of Saint Maximus and was published by Muratorius. If the two sermons are compared, it can plainly be recognized that it differs from the sermon attributed to Saint Augustine in the Common of Many Roman Martyrs in the Breviary. Both are placed by the Maurists in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine.

The same sermon was published under the name of Leo in several old editions, and also in the Basel edition of Paul the Deacon’s *Homiliary* of 1496, as the Ballerini brothers observed in volume I of the works of Saint Leo, page 387, Venetian edition of 1753. But they judged that it should not be attributed to Leo.

Accordingly, since it bears the name of Saint Maximus not only in the Ambrosian manuscript but also in Casinensis manuscripts 106, folio 19 verso, and 117, folio 64 verso, we think it should be attributed to this author, and not to Augustine or Leo, as we read it named in Laurentian I Plut. XIV, page 51, Vatican 1267, and Saint Peter’s Basel manuscript 105.

We note that in these manuscripts the title of the sermon is as follows: “On the Holy Innocents; on the feast of the holy Innocents.”

### ARGUMENT

599 [Col. 0689A] Martyrs are justified not by punishment but by their cause. The souls of the righteous rightly rest beneath the altar, because the body is offered upon the Lord’s altar. Among the others, Saint Cyprian stands beneath God’s altar; having completed his martyrdom in the priesthood, he wrote more than the others.

Whenever, brothers, we celebrate the martyrdoms of the saints [Note: [Col. 0689B] Codex Vallicellianus A 10: “of the holy martyrs”], so often we proclaim the praises of the Savior [Note: [Col. 0689B] Codices Vaticanus 1267 and Vallicellianus A 10: “we declare”]; and whenever we affirm their suffering, so often we preach the glory of Christ. For we do not marvel at what they suffered, but at the one for whom they suffered. Therefore it is not punishment that is honored in praise, but faith [Note: [Col. 0689B] Codex S. Petri 105 C: “but faith is in the person”].

Thus we magnify the martyrs [Note: [Col. 0689B] Codex Vallicellianus A 10: “Thus we magnify the martyrs, but especially those who, when Christ was born, attained the kingdoms of everlasting happiness.” Codex Vallicellianus B 5 agrees in the rest, but adds only “when Christ was born, at the very beginning,” and then “but observe,” etc.] not because they endured severe punishments, but because for the sake of justice they endured those same punishments. For we have seen many criminals suffer worse penalties, but they do them no good, because the cause makes martyrs righteous [Note: [Col. 0689C] Codex Vaticanus 1265: “criminals”], whereas their own conscience condemns criminals.

The blessed martyrs must therefore be held in the highest and most eminent place because of their faith. But observe what place they deserve among human beings, since they have deserved a place with God beneath the altar [Note: [Col. 0689C] Codex Vallicellianus A 10: “beneath the altar”]. For holy Scripture says: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony that they held, and they cried out” (Revelation 6), and so forth. “Beneath the altar,” he says, “the souls of those who had been slain.” What could be said that is more reverent or more honorable than to rest beneath that altar on which sacrifice is celebrated to God, on which victims are offered, on which the Lord is priest, as it is written: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109).

Rightly, then, the martyrs are placed beneath the altar, because Christ is laid upon the altar. Rightly the souls of the righteous rest beneath the altar, because the body of the Lord is offered upon the altar. [Note: [Col. 0689D] Who could fail to perceive from this that Maximus is a witness to the divine tradition concerning the sacrifice of the Mass and the real presence of Christ in the sacrament of the Eucharist? Moreover, no orthodox person is unaware in what sense the holy doctor said both that Christ’s blood is poured out upon the altar and that the members of Christ are laid upon the altar. Therefore I do not think that it is necessary to spend time explaining these matters. Compare volume II of the work *On the Perpetuity of the Faith*, concerning the Eucharist, book III and following, chapter 8 and following, p. 307 and following, Paris edition of 1672.]

Nor is it without reason that the vengeance for the righteous’ blood is sought there [Note: [Col. 0689C] Codices Vaticanus 1267 and S. Petri 105 C: “the righteous seek vengeance for their blood”] where Christ’s blood is also poured out for sinners. Accordingly, and as though by a certain fellowship, burial was decreed for the martyrs there where the Lord’s death is celebrated every day, just as he himself says: “Whenever you do these things, you will proclaim my death until I come” (1 Corinthians 11). This is so that those who died because of his death might rest in the mystery of his sacrament.

Not without reason, I say, a tomb was established there for those who were slain, as if in a certain fellowship [Note: [Col. 0689C] Codex 4 of the Minor Holy Cross in the Laurentian Library: “there a tomb is established for those who were slain, where …,” etc. Codex I Laurentianus likewise; but Codex S. Petri 502 C reads: “Not without reason, I say, a certain fellowship and tomb is established for those who were slain,” etc.], where the members of the Lord’s slaughter are placed, so that those whom the cause of one passion had bound together with Christ might also be joined by the holiness of one place [Note: [Col. 0689C] After the word “joined,” Codex Vallicellianus B 5 adds: “Thus Christ says: ‘Father, I desire that where I am, there my minister also may be.’ We read that many …” Codex Vaticanus 1267: “For we read that many …”].

We read that many of the righteous are cherished in Abraham’s bosom, and that some rejoice in the pleasantness of paradise [Note: [Col. 0689D] Codex S. Petri 105 C: “rejoice.” “Yet no one more deserved, apart from the martyrs, to rest there where both the sacrifice …”]; nevertheless, no one deserved it more than the martyrs—that is, to rest where Christ is both victim and priest [Note: [Col. 0689D] Codices 4 of the Minor Holy Cross and I Laurentianus: “that is, to rest there …”]. This is so that they might receive both propitiation from the offering of the victim and the blessing [Note: [Col. 0690B] Codices Vaticanus 1267 and S. Petri 106 C: “and the priest’s ministry”] and the performance of the priestly office [Note: [Col. 0690B] Codex Laurentianus: “receive”].

Among the other martyrs, therefore, whom we proclaim to stand beneath the altar of God [Note: [Col. 0690B] In the Laurentian codices cited shortly afterward there is no mention of Saint Cyprian. Instead, both attach the sermon concerning the holy Innocents, as follows: “We also proclaim that those blessed infants, the sucklings who confessed Christ—who became the firstfruits of the martyrs—not by speaking but by dying, deserved crowns. For there can be no doubt that those who went before the others in martyrdom intercede more than the others in martyrdom. Therefore it is said to them, as they ask for vengeance …” Codex Vaticanus 1267: “We proclaim that those blessed choirs of suckling infants also …”; “who became the firstfruits of the martyrs for Christ, confessing him not by speaking but by dying, and deserved crowns. For there can be no doubt that those who preceded the others in martyrdom intercede more than the others. Therefore it is said to them, as they ask for vengeance, after the reward has been given, that they should rest and wait until the number is completed,” etc. Codex S. Petri 105 C: “We proclaim that those blessed suckling infants also, who became the firstfruits of the martyrs for Christ, confessed him not by speaking but by dying, and deserved crowns. For there can be no doubt that those who preceded the others in martyrdom intercede more than the others in martyrdom.” In the remainder [Col. 0690D] it agrees with Vaticanus 1267. In both, as anyone can see, there is nothing about Saint Cyprian. Add to these the Vallicellian codices A 10 and B 5, in which there is not even a word about Saint Cyprian. Codex B 5 agrees more closely with Codex S. Petri.], blessed Cyprian also stands, pursuing the vengeance of all with richer eloquence.
