For there can be no doubt that the one who wrote more than the others in the priesthood intercedes more than the others in martyrdom. And although he received, together with all the others, the robe of splendid recompense, perhaps he ceases less from speaking because he understands that he has earned more.

Therefore it is said to those who ask for vengeance, after the gift has been given, that they should rest and wait until the number of their fellow servants is completed, and so forth.

You see, then, that the vengeance of the martyrs is delayed on our account. For while we delay, their blood remains unavenged. But this has happened because of our sluggishness: we do not live religiously as we ought, nor do we perform our work piously as is fitting. For if our justice in good works went before God, the number of our fellow servants that is awaited would already have been completed. No one doubts that the martyrs will receive vengeance after the judgment; even after the judgment they are honored with heavenly rewards.

## Sermon LXXIX: On the Holy Maccabees I

[Col. 0691]

### Notice

Of the two sermons on the holy Maccabees written by Saint Maximus, the distinguished Muratorius was the first to publish them, having read them in the Ambrosian codex. By searching four Casinensian codices, we likewise found them attributed to Saint Maximus: in codices 100, 142, folio 75 verso; 147, folio 117 verso; and 148; and also in two Laurentian codices, IV Plut. XX and CIX XIV, formerly belonging to the library of the metropolitan church of Florence. The Ballerini brothers included another sermon on the Maccabees, attributed to Saint Leo, in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Leo.

### Summary

One faith shone forth among the Maccabees, while diverse courage became evident in each individual. Saint Maximus praises this courage by describing their noble deeds; he also praises the courage of their mother Felicitas.

What shall I first undertake to proclaim, beloved, about the Maccabean brothers, whose feast is celebrated today? How shall I turn my discourse toward their praises, when it is neither possible for me to explain their distinguished merits [Note: [Col. 0691D] All the cited codices omit the words “in a discourse in their praise”] nor, presumably, to follow them [Note: [Col. 0691D] Codices 174 Aedil. of the church of Florence and the Casinensian codices: “nor, plausibly, to leave them behind”]? For just as one faith shone forth in all of them, so diverse courage became evident in each.

Truly venerable brothers, and brothers to be celebrated by every mouth [Note: [Col. 0691D] Codex IV Plut. XX Laurentianus, folio 87 verso, and the cited Codex 174: “and to be celebrated with every honor,” etc. Casinensian codices 100, 142, and 147: “and to be celebrated with the praises of all”], among whom there is confession in their words and triumph in their courage.

When these men are compelled by royal fear and the cruelty of tortures to abstain from forbidden foods and to partake in prohibited things, they all follow one another with a single willingness to die [Note: [Col. 0691D] All the Casinensian codices omit this phrase], because all had one hope of living after death.

How beautifully, and with what praiseworthy steadfastness, they shrink from touching swine’s flesh, which at that time was regarded as unclean by heavenly prohibition; their devotion was preparing them for the coming of the immaculate Lamb [Note: [Col. 0691D] The same Casinensian codex adds: “They were preparing themselves for the coming of the spotless Lamb! The very brave young men are seized and driven toward what is wicked and forbidden by various tortures of words,” [Col. 0692D] etc.].

Therefore the very brave young men are seized and driven toward what is wicked and forbidden by various tortures inflicted on their limbs. Yet they stand firm manfully and do not yield to tyrannical fury [Note: [Col. 0692D] Codex 174: “nor do they yield to the tyrant’s fury”], so that, by the marvelous providence of almighty God, those whom the generation of the flesh had produced as temporal and mortal brothers might be made eternal brothers through punishment.

Who, indeed, would not receive with complete amazement the fact that, for the authority of the divine law, boys display wisdom, adolescents do not fear torments, and young men despise both royal gifts and the allurements of life itself [Note: [Col. 0692D] The Casinensian codices: “young men despise royal gifts, etc.”]?

The persecutor therefore begins with the eldest [Note: [Col. 0692D] The same Casinensian codices: “with the firstborn”], so that by the punishment of the elders he might bend the minds of those who followed toward obedience to his commands. But what the impious man devises to cause fear benefits the brothers as an example.

Each of them understands [Note: [Col. 0692D] The Casinensian codices: “that he can and ought either to overcome these things”] that he can and ought to overcome what had already been trampled underfoot by the vigor of their brotherly spirit and fraternal devotion.

But what, above all, will the inadequacy of our discourse say about their venerable mother, for whom joyful hopes arise from so many bereavements, and who exulted in as many funeral torments as she had rejoiced in her children [Note: [Col. 0692D] Codices 174 and the Casinensian codices: “who exulted in the triumphs of as many funerals as she had rejoiced in children,” etc.]?

Blessed Felicitas acted, in a certain sense, as a double mother: those whom she had brought forth by bodily law into the present life, she gave birth to through the courage of her spirit for everlasting ages. Who among mortals would not marvel, brothers [Note: [Col. 0692D] The same Casinensian codices: “dearest brothers”], and whose heart would not tremble, that a mother trembled with all her entrails lest any of her sons should either fear or fail to deserve death in so magnificent a contest?

Amid the funerals of the slaughtered children, there was not merely no groan of sorrow in the mother’s breast; rather, beyond the affection of womanly devotion, that wondrous mother exulted in the victory of those whom she knew she had nourished no less with faith than with milk.

Thus the order of birth passes into the order of passion, so that, according to the most righteous rule of martyrdom, they might be transferred to heaven by the path through which the world had received them.

O new affection of piety! The sons are tortured, and the mother exults; and she believed that she would thereby be proved a true mother in the sight of the Lord if, amid the deadly punishments of her numerous offspring, she had stood there with her heart unbent and her eyes dry.

Indeed, she rejoices in herself because she recognizes the courage of her mind in her children, and because she was able to send her sons ahead through such a death, so that hell would claim nothing of them.

But after all these astonishing events, the woman, having died with the same confession as her sons, follows without fear those whom she had sent ahead with such devotion. It was most just in the sight of the Lord that the mother of so many martyrs should depart from this world not without the consecration of martyrdom.

Nor should we ask, brothers, by what particular punishment she closed her most glorious day; for all the punishments of her sons that we have heard tortured her maternal entrails, and she alone felt more sharply whatever each of them endured [Note: [Col. 0693D] Codex 4 Laurentianus: “Nor should we ask, brothers, which punishment most gloriously brought her day to its close, since …”].

## Sermon LXXX: On the Maccabees II

[Col. 0693]

### Notice

This second sermon on the Maccabees is found inscribed to Saint Maximus not only in the four Casinensian codices just mentioned and in the Ambrosian codex, but also in Vaticanus 6451, folio 154 verso, with these words: “Sermon of Saint Maximus, bishop, on the Kalends of August, on the holy Maccabees.”

### Summary

The Maccabees, tortured by sword, flames, and various punishments, were secure in the glory of eternity. Neither the affection of the mother standing by them bends, nor does the crowd of her dying children break their mother. Truly incomparable is the faith of the most glorious woman.

The unity of spirit in the New and Old Testament is also declared by the courage and faith of the Maccabees [Note: [Col. 0693D] Codices IV Laurentianus, Casinensianus, and Vaticanus: “the courage of the Maccabean brothers,” etc.]. Secure in the glory of eternity because God had promised it, they overcame the cruelty of the bloodthirsty king by a pious death.

For nearly all the Gentile world, through the testimony of the Gospel, believes that our Lord Jesus Christ came from heaven; but all Judea had long learned through the Law and the Prophets that he would be born on earth from a virgin. Hence, beloved, the Maccabean brothers, out of reverence for their ancestral law, submitted themselves to sufferings before the Lord of the law suffered.

Hence they despised death before hell was conquered through Christ [Note: [Col. 0693D] Codices Vaticanus and Casinensianus: “before hell was conquered by Christ”]. Hence they gave their own blood in honor of the Redeemer before the Redeemer poured out his blood for them.

Who could doubt that they would have been unable either to approach or to endure so many evils of the present world unless they had believed, with the fullest faith, in the blessings of the age to come?

No one, brothers—no one despises a tyrant unless he is lifted up by hope in a legitimate ruler; no one prefers death to life unless he believes that life exists after death; no one willingly endures torments unless he hopes for rewards after the torments.

Therefore, when Antiochus raged against the servants of God with unbridled madness, he ordered the most devout band of seven brothers to be brought with their mother before his tribunal, so that either their mother, tortured by punishments as the mother of so numerous an offspring, might be overcome, or, if his own death did not perhaps terrify one of the boys, a brother’s death might disturb him.

But the madman was mistaken, ignorant of the power of religion, in which the highest form of piety consists in preferring God to brothers, God to children, and God to parents [Note: [Col. 0693D] The Casinensian codices: “in which that piety especially consists,” or “etc.”].

He therefore ordered them, contrary to the heavenly decrees, to eat swine’s flesh; and when they refused, he applied various kinds of punishment. But the hearts of the faithful do not know how to yield to the will of the faithless [Col. 0694A].

They are therefore dealt with by sword, flames, and various punishments [Note: [Col. 0693D] The same Casinensian codices read: “They are therefore dealt with by sword, flames, and various punishments. One man’s head is stripped of its skin, another’s tongue is cut out; one is fried, another is mutilated in hands and feet,” etc.]. One man’s head is stripped of its skin, another’s tongue is cut out; one is fried, another is mutilated in hands and feet.

Yet amid the murderous hands of their torturers, neither does the affection of the mother standing by bend the sons, nor does the crowd of her dying children break the mother.

Thus, in the brothers and the very aged woman, there was one desire to die for the law of God, so that she might seem to have brought forth her sons more by the spirit than by the flesh, and they might be judged to have drawn from their mother not so much the substance of milk as of faith.

Who would not marvel, whether faithful or faithless, that an extremely aged woman does not lament the death of so many beloved children? Who would not be astonished that, amid the cruel punishments of her sons, a joyful mother insults the raging king [Note: [Col. 0694D] Codex IV Laurentianus: “a joyful mother, insulting the raging king,” etc.], and that the persecutor is tormented instead by the courage of the one whom, in his impious plan, he had intended either to defile through apostasy or to condemn to bereavement [Note: [Col. 0694D] Codices Vaticanus 6451 and Casinensianus: “whom, through impious persecution, he had intended …”]?

For what surpasses every miracle is that the mother said to the youngest son, whom she had received from the king to persuade him to yield:

“I ask you, my son, to accept death as one worthy of your brothers, so that, in the mercy of God, I may receive you with your brothers” (2 Maccabees 7) [Note: [Col. 0694D] The Casinensian codex: “so that, having become worthy …”].

Truly incomparable is the faith of the most glorious woman! She stands secure concerning the dead, anxious concerning the living. For she knew that she would lose this one son alone if he alone feared to be killed.

But the young man was not degenerate. He had patiently watched his brothers’ struggles, gladly listened to his mother, and not only did not fear the torturing king, but rebuked the savage man with a fitting reprimand.

And rightly, beloved, that wondrous woman—confident of her sons’ triumph and confident of heavenly recompense—insulted the king and exulted in the Lord. She believed that she was then giving birth more blessedly [Note: [Col. 0694D] Codex Vaticanus 6451: “being brought to birth”] when she saw her sons go before her to God through a glorious death.

Antiochus multiplied the punishments; but in place of the multitude of temporal torments, the faithful old woman counted the eternal rewards of the triumphant children. After their death, she herself lay down among their most beloved bodies, with a death she desired and a faith to be desired [Col. 0695A] [Note: [Col. 0695D] Here the sermon ends according to the text of the Ambrosian codex, but the two Laurentian codices, Vaticanus 6451, and the Casinensian codices preserve the conclusion.].

Nor was she terrified by any punishments, for she had already conquered every kind of torment in the bodies of her sons. She did not tremble at being killed, for she was hastening toward that life to which she knew she had sent her children ahead.

## Sermon LXXXI: On the Holy Martyrs Alexander, Martyrius, and Sisinnius I

[Col. 0695]

### Notice

On the authority of the Ambrosian codex, Muratorius attributed to Saint Maximus the two sermons that follow on the holy martyrs Alexander, Martyrius, and Sisinnius. Gallandius later published them in volume IX of the *Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*.

### Summary

Saint Maximus sets forth the reasons why the holy martyrs Alexander, Martyrius, and Sisinnius ought to be honored with every kind of veneration, and he describes their passion.

Although we rightly marvel at all the blessed martyrs whom antiquity hands down to us as worthy of honor, we ought especially to receive with complete veneration the holy Alexander, Martyrius, and Sisinnius, who suffered in our own times.

For I do not know why we have a greater affection for those whom our own conscience knows than for those whom history teaches us. We know that the former were martyrs through reading, but the latter through the contemplation of our eyes. We learn of the former’s passions through the report of fame; the latter’s punishments we retain through the testimony of their faces.

Therefore I ought to have greater affection where opinion encourages my faith. Greater affection, I say, I ought to have there where what I have seen compels me to believe more devoutly even what I have not seen. For when some things I had heard seemed impossible to me, I began to believe that they could have happened once I saw similar things happen.

And therefore the passion of our own time has granted us this: that it might present a grace now visible and confirm faith in the past. We ought, then, to receive the blessed men mentioned above with complete veneration, first because they deigned to illuminate the days of our life with their precious blood; second because they bestowed upon us no small privilege before God, showing what faith existed among Christians in our age, from whose fellowship martyrs deserved to arise; third because they had lived such holy lives that they found the crown of martyrdom in a time of peace.

For when no persecuting king was pressing upon them and no sacrilegious tyrant was threatening them, it was Christian devotion, not public persecution, that made them confessors.

While they were building a church in the region of Anaunia at their own expense and presiding over its holy altar—one of them serving as a deacon and two performing the office of clerics—the inhabitants of that region, among whom the Christian name had previously been unknown, wished, according to their customary sacrilege, which they call a *lustrum*, to pollute all the places. The holy men reproved them and clearly exposed and refuted their errors with reasonable correction.

Then the inhabitants, intoxicated more by fury than by wine, seized them and wounded them with the most savage slaughter, so that one of them, after many tortures, remained half alive and awaited and witnessed the outcome of his death. For they destroyed the church building, constructed a pyre from its beams, and delivered the blessed bodies to the flames.

Truly blessed are the bodies which the dreadful fire did not seize for the punishment of an idol, but which the holy flame received for the repose of the Lord’s house. A truly holy flame, which received the martyrs not to consume them in a harmful fire, but to prevent sacrilegious hands from reaching them.

In such a conflagration the entrails of the blessed were consecrated, not burned. What the Apostle says suits this passion: “He himself will be saved, but as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3). For these men were saved when they were consumed in the fire of their venerable confession.

This, then, is the whole cause of their passion, brothers, on account of which the holy men, having been given over to death, urged the rest to be like runners completing their course. Their exhortation made such progress that, when they departed from the world, their faith spread throughout every place of that region.

Thus, where Christ then suffered persecution in the three martyrs, he now rejoices there amid great numbers of Christians.

## Sermon LXXXII: On the Same Holy Martyrs II

[Col. 0695]

### Summary

Religious devotion made Alexander, Martyrius, and Sisinnius martyrs because they did not conceal the people devoted to superstitious ritual, but steadfastly reproved them. Let us imitate the example of the holy men. For if we see these things and remain silent, we make ourselves guilty through the consent and connivance of dissimulation.

Recently, when we were celebrating with the greatest festivity the feast of the holy Alexander, Martyrius, and Sisinnius, we especially praised this in their passion: that while they resisted sacrilegious people, they deserved to become martyrs, and while they opposed their superstitions, they won the palm of righteousness.

They were not handed over to death by people who were Christians; rather, they were dragged to punishment because they reproved the sacrilegious, because they were not Christians and devout.

Therefore, in a time of peace, when no persecuting king was pressing upon them, it was religious devotion, not public persecution, that made them holy martyrs. They did not fear to undergo danger to their own safety while they desired to provide for the safety of many.

For when they saw pagan people in their region polluting every place through their customary sacrilege, which they call a *lustrum*, by dreadful processions, and defiling innocent people—even those absent from the proceedings—either through complicity or connivance—for connivance defiles the one who, although he could have prevented the act by objecting, permitted it to happen as though through dissimulation—when the blessed men saw these things, they steadfastly reproved them and faithfully rebuked them. In this way they brought it about that they became martyrs there and made their persecutors Christians.

Therefore, brothers, because we have an example, let us imitate the holy men, if not through the martyrdom of suffering, then at least through the duty of Christian conduct. And because we have heard that some sacrilegious people are accustomed to perform a *lustrum*, let us rebuke the impious and correct those who err; for it is a share in martyrdom to do what the martyrs did.

But if we see these things and remain silent, if we silently endure them, we make ourselves guilty—not through the actual commission of the crime, but at least through the consent of dissimulation. For just as opposing sacrileges justifies the one who objects, so concealing what one sees defiles the one who remains silent.

Many wretched people are accustomed to say: “I do not know; I did not order it; it is not my affair; it does not concern me.” But, as I said, each frightened wretch speaks this way: he denies that he ordered it, although he did not wish to order that it not be done. For an evil that arises from custom is admitted when it is not restrained.

“It is not my affair,” he says. You are mistaken and do not understand. Do you not know that God’s affair belongs to everyone, and that what is committed by one is punished in many? For just as many are sanctified by the holiness of one, so very many are polluted by the sacrilege of one.

Therefore, an evil that is committed by another while you know of it concerns you, since it is held enclosed within your conscience.

But I do not know, brothers, what it is that makes us carry out God’s commands with such dissimulation. When the rulers of the world give orders, everyone obeys carefully; everyone vigilantly observes their commands. God gives orders, and we sleep through his commands.

How often has that same God commanded that the sacrileges of idols be destroyed, and yet we never wish to be concerned about this matter? We have always dissembled; we have always despised it.

Afterward an imperial command admonished us. See how great an insult to divinity this addition of human authority is. And what judgment is formed about us, who are compelled to live religiously not by devotion but by fear?

The rulers, indeed, as good Christians, promulgate laws for the sake of religion, but the officials do not enforce them properly. And therefore, once the ruler has been freed from guilt, the official remains liable, for if he enforces the severity of the law, he too is absolved from sin and will be granted eternal reward for the salvation of many.

## Sermon LXXXIII: On the Feast of the Holy Maccabees and Saint Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli

[Col. 0697]

### Notice

There is no reason why we should not regard this sermon as belonging to Saint Maximus. It is so similar in diction and style to the other sermons of the holy bishop that nothing more similar could seem possible. I am all the more confirmed in this judgment because I see that this same sermon is presented in full together with other sermons of Maximus in an old codex of the Laurentian Medicean Library, I Plut. XIV, p. 144, bearing the name of that same Maximus.

Some interpolator of the ancient records had the audacity to tear this very sermon into parts and, from them, arbitrarily construct two sermons on Saint Eusebius. Muratorius published them among the sermons of Maximus, but I judged that they ought to be relegated to our appendix.

### Summary

The particular reasons for which the Maccabees and blessed Eusebius fought are described. The martyrdom of each of the Maccabees and the passion of blessed Eusebius are recounted. Eusebius is not inferior: after refuting the perfidy of the Arians, he departed to God after his torments.

Beloved brothers, the devotion of a twofold festival invites us to gather with complete eagerness for the celebration of this present day. It is clear that we are keeping a festival of the triumph of the Maccabees and the victory of the confessor (2 Maccabees 7).

We have a general joy concerning the Maccabees, together with the others, but through blessed Eusebius we have a domestic, personal, and distinctive joy. Although they fought at different times and in different contests, one spirit fought in them all.

For who could doubt that they had one understanding, one mind, and one spirit, since they suffered for the law of the Lord, while this man endured suffering for the Lord himself?

Let us now consider more carefully the particular reason for which the Maccabees fought and that for which blessed Eusebius fought.

When, in ancient times, the Gentiles, kindled by the flames of the devil’s envy, burned against the servants of God, and when the especially savage heart of Antiochus was filled with impious madness, he ordered the Maccabean brothers and their most devout mother to be seized and brought before his deadly tribunal, so that through fear of death, terror of punishments, and offers of gifts he might persuade them to adopt his error.

But neither the threats of the world recall the most devout young men from their God, nor do royal blandishments lead them astray. Therefore, by the justice of divine providence, the first of them enters the arena of heavenly struggle, so that, being first in age, he might be first in suffering, and so that the order of birth among the brothers might preserve the order of triumph.

The king orders this eldest brother to be fried in a heated pan, but God cools him; his hands and feet are cut off, but he is entirely secure concerning the restoration of his body, because he knew that he suffered these things for the sake of the law of the one whom he believed alone possessed the power to form and restore the body.

For this reason the very brave young man is cut apart throughout his body and limbs, so that he might understand that, by God’s provision, he possessed as many martyrdoms as he had limbs. One loses his tongue, another is stripped of the skin of his head, so that the diversity of punishments might produce a diversity of rewards.

Cruelty, therefore, aggravated to every kind of savagery by the courage of the saints, rages. The hands of the executioners grow weary; their bloodstained eyes waste away; and impiety itself now blushes at what it has done. The order of the interrogation is reversed: the torturer groans, while the tortured man insults his torturer.

After six brothers had been struck down and cast down in this way, the seventh—the youngest, who was brought forward for examination—was introduced. That tyrannical king tried in vain to soften him with the gentlest speech, after so many and such great punishments had been expended.

He promised wealth, offered honors, and even pledged his friendship, if he could obtain apostasy from the boy [Col. 0699A]. But the steadfast youth despised both the king and the king’s gifts. Wandering through paradise in his thoughts and traversing heaven in his mind, he judged punishments more advantageous than gifts and chose to die for God rather than live with the tyrant.

Nor could royal promises bend the one whom his brothers’ torments had not bent. Indeed, as the outcome showed, the faithful boy seemed to be tortured more in this respect: that he was tortured later.

Meanwhile, the exceptional mother rejoiced, divinely inspired by the torments of her sons, confident that she would be adorned with as many crowns as funerals she had endured in her children. Who could hear these things without amazement? For the sake of God’s honor, natural affection grows cold in the mother’s breast; faith overcomes nature; and the woman, stronger than her sex, teaches her sons to love torments.

After sending her children ahead to God, she too, despising the world, succumbed to a most glorious death. It was truly fitting that the mother of martyrs should end her life through martyrdom.

[Note: [Col. 0699D] The Venetian edition, p. 156, following the Paduan edition of the *Anecdota* and Muratorius, volume IV, p. 85, continues as follows: “After these events, brothers, what my soul also desires …,” etc. All of this is absent from the cited Laurentian codex up to and including the words “from whom Eusebius was separated.”]

After these things, dearest, let us now recount as best we can what our most blessed father Eusebius endured in defense of the faith, so that we may perceive how great was the labor, and what merits raised him to such glory of confession. Thus, as our father’s account instructs us, he was snatched from this city and brought to Scythopolis, where he was handed over to the Arians to be slaughtered. It is not unknown, brothers, how much wickedness the freedom granted to an enemy to rage can exercise.

[Note: [Col. 0700D] Up to the words “the freedom granted to rage,” the codex agrees with the editions, but everything that follows is extraneous to it.]

To continue with what follows in his sufferings, it is said that, after that prophetic ascent by stairs, the Arians devised the following punishment for him: in the upper part of the house they prepared an exceedingly narrow room, so short, so low, and so cramped that it seemed less able to contain a man than to torture him; the Arian lodging was more a punishment than a resting place. For they say that it was so confined that the martyr, lying there, could not stretch out his foot; standing, he could not raise his head; he was always contracted, bent, and bowed, carrying nothing else except the free spirit of faith. His feet, fixed in one place, certainly grew numb, but by the steps of faith he walked through paradise; his bowed head lay there, but Christ raised his head within him.

The blessed martyr suffered these things in the lodging of the heretics—not because such treatment was owed to a martyr, but because Arian hospitality is of such a kind that its dwelling is the punishment of a prison, not the lodging of human kindness.

And although there is no mutual weariness for us in speaking and hearing about the sweetness of his deeds,

[Note: [Col. 0700D] “And although there is no weariness from the sweetness, etc.” These words and those above occur in Sermons 3 and 4 on Saint Eusebius, included in the appendix.]

yet the victory of the most blessed Maccabees must not be passed over in silence, since this same day also delivered them, rescued from the world, to heaven with a great triumph. And although that very courageous chorus passed to their God amid torments, Eusebius is not their inferior: he migrated to the same God after the torments, having refuted and conquered perfidy.

And so that we may perceive more clearly that Eusebius’ 614 victory was not inferior, those men fought for the ancient Law, whereas he served as a soldier for the new Gospel. They endured punishments for the commandments of God; Eusebius, however, contended for the truth of the very Godhead. They resisted King Antiochus so that they would not eat unlawful meats; he opposed the devil so that the bread of the Lord might not be defiled for us by the leaven of heretical teaching.

Let us therefore rejoice, brothers, giving thanks to our God, because under the devotion of this present day we rejoice in a double festival: receiving the triumph of Eusebius and marveling at the torments of the victorious Maccabees. Are not the Maccabees worthy of wonder? Through sharing one birth and one passion, we see that they were brothers in the world and are kindred in heaven; from the rich breast of their excellent mother they drew both the substance of life and the strength to conquer.

They grew to such perfection on their mother’s milk and teaching that wisdom was inseparable in their hearts, and strength in their bodies. Finally, Antiochus could neither terrify these outstanding young men, steadfast through their own faith and their mother’s exhortation, with the harshest punishments, nor draw them away with great promises, so as to turn them from reverence for their ancestral law. For such vigor was in their limbs, such spirit in their breasts, and such learning in their replies that, by scorning the punishments and refuting the impious king’s perfidy, they overcame both his terror and his fury.

Their venerable mother, having died with an equal confession and a similar death, departed from this world and went to her children with greater joy. Nor is it surprising that she endured the king’s savagery against herself with such courage, since she was able to endure it so bravely in her sons. Truly blessed was that woman, worthy to be celebrated by the praises of all: for the faith of her God, neither the affection of the flesh broke her when her sons perished, nor could either her sex or her old age call her back from the torments of her own body.

These, then, dearest, are the devout joys of the faithful on this day. Let us always offer such observances to blessed Eusebius and to the most glorious Maccabees, whom a different time, but the same faith and one day, brought forward into the eternal kingdom.

## SERMON LXXXIV. On the Feast of the Holy Martyrs Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla

[Col. 0699]

### NOTICE

615 Muratori was preceded in judgment concerning this sermon by the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius and by the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur. In his notes on the Roman Martyrology, where he commemorates the holy martyrs of Ravenna on the fifth day before the Nones of April, Baronius teaches that Saint Maximus should be recognized as its author. Since the testimonies of both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, 90 and 99, and of the Codex Sangallensis support the opinion of such distinguished men, we more safely ascribe it to that same holy bishop of Turin, against Codex X of the Laurentian Library, Pluteus XIV, and the Paris edition of Gillotius, no. 75 of the sermons, which attribute it to Ambrose. The title in Codex 99 of the Holy Cross, sermon 79, is: “On the Feast of the Holy Cantians”; in Codex 90 it is sermon 13: “On the Feast of the Saints Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla,” which is likewise found in the Sangallensis, sermon 13.

[Col. 0701A] **ARGUMENT.**—Christ granted them that those who were brothers by blood relationship should also become kindred in holiness. The story of their martyrdom.

Today is the feast of the most blessed Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla. How fittingly and pleasantly these three martyrs are called by almost one name! Nor is it surprising that those who are alike in passion should be alike in name, since they have one designation among human beings whose calling before God is one.

[Note: [Col. 0701C] Thus the cited codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and Codex X, Pluteus XIV, of the Laurentian Library supply the text.]

For they were called together by the Lord, not suffering at different times and in different ways, but all enduring martyrdom together in the same stroke.

[Note: [Col. 0701C] The same Codex X of the Laurentian Library reads: “For they were called unanimously.”]

This was granted to them by Christ through a kind of parental affection.

[Note: [Col. 0702C] The same Laurentian Codex X has *Quod quidem illis parentina quadam* (“This indeed [was granted] to them by a kind of parental [affection]”).]

Thus those who agreed in name might correspond in merit; those who were brothers by blood relationship might also become kindred in holiness; and the limbs whose substance was invigorated as one body might have their souls crowned by the confession of the same faith.

The history of the aforesaid blessed men relates that, at the time of their passion, when the persecutor was seeking them, they mounted a vehicle and, having joined the mules, wished to withdraw. As they were traveling not far from the city walls, one of the animals harnessed beneath the vehicle suddenly fell, and thus they were seized by the persecutors and taken to punishment. We must consider how glorious this event was and how it was arranged by the Divinity.

For just as Elijah, with his chariot attached, seemed to ascend to 616 heaven, so these men, with a vehicle brought near, arrived at martyrdom; and just as the chariot carried Elijah to rest, so it bore them to glory. Although that chariot was fiery, this one must not be regarded as inferior, since the former carried one prophet, whereas the latter supported three martyrs.

But someone may say: “It is more glorious to be carried in a fiery chariot than in an earthly one.”

[Note: [Col. 0702C] The codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and Codex X of the Laurentian Library read: “Nor was this altogether lacking,” etc.]

This was not entirely lacking in these holy men. For just as a fiery chariot carried Elijah, so an ardent faith was already carrying the martyrs. Christ, I say, was carrying them—he who is light, who is fire, of whom it is written: “Our Lord is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4).

Therefore, when the persecutor pressed the blessed men of whom we speak, they mounted the vehicle. Why? To flee? Far from it. Not to flee, but to reach martyrdom more quickly; not to hide, but to show themselves more openly as Christians to all who passed by.

Besides, they could have hidden more secretly among the crowds in the city, or each of them could have entrusted himself more safely to flight in different directions. But when someone, after gathering people together and arranging the vehicles and their equipment, goes out along the public road, that cannot be called flight but departure.

By this action the holy men, as though placed in a triumphal chariot, bore witness, saying: “Behold the persecutor; behold, we are setting out; behold, we are going ahead. Why are you sitting still? Why do you delay? Follow in our footsteps. For we do not wish to appear to be led unwillingly to punishment, since we declare that we are going ahead to glory.”

## SERMON LXXXV. On the Feast of Saint Stephen, the Protomartyr

[Col. 0701]

### NOTICE

617 We now bring this sermon to light for the first time. We copied it from a very ancient codex belonging to the library of His Eminence Francisco Xaverio de Zelada. It bears Saint Maximus’ own name at its beginning, and there is no reason to doubt that he was its author, since attached to it is found a homily on the feast of that same Saint Stephen, deacon and martyr, which we have published in its proper place. We have already stated that it was the incompetence of copyists of a later age either to combine one sermon from several discourses or to divide one sermon into several readings.

[Col. 0701C] **ARGUMENT.**—Blessed Stephen was given to the whole Church for its advancement: though still a layman, he deserved election to the diaconate, and, as a Levite, he deserved the primacy of martyrdom.

Yesterday we celebrated the feast of the Lord our Savior. Today, with the highest devotion, we venerate the passion of Saint Stephen the martyr. Yesterday was the day on which we were redeemed for our reward; today is the day on which we are summoned to follow an example. Thus the festival of yesterday’s solemnity was fittingly joined to today’s, so that the former might raise believers to life and the latter lead confessors to the crown.

Blessed Stephen 618, therefore, was given to the whole Church for its advancement. Though still a layman, he deserved election to the diaconate, and, as a Levite, he deserved the primacy of martyrdom. He still belonged to the common people, but he excelled in virtues; he held a humble position, but was exalted in faith; he was a disciple by rank, but became a teacher by example.

It is written about him in the Acts of the Apostles that he was appointed by the apostles to the ministry of the widows. In this fact—that he was placed in charge of the ministry—he earned the testimony of the most holy chastity. Blessed, therefore, will be, dearest brothers, the person who follows and imitates him, and who will obtain both the palm of purity and the crown of martyrdom. Concerning him, the reading from the Acts of the Apostles that was read to us today also says, etc.

## SERMON LXXXVI. Also, on the Feast of the Holy Martyrs I

[Col. 0703]

### NOTICE

Although the Maurists number this sermon among the Ambrosian works as no. 61 in the Paris edition of Saint Ambrose’s works (1690), they nevertheless judge it more likely that Saint Maximus was its author. They say that it is a general homily on the martyrs, praised by Gennadius and read as no. 12 in the Sangallensis codex. In the ancient codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, 90 and 99, the same sermon bears the name of Saint Maximus. Accordingly, we pay no attention to the copyists of later times—such as Vatican Codex 1269, p. 26, and Laurentian Codex 37, Pluteus XVII, p. 159—who attribute it to Saint Ambrose. We note that Muratori published it in volume IV of the *Anecdota*, p. 26, under the title “On the Feast of the Holy Martyrs”; it begins: “As we know, brothers, the festival of the servants always follows the vows of the Lord.” In the Urbevetanus codex and Codex IV of the Minor Convent Library, now in the Laurentian Library, the same sermon is read without the author’s name.

[Col. 0703A] **ARGUMENT.**—Saint Maximus compares the glory of the Lord’s resurrection with the holy martyrs. He adds that perhaps many of the martyrs also attained, or have attained, bodily resurrection with the Lord.

It is fitting and appropriate, brothers, that after the joy of blessed Easter, which we have celebrated in the Church, we share our joys with the martyrs and announce the glory of the Lord’s resurrection to those who share in the Lord’s passion. For those who are companions in disgrace ought also to be participants in joy.

[Note: [Col. 0703C] The Urbevetanus codex reads: “It is fitting and appropriate that we share our joys with the holy martyrs.”]

Thus the blessed Apostle says: “As you are companions in sufferings, so shall you be in the resurrection” (2 Cor. 1).

[Note: [Col. 0703C] Vatican Codex 6451 reads: “If you are companions in sufferings, so shall you be in the resurrection.”]

“If we endure,” he says, “we shall also reign with him” (2 Tim. 2).

[Note: [Col. 0703C] The Urbevetanus codex reads: “If we endure,” he says, “we shall also reign with him.”]

Those, therefore, who endured evils for Christ ought also to have glory 619 with Christ.

Let us announce, I say, to the holy martyrs the grace of the Lord’s Easter:

[Note: [Col. 0703D] Vatican Codex 6451 reads: “the glory of the Lord’s resurrection.”]

while we proclaim that the barriers of his tomb have been opened, may their tombs also be opened; while we say that his dead body suddenly came to life again, its veins warming, may their limbs, already cold, likewise be warmed by the heat of immortality. The same power raises the martyrs that raised the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0703D] Codex 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “For the same grace raises the martyrs.”]

For just as they experienced the way of his passion, so they also experience life.

[Note: [Col. 0703D] Vatican Codex 6451 reads: “so they will also experience the way of life.”]

For it is written in the Psalm: “You have made known to me the ways of life” (Ps. 15). This is certainly spoken in the person of the Savior at the resurrection: when, after death, he returns from the lower world to the heights, he begins to know the way of life that had previously been unknown.

The way of life was unknown before Christ,

[Note: [Col. 0703D] Codices 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, Vatican Codex 1269, and Vatican Codex 6451 read: “Before Christ’s coming the way of life was unknown.”]

because no one who had risen had yet opened it by his footsteps. But when the Lord rose, the way became known and was trodden by many, of whom the holy Evangelist says: “Many bodies of the saints rose again with him and entered the holy city” (Matt. 27).

[Note: [Col. 0704C] Vatican Codex 1264 reads: “rose again.”]

Therefore, when the Lord said at his resurrection, “You have made known to me the ways of life,” we too can now say to the Lord: “You have made known to us the ways of life.” For he made the ways of life known to us by revealing to us the path to life. He made the ways of life known to me when he taught me faith, mercy, justice, and chastity.

[Note: [Col. 0704C] Vatican Codex 6451 reads “charity” instead of “chastity.”]

For by these roads one reaches salvation. And although, when our body is dissolved,

[Note: [Col. 0704C] Vatican Codex 6451 reads: “And although, when our body is dissolved,” etc.]

the shadow of death surrounds us, life nevertheless does not abandon its steps. Even amid the very laws of hell, we walk fearlessly by the virtues of Christ.

Therefore the holy prophet says: “For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me” (Ps. 22). More clearly the Lord says this concerning the faithful person: “Whoever believes in me will not die,”

[Note: [Col. 0704C] Vatican Codex 6451 reads: “will not die forever,” and adds, [Col. 0704D] “and although he dies, he lives.”]

“and although he dies, he will live” (John 11).

Therefore, brothers, let us share with the holy martyrs the glory of the Lord’s Easter.

[Note: [Col. 0704D] Codex 6451 reads: “Let us share the glory of the Lord’s resurrection.”]

Let us share it, I say. Although they know everything better, let us nevertheless proclaim to them how he rose from the bosom of the tomb

[Col. 0704B] to the heights. Let them reveal to us how he returned from the depths of hell

[Note: [Col. 0704D] Codex 6451 reads: “from the depth of hell.”]

to 620 the tomb. Let them make known to us how, in a body already lifeless and cold, heat entered, spirit was infused, blood poured in, and the pulse of former vigor began to stir veins frozen by moisture. Let them make known to us how the loosened framework once again fitted together the scattered organs of the body into their former state, and how the life-giving spirit restored the harmony of the inner organs, now silent, to their former concord.

Let priests therefore proclaim what wonders the Savior performed after his resurrection in the world above. Let the martyrs reveal what refreshment he effected in the dead in the very midst of death.

[Note: [Col. 0704D] Here Codex S. Crucis Minor in the Laurentian Library continues, omitting the opening words “As we know.”]

The festival of the servants always follows the vows of the Lord,

[Col. 0704C] and the joy of the master of the household is accompanied by the joy of his faithful servants—namely, so that those who followed him in the likeness of his passion may also accompany him in the glory of his resurrection.

They accompany him also in the glory of the resurrection, as the Apostle says: “For if you are companions in sufferings, you shall also be companions in the resurrection” (2 Cor. 1).

Is there, then, a fellowship between the holy martyrs and Christ in his resurrection? There certainly is. For although they had not yet risen bodily, they had already risen in merit; although they had not yet received their limbs, they had already received grace. If they have not yet been delivered from the lower world, they have been delivered from sins.

[Note: [Col. 0705D] The holy bishop said that the martyrs, who had not yet risen, were indeed still held in the lower world—that is, in their tombs—but were nevertheless free from sins. This is to be understood of their bodies, not of their souls, which since death have enjoyed immortal light.]

For this is the first resurrection: to escape the darkness of sins and possess the light of righteousness. Nevertheless, perhaps many of those same blessed martyrs either will attain, or have attained, bodily resurrection with the Lord. For if we read that, at the festival of the first resurrection, when the Lord raised himself, many bodies of the saints rose again and came to life and entered the holy city, why should we not believe that, whenever the festival of his resurrection is celebrated, the saints also rise?

[Note: [Col. 0706D] This was indeed a distinctive opinion of Maximus: that on the annual solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection the bodily resurrection of certain holy martyrs is renewed.]

For where there is an unbroken solemnity of vows, there is also an unbroken grace of gifts.

But perhaps someone will say: “The tombs are closed and monuments have been built;

[Col. 0706A] how could they come forth from there?” To say nothing of the fact that all things are possible for God, and that he can lead forth a spiritual 621 body even when the inner chambers of the tomb are closed; to pass over all these matters, we nevertheless have the example of the apostle John. The tomb was able to receive and close him in, but it could not keep him. For it lost the body that had been deposited there; it did not retain it.

Here, when the doors of the tomb had been closed, he was removed by the grace of the resurrection 622, so that there would be a burial place, but no buried man would be found. Finally, when the priests sought the body in order to honor it, after the entrance had been opened, the tomb could not return the one it had received. Therefore, when the Savior rises, he raises his offerings with him.

## SERMON LXXXVII. Also, on the Feast of the Holy Martyrs II

[Col. 0705]

### NOTICE

The same highly learned Maurists, in the preface to this sermon, no. 60 of the Paris edition of Saint Ambrose’s works, persuade me not to agree either with the scribes of the codices or with the Roman Breviary, which attribute it to Saint Ambrose. In the Sangallensis and in Codices 90 and 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, we read that it is ascribed to Saint Maximus. One Urbevetan codex bears the name of Saint Gregory the Great.

[Col. 0705B] **ARGUMENT.**—Although the holy martyrs are silent in voice, they nevertheless instruct us by the virtue of their deeds and persuade us through the suffering of martyrdom. The martyr’s victory is the judgment of the persecutor.

If my bodily weakness could pursue as much as I must say and you ought to hear, we would all certainly be excused: I, for making known the command, and you, for carrying out the injunction. But since we are overcome by weakness and cannot speak as much as we ought, devotion of mind excuses us, though the act of preaching does not. That is: if our tongue falls silent in praising the Lord, let us nevertheless demonstrate his wonders through works of faith.

If we do not express his glory in words, let us fulfill his grace through deeds, since deeds take precedence over words. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever does and teaches, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

[Note: [Col. 0705D] Codex 99 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads: “Whoever does and teaches thus shall be called great,” etc. The same codex reads: “Whoever does thus and teaches thus,” etc.]

You see, therefore, that action comes first and teaching follows; indeed, doing good is the first instruction. When words fall silent, the excellent deed itself teaches a person by being seen. Even if it does not stir the ears by its voice, it can nevertheless pierce hearts by its virtue. For who, seeing a good deed, would not rejoice, imitate it, and, using it as a silent teacher, be instructed by its example?

[Note: [Col. 0705D] Both codices of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and the Urbevetanus codex read: “so that he may not rejoice, marvel, imitate, and, as it were,” etc.]

Thus deeds precede words; indeed, without deeds words are useless.

[Note: [Col. 0705D] The Urbevetanus codex reads: “For this reason the Lord first wished it to be done and then taught, lest words without good works should be,” [Col. 0706D] etc.]

For this reason the Lord also wished the deed to come first and teaching afterward, lest, without good work, words should be useless and a superstitious boast.

[Col. 0706B] We are therefore taught better by deed than by voice. Finally, although the holy martyrs are silent in voice, they instruct us by the virtue of their deeds; although they are silent with their tongues, they persuade us through the suffering of martyrdom.

Thus, although an eloquent speaker may teach me by his eloquence, I learn what is useful to me better from the example of the saints than from verbal argument.

[Note: [Col. 0706D] The Urbevetanus codex reads: “than from eloquence of words.”]

My eyes persuade me more quickly of what they see than the ear can convey what passes away.

[Note: [Col. 0706D] The Urbevetanus codex reads: “For forgetfulness quickly creeps over what is heard; the history of the eyes,” etc. Codex 90 of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem reads likewise.]

For forgetfulness quickly steals away what is heard, whereas the record of the eyes is always looked upon. Who would not at every hour and moment contemplate how the blessed martyrs then endured various punishments for the name of Christ and in a certain way triumphed over the very punishments themselves? For the more they suffered, the more they believed themselves to be most courageous.

[Col. 0706C] The martyr’s victory is the judgment of the persecutor, as it is written: “So that you may prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50). For when the martyr is judged and condemned, then he conquers and casts down his judge. By such a judgment he is not assigned to death but acquitted for rest. Thus, by the clearest reasoning, he has conquered rather than perished.

It is therefore established that the holy martyrs teach more through suffering than through speech, although their suffering itself is not without a voice. For we read that their souls cry out from beneath God’s altar, saying: “How long, holy and true one, will you not avenge our blood?” (Rev. 16).

The Lord also says concerning Abel’s blood to Cain: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me” (Gen. 4).

[Col. 0707A] Blood that has been innocently shed is therefore said to cry out, not so much by its voice as by its cause. So too the souls of the holy martyrs cry out when, through their very suffering, they commend their faith and innocence to our understanding.

**End.**

## SERMON LXXXVIII. Also, on the Feast of the Holy Martyrs III

[Col. 0707]

### NOTICE

[Col. 0707A] 623 We found this sermon attributed to our Saint Maximus in Codex Chisianus, shelfmark C VIII, p. 237 verso. Codex of the monastery of Subiaco, the Lectionary of the Canons of the Church of Padua, and two Breviaries—one of the Church of Velletri, the other for the use of the Gallican Church—provided a more correct version of it. Confirmed by this testimony, we do not hesitate to publish it under the name of the same holy bishop, although some codices, such as Vatican Codex 1273, p. 26 verso, Codex no. 6 A of the Basilica of Saint Peter, p. 250, and the Urbevetanus, p. 206, attribute it to Ambrose or Augustine. Its wording does not, in fact, seem unlike Maximus’ style of speech.

[Col. 0707B] **ARGUMENT.**—We ought to venerate our faith in the glory of the holy martyrs, for Catholic faith is the mother of martyrdom.

Rightly and as a matter of duty do those celebrate the distinctions of the blessed martyrs who, enlightening countless peoples by the power of their faith, felt the death inflicted upon them alone, but did not alone possess the benefits of their death. For the boundless mercy of our God, manifold in goodness and skillful for salvation, sets before us the arduous palm—precious to its few aspirants—and, though it finds few who seek it, looks to the advantage of the many in the triumphs of the few. [Note: Codex Vaticanus 1273: “the palm of virtue, rarely sought, precious in the triumphs of the few, he regarded for the advantage of the many.” Codex Urbevetanus: “but precious death in the triumphs of the few, for the many,” etc.] He wishes their merits to be our support; and, while commending the true faith to us through the hard contest of martyrdom, he makes the affliction of those who came before an instruction for those who follow. [Note: Codices S. Petri A 9: “while he commends to the Lord the contest of martyrdom.”]

How great is the concern of our God for us! He tests them in order to educate us; he crushes them in order to gain us; and he has made their sufferings our advancement. [Note: Codex Urbevetanus: “he wishes their sufferings to be our progress.”] Rightly, therefore, do we honor those who fight amid our dangers and serve our interests; who, through their contempt for light and life, teach us how much devotion we owe to our God. Let us know, then, that we do not debate the truth of religion without great peril, since we see it confirmed by the blood of so many. It is a matter of great danger if, after the oracles of the prophets, after the testimonies of the apostles, after the wounds of the martyrs, you presume to examine the ancient faith as though it were new; if, after such unmistakable leaders, you remain in error; and if, after the sweat of those who died, you contend in idle disputation. [Note: Codex S. Petri A 9: “you despise.”]

Let us therefore honor our faith in the glory of the holy martyrs. Let us rejoice, dearly beloved brothers, in our great faith, through which, while you receive exiles with overflowing charity, you may also deserve to have the martyrs themselves as intercessors. For this is the glory of the holy martyrs: although a portion of them may be scattered throughout the whole world in ashes, the fullness of their virtue nevertheless remains undivided.

Let us therefore honor our faith amid so many soldiers of Christ. For the mother of martyrdom is the catholic faith, in which that illustrious athlete signed his confession in blood and swore by his death. [Note: Codex Vaticanus: “For the mother of the martyrs is faith.” Codex S. Petri A 9 and Codex Vaticanus: “these illustrious athletes signed it in blood and swore by their death.”] Faith, I say, is the mother of martyrdom. Let us therefore honor our faith in the glory of the holy martyrs.

How is it our faith? Because, when endurance of death is accepted without hesitation, the hope of immortality is plainly affirmed by them. They would never have deliberately given up this life unless they had recognized with complete conviction that another life was incomparably more blessed. [Note: Codex Vaticanus: “another,” instead of “one.”]

In the sacred praises of truth there are both the greatness of their suffering and the authority of their reason, as well as the pledge of resurrection. [Note: Codex Vaticanus 1273: “and the authority of resurrection.”] For they perish willingly, to be restored to something better; through the narrow passages of tribulation, the way out into this fullness of joys is opened to them.

They reject the bloodstained judgments from the impious mouth; by hearing they repudiate them, and in their conduct they refuse them. [Note: Codex S. Petri omits “this”; then reads: “They reject the bloodstained judgments from the impious mouth; by hand they repudiate them, by hearing they reject them, and in conduct they shun them.” Codex Vaticanus 1273: “He rejects the judgments by hand, rejected them by hearing, and shunned them in conduct. That is, while avoiding the assault of suffering through humility. When the persecutor’s fury pressed upon them, the martyrs, still catechumens, prepared their spirit for heaven,” etc. Here we should understand the passage in this way.] Thus they challenge the onslaught of suffering with courage and turn it aside with humility. [Note: Up to this point the Chisianus codex is used; in various places it is corrected from the Sublacensis codex, which continues as follows. Yet what follows seems too far removed from Saint Maximus’ elegance and polished expression; hence it must be doubted whether he is the author.]

When the fury of persecution bore down upon them, although still catechumens, they prepared their spirit for heaven; they were reborn through death, released by condemnation, and consecrated by the sword. [Note: Codex Urbevetanus: “From this it is understood,” etc.] From this let us understand how effective the passion of the Redeemer was in taking away the sin of the world. Behold: the death of a human being is shown to confer innocence and life. From this let us understand how greatly the sacred death of the Son of God benefited everyone. Behold: human blood washes away original sin, and, what is more, no one now takes away what that blood conferred through his baptism. [Note: Codex Urbevetanus: “this blood conferred.” Codex S. Petri A 9: “what this blood may have conferred upon the baptized.” The present text reads: “After the cleansing of baptism, after the purity of pious rebirth bestowed upon us,” etc.]

After the cleansing of baptism, after the purity of pious rebirth bestowed upon us, after the angelic dignity of the wedding garment acquired by us, we fall back into the mud of sins and roll again in the mire of crimes; we soil the snow-white garment with the foul contagions of iniquities and lusts; and we stain the silk garment on which the seal of the divine image had been impressed. After the Lord’s singular indulgence, we defile what has been renewed, tear apart what was whole, violate what had been purified, and resume deeds that must now be cleansed not by water but by fire. [Note: Codex Urbevetanus and Codex S. Petri A 9: “having fallen back into the mire of sins and become entangled again in the ancient bog of crimes.” Codex S. Petri A 9: “and the silk garment.”]

Blessed is such a baptism, through which every sin departed from the catechumen in such a way that it could no longer return; through which he paid his debts so as no longer to fear the creditor; through which, by faith, he paid the enemy’s sins within himself and condemned them by his end; through which he sought innocence by devotion, found it through perseverance, and preserved it through death. [Note: Codex Vaticanus 1273: “he paid what was owed, so that he would no longer be held by the creditor.” Codex Urbevetanus: “which strips every sin from him in such a way that it can no longer return.” Up to this point Codex S. Petri A 9 extends.]

Since these things are so, dearly beloved, although every such witness of Christ is precious through confession, he is still more precious through his blood, more beautiful through his cruel wound, and whiter through his dyed garment. [Note: Codices Vaticanus and Urbevetanus: “whiter.” And although in whatever city a particular privilege of burial is believed to belong to him, etc.] Yet he is ours and belongs to all through the common benefit of intercession. [Note: Codex Urbevetanus: “Yet our support, and that of all, is common.”] For the overflowing affection of that aforementioned city, and its miserly faith, did not diminish his honor merely by claiming that his patron’s benefits were enclosed only within its walls. [Note: Codex Vaticanus 1273: “diminished.”] He who is spread abroad through his merits is not confined by places. [Note: Both Codex Vaticanus and Codex Urbevetanus: “that which is spread abroad through merits.”]

You invoked the martyr everywhere; everywhere he hears, since the one who is prayed to in the martyr hears. Therefore, under the direction of him who weighs your vows and distributes his gifts, the effective presence of the nearby advocate will be granted in proportion to the devotion of the faith with which he has been received. [Note: Codex Vaticanus: “more effectively.”]

For prayer that is aided by works of chastity, justice, and almsgiving surpasses the world, enters paradise, and flies up even to the presence of the supreme Majesty, borne there by the service of an angel, as an angelic voice testifies in a certain passage: “And when you were praying,” he says, “I offered your prayer in the presence of the glory of God” (Tobit 12). [Note: Codex Urbevetanus: “For blessed is the soul, dearly beloved, whose vow,” etc.]

Blessed is the soul, dearly beloved, whose vow, whose incense of compunction, and whose holocaust of supplication is smoky with no unbelief, polluted by no stench of carnal enticement, bloodied by no savagery, and stained by no hostility; but is fiery with faith, bright with conscience, fragrant with sincerity of heart, and perfected in harmony and charity. Through the service of the heavenly messengers it is carried even to the face of God. [Note: Codex Urbevetanus: “bloodied.”]

Since these things are so, let us honor the holy martyrs, leaders of the faith, intercessors for the world, heralds of the kingdom, and coheirs of God. But if you say to me, “Why do you honor what has already dissolved and been consumed in the flesh, for which God now has no concern?”—where then is that saying, dearly beloved, which Truth himself speaks through the prophet: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115); and again: “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored by me” (Psalm 49)? [Note: Codex Vaticanus: “which Truth himself speaks.” Codex 1273: “exceedingly,” instead of “very much,” as in the text. Codex Urbevetanus: “But your friends, O God, are greatly to be honored.”]

We ought to honor the servants of God; how much more the friends of God, of whom it is said elsewhere: “The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them shall be broken” (Psalm 33). [Note: Codex Vaticanus 1273: “The Lord,” it says, “guards all their bones, and not one,” etc.]

I therefore honor in the martyr’s flesh the scars received for Christ’s name. [Note: Codex Urbevetanus: “scars. I honor the living through the enduring memory of their virtue. I honor,” etc.] I honor the ashes consecrated by confession of the Lord. [Note: Codex Vaticanus: “the sacred ashes.”] I honor in the ashes the seeds of eternity. I honor the body that showed me that it loved my God, and that taught me, for God’s sake, not to fear death. Why, then, should I not honor that body, faithful people, which even the demons revere, which they afflicted in torment but glorify in the tomb? I therefore honor the body that honored Christ by the sword and that reigns with Christ in heaven. [Note: Codex Urbevetanus: “which Christ honored by the sword and which will reign with Christ in heaven.”]

### Sermon 89. Also, on the feast of very many holy martyrs IV

[Col. 0709]

### Notice

The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur commend the Lateran codices of the Constantinian basilica in the preface to the homilies of Saint Gregory the Great on the Gospels, no. 10, Venice edition of 1769, volume V, page 135. We too consulted these same codices for our collection of Maximus, and did not expend our effort uselessly. For in codex marked L A, page 152, before several sermons of the same holy bishop that had already been published, we found this one, not previously printed. Its inscription is as follows: “Here begin the sermons of Saint Maximus, bishop. On the feast of very many martyrs.”

[Col. 0711A] **Argument.**—If the just rejoice in the Lord, the unjust know how to rejoice only in the world. The charity of Christ must be preferred to the world; and the martyrs’ cause must be chosen if we wish to attain the martyrs’ palm.

When it is the day of the holy martyrs, what could more fittingly delight us than to speak of their glory? May the Lord of the martyrs help us, for he himself is our Lord. A little while ago, as the blessed apostle preached, we heard the voice of the martyrs saying: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” This is the voice of the martyrs. “Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or peril? Or sword? As it is written: For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are accounted as sheep for slaughter. But in all these things we overcome through him who loved us” (Rom. VIII). This is the voice of the martyrs: to overcome everything and to presume nothing of themselves; to love him who glories in his own, so that “he who glories may glory in the Lord.” They too knew what we sang shortly before: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you just” (Ps. XXXI). Rejoice and exult in the Lord. If the just rejoice in the Lord, the unjust know no joy except in the world.

But these are the first battle lines that must be overcome: pleasures must first be conquered, and pains afterwards. How can one overcome the world when it rages, who cannot drive it away when it flatters? This world flatters by promising honors, riches, and pleasures; it threatens by holding out pains, poverty, and humiliations. He who does not despise what it promises, how can he overcome what it threatens? Riches have their pleasure—who does not know it? But justice has a greater power to delight. Let riches, then, delight together with justice, until such a crisis of temptation occurs that riches and justice confront one another in temptation and you cannot retain both equally. If you put your hand to justice, let riches perish; but if you put your hand to riches, you must lose justice. Choose now; fight now. Let us now see whether you sang without reason, “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you just.” Let us now see whether you sang without reason, “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Rom. VIII).

Indeed, he passed over all the things by which the world flatters. Why? Because he was proclaiming the contests of the martyrs: those contests in which they conquered persecutions, hunger, thirst, poverty, disgrace, and finally the fear of death, the last enemy. But see, brothers, Christ’s whole art accomplishes this: the Apostle admonishes us to prefer Christ’s love to the world. How great are the hardships suffered by those who wish to seize another’s goods! “Or persecution?” he says. Even that does not break them: greed is not frightened. The greedy man plunders, fears punishment, and burns with anxiety in his plundering. Many endure hunger while acquiring and making profits; we instruct them to fast, and they make excuses about their stomachs. They can devote the whole day to counting coins, and go to sleep fasting. “Or nakedness?” What need have I to speak of nakedness? Every day merchants escape naked from shipwreck and sail again into danger. Why do people daily expose themselves to danger, except to acquire riches? Not even the sword prevents them. Fraud is a capital crime, yet an inheritance is broken up. If, therefore, temporal greed deserves this, why should Christ’s inheritance not deserve it?

The greedy man might say in his heart—though perhaps he would not say it with his tongue—“Who shall separate us from your greed? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution?” The greedy too can say to gold, “For your sake we are put to death all day long.” Therefore the holy martyrs rightly say in the psalm: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation, from an unjust man” (Ps. XLII). “Distinguish,” they say, “my tribulation: the greedy too are afflicted. Distinguish my distresses: the greedy too suffer distress. Distinguish my persecutions: the greedy too suffer persecution. Distinguish my hunger: the greedy too hunger in acquiring gold. Distinguish my death: the greedy too die for gold. What does ‘distinguish my cause’ mean? ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long’; they are not put to death for your sake.” The punishment is alike, but the cause distinct. Where, then, the cause is distinct, there surely is victory.

Therefore, dearly beloved, if we love the martyrs’ solemnity, let us love in them not their sufferings but the causes of their sufferings. For if we loved sufferings, we should find many who endure worse things for evil causes. But let us attend to the causes. Consider Christ’s cross: there was Christ, and there too were the thieves. The punishment was alike, but the cause unlike. One thief believed; the other blasphemed. The Lord judged between the two as from a tribunal: he consigned the blasphemer to Tartarus and placed the other with himself in paradise. Why was this so? Because, although the punishment was equal, the cause was unequal. Choose, therefore, the martyrs’ cause if you wish to attain the martyrs’ palm. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom is glory for ages of ages. Amen.

### Sermon 90. Also, on the feast of very many holy martyrs V

[Col. 0711]

### Notice

In the same Lateran codex, folio 194 verso, there also occurs a sermon ascribed to Saint Maximus, under the title: “On the feast of very many martyrs.”

[Col. 0711D] **Argument.**—Martyrs are truly to be called sacrificial victims: they offer God a sacrifice of praise, and their death is precious in the sight of the Lord.

We ought to rejoice and exult, brothers, because a great feast has been added to our feast and our vows have been heaped up with vows. For it is a great joy when, with the feast of the martyrs coming to us, a priest also arrives. I think this occurred through divine providence: since the victims of the Savior were to be ministered to, the pontiff of the Savior appeared, so that, since one would not suffice to unfold the glory of their proclamation, nor a second accomplish it, he might both adorn the martyrs with his service and instruct your holiness by his discourses and delight it by his blessings. We must therefore give thanks and rejoice that Christ has willed his victims to be praised by the twofold voice of priests, so that, in proportion to the glory rendered to God in their case, their merit might be praised among the people; and that, because they are more earnestly honored in heaven, they might be more abundantly magnified on earth.

Martyrs are truly to be called sacrificial victims, since by their suffering they have made God propitious to us and, like accepted libations, have conferred upon us the Lord’s propitiation by their death. In the martyrs there is indeed a sacrificial victim: not that by which a dumb animal is consecrated, but that by which faithful simplicity is consecrated. It is not, I say, the victim that is sunk into the earth with a mournful disposition, but that which is raised to heaven with a joyful mind. It is indeed a victim, but not in one who offers in order to profane the altar; rather, in one who knowingly offers himself in order to prove himself. Hence the prophet says: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. XLIX). The sacrifice of praise is truly martyrdom. What angels praise, peoples praise, and even the sufferer himself praises. For he understands its glory; unless he understood its praise, glory, and power, he would never offer himself as a libation, when others are afraid, for sacrifice. And so it is said, as though to the martyr himself: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise”; that is, as though it said: Offer in yourself; sacrifice yourself. Be for yourself both priest and victim, and by the priestly office offer the soul of your body with devotion of mind. Let the faith of the Christian bring it to God’s altar. For although the Christian’s limbs are laid low upon the earth, his spirit is consecrated in heaven by death itself, and life is bestowed where destruction is applied.

Hence the holy prophet says: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV). Truly precious is that death which is honored with the gain, as it were, of immortality; concerning which the blessed Paul also says: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. I). He counts it gain that, through the death of martyrdom, eternity succeeds frailty in him, life comes forth from destruction, and trials are ended by justice. “Precious,” he says, “in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV). Precious is the death of the saints; surely their life is more precious. If the death of saints is precious, the life of sinners is worthless; and of those whose life is worthless, their death too is undoubtedly shameful. Hence those who counted the Lord among sinners said: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. III). Ignorant of justice and enemies of truth, they attempted to condemn light along with darkness. They killed the Lord, creator of heaven and earth, with a most shameful death, because they suspended him on the gibbet with criminals, since both the death was shameful and its punishment seemed more dreadful than other punishments. The blessed martyrs followed this example and willingly followed his footsteps.

But the Lord’s death became glorious, and in his sight that of all the saints precious—those whose devout annual feast we celebrate today together with the arriving pontiff. O happy celebration of this day, which deserved to have pontifical service! Today the twofold joy of the solemnity has shone upon us: both from the patronage of the saints and from the arrival of this pontiff. Therefore, brothers, let us rejoice in the Lord, who in the immense clemency of his mercy has deigned to bestow such great benefits upon us, that, while we rejoice in the triumphs of those whose examples illumine us, we may be raised up by the protection of those whose merits delight us. [Perhaps *quae* is superfluous.] May boundless Divinity grant that with a pure heart and chaste body we may be able both to commemorate the gracious feast of this day and to receive the sacred mysteries from the hand of priests of high rank with an undefiled mouth; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

### Sermon 91. Also, on the feast of very many holy martyrs VI

[Col. 0713]

### Notice

This sermon bears Saint Maximus’s name in codex 108 of the Library of Saint Mark at Venice, from which codex we had it transcribed. That this too is to be regarded as belonging to the same holy bishop is, in our judgment, clearly confirmed not only by the authority of two other codices no less ancient, but also by the character of the style in which it is written, so similar to that of Maximus that, in our opinion, nothing more similar could be desired.

[Col. 0713C] **Argument.**—The martyrs, entering the contest of suffering with steadfast faith, attain in death itself a perpetual inheritance. Martyrdom is the forgiveness of sins, the summit of virtues, an occasion of righteousness, and an imitation of the Lord’s passion.

[Note: Lateran Basilica Homiliary: “We see the crown of all the martyrs shining.” The word *videmus* (“we see”) has been written above in a smaller hand, but apparently by the same hand.] The crown of all the martyrs shines, and so does that of those whose birthday of victorious glory is celebrated; they entered the contest of suffering with steadfast faith, knowing with certainty that Christ suffers in all of them and that they are immediately transferred with exultation of body to the kingdoms of heaven. While the nations shudder at death in sickness, they attain in death itself a perpetual inheritance, and through sufferings believe that there is a translation rather than an end. [Note: Lateran codex: “they believe there is a translation rather than an end.”]

This is the hidden wisdom which in your elect, O Lord, is not acquired by persuasion but is drawn by your martyrs from the divine fountain of power: for to live well is Christ, and to die is gain (Phil. I), triumphing in Christ and gaining release from their sins by their death. [Note: Lateran codex: “for to live is Christ, and,” etc.; “gaining their sins by their death.”] Yet whoever suffers in him does not die at all, for the death of confession is not death but the inheritance of life. [Note: Lateran codex: “for the death of confession,” etc.] Martyrdom, therefore, is forgiveness of sins, the summit of virtues, an occasion of righteousness, and an imitation of the Lord’s passion.
