O most blessed martyrs, who renounced the world! They preferred to be better at the end than at the beginning, since indeed their consummation makes a righteous beginning.

By your divine ordinance, almighty God, the most glorious martyrs deserved to be Christ’s witnesses; having also contemplated victory, they confessed Christ under scourges, in prisons, in workhouses, and in solitude, for confession must always be the companion of the just. O illustrious souls of the blessed martyrs and glorious victory! Among them even most devoted women conquered both world and sex together; fighting with the devil, they proved stronger than the men who tortured them, giving thanks to the raging executioner! [Note: Lateran Homiliary: “they gave thanks to the raging executioner.”] For almighty God expects faith from all persons rather than death. But the devil, who hates those who confess, unwillingly provides crowns. He makes martyrs of those whom he kills, and, while striving to conquer God’s servants, he himself is despised while he rages. [Note: Lateran codex: “He makes martyrs of those whom he kills,” etc.]

Therefore, O Lord God, your generosity has hitherto set martyrdoms before us, so that the adversary, by whom Adam was struck down, though now driven away, may be constantly struck down. [The text is corrupt: *quodam … elisus, cum jam amotos constanter elidi*; Lateran codex: “so that the adversary by whom Adam was struck down, though now driven away, may be constantly struck down.”] For you have willed not only to rescue humankind from the devil’s power through faith, but also to destroy its assailant through virtue. Thus we who rejoice that we have more readily been set free by Christ’s blood shed in death may speak of martyrdoms and afterwards triumph crowned in Christ. Through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

### Sermon 92. Also, on the feast of very many holy martyrs VII

[Col. 0715]

### Notice

This sermon too, bearing Saint Maximus’s name, occurs in the Venetian codex of Saint Mark mentioned in the preceding notice. Nor does its fluent, weighty, ornate discourse, furnished with a choice of sentiments—in a word, wholly worthy of Maximus—allow us to doubt that it should be attributed to that holy bishop.

[Col. 0715B] **Argument.**—Our Savior taught us courageously to despise terrors, persecutions, and tribulations. We must always change our conduct for the better; and, as we share Christ’s name, so we should imitate his work. The martyrs courageously resisted the raging pagan; you, relying on Christ’s help, must watchfully resist the deceiving devil.

We joyfully sing praises to the Lord our God while we celebrate the feasts of the holy martyrs, whom we have heard were strengthened by the aid of divine grace and unconquered amid torments. For he gave them strength and consolation—he who first deigned to undergo suffering both for them and for us—and gave them abundant exultation by promising them a reward in heaven. And now, when the Gospel reading was read, you heard the Lord’s consolation addressed to them: “When you hear of wars and reports of wars, do not be afraid; for these things must happen, but the end is not yet” (Luke XXI).

Therefore the Lord and our Savior forewarned his disciples and, through them, taught us also courageously to despise the terrors and persecutions and the various tribulations inflicted by persecutors, and to be comforted by the consolation of eternal life. Since these things frequently happen to us, as our sins require, we must always change our conduct and manner of life for the better: abandon vices, grow day by day in holy virtues, and endure with the greatest patience the insults and torments of this age, so that what is sung in the psalm may be said of us: “The saints shall go from strength to strength” (Ps. LXXXIII). Christ, who shed his blood for us, left us this example.

Therefore let every Christian consider by what name he is called, so that he may imitate Christ in all things, as far as he is able by the grace Christ generously bestows; so that, just as he shares that name, he may also imitate the work. Let him count the honors and dignities of this age as nothing for love of the heavenly kingdom. And if earthly means fail, let them by no means be acquired in the world through robbery and fraud. But if they are possessed, let them not be loved in the world through avarice; rather, through the generosity of almsgiving, let them be preserved in heaven as lasting possessions.

Therefore, Christian, be kindled with the holy martyrs by a like ardor of love; and, though at this time there may be no such necessity to fight against fleshly persecutors, let there nevertheless be steadfastness to fight against spiritual enemies and against the flesh. For although torments to be endured are not now inflicted by a pagan, temptations to be overcome are nevertheless offered by the devil. The pagan, raging with bloody hand, butchered Christ’s martyrs; but the devil, deceiving through subtle temptations, tortures Christ’s faithful all the more dangerously because he does so more secretly. Then the pagan, raging with a lion’s ferocity, compelled people to idolatry; now the devil, persuading with a serpent’s tooth, has infused the poison of faithlessness. The pagan, by killing the martyrs, sent them to the kingdom; the devil, by deceiving, leads people with himself to eternal fire.

They, therefore, conquered by enduring the tortures of the pagan executioner; you conquer by despising the countless temptations of the deceiving devil. They courageously resisted the raging pagan; you, relying on Christ’s help, watchfully resist the deceiving devil. Fight courageously to the end for the truth of the catholic faith, and confidently await the reward. Confess the triune Lord—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—of one substance, if you wish to possess the kingdom of heaven with all the saints. Do not be led astray from this saving confession by the enticement of temporal rewards, lest you be unhappily separated from Christ and tormented in the fires of Gehenna. For if you have learned to hold the world’s prosperities and adversities in contempt, even if torments are inflicted on you for Christ’s name, you will not fear at all. Only never trust in your own strength if you desire to be victorious. Let Christ, who is unconquered strength, be your sure hope, lest the Christian’s spirit be broken from hope of recompense. For just as steadfast and devoted strength is rewarded in a contest, so a faithful conscience is crowned in peace. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God in the unity of the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

### Sermon 93. On the feast of very many confessors

[Col. 0717]

### Notice

In the Homiliary of the Lateran Basilica, page 101 verso, this sermon’s title is: “On the feast of very many confessors, of Saint Maximus the bishop.” The same sermon is ascribed to the same holy bishop in Venetian codex 508, page 195. It is read without its author’s name in Vatican codex 4951, Urbevetanus, page 216, and Vallicellian codex XXV, page 156. What if its style also reveals Maximus as its author?

[Col. 0717A] **Argument.**—The holy confessors are called God’s friends because they kept his commands. Do you wish to be Christ’s friend? Observe what belongs to Christ. His friendship consists in virtue, not gain. Christ’s friend is not one who does not assemble at church on the Lord’s day.

It remains fixed in your minds, brothers, that we described the blessed confessors as having become friends of the Savior because they kept his will’s commandments and carried out all his instructions, just as the Lord himself says: “You are my friends, if you do what I command you” (John 15). We established that the Lord himself is a friend, for he said to his disciples: “I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends” [Note: [Col. 0717C] The word “my” is absent in the Lateran Homiliary.] “for a servant,” he says, “does not know what his master is doing” (ibid.). [Note: [Col. 0717C] The Lateran manuscript has: “Great, therefore, is the grace of friendship, which can know the Lord’s secret, which the servant does not know. Great indeed,” etc.]

Great indeed is the grace, because a friend enters the inner rooms of the chamber, while a servant waits outside at the door; the one searches out the secrets of the other’s heart, while the latter awaits his departure. Hence, in the Song of Songs, the Church says with rejoicing: [Note: [Col. 0717C] The Vulgate, chapter 1, reads: “The king brought me into his chambers.”] “The King brought me into his chamber” (Song 1). That is, [Note: [Col. 0717C] The Urbevetan and Lateran manuscripts have *quod*, “because,” instead of *quia*.] because, after the ignorance of pagan error, she was deemed worthy to know the mysteries of the Savior; and she who had formerly lain outside as profane is afterward received within as a bride.

“No longer, I say, shall I call you servants, but friends.” See how much the Savior bestowed upon his saints: by calling them friends, he made them his equals. [Note: [Col. 0717C] Vatican manuscript 4951 has *donaverit*, “may have bestowed,” instead of *donavit*, “bestowed.”] For friendship knows no rank. [Note: [Col. 0717C] The Lateran manuscript omits *sibi*, “to himself.”] Although one may be inferior in status in many respects, he is equal in affection; although he may precede in honors, he does not precede in duties. [Note: [Col. 0717C] The Vatican and Urbevetan manuscripts read: “Although he is inferior in status in many respects, he is equal in affection; although he precedes in honors, he does not precede in duties. For friends, rich and poor alike, show one another equal respect. The Lateran manuscript reads: ‘For although he is inferior in status in many respects, he is equal in affection.’”] For friends, rich and poor alike, show one another equal respect. [Note: [Col. 0717C] The Lateran manuscript: “For friends, rich and poor alike, show one another equal respect.”]

And although one is more powerful and the other more humble, the love of friendship nevertheless makes both equal to one another in noble affection, [Col. 0718A] whom rank had separated. [Note: [Col. 0717C] The Vatican manuscript reads: “Love makes them equal in noble affection, whom dignity had separated. Hence,” etc.] Why, then, do we think that these blessed saints became friends of the Savior? [Note: [Col. 0717C] The same Vatican manuscript omits “saints.”] Surely because they kept his will’s commandments, just as he himself says: “You are my friends, if you do what I command you” (John 15). Friendship itself is strengthened by willing and refusing the same things. [Note: [Col. 0717D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “For friendship itself is firm when there is the same willing and the same refusing.” The Urbevetan manuscript has the same, merely omitting *enim*, “for.” The Vallicellan manuscript reads: “Friendship itself is not weak when there is the same willing and the same refusing.”]

We may call those friends of God who desired justice as the Lord did and hated iniquity as the Lord did; [Note: [Col. 0717D] The Vatican manuscript adds: “who desired justice as the Savior did.”] [Note: [Col. 0717D] The Urbevetan, Vallicellan, and Lateran manuscripts read “hated [Col. 0718C] as the Savior did,” rather than “hated as the Lord did.”] therefore they are bound to him by the love of friendship. [Note: [Col. 0718C] The Vatican manuscript reads: “For this reason they are bound to him by intimate love.” The Lateran manuscript adds the preposition *ex*, “from” or “by.”]

From this passage we understand how we come to Christ’s friendship. For the Lord does not love anyone by chance; nor does he bestow affection freely upon just any person. [Note: [Col. 0718C] The Vatican manuscript reads: “For the Lord does not love anyone by chance, nor does he freely bestow affection upon just any person. If you wish to be Christ’s friend, observe the things that are Christ’s. If you wish to earn the Savior’s favor, keep the Savior’s commandments. He himself grants you the effect of his love if he sees that you love his commandments.”] [Note: [Col. 0718C] The Vallicellan manuscript reads *largitur effectum*, “he grants the effect”; the Lateran reads: “for he freely bestows affection upon any person.”]

Do you wish to be Christ’s friend? Observe the things that are Christ’s. Do you wish to earn the Savior’s favor? Keep the Savior’s commandments. He himself bestows the affection of his love upon him [Col. 0718B] if he sees that he has love for his commandments. [Note: [Col. 0718C] The Lateran manuscript reads: “He himself grants the effect of his love.”]

It is therefore in our power to become friends of God. [Note: [Col. 0718C] The Vatican manuscript reads: “to become a friend of our lords.”] For as we show ourselves toward the Lord, so too will the Lord be found by us. If we open to him the secrets of our hearts, he too discloses the secrets of his own heart. [Note: [Col. 0718C] The Vallicellan manuscript reads: “and he [discloses] his secrets to us.”] [Note: [Col. 0718C] The Vatican and Lateran manuscripts read: “he will lay them open.”] If we make known to him the consciousness of our sins, he too purifies us by revealing his knowledge. And the more ready we are for good works in imitation of him, [Note: [Col. 0718C] The same Vatican manuscript adds: “the more closely he will draw near to us in grace.”] the nearer we are to him in grace. [Note: [Col. 0718D] The Vallicellan and Lateran manuscripts read *erimus*, “we shall be,” instead of *sumus*, “we are.”]

For friendships in this world are established through some advantage—that is, through profit, benefits, or honors; [Note: [Col. 0718D] The Lateran manuscript reads: “either through profit, benefits, or honors.”] but the Savior’s friendships are established through virtue, not gain. A holy thing can be acquired through discipline, but it cannot be purchased for a price. [Note: [Col. 0718D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “It cannot be obtained by price. Let us therefore proclaim these blessed and praiseworthy men, who were friends of Christ and of one mind,” omitting the intervening material.] Since they are not won by deceptive flattery, [Col. 0719A] but summoned by a simple life, let us proclaim as blessed and praiseworthy those who were found worthy to be his friends [Note: [Col. 0719B] The Lateran manuscript reads: “We proclaim these holy confessors blessed and praiseworthy.”] and of one mind with him. [Note: [Col. 0719B] The same Lateran manuscript has *ut*, “so that,” instead of *et*, “and.”]

We too, therefore, brothers, ought to hasten to the Savior’s friendship and, following the example of the saints, do his will in all things.

But what shall we say about those whom we shall designate before God by this description—those who, invited to the Lord’s banquet on Sunday, despise the heavenly meal because of a worldly feast and abandon Christ’s table, while they delight in a human table? [Note: [Col. 0719B] The Vatican manuscript reads: “who, invited to the Sunday banquet, despise the heavenly meal because of a worldly feast and abandon Christ’s table; and while they delight in a human table, although all have been called by the Lord’s voice to the refreshment of life, each person refreshes himself with the wantonness of his own pleasure rather than assembling where a certain religious obligation summons him. For it is the duty of every Christian to assemble at church on Sunday.”]

For this is the first offense against Christ’s friendship: when he has called everyone to refreshment on Sunday, each person refreshes himself with the pleasure of his own wantonness rather than assembling where a certain religious duty summons him. [Col. 0720A] For it is a Christian’s duty to assemble at church on Sunday.

[Note: [Col. 0720B] We have restored this passage from the Vatican manuscript, correcting the Venetian manuscript, which reads: “for on that day they had read for this reason.” The Vallicellan and Urbevetan manuscripts also omit *leges*, “laws.” The Vallicellan has *judices*, “judges,” instead of *judicia*, “judgments.” The Lateran adds *ideo*, “for this reason,” after *nam*, “for.”]

For on that day the laws are silent and judgments are quiet, so that human salvation may receive the place of devotion: [Note: [Col. 0720B] The Vatican manuscript reads *peteret*, “might seek,” rather than *acciperet*, “might receive.”] it is not so much released from public activities as kept free from sinful crimes. [Note: [Col. 0720B] The same Vatican manuscript reads: “not so much kept from public acts as from sinful crimes.” The Lateran manuscript reads: “not so much in a holiday manner from public affairs,” etc.]

But what is worse is that the wretched person counts as an occasion for wantonness what was given for his salvation; and he not only fails to assemble at church because of his sins, but, devoting himself to vanities, piles up heavier sins for himself. [Note: [Col. 0720B] The Vatican manuscript omits *sibi*, “for himself.”]

May almighty God therefore free you, once you have been corrected—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# THIRD CLASS. SERMONS ON VARIOUS SUBJECTS

[Col. 0719]

## SERMON XCIV. On Miracles

### ADMONITION

The Maurist editors of the works of Saint Ambrose, Paris, 1690, p. 439, rightly and deservedly judge that this distinguished sermon should be attributed to Maximus rather than to Ambrose. For in many manuscripts, especially ancient ones, we see it adorned with the name of Saint Maximus. It appears in the Sangallensis no. 46; in the Ambrosian manuscript; in the manuscript of Saint Cross in Jerusalem, no. 13; and in the Bobiensis, with the title “On Miracles.” In later manuscripts—in Saint Cross in Jerusalem no. 47, no. 99; Vercellensis 66; Laurentian I, Plut. XIV; Laurentian 36, Plut. XIV; Laurentian 36, Plut. XVII; and no. 172 of the library formerly belonging to the fabric of the metropolitan church of Florence—it bears the title “On Miracles, or On the Two Little Boats.” In another Laurentian manuscript, X, Plut. XIV, p. 236, it is entitled “On Miracles, or on the Miracles that Jesus Performed in This World.” In Laurentian XXXVI it is entitled “A Sermon of Saint Maximus the Bishop on Luke, chapter V: ‘When the crowds pressed upon him to hear the word of God.’” It is also found in the manuscripts of the Basilica of Saint Peter, shelfmark 7 A, and in three Vallicellan manuscripts, 25, 7 A, and A 9. The same sermon is printed by Combefis in volume VII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 45, and by Muratori in volume IV of the *Anecdota*, as well as by several later writers. It must therefore be thought to have been rashly attributed to Saint Ambrose by some scholars.

[Col. 0719C] ARGUMENT.—Peter’s boat, which Christ boarded, is the Church; the other boat, which he left, is the Synagogue. The Church’s boat sails into the deep of the world, and Noah’s ark was its type. There is tranquility where Peter alone sails; there is a storm where Judas is also present. Where faith is whole, the Savior is watchful; where faith is mixed with faithlessness, he sleeps.

From this Gospel reading, which describes such great benefits being conferred through him, we can understand how many miracles the Lord Jesus performed. [Note: [Col. 0719D] The manuscripts of Saint Peter and Vallicella read “co-worker” instead of “worker.”] [Note: [Col. 0719D] The manuscripts of Saint Cross in Jerusalem and Novara read “upon the people.”] [Note: [Col. 0719D] Manuscripts 36 and Laurentian read: “so that the crowds of people, having been provoked,” rather than “so that the crowds of people, having been summoned.”] The crowds, urged to hear him, pressed upon him rather than asking him; they did not hope for the medicine of salvation through the grace of humility, but through the insolence of importunity. Thus, as they pressed upon him, as the Gospel says (Luke 5), the desert did not separate the crowds from the Lord Jesus, the Synagogue did not drive them away, and reverence for his divinity did not hold them back.

For this is the custom of the sick: while they hope for medicine for their illnesses, they are restrained by neither place, nor time, nor modesty from making importunate petitions; and the more abundantly the one who heals provides a cure, the more importunate is the sufferer. [Note: [Col. 0720D] Manuscripts 36 and Laurentian read: “the more importunate is the one who suffers.”]

Therefore, when the Lord Jesus, withdrawing from the crowds pressing upon him, could not remain on land, he saw two little boats on the sea and boarded Peter’s boat with all haste, so that the nature of the waters might repel the insolence of their importunity—for reverence for the teacher did not restrain it in the least. From there he began to pour forth the words of his teaching to the people from Peter’s boat.

See the Savior’s mercy: bodily he is separated from the people, yet through the usefulness of his teaching he is joined to them. Everywhere he shows mercy; everywhere he is beneficial. On land, through touch, he heals bodily illnesses; on the sea, through teaching, he cures the wounds of souls.

But let us examine what this little boat of Simon Peter is, which the Lord judged more suitable than the other for teaching—one that both keeps the Savior safe from insult and bestows words upon people so that they may believe. For we find that the Lord had already sailed in another boat and had been assailed by grave insults. He sailed with Moses on the Red Sea, when he carried the people of Israel across the currents of the waters; but he suffered grave insults, as he himself says in the Gospel to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me” (John 5). The Savior’s insult is the Synagogue’s unbelief. [Col. 0721B] Therefore he chose Peter’s boat and abandoned Moses’—that is, he rejects the faithless Synagogue [Note: [Col. 0721D] The same Laurentian manuscript reads: “he rejects the faithlessness of the Synagogue.”] and takes up the faithful Church.

Two little boats, as it were, have been appointed by God to fish for the salvation of human beings in this world, as in a sea, just as the Lord says to the apostles: “Come, I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4). Of these two little boats, one is left empty and vacant on the shore, while the other is carried out into the deep, laden and full. The Synagogue is left empty on the shore because it lost Christ together with the prophetic oracles; the Church, laden, is taken into the deep because it received the Lord together with the apostles’ teaching.

The Synagogue, I say, remains on the shore, clinging as it were to earthly works. [Note: [Col. 0721D] The same Laurentian and Novara manuscripts read: “clinging to earthly activities.”] But the Church is called into the heights, [Note: [Col. 0721D] Both manuscripts of Saint Cross in Jerusalem and the Novara manuscript read “is summoned back.”] as though examining the deep mysteries of heaven; [Note: [Col. 0721C] The Novara manuscript has *quia*, “because,” instead of *tanquam*, “as though.”] into that height of which the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11).

For this reason it is said to Peter: “Put out into the deep” (Luke 5)—that is, into the depth of discussions concerning divine generation. For what is as deep as what Peter said to the Lord: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16)? And what is as earthly as what the Jews said about the Lord: “Is this not the son of Joseph the carpenter?” (Luke 4)? The former, by a higher understanding, affirmed Christ’s birth as divine; the latter, with viperous minds, judged his heavenly generation in a carnal manner.

Hence the Savior says to Peter: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16). But to the Pharisees he says: “How can you speak good things, since you are evil?” (Matthew 12).

The Lord therefore boarded this one boat of the Church, in which Peter has been appointed teacher, as the Lord says: “Upon this rock I shall build my Church.”

[Note: [Col. 0721D] Everyone knows that Maximus frequently taught the primacy of Peter in the Church in his homilies. Nevertheless, since in this and the following sermon he has set forth the prerogatives of Peter and the Church with greater elegance, I shall summarize them here. First, it must be observed that, since the Synagogue has been rejected because of its faithlessness, one Church is to be believed in, chosen by Christ; in it, as in a boat, he appointed Peter in his own place as ruler, supreme governor, and teacher. Those who sail outside Peter’s boat, that is, outside the Church entrusted to Peter’s governance, cannot reach the harbor of eternal salvation. Peter’s boat, that is, the Church, is so secure from shipwreck by Christ’s providence that it presents those whom it embraces unharmed. Maximus asserts that Peter’s faith makes it safe, and that salvation cannot be lacking to anyone who firmly clings to his faith. At times the Lord seems to sleep in this boat, or Church, when he allows it to be shaken by storms and adverse waves; but he does this so that the successors in the apostolate may neither sleep nor presume upon themselves. For a certain fear is useful for arousing watchfulness and prayers; moved by these, the Lord stills the winds and sea by his command and restores the Church’s former tranquility.]

This boat sails into the deep of this world in such a way that, when the world perishes, it preserves unharmed all whom it receives. We already see its type in the Old Testament: just as Noah’s ark, when the world was shipwrecked, preserved unharmed all whom it had received, so Peter’s Church, when the world is consumed by fire, will present unharmed all whom it embraces. And just as, after the Flood had passed, the dove brought a sign of peace to Noah’s ark, so, after judgment has passed, Christ brings the joy of peace to Peter’s Church—for he himself is the dove, or peace, as he promised, saying: “And again [Col. 0722B] I shall see you, and your heart shall rejoice” (John 16).

But since we read in Matthew (chapter 8) that this same boat of Peter, from which the Lord is now bringing forth the mysteries of his heavenly teaching, was disturbed when the Lord was sleeping in it and the winds rose, so that all the apostles feared the danger of death, let us see why one and the same boat here gives teaching to the people in tranquility, while there it inspires the disciples with fear of death—especially since Simon Peter was also there with the other apostles.

The cause of the danger was this: Simon Peter was there, but the traitor Judas was there as well. Although the faith of the former founded the boat, the faithlessness of the latter nevertheless disturbed it. There is tranquility where Peter alone sails; there is a storm where Judas is added. [Col. 0722C] Although Peter was firm through his own merits, he was nevertheless disturbed by the traitor’s crimes.

While the disciples were afraid and Peter was anxious, the Lord slept. [Note: [Col. 0722D] The Laurentian manuscript reads: “while Peter awakened him, he slept.”] It may perhaps seem strange that the Lord slept while Peter was anxious: he slept for Peter, so that he might not keep watch for Judas. Thus, through the offense of one, the merits of all are shaken.

Christ falls asleep, and the winds are stirred up. For whoever commits sin immediately makes the Lord sleep for himself and raises up against himself a storm of worldly spirits. [Note: [Col. 0722D] The manuscripts of Saint Cross in Jerusalem, Laurentian, and Novara read “unclean spirits.”] But when the Lord’s serenity is at rest, a diabolical storm must arise. [Note: [Col. 0722D] The same Laurentian manuscript reads: “when the Lord’s serenity is at rest.”]

Therefore, if through the sin of one Judas all the apostles are endangered, let us beware by this example of the faithless one; let us beware of the traitor, lest through one many of us be tossed about. [Note: [Col. 0722D] Saint Cross in Jerusalem manuscript 99 reads: “lest many of us be tossed about.”] Indeed, let us cast such a person out of our boat, [Note: [Col. 0723D] The Laurentian manuscript reads: “let us cast him out of our boat.”] so that the Lord may not sleep but remain watchful in us; and while he is watchful, no storm of spiritual wickedness may shake us.

For where faith is whole, there the Savior teaches, watches, and rejoices; there are rest, tranquility, and healing for all. But where faith is mixed with faithlessness, there Christ is sluggish, asleep, and inactive; there are fear, storm, and danger for all. For according to our deeds, the Lord sleeps for us or keeps watch.

## SERMON XCV. On the Gospel Fishing

[Col. 0723]

### ADMONITION

While I was examining the Florentine manuscripts of the Laurentian Library, I encountered not only several that strongly confirmed me in the opinion that Maximus was the author of the preceding sermon; I also succeeded in discovering this sermon in three of them. Until now it had not been published; I now bring it to public light for the first time. The first of these three manuscripts is the one formerly belonging to the library of the fabric of the metropolitan church of Florence, no. CLXXII, p. 71; the second is in Plut. I, no. XIV, p. 80; the third is in Plut. XXXV, 2, XVII, p. 219. Not long afterward I also happened to discover this same sermon in the Casinensis manuscript CCCV, p. 116. Anyone who clearly sees that the similarity of the language corresponds to the authority of the manuscripts will admit that this sermon ought to be attributed to Maximus.

[Col. 0723B] ARGUMENT.—Saint Maximus gives a mystical interpretation of Luke, chapter V, and writes that the Church is a boat accustomed not to kill but to bring to life those whom it lifts above the storms of worldly affairs.

The time, brothers, urges us to expound the Gospel passage that was recently read, in which the Lord, still sitting in Peter’s boat, says to Peter: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.” [Note: [Col. 0723D] Laurentian manuscript 36 reads: “from now on you will be bringing men to life.”] From this conclusion we can understand the mystery of the entire reading.

For what reason was it that, when the disciples marveled at the boats filled with the catch of fish, the Savior did not promise Peter what he was learning, but pledged to him what he knew nothing about? That is, in the very boat in which he was, he would bestow an abundance of people to be brought to life in place of the fish that were quivering. For ordinarily people are not brought to life in a boat, but carried; they are not restored by a voyage, but tremble on foot.

See, then, whether this boat is not a boat entrusted to Peter to be sunk, but is the Church, which is entrusted to Christ to govern. [Note: [Col. 0723D] The Laurentian manuscript reads: “which is entrusted to Peter to govern, but is the Church.”] For it is the ship accustomed to raise people from the storms of worldly affairs, as from waves—not to kill them, but to bring them to life. For just as a sewn-together little boat injures and holds the little fish it lifts from the whirlpool, so the ship of the Church gives life to the people it rescues from the storm; when it catches them, it gives them life within itself. [Note: [Col. 0723D] The same Laurentian manuscript reads: “when it catches them.”] The Church, I say, gives them life within itself and, as it were, brings them back from death.

For this is what the word “to bring to life” means: nothing is brought to life unless it had shortly before been without life. Thus Peter is said to bring to life people wounded by the world’s storms and choked by the waves of the age, so that he who marveled at a boat filled with the number of quivering fish might marvel even more at a Church laden with a multitude of living people.

The whole sequence of the reading therefore contains a mystical meaning. For earlier too, when the Lord was sitting in the boat and said to Peter, “Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch,” he was surely teaching him not so much to cast instruments of fishing into the deep as to let down words of preaching into the heights. [Note: [Col. 0723D] The Casinensis manuscript reads: “But also what follows,” etc.]

Paul too penetrated this deep with the dart of his mouth, saying: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11), and the rest.

No, I say, was he teaching him to enclose little fish in a net, [Note: [Col. 0724D] The Laurentian manuscript reads: “he was teaching him to gather those little fish.”] but to gather people through faith. For faith accomplishes on earth what a net accomplishes in the waves. Just as a net does not allow those whom it holds to wander, so faith does not permit those whom it gathers to go astray. And just as there it brings those who have been caught to the boat in a kind of bosom, so here it leads those who have been gathered to rest in a kind of embrace.

But so that you may understand that the Lord was speaking about spiritual fishing, Peter says: “Teacher, we have labored all night and caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the net” (Luke 5)—as though he were saying: Since our fishing has accomplished nothing while we have kept watch in vain throughout the whole night, I shall now fish not with an instrument but by grace; not through the skill of art but through the urgency of devotion. “At your word,” he says, “I will let down the net.”

We read that the Word is the Lord Savior, as the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1), and the rest. Therefore, when Peter lets down the nets at the word, he certainly lets down his discourse in Christ; and when he unfolds the woven and arranged line at the teacher’s command, he expands more clearly ordered and fitting words in the Savior’s name, by which he can save not living creatures but souls. [Note: [Col. 0724D] The Casinensis manuscript reads: “‘All night,’ he says,” etc.]

“We have labored all night and caught nothing.” Peter had truly labored through the night: previously he had suffered darkness and, without Christ, could not see what he might catch. [Note: [Col. 0724D] The Laurentian manuscript reads: “he could not see what he might catch.”] But when the Savior’s light shone upon him, after the darkness had been scattered, he also began, through faith, to see in the deep what he could not see with his eyes. [Note: [Col. 0724D] The same Laurentian manuscript reads: “to perceive by faith what he did not see with his eyes.”]

Peter truly endured night until the day—which is Christ—stood beside him. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near” (Romans 13).

Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XCVI. On Hospitality

[Col. 0725]

### ADMONITION

This sermon was found by Edmund Martene and Ursin Durand in the papers of Mabillon and published in volume IX of the *Collection of Ancient Writers and Monuments*, pp. 133 and following. A similar sermon appears in the appendix to volume five of the works of Saint Augustine, no. 5; its opening is: “I have frequently admonished your charity.” As for the title, I now remember that in the homilies, no. 99, p. 351, I published one that is likewise entitled “On Hospitality.”

Finally, the reason I think this sermon should be attributed to Maximus is both its style and the authority of the very ancient manuscript 90 of the library of Saint Cross in Jerusalem. It is attributed to Saint Ambrose in Vatican Reg. 85, p. 44, where it reads: “Here begins a sermon on hospitality spoken by Saint Ambrose.” But who could fail to understand that nothing is less likely than that this sermon should be attributed to Ambrose, whose style is plainly known to have been altogether different?

[Col. 0725A] ARGUMENT.—The holy bishop commends hospitality to the faithful and exhorts them to this duty by the example of Abraham, who, after receiving three men—or rather angels—into his lodging, was heaped with many blessings.

We read in the book of Genesis that, when three men came upon him, Abraham hurried to meet them [Note: [Col. 0725C] The manuscript of Saint Cross in Jerusalem 90 reads: “he met them and prayed.” The Vatican Regius manuscript reads: “he meets them and prays.”] and, prostrating himself on his face, prayed that they would turn aside to his tent, so that through hospitality toward the saints he might receive the reward of blessing.

For he knew that this was the Lord’s command: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matthew 10), and the rest. [Note: [Col. 0725C] The same manuscripts of Saint Cross in Jerusalem 90 and Vatican Regius read “he says.”]

Abraham therefore hastened to receive the holy men so that, through sharing their lodging, he might be found worthy to share their holiness, and, while offering the service of human kindness, might receive a share in justification.

For this is the law of hospitality: that the guest who is received makes the one who receives him such as he himself is. [Note: [Col. 0725C] The same manuscript of Saint Cross in Jerusalem 90 reads *illum*, “him,” rather than *eum*, “him.”] The evangelist John most clearly indicated this concerning those who received the Son of God, saying: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1). [Note: [Col. 0725C] The same manuscript of Saint Cross in Jerusalem 90 reads: “he gave them.”]

You see, therefore, how great is the grace of hospitality: even the one who receives the Son of God in the lodging of his heart becomes a son of God. [Note: [Col. 0725C] The same manuscript of Saint Cross in Jerusalem and Vatican Regius 83 read: “so that he too may become a son of God.”] If, then, the one who receives the Son of God becomes a son of God, how much more does the one who receives a righteous person gain the grace of a righteous person?

For this is, as I said, the kindness of hospitality: that a holy man, when he arrives and shares a lodging, makes his host what he himself is. [Note: [Col. 0725C] The Vatican Regius manuscript reads: “so that when a holy man arrives,” etc.] Who would not wish to receive a holy man with such hospitality in his dwelling, so that, by sharing a habitation with him, he might share his holiness; and, although he may have been a sinner until that hour, by receiving a righteous person might himself become righteous, as the prophet David says: [Note: [Col. 0725C] Vatican Regius 83 has: “and with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the innocent man you will be innocent.”] “With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent” (Psalm 17).

Therefore, brothers, if Abraham our father, knowing [Note: [Col. 0725C] Vatican Regius reads: “knowing that this was.”] this grace of hospitality, hurried to meet the three men who came upon him, one of whom was the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0726C] Vatican Regius reads: “and prostrating himself on the ground,” etc.] and, prostrating himself on his face, prayed that they would enter beneath the roof of his tent, how much more ought we to go out to meet holy priests who arrive and receive them in our dwellings with every prayer, so that, according to David, we may be holy with holy guests.

Let no one now fear because of the awareness of his sins; let no one despair of forgiveness. Whoever receives a bishop as a guest has already become righteous. [Note: [Col. 0726C] In manuscript 90 of Saint Cross in Jerusalem this sentence reads: “has been made righteous.” Although shortly before . . . . you have committed, although . . . . you have been, while . . . . receives, you are restored through the merits of innocence.] [Note: [Col. 0725D] This must be understood in the spirit of the Lord’s saying in Luke, chapter 11: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.” Almsgiving has such great merit that it prepares the soul for repentance and faith, through which sins are cleansed, as is read concerning Cornelius in Acts, chapter 10. Hospitality, therefore, since it is an act of exceptional love, prepares the soul to obtain justice from God as its reward.]

Although shortly before he may have committed crimes, although he may have been guilty, while he receives an innocent man he is restored through the merits of innocence, as the prophet says: “With the innocent man you will be innocent.”

Therefore, brothers, since we are Abraham’s children, let us do Abraham’s works. He went out to meet three holy men; let us too go out to meet many priests. Although he was righteous, he received the blessed men as guests so that, being righteous, he might become more righteous. [Note: [Col. 0726C] The manuscripts of Saint Cross in Jerusalem 90 and Vatican Regius 83 read: “he received them as guests so that, being righteous, he might become more righteous; but because we are sinners.”] Since we are sinners, let us receive bishops, so that, with our sins washed away, we may be righteous.

Let us receive the saints, I say, so that our sins may be forgiven contrary to nature. For through hospitality, because Abraham the righteous had no sins, a son, Isaac, was given to him contrary to nature. [Note: [Col. 0726C] The same manuscript of Saint Cross in Jerusalem 90 reads: “who was given so contrary to nature, as I have said,” etc.] He was given so contrary to nature that cold old age despaired that he could be born, and his mother Sarah laughed.

Sarah laughed, I say, [Col. 0726C] because she was receiving a son not by nature but by grace; [Note: [Col. 0726C] The same manuscript of Saint Cross in Jerusalem reads: “and therefore a blessed offspring, whose birth was preceded not by groans but by joys,” etc.] hence a blessed offspring, whose birth was preceded not by pain but by joy. She certainly ought to laugh, since by God’s agency she received him. [Note: [Col. 0727A] The same manuscript of Saint Cross in Jerusalem reads *concepit*, “conceived,” instead of *suscepit*, “received.”]

Such, then, is the blessed hospitality of the saints: it always leaves joy with its guests. Sarah laughs because she was freed from barrenness; I laugh because I lay aside my sins. She was freed from a bodily defect; I, [Note: [Col. 0727D] The same manuscript of Saint Cross in Jerusalem reads “of the soul” instead of *enim*, “for.” Vatican Regius 83 reads: “I have been freed from the sins of the soul.”] for my part, have been cleansed from crimes. She rejoices that through hospitality she received Isaac as a son; I rejoice that I have obtained forgiveness together with righteousness.

But someone may perhaps say: Among those men who came upon Abraham, the Lord too was coming, and that is certainly true; for Scripture reports it so. But I say that even now Christ comes to us in his priests.

Let us therefore imitate Abraham, brothers. [Note: [Col. 0728D] The same manuscript of Saint Cross in Jerusalem reads: “our father Abraham; but why do I say Abraham?”] But why do I say Abraham? Let us imitate God our Father. [Note: [Col. 0728D] The same manuscript of Saint Cross in Jerusalem reads: “For if God wished people of different nations to dwell under the one hospitality of heaven,” etc.] Since God has willed people of different nations to dwell under one hospitality of heaven, why should we, who are brothers, not dwell together under one hospitality? Although he preferred to contain our diversity in the same house of the world, why should our holy unity not be held in the same dwelling? [Note: [Col. 0728D] Vatican Regius 83 reads *sede*, “seat” or “dwelling,” instead of *aede*, “house.”]

Here ends the sermon.

## SERMON XCVII. Begins on the Passage Written: “Raise Your Voice Like a Trumpet, and Announce Their Sins to My People.” Isaiah, Chapter 58

[Col. 0727]

### ADMONITION

In the work of the same Martene and Durand, at the place indicated in the preceding admonition, this sermon and the one that follows are likewise found inscribed to Saint Maximus.

[Col. 0727B] 649 ARGUMENT.—The priestly trumpet humbles sinners and strengthens the righteous. The walls of Jericho fell at the sound of priestly trumpets. These events were figures of the preaching of the priests of the present age.

Earlier we explained that the necessity incumbent upon us required us not to keep silent, and, lest others perish through their danger, we observed that we ought to rise up with a cry to sin [F.: “to preach”]. For we must cry out in the Church, lest we cry out in punishment. Thus the Lord says through the prophet: “Cry out vehemently; do not spare; like a trumpet raise your voice, and announce to my people their sins” (Isa. LVIII).

We are therefore commanded to cry out, and to cry out vehemently, sparing not our voice, lest we perish as regards salvation: “Do not spare,” he says—that is, do not pass over the sinner’s iniquity in silence, lest, while you take account of his shame, you fail to take account of his healing. For by keeping silent you have nourished his wounds, which you ought to have cut away by crying out, making them worse.

We are therefore commanded to cry out; and lest anyone say that he has not heard, or lest the voice escape anyone, priests are commanded to cry out vehemently. And, lest this perhaps prove insufficient, he added, saying: “Like a trumpet raise your voice” (Isa. LVIII).

We know that a trumpet sounds not so much for hearing as for terror, and that it brings not so much delight as dread. For a trumpet is necessary for sinners: it must not merely penetrate their ears, but also shake their hearts; it must not delight them with song, but correct them through what they hear. It should also exhort the energetic to justice and deter the sluggish from offenses. For just as in battle it casts down the mind of the fearful soldier but kindles the courage of the brave, so the priestly trumpet humbles the mind of the sinner, strengthens the soul of the holy man, and by one and the same sound bids the one be more courageous toward unity [Col. 0728B], while striking fear into the other, so that he may be more timid toward sin.

This, indeed, is the nature of the trumpet: to destroy the works of those who offend and to strengthen their deeds. Finally, the walls of Jericho, because they contained within themselves a sinful people, fell through the priestly trumpets. No battering ram struck them; no siege engine overcame them. Rather—and this is marvelous—the priestly terror of the sound overthrew them. Walls that had stood impregnable against iron collapsed at the sacred voice of the trumpets.

Who would not be astonished that in that event stones were split, foundations shaken by the blast, and everything so utterly collapsed that, although the victors injured nothing with their hands, nothing stable nevertheless remained among the adversary? Although no one touched those walls, they were nevertheless conquered: from outside, by the sound of the righteous, the dwellings of sinners gave way. Were they then to resist these men? Were they to protect them in any way? They opened defense to the righteous and denied it to the faithless.

Therefore, brothers [Col. 0728C], the sound of the priestly voice was already so powerful at that time, when it uttered I know not what amid the true confusion of the situation. How much power, then, do we believe the priestly living voice itself now possesses, when, while it speaks of Christ in words, it accomplishes something great in place of the Lord Savior’s command? When even the elements yielded to the sound of bronze, how could sensible things resist, when even insensible things were unable to endure sacred terror?

For we believe that hearts can be softened more readily by the words of priests than stones, and that sins can be dissolved more quickly than masonry was broken apart. The voice of a fitting spirit destroys the stain of sin more easily than material soundness dissolves a stone’s fortification.

Explicit.

## SERMON XCVIII. The Sequel

[Col. 0727]

On the preceding Sunday we discussed the walls of Jericho being conquered by priestly trumpets, and how, contrary to order and nature, an insensible thing yielded to sacred voices through a certain terrifying threat; and how everything collapsed at the sound of rebuke, so that the strongest defenses fell and the people, stripped of their sins, remained—so that the former might no longer resist and the latter might be more easily captured.

But we already stated that all these things were then done in figure. For what else do we believe the trumpets of the priests of that time to have been except the preaching of the priests of the present time? Through them we never cease to announce something stern to sinners in a terrifying sound, to foretell something grievous, and with a certain threatening din to strike the ears of those who offend.

Indeed, no one will be able to resist sacred voices; no one will be able to contradict them. For if sensible things tremble at the word of God, how much more should they tremble when even insensible things trembled then? Or how will the obstinacy of those people be able to resist that before which not even a sound siege engine could stand? For just as the crash of the trumpets reached into the people’s interior after the masonry walls had been destroyed, so now the preaching of priests, once evil thoughts have been destroyed, passes into the nakedness of the soul.

The soul is found naked before the word of God when all its activity of iniquity is scattered. That the soul is naked before God the Apostle says: “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. IV). Before the soul comes to know God and receives the faith of truth, it covers itself, as it were, with certain works of superstition and surrounds itself with a wall of wickedness, so that it seems able to stand impregnable within the defenses of its iniquities.

But when the sacred voice has thundered, its false security is immediately overthrown, its thought is dispersed, and all the defenses of superstition are dissolved, leaving it naked, as it is written: “The word of God penetrates to the division of spirit and marrow” (ibid.). Just as then the sound of the sacred voice destroyed and captured the rebellious people and avenged the wrath, so now the preaching of priests subdues and captures the sinful people and exacts vengeance. For blessed Paul says: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying thoughts and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and ready,” he says, “to avenge every disobedience” (II Cor. X).

See, then, whether there are not, according to the Apostle’s statement, certain weapons of words in the tongue of priests, by which vain thought is destroyed, inflated pride is captured, and rebellion is punished in prayer.

But what happened then around the city of Jericho, as we said, happened in figure. Indeed, this very thing has now occurred in reality. For we read that the priests of the time mentioned above went around that city continually for seven days [Col. 0730B], and that, when the hands of armed men could not conquer it, it was overthrown on every side by the sound of trumpets—not, I say, trumpets by which a dreadful soldier made a din, but those by which the consecrated priest rebuked.

For who would fear the trumpet of one whose sword he did not fear? During those days, therefore, the walls surrounded by priestly trumpets fell; during those days we read that the works of this world were completed. You see, then, that by this number seven the priests destroy not merely one city, but disperse the iniquity of the entire world.

For just as the designation of a single city represents the condition of the whole world, so the course of seven days signifies a span of seven thousand years. Through this period the trumpets of the preaching priests announce the destruction of the age itself and threaten judgment, as it is written: “For the world and everything that is in the world will pass away; but whoever does the will of the Lord remains forever.”

[Col. 0730C] **Note:** Saint Maximus seems to have followed the opinion of those who thought that the world would last seven thousand years. For they read in the blessed Paul, in Hebrews IV, that the Lord would take his rest after the seventh day, on which all his works would be completed. Taking those days—whose beginning was at the creation of the world—as thousands of years, they declared that the structure of the universe would not exist beyond that period. Yet when the apostles asked the Lord about the time when the kingdom of Israel would be restored, he replied: “It is not yours to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts I). And more explicitly, in Matthew XXIV, Christ stated that knowledge of the consummation of the age had been denied to the angels and reserved for the Father alone: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven, but the Father alone.” [Col. 0730D]

## SERMON XCIX. Begins concerning Zacchaeus

[Col. 0729]

### ADMONITION

In the St Gall manuscripts nos. 91 and 92 there are two sermons on Zacchaeus, which we publish in print as nos. 99 and 100, bearing the name of Saint Maximus. The same Martène and Durand published them in the place cited.

### ARGUMENT

Zacchaeus was richer in the substance of faith than in temporal treasure. Riches can help one attain Christ’s glory.

Frequently, dearest brothers, I had wished to preach the parable of this Gospel passage and to run through, in discourse of plainer eloquence, the grace of Zacchaeus the rich man; indeed, to be still more abundant in his praise, because he proved liberal toward his own salvation. For who would not praise the man who could give his riches away to himself and, by mastery over the possession of temporal wealth, acquire for himself an everlasting dominion? I say, give his riches to himself: for what we possess is another’s, unless we use it fittingly for salvation. Although what appears to be yours, it will not be yours if, when I depart from the world, it is kept in the world without benefit to me.

I had wished, therefore, to preach Zacchaeus’ riches and grace: truly a rich man, and rich forever, because he deserved to be richer in Christ than in the world. He was wealthier in the substance of faith [Col. 0730D] than in temporal treasure. Zacchaeus, therefore, is praiseworthy, because the rich are shut out from the glory of the heavenly kingdom, as the Lord says: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX). This man hastened to enter the kingdom by means of riches themselves, and to pass by that way and narrow opening of the needle with the twisting bulk of his limbs; and what was set before others for destruction benefited him for salvation.

But lest it seem strange that I have described the ugly limbs of a camel in a man: in a man there is a camel’s deformity, not in bodily ugliness but in the mind; not in the sluggishness of his bearing, but in the cowardice of his heart. For as a camel is misshapen by the unevenness of its limbs, so a man is deformed by the harshness of sins. This is what the Lord signifies in saying: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.” That is, it is difficult for a sinner to pass through that steep and narrow way of heavenly life after the perversity of his sins has been stripped off and made thin. For he who wishes to pass from a corrupt and sluggish bulk to the substance of that heavenly purity must greatly discipline and raise his habits to a higher plane; unless he does so, so burdened and large an animal will be obstructed in the narrow heavenly gate.

Zacchaeus, then, is to be praised, whom his riches were utterly unable to disentangle from the royal threshold. Or rather, he is to be praised because riches brought him to the threshold of the kingdom. Hence we understand that riches do not hinder, but help, in attaining Christ’s glory—provided that the person possessing them does not pour them out for self-indulgence, but distributes them for salvation. The fault does not lie in resources: riches are incentives to wickedness for the foolish, aids to virtue for the wise; to the latter an occasion of salvation is given, while for the former a stumbling-block of destruction is acquired.

## SERMON C. Likewise, on the sequel

[Col. 0731]

[Col. 0731B] ### ARGUMENT

Zacchaeus gave not half, but all; and he made restitution with manifold interest. He is to be imitated by us, and by the moneylenders of this time.

From the exposition on the preceding Sunday, I believe that all rich persons rejoice and congratulate those for whom Zacchaeus has opened the heavenly gate, formerly closed because of their wealth. For he opened the heavenly gate when he taught them to reach the kingdom by the very means by which they had been excluded from it: namely, that the wealth reproached in them as leading to destruction might serve for salvation.

Thus Zacchaeus conferred much upon the rich, making them possess their riches forever, so that those who were never poor here might not be beggars in the future, but by a profitable exchange might receive great things for small, heavenly things for earthly, everlasting things for temporal. It is indeed a profitable exchange to refuse to retain what one possesses, in order to obtain what one does not possess; and to suffer a certain loss in relinquishing money, in order to gain the perpetual profit of possessing grace.

Zacchaeus, therefore, although a tax collector who had acquired great wealth by lending money at interest and by the fraud of usury, immediately upon seeing Christ was so converted that he sought spiritual grace with greater desire than he had sought worldly money. He was so converted, I say, that, looking back on his former deeds, he himself condemned his frauds; and, cleansing his greed, first cleansed his conscience as well. For he says: “Behold, I give half my goods to the poor, and if I have taken anything from anyone, I restore it fourfold” (Luke XIX).

Perhaps someone will say: Why did this holy man, seeing the Savior present, give not all but half to the poor, when it is written, “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Mark X)? But if you examine carefully, he fulfilled this, for he gave not half but all. Take away what belonged to others, and nothing remains to Zacchaeus. Finally, the just man knew, in order that his liberality might be acceptable, how to dispose justly—namely, by restoring what belonged to others. For this is almsgiving acceptable to the Lord: that which is offered from one’s own native property, not that which is bestowed from fraudulent plunder. In generosity to the poor, not spoils but gifts are sought.

Besides, why is that a gift which one receives with joy while another loses with tears; over which one rejoices, while another groans? Whatever grace may help you who receive it, the complaint of those who groan certainly burdens you greatly. Even though you give away all [Col. 0732C], you perform a better act of almsgiving if you restore another’s property. Foreseeing this, holy Zacchaeus restored what he had taken, so that what he gave might be accepted. For he says: “If I have taken anything from anyone, I restore it fourfold.” See how he made amends for having sinned once! For he was a good moneylender: knowing what profit there was in divine gain, he restored with manifold interest the money he had received with interest. He is to be imitated by us all, and by the moneylenders of this time.

But, what is worse, many do not imitate his grace but imitate his interest: they know how to plunder; they utterly do not know how to restore. Although he voluntarily restored fourfold what he had received, they, even when compelled, do not restore what they have seized even once. They prefer to lose what is theirs through litigation rather than restore what is another’s through settlement.

Explicit.

## SERMON CI. On removing idols from one’s own possessions

[Col. 0731]

### ADMONITION

That this sermon was known before Muratori brought it to light in the Paduan edition, *Anecdota*, vol. IV, p. 99, is most certainly clear not so much from Baronius as from Gothofredus. For Baronius, in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for 31 January, not only mentions it, but reproduces in the very same words this description of impious sacrifices. Gothofredus, moreover, in his notes on title 10 of book XVI of the Theodosian Code, when mentioning laws enacted by the emperors against idolatry, aptly employs this testimony for his purpose. Muratori drew this sermon, like the next one, from the celebrated Ambrosian manuscript, where it is ascribed to Saint Maximus. Its title is as we have transcribed it: “On removing idols from one’s own possessions.”

[Col. 0733A] ### ARGUMENT

A person who sees his farmhand sacrificing to idols and does not forbid it sins. The evil of idolatry and the appearance of a soothsayer are described.

A few days ago, brothers, I urged your charity, as religious and holy persons, to remove every pollution of idols from your possessions and to root out from your fields the whole error of the Gentiles. For it is not lawful that you who have Christ in your hearts should have Antichrist in your dwellings; that while you worship God in church, your people should venerate the devil in shrines. Nor should anyone think himself excused by saying, “I did not order it done; I did not command it.” Whoever knows that sacrileges are being performed on his property and does not forbid their performance, in some measure commands them himself; by silence and failure to rebuke he gives consent to the sacrificer. For the blessed Apostle says that not only those who commit crimes, but also those who consent to their commission, are guilty.

Therefore, brother, when you see your farmhand sacrificing and do not forbid him to offer sacrifice, you sin: if not by granting the means, yet by allowing permission; if your command is not culpable, your will is nevertheless at fault. While you are silent, what your farmhand has done pleases you; if he had not done it, perhaps it would displease you. For the subordinate sins not only for himself when he sacrifices, but also for the *domnedius* [lord], who does not forbid him; if he forbade him, he certainly would not sin.

[Col. 0733C] **Note:** Muratori had already observed in the preface to the sermons of St Maximus published in vol. IV of the *Anecdota* that the word *domnedium* is derived from the corrupted speech of that age and has the same force as *dominum* (“lord”), and that St Paulinus of Nola used it in more than one place. See also Cange, *Glossarium mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, under *Dominaedius*. [Col. 0733D]

Idolatry, then, is a great evil: it pollutes those who practise it, those who live there, and those who look upon it; it reaches ministers, those who know of it, and those who are silent. When the farmhand sacrifices, the *domnedius* is defiled. He cannot fail to be polluted where he takes food which the sacrilegious cultivator has cultivated, bloody ground has produced, and a foul granary has stored. For everything there is defiled, everything impious, where the devil dwells—in the house, in the fields, and among the farmhands.

Nothing there is free from wickedness where everything is occupied with wickedness. When you enter the storeroom, you will find pale turf and dead coals in it: a sacrifice worthy of a demon, since dead things are offered in supplication to a dead deity. If you go out into the field, you see wooden altars and stone images: fitting service where senseless gods are served with rotting altars. If you rise early and see the farmhand wounded by wine, you should know that he is, as they say, a devotee of Diana or a haruspex; for an insane deity is accustomed to have a mad priest.

[Col. 0734B] **Note:** Those farmhands were called devotees of Diana (*dianatici*) who sacrificed to Diana, the divinity of fields; and *haruspices*, led by superstition, foretold the future from the inspection of the entrails of victims. Maximus describes the frenzy that seized them when they performed such sacrifices, and how impiously and foolishly they raged against themselves in order to render honor to a false divinity. [Col. 0734D]

Such a priest prepares himself with wine for the blows dealt in honor of his goddess, so that, while drunk, he may not feel his own punishment. They do this not only for intemperance but also as a technique, so that, carried away by the drunkenness of wine, they may feel their wounds less. A soothsayer is surely vain who thinks to establish piety by cruelty. How merciful toward foreign gods is he who is so bloody toward his own priests! To describe briefly the appearance of this soothsayer: his head is shaggy with artificial locks, his breast is bare, his legs are half-covered by a cloak, and, equipped for battle after the manner of gladiators, he carries iron in his hands. Yet he is worse than a gladiator, because the latter is compelled to fight another, while the former is forced to fight himself; the one seeks another’s entrails, the other tears apart his own limbs; and, if it can be said, a trainer urges the former to cruelty, a deity the latter. Wearing this dress, then, and bloody with this slaughter, judge whether he is a gladiator or a priest. Therefore, as the public crime of gladiators was abolished by the devout action of religious rulers, so let these mad gladiators be removed from your own homes by the observance of Christianity.

## SERMON CII. On the same subject

[Col. 0733]

[Col. 0733C] ### ARGUMENT

He who knows that idols are being sacrificed to on his land and does not forbid it certainly becomes a participant in sacrilege.

We believe that you profited not a little from the exposition on the preceding Sunday, since by our preaching we cleansed your hearts from every defilement of idols. For our hearts are cleansed when our conscience is not held polluted by the filth of the devil. The person who does not permit sacrileges to be practised on his property does not have a polluted conscience. But whoever knows that idols are being sacrificed to on his farm and does not forbid it, although he himself remains far away in the city, is nevertheless touched by that impious pollution. Although the farmhand stands at the altars, the execrable contamination returns to the *domnedius*. For he becomes a participant in it, if not by consciousness, certainly by knowledge.

We believe, therefore, that we have made progress when you prohibit the cult of sacrilege on your possessions; for we say that a Christian man’s possession—that is, a clean man’s possession—should be clean. Solomon says: “A clean man is a precious possession.” If, then, a pure man is compared to a most precious possession, how much more valuable is that possession if it is sound and pure and is not cheapened by any contamination of the devil! But we must understand why a clean man is called a clean possession: namely, because he is made precious not by the frailty of his body but by the purity of his integrity, and because for that very purity of mind the Lord deigns to possess him, as the prophet says in the person of the saints.

(In the Ambrosian manuscript, where this sermon is found, several leaves are missing.)

## SERMON CIII. On the watchman appointed for the children of Israel

[Col. 0735]

### ADMONITION

It exists in the Ambrosian manuscript mentioned above, and is printed in Muratori, *Anecdota*, vol. IV, p. 102.

[Col. 0735A] ### ARGUMENT

If a preacher chooses to dissemble, keep silent, and conceal, he neither corrects his brother by silence nor despises himself by not preaching. The watchmen established by the Lord are none other than priests.

Sometimes, brothers, when we preach, our discourse seems rather harsh to many; and what we set forth according to the rule is received by some as though it proceeded from the austere severity of our own character. For they say: “How harshly and bitterly the bishop preached,” not knowing that necessity is greater for priests than willingness. I say necessity of speaking is greater: not because the will to pursue truth is lacking, but because the penalty appointed drives away the silence of keeping quiet. We endure necessity while we fear; and thereby we are compelled to be able more than to will, and we press fearful things upon others because we ourselves fear for our own safety.

This, however, is the condition of a preacher: he must not keep another’s sins silent if he wishes to avoid his own sins; he must correct his brother by rebuke, so that he may not lose the priest in himself. But if he chooses to dissemble, to keep silent, to conceal, he neither corrects that man by silence nor despises himself by not preaching. It is better, therefore, to correct sin by rebuke than, by silence, to take upon oneself the offenses of the sinner. For we are placed in this office so that, if we do not tell offenders their crimes, the guilt of those very crimes may also entangle us.

For thus the Lord certainly says through the prophet: “And you, son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; and you shall hear a word from my mouth. When I say to the sinner, ‘You shall surely die,’ and you do not speak, so that the wicked man may beware of his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but I shall require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. III), and what follows. The judgment is plainly evident and manifest: it stains the watchman with the blood of the criminal because he kept silent. Nor is it content that the wicked man should be condemned by his own iniquity, unless it also declares guilty the person who refused to rebuke that same iniquity.

See, then, how great is the evil of the offender: the offender himself sins, and the priest is accused. He kills himself by his sins, and his blood is required from the bishop’s hand. We must therefore speak and cry out, lest on the day of judgment that same sinner excuse our silence and he who pretends to be a participant in holiness then accuse us of being his companion in error: “And you, son of man,” he says, “I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel.”

What is a watchman? A watchman, certainly, is one who stands as it were on a lofty citadel, looks out over the neighboring people lest some enemy suddenly creep upon them, and, diligently caring for them, ensures that the people enjoy the sweetness of peace. If he suddenly sees anything adverse, he immediately gives notice and announces it steadfastly, so that both the citizen may be prepared to avoid the danger and the enemy may flee when discovered. But if, when the adversary presses, the watchman dissimulates, keeps silent, or neglects his duty, the people are unexpectedly overtaken, the advancing enemy rages, and therefore all blame is ascribed to the man who refused to speak so as to save many, but preferred silence so that he himself might perish with many.

Whom, then, are these watchmen established by the Lord, if not the most blessed priests? Placed as it were on a lofty citadel of wisdom for the protection of peoples, they see from afar the evils that are coming and, while still distant, discern future punishments—not with the sight of bodily eyes, but with the vision of spiritual prudence. Therefore they cannot be silent but are compelled to cry out, lest the hostile devil invade Christ’s flock through their silence.

For behold, we foresee the day of judgment approaching, and already in thought pronounce the punishments of sinners. Therefore we announce to each person that he should turn away from his way of impiety: to the drunkard, that he should pursue sobriety, because hostile lust is the companion of drunkenness; to the greedy man, that he should distribute his money, lest by keeping it he seem to possess riches not to use them but to worship them. For whatever a person loves, that he worships, preserves, and in some way venerates. See then, greedy man, lest the vessels of your table become an idol to you, since you do not use them as a master but guard them stored away as a slave.

## SERMON CIV. Rebuke to the people, and on the Lord’s saying: “To him who has, it shall be given,” Luke VII; and “We sang to you, and you did not dance,” Matthew XI

[Col. 0735]

[Col. 0735D] **Note:** The Vulgate reads, in verse 17, “We sang to you, and you did not dance.”

### ADMONITION

In the ancient manuscripts of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, no. 40 of 90 and no. 84 of 99, and also in the Ambrosian and Laurentian manuscript 10, Plut. XIV, this sermon bears both the title which we give and Maximus’ name. For this reason we judge that its author was not Ambrose but Maximus.

[Col. 0735D] ### ARGUMENT

Saint Maximus says that it is perhaps superfluous to press the preaching of the Lord’s cup upon one who does not retain the Lord’s command in his heart. He then explains the cited testimonies of sacred Scripture, and finally writes that the blessed Virgin Mary is the Ark of the Covenant.

I had often resolved within myself, brothers, to withhold from you the words of the Lord’s preaching and [Col. 0736D] not to distribute so frequently the mysteries of heavenly discourses. For it is of no benefit to offer food to one who refuses it or to present drink to one who is not thirsty, since he swallows what you offer not so willingly as he rejects it disdainfully, as though it were turbid; and thus it happens [Note: [Col. 0736D] Cod. Laurentianus 10 Plut. XIV: “and of the people.”] that the purity of the cup is spoiled and that the disdainful drinker finds reasons for his offense.

So too, then, it is perhaps superfluous to pour into your charity the preaching of the Lord’s [Col. 0737A] cup, since your soul, with its inner organs closed, drinks it not so thirstily as it spills it dissemblingly. For he spills the Lord’s command who hears it with his ear but does not retain it in his heart. Carrying it, as it were, on the surface of his body and not sending what he has heard into his interior, he forgets it, pours out the sequence of the preaching, and thus returns home empty who had gone out from the church [Note: [Col. 0737D] Laurentianus: “unjust.”] laden.

Tell me, then, [Note: [Col. 0737D] b The same Laurentianus codex: “which of you, when …”] which of you, when he has returned to his lodging, says: “Today we heard the bishop discussing almsgiving; he preached something useful: we ought to have mercy on the poor. He also spoke about the execrable worship of idols; let us make inquiry lest, without our knowing it, there be an idol in our property. He also admonished us that the catechumen ought to hasten [Col. 0737B] [Note: [Col. 0737D] c Codices of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme and Laurentianus 10: “to the grace of faith.”] to the grace of God. Let us offer our household so that whoever is faithful may receive the faith, lest perhaps an account of their salvation be required of us, since their life depends upon our judgment”? 662

No one thinks about the things of God; no one speaks about the day of judgment, as though we were either going to live forever or going to die entirely. [Note: [Col. 0737D] d Thus the codex of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme: “we shall live through everything.”] Believe me: we live in this age in such a way that we die in body; we die in such a way that we live in order to render an account. Meanwhile the human being dies, but the cause of his deeds does not die. Since the cause remains alive, it is necessary that the person responsible for his cause not be absent, as the prophet says: “Behold the man and his works.”

I had therefore wanted to withhold from you the words of the Lord’s preaching—not because I was doing this in anger, but in order to preserve the evangelical saying. For the Lord says: “To the one who has, it will be given, and from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Matt. XXV; Mark IV). He therefore commanded that something be given to the one who has, and that to the one who does not have not only should nothing be given, but even what he has should be taken away.

Perhaps this saying seems superfluous to you; but I say that the Lord commanded rightly and wisely. “To the one who has,” then, it is commanded that something be given. Clearly he deserves to receive who has labored so that, through his own diligence, he might acquire spiritual riches for his soul. Suppose that someone, with a strong resolve for continence, has begun to guard the virtue of chastity: he deserves to hear what reward chastity will have in the future, so that, by adding the glory of reward to the observance of virtue, he may more easily overcome the struggle he has begun.

Another person, ready to show mercy, ought to hear that God will show mercy to him. And he who has exchanged this earthly substance for heavenly riches must, by hearing of the recompense of heavenly rewards, necessarily pursue the Lord’s work more readily and willingly, and add an increase of liberality to the good of mercy that he possesses. Therefore the Lord says: “To the one who has, it will be given”—that is, the one who is rich in good works will be enriched still more by evangelical preaching.

But if you preach to a fornicator and tell him that he ought to remain a virgin, and tell a miser that he ought to sell all that he possesses and give it away, it is folly for him. He considers this preaching [Col. 0738A] ridiculous. Thus the Apostle says: “The natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit” (1 Cor. I), “for they are folly to him.” To preach what is perfect to such people is like wanting to dress a beggar buried under rags in silk, or delight a hungry peasant with a pastry: both must reject such an offering.

Silk displeases the one who needs clothing suitable for the cold; the pastry is bitter to the other, while he seeks food that will satisfy his hunger. From such persons, then, what is theirs must rather be taken away, as the Gospel says: “Even what he has will be taken away from him” (Matt. XXV). That is, the fornicator must be compelled to cast off the rags of his corruption, and the miser must be forced to expose the bread of his greed.

I fear, brothers, that this evangelical reading applies to many of you. It says: “We sang to you, and you did not dance; we lamented, and you did not weep” (Luke VII). We announce to you, therefore, the joy of the heavenly kingdom, and your hearts do not leap up with any movement of gladness. [Note: [Col. 0738D] The codex of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme: “We preach.”] We have preached the grievous judgment, and your senses do not break forth into tears of repentance.

For it is a kind of unbelief, in divine matters, neither to rejoice in what is favorable nor to weep over what is adverse. The Lord therefore asks a dance from you—not, of course, the twisting movement of the body, but the holiness of faith lifting itself upward.
