Just as one who dances bodily is at one moment suspended in the air, at another thrown higher, and at another surveys different places through alternating leaps, so one who dances spiritually, when faith intervenes, is at one moment raised to the heights of the air, at another lifted to the higher regions of the stars, [Col. 0738C] [Note: [Col. 0738D] Both codices of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme: “lifted up.”] and at another surveys paradise and heaven through the various leaps of his thoughts. And just as one who dances bodily, exercising himself through the movement of his limbs, acquires a circle for his dancing, so one who dances spiritually, moving himself with the liveliness of faith, takes for himself the circle of the whole world.

Let people dance, as is customary, at their vows—that is, dance or sing especially at weddings. We too have weddings of our vows, at which we ought to dance or sing. Our vows are celebrated when the Church is joined to Christ, as John says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III). For the sake of these weddings, then, it is fitting for us to dance.

Indeed, King David, both king and prophet, is said to have danced before the ark of the covenant while singing many songs (2 Kings VI). Raised up by joy, he broke forth into dancing. For in the spirit he foresaw Mary, sprung from his lineage, to be joined to Christ’s bridal chamber. Hence he says: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Ps. XVIII). Therefore he sang more than the other authors of prophecy, because, more joyful than all, through these joys he was marrying his descendants and inviting them to their own vows with an accustomed sweetness. He taught us what we ought to do at those very weddings, since he danced before the ark with such exultation before the wedding itself. [Note: [Col. 0738D] Codex 90 of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme: “we ought to do.”]

Therefore the prophet David danced before the ark. And what should we call the ark but Saint Mary? For the ark carried within it the tablets of the covenant, whereas Mary carried the heir of that very covenant. The one retained the Law within itself; the other retained the Gospel. The one had the voice of God; the other [Note: [Col. 0739D] Thus both codices of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.] the true Word. Yet the ark shone within and without with the radiance of gold; and Saint Mary likewise gleamed within and without with the splendor of virginity. The one was adorned with earthly gold, the other with heavenly gold.

## SERMON CV. On the Cup of Cold Water

[Col. 0739]

### ADMONITION

665 Up to this point this sermon lay mutilated in volume IV of the *Anecdota*, which the editor Muratori himself had found incomplete, together with many others, in a very ancient Ambrosian codex. Its beginning was missing as far as the words “he loves and commends.” To restore it to him, we received it through the kindness of the most distinguished Stefano Borgia, secretary of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith. He extracted a complete and finished copy from Codex Beneventanus III, p. 118, bearing this title: “Sermon of Saint Maximus, bishop, on a cup of cold water.”

[Col. 0739A]

### ARGUMENT

God promises a heavenly reward even for a cup of cold water; he invites the poor and incites the rich. He does not seek the value of the gift, but the devotion of the one who offers it. What is the spiritual meaning of this kind of promise.

The most merciful God, Savior of the human race and most abundant distributor of incorruptible gifts, in order to find more people to whom he may lavish his gifts, promises his faithful a heavenly reward even for a cup of cold water, saying: “Whoever gives one of these little ones a drink, only a cup of cold water in my name, amen I say to you, he will not lose his reward” (Matt. X).

Observe, brothers, how our Lord both loves and commends his little ones with special care. For he promises that he will grant a reward for that water alone which a religious hand has offered to his servants, who are indeed considered little ones in this world. By the very fact that it is offered to those who believe in Christ in honor of his name, [Note: [Col. 0740D] “Or should it read: ‘By this very fact … by which it is offered to believers?’ EDITOR.”] the water itself becomes more acceptable to God.

He therefore says: “Whoever gives a drink, only a cup of cold water in my name.” We see many people, brothers, who bestow very great wealth and magnificent gifts upon their relatives, friends, or patrons, not so much with a view to heavenly grace as from the practice and necessity of human society. It is clear that these gifts will perish with this world, since they are given not to God, who remains forever, but to mortal people who are soon to depart from here. Whatever is spent for the ambitions of this age must necessarily slip away with the age.

But our Lord, the consoler of his poor and humble ones, does not demand alluring ornaments of glittering gems, nor costly silken garments; rather, he promises a reward even for cold water. He asks for cold water so that every poverty may abound in religious mercy toward the needy. “Whoever,” he says, “gives a drink, a cup of cold water, will not lose his reward.”

This saying, beloved, both invites the poor to obedience to the heavenly commandments and urges the rich to it. For what poor person can lack water to offer to the thirsty? Or what faithful rich person would not desire to give better things, when he sees that with the most munificent God great rewards are bestowed for small gifts?

In this fellowship, it is not the value of the gift that is sought, but the devotion of the giver. Thus that needy and most devout woman (Mark XII), who was putting two small coins into the treasury, was preferred by the Lord’s judgment to all the rich. And rightly so, brothers, because the most wise Judge was seeking not the abundance of the work but the affection of the worker. He was not considering how much the rich person brought forth for God’s gifts from his overflowing storehouses, but how much sustenance remained with the woman who had left nothing for herself.

The rich offered gifts to the great God in such a way that they would not cease to be rich. But the poor woman, with such great generosity of faith, preferred God to herself that, despising her poverty, she offered everything she had. Therefore she put in more than all the others, because she reserved less for herself than all the others.

“Whoever gives,” he says, “a cup of cold water will not lose his reward.” What poverty, then, can remain without a reward under the generosity of so merciful a Judge, with whom even water, when offered, produces a reward? Water is abundant and, by its very inundation, extremely cheap; but when it is offered under the profession of religion, the confession of Christ makes it precious.

Hence, beloved, it is for you to consider what and how great the rewards of heavenly riches must be for one who gives food, clothing, or money, since it will not be without effect to have offered a cup of water. The rich must certainly beware lest this kindness of Christ make them slower to give, since the offering of water produces a reward especially for those who have nothing else that they can offer to the poor. For what kind of religion, or how great a devotion, is it to have abundant possessions and, from a small and insignificant deed, to want to purchase heaven?

After these matters, beloved, if we direct our understanding toward spiritual meaning, we shall find another water that has power to refresh the hearts of the righteous with very pleasing grace. Therefore, whoever receives the discourse of holy men preaching God with a believing ear will strengthen by its simplicity all their inner faculties, which indeed thirst for life, and will strengthen the faith of those who hear.

Thus the Lord Jesus himself (John IV), when he had sat down, weary and thirsty, beside the well—he who truly thirsted for the salvation of mortals—was given drink by the abundant faith of the Samaritan woman and of the crowds coming out of the city. 668 For although the Lord watered the dryness of their minds with his saving discourse, spiritual words nevertheless have such a nature that, if their effect follows, by a kind of reciprocal gift they refresh both the hearer and the speaker.

And so it happens that when the defender of truth sows the evangelical seed, if the one receiving it pours over it the moisture of faith, the most abundant harvest of heavenly fruits is nourished. Hence, brothers, both aspects contribute to our salvation: that we practice mercy most readily and commend obedience to those who teach holy things, so that we may hope for a full and perfect reward when the Lord repays us.

## SERMON CVI. On the Five Loaves and Two Fish

[Col. 0741]

### ADMONITION

This sermon is attributed to Saint Maximus in Muratori, volume IV of the *Anecdota*, no. 21; and from its similar manner of composition it can plainly be recognized as the work of the same holy bishop.

[Col. 0741A]

### ARGUMENT

Although you have said very much about divine Scripture, more nevertheless remains to be said. More is taken away from the Lord’s table than is brought to it.

After the solemnity of a festive celebration, what remains is usually sweeter, and the leftovers from a great banquet are customarily more pleasing to taste. Therefore we too, as we celebrate the Lord’s birth, ought more gladly to receive what has been most abundantly reserved for us from the preparations. We cannot fear disgust at the leftovers, because the Savior’s banquets are always complete and always undefiled; they are not diminished by any contamination. But whenever something is taken from them, they are renewed again in their own excellence by heavenly vigor.

It is therefore a great food, from which you may take as much as you wish while everything you have taken remains intact. Divine Scripture has such vigor that, although you have said very much about it, more nevertheless remains to be said. The more deeply the preacher’s discussion has extended itself, the more the holy mind finds a corresponding height for discussion. Hence the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. XI).

We must not therefore fear that, after so great a banquet, we shall suffer disgust and hunger. We have spent everything in devotion, yet by grace everything has remained; and, to make what I have said less surprising, after everything has been spent, everything has remained.

Recall the evangelical Scripture that was read recently, and you will find that more is taken away from the Lord’s table than is brought to it. Five loaves were brought, and twelve baskets of fragments were carried away. More, then, is found by those who gather the leftovers than was brought by the one who supplied the food for the banquet.

Finally, after the five thousand men had been filled, scarcely twelve apostles carried away twelve baskets—what one boy had brought in his hand before anything had been spent. Thus bread is multiplied in the Lord’s hand while it is broken; it grows while it is diminished; while it is distributed, it increases. Through this more profitable expenditure, the created food nourishes and benefits the peoples; what seemed less in the hands of the servers grows in the mouths of those who eat.

Finally, Saint Andrew says: “There is one boy here who has five loaves and two fish” (Luke IX), and so forth. In a wondrous manner, therefore, through the blessing of Christ the Lord, the solid nature of bread flows, abounds, and overflows; through a kind of channel of vigor it becomes for those who eat not a fountain of waters but of foods.

We read in the prophets that the same Lord brought forth drink for the thirsty from a hard rock. Behold, now he has produced for the hungry, flowing from dry bread, the fullness of satisfaction. There he dissolved the rock into waves; here he multiplied the food into abundance.

All these things, as I said, are to be compared figuratively with the evangelical Scriptures. Through a few verses they refresh Christian peoples and never fail; through their blessing they feed hungry souls, and when they have satisfied them, they abound still more. For who, once refreshed by the evangelical commandments, would not give thanks for them as one enriched by these commandments, possessing a treasure by which he himself may always be satisfied and may also fill the mouth of another who is hungry?

## SERMON CVII. On the Words of the Gospel of Mark, Chapter VIII: “When a Great Crowd Was with Jesus and They Had Nothing to Eat”

[Col. 0741]

### ADMONITION

I trust that readers will be grateful to me when I bring this exceptional sermon, wrought with much learning, into a more brilliant light than it has hitherto possessed in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine, no. 81. Regarding it, the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur taught that it was first left anonymous by the Louvain scholars among the Augustinian works, and then rejected by Verlinus and Vindingus because it deals with the Eutychian heresy, which arose after Augustine. Their judgment is certainly fair and correct.

But if it cannot be reconciled with Augustine, will it conflict with Maximus? On the contrary, since the holy bishop of Turin clearly understood that hidden iniquity and opposed it learnedly and solidly in his writings, and since he condemned so dreadful a heresy at the Council of Milan, Saint Maximus himself must be established as the author of this sermon.

Let no one object that the same battle against Eutyches could have been waged by another writer, or that no documents can be produced to confirm my opinion. All such objections fall away as insignificant if this sermon is compared with the preceding one. In that sermon Maximus discussed the miraculous multiplication of the five loaves and two fish, as related in Matthew, chapter XIV; here he explains the passage in Mark, chapter VIII, where it is related that Christ the Lord filled a great multitude of people with seven loaves and a few fish.

In both sermons, hidden mysteries connected with one another—the calling and rejection of the Synagogue, the illumination of the nations, and the new beginnings of the rising Church—are wonderfully explained. Since there is therefore such close connection, the same spirit of understanding, and finally the same form of expression, why should we not likewise acknowledge Saint Maximus as the author of this sermon?

In the chapters or readings of the Gospels now being published for the first time, the same interpretation of this passage from the Gospel of Saint Mark is attributed to Saint Maximus; it is very close to what is said in this sermon. The style also contributes evidence, for it is plainly Maximian, as is the method of adducing passages of sacred Scripture, which was peculiar to Maximus.

[Col. 0743A]

### ARGUMENT

In our Redeemer, the distinct operation of divinity and humanity must be considered, and the error of Eutyches must be detested; he dares to teach that there is only one operation in Christ. The multiplication both of the fish and of the seven loaves is explained at length and mystically.

Our Lord Jesus Christ has shown the height of his divinity and the mercy of his humanity in many different ways in the holy Scriptures, as he is accustomed to do in mysteries and sacraments, so that those who ask may receive, those who seek may find, and to those who knock it may be opened. For all the miracles that he displayed in this world under the conditions of our frailty benefit us. The Lord did not perform them without purpose, as though pointlessly and vainly. Christ is the Word of God, who speaks to human beings not only with words but also with deeds.

This passage also, which has been read today from the Holy Gospel, seeks someone to understand it; and once it has been understood, it produces spiritual joy. In this reading too, we must consider simultaneously, in one and the same Redeemer, the distinct operation of divinity and humanity, [Note: [Col. 0743C] By “distinct operation” Maximus means not confused. For he is opposing Eutyches, who had affirmed confusion, though not sufficiently explicitly in words, yet in reality. Whoever had maintained that the two natures, divine and human, and their properties were confused in Christ after the union had certainly maintained what necessarily follows from this: that the operations of the two natures were likewise confused in the same Savior. This is entirely clear from many other ecclesiastical documents, and especially from the celebrated letter of Saint Agatho, pope, to which the Sixth Ecumenical Synod willingly adhered. In it, speaking about the Eutychians, he says: “They confuse the mystery of the holy Incarnation because they say that there is one nature of Christ’s divinity and humanity; they contend that he has one personal will and operation, just as he has one nature. But the apostolic Church of Christ, the spiritual mother established by God of your imperial power, confesses one Lord Jesus Christ existing from two natures and in two natures. It defends that his two natures, divine and human, remain unconfused in him even after inseparable union, and it recognizes each form of Christ’s natures as perfect according to their natural properties; it confesses that everything belonging to the properties of the natures is twofold. Consequently, according to the rule of the holy Catholic and apostolic Church, it also confesses and proclaims that there are in him two natural wills and two natural operations.” See act 4 of the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, p. 1084, volume III of the *Councils*, Paris edition, 1714.

Hence Saint Leo, in that divine letter to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople—in which the Council of Chalcedon testified that Peter had spoken through Leo—refutes the heretical Eutychian doctrine concerning Christ’s divine and human operations in these terms: “Each form acts, in communion with the other, according to what is proper to it: the Word doing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines forth in miracles; the other submits to injuries,” etc. Letter 25, elsewhere 26, chapter 4, volume II of the works, Rome edition, 1755, p. 20.

674 Saint Agatho used this passage of Saint Leo in the very letter to the emperors that I have just mentioned, a letter so highly celebrated by the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, p. 1099.

Now that Eutyches said that the two natures in Christ, and their properties, were confused is attested by Saint Flavian in his first letter to Leo, chapter 3, volume II of Saint Leo’s works, p. 100, and in another letter found in the same place, p. 16, where he says that Eutyches maintained: “Before the incarnation of our Savior Jesus Christ there were two natures, divinity and humanity; but after the union there was one nature”—not knowing what he says or concerning what he makes his assertion. For the union of the two natures that came together in Christ did not confuse their properties in the union; rather, the properties of the two natures remain entire even in the union.

Compare Saint Leo, *Letter to Flavian*, chapter 3, p. 120, and chapter 4, pp. 122 ff., and Letter 22 to Theodosius Augustus, p. 107, where, indicating the Eutychians, he says: “We condemn the blasphemies of those who, by a novel invention, attempt to say that from the time the flesh was assumed, all the things of the divine nature were changed into the human, and all the things of the human nature into the divine—a claim that no heresy has ever dared to make. For by this kind of confession they assert that both the nature of divinity and the nature of humanity were changed into something else, and they do not affirm the Son to be either perfect God or perfect man according to the truth.” Read what follows concerning the two operations in Christ, namely the divine and the human. More documents of the ancients could be produced in the same sense, but there is no need, since these seem sufficient to me.] and the error of Eutyches, which must be detested in every way, for he dares to teach that there is only one operation in Christ.

For if one says that he was merely human, he will deny the glory of the Creator; but if one says that he was merely God, he will deny the mercy of the Redeemer. Namely, when the Lord has pity on the crowd, lest it fail through hunger or the labor of a longer journey, let us recognize the feeling and compassion of human frailty; but when he satisfies four thousand people with seven loaves and a few fish, we believe this to be the work of divine power.

Therefore let your holiness attend, because this is what has been set before us to discuss with your charity: what is the meaning of this mystery, that sacred Scripture testifies that he demonstrated himself to his disciples as God in the manner in which the Gospel relates it. For the evangelist says in today’s reading: “When a great crowd was with Jesus and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples and said to them: ‘I have compassion on the crowd’” (Mark VIII).

But let us investigate what he says above: “In those days, when there was a great crowd.” Previously the Jews had approached the Savior, accusing his disciples because they ate with unwashed hands. The Lord rebuked them, because it is the evil things that proceed from the heart that defile a person.

Leaving them, he came to the borders of the Gentiles, where the Canaanite woman, who is the mother of the Gentiles, pleaded with the Lord on behalf of her daughter—that is, on behalf of the Church. She persisted in asking until she received what she sought. After this he again healed a mute and deaf man.

Therefore, in those days, when a multitude of people had gathered and they had nothing to eat—because the Gentiles did not have the Law, that is, the five books of Moses and the prophets, nor the preaching of Saint John, because the Gentiles came to the Redeemer not through the Law but through faith—they persevered for three days. This means in the Lord’s birth, passion, and resurrection, or in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

To persevere means to remain in confession, as the Lord himself says: “But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Mark XXIX). The Lord therefore says: “They have nothing to eat, because they do not have the Law; and I do not want to send them away fasting, lest they fail on the way” (Matt. XV), so that those who believed in Christ through faith might be saved through faith in Christ.

Some of them had come from far away. The Gentiles were far from God because they wandered among idols; and now everyone who sins is far from God. His disciples say: “From where could anyone satisfy these people with bread here in the wilderness?” (ibid.). Unbelief still held the apostles, until the mysteries were revealed; they did not remember what he had done with the five loaves and two fish.

Jesus asked them how many loaves they had. They said, “Seven.” And he ordered the crowd to sit down upon the ground. Taking the bread, he gave thanks and [Col. 0745B] gave it to his disciples to distribute. He likewise blessed the fish and set them before them. They ate and were satisfied, and they took up seven baskets full. Those who ate were about four thousand, besides women and children (ibid.).

We clearly believe that the Lord’s miracles were performed in the present event; but, with the grace of God granting it, let us inquire into what lies hidden in its mystery.

In the earlier reading, concerning the five loaves and two fish, he satisfied five thousand people; here he satisfied four thousand with seven loaves. There the disciples make a suggestion to the Lord, saying: “The place is deserted, and the hour has passed; send the crowds away, so that they may go into the villages and buy food for themselves” (ibid.). Here the disciples are completely silent; but the Lord himself is concerned for them. 672

Let us see why they are silent. It is because they had not yet been sent to preach to the Gentiles, but rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. That earlier parable therefore pertains to the Jews; this one, however, to the Gentiles.

There were five loaves there—that is, the five books of Moses. Here, however, there are seven loaves, which are the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit, as the holy prophet Isaiah says: “The Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and he will fill him with the Spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. XI).

There, twelve baskets were full of the Holy Spirit; here, the seven Churches, or the seven golden lampstands. There, two fish, which are the two Testaments, or the one book of all the prophets, or the preaching of Saint John; here, an indefinite number is given, representing the gifts of graces, as the Apostle says: “To one through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another prophecy, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of utterances. All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes” (1 Cor. XII).

There they recline upon grass, and here upon the ground. In both places there is one way of life, one grace, one power, one divinity. There they recline upon grass—that is, upon works of the flesh that have been put to death, because, as the prophet says, “all flesh is grass” (Isa. XL); here they recline upon the ground, that is, they trample upon earthly works.

There, five thousand were nourished, a number that pertains to the Jews; for after the Lord’s ascension, when Peter was speaking, five thousand were baptized. Here, however, there are four thousand—that is, all the Gentiles from the four quarters of the earth are filled with the grace of the sevenfold Spirit unto eternal life.

And therefore, beloved, we who believe in our Lord Jesus Christ not through the Law but through faith, who have been redeemed not from works but by grace itself, who have been filled not from five loaves—that is, from the five books of Moses—but from the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, just as blessed Isaiah prophesied, saying: “The Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and he will fill him with the Spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. XI)—let us remain in this sevenfold grace of the Spirit, in which we have been called and filled with the gift of the Holy Spirit through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CVIII. On the Canaanite Woman

[Col. 0745]

### ADMONITION

In the paper codex Chisianus of the fifteenth century, the sermon that we publish as number CVIII is attributed to Saint Maximus.

[Col. 0745C]

### ARGUMENT

On the great faith, patience, and humility of the Canaanite woman. Just as she remained steadfast in prayer, so let us persevere in all good works.

These cities to which the Lord came signify [Col. 0745D] this world, into which the Lord came for our salvation, to free us from the power of the devil. And this woman signifies the holy Church gathered from the Gentiles. This woman is called a Canaanite because she was born from the stock of Canaan, who was the son of Noah and was cursed by his father.

Let us hear what this woman cries out after the Lord: “Have mercy on me, Son of David; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon” (Matt. XV). This woman had such great faith that she did not bring her daughter with her to the Lord, nor did she invite him to come to her; rather, she firmly believed that, if God willed it, he could give health to her daughter.

By this woman’s daughter we must understand every sinful [Col. 0746C] soul, which is daily tormented by the devil and is subject to vices and every evil work. Those who are teachers of the Church must always admonish and rebuke those who do the works of the devil, and they should pray for them, just as this woman prayed for her daughter.

[Col. 0746D] But the Lord did not answer her a word. For such reasons the Lord did not wish to answer the woman. First, to test her constancy, so that she might persevere in prayer. Second, to remove the Jews’ excuse, lest they say: “The Christ was promised to us, yet this man teaches the Gentiles and heals them; therefore we do not wish to believe in him.” Third, to test the disposition of the disciples and provoke them to mercy.

And the disciples approached and begged him, saying: “Send her away, because she is crying out after us.” As if they were saying: “Forgive sins and grant virtues.” After the woman heard the holy apostles pleading for her, she immediately came to the Lord with great confidence, 675 and worshiped him, saying: “Lord, help [Col. 0747A] me.”

He answered and said: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” This means: “It is not right that the teaching of God should be taken away from the Jews, who have always worshiped the Lord, and given to you, who are Gentiles and pagans, and have always served the devil.”

Yet the woman wisely understood what the Lord had said and answered humbly in this way: “Yes, Lord.” That is to say: “I know and believe, Lord, that it is as you say. Certainly we are not worthy to receive the children’s bread, since we have always worshiped idols. But I say this because you have deigned to come into the world to show your grace to us Gentiles: even the little dogs eat of the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”

676 She had faith, because although she was a Gentile, she believed that the Lord could give health to her daughter. She had patience, because when the Lord rejected her, she persevered in prayer for as long as necessary, until she received what she sought. She had humility, because when the Lord compared her to dogs, she compared herself to little dogs.

After our Redeemer saw that this woman’s faith was so great, he said to her: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.”

We must receive an example, dearest brothers, from this woman: just as she remained steadfast in prayer, so let us persevere daily in every good work; and just as she prayed to the Lord, so let us pray to God that he may deign to free our minds from the devil’s snares.

# SERMON CIX. On Fraternal Correction

[Col. 0747]

## NOTICE

We have copied this sermon, which is numbered 109 and adorned with the name of Saint Maximus, from the Casinensis manuscript XII, p. 334.

[Col. 0747B] **SUMMARY.**—Maximus extols the apostle Paul with the highest praises and, explaining his testimony in 2 Corinthians VI, shows that in the same heart, within the dwelling of a single breast, injustice and justice cannot inhabit together.

The most blessed Paul, dearest brothers, whom heavenly election appointed as teacher to all the nations because of the blameless conscience of his heart and the perfection of his holy doctrine, rebukes, instructs, and corrects the Lord’s people—now with apostolic vigor, now with the authority of a teacher, and always with paternal affection and compassion. This glorious man truly has this purpose: not to make his disciples excessively negligent through excessive flattery, nor, on the other hand, to disturb them through harsher rebuke. Rather, he presents his discourse with such weight and moderation that, through an unoffending art of teaching, he healthfully recalls, chastises, and encourages each person who has strayed from the right path.

[Col. 0747C] For the most prudent teacher, like a truly spiritual bee, wished to cast his stings and offer his honey according to the variety of sinners. But we, brothers, who lack virtue and are accompanied by sins of many kinds, set before your hearing the sharp stings of more severe correction, softened by apostolic authority’s affectionate concern. For wounds of the human body are treated better with sweetness than with bitterness.

Thus the Apostle says, among other things, writing to the Corinthians concerning the same recompense: “As to children I say: be enlarged yourselves, and do not bear the yoke with unbelievers” (2 Cor. VI).

“As to children,” he says, “I speak.” See how, although they are sinners, the Apostle calls them children, so that no one, deterred by shame over a sinful [Col. 0747D] conscience, may hesitate to rely on the love of so great a father. For when Paul rebukes, he is not exercising the hatred of an angry man but fulfilling the duty of one who loves. A rebuke that proceeds from a friend’s mouth carries desirable healing in the wound. As that wisest man, Solomon, says:

[Note: [Col. 0747] In the Vulgate he reads: “The wounds of a lover are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates.”]

“The wounds of a friend are better than the willing kisses of an enemy” (Prov. XXVII). What else can the wounds of friends be except words by which sinners are struck?

“Be enlarged,” he says—that is, see to it that perhaps the way on which you hasten toward the heavenly kingdom is not enclosed by the thorns and brambles of unbelief and crimes. Rather, act so that the royal road, which the pleasure of this world and the obstacle of sins make narrow, may be widened for you through the practice of faith and virtues.

“Do not,” he says, “bear the yoke with unbelievers.” Everyone bears the yoke with unbelievers who conspires toward a person’s destruction and death. Whoever associates himself with dishonorable and shameful people bears the yoke with unbelievers; whoever, after confessing Christ’s name and embracing the faith, is drawn back by diabolical superstition to sacrilegious pleasures bears the yoke with unbelievers.

And, brothers, he bears a most dangerous yoke who, having rejected integrity of life and broken the bonds of divine fear, wholly immersed in earthly things, miserably submits his captive neck to a savage way of life. Concerning the impious it is written that they refused to look toward heaven and heavenly things, as the prophet says: “They set their eyes to turn down toward the earth” (Ps. XVI).

[Col. 0748C] Consider further how the order of apostolic teaching is developed. For he says: “What partnership has justice with iniquity? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? What agreement does Christ have with Belial? What share does the faithful have with the unfaithful? And what agreement does the temple of God have with idols?”

“What partnership,” he says, “has justice with iniquity?” (2 Cor. VI). Brothers, in the same heart, within the dwelling of a single breast, iniquity and justice cannot dwell together. There is an unceasing war between them, and one must necessarily be driven out by the other.

In vain does any unjust person sometimes display in himself the appearance of integrity. In a soul frequented by iniquity, justice is feigned. Many do not sometimes appear just for the sake of justice itself, but, in order to cast a shadow of holiness over their iniquities, they place before them the coverings of a deceitful equity.

But those will truly be just in whom iniquity—utterly hateful to God—never secretly takes root. Concerning them the venerable patriarch David also says: “Blessed are they who keep judgment and practice justice at all times” (Ps. CV).

Then follows: “What fellowship does light have with darkness?” Let every hearer understand that [Col. 0749A] one and the same person cannot be both bright and obscure—that is, the same person cannot at once be deceitful and sincere, proud and humble, cruel and gentle, lustful and chaste, treacherous and faithful, envious and friendly. Just as light has no fellowship with darkness, so there is no communion between virtues and vices.

You have likewise: “What agreement does Christ have with Belial?” That is, Christ and the devil cannot meet in one place and in the same mind. Thus that most faithful Elijah said to Israel when it was transgressing: “How long will you limp between two sides? If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal is God, follow him” (3 Kings XVIII).

If, then, the prophet so vehemently condemns a people wavering between error and truth, how do we suppose that we, brothers, can limp along with uncertain steps, both following vices and loving virtues? How can we, marked by one and the same Spirit, serve Christ and do the devil’s will?

Is it not the devil’s will to lie in wait for the innocent, form factions, slander friends, envy those who are better, violate faith, and attack justice? Conversely, Christ’s portion is to fear God, love goodness, help the unfortunate, pursue peace, preserve patience, and keep charity unharmed in all things.

[Col. 0750A] You have after this: “What share does the faithful have with the unfaithful? And what agreement does the temple of God have with idols?” What fellowship, brothers, can there be between the faithful and the unfaithful, when one treads the left-hand path and the other walks on the right; one moves toward life and the other toward death; one follows Christ and the other accompanies the devil? What could things so different ever have in common?

Who, moreover, could doubt that the temple of God can have no agreement with idols? Hence the Apostle says to the faithful whom he forbids to participate in idols: “You are the temple of the living God” (2 Cor. VI).

Therefore, if we are the temple of God, let us not become the devil’s tomb and a receptacle of vices. If we truly receive Christ into our heart, let us drive Christ’s enemy far from us with all the strength of faith.

These things, dearest brothers, we have brought forward from the apostolic reading for our common progress, so that, avoiding what is unjust and treacherous with every effort and every endeavor, we may always pursue what is pleasing and acceptable to our God.

# SERMON CX. On the Pursuit of Chastity

[Col. 0749]

## NOTICE

679 We have also seen this sermon, numbered 110, attributed to Saint Maximus in the same Casinensis manuscript XII, p. 335. Anyone who reads it can plainly see that it should be entitled “On the Pursuit or Guarding of Chastity.”

**SUMMARY.**—Above all other virtues, chastity must be praised by us; above all others, Christ chose it by a particular grace when he was born from a virgin. Let us look more carefully and think more holily, lest an undisciplined gaze steal upon an idle heart.

How great and how necessary a benefit we can derive from the holy Scriptures, the most blessed Paul teaches us, saying: “Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for reproving, and for instructing” (2 Tim. III). What a splendid and wondrous judgment the teacher of the Churches has proclaimed from the divine utterances, which direct and shape the hearts of mortals toward the fullest perfection of life! The heavenly word is certainly useful for teaching, reproving, and instructing.

It is useful for teaching when it sets right the perverse habits of the undisciplined through the soundness of holy instruction. It is useful for reproving when it refutes the errors of heresy by the pure and unalloyed truth of its assertions in the Church of God.

Every believer, through the admonition of the divine law, recognizes his fault, lest he incur guilt unknowingly and ignorantly; and through its severity we are terrified, lest in damnable presumption we dare to commit what is forbidden. Through its further instruction we perceive God as the future judge of our good and evil deeds, and confess him as their avenger.

Thus in the holy Scriptures there are instruction in uprightness, correction of faults, and education in truth.

It is appropriate, then, that we say something to your charity about the observance of modesty and the guarding of chastity. Above all other virtues, chastity must be praised by us, for above all others Christ chose it by a particular grace when he was born from a virgin.

Therefore we must adopt the teaching of the holy Gospel, which no believer is unaware was divinely inspired. There I find written, and there we all read: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V).

See, dearest brothers, how vigorously our Lord, the reformer of all depravity, restrains the wantonness of human looks, and with what precipitous force he anticipates the incitements of slippery flesh, lest the worst fruit follow from an evil seed! How far does he wish lust to be from the human heart, when he so carefully restrains and chastises lustful eyes?

“If anyone,” he says, “looks at a woman in order to desire her, he has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

And, as I think, the Lord anticipates diabolical temptations so carefully that a religious man, if he should perhaps loosen his eyes when he sees a beautiful woman, may discover himself to be sinning before he sins, and may understand that, through the service of his eyes, he has incurred blame before committing the sin.

And this, beloved, is not so that a wretched man may incur the sentence of condemnation, but so that, once it has been driven away by the compunction of a sighing heart, he may not neglect to avoid the fault he foresees.

Oh, truly salutary physician of human weakness! So that he may not find in a man, with injury to the man, something to cure, he applies medicine in advance of the wound. And because he does not wish any of his believers to burn with the deadly fevers of sins, the remedy of paternal compassion heals before weakness arises, as the blessed prophet David says: “My God, his mercy will come before me” (Ps. LVIII).

The salvation of the human race knows very well how to cut away the harmful beginnings of a savage conception; at the very gate of sinning it shuts out the devil’s stealthy entrance.

The one and same Son of God is Lord of our nature and teacher of chastity. And why should I call him the teacher of chastity, when he himself is incorrupt purity, himself inviolate chastity? For in whose mouth no deceit was found, whose heart and flesh rejoiced in the living God, not even in his eyes could there be found a trace of sin.

Therefore, brothers, because our frailty is corrupted by sins of many kinds, and that dreadful judgment is being prepared for our life, let us look more carefully and think more holily, lest the undisciplined gaze of wandering eyes steal upon our idle heart.

We received eyes so that they might provide light for the body, not so that they might bring blindness upon the soul.

681 And after all this, the ministers of light must not be lighter than darkness. For the Lord says to each of us: “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be!” (Matt. VI).

And therefore, dearest brothers, Holy Scripture must be read again and again, through which we may be taught uprightness, restrained from greed, and instructed by the salutary rules of true faith, just as the Apostle says: “Be enlarged yourselves, and do not bear the yoke with unbelievers” (1 Cor. VI).

# SERMON CXI. Against Depravity in Speech

[Col. 0751]

## NOTICE

This third moral sermon stands in the same Casinensis manuscript XII, p. 331, explicitly marked with the name of Saint Maximus the bishop both in its title and in the margin. No one can doubt that it came from the same source as the two preceding sermons, since it displays the same manner of speaking and the same use of Scripture, in which Saint Maximus particularly excelled.

[Col. 0751B] **SUMMARY.**—Since in the preceding discourse Saint Maximus exhorted the faithful to holiness of heart through diligent guardianship of the eyes, here he rebukes license in speech and reveals the worst effects of corrupt language.

It is fitting and necessary for us, brothers, to review the apostolic admonitions for our common instruction and correction, and to examine salutary commands in simple words, as it is written: “Blessed are those who search his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart” (Ps. XVIII).

Thus the glorious Paul says: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth” (Eph. IV).

How beautifully and magnificently the splendid teacher of heavenly disciplines, with almost a single stern sentence, corrects the unbridled excess of evil-speaking and the insolence of a wanton tongue! Therefore, dearest brothers, see how the teacher of the nations and excellent cultivator of the Lord’s vineyard cuts away with the sickle of his command all the branches of vices that are destined to burn.

By saying, “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth,” he removes at once all the harmful refuse of our heart and mouth. He acts so that, if some evil should perhaps strike someone’s heart at the devil’s prompting, it may not find in him the means of expression through speech. For all the poisons of hidden thoughts, if they are not brought forth in words, immediately vanish as though deprived of strength.

Thus prophetic speech bears witness to the expression of a wicked heart’s purpose, saying: “He conceived sorrow and gave birth to iniquity” (Ps. VII)—that is, the impious and unjust man gives birth with his lips to the wickedness he had conceived in his heart.

Take away, then, the birth of evil in speech, and whatever sadness has been conceived in a human heart will have no power to be born, like an abortive fetus, but will soon die within its own womb.

“Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth,” because beyond doubt blasphemy lies in evil speech. Remove, therefore, the whispering of wicked words, and envy will have no means of stimulating its malice. Remove the shameful mystery of soft lips, and no snare will be laid for simple men by flatterers. Take away the workmanship of a cunning tongue, and avarice will remain empty of criminal malice [Note: [Col. 0751D] So in the manuscript.] For the insane hunger of a greedy heart is not fed unless evil speech advances toward its prey.

“Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth.” How fitting it is that we should be far removed from evil works when we are not even permitted to offend in speech!

For in what follows the most blessed Paul says: “Fornication and impurity must not even be named among you, nor indecent speech, nor buffoonery, which is inappropriate” (Eph. IV).

For this reason the Apostle forbids all these things to be named among the faithful: lest either the habit of evil speech drag them into the worst deed, or, through the obscenity of shameful language, the holy tongue dedicated to the praises of God become defiled.

Who could endure [Col. 0752C] hearing divine utterances come forth from one and the same mouth at one moment, and the words of demons at another? Who could endure the same tongue singing psalms to God and singing to the devil?

And so that we may more fully recognize how many and what kinds of incitements there are to evil speech, let us recall a few examples from the holy Scriptures.

Evil speech came from the mouth of Simon Magus when, after offering money to the apostles, he requested that the grace of God be sold to him. Evil speech came from the mouth of the Egyptian woman who, through shameful words, inflamed the chaste Joseph toward intercourse with her. Evil speech came from the mouth of the exceedingly greedy King Ahaz, 683 who, inflamed by the flame of insane desire, demanded another man’s vineyard with shameless speech and, through the evil-speaking of his wife Jezebel, obtained possession of what did not belong to him by the death of the murdered poor man.

Evil speech came from the mouth of Judas the betrayer when, through impious conversation, he sold the Lord’s blood to the leaders of the Jews.

Hear further, beloved, how great a discipline of not only the mouth but also the eyes is formed in human beings through the divine utterances.

As has been said, the Apostle declares: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth” (Eph. IV). And the Lord says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery in his heart” (Matt. V).

You perceive, brothers, [Col. 0753A] with what care and concern we are forbidden either to speak shamefully or to look shamefully; with what agreement between the commandments the good Lord and his faithful servant destroy the instruments of our sins.

The one restrains the eyes, the other the tongue, because through the eyes lust slips into the human heart, and the heart’s desire is fulfilled through the service of slippery speech.

Through these commands, therefore, Christ cleanses the defiled gaze, so that sin may not pass through the eyes into the inner chambers of our breast; and the Apostle corrects our tongue, so that a shameful desire may not be brought to completion by even more shameful speech.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us be watchful in every way lest evil or shameful speech proceed from our mouth, so that our prayers, which we ask to be received in heaven, may be conveyed to God by a chaste tongue.

# SERMON CXII. On the Centurion’s Servant in the Gospel

[Col. 0753]

## NOTICE

[Col. 0753]

Although the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, the editors of the works of Saint Ambrose, explicitly indicated that this discourse should not be attributed to Ambrose, they nevertheless placed it at the end of his sermons as number 63. We were afraid to transfer it into our collection until we saw with our own eyes that it was attributed to Saint Maximus under number 94 in manuscript 99 of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, as well as the judgment of the very learned Cardinal Besutius.

He writes: “The last sermon which I believe to be Saint Maximus’s is on the centurion’s servant in the Gospel, at the dedication of a basilica, beginning: ‘We read in the holy Gospel,’ etc. . . . It is not, however, a sermon for the feast of the dedication of a church, as we now understand it, but a sermon delivered to the people when a basilica had been newly built by the count who was there called both the emperor’s count and count. In it he also praises two men, Vitalianus and Majanus, who, although of modest status and limited means in the world, nevertheless had the basilica’s tabernacle constructed. The testimony of the Sangallensis manuscript, number 75, also supports this.”

[Col. 0753B] **SUMMARY.**—What Maximus treated in this sermon is sufficiently established by the preceding judgment of the most eminent Besutius.

We read in the holy Gospel that, when a certain centurion’s servant, who was more precious to him, was suffering from a severe illness of paralysis, and the centurion asked the Savior through the Jewish elders to heal his pains—for, as Scripture says, he was at the point of death—the Jews, among other things, said to the Lord in order to commend him more highly: “He is worthy that you grant this to him, for he loves our nation, and he himself built our synagogue” (Luke VII and following).

If, then, the man who built a synagogue is commended to the Lord, how much more commendable is the man who built a church? And if he deserves grace who provided a dwelling for impiety, how much greater grace does he deserve who prepared a dwelling for religion?

And if he is visited by heavenly mercy who built a place where Christ is always denied, how much more ought he to be visited [Note: [Col. 0753D] The manuscript of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads: “who had the tabernacle skillfully made.”] who caused a tabernacle to be built where Christ is preached daily?

In the centurion, the Lord approved not what work he had done but with what intention he had acted. For since he had carefully built a synagogue at a time when they were not yet Christians, it is understood that, had they been Christians, he would have built a church with far greater care.

Yet although he builds a synagogue, he preaches Christ. In that very work he urges the Pharisees that they ought to receive the Savior, and he shows that he added the tabernacle for this reason: so that there they might speak of the Lord’s glory in many ways.

For if the founder of the synagogue believes in Christ, the inhabitant of that synagogue ought to believe much more. Therefore, if the centurion was justified because of a fragile or earthly work, surely our illustrious and provident count ought to be justified because of so enduring and heavenly a work. Just as this count is superior to the centurion in dignity, so he ought also to be more devoted in faith.

He is a wise and religious count, who, as much as he serves the emperor in war, serves the Savior; and as eagerly as he hastens to rescue captives from the hands of enemies, so much more eagerly does he hasten to free himself from the devil’s sacrilege.

There he kills the enemies of an earthly king; here he pursues the adversaries of the heavenly Lord. There he conquers barbarians; here, demons. He is wise, I say, because just as he is the emperor’s count, so he desires to be Christ’s count as well.

For by acting wisely and religiously, he desires his dignity to be perpetual, in accordance with what is written in the prophet: “And you, O good kings, make your ways and your pursuits good, and hear the voice of the Lord your God, and the Lord will repent of the evil which he has spoken against you” (Prov. XXVI).

Therefore, when the centurion asked the Lord to rescue the sick man from death, and the Lord wished to go to the centurion’s house where the servant lay, the centurion said: [Col. 0754C] “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.”

The centurion excuses himself and says that he is unworthy for the Lord to enter beneath his roof. Behold, our count is worthy, beneath whose roof the Savior enters today.

Let us see what grace the centurion’s excuse possesses. For he says: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, [Note: [Col. 0754D] The manuscript of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme reads: “but only say the word, and my servant will be healed. O faith,” etc.] but only say the word, and my servant will be healed” (Matt. VIII).

O Christian faith, which has learned to obtain everything through humility! Behold, the religious centurion becomes more worthy to receive salvation when he declares himself unworthy; and while he considers his house unworthy of such an honor, he makes it more honorable and pleasing.

He was a man of great and perfect faith, for he understood that Christ was the Lord of heaven, while he feared that the narrowness of his lodging might not be able to receive him.

686 Therefore, while the centurion objected, the Lord did not go to the house. The Lord did not go, but the Lord’s medicine went; the Savior did not visit the sick man, but the Savior’s health visited him.

What shall I say about our holy brothers, Vitalianus and Majanus? I know that they do not seek glory from human beings, but from God alone. Yet even if I keep silent, their works themselves speak their praise; for whatever we praised in others a little earlier belongs to their praise as well.

For although many built this tabernacle, these men nevertheless carried out the expense with one accord. And at what expense, since they are of modest status and limited means in the world? At that expense of which the Apostle says: “the abundance of faith and the riches of simplicity” (2 Cor. VIII).

For poverty itself is always rich for holy men. Hence I believe that these blessed men built this church no less with prayers than with expenditures. For it was fitting that Christ’s work should grow more through prayers than through masonry.

They spent all their substance on the construction of this work, and yet they themselves certainly lack nothing. This is plainly, as we said, rich and wealthy poverty, which spends everything and possesses everything.

But this poverty is blessed by God, like the widow of whom the Lord says in the Gospel (Mark XII): “This poor widow has put in more than all the others; for all these gave gifts to God from their abundance, but she put in all the living she had.”

# SERMON CXIII. On the Words of the Gospel: “Come to Me, All You Who Labor and Are Burdened.” Matthew, Chapter XI

[Col. 0755]

## NOTICE

[Col. 0755]

We have drawn this mutilated sermon, as it lies in the Ambrosian manuscript, from Muratori’s *Anecdota*, vol. IV, p. 109; following Muratori, we also publish this fragment.

[Col. 0755B] **SUMMARY.**—The Lord Christ sets before his disciples, in himself, examples of holy teaching to imitate. What his yoke and burden are like.

When the Only-Begotten of Almighty God wished to reveal to human beings who and how great he was, and had proposed to open to mortals the source of his goodness, he said: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. XI).

These words, dearest brothers, concerning the mutual knowledge of the Father and the Son undoubtedly show that their substance is one and indivisible.

Now listen more attentively, brothers, to the nature and extent of the divine power and the wisdom of heavenly teaching possessed by our Lord and Redeemer, and to the incomprehensible goodness of his most merciful heart.

For after he confessed that everything had been delivered to him by God his Father, as the Gospel discourse testifies, and no one, etc. 687

*(A page is missing. The fragment continues.)*

. . . . . the simple from the deceitful, the peaceful from the angry, the humble from the proud.

Therefore Christ refreshes us—or rather, remakes us—when he either anticipates crimes that are about to be committed through stricter admonitions or forgives those already committed through the gift of his indulgence.

“Take my yoke upon you,” he says, “and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI).

Christ is truly gentle because for this reason he descended from heaven: so that, through his reproaches and injuries, he might always grant indulgence to sinful mortals. And he is truly humble, since, in order to be able to die for the dead, he deigned to join to himself a carnal nature.

“I am gentle,” he says, “and humble of heart.” The Lord professes himself humble of heart [Col. 0755D] because that humility is truly holy which proceeds from the purity of a religious mind, not that which descends from a vicious breast trembling with conscience.

“Learn from me,” he says, “because I am gentle and humble of heart.” How well such a teacher teaches, who sets before his disciples in himself examples of holy teaching to imitate!

But you, dearest brothers, direct your attention always not to human frailty but to him who spoke what he did and did what he spoke.

“Take my yoke upon you,” he says, because 688 “my yoke is easy and my burden is light.”

The yoke of Christ, brothers, dissolves all the bonds of the devil’s yoke. The yoke of Christ does not scar the neck but adorns it. The yoke of Christ does not press down our heads but restrains them. The yoke of Christ, cutting furrows with the plowshare of faith, cuts down the grass and thorns of every vice. The yoke of Christ joins God and human beings in eternal fellowship through the harmonious bonds of charity.

What more shall I say about the Lord’s burden? It is of such a kind that it turns away from our necks the weight of all sins. For Christ’s burden is chastity; Christ’s burden is humility; Christ’s burden is patience; Christ’s burden is contempt for the world; and, for confessing his name, the blessedness of martyrdom’s torments.

These are the most healthful burdens of life that the Savior places upon us, lest we be crushed by the deadly weights of this world.

Therefore, let us submit our heads to the evangelical yoke with more devoted zeal, and let us also place our shoulders beneath the delightful burdens of holy conduct, so that our almighty God may deign, as one truly good and truly gentle, to rescue and free us from the harshest yoke of diabolical captivity and from the burden of wretched servitude.

# SERMON CXIV. On These Words of the Gospel: “Who, Do You Think, Will Be Greater in the Kingdom of Heaven?” etc. Matthew, Chapter XVIII

[Col. 0755]

## NOTICE

[Col. 0755]

In this place of the Gospel, we have shown that Saint Maximus is the author of the homily whose beginning is “If you listened carefully to the Gospel reading,” etc., which we published as number 85, col. 283 of this volume. Therefore this sermon must likewise be attributed to him. The homily follows there in the aforementioned Casanatensis manuscript under the heading “Likewise, concerning the foregoing,” and it is composed in a similar style of writing.

**SUMMARY.**—With a child placed in their midst, the Lord wishes us to live in the present world according to the same example, without malice and without deceit. The patriarchs and apostles are called children by the Lord, and we must imitate their example. A millstone is to be hung around the neck of those who cause scandal, especially heretics and Jews.

The disciples, still ignorant of how great was the glory of humility, were contending over precedence in merit or honor, saying to the Lord: “Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven?” (Matthew 18). The disciples were disputing who would be greater in the kingdom of heaven, although undoubtedly in God’s sight the greater is the one who is more humble, as he himself says: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23). Therefore, not without good reason, to put an end to this unnecessary contention of his disciples, he says: “Jesus called a child, set him in their midst, and said: ‘Amen, I say to you, unless you turn and become like children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven’” (Matthew 18).

Having set a child in their midst, the Lord exhorts the disciples by his example, showing that no one can enter the kingdom of heaven unless he becomes like a child. But the Lord did not offer the example of children, nor command us to become like children, so that we should become like them in age, since one who is already old cannot return again to infancy; rather, he commanded this so that we might imitate the childhood and innocence of children.

The blessed Apostle knew in what way we are commanded by the Lord to be children when he says: “Do not become children in understanding, but be infants in malice, so that you may be mature in understanding” (1 Corinthians 14). A child or infant does not know the malice of the world; he does not know how to commit sin; he does no evil to his neighbor; he does not hold onto anger; he hates no one; he does not seek riches; he does not marvel at the glory of this world; he always follows his father and does not leave his mother.

For this reason, then, the Lord wishes us to become like children, so that, following their example, we may live in the present world without malice and without deceit. Let us flee sin; let us do no evil to our neighbor; let us not retain anger; let us not seek riches or the glory of this world. Let us always follow the Father—that is, God, whose adopted children we have already begun to be—and let us not leave our mother—that is, the Church, through whom we have been spiritually born to God. In the lap of this mother, like little children properly placed in their father’s bosom, let us rest. Let us be nourished daily by her saving teaching, so that we may grow in the faith and grace of baptism, according to what Peter testified in his Epistle, saying: “As infants, desire milk, so that by it you may grow” (1 Peter 2).

Saint John also shows us in his Epistle how we ought to be children when he says: “I write to you, children, because you have come to know the Father” (1 John 2). We are therefore commanded to be children in this respect: that we recognize the Father, and that we live in this world innocent and simple, like doves.

Since the Lord therefore wished this likeness of children to exist in us, he rightly says in the present passage: “Unless you turn and become like children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” Whoever, then, humbles himself like this child is the greater in the kingdom of heaven. The Lord plainly declares that whoever imitates the child’s humility and innocence will be the greater in the kingdom of heaven.

Finally, the Lord himself, in order to show us perfectly in himself an example of humility, also deigned to become a child by assuming flesh, according to what we read written about him: “For a child is born to us, and a son is given to us, whose rule has been placed upon his shoulders” (Isaiah 9). For this reason the holy patriarchs and apostles are also called children by the Lord, according to what we read written about them: “Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me” (Isaiah 8), because they remained like children, without deceit and without malice.

Let us therefore imitate the example of such children—that is, of all the saints—so that we may deserve to enter the kingdom of heaven with them. Let us imitate the humility of the Lord himself, who, for the sake of our salvation, deigned to become a child, so that we might reign with him. And rightly he added: “Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me,” showing that whoever faithfully receives a servant who believes in Christ and lives according to the innocence of a child receives Christ himself.

The Lord said that he himself was received in the receiving of such a person, lest we hold in contempt any servant of God who lives humbly. Therefore he added, saying: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea.”

It was necessary that, after the reward of devoted faith, condemnation should follow for unbelief. Just as punishment is owed to those who cause faithful people to stumble, and from this we recognize how grave a sin it is to cause scandal, since the Lord says that it would be better for such a person to have a millstone hung around his neck and be plunged into the depths of the sea than to cause one of the little ones who believe in Christ to stumble. Thus, once the scandal of sin has been forestalled, if possible, by this sentence, we should prefer to live without scandal in the present life rather than incur, with scandal, the eternal punishment of that death.

If, then, the Lord says this about one who causes one of the little ones to stumble, what punishment do we suppose the heretics will have, who by their perverse and faithless teaching cause scandal not to one person but to the entire Church? And although the Lord’s saying about the millstone can also be understood simply, nevertheless, according to its mystical meaning, something more can be understood in the signification of the millstone.

Animals that are usually yoked to a mill customarily have their eyes closed. Therefore, by the signification of the mill, the labor of the present life is indicated. In the ass, however, the Gentile is represented: without knowledge of God and the light of faith, he lives in the labor of the world like a blind animal. The depth of the sea signifies the deep error of the world. Hence he rightly said that it would be better for such a person who causes scandal to have a millstone hung around his neck and to be plunged into the depths of the sea.

In this, above all, he seems to signify the Jew, who is known to suffer scandal because of the cross of Christ and the preaching of his name. It would therefore be better for such a person if, in the blindness of Gentile error, he were, as it were, plunged into the depths of the sea, than that, under the preaching of the Law—by which the Jew supposes that he recognizes the light of truth—he should be scandalized by Christ or by his apostles, whom he calls little ones. For it is easier for a Gentile without the Law not to believe in Christ than for a Jew living under the Law to deny the Lord of the Law.

We can also understand the two Testaments to be signified by the millstone, by which everyone who causes scandal, bound by a just sentence, is plunged into destruction and death. We recognize that this sentence concerning the millstone was fulfilled especially in the Jewish people. Since they often stirred up scandal against the Lord and against his apostles, they were plunged into the depths of the sea by hearing those same two Testaments, as though toward a certain remedy of salvation, after losing their own kingdom—that is, they were dispersed among the gatherings of diverse nations. They inhabit the error of this world as though in the depths of the sea, because they do not know the Creator, the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, to whom belong salvation and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 115. On the Arrival of the Rich

Whoever, with the Lord’s support, has earnestly desired the saving commandments of God and has striven to bend the pride of his haughty mind, which is hateful to everyone—can conquer the devil; he can restrain avarice, the root of all evils; curb luxury, the enemy of good virtues; mitigate envy, the enemy of holy chastity; refuse the destructive profits of usury; refrain from burdening the guardian of peace, justice, with gifts; shudder at the harmful schemes of factions; avoid the inglorious and sometimes bloody pursuit of unlawful honor; restrain the incentives to discord and the curses of an insulting tongue; and likewise drive from the Christian mouth lies, which stain life, wound the soul, and shatter friendships. He can also flee from every superstition and every sacrilege involving demons and idols, through which the goodness of the almighty true God is especially offended, by the love of that God.

# SERMON 116. On the Arrival of the Rich

For whoever abounds in his own goods does not seek the treasures of the world. For one’s own goods are integrity, sobriety, mercy, and chastity—goods more precious than all gold, so that you may know that metals themselves are less valuable than these. Talents of gold can be dug out; vessels of silver can be acquired; integrity alone cannot be dug out. Integrity is not extracted but acquired, because it does not consist in price but in virtue.

You, then, who possess gold, let us compare our goods with one another, if you please. When you set out abroad, your treasures remain at home; because they are far from you, you are always anxious and always uncertain lest, when you return home, you no longer possess what you possessed before. Thus, while you are always afraid of losing them, you are naked and poor in your own conscience.

But wherever I go, my riches follow me, and my goods cannot be separated from me, because they are retained not in an earthly cavern but in the treasure of the heart. When you depart from the world, leaving your riches behind, you have lost them; but when I am required to depart from this world, I carry my riches to paradise. After death, your riches will be followed by fire and darkness, as happened to that rich man clothed in purple; my riches will be received by Abraham’s bosom and blessedness, as happened with Lazarus.

# ADDITIONS

## NOTICE

Since two sermons on Pentecost, which had been omitted from the sheets and indicated on page 521, were finally discovered and ought to be added [Note: We have restored these sermons to their proper place, as was fitting. See columns 609–642 of this volume, under numbers 54 and 55. EDITORS.], it happened that, on the very threshold of completing the edition, those excerpts from the works of Saint Maximus that had long been awaited from manuscript codices of the library of the king of France finally arrived.

We wish to warn readers that, concerning the first matter—the two sermons to be added, which would have been the seventh and eighth on Pentecost—we are now publishing both for the first time from the very ancient codex of Saint Dalmatianus, often cited above; the testimony of the Turin codex is added, in which they occur as Homilies 16 and 17 under the heading “Also, on Pentecost.”

As for the French codices, we stated in the preface, on page 24, that we hoped for more from them. Yet although the most diligent and learned Father Petrus Paulus Druon, of the Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur, selected for this purpose by the distinguished prelate Joseph of Auria, archbishop of Seleucia and papal legate to the king of France, devoted a great deal of time and labor to examining almost innumerable manuscript volumes, the result did not wholly answer his great care and efforts.

Some of the sermons sent by him have therefore already been printed in our collection; some occur in the body and appendix of the works of Saint Augustine; others are found in all editions of Saint Leo the Great. What remains differs entirely from the diction of Maximus of Turin, as will be clear from certain excerpts. We shall give the beginnings and endings of each, as they stand, preserving the order of the Parisian manuscript.

## SERMON 1, On the Advent of the Lord

[Column 759D]

This is said to have been drawn from codices 3786 and 3802. It begins: “Perhaps, brothers, it moves you,” etc., preceded by the preface: “Therefore, since the season requires it, we ought to refresh ourselves with spiritual banquets,” etc. We lack none of it, as can be seen on page 5.

## SERMON 2, On the Nativity of the Lord

“You have heard, dearest brothers, how the blessed Evangelist has related to us today the mystery of Christ’s generation,” etc. It ends: “Therefore we celebrate the feast day not because of human devotion but because of divine condescension,” etc.

The excerptor notes that it was taken from codex 3783, of the eleventh century, and that in several other manuscripts it is attributed to Saint Maximus. In truth, however, it should rather be called a patchwork assembled from various passages, a considerable part of which is read in Sermon 1 on the Nativity of the Lord, which we placed among the spurious works attributed to Saint Maximus of Turin in the appendix, page 26.

## SERMON 3, On the Nativity of the Lord

[Column 761A]

“For this reason the Fathers instituted the day of the Lord’s Nativity as a votive solemnity,” etc. It ends: “For this reason we ought to observe each feast with solemn celebration as the year’s cycle comes round, so that what happened—that Christ was born—may be recalled.”

Codex 3786 is indicated as the manuscript from which it was copied, and the testimony of six other codices confirms its attribution to Saint Maximus. Were it not burdened by the same absurdities, it would at least have a place among the doubtful works; but it ought not even to be transferred into that class. Besides, it appears to be a fragment rather than a sermon.

## SERMON 4, On the Nativity of the Lord

“I would rightly and most fully praise the most chaste womb of the Virgin Mary, the Virgin Bride’s closed chamber of the womb, the inner chamber sealed by modesty,” etc. It ends: “Rejoice, therefore, Joseph, and rejoice exceedingly in Mary’s virginity at the birth of the Redeemer and the manifestation of the Savior; and thus Joseph was separated from intercourse with his wife, so that he might be called the Savior’s father,” etc.

We have received this from codex 3786 of the royal library, with, it is said, confirmation from several other manuscript codices. The Maurists placed it in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine, Paris edition, page 323. We reject it completely, and anyone who has even lightly tasted the work of Saint Maximus of Turin will agree with us.

## SERMON 5, On the Nativity of the Lord

“I ask you, dearest brothers, to receive with willing hearts the sermons that the Lord will grant on this most sweet day,” etc. It ends: “And may the merciful Lord admit all of you into the heavenly granaries where the grain is to be gathered; to him be honor,” etc.

This sermon was taken from the same codex mentioned above. It is likewise found in the same appendix to Saint Augustine, and appears in the Antwerp edition, column 159. The Maurists, who knew the works of Saint Maximus extremely well, did not even suspect that it belonged to him.

## SERMON 6, On the Nativity of the Lord

[Column 761C]

“Today truth has sprung from the earth; Christ has been born from the flesh. Rejoice solemnly, and, reminded today also of the everlasting day, contemplate it; desire eternal gifts with the firmest hope,” etc. It ends: “He who for your sake took the form of a servant—may we receive freedom in him who for our sake sprang from the earth; in him may we possess heaven,” etc.

The Maurist Fathers gave it a place among the genuine sermons of Saint Augustine, as is evident from the Antwerp edition, column 623; it is Sermon 9 on the Nativity of the Lord.

## SERMON 1, On the Epiphany of the Lord

“It is a just and reasonable service of true devotion, dearest ones, to rejoice with all one’s heart on the days when the works of divine mercy are bestowed,” etc. It ends: “Lest the mystery of faith or the penalties of sufferings to be endured should be disturbed by the diversity of circumstances, since no one could be justified unless they believed the Lord Jesus Christ to be true God, true Lord, and true man,” etc.

No other codices support this sermon besides another codex, namely 1646, written in the eleventh century, as is said. Indeed, it was published among the sermons of Saint Leo the Great as number 33, “On the Fourth Epiphany,” in the Roman edition of 1753, page 84.

## SERMON 2, On the Epiphany of the Lord

“Today’s feast, dearest ones, is illumined by the appearance of our Lord and Savior, as you know [the manuscript reads: ‘as you know’], and this is the day on which a guiding star led three Magi to recognize and adore the Son of God,” etc. It ends: “For the delay of vengeance grants an opportunity for repentance,” etc.

It was likewise published as the preceding sermon, on page 88, number 5, “On the Epiphany of the Lord.”

## SERMON 3, On the Epiphany of the Lord

“The solemnity of this day, known throughout the whole world, brings us what kind of festivity, and what does it commemorate by its annual repetition?” etc. It ends: “Recognizing and praising Jesus Christ, and honoring him as though in gold, frankincense, and myrrh, it remains for us,” etc.

The Maurist Fathers did not hesitate to publish this sermon, copied from the same codex 1646, among Augustine’s genuine works in the cited volume, page 914.

## SERMON 1, On Lent

“Some days ago, while preaching the devotion of holy Lent,” etc. It ends: “For the former nourishes the body for a time, but the latter refreshes the soul eternally,” etc.

Supported by the testimony of numerous codices, we gave it a place among the homilies of Saint Maximus as number 38; it is found on page 109. In the Paris codex it is listed as numbers 3785 and 3777.

## SERMON 1, On the Octave of Easter

“Let us rejoice, dearest brothers, on the day of Christ’s resurrection; the joy of all is common, our joy is common, fully common, because when he rose, we all rose,” etc. It ends: “It is therefore not surprising that those who were so cruel toward the Savior proved so cruel toward their descendants.”

This sermon and the one following, which a French Benedictine monk reported as copied from codex 3814 of the royal library, together make up the complete sermon that we reprinted in this collection from Muratori, *Anecdota*, volume 4; it is the first sermon on the solemnity of Easter, column 741.
