The beginning, “We ought to rejoice,” through the words “time consumes antiquity,” was omitted. Everything else agrees perfectly.

## SERMON 2, On the Octave of Easter

“Not without good reason did Saint David command that we rejoice and be glad on this day, on which the joys of the whole world are celebrated,” etc. It ends: “As the blessed Evangelist says: ‘He was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world,’” etc.

## SERMON 1, On the Ascension of the Lord

“Everything that our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brothers, performed in this world amid our frailty—miracles—benefits us,” etc. It ends: “But rather let him acquire with himself a body sanctified in heaven,” etc., “more glorious by nature,” with the help of him who lives and reigns, etc.

It is unnecessary for me to say more at length about this sermon, taken from Parisian codex 3781. To learn what judgment should be formed, see the judgment of the Maurist Fathers in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine, number 176, Antwerp edition, column 213.

## SERMON 1, On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist

“After that most holy day of the Lord’s Nativity, we read of no human being’s birth being celebrated except that of the blessed John the Baptist alone,” etc. It ends: “Who, I ask, unless by obeying teachers, resisting vices and injustices arising from desire, turning away from sins, and redeeming them by fasts and almsgiving,” etc.

Like the preceding sermon, it was published by the same editors in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine, number 63, page 563. The authority of the Parisian codex 3785, which bears the name of Saint Maximus in its inscription, therefore moves us not at all.

## SERMON 1, On the Vigil of the Apostles Peter and Paul

“Today, with the Lord’s help, we celebrate the natal day of the apostles, whose memory the whole world embraces,” etc. It ends: “The magician flies; he seeks the heights so that he may fall more deeply; you apply your head to the earth so that, having been slain, you may possess heaven, by God’s provision,” etc.

After so many outstanding sermons of our Saint Maximus on the holy apostles Peter and Paul, we would seem to have lost all sense of judgment if we attributed this wretched heap of words to him. It is rightly noted that the sermon was copied from a fourteenth-century codex, number 3817, for it corresponds to the wretchedness of that age.

## SERMON 1, On the Nativity of Saint Laurence the Martyr

“The new feast of blessed Laurence, dearest brothers, continually kindles the Church of God with the joys of spiritual gladness,” etc. It ends: “Instead of the flame he brought forth, may he rejoice before the almighty Lord in the illumination of incorruptible light,” etc.

We have already published it among the homilies on the saints, column 341. Nothing else needs to be added except that we should note that our judgment is confirmed by Parisian codex 3809.

## SERMON 1, On the Nativity of Blessed Mary

[Column 763A]

“Although the merits of all the saints, dearest brothers, are venerable to our devotion, nevertheless the nativity of glorious and ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, must be venerated by us with our whole affection,” etc. It ends: “You have this blessed and most glorious Virgin and Mother as the helper of your struggle, under whose protection you may take refuge,” etc.

The feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary began to be celebrated in the Church only in the eighth century. It contains nothing of the vein of Maximus; rather, its author composed it with childish and tasteless opinions. I am not surprised at the ignorance of the copyist, who in Parisian codex 3820 ascribed it to the most eloquent holy bishop of Turin.

## SERMON 1, On the Dedication of a Church

“Today, beloved brothers, let us celebrate with devoted minds and all our strength the anniversary feast of the consecration of this holy church,” etc. It ends: “And let us rejoice in so great a feast, so that we may deserve to be found participants in heaven,” etc.

We placed it in our appendix to Saint Maximus among the spurious writings, column 78, since the manner of its discourse differs completely, in style and ornamentation, from the diction of the holy bishop of Turin. Just as we considered the testimony of Vatican Codex Regina 539 worthless, so the authority of Parisian codex 3822 does not withdraw us from the same judgment.

[Note: See this sermon and the following one in the present edition, pages 759–760. EDITORS.]

## SERMON 1, On the Arrival of the Rich

“Whoever, with the Lord himself assisting, has earnestly desired God’s saving commandments and has striven to bend the pride of his haughty mind, hateful to all, to restrain avarice, the root of all evils,” etc. It ends: “to flee, through love of the true God, from all superstitions of demons and sacrileges of idols, through which the goodness of the Almighty is especially offended,” etc.

## SERMON 2, On the Arrival of the Rich

“For whoever abounds in his own goods does not seek the treasures of the world; for one’s own goods are integrity, sobriety, mercy,” etc. It ends: “My riches, after the example of Lazarus, will be received by Abraham’s bosom and blessedness.”

Both sermons are said to have been taken from the same Parisian codex, number 3776, but they should rather be called fragments, which do not deserve to be adorned with the name of Saint Maximus. Nevertheless, we present them as a specimen of the tasteless author from whom certain sermons emerged after being copied and rejected.

# [TRACTATES OF SAINT MAXIMUS]

## PREFACE TO THE TRACTATES OF SAINT MAXIMUS

Jacques Sirmond, exceptionally diligent in investigating the writings of the ancient Fathers, found the following three sermons or tractates attributed to Saint Augustine in the Floriacensis codex. He found them under the same inscription in the very ancient Remigian codex. He compared them with three other sermons, formerly inscribed among Augustine’s sermons *On the Season*, which the monks of Saint Maur placed in volume 5, appendix, numbers 237, 238, and 239, and he judged them not dissimilar in style.

Moreover, Ivo of Chartres mentions them in his decree *On Baptism* and attributes them to the divine Augustine. But Ivo calls the sermon whose opening is “We promised”—the second in our order—a third homily; and he subsequently calls the homily beginning “Thus far”—which is the third sermon, or tractate here—a fourth homily.

In the Remigian codex, the sermon “We promised,” which there is evidently fifth in order, begins as follows: “Therefore, in the first and second preaching we spoke only about these things,” etc.; “but now we are going to speak about the inner mysteries,” etc.

Leidrad, bishop of Lyon, transferred a considerable amount from the sermon beginning “Every word of God,” etc., into a book that he composed on Baptism at the command of Charlemagne. The book was published in the previous century in volume 3 of the *Analecta*, but he names no author. See volume 6 of the Antwerp edition of Saint Augustine, 1700, columns 768 and following.

But whatever others may have thought about these tractates, we attribute them to Saint Maximus of Turin, relying on three very ancient manuscript codices that agree in their inscription and in designating the author. The first is a codex formerly belonging to the abbey of Saint Dalmatianus. The second is the codex of Appannis. The third, finally, is the codex of the Major Church of Turin, in which they occupy numbers 5, 6, and 7 among the sermons on Baptism.

The title “Tractates” is appropriate to them, since they discuss the mysteries contained in that sacrament. At that time the practice was in force in both Eastern and Western Churches that baptism should be solemnly administered to adults on Holy Saturday. This custom of the bishops, indeed the discipline of the Church, is sufficiently demonstrated by the *Catecheses and Instructions* of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem and by the books *On the Mysteries* and *On the Sacraments*, published under the name of Ambrose, to omit other evidence.

Saint Maximus, therefore, with the facility in extemporaneous teaching by which he was endowed, delivered these three tractates on this occasion in order to instruct his people in the Christian religion. In them he explained to his neophytes many, though not all, of the mysteries of so great a sacrament.

In the first tractate, at its very beginning, he explains why he had previously kept silent before these catechumens about the marvelous gifts of God bestowed in baptism, and says that they were not yet considered worthy to be admitted into the more secret recesses of the holy religion. From this it is clear that the Church’s discipline—which they called the discipline of the secret, or *arcani*—had not been relaxed in Maximus’s days but was maintained in full observance.

The instructions that bishops gave to catechumens have been so fully explained by writers who dealt with the catechumenate that it would be superfluous to linger over a well-known matter. Maximus therefore passes over the first prayers performed by the priest, the minister of baptism, in preparation for the sacrament; he omits the petitions and exorcisms of those to be baptized; he also omits the threefold breathing upon the face and the placing of salt in the mouth, rites that are most ancient in the Church; and he begins to explain what the anointing of the ears signifies.

He teaches that the ears are anointed before the other parts of the body because the entrance of faith and of the whole of holy doctrine into the soul is through the ears, and understanding arises from hearing. Therefore our sanctification ought to begin with those organs through which the first seeds of eternal truth are received and implanted in the soul. No one can perceive the teaching of faith without hearing—a teaching by which he is enlightened and recognizes that he has been living in profound ignorance of the grace of the author; consequently, he rises to love God, his author and the giver of all good things.

From several statements of Sacred Scripture, Maximus infers that the sanctification of our ears is to be desired, and that the ears must be guarded with great care, lest the purity of heavenly wisdom be corrupted by evil speech.

It should further be observed that Maximus says that this anointing is performed with blessed oil, and not with saliva, as the Roman Ritual prescribes. Different customs were observed in different regions concerning this matter. According to Leidrad [Note: *The Book on Sacramental Baptism to Charles the Great*; see Trombellius, *On Sacred Matters*, dissertations 1 and 2, “On Baptism.”], some touched the ears and nostrils of catechumens with holy oil, others with spittle, and still others with neither oil nor spittle.

Indeed, neither in the book *On the Mysteries* attributed to Ambrose nor in the work *On the Sacraments*, whoever its author may have been, is there any mention of the material with which that mystery of opening—so they call it—was performed. There is merely mention of the touch of the fingers accompanied by the word *ephphatha*, that is, “open,” which Christ used when he was about to heal the deaf and mute man.

After explaining the anointing of the ears, Maximus also discusses at length the anointing of the nostrils, likewise prescribed by the Church for catechumens so that they might be more prepared to receive baptism. The holy bishop considers the organ of the nostrils, formed by God especially for human beings so that they might draw in and expel breath; by the movement of the air, the whole body is enlivened, and when that movement is obstructed, life cannot continue.

Since the catechumen in baptism devotes himself wholly to God and promises to hold fast to his faith and commandments, he receives in the sanctification of his vital breath a certain strength and firmness in goodness. Thus, with Saint Job, chapter 27, he can say:

“As long as my breath remains in me,  
and the spirit of God is in my nostrils,  
my lips shall not speak iniquity,  
nor my tongue utter deceit . . .  
until I perish, I will not depart from my innocence.  
I will not abandon the righteousness that I once began to hold.”

Considering another property of the oil with which the nostrils are anointed—namely, its fragrant smell—Maximus teaches that through it the sense of the mind, or understanding, is perfected. Thus Christ may always be preferred to all earthly things, and those reborn in the font of baptism may delight in his sweetness and love; and, after the fragrance of heavenly ointments—that is, of the virtues—they may profess that they will run.

Having dealt with these matters first in the treatise, Maximus proceeds to explain another group of rites that were customarily employed in the administration of baptism. In particular, he turns to those articles of faith concerning which the catechumen, when questioned, was required to make a distinct confession. I will by no means pass over in silence the fact that Maximus says nothing about the anointing with holy oil which, before the profession of faith, was performed in the form of a cross on the breast and shoulders of the catechumens; he mentions only the pledge given by the catechumen that he would renounce the devil, all his works, and all his pleasures.

To speak frankly, the preliminary commendation of the sacred font is splendid. He calls it the fountain of life, the fountain of redemption, a fountain sanctified by heavenly power, and sanctified in such a way that, by washing away very many sins, it sanctifies human beings. Maximus then continues, warning his faithful not to conceive with their eyes, but with their minds, how highly the substance of those waters ought to be esteemed. Their effect is not to be measured by nature, but by the special grace of God, by the power of the Holy Spirit, and by Christ himself, who consecrated the waters through his baptism. For whenever divine power intervenes, the powers of all the elements and of all natural things are elevated so as to produce greater effects.

Since, therefore, the grace of sanctification is perpetually joined to this water, Christ the Lord added the command that all nations should be washed by it, to such a degree that no one is saved unless he has been washed in this baptism. For he said in the Gospel of John, chapter III: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” Finally, in order to reach his intended subject, Maximus addresses them as follows:

“In this font, therefore, before we immersed you in your whole body, we asked: ‘Do you believe in God the almighty Father?’” etc.

The protestation, or confession, of faith in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, and in the Holy Spirit—which was required of those who were immediately to be baptized—is so ancient in the Church that those who trace it back to the apostles rely upon the testimonies of the Acts of the Apostles, chapters VIII and XVI. The Fathers of earlier centuries also mention it, including Dionysius of Alexandria, Epiphanius, Cyril of Jerusalem, and others whom we pass over.

Since the first approach to God is to believe that he exists, as Paul says, Maximus teaches those approaching baptism—in which the entire Trinity accomplishes our sanctification—that they must confess one God and three distinct Persons: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For baptism is administered in their name, according to the Lord’s command.

Saint Maximus, who instructed those recently converted from idols in the Christian faith, earnestly warns them that, since three Persons are proposed to them for belief, they must not suppose that there are three gods. “Let no one,” he says, “when he hears of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, think that we confess three gods. May such sacrilege be far removed from our faith, because we have learned, with God himself bearing witness, that there is only one God,” etc.

He then continues by demonstrating that the three Persons have one essence and share common properties among themselves. “We therefore hold and believe in three Persons—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—of one power, one substance, one eternity, one will, and likewise one divinity; and we venerate the whole Trinity under the designation of one God.”

Having thus established the first foundation of faith in the confession of the Trinity, Maximus proceeds to clarify the other articles contained in the catechumens’ confession [697]: namely, that the Church is holy and that in it there is forgiveness of sins.

The holiness of the Catholic Church must certainly be believed, because Christ the Lord is its head, its sacraments were instituted by him, and its members, who compose the Church, are holy. Nevertheless, Maximus says that one must not believe in the Church as one believes in God. Rather, those who are in the holy and Catholic Church are the ones who believe in God; and, believing in him, they must also believe that he himself was the founder of the holy Church.

For if there is forgiveness of sins in the Church, as must be believed, the Church does not possess this power from itself. It is certain that Christ bestowed it upon the Church in Peter, to whom he gave the power to forgive all sins.

Many hold that such a confession was required for the reception of baptism as a response to the Novatian heresy, since Saint Cyprian wrote in his letter to Januarius: “We understand that the forgiveness of sins is granted only in the Church.”

After this, the holy bishop mentions that the faithful also promised to believe in the resurrection of the flesh and in eternal life. Maximus frequently treated this article of faith, calling it the summary of the whole religion and the culmination of the mysteries, since all other matters are directed toward the attainment of blessedness in the life to come. For, as Christ says, “God is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Mark XII and Luke XX). Nor did the Son of God become human, die, and rise again in order to acquire for us some earthly happiness, but in order to make us sharers and co-heirs in his heavenly possession.

We cannot enter upon this inheritance except by rising again; and in expectation of it all the consolation of this most wretched life flows. Therefore Maximus said: “For the whole hope of Christians consists in this: that we believe in truth that the resurrection of this body, and not of another, will take place.”

Just as an unfailing crown and a very great reward are promised to those who believe perfectly, so unbelievers and the undeserving, driven from the kingdom of God, will be assigned to eternal flames for punishment. “For in this,” says Maximus, “the saying of our Lord Jesus Christ bears witness. In the Gospel he pronounced concerning sinners: ‘Then the impious will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.’”

This teaching of Maximus is the teaching of all the holy Fathers, as the most learned Trombellius demonstrates at length in Dissertation 6; we refer readers to him.

Our holy bishop concludes this treatise by discussing the third immersion, by which the laver of regeneration was administered at that time. He had previously said that new Christians were immersed three times in honor of the most holy Trinity, which accomplishes sanctification in those who are to be regenerated. Just as it was commanded that baptism be conferred in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so, to represent the mystery, it was fitting that a triple immersion correspond to the invocation of the three divine Persons.

Here, however, he gives another reason for the third immersion in baptism and teaches that it was instituted in memory of the Lord’s burial: just as Christ lay three days in the tomb and afterward rose again, so those who are immersed three times in the waters and, as it were, buried there must rise again to a new life of holiness, so that, freed from sins, they may never fall back into them.

“Rightly,” he says, “you were immersed three times, having received baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, who rose from the dead on the third day. For that immersion repeated three times expresses the type of the Lord’s burial, through which you were buried with Christ in baptism and rose with Christ in faith, so that, washed from sins in the holiness of virtues, you might live Christ by imitating him.”

We have now come to Maximus’s third treatise on Baptism. In the first place he discusses confirmation, and in the second, the washing of the feet.

No one is unaware that in the earliest times the Church customarily conferred the sacrament of confirmation upon the faithful immediately after baptism [Col. 0767]. “When baptism has been completed,” says the holy bishop, “we pour chrism—that is, the oil of sanctification—upon your head. Through this it is shown that a royal and priestly dignity is conferred by the Lord upon those who have been baptized.”

It may seem surprising that Maximus said nothing about the principal effects of this sacrament, which are character and grace, and discussed only a secondary effect: that those who have been confirmed are raised to a certain royal and priestly dignity. Nevertheless, Maximus should be considered to have done this deliberately.

He remembered that the Apostle had written to the Corinthians: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians III), because those who had recently converted to the faith, like newborn infants, were unable to receive stronger food—that is, more advanced teachings concerning salvation—and therefore he sought to nourish them with easier instruction.

Maximus conformed himself to this example and admonition. His discourse was addressed to people who shortly before had served idols, who had pursued nothing but wealth and worldly vanities, and who had preferred the humble following of Christ to secular pomp. They therefore had to be taught that the Christian religion contains something august.

Accordingly, he teaches that the Christian religion establishes a kingdom, both in the present life and in the life to come, for those who profess it fully, and consecrates them so that they may offer themselves to God as a pure and holy sacrifice.

He therefore warns that these splendid gifts [699] are obtained through chrismation, since through it a certain fullness of grace is conferred. Strengthened by it in goodness, we come to regard all earthly things as worthless, are inflamed with desire for the heavenly kingdom, and strive to make the soul purer, so that our offering may become more acceptable and pleasing to God.

“It is certainly wondrous,” says Maximus, “that through that chrism you have attained the kingdom of future glory and the priesthood. Yet it is not I who declare that this dignity has been conferred upon you, but the Apostle Peter—or rather, Christ through Peter.”

There was once disagreement as to whether this pouring of holy oil upon the head, which was performed for neophytes scarcely emerged from the waters and is also discussed by Ambrose in chapter 6 of *On the Mysteries* and by the author of *On the Sacraments*, book I, chapter 3, was the sacrament of confirmation; or whether confirmation was completed by another anointing accompanied by the imposition of the bishop’s hands.

This is not the place to discuss controversies on which many Catholic authors have written with great learning. As far as Ambrose is concerned, however, we say that the evidence presented in the notes by the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur has considerable weight. They prove that nothing other than holy confirmation can be understood by the anointing of the head, whose effects are clearly identified in chapter 7 of *On the Mysteries*:

“Recall,” he says, “that you received the spiritual seal, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength,” etc.

He continues by enumerating other gifts of the Holy Spirit conferred with the fullness of grace, so that the baptized person may become Christ’s soldier and present an unconquerable breast to the enemies of the faith.

As for this passage of Maximus—“When baptism has been completed, we pour chrism, that is, the oil of sanctification, upon your head”—it is clear that he is speaking of confirmation, since he expressly mentions chrism, which only bishops prepare and use to confirm Christians. He calls it the oil of sanctification, whose operation belongs exclusively to the sacraments.

The omission by Maximus of the imposition of hands presents no obstacle. For, as Saint Thomas teaches (*Summa theologiae*, Part III, question 72, article 2), even in apostolic times, when visible signs had ceased—that is, when the Holy Spirit no longer descended visibly through the imposition of hands—the apostles commonly used chrism in the administration of the sacrament, when such visible signs were not displayed.

The holy Doctor proves in the same article that chrism is a suitable matter for the sacrament of confirmation, for this reason: the grace of the Holy Spirit is signified by oil. Thus Christ is called “anointed with the oil of gladness” (Psalm XL) because of the fullness of the Holy Spirit that he possessed [lacuna] and therefore oil is suitable as the matter of this sacrament.

Balsam is added because of the fragrance of its odor, which spreads to others. Hence the Apostle says, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter XI: “We are the good odor of Christ to God.” Thus Saint Thomas.

It is established that the Greeks used chrismation alone in administering confirmation. At the Council of Florence, where other articles of faith were defined for the restoration of union between the Greeks and the Latin Church, nothing was altered in this matter. The Greeks therefore retained chrism as the suitable matter of confirmation, while the Latins remained with their position that chrismation and the imposition of hands are integral and constitutive parts forming the appropriate matter by which the sacrament is completed.

See Cardinal Orsi, *Dissertation on Confirmatory Chrism*, chapter 4 and following, page 208 and following, Milan edition, 1733.

After explaining the mysteries of baptism and confirmation, Maximus begins a discussion of the washing of the feet. First he warns that it was performed by the bishop for those to whom he had previously administered baptism and chrismation.

Ambrose discussed the same washing in chapter 6 of *On the Mysteries*, as did the author of *On the Sacraments*, book III, chapter 1. We must examine what Maximus thought about this mystery.

“For we have washed,” he says, “the feet of each one of you, in imitation of ourselves—or rather, urging you to imitate our Lord and Savior himself—so that, just as we have washed your feet, you too may wash the feet of your brothers and guests.”

After recounting the washing of the feet performed by Christ, by which he taught the apostles the highest form not so much of submission as of mutual charity, he concludes:

“Consider, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, what misery and madness it is for a servant to disdain washing the feet of a fellow servant, or for a disciple to disdain washing the feet of a fellow disciple, when the Lord and master of all servants and disciples deigned to wash the feet of servants and disciples.”

Let us now hear Ambrose in *On the Mysteries*. After repeating the Lord’s words to Peter, he says:

“Peter was clean, but he had to have his sole washed; for he bore the sin of the first man by succession, when the serpent tripped him up and persuaded him into error. Therefore his sole is washed, so that hereditary sins may be removed; our own sins, however, are forgiven through baptism.”

It is well known how learnedly and skillfully the Benedictine monks mentioned above explained this passage of Ambrose against the heretics who abused it in order to eliminate the necessity of baptism as a remedy for original sin. For our purposes it is sufficient to have shown that Ambrose attributed some sanctifying power to the washing of the feet.

The author of *On the Sacraments*, book III, chapter 1, appears to have followed the same opinion. First he says that the Roman Church does not have this custom of washing the feet [701], perhaps because of the multitude of those approaching baptism. He then continues:

“Nevertheless, there are some who say—and attempt to offer an excuse for it—that this should not be done as a mystery, nor in baptism, nor in regeneration, but that the feet should be washed as one washes those of a guest. One thing belongs to humility; another to sanctification.”

Since, therefore, Saint Ambrose in his book *On the Mysteries* and the author of the work *On the Sacraments* had one view concerning the necessity of obeying the Lord’s command—namely, performing the washing of the feet after baptism—and concerning its effect, while Maximus had another—for the former attributes to it the power of sanctification, whereas the latter attributes only the merit of humility—this evident disagreement silences all those who, without examining Ambrose’s books *On the Sacraments*, judged them not unworthy of Maximus.

The question has now been settled, and after Mabillon there is no longer room for the conjectures of Robert Sala and Dominicus Maria Manzi, who based their argument on the fact that writings attributed to Saint Maximus were found in the Codex Sangallensis after the homilies and sermons, and that they display a certain form of sermon. We acknowledge that this argument is not easily dispelled by the Subalpine codices.

Two other treatises follow these, one against the pagans and the other against the Jews, drawn from Codex Veronensis 49. We now publish them for the first time. We admit that they have come down to us anonymously; nevertheless, substantial considerations move us to attribute them to Maximus.

First, they are extant in the same very ancient codex that contains the Chapters of the Gospels, or *Expositions of the Gospels*. In asserting that the author of these works is our Maximus, we are supported by the clear testimonies of Gennadius and Trithemius [Col. 0769].

Second, it is evident that the author of the treatises generally used passages from the divine Scriptures according to the Old Italic version, just as Maximus used them in his homilies and sermons. If you examine his manner of expression and, as they say, his style, you will find in these writings the Maximian force and solidity displayed by his other works.

What recommends this attribution even more, however, is the author’s constant use of sacred utterances and their apt interpretation. No one will deny the holy bishop of Turin the praise of this wisdom: he was thoroughly familiar with the divine books and excelled in understanding them.

All doubt is removed by the fact that matters elsewhere transmitted by Saint Maximus are found reproduced in these treatises. This kind of evidence is so strong that nothing stronger could be desired. It is greatly to be lamented that, through the extreme antiquity of this codex, the form of the characters has completely deteriorated in many places. Had it remained intact and perfect, these writings would have to be counted among the most precious monuments of ecclesiastical teaching.

We shall briefly outline what each treatise contains.

At the beginning of the first, Maximus declares war upon the pagans as enemies and attacks the doctrine of fate, by which they said that everything came about. He ridicules their folly: although they considered themselves subject to necessity, they nevertheless performed sacrifices to their gods and sought through prayers and worship to make them favorable toward themselves.

The holy bishop proves how great their madness was from the fact that they sought help and protection from images that themselves required the protection of those who supplicated them, lest they suffer injury or damage. He says that imaginary powers can accomplish nothing, since they are powerless in themselves. It is enough to look at the material of which they are made to recognize them as works of human hands, or rather as fabrications of people out of their minds.

Lest the pagans suppose that Christians’ prayers and offerings in their temples should be mocked on the same grounds, Maximus teaches that we imitate the blessed apostles. Hoping for everything from the Lord, the maker of heaven and earth, they commanded the elements, diseases, and even death itself in his name and through faith in him, and obtained whatever they asked from God.

For we know whom we are entreating: the first cause of all things, the supreme author of the world, and its ruler, who dwells in heaven, to whom all these lower things are subject and minister.

The pagans, by contrast, parade a multitude of divine names, but there is no one among them who possesses power or can benefit or harm created things. What, then, is the purpose of such a vast offspring of deities? Do they each thunder with the same authority, or do the lesser obey the greater? If you distribute power and kingship among many gods, there will be no supreme ruler—and therefore no God. But if you say that they are unequal, what kind of divinity is it whose inequality human beings define and whose boundaries they set?

“I alone am,” says the Lord, “and there is no other God besides me” (Deuteronomy XXXII).

There is one holy God, a pure spirit, a simple unity, sustaining and ordering all things by his majesty. He has no beginning; he has always existed from eternity and will always exist in eternity.

Do the pagans set forth holiness, chastity, or justice for worship in their shrines when they burn incense and pour libations to Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, Apollo, Vulcan, and the rest? Were these not depraved and criminal men, deserving hatred rather than honor? It is well known how much wickedness they committed in adulteries, plunderings, frauds, and other crimes. Why, then, are such and so many offenses bestowed upon religion and worship as the highest virtues and merits?

The pagans [703] place some of these distinguished gods in heaven, others among the stars and the elements, and still others as guardians in the dwelling places of hell. Those gods must certainly be considered fools who were exiled from heaven, the dwelling place of perfect blessedness; or else they must be called unhappy if, expelled from it, they were forced to live elsewhere.

Yet the pagan fabrication surpasses all madness: they raised the most impure and criminal women to heaven and called them the mothers, daughters, or wives of the gods. What more wicked or shameful offspring could have been imagined than Juno, Venus, Diana, and the others? Women whom unrestrained lust and depravity of character had made a disgrace to their sex were, through human malice in a world wrapped in darkness, made equal to the heavenly beings.

Maximus then invites the pagans to compare their heroes with ours. Can they find among any of theirs a just Noah, a faithful Abraham, a holy Elijah, or the like? Christians, however, venerate these men not as gods but as servants of God, just as they venerate the apostles whom Christ first called to follow him.

We call this Lord our Lord, believe and adore him as the Son of God. By nature he is God and eternal God. In compassion for the human race, deceived by the devil and driven into condemnation, he put on this flesh of ours and, taking the form of a servant without changing the condition of his divinity, fully pleasing to the Father, accomplished universal salvation and freedom by paying the price of his blood.

Maximus therefore concludes that nothing in the Christian religion is absurd and nothing unworthy of holier conduct, since one God is worshiped and one Lord, our lawgiver, is heard. For those who obey him, unending happiness has been established in heaven.

To summarize briefly the principal points of the other treatise, against the Jews: although its beginning is mutilated, it can nevertheless be gathered from the surviving text that Maximus immediately set before the Jews the image, or outline, of the distinction between the two peoples in Cain and Abel, the first children of Adam.

“Cain,” he says, “the elder by birth, represented the people of the Jews. He was rejected on account of his crime; Abel, younger by birth, was chosen, and he represented the Christian people.”

Maximus confirms this same differing fate of the two peoples—so that the Jews might understand that they had been rejected, while we had been chosen—by the examples of Ishmael, the elder son born of the slave woman Hagar, and Isaac, the younger son born of the free woman Sarah, as well as Esau and Jacob, born of the same birth.

[Note: See Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book XVI, chapter 26 and following.]

Scripture testifies that Ishmael was expelled from the house of his father Abraham together with his mother, and that God said concerning Isaac’s sons: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Malachi I; Romans IX).

These events are not so much symbols as prophecies of things to come, especially in the words spoken to Rebecca:

“Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples will be divided from your womb.”

Thus the Jews descended from Esau might recognize that they had received rejection from their ancestor, and that, by departing from the divine commandments, they had imitated him.

Abraham was justified by faith. Although the command to sacrifice his son was laid upon him, he nevertheless believed that his offspring would produce the shoot through which all nations would be blessed—namely, Christ the Son of God.

He is the very one in whom all things were created, as Moses testifies in the words with which, at the beginning, according to Maximus, he designated the Son, in whom God the Father made heaven and earth:

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis I).

Relying upon this truth, the Apostle said that in Christ all things were created that are in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible. Saint John wrote: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made” (John I).

Maximus proves through so many and such clear prophecies of the holy prophets that this Word, clothed in human flesh in time, must be believed to be the Savior promised to the world. The Jews ought to have believed these prophecies, unless they were afflicted by blind unbelief and hardness of heart.

Isaiah prophesied that a virgin would bear a son whose name would be Emmanuel, that is, “God with us”; and this son was conceived in the virginal womb of Mary. It was fitting that, at his birth, nothing should shine forth except what was immaculate, pure, and accomplished through the power of the Holy Spirit.

The Scriptures therefore testify that Christ was born of the Virgin Mary. His works and teaching so clearly manifest him as holy and the Son of God that the blind man whom he enlightened declared before the unbelieving Jews that, unless this man were from God—that is, unless he possessed within himself the power of God—he could not have restored sight to his eyes.

What, indeed, was holier than his teaching, or more equitable than his laws, since he most earnestly commends all love toward God and neighbor, and all his commandments are directed toward this end? [Col. 0771]

Jews who proudly boasted that they had Abraham as their father and carried the sign of his covenant in their flesh received this answer from Maximus: Abraham was justified not by circumcision. Scripture says that he believed the word of God and obtained his blessing. If, then, they are regarded as Abraham’s sons, let them imitate him by believing in the Redeemer.

“For they vainly expect,” says the holy Doctor, “the reward of salvation from circumcision, since it was given as a sign of their race. Before it, Abel, Enos, Enoch, Noah, and Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, were called righteous by faith and were not circumcised according to the flesh.”

Since Christ is the end of the law [705], that ancient circumcision must be regarded as a symbol by which the faithful are to avoid the enticements of the flesh, flee the vanities of idols, and impose restraint upon the desires of the world.

“In Jesus Christ,” the Apostle wrote to the Galatians, “neither circumcision has any value, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Galatians V).

For Christ, the heavenly man, as the Apostle calls him, calls his followers to heavenly things, not earthly things. He commands them not carnal but spiritual works, by which, always keeping God before their eyes, they may do everything for his glory.

Vivified by this spirit, they experience the yoke of his law as easy and the burden of his commandments as light. For Christ’s help is never lacking to those who love him, so that they may merit eternal salvation for themselves.

Maximus refutes the Jews, who boasted that the Messiah would be a future king and would come with glory and majesty, by means of many oracles of the New Testament. He demonstrates that some of them were perfectly fulfilled at Christ’s first coming; the rest remain to be fulfilled at his second coming, when, as Augustine says [Note: *City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 45], “he will come with the splendor of power.”

How many and how great lessons of heavenly wisdom did they hear from him? How often did they marvel at his divine powers? How frequently did they see him restore the weak to strength, the sick to health, and even the dead to life?

Yet after all these things, the impious blasphemed Jesus, saying that he had a demon; and, seizing stones, they rushed upon him in fury. So far did envious hatred and blind treachery prevail among them that they subjected the just and innocent, the benefactor and savior, to the punishment of the cross and drove him from among the living.

Having dealt with these matters not so much in words as through the testimonies of Scripture, Maximus gathers all the arguments into one body by which he demonstrated against the Jews that Jesus Christ, true God and true man, is to be heard and adored as our Redeemer. Finally, he exhorts them, so that they may recover from their hardness and behold in Christ the light of truth, by the promise of eternal life.

[Col. 0771]

## TREATISES OF SAINT MAXIMUS (C, G, S)*

### FIRST TREATISE: ON BAPTISM

[Note: [Col. 0771B] Sirmond’s title is: “Sermon on the Neophytes. Let the ears and nostrils be anointed with holy oil by the priests.” The variant additions derive from him.]

[Col. 0771A] 709 [Note: [Col. 0771B] “Dearest brothers.”] Every word of God, brothers, ought indeed to be heard with complete attentiveness and diligence of mind, but especially this word which we are to deliver to your charity today. For this reason, having now dismissed the catechumens, we have retained you alone to listen: because, in addition to those matters which all Christians ought commonly to observe, we shall speak in particular about the heavenly mysteries, which cannot be heard except by those who, through the Lord’s gift, have already received them. Therefore you ought to hear what we say with so much greater reverence as these matters, entrusted only to baptized and faithful hearers, are greater than those which even catechumens are accustomed to hear.

But you ought not to wonder, dearest brothers, that amid the very mysteries we have said nothing to you about the mysteries without immediately interpreting what we have handed on. [Note: [Col. 0771B] After this, the edition has: “which we certainly did not do through negligence—for that would be sacrilege in matters so sacred and divine—but out of reverence. We employed …”] For we have shown honor to such sacred and divine matters by silence, and amid those sacred rites of the mysteries we refrain from the office of teaching, so that by keeping silent we may venerate all the more the majesty of divine grace, which cannot worthily be explained by any human words.

But since it is necessary that your love be instructed and taught in all things, [Note: [Col. 0772B] “The rite having now been completed.”] when the order of the mysteries has been completed, we explain to you what we previously handed on, lest, while you understand less of the dignity of the divine mystery, you should esteem it less highly. If you understand it, you will see that everything regarded as precious in this world is utterly worthless in comparison with so great a sacrament. [Note: [Col. 0772B] “‘Is’ is omitted.”] Let each of you therefore recall the individual forms of the mysteries which, through our ministry and by the Lord’s gift, you have received, and now understand wisely what you then received simply and faithfully, so that you may better preserve what you have understood.

First of all, certainly, we anointed your ears with the oil of blessing; but recognize for what reason, according to ecclesiastical tradition, this is done by all the Catholic priests of Christ. The entrance of faith and of the whole sacred teaching is admitted into the soul [Note: [Col. 0772B] “‘To the soul,’ likewise below.”] through the ears, and understanding arises from hearing. For no one can know the sacraments of faith unless he hears the preacher, as the blessed Apostle affirms when he says: “How, then, will they hear without a preacher?” and again: “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (Rom. 10). Rightly, therefore, by that oil the organs of the senses are sanctified, without which faith cannot reach the soul.

At the same time, those who are approaching baptism are instructed to guard their ears, undefiled by every evil and shameful word, to the end, so that, like the deaf, they may not hear one who slanders his neighbor [Note: [Col. 0773D] “Or one who speaks obscenely or immodestly.”] or one who speaks obscenely and immodestly, fulfilling that saying of divine Scripture: “Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Ecclus. 28:28). And elsewhere: “Do not believe every empty report.” And again: “Give your heart to discipline, and prepare your ear for words of wisdom” (Prov. 23; Ecclus. 2).

Therefore the holy anointing applied to the ears signifies that they should turn away from and flee all speech outside the discipline of Christ, as though it were speaking against Christ’s teaching, [Note: [Col. 0773D] “Speaking against it.”] and devote themselves solely to hearing the words of God, because [Note: [Col. 0773D] “By that oil having been applied.”] by the oil with which they were anointed they have consecrated their hearing to the sayings of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0773D] “They have consecrated it.”]

For the Savior himself speaks to the Father and glories in the obedience of the people who believe in him, saying: “You desired neither sacrifice nor offering, but you perfected ears for me” (Ps. 39). The ears of Christ’s faithful are truly perfected when they desire to hear nothing besides Christ and the things that belong to Christ. [Note: [Col. 0773D] “Hence also in the Gospel.”]

Therefore, when the same Lord was speaking in the Gospel about the mystery of the heavenly kingdom, he said: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 11; 13; Mark 4, and elsewhere). For although everyone commonly possesses ears, the ears of hearing are not common to all. Whoever despises the words of God—although he cannot despise them unless he first hears them—nevertheless, because he despises what he hears, is not said to have heard, since he rejects what he has heard as though it had not been heard. Thus such people have ears, but not ears that are called ears of hearing, [Note: [Col. 0773D] “That are called so.”] rather ears that hear so as not to hear; [Col. 0773C] that is, so that they may despise what they have heard as though, as we said, they had never heard it.

But Christ says that only those have ears of hearing who, when they hear with their ears, firmly commit what they have heard to their minds, and carry out in their deeds what they have entrusted to their minds. [Note: [Col. 0773D] “They entrusted [it].”] Of such hearers the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear” (Matt. 13). And again: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house upon rock; and the rain fell, and the rivers came, and the winds blew and struck that house, and it did not fall, because it had been founded upon solid rock” (Matt. 7 and following).

Again, concerning those who hear badly—who indeed have ears, but not for obedience—he declares: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand; [Note: [Col. 0773D] “And the rain fell, and the rivers came, and the winds blew.”] and the rain fell, and the winds blew and rushed upon that house, and it fell, and its ruin was great” (ibid.).

You see, then, how great is the difference between one who hears well and one who hears badly—that is, between one who keeps the words of God [Note: [Col. 0774D] “And between one who heard him as though never hearing.”] and one who hears them and, as though they had never been heard, [Col. 0774A] despises them. [Note: [Col. 0774D] “Despises them.”] Wisdom is attributed to the one who obeys and acts; folly to the one who despises. The former builds upon a solid foundation; the latter’s empty building, without a foundation, is described as easily collapsing. In the one there is stability; in the other, ruin—and great ruin. For no one falls more grievously than the person who, after hearing the word of God, turns to the sins for which eternal punishments have been prepared.

But you, after your ears have been anointed with blessed oil, have been marked out among the number of wise hearers, so that, rightly retaining the words of God—that is, fulfilling what you have heard—you may on the day of judgment hear Christ say to you: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

Do not think that it was done idly or without a definite sacramental purpose [Col. 0774B] when we also anointed your nostrils with the oil of blessing. This is understood to be done so that those who come to baptism may be admonished to preserve the sacrament of so great a mystery inviolate and entire until death: as long as they draw the breath of this life through their nostrils, they must not depart from the worship and service of Christ our Lord.

Hence the holy man Job also says: “The Lord lives, who has taken away my judgment, and the Almighty, who has brought bitterness upon my soul; for as long as my breath remains in me and the spirit of God is in my nostrils, my lips shall not speak iniquity, nor shall my tongue utter deceit. Far be it from me to judge you righteous; until I perish, I will not depart from my innocence. I will not abandon the justification which I once began to hold” (Job 22).

But a subtler meaning is also signified in this anointing of the nostrils. [Col. 0774C] The fragrance of that oil, which has been blessed in the name and power of Christ, summons you to spiritual smelling, so that you may perceive Christ, not with the senses of the body but of the mind, with inestimable sweetness; and, delighted by the knowledge of his mouth (oris eius), [Note: [Col. 0774D] “By knowledge of his fragrance.”] following his footsteps, you may be able to say what the congregation of believers says to God: “We run after you in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song 1).

The Apostle commends this fragrance to Christians when he says: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us the fragrance of the knowledge of himself in every place, because we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2).

Consider how greatly the apostles advanced by sensing the fragrance of Christ, [Note: [Col. 0774D] “And by surpassing others through the urgency of preaching and holiness of life.”] and how, by the zeal of their preaching and holiness of life, they surpassed all others: while they spread the fragrance of Christ’s sweet perfume [Col. 0774D] in every direction, [Note: [Col. 0774D] “‘Everywhere’ (ubique) in place of ‘in every direction’ (undique).”] they themselves also became a good fragrance to God.

We desire this also to be fulfilled in you, beloved brothers: when you yourselves have received the good fragrance of the knowledge of Christ, may the sweetest fragrance to God also rise from the holiness of your life. Through the Lord, etc.

## TREATISE II. ON BAPTISM

[Note: [Col. 0775D] The title in the edition is: “On the mystery of baptism.”]

[Col. 0775]

[Col. 0775A] 713 [Note: [Col. 0775D] The manuscript of Appannis begins thus: “In the preceding treatise, if your holiness remembers well, we promised to speak about everything, etc.”] In the first treatise we promised to speak about all the mysteries which you have received through our ministry and Christ’s grace, lest any charge of ignorance or negligence should arise against us. But we took account of your labor and memory, providing that either your mind, wearied by listening, might not be able to understand everything, or that your memory, burdened by learning many things at once, might quickly lose even what it had understood.

Therefore, in our first instruction we spoke only about those matters which, before you came to the holy font, we handed on to you according to the institutions of the Catholic rule. We interpreted, as the Lord deigned to grant, what was signified by the anointing applied to different parts of your body, which signifies different meanings, when we showed that through the oil of sanctification you had been prepared for the hearing [Col. 0775B] [Note: [Col. 0775D] “Clearly, for the hearing of faith.”] of faith, had been called the good fragrance of Christ, and had been admonished [Note: [Col. 0775D] “Had been instructed that you must renounce the devil.”] to renounce the devil with your whole heart.

Now, however, we shall speak about the inner mysteries celebrated in the holy font itself. After you had made the most certain pledge by which you promised to renounce all his pageants and works, and every diabolical fornication, [Note: [Col. 0775D] “Descending into the font, the sacred font.”] you descended into the sacred font—the font of life, the font of redemption, the font sanctified by heavenly power—and so sanctified that it sanctifies human beings by washing away their many sins.

For you must not judge those waters by your eyes, but by your mind. For although the substance of that water belongs to the common nature of water, [Note: [Col. 0775D] “Yet its special effect proceeds from the grace and power of God, who created the waters by which bodily and visible impurities are washed away. He therefore sanctified the waters, through which, by the secret power of his might, he would wash away sins that are not seen.”] its effect nevertheless proceeds from the grace and power of God, who created the waters so that, by the secret power of his might, they might wash away sins that are not seen.

For the Holy Spirit operates in that water, so that those who before baptism were held guilty of various crimes and were destined to burn with the devil in the gehenna of eternal fire might, after baptism, deserve to enter the kingdom of heaven. [Note: [Col. 0776D] “May deserve it.”] Hence the Lord, expressing the power of so great a sacrament in the Gospel, says: “Unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3).

In this font, therefore, before we immersed your whole bodies, we asked: “Do you believe in God the almighty Father?” You answered: “I believe.” Again we asked: “Do you also believe in Jesus Christ, his Son, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary?” [Note: [Col. 0776D] “Who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.”] Each of you answered: “I believe.” Again we asked: “Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit?” [Note: [Col. 0776D] “Again we asked: ‘And in the Holy Spirit.’”] You answered likewise: “I believe.”

We did this according to the command of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, who, when he ascended to the Father in heaven, charged his disciples, that is, the apostles, saying: “Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. 28).

When anyone hears “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit,” no one should suppose that we confess three gods. Far be such sacrilege from our faith! [Note: [Col. 0776D] “Who” in place of “because.”] For we have learned from his own testimony that there is only one God. “I am God,” he says, “and there is no other besides me; a just God and a Savior, there is none besides me. Turn to me, and you shall be saved, because I am God from the end of the earth, and there is no other besides me” (Isa. 45; Hos. 13). And in another book: “Hear, O Israel: The Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6). And again: “The Lord your God is here, in heaven above and on earth below, and there is no other besides him” (Deut. 4).

We therefore hold and believe in three persons, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—of one power, one substance, one eternity, one will, and likewise one deity—and we venerate the whole Trinity under the name of one God. To believe in several gods is the impiety of the pagans.

And again: not to believe that there are three persons of one substance, in one deity and equality, or co-eternity, is heretical madness, since this authority of Christ, which we have cited, is manifest: “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

But when we asked: [Note: [Col. 0776D] “ ‘Do you believe in the holy Church,’ without the preposition ‘in’; then it adds remission of sins and the resurrection of the flesh.”] “Do you believe [that] the holy Church and the remission of sins [exist]?” 715 we did not ask in such a way that you should believe in the holy Catholic Church as one believes in God. [Note: [Col. 0776D] “So also, ‘in the Church.’”] It is holy and Catholic because it believes rightly in God. Therefore we did not say that you should believe in the Church as in God; rather, understand that we are saying, and have said, that while living in the holy and Catholic Church you should believe in God.

You should also believe in the resurrection of the flesh, which is to come. Just as, therefore, you believed in the mystery of the Trinity and received the one God under the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; just as you believed that your sins ought to be forgiven, and now through baptism believe that they have been forgiven; so also believe that the resurrection of the flesh is to come. [Note: [Col. 0776D] “ ‘Is to be,’ is lacking.”] This, certainly, you promised that you would believe.

For the whole hope of Christians consists in this: that we believe that the resurrection will truly be of this body, not another. And just as we now stand in the Church before the altar of God, so we should believe that on the day of judgment we shall stand [Note: [Col. 0777D] “We should believe that we shall stand.”] before the tribunal of God, as the blessed Apostle Paul says: “We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his own body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5). And this is what unbelieving souls do not believe will happen.

There are some who promise with their lips that they believe, but despair in their hearts. They do great injury to almighty God, since they do not believe that human beings can be raised and brought to life by him after death. But we who give credence to the divine utterances cannot doubt our resurrection. For we believe that God, who made human beings when they did not yet exist, can easily remake those who once existed.

He who made heaven, earth, and the seas, and all that is in them, and all the elements from nothing—how could he not restore human beings, whom he made for this reason: that in this life they might do what would be judged in the other, and might deserve either rewards for a good will or punishments for an evil one?

For this is the faith of Catholic Christians: that we believe we shall rise with the same soul which we now possess, having as a fitting example of our future resurrection our Lord himself, the Word of the Father. [Note: [Col. 0777D] “Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, the Word of the Father, is a fitting example of the resurrection.”] Since he is God and the Son of God, [Note: [Col. 0777D] “God the Word.”] or the Word, and according to the substance of his divinity co-eternal and consubstantial with the Father, he therefore took on a human being of our nature. In that nature he willed to be born of a virgin, and afterward to suffer and die; and on the third day he rose again, [Note: [Col. 0777D] “And ascended into heaven.”] and ascended into heaven, so that he might kindle in us the hope of resurrection, so that we may believe that we shall be raised from the dead just as we confess that Christ rose from the dead. [Note: [Col. 0777D] “That he rose from the dead.”]

Hence the blessed Apostle rebukes the minds of unbelievers, saying: “But if Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how can some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?” (1 Cor. 15).

Hold this, therefore, steadfastly, and believe what is affirmed by the divine utterances: that there will be a resurrection in which glorious immortality will be given to all the saints who love Christ and do his will, so that they may rejoice forever in the sight of God with the angels and heavenly powers.

But unbelievers and sinners, and those who do not do the commandments of God, will rise for this purpose: that their flesh, having been made immortal, may be assigned to eternal fires, so that it may burn forever and never cease burning. For this too is attested by the saying of our Lord Jesus Christ, who pronounced in the Gospel concerning sinners: “Then the wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25).

Now, after you promised that you believed these things which we have said thus far, [Note: [Col. 0777D] “The third time, your heads.”] we immersed your bodies in the sacred font a third time. This order of baptism is celebrated with a twofold sacramental significance. You were rightly immersed three times because you received baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, who rose from the dead on the third day. [Note: [Col. 0778D] “In the name of the Trinity. You were rightly immersed three times because you received baptism in the name of Jesus Christ.”]

That immersion repeated three times expresses the type of the Lord’s burial, through which you were buried with Christ in baptism and rose with Christ in faith, so that, washed from sins, you might live Christ by imitating him.

Hence the blessed Apostle says: “Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be united with him in resurrection, knowing this: that our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, and that we might no longer serve sin” (Rom. 6).

Consider, brothers, [Note: [Col. 0778D] “Dearest brothers”; thereafter “us” is omitted.] under what condition the Apostle said that we were baptized: “so that we might no longer serve sin.” What can be so great—not negligence, I say, but madness—as that, after receiving the forgiveness of sins through baptism, you should wish to bind yourselves to sins; that, having been made holy from sinners, you should again wish to become sinners from holy persons; and that, after that sacred font, in which one may be washed only once, you should return again to the filth of vices?

Pay attention, therefore, beloved, so that what you have received, and what cannot thereafter be received again by you, you may preserve whole and undefiled to the end; and, having once been made free from sin, may henceforth withdraw forever from every sin. For Christ, who in his mercy cleansed you when you were polluted and defiled by the devil’s persuasion, does not wish those who have been cleansed to be defiled again.

To him be glory and honor, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## TREATISE III. ON BAPTISM

[Note: [Col. 0775D] The title in the edition is: “On the mystery of baptism.”]

[Col. 0777]

[Col. 0777D] Up to this point we have spoken about the mysteries which are celebrated either before the sacrament of baptism or in baptism itself. Now we shall treat of those things which are completed [Note: [Col. 0778D] “‘In’ is omitted.”] in the baptized through holy instruction. For when baptism has been completed, we pour chrism—that is, the oil of sanctification—over your heads, by which it is shown that the Lord confers upon the baptized the dignity of kingship and priesthood. For in the Old Testament those who were chosen for the priesthood or kingship were anointed with holy oil and with anointing of the head; some received from the Lord power to reign [Note: [Col. 0778D] “To reign among the people of God.”], others power to offer sacrifices.

We read that holy David and the other kings were anointed by the prophets, and that by the oil of sanctification [Note: [Col. 0779D] “By the oil of sanctification.”] they were changed from private persons into kings. Likewise, we read that holy Aaron was anointed by Moses and consecrated with holy oil from a layman into a priest of the Lord. Hence it is sung in the psalm: “Like the ointment on the head which ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” (Ps. 132).

But in the Old Testament that oil conferred a temporal kingdom and a temporal priesthood, for their life of service was limited to the course of a few years. [Note: [Col. 0779D] “At this point . . . . . the text ends.”] This chrism, however—that is, this anointing which has been placed upon you—has conferred the dignity of that priesthood, [Note: [Col. 0779D] “It conferred upon you the dignity of that kingdom, of that priesthood, etc.”] which, once bestowed, is never to end. [Note: [Col. 0779D] “You may perhaps wonder.”]

It is certainly astonishing what we have said: that through that chrism you have obtained the kingdom of future glory and the priesthood. [Note: [Col. 0779D] “‘Not I say it to you’; ‘but’ (verum) is lacking; then: ‘Christ through the Apostle.’”] But it is not I who declare that this dignity has been bestowed upon you; it is the Apostle Peter—or rather, Christ through Peter. For this is how he speaks to the faithful, that is, to those who have been washed in baptism and consecrated with chrism: “But you are a royal and priestly race, a holy nation, a people for possession, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Pet. 2).

Consider, therefore, the honor which you have received in that mystery, and beware lest, after your sins, through baptism, have made you sons of the kingdom, by sinning again—God forbid—you should wish to become sons of gehenna. [Note: [Col. 0779D] “How do you suppose God becomes angry, if after his benefits and the forgiveness of sins you wish to return to sinning, and, having been adopted as sons of God, you again, like servants, despising God, wish to do the devil’s will?”]

When all the sacraments had been completed, we also handed on to you Christ’s commandment, both by example and by word. [Note: [Col. 0779D] “We handed on to you the commandment and example.”] For we washed the feet of each one of you, urging you to imitate us—or rather, our Lord and Savior himself—so that, just as we have washed your feet, you too should wash the feet of your brothers and of your guests.

We teach you not only to be hospitable, but also humble, honoring those whom you have received into your homes in such a way that you are not ashamed to perform toward them the service of servants. [Note: [Col. 0779D] “To fulfill the service of servants. If anyone considers this insulting and, inflated with the devil’s pride, disdains to carry out the Lord’s command …”]

No one should consider this insulting or, inflated with devilish pride, disdain to carry out the Lord’s command; [Note: [Col. 0780D] “Even though he may be noble in this world, let him not be ashamed to wash the feet of poor and despised Christians in this world—he who both commanded and did this, indeed deigned to do it before he commanded it.”] even if he is noble in this world, he should not be ashamed to wash the feet of a poor and despised Christian in this world. For he both commanded this and did it—indeed, before he commanded it, he deigned to do it. He first supplied the example, so that he might commend the command more easily.

For thus we read concerning the Lord Jesus in the Gospel: “Knowing,” he says, “that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going to God, he rose from supper, laid aside his garments, and, having taken a towel, girded himself. Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the feet of the disciples and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded” (John 12).

And again: “After he had washed their feet, he took his garments; and when he had reclined again, he said to them: ‘Do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If, then, I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, how much more ought you to wash one another’s feet? For I have given you an example, so that, just as I have done to you, you also should do. Amen, amen, I say to you: a servant is not greater than his lord, nor an apostle greater than the one who sent him. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them’” (ibid.).

Consider, therefore, dearest brothers, how great is the misery and madness of someone who disdains to wash the feet of a fellow servant, a disciple of a fellow disciple, when the Lord and teacher of all deigned to wash the feet of his servants and disciples. [Note: [Col. 0780D] The manuscript of Appannis has “deigned.” “He humbled himself to those beneath him, while we disdain to humble ourselves to our equals and often our betters. This arises from no other cause …” The edition of Augustine likewise has this reading.]

This arises from no other cause than unbelief concerning the future. For if we truly and wholeheartedly believed that through these commands of the Lord, which we observe during the brief span of our whole life, we would attain eternal and heavenly rewards, we would not merely refrain from being ashamed to perform every work of humility; we would even glory in doing so.

Therefore firmly commit to memory what you have heard from us—and what you promised to us, or rather to the Lord. Let no tribulation of this present life ever take from you the remembrance of your pledge. [Note: [Col. 0780D] “Fulfill all the commands you have heard; fulfill everything you have promised.”] Fulfill everything which you have heard commanded.

Do not become like the Jewish people, who, when they heard the commands of God, rightly said: “Everything which the Lord has commanded us we shall hear and do” (Exod. 19); but neglected what they had promised well. They pleased God [Note: [Col. 0780D] “ ‘When’ in place of ‘because.’”] because they promised that they would keep his commands.

Thus we read that the people of Israel said to Moses: “Come near, and hear everything that the Lord our God says to you; and you shall speak to us everything that the Lord our God says to us, and we shall hear and do it.” [Note: [Col. 0780D] “All that the Lord speaks to you, etc.”] And the Lord said to Moses: “I have heard the voice of the words of this people, everything that they have said. Who will grant that their heart may be such within them that they may fear me and observe my commandments all their days?”

They therefore pleased God, as we said, [Note: [Col. 0780D] “‘Since’ (quandoquidem) in place of ‘because’ (quoniam); likewise shortly afterward.”] because they promised that they would carry out his commands; but they displeased him because, after his commands had been given to them, they transgressed by failing to keep what they had promised.

Concerning them the prophet says: “They loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him” (Ps. 77). This is what it means to love him with the mouth and not with the heart: they promise that they will do the will of God, but they lie with their tongue and flee to doing the devil’s will, provoking almighty God to anger, for he does not permit himself to be mocked.

Since he sees the deeds of human beings, however secretly they may be done; since he hears every word, however privately it may be whispered; since he understands and knows the thoughts of all people, he will judge with the utmost severity.

He does not always punish his despisers here because he has decreed that there will be a judgment in the future, where eternal condemnation and everlasting punishment are reserved for sinners. There will be “weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8); where, as the Lord himself says: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (Mark 9).

[Note: [Col. 0781C] “But we, dearest brothers, believe in the name of the Lord that you do not hear our words, or rather the divine words, only fleetingly …”] But we, dearest brothers, believe in the name of the Lord that you do not hear our words—or rather, the divine words—only fleetingly, because what we say to you we borrow from the holy and divine utterances. We hope in the Lord that you will do everything you have promised, [Note: [Col. 0781C] “With God assisting you in holy works, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ himself, to whom belong glory and honor, etc.”] with the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ assisting you in those holy works. To him be glory and honor with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

The end.

## TREATISE IV. AGAINST THE PAGANS

[Col. 0781]

[Col. 0781B] 721 It is customary for the servants of God to undertake every good work, whether in word or deed, in the name of Christ, so that it may be accomplished for the glory of God, as the Apostle admonishes and says: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of Christ” (1 Cor. X).

Today, with the Lord’s help, in the name of Christ our Savior we draw up the battle line against the pagans and carry heavenly weapons, intending to strike the enemies of Christ with the darts of truth, to overthrow the hostile forces and the camps of perfidy, and repeatedly to bring down, with the battering ram of faith, their needless towers. We follow Christ as our leader—namely, the Lord Christ, who both through Jesus son of Nun, the successor of Moses, destroyed the walls of the proud city Jericho, and through his apostles cast down to their foundations [Col. 0781C] the arrogance of this world, which exalts itself against the knowledge of God.

Come now, let us examine these pagans and bring their assertions into the open. The pagans say that everything happens by fate, [Note: Four opinions of pagan philosophers concerning fate are reported. The first recognizes fate in nature, by which all things are generated. The second uses “fate” for the enduring succession of causes necessarily linked together. The third calls the stars fate. The fourth takes fate to be the execution of the divine plan. The divine Augustine, in *The City of God*, book V, chapter 8, discusses the monstrous doctrines of the Stoics concerning fate. Cicero, Seneca, and many others had dealt with this before him. According to those philosophers, each of these opinions imposes a certain necessity upon events and actions, whether human actions or operations. See, among recent writers, Monilia in his distinguished work against the Fatalists.] and that neither prayers nor supplications have any power. They also say that idols are worshiped in honor and likeness of the gods, or that all the elements are themselves gods and goddesses, dwelling in the heavens, in images, and in the stars.

We see, therefore, brothers, that these pagans and astrologers are truly foolish, and that these stars, armed with empty weapons, will fall without delay in this battle. For they think that, clothed in the proud and lofty arms of their arrogance, [Note: To designate the enemies of God, he calls the pagans *allophylos* (ἀλλοφύλους), “of another race,” just as he mentions them in the homily on Lent beginning, “I believe that you have understood.” These peoples served in the army of King Geth and waged war against King Saul. Again, Maximus calls the barbarian hostile bands threatening Taurinus *allophylos* in the homily on the Nativity of the Lord, whose opening words are: “While celebrating with due honor the most solemn nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, brothers,” etc. Likewise in the homily on the Epiphany beginning: “For the venerable, brothers, feast of the Lord.” Eusebius of Caesarea has similar material in his commentary on Psalm LXXXVI, p. 841, vol. I of the *Collection of the Ancient Fathers*, Paris, 1706. He observes that ἀλλόφυλοι means the same as “pagans.” The passage written by Saint Hilary of Poitiers concerning the *allophylos* in Psalm LIX, no. 12, p. 123, vol. I of the Venetian edition of his works, 1749, is also relevant. I pass over the others, lest I be lengthy.] can disturb the battle line of God and Israelite courage, and they do not think that they can easily be overthrown by David’s stone.

This stone is Christ our Lord, who gave David the victory [Col. 0782B] and cast down with mighty power Goliath’s proud brow, raised high through the arrogance of his insolence. This is our God; this is Christ, “the Lord who shatters wars”; the Lord is his name (Judith XVI). He has always been accustomed to be the helper of his servants who fight for his name and undertake battle for the truth.

The pagans therefore say that everything happens by fate, and that, concerning the whole human race, whatever fate has established or decreed is fixed and immovable, and that neither prayers nor supplications have any power. To them we first say briefly—as though with a single plow of faith and secure truth we were cutting all around and overturning the forest of their error: If, then, prayers and supplications have no power, O pagans, and everything is fixed, as you say, according to what fate has given or decreed, why do you worship gods and goddesses? Why do you sacrifice to idols? [Col. 0782C] Why do you bring prayers, incense, victims, and every kind of offering into the temples, if everything is fixed and decreed, and nothing is granted or obtained through prayers or petitions? Why, then, do you plead?

But they say: “We do these things so that they may not harm us.”

To them we reply: How can those who cannot bestow anything cause harm?
