[Note: “Holiness, moreover, is knowledge of the gods who are to be worshiped; for what reason they should be worshiped I do not understand, since no good has either been received or hoped for from them.” Cicero, *On Divination*, book I.]

And because they truly can neither harm nor benefit, the guarding of dogs around those gods whom you call yours, and the vigilance of their guardians, testify to this. For whenever thieves find them, they carry them off and smash them to pieces.

You say that everything happens by fate; but what you call the work of fate, according to I know not what uncertain opinion, I say happens by the will or permission of God, because God [Col. 0783A] the Father “has placed all things in his power” (Acts I), and nothing happens that the Lord himself has not willed or permitted to happen.

Do you wish to see what our prophets and apostles accomplished—not by the power of fate, but by faith, by the help of the supreme God, and by the divine power of Christ? Behold, they restored even those who had been shattered, whom you say were afflicted by fate; likewise they healed the sick, raised the dead, gave sight to the blind, and made the lame stand. They asked nothing from fate, but fulfilled everything, as I have said, through the sincerity of faith, divine resources, and mercies.

You say that everything happens by fate? But “the fool speaks foolishly, and his heart understands vanity.” And, as Tullius says in the *Hortensius*: “My grandmother used to say what you say—that everything happens by fate; but my mother, a wise woman, did not think so.”

And we can say truthfully that [Col. 0783B] our grandmother—that is, ancient error and pagan folly—used to say this. But our mother, the wise woman, namely the Church, who gave us spiritual birth, never thought so. She knows that the Son received all power from the Father in heaven and on earth.

Therefore his disciples performed such mighty works in his name. He also said: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (John XVI). Certainly, when he said this, he opposed the errors and demons who invent fates and insist that prayers have no power, lest God be entreated and their works be destroyed. Therefore the Lord drew the people to himself, so that faith in God might have the greatest power and disbelief might not prevail.

You say, shameless man, that everything happens by fate? You add that neither prayers nor supplications have any power? But how greatly [Col. 0783C] the prayers and supplications of the faithful avail is proclaimed by the sacred records of all the divine books, and access to salvation is readily granted to those who wish to know. Therefore nothing is accomplished by fate; everything is governed by the providence of the Maker of the world.

As for the idols, or the elements that the pagans consider gods, listen briefly, brothers, as our blessed prophet mocks these pagans concerning their useless objects and says: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands: they have mouths, but they do not speak; they have eyes, but they do not see; they have ears, but they do not hear” (Psalm CXXXIV), and so forth in what follows there.

I ask you, pagan: would you wish to be such as those whom you worship—without soul, without sense, without movement, without any vital understanding? Do you regard this as a curse? Then cease worshiping those whose likeness troubles you and whose worship you consider honorable.

But the pagans say: “We worship and venerate the sun and moon, or the stars, and all the elements.”

To them it is again said: [Col. 0783D] “But vain are all human beings in whom there is not the knowledge of God; and from the visible good things they were unable to understand him who is; nor, by attending to the works, did they recognize who was their craftsman. Instead, they considered either fire, or spirit, or swift air, or the circle of stars, or the excessive water, or the sun, or the moon to be gods” (Wisdom XIII). [Note: The Vulgate adds: “the rulers of the world, gods,” etc.]

If they judged these things divine because of their beauty, let them know how much more beautiful than these the Lord is; for the Creator of beauty established all things. [Col. 0784A] Or if they marvel at their power and works, let them understand from them that he who established these mighty things is mightier than they.

And the Apostle Paul says: “For the invisible things of God, both his eternal power and divinity, are understood and seen through the things that have been made since the creation of the world, so that they are without excuse. For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools. And they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of a corruptible human being, and of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents” (Romans I), etc.

Therefore, he says, “they considered either fire, or spirit, or swift air, or the circle of stars, or the turbulent water, or the sun, or the moon to be gods.”

[Col. 0784B] The pagans worship fire and call it a god, although water extinguishes it and a throw of earth suppresses it. The pagans worship fire, which is nourished by the fuel of wood. The pagans worship fire, although they are destined to burn in eternal fire.

But perhaps they worship lightning. Why do they worship these things? They are moved not by their own motions but by God’s command, just as the sun and moon, the rains and courses of the stars, the movements of the winds, and the passage of the clouds are.

They therefore venerate the air and the spirit of the winds. But these things serve the Lord of all, as it is written: “He will blow with his spirit, and the waters will flow” (Psalm CXLVII). [lacuna] “fire, hail, snow, ice, storm-wind, which carry out his word” (ibid.).

The pagans worship the circle of stars, perfected by God the Craftsman and arranged with [Col. 0784C] distinguished beauty for the adornment of the world.

They worship the water, which is poured out through the Creator’s generosity for the use not only of human beings but also of cattle and all other things.

They worship the sun and moon, although we see the sun, both at its rising and at its setting, run its course in the manner appointed for it. From this it is understood that no one can run continually and persist in his service unless he is under the Lord and has one who commands him.

Nor would the moon undergo increase or decrease except by the will and decision of the Creator; and if the sun were in its own power, it would shine with perpetual light. [lacuna] to serve, and the stars to follow their own order; the sea, too, to be kept within its boundaries.

And therefore the most holy prophet cries out, [Col. 0784D] saying to the Lord our God: “How magnificent are your works, O Lord! You made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with your creation. This sea is great and spacious; there are creeping things there without number, animals small and great” (Psalm X).

725 This is the Lord our God, of whom one of the saints said: “He hung the heavens aloft in sublime height, solidified the earth, cast down by its massive weight, spread out the seas in their freely flowing waters, and arranged all these things, full and adorned with their proper and fitting instruments.”

When, therefore, you see [lacuna]

[Col. 0785A] The pagans also worship mountains, trees, springs, and rivers, where oxen, sheep, and every kind of animal graze, walk, and crawl.

For their statues and idols, though honored with due reverence, are covered by spiders, pierced by moths or worms, inhabited by mice, and trampled by flies. They neither defend themselves from fire or rain nor avenge themselves against robbers or thieves.

Therefore Saint Cyprian rightly said to the pagan Demetrian: “Be ashamed to worship those whom you yourself defend; be ashamed to hope for help from those whom you protect. For what could those who worship them receive from them, when they cannot defend themselves against those who do not worship them? Just as it does not matter to them by what means they are worshiped, so they do not perceive by what means they are harmed.”

[Col. 0785B] But the pagans say: “We worship the gods, or goddesses, who are said to be in heaven.”

To them we reply: If you mean and worship those gods whom we hear recited in your books—namely Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, Apollo, Vulcan, Aesculapius, and countless others—and if you call Juno, Minerva, Diana, Cybele, Latona, and the rest goddesses, then, if you call all of these gods, why do you place some among the stars and not others?

For you say that Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and Mercury are in heaven, but you do not say this of Neptune, Apollo, Vulcan, Aesculapius, and the others. Or perhaps the latter committed some sin while the former committed none, and for that reason you assert that the former possess the heavenly regions, although it is more evident that all of them [lacuna] human beings and [lacuna] among human beings.

[Col. 0785C] Behold, we know that Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and Mercury, among others, committed unspeakable crimes. Does not your leading poet Virgil, [Note:

* Aeneid*, book VIII, line 319.]

—the poet whom you venerate above all and whose verses you still honor today—thus proclaim concerning Saturn, saying:

“Fleeing Jupiter’s weapons and an exile from his lost kingdom”; hence Latium also received its name from his hiding place, because he had hidden safely in those regions—that is, because he had fled and hidden in the territory of Italy. And again he says:

726

“Faunus is the father of Picus; and he traces you,

Saturn, as their ancestor, you, ultimate source of the blood.” [Note: Virgil, book VIII, line 47.]

He was the first to introduce the impressing of letters and the minting of coins in Italy; hence the treasury is called Saturn’s treasury. He was also a cultivator of rustic life; hence he is depicted carrying a sickle.

[Col. 0785D] When he was seized by insane fury, he devoured his own sons. He also escaped with his head covered, so that he would not be recognized, and is represented in this manner in your shrines.

Jupiter, his son, was taken away from his mother. [lacuna] [Col. 0786A] [lacuna] the island has a tomb. [lacuna] he lies despised. [lacuna] Hence Virgil said: “cre[lacuna] in the middle lies an island.” [lacuna] He briefly recalls his crimes, saying: [Note: [Col. 0785D]

“But I, who walk as queen of the gods,

Moreover, should he, as a suppliant, offer honor at the altars? [*Aeneid* I, line 50.] “Both sister and wife of Jupiter, and,” he says, “the honors of the abducted Ganymede.” See how detestable—indeed, how utterly abominable—this Jupiter must be regarded, since he wished to have his sister as his wife, to say nothing of his other crimes. Alas! The names of piety that are considered holy among saintly human beings have become vile sacrileges among the pagan gods.

For what shall I say about Mars, who was born among the Thracians [lacuna] [Col. 0786B] [lacuna] of the infernal regions, but [lacuna] is said to possess? Yet you are not ashamed to say that the sun had a daughter and that the moon loved Endymion. What believer would not grow angry at such madness of yours? Who would not judge you, persisting in such things, worthy of every punishment?

You likewise say that Saturn is the son of Heaven, and again that Jupiter is his son; or rather, you lie that he begot Minerva from his head, [lacuna] from his thigh, and many other things. [lacuna] For your goddesses, [lacuna] whom you assert to be worthy of veneration, are comprised within the vice of obscenity. [Col. 0786C] Of these, you say that Venus alone is in heaven and you place her among the stars. [Note: [Col. 0786D] Cicero explains from what source these names of the gods derive in Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods.] Why not, I ask, Juno, Minerva, Diana, or the others as well? [727] Is it because you say that Venus is beautiful, and for that reason declare that she dwells in heaven, while you assign [lacuna] of ugliness to earthly dwellings?

Why do you place that most shameless woman among so many men in heaven? What does she claim for herself? Is she someone’s wife, mother, sister, or daughter? But if she is none of these, and you say that she is in heaven solely because of her beauty—although she was a prostitute—see how wicked it is to say that a criminal beauty is in heaven, while you do not say this of Minerva, whom you call chaste and wise. It is clear that you are carnal rather than spiritual. [lacuna]

[Col. 0786D] [lacuna] the religion which [lacuna] your ancient [lacuna] lights with [lacuna] pictures and images, and you delight in such [lacuna] of yours.

[Note: [Col. 0786D] Stage spectacles were first brought from Greece into Italy. I say this because history, which refutes those who deny it, shows that the Romans did not introduce into the worship of their gods those same games, in which the poets’ fictions reign, through uninstructed devotion; rather, the gods themselves, so that the games might be solemnly presented to them and consecrated to their honor, brought this about by ordering it harshly and, in a manner of speaking, extorting it, [Col. 0788D] and by [lacuna].]

Why do the most impure actors today, amid your applause, represent in the theaters that shameless Venus herself and the adulterer Mars, and that Jupiter, the chief of vices, transformed—with all his thunderbolts, that is, his magical arts—into earthly loves with [lacuna], now streaming down in a shower of gold [lacuna]?

For “all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law” (Romans II). Yet the pagans are not ashamed to speak of so many gods and goddesses, saying that Saturn begot Jupiter or the others. But if the gods were born then, why are they not born even today? Unless perhaps, as the holy Cyprian also said, either Jupiter has grown old or Juno’s capacity for childbirth has failed. [Col. 0787B]

The pagans also observe the flight of birds and the calls of ravens or jackdaws, and in their entrails [lacuna] [lacuna] they inquire, but we know that what [lacuna] threatens cannot be avoided, nor can we [lacuna] the dangers that impend. To them we say: if future events can be avoided through observation, then human beings are not governed by fate or by an immovable decree, since by their own choice and caution they can avert what threatens them. But they say: “They cannot be averted.” Let us say to them again: Why, then, do you inquire? Why do you perform sacrifices in vain? Why attend to the calls of birds? Why watch their flight? [lacuna]

Do you wish to know how much prayers avail, how pleasing to the Lord God are the prayers of the faithful? Search our books, books that are clear and transparent in their truth. Inquire about Noah; inquire about Moses; inquire about Joshua, son of Nun; inquire about Elijah or Elisha; inquire about Jonah, or about the other holy prophets and blessed apostles, the disciples of Christ, to whom the Lord granted everything that their faithful prayer requested. From them, then, you will learn how much can be obtained from God by you. [lacuna]

And [lacuna], after [lacuna], having endured shipwreck amid raging waves and the crashing [lacuna] of storms raging everywhere, through the dangers of the sea and the terrifying crests of towering waters, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, escaped safely; and whoever, having poured out prayers to the Lord, deserved to be preserved unharmed with all his companions, so that the storm itself marveled that, while everyone everywhere was perishing, one person alone with his companions had survived. Let the pagans say, if they can, [Col. 0788A] what fate could have accomplished here: did fate kill everyone in that flood, or did fate grant life to this one man?

[Note: [Col. 0788D] Here Maximus points to the patriarch Noah, who, as recorded in Genesis VII, escaped safely from the waters of the Flood. Scripture says: “Noah alone remained, and those who were with him in the ark.”]

If fate killed everyone, why did it not kill this man also? If fate granted this man life, why did it not grant it to everyone? In truth, the power and might of almighty God undoubtedly accomplished these things: he assigns punishments to the obstinate and contemptuous, and salvation to the just and to those who observe his commandments. [lacuna]

What shall I say of him who is known not to have fallen short of his teacher Moses in any excellence of virtue, and who, setting out to conquer the city of Jericho, by his prayers—like a kind of thunderbolt—cast down Jericho’s walls without delay and demolished them to their foundations? He also halted the sun’s swiftest courses above Gibeon by praying (Joshua X), and by his command restrained the moon’s paths above the battle lines until he had overcome all his enemies. [729]

What shall I say of the most holy Elijah, who by the merit of his faith carried the key of the rains upon his lips, by which he closed [lacuna]?

[lacuna] did not abandon the belief of the shipwrecked; he received from the Lord everything he requested, and, like a faithful ship, was saved and brought to shore, presenting it intact just as he had received it. All the holy [Col. 0788C] prophets, through the merit of their faith, performed many acts of virtue and many wonders, as we have said. The blessed apostles also restored those whose strength had been broken; they asked nothing from fate, but healed the sick and raised the dead. They accomplished everything by God’s power and through Christ’s help.

[lacuna] let us say to the pagan gods, [lacuna] most beloved [lacuna]. [lacuna] and of our faith [lacuna]. Let us speak: there is one [lacuna] Lord God, and the holy [lacuna] says [lacuna]. He forms all things that exist by the word of his majesty and wisdom, and completes them by reason [Col. 0788D] and almighty power. He cannot be seen; he is more glorious than sight can perceive and greater than sense can estimate. Therefore we estimate him worthily when we call him beyond estimation.

This, I say, is the Lord our God. Even the pagan philosophers, overcome by reason, although they do not venerate him, nevertheless acknowledge him as God. They do not venerate him because, to the injury of the Creator himself, they assert that there are many gods and, as we have said, offer the Creator’s honor to creatures. [Col. 0789A]

[Note: [Col. 0789D] The Apostle spoke of these things in Romans I: “They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, [Col. 0790D] and serpents. Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts for impurity,” and so forth.]

Therefore, whether they wish it or not, even the philosophers, constrained by the truth, assert that our Lord God is invisible and all-powerful. Among them, the distinguished Sosthenes denies that the form of this world can be seen and says that true angels stand beside God’s seat. Plato agrees with him in the same way: while proclaiming one God, he calls the others angels or demons. Hermes Trismegistus likewise acknowledges one God and confesses him to be invisible [730] and incomprehensible. This God, then, we confess in truth, know, and acknowledge.

We confess the almighty God, whose work is the world; who hung heaven like a vaulted chamber; who founded the earth upon the waters; who spread out the seas in their fluid expanse; and who, with wondrous balance, himself the Maker, sustains the entire mass of this world, composed on every side. He himself [lacuna] the vapor-bearing [lacuna] of the sun; he himself kindly and usefully prepared all living creatures with all their offspring. He himself [lacuna] springs, rivers, and hollow torrents; he himself the broad sea [lacuna] fields of the sea [lacuna] far and wide with waves [lacuna], and all things visible and invisible [lacuna]. He completed all things through Christ his Son, our Lord, as it is written: “All things were created in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible” (Colossians IV), as the apostle Paul bears witness.

Therefore, brothers, one God alone is to be worshiped, as it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Matthew IV). He alone is to be loved, as Scripture says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your understanding, and your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew XXII).

Who, I ask, is our neighbor, if not our Lord Jesus Christ, who, although he existed in the form of God, assumed the form of a servant? “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). He also said: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII).

And because it has been determined before God that one person cannot be a servant of both kingdoms, devote every effort to entering into the covenant and laws of the good king.

For this reason, when the true prophet was present with us and saw certain wealthy people negligent in the worship of God, he revealed the matter in this way [lacuna] and the rest, up to this point, St. Peter continues.

Christ therefore said: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” [Col. 0790C] (John XVII). Brothers, eternal life consists in this knowledge. For hear Scripture, which reports concerning the supreme God the Father and his Son Jesus Christ: “In the beginning,” it says, “was the Word”—that is, the Son—“and the Word was with God” (John I), with his begetter [lacuna].

Again we insert St. Peter’s exposition: “Acknowledge,” he says, “the truth, and separate yourselves [lacuna] deceiving [lacuna] [lacuna] writings [lacuna].” [Col. 0791A]

Of the gods [lacuna] [lacuna].

As one [lacuna] has many under him—you speak, for example, of prefects, consuls, tribunes, and the other authorities—so we suppose something similar, provided that the one God is greater than all, and that those whom you call gods have been appointed in this world in the likeness of the authorities we have mentioned. They are subject to the greater one, while we, because they are in this world, regard them as administrators.

Hear, then, you pagans, how in these very arguments that you advance for deception you confess the reasoning of the truth. You say: “Since God holds the judgment of Caesar”—[sic]—“and those who are called gods preserve the appearance of authority, then observe the example of Caesar, as you have proposed. Know that just as none of the judges or administrators—whether prefects, proconsuls, commanders, or tribunes—is permitted to assume the name of Caesar, since otherwise both the one who assumed it and those who bestowed it would perish together, so you must understand the same thing here. If anyone bestows the name of God upon another besides him, and that person accepts it, both will suffer one and the same destruction—perhaps a far worse one than the servants of Caesar.” For the one who commits an offense against Caesar will receive temporal destruction; but the one who offends against the one who alone is the true God will suffer forever [lacuna]. [Col. 0791C]

[lacuna]

Other pagans say: “We do better still, since we give thanks both to the supreme God and to all those who are with him.” To them it must be said: This is like someone who, seeking a cure for his illness, calls both a physician and a poisoner, although poisoners can indeed harm him, while the true physician can heal him. But the true physician refuses to mix their poisons with his medicines, lest either harm be done to what is good or health [lacuna].

In the end, the elements are compelled, wearied by the crimes of the impious, to act [lacuna] against the goodness of the Creator. [733] Hence either the produce of the earth is corrupted, or the balance of the air is disturbed, or the sun’s heat burns with excessive intensity, or an immense force of rains or frosts is poured out. In [lacuna], and the face of death passes through in various forms. For creation would hasten to move against the impious in vengeance; nevertheless, God’s goodness restrains it [Col. 0792A] and holds it back from indignation against the wicked, commanding it to obey his mercy rather than be inflamed by human sins and crimes.

For God’s patience waits for the conversion of human beings while they are in this body. But if they persist in impiety until the end of life, then, when the soul—which is immortal—departs, it pays immortal punishments for its persistence in impiety.

“But we,” says the holy Peter himself, whose discussion from the history of blessed Clement, his disciple, we have taken up and joined to our own words for assistance—“we have been sent for this purpose: to disclose to you the hiding places of the ancient serpent, and, dissolving your enmities, reconcile you to God [lacuna] and make you pleasing to him [lacuna].”

But perhaps [lacuna] nothing and [lacuna] God [lacuna] we can arrive at knowledge [lacuna] how he governs human affairs [lacuna].

Through this God is shown to have not only care for human beings but also a certain great affection for them, since he has consigned such splendid elements to their service.

“But,” you will say, “what harm is done to God if these things too are worshiped by us, if one of you gives honor [lacuna]?”

[lacuna] or another [lacuna]. God is not [lacuna] [Col. 0792C] [lacuna]. Since you were able easily to detect these matters, but were unwilling to direct your attention toward examining them, it is certain that you are hindered from knowing God not by impossibility but by the vice of laziness. For if you had wished to do so, from these very useless images you would surely have received a path to understanding [lacuna].

For Jannes and Jambres also practiced magic against Moses [lacuna].

It is [lacuna] permitted by the devil for a time to do certain things in order to deceive unbelievers, so that [lacuna] the minds of the faithful [lacuna] in faith, and so that they may be perfected in the love and fear of God and not be overcome by evil [lacuna].

The soothsayers also speak of future and hidden things, and [lacuna]. Sometimes, by worshiping [lacuna], they declare future and hidden things. They do these things not by divinity but by malignity or curiosity, and, as has been said, in order to lead astray and deceive. They are wandering and insincere spirits, flying about and investigating.

For truly those are holy servants, and truly those are ministers of God, who perform signs that bring salvation, give life to the dead, and drive out demons. Thus they are known truly to belong to God: by his light they enlighten the blind, by his power they heal the sick, and by his mercy they raise the dead. In Christ’s name, in imitation of him, they both do and have done many things through the power of faith. [Col. 0794A]

Therefore let us pursue their charity and follow their innocence, so that we may preserve their forgiveness and gentleness. Assisted by the eternal God, let us always offer honor and eternal praises to his eternal and blessed Son, worshiping and confessing the Father and the Son in the Holy Spirit, to whom be glory and majesty forever. Amen.

Thanks be to God, always.

# TREATISE V: AGAINST THE JEWS

[Col. 0793]

[Col. 0793B] 735 The Jews speak according to the letter, not according to [lacuna]. Reason urges us [lacuna], brothers, to speak for a little while [lacuna] against the Jews, or [lacuna] to them in the presence of your holiness [lacuna]. First, then, I must show that this people was rejected by divine providence from the beginning of the world, while the succeeding people was chosen and taken from the nations—that is, the Christian people. To establish what we say more certainly, let us begin with the very first man, Adam.

Adam fathered Cain and Abel. Cain, the elder by birth, represented the Jewish people. He was rejected because of his crime, while Abel, the younger, was accepted, and he represented the Christian people. For God rejected Cain’s sacrifice, but accepted Abel’s sacrifice. Abel himself was killed [Col. 0793C] by Cain, and another son of Adam was born in his place, named Seth. Consider the mystery. Abel is interpreted as “mourning,” Seth as “resurrection.” Therefore, in these two younger brothers [lacuna].

[lacuna] because he is commanded to leave his former errors and ancient vices, to depart from there, and to become a great nation—that is, the faithful Christian people spread throughout the whole world. Hence Scripture announced, saying: “The nations [of Christians?] shall be at the head, but the unbelieving people at the tail,” that is, the Jews.

Abraham fathered two sons, Ishmael and Isaac. Ishmael, the elder by birth, was born of the slave-woman Hagar; Isaac, the younger, of the free woman Sarah. Our apostle Paul, who himself had believed as one of the Jews, said: “We are no longer children of the slave-woman, but of the free woman” (Galatians IV). [lacuna] You see that the former is rejected and the latter accepted.

[Col. 0794B] Jacob himself also blessed the sons of Joseph, his younger son. Now you understand that in Joseph, the younger son, he represented the Christian people. Jacob therefore blessed those two boys and placed his left hand—that is, his left hand—on the head of the elder, and his right hand on the head of the younger, to show that the younger would become more honored and greater.

Moses too received the tablets, but because of the people’s sin he threw them down; then he received and preserved a second set that had been written anew,

[Note: [Col. 0793D] Moses therefore cut out two stone tablets like the former ones, and rising during the night he went up Mount Sinai, as the Lord had commanded him, carrying the tablets with him. Exodus XXXIV.]

and in the sacred books [lacuna], [lacuna]:

[Note: [Col. 0793D] “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your people and from your brothers; you shall listen to him, just as you asked the Lord your God at Horeb, when the assembly was gathered and you said, ‘I will no longer listen to the voice of the Lord my God,’ etc.”]

“A prophet from your people and from your brothers; listen to him as you listened to me. For every soul that does not listen to that prophet shall perish from his people” (Deuteronomy XVIII). He called Christ “the prophet,” because he is the prophet of his Father and God. But he is Lord and God of every creature.

Moses spoke of him again in the book of Genesis (chapter I): “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Here he identifies the Beginning with the Son, in whom God the Father made heaven and earth. Our apostle Paul, confirming Moses’ statement, said that in Christ all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions (Colossians I), and so forth, as follows there.

“In the beginning, therefore, God made heaven and earth.” The Beginning is Christ, who spoke through Solomon:

[Note: [Col. 0794D] This passage is taken from Proverbs VIII, where we read: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything, from the beginning,” etc.]

“The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works” (Proverbs VIII). [lacuna] [Col. 0794D] or the globe of the earth was founded [lacuna] he might prepare heaven [lacuna] Christ the Lord, the Son of God, is himself [lacuna].

[lacuna] he said [lacuna] “Let there be a firmament,” and the firmament was made; “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, so that they may shine upon the earth”; and he made two lights, the greater and the lesser. The greater light was made for the beginning of the day, and the lesser light for the beginning of the night (Genesis I).

God therefore spoke, and God made. Listen further: God says, “Let us make man in our image and likeness”; and God made man; “in the image of God he made him” (Genesis I).

[Col. 0795A] Perhaps the Jew says: “God spoke to the angels.” He is refuted by what follows: “And God made man.” For it was not the angels who, as he says, made man, but God made man. God spoke, and God made—that is, the Father commanded, and the Son fulfilled.

Consider also what is written about Abraham (Genesis XVIII), that God appeared to him at the oak of Mamre. Later Scripture says, in the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (the same place), that the Lord rained fire and sulfur upon those cities from the Lord. Thus there are the Father and the Son: from that Father—that is, by his command—the Son rained fire and sulfur.

In the Son, therefore, God made heaven and earth, although he existed before heaven and earth. Were not the angels, archangels, and all the spiritual powers and authorities made before them? Therefore, when it says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” it is clear that he spoke in Christ. In reference to him David also said: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Psalm XXXII).

This is the Son of God, of whom David himself again said in the second psalm: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” Consider the second mystery: in the second psalm this is said [lacuna] the second Son [lacuna] but by day [lacuna]. Most certainly God begot the Son whom he begot—not as human beings beget, but as it was fitting for God to beget: impassibly and incorruptibly, from himself. One begot one; the solitary, the solitary; God, God; king, king; the unbegotten [Note: “Unbegotten” is used here to mean “not made.”] the unbegotten; the Father, the Son; the Author, the Word; the creator, the creator; eternal, eternal; Spirit, Spirit; light, light; radiance, radiance; pious, pious; good, good; merciful, merciful; perfect, perfect.

To this Son David again spoke, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0795D] The Vulgate reads, in Psalm XLIV: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom,” etc.]

“Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of righteousness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Psalm XLIV).

See how, speaking to God, he said to him: “God, your God, has anointed you”—that is, your Father has anointed you, the Son, with the oil of eternal joy, of the eternal sacrament and heavenly mystery, or further [lacuna].

“ The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Psalm CIX) [lacuna]. This king had a Lord to whom his own Lord God had said: “Sit at my right hand.” Who is this Lord to whom God the Father spoke, if not our Lord Christ, his Son?

Hear the Father again speaking of his Christ: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ; I shall clothe his enemies with shame” (Psalm CXXXI). “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ”—that is, the Church shining with his light and burning brightly: the number of the faithful who, having received the light of truth and belief in their hearts, do not abandon the darkness of unbelief [Col. 0796A] and ignorance.

“I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.” Again, in holy John, we understand the lamp to be spoken of as illuminating the people concerning this Lord and Savior and his future coming in the flesh.

The most holy Isaiah also spoke: “Strengthen,” he says, “the weak hands and the feeble knees”; and shortly afterward he says: “Our God will render judgment; he himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear” (Isaiah XXXV), and so forth.

Baruch also spoke of Christ:

[Note: [Col. 0795D] The Vulgate reads: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him. He discovered every way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings.”]

“This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. He discovered every way of wisdom and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel, his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III).

Thus it was not God the Father who appeared and lived among human beings, but the Son of God. Concerning the coming of his incarnation, Isaiah again announced: “God has revealed his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the nations shall see him, the salvation sent by God, upon the earth” (Isaiah LII).

He repeats this again and says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted as “God with us” (Isaiah VII). “God with us”—that is, God in a human being, the Word in flesh, majesty in a body.

He descended like rain upon a fleece (Psalm LXXI), without display, without uproar. The heavenly king entered the world in humility, intending to give everyone the triumphs of immortality and peace. He assumed a human body so that, for a time, he might cast a shadow over his radiance through the veil of the body, and so that God might speak to human beings through a human interpreter.

[Col. 0796C] In that temple of the body was God, so that he might make mortal humanity immortal.

But the Jew does not believe; nor does the pagan believe, for they do not believe that a virgin gave birth without union with a man. Let them hear and believe concerning the Savior’s birth from a virgin, what the holy angel sent by God the Father said to that most holy Virgin Mary: “The Holy Spirit,” he said, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke II).

That immaculate Spirit—that is, the pure, holy, secure Son of God—assumed human flesh from holy Mary and, by his own power and capacity, made flesh for himself. For if he granted this to certain birds, that they should conceive from wind or dust without males, and if they observed this, how much more could he himself, as has been said, [Col. 0796D] fashion a body for himself? And if birds produce living young from eggs by the shadowing of their wings, and the earth without intercourse produces certain animals, such as worms and other creatures, how much more could God, by wondrous means, build for himself among human beings a temple of his own body?

[Note: Saint Maximus says the same concerning the generative power of the earth in his homily on Palm Sunday: “For the worm is produced without any external admixture of an alien body, but from earth alone and pure,” etc.]

If he had wished, he could have made a body for himself from stone, wood, water, or earth, since he had also fashioned the first man Adam from the clay of the earth. He chose to assume human flesh in order to show that he had come for human beings.

For this reason he also willed to be born in our likeness, to die, and to rise again, so that he might show us in himself both how to die and how to rise again, and might reveal to us the hope of the resurrection to come.

[Note: [Col. 0797D] Saint Maximus pursued this same truth, almost in the same words, when explaining the article concerning the resurrection of the flesh in his homily on the handing down of the creed.]

But the Jew says: “Then God had to be born from a woman.”

[Note: [Col. 0797D] Saint Maximus said in Homily I on the Nativity of the Lord: “Thus the Word became flesh—not so that God might be emptied in man, but so that man might be glorified into God.”]

Christ’s flesh was born from a woman, whom God had made; yet the majesty of Christ cannot be defiled in the flesh. For if the shining sun is not polluted by any touch, how much less could the Lord of the sun be polluted, even though the pure touched what was pure.

We have him himself as the guide of our journey, because he is the way to the Father; the prince of light, because he is the truth, who poured into us the light of truth; the author of salvation, because what was made in him is life, and with the Father he gives life to all. Through him we always give thanks to God the Father, brothers.

But the unbelieving Jews still sometimes dare to disparage the Christian faith and insult God’s faithful people. Therefore we must once more review the divine books, which will confound them by their manifest truth and make them understand that they are plainly without hope and without faith.

These are the Jews whom holy Stephen rebuked in a clear voice, saying: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who announced the coming of this Just One, and you have become his betrayers and murderers” (Acts VII).

This is what holy Stephen said. Blessed Paul the apostle likewise says of them: “Always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth.”

[Col. 0797C] “Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth—people corrupted in mind and disapproved in judgment” (II Timothy III).

They say: “We have circumcision, and we are children of Abraham.” To them the Lord rightly said: “If you were children of Abraham, you would certainly do the works of Abraham.”

“We have circumcision,” they say. To them we reply: “Would that you had the fragrance of Abraham’s faith, and not of your own faithlessness!” You are rather children of vipers, carrying poisons within yourselves: you inflict death upon your parents, and by killing others you prepare destruction for yourselves.

The prophet David says of you, O Jews: “They went astray from the womb; they spoke falsehood. Their wrath is like the wrath of a serpent” (Psalm LVII).

Our apostle Paul also says: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame; they set their minds on earthly things” (Philippians III).

Therefore they went astray from the womb and spoke falsehood; their wrath is like that of a serpent. With viperous bites you shed the entrails and blood of your parents, and, slipping on the treacherous ground of your crime, you rolled about in the wounds of others. By despising the precepts of the law, you fell through various guilt of crimes, as though down many precipices, by different catastrophes.

See now, if you can, how foul and disgraceful is one who stains himself with the blood of others. For we read [lacuna] which contains no understanding of [lacuna] my light, nor shows through the spirit [lacuna]. The Lord says to them: “You are born from the devil as father, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (John VIII).

For the devil, having changed himself into a serpent and using deceitful tongues, deceived the pious and still-untutored innocence of the first human beings in paradise through contrived wickedness. These people, following his madness, a serpentine generation, still strive to deny Christ, the Son of God.

Against them, with the help of the same Lord Christ, we have undertaken this disputation. We must still say to them: What is this that you claim when you call Abraham your father and assert that you have received his circumcision?

Abraham was justified by faith, not by circumcision. For Scripture says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called God’s friend” (Romans IV).

Abraham therefore was justified not by circumcision but by faith. He believed the word of God, was justified, received blessing from God—both he and the offspring of his faith.

Consider this, lest you think circumcision is the mark of the faithful. Before Abraham, all the holy ones were uncircumcised; they pleased the Lord by purity of mind, and more truly displayed the Christian people in themselves.

Run through the order set out in the sacred Scriptures, and you will find that all were as we say. First there was Adam himself, formed by the hands of God, who remained uncircumcised; then righteous Abel, Enos and Enoch, Noah and Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God. All were righteous, and, as we say, were neither circumcised according to the flesh nor subject to distinctions among foods.

As for Abraham, who is said to have received circumcision, that circumcision does not possess the reward of salvation; it was given as a sign of lineage [lacuna] the children of Israel, a second time [lacuna] had already first been circumcised [lacuna]. It must be understood spiritually: through the law—that is, through the precepts of the law—one must be circumcised from the worship of idols; then one must be circumcised through the Gospel.

The Jews still say: “We are children of Abraham.” To them we reply: “You are children of Abraham,”

[Note: In the homily beginning “Not inappropriately some days ago,” Saint Maximus says that Hagar was a type of the Synagogue and cites this same passage of the Apostle.]

but of the slave-woman, concerning whom it is written: “Cast out the slave-woman and her son, for the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman” (Genesis XXI; Galatians IV).

We, in the glory of God, are children of the free woman. Your father is Ishmael, from whom you derive your lineage; our father is Isaac, from whom we derive ours.

[Note: [Col. 0798D] Saint Augustine teaches the same in The City of God, book XVI, chapter 26.]

“In Isaac,” he says, “your offspring shall be called.” That most holy Isaac, whom his longing parents [lacuna], concerning whom it is said: “In your offspring all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis XX). It did not say, “in your offspring,” which is Christ [lacuna].

[Note: [Col. 0799D] In Homily I on Easter, which begins “The benefits of our God,” he said that this same Isaac, whom his father was to sacrifice, was a figure of Christ.]

This is the most holy Isaac, who was led patiently to sacrifice, the cherished offspring of a most merciful father. As we have said, bearing the image of Christ, he neither resisted his father’s command nor refused to undergo sacrifice.

This father, then, is proved to be ours. Your Jerusalem, the earthly city, is your mother; our Jerusalem, the heavenly city, is our mother. That one is yours, and it perished; this one is ours, and it remains forever. You are the former, we the latter—just as Ishmael came first and then Isaac; because “the first shall be last, and the last first.”

It is written:

[Note: [Col. 0799D] Saint Maximus alludes to these words: “He shall be at the head, and you shall be at the tail. And all these curses shall come upon you,” etc., “because you did not listen to the voice of the Lord your God, nor keep his commandments and ordinances which he commanded you,” etc.]

“The nations [of Christians?] shall be at the head, but the unbelieving people at the tail” (Deuteronomy XXVIII).

Isaac himself also fathered two sons, Esau and Jacob. Concerning them it had been said by a divine response to Rebecca, Isaac’s wife: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your womb; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger; for I loved Jacob, but hated Esau” (Genesis XXV).

But this has already been mentioned above. Jacob himself is also described as having had two wives: Leah, the elder by birth, whose eyes were weak; and Rachel, the younger, who was beautiful.

That Leah bore the figure of the Synagogue: she was weak, as has been said, in her eyes. Why weak in her eyes? Because the sight of the Synagogue was failing, and it often lamented itself in its unbelieving children.

Rachel, on the other hand, bore the figure of the Church. Of her it is written:

[Note: [Col. 0799D] In the Vulgate, Song of Songs I reads: “Your eyes are like those of doves.”]

“Your beautiful eyes are like doves” (Song of Songs I).

And again our apostle Paul says of her: “Having no stain or wrinkle or anything of the kind” (Ephesians V). Her sight was clear and spiritual.

Understand also how what the apostle speaks in mystery suits the Christian people: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly” (I Corinthians XV). “As was the earthly, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are the heavenly.” And “the law, when understood according to the letter, kills, but the spirit gives life” (II Corinthians III).

Moses, as we have recalled, received the first tablets, broke them, and threw them down, in order to show that your stony heart was broken and rejected, while the Christian people’s heart was suited to and worthy of being preserved by the divine laws.

Hence Scripture says of the Christian people: “They show the work of the law written in their hearts” (Romans II).

Understanding all these things, and considering still greater matters from the law and the prophets, the holy apostle Paul separated himself from you and did not wish to be yoked together with unbelievers, because “there is no fellowship between light and darkness, nor is there a share between the faithful and the unbeliever” (II Corinthians VI).

He turned especially to Christ, because he had been admonished by him to [lacuna] the oath of belief [lacuna] depart [lacuna] the Christian people [lacuna].

But the Jews say [lacuna] [lacuna] the sign of salvation among us [lacuna]. With the Lord’s sign all males and females alike are marked; with the Lord’s sign we are marked on the forehead, upon the two doorposts, with the blood of the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. Concerning him it had already been written in the law, and it is recognized as fulfilled in the holy Gospel, when you cried out, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew XXVII).

But it is beneficial for us to say this: “His blood be upon us and upon our children”—for you unto condemnation, but for us unto salvation. For you say it with one intention, we with another: you in rage, we in prayer; you in insult, we in humble supplication; you out of hatred, we out of love; you as grieving, we as always rejoicing.

You chose a robber, because every creature turns toward what resembles itself; we chose to serve the Lord. “We,” says the apostle, “belong to the Lord.”

You followed the robber who reproached the Lord; we followed the robber who worshiped and confessed the Lord upon the cross: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” The Lord said to him: “Amen, I say to you: today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII).

O blessed robber, who suddenly deserved such holiness and, at the very moment of death, passed into the light!

[Note: [Col. 0800D] In two homilies Saint Maximus extols the faith of the converted robber and eloquently teaches that he was transferred from the cross to paradise.]

Those two robbers also represented, one your image and the other ours.

You killed the Lord, and you rejoice. You killed him, indeed, but you did not kill him; you killed him by your will, but you did not kill him in reality, because Christ remains forever.

His body did lie in the tomb, but Christ reigned in heaven. For [lacuna] could not contain [lacuna] he is not enclosed in the tomb together with the body; much less could he be enclosed there divinely.

Christ therefore lives forever, just as the holy angel Gabriel also said to the glorious Mary: “He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke XI).

And in the seventy-first psalm it is said of him: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace.”

When he said:

[Col. 0800D] [Note: [Col. 0800D] What follows concerning the holiness of the Lord Christ’s commandments presupposes earlier material omitted by the copyist.]

“Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also; and to him who wishes to go to court with you and take your tunic, surrender your cloak as well.”

What is more just, what more useful, than to overcome impatience with patience, and to be overwhelmed by losses rather than to sin by seeking gain?

[Col. 0801A] For these are the Lord Savior’s commandments of righteousness, set forth in the holy Gospel. And, not to prolong the whole account, a little farther on it says: “and abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away” (Psalm LXXI).

“Abundance of peace,” because he himself is the purest fountain of peace, in whom there are no turbulent quarrels, no bitterness of wickedness, but every fullness of sweetness and every tranquility of goodness.

Of him the prophet David said elsewhere: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet. Blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Psalm XXXIII).

For the Lord said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you. By this all people shall know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John XIV).

Again he said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God. Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V).

“And abundance,” he says [lacuna] [Col. 0801B] [lacuna]. But afterward it is exalted and raised up when, with the Lord’s help, it is led to the heavenly kingdoms.

The psalm continues: “And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth” (Psalm LXXI)—that is, among all nations and throughout the whole world, wherever the expanse of Ocean spreads far and wide and encloses the boundaries of all lands.

It continues: “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall, and his enemies shall lick the earth” (the same psalm).

Those Ethiopians are the spirits of darkness, who, at the sight of the Lord—that is, at his coming—were disturbed [lacuna] [Col. 0801C] [lacuna]. But how are they said to lick the earth, as these people also [lacuna] and lick the earth? Is this because they love the earthly letter and carnal cunning, but do not seek spiritual grace?

The psalm continues: “The kings of the earth and the islands shall offer gifts. The kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents” (the same psalm).

Thus East and West are represented, as was again manifested in the holy Gospel when the Magi came bearing gifts—gold, frankincense, and myrrh: gold offered as precious faith to the king; sweet frankincense, a sacrifice of praise, to God; and myrrh as a sign and service of burial.

Again: gold for the king, frankincense for the priest, myrrh for the sacrifice, because the Lord Christ is king, priest, and sacrifice.

Because he is king, he says: “I have been appointed king by him” (Psalm II).

As for his priesthood, the Father says to him: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm IX).

The apostle Paul calls him a sacrifice, because he “offered himself as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant odor” (Ephesians V).

Gold, frankincense, and myrrh: the king seeks gold—that is, chosen hearts; God seeks frankincense, pure and good prayers as a fragrant offering; myrrh is for the burial of his saints.

Thus peoples from every direction bring gifts to Christ.

[Col. 0802A] The psalm continues: “And all the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Psalm LXXI).

We see this fulfilled, because everywhere the name of the Lord Christ is worshiped by all kings—at least by Christian kings—and by all nations.

But if there are some kings or nations unwilling to worship him, as you Jews are, the eternal prison remains; God’s judgment remains. “God,” says the prophet, “will come openly; our God will come, and he will not delay” (Psalm XLIX). He who came hidden in humility will come openly in power.

Then every flesh—that is, every human being—will see him, because we shall all stand before Christ’s tribunal, so that each may receive what belongs to his body according to what he has done, whether good or evil (Romans XIV).

For in that same psalm, at its beginning, he says: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Psalm LXXI), because the king and the king’s son is the Lord Christ.

At the conclusion of the psalm he says: “His glory shall fill the whole earth; let it be, let it be” (the same psalm).

And we, agreeing with the holy prophet and with the Lord’s voice, say: “Amen, amen”—that is, truly and faithfully. This repetition of the words contains within it a confirmation of the truth.

Thanks be to God.

The Jews are therefore plainly refuted. With God’s help, let us speak against them in this way—not with a desire to harm them or destroy them once defeated; far be that from us. A spiritual battle is being waged for the salvation of human beings; our weapons must not be carnal, but powerful through God.

Thus we desire to save them and, under the rule of our king Christ, [lacuna] convert [lacuna]. Let us not seek quarrels, then, because we are seeking the truth. We serve under a peaceful king and pursue the camp of peace.

[Col. 0802C] Therefore, as I said, we wish to lead them from the stormy waves of error to the harbor of salvation, and through the court of truth to introduce them into the royal house of our Lord, so that enemies may become friends and antichrists Christians.

Let them see the spiritual pasture; let them see, if they deserve it, the heavenly banquet; let them see the Lord’s table, and sing with us, together with the most holy prophet David:

“The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has settled me” (Psalm XXII).

And again: “How lovely are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm LXXXIII).

But the impious Jews resist this persuasion and prefer to die rather than be defeated, saying: “We worship one God, as it is written in the books of Moses”:

[Note: [Col. 0801D] Another passage from Isaiah XLIV and XLV: “I am the Lord, and there is no other; apart from me there is no God.”]

“You shall have no other gods besides me, and you shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone”; and: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy VI).

“This commandment,” they cry, “was given to our fathers, and we ought and must keep it.”

To them we say: “Then tell us why your fathers, abandoning this one God, turned to idols? They made a calf at Horeb and worshiped a carved image, exchanging their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass” (Psalm CV). “And they served the host of heaven.”

They reply: “Let them answer for themselves; we know nothing.”

To them we say: “Listen, then, and learn. This admonition was given by God in order to turn them back to himself” [lacuna] [Col. 0803A] [lacuna] [lacuna] [fragment uncertain]. From there they made groves for themselves (II Kings XXI), from there they presumed unlawful sacrifices, from there many gods, false inventions, and empty idols.

Therefore, wishing, as we have said, to turn them from such errors to the worship of his majesty, the Lord frequently thundered through the sacred utterance, saying: “You shall have no other gods besides me, and you shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone”; and: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy VI).

For, so that you may know with certainty what the Christian faith is, we believe in, worship, and revere that one invisible, incorporeal, immortal Lord, without origin and without end [lacuna].

[Col. 0803B] [lacuna] [lacuna] [lacuna] [lacuna] may deserve [lacuna]. We are devoted to proclaiming the truth; therefore, after what we have said, we still draw upon divine testimonies, so that we may prove that Christ is God and the Son of God, as we have already explained in part.

Almighty God the Father says to Moses in Deuteronomy (chapter XVIII) concerning Christ his Son: “I shall raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you; I shall put my word in his mouth, and he shall speak to them whatever I command him. And if anyone does not listen to that prophet, I myself shall punish him.”

[Note: [Col. 0803D] The Vulgate reads: “I shall raise up for them a prophet from the midst of their brothers, like you; and I shall put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command them. But whoever refuses to hear his words, which he shall speak in my name, I shall be his avenger.”]

Again, in the Books of Kings we read: “I shall raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do everything that is in my heart” (I Kings II).

And in the Gospel the Father himself says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew XVII).

[lacuna] he said; and [lacuna] him [lacuna] he says, “listen to him” [lacuna] [lacuna] the word is suitable to them and fitting for them. He is proved to be that one, the prophet who is Christ the Lord, the Son of God.

He is called the Father’s Prophet, but he is Lord of the Father’s prophets; rightly a Prophet, as the herald of his Author, while himself granting the grace of prophecy to the others.

For just as he is called Prophet and Angel by the Father, so it is written: “Behold, I send my Angel before your face, who shall prepare your way. Observe him and obey him, and do not be disobedient to him; for he will not fail you, because my name is in him” (Exodus XXIII).

Hence the Lord Christ himself also said in the holy Gospel: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; when another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John V).

David said: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Psalm CXVII).

But it is said [lacuna] [lacuna] the writings of the other prophets, and from them let us seek the rule of truth and repeat what we have already brought forward.

[Col. 0804A] Blessed Moses, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, said in the book of Genesis (chapter I): “In the beginning God made—”

God—heaven and earth. Observe at once that he began “in the beginning,” and called it “beginning”—which we understand to mean Christ, called the Beginning—in whom God the Father made heaven and earth. He made heavenly and earthly things alike in Christ, that is, by his power: he made them in the one who ministered at the command of the one giving orders; in him he made whatever was commanded and fulfilled it, because it is written of the Father: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and all things were created” (Ps. 32). Therefore, “in the beginning,” that is, [lacuna], God made heaven and earth [lacuna], “he created me at the beginning of his ways, for his works” [lacuna].

[Col. 0804B] Before the ages he founded me. And again, in the person of Wisdom, Christ himself says of himself through the prophet: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature” (Sir. 24). Therefore, in this Son and through this Son, as has often been said, God the almighty Father made all things, just as he said again in the psalm: “In the head of the book it is written of me” (Ps. 39).

But the Jew says: “The one who spoke also himself made.” To him we reply: “And what necessity was there for him to speak? If there were no other who could hear and act, was he saying to himself, ‘Let it be’?” But the Jew says again: “He spoke to the angels.” To him we reply: “But [lacuna] the angels made [lacuna], but it says, ‘and God made’ [lacuna].”

The Jew says: “How [lacuna] can God have a son?” [Col. 0804C] [lacuna] the invisible Jew, and in [lacuna] to whom again we reply as the Lord did: “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said: You are gods, and all of you are beloved sons of the Most High’?” If he called those to whom the word of God came gods and sons of the Most High, “and Scripture cannot be annulled”—[Note: [Col. 0804D] The text of St. John continues as follows: “Whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, you say, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?”]—“do you become angry with me,” says the Lord, “because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’? If I do not perform the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do perform them, even if you do not wish to believe me, believe the works” (John 10).

Next we ask: “What, in the Jews’ view, does that statement mean which David unquestionably uttered in the person of Christ: ‘The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you’?” And again, in the person of the Father, that most holy prophet David himself says to the Son: “With you is the Beginning on the day of your power, amid the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109).

“Whom did he beget?” [lacuna] he says. Therefore, do you believe that [lacuna]? We reply: Thus the prophet [lacuna], and we likewise believe: he begot [lacuna], but so that [lacuna] [lacuna] of the holy divine generation [lacuna], so that, as God begets, the Lord begot the Lord, light begot light, splendor begot splendor, the powerful begot the powerful, king begot king, one begot one, [Col. 0805A] alone begot alone, eternal begot eternal, power begot power, creator begot creator.

We have already said these things, and we say them as best we can. But that which is the Father and the Son, the Son of the Father, the Word of the Father, the power and wisdom of the Father, in whom and through whom the Father made all things, is inexplicable and ineffable.

Understand this Word to be the Son of God, whom he sent for the salvation of the world, as the prophet said: “He sent his Word, and healed them” (Ps. 106). Therefore, the Son of God is called the Word of the Father—not as you understand it in a fleshly and blameworthy sense, as though we were saying that God begot him carnally. For hear the holy prophet Isaiah speaking of Christ: “And who will recount his generation?” (Isa. 53). Can it be said or explained how the Father begot the Son, or how God brought forth the Word? [lacuna] I wish to understand [Col. 0805B] how you believe these things concerning Christ. To him we reply:

“Listen. It is written with the Father speaking: ‘With you is the Beginning on the day of your power, amid the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you’” (Ps. 109). The one who says “you” shows that another exists; that is, his Son, second in relation to himself, to whom he says “you.” The one who says “you” declares that there are two persons: the person of the speaker and the person to whom he speaks.

“From the womb,” he says, “before the morning star, I begot you.” Here I understand “womb” in the sense of majesty: the ineffable fullness and profound mystery, the incomprehensible wisdom of God. “Before the morning star I begot you”—or, before the adornment of heaven, or before the beginning of the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0805D] Among the divine Persons there is no priority of time, since all three are coeternal. Only an order among them is conceived: namely, the Father, then the Son, and afterward the Holy Spirit. Since the Son is truly a begotten Person, the Father, the beginning of generation or origin, must precede in the conception of him. And because the Holy Spirit is breathed forth from the love of the Father for the Son and of the Son for the Father, the breathing of both is regarded as the beginning of the Holy Spirit—not, however, as later in nature or subsistence, but as coeternal. Maximus indeed confesses him to be coeternal in many passages, so that there is no reason to fear that he used τὸ initium (“the beginning”) in a sense differing from the one we have judged.] For the Holy Spirit himself is called the morning star, [lacuna] who pours the light of truth and of sound faith into human minds, and who very often announced through the prophets the coming of Christ, the eternal Sun, as the morning star.

For this Lord Christ, the Son of God, was seen by many holy men even earlier, and is recognized as having appeared previously: by Abraham, Jacob, and Moses, and by the children of Israel in the pillar of fire and cloud. Concerning him God the Father had said: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you” (Mark 1). He himself also appeared to Joshua the son of Nun, and said: “I am the prince of the army of the power of the Lord” (Josh. 3). Certainly he is also the Son of the Father; and he is called his Angel, that is, messenger, as well as prophet, priest, servant, advocate, power, wisdom, and so forth.

Since he appeared to Abraham, hear Scripture saying (Gen. 22): “The angel of the Lord called Abraham from heaven and said: ‘Abraham, Abraham, do not stretch out your hand against the boy’” [lacuna]. [Col. 0805D] [lacuna] [lacuna] [lacuna] [lacuna] [lacuna] [lacuna] [lacuna] [lacuna] [lacuna] [lacuna] Therefore, in what follows [lacuna] you will find it written [Col. 0806A] that “the Lord rained fire and sulfur from the Lord upon the two cities, Sodom and Gomorrah” (Gen. 19).

Do you hear that the Lord rained from the Lord? Which Lord? From which Lord, if not the Son from the Father? For he himself also appeared to Jacob and wrestled with him. Hence Jacob himself said: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” (Gen. 32). Certainly he had seen Christ in the form of the body which he would afterward assume, and with whom he had wrestled.

For it is written of the Father: “No one has ever seen him, nor can anyone see him” (John 1). And again, God the Father himself says: “A man cannot see my face and live” (Exod. 33). [Note: [Col. 0806D] He says again: “You will not be able to see my face, for no human being shall see me and live.”]

That Angel of the Lord, who is Christ, appeared to Moses in the bush, in the fire. He himself said: [lacuna] “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and of Jacob.” He was called the Angel of the Lord when he first appeared in the fire; he himself [lacuna] afterward is said (Exod. 3) to have said: “I am the God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob” [lacuna]. He appeared [lacuna] to Joshua the son of Nun, standing on the bank of the river near Jericho [lacuna]—the Lord Christ himself, holding a sword in his hand. When Joshua said to him, “Are you for us, or for our adversaries?” the Lord said to him: [Note: [Col. 0806D] When Joshua was in the field of the city of Jericho, he raised his eyes and saw a man standing opposite him, holding an unsheathed sword. He went toward him and said: “Are you for us, or for our adversaries?” He replied: “No; but I am the prince of the army of the Lord, and now I come,” and so forth.] “I am the prince of the army of the power of the Lord” (Josh. 3).

This is the prince seeking a principality, and he is the king appointed by the Father, as he himself testifies and says: “But I have been appointed king by him” (Ps. 2).

And in a certain psalm David spoke in the person of Christ himself, saying: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High; call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you will glorify me” (Ps. 49).

In these little verses he warns that a sacrifice should be offered to God the Father and that he himself should be invoked, so that he may help his suppliants—as though he were saying: “Render to the Father the service of praise, and I will provide you the aid of one who protects; honor the begetter, and you will find me your helper.” Hence in the holy Gospel he himself also said: “I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me” (John 8).

We Christians therefore believe and confess one God, the Father, and one Lord of ours, Jesus Christ, his Son, of whom both the Law and the Prophets spoke. Through him we pray to God the Father, and we give thanks to him, because the Savior himself also commanded us in this way, saying to all who wished to believe: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17).

Therefore, knowing the commands of our Savior Christ, let us always praise through him the one God, the Father, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

[Col. 0807]

# Expositions of Saint Maximus, Bishop of Turin, on the Chapters of the Gospels. (C, G, S)*

## Notice

751 Formerly, Gennadius, in the Catalogue which he was the first to compile concerning the works of Saint Maximus of Turin, noted that Maximus had wisely expounded many chapters from the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles. After him, John Trithemius, a most learned Benedictine monk and another cataloguer of the works of Maximus, mentioned the chapters of the Gospels first. Until now, those readings have lain buried in such darkness that none of the later writers remembered them, nor did any commentator on Sacred Scripture give any indication that he had examined or seen them.

Nevertheless, some hope had dawned for us that Saint Thomas, who composed a Catena from the opinions of the Fathers on the four Gospels, might include some interpretations of Maximus. He does indeed contain a few, especially on Luke, but he did not derive them from the readings with which we are concerned. Yet this silence of a later age in no way prevents us from asserting that Maximus was the author of these readings. For it is well established that, in the course of time, many writings of the Fathers have been discovered which had lain hidden in ancient manuscripts and awaited the care and diligence of more recent critics. Among those who distinguished themselves in publishing such works were Sirmond, Mabillon, Leo Allatius, and Lucas d’Achery, Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur—to omit many others—and they strengthened ecclesiastical learning with great resources.

Apart from those two testimonies of Gennadius and Trithemius, we are also moved by arguments which carry considerable weight with us. First, the same themes that Maximus illustrated in his homilies and sermons present themselves here. Second, there is his constant use of the ancient Itala version of the divine books, which is characteristic of Maximus. Third, there is the admirable connectedness of Sacred Scripture; whether he explains the literal or the mystical sense, he displays not merely a perfect understanding of the word of God but also an exceptional sharpness of mind. Fourth, there is the style of the expositions: although it is somewhat plainer, many of his modes of expression shine through, so that they seem to have flowed from the same source. Fifth and finally, we add the singular agreement of these works with Maximus, whether one regards his homilies or his treatises; such agreement would be exceedingly difficult if another mind and hand had produced them.

These chapters, interpolated in various places, have come down to us from the manuscript of Verona, marked number 49; we have supplied some lacunae from the sentences indicated in Scripture. We have also corrected a considerable number of copyists’ errors, which must be attributed to the antiquity of the times, so that, insofar as we were able, we might restore a purer and more complete text. We hope that we shall do something pleasing to those devoted to sacred studies by placing at their disposal Saint Maximus, who rendered the finest service in interpreting the Gospels. Perhaps someone will arise who will rescue from oblivion Maximus’s Expositions on the Acts of the Apostles as well.

## I. On the Gospel Reading, Mark 6:38

[Col. 0807A]

Today it was read in the holy Gospel that the Lord Jesus fed five thousand men in the wilderness with five loaves and two fish.

[Note: [Col. 0807B] Saint Maximus expounds this same Gospel passage in a sermon entitled “On the Five Loaves and the Two Fish,” which begins: “The sweetness of what remains after the solemn celebration of the appointed days is usually greater,” etc.]

Everywhere the Lord Jesus heals all and feeds all. In him the blind find eyes, from him the deaf receive hearing, lepers are cleansed, the dead are raised, demons are driven away, and paralytics, with their limbs restored, are strengthened again. The lame run with firm steps, and all glory in his gifts. Even the waters of the sea and the swelling waves reverence him with obedient service as he walks upon them, their movements fixed and stilled.

Therefore today, as it was read, five thousand men are fed by the Lord from five loaves and two fish, [Col. 0807B] and twelve baskets full of fragments are gathered. Let us consider, brothers, the wonders of the Lord Jesus. He touches the loaves, and just as he multiplies the rains over the earth, so all things increase into abundant multitude. The bread grows, and in wondrous ways a shining harvest of fragments arises amid the crowds of those eating. Everything becomes full; the peoples are satisfied; and twelve full baskets are still gathered, [Col. 0808A]

corresponding to the number of the twelve beloved disciples, so that the Church may always abound in the apostles’ truth and be filled with the loaves of their teaching.

And so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0808B] The twelve apostles and the teachers who follow them are represented by the twelve baskets: outwardly they are despised by men, but inwardly they are heaped with the remnants of saving food. Bede, On the Gospel of Mark.]

## II. Also on the Gospel Reading, or on the passage where the Lord says, John 7:28: “Let whoever thirsts come to me and drink; whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

The most holy prophet David rightly spoke to him, whom he saw in the Spirit, suspended in devout thirst and kindled by immense ardor:

“As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Psalm 41).

That blessed sister of Martha, Mary, also burned with such ardor; the Lord nourished her with sacred words. [Col. 0808B] [lacuna] She by no means departed [lacuna] This good woman undoubtedly possessed the portion that could never be taken away from her. For she could never lose what the Lord had granted her to possess through his favor, since he himself gives spiritual water to those who thirst. Today he was saying:

“Let whoever thirsts come to me and drink” (John 7). [Col. 0809A]

This Mary, whom we have mentioned, appears, as it seems to me, to represent the person of the faithful Church. She prefers to cling to the Lord; the Lord continually builds her up by his address; she is drenched by the frequent overflowing of Christ’s springs. The Lord does not disdain her as she sits beside him and clings to his footsteps, but rather comforts her. He also deigned to wash the disciples’ feet, so that what Abraham had once done for him, he himself might take care to do for the sons of Abraham.

Does it not seem to you, I ask, that this Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet, [lacuna]—we say that she loses her person—[lacuna]? In the Psalms the divine word addresses her:

“Hear, O daughter; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house; and the king will desire your beauty, for he is your Lord God, and you shall worship him” (Psalm 44). [Col. 0809B]

Therefore, as has been said, the Church is watered from Christ’s springs. For the Lord Christ loves and has loved the Church, as the Apostle affirms, saying:

“Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, in order to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life” (Ephesians 5), etc.

Therefore, “let whoever thirsts come to me and drink.” Let us drink, I beg you, brothers, those heavenly waters flowing from Christ’s springs, and let us sing to that same Lord our new song. For the renewed people of the Church should sing a new song as well.

Let us proceed along the royal road, singing psalms, so that we may reach the Father of the Lord. You say to me: “What is this royal road?” Hear the Savior himself saying:
