“I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). [Col. 0809C]

It is called the royal road because he himself is our king. The prophet says:

“O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son” (Psalm 71).

This is the royal road; this is the fountain of life from which, while we live, the soul receives the satisfaction of every good. Again, the prophet spoke from the Lord’s own person, saying:

“Come, children; hear me. I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Psalm 33).

“Come, children.” He says “children” because “to all who received him he gave power to become children of God” (John 1).

Therefore, come, children; hear me. Come to me, the way, so that, freed from the errors and winding paths of the world, you may travel by a sheltered route to the Father.

“I am,” he says, “the way,” in which there are no tortuous turns of wickedness, no malice of perversity, no rocky or thorny places; rather, everything is clear, everything pleasant, everything innocent and safe, where the footprints of the faithful soul are not injured.

There is nothing harsh with the Lord, brothers; there is nothing dreadful with Christ, where paternal mercy has prepared everything pleasant.

Therefore, from this person the evangelist teaches (Matthew 9) that it is better to enter the kingdom of God with one eye, one hand, and one foot than, possessing two eyes, two hands, and two feet, to be cast into the gehenna of fire, “where their worm will not die and the fire will not be extinguished.”

Whoever hears this will undoubtedly be crushed—and would that he be terrified even more intensely—for by fearing the divine commandments he is freed from sin. For, as Scripture says, the fear of God drives out sin (Ecclesiasticus 1). Whoever is without fear cannot be justified.

Therefore, if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you (Matthew 5). For it is better to endure a wound to the body than to suffer the shipwreck of chastity, where the soul will perish together with the body.

But lest this amputation trouble you, whoever you may be, through a fragile understanding, and make you think that you must cut off the members of your body, especially those that are necessary: the Lord plainly commanded not that the members be cut away, but the vices; all impulses must be broken, as must the assaults of sins. Thus, wherever the enemy drives the mind toward the precipice of condemnation, there, with the wall of chastity resisting him, the devices of his sin may perish.

“If your right eye causes you to stumble”—that is, if you take illicit pleasure in seeing what could destroy you and prepare swords for you through inquisitive eyes—when instead you ought, with commendable modesty, to guard your eyes even with your fingers, cover them with the beautiful veil of chastity, and not release them to any wanton vices, but snatch them away, as has been said, and subject your sight to the reins of divine power, lest the soldier of Christ be conquered by the loose allurements of his thoughts, or the chaste woman be held by playful eyes in serpentine coils.

These things must be avoided, dearest ones. The Lord says:

“I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8). [Col. 0810C]

Let us therefore choose the radiant light rather than the error of darkness, so that, remaining in the light and aided by the light, we may be filled with the shared joy of a good conscience, always giving thanks to the Lord, [Col. 0810C] who is blessed forever. Amen.

## III. Also, the Gospel reading recited was Mark 4:14: “Whoever speaks sows the word.”

[Note: [Col. 0809D] The Vulgate reads: “The one who sows sows the word.”]

From this, dearest ones, let us speak about the Lord’s word, with the Lord himself assisting us:

“Whoever speaks sows the word.”

It is entirely certain that whoever speaks sows the word. He scatters words like seeds, but God grants the growth. Consider the comparison: while seed is held in the hand, it remains by itself; but once it has been thrown and sown, and has been watered by heavenly rain, it is rooted and grows by divine providence.

So also, while we hold the word in our mouth, it remains by itself; but once it has been thrown out and, so to speak, sown, through God’s grace it takes root in the hearts of individuals, grows, and multiplies in fruits.

Therefore it was rightly said:

“Whoever speaks sows the word.”

And what fruits the seed of God, the spiritual word, produces, hear:

“The fruit of the Spirit,” he says, “is hope, charity, joy, peace” (Galatians 5), and so forth.

The earth of the heart, which receives the Lord’s seed, bears fruit both in the body and in the spirit. Hence the Apostle Paul also said to his hearers:

“We have sown spiritual things among you; is it a great thing if we reap your bodily things?” (1 Corinthians 9).

Therefore, let the field of our breast be made fertile, so that it may receive the Lord’s seed and enrich us with a fruitful harvest. Let there not be thorns and thistles of worldly ill will in the earth of our heart, lest a harmful growth kill the good seed. Let there not be rocky places or the barren destruction of stones among you.

For the Lord rejects such a way, saying:

“I will inhabit them and walk among them” (2 Corinthians 6).

Rather, as I said, let the earth of our heart be good, producing fruits thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold—that is, let it multiply in every good thing and contain within itself the fruits of grain, wine, and oil.

The fruit of wine is faith and confession of the passion and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, who “washed his robe in wine and his garment in the blood of the grape” (Genesis 49), and drenched the winepress with the salutary fervor of the vintage. Living by the sacrament of his cup, they are so intoxicated by its spiritual fervor that they do not feel the storms of the world, its insults, or the punishments inflicted by persecutors, so that they proclaim and say:

“How glorious is your inebriating cup!” (Psalm 22).

Therefore, the fruits are grain, wine, and oil. The fruits of oil are joy, peace, sweetness, and serenity of mind, which, like oil, rises above and excels. Hence we are commanded to anoint the head, so that the head of our heart may shine with the splendor of faith.

May our mind therefore always abound in these spiritual goods, so that through the Son we may always give thanks to the Father. Amen.

## IV. Also on the reading of the holy Gospel, Mark 6:31

It was recited that, after John the Baptist had been killed by the wicked Herod, the Lord addressed his disciples and told them to go into a deserted place and rest for a little while.

John was killed by Herod: a holy man by an unrighteous man, a kind man by a wicked man. But let the enemy not rejoice, for “the righteous man, however death may overtake him, will be at rest” (Wisdom 4).

The prophet rightly said:

“How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly against your saints!” (Psalm 73).

Yet he was commanded to be killed at a banquet. What do luxurious banquets not force mortal hearts to do? What do boastful spectacles not compel reckless minds to undertake?

O crime! Amid the pouring of wine, the shedding of the blood of a righteous man is demanded. It was not enough for that unspeakable lust that such luxury was being practiced at the banquet: a holy man is killed.

A wanton girl, by dancing, ensnared the mind of the wicked Herod. She had learned from her wicked mother to pursue immodesty. Such a girl pleased Herod, to whom luxury could more readily be pleasing than an adulteress.

The devil found a means by which to kill the man of God: he caused the one who condemned luxury to be slaughtered by luxury itself.

But the wretched man does not know that “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115). It is so precious that, by dying, he possesses eternal life.

When the Lord heard about John, he went with his disciples to a deserted place. He gathered his flock to himself, lest they be harassed by the ferocity of wolves, and lest Herod, the persecutor of justice, again find people whom he might destroy.

He went into the wilderness to reject the company of the wicked and to display the wonders of his virtues.

The wilderness signifies the Church, which did not yet possess the cultivation of the apostles or the fruits of the divine word, but was still uncultivated and bristling with the thorns of vices and ignorance. Of it it was said:

[Note: [Col. 0811D] The Vulgate reads in the Epistle to the Galatians: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband.”]

“Rejoice, thirsty wilderness, and the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband” (Isaiah 54; Galatians 4). [Col. 0812A]

The Lord Jesus came there and multiplied the five loaves, so that the Church of God might abound in the manifold gifts of divine grace. We may understand those five loaves that are multiplied as the five bodily senses, which are multiplied into spiritual senses.

The two fish are the New and Old Testaments, by which human beings are nourished—but together with the bread, that is, with Christ, who is the bread of life.

Therefore he blessed and broke the loaves and gave them to his disciples to set before the people, and he divided the two fish among all (Mark 4). The loaves continued to increase, and the fish likewise multiplied; five thousand men were filled with the sweetness of Christ’s gifts.

They also gathered twelve full baskets of fragments. These twelve baskets signify the radiant fullness of the twelve disciples, just as in another passage the seven full baskets that were taken up, sevenfold in number, displayed an image of the Church.

For there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit by which the Church is fortified and restored. They are enumerated by the Apostle (1 Corinthians 12).

Christ gave this gift, this inheritance, to his people, so that whoever follows him may always be satisfied with heavenly goods from his abundance. Amen.

## V. Also on the Gospel reading, Matthew 9:18

A certain ruler came and worshiped the Lord, saying:

“Lord, my daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.”

And the Lord rose and followed him, and so forth. [lacuna] of the ruler, brothers. For he was saying within himself:

“God has sent his Son and has given everything into his hand.”

Therefore he said:

“Come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.”

Christ, who is life, gives life to the dead, heals the sick, cleanses lepers, drives out demons, strengthens paralytics, grants movement to the lame, illuminates the blind, and performs many wonders.

The girl had died and was already on the point of departing for the abodes below. But when the loving father of the girl saw her bloodless limbs, he sought the protection of the Lord Christ against the destruction and robbery of death.

The most merciful Lord gladly heard the request of the petitioner.

“And rising, he followed him.”

He says “rising”; therefore shortly before he had been sitting, waiting to see whether anyone would come to ask for his gifts.

“And rising, he followed him.”

The father was hurrying for his one daughter; the Lord was also hurrying for his one servant-girl, caring more for everyone than each person cares for his own.

And behold, in the crowd was a woman whom a troublesome illness had often bowed down and whom a discharge of blood had afflicted most severely; she no longer possessed bodily strength, but, exhausted of all human resources, retained faith alone in her heart. I think the Lord’s coming had suddenly made this faith known to her senses.

She approached, saying within herself:

“If I touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved” (Matthew 20).

She said this within herself so that she might be healed more quickly within herself. Christ was present to her thought, and immediately, at the very touch of the fringe, she was healed.

She touched the fringe and obtained a cure; through the solace of a small garment she found great healing. Thus the Lord Christ, rewarding the faithful, grants great things through small ones.

He then came to the ruler’s house and said to those who were mourning:

“The girl is not dead, but asleep.”

O Lord Jesus, how is the girl not dead but asleep, when there is no spirit of life in her?

“To me,” the Lord says, “she is asleep, for I shall raise her.”

And taking her hand, he raised her. Restoring her alive through the light of his splendor, he commended her to her devoted parents in the sight of all.

He is the one who will bring about the resurrection of all alike. To him be glory forever. Amen.

## VI. Also on the reading of the holy Gospel in which the woman with the discharge of blood is healed, Matthew 9:20

Our Lord and Savior Christ, whose wondrous works we heard today in the holy Gospel, says:

“I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). [Col. 0813B]

Let us therefore approach him, brothers, so that, walking through him along so blessed a path, we may be able to reach the Father.

Let us approach him as this woman approached him faithfully today, and let us touch him through faith.

Although the Lord Jesus is always surrounded by crowds—not only by apostles and prophets, but also by martyrs and all the righteous, together with the multitude of all the angels and heavenly powers—nevertheless, if we touch the fringe of his garment, and through that garment, that is, through the veil of his body, [lacuna] the propitiatory [lacuna] invoke the help of his majesty, and, aided by his heavenly gifts, carry out our work, then immediately we too shall be saved from our weakness. Nor will the flood of blood—that is, the dangerous storm of carnal vices—destroy us any longer.

This faithful woman did so; the holy Gospel related her story shortly before. Let us consider what this woman’s person signifies.

This woman, as it seems to me, displayed in herself a figure of the whole of human frailty. Previously placed in the affliction of the flesh—that is, established in the vices of sins—she could not otherwise be healed unless she received remedies from Christ.

Or again, she displayed in herself an image of the Synagogue, which for a long time had suffered from the blood of its members—that is, from the circumcision of its children. She had indeed spent much on physicians, that is, on the scribes and Pharisees, whose false and empty doctrinal sayings she sought, and from them she became even weaker.

After she saw Christ the Savior coming for the nations, she chose the better portion, passed over to faith, and began to think within herself, saying:

“If I touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved.”

Immediately, believing that God was present in the body, she ran to Christ with the strength of faith; touching the fringe of his garment, she received the fullest remedy of salvation from the divine springs.

Therefore the Lord said to her:

[Note: [Col. 0813D] The Vulgate reads: “Take courage, daughter. Your faith has saved you.”]

“Stand firm, daughter; your faith has saved you. Go in peace”—that is, walk securely in peace. Reject the wars of vices that were tearing your soul apart; always hold fast to the peace of faith and the fear of God, and be healed of your wound.

Every human being bore within himself the wound of sins, not only those from the Jews but also those from the nations. Coming to Christ, he is saved by him; through faith and the help of his blessing he is fortified.

To him be glory and dominion forever. Amen.

## VII. Also on the holy Gospel, Luke 11:27

As the Lord was speaking to the crowds and sowing words of piety and salvation in the hearts of all, a certain woman from the crowd cried out to him and said:

“Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that nursed you.”

The Lord said to her:

“Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.”

“Blessed,” she says, “is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that nursed you.”

This woman, brothers, moved by a devout understanding, praised the mother’s womb and praised the breasts of the mother; truly filled with the Holy Spirit, she rightly offered praise to the mother who had borne such an offspring and nursed such a child.

The Lord himself had certainly conferred an extraordinary blessedness upon that mother, because he had chosen her womb for his majesty as a kind of royal dwelling in which the heavenly King might descend.

She deserved to be the blessed and most blessed mother of the Lord, and, taken up from being a handmaid, she received the name of mother.

“Blessed,” she says, “is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that nursed you.” Blessed is the womb that bore the world’s Maker; blessed are the breasts that nursed the Lord of the world.

And the Lord said:

“Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.”

Those who hear the word of God—that is, Christ, the Word of God—“and keep it,” that is, keep his commandment.

Christ the Lord is the Word of God, who “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John 1).

Therefore blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it—that is, who keep the commandment of God and preserve it with careful observance.

The highest and perfect blessedness consists above all in fulfilling what is said.

Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it, because with attentive ears they preserve the divine words in their whole heart and make manifest by the works of their deeds that they have fulfilled in themselves what divine preaching had often commanded.

Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it, where it is said:

“You shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not covet; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not swear falsely. Honor your father and mother, and do not do to another what you do not wish for yourself; and whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same good things for them.”

Blessed, he says, are those who hear the word of God and keep it, so that by keeping and doing it they may obtain their reward.

After this, the Lord is reported to have said:

“This wicked generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Luke 11).

This most holy prophet Jonah carried within himself a figure of the Lord’s passion and resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0813D] In the homily on Easter beginning, “Although the benefits of our God are great and wondrous,” etc., Saint Maximus has a particular discussion of Jonah among the figures prefiguring the resurrection of Christ the Lord, and expresses the same ideas in other words. [Col. 0814D]]

When the sailors once cast him headlong into the sea, he was received by a sea creature and, snatched into its slimy throat, entered the gate of the beast’s belly. Held for three days and likewise three nights in the darkness of a fleshly prison, he was finally restored to the light and, as we said, displayed the future sacraments of the Lord’s mystery.

The Lord recalled this very event and signified by it his passion and resurrection. [lacuna]

And concerning the queen of the South, who came to hear Solomon’s wisdom (the same passage), let the Jews blush and be confounded: a woman seeks the wisdom of a man, while the scribes and Pharisees despise the wisdom of God.

She travels from afar to learn from Solomon, the son of David; these men despise the one who is present, both the Lord of Solomon and the Lord of David, although David himself says:

“The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 109).

Then, concerning the Ninevites who repented at Jonah’s preaching:

[Note: [Col. 0815D] Saint Maximus discusses the repentance of the Ninevites in a homily beginning, “We read in the prophets that, when destruction divinely threatened the city of Nineveh,” etc. Also in another whose beginning is, “We said on the previous Sunday,” etc.]

“And behold, something greater than Jonah is here.”

The Ninevites repented when a servant preached, but the Jews despise the Lord when he preaches and do not wish to repent, because they do not deserve to be saved.

Truly they are deaf adders, stopping their ears (Psalm 57), who do not listen to the voice of charmers or to the medicine compounded by the wise man. The Wisdom of the Father, the Lord Christ, repeatedly instructed them through Moses and the other prophets, but did not at all bring them back to the straight path of life, because he did not wish to break again the free will which he had given to humanity, lest he violate the freedom of the soul that he had recently granted, as we have said.

Therefore he left each person to his own judgment, reserving for himself the future examination, so that the guilty might be punished and the one who did not wish to commit a crime might be saved from punishment.

Therefore, brothers, let us search the words of the divine discourse with the full attention of our minds. And let us always offer praises and thanks through Christ our Lord to God the almighty Father, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

## VIII. Also on the Gospel reading, Luke 18:10

It was read concerning the Pharisee and the publican. When I consider the merits, prayers, and persons of these two men, I am filled with admiration for the goodness of God and the just judgment of Christ.

Pride was confounded; humility deserved to be justified. Tears found mercy; boasting was rejected. The Pharisee, who had rejoiced, was put to shame; the publican, who had wept, rejoiced and heard the judgment:

“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18).

And:

“Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Psalm 125).

And:

“The Lord is always near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit” (Psalm 33).

Let us consider, brothers, the text of this reading.

“They went up,” he says, “into the temple to pray, the Pharisee and the publican.”

It is rightly said, “They went up” [lacuna] and yet [lacuna] whoever raises his mind to God will be justified only in humility.

Let us therefore consider. Those men went up into the temple to pray. The Pharisee prayed to himself, saying:

“God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity: robbers, unjust, adulterers, or even like this publican,” etc.

But the publican stood at a distance and did not even wish to raise his eyes toward heaven; rather, he beat his breast, saying:

“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

And this publican went down to his house justified, rather than that Pharisee, because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.

First, in these two men I understand the persons of two peoples to be signified: the Jews and the nations.

The Pharisee therefore said:

“God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity: robbers, unjust, adulterers, like this publican.”

You would rightly give thanks [lacuna] you do not accuse at all [lacuna]. You would give thanks rightly if you had not exalted yourself with proud words. For when you accuse others, you condemn yourself, because you ascribe praise to yourself from the faults of others.

“Do not be high-minded, but fear.”

“God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity: robbers, unjust, adulterers, even like this publican.”

Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls. And God is able to make him stand (Romans 14).

You continue:

“I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess.”

This is hateful boasting in one’s own praise.

“I fast twice a week.” Let the one who fasts not judge the one who eats, and let the one who eats not despise the one who fasts, because the one who eats eats for the Lord and gives thanks to God; and the one who does not eat does not eat for the Lord and gives thanks to God (the same passage).

And yet, to whom are you saying these things? Do you not understand that you are speaking to him who knows everything, even before it happens?

“I give tithes of everything I possess.”

You give tithes, but you receive more than you give. You possess too much. Many crops increase for you through the divine rains, and although you give a small amount from much, you still reproach.

But the publican stood at a distance, bearing, as we said, the person of the nations, because the nations were held farther from God by their sins.

Therefore he stood at a distance and did not wish even to raise his eyes toward heaven. You see: the conscience of the petitioner has become his own judge. He punishes his sins within himself; he does not dare to come nearer; he does not dare to raise his eyes toward heaven; nor does he wish with polluted eyes to see the radiant light, because serene light stings and strikes eyes fixed in sorrow.

And so, bending toward the earth, he beat his breast, saying:

“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

And the Lord said:

“Amen, I say to you: this man went down to his house justified rather than the Pharisee, because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted.”

Therefore, brothers, let us also pursue humility and, with a gentle heart and humble prayer, beseech the Lord, so that we may obtain the help of his mercy, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

## IX. Also on the Gospel reading, Matthew 21:1

The Lord Jesus sent his disciples to bring him a young donkey on which he might sit, and the disciples went. When they found the young animal tied up, they untied it and led it to the Savior, and he sat upon it.

[Col. 0817A]

763 Listen, brothers: the truthful prophecy of the holy Isaiah was fulfilled in our Lord Jesus Christ. For Isaiah himself, the prophet full of the Holy Spirit, spoke about the Savior, saying:

“Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; behold, your King comes to you, meek and gentle, sitting upon a young donkey” (Isaiah 62; Zechariah 9).

What shall we say, brothers? First, we must admire the Lord’s great humility. Knowing that worldly ambition is useless, he did not delight in horses neighing with proud necks, nor in those moving with lofty strides; rather, he wished to be carried on the back of a lowly young animal.

He showed that he loves not the exalted and self-aggrandizing, but the meek and those regarded as worthless, who are considered, as the Apostle says, like the refuse of the world:

“God chose the lowly things of this world to confound the strong, and God chose the things that are cast aside and are not, to destroy the things that are” (1 Corinthians 1).

Therefore the disciples bring the young donkey, untying it.

Here, dearest ones, there is a great mystery. This young donkey signifies the people of the nations, who were regarded as lowly and cast off and were held bound by the chains of sins.

It is untied by the disciples, who were appointed by the Lord’s command for the salvation and freedom of the nations, and it is brought into the service of the Savior—that is, into the mystery of faith—so that it may carry the Lord within itself, and so that he may rest and dwell in it.

Through his dignity he will make a most precious people from a very lowly multitude, a royal and priestly race. He will order minds that were formerly sluggish by his vigilant command and submit them to the honorable yoke of devotion, so that they may serve him; and those in whom the Lord sits will be honored by others.

This is what we see today: religious people who honor the Lord, carrying Christ within themselves and possessing his discipline in their conduct, are honored by the other peoples.

Thanks be to God.

## X. Also on the reading of the holy Gospel, Matthew 14:20
Recited was the passage in which the Savior fed five thousand men with five loaves, and with two fish, and twelve full baskets were collected. Then there is the account of how once again he fed four thousand men with seven loaves, and seven baskets full of fragments were collected. A mute and deaf man is also healed: the Lord spat, touched his tongue, and put his fingers into his ears; then, looking up to heaven, he groaned and said, “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened”; and the bond of his tongue was loosed, his ears were opened, and he spoke correctly (Mark 7). He also heals a blind man by laying on his hands [Col. 0817D], and performs the other miracles of healing.

Everywhere, brothers, Christ the Lord is health to all: he feeds all, heals all, gives life to all, assists all, and has mercy on all, since he is the God of every creature. Sent by the Father, he graciously deigned to heal the sufferings of his image, removing the various afflictions of diseases. He blesses the loaves and likewise the fish, to show that he is the maker of land and sea, who by divine generosity grants all things both on land and in the waters. Twelve baskets and seven full baskets are gathered, so that it may be recognized that both the number of the apostles and the abundance of the churches overflow with Christ’s generosity.

[Col. 0818A] Then a mute and deaf man is healed; two impaired members receive medicine. The Lord spat, touched his tongue, put his fingers into his ears, and said, “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened”; and immediately the doors of his mouth and his ears were opened. His voice found a means of breaking forth, and his ears found a means of hearing sound. The impediments of his tongue were driven away, and the coverings of his ears fell. Through the Savior’s miracles he was found worthy both to give thanks to the Lord with his mouth and to hear the word of God from the preacher. He received faith through hearing, believed in his heart unto righteousness, and confessed with his mouth unto salvation.

And what of the blind man? The blind man too is healed; through the Savior’s hands he receives the brightness of his eyes. Darkness yields to light, and every blindness is driven away by Christ’s powers. Light is restored to the one who longs for it; and, having received so bright a splendor, the blind man rejoices, raises his opened eyes to heaven, and, receiving the sweetness of sight, gives thanks to God for all things. In Christ’s hands all blessings remain.

After first laying his hands upon him, he asked the blind man whether he saw anything. He said, “I see people as though they were walking trees” (Mark 8). His sight was still wavering; his vision was still clouded. Then, laying his hands upon him again and removing every confusion of darkness, he received clear light with a gentle radiance.

Let us always give thanks to our Lord Jesus Christ, whose dominion is forever and ever. Amen.

## XI. Also, on the Gospel reading, Mark 12:42

It was recited today that, when the Lord had sat in the temple opposite the treasury, he saw the crowds putting money into the treasury. He saw the rich putting in much [Col. 0818C], and one very poor widow putting in two small coins. Calling his disciples, he said to them: “Amen, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all the others. For they all contributed from what they had in abundance; but she, from her poverty, put in all the sustenance she had.”

O lover of mercy, who praises not the resources of the rich but the poverty of the poor! He especially commended the poor woman’s deed above all others, and declared her small offering more valuable than the wealth of those who had abundance, because he approves not the quantity of money but the devotion of the mind.

O blessed and righteous widow, who was worthy to be praised before the day of judgment! She put two small coins into the treasury, and by the gift of such a tiny alms acquired a great reward. And, as it seems to me, lifted and suspended by these two coins as though by two wings, she reached higher things. She found a place in heaven, though she endured hardship in this world.

The Lord also provided this testimony in the sight of the disciples, to prove that even a small almsgiving has a great reward with the Lord. The blessed Apostle says the same: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows with blessings will also reap with blessings” (2 Cor. 6).

[Note: [Col. 0817D] “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly,” etc. Thus the Vulgate.]

For God loves a cheerful giver. Whoever shows mercy will obtain mercy, and whoever shares with the needy will be heaped with heavenly rewards. David says: “I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread. All day long he shows mercy and lends, and his offspring will be blessed” (Ps. 36).

Therefore blessed Isaiah the prophet admonishes everyone and urges them to works of mercy, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0819D] “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless and poor into your house. When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. Then your light will break forth like the dawn, and your health will quickly arise, and your righteousness will go before your face, and the glory of the Lord will gather you” [Col. 0820D]. Thus the Vulgate.]

“Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless into your house. If you see a naked person, clothe him, and do not despise the members of your own offspring. Then your early light will break forth, your garments will quickly arise, righteousness will go before you, and the brightness of God will surround you” (Isa. 58), and so forth.

Therefore, brothers, from what the Lord graciously grants, let us give food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, lodging to the stranger; let us provide service to the sick and comfort to the afflicted. In the treasury, let us labor more frequently, according to our ability. For the eyes of the Lord always look upon us and are always present; in every place they observe the good and the wicked, and each person will render an account according to his works. To him be glory forever. Amen.

## XII. Also, on the Gospel reading, John 11:1

We heard today in the holy Gospel that Lazarus, who had been dead four days, was raised by the Lord, while the Savior himself prayed to the Father and said: “Father, I thank you because you have heard me; and I knew that you always hear me. But because of the people standing around I said this, so that they may believe that you sent me.” And afterward [Note: Perhaps, “he cried out.”] he wept: “Lazarus, come outside!” And immediately the man who had been dead came out, his feet and hands bound with strips of cloth, and his face wrapped in a cloth. He commanded that he be unbound and allowed to go (John 11).

Listen, brothers: Lazarus’s dead and lifeless body lay in the tomb, and his weak limbs, in which life had not been present for four days, were gradually dissolving in the grave. Christ prays to the Father, and the dead man receives strength; he entreats the Begetter, and the man is made firm. Then he cries, “Lazarus, come outside!” Death is terrified, hell trembles, and immediately at the Savior’s voice the animated body is shaken forth; the limbs wrapped in linen grow warm with vital movement.

The Lord commands him to be unbound and depart, lest he be thought a phantom. He commands him to be unbound so that the already-moist bindings and the body might be recognized, and that the newly restored limbs might be seen with their fresh pallor.

The Lord displayed in Lazarus a sign of the future resurrection, as also in the son of the widow and in the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue. For, dearest ones, all the dead could have risen together at one word of the Savior, unless he had called each one individually. Therefore he said to each: “Lazarus, come outside”; “Young man, I say to you, arise.” “I say to you,” he says, “for the present only: you, arise”; “Talitha cumi,” which means, “Girl, arise.” Thus he called each one individually, as I have said.

And he willed that what is seen in individuals should be understood as destined to occur generally in all. He is our Lord, who will come to judge the living and the dead; all will hear his voice, and those who have done good will rise to the resurrection of life, while those who have done evil will rise to the resurrection of judgment (John 5). To him be glory and dominion forever. Amen.

## XIII. Also, on the holy Gospel, Matthew 26:7

It was said that, while the Lord was reclining at a meal, a sinful woman came carrying an alabaster jar of ointment. Standing at the Lord’s feet, she watered them with her tears, wiped them with her hair, kissed them, and anointed them with ointment.

She did not dare to intrude shamelessly upon his most holy gaze. Since she stood in the darkness of sins, she could scarcely endure even the slightest rays of that gaze. She stood at his feet, worshiping the last part of his body, and, as though beneath the shade of his feet, sought relief from the burning of her sins. Believing that he had assumed a body for the remission of sins, she kissed his feet, watered them with her tears, and wiped them with her hair—feet with which he had gone through various places and had offered himself, a saving light, to every kind of infirmity.

Therefore this sinful woman repented and sought forgiveness through the very things—her eyes, hair, and lips—with which she had chiefly contracted the vices of sin. But the Lord, who always wishes to heal the sicknesses of the penitent, said to her:

[Note: [Col. 0820D] “Therefore I say to you, her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). Again: “Your sins are forgiven.” Thus from the Vulgate.]

“Your sins will be forgiven”; and again: “Many sins will be forgiven her, because she loved much” (Matt. 26).

O immeasurable compassion! He returned joy for weeping, and this heavenly physician heals the sick woman in her evils, so that where there had been despair over her offenses, there might be security of joys. He further said: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace. Flee the battles of vice; walk [Col. 0820C] in the peace of chastity, humility, sobriety,” and so forth.

## XIV. Also, on the Gospel reading, Matthew 5:14

The Lord said: “You are the light of this world. A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and place it under a measure, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to everyone in the house,” and so forth.

Therefore, he says to the disciples, “you are the light of this world: a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.” It is certain that a city set upon a mountain shines for everyone, is bright to everyone, and cannot be hidden.

The Lord spoke this figuratively, in parables, concerning the disciples. For the city set upon a mountain signifies the soul joined to Christ, which is established in him and, raised up by his faith, rises conspicuously above others. The soul is therefore called a city because divine laws and ordinances have been inscribed in it: “They show,” he says, “the work of the law written in their hearts” (Rom. 2).

Therefore a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden. Christ is called the mountain by the holy prophet Daniel. “It came,” he says, “upon the earth and became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth” (Dan. 2), growing in the minds of believers. He is also called the stone [Dan. 117] placed at the head of the corner, the cornerstone, which joined and united two peoples, like two walls coming from opposite directions—from circumcision and from uncircumcision—in one faith.

And rightly is he at the head, because he is the head of the Church; he is also called its foundation. For the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3).

[Col. 0821A] Thus he is both the stone at the head and the foundation below. Why below? Because Christ is both from above and from below: he is God and man, Word and flesh, living eternally and dead for a time; one aspect of Christ is impassible, another passible; one is before the ages, another in time.

Therefore he is called the mountain, the stone, and the foundation. He was also the rock: “and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10). Upon this rock every wise person builds his house—that is, the house of his soul. The winds come, the rain descends, and the rivers strike against that house, yet it does not fall, because its foundation is upon the rock.

Therefore, as we had begun to say, a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden. It continues: “Nor do they light a lamp and place it under a measure, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to everyone in the house.”

The lamp placed on a lampstand is the mind established in the substance of the body; it shines and rises above, especially if the oil of charity or chastity is not lacking in it, as it was in blessed John the Baptist, of whom it is written: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5). He burned and shone: he burned with the warmth of the Holy Spirit and shone with the light of Christ.

Hear this lamp crying out concerning Christ and saying: “This is the Lamb of God; this is the one who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). Again he says: “The man who came after me was made before me; I am not worthy to carry his sandal” (ibid. 27).

Therefore the mind of blessed John shone with the light of Christ, because, as it is written, all the saints receive from his fullness grace upon grace (John 1). All the saints receive from his light, yet it is not divided into parts, nor is the majesty of Christ’s light diminished.

For if the light of a lamp is used to light, for example, a thousand torches or a great many lamps, that fire is not diminished, nor is it divided from itself into parts, how much more is Christ’s majesty complete, and his fullness abounds in all; it is not divided, but is wholly present in all.

For even when our speech is spoken, it is heard by everyone, yet it is not divided among individuals; it remains wholly and entire in everyone. And if we all read a verse written on a wall, we do not divide it into parts; it remains whole in each person’s understanding.

And therefore, brothers, we have said that the saints, always shining with the light of Christ, cried out, saying: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me—Christ?” (2 Cor. 13).

And therefore they give light to everyone in the house—that is, in the house of this world. For in a great house, as it is written, there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware (2 Tim. 2).

Thus all the saints are appointed for the illumination of human beings, and the apostles and prophets were appointed so that, with the Lord’s gift, the edifice of the Church might be built through them. To our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ be glory and dominion forever. Amen.

## XV. Also, on the holy Gospel, Matthew 17:1

It was recited in the holy Gospel as follows: “After six days,” he says, “Jesus took Peter, James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves, and he was transfigured before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became white like snow. And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him. Then Peter answered and said: ‘Teacher, it is good for us to be here. Let us make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah,’” and so forth.

“After six days,” he says: after six days we understand the seventh day to be the Sabbath. The first day is the Lord’s Day, the second day the second weekday, and so with all the days. After six days, as stated, the Sabbath is counted.

This day indicates rest, because on the seventh day God also rested from his works. Therefore, on this sanctified day, the Lord showed that all the saints, both those in the Law and those in the Prophets, would be present with the blessed apostles in his glory and would remain with him.

Moses the lawgiver, who described all the saints from the beginning of the world: therefore all the saints will rise with him. Elijah represents the number of the prophets. With him, all the prophets—those who died and were buried—will be found alive and will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air.

Thus the three apostles—Peter, James, and John—represent believers with them, including all who follow the faith of Peter, James, and John. Concerning these it is written: “Peter, James, and John, who seemed to be pillars” (Gal. 2). They are rightly called pillars, since they supported the building of the Church and raised it from lower things to higher things, so that they might seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.

Thus there are two—Moses and Elijah—and three apostles, so that every word might stand on the testimony of two and three witnesses. The Lord himself also said: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. 18).

Here too the Lord showed that those who do not accept the Law and the Prophets will be confounded, because he joined them to himself and associated them with the number of the apostles.

Moses wrote about the Lord (Exod. 17), and, as a type of Christ, raised his hands on the mountain against Amalek, just as Christ raised his hands on the cross to conquer the devil. Again, Elijah (1 Kings 17), in order to raise a dead man, stretched himself out—something the Lord did on the cross, to drive away death and restore life.

Let us see what follows. Saint Peter says to the Lord: “It is good for us to be here; let us make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” Peter said this according to the affection of a good disciple, who loved the Lord’s servants and friends, Moses and Elijah.

And behold, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and a voice came from the cloud saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” As if it were saying: “Three tents are not to be made; rather, this is my most beloved Son, whose tent will be one—that is, one Church spread throughout the whole world, after the likeness of the one city Jerusalem, which is in heaven.”

In this Church Moses and Elijah, Peter, James, and John will be present, always bearing witness to the Lord, together with all the patriarchs and prophets and holy apostles. With them may all of us who believe always rejoice and glory in the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and through him always give thanks to the Father; to him be glory forever. Amen.

## XVI. Also, the Gospel reading, Luke 12:50

The Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled? I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how constrained I am until it is accomplished?” and so forth.

“I have come,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” The Lord casts fire upon the earth of our breast, to cultivate the field of our heart and burn up the thorns and thistles of sins, so that the coldness of our wickedness may be driven away and all things fruitful and prosperous may arise in us through the warmth of the Holy Spirit.

For take a comparison from this earthly fire. A certain author of secular literature says:

[Note: [Col. 0823D] Virgil, Georgics, book 1.]

“Frequently, too, it is useful to burn sterile fields  
and consume the light stubble with crackling flames:  
whether from this the earth conceives hidden powers  
and rich nourishment, whether through the fire  
every defect is boiled away and useless moisture  
sweated out; or whether that heat opens  
more passages and hidden vents, through which the sap  
may come into the new grass;  
or whether it hardens the soil more  
and tightens its gaping veins.”

If this is what that earthly and bodily fire accomplishes, how much more does that heavenly and holy fire, which penetrates the hidden recesses of the soul so deeply that, passing even through the whole substance of the body, it makes the entire person clean and fruitful! This fire produces in a human being such fruits as the Apostle Paul describes, saying: “The fruit of the Spirit”—that is, of that fiery Spirit—“is charity, joy, peace, patience, goodness, faith” (Gal. 5), and so forth.

“Charity,” he says, at the beginning, because the coldness of iniquity never extinguishes the fire of charity. Thus divine Scripture says again: “Many waters cannot extinguish charity, nor will rivers overwhelm it” (Song 8), [uncertain text: “so that it may not be for it a rock and a tower cut out”].

“I have come,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” It is kindled through good will and through the mind’s good purpose, which in some way increases and inflames that divine fire within itself.

This fire is further kindled in us by the frequent breathing forth of the divine Scriptures. Hence the holy Apostle, knowing this, commanded his disciple Timothy, saying: “Attend to yourself and to reading; remain in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you” (1 Tim. 4).

And “you,” he says, “will be saved, shining with the fire’s saving power, and you will illuminate the others who hear you.”

Then the Lord continued, saying: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how constrained I am until it is accomplished?” (Luke 12). [Col. 0824A] The Lord was speaking here of his Passion.

He added further: “Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth?” [Note: [Col. 0823D] The Vulgate reads: “Do you think that I have come to bring peace on earth?”]

“No, I tell you, but division.” For from now on there will be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three: father against son and son against his father; mother against daughter and daughter against her mother; mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law” (ibid.).

This division is made by believers against unbelievers. When some consent to the Lord’s faith and others dissent, they are separated from the faith; and this separation saves the believers but condemns the unbelievers.

For it is right that the believer depart, since fellowship cannot exist between light and darkness, nor can the sweet be mixed with the bitter, nor the faithful with the unfaithful.

Therefore, brothers, let us persevere in the Lord’s faith and take pains to lead unbelievers to the Lord’s faith, so that all may be saved in Christ. To him be glory and dominion forever. Amen.

## XVII. Also, on the Gospel reading, Mark 2:15

It was recited that the Lord held a meal at Levi’s house with tax collectors and sinners. The Lord did not exclude tax collectors and sinners, so that at least through the occasion of the meal they might be instructed. The just and pious Lord, who had come to heal everyone, did not repel the impious and unjust, just as he himself had said: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9).

To those afflicted by many fevers of desire he poured in the refreshing remedies of his words. There was an abundance of food and drink; but the Savior, seeing them intent upon these things, joined them at an earthly meal so that he might urge them to hasten to heavenly banquets, where there are those delights that are not temporary but eternal, which neither eye has seen nor ear heard nor the human heart conceived, which God has prepared for those who love him (Isa. 64 and 1 Cor. 1).

“Those who are well,” he says, “have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” You who are sick in soul, held by whatever disease of vice; you who have the fevers either of pride, lust, evil desire, anger, or greed—run to Christ the physician and, pleading, say to him: “I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you’” (Ps. 40).

So that he too may say [lacuna: surviving text begins] “if you hear my words … you love and do not …” [lacuna], you will feel the help of divine assistance as medicine if you devote the devotion of your mind to the divine commandments with complete observance.

It is a great and good thing, brothers, to obey the heavenly command; salvation is acquired precisely where hearing serves obedience.

Therefore let us obey the divine commandments, so that, having obtained the substance of good things, we may always give thanks to the Father through the Son. To him be glory forever. Amen.

## XVIII. Also, on the Gospel reading, Luke 15:12

We heard today recited in the holy Gospel the account of two sons, the younger and the elder, to whom their father had distributed his property; and how the younger, having gone away from his father and living prodigally in sins, lost everything, and afterward, led to repentance and greatly afflicted, returned to his father. His father ordered a robe, a ring, and sandals to be given him, and a calf to be slaughtered at the banquet for his redemption [lacuna]. [Surviving text:] “when … [he came] … console … ‘Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But it was necessary to feast and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and came to life again; he had perished and has been found.’”

These two brothers, as it seems to my inadequacy, dearest ones, signify two peoples. The elder may be understood as the ancient people of the patriarchs or prophets, who persevered in serving God the Father. The younger signifies the people of the nations, who, distancing themselves from God and departing as though into a foreign land, lived amid many errors. Later, coming to the father in repentance and supplication, they received the first robe—that is, the first ornament of redemption—because it is written: “You will make the nations the head” (Deut. 24).

The ring on the hand is a sign of betrothal. According to the Apostle, the bride, betrothed to one man, is presented as a pure virgin. The sandals on the feet are also a sign of marriage, since the feet of Christ’s bride are shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace.

The calf too is ordered to be slaughtered at the banquet. The fattened calf is our Savior, whom the Father willed to be sacrificed for the redemption of the human race.

As for the statement that the elder brother became angry over the younger brother, anger there stands for astonishment, because the ancient people of the righteous were astonished at the reception of the nations. And although some of them were truly angry—that is, the Jewish people—nevertheless they are admonished by the divine commandments that they ought to rejoice, because a small-minded consideration of human weakness ought kindly to accept the plan of the indulgent God.

Therefore, let the people of the nations, converted to the Lord, rejoice that they have been saved by the Lord’s kindness, and let them always give thanks to God the Father through his Christ. To him be glory forever. Amen.

## XIX. The reading of the holy Gospel, Luke 16:19

We heard today recited in the holy Gospel:

“There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day. And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores, longing to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table. But dogs also came and licked his sores.

“Now it happened that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell. Lifting up his eyes while he was in torment, he saw Abraham from afar and Lazarus in his bosom. And he himself cried out and said: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.’

“And Abraham said to him: ‘Son, remember that you received good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, while you are tormented. And in all these things a great gulf has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross from there to here.’”

Let us consider, brothers, that a rich man and a beggar are presented. The rich man’s name is suppressed, and he is without a name, like a body without a head: the name is recognized in the head. He is rightly without a name because he was without a head, since he had neither faith in Christ, who is the head, nor mercy in himself.

Then Lazarus the beggar is named; nevertheless, his name is contained in the Book of Life, and the Gospel does not conceal it.

1. That rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day also died, and was buried in hell.

2. Lazarus the beggar died and was carried by angels and placed in Abraham’s bosom.

3. God’s judgment was immediately shown in both: after many labors and pains, the poor man received the refreshment he had desired; and the rich man, after his arrogance, received fitting torments.

When the rich man saw Lazarus resting in Abraham’s bosom, he cried out and said: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger, so that he may cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.”

And Abraham said to him: “Son, remember that you received good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, while you are tormented.”

The rich man sought to have himself touched by the dew of Lazarus’s fingertip, but it was not permitted him, because it is written: “In death, who will remember you? And in hell, who will confess to you?” (Ps. 6).

Even now, if the rich wish, let them consult the poor. They have and see many Lazaruses. When they show them mercy, they prepare refreshment for themselves in the future, because whoever shows mercy will obtain mercy.

For the one who has not himself been merciful cannot deserve God’s mercy. Let them be more humble in prosperity; arrogance has [lacuna]. [Surviving text:] Above all, let them not be proudly minded about the world, nor hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who grants us all things.

Therefore the Apostle teaches them to be rich in good works, generous, ready to give, and sharing with others, storing up for themselves a good treasure for the future, so that they may seize true life (1 Tim. 6).

There are many rich people who are not blameworthy, who seem to possess what they have not for themselves alone but for many; they generously distribute it to many and give it out well to many.

He is truly rich in God who gives to the poor person sighing, not to the dancing actor. There are many rich people among bishops, presbyters, and deacons; but whoever properly administers his wealth can incur neither the guilt of luxury, nor the stain of crime, nor the punishment of condemnation.

Certainly, God wished some to be rich so that there would be people to give to the poor; and for this reason he made some poor, so that they might receive what they need from the rich.

For God’s plan is holy in all things, to be revered in everything, and always to be praised. To God the Father be glory forever. Amen.

## XX. Also, on the reading of the holy Gospel, Mark 8:3

“Behold,” he says, “a sower went out to sow,” and so forth.

The Lord Jesus came into the world, going forth from the Father himself, saying: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16).

Therefore he says of himself: “Behold, a sower went out to sow.” He went out to sow the Gospel in the world, to sow faith, justice, truth, peace, chastity, humility, and the other virtues.

But the devil, by contrast, began to sow his own things: pride, anger, lust, murders, adulteries, thefts, and the other vices, which in the divine writings are called weeds.

When the disciples said to the Lord Jesus, “Did you not sow good seed in your field? Where then did the weeds come from?” the Savior said: “An enemy has done this” (Matt. 13). By “the enemy” he meant the devil, who introduces enmity between God and human beings—that is, sins—by which he separates human beings from God.

He was the one who also deceived those first human beings, Adam and Eve, placed in paradise. Having changed himself into the form of a serpent, he approached them with slippery entanglements and conversations seemingly human, and deceived their inexperienced souls through heedless credulity.

He is also the one who now injects wicked thoughts, destined to burn with him at Christ’s judgment.

Therefore let us consider, brothers, the seeds of the Lord Jesus Christ and the seeds of the enemy, the devil. When each person sees thoughts and desires of piety, mercy, humility, chastity, patience, and other good things rising in his heart, let him know that they are Christ’s seeds.

But if he perceives a desire for adultery, fornication, theft, fraud, or other evils, let him understand that they are the devil’s seeds.

Therefore let him prepare his heart for God and not for the devil, as the prophet says in the Psalms: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make music to you in your glory” (Ps. 56), as though saying: Having received the seeds of your righteousness, I offer you the fruits of praise and blessing.

“Behold,” he says, “a sower went out to sow.” And as he sows, some fell beside the road, some on rocky ground, some among thorns, and some on good soil.

What fell beside the road: the birds come and take it away. Whoever does not walk on the way, which is Christ, is placed outside the way and cannot retain within himself the seed of God’s word; it is snatched away by the birds—that is, by wandering spirits.

Whoever has a rocky mind—that is, hardness weighed down by unbelief—does not retain the roots of God’s word within himself; it soon withers because it does not produce enduring fruits from the depths of the heart.

But what fell among thorns is constricted by the density of thorns—that is, by the barbs of worldly thoughts—which suppress the word, so that it cannot become fruitful.

But what fell on good soil overflows with fruits and grows abundantly, producing, as the Lord says, thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold fruits: the fruits of hope, faith, and charity; the fruits of widowhood, virginity, and martyrdom.

By these fruits the Church grows well and prepares its harvests worthily for the heavenly storehouses, as is said generally of all the prophets, apostles, and various teachers.

Thus the Lord rightly says: “Whoever speaks sows the word.” And so it is, because whoever speaks the word scatters words like seeds, but God grants the growth.

For the Apostle Paul also said: “We have sown spiritual things among you” (1 Cor. 9).

Since, therefore, whoever speaks sows the word, and just as seed, when it is thrown upon the earth, is watered by heavenly rain, takes root, and grows in the hearts of individuals, so from it arise those fruits that have been named: the thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruits of good will.

## XXI. Also, on the Gospel reading, Mark 7:25
“In entering,” he says, “the Lord Jesus went into a house and wanted no one to know it, yet he could not remain hidden,” and so forth. First let us consider this, brothers: “The Lord,” he says, “entered a house, wanted no one to know it, and yet could not remain hidden.” If he wanted no one to know, why could he not remain hidden? Clearly, the Lord does not wish to show himself in such a way that he nevertheless does not wish to remain hidden. For is it because the divine substance is not now seen by our eyes that it is absent from us, or does not wish to be present to us? He himself pours the light of his knowledge into all, he who is the true light, enlightening every human being who comes into this world.

He entered a house, but he was not absent in public; he was in the body, but he was not absent from heaven; he was seen [lacuna], of whom the prophet David speaks in the psalm, saying: “He stretches out heaven like a skin; he touches its upper parts in the waters; he makes the clouds his ascent; he walks upon the wings of the winds; he makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Psalm 103). Therefore he is the one who, with the Father, created the world.

“A certain Syrophoenician woman,” he says, “of gentile origin, came to him and begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter” (Mark 7:25). This woman, if we speak allegorically, was both gentile error and ancient ignorance; she had begotten a daughter subject to a demon, a miserable and infirm offspring, which did not possess a manly—that is, a strong—understanding in faith, but was unstable in unbelief.

When this woman ran to the Lord and begged him, the Savior said: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” But she replied and said: “Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their master’s table” (Mark 7). She compared herself to little dogs longing at their masters’ table. She humbled herself not merely before the master, but also before the master’s servants and children, comparing herself to puppies.

And the Lord said to her: “Go; because of this saying the demon will leave your daughter.” You see, therefore, that if anyone comes from the error of paganism to Christ, recognizes him as Lord and Savior, and benefits himself, he also obtains salvation for his children, so that, rescued from the power of demons, they may receive the reward of liberation.

Then it was recounted that the Lord put his fingers into the ears of a certain deaf and mute man, touched his tongue with his spittle, and immediately he spoke and recovered his hearing. Nothing is impossible for God (Romans 10). Whatever he touches is effective; whatever he looks upon lives. The tongue felt, and the ears felt, the benefit of their Lord; they were freed from hindrances, and the inactive organs received their proper use [lacuna].

“Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened”: with the Lord’s command, the benefits followed. The bond of the tongue was loosed. With his spittle he touched the man’s tongue; from the substance of his flesh he bestowed health; with the fingers of his hands he once again poured hearing into his ears. Through the bodily members the power of the Divinity was at work.

Even now he makes the deaf hear—that is, makes unbelievers believe—“for faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God.” He makes the mute speak: those who did not know how to speak the word of truth he makes teachers and masters in the Church, preachers of the truth, so that they may also penetrate the ears of others with their teaching, open them by piercing through, and make the tongues of their hearers eloquent. Thus, strengthened in the unity of faith, may all rejoice forever in the Lord Jesus Christ himself, to whom are glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

## 778. XXII. Also, on the Gospel reading, Mark 8:1–26.

[Col. 0829B]

It was said today, as the holy Gospel was being read, that the Lord Jesus Christ satisfied the people with seven loaves and a few fish, and that seven baskets full of fragments were gathered. Our heavenly King, the Lord Jesus Christ, feeds his people both from the land and from the sea. All are satisfied with seven loaves. Why do we think that this number was written in connection with the loaves? I believe that, by the gift of Christ’s grace, seven Churches have been established, through whose sevenfold number all peoples are fed in Christ. Moreover, seven baskets remain, full to overflowing, because the grace of the Churches is never diminished, but is always increased by the generosity of the Holy Spirit.

This sevenfold Church contains within itself the number of perfection, just as the seven days complete the perfection of the world, and seven thousand years are said to have been appointed for the consummation of the world itself. For in the Apocalypse (chapter 5) the Lord’s seven eyes are mentioned, watching over the world, as well as seven stars in God’s hands. Thus the seven full baskets are shown to remain, so that the Churches may always be known to be full of Christ’s grace.

Likewise, in what follows, it was said concerning the blind man who was restored to sight that the Lord Jesus Christ again healed a man blind from birth in this manner: “He spat into his eyes, laid his hand upon him, and asked him whether he saw anything. And he said: ‘I see people like trees walking about.’ And again he laid his hand upon him, and he saw everything clearly.”

This blind man, whose birth had not given him light, but had brought him the shipwreck of sight at the very moment of his birth, now receives healing from the Lord: the true light of our Savior illuminated his eyes and his darkness, removed the captivity of his sight, and granted him the vision of free light. After long darkness, struck by the force of the light, he first saw with wavering eyes as though trees were walking about; then, after the repeated [lacuna].

## XXIII. Fragment on the words: “The names of the twelve apostles are these: the first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother,” and the rest, Matthew 10:3.

[lacuna] as the first [lacuna] [Col. 0830A] received [lacuna] this first received [lacuna] Simon, who is called Peter; son [lacuna] and Israel names [lacuna] Moses did not say “the first” [lacuna] in simple speech [lacuna] Simon [lacuna] now, however, bestowing great [lacuna] and singular honor upon blessed Peter, the Evangelist says: “First, Simeon, who is called Peter.” Peter is interpreted as “clothed over,” namely, with the purity of grace that is above what is in the Law; for this reason he was the shepherd of the Church, and furthermore the shepherd of the flock. For Jesus said to him: “Feed my sheep” (John 21).

Thus, as disciple, foundation of the Church, apostle, and martyr, he was crucified head downward at Rome; [Col. 0830B] for all these things he was crowned doubly. Therefore he is rightly interpreted as “Peter,” that is, “clothed over.”

Andrew, his brother, is interpreted as “obstructed” [lacuna] by guards [lacuna] then [lacuna] is interpreted as “surrounded” [lacuna] [lacuna] enduring pain; for in this [lacuna] death, and he despised pain. When his head was cut off by Herod [lacuna] in this he surrounded him [lacuna] the wicked devil, when he swiftly passed from this world into the heavenly kingdoms.

“And John his brother.” [Col. 0830C] John is interpreted as “obedient to the Lord.” And who obeyed the Lord as did John, who was commanded to follow him and reclined upon the Lord’s breast? He was also surnamed, together with James, “son of thunder,” as though, by spiritual and heavenly power, he would thunder in the last days in the holy Church.

After these came Philip, who is interpreted as “confused,” yet living. Hence Paul also says: “We have become a spectacle to this world,” and “as refuse” [lacuna].

Now Bartholomew is interpreted as “most beloved son.” Therefore he called him to the apostolate and [lacuna] would name him his most beloved son. Would that all of us also [lacuna] live in the adoption of sons, so that we may be counted among God’s most beloved children.

Then Thomas, who is interpreted as “abyss,” or “depth,” or “inscrutable,” like a vessel of the Holy Spirit, like a temple of the Paraclete, who searches all things and investigates every depth in the things that have been made, both in angels and in human beings.

[Col. 0830D] And Matthew, who is interpreted as “gift of life.” The magnificent Matthew became a double gift of life to this world: both because he was an apostle and because, as an evangelist, he wrote this Gospel uniquely in Hebrew for the Hebrews, and uniquely for the gentiles, through which this Gospel was announced to the gentiles.

“But Matthew,” he says, “the tax collector” [lacuna] from his father, or from his grandfather, or from royal [lacuna] lineage you name [lacuna]. But you name yourself a tax collector [lacuna].

[Col. 0831A]

O blessed Matthew, why do you accuse Matthew, O blessed evangelist? Why do you rebuke the evangelist? O blessed apostle and truest disciple of the Lord, why do you not spare yourself?

“I,” he says, “am called Matthew the evangelist, and I am certainly an apostle. I do not therefore accuse Matthew, but rather glorify him greatly, so that he who was a tax collector might become an apostle. Nor do I rebuke the evangelist; rather, as a marvelous herald of the truth, I praise him. It is not so very remarkable for someone to be good among the good; but it is exceedingly glorious for someone to be shown good among the wicked.

“I call myself a tax collector, so that all may believe that this writing of mine is entirely truthful, and that my proclamation is without flattery. [lacuna] for I do not speak about myself [lacuna] I shall speak about another. If I do not flatter myself, how could I flatter [Col. 0831B] this one about whom I am making this proclamation—that is, the Only-Begotten God?”

Matthew the tax collector.

James, son of Alphaeus, is interpreted as “one who circumvents doctrine.” Not only here, but all the blessed apostles, through spiritual doctrine, first circumvented the devil and then all the wise men of this world. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.

Thaddaeus was called Lebbaeus by his parents at the beginning; this means “heart,” “discipline,” and “mind,” and he received an increase of this name. When Thaddaeus was called by the Lord, he was called by a name meaning “praise of life,” as though praising eternal life greatly, or praising and proclaiming the Lord himself, who is the eternal life of all.

Then Simon the Cananaean, which means “obedience,” or “prepared,” as blessed Simon was, and all the apostles were both obedient and prepared. Therefore he obeyed [Col. 0831C] the Lord quickly and followed him readily, just as the others did.

And we too, beloved brothers, must be obedient and prepared [lacuna] for it is necessary to speak a good word [lacuna] [Col. 0832A] walking in the footsteps of the most blessed apostles [lacuna] so that we may obtain rest on the day of concealment.

But let us not pass over Judas in silence, since the blessed evangelist did not omit him. “Judas,” he says, “Iscariot, who also betrayed him,” last of all, properly and fittingly, as though he himself had prepared this for himself, or as though he himself had arranged it for himself. And it is not merely a great thing that he is named last; there is also an infinite patience in the fact that he is named at all.

Judas is interpreted as “one who confessed voluntarily.” What did he confess? That he had betrayed righteous blood. “I have sinned,” he says, “because I betrayed righteous blood” (Matthew 27). You confess, Judas, but you confess too late, and you confess badly.

“Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him”: not only is he himself confounded and dishonored because of his [Col. 0832B] evil audacity, but his province and region as well, in which he was born and which is called Iscariot, is named on his account, suffers reproach, and bears a curse because it produced such a man.

Thus, just as the provinces and nations of the saints are greatly exalted and honored on account of them, so the lands of the unjust are remembered among later generations for the greater rebuke of those who originated there.

Jesus now sent these twelve apostles to illuminate the darkness, straighten what was crooked, seek what was lost, illumine this world, and turn all people onto the way of life. Jesus sent these twelve to teach everyone reverence, to illumine everyone by faith, to commend to all the Father’s unique sovereignty, to demonstrate to all the obedience of the Son who was sent, and to reveal to all the unique illumination of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete.

[Col. 0832C] Jesus therefore sent these twelve, commanding them and saying: “Do not go among the gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matthew 10:5).

# APPENDIX OF THE WORKS OF SAINT MAXIMUS, BISHOP OF TURIN, CONTAINING DOUBTFUL AND SPURIOUS SERMONS, AS WELL AS TWO LETTERS

[Col. 0831]

## PREFACE TO THE APPENDIX

1. The Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, who must always be commended for their editions of the holy Fathers, did not entirely reject writings that were spurious or uncertain. Since they judged that some usefulness could also be derived from them, they placed the inferior material after the more carefully selected harvest, in a separate volume. Following these guides, and having previously exhausted as many manuscript codices as we could, we have decided to publish at the end of our collection not a few works attributed to Saint Maximus, although we know that they cannot be established as his.

And because not all of them bear the same marks of spuriousness, but some bear more and others fewer, we divide our appendix into two parts, the first containing doubtful works, the second inferior ones. For several reasons for doubting an author arise: either when the number of dissenting manuscripts is greater; or when those that support the attribution do not deserve complete confidence; or when a different manner of expression and connection of ideas is recognized; or finally when the same things said elsewhere are stitched together with a few additions or alterations.

Whenever one of these causes occurs, it will be sufficient for us to doubt that the work belongs to Maximus and to place it in the first class. It will suffice to have said this about them, since we shall give the reasons for each individual work in its proper place.

As for the second part of the appendix, much weightier considerations move us to erase from the catalogue of Maximian works those whose statements do not correspond to the facts, whose chronology does not fit, or whose style is so uneven and so low that it is wholly impossible that the same author could have been at one time lofty and outstanding, and at another foolish and crude.

We must explain why we consider those four sermons on the praises of Saint Eusebius of Vercelli, edited by Muratori from an Ambrosian codex, to be spurious. First of all, some material has been transferred into this first sermon from Saint Maximus’s second homily, in which Saint Eusebius of Vercelli is discussed. But what chiefly deters me from attributing it to the bishop of Turin is a passage in that same sermon which plainly contradicts not only the records of history but also orthodox doctrine.

The passage comes down to this: Dionysius, bishop of Milan, was captured by an Arian trick and carelessly subscribed to their demands. Eusebius of Vercelli took this very badly and, in order to ward off the disgrace of Dionysius, falsely claimed that he was a heretic and pretended that he approved whatever pleased the Arians. Yet he expressed wonder that, while they preached that the Father ought to be placed above the Son, they nevertheless thought that Dionysius should be given first place in signing—although that honor ought to be accorded to one who would regard Dionysius himself, once his former hearer, as a son.

The Arians, who desired nothing more than to add Eusebius as a partner to their impiety, were consequently delighted and eager to have Dionysius’s name erased from the document. They asked Eusebius, since the more honorable place was now vacant, not to refuse to sign first himself. Eusebius replied to their request that they should not hope that he would ever pollute himself with their crimes.
