It was enough for him that he had eluded their devices and achieved the result that Dionysius would not be regarded as a participant in their perfidy.

I cannot even guess where the author of that sermon obtained this tale. For I see that there is absolutely no ancient writer who committed anything of the sort to writing.

Athanasius, whose authority is especially outstanding in this matter, in his *Apology for His Flight* [Note: [Col. 0833] No. 4, p. 255, vol. I, part 1, Padua edition, 1777. Similar things are written by him in the *Apology to Constantius*, no. 27, p. 247, and in the *History of the Arians to the Monks*, no. 33, p. 287.], is so far from asserting that Dionysius subscribed after being ensnared by Arian deceit that, on the contrary, he teaches that Dionysius was driven into exile because he had not consented to the Arian heresy and had not subscribed to the false accusations and calumnies that they had contrived against Athanasius himself.

Hilary of Poitiers, moreover, a truly weighty writer and a contemporary of those times, does report that Dionysius wrote when the Nicene faith was presented by Eusebius; but he does not likewise report that Dionysius subscribed to Athanasius’s condemnation. For in the first book addressed to the emperor Constantius [Note: [Col. 0833] No. 8, p. 427.] he says:

> “When Eusebius was summoned to subscribe against Athanasius, he said that the matter of priestly faith ought first to be established, since he had discovered that some of those present were polluted by heretical corruption. He placed before them the faith set forth at Nicaea, which we mentioned above, promising that he would do everything they demanded if they would write a profession of faith. Dionysius, bishop of Milan, was the first to take the document and began to write his profession; but Valens violently snatched the pen and document from his hands, shouting that nothing could be accomplished by it.”

Who could fail to see from this that Dionysius wrote nothing except the Nicene faith, while Valens, the Arian bishop of Mursa, raged and therefore violently tore the pen and document from Dionysius’s hands? If there was any promise concerning the condemnation of Athanasius, Hilary writes that it was made to the Arians not by Dionysius but by Eusebius, on the condition that the establishment of the Nicene faith should first be discussed. I shall speak of this shortly.

Ambrose does not disagree with Hilary [Note: [Col. 0833] Letter 63, no. 68, p. 1129, vol. III, edition of 1751.]. The account of Rufinus runs as follows:

> “A council of bishops was convened at Milan. Many were deceived. But Dionysius, Eusebius, Paulinus, Rhodanus, and Lucifer, declaring that there was deceit in the matter and asserting that they were seeking a subscription against Athanasius for no other reason than to destroy the faith, were driven into exile.”

These things plainly agree with what Socrates reports in book 2 [Note: [Col. 0833] Chapter 35, p. 115, Turin edition, 1747.], Sozomen in book 4 [Note: [Col. 0834] Chapter 9, p. 128, same edition.], and Theodoret in book 2 [Note: [Col. 0834] Chapter 15, p. 128, same edition.].

I am not unaware that Sulpicius Severus gives the following account in book 2 of his *History*:

> “They assembled at Milan, where the emperor was then present. The same dispute concerning the condemnation of Athanasius yielded nothing on either side. Then Eusebius of Vercelli and Lucifer of Caralis in Sardinia, bishops, were sent into exile. But Dionysius, bishop of Milan, subscribed that he consented to the condemnation of Athanasius, provided that the matter of the faith should be investigated among the bishops. But Valens, Ursacius, and the others, fearing the people, who were preserving the Catholic faith with remarkable zeal, did not dare to make their abominations known; they gathered inside the palace. From there they issued a letter in the emperor’s name, filled with every kind of depravity. When the letter was read in the church, the people rejected it. Dionysius was driven from the city because he had not agreed, and another bishop was immediately substituted in his place.”

This is his account.

Everyone can now see what the disagreement is: many writers, and especially weighty and distinguished ones, deny that Dionysius subscribed to Athanasius’s condemnation; whereas scarcely two affirm it, both of whom were less precise, and one also later in date. For my part, I agree with Hilary and Athanasius, with the contemporaries of those times and with those well informed about the facts.

Why should I not entirely agree with them, especially with Athanasius, who knew very well what had been done for or against him and who recorded its history? If someone should perhaps prefer to agree with Sulpicius and with Lucifer of Caralis, whom I shall discuss later, I shall not now offer much resistance. For why should I resist, when I shall concede nothing that can serve the interests of the opposing side?

What can be concluded or established from Sulpicius’s passage except that Dionysius subscribed his consent to Athanasius’s condemnation after Lucifer and Eusebius had departed into exile? But how can anyone reconcile this with the things that the author of the sermon now under discussion confuses and distorts?

If Eusebius had departed, how, I ask, could this Eusebius, while present, have approached the Arians, lied that he was a heretic, and finally forced them to erase Dionysius’s subscription so that the vacant first place might be left for him to sign—the very actions that the author of the sermon asserts so confidently?

But suppose that Eusebius remained at Milan until Dionysius’s exile. That is false, if one follows Sulpicius and Hilary [Note: [Col. 0834] He writes that the sentence against Eusebius was issued by the impious Arians long before they entered the Church; but he does not likewise write that the sentence against Dionysius was issued at that time. Book 1 addressed to Constantius, no. 8, p. 427.], to whom, as is proper, I attribute very great authority. Still, suppose that Eusebius remained at Milan while Dionysius remained there; suppose also that Dionysius, as Sulpicius relates, subscribed that he consented to Athanasius’s condemnation, provided that the matter of the faith should be investigated among the bishops.

Let these things be true; I shall tolerate them. But what cause could arise from them for Eusebius to be so greatly disturbed—as the author of the sermon, in his dream, has invented—and to think with such anxious care about erasing Dionysius’s subscription, if Eusebius himself, according to Hilary, had publicly declared that he would willingly do what Dionysius had written?

Hilary’s account has already been demonstrated shortly before. “When Eusebius was summoned to subscribe against Athanasius, he said: ‘The matter of priestly faith ought first to be established …’ He placed the faith set forth at Nicaea before them,” promising that he would do everything they demanded if they would write a profession of faith [Note: [Col. 0834] Hilary, book 1 addressed to Constantius, no. 8, p. 427.].

Am I to believe that Eusebius was so inconsistent that what he himself, according to Hilary, promised the Arians—without danger to piety being betrayed and without dishonor to himself—he would have judged, if written by Dionysius, to be dishonorable to Dionysius and harmful to religion?

Surely it does not even enter one’s thoughts that a promise made orally should be free from guilt, while the same promise, once committed to writing, should not be. Thus Hilary, in the book he published against Constantius [Note: [Col. 0834] No. 26, p. 460.], says:

> “Do you think that Christ judges only through letters, and that God needs a little document in order to examine the will?”

Therefore, with Athanasius, Hilary, Rufinus, Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret as witnesses, Dionysius did not subscribe [5]. And although Sulpicius, disagreeing with such illustrious men, asserts that he did subscribe, he nevertheless states that he subscribed under a condition that cannot be blamed—the same condition under which Hilary says that Eusebius acted when he promised the Arians that he would do against Athanasius what they desired.

Why should I concern myself with the author of the sermon under discussion, who not only asserts, contrary to so many distinguished Fathers of such ancient authority and eminence, and contrary to the testimony of so many illustrious historians, that Dionysius subscribed, but also—contrary to Sulpicius’s account—claims that Dionysius, as though by his subscription he had inflicted a wound upon the cause of religion [Col. 0835], and praises in Eusebius things that no writer had ever imagined and that no Christian, much less a bishop, could carry out without loss to piety and truth?

Indeed, I am astonished that this escaped the monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, otherwise extremely learned men, when they discussed this sermon [Note: [Col. 0835] In the appendix to the works of Saint Ambrose, note on sermon 56, vol. IV, p. 577, Venetian edition, 1751.]:

> “Apart from the title of martyr attributed to Saint Eusebius, the rest of the sermon agrees sufficiently with the history of that bishop.”

For what that history contains has been established from the works of the Fathers and historians. In them there is not even a word about Dionysius’s being trapped through simplicity, or about Eusebius’s pretending—as the author of this sermon asserts—that he was a heretic. On the contrary, there are statements that disagree with this sermon so completely that they plainly demonstrate that what is read in it concerning Eusebius’s simulation, Dionysius’s erased subscription, and related matters is full of falsehoods.

But Lucifer of Caralis, who took part in the Council of Milan, teaches in the second book addressed to Constantius that Dionysius, deceived by Constantius, subscribed to Athanasius’s condemnation [Note: [Col. 0835] p. 203, vol. IV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons edition, 1677.]. For that bishop says, addressing the emperor:

> “How will you be able to deny it, when you sent into exile the most holy Dionysius, bishop of Milan, who, believing your false assertion, had already condemned Athanasius because he refused to be an Arian?”

Let these be Lucifer’s words, if you will; but from whom did he receive them? He himself was not present, since, as we have observed, he had already been driven into exile together with Eusebius.

Who would persuade himself that he used better witnesses than Athanasius, whose case was at issue and who repeatedly, without hesitation, denies that Dionysius subscribed? But let Lucifer see Dionysius subscribing.

What? Did Lucifer say that Dionysius thereby became a participant in Arian impiety? Or that Eusebius feared that Dionysius’s faith and reputation might be placed in danger? Or that Eusebius lied to the Arians, claiming that he agreed with heretics and approved what pleased them? Or that he so arranged his speech that the Arians would understand that, if they erased Dionysius’s subscription, Eusebius himself would subscribe first to Athanasius’s condemnation?

But if Lucifer nowhere said anything of this sort about Eusebius, what support can anyone hope to find in him for defending the author of the sermon, who heaps together such inventions? What if Lucifer, who was so stern and vehement that he did not think much lesser matters should be tolerated, had attacked Eusebius fiercely if Eusebius had resorted to devices, simulations, and lies touching the faith?

But enough has been said about that sermon’s disagreement with the records of the Fathers and historians. It remains for me to show that it also opposes sound and orthodox doctrine.

We already know what Scripture says about those who speak lies (Psalm 5:7; Wisdom 1:11), and that divine command of Christ remains firm (Matthew 5:37): “Let your speech be, Yes, yes; No, no; for whatever is more than this proceeds from evil,” as Christ himself warned [Note: [Col. 0835] See Saint Augustine, *On Lying*, chapter 8, no. 6, p. 310, vol. VI of the works, Antwerp edition, 1700.].

Therefore, by the consensus of the Fathers, a principle has been established and continuously handed down to us: it is permitted to no one, under any circumstances, to lie.

I would present the complete and fully ordered succession of these Fathers if I did not fear that it would be longer than the brevity of a preface permits. I shall therefore impose a limit and mention only those who may stand for all the rest.

I shall begin with Athanasius. Since he detested the simulation of error among the Meletians [Note: [Col. 0835] Letter to the Bishops of Egypt and Libya, no. 22, p. 231, vol. I, part 1.], how could he have thought that such simulation was to be tolerated in a Catholic? He both knew and confessed that Peter had rightly been rebuked by Paul for his simulation [Note: [Col. 0835] Compare Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, chapter 2, verse 12]. Would he then have judged that Eusebius, pretending to be a heretic, should either be praised or at least excused?

Basil follows, whose answer to question 76 in the *Shorter Rules* is this [Note: [Col. 0835] p. 44, vol. II, Paris edition, 1722.]:

> “The judgment of the Lord, who expressly said that a lie is from the devil, permitting no distinction among lies, does not allow one to lie for the sake of some useful purpose.”

The things he discusses in *Morals*, rule 24, lead to the same conclusion [Note: [Col. 0835] Ibid., p. 255.].

There is much of the same kind in Augustine. But it is especially important to note what is read in his book entitled *On Lying* [Note: [Col. 0836] Chapter 7, p. 312 and following, vol. VI of the works, Paris edition, 1700.]:

> “No one can prove that one ought ever to lie unless he can show that some eternal good can be obtained through a lie. But since each person departs from eternity in proportion as he departs from truth, it is utterly absurd to say that by descending from it one can reach some good; or, if there is some eternal good that does not embrace truth, it will not be true, and therefore what is false will not be good.”

Yet there were Fathers who defended the view that some good could rightly be obtained by lying. I shall grant that there were some; but I know that they were deceived by Origen’s error. And after considering their works carefully and for a long time, I have clearly discovered that they were never led to the point of saying that, for the sake of obtaining any advantage, however great, someone could pretend without enormous guilt that he agreed with heretics and approved what pleased them.

Such was the perversity of the Priscillianists that they said it was lawful for them to lie about their religion, provided either that their number increased or that they protected their sect from suffering any loss [Note: [Col. 0835] See Saint Augustine, book 6, *Against Lying*, addressed to Consentius, chapter 1 and following, p. 327 and following, vol. VI.].

> “The true martyrs, the holy martyrs, certainly did not understand matters in this way. They saw and held to what is written: ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation’; and ‘no lie was found in their mouth.’ Thus they departed blameless, where they will no longer need to beware of being tested by liars” [Note: [Col. 0836] Saint Augustine, ibid., chapter 2, p. 329.].

The following conviction was deeply fixed in their minds, a conviction that Augustine later expressed in the book entitled *On Lying*:

> “The first thing to avoid, and to flee far from, is the capital lie committed in the teaching of religion; no one ought to be driven to such a lie under any condition” [Note: [Col. 0836] Chapter 14, p. 312.].

Therefore the martyrs themselves were certain that it was preferable to suffer anything [Note: [Col. 0836] See Saint Augustine, *Against Lying*, addressed to Consentius, chapter 2, no. 3, p. 328.] rather than fall into that disgrace and crime of falsely claiming that they were bound to the religious rites of others. Indeed, they preferred even to perish rather than fail to confess openly the holy religion that they worshiped in their hearts.

What of those who, although they themselves had not sacrificed to lifeless gods, had nevertheless received certificates on which it was falsely written that they had sacrificed, and who therefore ought to be regarded as having gone free? What if the holy martyrs detested them so greatly that they enrolled them among the lapsed [Note: [Col. 0836] Compare Saint Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, p. 133, Oxford edition, 1682.]?

Finally, who would deny that those guardians of the Christian sacred things who, when ordered by pagan prefects of the cities to hand over the divine Scriptures, gave them books that contained nothing about religion, while pretending or lying that those books contained the divine Scriptures—who, I ask, would deny that the Fathers rightly condemned such guardians of the sacred things for betrayal [Note: [Col. 0837] Saint Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book 3, chapters 16 and 17, p. 316, vol. IX of the works, must be consulted.]?

Although they had taken care that the divine Scriptures should not fall into the hands of the enemies and be burned unjustly in the flames, they had nevertheless taken that precaution by a lie, than which nothing is more unworthy of Christian faith and integrity.

Now, since it is perfectly clear from what we have pursued thus far that those who judge it lawful to lie in order to obtain some good, even a great one, conflict with the doctrine of Scripture and the Fathers—and that this form of conflict is all the more atrocious when they judge a lie permissible because it touches the dogma of religion—who would not admit that the author of the sermon with whom this whole discussion is concerned conflicts with the doctrine of Scripture and the Fathers?

For he invented the claim that Eusebius of Vercelli had lied that he was a heretic, had said that he approved what pleased the Arians, and had pretended that he wished to subscribe first. Nor did he merely invent this; he also extolled it as though it were rightly done, so that he seems to have praised a bishop lying in so serious a matter because he dreamed that such a great lie could protect the reputation and good name of Dionysius of Milan.

Someone may ask: If, as can be understood from Hilary, Eusebius was permitted—although he would never have carried it out—to promise the Arians that he would do everything they desired, provided that they had first professed the Nicene faith, why was it not likewise permitted to someone seeking to safeguard Dionysius’ reputation to lie that he was a heretic and to pretend that he approved what pleased them?

The cases are wholly dissimilar. For whoever, although inwardly at variance with heretics, nevertheless by words, signs, or gestures either affirms or pretends that he agrees with those same heretics in doctrine binds himself, as we have seen, by a grave lie and becomes guilty of treachery, since he denies the faith which he ought to profess. But whoever tells adversaries that he will do something for them, on a condition that everyone can see will be rejected by those same adversaries, is far removed from the charge of lying; for he plainly shows that he will no more do it than it is certain that the adversaries themselves will reject his condition.

Eusebius, of course, knew how firm Athanasius was in defending the Catholic faith and how steadfast he was. He could not be induced to condemn its champion and the defender of the holy religion. Therefore, when he said that he would do everything the Arians desired, provided that they had first professed the Nicene faith, he did not mean that, while that same faith remained unharmed, he would pronounce judgment against Athanasius—a judgment which he knew with certainty would be full of injustice and wickedness. Rather, he meant to make it perfectly clear that he would do no more against Athanasius than they stubbornly refused to obey the decrees of the Nicene Council. Moreover, there was this further consideration: the Arians, seeing that they could obtain nothing against Athanasius unless they accepted that condition, would eventually cease to demand his condemnation.

I return to the author of the sermon under discussion. It was not enough for him to introduce Eusebius as lying about, or pretending to be, a heretic. He added Paul, as though that apostle himself had urged Eusebius, by his example, to lie or pretend in impiety and treachery. Thus, in the height of ignorance, he writes:

> “As Saint Paul says: ‘I became as a Jew to the Jews, in order to win the Jews’; so Eusebius lied to the heretics that he was a heretic. For he said that he agreed with their treachery,” and so forth.

But what he adduces from Paul is altogether different. For this teacher of the nations neither did nor said or pretended that he would do anything contrary to sound doctrine and true piety toward God. He did only this, in order to win the Jews for Christ: at times he adopted certain rites and ceremonies of the old law [Note: See Saint Augustine, Letter 15, alternatively 9, to Jerome, no. 6, p. 65, vol. II of the works, Antwerp edition of 1700, and Letter 72, alternatively 19, no. 26, p. 151.]. Although these rites had ceased to be valid once the New Testament had been introduced, they were not yet deadly.

But what the author of the sermon unjustly attributed to Eusebius was wholly—because of the lie or pretense that he approved a heretical doctrine—as full of the error of the Priscillianists as it was of crime and impiety. What if the author of that sermon, although thoughtless, was nevertheless so unjust to the great apostle that he made Paul himself guilty of the very pretense for which we read that Peter was rebuked by that same Paul?

Since writings so injurious to so great an apostle and to Saint Eusebius, so consonant with the error of the Priscillianists and so foreign to Christian sincerity, faith, and religion, are contained in that sermon, it is truly astonishing how they could ever have seemed acceptable to Tillemont by any reasonable argument [Note: *Mémoires pour servir à l’Histoire ecclésiastique*, vol. VII, title “Saint Eusebius of Vercelli,” article 9.]. To make them less intolerable, Tillemont presented them somewhat differently from what the context of the sermon permits. I do not concern myself with the purpose for which he did so. He says that the sermon itself is the work of an ancient author, but he does not likewise say who that author was.

Many others, especially the monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, explicitly deny that it was written by Ambrose, observing that the discourse and style are unlike Ambrose’s. I agree with them all the more strongly because I see that the holy bishop, who occasionally dealt with Eusebius and Dionysius in his genuine works, never affirmed or even suggested anything that appears related to the monstrous story celebrated by the author of this sermon.

I know that some, after removing this type of sermon from Ambrose, decided that it should be attributed to Maximus. The same Benedictine monks rejected their view on the ground that the sermon was delivered in the Church of Vercelli in the presence of Exuperantius, a disciple of Eusebius of Vercelli. That is something. Yet a much weightier argument can be drawn from a comparison with the homilies of Maximus.

There are two genuine homilies of this holy bishop concerning Saint Eusebius. The first is no. 77 in our series *On the Saints*, and the second is no. 78. In both, Saint Eusebius’ religion, piety, holiness, zeal for religion, and firmness and constancy in asserting the truth of the faith against heretics are celebrated in such a way that he never appears deceitful, double-minded, or insincere in anything. Can anyone prudent really be persuaded that Maximus, who spoke so chastely, so magnificently, and so abundantly about the virtue of Saint Eusebius, was eventually driven to write that Eusebius had lied that he was a heretic and had agreed with the Arians’ treachery?

Furthermore, Maximus treats Eusebius in a way that plainly indicates that he knew what Eusebius had done; nor does he anywhere hint that he was less experienced in carrying out ecclesiastical office. What of the author of the sermon? He confesses that he is ignorant of Eusebius’ deeds, unskilled in Sacred Scripture, and inexperienced in priestly functions. Even if he said nothing else, I would believe him: he perverts and confuses everything so completely that scarcely anyone could seem more ignorant, uninformed, or inexperienced in doctrine and history. Yet there will still be people who dare to say that he and Maximus were one and the same author? For my part, I shall take care not to dare it. For I have discovered that they were so certainly not the same that I have also clearly learned that this author himself lived later than Maximus. Whatever in his sermon is appropriate and truthful concerning Eusebius, he copied almost entirely, as I see, nearly word for word from Maximus’ homily 78 *On the Saints*. This is plainly the work of a plagiarist, and therefore of someone later than Maximus.

But someone may perhaps say: Saint Exuperantius, Eusebius’ hearer and also bishop of the Dertonensians, was older than Maximus. The former attended the Council of Aquileia in the year 381 [Note: See the acts of that council after Ambrose’s Letter 8, vol. III of the works, pp. 821 and 843, Venice edition of 1751]; the latter attended the Roman council under Hilary eighty-four years later, that is, in 465 [Note: Vol. II of the *Councils*, Paris edition of 1714, p. 799.]. Now the author of the sermon that we are discussing lived with Exuperantius, for he dealt with Eusebius’ praises in his presence. Therefore, he too was an author older than Maximus.

Nonsense—as though a man convicted of plagiarism could not have represented Exuperantius as present, even if Exuperantius had died long before. There are hundreds of examples of authors of this sort who, either to add reputation and value to their work or to practice their writing, composed booklets, speeches, and sermons containing many things as though they had happened, although in reality they had never happened.

For the present, I hold this certain: the author of that sermon took it from Maximus, and he who took it from Maximus could not have been older than Maximus himself. Enough has been said about the first sermon, which we relegated to the appendix of spurious little works.

It remains for me to explain what should be decided concerning the authors of the other sermons that follow shortly and concern the same subject, Saint Eusebius. In the first place, I assume without hesitation that none of them was written by Maximus. For the second in numerical order, if style and eloquence are taken into account, is evidently not the work of a bishop distinguished for his speaking ability, but perhaps of a monk who was plainly a beginner in this field and had scarcely begun declaiming at school.

I shall give the clearest possible evidence for this judgment. For this is how the sermon itself begins:

> “Although my inexperience, my shame, and my ever-trembling first efforts hold me back from presenting to your charity the sermon that I owe you, brothers, the venerable man, the bishop who is present, may nevertheless give confidence to my trembling. Your affection, whose love for me has been tested from my very infancy, excludes the force of fear from my mind; and in every respect the grace of the blessed memory of our lord and father, the confessor, urges me on. In him the office of pious devotion pleases more than a display of words, because of his heavenly training in the virtues. Although what I say may be slight and insignificant, I do not doubt that it will please him when spoken by one whom he himself nourished in his Church, born and brought forth there, with the rich, life-giving milk of the spirit.”

Who, moreover, would not see how enormously all this differs from the oratory of Maximus—not only from Maximus’, but from that of any moderately competent sacred orator who is not delighted by the empty sound of words and whose speech contains scarcely any substantive thought?

Some may perhaps think that this second sermon should be attributed to the same unknown author as the first. I am not concerned whether that opinion is true or false. I wish only to point out that a large part of the third and fourth sermons in our series was compiled from one sermon preserved in Codex 172 of the library of the *Aediles of the Greater Church* at Florence, now the Laurentian Library. That sermon bears both the name of Maximus and the title *On the Feast of the Holy Maccabees and of Saint Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli*, and we published it among the genuine works in column 611.

We learned this by comparing those two sermons with the latter one. Since these sermons consist partly of Maximus’ words and partly of words belonging to someone else, who could think that they should be counted among the sincere and genuine works of that bishop?

I admit that Muratori attributed them to Maximus himself. But that editor—whom otherwise I esteem as highly as I ought—found them in an Ambrosian codex and published them under the name found in the codex, without considering it necessary to argue at length whether they had truly been written by Maximus or had instead been attributed to him.

Furthermore, Gennadius, whose authority must necessarily carry weight because of his antiquity, when compiling a catalogue of Maximus’ works, mentions only two either treatises or sermons concerning Saint Eusebius, as we have shown elsewhere. Anyone may read them above as homilies *On the Saints*, nos. 77 and 78. These four sermons that we rightly relegated to the appendix cannot in any way be compared with them in seriousness, order, or elegance.

Of the remaining sermons transferred to this class we shall touch briefly on a few points, since their spuriousness becomes much clearer. Among them is a sermon recovered from the homiliary of the archives of the Lateran Basilica and inscribed to Saint Maximus. Its title is *On the Feast of a Certain Confessing Bishop*, and it is found on page 196.

It perhaps consists of three sections by three different authors. The first, beginning with the words “This man is the householder, the Lord Christ,” and continuing to “Neither has ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart,” is very far from Maximian eloquence and offers a crude explanation of the Gospel passage.

The second section, which begins with the words “But this man, journeying abroad, entrusted goods to his servants,” and continues to “So that there is no longer anything external to grieve over because of corruption,” is entirely from a homily of Saint Gregory the pope, found in the *Roman Breviary* for the Common of a Confessing Bishop. It is homily 9 in the Venetian edition, p. 173.

The third and final section begins, “Therefore, the deposition of this saint,” and was published by the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur among the Ambrosian sermons as no. 57.

After this sermon comes another, *On the Dedication of a Church*, drawn from Codex 539 of the Vatican Regina Library. Its manner of speaking is not only wholly unlike the purity of Maximus’ style, but its frequent use of lowly thoughts and street-level expressions also urges us to remove it from his works. This is even more strongly confirmed by the fact that what the author says about the rite of consecrating churches must be assigned to a period later than Saint Maximus’ time.

For it is certain that the order of those prayers, the presence of fellow priests, and the entire liturgy presented in the sermon reveal a more recent institution. By the same critical rule we also removed from the Maximian collection a sermon dealing with the offering of first fruits and tithes, since these were scarcely heard of in the Church in Maximus’ time.

Only collections were made, as is clear from many sermons of Saint Leo the Great; these were distributed for the adornment of churches and the relief of the poor. Nothing else emerges from the sermon that seems to belong to Maximus, since scarcely anything in it can be seen that is not plainly written without polish.

Add to this the piled-up passages from Sacred Scripture, illuminated by no explanation, contrary to Maximus’ custom. This sermon was copied from a Beneventan codex, as was the one that follows immediately, *On the Honor Due to Parents*. Although the things it contains are true, its discourse nevertheless collapses, worked out with no elegance and adorned with no beauty of expression. I would call some beginner, not Maximus, the author of this preliminary effort, one reaching the tenth or eleventh century, when human letters lay uncultivated and almost lifeless.

An even worse piece follows the foregoing in this class: a certain discourse on the holy Resurrection of Christ, found under the name of Saint Maximus in Casinensis Codex 123. You will scarcely have tasted its first draught before you immediately judge how insipid and wretched the rest is—namely, that the writer fell into those times when almost everyone, having abandoned the springs of the Latin language, pursued muddy streams.

No more certain evidence can be offered to establish that collections of this kind—homilies and sermons—were made after elegance and purity in Latin writing had already been corrupted, when good and bad were indiscriminately mixed together.

Nor need confirmation of this truth be sought farther than the following sermon, *On the Feast of Saint Stephen, the Protomartyr*, likewise taken from Casinensis Codex 106, page 16. That codex contains several other genuine works of Maximus and of other Fathers; it also contains some spurious ones. This does no harm to the others, since they are supported by such numerous and illustrious marks of authenticity that anyone who doubted their authors would rightly be accused of frivolity.

One point alone remains to be noted, as we have observed: such unfortunate productions are usually found in only one or another codex, which readily creates doubt about their spurious attribution.

Three homilies that we brought forth from the paper Codex Chisianus belong to this class of spurious works. Although it is written in a neat hand, it is full of errors. Two sermons also belong here, which the most courteous Francesco Antonio Frisius, canon, already praised elsewhere, supplied to us from a codex of the Basilica of Saint Ambrose at Milan. We shall give their titles in the index to be added shortly.

Whoever has read the first of these homilies might think that he had read the others as well. The same sterility of ornamented expression, strength, and learning reveals the commentator’s poverty and produces weariness and disgust. Who, unless he were dull and utterly ignorant of Maximus, would wish to think so poorly of him as to attribute these patched-together absurdities to him?

The third homily is even more unfortunate than the two preceding ones, since its author appears to have fallen into a factual error. What Saint Matthew wrote about Herod lying in wait for the Lord Christ and about the angel’s warning to Joseph in a dream, he says was reported by Saint John the Evangelist.

There is nothing in it except what has simply been imagined and expressed in childish fashion. What it says about Herod’s embassy to the Roman senate contradicts the Gospel narrative. For from Matthew we learn that, after being deceived by the Magi—whose return he had awaited in order to discover where Christ had been born—Herod ordered all infants in Bethlehem and throughout its territory, from two years old and younger, to be killed.

That monstrous slaughter was carried out not after two full years had elapsed, but when scarcely two or three months had passed. We pass over the remaining details, which confirm its putrid spuriousness.

At last we have reached the final sermons copied from a codex of the Basilica of Saint Ambrose at Milan. The first concerns the *Feast of the Dedication of a Church* and explains the passage from chapter 10 of John: “The feast of the Dedication took place at Jerusalem,” and so forth. The other bears the title *On the Octave of Saint Stephen* and explains Matthew’s account of the didrachma found by Peter.

We attributed neither to Maximus, since in them there is no trace of his eloquence, his selection of subject matter, or his understanding of Sacred Scripture. We send them, together with the other unfortunate sermons heaped together above, to the later centuries.

For this reason, and also by applying stricter rules of criticism, we omit publishing five sermons taken from Bobbian codices. Two concern the Nativity of the Lord; the next two concern the blessed Mother of God, Mary; and the last concerns the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

There is no need to discuss each one in separate observations, since they all suffer from the defects of a later age: inelegance, childish simplicity, and—something even more absurd—the use, in the sermons about the Virgin Mary, of expressions that are not merely humble but wholly out of keeping with the dignity of the subject. It is not at all believable that Saint Maximus, who always spoke with the greatest refinement, used such expressions. We therefore leave them hidden in darkness.

Two sermons and three homilies copied from a Neapolitan codex of the library of Monte Oliveto must be placed in the same collection. The titles of the sermons are as follows.

The first sermon is *On Fasting*, and begins: “I want you, dearest brothers, to be moved by the higher concern: why should we observe the Lord’s Lent?” and so forth.

The second is *On Works of Mercy*, whose beginning is: “See, brothers, why you are called Christians,” and so forth.

In third place follows a homily on Luke chapter 6: “Be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful,” and so forth. It begins with the words: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged,” and so forth.

The fourth place is occupied by a homily on Mark chapter 8: “When there was a great crowd with Jesus and they had nothing to eat,” and so forth. It begins in this way: “The Lord Jesus Christ, God before the ages,” and so forth.

Finally, I shall mention a homily on the Gospel according to Luke chapter 5: “When the crowd pressed upon Jesus to hear the word of God,” and so forth. Its beginning is: “Concerning the fish which, at the Lord’s command, they caught after lowering the nets,” and so forth.

Why I judge that these little works must be omitted altogether I shall briefly explain. The first sermon by itself shows how unworthy it is of Maximus as author. It is so entangled in obscurity and so filled with absurdities plainly worthy of children’s exercises that it is intolerable.

Although the second contains neither so many gaps nor such great confusion, nothing nevertheless occurs in it that is not unlike Maximian speech. The homilies follow.

The first of them is partly excerpted from the second book of the great Augustine *On the Sermon on the Mount* [Note: Chapter 8 and following, nos. 59 and following, vol. III, part 17, pp. 16 and following, Antwerp edition of 1700], and perhaps partly from elsewhere; but certainly not from any work of Maximus, since nothing could be imagined more alien to him.

In the second I do not see what it contains that is distinctive of a homily. It is a continuous explanation of a Gospel passage, but the discourse is neither elegantly developed in connection and order nor arranged for the shaping of morals. It is composed in such a way that one might recognize its author not as Maximus but as Dionysius the Carthusian, or someone like him—someone more devoted to the letter than to moral meaning and who treated the subject more narrowly and constrictedly. Maximus, by contrast, was accustomed to write both more polishedly and more expansively.

I say the same about the third homily. Since these little works are of such a kind that they can bring no benefit to anyone and add nothing of distinction to this edition, I am not afraid that someone will reproach me for judging that they should be completely rejected. This is especially so since I have followed the example of the highly learned monks of Saint Maur, who, although they mentioned many sermons falsely attributed to Saint Ambrose, nevertheless judged that, since they contributed neither to the honor of their Ambrosian edition nor any useful content, they should be removed even from the appendix of spurious works.

Finally, I must discuss two letters which, following Erasmus [Note: See Erasmus’ Frobenian edition of 1517 and Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. II, book IV, chapter 3.], all editors of Jerome’s works contend were falsely attributed to Jerome. One is said to have been sent to some unknown sick man; the other to a friend, concerning the perfect man.

In undertaking this discussion, I was prompted by John Martianaeus, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur, and by Dominicus Vallarsius, a priest of Verona. Martianaeus, whom I named first, wrote in volume V of Jerome’s works, which he published not long after the beginning of this century, that the letter to a friend concerning the perfect man ought to be attributed to Saint Maximus, although he relied on no witness, no evidence, and not even a conjecture.

Vallarsius was bolder than Martianaeus. Although he did not dare to affirm with certainty that the first letter, to the sick man, had been written by Maximus, he nevertheless judged it probable that it had been composed by Maximus or at least by someone who held episcopal rank. Concerning the other, the letter to a friend about the perfect man, he confidently declares—fearing nothing so much as to appear doubtful:

> “This is Saint Maximus of Turin’s, as no one now denies.”

Dominicus Mansi, otherwise a learned man who later became archbishop of Lucca, agreed with these two editors of Jerome’s works [Note: In the notes to Fabricius’ *Bibliotheca mediæ et infimæ ætatis*, Padua edition of 1734, vol. V.].

There are, however, many reasons that prevent me from thinking that authority should be attached to their view. In the first place, why should I be influenced by men who, although modern, make arbitrary judgments about matters removed from our memory by great antiquity, while ancient monuments and writers remain silent?

Moreover, since Maximus’ discourse and style differ so greatly from those displayed by the two letters that nothing could be more unlike them, how could I bring myself to believe that either letter ought to be attributed to Maximus? There is no reason to discuss so evident a matter at greater length.

Let readers compare these letters with Maximus’ genuine works. I promise myself that there will be no one who can say that he has read anything in the letters themselves worthy of Maximus.

Nevertheless, in this appendix we have decided to print them again, with many variant readings supplied and corrected from Codex IX, Pluteus XIX of the Laurentian Library, and from the Roman edition of Saint Jerome’s *Letters* printed by Peter de Maximo in 1468. This necessary work of correcting the text was omitted by Vallarsius.

[Col. 0843]

*[SERMONS (C, G, S)]*

## FIRST CLASS

## SERMONS ON THE LITURGICAL YEAR

### SERMON I. On the Advent of the Lord I

#### NOTICE

Two Casinensis codices, 106 and 117, and the Neapolitan codex of Monte Oliveto present this first sermon under the name of Saint Maximus. The latter gives it the title *On the First Sunday of Advent*. I think that some material from Saint Maximus’ first homily before the Nativity of the Lord was incorporated into this sermon; where the remainder came from, I do not know. I suppose that it came from Maximus’ writings, for the style of the entire discourse does not seem uniform to me.

#### SUMMARY

[Col. 0843A] Especially on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, it is fitting that we should be adorned and radiant with good works. Above all, we must flee drunkenness, resist anger, and drive hatred from our hearts.

By the favor of the Divinity, dearest brothers, the day will soon arrive on which we must celebrate with joy the birthday of the Lord our Savior [Note: From Casinensis Codex 117 and the Neapolitan Codex of Monte Oliveto: “the day has now arrived on which …”]. Therefore I ask and exhort you to labor, with God’s help, as much as we can, so that on that day, with a sincere and pure conscience, a clean heart, and a chaste body, we may approach the Lord’s altar and be found worthy to receive his body and blood, not for judgment but rather as a remedy for our soul [Note: The word “rather” is absent from the same codex; the Monte Oliveto Codex reads “to receive.”].

For our life consists in the body of Christ. The Lord himself said so: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6). Therefore let the person who wants to have life change his life [Note: Likewise the codex: “who wishes to receive life.”]. For if he does not change his life, he will receive life for judgment; and by that very life he will be corrupted rather than healed, and killed rather than given life.

The Apostle says: “Whoever eats the Lord’s body and drinks his blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11).

Although it is fitting that we should be adorned and radiant with good works at all times, our works ought especially to shine before people on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, as the Lord himself said in the Gospel.

Consider, I ask you, brothers, when some powerful or noble man wishes to celebrate his own birthday or that of his son, with what care, many days beforehand, he orders everything dirty that he sees in his house to be cleaned, throws out whatever is useless or unsuitable [Note: The Casinensis Codex reads “throws out”], and orders whatever is useful and necessary [Note: The same codex reads “orders to be provided”] to be brought forth. If the house is dark, it is whitewashed; the floors are cleaned with brooms and adorned by being sprinkled with various flowers; and everything that contributes to joy of spirit and bodily delight is provided with the greatest care.

Why is all this done, dearest brothers, except so that the birthday of a mortal man may be celebrated with joy [Note: The same Casinensis Codex and the Monte Oliveto Codex read “the day of the birthday”]? If, then, you make such preparations for your own birthday or that of your son, how great and what sort of preparations ought you to make when you are about to celebrate the birthday of your Lord? If you prepare such things for one who will die, what ought you to prepare for the eternal one?

Therefore, whatever you do not want to find in your house, labor as much as you can so that God will not find it in your soul. Certainly, if an earthly king, or any householder, invited you to his birthday celebration, in what sort of clothing would you take care to appear? How new, clean, and splendid would it be—clothing whose age, cheapness, or any ugliness would not offend the eyes of the one inviting you [Note: The same codices read “clothing.”]?

With such zeal, therefore, as far as you are able, and with Christ’s help [Note: The same codices read “with Christ’s assistance”], strive to come to the solemnity of the eternal King—that is, to the birthday of the Lord our Savior—with your soul composed by various ornaments of virtue and adorned with the jewels of simplicity and the flowers of sobriety, with purity shining, charity radiant, and almsgiving bright [Note: The same codex reads “shining … radiant … bright”—respectively, “clean,” “splendid,” and “white.”].

For if the Lord Christ sees you thus prepared celebrating his birthday, he himself will deign not only to come to you and visit your soul [Note: The Casinensis Codex reads “to visit and also to dwell”], but also to rest there and dwell in it forever. As it is written: “I will dwell among them and walk among them” (Leviticus 26). And again: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone rises and opens to me [Note: The Casinensis Codex reads “I will enter”], I will enter to him, and I will dine with him and he with me” (Revelation 3).

How happy is the soul that, with God’s help, takes care to govern its life in such a way that it may be found worthy to receive Christ as guest and inhabitant [Note: The same codex reads “to welcome”]. Conversely, how unhappy is that conscience—one to be mourned with a whole fountain of tears—which has stained itself with evil works so thoroughly that Christ cannot rest in it, but the devil begins to rule there!

Such a soul, unless the medicine of repentance soon comes to its aid, is abandoned by the light and seized by darkness; it is emptied of sweetness and filled with bitterness; death attacks it, and life rejects it. Yet let the person in such a state not lose confidence in the Lord’s mercy or be broken by deadly despair; rather, let him flee quickly to repentance.

While the wounds of his sins are still fresh and hot, let him apply healing remedies to himself, because our physician is almighty. He is so accustomed to healing our wounds that, after his medicines, not even the traces of scars remain.

Therefore you ought to abstain from every defilement for many days before his birthday. Whenever you plan to celebrate the Lord’s birthday or the other solemnities, flee drunkenness above all; resist anger as the most savage beast; drive hatred from your hearts like deadly poison; and let there be such charity among us all [Note: The same codex reads “let such charity be in you”] that it reaches not only to our friends but even to our enemies, so that we may confidently say in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6).

For whoever knows that he hates even one person—I do not know whether he can approach the Lord’s altar with confidence, especially since the blessed John the Evangelist cries out in terror and says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3). It is for you to judge whether a murderer ought, before doing penance, presume to receive the Eucharist.

Saint John adds still further and cries out, saying [Note: The same codex reads: “Whoever hates his brother walks in darkness and does not know …”]: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness; he does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (ibid. 2). And again: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar. For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (ibid. 4).

Whoever keeps hatred or anger in his heart and, beneath such thunder, is neither frightened nor awakened ought to be considered not asleep but dead.

Therefore, dearest brothers, reflecting on these things daily, let those who are good strive, with God’s grace, to persevere in good works: “For it is not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered to the end, who will be saved” (Matthew 10).

But those who recognize that they are slow to give alms, quick to anger, and rash in practicing every kind of wickedness [Note: The Casinensis Codex and the Monte Oliveto Codex read “rash in exercising anger”] should hasten, with the Lord’s help, to rescue themselves from evil, so that they may be found worthy to accomplish what is good. Thus, when the day of judgment comes, they may not be punished with the impious and sinners, but may be found worthy to reach the eternal rewards with the just and merciful [Note: The Casinensis Codex and the Monte Oliveto Codex add: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”].

### SERMON II. Again, On the Advent of the Lord II

[Col. 0845]

#### NOTICE

In three Casinensis codices—103, folio 1 verso; 106, folio 57 verso; and 117, page 3—the title of this sermon is *On the Third Sunday of Advent*. We stated on page 394 of this volume that it should be assigned to a period later than Maximus.

In Codex 106, Maximus’ name can now be seen to have been erased and Augustine’s name substituted for it. The style of this sermon also differs from that used by Maximus.

#### SUMMARY

[Col. 0845C] At Christ’s birth, the prophecies of the prophets were fulfilled.

We are taught from the prophetic reading from which tribe Christ was to be born. That he would come according to the flesh from the stock of David [Note: Col. 0846D; Codex Casinensis 106: “would be”], through the Holy Spirit, was thus foretold in the Psalms: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not disappoint it: ‘From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne’” (Psalm 131). And again: “Once I have sworn by my Holy One: if I lie to David, his seed will remain forever, and his throne like the sun in my sight, and like the perfect moon forever, a faithful witness in heaven” (Psalm 88).

Likewise, in the Book of Chronicles: “And the word of the Lord came to Nathan the prophet, saying: [Note: These words are omitted between asterisks in Codex Casinensis 117.] *Go and say to my servant David*: Thus says the Lord: I will announce to you that the Lord will build you a house. And when your days are fulfilled, so that you go to your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall be from your sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build me a house, and I will make his throne firm forever. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me; and I will not remove my mercy from him, as I removed it from him who was before him. I will establish him in my house, and he shall reign forever, and his throne shall be firmly established forever” (1 Chronicles 17).

Whoever thinks that all these things were fulfilled in Solomon seems to be greatly mistaken. For what is to be understood differently in Solomon is what was said: “And when your days are completed and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, who will come forth from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom” [Note: Codex Casinensis 117: “his kingdom.”] (2 Samuel 7). Can it be believed that this was prophesied concerning that Solomon? Certainly not. For he began to reign while his father was still alive. But here it says: “When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed.” From this it is understood that another was promised, who had not been foretold as one to be raised up before David’s death, and who would build the house of the Lord—not from walls made by human hands, but from living and precious stones, that is, from holy and faithful people.

And regarding what follows—“His house is faithful, and his kingdom shall be before me forever” (ibid.)—let anyone pay attention and see that this was not foretold concerning Solomon [Note: Col. 0846D; Codices Casinenses 106 and 117 read “pronounced”]. Solomon’s house was full of foreign women worshiping idols, and he himself, seduced and captivated by them, became a king of idolatry. Although he had been good at the beginning, he had an evil end.

Who, then, is this whose house is faithful forever, and who was promised as one to be raised up after David’s death? He is certainly the one concerning whom David himself, [reading uncertain: “aestuan.”] cries out in Psalm 88, saying: “But you have delayed your Christ.” It is therefore neither Solomon nor David himself, but Christ has been deferred.

Behold, the prophecies foretold above have appeared as fulfilled not in Solomon but in Christ the Lord, who arose from the family of David. Concerning him the Lord himself says through Jeremiah: “And I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king, and he shall be wise, and he shall execute judgment and righteousness upon the earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely; and this is the name by which they shall call him: ‘The Lord our righteous one’” (Jeremiah 23). [Note: Codex Casinensis 117: “in those days.”]

Isaiah likewise speaks of Christ, because he was born according to the flesh from the seed of David. Thus he says in what follows: “On that day the root of Jesse, which stands as a sign for the peoples, the nations will seek, and his tomb shall be glorious” (Isaiah 11). The root of Jesse stands as a sign for the peoples because Christ will imprint the sign of the cross upon their foreheads. “The nations will seek him,” since it is plainly seen that this has been fulfilled. His tomb is so glorious that, apart from the fact that we who have been redeemed through his death display his glory, the place itself, shining with miracles because of its glory, draws the whole world to itself.

In Hebrew this passage reads: “And his resting-place shall be glorious.” This is certainly because, when his flesh died, it did not see corruption, in accordance with the Psalm’s statement: “For you will not abandon his soul to the underworld, nor will you give your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm 15).

This is the one who is promised through Nathan from the seed of David, and who is likewise proclaimed through the prophet Isaiah in these words: “A branch shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 11). This branch from the root of Jesse is the virgin Mary, who sprang from the root of David and bore the flower, the Lord and Savior. Concerning him it also follows: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him” (ibid.).

These great gifts of the Spirit are proclaimed concerning him because the Holy Spirit does not dwell in him in measure, as in us, but in him is the whole fullness of divinity and grace.

He is the one who does not judge according to the sight of the eyes or the hearing of the ears; rather, “righteousness is the belt of his loins,” [Note: The Vulgate reads: “and faith is the belt of his kidneys.” These words are omitted in Codex 227.] “and faith is the belt of his loins” (ibid.).

In his Church the wolf dwells with the lamb: the very one who used to snatch prey from it, when he is converted to it, dwells with the innocent. In his fold the leopard lies down with the kid. That is, the cunning are mingled there with sinners; the calf from the circumcision, the lion from secular power, and the sheep from the common people dwell together, because in the faith there is a common mingling of all.

The little child who threatens them is certainly the one who humbled himself for us as a little child. The ox and the lion will eat straw together because the ruler and the subject peoples share a common teaching. “The infant shall delight over the hole of the asp” (ibid.), while the nations that once used to proclaim poisons are converted, and even little children delight in hearing the faith of Christ.

The den of the basilisk is the hearts of unbelievers, in which that twisting serpent rested. When the child was weaned, he seized it and dragged it away captive, so that it might do no harm on his holy mountain, that is, in the Church.

Now, because prophetic utterance bears witness concerning Christ who was born from Moab, Isaiah himself also testifies: “I will set a lion upon those who have fled from Moab, and upon the remnant of the land. Send forth, O Lord, a lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isaiah 15:9 and 16:1). [Note: Vulgate 15:9: “For the waters of Dibon are filled with blood; for I will bring additional things upon Dibon, upon those who have fled from Moab, and upon the remnant of the land.” Chapter 16: “Send forth a lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth,” etc.]

For from this nation of the Moabites came forth the immaculate Lamb who takes away the sins of the world and rules over the entire earth. The rock of the desert signifies Ruth, who, left destitute by the death of her husband, bore Obed from Boaz; Obed begot Jesse, Jesse begot David, and from David’s stock Christ was born.

By “the mountain of the daughter of Zion” he either means, historically, the city of Jerusalem itself, or, according to the tropological interpretation, the Church, consoled upon a watchtower—that is, exalted in virtues.

## SERMON III. On preparation for the Lord’s Nativity

[Col. 0847]

### ADMONITION

This sermon was published by the Maurists in volume V of the appendix to the sermons of Saint Augustine, sermon 116, and attributed to Saint Caesarius. But in Codices Casinenses 106 and 117, and in the Beneventan and Neapolitan codices of Monte Oliveto, we read the same sermon ascribed to Saint Maximus, as also in Dominicus Maria Mansi’s edition in the *Miscellanea* of Baluze. Yet anyone who pays attention will easily recognize that this style is not Maximus’s.

### SUMMARY

[Col. 0847C] Let us prepare, with Christ’s help, for the day of the Lord’s Nativity, as though for a nuptial and heavenly banquet, cleansed from every form of luxury and adorned with good works.

Most beloved brothers, as we are about to receive with the most faithful devotion this holy, desirable, glorious, and unique solemnity—that is, the Nativity of the Lord and Savior—we must prepare ourselves with his help [Note: Col. 0848D; Codex Neapolitanus of Monte Oliveto: “with all our strength”] and carefully examine every hiding-place of our soul, lest perhaps there be some hidden sin within us that both confounds and gnaws at our conscience and offends the eyes of the divine majesty.

For although Christ our Lord rose after his Passion and ascended into heaven, he nevertheless observes how we conduct ourselves, and carefully considers how each of his servants strives to prepare and compose himself for celebrating his Nativity without avarice, anger, pride, or luxury. According to how he sees each person adorned with good works, so he will distribute to that person the grace of his mercy.

For if he sees someone clothed in the light of charity, adorned with the pearls of justice and mercy, chaste, humble, merciful, kind, and sober, if he recognizes such a person, he will distribute to him, through the ministry of his priests, his body and blood not for judgment but for healing.

But if he sees someone adulterous, drunk, greedy, and proud, I fear that what the Lord himself said in the Gospel may be said to him: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” And, God forbid, what follows may happen: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 22).

Behold what sentence will befall on the day of judgment the person who, without the remedy of repentance, approaches the Lord’s festival polluted by the filth of vices.

For on the Lord’s Nativity, most beloved brothers, he was joined to his bride as though at a spiritual wedding. Then truth sprang up from the earth; then righteousness looked down from heaven. Then the bridegroom came forth from his chamber—that is, the Word of God came forth from the virgin womb. He came forth with his bride, the Church, that is, he assumed human flesh.

Invited, therefore, to such holy nuptials, and about to enter the banquet of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, consider with what garments we ought to be adorned. And so, with God’s help, let us cleanse as much as we can both our hearts and our bodies, so that that heavenly inviter may find nothing filthy, nothing foul, nothing dark, nothing unworthy of his eyes in us.

These things, therefore, dearest brothers, we must consider not casually but with great trembling. For we have been invited to a wedding at which we ourselves, if we act rightly, shall be bridegrooms. Let us consider to what kind of wedding, to what kind of bride, and to what kind of banquet we have been invited.

We have been invited to a table where the food of human beings is not found, but where the bread of angels is set forth. Therefore let us see to it that perhaps within, in the soul where we ought to be adorned with the pearls of good works, we do not appear wrapped in the old rags of vices; and that when chastity makes those who are good in God’s sight white, luxury does not make those who are evil filthy.

Therefore, whenever either the Lord’s Nativity or the other festivals arrive, as I have often admonished you, abstain not only from the unhappy companionship of concubines but also from your own wives, and make yourselves strangers to every form of anger, so that past sins may be redeemed through almsgiving and repentance. Let no hatred be held in the heart against anyone.

What vanity used to waste through the throat, let justice begin to distribute to the poor through mercy. What luxury or gluttony dissipated in the world, let piety gather up in heaven.

Although it is beneficial that we should always give alms, nevertheless, especially on holy solemnities, let us distribute generously according to our means; above all, let us invite the poor to our banquets more frequently. For it is not right that on a holy solemnity, among a Christian people belonging to one Lord, some should become drunk while others are tormented by the danger of hunger.

We and all the people are servants of one Lord. We have been redeemed at the same price. We entered this world under equal conditions, and we shall depart from it by a similar exit. If we act rightly, we shall likewise come together to one blessedness.

And why should the poor person not receive food with you, when he will receive the kingdom with you? Why should the poor person not receive at least an old tunic, when he will receive with you the robe of immortality? Why should the poor person not deserve to receive your bread, when he has deserved to receive the sacrament of baptism with you? Why should he be unworthy to receive the leftovers from your food, when he will come with you to the banquet of angels?

Listen, brothers; listen not to my command but to the Lord’s common command. For he says in the Gospel: “When you prepare a breakfast or a dinner, do not invite the rich, who may invite you in return and repayment be made to you; but invite the poor and the lame, and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you; but you will be repaid in the resurrection of the just” (Luke 14).

But someone says: “Then ought I not to invite friends or relatives to a banquet?” Relatives and neighbors should indeed be invited, but they should be invited less often; and banquets should be prepared for them not too lavish or luxurious, but so frugal, sober, and proper that something remains with which the poor may be refreshed and something may be distributed to those in need.

Then, when the day of judgment comes, may we not hear with the wicked, who now despise the poor: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire”; but may we deserve to hear with the just and merciful: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom; for I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matthew 25).

May that desirable voice also be directed to us: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord” (ibid.).

But so that these things we have suggested may remain more firmly fixed in your loving hearts, let us briefly repeat what has been said. This is what we have urged, brothers: because the Lord’s Nativity is near, let us prepare ourselves through Christ’s help as though for a nuptial and heavenly banquet, cleansed from every form of luxury and adorned with good works. Let us distribute alms to the poor; let us cast anger and hatred, as the devil’s poison, out of our hearts.

Preserve chastity faithfully even with your own wives. Invite the poor more frequently to your banquets. Rise earlier for the vigils. In church, standing, either pray or sing psalms. Do not yourselves utter idle or worldly words from your mouths, and correct those who wish to utter them. Keep peace with everyone, and restore to harmony those whom you recognize to be at variance.

If, with Christ’s help, you faithfully wish to fulfill these things, then in this age you will be able to approach the Lord’s altar with a secure conscience, and in the future happily attain eternal blessedness, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On the Nativity of the Lord I

[Col. 0849]

### ADMONITION

Although the beginning of this sermon is excerpted from Maximus’s fifth homily on the Nativity of the Lord, we have nevertheless attributed the sermon as a whole to some uncertain author, because the style of the remaining portion seems different to us. Only in Codex Casinensis 106, page 12, is it attributed to Saint Maximus; in Codex 106 of the archive of Saint Peter, letter C, page 4, to Saint Augustine; in the other codices we have seen, to no one.

### SUMMARY

[Col. 0849C] Let us celebrate the coming of God and man and the festive day of divine condescension, so that we may return to God.

Today, most beloved brothers, Christ has been born; we have been reborn. Today the Savior of the world received from his mother the time of birth, although from the Father he has no time of birth. He who is eternally the Creator of all things today, by being born from a mother, became our Savior. Today he was born for us within the turning course of time, so that he might lead us to the Father’s eternity.

God became man so that man might become God. So that man might eat the bread of angels, the Lord of angels today became man.

Today that prophecy has been fulfilled which says: “Drop dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one; let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Savior” (Isaiah 45).

Therefore the one who had made was made, so that the one who had perished might be found. Thus in the Psalms man confesses: “Before I was humbled, I sinned” [Note: Col. 0849D; Codex of Saint Peter: “I sinned”] and again: “I went astray like a sheep that had perished” (Psalm 118).

Man sinned and became guilty; God the man was born so that the guilty might be freed. Man therefore fell, but God descended. Man fell miserably; God descended mercifully. Man fell through pride; God descended with grace.

Thus the Mother of the Lord heard from the angel: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you” (Luke 2).

He who was first born without a mother in heaven was born today without a father on earth. Christ was born: God from the Father, man from his mother; from the Father’s immortality, from his mother’s virginity; from the Father without a mother, from his mother without a father; from the Father without time, from his mother without seed; from the Father the beginning of life, from his mother the end of death; from the Father ordering every day, from his mother consecrating this day.

For he sent John the man before him, so that John might be born when the days began to grow shorter; and he himself was born when the days begin to grow longer, [Note: The same codex: “so that this might be prefigured from it.”] and by this was prefigured what John says: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3).

Human life must decrease in itself and increase in Christ, so that the one who lives [Note: The same codex: “may now no longer live for himself.”] may no longer live for himself but for him who died and rose for all; and so that each of us may say what the Apostle says: “I live, yet it is no longer I; Christ lives in me.” [Note: Codex Vaticanus Palatinus: “I live, yet it is no longer I.”] “He must increase, but I must decrease” (Galatians 2).

Let all his angels praise him worthily [Note: Col. 0849D; the same codex reads “They praise”], for he is the eternal and incorruptible food that gives them life by nourishing them; for he is the Word of God, by whose life they live and by whose goodness they always live well. They worthily praise God in the presence of God and give glory to God in the highest.

But we, his people and the sheep of his pasture, according to the measure of our weakness, reconciled by good will, deserve peace. For the true and present-day voice of those angels is the one they joyfully poured forth when the Savior was born for us: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2).

They praise appropriately; let us also praise obediently. They are his messengers; we too are his sheep. He filled their table in heaven; he filled our manger on earth. Their table is full because “in the beginning was the Word” (John 1); our manger is full because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Let us therefore celebrate the Lord’s Nativity, most beloved brothers; let us celebrate the coming of God and man, so that we may return to God. Let us therefore celebrate the festive day—not of human devotion but of divine condescension; not of weakness but of eternity; not of the Lord’s formation but of his reformation—that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON V. On the words of Matthew, chapter 2: “When Herod had died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: Rise, and take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel; for those who sought the child’s life have died.”

[Col. 0851]

### ADMONITION

We have observed that the manner of writing in this sermon is not like that used by Saint Maximus. Therefore we think that the scribe of the thirteenth-century codex of the Lambach library rashly attributed it to that holy bishop.

### SUMMARY

[Col. 0851B] Herod’s illness and cruelty are described, and the Gospel passage is expounded.

Herod, who had made himself the author of such great crimes that he did not even withdraw his hand from persecuting the Lord himself, could not remain unpunished. He had fraudulently been the first foreigner to obtain the kingdom of the Jews; he had not only inflicted many evils upon the Jews [Note: See Flavius Josephus, *History of the Jews*, book XVII, chapter 7, volume I, page 847, edition of Sigibert Avercamp, 1726], but had also become a parricide against his own sons. On top of all the evils that would take too long to recount, when he heard that the Savior of the world had been born, moved by envy—that he might destroy the one whom he had heard was born to reign—he ordered all the boys in Bethlehem and throughout its entire territory to be killed.

Such madness had inflamed his mind that neither the multitude of the dying nor the innocence of the children caused his cruelty to cease. For this he was struck by divine vengeance and suffered an incurable illness.

He had fever, extremely violent sighs, continual shortness of breath, and also spasms throughout his whole body. Dropsy had wasted his body, so that his footsteps were burdened by the swelling of his feet. His internal organs were also burned by such pain that they seemed to be dissolving through the natural excretory process.

The itching throughout his body was also so intolerable that even his private parts became putrid and swarmed with worms. He also suffered such foul breath that scarcely any physician could approach him to administer medicines.

Finally, while he lay in this illness, he is said to have ordered some physicians to be killed because they were unwilling to do what might have helped his health. In addition, he endured intolerable hunger and thirst; and, what was more grievous, every food and drink was repulsive to him.

He suffered such sleeplessness that he passed his days and nights without sleep. If he happened to fall asleep briefly, he suffered a nightmare, so that he regretted having fallen asleep.

But because he burned with excessive love for the present life, he ordered himself to be carried across the Jordan, where there were hot springs said to bring relief even to the sick. But although they were useful to others, they benefited him nothing, so that it might be understood that he had been struck by the will of God.

The physicians also thought that he should be placed in a bath of warm oil. When he had entered it, his entire body is said to have become so relaxed that his eyes turned like those of the dying, his voice was cut off, and his senses disappeared.

When, after a short while, he had been roused by the voices of his friends and servants and had recovered his senses, he ordered himself to be carried to Jericho. When he had already despaired of life, he ordered all the leaders of the Jews, summoned to him from their individual cities and fortified towns, to be shut up in custody.

Calling his sister Salome and her husband Alexander, he said: “I know that the Jews will rejoice at my death. But I shall be able to have an honorable funeral from the mourning of those who lament if you are willing to obey my commands. As soon as I breathe out my spirit, kill all the leaders of the Jews [Col. 0852B] whom I have shut up in custody; thus those who wish to rejoice at my death will be forced to mourn the destruction of their fellow citizens.”

And so that they might not withdraw their hand from shedding their blood, he ordered five hundred silver drachmas to be given to each of them.

When he was afflicted by great pain, he ordered his son Antipater—whom he had bound in chains because he had plotted his father’s death—to be killed; and, when he heard of his death, he rejoiced.

Now, overwhelmed by such great evils and having realized that he could not continue to live, he wished to hasten his death. Therefore one day, when he had sat down, he aimed a blow at himself and would have struck himself with his own hand and immediately ended his life, if one of his friends, who was standing nearby, named Achiabus, had not pulled his hand back.

Such, then, was the end of Herod, who, out of hatred for the Savior, had shed so much innocent blood.

When he had died, behold, an angel of the Lord again appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: “Rise, and take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel; for those who sought the child’s life have died.” And he rose, took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel (Matthew 2:19 and following).

And because the angel did not say “the dead man” but “the dead,” we understand from the angel’s words that many of the leaders of the Jews had agreed with Herod. Therefore divine vengeance brought it about that many of them perished with him, since they had consented with him to the Lord’s death.

Spiritually, however, Herod’s death signifies the end of the envious contention with which Judea now rages against the Church. But the fact that, after Herod’s death, the child Jesus returned to the land of Israel signifies that, toward the end of the age, he will return to the Synagogue when it has believed in him through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch.

Thus, when he is ordered to be carried into Egypt and commanded to flee by night, night is mentioned. But when he returns to the land of Israel, there is no mention of night. Those whom he now abandons in darkness because of unbelief he will receive into the light of faith toward the end of the age.
