“But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there.” Archelaus was one of Herod’s sons, whom Herod had appointed to reign in Judea after him. Later, when the Jews accused him of arrogance, he was banished by a decree of the Senate to Vienna, a city of Gaul, and there ended his life.

Archelaus, however, whose name is interpreted as “victorious lion,” signifies the Antichrist, because for a time he will have victory among his own people and will appear as a terrifying lion.

Joseph therefore did not wish to go into the region where Archelaus reigned, because Christ will not dwell by faith among the Jewish people who are going to believe in the Antichrist. After Archelaus’s death Christ returns to the land of Israel, signifying that after the Antichrist has been killed the Synagogue will believe in him, as the Apostle says: “When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11).

But let us hear where he dwelt who remains and will remain in the Church: “And being warned in a dream, he withdrew into the region of Galilee; and coming, he dwelt in a city called Nazareth.”

Because Nazareth is interpreted as “flower” or “young shoot,” it signifies one that possesses both the flower of purity and the young shoot of virtues. The bridegroom admires the beauty of this young shoot in the Song of Songs, saying: “Who is this that comes up through the desert like a column of smoke from the spices of myrrh, frankincense, and every perfumed powder?” (Song of Songs 3). Again, the bridegroom says to her: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2).

And because the Church passes from love of the present life to heavenly desire, Nazareth of Galilee is rightly named, since Galilee is interpreted as “migration.”

But concerning what follows—“so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: He shall be called a Nazaraean” (Matthew 2)—this testimony, as we have said, is not found in the Septuagint translators.

Some wish to say that it was written in the book of the prophet Isaiah, where it says: “A branch shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 11). But we have said that if the evangelist had set down a definite testimony from the Scriptures, he would not have said “through the prophets” but “through the prophet.”

For all the prophets call the Lord a Nazaraean when they proclaim him as Christ. He is the one of whom it is said through Daniel: “When the Holy One comes, anointing shall cease”; and David says: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Psalm 15). And again: “Know that the Lord has made his Holy One wonderful” (Psalm 4).

## SERMON VI. At the Vigil of Easter

[Col. 0853]

### ADMONITION

Although the Maurists are uncertain whether this sermon should be attributed to Maximus, we agree with them. See them in the appendix to the works of Saint Augustine, no. 158, page 198, Antwerp edition, 1700.

### SUMMARY

[Col. 0853B] Joseph of Arimathea’s acts of piety toward the dead Redeemer are expounded; Peter’s love and faith, as well as Mary Magdalene’s, in seeking Christ in the tomb are commended.

After the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ and his resurrection, in which the substance of our faith consists, a certain Joseph appears, formerly a lover and disciple of the Lord, who, according to the circumstances of the time, provided funeral rites for the dead man, since the fury of the persecutors prevented even acquaintances from showing mercy.

Saint John narrated the event thus: “Joseph,” he says, “secretly asked Pilate, because of fear of the Jews, and requested the body of Jesus; and Pilate permitted it” (John 19).

While fear and devotion contended in his religious heart, he immediately devised something that would satisfy both faith and fear: secretly requesting that the slain man be committed to the earth, while avoiding the madness of the Jews.

The judge preserves the same disposition toward the dead man that he had shown toward him when he heard him: the one whom he had reluctantly handed over to punishment, he willingly handed over to burial.

But after Jesus’ body had been buried, he immediately reclaimed his power, and the majesty that had come was destined to return. For the one whose birth had shown him to be a son of man, his death revealed to be God.

When Mary Magdalene came to the tomb—she who, remembering the Savior but having lost faith, was driven by devotion into tears—she saw that the stone had been rolled away from the entrance. When she did not find the Lord in the tomb, she began to grieve more bitterly because she had lost even the dead man.

Then she quickly ran to Peter, his disciple, whom greater concern for the Lord’s death touched in proportion to his merit and faith. She announced that the tomb was empty; the body was sought as having been taken away.

But Peter, who before the cross had been aware of the resurrection of the Son of God, which he himself had foretold that he would suffer, did not weep or grieve at such a message. Rather, preserving his customary conduct in divine matters, he hastened to test what he had believed.

He therefore hurried to the Lord’s tomb at a swift pace, destined to return more joyful if he did not find the one he was seeking.

The blessed evangelist also proves from what follows the power of the one who rose: “Simon Peter came,” he says, “and entered the tomb; and when he did not find the Lord, he saw the linen cloths lying there, and the napkin that had been over his head” (John 20).

God was now manifest, about to carry into heaven the one he had made alive; he emptied both death and the tomb. For when the linen in which the corpse had been wrapped was set aside, the majesty, now clothed in a living body, left the vestiges of death to the earth.

Therefore Peter, seeing that the resurrection foretold by the Son of God had been fulfilled, departed secure, although he had come anxious.

But Mary, unaware of the resurrection, did not cease pouring out tears, not knowing that this was the glory of the Lord’s body, which she thought an injury.

The angel rather restrains than consoles her empty grief, as the evangelist also testifies: “Mary,” he says, “why are you weeping?” (ibid.).

If you understand the intention of the divine speech with spiritual discernment, he does not ask the cause of her tears as though ignorant, but rebukes the mourner’s excessive weeping.

“Mary,” he says, “why are you weeping?” Since the empty tomb indicated not the loss of a corpse but the merit of the risen one, the power of Jesus Christ had claimed his body for itself, not any crime.

At the same time he censures Mary for pouring out tears when she ought to have rejoiced. “Why are you weeping? Or whom are you seeking?” The angel instructs the ignorant woman with sound counsel not to seek the living among the dead.

Because this woman did not recognize that the one she was mourning had come back to life, even when corrected, she is later recalled from her unnecessary tears by the voice of the risen one.

For Jesus addresses Mary in similar words: “Woman,” he says, “why are you weeping? Or whom are you seeking?” This is what he means: “Now that I am alive, why do you shed tears for the one who was dead? Or, now that I am present, whom are you seeking?”

When she was addressed a second time, she recognized Jesus through the power of the divine majesty at work and found alive the Jesus Christ our Lord whom she had been seeking as dead. To him, with the Father, be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON VII. It begins happily, then as above; on the day of the Lord’s Ascension

[Col. 0853]

### ADMONITION

In the Lambach library codex mentioned immediately above, this sermon, which contains an exposition of the Creed, is read ascribed to Saint Maximus. But the exposition transmitted by Maximus, which we published above as Homily 87, is entirely different in its language and style.

### SUMMARY

[Col. 0853D] On the wording of the Creed; on the fraud of heretics in transmitting it, especially the Patripassians, Sabellians, and Arians. We must neither take anything away from the Creed nor add anything to it. The Creed can be retained more effectively if it is not written down.

Having thus far celebrated the mysteries of the scrutinies, an inquiry was made—through exorcism—to ensure that no impurity remained clinging to anyone’s body; sanctification was sought and applied not only to the body but also to the soul. Now the time and day have come for us to hand on the Creed. The Creed is a spiritual seal; the Creed is the meditation of our heart and, as it were, an ever-present safeguard—indeed, the treasure of our heart.

First, therefore, we must understand the meaning of the name itself. *Symbolum* is said in Greek, but in Latin it means “consolation.” Merchants, in particular, customarily use the word *symbolum* when they pool their money, so that, gathered together from the contributions of individuals into one sum, it may be preserved whole and inviolate, and no one may attempt to commit fraud against the contribution, nor may anyone engage in trade [lacuna]. [Col. 0854D–0855A] Something is omitted here, for the sense remains suspended. Finally, among the merchants themselves this is the custom: if anyone commits fraud, he is rejected as fraudulent.

Thus the holy apostles, coming together as one, composed a brief summary of the faith, in which we may grasp briefly the entire sequence of the faith. Brevity is necessary, so that it may always be retained in memory and recollection. I know that in some regions, especially in the East, while some devote themselves—as it were—to fraud and others to diligence concerning what was first handed down by our forebears, the heretics intend fraud, while the Catholics intend diligence. As the former fraudulently try to insinuate themselves, they have added what is unnecessary; while the latter strive to guard against fraud, they seem, through a certain piety and carelessness, to have advanced beyond the boundaries established by their forebears. Therefore the holy apostles, coming together, composed the Creed.

Briefly, seal yourselves. When they had completed the doctrine of the Divinity in this Creed, the teaching of the eternal Divinity was comprehended. And our faith is this: that we believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in equal manner. For where there is no distinction of majesty, there ought to be no distinction of faith either.

I have often warned you that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, alone assumed flesh in this manner: possessing a rational and perfect human soul, he also assumed the form of a body and the reality of this body, and became human; yet he possesses the special privilege of his generation. For he was not born from the seed of a man, but was generated by the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, acknowledging the prerogative of his heavenly author. He became human in order to take our weaknesses upon himself in his flesh, but he came with the privilege of eternal majesty.

Therefore let us recite the Creed. And when you have recited it, it is complete, for Scripture says this. Should we, with presumptuous minds, advance beyond the faith of the apostles? Are we more cautious than the apostles?

But you say to me: “Heresies arose afterward.” For, as the Apostle says, “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may be revealed” (I Cor. 9). What follows from this? Consider the simplicity; consider the purity.

When the Patripassians arose, they thought that Catholics too ought to add to this section the words “invisible” and “impassible,” as though the Son of God had been visible and passible. If he was visible in the flesh, certainly it was the flesh that was visible, not the Divinity; it was the flesh that was passible, not the Divinity. Finally, hear what he says: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21). Our Lord Jesus Christ says this in his Passion; he spoke according to his humanity, he spoke according to the flesh, as though the flesh were saying to the Divinity: “Why have you forsaken me?”

Therefore, although our forebears were physicians, they did not wish to apply medicine to an illness once health had been restored. The question, then, is not whether medicine was necessary at that time; let the grave illness of certain souls seek whether it had to be sought then. Now it is not necessary, since the faith is intact against the Sabellians. The Sabellians were excluded, especially in the regions of the West.

From that remedy the Arians devised a form of slander for themselves. Because we hold the Creed of the Roman Church, they therefore judged and asserted that the almighty Father was “invisible” and “impassible”; or, because the Creed says this, they would designate the Son as visible and passible. What follows, then? Where the faith is intact, the apostles’ instructions suffice; the precautions of priests are not required. Why? Because weeds are mingled with the wheat.

Thus in the Creed say: “his only Son, our Lord”—the only Son, not the only Lord; there is one God, there is one Lord. [Col. 0855D] But lest they slander us and say that, by calling the Son “only,” we are also speaking of one person as our one Lord, understand that, after speaking of the Divinity of the Father and the Son, we proceed to his incarnation, through which he was born, suffered, and was buried. You have his Passion and burial:

“On the third day he rose from the dead.” You also have his resurrection. “He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father.” See, then, that the flesh could diminish nothing from the Divinity; rather, a great triumph for Christ was gained through the incarnation.

For in what way, when he rose from death, does he sit at the right hand of the Father? It is as though he had brought back to the Father the fruit of his good will. You have two things: he rose from death, and he sits at the right hand. Therefore the flesh could bring no detriment to the glory of the Divinity.

You have two possibilities: either, as a second prerogative of his Divinity and of the substance of his generation, our Lord Jesus Christ sits at the right hand after rising from death; or, certainly, as an eternal victor who obtained a good kingdom for the Father, he claimed the prerogative of his victory. “He sits at the right hand of the Father; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.”

He himself will judge us. Take care, therefore, not to detract from the one whom you will have as your judge. Why this mystery? Is there not one judgment of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? Is there not one will? Is there not one majesty? Why are you told that the Son will judge, unless so that you may understand that nothing is to be taken away from the Son?

Therefore see: you believe in the Father; you believe in the Son; and what comes third? “And in the Holy Spirit.” Whatever sacraments you receive, you will receive them in this Trinity. Let no one deceive himself. You see, therefore, that the venerable Trinity possesses one operation, one sanctification, and one majesty.

Now receive an explanation of how we believe in the author, lest you perhaps say: “But it also has the Church; it also has the forgiveness of sins; it also has the resurrection.” What follows? The reason is the same: we believe in Christ in the same way that we believe in the Father, and we believe in the Church, the forgiveness of sins, and the resurrection of the flesh in the same way. What is the reason? Because whoever believes in the author also believes in the author’s work.

Finally, lest you think this is our own invention, receive the testimony: “If you do not believe me, believe at least the works” (John 10:38). Thus you have this: your faith will shine forth more fully if you judge that true and complete faith should be given to the work of your author: “the holy Church and the forgiveness of sins.”

Believe, therefore, in faith that all your sins are forgiven. Why have you read in the Gospel that the Lord said: “Your faith has saved you” (Mark 10:52)?

“The forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh.” I believe that the flesh too will rise. For what purpose was it necessary for Christ to assume flesh? What purpose was there in Christ tasting death, accepting burial, and rising again, unless for the sake of his resurrection? This entire mystery concerns your resurrection. If Christ has not risen, our faith is vain; but because he has risen, our faith is therefore firm.

We read that if anyone violates his Creed, he is to be regarded as wicked and detestable. Much more, then, must we beware lest anything be taken away from the Creed of our forebears, since you have in the book of the Apocalypse of John (ch. 22): “If anyone adds to it or takes away from it, he brings judgment and punishment upon himself.” If nothing is to be taken away from the writings of a single apostle, how shall we defile the Creed that we received as handed down and composed by the apostles? We must take nothing away and add nothing.

This, moreover, is the Creed held by the Roman Church, where Peter, the first of the apostles, sat and brought the common judgment. Thus, just as there are twelve apostles, so there are twelve articles.

Briefly, seal yourselves.

“I believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.” [Col. 0856D] Behold these four articles. Let us examine the others:

“On the third day he rose again, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead.” Behold four other articles—eight articles in all.

Let us examine the remaining four:

“I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life. Amen.”

Behold: corresponding to the twelve apostles, twelve articles have been comprehended.

I want you to be warned of this: the Creed ought not to be written down but retained. But what do you say to me? “How can it be retained if it is not written down?” It can be retained more effectively if it is not written down. How? Listen.

What you write down, you treat as secure, as though you had bound it up; you will not begin to review it through daily meditation. But what you do not write down, you fear that you may lose, and you will begin to review it daily. This is a great safeguard.

When stupors of mind or body arise, when the adversary’s temptation comes—he never rests—when some trembling of the body or weakness of the stomach occurs, recite the Creed and examine it within yourself; especially, review it within yourself. Why? So that you do not do it merely from habit, and, when you are alone, recite it as you do where believers are, and begin to recite it among catechumens or heretics. Explicit.

## SERMON VIII. On Pentecost

### Admonition

The first part of this sermon, up to the words “the thirsting hearts of the peoples,” is found in Codex M. E. of Turin, where it also bears the name of Saint Maximus with the title: “Likewise, a homily on Pentecost, XIX”; it is noted that two folios are missing. The same sermon is read in full among the Maurists, *Appendix to the Sermons of Saint Augustine*, class 2, no. 182, Antwerp edition, 1700. Since, however, the second part of the sermon, whose beginning is “Let us inquire at this point,” appears to differ from Maximus’s diction, we think that, together with the Maurists, it should rather be attributed, with the Maurists, to an uncertain author than to Maximus, as the writer of the aforementioned codex attributes it.

### Argument

The Holy Spirit is one God in substance, another in person, and unique in equal compassion. On the day of Pentecost he was present with his faithful through the presence of his own majesty. The question is what can still be added to the apostles’ perfection through participation in the Holy Spirit.

After that singular and remarkable victory by which he fought as the world’s public champion and conquered, after he had rescued the frailty of our condition not only from the underworld but also raised it to the heights of his kingdom, on this day, in accordance with his holy word, he gave the Holy Spirit, of whom he had already said to his apostles: “And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14).

Another, certainly, not lesser; another Paraclete, that is, one of similar glory or nature and of the same substance. Thus the disciples’ faith, prepared by a truthful promise to await so great a gift, would recognize as true God the one whom it remembered had been promised by the Lord in the place of God.

“And another,” he says, “Paraclete”: understand a companion of the majesty, whom you see set alongside that majesty. “And I will ask,” he says, “the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete.” How well, under the title of a promise, he has presented the distinction of the Trinity! The Father is the one indicated as being asked; the Son is the one understood to ask; the Holy Spirit is the one promised as being sent by the Father.

How great and ineffable is the Redeemer’s compassion! He carried a human being to heaven and sent God to earth. How great is the care of the author for the restoration of his work! Behold, once again a new medicine is sent from above; behold, once again the majesty deigns to visit its sick by its own agency.

Behold, once again divine things are mingled with human things, that is, the “vicar of redemption.” [Note: The Maurist edition reads *vicarius Redemptoris*, “the vicar of the Redeemer.”] Thus the benefits begun by the Lord and Savior may be brought to completion by the particular power of the Holy Spirit; what he redeemed, this one may sanctify; what he acquired, this one may guard. In this way the unity of the Godhead is demonstrated through the unity of grace and gift, so that the Holy Spirit, one God in substance, another in person, and unique in equal compassion, may be worshiped.

Therefore on this day the Holy Spirit descended upon the temples of his apostles, prepared for him, like a rain of sanctification—not now as a sudden visitor, but as perpetual Consoler and eternal inhabitant. For just as he had said of himself to his apostles: “Behold, I am with you every day, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28), so also concerning the Holy Spirit he says: “The Father will give you the Paraclete, that he may be with you forever.”

He was therefore present on this day with his faithful, no longer merely through the grace of visitation and operation, but through the very presence of his majesty. And into the vessels there flowed no longer merely the fragrance of balsam, but the substance itself of the ointment, whose fragrance would fill the breadth of the whole world, so that those who drew near to their teaching might become capable of and participants in God.

He therefore sat upon each of them like fire, concerning which our Savior testifies: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12); and concerning which it is said: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4). Thus he drenched his apostles with the fountain of living light, so that afterward they might illuminate the whole world like twelve rays of the sun and an equal number of lamps of truth, and, filled with new wine, might fill and water the thirsting hearts of the peoples.

Let us inquire at this point what, after the Lord’s resurrection or ascension, could still be added to the apostles’ perfection through participation in the Holy Spirit.

There was faith in them, certainly, but the steadfastness of confidence was lacking. They could indeed already proclaim Christ throughout the world, but they were not yet able to fight for Christ unto death; so much so that no disciple was crowned with the palm of martyrdom before the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Moreover, the Lord Jesus had already withdrawn from their eyes. While visibly teaching them face to face, he had strengthened them by his preaching and instructed them through miracles of power. When they were with him, they readily believed what they saw: faith was assisted by sight, confirmed by present works, and nourished by signs and miracles.

But after the Lord Jesus had been taken from their eyes and withdrawn into heaven, their astonished and trembling minds were not yet sufficient, as they should have been, to contemplate heavenly and eternal things; nor were their narrow hearts yet strong enough to bear the greatness of divine thoughts, so that they could understand Christ—how he was the Word, God with God—as the Lord himself, while still present in the body, clearly indicated to them, saying: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16).

You see that, after the departure of the supreme and worshipful Power, the disciples’ hearts were enlarged to sustain the greatness of divine light and the understanding of truth. God, therefore, is able, after his generosity, to heap up grace, increase wisdom, and strengthen steadfastness.

Let us see, then, how much they lacked in greatness of spirit and perfection before the visitation of the heavenly Consoler.

First, when they had seen him walking upon the swelling ridges of the sea, with the waves beneath his feet, while the unstable path of the waters was made firm under the divine feet by the serving wave, they were troubled and said: “It is a phantom,” and out of fear they cried out.

But after the infusion of the Holy Spirit they no longer say, “It is a phantom”; rather: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” And again he says: “He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). The Apostle also says: “For he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Col. 1).

One of the disciples, Thomas, however, not yet enriched by the blessing of this gift, sought God in a body already glorified, already heavenly, through the wounds of the flesh; and, in order to believe in incorruptible Divinity, he needed the testimony of the nail marks and scars: “Unless I see,” he says, “the mark of the nails in his hands and put my hand into his side, I will not believe” (John 20).

But another, already filled with the instruction of the Holy Spirit, confidently cries out: “What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life—and we announce to you the eternal life that was with the Father and appeared to us” (I John 1).

And again, elsewhere, the Apostle Paul, enriched by the inpouring of such majesty, confidently declares: “Even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (II Cor. 3).

Blessed Peter, when the Lord’s Passion was already near, not yet strengthened by the divine inspiration of the Paraclete, unwilling to be separated bodily from Christ, drew his sword against the traitor and the soldiers, and thought that force should be repelled by force.

But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, no longer seeks Christ on earth. With heaven opened, he saw the glory of God; nor does he think about vengeance, but he prays and pleads for his persecutors: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7).

Before the coming of the Holy Spirit, at the very time of the Lord’s cross, some of the disciples fled, while others were terrified by the voice of a single servant girl. Fear penetrating their trembling hearts, they were compelled to deny their Lord.

But after the illumination and strengthening of the Holy Spirit, tortured in custody and afflicted by beatings, they went away rejoicing because they were worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Christ. Those who had earlier denied him with an oath, “We do not know this man,” now glory in punishments endured for his sake. With the Holy Spirit working within them, they considered whatever they suffered for the love of Christ too little.

Those who had earlier been frightened by words were now strengthened by penalties and torments. They confessed Christ the Lord no longer with their voices but with their conduct, and testified to the greatness of their love by the shedding of their blood. Meanwhile, warmed and set ablaze by the pure wine of the Lord’s love, they exclaimed: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

Thus the blessed apostles, burning with that fire of faith of which the Lord himself says, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12), were thought by the impious crowd to be drunk and full of new wine. They said to one another: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2).

Yet they were filled with new wine, because they had already been renewed by the Holy Spirit; and there appeared in them what the Lord himself had said: “New wine must be put into new wineskins” (Matt. 9).

Let us not think, however, that only the apostles received this new wine at that time. Hearts of the faithful and the souls of converts are also inflamed by this wine and daily become drunk with this splendid cup.

We frequently see this happen when, out of desire for salvation, people leave their parents and homeland; they depart, compelled by no one, from their land and kindred, and, having died to this world, seek other parents spiritually for their souls. Free people come under the yoke; those who shortly before were distinguished and exalted pursue humility, disdain pride, and desire to become what they had previously despised. They begin to hate what they once were. Guests of the present, seekers of the future, they sigh for that eternal homeland, despising the falsity of temporal things.

Drunk with and wholly transformed by this spiritual wine, spiritual souls prefer abstinence to luxuries, vigils to sweet sleep, and poverty to riches. They reckon arduous labor against vices a most delightful pleasure. What was contemptible becomes sweet to them, and what was previously precious becomes worthless.

They love their enemies and do good to those who hate them. They are not overcome by the angry, are not provoked by insults, and are not irritated by injuries. Because of the fervor of the Holy Spirit and the eternal reward, they feel none of these things at all.

With this spiritual wine the martyrs were warmed when, casting away and throwing behind them all the allurements of the world, they went toward suffering, forgetting their possessions and affections, their inheritances and marriages. They overcame the natural affection armed against them by the tears of their little children: parents shouting aloud, throwing dust upon their heads, and mothers tearing their faces with their loosened hair.

But they, as though drunk, saw and recognized none of these things, nor did they recognize their own. For once the Holy Spirit had been poured into their inmost hearts, they hastened toward pains and punishments as though toward consolations and rewards.

We do indeed celebrate each year the anniversary of the coming of the Holy Spirit. But let us act in such a way that every day we invite him to us through chaste works and chaste hearts.

We ought to be pure and cleansed in our senses and thoughts; we must guard our mouths and hearts in such a way that we may always make ourselves worthy of his visitation and illumination, and appear free from every impurity of thought. For, as I have said, “perverse thoughts separate from God” (Wis. 1).

Let us strive to be free from every form of slander and every kind of malice, because “wisdom does not enter a malevolent soul, nor will it dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1).

Through anger and pride, the souls of the negligent are stripped of the protection and safeguarding of the Holy Spirit. Let us therefore not grieve the Holy Spirit through such passions; rather, let us summon him to the seat of our heart through the grace of humility and the gentleness of peace, and gladden him by our works and progress. For he says: “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66).

If, then, we desire to merit the entrance of so great a visitor, let us first cleanse the house of our soul from the unworthy passions of carnal desire, from the abomination of pride, from the stench of boasting, and from the horror of tepidity, concerning which the Lord himself says: “Would that you were cold or hot; but because you are lukewarm, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. 3:16)—that is, to spit you out from the inmost depths of my heart.

Let us therefore prepare this house every day for the coming of the sacred King, and adorn it with the varied flowers of praiseworthy conduct. Let us fill it with the pleasant and precious incense of chastity, faith, and compunction, with the balm of goodwill and the frankincense of charity. Thus, once vices have been cut away and virtues grafted in, and the dwelling of the devil within us destroyed, we may be transformed into a temple of God, so that such a blessed guest, delighted by a spotless dwelling, may establish in us a lasting and perpetual abode.

For this reason he descended to us: so that we might be able to ascend to him. To him be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. [Col. 0860D] Amen.

## SERMONS ON THE SAINTS

## SERMON IX. Begins: On Saint John the Baptist I

### Admonition

I have not dared to attribute this sermon to Saint Maximus, although it is ascribed to him in a manuscript at St. Gall, because it differs from Maximus’s elegant and polished style, and because it is attributed to him in no other manuscript.

### Argument

Nothing greater can be said in praise of John the Baptist than that his praise is found in the Gospel. For this reason, the author of the sermon expounds at length what is read about him in the Gospel.

The Apostle Paul, when he wished to commend Luke, the author of the Gospel, to the Corinthians, thought that he could offer no greater testimony than to say that his praise was contained in the Gospel. Writing about him, he says: “We have also sent with him the brother whose praise in the Gospel is spread throughout all the churches” (2 Cor. 8). Thus, dearest brothers, following the example of the chief Apostle, as we now undertake to say something among you in praise of John the Baptist, whose feast we are celebrating in honor of the Lord, we can bring forward nothing greater than to say that his praise is in the Gospel; and you should consider that nothing better is contained in this statement.

For it is already an immense and immeasurable thing to be proclaimed in the Gospel, since the question is not so much whether someone is praised as by what authority he is praised. Moreover, this is conveyed by a great witness. For to be praised badly by the wicked is to be censured, since perverse praise is a form of censure; or, by right, he should be judged especially praiseworthy whose praise is in the Gospel, since those things praise him which themselves cannot adequately be praised. And this is true. For if those to whom good and wise men bear testimony are rightly considered good, what, then, must we suppose those to be who are praised by Christ Jesus?

But before we come to the testimony of the Lord’s title itself, let us see what was said and written about him before his birth, so that from this we may understand how great a man he must be considered who was proclaimed long before he was born and whose praise began before his life. First, the evangelist Mark began his Gospel with that prophecy [Col. 0861B] which proclaimed his birth and virtue as worthy of the highest honor—believing, evidently, that the Gospel had its beginning in the fact that John had received praise, especially since whatever he said in praise of the Lord’s forerunner redounded entirely to the Lord’s praise.

He began in this way (chap. 1): “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way.” He whom the Lord called an angel must be considered to possess more than human worth: “Behold,” he says, “I send my angel before your face.” He had not yet been born into this world, and already he was called an angel by the Lord.

Truly he was a man of outstanding and almost unique testimony, who, even before his earthly birth, deserved by heavenly dignity to have his coming preceded by honor; plainly worthy to be the Lord’s forerunner, since he had even anticipated himself in titles: “Behold,” he says, “I send my angel before your face” (Mal. 3; Matt. 11; Mark 1).

Let us consider by what designation he has honored each person, and we shall find one called a simple man, another a just man, a son, a faithful servant, and scarcely anyone called an angel—not because the angels are not servants of God, but because they are distinguished from human beings by rank and likewise by honor. Human beings are servants, and angels are servants; yet we human beings were made by the Lord so much lower than the angels that those whom their very dwelling and blessedness distinguish from human beings are not made comparable even by sharing the same name. Therefore the Lord did not call John holy, or good, or chosen, but an angel.

Why, then, an angel? Clearly, so that He might grant him a title corresponding to the loftiness of his virtues; and so that he who had exceeded the measure of human merit might receive the name of heavenly dignity, attaining through the magnificence of faith as much honor as the heavenly beings possessed by nature.

There is no doubt about this; for the evangelist adds—after the Lord had called him an angel above—“who will prepare your way.” Therefore he alone deserved to be called an angel because he alone was worthy to prepare the Lord [Col. 0861D]. For this is a great and singular testimony: the office of preparation is entrusted to him.

Just as, in earthly duties, every person most skilled at preparing what is necessary for a lord’s arrival is appointed by a worldly master—knowing, of course, what he ought to provide for his arriving lord, what to prepare, what dwelling, what vessels for service, and what delights for the banquet, lest the master of the household, on arriving, find either a dark habitation or dirty furnishings displeasing—so holy John, when he was sent by the Lord to prepare, was first instructed by the One who sent him. In order that he might prepare what was pleasing to God, he himself had long before become pleasing to Him; and, intending to provide ways and dwellings for Christ, he himself first became Christ’s way and dwelling. For he could not have known the Lord’s delights unless he had long experienced the things by which the Lord is delighted.

After long practice and prolonged instruction, he received this most fitting reward of tested familiarity: that he should understand himself to be preparing the Lord in the manner in which he had prepared himself for the Lord.

But lest anyone think that we are saying this merely by reasoning or conjecture, let us see whether the Lord Himself also testifies to what we assert on the basis of the Lord’s judgment concerning him. We read in the Gospel of Luke that the angel of the Lord said to his father Zechariah: “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for behold, your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear a son, and you will call his name John, and there will be joy and exultation for you, and many will rejoice at his birth. For he will be great before the Lord, and he will drink neither wine nor strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (Luke 1).

Here is the very thing we mentioned above: long before this office of preparing the Lord, he was already the Lord’s vessel, way, and house: “For he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.” Therefore, without doubt, he possessed the Holy Spirit, whom he received at the very beginning of his birth.

Truly blessed and of extraordinary beatitude was he to whom, as he emerged from the womb and was about to breathe this common air, it was granted to draw in the Lord before he encountered the light. Thus God made him worthy of preparation, because God’s Spirit had dwelt in him. He was taught by that Spirit and instructed by it—not by hearing but by experience, not by reading but by recognition, not by sowing but by familiarity—in all the things that pleased the Lord. While he himself was pleasing, he came to know those things, so that it was no wonder that the one who possessed within himself the One who was preparing him should himself become a preparer.

The same things must be repeated more often so that, once repeated more fully, they may be understood. Just as infants, who need to take in food, cannot do so without much and repeated tasting, so we cannot grasp the force and greatness of heavenly utterances unless we receive them gradually.

“Therefore,” he says, “he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.” We have explained what it means to receive the Holy Spirit immediately from the womb. But since receiving is less than being filled, the evangelist, in order to explain the magnificence of the sacred gift, did not say, “He will receive the Spirit,” or “The Spirit will enter him,” but said, “He will be filled with the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0862C].

What does “he will be filled” mean? I think that something is said to be filled in such a way that no emptiness remains in what is filled. So holy John was filled with the Lord’s Spirit in such a way that he could receive nothing else within himself besides that with which he was being filled. Once everything that normally occupies the vacant senses of human beings had been excluded, only that fullness which had filled him reigned within him—and so it happened.

For never did any sign of lust, greed, anger, gluttony, or even that somewhat weaker kind of affection appear in him. If lust tried to approach, it was subdued by chastity; if wickedness, it was restrained by kindness; if laxity, it was overcome by severity. For once the human being had been sanctified inwardly and outwardly, nothing worldly could enter him, since the Lord had filled everything within him.

Indeed, the Gospel reading with which we began teaches this in what follows, saying: “John was in the desert, baptizing and preaching the baptism of repentance” (Luke 1). Why, then, in the desert? For a crowd would seem more suitable to this office, since one who preaches to many is heard by many [Col. 0862D]. But the dwelling of the man whom the Holy Spirit had filled at the very beginning, in order to preserve the purity of the sacred gift completely, was more suitably the desert. The place itself separated him from fellowship with human defilement, so that he might bring healing to the sick without experiencing the contagion of sickness in himself.

Thus, to the one baptizing, no one, I think, came except someone already purified or about to be purified. Truly blessed was he whose sanctification from the womb was attended only by a choir of the sanctified; when their uncleanness had been washed away through repentance, a people aspiring to a bright manner of life adhered to the man of bright conduct, giving him no less a gift in the future than honor in the present. A crown of purified people surrounded him, so that he himself might be the cause of purity for all: plainly worthy to wash others in the water of repentance for the remission of their sins, himself washed by the Spirit in whom the Lord had caused the fountain of purity to flow.

This, then, was the meaning of what the Gospel had proclaimed: that he was filled with the Holy Spirit from birth. For by that fullness of the divine gift the office was already being prepared for him, namely, that the river of sacred generosity should flow so abundantly in him that it would overflow upon others.

The things written about him elsewhere likewise belong to the same subject. “A leather belt,” it says, “around his waist; and his food was locusts and wild honey” (Matt. 3; Mark 1).

“A leather belt,” it says, “around his waist.” Even things that seem small in outward form in the Holy Scriptures are nevertheless to be revered as containing a great mystery. Since what the Lord speaks is undoubtedly divine, while the same thing cannot be both insignificant and divine, even those things that appear small in the Holy Scriptures must be understood to be great for this very reason: that they are divine.

Although they may appear slight and feeble, the fault lies not in them but in us. Since we do not understand the force of the sacred utterances, we think insignificant the things that are great. Hence it must clearly be understood that those things are not feeble which are found, upon consideration, to be great; rather, we are feeble, since we regard as feeble what is great.

Thus it is with what we mentioned above: “A leather belt,” he says, “around his waist.” What seems more insignificant in appearance? What advantage is there in saying that it was leather, or that it was around his waist? As if nearly everyone who wears belts did not wear them around the waist, or as if people could not gird their hands, feet, heads, or necks with such a belt.

But this is precisely what makes the Holy Scriptures more wondrous: under the covering of lowly words they conceal immense and immeasurable riches, and their inner meanings are great even when the surface appears to promise nothing of the sort. The Lord evidently wished to show by this very fact how great the force of sacred majesty is, since He had placed the greatest treasures even in the lowliest things and had made great things out of objects of humble appearance.

“A leather belt,” he says, “around his waist.” We see that the Holy Scriptures very frequently mention belts and waists. Let us therefore examine what sacred reading usually signifies by waists and belts, so that when we have recognized what is meant by the belt, we may also understand what a leather belt signifies.

We read in Exodus (chap. 12) that, among the other preparations for the paschal feast, the Lord especially commanded this: all who were to celebrate the Lord’s solemnity were first to gird their waists. For evidently one would be unworthy to partake of the holy food of immortality who had not first merited communion in the sacred body by girding his waist.

**End.**

## Sermon X. Also, on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist II

[Col. 0863]

### Notice

I see a great difference between the style of the author of this sermon and that of Maximus. Therefore I agree neither with Muratori, who counts it, having transcribed it from an Ambrosian manuscript, among the Maximian sermons in volume 4 of the *Anecdota*, nor with the others who, following Muratori, ascribe it to Maximus. Some attribute this sermon to Saint Ambrose.

### Summary

John the Baptist was born in prophecy and was slain in reality. His birth and that of Christ had something in common.

In praising the holy and most blessed John the Baptist, whose nativity we celebrate today, I do not know what I should proclaim above all: whether that he was born wondrously, or that he was slain even more wondrously. For he was born in prophecy and slain in reality; by his birth he announced the Savior’s coming, and by his death he condemned Herod’s incest.

For this holy and just man, who had been brought forth by promise beyond the ordinary birth of human beings, obtained this from God: that he should depart from the world by the common death he shared with others, but should lay down the body he had received by the Lord’s gift while confessing the Lord. Thus John fulfilled God’s will in every respect, since he was both born and died for the Lord’s work.

To review briefly the course of his birth: his father Zechariah and his mother Elizabeth were worn out by old age and had no joy in offspring. The flourishing time for bearing children had also passed them by, so that even their hopes of receiving a child had now failed. Then they were granted a sudden promise through an angel, and holy Gabriel announced that John would be born, saying: “Do not be afraid, Zechariah; behold, your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will conceive and bear a son” (Luke 1).

“Your prayer has been heard,” he says. From this we understand that Zechariah begot John more through righteousness in prayer than Elizabeth received him through the power of procreation. From this, I say, we understand that John was created by supplication, not by desire.

For when the inward parts of the mother’s womb had grown cold through old age, and her weary bodily members had already lost the grace of fertility, against the body’s impossibility and against the barrenness of her womb, Elizabeth’s womb swelled at Zechariah’s prayers, and she conceived John not by nature but by grace. Therefore it was fitting that a holy son should be born who was generated not so much by embraces as by prayers.

We should be less surprised that John merited such grace in his birth. For the forerunner and precursor of Christ ought to have something resembling the birth of the Lord the Savior. The Lord was born of a virgin, while John was born of a barren woman; the former was brought forth from an undefiled young woman, the latter from an old woman already weakened by age.

His birth, therefore, also possesses something of glory and wonder. Although a woman’s childbirth may seem less extraordinary than a virgin’s, just as we marvel at Mary because a virgin gave birth, so we marvel at Elizabeth because an old woman gave birth.

I believe that this event contains a mystery: John, who bore the figure of the Old Testament, was born from an aged woman whose blood had already grown cold; while the Lord, who was to proclaim the Gospel of the heavenly kingdom, was born from the bloom of a fervent young woman.

Mary, conscious of her virginity, marvels at the fetus enclosed within her womb; Elizabeth, conscious of her old age, is ashamed that her womb will become heavy with childbirth. For the evangelist says: “She kept herself hidden for five months” (Luke 1).

But how wondrous it is that the same archangel Gabriel performs the service of announcing both births. He comforts the unbelieving Zechariah and encourages the believing Mary. Because Zechariah doubted, he lost his voice; because she immediately believed, she conceived the saving Word.

This also seems by no means to be omitted from John’s praises: although not yet born, he already prophesied; while still enclosed in his mother’s womb, he confessed Christ’s coming through rejoicing, since he could not do so by voice. For Elizabeth says to holy Mary: “As soon as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy” (ibid.).

John rejoices before he is born, and before he recognizes his appearance in the eyes of the world, he already recognizes the Lord of the world in spirit. In this I believe the prophetic statement is fulfilled, which says: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. 1). Therefore we should not marvel that, when shut up in prison by Herod, he always made Christ known to his disciples, since, even shut up in the womb, he proclaimed the same Lord through his movements.

*(A page is missing; the following fragment then occurs.)* [lacuna] “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14).

We therefore celebrate John’s nativity on the same day on which we also attend to the beginning of the harvest [Col. 0865A]. Great are both births: the one drove away the poverty of the womb, and the other drove away the hunger of sinners. Because of this, a wasting disease no longer torments me, nor does a pestilential conscience consume him; I experience nourishment alike in my senses and in my inward parts. Indeed, John himself is our harvest, for from his prophecy we bring forth the fruit of salvation, and from his words, like a heavy stalk, we take the grain of salvation.

Concerning this grain it is written in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the ground, dies, it remains alone” (John 12), and so forth.

## Sermon XI. On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary I

[Col. 0865]

### Notice

Combefis was the first to publish this sermon under the name of Saint Maximus in his *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume 8, page 45. It was taken from the manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; afterward Andreas Gallandius reprinted it in volume 9, page 394, of the new *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Since we lack the testimony of other manuscripts and collections, we can offer no stronger argument concerning its authenticity. Its being falsely attributed to Maximus is made plain by the dissimilarity of its style. Anyone who reads it will clearly recognize that it ought to be entitled *On the Annunciation*, not *On the Assumption*.

### Summary

In an indescribable manner the blessed Mary became both mother and virgin: a virgin before marriage, in marriage, while pregnant, in giving birth, after being given to a husband, and a mother not by a husband.

Knowing, dearest brothers, that we owe much to our Creator because we were created, and more because we were redeemed, let us honor the price paid for our redemption. Let us celebrate with acts of devotion, even if not with merits, that most sacred womb from which God appeared united to man. Let us remember that the radiance of her childbirth dispelled the darkness of our error, because what the first mother, through the disobedient arrogance and gluttony of the first man, had lost through the negligence of our ancestor, the childbirth of this sacred Virgin not only restored when it had been ruined but also bestowed eternal things.

For this reason let us honor with every kind of praise the woman who, while conceiving her Creator from heaven, bore our Redeemer into the world. And because she is appointed as the counterpart and model of our mother, the Church, may she herself watch over it amid the burning storms of the world, and may she also cherish it through daily prayer amid the world’s courses. For there is no doubt that she who merited to be the price for those to be freed can grant assistance.

Meanwhile, let our prayer be directed more earnestly to the Lord, so that with due devotion we may honor the womb which He entered in order to sanctify it for the sake of His name. May it benefit us as a remedy that through her He gave Himself to us as the price.

The blessed Mary is rightly exalted by us as unique, since she offered the world a unique exchange. Rightly did she rejoice even among women when she carried in her chaste womb the unique medicine. She felt the weight of pregnancy, yet had not lost the modesty of chastity; she marveled at the signs of childbirth, although, as a virgin, she had known no defilement.

O richly fruitful virginity, which by a new and unheard-of kind of birth could become both mother and virgin! For she bore and carried Him in whom she herself was created, since Mary’s Creator is the very one born from Mary. Thus, in an indescribable manner, blessed Mary remained mother and virgin: while receiving the fruit of pregnancy, she suffered no loss of integrity.

In her the heavenly providence arranged the circumstances of the matter itself so that she displayed obedience to the command more than she recognized her own honor from the angel. Nor does she reject the messenger’s testimony when she understands the dignity of the angel announcing to her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

She believed what she heard when instructed, and, sanctified, she merited what she believed. Finally, she raised herself so high toward the heights of heaven that she received the Word who was in the beginning with God—that is, the Son—from the highest citadel of heaven.

When she united the mystical secret of divinity with our flesh and weakness, divinity lay hidden in humanity so that humanity might not perish in divinity. It is hidden beneath the veil of assumed flesh.

He redeemed the lost more dearly than those who had been defended and captured by the threatening enemy. Immeasurable compassion, and majesty deserving proclamation beyond what can be expressed: the maiden’s womb was filled with the Holy Spirit, and the virgin’s unmarried womb swelled as the seed of the Word grew within it.

The sacred mystery of her womb was filled, I say, filled with the Spirit’s fruitfulness; and there was hope in the childbirth where there had been no pleasure in intercourse. The most precious Mother was astonished and silently marveled within herself at the novelty of what had happened. She was troubled by the heat of uncertain thought and, struck by the magnificence of the angelic greeting, was wondrously overcome.

Knowing her own integrity, she marveled at the fruitfulness of her womb. O blessed Mary! O glorious mother! O exalted mother in childbirth, in whose womb the Creator of heaven and earth was entrusted.

O blessed kisses impressed upon nursing lips, when, amid the sure signs of infancy, her true son, as was fitting, played with her as his mother, while the true Lord from the Father gave commands. For by conceiving her Creator, you brought him forth—poor in time, though you had possessed him as Creator before time.

O blessed childbirth, praiseworthy to the saints, necessary for the lost, fitting for the defeated! After enduring many injuries in the flesh he had assumed, He was finally scourged with lashes, given gall to drink, and fastened to the cross; in order to show that He had a true mother, He demonstrated by suffering torments that He was truly human.

But you, blessed and glorious Virgin Mary, are praiseworthy in these things and because of them: you merited the gift of fruitfulness without losing the privilege of virginity [Col. 0866C]. You are blessed among women; you are chosen above all the companies of virgins; you follow the Lamb wherever He goes.

Through shining lilies and blossoming roses, you invite virgin choirs, estranged from the incitements of the allurements of the flesh, to come to the fountain of everlasting life and drink. You have attained the first dignity in that most blessed region of the saints; wandering with dew-covered feet amid the delights of paradise, proceeding with tender knees among the grassy choirs, and with fortunate palm gathering unfading violets.

Joined to minds holy without end and associated with angels and archangels, you never cease to cry out with unwearied voice: “Holy, Holy, Holy.”

But what can I say, poor in understanding, when whatever I say about you is certainly less than your dignity deserves? If I call you the mother of nations, you surpass the title; if I call you the form of God, you are worthy of it; if I call you the nurse of heavenly bread, you fill Him with the sweetness of milk.

Nurse, then, mother, our food; nurse the heavenly bread; nurse the food of angels; offer your breast to Him who suckles, so that on your behalf He may offer His cheek to the one who strikes. As a mother, minister to Him temporal substance, so that He Himself may grant everlasting life to us and to you.

Nurse, then, Him who made you—who made you such that He Himself might be made in you. Nurse Him who gave you the fruit of fruitfulness by His conception and did not take away the dignity of virginity by His birth. Before He was born, He made you a mother, so that He might proceed from His bridal chamber, where He could be seen by mortal eyes.

How great was this condescension: that the King should be created from you, whom He created; that He should be carried in the hands He created; that He should suck the breasts He filled?

What praises, then, shall we speak of God’s love, what thanks shall we give Him, who loved us so much that for our sake He became human, entered the womb of our condition, endured the insults of a newborn infant, and underwent all that human life requires?

Giving our Creator as many thanks as we are able, let us therefore celebrate with joy the nativity of the most precious Mother. For it is right that we serve her with the greatest devotion, through whom the marks of virginity have blossomed. She was a virgin before marriage, a virgin in marriage, a virgin while pregnant, a virgin in giving birth, a virgin after being given to a husband, and a mother not by a husband.

The almighty Son of holy Mary in no way took away at His birth the virginity that He chose when He was to be born. Let virgins rejoice, then: a virgin bore Christ. Let them not think that anything they have known has been destroyed by this; she remained a virgin after childbirth.

Let widows rejoice as they celebrate the virgin’s nativity: the widow Anna recognized the Virgin Mother. Let married women rejoice as they attend the solemnity of blessed Mary: the married Elizabeth was greeted by the Virgin Mother of the Lord.

Let boys rejoice who vow continence to the Child. He Himself preserved the integrity of childhood, who brought fruitfulness to His mother without taking away her virginity. To Him be honor forever and ever. Amen.

## Sermon XII. Also, on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary II

[Col. 0867]

### Notice

This sermon was recovered from a parchment folio manuscript of the library of Modoetia, marked B XI, from the twelfth century, and sent to us by the distinguished man Antonio Francesco, a canon theologian from Frisia. We place it among the spurious works, since it displays nothing of Maximus’ elegance and dignity. Nor should this sermon have been entitled *On the Assumption*.

### Summary

How holy, how beautiful, how chaste the blessed Virgin Mary was: ever a virgin, before childbirth, after childbirth, conceiving, giving birth, and nursing.

The celebration of this day reminds us that we ought to linger in praise of the Virgin. For it is truly fitting that on the day of such a mother, the tongue of flesh should not be silent about the Lord’s praises.

On this day, blessed Virgin Mary, that heavenly bride, appropriately proclaims freely: “You have held my right hand, and in your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me” (Ps. 72). Today, I say, she may also fittingly hear from her bridegroom: “Come, my nearest one, my beautiful one, my dove. For behold, winter has passed, the rain has gone away” (Song 2).

And blessed Mary herself now replies: “The flowers have appeared on the earth, for the time of pruning has come” (ibid.). “My soul has rejoiced in the Lord; it will delight in His salvation” (Ps. 34). “And my soul will glory in the Lord. Let the meek hear and rejoice” (Ps. 33). “And I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26).

Let us therefore see, brothers, what sort of virgin this is to whom the Holy Spirit deigned to come; how beautiful she is whom the Lord chose as His bride; how chaste she is, so that she could be a virgin after childbirth—she who is the Lord’s temple, that sealed fountain, and the closed gate in the house of the Lord.

The Holy Spirit descended upon her; the power of the Most High overshadowed her; from her Christ, powerful in virtues, came forth. She was undefiled in intercourse, fruitful in childbirth, a virgin in chastity. She conceived as a virgin, not from a man but from the Holy Spirit. She gave birth not in pain but in joy. She nourished the food of angels and human beings.

Certainly blessed and worthy of all praise is she who, without human seed, brought forth the heavenly bread of the world and gave birth to the Savior for the world.

O covenant of faith! O secret of faith! The angel promises a son to a virgin who rejoices and desires to become a mother. Truly this is a great and saving mystery: she gave birth in such a way that she could be called both mother and virgin.

Nurse, Mary, your Creator; nurse the bread of heaven; nurse the price of the world. Offer your breast to Him who suckles, so that on your behalf He may offer His cheek to the one who strikes. As a mother, provide Him with temporal substance, so that He may grant everlasting life to us and to you.

Nurse, then, Him who made you—who made you such that He Himself might be made in you. Nurse Him who, when conceived, gave you the fruit of fruitfulness and who, though God, did not take away the state of virginity by His birth.

See, brothers, how fittingly virginity consecrated to the Lord serves Him, since He deigned to love it so much that one and the same woman could be called both virgin and mother. What grace is more worthy of preference and proclamation throughout all ages? She alone obtained the dignity of a mother and did not lose virginal modesty.

Finally, she marveled that she was to give birth without having known a man, since she had known no bridal chamber. O how blessed is this mother, who conceived without defilement and gave birth without pain to the medicine of salvation.

Blessed, I say, is the mother through whom the life of our race was restored; she received offspring from heaven and gave birth to the Savior for the world. For in a wondrous and ineffable manner she bore the Creator of all things and her own Creator.

An intact virgin was chosen, to whom the fruitfulness of a mother would be given; and she became a fruitful mother in whom the integrity of a virgin was preserved.

Let us therefore conceive of a virgin who conceived flesh without the desire of the flesh and gave birth to a man without a man. And if we wish to seek the reason for this event, we collapse in the very act of our inquiry, since it is written: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isa. 55).

For blessed Mary herself, whose nativity we celebrate today, gave birth by believing and conceived by believing. When the angel had announced the divine birth to her, she, conscious of her own chastity but unaware of the divine dispensation, replied to the angel: “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1). The angel answered her with a peaceful countenance: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (ibid. 1:35).

Do not dread childbirth, Virgin, and do not fear or greatly dread what you have never experienced. Only believe, and you have conceived; love, and you have given birth. For the Holy Spirit will come upon you; therefore there is nothing for you to fear. And the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore you have reason to rejoice.

Pain in childbirth would follow only if desire had preceded conception. But now the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you—that is, He will refresh you under the shelter of the Holy Spirit, so that you will not be terrified by the heat of desire.

“Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). When Mary heard these things, already pregnant with the seed of faith, and conceiving Christ in her mind before conceiving Him in her womb, she answered the angel: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).

Immediately, as the Virgin’s assent was revealed, the heavenly bridegroom entered her immaculate body, and He whom the whole world cannot contain was poured into the limbs of an unmarried girl.

For hear, brothers, how the gate through which the Lord entered was always closed, as the prophet Ezekiel saw in a divine vision. “I turned,” he says, “toward the way of the gate of the outer sanctuary that faces east, and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: The gate that you see shall be closed and shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it; and it shall remain closed forever” (Ezek. 44).

Here he clearly shows us that holy Mary was always a virgin and remained a virgin: a virgin before childbirth, a virgin after childbirth; she conceived and is a virgin, she gives birth and is a virgin, she nurses and is a virgin.

Blessed Mary could be a mother; she could be a woman. Great is the merit, great the gift, great the grace: a handmaid bore the Lord, a creature bore the Creator. With fruitful womb and intact generative organs, the virgin mother brought forth the Lord upon earth—conceiving as a virgin, giving birth as a virgin, remaining a virgin, a pregnant virgin, a mother who had given birth, an everlasting virgin.

Why do you marvel at this, O human being? It was fitting that God should be born in this way when He deigned to become human.

Amid these things, therefore, let us devote ourselves wholeheartedly to the aid of the blessed Virgin. With every effort let us implore her protection; and while we honor her with humble devotion on earth, may she deign to commend us through earnest prayer in heaven.

May He deign to grant this, who as perfect Trinity lives and reigns, God, forever and ever.

## Sermon XIII. On the Nativity of the Holy Martyrs Nazarius and Celsus I

[Col. 0869]

### Notice

William Cave, who knew of this sermon among the Ambrosian works, writes that Saint Maximus was its author; he cites the 1569 Paris edition of the works of Saint Ambrose, no. 93. We think it more appropriate to place it among the doubtful sermons of Maximus. Nor do we omit warning that part of this sermon—from the words “Thus, rightly and as is our duty” up to “you contend in an idle dispute”—was taken from Sermon 83 of Saint Maximus, *On the Nativity of the Holy Martyrs III*, column 623; the remainder was attached by an uncertain author.

### Summary

In the glory of the holy martyrs we venerate our faith. Blessed Nazarius, born of parents of no low standing, after countless signs of virtue and after traversing innumerable regions for the preaching of Christ, finally, having completed the contest of martyrdom, was consecrated by the sword together with the boy Celsus.

Even if we were rendering the pious dues owed by our vows to martyrs from a foreign region, we would nevertheless be shown to be consulting our own interests and advantages. For faith would make them ours, and, however remote their boundaries, they would procure for us the patronage we hoped for. Such benefits of devotion depend upon zeal, not upon places. Therefore, among God’s household, you will merit as much intercession as you have shown veneration. It is necessary, then, that religious devotion reconcile strangers to us, rather than that, through the negligence of an irreligious age, it estrange from us those who are perhaps our own.

Let us recognize, beloved, the more abundant generosity of divine gifts toward our Church. The peoples of individual cities rejoice if they are fortified by the relics of even a single martyr. Behold, we possess peoples of martyrs. Let our land rejoice—the nurse of heavenly soldiers and the fertile mother of so many virtues. Rightly, therefore, and as a duty, the distinctions of these blessed martyrs are celebrated by the children of their mother, the Church. By illuminating countless peoples through the power of their faith, they alone indeed experienced the death inflicted upon them, but they did not alone possess the benefits of their death. For the immense mercy of our God, manifold in goodness and skilled in salvation, while setting before us the difficult palm of virtue, precious because sought by few, looks to the advantage of many through the triumphs of a few. He wishes their merits to be our intercessions. At the same time, while commending true faith to us through the harsh contest of martyrdom, he makes the suffering of those who preceded us an instruction for those who come after.

How great is the concern of our God for us! He puts them to death in order to instruct us. He crushes them in order to win us, and wishes their torments to be our progress. Therefore we rightly honor those who fight through their own dangers and serve as soldiers for our benefit; those who, through their contempt for light and life, teach us how much affection we owe our God.

Let us understand, then, that we do not doubt the truth of our religion without great peril, since we see it confirmed by the blood of so many. It is a matter of great danger if, after the utterances of the prophets, after the testimony of the apostles, after the wounds of the martyrs, you presume to examine the ancient faith as though it were something new; if, after such manifest leaders, you remain in error; and if, after the sweat of those who died, you contend through idle disputation.

We therefore congratulate you, dearest brothers, on your great faith, through which, while you receive exiles with overflowing charity, you have also deserved to have the inhabitants of paradise and citizens of heaven. Thus blessed Nazarius, martyr of Christ, although the holy Church of Milan retains his entire body with itself, has nevertheless transmitted him wholly to the world in blessing. For this is the glory of the holy martyrs: even if a portion of them is scattered throughout the world in ashes, the fullness of their power nevertheless remains entire in them.

We therefore venerate our faith in so great a soldier of Christ; for the martyr’s mother is the Catholic faith, in which the illustrious champion, having shed his blood, trampled death for that very faith. The faith, I say, is the mother of martyrdom. Let us therefore venerate our faith in the glory of the holy martyrs.

How is it our faith? Because, while these men unquestionably endure death, the hope of immortality is clearly affirmed. They would never have spent this life with such steadfastness unless they had perceived with complete conviction that another life existed, incomparably more blessed. In the holy heralds of truth, therefore, there is the authority of the resurrection. They willingly perish in order to be restored to something better; through the straits of tribulations, an exit is opened for them into the vastness of joys.

Hence blessed Nazarius, whose glorious victory over the enemy of the world the universal Church today celebrates with festive rejoicing, although he was born in the time of paganism from parents of no low standing, suddenly began, while still a sacrilegious boy, to detest both his father’s military service and his teaching. Then, from his innocent mother—already distinguished by the titles of Christian faith and diligently devoted to Christ—he earnestly requested that the streams of sacred regeneration be shown to him, anticipating them through a faithful spirit and faith already established.

For although he had not yet received baptism, he was perfected amid the beginnings of religion; although the laws had not yet been revealed to him, he was full of God and suddenly became God’s possession and dwelling place. Thus he deserved to raise the summit of a tower reaching even to heaven before he had laid its foundation. Not yet conscious of the sacraments, he had already been chosen for sacrifice.

What can we unhappy people say in reply to this? After the radiance of baptism, after the whiteness bestowed upon us through sacred regeneration, after acquiring the angelic dignity of the wedding garment, we have fallen back into the filth of sins and rolled again in the ancient mire of crimes. We stain upon the earth the snowy garment and soil it with the contagions of lust. We have defiled with the stains of deadly corruption the silk garment on which the seal of the divine image had been impressed. After the singular indulgence of our God had renewed us, we disgrace it; we tear apart what was whole; we violate what had been cleansed; and we return to deeds that must now be purged not by water but by flames.

What was that gift of divine grace, and how remarkable, which, after receiving the saving washing, after countless signs of virtue, after traversing innumerable regions everywhere for the preaching of Christ, while nearly the whole world raged against him through various tortures because of his confession of the supreme God, and while he was now being confined for cruel punishments and now carried into exile in the most distant lands—what was that gift by which, with the breast of a most vigorous champion of Christ, he overcame every torment and carried away a valiant trophy from his prostrate enemy?

Amid the bloody commands of Caesar, thrown into the currents of the vast sea, he was granted by divine providence to walk upon the waters. With nature itself astonished, setting his suspended steps upon the new paths of an unfamiliar route, he trod the swelling backs of the sea. You would have seen the sea’s waves lying beneath the merits of the saint, and him, strengthened by angelic words of encouragement, exulting in the praises of Christ Jesus.

Behold, the profane enemy could never have benefited the blessed martyr so much by his service as he benefited him by his hatred. But at last, when the contest of his struggle had been completed, Nazarius was released from this life by a cruel sentence and consecrated by the sword, together with the boy Celsus, whom he himself had taken from the polluted world and offered to God as a holocaust.

Happy was he in such an end: through it every fault departed from him in such a way that it could not return; through it he paid what he owed, so that he would no longer fear the creditor; through it, by faith, he closed the sins of his enemies within himself and condemned them by faith. Through it he sought innocence by devotion, found it through perseverance, and preserved it through death.

Since these things are so, beloved, although this great witness of Christ—precious through his confession, more precious through his blood, more precious still through his cruel wound, and whiter in his blood-dyed garment—although by the privilege of his tomb he is considered the particular possession of the Milanese, nevertheless he belongs to all through the communion of intercession. For the overflowing charity and miserly faith of this city would have done this martyr great injustice if, while claiming him for themselves, they had believed that the benefits of his patronage would come only to those within their own walls.

What is spread abroad through merits is not confined by places. You have invoked the martyr everywhere; everywhere he hears you—the one who is honored in the martyr. Therefore, under the governance of him who weighs your vows and dispenses his gifts, the nearby presence of an effective advocate will be granted in proportion to the devotion of the faith with which he has been received.

For prayer that is aided by works of chastity, justice, and almsgiving surpasses the world, penetrates paradise, and flies up even to the sight of the highest Majesty, with an angel presenting it. As the angelic voice testifies in a certain passage: “And when you prayed,” he says, “I offered your prayer before the presence of the glory of God” (Tobit 12).
