Blessed is the soul, beloved, whose vow, whose incense of compunction, whose holocaust of supplication is smoky with no unbelief, polluted by no stench of carnal allure, bloodied by no savagery, stained by no contentiousness born of idleness, but is fiery with faith, bright with conscience, fragrant through the sincerity of the heart, and perfected in harmony and charity, and which is carried through the service of the heavenly messengers even to the face of God.

Since these things are so, let us honor the blessed martyrs: leaders of the faith, intercessors for the world, heralds of the kingdom, coheirs of God. But if you say to me that you are honoring flesh already dissolved and consumed, for which God no longer has any concern—where then, beloved, is what Truth itself speaks through the prophet: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115)? And again: “Your friends, O God, have been greatly honored” (Psalm 138).

We ought to honor God’s servants; how much more, then, God’s friends? Of them it is said elsewhere: “The Lord guards all their bones, and not one of them will be broken” (Psalm 33).

I honor, therefore, the scars received in the martyr’s flesh for the name of Christ. I honor the memory of the living through the perpetuity of his virtue. I honor the ashes consecrated through the confession of the Lord. I honor in the ashes the seeds of eternity. I honor the body that my Lord showed himself to love, and that taught me, for the Lord’s sake, not to fear death.

Why, then, should the faithful not honor that body which even demons revere, which they afflicted by torture, but which sits glorified in the tomb? I therefore honor the body that Christ honored by the sword, and that will reign with Christ in heaven.

## SERMON XIV. Likewise, on the feast-day of the holy martyrs Nazarius and Celsus, II.

[Col. 0871]

### WARNING.

We doubt whether Maximus is the author of this sermon, as Cave maintains. The Maurists, in the appendix to the works of Saint Ambrose (1690), sermon 52, p. 574 of the Venetian edition of 1751, deny that Ambrose could have composed sermons on Saints Nazarius and Celsus, since the bodies of these martyrs were discovered at the end of his life.

### SUBJECT.

[Col. 0871B] Saint Nazarius is commended because by his exhortations he brought the boy Celsus to Christ.

You have heard, dearest brothers, from the reading of the Gospel that the Lord called the apostle Philip to follow him. He immediately found Nathanael and urged him to come with him to the Lord. This event is most fittingly suited to today’s feast, because, just as the apostle Philip called Nathanael, so the blessed martyr Nazarius brought the boy Celsus to the Lord. For to him too the saying most fittingly applies: “Behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1). Boys are accustomed to be without deceit and guile; hence elsewhere the Lord says: “Unless you become like this little child, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18).

[Col. 0872B] We must therefore imitate what we celebrate in today’s feast, so that whoever has been called to Christ by God’s grace may draw and invite others along with him, and may show love to his neighbors without deceit or fraud. For there is deceit if someone speaks to his neighbor with his mouth yet keeps anger in his heart. Whoever does this cannot be a true Israelite, because he will not deserve to see the Lord. For it is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers; blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5). Let each person question his own conscience; and if he has received from his neighbor an injurious word or any other slander, let him forgive it for God’s love, so that, with Saint Nathanael, he may be worthy to see heaven and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man. May he himself deign to grant this.

## SERMON XV. On Saint Vincent, martyr.

[Col. 0871]

### WARNING.

We place this sermon, copied from the second manuscript of Saint Dalmatius, among the doubtful works of Saint Maximus, although we already have it published in the appendix to the sermons of Saint Leo and Saint Augustine. For the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur teach in their preface that in some printed books it was attributed to Augustine and in others to Leo the Great. They themselves assign it to neither, judging it to have been composed by some Spanish author, as Quesnel likewise does in his notice. Since the testimony of the manuscript mentioned does not make us more certain of its author, we admit it in this class; yet we note that the text in the manuscript of Saint Dalmatius, which contains sermons of Saint Maximus, is purer than that in the said appendix, as those who compare the two will find.

### SUBJECT.

[Col. 0871D] Vincent, preacher of truth, is conquered neither by the penalties of tortures nor by the confinement of a dark prison. His body is neither torn by beasts nor concealed in the deep, but is restored to the shore and made famous by proclamation.

However much, dearest brothers, the one and the same faith may make the most glorious sufferings of the martyrs—whose places have been allotted in regions set apart—venerable to all with undifferentiated honor, yet in this service of holy veneration those also claim a dignity of their own who have raised up the Church of God by outstanding examples and aided it by their patronage. Among them we rightly proclaim with Catholic devotion the blessed deacon Vincent, by whose preaching and death we have learned that Christ was preached to unbelievers. In order more diligently to commend the devotion of the faithful to God, he at last faithfully offered himself to death with the loftier affection of burning charity, that he might leave to those following him the strength of faith, founded upon that most firm rock which is Christ, as an example to imitate; and that the seed of apostolic preaching, scattered through him, might afterwards be stored in the heavenly granaries, enriched with continual fruit for many through the help of his intercession and his perfect consummation.

Let his own people, therefore, venerate him more abundantly, whom even strangers admire, so that he may show himself more generous in benefits to those by whom he recognizes himself to be more beloved in rejoicing; and that joy in his solemnity may be fuller, from which a greater effect of faith has grown. For his spirit shone with so great a gift of virtues that, supported by the office of the most sacred ministry, in which he was to follow the Son of God, our Lord, in his passion he first administered for salvation the same cup. Happily intoxicated by its draught, he fearlessly faced the madness of the rabid enemy raging against Christ, endured it with composure, and mocked it more securely, knowing himself prepared to resist but not knowing himself exalted so as to conquer. Armed beforehand with spiritual weapons by the love of him whom he resisted, he also, by that one’s help, courageously conquered through invincible endurance whatever punishments the wrath of his raging foe devised against him.

Therefore neither the fiery plate of a frying-pan, nor the rack, nor the claws, nor iron hands, nor the fearful force of those striking him, nor the pain of limbs torn apart, nor the roar of fire, nor Dacian’s casting of crackling salt into his open entrails, could in any way subject him to its command. But when the swelling of that man’s mad frenzy had grown so great that, delightedly puffing himself up, he imagined that he had either conquered or killed one subdued by such immense pains of suffering, he was disappointed in the hope he had conceived: where he seemed to appear victorious, there he was compelled to blush as vanquished. For the more severely God’s martyr was pressed by punishment, the more greatly the constancy of his confession exulted.

It is fitting, brothers, to recount more clearly the final events of his passion, so that your holiness may observe by what deceits the devil brought his servant to his end and how Christ preserved his servant to the end. There is indeed something marvellous in this: as greatly as Vincent was outwardly oppressed and crushed by many kinds of punishment, so greatly was he inwardly enlarged as the inner man exulted; and as greatly as the other was outwardly puffed up by the boastfulness of temporal power, so greatly, perceiving himself inwardly despised, was he choked and tormented in his inner man. For he saw that the hands of the executioners, raging to exhaustion, could find no further place for a wound upon him, and that the spirit alone, still vigorous, rebuked his folly precisely insofar as it challenged him by the standard of truth. Therefore, believing that he would avert the cause of his shame if he removed the person who had despised him from sight, he ordered him removed from public view.

Yet even so he was not to lack torture: shards of a broken pot were spread beneath him where he lay, so that the force of the sharpness beneath the body laid upon it might tear the severed mass still more, and his limbs, returned to tortures, might receive the fragments confronting them to cut them. Blind cruelty, however, is mistaken in its expectation of victory. For divine goodness, accompanying its beloved more abundantly in confession, brought a new light into the darkness and made the gloomy prison a splendid dwelling. God’s healing hand cherished his torn limbs and supplied the injuries of his weary side with a more beautiful increase of his former holiness. The guards, struck by the extraordinary brilliance of this light, stood amazed; indeed, the mind of the pallid doorkeeper was terrified by the sound of angels singing hymns to God. The attendant, half-dead, ran to the governor; the report of the messenger was about to strike him more grievously than the blow of a sword. And when the greatness of the matter would not allow him to keep silent about what he had seen, terror seized the judge, pain tore him, fury inflamed him. “Quickly,” Dacian said, “let Vincent be brought out of prison, lest, while we persist in punishing the rebel, we seem rather to crown him with victory.”

Accordingly he was brought out from the abyss of that grim prison, certainly fairer through heavenly grace and, if he were still to suffer, stronger. But when the envious mind understood that the longing of one hastening to the call of the heavenly kingdom could be broken by no kind of punishments or death, it ordered the supports of a softer bed to be placed beneath him and him to be cherished with gentler rest. This was so that, if the executioner were withdrawn for a little while and he peacefully breathed out his soul, it might be said that he had not been killed but had died—as though punishment had not slain him when punishment itself had perished along with him.

Meanwhile the heavenly court received blessed Vincent and granted him the gift of blessed happiness. At his entrance the angelic spirits rejoiced and all the saints together congratulated him. And we give you thanks, Lord Jesus, because a soul worthy of your fellowship, which steadfastly endured punishment, fled false compliance, and which was content that its persecutor should rage, disdained that he should spare it.

When, therefore, he learned of the saint’s departure, the insane judge Dacian—unaware that Christ had conquered in Vincent—promised himself revenge by exposing his corpse, though he groaned at the victory won through Vincent’s virtue. Deceived by the pride of his fury, he ordered the lictors to throw it out to be devoured by wild beasts and dogs, so that he might fill with such food the bellies of those whose mind he himself bore. But, as divine benefits increased, so that a greater victory might be granted to Vincent [Note: At [Col. 0873], a word seems to be missing here, unless one prefers to read “of a greater victory.” EDIT.], a raven, a bird friendly to corpses, was sent to guard while fasting the exposed food of the body.

But here, brothers, observe the distinct services rendered according to their merits. Elijah of old, cautiously avoiding the impious hands of Ahab and Jezebel, was fed in the wilderness by ravens bringing him food. But Vincent, champion of truth, slain by Dacian’s fury, was exposed to be consumed by beasts, yet was kept unharmed by the raven’s service. By divine appointment, then, Elijah obtained from the ravens what would feed him; Vincent was granted, with the raven likewise serving him, that he should not be eaten. To show that it had been appointed from heaven as his guardian, it vigorously drove away from afar the other birds that approached. Among them it even drove far off a huge wolf that came nearer, beating it with wings and feathers as though it presumed with sacrilegious audacity to defile the treasure entrusted to it. Yet the wolf, stupid in its very bearing, showed that it had come not now to inflict injury but to increase the splendour of the miracle. O shameless fury! O foolish madness! The raven serves, the wolf reveres, Dacian persecutes; nor is he ashamed, still fierce, to wish to destroy one whom the tamed fierceness of a beast laboured to protect.

Therefore, to conceal the martyr’s praise, he chose no longer a secret place but the deep sea, believing that not barriers but seas would preserve his glory from being hidden—as if the Lord of the element were not the same one through whom the recesses of the prison had long before shone with heavenly radiance for him. The body was handed over to sailors to be submerged in the waves, so that at least the waters might succeed in helping to overcome Christ’s soldier, when even land had failed. After they had sailed over a great part of the sea’s depths, God’s mighty right hand caught up the body cast among the swallowing waves; and the hand that had borne his spirit to heaven soon restored his body to a tomb.

Thus, dearest brothers, the preacher of truth is conquered neither by the penalties of tortures nor by the confinement of a dark prison. He is not torn by beasts, not concealed by the deep, but restored to the shore and made famous by proclamation; so that he who had truly confessed the name of the Deity might truly experience the aid of Divinity as present to him. The grace of his precious death so adorned his life, glorious in virtue, that what he had taught by living he steadfastly proved by dying. And it followed that through death he should attain to the vision of him to whom he had always borne witness by the conduct of a praiseworthy life, knowing that from contempt for the present life arises the glory of eternal blessedness; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen. Here ends.

## SERMON XVI. On the feast-day of Saint Lawrence.

[Col. 0873]

### WARNING.

In Vatican manuscript 1273, p. 16, and in the Subiaco Homiliary, this sermon, interpolated in certain places, is ascribed to Saint Maximus. We arrange for its complete publication from manuscript 39, Plut. XVII, fol. 173 verso, in the Laurentian Library, where it bears the name of Saint Fulgentius, bishop.

### SUBJECT.

[Col. 0875A] After eloquently describing Saint Lawrence’s brave and noble deeds, the author of the sermon says: let us learn to despise avarice, love mercy, feed the poor, store up money in heaven, fight for Christ even unto death, burn with inward charity, and endure tribulations for righteousness’ sake patiently, as though they were coals.

To present a sermon to your charity, both the feast of the holy martyr and the authority of the holy Father command me sweetly and invite me to obedience. I trust that my humility will be divinely assisted. For God, who then fed blessed Laurence, will deign to feed his own faithful as well. Through him he gives bread to the poor; through that same man he will deign to grant us a sermon. Just as the blessed Father’s command is present, so his prayer will not be absent. For he does not cease to pour out prayer to God, so that what he has commanded may be sufficiently fulfilled—he whom God has made illustrious both in name and in honor, and just as he bestowed upon him exceptional dignity, so he infused his heart with the most generous charity. We are therefore greatly encouraged in hope when we are helped by his prayers before God.

We rejoice greatly in the Lord, brothers, as we behold the gathering of this devout multitude. Seeing the abundant assembly produced by your expectation, we recognize the inward affection of your charity. Charity, however, does not come from oneself; it is bestowed for salvation by Christ. Christ gave it to his martyrs, and he gives it to his faithful. Therefore, just as Christ’s charity conquered in his martyrs, so it brings the faithful to the solemn celebrations of the martyrs. You show that you love this same charity in the holy Laurence, to whose feast you hasten with delight.

For blessed Laurence, clothed in the strength of charity, fought the good fight, finished the course, kept the faith, overcame through suffering, and triumphed when killed. There is, however, a certain opinion among worldly men, by which it is commonly said: “Among warriors, a victor, when killed, is therefore called vanquished.” The world says this to its lovers, but Christ speaks differently to his faithful. In the holy Church one finds what annuls that opinion, so that the man who was victor when killed is not called vanquished.

For it is one thing to be killed for the world and another to be killed for Christ. He who is killed for the world is defeated when he is killed. Hence he is rightly called vanquished, even if he is killed after victory. This man, therefore, is found killed not as victor but as one who was overcome, because unless he had been conquered, he would not have been killed. But he who is killed for Christ is not conquered, although he is killed; rather, he is truly killed as victor, because when he is killed he is made victorious. A crown, moreover, is given to victors. How, then, can that victor be denied to have been killed who, precisely because he is killed, is crowned by the just Judge?

Behold, blessed Laurence the martyr was indeed killed, yet he was not defeated. He remained victorious when killed, because he is found to have been killed for the One who cannot be defeated. For Christ the Lord is unconquered, and the martyr preferred to be killed for him. If he had feared being killed for the unconquered One, he would not have attained victory; indeed, if he had not been killed, he would have been miserably defeated. Therefore, by dying for the faith of Christ, he conquers—the man who would have been defeated by living without faith.

It is written: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Romans I). Therefore, if this martyr had taken pleasure in living after abandoning the faith, he would have lived in vain bodily, since spiritually he would have died in his soul.

[Note: In the cited Laurentian manuscript these words are lacking, up to “lives by faith.”]

The body lives from the soul, and the soul lives from faith. Christ, moreover, deigns to dwell through faith in the hearts of his faithful. The Apostle says that Christ dwells in our hearts through faith in the inner person (Ephesians III). Therefore, while faith remains, Christ remains in a person. When faith departs, Christ departs from the person. When Christ departs, life departs from the person.

The Apostle teaches that Christ is our life, saying: “When Christ, our life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians III). Thus the body is vivified by the soul to no purpose if, when Christ departs, the soul dies. For the Lord himself, to show that faith is the life of the soul, called unbelievers dead, saying: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew VIII).

What benefit, then, is there in seeming alive in the body when one has been killed in the soul by the death of unbelief? This blessed Laurence, full of the Holy Spirit, reflected on these things, and, so that he might always live in soul, he did not fear bodily death in the least. For he remembered that the Lord had said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (ibid., X).

Blessed Laurence therefore knew that, when the soul dies, the body too would perish with it in eternal punishment; and that, when the soul lives, the body too would live with it in eternal rest and happiness. For this reason he willingly and courageously chose to undergo bodily death, since in that very temporal death he found eternal life for both soul and body.

[Col. 0876B] He is not, therefore, that victor killed as vanquished, whose bodily death became so fully a triumph that through that death he became immortal.

[Note: Up to this point we have followed the reading of two manuscripts, namely the Vatican and the Sublacensian, adding only the name Laurence in places where “the blessed martyr” was read; from here onward we continue according to the Laurentian manuscript.]

Let us now consider the course of his contest, so that from it we may learn how he overcame the enemy. From his bishop, the blessed Xistus, soon to become a martyr, he received the Church’s resources to be stored away with careful attention. In order to do this, what suitable person could he seek, and what safest place could he find for storing those resources? He feared entrusting them to any prominent person, because everyone feared Caesar Decius. What, then, remained except for him to consider raising to heaven what he could not preserve on earth?

But bearers had to be sought through whom everything could be carried to heaven. He found Christ’s poor, whom he could have as faithful bearers and suitable guardians. Whatever he placed in their hands, he stored up in heaven; indeed, whatever he entrusted to the poor, he entrusted to Christ himself. He found a great plan: not to entrust the Church’s resources to a man subject to the emperor, but to entrust them to Christ, to whom the emperor himself was subject.

Whatever, therefore, is deposited with Christ is the only thing guarded without danger. Saint Laurence is found to have made excellent use of this plan, since he took care to find such a place for storing the Church’s resources. He showed himself so secure about the place where he had deposited everything that he led those same poor men before Caesar, and Caesar’s savagery had no power to harm them.

Behold what strength Christian poverty possesses, so that it can always overcome every power of the world. Blessed Laurence knew that he had undertaken a conflict against Caesar Decius, in which he had to fight not with earth but for heaven. He also knew what Scripture says:

“Hide almsgiving in the heart of the poor, and it will plead for you against every evil” (Ecclesiasticus XXIX).

[Note: The Vulgate reads: “Enclose almsgiving in the heart of the poor, and it will plead for you against every evil.”]

Thus secure, he arranged the most salutary counsel of Holy Scripture into a battle of humility and gentleness, so that he might attain true victory. He assembled an army, distributed its pay, prepared himself for the coming contest, drew up the battle line, and led against Caesar Christ’s soldiers, who knew how to fight not with iron but with faith and prayer.

Behold, faith and unbelief, mercy and greed, gentleness and savagery are now engaged in battle. The fiercest conflict between vices and virtues is being waged; and because greed could not overcome mercy, unbelief attempted to conquer faith, and savagery to overthrow gentleness.

Laurence was therefore handed over to Valerian and assigned to be killed by fire. He was roasted alive on a gridiron, but was not deprived of divine refreshment. Then Laurence began to mock his adversary as one victorious in Christ, when by divine ordinance he perceived that the coals supplied him not pain but refreshment.

At last he answered Valerian, saying: “Learn, wretch, how great is the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, for these coals provide me not pain but refreshment.”

O truly wondrous power of the Lord and Savior, who inflamed his martyr with the fire of charity more fiercely and armed him against the fire of his persecutor! For unless Laurence were burning with heavenly fire, he could not overcome earthly fire. He did not fear the flames applied to his body because inwardly he was burning with spiritual flames. First kindled by the fire of charity, he conquered the fire of greed; then, burning with the fire of confession, he did not fear the heat of burning.

He presented his body as a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God. In him was also fulfilled bodily what is written spiritually concerning the righteous in the Book of Wisdom (chapter III), where it says:

“Because God tested them and found them worthy of himself; as gold in the furnace he tested them, and as a sacrifice of a burnt offering he accepted them.”

“Burnt offering,” brothers, is a Greek expression, not a Latin one. What is called *holocaustum* in Greek is called in Latin *totum incensum*, “wholly burned.” Thus *holocaustum* was the name given to the sacrifice that was entirely consumed on the altar.

Christ’s charity therefore presented blessed Laurence as a burnt offering, which the persecutor’s cruelty set on fire. Valerian roasted Laurence, but the most holy martyr offered himself to God as a burnt offering and sacrifice. The judge’s impiety killed Laurence, but glorious suffering perfected him as a burnt-offering sacrifice; and thus God gladly received his martyr as a living sacrifice.

Laurence knew that Christ had said: “Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there also will my servant be” (John XII). He served in the diaconate; he followed in martyrdom. He became the intermediary between Xistus and Hippolytus. And because he had learned from the Apostle that what is owed must be repaid to everyone, as Christ’s faithful minister he repaid to each what he recognized himself to owe: he served Xistus, and gained Hippolytus.

To Bishop Xistus he showed devoted humility; to the pagan Hippolytus he offered pure charity. In Xistus he honored the dignity of the priesthood; to the pagan Hippolytus he proclaimed the truth of the Christian faith. From Xistus he learned to suffer for Christ; to Hippolytus he granted the confession of Christ.

The order of the Church was preserved there: in martyrdom the bishop was found first, the deacon second, and the layman third.

Deacons commonly precede bishops in the order of procession, but not in the order of suffering. Now, however, the Lord arranged it so that the bishop should go before and the deacon follow; and with the deacon going before, the layman should follow as well.

Let us all therefore rejoice in this feast and, as far as the Lord helps us, imitate the virtues of the saints. Every rank has here something from which it may truly be instructed; every profession has something it may imitate for salvation. Bishops and presbyters should consider Xistus; deacons should attend to Laurence; laypeople likewise should contemplate Hippolytus.

May the joy of this feast benefit all as an example of virtue. Let us all learn to despise greed; let us learn to love mercy; let us learn to feed the poor; let us learn to store money not on earth but in heaven; let us learn to fight for Christ’s name even unto death; let us learn to burn with inward charity; and let us learn patiently to endure tribulations for justice as though they were coals.

For the righteous there is a certain burning that consists in temporal affliction, concerning which it is said: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation through tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclesiasticus XXVII).

Therefore, beloved, let us love Christ the Lord and, strengthened by his power, let us burn spiritually with the fire of holy charity, so that we may overcome the kindling of carnal desires. Thus it will come about that we are not wearied by the fires of tribulation, but are lifted up by the unconquerable refreshment of divine power. In this way we shall be led to that rest where, with the holy martyrs, we may rejoice without end.

## SERMONS ON VARIOUS SUBJECTS

[Col. 0877]

## SERMON XVII. On Solomon. On chapter XXX of Proverbs. On the difference between Solomon and the other prophets.

### ADMONITION

Ceillerier, following the Maurists in reviewing the works of Maximus, judges that this sermon should be attributed to Maximus himself. We are doubtful, since both the style of the discourse seems less like Maximus’s style and, apart from one Vatican manuscript, we have found no manuscript—although we have examined quite a number—in which it is attributed to Maximus himself. Some think that this sermon is rather a fragment of a work of Maximus; as to that matter, I am not concerned.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0877C] The other prophets spoke by the spirit alone; Solomon, however, spoke both from the spirit and from the wisdom associated with it.

Before the coming of Christ our Savior, many prophets, having conceived the Holy Spirit, announced things to come. Among them Solomon too is counted in his proper place and order according to the times; yet there is some distinction between him and the others. Therefore, the other prophets spoke by the spirit alone, whereas Solomon spoke both from the spirit and from the wisdom associated with it.

Finally, this is confirmed by the statement that we have heard recited from his words: while he professes his ignorance concerning certain mysteries, he seems to distinguish between the wisdom granted to him and the spirit. He says:

“There are three things impossible for me to know, and a fourth which I do not know: the path of a ship sailing, the ways of a serpent upon a rock, and the tracks of an eagle flying; and the fourth, which I do not know, is the way of a man in his youth. Such is the way of an adulterous woman, who, after she has washed herself, says that she has done nothing wrong.”

[Note: The Roman edition of the works of Saint Ambrose, 1581, volume II, page 403, attests this reading. While he openly declares his ignorance of certain mysteries, he appears to distinguish between the wisdom bestowed upon him and the spirit. He therefore says: “There are three things impossible for me to know, and a fourth which I do not know: the path of a ship sailing, the ways of a serpent upon a rock, the tracks of an eagle flying, and the fourth, which I do not know, the way of a man in his youth. Such is the way of an adulterous woman, who, after she has washed herself, says that she has done nothing wrong.”]

He says, then: “There are three things that I do not understand: the way of a ship upon the sea, the path of a serpent on a rock, and the track of an eagle flying in the air; the fourth, which I cannot investigate, is the adulterous woman, who, once she has washed herself, believes that she has not sinned at all” (Proverbs XXX).

These words seem, in their ordinary sense, to have been gathered from common speech, but they contain holy mysteries throughout: three concern Christ, and one the Church.

For when he said that he could not discover the way of the sea, this statement is not without mystery. Who could gather amid the waves the path by which a ship had passed?

[Note: The same edition reads: “Who could show or prescribe, amid the waves, the path which the ship had traversed? For by passing through them the ship cleaves the waves, and immediately the wave closes again, so that it appears that the ship has passed, but it is not known where.” The ship is made of wood and fastened with iron so that it may be raised more firmly amid the waves, and so forth.]

By its passage a ship cleaves and tramples the waves, so that it is known to pass but cannot be seen where it has passed. It may leave an appearance, but it cannot leave a footprint.

Christ is the ship in which the souls of all believers embark. So that it might possess complete firmness amid the waves, it is fashioned from wood and fastened with iron—that is, Christ upon the cross. But he speaks of a ship without a track because the powerful Word of God penetrated through the ear into the inward parts; having assumed humanity, he was born among human beings, and the Virgin Mary gave birth to him.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “The living and effective Word of God penetrates through the ear into the inward parts without injury; and, having assumed humanity, the Word is born among human beings without diminishing himself, and the Virgin Mary gives birth without corruption. The ship passes … footprints remain, because he came,” and so forth.]

The ship passes through the sea and leaves no track in the waves: Christ came from heaven, was conceived through the ear, and at the appointed time was carried in the womb. After she had given birth, the Virgin Mary remained such as she had been before she conceived the Word through her ear.

[Note: The same edition reads: “Having conceived through the ear and carried him in her womb.” “Justly … he establishes a distinction between the spirit and the wisdom infused into him, while through the Holy Spirit he indicates the mystery that he did not know. Finally … upon a rock. It is common and evident to everyone,” and so forth.]

Solomon therefore rightly says that he is ignorant, distinguishing the Holy Spirit from wisdom, and indicates the mystery that he does not know.

Next he professes that he does not see the path of a serpent on a rock, which is commonly evident to all. In summer, when the earth is loosened into dust, a serpent emerging from its hiding place can mark a path in the corrupted ground through the imprint of its body; but when it reaches rock, it does not make in stone what it made in dust.

So too the serpent, the devil, at the world’s very beginning found corruptible earth in Adam and Eve, who willingly listened to what he said. He made a path in their ears; he made one also in their feet, with which they had been forbidden to travel to the tree; he made one in their hands, with which the apples were touched; he made one in their sides, before the marriage that had not yet been permitted, but was celebrated.

[Note: The same edition reads: “In their sides, while they did not remain as they had been granted,” and so forth.]

At that time the serpent could make a footprint in primitive humanity as in dust. He came to the rock, which is Christ—for Adam had been made such as Christ is from the womb—and saw a likeness covered by a body, but could not recognize the majesty. He could even approach him to test him, but Christ neither obeyed nor became angry, because anger is the devil’s work. When the devil’s words were despised, the serpent made no footprint on the rock.

Third, he testifies that he did not understand the eagle’s tracks.

[Note: The same edition says that he declares, namely, that he did not understand the tracks of the flying eagle.]

The eagle is understood as Christ, who descended from earth in his flight. This species of animal is not nourished unless the chastity of its mother has first been established, so that, with eyes opened, it may gaze upon the whole sun without blinking.

This animal is rightly compared with the Savior, because when it wishes to seize something, it does not walk upon the ground by its tracks but chooses a lofty place. So Christ, suspended upon the lofty cross, made a charge against the underworld with a thunderous sound and terrifying flight.

[Note: The same edition reads: “He made an assault from the underworld …” and so forth.]

Seizing the saints, he returned to eternal things.

Fourth, in what he says about the adulterous woman, the woman here is understood as the Church. Once she had followed idols and gone whoring after foreign gods; but, once truth was known, [uncertain: “dwellings,” or preferably “uncleannesses”] formerly gathered—once she had been washed from sin in baptism and laid aside worldly conduct—she died to the devil and was reborn to God.

[Note: After these words—“is reborn to God”—the Vatican manuscript ends. The Roman edition adds: “As the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: ‘Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.’ Finally, she rightly says that she has done no evil, because through the sacrament of regeneration her sins have been abolished as though they had never been committed; nor are they in God’s memory, as the prophet Ezekiel testifies, saying: ‘He shall surely live and shall not die; he shall not remember against him any of all his sins that he has committed.’ For this reason Christ gave himself over to death, as the Apostle writes to the Ephesians, in order that he might present to himself a glorious Church, without spot or wrinkle.”]

## SERMON XVIII. On the dedication of a church I

[Col. 0879]

### ADMONITION

There are four Laurentian manuscripts—namely, 39 Plut. XVIII, 42 Plut. XVI, 172 of the former library of the metropolitan church of Florence, and 174 of the same library—in which this sermon is attributed to Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin. We mention several among the many that name Saint Augustine as its author. It is indeed found in manuscript 40 F of Saint Peter’s, page 74, with the title: “Sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, on the Dedication of a Temple or Altar.” Manuscripts Vallicellanus 25, Farfensis, that of the Lateran Basilica page 219, Albanus, and others likewise include it under the same name. In Vatican manuscript 3836, page 190, it is anonymous, with the heading: “Here begins a homily on the dedication of a church.” In the Roman breviary its first part is read in three lessons for the feast of the Dedication of a Church, adorned with the name of Saint Augustine. But since the monks of the congregation of Saint Maur did not find in it the characteristic vein of the holy Doctor, but rather that of Saint Caesarius, they placed it among the spurious sermons as number 229. We too, uncertain of its authenticity, have likewise transferred it to our appendix.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0879C] Whatever is done in temples made by human hands is completed entirely in us through spiritual edification. Let us diligently strive, as far as we can with God’s help, to guard our consciences.

Whenever, dearest brothers, we celebrate the feast of an altar or temple, if we attend faithfully and carefully and live holily and justly, whatever is done in temples made by human hands is completed entirely in us through spiritual edification.

[Note: Vatican manuscript 3836 reads: “if we attend.”]

For he did not lie who said: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians III); and again: “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Corinthians VI).

By what merits, through God’s grace, have we deserved to become God’s temple? Let us labor as much as we can with God’s help,

[Note: The Lateran manuscript reads: “with his help.”]

so that our God may not find in his temple—that is, in ourselves—anything that would offend the eyes of his majesty. Rather, let the dwelling of our heart be emptied of vices, closed to the devil, and opened to Christ. Let us labor so that by good works we may be able to open the door of the heavenly kingdom for ourselves with keys.

For just as by evil works the door of life is closed to us, as though by bolts and bars, so without doubt it is opened by good works.

And therefore, dearest brothers, let each person examine his conscience. When he recognizes that he has been wounded by an old crime,

[Note: Manuscript 40 F of Saint Peter’s and the Vallicellan manuscript read: “by some old crime.”]

let him first strive to cleanse his conscience through prayers, fasts, and almsgiving, and then presume to receive the Eucharist. For if, recognizing his guilt, he withdraws himself from the divine altar, he will quickly attain the forgiveness of divine mercy. For just as “the one who exalts himself will be humbled,” so, conversely, “the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

Whoever, as I said, recognizing his guilt, wishes humbly to remove himself from the altar of the Church for the amendment of his life

[Note: The Lateran manuscript reads: “he himself humbly from the altar of the Church.”]

need not fear being entirely excommunicated from that eternal and heavenly banquet.

I ask you, brothers, pay close attention. If no one presumes to approach the table of any powerful man in torn and soiled clothing, how much more should each person struck by the poison of envy or hatred, or filled with the fury of anger, withdraw himself with reverence and humility from the banquet of the eternal King—that is, from the Lord’s altar—because it is written: “Go first to be reconciled with your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew V).

[Note: The Vallicellan and Saint Peter’s manuscripts add: “and then, coming, offer.”]

And again: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matthew XXII).

For the text of the Gospel reading says that a certain man made a wedding feast for his son

[Note: The Lateran manuscript adds: “and entered to see those reclining together.”]

and entered to see those reclining together. When he saw there a man who did not have a wedding garment, he said to him: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” When the man was speechless, he said to the attendants: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Behold what sentence the person will deserve to hear who presumes to approach the wedding feast—that is, the Lord’s altar—either drunk, adulterous, or retaining hatred in his heart.

[Note: The same Lateran manuscript reads: “deserves to hear.”]

[Note: The Saint Peter’s manuscript reads: “presumes to approach.”]

May God avert this from us, dearest brothers, and grant that we may either never wish to commit these evils, or, if they have been committed, hasten to heal them without delay through repentance or reconciliation, and cleanse ourselves through more generous almsgiving. Otherwise, if we come before the tribunal of the eternal Judge bearing the wounds of our sins, we may perhaps be separated by perpetual excommunication from that eternal Church and from that heavenly Jerusalem.

Consider, then, I ask you, brothers: if someone were expelled today from the assembly of this church for some crime, how great would be the pain and tribulation of his soul? Yet if it is unbearable pain to be expelled from this church—where the person expelled can eat and drink, speak with people, and retain hope that he may once again deserve to be recalled to the church—what do we think the pain will be if someone is separated for his crimes from the Church that is in heaven, from the assembly of angels or the congregation of all the saints?

[Note: Manuscript 40 F of Saint Peter’s reads: “which is in heaven, that is, from the assembly of angels or of all the saints.”]

[Note: The Vallicellan manuscript reads: “to whom even this alone will not suffice.”]

Such a person is not merely cast outside as punishment; he is also shut out into the outer darkness, where he will be consumed by eternal fire. Whoever has deserved to be excommunicated from that heavenly Jerusalem will have not only this punishment—that he will be unable to eat or drink—but will also endure the punishments of hell, where there are weeping and gnashing of teeth, howling, lamentation, and repentance without any remedy; where there is that worm which will not die and the fire which will never be extinguished; where death is sought and not found, because those to whom life was offered in this world and who refused to accept it will seek death in hell and will not be able to find it.

[Note: The Saint Peter’s manuscript says: “He will have not only this punishment, but will also endure the flames of hell, where there are weeping,” and so forth.]

There will be night without day, bitterness without sweetness, darkness without light. There neither riches, nor parents, nor spouses, nor children, nor neighbors will be able to offer help. The sinner will find nothing there except what he has sent on from this world through almsgiving, by living chastely and justly.

[Note: The same Saint Peter’s and Lateran manuscripts read: “except what he has sent on from this world by living chastely.”]

Considering these things, dearest brothers, let us, with God’s help, strive to approach this altar so chastely, soberly, and peacefully that we may not deserve to be excluded from that eternal altar.

Whoever comes to this altar with a chaste body and a pure heart, with a secure and clean conscience, will reach that altar which is in heaven through a blessed migration.

Finally, dearest brothers, what I commend to you is neither difficult nor burdensome.

[Note: The same Saint Peter’s and Lateran manuscripts read: “neither difficult nor burdensome, what I suggest.”]

This is what I say, and what I often see you doing: whenever men wish to receive communion, they wash their hands, and all women present clean linen cloths in which they may receive Christ’s body.

[Note: The same Saint Peter’s and Lateran manuscripts add: “It is neither difficult nor burdensome.”]

What I say is not difficult, brothers. Just as men wash their hands with water, so let them wash their consciences with almsgiving. Similarly, just as women present a clean cloth in which they may receive Christ’s body,

[Note: Saint Peter’s manuscript adds: “let them present themselves as recipients.”]

so let them present a chaste body and a pure heart, so that with a good conscience they may receive the sacraments.

I ask you, brothers: is there anyone who would wish to put a garment into a chest full of filth?

[Note: Saint Peter’s manuscript reads: “his garments.”]

Even if an expensive garment is not placed in a chest full of filth, with what face is Christ’s Eucharist received in a soul polluted by the filth of sins?

[Note: The same Saint Peter’s and Lateran manuscripts read: “in a soul which is polluted by the filth of sins.”]

And since we have begun to speak through these very true examples, I will also point out something you know well.

[Note: The Lateran manuscript reads: “and I make known this thing which you know well.”]

I do not think there is anyone who would allow a live coal or any spark to be enclosed in his chest, where he keeps his precious garments. Why is this, brothers? Because he fears that the clothes he wears on feast days might be burned.

I ask you, brothers: you who do not want to enclose a spark of fire in your chest,

[Note: The same Lateran manuscript reads: “in his chest.”]

why are you not afraid to kindle in your soul the flame of anger?

But why this happens we clearly and plainly recognize. We do not put fire into a chest because we love our clothing. But we do not extinguish the flame of anger because we not only fail to love our soul, we even hate it,

[Note: The same Saint Peter’s manuscript adds: “our souls.”]

according to what has been said: “The one who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm X).

And therefore, dearest brothers, considering these examples with the greatest attention, let us diligently strive, as far as we can with God’s help, to guard our inner little chests—that is, our consciences.

[Note: The Lateran manuscript reads: “our inner chests.”]

Then, when the day of judgment comes, in that eternal and blessed Church where the wicked will never be able to dwell and from which the good will never depart,

[Note: The same Lateran manuscript reads: “from which the good will never depart.”]

may we not appear cast outside into the outer darkness in old rags, but, clothed in the robe of immortality, adorned with the jewels of chastity and justice, and dressed in the radiance of almsgiving, may we deserve to hear:

“Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matthew XXV), and:

“Good and faithful servant, enter into the joy of your Lord” (ibid.).

May the Lord lead us to that joy under his protection, he who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIX. Also on the dedication of a church II

[Col. 0883]

### ADMONITION

Since this sermon is adorned with the name of Saint Maximus in the Laurentian manuscripts mentioned above and in the Gotwic manuscript, but is attributed to Saint Augustine in the same manuscripts of Saint Peter’s, the Vallicellan manuscripts, the Lateran manuscript, and Casinensis 115, page 185; and since the Maurists refer it to the appendix of Saint Augustine’s sermons as number 231, while in the *Bibliotheca maxima Patrum*, volume VI, page 675, edition of 1677, it is attributed to Eusebius Gallicanus, we are entitled to place it likewise in the appendix.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0883A] Certain figures of the Old Testament prefigure the Church of Christ, especially the Queen of Sheba, concerning whom the author of the sermon speaks at length.

Those rightly celebrate the festivals of the Church who acknowledge themselves to be children of the Church. For she is the mother of all believers, [Note: St Peter manuscript A 9 and the Cassinese manuscript read: “who regenerates those begotten for death.”] who regenerates those born for death into salvation, through whom Christ restored more to grace than was lost in nature. [Note: The Lateran manuscript reads: “and the transgressor Adam.”] And it received the degenerate offspring of the transgressor against God into the adoption of divine fatherhood; and it restores as heirs of heaven those who had been disinherited from heaven. [Note: The St Peter, Cassinese, and Lateran manuscripts read: “restored [them] as co-heirs.”] [Note: From manuscript 23, Plut. XVII, shelf b, of the Lateran Library: “This is indeed the one called after the Synagogue.”] This is the one called after the Synagogue, but promised before the Synagogue. [Note: The St Peter manuscript reads: “This too was prefigured in the first human beings.”] For she was already prefigured in the first man. Just as Eve was fashioned from Adam’s side, so the Church, redeemed from Christ’s body and wound, grew. [Note: The same St Peter, Cassinese, and Lateran manuscripts read: “She, preserved within the ark while the flood overflowed, [prefigured] the benefit of the cross, etc.”] She, preserved within the ark while the flood overflowed, prefigured through the benefit of the cross [Note: Manuscript 23 reads: “the benefit of the cross.”] the mystery of baptism. This is the barren Sarah who, in old age and when hope had been abandoned, foresaw fertility through her only pledge. [Note: The Laurentian and Lateran manuscripts read: “she foretold that she would be made fruitful.”] For the Church brought forth the one people beloved by God when the world was already growing old. This is that queen of whom David says: [Note: The St Peter, Vallicellian, and Lateran manuscripts read: “to God through David.”] “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold and surrounded with variety” (Psalm 44); that is, surrounded by the precious beauty of diverse virtues. [Note: The Vatican manuscript 3836 and the Laurentian manuscript read: “precious.”]

This is that queen who came from the regions of Ethiopia to hear Solomon’s wisdom. [Note: The same Vatican 3836, St Peter, Vallicellian, and Lateran manuscripts read: “But here she comes from one region,” instead of “Behold, this one.”] Behold, she comes not so much from one region as from all the parts of the world, seeking kings. [Note: The same St Peter and Lateran manuscripts read: “she comes seeking kings.”] As the evangelist also recalls: “The Queen of the South will come from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon” (Matthew 12). The Church comes to her Redeemer and teacher, so that from the folly of error she may receive the teaching of truth. [Note: The Gotwicensis manuscript reads: “Kings.”] Of this the history of Kings writes more fully, as we have heard, saying: “And the queen of Sheba entered Jerusalem with a very great retinue” [Note: The Lateran manuscript adds: “and with great riches.”] “and with riches, with camels bearing spices, and exceedingly great quantities of gold and precious stones” (1 Kings 10). She came to Solomon and spoke to him about everything that was in her heart.

Therefore, in the figure of that queen, [Note: The St Peter and Cassinese manuscripts read: “of this queen.”] the Church comes from the nations, from the ends of the earth, putting an end to earthly desires and vices, to hear the wisdom [Col. 0884A] of Solomon—that is, of the peaceful man, our Lord Jesus Christ, [Note: The Laurentian, Vallicellian, and Laurentian manuscripts read: “who made both one.”] who made both one, destroying enmity between God and humanity in his flesh. She comes after the ancient and profane superstitions to hear and learn about the enlightenment of faith, the coming judgment, and the immortality of the soul; [Note: Cassinese manuscript 185 reads: “the enlightenment of faith and the future judgment.”] about the hope of reward and glory. [Note: The Laurentian, St Peter, and Cassinese manuscripts read: “about the hope of resurrection and glory.”]

Thus she comes into Jerusalem with a great retinue—that is, no longer with one people alone, the Jewish people, just as previously the Synagogue possessed only the Hebrews, [Note: The Lateran manuscript reads “Jews” instead of “Hebrews.”] but with the peoples and diverse nations of the whole world. Thus she comes offering gifts worthy of Christ: gold and precious stones, carried by camels—that is, by those coming from the gentile people, [Note: The Lateran manuscript reads: “who had previously been misshapen by the ugliness of vices.”] who had previously been distorted by the ugliness of vices, bent beneath the burdens of evil [Note: The St Peter manuscript reads: “burden.”] and deformed by the perversity of sins. [Note: The same St Peter and Lateran manuscripts read: “With these gifts, therefore.”]

With these as gifts, this queen enters before Christ the peaceful king, bringing with her the gold of faith, [Note: The St Peter manuscript adds: “and the incense of purity, namely the distinguishing marks and adornments of diverse virtues. And she spoke, etc.”] the incense of purity, the splendors of precious gems—that is, the distinguishing marks and adornments of virtues. [Note: The Lateran manuscript reads: “the distinguishing marks, namely the adornments,” referring to morals.] And she spoke to him about everything that was in her heart, [Note: The St Peter and Cassinese manuscripts add: “in her heart. The same manuscript reads: ‘She opened to him, etc.’”] that is, she opened her heart to him and revealed to him the secrets of her conscience in confession and repentance for her former sins.

Let us see what this queen does. The queen of Sheba, I say, seeing all Solomon’s wisdom, the house that he had built, the food of his table, and the burnt offerings that he offered in the house of the Lord, “had no longer any spirit” (1 Kings 10). What reason was there for such a powerful queen to marvel so greatly at the house, expenses, and royal foods? Therefore, in this passage we must seek out matters of greater significance.

[Note: The Lateran manuscript reads “saw” instead of “sees.”] Thus the Church gathered from the nations sees the wisdom of Christ. That is, after the carnal institutions of the gentiles and the human and animal teaching of philosophers, she received an understanding of salvation and life [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “of salvation and life. She observed the wonders of spiritual goods and recognized the true maker of heaven and earth,” with which the St Peter and Lateran manuscripts agree.] and observed the wonders of spiritual goods. She recognized the true maker of heaven and earth, the most powerful creator of the human race, of whose wisdom it is said: “You have established all things by measure and number and weight” (Wisdom 11). She also saw the house that he had built—that is, the incarnation of the assumed human being—[Note: The Laurentian, St Peter, and Lateran manuscripts read: “about which house he says.”] concerning whom the Apostle says: “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2). [Col. 0885A]

She saw the foods of Solomon, that is, [Note: The Laurentian manuscript reads: “as it were those things”; the Lateran manuscript reads: “that is, she saw those things of which he says.”] those things of which he said: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 4). The food of Christ is our salvation. He is refreshed by heavenly banquets, by our progress. We are his food when, having been acquired for the Church, we pass into his members, [Note: The Laurentian manuscript reads: “into his members and body we pass. The St Peter manuscript reads: ‘into his members and body we pass, as the sacraments of his altar are his food, etc.’ The Lateran manuscript reads: ‘into his members and body we pass; or, the foods are the sacraments of his altar.’”] and pass into his body; or his salutary food is the heavenly sacraments, of which it is said: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 77).

She also saw his burnt offerings, undoubtedly the ministries [Note: The same Laurentian, St Peter, and Lateran manuscripts read: “mysteries.”] of prayers and supplications, [Note: The St Peter and Lateran manuscripts read: “and she was astonished. There she saw, etc.”] and she was astonished when she saw the immeasurable riches of her Lord. She said to the king: “True is the report that I heard in my land about your words and about your wisdom; I did not believe those who told me until I came myself and saw with my own eyes, and discovered that even half had not been told me; [Note: The St Peter and Lateran manuscripts read: “which I heard.”] your wisdom and works are greater than the report I heard” (1 Kings 10). [Note: The Laurentian manuscript reads: “Your wisdom is greater.”]

When this queen, therefore—whether the Church or any holy soul—comes into the eternal Jerusalem, [Note: The Lateran manuscript reads: “has come.”] that is, the vision of peace, and enters the blessed rest and glory of the heavenly promises, she will see things far greater and more magnificent than were announced to her on earth through the sacred Scriptures, through the prophets and apostles. For now she sees “through a mirror and in a riddle,” [Note: The St Peter and Lateran manuscripts read: “as through a mirror and in a riddle.”] but then she will see with her own eyes, that is, face to face.

When, I say, every faithful and holy soul in that age is presented before the divine presence, filled with the fruits of good works, [Note: All the manuscripts cited read: “full of the fruits of good works.”] presenting itself as an example, [Col. 0886A] bringing before its God gifts worthy of heaven and capable of attaining heaven, gifts in abundance—gems of mercy, pearls of justice, [Note: The Laurentian manuscript reads: “the adornments or worshipful objects of diverse virtues”; the St Peter and Lateran manuscripts read: “the worshipful objects of diverse merits.”] the merits of diverse fragrances, that is, spices of compunction and sweet-smelling balsams of chastity—it brings, as I have said, exceedingly abundant gold, [Note: The same Laurentian manuscript reads: “exceedingly great and unlimited.”] that is, preserving in itself the complete and devoutly immeasurable price of the Redeemer, [Note: The St Peter, Cassinese, and Laurentian manuscripts read: “reinscribing in itself the complete price of the Redeemer, through devout and immeasurable offerings of heart and body.”] pleasing him through spiritual offerings of heart and body, so that it may take up the voice of prophetic exultation and be inserted among the heavenly wonders: “I will enter your house with burnt offerings” (Psalm 65).

Then the blessed and illustrious soul, established within the astonishing rewards which it sees [the reading *vitas* is uncertain], will be able to use before God the ineffable words of this queen, saying: [Note: The Laurentian manuscript reads: “the illustrious soul, placed amid the astonishing riches of its Rewarder, may use the ineffable words of this queen before God, saying: ‘Your works are greater than the report I heard concerning your words’; that is, it says, etc.” The St Peter manuscript reads: “the illustrious soul, placed amid the astonishing riches of its Rewarder, will be able to use the ineffable words of this queen before God, saying: ‘True is the report that I heard,’ etc. The Lateran manuscript likewise reads this, but has: ‘will be able to use before God, saying.’”] “True is the report that I heard in my land about your words; your works are greater than the report I heard.” That is to say: “O Lord, I dared to hope for great things from your rewards, but I received greater things; [Note: The St Peter manuscript reads: “The manifest greatness of the sweetness that I behold surpasses the capacity of my thought; it exceeds the fulfillment of my expectation.” The Cassinese manuscript reads: “The manifest sweetness that I behold surpasses the greatness of my thought; the fulfillment of expectation exceeds the feeling.” The Lateran manuscript reads “feeling,” and otherwise agrees with the Cassinese. It then adds: “and truly what God prepares, etc.”] the abundance of your sweetness that I behold clearly surpasses the magnitude of my thought. The fulfillment surpasses the sense of expectation, and truly what God prepares for those who love him is not grasped by faith, is not reached by hope, is not contained by love; it surpasses desires and vows. It can be acquired, but it cannot be measured.”

[Note: The Lateran manuscript reads: “A person will see his merits diminish because of the unsuspected abundance of rewards.”] A person will see his merits grow through the inseparable abundance of rewards. [Note: The St Peter manuscript reads: “through the insuperable abundance of rewards.”] He will have the fruit of receiving, but will not have disgust from satiety. [Note: From the St Peter and Lateran manuscripts, the word “satiety” appears to have been written in place of the reading “association.”] May he bring us to these blessings who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SECOND CLASS

[Col. 0885]

### SERMONS

### SERMON XX. On Saint Eusebius, Bishop and Martyr of Vercelli I

#### ADMONITION

What we think about these sermons, published by Muratori in volume 4 of the *Anecdota*, we have sufficiently explained in the preceding preface. They were also published by the Venetian printers and by Andrea Gallandi, whose reading we follow.

#### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0885D] Saint Eusebius’s blessed disciple Exuperantius was like him. The virtues of Saint Eusebius, especially his courage: he taught the monks to be the same as the clergy; he resisted the fraudulent practices of the heretics in order to preserve the faith unharmed; he died a martyr through the treachery of the Arians, and is to be numbered among the chorus of the Maccabees.

To add anything to the praise of the holy martyr Eusebius is to detract from it; for he was a teacher of doctrines so ineffable that his merits can more easily be recognized than explained in words. Therefore conscience retains of him as much as speech and narrative cannot express. His deeds, then, should not be embellished with words but touched upon in brief statements, especially since we know that we ought not to set forth in speeches what we see already adorned with virtues, since the Apostle says: “The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power” (1 Corinthians 4).

Therefore, to wish to add something to his merits is to detract from them—especially for me, who am both ignorant of his deeds, unskilled in sacred letters, and inexperienced in priestly functions. These matters could have been proclaimed more easily through the accustomed practice, more authoritatively through the experience, and more brilliantly through the teaching of my holy predecessor. I mean the especially blessed lord and father Exuperantius, who was his assistant in the priesthood, his companion in martyrdom, and his partner in labor.

In his face we believe that we see Saint Eusebius also, and as though in a mirror we contemplate an image of his goodness; for we readily recognize what kind of teacher he must have been when we see that he had such a disciple. But since the glory of a similar confession accompanies him, he prefers to keep silent about his father’s praises, lest he seem likewise to boast of his own.

What, then, shall I proclaim about the glory of the martyr Eusebius, when this whole people is his glory? And since Scripture says, “A wise son is the glory of his father” (Proverbs 10), how great must be the glory of one who rejoices in the wisdom and devotion of so many sons? [Col. 0887B] For in Christ Jesus he himself begot us through the Gospel.

Whatever virtues and grace can exist in this holy people is found in the teaching of Saint Eusebius. From this clearest fountain of virtues flowed the purity of many streams. For because he was powerful in the vigor of chastity, he established the commitment to virginity; because he gloried in the austerities of abstinence, he introduced the disciplined service of monks; because he was endowed with the attractions of gentleness, he stirred the affection of all the citizens toward God; because he shone through the administration of the episcopate, he left many of his disciples as heirs of his priesthood.

Although some leave their children treasures of gold and silver, no one left richer heirs than Saint Eusebius, since all of them became either priests or martyrs. To say nothing of the rest, this too is remarkable: in this holy Church he established that the monks should be the same as the clergy, and that priestly duties should be contained within the same retreats in which singular chastity was preserved, [Col. 0887C] so that in those men there might be contempt for worldly things and the careful discipline of Levites. If you saw the beds of the monastery, you would judge them to resemble an Eastern monastic establishment; if you observed the devotion of the cleric, you would rejoice in the discipline of an angelic order.

I do not think I should pass over entirely the fact that, when the detestable treachery of the Arians had disturbed all Italy together with the whole world, and the priests of that plague had taken captive the simplicity of Saint Dionysius the martyr, so that they held his signature as a bond, Eusebius freed him from their hands by his wisdom.

For just as the holy Apostle Paul says, “To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews” (1 Corinthians 9), so Eusebius pretended to be a heretic to the heretics in order to free his son from heresy. For he said that he agreed with their treachery and approved what they approved; but he declared himself deeply offended that they had placed his son Dionysius before him in signing. [Col. 0888A] “You,” he said, “who say that the Son of God cannot be equal to God the Father—why have you placed my son before me?”

Moved by this reasoning, they immediately erased Saint Dionysius’s signature, granting blessed Eusebius the first place for signing. Rebuking and mocking them, he said: “I neither pollute myself with your crimes nor permit my son to share in them with you.”

Thus, since the Gospel says that in this generation the sons of darkness are wiser than the sons of light, behold, among these very darknesses a son of light was found wiser than they. Then, gravely indignant that their wickedness had been deceived, they harassed him with new sufferings through the emperor Constantius. After many insults, they banished him into exile in the region of the East, where he suffered so greatly that he carried off the invincible victory of martyrdom.

Among the other kinds of suffering, it is said that he endured this painful punishment: when the Arians questioned him and he refused to admit that he shared their treachery, he was dragged down the sloping flight of stairs all the way to the bottom with his feet uppermost. Then, summoned again to the top and questioned a second time, when he gave the same answers, he suffered the same treatment; and frequent questioning was repeatedly followed by this kind of punishment.

In this passion of Saint Eusebius the martyr, although his head was battered, his body bruised, and his limbs broken, his spirit remained unconquered in faith. For the more the Arian treachery tore him physically, the more Catholic integrity spiritually strengthened him.

We may say that this ascent and descent of the stairs was what Jacob prophetically saw in his dream. Just as Jacob saw those stairs reaching from below all the way to heaven, so through these stairs Eusebius ascended to heaven, while the Arians descended into hell.

Therefore, brothers, I think Saint Eusebius should be numbered among the chorus of the Maccabean martyrs. For they endured martyrdom in their individual limbs, whereas he confessed the Lord through the suffering of his whole body; and their grace was not unequal, since one day joined them together in martyrdom. [Col. 0888C]

*(Gallandius notes that this sermon is mutilated because several pages are missing from the archetype manuscript, and he appends the following fragment.)*

Among these matters, dearest brothers, it is especially fitting for us to rejoice over the Maccabean brothers, whose sorrowful passion but joyful victory has filled today’s festival with manifold gladness. For, confessing one Lord, the champions of the evangelical faith and guardians of the ancestral law triumphed in the contest for the one God.

Just as the Maccabees overcame tyrannical tortures for the honor of almighty God, so blessed Eusebius, repelling the insult offered to his God, could not be overcome by the punishments of his persecutors. Therefore, on this day let us rejoice over the saints’ death, because we do not doubt that after death they deserved everlasting life.

### SERMON XXI. Also on Saint Eusebius, Bishop and Martyr of Vercelli II

[Col. 0887]

#### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0887D] Saint Eusebius defended the indivisible unity of the Word with the Father. Driven from the Church by the hands of wicked men, he carried the Church with him wherever he went. On the struggles and hardships that he endured; on the courage of the mother of the Maccabean martyrs, and on the most grievous punishments by which they were killed.

When we gather to perform the duties owed to the revered memory of our common father Eusebius, in honor of his confession, we render religious service to the author of the confessors’ perpetual glory. For whatever devotion we offer toward God’s chosen ones, we offer entirely to God, who sanctifies his chosen.

Who would not venerate the memories of the holy confessors with a full and perfect love, concerning whom our Lord and Savior says: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10)?

It is therefore greatly beneficial for us to contemplate the merits of blessed Eusebius, whom the coeternal Son confesses before the eternal Father in return for the faith he preserved. Consider, then, dearest brothers, how great a glory blessed Eusebius prepared for himself by living for Christ and not fearing death for Christ, as the Apostle says: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1).

Christ was indeed his life, because as he walked along the path of spiritual virtues, he did not know how to live apart from Christ. Death was also gain for him, because if he passed from the world at the cost of his present life, he knew that, going to Christ, he would gain the riches of heaven.

Thus this most glorious confessor sought Christ while living and acquired him while dying. He sought Christ while living when, keeping Christ’s salutary commandments, he asserted the indivisible unity of the Word with the Father. He acquired him while dying when, through the death of his body, he passed into fellowship with Christ’s kingdom. And because he did not deny that the Father and Son have one substance, as they truly do, [Col. 0889A] he endured exile, prison, blows, hunger, and thirst. Faithfully overcoming all these things, he found the life that he loved and triumphed over the death that he did not fear.

For what else is it to trample down death than to possess life faithfully after death by living, and, undergoing death in faith, to preserve the memory of the holy name? Behold, ages yield to ages; generations pass away in succession. But blessed Eusebius, surpassing all the courses of our ages, remains perpetual in the confession of Christ and continuous in our devotion. Nor is there any doubt that unfailing life accompanies one who lives piously and holily, and that eternal honor follows him.

This is Eusebius, worthy of veneration, brothers. While defending the faith, which was wandering among the treacherous, through his own faithful wandering, he earned fellowship with the heavenly city as he journeyed toward the homeland of true faith. He was indeed driven from the Church by the hands of the wicked, but this most faithful man carried the Church with him wherever he went.

Or was the Church not in him, whose Catholic and most courageous heart the eternal founder of the Church inhabited?

But let us now see what struggles the excellent confessor underwent for the faith and what hardships he endured. For it is said that he was confined in such a painful dwelling that the house was shorter than a man and the prison narrower than a prisoner, so that for one standing and lying in such a dungeon it would be a deadly punishment if the cramped conditions of that most miserable habitation performed whatever tortures a cruel executioner could exact from the holy body.

Besides this, he was afflicted by hunger and thirst, but the champion of saving faith did not know how to grow weary through the necessity of want. Eusebius did not know, I say, how to be overcome by lack of food and drink, for the Word of God was living bread to him, and the Holy Spirit watered him with the dew of his abundance.

What substance of soul and body could be lacking to him who confessed the one and coeternal divinity of the almighty Father, his Only-Begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit, and who was nourished forever at the evangelical breasts?

What, then, was lacking to this man’s martyrdom, who endured so many contests of martyrdom?

Our joy is increased further by the fact that today the birth into glory of the Maccabean brothers is celebrated as well. Their mother, fruitful for God, brought them forth through a religious birth (2 Maccabees 7), nourished them with devout milk, and advanced them through faithful instruction, [Col. 0890A] so that it might be evident that this most noble mother imparted to her children not only the nature of an earthly body but also infused the purpose of a heavenly spirit.

Although the brothers differed in age and were also distinct in the variety of their limbs, their brotherhood nevertheless remained harmonious and could not disagree in its confession of the divine name. For this reason that remarkable woman rejoiced more gloriously to lose her sons than to have borne them.

Certain of God’s promises and secure in her faith, she stood undaunted and unconquered amid the torments of her dying children. Even when the tyrant offered the life of the youngest son, she despised it, knowing that through the reward of present death he would purchase the unending ages of eternal life. The mother taught that, when God’s honor is at stake, one should spare one’s children rightly, but should not spare them at all.

Who would not, utterly astonished, marvel at such a woman, who, forgetting the natural affection proper to a mother amid the bitterest death of so many sons, preserved an unwavering devotion to God?

What shall I say about the bravest young men, or in what words can one best express how great was their virtue and faith, since they obeyed their mother urging them toward death rather than yield to the king, who at one moment inflicted wounds and at another promised gifts?

The young men were marvelous in their punishments, but each was oppressed by his own tortures. The mother, however, was much more marvelous, for she was able to stand firm even while the torments of so many sons tortured her all at once.

The first of them was roasted in a frying pan heated by flames; but the affection burning with a natural fire in all the mother’s entrails roasted her still more. The head of another, as we have read, was pitiably stripped of its skin together with its hair; but she, lest her son be overcome by such punishments, hung suspended in maternal concern, as though her hair were tied at the crown of her head. The tongue of another was cut out by the hands and sword of the impious; but against the raging tyrant the tongue of the mutilated son lived more powerfully in the mother.

And what more is there, dearest brothers? Just as the mother of all her sons was afflicted by their tortures, so she was adorned by all their victories. She was then slain by the sword—[Note: The text reads *gentili mors*; the editor suggests reading *mox*, “then.”]—and departed through a desirable death, so that she who taught that one must die for God’s honor might herself honor God by her death.

Therefore let us now rejoice with all our joy, because the Maccabean offspring, for the defense of the ancestral law, and Eusebius, the defender of evangelical truth, ever faithful to God through his most blessed death, have consecrated this day for us to complete gladness.

### SERMON XXII. Also on Saint Eusebius and on the Maccabees, Delivered at Vercelli III

[Col. 0889]

#### ADMONITION

What we said in the admonition to the sermon “On the Feast of the Maccabees and Saint Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli,” above, column 611, should be consulted, and the variant readings noted there; we publish this sermon as it appears in Gallandius.

#### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0889C] Eusebius, previously unknown, suddenly becomes, through the concordant wishes of the people, both a priest of Christ and the father of the city of Vercelli; concerning his college of fellow priests and other notable things accomplished by him. On the courage of the Maccabees.

Although my lack of skill and modesty deter me from offering the sermon owed to your charity, brothers, and my always hesitant beginnings frighten me, the love of the venerable bishop who is present gives confidence to one who trembles. [Col. 0889D] Your affection, tested from my earliest beginnings, entirely drives away the force of fearful anxiety; and above all, the grace of our lord and father, the confessor of blessed memory, urges me on. For, in the instruction of heavenly virtues, he takes greater pleasure in the service of devout dedication than in a display of words.

Though I say little and insignificant things about him, I do not doubt that what is said will please him when spoken by one whom he himself nourished in his Church, born and begotten there, with the life-giving light of spiritual milk. Indeed, pious parents are delighted by the babbling speech of their infants’ still unblemished tongues, when nature first prompts the little ones to speak, and by a certain sweeter joy of infancy itself.
