Their manner of speaking is especially sweet when, with lips still trembling, they cannot express in broken words what they desire. [Col. 0890C]

Therefore, brothers, although I am weak in understanding and poor in speech and cannot match the heavenly merits of this most reverend man, one consideration nevertheless consoles me greatly: the greatness of my bewildered intellect is excused by the abundance of his love, and no offense arising from presumption will wound me where devotion commends inexperience and love overcomes embarrassment.

Who, then, dearly beloved, would not burst forth with his whole heart in praise of blessed Eusebius? [Col. 0890D] Even if our tongue were silent about his glory, the monuments of his countless virtues bear witness to it throughout almost the whole world. For this is the man of whom divine judgment showed such a remarkable favor that, as the report of faithful fathers has also brought to our knowledge, when he had come here as an unknown stranger, the people’s wishes suddenly agreeing, he became both a priest of Christ and the father of our city.

Nor could the fact that he seemed unknown harm his election, since the one whom human judgments failed to recognize could not be hidden from the foreknowledge of almighty God. Finally, do you wish to know by what special grace of heavenly calling he was consecrated? Behold: the integrity of his life and the perfection of his faith made him both an exceptional priest and a most glorious confessor.

He taught various dispositions among those living together within the enclosure of a single dwelling to come together in one harmony. [Col. 0891A] Such was his measure and discipline of life that, as daily progress increased, that habitation no longer seemed a gathering of different clerics but a fellowship of fellow priests. Indeed, as though from a seedbed of excellent growth, the peoples of very many cities sought and received from his institution the choicest pastors.

For, with so great a leader going before them, there was in all things tireless diligence in spiritual duties, the soundness of frugality and sobriety, the sweetness of charity, the grace of gentleness, and the guardianship of chastity. Even if our generation, brothers, cannot fulfill all these things, posterity nevertheless has in this excellent father someone whom it may admire.

What shall I say of this? By his assertion of the saving faith, he deserved to endure banishment, exiles, and manifold punishments; strengthened by the disciplines of fasts and vigils, and never turned aside from the way of truth, he triumphed over the authors of false belief with the most steadfast courage of heart. 73

Hence, dearly beloved, his death is more illustrious than his whole life; hence his priesthood, while the devotion of the faithful endures, does not experience the common decline of mortals. [Col. 0891B]

What, moreover, should I say especially about the seven most blessed brothers, the Maccabees? Having trampled underfoot the terror of the raging Antiochus, they did not abandon the legal commands of the Old Testament, but reached the company of the eternal King and the blessed glory of the Gospel. And just as their birth was the kinship of one womb, so their victory was the brotherhood of one faith.

Like that seven-branched lampstand which once shone with seven lights in the Temple, they sent forth the torch of the world through the lamps of their seven sufferings. And just as the priest’s care then supplied oil to that lampstand so that its light might continue, so the almighty Lord poured out upon these men, from the treasury of his glory, the anointing of the Holy Spirit to illuminate their faith.

Amid all this, the venerable mother, while rejoicing most greatly in the death of such sons, mourned with one and only one sorrow: lest any of her beloved children should be unwilling or afraid to be killed for the sanctification of the divine law. [Col. 0891C]

What a marvelous event it is that, for the increase of our present joy, the assumption of our holy Eusebius and the victories of the Maccabees have come together on one day! How alike their battle! How equal their triumph! The anxious mother presented them to the raging Antiochus; the Church, mother of all believers, brought him forth into spiritual combat when the devil was raging. [Col. 0892A]

The Maccabees endured many kinds of torture patiently and courageously, lest their hearts devoted to God be polluted by the flesh of swine, which was then forbidden. But our most blessed father Eusebius endured countless and exceedingly grievous tortures from the heretics, lest he stain the conscience of his purest heart with the pollution of Arian false belief.

The first of those seven brothers, as you have heard, because he remained steadfast, had his hands and feet cut off. 74 Eusebius, however, persevering in the truth of the faith, consented neither by the movement of his feet nor by the subscription of his hand to the heretical will.

The second of them, so as not to lose the head of true salvation, was content to have the skin stripped from his head. But the venerable Eusebius, while offering his own head to persecutors on behalf of the members of the Church, did not lose the covering of his heavenly head.

The third of the Maccabees, when called upon, steadfastly thrust out his tongue to be cut off by impious hands, so that the tongue which had spoken on behalf of the whole body might go before his entire body to God. Eusebius, however, armed his tongue against the tyrant, for the faith and for the overthrow of diabolical error, not fearing to lose what he knew could not perish for him even if lost. [Col. 0892B]

The fourth, fifth, and sixth, as was read, rebuked King Antiochus in sharper words, without any description of their punishments. Eusebius, likewise, amid countless tortures and various sufferings, spoke with such courage and grandeur that the impious hearts of the false believers were tormented by the rebuke contained in his words.

The seventh, persisting in the defense of his ancestral law, rejected with marvelous greatness of spirit Antiochus, full of deceit and promising honors and riches. But neither ambition for priestly honor nor the poverty of exile turned Eusebius away from defending the true faith. Rather, through holy poverty he sought out unspeakable riches, and preserved his priesthood by accepting the loss of that priesthood.

The most glorious mother also, because her sons would not yield, overcame the enraged Antiochus; and the Church of Christ, while Eusebius conquered false belief, crushed the devil himself, the author of impiety, when truth was restored to the world. [Col. 0892C]

This, then, is the fellowship of blessed combat and glory shared by the most blessed confessor and the Maccabee brothers. Each year we must increase and honor the solemnity of this day, on which the defenders of the Old Testament passed into eternal blessedness and the champion of the new Gospel was taken up.

## SERMON XXIII. Likewise on Saint Eusebius and the Maccabees, IV

[Col. 0891]

### Argument

[Col. 0891C] Again, the glorious deeds accomplished by Eusebius are recounted; especially the fellowship of priests established through his work, together with the confession of faith and the punishments inflicted upon the Maccabees.

Although, dearly beloved brothers, I am an unworthy son and the least servant of our blessed father, the high priest and confessor Eusebius, I nevertheless discharge, according to my ability, at least a small service in return for his distinguished merits and virtues. Even though he, now active in heavenly things and joined to the evangelical assembly, does not require this, we, mindful of our own obligations, offer what we owe.

I dare to do this with the greatest confidence because I do not doubt that, although I speak humble and insignificant words, he weighs the speech of his servant and fosterling not with the judgment of an examiner but with the affection of one who loves. [Col. 0891D]

Therefore, with every joy, we offer service to our father, duty to our priest, and honor to our confessor.

When, by God’s dispensation, he had assumed the rank of supreme pontiff in this city, he gathered all his clergy together with him within the enclosure of a single dwelling, so that he might present himself to his entire clergy as a heavenly mirror of spiritual instruction, and so that those whose religious purpose was one and undivided might have a common life and sustenance.

Thus, in that most holy fellowship of life, they became for one another both judges and guardians of their conduct. While each preferred the humility of another, marveled at his self-restraint, revered his chastity, praised his patience, proclaimed the goodness of his compassionate spirit, and admired his fasts and vigils, all learned from one another what each individually did not possess. [Col. 0892C]

Although these things were so, the fullness of every virtue nevertheless flowed into the hearts of all from the fountain of that great Eusebius. Thus, while they mutually stirred one another to the divine commandments by their examples, that dwelling seemed to contain not so much a gathering of human beings as an assembly of virtues.

When Arian impiety was disturbing the Christian faith and the peace of the Church throughout the world, and rebels against the Godhead, through royal terror, exiles, and various punishments, were forcing simple priests into agreement with their false belief, our Eusebius, establishing his foundation upon the rock, shone forth as such a great and steadfast man that no error could engulf him amid the roar of the world’s waves, and no power could terrify him. [Col. 0892D]

For, as the report of our fathers has taught us, he was shut in and yet opened up in such a narrow and cramped prison that, whether standing or lying down, he had no freedom to stretch out his body. He was pressed by the painful dwelling so that he could not raise his bowed head; yet, by the merit of his suffering, he lifted his head toward heaven.

He was likewise constricted by the prison’s narrowness, so that he could not relax his weary knees into rest; but, walking along the paths of truth, he extended the traces of his incorrupt faith through the pleasant places of Paradise. 75

Food and drink were also withheld from him, as his own writings testify; but he was not wearied by hunger for bodily nourishment, since by confessing the eternity of Christ he lived by the heavenly bread of the Word. He could never be compelled, by the authority of the false believers or by bodily necessity, to subject the state of his faithful soul. [Col. 0893A]

And although blessed Eusebius, in so great a battle for the faith, overcame every adversity with the help of the God whom he served, he nevertheless bore more tolerably all those cramped conditions of lying down and that deprivation of hunger—[the defective text continues: “which had trained him; a harder bed and the continued fasts of a holier purpose”].

[Note: [Col. 0893] The whole of this phrase seems defective and could not easily be restored. EDIT.]

[Note: [Col. 0893] The whole of this phrase seems defective and could not easily be restored. EDIT.]

Here he truly both says and teaches with the apostle Paul: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or hunger?” (Romans 8), and so forth.

Rightly, he could not be separated from Christ by tribulations and distress, since he could not be forced to separate the Son from the Father.

And although there can never be mutual satiety for us in speaking and hearing about the sweetness of his deeds, the victory of the most blessed Maccabees must nevertheless not be passed over in silence (2 Maccabees 7), since this same day also rescued them from the world and carried them with great triumph to heaven.

Although that most courageous band passed to its God amid tortures, Eusebius is by no means inferior: after refuting false belief, he migrated to the same God, victorious after his sufferings. [Col. 0893B]

And so that we may perceive more clearly that the victory of our Eusebius was not inferior, they fought for the ancient Law, whereas he fought for the new Gospel. They indeed submitted to punishments for the commandments of God, but Eusebius contended for the truth of the Godhead itself. They resisted King Antiochus so that they would not eat meats that were then unlawful; he resisted the devil so that the bread of the Lord might not be polluted for us by the leaven of heretical speech. 76

Let us therefore rejoice, brothers, giving thanks to our God, because under the devotion of this present day we are gladdened by a double celebration: we look up to the triumph of Eusebius and marvel at the victorious sufferings of the Maccabees. [Col. 0894A]

Are the Maccabees not marvelous—those whom, through sharing a common birth and common suffering, we see to have been brothers in this world and kindred in heaven? From the rich breast of their excellent mother they suckled both the substance of life and the strength to conquer.

They grew to such perfection on their mother’s milk and teaching that wisdom in their hearts and courage in their bodies were inseparable. Finally, Antiochus could not turn those most distinguished young men, steadfast through their own faith and their mother’s exhortation, away from reverence for their ancestral law either by the most savage punishments or by great promises.

Such vigor was in their limbs, such spirit in their hearts, and such learning in their answers that, by scorning punishments and refuting the king’s false belief, they overcame both his terror and his fury.

The venerable mother, having died with an equal confession and a similar death, departed from this world and migrated joyfully to her children. Nor is it surprising that she bore the king’s savagery bravely in herself, since she was able to endure it with such courage in her sons. [Col. 0894B]

Truly blessed was that woman, deserving of praise from everyone, whom, for the faith of her God and at the deaths of her sons, no affection of the flesh broke, and whom neither sex nor old age could recall from the tortures of her own body.

These, then, dearly beloved, are the faithful joys desired for this day. Let us always offer such services to blessed Eusebius and the most glorious Maccabees, whom a different time but the same day and one faith carried into the eternal kingdom.

## SERMON XXIV. On the Feast of a Single Pontifical Confessor

[Col. 0893]

### Admonition

Concerning the authorship of this sermon, consult what we wrote in the preface to the appendix.

### Argument

[Col. 0893C] Since the Lord distributes his gifts to each person as he wills, it is not the quantity but the use of heavenly grace that is weighed in the account rendered to God.

It is written in the Gospel reading that a certain man, going abroad, called his servants and handed over his possessions to them. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability; and he departed at once (Matthew 25).

This man, the master of the household, is the Lord Christ, who, victorious after the resurrection, ascended to the Father and, having called the apostles, entrusted them with evangelical teaching. He gave more to one and less to another, not according to generosity or parsimony, but according to the abilities of those receiving it. In the same way, the Apostle says that he gave milk to those who could not receive solid food. [Col. 0893D]

Finally, he received with similar joy both the servant who had made ten from five talents and the one who had made four from two, considering not the size of the profit but the zeal of the will.

By the five, two, and one talents, let us understand either the different graces entrusted to each person, or, after examining the first, all the senses; in the second, understanding and works; and in the third, reason, by which human beings are separated from beasts.

The one who had received five talents went away, put them to work, and gained another five. Having received earthly senses, he doubled for himself the teaching of heavenly things: from created things he understood the Creator, from bodily things incorporeal realities, from visible things invisible realities, and from transient things eternal realities.

Likewise, the one who had received two gained another two. According to his ability, he doubled in the Gospel whatever he had learned in the Law; or he understood in the present life both knowledge and works as a figure of future blessedness.

After a long time the master of those servants came and settled accounts with them. The long time is the period between the Savior’s ascension and his second coming.

The one who had received five talents came forward and offered another five, saying: “Lord, you gave me five talents; behold, I have gained another five.” His master said to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.”

The one who had received two talents also came forward and said: “Lord, you gave me two talents; behold, I have gained another two.” His master said to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.” [Col. 0894C]

To both servants, as I have already said—to the one who had made ten from five talents, that is, who had spiritually multiplied the five bodily senses and had lived the active life well; and to the one who had made four from two, that is, who preached to his brothers what he understood, completed the works, and led those same neighbors to the faith of Christ through his good example—the master of the household speaks graciously, saying: “Well done,” which means, “Rejoice rightly.”

It should be noted that everything possessed in the present life, although it may seem great and abundant, is nevertheless little and small in comparison with future things. “Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much,” that is, in eternal rest.

What greater gift can be given to a faithful servant than to be with the Lord and to see the joy of his Lord? Once placed in eternal blessedness, whatever he did not possess by merit he will possess in charity; and he will have such joy in another’s more eminent glory as though that glory appeared to be his own. [Col. 0894D]

“Enter,” he says, “into the joy of your master,” as though he were saying: “Receive what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man.”

But this man going abroad handed over possessions to his servants because he granted spiritual gifts to the holy faithful. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another he entrusted one.

For there are five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Thus the five talents express the gift of the five senses, that is, external knowledge; the two signify understanding and action. The name of the one talent signifies understanding alone.

But the one who had received five talents gained another five, because there are some who, although they do not know how to penetrate inward and mystical realities, nevertheless, with the heavenly homeland in view, teach the right things they can from the external gifts they have received. While they restrain themselves from the wantonness of the flesh, from the pursuit of earthly things, and from the pleasure of visible things, they also restrain others from these things by admonishing them. [Col. 0895A]

There are also some who, enriched as though with two talents, receive understanding and action: they understand subtle things concerning interior realities and perform marvelous works in exterior matters. By preaching to others through both understanding and action, they bring back, as it were, a doubled profit from their business.

It is rightly said that another five or another two have come as profit, because, since preaching is offered to both sexes, the talents received are doubled, as it were.

But the one who had received one talent went away, dug in the ground, and hid his master’s money. To hide a talent in the ground is to entangle the intellect one has received in earthly activities, not to seek spiritual profit, and never to raise the heart above earthly thoughts.

There are indeed some who have received the gift of understanding but savor only the things of the flesh. The prophet speaks of them: “They are wise to do evil” (Jeremiah 4); but they do not know how to do good. 78

But the master who bestowed the talents returns to settle accounts, because he who now mercifully grants spiritual goods will strictly demand an account of merits at the judgment. He considers what each person has received and weighs what profit each has brought back from the talents received. [Col. 0895B]

The servant who returns doubled talents is praised by his master and led to eternal reward, when the master’s voice says to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.”

All the goods of the present life are indeed little, however abundant they may seem. But the faithful servant is then set over many good things when, after every affliction of corruption has been conquered, he rejoices in eternal joys in that heavenly dwelling.

He is then perfectly admitted into the joy of his master when, taken up into that eternal homeland and joined to the companies of angels, he rejoices inwardly in the gift in such a way that he has nothing outwardly left to grieve over because of corruption. [Col. 0896A]

We therefore celebrate the solemnity of the deposition [F. depositionis] of this holy man, to whom, we know, the talents mentioned above were entrusted.

What is a deposition? Not only that deposition which was carried out by the hands of clerics for burying the remains of his limbs in the earth, but also that by which a human being, released from bodily bonds and departing freely toward heaven, returned to his Lord the talents entrusted to him, doubled.

That is truly the deposition in which we cast away desire, cease to commit offenses, and lay aside sinning. Therefore this day is prepared as a very great celebration, because the true and highest festival is to be dead to vices and to live for righteousness alone.

It is also called a birthday, because, liberated from the prison of sins, we are born into freedom for the Savior.

As I have said, then, we celebrate the birthday of this father of ours, the confessor. In his praises the first thing to be said is that he was blameless in his priesthood: gentle and innocent, so that he might at the same time be wise. [Col. 0896B]

He was so gentle that severity was mingled with gentleness in him. He was so humble that, in that very humility, he surpassed others through the authority of greater reverence.

Thus he was innocent and wise. He fulfilled the Lord’s saying: “Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10).

He was innocent in the administration of the holy Church and wise in the suffering he endured for the Catholic faith. For, like a serpent when it suffers persecution, he always protects his head with cunning and disregards its other members.

He had read the Apostle’s statement: “The head of a man is Christ” (1 Corinthians 11). Here we understand what sort of man this blessed confessor was. Therefore, in accordance with his merit, he earned the highest priesthood here, and afterward received from the Lord the crown of confession.

Through the help of him who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXV. On the Dedication of a Church

[Col. 0895]

### Admonition

In the codex of the Vatican Regina collection, no. 539, this sermon is attributed to Saint Maximus. We assign it to this class because that most holy bishop was accustomed to use a more elegant manner of expression, and because the sermon appears to us to have been composed in a later period.

79

### Argument

[Col. 0895C] The festivals of church dedications deserve no less observance than the birthdays of the saints. Let us solemnly celebrate today’s dedication with psalms and rejoice in so great a festival.

Today, dearly beloved brothers, let us celebrate with devoted minds and every effort the anniversary festival of the consecration of this holy church. Let us therefore knock, most dear ones, with pious affection and devoted hearts, entreating the Lord’s mercy, so that he may grant us the happiness of his clemency and the remission of forgiveness, and open the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, that in the heavenly temple and in the higher and eternal Church we may eternally enjoy the fellowship of the saints. Therefore, brothers, it is holy and pleasing to God that we venerate the dedication of this church with exceptional devotion. Rightly, then, do those who recognize themselves as children of the holy Church of God reverently honor the festivals and consecrations of holy churches. For she is the mother of all believers, who regenerates those born for death into life.

Therefore, dearly beloved, [Col. 0895D] all who are reckoned by the Christian name and called children of God ought above all solemnly and becomingly to celebrate the consecrations of new churches, to venerate them with the greatest devotion, and with every effort to implore the Lord’s help in them. For there is no doubt that the almighty Lord dwells in temples made by human hands, spiritually visits the hearts of those who gather there and reverently honor their dedications, helps all who entreat him there, and comes to the aid of their needs.

Accordingly, the solemn dedications of new churches in the New Testament and in the present age are to be honored with greater glory and veneration than the observance and institution of the law of the Old Testament established. For just as a greater redemption was afterward accomplished among the [Col. 0896C] Christian people through Christ’s blood, so a greater and much more abundant veneration of the dedications and consecrations of churches is to be prepared and faithfully embraced—churches in which the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, sacrificed daily, are received by the faithful.

Each believer must also consider how great is the consecration of a church’s dedication, and how great the prayer offered in it by the bishop or by the other priests and ministers; how, through the mystery of dedication and consecration and through the intention of the prayer, the hearts of the faithful are kindled; and how diligently all should venerate the festivals of the temple’s consecration. For with knees bent, the supreme pontiff and the other priests and ministers of God perform the litany; afterward they offer the remaining prayers, as the ecclesiastical order teaches.

In the consecration of a new church, the bishop, his fellow priests, and the remaining ministers implore the majesty of the Lord so that the prayers of all who come there may be heard by the Lord; the anxieties of all who pray there may be released; the sins of those who entreat him may be forgiven; [Col. 0896D] illnesses may be healed; vows may be accepted; desired things may be obtained; petitions may be granted; and all who continually flee to it and pray in it may be freed by the Lord from every evil and preserved by him, or mercifully delivered unharmed from all evils. The other things contained in the sequence of the prayers for the dedication and consecration of the church likewise express the same manner of entreaty.

Many saints who now rejoice in heaven among the hosts of the saints consecrated temples of God in the present Church [Note: [Col. 0895] The sequence of the prayer seems to require that we read *consecraverunt* (“they consecrated”) instead. EDIT.], whose buildings together with their consecrations still remain, and whose walls appear to stand to this day. No one, therefore, should doubt that their prayers are heard by the Lord and that what they obtain is fulfilled, since their souls are in heaven, equal to the souls of the saints [Col. 0897A].

For if, while living in the flesh, they planted and built churches and consecrated them with their prayers, and certainly deserved to obtain by their holy prayers the things they sought during their dedications, how much more, now that they reign with the Lord, do their requests and attainments overflow through their merits upon those who come devoutly to the same temples to pray, gather to honor the festival of their dedication, or reverently celebrate and venerate it? For just as those saints mentioned above, or all the holy fathers, received an everlasting reward for these deeds and deserved to attain eternal glory, so now all who imitate their footsteps undoubtedly deserve, with the Lord’s favor, to attain eternal rewards.

For this reason, all must carefully consider that they should imitate their footsteps insofar as they can, and humbly gather at the churches that they consecrated, or that their successors afterward dedicated or dedicate daily, so that they may be able to obtain for themselves what they request—not only through their own good intentions and good deeds, but also through the prayers of the [Col. 0897B] priests who dedicate those churches and of the saints whose relics they place there and who are venerated in those churches. Thus they may deserve to obtain what they ask.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we exhort you not to undertake these things in vain or permit them to cease. For if you reverently honor the dedications of new churches and celebrate their solemnities with the greatest devotion, you will rejoice, with the Lord’s help, to obtain mercifully what those holy priests themselves requested in those church dedications for you and for all who pray there: namely, that your prayers may be heard in the places consecrated by them and in the churches of God; that what you strive to obtain in them may be granted; that you may be freed from the troubles of the present age, from all tribulations, and from sins; and that, concerning the things belonging to heaven, the fellowship of the saints, and everlasting rest, you may, through the Lord’s mercy, obtain them sweetly. Moreover, whatever you [Col. 0897C] humbly and faithfully ask for in them, you will be able to attain, with the Lord mercifully granting it.

If, then, our Lord and teacher Jesus Christ deigned to come to the festival of the temple’s dedication, how much more ought we to come to the festivals of the dedications of churches, and solemnly and reverently celebrate them in mind and heart, as we are able and as the Lord grants? For you heard, dearest brothers, from the Gospel reading that the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem, that it was winter, and that Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s portico (John X).

The *encaenia* were called the solemnities of the consecration and dedication of the holy temple, which the people of God, following the tradition of their fathers and ancient custom, were accustomed to celebrate each year. Imitating their example today, according to the custom of the Christian world, we strive to make the annual day of the dedication of our church solemn with divine praises, vigils, other good practices, and prayers.

For the festivals of the dedications of churches are no less to be honored and venerated [Col. 0897D] than the birthdays of the saints, since in those churches dedicated to God many saints deserved, by praying and lawfully striving, to attain glory and the fellowship of the saints. If, then, our Lord and teacher Jesus Christ wished to come to the dedication of the new temple, to the festival of the consecrated temple, and to the day of its consecration, and strove to celebrate that festival solemnly with the other people, although he was burdened by no weight of sin, how much more ought we, who are weighed down and oppressed by the burdens of many sins, together with the other peoples subject to us, suitably to come to the festivals mentioned above and celebrate them solemnly, so that, with the Lord’s favor, we may deserve to obtain what the holy priests who consecrated them entreated and requested?

We ought to celebrate this festival with the greater devotion because we know it to be especially pleasing to our [Col. 0898A] Redeemer. The festival of the temple’s devotion was indeed exceedingly pleasing to the Lord, since he himself wished to enter the temple on that occasion and speak to the people, and deigned there to disclose the mysteries of his divinity.

For suitably, in churches dedicated to God by bishops and priests through divine prayers, countless signs visibly occur, but invisibly miracles of greater power emerge. Bodies are healed outwardly, but the wounds of the soul are released inwardly. What the grace of the Lord visibly displays outwardly is what divine power invisibly accomplishes spiritually within. For it is much greater for souls to be renewed inwardly and raised from their wounds than for bodies to be healed outwardly. One thing is shown carnally to bodily eyes; the other is invisibly accomplished by divine power.

We also see many signs performed in our times at the dedications of churches. Therefore we ought solemnly to venerate the dedications and solemnities of the consecrations of new churches, so that, just as we see the bodies of others [Col. 0898B] healed and restored in them, our souls too may be healed, inwardly renewed by the Lord’s mercy, and raised from sins. May sins also be released, and may divine mercies be implored.

In churches dedicated to God, the blind are visibly illuminated, but the hearts of the faithful are invisibly enlightened there by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Lepers are visibly healed, but invisibly the hearts of those who have been stained by various teachings and thoughts, or by heresies, are touched spiritually in churches dedicated to God and turned either to the catholic faith or to right action. The deaf also visibly receive hearing in the holy places mentioned above, but invisibly the ears of their inner hearts are opened by the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit, so that they may be able to hear and understand the things that belong to God.

Likewise, the other things visibly displayed in miracles at places dedicated to God appear to contain the meaning assigned to them. Therefore, brothers, if we wish to obtain or receive such benefits, we and you, or all of us, ought humbly to gather at churches consecrated by divine [Col. 0898C] prayers, reverently venerate the festivals of the dedications of new churches, and solemnly celebrate them, so that, with the Lord’s favor, we may deserve to obtain and receive in them the benefits mentioned above, or even greater ones.

O how venerable is the day on which the walls of this temple were consecrated by divine prayers! O beloved and blessed day on which this house was dedicated to the Lord through divine worship and sacred actions, so that the Lord’s name might be invoked in it forever, the prayers of all who devoutly entreat him there might be heard by the Lord, the vows of their petitions might be obtained through prayer, and the remedies of eternal salvation might be received!

O most sacred day on which the walls of this building [F. *aedis*, “edifice”; the reading *hujus diei*, “of this day,” is evidently corrupt] were smeared with sacred anointings of holy chrism, so that thereafter the offerings of the people might be presented to the Lord, and the priests of the Lord might consecrate sacrifices in it; so that what previously was not permitted to be done in it might become permitted after the consecration of this day, and what previously no one was permitted to perform in it might afterward be lawfully performed by all priests [Col. 0898D] in priestly fashion!

O day to be embraced and loved with every effort, and reverently honored by all, on which the altars of this temple of the Lord were smeared with divine anointings, reverently anointed by the bishop with the anointing of holy chrism, and consecrated by divine prayers, so that in times to come priests might sacrifice offerings upon them and lawfully and priestly prepare the Lord’s body upon them through divine prayers; so that what before their consecration was not lawful to touch in them might afterward be done after their consecration [Note: [Col. 0897D] The passage is corrupt. EDIT.]. Thus may the lawful consecration of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ benefit us for present and everlasting salvation, and may it also become an expiation for the other peoples and for us, and mercifully grant the rewards of eternal blessedness!

O truly beloved and solemnly honored blessed day of today’s festival [Col. 0899A] and of the dedication of this holy temple, on which the foundations, pavements, and roofs of this temple were dedicated by the bishop through divine prayers, so that what had previously been called a house might afterward be called a church for worship and assembly; so that those who religiously gather there and devoutly pray in it might receive what they ask for according to their righteous desires, obtain pardon, find consolation, guard themselves there always from idle speech and vain thoughts, devote themselves to prayer, direct the ears of heart and body toward the Lord, implore the Lord’s mercy, and receive the rewards of eternal life!

For among our fathers the dedications of churches and their solemnities were held in as much veneration as the days of the Lord’s own Resurrection and Nativity, or Pentecost. For, as we read, certain holy fathers, seeking relics of the holy martyrs in whose honor they desired to have churches, but not finding them—for their bodies had not yet been discovered and they could not [Col. 0899B] possess their relics—nevertheless built churches, raised altars in them, and consecrated them through divine worship and prayers in honor of those saints whose relics they desired to possess.

They placed cloths upon the already consecrated altars and afterward laid them upon the dead; and the dead, in the names and merits of those saints in whose honor the altars had been consecrated, were immediately restored to life and made healthy as before. Therefore—[text uncertain: something appears to be missing, or the words *ut res* are redundant; Note: [Col. 0899D] EDIT.]—no one can recount or write how greatly the consecrated temples and altars are to be honored and venerated, since in them and concerning them these and countless miracles are read of and most wondrously and clearly displayed.

For I cannot, because of their multitude, either remember, write, or judge how many miracles have openly been performed in our times by God’s mercy at the solemnities of church dedications, through wondrous means and most evident signs, and have been most clearly displayed and revealed before our eyes. Therefore the dedications [Col. 0899C] or reconciliations of new churches are to be honored with every effort and most devoutly venerated by all, so that similar or even greater things may occur in them in times to come, and the Lord’s name may be magnificently praised by all people in every progeny and generation.

But if the pagans celebrated the dedications of their idols with festivals, and still [do so; reading uncertain]—as we read concerning Nebuchadnezzar and many other pagans—how much more ought Christians to honor the solemnities of the dedications of holy churches, reverently venerate them, and solemnly celebrate them? In these churches the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood are prepared by priests through divine prayers, and greater miracles and signs than among the idols of the pagans are daily displayed with immeasurable clarity by the grace of the Lord.

O how venerable and reverently to be honored is the consecration of this holy church’s festival today, in which angels visit those who pray and seek the Lord with their whole heart, and wondrously protect and guard them, as the [Col. 0899D] prophet says: “In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you, and I will confess your name” (Psalm CXXXVII)!

O how venerable is this place dedicated to the Lord, in which the heavenly spirits—angels and archangels, thrones and dominions, principalities and powers—ceaselessly penetrate the hearts of the faithful spiritually day and night; incite everyone to right action at the divine command; and, inciting and accompanying them toward everlasting eternities, often visiting them and guarding them in harmony, lead them onward!

How much better it is to pray and offer sacrifices in churches dedicated to God than in other unconsecrated places is shown in the prayers of the church’s dedication, and the signs and miracles themselves that are divinely performed there through the prayers of those saints in whose memory and honor the churches are dedicated most clearly [Col. 0900A] declare and openly demonstrate.

Who has ever seen so many signs and miracles performed in unconsecrated places as in places consecrated and dedicated by bishops and priests through divine prayers? Let anyone say so, if he wishes, so that he may be answered; and if he does not wish to say so, let him be ashamed and remain silent forever. If he is unwilling or unable, because he has a blind heart, to recognize this spiritually, let him at least learn it from the signs and many miracles divinely performed there.

But signs and miracles, as the Truth himself says, are not for believers but for unbelievers. One thing is not forbidden in houses and churches that have not been consecrated; another is by no means permitted. It is not forbidden to pray everywhere, because the Lord is prayed to everywhere and is found by those who seek him rightly. But in consecrated churches we receive our petitions more often, as we ourselves know and have frequently learned by experience, than in other unconsecrated places, as is made clear by the most evident signs in the case of many who are sick and afflicted.

For in churches and oratories dedicated to God we very frequently see the blind illuminated, the [Col. 0900B] lame restored, lepers cleansed, and countless other signs most clearly performed. In other places, however, we do not find these things happening in the same way, except through the devotion of going or returning to holy places, or through persevering in good devotion.

We neither read nor truly know that sacrifices may be offered or the Lord’s body prepared justly in other places, except in places dedicated to God by bishops—unless there is a cause of hostility or the greatest necessity. Even then this is not to be done in residences or unconsecrated houses, but in tabernacles dedicated by bishops and upon altars anointed by pontiffs with sacred unction and consecrated by divine prayers.

We read that this was granted by the ancient fathers and our holy predecessors only in the case of the greatest necessity, when people were situated far from a church, lest they remain without the solemnity of Mass and without receiving the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—not on any other pretext, nor through laziness or presumption.

Otherwise, except as stipulated above, it is not permitted to celebrate the solemnities of [Col. 0900C] Mass in unconsecrated places; and even in the cases of the greatest necessities mentioned above it is in no way permitted except for those necessities. For the divine law, expressly commanding this, says [Note: [Col. 0900D] The Vulgate reads: “Take care that you do not offer your holocausts,” etc.]: “See that you do not offer your holocausts in every place, but in the place that the Lord your God will choose” (Deuteronomy XII). And elsewhere: “He offers rightly, but does not divide rightly” (Genesis IV).

He offers rightly who, forestalled by necessity or illness, cannot come to church or go where God is worshipped; but he does not divide rightly who celebrates Mass in unlawful and entirely unconsecrated places. It is much better not to sing or hear Mass than to sing or hear Mass in unlawful places. For whoever does what is unlawful and does what is forbidden errs greatly and sins exceedingly. Unless he canonically and rightly repents of this in the present age, he will undoubtedly receive the greatest condemnation for it at the future judgment.

Many other countless examples of these matters are found in the legal books mentioned above and in other canonical and divine books. Because of the length of the [Col. 0900D] discussion, we have postponed inserting them here, and because of the weariness and labor of writers and readers we have not included them here. If anyone wishes to find more important and more numerous examples, he will be able to find them sufficiently by reading and diligently searching the books mentioned above.

For us, however, it is enough to believe the examples already cited, obey the Lord’s commands, avoid violating the decrees of the holy fathers, and shun what is unlawful. In the canons, therefore, we read that the matters mentioned above are strongly prohibited by the holy fathers, and we know that it is unlawful to do them. Let no one do what is forbidden without unavoidable necessity, for unless he corrects himself and amends his conduct through satisfaction, he will not escape certain condemnation. No one acts against the prophets, the Gospels, or the decrees of the holy fathers without danger.

Let us therefore see, dearest brothers [Col. 0901A], that we do not act against the statutes of the holy fathers. Let us run to the churches dedicated to God, and there let us pray and offer sacrifice, so that we may receive there the remission of our sins and find consolation in our anxieties by entreating the saints who are honored there. Let us conduct our ministry in consecrated places more justly and more holily, so that we may be found not despising but obeying the Lord’s commands.

Let us hasten devoutly to run to the churches, reverently honor their *encaenia*, and with every effort praise the Lord on today’s festival of dedication, so that we may be able to attain God’s grace. For our ancient fathers rebuilt ruined temples and restored old or damaged altars; they devoutly celebrated their consecrations becomingly and solemnly, calling many companions together and having them join them. They adorned the temples of God with golden crowns and decorated the altars themselves with purest gold and most precious gems.

With the same good zeal and most willing intention, they also constructed the [Col. 0901B] walls with purest gold and restored both the ceilings and the pavements and the doors with purest gold. They reverently and piously honored the dedications of the temples in which they performed the divine office by living in them for eight days; during those eight days they continually devoted themselves to hymns, songs, and other divine praises in honor of the temples’ dedications. Spending eight days solemnly in every form of worship, they always gave thanks and praise to the Lord, humbly sought pardon for their own crimes and for those of the whole people, and praised the Lord with the greatest zeal, stretching out their hands toward heaven, with the utmost concentration and devotion.

We, however, whom the Redeemer of the world finally redeemed with his most precious [Col. 0902A] blood, ought much more to praise him and greatly to venerate the dedications of our churches. We ought always to give him thanks, since he shed his blood for us, redeemed us from the gates of hell, and proclaimed and gave us eternal life.

For if we are found more remiss and less useful than they in the matters mentioned above—in the veneration and observances of the churches—we shall in no way be able to attain the glory that they received. How much less, then, will we be able to attain the glory that the Lord afterward promised us, “which no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians II)?

Therefore, dearest brothers, we ought greatly to venerate the dedication of churches and their solemnities, lest, God forbid, we hear with the negligent that sentence: “Cursed is the one who performs the work of God negligently” (Jeremiah XLVIII). May we instead deserve to hear from the Lord the saying that the Lord himself promised in the Gospel to the faithful of the holy Church of God, to righteous souls, and to those who lovingly [Col. 0902B] devote themselves to divine worship: “Well done,” good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew XXV).

O how great a mystery and how wondrous a sacrament is honored today on earth! We all venerate today the *encaenia* of the holy Church of God, and on earth we sing psalms to the Lord God with human voices, while the angels above sing heavenly hymns. We also pray on earth; the angels praise the Lord in heaven. We rejoice on earth; the angels and saints of God rejoice in heaven over so great a solemnity.

Let us therefore solemnly honor today’s dedication on earth with psalms, and rejoice over so great a festival, so that we may deserve to be found participants in heaven.

*Explicit.*

## SERMON XXVI. On Firstfruits and Tithes

[Col. 0901]

### ADMONITION

[Col. 0901]

Since the style of this sermon, attributed to Saint Maximus in Beneventan Codex I, page 11, is very unlike the Maximian style, we count it among the spurious works.

### ARGUMENT.—[Col. 0901C]

The author endeavors to demonstrate from Scripture and reason that the firstfruits of all crops and fruits are to be offered to God as the supreme Lord.

We ask, dearest ones, that you listen attentively to what is said for your salvation. The order of Scripture is arranged at length; but so that you may retain at least a little of it in memory, we commend to you a few things from among many.

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Distribute all your tithes.” Through the prophet he says: “Bring the whole tithe into my storehouse, so that there may be food in my house; and test me in this, says the Lord” (Malachi III). And in Exodus (chapter XXIII): [Note: [Col. 0901D] The Vulgate reads: *fraudulenter*, “fraudulently.” The Vulgate has: “You shall bring the firstfruits of your land into the house of the Lord your God.” Elsewhere the Vulgate reads: “And indeed those who receive the priesthood from the sons of Levi,” etc.] “Bring the firstfruits of your land into the house of the Lord your God.”

The apostle Paul says: “Those who receive the priesthood from the sons of Levi have a commandment to take tithes from the people according to the law” (Hebrews VII), that is, from their brothers; “for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians IX).

Solomon said: [Note: [Col. 0902D] The text is emended from the Vulgate: “Some distribute their own goods and become richer; others seize what is not theirs and are always in poverty.”] “Some divide spoils and become richer; others seize what is not theirs and are always in poverty” (Proverbs XI).

Jesus son of Sirach said: “In every gift make your face cheerful, and sanctify your tithes with rejoicing. Give to the Most High according to what he has given; and with a good eye make an offering from the work of your hands, for the Lord is one who repays, and he will repay you sevenfold” (Ecclesiasticus XXXV).

Augustine said: “For these tithes are the taxes owed to needy souls. If you give a tenth, you will receive not only an abundance of fruits but also bodily health.” Tithes are indeed required as a debt. What if God were to say: “Indeed, you are mine, O man; the land that you cultivate is mine, the seeds that you scatter are mine, the animals that you weary are mine, [Col. 0902C] the warmth of the sun is mine. Since everything is mine, you who supply the labor of your hands deserved only a tenth; but keep nine parts for yourself and give me the tenth. If you give me the tenth, I will multiply the nine parts.”

Even the holy fathers, before the law was given, took care to offer a tenth to God. Thus Abraham offered tithes of all that he possessed to Melchizedek; and Jacob said: “If my God is with me, I will offer you tithes of all that you give me” (Genesis XXVIII).

Hence it is also said: “You shall not delay offering your tithes and firstfruits to the Lord” (Exodus XXII). Solomon likewise says: “Honor the Lord from your substance and from the firstfruits of all your crops, so that your storehouses may be filled with abundance and your winepresses overflow with wine” (Proverbs III).

The Lord God is not in need and does not seek a reward, but honor. For our God, who deigned to give everything, deigns to ask a tenth from us—not for himself, but plainly because it will benefit us. Therefore, through the prophet he said: “You shall not delay offering me the firstfruits of your threshing floor and winepress.” If you give it late, it is [Col. 0902D] sin; how much more so if you do not give it.

Give tithes from your business and your craft. Since by giving tithes you can earn both earthly and heavenly gifts, why do you defraud yourself through greed of a double blessing? For this is the Lord’s most just custom: if you do not give him a tenth, you will yourself be reduced to a tenth. Will you give to an impious soldier what you refuse to give to a priest?

God is always ready to do good, but human wickedness prevents it. Tithes are indeed required as a debt. Whoever refuses to give them has invaded another’s property. And however many poor people in the places where he lives may have died of hunger because he did not give the tithes, he will appear guilty [Col. 0903A] of as many murders before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, because he kept for his own uses what the Lord had assigned to the poor.

Therefore, whoever wishes either to acquire a reward for himself or to deserve the forgiveness of sins should, after paying his tithes, also strive to give alms from the nine parts. Whatever remains from the nine parts, except for reasonable food and clothing, should not [Col. 0904A] be kept for luxury or worldly profit, but stored up through almsgiving in the heavenly treasuries.

For whatever God gives us beyond what is necessary, he did not give to us for ourselves alone, but transmitted it through us to be distributed to others. These things, brothers, listen to willingly according to your custom, and with Christ the Lord’s help strive to fulfill them.

## SERMON XXVII. 87 On Honor and Love toward Parents, and on Tithes

[Col. 0903]

### ADMONITION

[Col. 0903]

This sermon too is attributed to Saint Maximus in the same Beneventan codex. The Maurists place it in the appendix of Saint Augustine’s sermons, no. 276, and believe it to have been written by Saint Caesarius.

### ARGUMENT.—[Col. 0903A]

An order must be observed in giving alms: first, necessities are to be supplied to one’s parents, and tithes are to be paid. There are two kinds of almsgiving.

We read, dearest brothers, that the Lord admonishes us through the prophet [Col. 0903B], always to show both honor and love toward our parents. And if it should happen that they are suffering from some poverty, we are commanded to relieve their needs according to our ability. For he says: “If you see someone naked, cover him, and do not despise the members of your own seed” (Isaiah 58). By “the members of your own seed” in this passage he wished our parents to be understood.

But someone may say: “Who is there that hates his parents, so that the Lord would admonish us about this as something of great importance through the prophet?” Without doubt, brothers, the Holy Spirit knew that there are some people who, after attaining some honors or riches acquired from whatever source, despise their poor parents so thoroughly that they do not even deign to see them. Whoever does this should have no doubt that he has committed not merely a sin but also a grave crime. And perhaps it happens that, through riches and pride, such a person commits great crimes or sins, while his parents, precisely because of their poverty and humility, maintain righteousness. With what face does he disdain to attend to his innocent and righteous parents, when he himself is a sinner and unjust?

If anyone [Col. 0903C], therefore, is able, and has parents who are poor, let him first provide them with necessities, and then give alms to needy strangers; for if he does not give to the other poor at that time, someone else will give. But if you give nothing to your poor parents, it is difficult for someone else to give to them.

This is the just and proper order of almsgiving: first provide sufficient and moderate food and clothing for yourself and your own—not splendid or luxurious. Then, as I said, if any of your parents are poor, give as much as you can. Then do not allow your male and female servants either to go hungry or to suffer cold. And after this, whatever God, as I said, has given you beyond food and clothing, store not in an earthly treasury, where thieves break in and steal, but in the heavenly treasury, so that where your treasure is, there your heart may also be.

And when the priest cries out, “Lift up your hearts,” let us confidently and truthfully answer, “We have them with the Lord.” For whatever God [Col. 0903D] has bestowed—apart from moderate and reasonable food and clothing—whether from any kind of military service or from agriculture, he did not give to you specifically, but sent it through you to be distributed to the poor. If you do not wish to give, know that you are taking away another’s property; for, as I said, the only thing that is truly ours is what is reasonably sufficient for us and our own. Whatever remains over, our God, as I said, has sent to be distributed to the poor. Thus we ought not only to give tithes, but also faithfully to distribute from the nine parts whatever remains after taxes have been paid and our expenses have been met, as though it had been sent on to others.

If we do this, what we give is truly ours; [88] but if we do not, even what we keep is not ours; nor are we ourselves our own, who seem to keep these things. And yet, brothers, I do not see with what face we fail to offer a small portion to the one from whom we received everything. If God should wish to settle accounts with us and say:

“I made the land that you cultivate; I made you yourself [Col. 0904A], who cultivate it, and your servants; I created the animals that assist you in cultivating it; I supply the warmth of the sun; I distribute the rain in its seasons. But for a just accounting you ought to reserve the tithes for yourself and the nine parts for me. Yet I do not ask this: I wish to be merciful, and I provide sevenfold, so that just as I have [Col. 0904B] had mercy on you, so you may have mercy on the poor.”

If, then, brothers, God should wish to settle this account with us, is there anything we could answer?

And although God admonishes us about these matters in many passages of the holy Scriptures, nevertheless through the Apostle he cries out and admonishes us in particular, saying:

> “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these.”

[Note: [Col. 0903] The Vulgate reads: “But having food and with which to cover ourselves, with these we are content,” and so forth.]

“For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the devil’s snare, and into many foolish, useless, and harmful desires, which plunge people into destruction and perdition; for greed is the root of all evils. Some, desiring it, have been shipwrecked and have entangled themselves in many troubles. But you, man of God, flee these things; pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, and charity” (1 Timothy 6).

I ask you, brothers, even if we say nothing about the rest of the Scriptures, this apostolic sentence is sufficient for every Christian. I truly tell you, brothers, that whoever does not rise from the sleep of avarice under such thunder must be considered not asleep but dead.

And therefore, brothers, since because of this bodily weakness many of us are [Col. 0904C] continually troubled and pierced by sins, like flies buzzing around us, let us hurry amid the storms of this world to the harbor of God’s mercy. Perhaps someone asks how he can reach this harbor. Let him hear Christ saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5). And again: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11).

Therefore, if we wish to escape from the sea of this world, we ought always to keep before our eyes the Apostle’s just judgment. Let it be enough for us to have reasonable food and clothing—not splendid, not luxurious. Whatever more God gives should not be withheld from the needs of the poor, because it is shown to have been sent through us to them. And if we do not give what is superfluous to us, we have seized another’s property. How many poor people will have died of hunger with our conscience as their cause, and will bring charges against us before Christ’s tribunal!

There are, indeed, two kinds of almsgiving: one consists in distributing to the poor; the other in forgiving our neighbors or brothers [Col. 0904D] whenever they have sinned against us. With God’s help, let us do both, because one without the other profits nothing. Conversely, if you forgive those who sin against you but refuse to give as much as you can to the hungry, as I said, one cannot profit you without the other.

Let us, brothers, prepare these two kinds of almsgiving for ourselves as though they were the oars of spiritual wings, so that, rejecting and casting off every desire for earthly things, and supported by the free feathers of the virtues, we may be able to fly happily and arrive as spiritual doves at our true homeland, that heavenly Jerusalem. This accords with what the Psalmist desires and begs when he says: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? And I shall fly and rest” (Psalm 54)?

It is certain, brothers, that unless each person strives [Col. 0905A] to free the wings of his soul from the glue of sins and from the very great [F. *nimiis*, “excessive”] impediments and snares of this world, he will never be able to reach true rest.

Let us, brothers, with God’s help, strive, if we cannot entirely remove the impediments of this world from ourselves, at least to restrain them insofar as our strength permits, or to withdraw from them, so that some intervals of time may remain for us in which we can devote ourselves to reading or prayer. For if worldly occupation takes all our time away from us, we must fear that what is written may [Col. 0906A] come upon us: “The impediments of this world made them wretched.”

Let us therefore labor more earnestly, with the Lord’s help, so that in us too, at least in some measure, what is written about the blessed man may be fulfilled: “He will meditate on the law of the Lord day and night” (Psalm 1).

May the Lord, through his merits, deign to grant this to your holy charity. He lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXVIII. On the holy resurrection of Christ

[Col. 0905]

### ADMONITION

It is indeed rash—and this becomes perfectly clear to anyone who compares it with the genuine works—that this sermon too was attributed to Saint Maximus by the scribe of the Casinensis manuscript 123.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0905A] The day of the Lord’s Resurrection provides the faithful with a cause for joy: while Christ, triumphing over death, returned to life that can never perish, he showed us that the same resurrection and glory would not be denied us.

[Col. 0905B] I cannot express with my mouth, dearest brothers, what I conceive in my mind, and my tongue cannot explain the joy of my heart. Yet this afflicts not only me, who desire to relate what I feel; you too suffer the same with me, exulting more in your inward consciousness than expressing it in speech.

It seems to me that this day is brighter than the other days, that the sun has shone more brilliantly, and that all the stars and even the elements rejoice—those which, when the Lord was suffering, had withdrawn their proper light and had refused to look upon their crucified Creator and Lord. Behold, now, as he rises victorious from the underworld, he calls them forth to serve him with a new display of his splendor.

Heaven believes, earth believes, and the net that fished throughout the whole world was unable to hold the Jews. “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 117).

Just as Mary, the Virgin Mother of the Lord, holds primacy among all women, so this day is the mother of all days among the other days. I speak of nothing new, but of something confirmed by the voices of Scripture.

This [Col. 0905C] is both one of the seven and beyond the seven. This is the day called the eighth; hence in certain titles it is superscribed, “For the eighth.” This is the day on which the Synagogue comes to an end and the Church is born. This is the day whose number saved eight souls in Noah’s ark.

Indeed, it would be necessary to explain innumerable things. The day would not run out if I wished to expound the whole mystery of the day. I say only this: all the grace of the Sabbath, and that ancient practice of the Jewish people, has been changed in the solemnity of this day.

They did not perform servile work on the Sabbath. Let us not perform servile work on the Lord’s Day, that is, on the day of the Resurrection, because we do not serve sins and vices; for whoever commits sin is the slave of sin.

They did not go out from their houses. Let us not go out from the house of Christ, for we are in the church.

They did not kindle a fire on the Sabbath. Let us, on the contrary, kindle in ourselves the fire of the Holy Spirit and burn away every vice of sins. Concerning this fire the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what [Col. 0905D] do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12). The Lord [Col. 0906A] desires this very fire to burn within us, so that, in accordance with the Apostle, the Holy Spirit may boil fervently and charity may not grow cold.

They did not travel on the Sabbath; for they lost the one who said, “I am the way” (John 14). But we say: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk [Col. 0906B] in the law of the Lord” (Psalm 118). And again: “I have chosen the way of truth.” And: “Teach me the way of your ordinances” (ibid.).

They crowned the Lord with thorns. But if we are precious stones, we crown our Lord. Diadems adorn the heads of the rulers of this world; we are placed upon the head of our King so that we may ourselves be adorned by the Head.

They did not receive Christ, and they are going to receive Antichrist. We receive the humble Son, so that afterward we may possess him in triumph.

And finally, our goat is sacrificed before the Lord’s altar; their goat, Antichrist, spat upon and accursed, is cast into the wilderness.

Our robber entered paradise with the Lord; their robber, a murderer and blasphemer, dies in his sin.

Barabbas the robber is released for them; Christ is put to death for us.

For all these things, dearest brothers, let us sing together with harmonious voice: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 117).

Today Christ opened the flaming sword and the gate of paradise, which no one had been able to break through, saying [Col. 0906C] to the angels: “Open for me the gates of righteousness, and entering through them I will confess to the Lord” (ibid.). Once it has been opened, it is never closed to believers.

From the time when the Lord suffered until the present day, this gate has been both closed and unlocked. It has been closed to sinners and unbelievers; it has been unlocked for the righteous and believers. Through it Peter entered, through it Paul entered, through it all the saints and martyrs entered; through it every day the souls of the righteous enter from the whole world.

For what are the gates of paradise but the gates of the Church? We enter through the gate of paradise. Thus we ought to live so that we are not cast out of that house and, having been driven outside, devoured by the beasts whom the prophet, fearing them, mentions elsewhere: “Do not hand over to the beasts the soul that confesses you” (Psalm 73).

Behold, now the Lord, standing at the gate of paradise, speaks to us who are gathered in his house, and says: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Psalm 117).

May he himself deign to grant this, who lives and reigns [Col. 0906D] forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXIX. On the feast of Saint Stephen, the first martyr

[Col. 0905]

### ADMONITION

[91] The same judgment should be formed about this sermon, copied from another Casinensis manuscript, 106, page 16, and attributed to Saint Maximus.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0905D] What is commended is not so much the martyr’s courage while he was being crushed by stones as his admirable charity in praying to God for his persecutors.

Among the most splendid ranks of martyrs and the purple choirs of martyrs stained by Nazarene blood, Saint Stephen shone with such brilliance that, while he was still receiving the divine reward, heaven [Col. 0906D] itself lay open.

That illustrious athlete of God, anointed with the Spirit of God, first entered the arena of combat and attained such glory of victory that he was the first to receive the crown. A faithful soldier of Christ, a strong standard-bearer among the martyrs, he soon passed through the ranks of the devil after Christ and triumphed gloriously, illustrious in the bright splendor of martyrdom.

For by following the Lord Christ he earned precedence in martyrdom; and when he reached the signs of the cross, the palm was sent to him first from heaven. As he hastened to die, he was the first to desire to be crowned.

Finally [Col. 0907A], he answered them in this way:

> “Stiff-necked men, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of Christ” (Acts 7).

Behold, the hands of the wicked are being prepared for murder; the weapons of fury are already revealed; the martyr is already surrounded by a blade of stones, and weighted destruction hangs over his innocent head.

But he said: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears.”

Here he does not flatter but attacks; he does not caress but provokes; he does not tremble but incites: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears.”

Look, martyr, at the hail that is near; observe the twisting air; behold the heaps of stones burning with heat. Let us now see their panting mouths. Look now upon their dripping eyes.

And behold, the deadly line approaches; it advances; already the stones are being hurled:

> “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did.”

When he said these things, they seethed in their hearts and gnashed [Col. 0907B] their teeth against him.

But the strong pillar of God, seized amid hands bearing stones and held in the tyrant’s pincers, firmly grounded in faith, guided by hope, established in charity, was set aflame and hung suspended, struck and driven onward, shattered and strengthened, beaten and not conquered.

Blessed workshop of faith, which constricted the martyr so tightly that, in the commands [perhaps “rights”] of majesty, he could behold such things. “Behold,” he said, “I see the heavens opened, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7).

The seat of God was revealed, and the sides of heaven hung open, cleft through the furrowed air. The bright vault and expanse of heaven yawned open.

Finally, when twisting whirlwinds of stones barked over him and revolving heaps were hurled against him, he prayed in this way for those raging against him:

> “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”

The roaring lion wanted to devour him, but the sheep of Christ did not lose its gentleness. The lion indeed opened its jaws, but could not swallow the martyr. The Jew carried out the execution born of his fury, but our David [Col. 0908A] snatched his sheep from the mouth of the raging beast.

For thus it is sung in the psalm:

> “Unless the Lord had been with us when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Psalm 123).

O Judea, drunk with the blood of the prophets, are you not yet filled—from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah? The rivers of your crime foam, and do they not satisfy you?

For thus the Lord rebukes the Jews:

> “So that all the innocent blood that has been shed upon the earth may come upon you, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matthew 23).

You stained the world, still crude in Abel, and there you poured out your fountain. You boiled over in the vein of this blood, and are you still thirsty? Do you burn for the death of a martyr? Do you still pant for the blood of a confessor? Has the wave of your fury not yet dried up? Does the channel of your crime still flow?

Put an end to your crime at last; spare at least the martyr.

But they were stoning Stephen as he called upon the Lord and said:

> “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7),

because he was pouring out his blood for you.”

“Saul was consenting to his death” (ibid.), as Scripture [Col. 0908B] says, and he guarded the garments of those killing him. He was not merely consenting but an instigator; not merely a companion but a patron.

And you, Saul, ravenous wolf, drinking another’s blood—wait a little and you will see your own blood. You are a thief, and you too, together with the Jews, will suffer what you inflict upon another. You guard the garments of those stoning him; you will feel the fury of those raging. You will see those hands inflicted upon the martyr, and they will not spare you.

You envy Christ; you too will yet die for him in the world. You impose punishment upon the martyr; you will feel vengeance in return.

And indeed he felt it, because he too shed his blood for Christ. Now we have the Apostle Paul, a preacher of Christ, who had previously persecuted Christ’s members.

Let us therefore now, brothers, venerate Saint Stephen, the first martyr and the example of truth, with festive devotion. Standing upright, let us offer prayer to him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXX. On the feast of the dedication of a church

[Col. 0907]

### ADMONITION

[93] From the canon Antonio Francesco Frisi, whom we have commended, we have also received this sermon on the dedication of a church, attributed to Saint Maximus in a very ancient manuscript of the Basilica of Saint Ambrose in Milan. We place it among the spurious works, because, according to the canon Casola, as the same Frisi reports, it should rather be attributed to the venerable Bede than to Maximus, and its diction differs from that of Maximus.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0907C] We ourselves are called, and are, the temple of God. Let us seek God in goodness and simplicity of heart. Christ is consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit. The perfidy of the heretics, especially of Arius and Sabellius. The Encaenia concern the final dedication of the temple; these things were done as a figure of us and were certainly written on our account.

We have heard from the Gospel reading (John 10), dearest brothers, that the Dedication took place in Jerusalem. The Dedication, moreover, was what the solemn celebrations of the temple’s dedication were called—celebrations which the people of God, following the ancient tradition of the fathers, were accustomed to observe every year. Following their traces today according to the custom of the Christian world, we too have taken care to celebrate solemnly, with divine praises and vigils, the annual day of the dedication of our church. We ought to celebrate this festival with all the greater devotion because we have learned that it is especially pleasing to our Redeemer. And so, on that occasion, he himself deigned to enter the temple, address the people, and disclose the mysteries of his divinity:

“Now the Dedication took place in Jerusalem, and it was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s portico” (ibid.).

If, then, he wished to walk in the place where the flesh and blood of brute animals were offered, how much more gladly will he visit our house of prayer, where the mysteries of his own flesh and blood are celebrated? If he did not disdain to walk in the portico where a formerly mortal and earthly king—although exceedingly powerful and wise—used to stand in prayer, how much more does he desire to visit and enlighten the inward places of our hearts, provided that he perceives them to be Solomon’s portico—that is, provided that he sees them possessing his fear, which is the beginning of wisdom.

Nor should we think that only the house in which we gather for prayer or to celebrate the sacred ministries is the Lord’s temple. We ourselves, who gather in the Lord’s name, are much more called his temple and truly are his temple, since the Apostle plainly says: “For you are the temple of the living God, as God says” (2 Corinthians 6): “I will dwell in them, and I will walk among them” (Leviticus 26).

If, therefore, we are God’s temple, let us be diligent and strive through good actions so that he himself may more often deign both to come and to make his dwelling in his temple. Let us beware of winter’s example, lest, when the Lord comes, he find our hearts numb with respect to the warmth of charity and therefore, offended, quickly leave them. For why did the evangelist consider it relevant to mention that it was winter, unless he wished by the harshness of the winter winds to signify the hardness of the Jews’ unbelief? And because the saying that he spoke suited many of those whom he then found in the temple: “Because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24).

As he subsequently declares openly, saying: “Then the Jews surrounded him and said to him: How long will you keep our souls in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10). They did not say this while seeking the truth of faith, but while plotting against the one whom they questioned and constructing an accusation. For orthodox faith confesses Christ to be true God and true man, whereas they believed that he would be merely a man, and not also God.

They remembered that the Lord had sworn to David concerning Christ’s humanity that he would sit upon his throne, from the fruit of David’s womb (Psalm 131); but they had forgotten what he himself had sung through that same David concerning Christ’s divinity: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son” (Psalm 27). Thus they believed that Christ would be born from David’s line and would come as a king superior to all others. In such madness their descendants likewise continue to err even to the present day, until they receive the Antichrist in place of Christ.

Even if the Lord Jesus had answered that he was the Christ, they were thinking of handing him over to the governor’s power for punishment, as though, resisting Augustus, he were unlawfully claiming an empire for himself.
