But he, concerned for our salvation—for whose sake these things were to be written—tempered his answer in such a way that he both closed the mouths of his accusers and proceeded openly as Christ before the faithful. They were asking about Christ as man; he, however, was openly recounting the mysteries of his divinity, which is equal to the Father.

Let us therefore surround him too, dearest brothers—not by attacking him with the plots of the Jews, but by repairing in ourselves a peaceful dwelling for him as his most faithful household. Of us it may rightly be said: “The Most High has sanctified his tabernacle; God is in its midst; it shall not be shaken” (Psalm 45). Let us ask him, not in our madness, “How long will you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” For what could be more insane than that they should complain that the teacher of truth was keeping their soul in suspense because he had not openly disclosed the secrets of his majesty to them in their unbelief and opposition?

Rather, as Scripture admonishes (Wisdom 1 and following), let us think of him in goodness and seek him in simplicity of heart. “For he is found by those who do not put him to the test; and he appears to those who have faith in him.” Let us say to him in supplication: “You are Christ, the only-begotten Son of God; in your divinity you are both coeternal and consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit. We have come to know that in time you became a participant in our substance. Grant that what we now venerate in devout faith we may contemplate fully in the vision to come.”

For this is the one salvation and life of our soul: to behold your face and to see your light perpetually. Nor should we doubt that he hears us when we pray for what he himself commanded us to ask. For how could he be thought to deny his servants, when they humbly entreat him, gifts that he did not refuse to disclose even beyond what his rebellious people requested?

When they asked him whether Christ was a man, he did not keep silent about his being not merely a man but also God, Christ, and the Son of God. For he answered them, saying: “I speak to you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name, these bear witness about me. But you do not believe, because you are not among my sheep” (John 10).

Therefore, when he testifies that he does his works in the Father’s name, he certainly indicates that he is to be believed to be the Son of God. But they are held guilty of a double offense: they could be brought to faith neither by the words he spoke nor by the deeds through which he established the truth of his words. And rightly they are said not to be among his sheep, since they did not follow the shepherd who was good with the simplicity of sheep, but rather strove to persecute him with the savage fury of beasts.

Yet because there are some who observe the faith in words alone and conceal bestial hearts beneath the appearance of sheep, the shepherd himself next teaches what the life of his sheep is and what their reward will be:

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish” (John 10).

Whoever desires to avoid eternal destruction and see perpetual life must follow Christ’s voice—not merely by hearing and believing, but also by living well. When he says that he knows his sheep, this signifies that he chooses them and predestines them for the heavenly kingdom. Hence Solomon says: “For the Lord knows the paths that are on the right” (Proverbs 4). Conversely, concerning the reprobate the Apostle says: “Whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14).

Beautifully, concerning those who hear his voice and follow him, he says: “And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish” (John 10). The martyrs appeared to the eyes of the foolish to die. They appeared to perish when, overcome by various kinds of punishment, they surrendered mortal life. But they shall not perish forever. They shall not see death forever—once released from the prison of the flesh, they immediately receive the rewards due to their struggle.

The text further adds openly: “No one shall snatch them from my hand” (ibid.). Impious persecutors tried to snatch Christ’s faithful confessors from his hand when they either compelled them through tortures to deny the faith, thereby making their souls alien to Christ, or, defeated by those who were dying, nevertheless cast their lifeless bodies into the waters to be dissolved or into the fire to be burned, as though they could deprive Christ of the power to raise them again.

But no one snatches them from the hand of him of whom, as he says elsewhere, “all things have been handed over by my Father” (Luke 10). For he helps those who are struggling to conquer, crowns the victorious so that they may reign forever, and in due time will restore to them immortal the flesh in which they struggled.

By these words he also rebukes the recklessness of those who prepared the snares of death for themselves, clearly showing how foolishly they acted through schemes against the destruction of one who could give immortal life—one from whose hand no one could snatch anything belonging to those whom he foreknew as his own before the ages.

But lest he seem by speaking in this way to be seeking his own glory, he refers all his power to the glory of the Father, when he adds: “My Father, what he gave me, is greater than all” (John 10). What the Father gave to the mediator between God and humanity, the man Jesus Christ, is greater than all: namely, that he should be his only-begotten Son, in no respect unlike his begetter in nature, inferior in power, or later in time. This equality, which the Lord himself possessed in divinity with the Father before the world existed, he received in his humanity from the time of his incarnation.

“And no one can snatch [them] from my Father’s hand.” Above, concerning his sheep, he says: “No one shall snatch them from my hand”; now he adds: “No one can snatch anything from my Father’s hand.” He plainly gives us to understand that his hand and the Father’s are one and indistinguishable—that is, that his power and the Father’s are one. For this reason Christ is to be believed to be not like the others, sanctified by grace in time, but eternally the true Son of God.

He makes this even clearer in the following statement: “I and the Father are one” (ibid.). “We are one,” he says. We have one substance, one divinity, one eternity, perfect equality, and no dissimilarity.

By these words he not only explained the Jews’ present question—whether he was the Christ—but also showed how greatly the perfidy of the heretics that he foresaw would arise must be detested.

Only Arius says: “Christ is merely man; he is not God.” But when Christ himself says, “I and the Father are one,” it is manifest that a mere man cannot be substantially one with God the Father. And because Christ is what the Father is, the heresy of Photinus must be avoided, for it forbids this belief.

Arius also says: “Christ was made by God; he was not born from God, and therefore must be believed to be less than the Father.” But Christ himself contradicts him: “I and the Father are one.” Who could fail to see that no creature can naturally be one with him who created all things? Since Christ is naturally one with the Father, Arius’s perfidy—which asserts that he is a creature—must be condemned.

Sabellius, moreover, says: “The Father and the Son must not be confessed as two persons. The Father himself is Father when he wishes, and Son when he wishes; nevertheless he is one.” Christ himself condemns this view in the statement just mentioned. For it is clear that “I and the Father” could not be said of one person, nor is “we are” appropriate to one.

Therefore, casting aside the error of Sabellius along with the others, we must follow the apostolic faith of blessed Peter, who confessed the Lord and said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16).

We have now briefly passed through the Gospel reading in explanation, insofar as the Lord granted us to do so. But it is fitting to speak more fully to your fraternity about the solemnity of the Dedication, which the people of Jerusalem celebrated then and which we celebrate today.

First of all, it must be noted that the Dedication which we have learned from the Gospel reading took place not at the temple’s first dedication but at its final one. This is easily inferred from the fact that it is reported to have occurred in winter. The temple’s first dedication was carried out by Solomon in autumn; the middle one by Zerubbabel and Jesus the priest in spring; and the final one by Judas Maccabaeus in winter. At that time, it is recorded, a special decree was established that the same dedication should be recalled every year through solemn observances. We have just heard, when the Gospel was read, that this practice was observed up to the time of the Lord’s incarnation.

This was the reason for the second and third dedications. Solomon completed the temple that he built for the Lord in seven years. In the eighth year, on the tenth day of the seventh month—which we call October—he dedicated it with great glory. That day had already been established by the Law as a solemn day, so that every year the entire tabernacle was to be purified with greater sacrifices.

Finally, Zechariah, the father of blessed John the Baptist, serving at the altar with these same rites of purification, was instructed by the angel concerning the Lord’s birth and the joy of human salvation.

But after four hundred and thirty years the Chaldeans burned this temple, and, after destroying the city of Jerusalem, led the people of Israel captive into Babylonia. After seventy years, when the Persians were ruling, the people were sent back to their homeland, and the temple was rebuilt over forty-six years. On the third day of the twelfth month, which we call March, the work was brought to completion.

The leaders of the people then in charge of the work were, as we have said, the most vigorous: Zerubbabel, of royal blood, and Jesus the high priest; and also the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, who assisted them and strengthened the people’s courage against the plots of the enemies who were hindering the work.

Then, about three hundred and fifty-six years later, the most wicked Antiochus of the Greeks, having seized Jerusalem through deceit, profaned the same temple with the filth of idols. He removed and smashed the Lord’s golden altar, the table of the Presence, the lampstand of light, and the other golden vessels of the temple that he could find. He also set up an image of Jupiter in the temple and compelled the people through tortures to sacrifice to idols.

In that persecution many of the people were slaughtered for guarding the divine Law. Among them was that mother of seven sons, deservedly famous, who with her offspring earned a martyr’s crown for the Lord, nobly enduring for him.

But Judas Maccabaeus, being of priestly descent, gathered an army of righteous men, took up arms against Antiochus’s commanders, and drove them from Judaea, bringing the most savage persecution to an end. He cleansed the temple of the idols’ images, made new altars and the other vessels and furnishings, restored them to the temple, and dedicated them together with the temple, which he had purified and renewed, on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, which we call December. It is clearly beyond doubt that this falls in winter.

As we have said, he established a decree that every year the day of the Dedication should be celebrated with festive devotion as the commemoration of the temple’s renewal and dedication.

All these things, as the Apostle teaches (1 Corinthians 10), were done as a figure of us and were certainly written for our sake. Therefore, we must examine them more diligently in a spiritual manner.

King Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” typologically designates our Redeemer himself. Isaiah says of him (chapter 9): “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of his peace.” The temple that Solomon built is his Catholic Church, which he gathers from believers throughout the world, as though from living stones, into one structure of faith and charity.

The fact that the temple was built over seven years signifies that throughout the entire span of this age—which unfolds through seven days—the holy structure of the Church never ceases to grow.

The fact that the temple was dedicated in the eighth year, and that Solomon the king, with the children of Israel, displayed that famous and greatest solemnity when the period of dedication had been completed, mystically indicates that, when the number of the elect has been completed at the end of the world, the festival of the long-desired immortality will follow. Once the miracle of the universal resurrection has been accomplished, all who belong to the kingdom of the peaceful king—that is, of the true Solomon—will immediately enter with him into the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland.

Because our Lord wished to rise from the dead on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day of the week—the number eight rightly signifies the future festival of our resurrection as well.

The temple, burned by enemies and restored again through the Lord’s mercy, and the temple, defiled by idolatries and cleansed anew through the aid of heavenly mercy, signify the various events of the holy Church. At one time it is oppressed by the persecution of unbelievers; at another, freed from persecutions, it serves the Lord in tranquil obedience. At present, the ancient enemy endangers some of its members through his plots; those whom he seemed for a time to have destroyed, once chastened through repentance, the Church has received again.

The fact that the temple was built a second time over forty-six years refers specifically to the signification of the Lord’s body, which he assumed from the Virgin. Concerning this he said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2). For after his body had been destroyed in the Passion, he himself raised it to life on the third day.

Indeed, those who report it say that the human body is formed in the differentiation of its members on the forty-sixth day after the beginning of conception. Therefore it did not happen by chance, but was arranged by divine providence, that the temple should be built in that number of years in which the Lord’s body—which the temple prefigured—had to be perfected in the Virgin’s womb according to that number of days.

The fact that it was decreed that the Dedication should be celebrated every year certainly admonishes us always to retain in our minds the memory of the Lord’s Resurrection, which we believe has already occurred, and of our own resurrection, which we hope is still to come. We must live in such a way that we may deserve to rise not for judgment but, as the Lord promised those who have done good, for life.

Nor should we pass over without examination the fact that, when Solomon dedicated the temple and had completed his prayers, fire came down from heaven and devoured the burnt offerings and sacrifices.

We are the burnt offerings and sacrifices of the true Solomon; all his elect are the burnt offerings and sacrifices of the supreme King. Concerning them the Apostle Peter says: “Christ also died once for our sins, the just for the unjust, that he might offer us to God; put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit” (1 Peter 3).

The heavenly fire is the fervor by which the citizens of the heavenly homeland rejoice in burning always with love—in their mutual blessedness and in the splendor of their Creator as they behold him. Hence certain ranks of the heavenly powers, which burn with incomparable love because of their singular closeness to their Creator, are called by the special name Seraphim, that is, “burning ones” or “those who set aflame.”

When, therefore, the temple’s dedication has been completed, fire descending from heaven devours the sacrifices offered to the Lord. So, when the time of our resurrection has been fulfilled, and faithful servants aflame with true love have entered into the joy of their Lord—the love with which the angelic powers are now inflamed—their minds too will be absorbed by the sight of their Redeemer.

Even now, there is no doubt that many of the elect in the heavenly city have been wholly absorbed by the face of love. But then this will be fulfilled much more perfectly, when they have received back their immortal flesh, and when all their servants and brothers have been received into the same blessedness—those whom we still see struggling on earth. They will no longer have any reason to direct the gaze of their thoughts outward, even for a moment, since they will have God within them, rejoicing in his eternal vision, and their neighbors with them, eternally rejoicing in their happiness. There the Lord’s first and greatest commandment will be fulfilled completely:

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22).

For the more closely they behold the present face of God, the more ardently they devote themselves wholly to love; and the more they recognize that all their neighbors are elect and beloved by God, and perceive that their hearts are filled with sincere love no less than their own, the more they delight in loving them no less than themselves.

It must also be noted how Scripture concluded the dedication and the festival that followed. [Note: The Vulgate has: “Therefore, on the twenty-third day of the seventh month, he dismissed the people to their tents, rejoicing and exulting over the good that the Lord had done for David, and for Solomon, and for Israel his people.”]

“And Solomon dismissed the people, and they departed to their tents, blessing the king, rejoicing and cheerful in heart over all the good things that the Lord had done for David his servant and for Israel his people” (2 Chronicles 7).

After the gift of the resurrection has been completed, the Lord will dismiss his elect, rejoicing, into eternal tabernacles—not removing them any further from his presence, but admitting them from the peril of judgment, which, as the Apostle teaches, we know will take place in the air, into the habitation of the heavenly homeland. There each will receive, according to his merits, the promised seat of the kingdom.

The fact that the people are said here to have departed to their tents is certainly what the Lord says in the Gospel: “There are many dwelling places in my Father’s house” (John 14).

It is rightly said that they departed to their tents while blessing the king, because this is surely the sole, most peaceful, and happiest activity of the citizens above: to sing hymns of thanksgiving to their Creator. Hence it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83).

For this reason the same prophet completed the final seven psalms of the Psalter with praises of divine sweetness. Before the end of the Psalter, he completed the eighth psalm by blessing God for the victory of the battle in which he had struck down the giant. There he plainly indicates that all who here overcome the contests of the evil enemy will there, in true rest, sing the praises of their Redeemer and Helper.

“They departed,” he says, “blessing the king, to their tents, rejoicing and cheerful in heart over all the good things that the Lord had done for David his servant and for Israel his people.”

The righteous, rejoicing over the blessings they receive from the Lord, enter the tents of the heavenly dwelling places. For however severe the burdens and long the labors of this age may have been, everything that ends in eternal blessedness naturally appears brief and light.

Therefore, dearest brothers, each of us ought to strive as much as he can in building the house of God: exhorting, entreating, rebuking, and laboring himself through pious actions. Let him do so lest, if the heavenly King now sees anyone idle in the work of his temple, he make that person shareless in the time of the dedication of his great solemnity.

Let us strive through mutual assistance in charity, so that Jesus Christ our Lord may bring us all, cheerful in heart and tireless in the works that he has commanded, into the presence of his eternal vision. He lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

SERMON XXXI. On the octave of Saint Stephen. Gospel according to Matthew, chapter 17: At that time, when the Lord Jesus came to Capernaum, those who received the didrachma approached Peter and said to him: Does your master not pay the didrachma? And the rest.

[Col. 0913]

ADMONITION.

Since the style of this sermon too appears to us very unlike that of Maximus, we relegate it to the spurious works, although Frisius found it similarly adorned with the name of St Maximus in the Milanese manuscript, of which we made laudatory mention in the preceding admonition.

ARGUMENT.—[Col. 0913B] After the Gospel reading has been explained literally and mystically, the author of the sermon says: “This fish, which first rose to Peter’s hook, can fittingly signify Stephen, the first martyr.”

For in the time of Augustus Caesar Judaea became tributary, and at his command every person declared his tax assessment in his own district and city. Hence Joseph, ascending with blessed Mary from Galilee to Bethlehem, a city of Judaea, in order to declare the tax assessment there, because he was of the house and family of David. But because the Lord had been brought up in Nazareth, which is a town of Galilee subject to the city of Capernaum, the tax was demanded from him; for all newcomers who came there declared their tax assessment.

And because they did not dare to approach the Lord because of the greatness of his miracles, they approached his disciple Peter indirectly and asked whether his master paid the didrachma. They asked either with a straightforward intention, in order to receive the tax, or indeed maliciously, in order to discover whether he would pay the tax or resist Caesar’s will, so that they might find an occasion to accuse him.

And because the tax collectors had approached Peter apart from the others, when the Lord came into the house, before Peter could mention anything to him, he anticipated him. Thus, when the holy apostles recognized that he understood the things that had happened in his absence, they would not be scandalized by the demand for the tax. For he said: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax? From their sons or from strangers?” And he said: “From strangers” (Matthew 17).

For the Lord according to the flesh was a king’s son. He was a king’s son according to the flesh because he had been begotten from David’s line; according to the Spirit, because he was the Word of God the almighty Father. Therefore, because a king’s son ought not to pay tribute to anyone. But because he assumed the flesh of our lowliness, he therefore paid tribute.

But we wretched and unhappy people render nothing worthy of so great a majesty. For he paid the tax for us and underwent the cross. Yet we too do not pay tribute, and, as though not paying tribute, we are like sons of a king exempt from taxes. Therefore we ought always to strive to render him the tax of good works.

He said to him: “Then the sons are free” (Matthew 17). For if in every kingdom and nation the king’s sons are free and exempt from taxes, how much more is that Son of the eternal King, under whom all the kingdoms of the earth are established?

It follows: “But lest we scandalize them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. When you open its mouth, you will find a stater; take it and give it to them for me and for yourself” (ibid.). Blessed Jerome says: “What should I first admire in this passage? I do not know—either the Lord’s foreknowledge or his power. His foreknowledge is admirable, since he knew what was happening in the depths of the sea, what the fish carried in its mouth, and which one from so great a multitude would first rise to the hook. His greatness and power are likewise admirable, if at his command a stater was immediately created in the fish’s mouth; for by his word alone he brought about what was to happen. For by these signs he is shown to be he of whom the prophet says: ‘His eyes behold the depths of the abyss’ (Daniel 3).”

But the Jews’ unbelief is greatly to be wondered at, because, though they were rational human beings, what was found in the fish’s mouth was not found in theirs: namely, the stater of fairness and justice. For if this passage is understood simply, it edifies the hearer; for these words show that the Lord was so poor that he did not have anything with which to pay for himself and his disciple. In this action he taught that poverty should be pursued.

But perhaps someone objects: “Why then did Judas carry money in the bag?” The brief answer is this: the Lord considered it wicked to divert the property of the poor to the use of himself and his disciples. In this action too he left us an example, that what we have once vowed to God or to the poor we must by no means divert to common uses.

Allegorically, the sea signifies this present age, according to: “This sea, great and wide” (Psalm 103); and again: “I have come into the depths of the sea” (Psalm 68). Capernaum, however, signifies the Synagogue; the tax collectors, the scribes and Pharisees. The hook signifies the preaching of Peter and the others. By the fish that first rose to Peter’s hook, Cornelius may fittingly be understood, since he was the first of the Gentiles to believe through Peter’s preaching. By the stater, which [represents] two didrachmas, [there is a lacuna in the text] the teaching of the two Testaments.

For when the Jews wished to bind the Lord (Acts 10) under legal bonds, saying that it was not lawful to heal on the sabbath, and to condemn him to death as a criminal, what else were they doing but demanding the tax of our redemption? But while they demanded it, the Lord commanded Peter, who is the teacher of all preachers, to cast the hook of holy preaching into the sea of the Gentiles. When he cast it, Cornelius, the first fish, rose to his hook, carrying a stater in his mouth, though it was hidden: namely, the confession of true faith and the work of the two Testaments. Of him it is written: “He was a just and good man, fearing God and giving many alms to the people” (Acts 10), etc.

When blessed Peter came and preached, he made manifest the stater that had been hidden, because Cornelius confessed Christ the Son of God and was reborn in the water of holy baptism. Moreover, in saying, “Take it and give it to them for me and for yourself” (Matthew 17), he shows that through Peter and his successors the teaching of the two Testaments was to be made known to Jews and Gentiles. Thus, “Take it and give it to them for me and for yourself” must be understood: for me as lord, for you as servant; for me as author, for you as minister of salvation.

Alternatively, this fish, which first rose to Peter’s hook, can fittingly signify Stephen, the first martyr. He carried in his mouth the stater: the confession of true faith and the teaching of the two Testaments. For, standing in the council, he confessed the Father and the Son, saying: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God” (Acts 7). Also, standing in the council, he interpreted the Law of the Old Testament in the Son of God. Thus, when Peter preached, Stephen swallowed the first hook, because he was the first to attain the palm of martyrdom.

[Col. 0915]

[HOMILIES. (C, S)*]

FIRST HOMILY. Third Sunday of Advent: Gospel according to Matthew, chapter 11: At that time, when John in prison heard of Christ’s works, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: “Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?” And the remainder of the same reading, by blessed Bishop Maximus.

ADMONITION.

[Col. 0915]

A paper manuscript of the Chigi Library, shelf-mark A VI 181, sixteenth century, small folio, written in very neat characters but corrupt in quite a few places, provided us with three homilies, which we have placed at the end of this appendix. Anyone who considers their style will readily recognize that Maximus is not their author.

ARGUMENT.—[Col. 0915B] The words of the Gospel are expounded literally and allegorically.

Saint John the Baptist, the forerunner of the Lord and Savior, was imprisoned by Herod because of the truth [Col. 0915C]. When he heard of Christ’s works and miracles, as the Gospel reading makes clear, he sent two of his disciples to Christ. They questioned their master because they still doubted in faith, so that, seeing the signs the Lord performed, those disciples might believe both their master’s prophecy and Christ’s teaching. Blessed John said to them: “Go, tell him: ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’”

This should be understood as what Saint John sent to Christ, saying: “I know that you were born for everyone, but I do not know whether you will deign to die for everyone. For, so that I may know—when I am killed by Herod and descend to the underworld—whether I should announce to the dead in the underworld that you are coming for their redemption, just as I announced your coming to the living, and whether you have determined to send [me] to complete these mysteries.””

Our Lord answered what he had been asked, but rebuked the messengers’ faithlessness, saying: “Go and report to John what you have heard and seen: the blind see, the lame walk, [Col. 0915D] lepers are cleansed, and blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me.” By saying this, he meant: “You see me performing such great miracles; nevertheless, understand this: I am dying for everyone. But blessed will be the one who is not scandalized by me—that is, who does not believe, when he sees me dead, that I am merely and purely human.”

What the Lord says—“the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed”—should be understood spiritually in this way. Certainly, before Christ’s coming all human beings were blind and were in darkness, since they did not see the light of truth. They were lame because they ran after the devil every day. They were lepers because they were filled with various filthinesses of sins. They were deaf because they did not have open ears for hearing the word of God. They were dead because they always lay in many sins and vices. They were poor because they were strangers to good works.

But after the Lord, in his mercy, deigned to come into this world, he illuminated all who were blind. He made the lame walk, because he commanded all the elect [Col. 0916B] to follow his footsteps. He cleansed the lepers, because he purged the human race from many evils. He made the deaf hear, because he opened human ears to hear the word of God. He raised the dead, because he brought sinners, who lay in their sins, to true repentance. He preached the Gospel to the poor, because he taught the doctrine of life to those who were strangers to true repentance.

They were dead in their sins.

When they had departed, Jesus began to say to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” A reed is a cane, and it has three characteristics. First, it grows in green or watery places. Second, it bends in another direction whenever it is touched by any breeze. Third, it is beautiful on the outside but hollow within. By the reed is signified the carnal mind, which rejoices excessively when it has prosperity and is excessively saddened when it has adversity—like a cane that bends in whatever direction under any breeze.

But Saint John was not like this, because he was born of chaste parents, loved chastity, and preserved it; and the holiness that he displayed in his clothing he possessed in his heart. He did not delight in prosperity or praise, nor did he fear adversity. In praising him the Lord continues to say [Col. 0916D]: “What did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses.”

Saint John was not dressed in delicate garments, but his garments were made from camel’s hair. For a rough haircloth is made from camel’s hair. Certainly, brothers, if it were not sinful to have delicate garments, the Lord would not have praised John for the roughness of his clothing. Those who have delicate garments serve an earthly king. They do not wish to endure hardship for God, but instead pursue the riches and pleasures of the world; and for love of praise, or through fear of persecution, they chastise sinners in order to acquire good things from this world.

“But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.” It is the prophet’s office to preach what is to come, but not also to point it out with his finger. John, however, was more than a prophet, because he pointed out with his finger the one whom he had foretold, coming to baptism, saying (John I): “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

After the Lord had shown that Saint John was more than a prophet [Col. 0917A], he added, saying: “For this is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you’” (Mark I).

For “angel” is Greek; in Latin it is called *nuntius*, “messenger.” Properly, the one sent to announce the heavenly Judge is called an angel. All who preach Christ and announce the word of God, or who are designated by the name of priest, can be called angels, as the prophet Malachi says (chapter II): “The lips of priests guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.”

Nevertheless, dearly beloved brothers, if you wish—and if you are able—to merit the dignity of this name, each one of you, insofar as he has received so great a grace of divine providence, has certainly become an angel if he first turns someone back from wickedness; if he urges his brother, as far as he is able, to do good works; and if he announces to one who is wandering either the eternal kingdom or eternal punishment.

Therefore, my brothers, if you are hastening toward God, see to it that you do not come to him alone. Awaken your neighbors along with yourselves to eternal joys, and turn idle conversations toward the study of reading. Consider how quickly the days of this life flee, and observe how sternly the Judge who will judge the whole world is coming. Certainly, if you announce the Lord according to your abilities, by words and good works, you will receive eternal joy with the holy angels—which may he himself deign to grant.

## HOMILY II

On the Gospel of Saint John, chapter II: “At that time a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee.”

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0917A] Why did Christ the Savior come to a wedding? [Col. 0917B] Concerning the miracle performed by him of changing water into wine, and concerning the spiritual meaning of the six water-jars.

Whenever, dearly beloved brothers, we read that our Redeemer came to a wedding, we must not suppose that he did so for the pleasure of the appetite, as the scribes and Pharisees did, who said that he was a glutton and a friend of tax collectors. Rather, we must believe that he came for the purpose of winning souls.

Just as a learned fisherman and a wise hunter casts his nets in a place where he knows that many fish, birds, or animals will come, so that he may catch some of them when many have gathered, so the Lord wished to come to a banquet or wedding where many were assembling, in order to catch some of them through the word of his preaching.

In the spiritual sense, when the Lord came into the world, the wine failed, because the Jews had lost the sweetness of the law that they had previously possessed.

Jesus says to her: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come” [Col. 0917C] (John II). We must not suppose that the Lord dishonored his mother, since he commands that parents be honored. Rather, he says this to her in order to raise her mind toward the power of his divinity.

It is as though the Lord were saying to her: “Woman, what does your humility have in common with a miracle? What you are asking belongs to divine power: works of power and miracles.” My hour has not yet come—that is, the hour of my Passion has not yet come, when I will openly reveal what the humanity that I received from you is capable of.”

That hour was fulfilled when, hanging on the cross, he said: “Woman, behold your son,” as though he were saying: “Behold what I assumed from you: it can suffer and die. The miracle you seek cannot be performed without divinity.”

His mother says to the servants: “Whatever he tells you, do” (ibid.). Holy Mary understood from those words that the Lord was saying that he had not been angered, and therefore she confidently told the servants to carry out her son’s commands.

Now six stone water-jars had been placed there for the purification of the Jews [Col. 0917D], each holding two or three measures. It was the custom of the Jews, and especially of the Pharisees, to have vessels filled with water prepared at banquets and weddings for washing the hands or for anything else that might be necessary.

Jesus says to them: “Fill the water-jars with water.” And they filled them to the top; they were changed into wine. Certainly, dearly beloved faithful, the Lord could have filled the empty water-jars with wine, since he created all things from nothing before they existed. But he first commanded that they be filled with water, and afterward changed it into wine.

This signifies that, when our Lord came to earth, he gave no other law than the one he had given through his servant Moses; rather, he opened the spiritual understanding that had been hidden within that very law.

In the spiritual sense, however, these water-jars signify the hearts of the holy teachers, who possess water within themselves—that is, knowledge of the Scriptures. The fact that they were six and made of stone signifies the hearts of the saints, which are always firm and strong against the temptations [Col. 0918A] of the devil. These six water-jars also signify the six ages [Col. 0918B] of the world.

The first age of the world was from Adam to Noah. The second was from Noah to Abraham. The third was from Abraham to David. The fourth was from David to the Babylonian captivity. The fifth was from the Babylonian captivity to Christ’s coming in the flesh. The sixth age is the one that now continues, from the Lord’s coming to the end of the world.

In all these ages almighty God sent holy men who continually preached the divine utterances.

In the first age of the world we read that God made man from the earth in his image and likeness; and from his side, while he slept, he took one of his ribs and made Eve. After this he placed them in paradise and commanded them to eat from every fruit of paradise, but he commanded them not to touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Later, deceived by the serpent—that is, by the devil—they ate the fruit that had been forbidden to them. Therefore the Lord became angry and cast them out of paradise.

Whoever hears these things and fears to transgress the Lord’s command finds, in the first age, a water-jar full of water. If he finds it, he understands spiritually that through Adam our Lord is signified, for he received flesh from the Virgin; and through Eve he understands the holy Church, which was formed from the Virgin and from the side of Christ hanging on the cross. Immediately the water-jar that had been full of water is changed into wine.

In the second age we read that the Lord commanded Noah to make an ark because of the flood. He intended to send the flood upon the earth because all human beings had abandoned God’s commands and were doing evil. Whoever hears these things and desires to be saved with the few rather than perish with the many finds, in the second age, a water-jar full of water.

If he wishes to understand it spiritually, Noah, who built the ark, signifies our Lord, who was the builder and ruler of the holy Church; and the flood that he intended to send upon the earth to destroy sinful human beings signifies baptism, in which sins are destroyed. Whoever understands these things spiritually in this way has the water-jar that he formerly possessed full of water changed into wine [Col. 0918D].

In the third age we read that he commanded Abraham to leave the land of his kindred and his father’s house; and he came into the land that God would show him. As soon as God commanded him, he did this.

Whoever hears these things and considers in his heart with how much devotion he ought to obey God has, in the third age, a water-jar full of water. If he wishes to understand it spiritually, Abraham signifies God the Father, and the water-jar is changed into wine—the jar that previously had been full of water.

In the fourth age we read that David was king, and that he was humble and merciful, and endured much suffering and tribulation from King Saul. Whoever hears these things and wishes to follow David’s humility finds, in the fourth age, a water-jar full of water.

If he wishes to understand it spiritually, by Saul the Jewish people, who persecuted the Lord, and by David our Lord, who deigned to pray for his persecutors, he has the fourth water-jar changed into wine, though previously it had water [Col. 0919A].

In the fifth age we read that the Jewish people transgressed God’s command, and for this reason the Lord delivered them into the hand of the king of Babylon, who led them captive to Babylon and destroyed the city of Jerusalem. Whoever hears these things and fears to sin against the Lord, lest weakness or some tribulation come upon him, finds, in the fifth age, a water-jar full of water.

If he wishes to understand it spiritually, the Israelite people signify the human race; Babylon signifies hell; and the king of Babylon signifies the devil, who always desires to drag the human race into hell. Whoever understands it in this way has his water-jar changed into wine—the jar that he had possessed full of water.

In the sixth age we read that our Redeemer deigned to become human for everyone; on the eighth day he was circumcised, and on the thirty-third day he was presented in the Temple. Whoever hears these things and considers in his heart with how much devotion he ought to observe God’s commands finds, in the sixth age, a water-jar full of water.

If he wishes to understand it spiritually—that we cannot enter the kingdom of God unless, in this present life, we have been purified through confession and almsgiving—he has a water-jar changed into good wine.

Each of these six water-jars held two or three measures—that is, two or three units of measure.

The servants who filled the water-jars signify the holy apostles and teachers of the Church, who preach God’s commands. Of them it is rightly said: “And they filled them to the top” [Col. 0920A]. Certainly, from the beginning of the world there was never a time when there was not someone faithful to God who daily made him known through teaching, good example, or preaching.

And Jesus says to them: “Draw some out now and take it to the master of the feast”; and they took it (John II). The master of the feast is the steward of the household, and he signified the teachers of the holy Church, who knew how to distinguish between the Old and New Testaments and between good and evil.

The master of the feast calls the bridegroom and says to him: “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when they have become drunk, then the inferior wine” (ibid.). Many say that this bridegroom was Saint John the Evangelist, who, because of the miracle he saw, left the wedding and followed the Lord.

“This was the beginning of signs that Jesus performed in Cana of Galilee. He revealed his glory, and his disciples believed in him.” Before this miracle took place, the disciples of our Redeemer believed that he was merely and purely human; but after they saw it, they believed with great confidence [Col. 0920B] that he was true God and true man.

And let us, dearly beloved brothers, believe in his works at all times, carry out his commands, and always announce his teaching to others, so that in the future we may rejoice with him. Through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

## HOMILY III

On the Gospel according to Matthew, chapter II: “At that time, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream,” and so forth.

[Col. 0920]

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0919B] Concerning Joseph’s withdrawal with Mary and the child Jesus into Egypt, and concerning the reason why Herod delayed the killing of the children of Bethlehem.

This holy [Note: [Col. 0919D] Read “Matthew.”] evangelist John, dearly beloved brothers, reveals to us the schemes of Herod, who had promised that he would come and worship the Lord. But this promise did not proceed from a good heart, as though he wished to worship the Lord. He made the promise because he wanted to kill him, just as he killed many children.

But the angel of the Lord, who is a minister in heaven, seeing Herod’s schemes, appeared to Joseph in a dream and warned him to take the child and his mother and flee into Egypt, lest Herod be able to carry out his fury against the Lord, as he had done against the children.

Saint Joseph, the Lord’s bearer and foster father, guardian of chastity, immediately upon being warned by the angel rose with great diligence and concern and fulfilled God’s commands. The evangelist makes this clear when he says: “He rose, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew into Egypt; and he remained there until Herod’s death.”

Here, dearly beloved brothers, we can understand that Joseph himself was holy and good, because he did not fear the darkness of night; he did not wait for daylight, nor did he turn aside in another direction through distrust of any faithless people. That very night he rose, took the child and his mother, and went [Col. 0919D] into Egypt; and he remained there until Herod’s death.

Then Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the Magi, became very angry, and sent men to kill many children who were in Bethlehem and throughout all its territory, from two years old and under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the Magi (Matthew II).

After Herod saw that his schemes had accomplished nothing, he became very angry and ordered that all the children who were in Bethlehem of Judea should be killed. He supposed that, if all the children were killed, the one he was seeking could not escape.

That wretched man did not consider that “there is no wisdom, no prudence, and no counsel against the Lord.” When Herod himself ordered all the children to be killed, he commanded that all children who were two years old—and even children only one night old—should be killed [Col. 0920B].

He carried out this massacre two years after Christ’s birth, because ecclesiastical history relates that at that time Herod himself, who had heard from the Magi that the King of the Jews had been born, received a summons from the emperor ordering him to go immediately to Rome. For he had been accused with great force by his enemies.

Nevertheless, when he had appeared before the emperor and before the entire Roman senate [Col. 0920C], he most honorably and wisely cleared himself of everything that had been said against him. He was indeed highly gifted and eloquent.

After this had been done, he was exalted by the emperor with still greater glory, to such an extent that the emperor gave him a royal crown and granted him the power to rule in Judea. When he had returned to Judea in great glory after two years, he suddenly recalled what he had heard from the Magi—that the King of the Jews had been born—and sent men to kill all the children who were in Bethlehem.

Then what had been spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled: [Note: [Col. 0919D] The Gospel supplies what is lacking: “Then what had been spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled, saying” [Col. 0920D]: “A voice was heard in Rama, weeping and much wailing. Rachel weeping for her children, and she learns, [Note: [Col. 0920D] The author added this word, which is not found in the Gospel text.] and she did not wish to be comforted, because they are not” (Matthew II).

In this passage Rama is not the name of a city or of any place, but means “on high.” It is as though he were saying: “On high a voice and much wailing were heard,” because Rachel—that is, the holy Church—mourns her children. That is, the holy Church groans over the persecution of the faithful and does not wish to accept that consolation, so that those who have been crowned through martyrdom and reign with Christ might return again to fight the battles of the world.

Someone may also understand it another way: the holy Church daily mourns over those whom it cannot recall to repentance.

But we, dearly beloved, insofar as God has granted us the ability, should maintain an innocent life. Even if we cannot be martyrs in the body, let us follow the martyrs in mind. Certainly, if we abstain from evil desires and wicked thoughts, and if we do what is right, we can belong to the number of those who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. May he grant this to us, he who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

[Col. 0921]

## LETTERS

### LETTER I. FIRST LETTER

To a sick friend [Note: [Col. 0921C] In the Laurentian manuscript the following title is prefixed to the letter: “Jerome’s consolatory letter to a sick friend, in the form and manner of a dialogue.”]

### FIRST NOTICE OF DOMINICUS VALLARSIUS IN VOLUME XI OF THE WORKS OF SAINT JEROME

[Col. 0921]

109 This seemed, long ago, to Erasmus not unlike the style of Tertullian, insofar as, Vallarsius says, one may discern from its fragments. For it is rather affected and somewhat harsh, although it contains weighty thoughts.

Others perhaps think—and with even greater conformity to the wording of the letter that follows, which no one now denies to be by Saint Maximus of Turin—that it approaches that letter so closely that it should nevertheless not be assigned to him with certainty.

For my part, although I would not yet dare to give a definite judgment on this matter, I nevertheless think that the person who wrote this was acting the part of a bishop, since at the very beginning he says that he is “occupied by the religious obligation of the Lord’s affairs.”

### SECOND NOTICE

Among the spurious works of Saint Maximus we also place the letters once attributed to the holy Jerome and published under his name—two letters in all. In the preface, compare the weight of the arguments that drove us to this judgment against the opinion of Vallarsius and others.

Nothing remains for us to add except that we have taken the variants from Codex X of Pluteus XIX, membranaceous, in folio, fifteenth century, page 265, of the Laurentian Medicean Library, and from the Roman edition of the Letters of Saint Jerome published by Petrus de Maximo in the year 1468.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0921A]

Although I know with complete certainty that your experience has no need of the relief and support of another’s consolation—for you yourself sustain and treat and set in order the illnesses and hardships of your weakened body, and the numbness of your stiffened limbs, by the happiness of a vigorous and burning spirit, and with medical skill—nevertheless, amid adversity a defense, amid illnesses a remedy, amid cares a consolation, and amid waves the oar of another’s hand is always sought and desired.

For there is no doubt that the fruit of fraternal consolation is part of the greatest remedies: [Note: [Col. 0921C] The same Laurentian manuscript reads: “and the kindling of words that console with the sweetness of their sayings, a relief.” The Roman edition reads: “and the kindling of words that console with the sweetness of consolations, a relief.”] and the kindling of words, [Note: [Col. 0921C] In Vallarsius there was formerly *dulcedine consolationis* (“with the sweetness of consolation”), an expression also used by Saint Cyprian at the end of the first letter to Donatus, by Aulus Gellius in book XIX, chapter 9, and by Boethius in book II of *The Consolation*, as well as by Sidonius in book V, letter 17, and others. Nor, in fact, should that reading have been changed.] with the sweetness of those who console, introduces relief to weary spirits.

And although it does not set a person in order in the bodily limbs, it nevertheless does so in the recesses and hidden places of the spirit through spiritual devotion; it brings health like a physician, and assists the efforts of exhausted strength under the burden of prolonged pressures—especially since it is written: “A brother helping a brother will be exalted” (Proverbs XVIII).

For this reason, since the religious obligation of the Lord’s affairs [Note: [Col. 0921C] The same Laurentian manuscript reads: “so occupies me.”] keeps me so occupied that I have no opportunity, through bodily attendance, to bring light to your hardships, I have decided, as you requested, to relieve such prolonged trials with whatever consolation letters can provide—or rather, to visit you with the benefit of salvation and advance a mind grounded in Christian virtue toward the greatest strength.

We who strive to seize the spoil of the heavenly kingdoms and the reward of everlasting recompense cannot become victors without some struggle. For delicate virtue, ignorant of combat, has never climbed to the palm-bearing summit of victory, nor received a prize for conquered adversities—especially one who judges the life of his body, however worthless, dearer than victory.

Nor is the one for whom life arises from death shaken by fear of death. For him it is precious even to shed blood; it is a source of happiness to fight against unhappiness; it is the highest state of health to endure bitter wounds; he considers even the loss of limbs a great gain.

[Note: [Col. 0921C] The Roman edition reads: “And what is the final point?”]

And I shall say what is the final point: it is glorious for him, in the very struggle, to return his palm-bearing soul to its creditor.

[Note: [Col. 0922C] The manuscript and edition read: “For reason is better concluded in this way: if what is owed to nature is paid by virtue.”]

For it is better, as reason determines, if what is owed to nature is paid to virtue [Col. 0921C].

Therefore, brother, all those things must be endured—must indeed be endured—through which the Lord has wished to test you by prolonged affliction and to appoint you to great rewards.

## CHAPTER II

INFIR. [Note: [Col. 0922C] The same manuscript and edition read: “INFIR. Who, you said, could endure these things now that his strength has been brought low?” and so forth.] What spirit, with its strength now brought low, could endure these inevitable misfortunes, the assaults of destructive calamity, and these hostile illnesses, which, as I see, will soon die together with the body itself?

HIERON. The one whom a storm finds amid the waves must necessarily engage and struggle with dangers. And although no one willingly suffers or endures danger, nevertheless, under the weight of danger and compelled by necessity, he perseveres.

INFIR. But another anxiety has come upon me. With grief doubled, it envelops my senses and imposes on me, through biting cares, cares that cannot be unraveled. For it troubles me that, amid such trials and in the struggle against so obstinate an illness, I alone should have been compelled to fight, when I know that others have been corrected by gentler blows and have emerged victorious after a brief struggle.

Why did the Lord not impose a struggle on me together with the others? Why did he not chastise me as he did the others?

HIERON. First, since you have been placed in so arduous a struggle, you must not think about lesser things. Lesser battles have lesser rewards.

[Note: [Col. 0922C] The manuscript reads: “Where, finally, stronger things are commanded to the strong,” and so forth.]

Where, finally, strong commands are given to the strong, a stronger recompense of reward follows the stronger man; and therefore a strong man considers it disgraceful to be matched with an inferior.

Great is the one who has conquered great things [Col. 0922B]. It is the mark of the greatest devotion to endure the greatest things; it is the mark of immense virtue to overcome immense things.

For the one who has been most severely troubled by the *kaûma* (*cauma*, Greek καῦμα), the heat of battles, and whom conquered adversities have made victorious, excels others in merit before the king.

Finally, the prize appropriate to the quality of the struggle is present within the very conflict, appointed according to the victor’s merit. Kings impose military burdens according to their soldiers’ strength; physicians provide remedies according to the causes of illness. The one who must be cured does not tell the physician by what method he should be treated; nor does the soldier choose where he should be sent; nor does the servant choose by what beating he should be punished.

For what depends upon the judgment of a superior is not in the power of a subordinate. Therefore, since we are ruled by heavenly power and live amid the manifold miseries of the world for the sake of correction, it is not ours to choose either the blows of the Lord’s power or other struggles that we might conquer by enduring them—just as it is not the servants’ place to choose from their masters the kinds of scourges they will receive.

The permission of the one who depends never depends upon the will of the one who strikes. It belongs to authority to correct; it belongs to one’s condition to submit. It belongs to the king to impose the burden, and to the soldier to endure it.

Indeed, since nothing unjust is done by the king himself, when he assigns the sweat of warfare to his legions according to their strength, he sends the strong to strong tasks and commands what is suitable for the weaker, so that neither an inferior is prevented from fighting against a stronger opponent beyond his own strength, nor is the latter humbled by a struggle against an inferior opponent, with his merits impaired.

While this is being done—so that no one may be diminished or certainly defeated in another’s place—he wishes all to be victorious.

[Note: [Col. 0923D] The manuscript reads: “Nor is the physician unjust.”]

Nor is he an enemy, the physician who strikes in order to remove danger and to exclude one wound by means of another. Nor does paternal affection act against a person if it teaches children through embraces of the rod. For a father’s blows are exercises of harmless affection.

Therefore, since correction is the purpose of correcting love, and since it descends from affection, love the striking physician, whose wound is the mother of healing. Affection produces nothing impious, so that, having embraced the virtues, the person spiritually healed may contain within himself the fruit of affection.

“I am the Lord,” he says, “I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deuteronomy XXXII).

## CHAPTER III大小规律
INFIR. But you said: “So piety strikes?”

HIERON. It certainly strikes; otherwise it might be judged impious if it did not correct the delinquent. Since there is something in a person that needs curing, it strikes in order to cure, just as a physician’s hands, [Note: [Col. 0923D] Codex: *quae multam laedendo conferunt sanitatem*—“which, by causing much injury, bring about health.”] while causing much injury, bring about health—not without the patient’s murmuring. In the same way, while we are under the care of the blows of the healer, amid the very constrictions of sorrow, we murmur against the Lord as wounded patients do against a physician: they are being cured, and they suffer. [Col. 0923B]

Take up, then, brother, take up [Note: [Col. 0923D] Codex and edition: *sustinentiae remedium tuum*—“the remedy of endurance that is yours.”] the remedy of endurance, by which you may lighten the burden heavy with trials and overcome dangers by enduring them. Let a steadfast spirit console and heal the limbs that lie prostrate. Let virtue hold the kingdom within the body imprisoned by anxieties, so that the soul enclosed by dangers may remain vigorous through the freedom of virtue itself, [Note: [Col. 0923D] Codex: *quae in conflictum tentationis variae*—“which [is] for the conflict of varied trial.”] which, in the conflict of temptation, was long ago commanded by the legal trumpets to prepare itself in various ways and, at the very trace of the Lord’s service, to arm itself against hostile calamities.

“My son,” he says, “when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for trial” (Ecclesiasticus 2). [Note: [Col. 0923D] Codex: *Ergo cum tentatio mei utilitatibus praerogetur, non est mirandum si nobis ejus ardor accedat*—“Therefore, since trial is prolonged for my benefit, it is not surprising if its heat comes upon us.”]

Therefore, since trial is prolonged for our benefit, it is not surprising if its heat comes upon us. Thus the most blessed Peter warns and says in his letter: “Do not be surprised at the fiery trial that comes upon you, which is taking place for your testing, lest you fall among the various waves of the world” (1 Peter 4). [Col. 0923C]

The Christian life is shaken and tested by frequent storms, and under countless pressures it is nourished and grows. The most blessed and illustrious prophet Solomon bears witness to and proves this: “Join yourself,” he says, “to the Lord and endure, so that your life may increase at the end” (Ecclesiasticus 2).

The voyage of our life rejoices when storms drive it; it is disturbed only by calm. Its course grows numb when the winds cease; it is endangered if it is not tested by dangers. For it is uncertain whether someone belongs to the Lord if pressure, the mother of glory, does not purify him by tossing him about, nourish him by weighing upon him, test him by disciplining him, and heal him by striking him. Since divine love imposes blows and various trials upon us, and, like a physician, provides a remedy from opposites and comes to our aid by torturing us, he does not prove that he belongs to the love of the Lord who has not deserved to submit to medicinal wounds. [Note: [Col. 0924D] Codex: *ad amorem pertinere divinum*—“that he belongs to divine love.”]

But perhaps you say: “If God is my lover, why then do the scourges of my lover sadden me through grievous laceration and trouble me by wounding me? If he who loves me torments me with the embraces of scourges, then false love is already exercising the role of hatred; let him hate me instead, so that he may not torment me.” [Col. 0923D]

Rather, take care that he not hate you; ask that he deign to love you. Love corrects, whereas hatred threatens punishment. Love is accustomed to provide discipline; hatred, once judgment has been pronounced, recounts the offense. This hatred of the human race is propagated from God into humanity. Thus what God hates or becomes angry about belongs to humanity: he hates when he is offended, and he becomes angry when the offended party is not entreated. For a person provokes the Lord to hatred of him when, by hateful deeds, he makes himself hateful and refuses to entreat him when offended. [Col. 0924A]

Nevertheless, God loves the human being as a craftsman loves his work, but he hates the evil deeds by which his work is pressed toward ruin and driven into [Note: [Col. 0924D] Codex and edition: *labinam*—“a collapse.”] collapse. And whoever hates evil deeds cannot love the perpetrator of evil deeds, as the most holy Solomon declared: “The ungodly and his ungodliness,” he says, “are hateful to God” (Wisdom 14).

Therefore, in this world that is perishing as the years decline, whose old age sunset presses down upon and swallows up, it is better to endure medicinal blows out of love for the Lord than, out of hatred, to await an incurable wound and lead a condemnable life under the thunderbolt of judgment. It is better to pass through the hands of a physician and endure brief torment than to reject the physician and incur punishment that will be inflicted by eternal torturers.

Or, if you are still astonished that the medicine of our lover consists in scourges, you ought also to wonder that remedies torment those whom the physician loves—he who, by causing harm, removes what causes harm. Certainly, one who seeks to remove harmful things cannot himself be harmful; and therefore he heals by wounding, so that health prepared through sorrows may be more precious. If medicine did not lacerate the person to be healed, the merit of health would always delight in voluntary wounding. If the care of harmful remedies did not consist in precious aids that bite, the necessity of treatment would not compel the patient into sorrow. Thus healing is accomplished through remedies that cause pain, so that health purchased at the price of sorrow may be held more precious and welcome. [Col. 0924B]

Therefore, the one who is to be loved cannot fail to be reformed by any test; [Note: [Col. 0924D] Codex: *qui corrigendus est, amatoris verbere non potest non probari*—“the one who must be corrected cannot fail to be tested by the lover’s scourge.”] the one who must be corrected cannot fail to be scourged by the lover’s blow; the one who must be healed cannot fail to be wounded by the healer’s painful treatment.

Why are you astonished as though at a miracle? The person whom fire and iron are treating expects help from dangers. For many things are healed only after being struck. There are many whom physicians cannot cure without iron. Physicians, when asked, grant health through various torments and often administer extremely bitter draughts, as the illness requires, for the sake of a remedy to people who do not thirst for them; these are swallowed only with wrinkled brows. For if you observe the drinker’s face, he drinks sadly and anxiously so that he may live happily and in good health. [Col. 0924C]

O rational yet sufficiently inconveniently convenient perversity of medicine! A person is compelled to drink what he does not thirst for, although sometimes what he thirsts for is his remedy. And because physicians sometimes prescribe abstinence from food, they relieve the body by imposing a fast, so that, restored by that very exhaustion, it may be made strong.

They tend, bind, mend, and heal sudden wounds brought into the camp by accident; by making the patient sorrowful they make him joyful, by tiring him they strengthen him, and by wounding him they heal him. For while, by attaching the skin of the surrounding parts to the wound with certain clasps, they insert health into it, they promise life through consolation and restore it through treatment. [Note: [Col. 0924D] Codex: *inferunt sanitatem*—“they confer health.”]

But these things we have mentioned are comparatively mild. Among physicians there is also the remedy of removing weakened decay with a scalpel and cutting dead parts from a living person. Although one limb is amputated not without sensation throughout the body, the person nevertheless consents to his own losses so that he may live. Sometimes the skin is removed and the bones themselves scraped, lest the whole person, perishing, be scraped away. At times a worm-infested and feverish swelling is cut open with medicinal iron. Fire burns in order to cool; powder bites and lacerates in order to heal.

What more need be said? Under medical compassion, a person is tormented greatly so that he may live greatly. Here is a necessary danger in which faithful torment is a benefit. The one whom the physician treats is certainly endangered, but the one who rejects him both perishes and is deceived. To the former, although under torment, life is promised; to the latter, hope of living is denied. Therefore, when necessity demands it, it is better to be endangered than to perish. To suffer harm through inconveniences with profit is better than to perish through the refusal of inconveniences; [Note: [Col. 0925D] Codex: *id est sanius est remedio noceri quam non posse curari*—“that is, it is healthier to be harmed by a remedy than to be unable to be cured.”] that is, it is better to be harmed by a remedy than to be unable to be cured.

## CHAPTER IV

I speak of this in relation to the heavenly physician, and I refer it chiefly to spiritual healing, not merely to that treatment which, by an art destined to perish, is concerned with mortal limbs. It is therefore better for us to be rebuked and chastised by the Lord and to be healed under his blow than to be removed from his medicine as incurable. [Col. 0925A]

For God keeps from his presence those whom he sees afflicted by the iniquity of an incurable disease and, like dust or chaff scattered and dispersed by the force of a whirlwind, scattered through vices—just as he himself speaks in his own voice, saying: “Let the wicked depart from me, for I do not wish to know their ways; because their lamp has been extinguished, and they will have groaning in their life. For they will be like chaff that flies before the wind and like dust that is lifted by storms” (Job 21). [Note: [Col. 0925D] Codex and edition: “He does not wish to know their ways, who altogether refuse to keep the one way through hardships to the lofty height. To the one, etc.”]

He does not wish to know their ways because they do not wish to follow the way that leads to the heights. For there is one way to the one Lord, to be followed in Christ; through trials that press in upon it, it leads into the spaciousness of enduring security. [Col. 0925B] The palace of heaven lies open to this way alone; the others, winding through the curves of pleasures, make for a fiery region.

Concerning these Solomon testifies in his own voice: “There are ways that seem right to human beings, but at their end there is sadness and pain” (Proverbs 14). Along these ways those rush headlong whose journey through an enemy life flatters them with deceptive allurements; deaf time deceives them, destruction receives and encloses them. As a storm drives a doomed ship upon the rocks, so unhappy prosperity leads those who are prone and slipping toward destruction.

And just as, when someone is walking with confident steps, a sudden accident twists the protection of his feet through the slipperiness of marble or a displaced pavement slab, so those whom the uncertain path of worldly success and a life wrongly considered joyful leads on must be driven by sudden accident into an irrevocable fall. As the most holy Solomon testifies and cries out: “As one who falls on a pavement, so swiftly will the downfall of the wicked come” (Ecclesiasticus 20). [Col. 0925C]

These, beyond doubt, are those who do not deserve to be shaken by the ventilated [Note: [Col. 0925D] Codex: *ventilatis fatigationibus*—“by the weariness of troubles.”] blows of any misery—blows by which eternal sickness is nourished—nor to be scourged with the saints while the Lord chastises them, with whom they will reign after the scourges. David asks that mention be made of them in this verse: “They are not in the troubles of men, and they will not be scourged with men; therefore pride has taken hold of them” (Psalm 72).

You see, then, that those who do not deserve it are despised by the medicinal scourge, while those who do deserve it are chastised in friendship. God, the parent of all, as a faithful physician toward those entrusted to him and as a father toward his children, strikes those whom he loves so as to correct, not to kill. Therefore blessed is the one who is beaten where the wound is one of love. Blessed is the one whom the remedy of heavenly scourging heals, corrects, reforms, and restores, while the blessed and illustrious prophet David proclaims and cries out, saying: “Blessed is the one whom you correct, Lord, and teach from your law” (Psalm 93). [Col. 0925D]

Therefore, since by divine permission we are subject to illnesses of various painfulness [Note: [Col. 0926D] Codex and edition: *angoribus subjacemus*—“we are subject to the anxieties of illness.”] and carry a life that is to be healed through prolonged calamity, let us endure with equanimity, as a test of our virtue, the miseries foretold long ago. Let us bear with mental joy the unhappy and manifold accidents, anxieties, and tears that we encounter from birth.

Nor is it surprising that human life is so devastated in the world by the various massacres of frequent evils, in which no one is born laughing and no one begins the light of life except with tears. When our mother’s womb displayed its tent to the world, we learned the world through weeping, so that we might taste, as it were, the first fruits of evils in the first place through tears. [Col. 0926A]

The prophet Solomon testifies to this declaration: [Note: [Col. 0926D] Codex: *Salomon propheta hac probatione testatur: Et ego, inquit, etc.*—“The prophet Solomon testifies to this by this statement: ‘And I,’ he says, etc.”] “I,” he says, “was born and received the common age of humanity, and I fell upon the earth fashioned in the same way. I uttered my first voice, like everyone else, weeping. I was nurtured in swaddling clothes and in great cares. No king had any other beginning of birth. There is therefore one entrance into life for all, and a similar departure” (Wisdom 7).

For whoever has come must pass away where he has led his life as a stranger, especially since Solomon declares: “There is one entrance into life,” he says, “and a similar departure.” What prosperity or joy, then, can meet us when we first learn to weep and, amid the very cradles of infant infancy and at the very threshold of life, encounter nothing new about the world except weeping? [Note: [Col. 0926D] Codex: *nec aliud mihi de mundo, quam fletus occurrerit*—“and nothing else from the world has met me except weeping.”] We have trodden the lights of the world with weeping; we shall indeed weep as we pass away.

O narrow and exceedingly anxious span of mortal life, in which the end is named together with the beginning, and we take up our beginning together with its end! The one who is born has already been seized by death. The dead are witnesses, since they do not deny that they are destined to die. [Col. 0926B]

Therefore, since we have come only to depart, like travelers, let us overcome by bearing whatever happens within the lodging of the world as we pass through it: [Note: [Col. 0926D] Codex and edition: *transeuntes, ferendo mala imposita, bona devotione portata vincamus*—“as we pass through, let us overcome by bearing the evils imposed with good devotion.”] Evils imposed upon us are overcome when borne with good devotion.

For evil does more harm if it is borne badly; even good things injure us if they are borne badly.

There, certainly, the consolation of virtue is needed—under contemplation, of course, of the heavenly reward—where the end and departure of life are desired just as the protection of the harbor is desired by those at sea. Who, amid the anxieties of a wandering world and the hardships of afflicting diseases, would not desire death more than a sufficiently long and languid life, when Solomon says: “Death is better than a bitter life, and eternal rest than continuing weakness” (Ecclesiasticus 30). And elsewhere: “It is better for you to die than to live” (ibid. 40). For death gives rest to every human being. [Col. 0926C]

Certainly, amid rampant evils, an end is necessarily thirstily desired. But just as it was not ours to be born, so it is not within our power to die. Otherwise, if dying were within our power, not dying would also be within our power. Amid the narrow straits of death we ask for rest because, amid evils, it is a consolation drawn from the good not to be silent about it: like sailors, for whom, amid dangerous and anxious voyages, it is a refreshment to speak of the safety of the harbor. Even if it is not permitted to reach it more quickly, as greatly as the spirit desires, it is nevertheless pleasing—and very beautiful—to wish for better things.

But since it is not within our power to possess the better things that arise from death, let us await better things while meanwhile carrying on a good struggle amid evils. A good struggle is not to yield to evils, but to bear evils through the good of virtue, so that we may be carried, exalted into better things born from death and free from disease and death.

For without the guidance and spur of unhappiness one does not reach the triumphs of immortal glory, because the journey to port is completed through dangers. No one can first be called a victor unless virtue has found him victory: virtue sees everything that is feared struck down beneath it and, unconquered, drags it away captive.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0926D]

The world exists among these things like a sea impatient by nature and swollen even without winds, raising, in the very calm, threatening and terrifying waves. Although its harmless magnitude does not injure those who sit upon it, it nevertheless has something fearsome about it, and dangers and the blows of waves are often not absent for sailors. No helmsman, after all, has ever spread out all the folds of the sea in complete security.

And in this world, where we seek the rough and turbulent course of this life, we are frequently touched by the threats and causes of evils—especially those whom heavenly service has marked and enclosed within the royal camp. [Col. 0927A] We have already said that the world may be compared to the sea, in which prosperity is rare and turbulence dense; one trembles and fears, diseases too are not absent, and the harbor alone is the place of security.

From here and there hostile assaults of calamity press upon us; but to endure as far as the harbor—that is, the end—is the work of virtue. Amid dangers the helmsman protects and preserves the ship. Amid calamities the governing spirit steers and directs the human being.

Someone may guide a manageable ship when dangers have been somewhat tempered; but that ship is awaited and received with greater triumphs which has powerfully shaken off blind waves onto the crest amid a turbulent current. This ship is received by triumphal security.

A soldier established in the army is splendid in his armor; but the sluggish and empty person, inactive in distorted virtue, grows squalid. On the field he is known neither to himself nor to another. He lacks praise, and he lacks rewards. [Note: [Col. 0927D] Codex and edition: *Et ideo novicum debet esse periculum*—“And therefore danger must be something new [or unfamiliar].”]

Therefore danger ought not to be harmful where a reward is born. A soldier should not be recalled or made fearful where the palm of victory follows. He is wretched through his very good fortune who, amid the misfortunes through which glory is generated, has never deserved to engage in combat. Nor has the person learned his own virtue whom calamity has not shaken. [Col. 0927B]
