Indeed, with inactive limbs, a soldier lies ignorant of and unknown to himself, having never panted amid the glorious heat of burning wars and never found triumphs through sweat. Nor does the happiness of rewards follow one who [Note: [Col. 0927D] Codex: *sarcinam gestare non novit armorum*—“does not know how to carry the burden of armor.”] does not wish to carry the burden of armor.

Therefore, what generates reward ought to be put into practice, and what gives birth to glory ought to be desired. Since we must fight with various weapons of temptation, if anything emerges that tests our strength, shakes our limbs, or proves our soul, let us seize it as an opportunity for service and embrace it with virtue.

The strength of an immovable spirit and the unconquered firmness of an unshaken mind must be such that it resembles the rock in the sea which nature established amid the waves: it is repeatedly beaten by the collision of swelling waters, yet is not moved.

Thus, when adversities summon a person to battle and calamity presses and compels him into combat, let a happy spirit bring him forth armed with the shield of virtue; let it keep him safe and secure amid dangers, show him happy amid misfortunes, cheerful amid anxieties, healthy amid grievous illnesses, and, through the spear of endurance, make him victorious once calamity has been conquered. [Col. 0927C]

Disease is overcome in the body if the spirit learns to endure. Therefore, where the body lies weak, greater virtue must be cultivated in its inner recesses, and what neither weariness may shake nor age bend must be prepared. [Note: [Col. 0928D] Codex: *nec lassitudo dejiciat, aut, etc.*—“nor let weariness cast down, or, etc.”]

## CHAPTER VI

Hold fast, then, brother, hold fast the unconquered strength of faith; hold fast the immovable Christian defense, founded upon the firmness of heavenly vigor. Amid languishing and sufficiently rigid limbs, carry unharmed and strong the shield of faith and soul, and you will overcome sluggish disease and destructive weakness.

Meet evils as they batter you with the barriers of virtue. Conquer while you are beaten; for Christian power is nourished by hardships and advanced by adverse evils. It belongs to Christian service to be shaken by calamities and tested. It belongs to it to expand happily amid misfortunes and narrow straits, to grow under pressures, and, by maturing, to trample down pressures. [Col. 0927D]

It belongs to it to nourish its own defense through frequent exercises and to contend with dangers. It belongs to it to sail toward the harbor of perpetual happiness through the burning dangers of the world and, beneath the blows of medicinal discipline, to reign powerfully through necessity itself.

Ours, I say, is to be raised by the exercise of calamity to the summit of glory and, under evils that press upon us, to advance toward good rewards. Among us weakness, or any kind of pressure, is evidence of power and, certainly, the mother of crowned virtue.

Thus the most blessed apostle Paul, placed in battle against diseases amid various blows, different scourges, and stormy assaults, [Col. 0928A] as a heavenly soldier powerful in weaknesses, glories and says: “Therefore I will most gladly glory in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Corinthians 12). “For this reason I am pleased to glory in weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, in deficiencies, and in anxieties for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then I am powerful” (ibid.). And again: “As often,” he says, “as I am weak, then I am more truly tested and find my satisfaction in my weaknesses.”

And again, when he asked that the thorn of the flesh be removed from him, he learned that virtue could be nourished in weakness. He says: “A thorn of my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to strike me with blows, so that I might not be exalted. For this I asked the Lord three times that it depart from me, and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (ibid.). [Col. 0928B]

[Note: [Col. 0928D] Edition: *Nunquid igitur virtus documentis mollioribus eruditur*—“Is virtue, then, ever instructed by milder lessons?”]

Virtue, therefore, is never instructed by milder lessons, since the examples of the greatest virtues would otherwise have perished. Our ship rejoices in agitation when it is raised in whirlwinds, when it is beaten by raging waves, and when this rough voyage, as adverse things emerge, does not spare it but challenges its devoted virtue to continual combat.

For we cannot be happy before the Lord except by being purified through misfortunes and earthly squalor. That person should be judged wretched and sick who, languid with pleasures, rolls about and lies amid enticements. Let the person know himself unhappy who wanders among the delights of vices, pierced by enervating prosperity. [Col. 0928C]

Wretched and unhappy is the one who has not been tested by unhappiness. He lacks the gift who lacks the struggle as well. Whoever feared the weapons of adverse combat never deserved to receive the name of victor. Undoubtedly, it belongs to a prostrate spirit to fear fearful things; it belongs to the humble and inactive to pursue what is safe.

Good cast into leisure without struggle is incomplete and weak. Its vigor lies weakened and enervated; the spirit lies sick; its brightness lies obscured. Therefore the bravest soldier must always stand in the battle line and seek an opportunity through which virtue may shine forth after being tested. [Col. 0928C]

For the lover of battles, wounds are ornaments. Therefore, to learn virtue and to despise hardships, experience is necessary—experience that nourishes strength. A body is solid, and its mass of limbs robust, when frequent use has exercised it.

Farmers, after all, possess muscular strength through frequent labor; their hands are hardened as, with bent bodies, they seek the harvest through sweat among thorns and thistles. The art of navigation, whose ship a storm has often twisted while it presses toward port amid dangers, has learned to cross waves and fight with the tempest.

An army lacerated by the repulsion of weapons is strong and seeks victories amid wounds, wishing to please its own king. Runners have agile limbs, and practice has taught and trained them. What more need be said? Everyone rises to more perfect attainments through the addition of trials and, as a victor, seizes the reward.

## CHAPTER VII

Therefore, while at first we endure small and moderate things, we must learn to bear greater or even the greatest things. For it is the mark of our service to set a shining step through difficult places, to be carried through hardships, and to endure the harsh judgment of miseries with hard strength. [Note: [Col. 0928D] Edition: *specimen fulgidum per ardua, etc.*—“a shining example is to set one’s step through hardships, and so forth.”] [Col. 0928D]

The way to heaven is placed before us through rough ground, narrow passages, harsh windings, and difficult places; whoever did not wish to be tested did not follow this way. God calls to heaven the strongest soldier; pressures, accompanied by glories, lead him onward, and rewards receive the victor who is destined to reign.

Does he meanwhile impose upon us anything precipitous that exceeds the measure of a balanced burden? Does he thrust upon us anything that surpasses the capacity of our virtue? The most faithful governor orders a burden to be imposed according to our strength. Paul’s proclamation testifies to and proves this: “God is faithful,” he says, “and he will not allow you to be tested beyond what you are able to bear” (1 Corinthians 10). [Col. 0929A]

Let us believe that the Lord acts and governs in the same way as teachers of athletic games govern their students: they impose and assign the greatest labor to those whom they see excelling the others in skillful abilities. We likewise regulate the burden placed upon animals subject to our authority according to the quality of their strength. We impose strong tasks upon the stronger and small ones upon the weak, so that practice, that nourisher of virtue, may raise them and advance their strength to the greatest vigor of youth.

In this way our beginners are struck by light blows, so that thereafter, out of love for divine virtue, they may prepare their accustomed strength for heavier ones. Although this principle abounds in many divine teachings, let us also use an example from worldly affairs; it is not harmful to use things foreign to us in that respect in which they are our own.

Do you suppose that the Spartans hated their own children, whose character and tender limbs—still inexperienced, of course, in labor—they put to the test, and whom paternal affection itself encouraged, by applying public scourges, to bear the blows of lashes bravely? They even pleaded with and begged their lacerated and half-dead children to persevere in presenting wounds to wounds. [Col. 0929B]

What wonder, then, if God allows you, his noble children and his own household, to be harshly tested for the sake of the splendor of virtue that must be cultivated, since he is going to bestow perpetual kingdoms upon victors? He promises the rewards of labor against every evil in this way, saying: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10). And again: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11).

The brief span of perishing time is the price of eternity. [Col. 0929D] [Note: Codex: *Devotio tribulationis cultura reddetur*—“The devotion of tribulation will be repaid, made fruitful by everlasting fruits.”] Devotion amid tribulation will be repaid, made fruitful by everlasting fruits. Among us, kingdom is sought through fruitful captivity; security is purchased by dangers; rest is acquired through sweat. For, as the Apostle says, “power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12).

It is certainly more advantageous to be troubled bodily by languishing affections than, with healthy limbs, to carry a conscience harassed by blind punishment. Many are sick from sins precisely because their limbs are empty of illness. For while they are free from bodily weaknesses, the body must necessarily flow in diseased laxity and be dissolved by a deadly illness, wickedly leading the person headlong through vices and forests of error. [Col. 0929C]

## CHAPTER VIII

Do you judge those free, or free from diseases, whom barbarous pleasures have bound? They do not have a chain, but savage luxury holds them in bonds with biting force. Thus they have fallen into the snares of savage pleasures like birds captured by the deceit of bird-catching; the more they try to escape, the more they entangle themselves in countless knots and plunge into deeper recesses.

Are those truly healthy whom an insane disease has enveloped and tossed about? Rather, the person whom God corrects by any blow is whole; by chastising him, God testifies that he loves humanity: “Those whom I love,” says the Lord, “I rebuke and chastise” (Revelation 3).

Therefore let no one judge himself healthy because he lacks either diseases or filth and is not comforted by the remedy of weakness. Those are wretched who grow sluggish in the idle tranquility of excessive happiness; a counterfeit health flatters them in order to deceive and mislead them. Eternal sickness will hold them, and an eternal torturer will later torment the whole person. [Col. 0929D]

For them there are as many roads as pleasures occur to them. Their path is whatever desire, their companion, dictates amid perishable dangers. Seized by the winding paths of dragging vices, the wretched are rolled toward destruction in a varied fall, traveling an utterly uncertain road from which they will not return. They direct their spirit outward, like streams that never return to their own source.

They lead this life, which they suppose to have an end as its companion, along prosperous courses; but their steps end utterly badly in the final stages, while they stand harshly at the end. What does it profit to have run prosperously through dangers if, after the course, one happens to perish?

In vain, then, does a ship run through a proud and raging sea toward port with favorable success amid friendly waves, if it arrives through shipwreck and the harbor receives a doomed vessel. It is therefore more advantageous to reach the harbor of glory under the guidance of any pressure than, after completing a voyage of diseased ease in a delicate vessel, to go out into punishments.

Thus poverty is often preferable to wealth, disfigurement to beauty, insult to praise, servitude to power, weakness to strength, captivity to freedom, and humility to dignity. The illustrious prophet David expressed such a verse: “It is good for me, Lord,” he says, “that you have humbled me, so that I may learn your justifications” (Psalm 118). [Col. 0930A]

Therefore it is better to be humbled by the heavenly judgment of discipline than to be condemned with the world, as the Apostle says: “When we are judged by the Lord, we are corrected, so that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Corinthians 11).

Therefore let us bear without murmuring what is imposed for our benefit out of love for the Lord. It is administered as a remedy by the physician and as discipline by the Lord. It is part of the physician’s art sometimes to heal with fire and iron. What wonder, then, if the Lord, the physician of our souls, shakes us with storms, exhausts us through illnesses, and purifies us through calamities? [Col. 0930B]

It is an expression of our strength to be purified like vessels through fires and flames. Divine Scripture testifies to and proves this: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests just people” (Ecclesiasticus 27). And elsewhere it says: “Gold, silver, iron, lead, and everything that has passed through fire will be purified” (Numbers 31).

Vessels never say to the potter: “Why do you test us at the discretion of flames, and burn and prove us with consuming fires?” Unless the arbiter of fire has pronounced them most suitable by his judgment, they cannot be put to use.

We too, unless the judgment or testing of temptations has purified us, are found useless by the potter of our limbs—he who burns us in order to heal, tests us in order to free, and afflicts us in order to save. For nothing is so polluted or filthy that it cannot be expiated by purifications from vices.

Indeed, we have often seen people soiled by reproach come into brightness, and iron covered with rust shine again in its former appearance. We have seen gold and silver purified by the discipline of flame, and trees cut back revive through the most pleasing cultivation and be adorned with lovely shoots. We have seen sterile things restored to fertility, and, once the trunk has been exhausted, root and abundant fruit accompany it. [Col. 0930C]

So too in us, whatever was perhaps seething under the pressure of sins, whatever the stain of squalid antiquity obstructed, has been driven out by the light of illness. And therefore, brother, bodily illness has made you healthy through medicinal treatment. Only the material of flesh in you needs the strength of health; and lest it should perhaps trouble you, it is troubled by a beneficial disease.

This is what the dog-star of old age strikes in everyone, destined to lose its own bloom as grass withers, as it is written: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isaiah 40).

Let us therefore endure with equanimity if the body—which we read will perish like grass with its flowers destined to fall—is tossed about, exhausted by afflicting evils. Its health is accustomed to bring illness upon the soul and, contrary to spiritual benefits, to draw out savage and barbarous pleasures.

Indeed, the flesh, when unrestrained, has often stripped the soldiers of chastity of their armor. It is therefore for our benefit if we are chastised by long and biting scourges, though we are attacked by its chastity. [Note: [Col. 0930D] Codex and edition: *sanitate impugnamur*—“by whose health we are attacked.”]

Foolishly we love the flesh; we do not grieve over the soul’s prison and burial. Let us therefore despise the frailty of that flesh and seize whatever happens with the embraces of devotion as a treasure.

It is fearful for a Christian soldier to wish to remain in calm like one who is joyful. It is the mark of a cast-down mind to fear the whirlwind; by contrast, it is the mark of courage not to tremble amid opposites. It belongs to unhappiness not to know adversity; it belongs to happiness to know how to meet adversity and how to fight.

Since all the blows by which we are shaken, as we have already said, arise from a divine gift, let the person who does not know how to be troubled by trials recognize that he is a stranger to the love of God, since the legal trumpet repeatedly impresses this upon our hearing in various verses and says: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 13). [Col. 0931A]

And elsewhere: “My son,” he says, “do not neglect the discipline of God, and do not grow weary when corrected by him. For God corrects the one whom he loves” (Proverbs 3). And again: “Do not despise the correction of the Lord. For he himself gives pain, and he himself gives relief; he strikes, and his hand presents healing” (Job 5).

## CHAPTER IX
But perhaps you say:

**THE INVALID.** If only, as with others, I might be allowed to be tested at intervals in the hope of recovery! If only I were permitted to taste health briefly, through some kind of interruption or change for the better! What does it mean that illness should so occupy and remain confined within my limbs that it has shut out health, never to return? What does it mean that this destructive companion should drag my shaken limbs onward to the end of life, and itself too be dragged along, to be excluded in death together with those limbs? What does it mean [Note: [Col. 0931D] The manuscript and edition read, “that the bodily members have been deprived of the sense of health.”] that throughout the whole span of life my limbs should be frustrated of the experience of health? When cold has been introduced into my veins, their warm vigor has vanished into chill; the walking that nature had granted, inward torpor has shut out. Indeed, no journey, even a very brief one, is tasted for the exercise of this wasted body. The knees are not bent in their accustomed way for prayer; the uneven order of the fingers, thrown into confusion by inner numbness, is prevented from touching the things it usually touches. Why say more? Every function of the body, once accustomed to be present at the stations of the sinews, now lies enclosed in such coldness. Alas! Was I alone destined to be chastised in this way? Was I alone to be subjected to blows so destructive and wrapped in prolonged evils?

**JEROME.** I beg you, brother, to restrain these murmurs with the reins of patience and to confine your complaining voices in silence, while prophetic consolation addresses you in these words: “Join yourself to God,” it says, “and endure, so that your life may increase at the last. Accept whatever is brought upon you, and endure in suffering; maintain patience in your humility, because gold and silver are tested in the fire, but receptive persons (*receptibiles*; manuscript: *receptabiles*, “acceptable persons”) in the furnace of humiliation” (Ecclus. 2). When I review the laws and songs of the prophets, my ears also, unless I am mistaken, apprehend excellent sayings from worldly authority—sayings stolen, as it were, from divine law—which ought necessarily to be inserted into the precepts of the Law. For it does no harm to use what belongs to others in that part in which it is also ours.

The first saying is this: “Fire tests gold, and misery tests good men.” And elsewhere: “Nothing seems more unfortunate than the man to whom nothing adverse has ever happened. He has not been permitted to test himself, since everything has flowed according to his wishes.” And elsewhere: “I judge you miserable because you have never been miserable. You have passed through life without an adversary: no one will know what you were capable of, nor will you yourself. For self-knowledge requires experience. No one has learned what he can do unless he has been tested.” And elsewhere: “To remain fortunate for a long time and to pass through life without sickness of soul—is this not to be ignorant of one half of the nature of things?”

Therefore let us endure with a joyful spirit the miseries that arise, through which unknown things are learned, happiness is born, and virtue too is purified when shaken—whether because we ought to suffer, or because we are already being held captive. Unless flame adds brilliance to gold, it remains darkened by its dross and suffers the disgrace of its impurities. So the person who has not been shaken by the trials of misery lies ignorant both of the parts of happiness and of his own virtue.

Rightly Solomon bears witness in these words: “He who has not been tested in anything does not know what kind of person he is” (Ecclus. 34). Therefore bless the Lord in the time of tribulation, whom you praised in the time of health. Use the songs of the prophetic voice: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33). Let that voice especially of the blessed Job be drawn forth from you in steadfast proclamation—a voice by which exhausted strength rejoices in abundant nourishment and rises again, restored like a newly planted shoot: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” (Job 2). “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1).

It is therefore wholly contrary and opposed to the time of testing to murmur against the Lord: he either afflicts the destructive stain of our life with the agitation of sufferings in order to free us, or he winnows us in justice in order to crown us; and by the torment of our limbs he either punishes sin or tests righteousness, so that it may conquer. Therefore, to bring back to the consolation of your sufferings the merit you possess through the triumph of an ancient trial, let us employ the most just examples.

**CHAPTER X**

Although it is evident that the merits of persons differ by long degrees, it is not unjust to compare the struggle of a Christian with the contests of victorious righteousness. What you appear to endure in this world is insignificant if you consider what Job, the friend of the Lord, was able to endure with the Lord’s permission. God measured it out so that it would correspond and be suited to his strength. [Note: [Col. 0931D] The edition reads: “Could you, who are unequal to him in righteousness, be equal to him in the succeeding titles of honor?”]

Could you, who are unequal to him, be equal to him in the titles of righteousness that follow? You are shaken less than that righteous man, but you are wounded more severely than others; his wounds are great, but yours are not lesser. For you yourself are great, since you follow one who is great.

There was one patriarch, Job, an unconquered worshiper of majesty, wealthy and rich in the resources of equality, whose Lord displayed his illustrious merits when he anticipated the savage weapons of the hostile faction with a proclamation of praise: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth: a blameless man, a true worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil work and remaining in his innocence and simplicity of heart?” (Job 2).

Therefore, when by divine permission he was struck by hostile arrows, and the repeated, savage assault of the robber pressed hard upon him, he defeated the blows as they arose with the shield of patience. Against the savage forest of advancing evils, full of arrows and crosses, he stood firm with the barriers of righteousness.

When that man’s possessions had been taken away by the enemy’s storm, he felt no loss, because he found profit in his losses, carrying the Lord enclosed in the recesses of his heart. When sudden force shook the building at its corners and twisted it into collapse, he was deprived of his children, yet remained steadfast and immovable in faith. When his innocent limbs, filled with the Lord, were infested with legions of beasts, and a destructive mass of worms wandered through tunnels in his pierced flesh, while his body was struck by hostile blows, the righteous man remained sound within his wounds and carried on his warfare. The hostile fury that gnawed at him with pestilential sores, he endured with tranquility of mind until the enemy storms yielded. The righteous man conquered by being beaten; the enemy failed by striking.

To that man the service of his household servants was denied; around you, your attendants perform their services. Friends console you and grieve through their frequent visits; if nature allowed it, they might perhaps carry this burden with you. There is one virtue of the soul—one, brother—which, rescuing us from the storms of this life as though from the sea, brings us into the harbor of tranquility.

Look: the day hastens toward sunset in its downward course. Look: the unclean world, soiled by the filth of old age, turns toward collapse. [Note: [Col. 0932D] Another reading: “You.” The manuscript and edition read: “Look, we.”]

Look: heaven receives the victorious through death’s assistance. As we escape, all things perish, and, with their setting already near, are swallowed up never to return. For us, after the world has been destroyed and the body has died, all things are healed. We shall rejoice in the soundness of our limbs, where life will be troubled by no disease.

Therefore, in you, brother, let the most excellent mind, with illustrious leadership, govern and direct the impeded functions of the body, so that this bodily calamity may become a welcome opportunity for virtue. For a tree is neither solid nor strong unless it is tested by the assaults of constant storms, its trunk shaken and bent this way and that, or unless the blast of turbulent winds often strikes it; through these very disturbances it is compressed and pressed down, and, with its roots fixed, is strengthened more securely.

So we are protected by the biting whips of frequent evils when stretched out, corrected when scourged, tightened when beaten, and rid of our foulness while we are shaken by prolonged falls. Therefore, amid ever-increasing pains and limbs afflicted by monstrous miseries, let strong and sound virtue reign with heavenly vigor, by which adversities may be endured, and those things carried which are called misfortunes.

In the midst of afflictions the wise man rejoices and grows by an equal support of consolation; by his aspiring reason he expands and lives. He does not know what he suffers who remembers unconquered virtue, who, under the leadership of reason, has discovered that many have been crushed by evils and have been increased and nourished by the very evil that befell them, with reason as their teacher.

Therefore the consolations of reason lie open before you, so that the calamity of the body—and the entire mass of the body lying captive—may now be regarded as an advantage. But the resurrection will come, restoring you sound and recovering every limb that has been seized in you. Meanwhile, let your tongue be daily nourished by the theme of praising the Lord, so that it may recount the abundance of praise in the heavenly kingdoms. May the Lord cherish you with heavenly medicine and permit you to endure beneath such a burden with inflexible virtue.

**LETTER II. To a Sick Friend, on the Perfect Man**

[Col. 0933]

**FIRST PREFATORY NOTE**

123 Vallarsius writes, in the place indicated above, that Saint Maximus of Turin is the author of this Letter: “Although no one now denies it, even though Saint Agobard, a writer of the ninth century, in Book Against Felix, chapter 20, does not doubt that it belongs to Jerome when, quoting from it the passage that we shall note below in its proper places, he says: ‘The reader has, on the same subject, a sufficiently polished and lucid statement of blessed Jerome, when he was treating that passage of Holy Scripture where it is said: “I will place,” and so forth.’”

Erasmus, on the other hand, says: “This letter was indeed the work of an eloquent and learned man, and was carefully composed; but it differs so greatly from Jerome’s style that neither could this writer have imitated Jerome’s diction, had he wished to do so, nor could Jerome have imitated his.”

In most manuscripts it bore no name; in some, the name of Ctesiphon had been added. Nor is any mention made in the letter itself of the person to whom it was written. The author does, however, mention Saint Ambrose and the discovery of the bodies of the holy Gervasius and Protasius.

**SECOND PREFATORY NOTE**

[Col. 0933]

How unworthy this letter is of Maximus has also been demonstrated by us in the preface to the appendix. The variant readings of this letter, which we have appended, are taken from manuscript 9, Pluteus XIX, of the Laurentian Library at Florence, page 337.

**CHAPTER I**

[Col. 0933B]

Look, I am writing to you again, and I find nothing worthy for your wisdom to read. And what wonder is it if, in your absence, my intellect—deprived, as it were, of the sun—grows cold in a chilly heart, and my mind, estranged from the light, grows numb, suffocated by the darkness of folly [Note: [Col. 0933D] The manuscript reads “darkened.”]—and if I am the less wise the farther I am separated from you?

But if, for the present, anything in my speech should please you [Note: [Col. 0933D] The same manuscript: “whatever pleased you in my speech.”], it will be granted to me through your prayers. Finally, so that you may recognize all my folly more carefully, I even treated my stomach, after it had received that wax treatment [Note: [Col. 0933D] The Roman edition reads *cerotum*, “a wax dressing.”], while you were absent—although I deserve to suffer worse from the one to whom, after your holy ministry and angelic service, I applied the hands of physicians, as though there were no prophet in Israel.

If I had suffered anything, it ought to have been easier for me to return to you than to think like a pagan; and it would have been better to endure even the labor of the most difficult journey than to be deprived of the precious sight of your presence, so that any compensation would have been preferable to my going to the fly-god of Ekron.

This is what the world suggested to me in your absence [Note: [Col. 0933D] The same Roman edition reads: “had no counsel in me.”], a world that, in your presence, has no counsel over me. You had made me a senate of prophets, not a gathering of Sirens. But now, for the destruction of your holy work against me, the entire senate of folly has entered into me and deals with me in fourfold form.

For it exacts interest from one who is absent, which it did not dare to demand when you were present, so that you may understand that, if I possessed any wisdom before God in your presence, what I possessed was yours. Thus the people of Israel fornicated when Moses was absent (Exod. 32); thus, while the Lord slept in the boat, the apostles were thrown into confusion by the storm (Matt. 8); thus, at Bethsaida, the porticoes overlook the man who has no water in the healing pool [Note: [Col. 0933D] The Roman edition reads, “not clinging to the water,” and so forth.] (John 5).

[Note: [Col. 0933D] Another reading: “Although here I also observe another kind of fault.”]

How great another kind of fault I also perceive here! I cared for the little body while the soul was languishing; I tended the outward man while the inward man was sick; I came to the aid of human things while divine things were failing, bent by the fault of common custom, through which we are all cautious in small matters and negligent in great ones. This happens because we do not know where true life is.

124 This sun deceives us, evidently; this day misleads us; this expanse of time surrounds us. The world leads us astray, while we think that nothing is greater than the sun, and suppose that light is what we see with our eyes; while we judge the man we see to be the man himself, and believe that the world creates life, ignorant of where man is, what man is, and what the life of that man is. If we understood this, we would not be generated for one thing and live for another. Thus, having abandoned the origin of life, we have also lost the rule of living. First, then, let us hear where this man of whom we speak is.

**CHAPTER II**

Since the division itself has generated a certain discussion for us [Note: [Col. 0934D] Perhaps “the man.”], understand that the man is contained within this body, fashioned by the hand of God the Craftsman from the clay of the earth, as though in a kind of little vessel [Note: [Col. 0934D] The manuscript and edition read: “Understand that he is contained within this body, formed by the hand of God the Craftsman from the clay of the earth, as in a certain earthen vessel.”], as the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4). Infused everywhere throughout this body, he has borrowed from the flesh the vital sense that does not fail him.

He rules; he is not ruled. He possesses rather than is possessed, so that he does not receive life but supplies it. For when the fluid spirit animates this earthly and sluggish matter, taken up for the use of service, the spirit becomes lord of the body, not a man subject to the body.

Finally, this little vessel of which I have spoken lives while he himself is present and dies when he departs [Note: [Col. 0934D] Another reading: “for him,” though these words are absent from both the manuscript and the edition.]. This visible and perishable thing, then, is either the dwelling, the minister, or the sheath of that inward being. But he who truly is man, since he is the second element in the division that has been made [Note: [Col. 0934D] Another reading omits “since.” The manuscript and edition read: “since he is the second place of the division,” and so forth.], must himself be invisible, and all that belongs to him invisible as well.

If he is sick, the hands of physicians cannot reach him; if he fails, he is not restored by the juices of herbs. Nothing bodily can enter him; only something like his own substance descends to him. He is cured by a word and grows strong through obedience.

Thus, when the blessed and wealthy man of the church of Laodicea, well sighted and well clothed according to the outward man, seemed to himself to be such, he was rebuked by the Lord and told: “You do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Rev. 3). Yet, as I have said, he was considered neither without clothing, nor without eyes, nor without riches. But our invisible God saw that invisible man to be in poverty, blindness, and nakedness; and he deigned to urge him to purchase from him gold refined by fire, and a white garment in which he might be clothed most gloriously, and eye-salve by which he might recover his sight.

He therefore has eyes of his own, in addition to these bodily ones, which he may either lose or restore; and he is naked beside himself, so much so that he needs clothing. Yet, in a remarkable way [Note: [Col. 0935D] The manuscript and edition read, “to a beggar.”], the Lord speaks to him as to a physician and commands him to purchase riches from him. With what resources, if he is both naked and poor, will he buy that most noble garment or that purified gold already tested by fire? From where can the expense of such a transaction come?

Clearly, it will come if he either cherishes the profits of the outward man, or, by not using those things through which he appeared outwardly rich, becomes wealthy; and if he blinds the eyes of the body, by which he was seized by worldly passion, through contempt for the corrupted universe. Thus that invisible man—who truly is man, as we have said—is raised by contempt for this outward man, clothed by nakedness, and illuminated by blindness.

Thus Jacob saw not only the positions but also the merits of his grandsons Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen. 48) through incorporeal blindness [Note: [Col. 0935D] The manuscript and edition read “bodily blindness.”]. For when his son Joseph, who was presenting the children mentioned above, judged that he could not see even what was before his feet [Note: [Col. 0935D] The manuscript and edition read: “and could not see even before his feet.”], he perceived from his father’s response that Jacob also foresaw what was to come [Note: [Col. 0935D] The manuscript and edition read: “that those things also which were to come,” and so forth.].

But just as the inward man makes this outward man live by his own life and animates him by irrigating him from the fountain of his own nature, so in turn the outward man, through the corruption of his mortal matter, kills the inward man if he binds him to unlawful desires. And when one appears to be of the other’s nature, each passes into the substance of the victor, so that either the spiritual man (*spiritualis*) renders even the flesh spiritual through his virtues, or the conquering flesh makes the soul fleshly. [Note: [Col. 0936D] The manuscript reads: “that is, so that the soul may also impart spiritual qualities to fleshly substance by its virtues.”]

Therefore, when the Lord, angered, was considering the destruction of the human race, he said: “My Spirit shall not remain in human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6). And since we are all clothed in flesh, there is no doubt that we are not “in the flesh” if we do not walk according to the flesh. From this also arises the fact that a man is not always reckoned by this name of “man.” According to his virtues or his vices, he assumes different forms and names.

Thus the prophet says: “Do not become like a horse or a mule” (Ps. 31). There are therefore human beings who, before the Lord, are horses and mules. The Lord also says: “Do not throw your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7). There are therefore human beings who are swine. And again the Lord himself says: “Behold, I am sending you like sheep among wolves” (Matt. 10). There are therefore human beings who are wolves, and conversely there are human beings who are sheep.

The Lord also says to Peter: “Feed my sheep” (John 21); and earlier he himself said: “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of human beings” (Matt. 4). There are therefore human beings who are fish. But these forms appear to belong to actions, not bodies. The condition of our body is fixed, as is that of all living creatures; but since before God we are judged not by the condition of our body but by the merits of our life, it is clear that every person forms for himself, in his mind, a condition and a name. This is certainly produced by the fault or virtue of that invisible man whom we are describing.

It is his own fault if he has allowed himself to be subjected to subjects [Note: [Col. 0935D] The edition reads: “if he has allowed himself to be subject to those who are subject.” The manuscript reads: “if he has known himself to be subject to those who are subject.”]; if, contrary to the divine arrangement, servitude exists in domination and domination in servitude.

But lest I seem—since, by removing the wall a little, as it were, I have reached that invisible man in my discussion—to destroy the body altogether, which possesses so great a sacrament that the Lord came in this very thing, namely, in our frail and infirm condition, I have neither done nor am doing this. Rather, I have tried to show that the life of this outward man consists in the life of that inward man; and again, that the death of the inward man descends upon this one from death: when poison has been administered through vices, this outward man has nothing of life unless he has been irrigated by the inward man. One passes into the nature of the other, as I have said, either infected by vices or cleansed by virtue.

Therefore, since I have now shown, briefly as permitted, both where man is and what man is, let us see what the life of that man is. [Note: [Col. 0936D] The manuscript and edition read: “But surely this worldly life, which has evils for goods and goods for evils.”] For if this worldly life—which has evils for goods and goods for evils, and which the whole world follows and worships—is not found in abundance of riches, nor in the height of power, nor in the cunning of authority, nor in the pomp of eloquence, nor in strength made glorious through battles, nor in merchandise increased by the exchange of provinces and by wandering from place to place, nor in the enticement of beauty, nor in the solicitation of gifts, nor, finally, in all those things that we see—for all these things perish, and one can live happily even according to the world without them—then true life, life worthy of reverence [Note: [Col. 0936D] The manuscript and edition read: “life to be reckoned: to know God.”], is to know God, fear his power, love his goodness, admire the world in its Maker, despise the tempter, and be content with modest food according to nature’s need, protected by cheap clothing either for the sake of modesty or against the harshness of the season.

In this way one should make use of the rest of creation, not from one’s own abundance or for the necessities of life, but as an aid to this light [Note: [Col. 0936D] The manuscript and edition read: “or as an aid to this light.”]. For whatever is more than this is from evil: to love every human being as a brother, to harm no one, to serve everyone, to bear the form of a servant together with the Lord, who, apart from the service contained within us, serves us daily in the world by bringing forth the sun, sending out the light, pouring down the rains, changing the seasons, and either producing or ripening the crops.

For he serves us in the face and abundance of the whole creation, since he created everything for us. But, to return to the duties owed to human beings: to clothe the naked, feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, visit the sick, sympathize with the sorrowful, bury the dead, possess nothing as one’s own, but judge all one’s goods to be held in common with everyone—and then to live more fully for oneself when one is thought to live for others, and to store up for oneself when one is believed to distribute to others.

Yet these are still only the outlines of the outward man.

**CHAPTER III**

The life of the inward man, moreover, consists in knowledge of divine things—not in knowing through what part of the earth the heavens turn, nor whether the stars are swept along in an opposite course, nor whether the fullness of the moon produces its increase from the Ocean, nor whether the roundness of the world itself suspends its globe, or whether it binds it with four projecting angles, nor whether there is one world or several. [Note: [Col. 0936D] The manuscript and edition read: “For these things do not tend toward the soul’s benefit.”]

For these matters do not tend toward the soul’s benefit and are judged foolish before God. Rather, the inward man lives and is nourished when he is occupied with those sound thoughts.

What are these sound thoughts? Without doubt, they are present when our mind remembers its Creator; when, through a kind of return to its senses, it reveres and contemplates its Maker; when, intending to see him in his works, it marvels at his works; as blessed Paul says: “His invisible things, understood and perceived through the things that have been made from the creation of the world, and also his eternal power and divinity” (Rom. 1).

That is, we extend ourselves from the immense visible things of creation to the whole of the invisible Creator; and, while through these things we learn that he is beyond estimation, we esteem him. As, unfolding his height through the gift of the Holy Spirit—for he alone admits us into himself, who is from him—we look upon all the beginnings of the rising creation as though they were made before us by him; and, as though God were still making them, we contemplate the things God made.

Traversing the whole origin of the world, we become, as it were, older than we are in age; and although all things were made before we existed, we nevertheless reckon the nature of all things as though it had been generated through us, while we are inscribed into the Creator. We entered into it not to serve, but to rule.

Thus separated from worldly wisdom, which attributes everything either to chance or to atoms, we are raised by divine meditations and separated from those who either said that matter had always existed [Note: [Col. 0937D] The manuscript reads: “and wished to understand God only as the craftsman of things, not their author,” and so forth.] or who wished God to be understood only as the craftsman of things, not their author; and from those who worshipped the elements themselves as gods; and from those who introduced families of gods according to sexes, ages, and functions, as though introducing a kind of populace subject to the senses.

Separated from them through the Holy Spirit and led upward into higher things, living the true life—that is, possessing true wisdom, which lacks this folly [Note: [Col. 0937D] The manuscript reads: “which lacks this folly”; the edition: “because it lacks this folly.”]—let us remember that the world was made by God from nothing, and that all living creatures came into being through God, with the Word as craftsman, although they did not previously exist. For only he has the right to call things that are not as though they were.

And the very human being, for whom so great a possession was being prepared, he who formed the universe deigned to make in his own image—not some Prometheus from a fable, but God himself, with his own hand from the clay of the earth, so that no part of him might remain empty within us. This thought, as I have said, is the life of the soul, because the first principle of living is not to be ignorant of whom the soul ought to serve: lest, deceived, it worship another instead of him; lest it adore the ministries of its life as though they were the authors of life; lest it admire the elements so greatly that it judges them unworthy of belief as created things, when the one who produced such marvelous things is more worthy of admiration.

O how majestic [Note: [Col. 0937D] Another reading: “narrow”; the manuscript and edition read: “majestic.”] this divine thought is, and how full of life! O how greatly it kindles the human being toward every pursuit of goodness! O how greatly it commends to him the majesty of his Creator, when he considers that nothing in the whole creation except the human being was formed by God’s hand—not the earth, not the seas, not the heavens, not even the stars, so pure, so clean, so bright; but that the human being alone, formed from a certain mud, a heavier and dirtier element, was shaped by that hand whose palm measures the heavens according to measure, whose handful encloses the immeasurable spaces of the outspread earth.

How great, then, was the dignity of his having once existed! Yet let us also see how the Creator’s goodness applauds him further by not making him from the stars. For if he had been created from them, he would derive his distinction from the brightness of his material rather than from the Creator’s condescension, and he himself would seem lesser because of the origin of his body.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] The manuscript reads: “If, made from heavenly things, he were brought down to the earth for the cultivation of the land.”]

If he were made from heavenly things and brought down to earth for the cultivation of the land, it would be more glorious for him to be raised from the soil and placed among the stars. Our God, I say, wanted what we are to be his own—strictly his own. We owe nothing to matter, nothing to the elements, nothing to any principles, whether great or small.

If the mind recalls and considers all these things within itself, they become more moderate and narrower than their beginnings. [Note: [Col. 0937D] The manuscript reads: “But when, through the contact of God’s hand, we ceased to be what we had been.”]

But when, through the contact of God’s forming hand, we ceased to be what we had been, and nature, subjected to a new quality of matter, was glorified by its transformation according to the elements for the sake of its Maker, and our body began, if it is permissible to say so, to be a new element among the elements [Note: [Col. 0938D] The manuscript reads: “to have begun to be an element.”], we were immediately made higher than all the bodies of the world—not by the substance of our nature, but by the power of the Creator, through which there arose from what had been subject to the other creatures that which was to command all creatures.

Indeed, if you look at the metal of our flesh and body, you will find nothing lower, nothing cheaper, nothing more subject to every injury and suffering. Earth alone among the elements appears to be the servant of the others; alone it experiences within itself the powers of all things, not without harm to itself—whether it is scattered as dust by the winds, soaked and swallowed by the waves, or baked and consumed by the fires of the stars. Thus a human being cannot merely glory in being from the earth, but can even be ashamed of it.

But if we contemplate our condition [Note: [Col. 0938D] The manuscript and edition read: “since he made it superior to the other animals when God formed it according to his image,” and so forth.], since God introduces it as superior to the other living creatures by shaping it according to his own image, we shall find that the earth itself—that is, the seed of our body—could have rejoiced, if there is any sense in it, because, transformed for our sake, it became happier than it had arisen, since in us it received the image and likeness of the Creator.

The hand of God touched it, although the earth itself did not deserve that contact when it was made for his sake. For what is more glorious than this condition? What could we know more sublime? What has been distributed into limbs with such care? What has been bent so beautifully through its joints? What has been raised so sublimely into the mouth and eyes? What has been modulated so vocally into words? What has been animated so vigorously in the heart? What is richer in sensation? What more secret in thought? What more expansive in speech? What stronger in intelligence? What better equipped in disposition? What more tenacious in memory? What gentler in affection? What more elevated in reflection?

It is clear that he adorned that first-formed human being, already beautified with every dignity, with the form—or rather, the condition—of his Son, our God, who was to come at the end of the ages for our redemption, in this body. To this human being the planter of all things had also granted Paradise at that time, like a most delightful estate, beautified with urban features and planted with rural produce, under the law of death. But the prime sower begrudged him this, and, deceiving the credulous newness of the first human beings, secretly immersed his poison in our bodies. From the two substances he dissected the single and perfect nature of the human being by a kind of discordant division, so that, although we had one mind—the one produced by the kinship of soul and body—a different will might be generated through corrupted nature against the soul.

Thus the Apostle also says: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin that is in my members” (Rom. 7). And elsewhere: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These oppose one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish” (Gal. 5).

**CHAPTER IV**
Hence also our Creator, who had made either us for ourselves or the world for our sake, offended by those first human beings, poured out curses upon each one according as the gravity of the crime required. And although he was angry, nevertheless, like a merciful father, he immediately revealed the mystery of our salvation. Nor would it have been fitting to think of a remedy for our salvation at any other time than when death had been discovered. Thus, among the wiser physicians, a doctor is applied at the outset to death, so that, once the source of the illness has been detected, a health-giving remedy may more readily come to the rescue.

Our Lord and Savior, therefore, was not promised only then, when Isaiah cries, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. VII), nor only when it was said to Abraham, “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son” (Gen. XVIII). For by then it was almost too late, and so many thousands of patriarchs seemed to have died without hope; yet they could not have had life if they had not hoped that the Lord would come, as the Apostle says: “For in hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope, but what is hoped for” (Rom. VIII). [Note: [Col. 0938D] Another reading: “in what manner”; thus the manuscript and edition.] And what hope could there have been if it had not been promised?

Indeed, just as that beast, wiser than all beasts, brought knowledge of death to the first human being, so it was necessary that the Lord, true Wisdom, should already at that time know the life-giving aid; and so he did. Nor did he cease to make it known, lest so great a work of his, repelled by a single attack of the enemy, should seem to have been created more for ruin than for honor, and lest he who could have overwhelmed so great a work by another’s power should be considered stronger than the one who had ineffably made his work surpass all creatures, if he had either been unable to preserve it or had been unwilling to restore it.

I say, he defended himself against this envy. That Creator and Redeemer of ours defended himself, and at the same time showed that he both could and would do so, since neither power was lacking to his might nor condescension to his mercy. This is all the more worthy of our adoration because, in the very storm of our error, he did not stop; rather, even while provoked, he broke forth more greatly: where we deserved punishment, the hope of redemption was shown; and where we were in the bitter danger of shipwreck, the harbor of salvation was opened. Thus, in a new manner, what had been the occasion of anger began to become the origin of clemency.

[Note: [Col. 0939D] Manuscript and edition: “Thus, by a hidden operation.”]

If, by a hidden operation, he was revealing that he wished our weakness to be an argument for his strength, he was also showing how greatly he loved us when we sinned against him—those whom he could not forget even after their errors; indeed, those whom he would redeem at a higher price than he had created.

Let human cruelty now seek out for criminals either private workhouses or public prisons, and, angry, sigh over iron handcuffs and hard fetters fastened to a rigid beam; let it unleash its ingenuity upon countless forms of punishment. Let every judge test the chastity of his own mind by endangering another, becoming more devoted to cruelty the more removed he is from the crime. For those who are purer of guilt are commonly more savage toward the guilty. These men pursue crimes, or the contagion of criminals, with greater zeal because they have avoided association with wicked deeds more carefully and less negligently.

O wretched men, endowed with every kind of blindness, who adorn good with evil, who exalt self-restraint under the appearance of cruelty, [Note: [Col. 0939D] Manuscript and edition: “they exalt it and commend their own integrity by another’s misfortune.”] and commend their own cruelty by another’s misfortune—when they lend support to their virtues through the destruction of the wretched and applaud the torments of the guilty as evidence of the judge’s innocence.

## CAP. V.

But our God, against all hope and almost against all expectation, drew good from evil through the riches of his mercy, generating and strengthening mercy within anger. He willed the seed of sin to issue in the fruit of pity; and he who ought to have destroyed us because of our transgression promised that, because of his mercy, he would restore us. At the very time when we deserved punishment, he displayed the proof of salvation, so that we might understand how much it is worth to give when one has not been injured, if one gives so much when angry.

Thus, in the first human being, as he was speaking, he immediately promised us judicial assistance; immediately he brought forth good things from his good treasury; immediately he proclaimed to the angels themselves, who were ignorant of it, the sacrament that was to be fulfilled at the end of time; and he promised the earthly Adam an Adam from heaven.

For when he struck the serpent with a curse suited to its deserts, he commanded it to have the earth for food and to crawl upon its belly. And because it itself had brought about that death, he added, saying: “And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and the seed of the woman. She shall crush your head, and you shall watch her heel” (Gen. III).

[Note: [Col. 0939D] In Agobard, who cites it as though from Jerome: “and you shall lie in wait for his heel”; immediately follows what he then marveled at, namely, that the one who, as the evangelist says, was made in the flesh, the one who is the Word, etc.]

Do you not consider, do you not see, that even then he was threatening the serpent in reference to Christ? For I accept no other seed of the woman whatever than that of which the Apostle says, “made of a woman, made of flesh” (Gal. XIV); that which, as the evangelist says (Luke III), “was thought to be the son of Joseph,” but was not—that very one who was the Word made flesh (John I).

For if we consider the ordinary and natural process of generation, women do not have seed; indeed, no woman conceives without a man. And therefore, since the seed of human generation in Adam had already been corrupted by transgression, heavenly seed was promised—not, as the Apostle understands it, from the corruption of man, but from God:

[Note: [Col. 0939D] In the same source: “that it might become flesh in a woman, and the elements …”; [Col. 0940D] the Laurentian manuscript has: “that it might become flesh from a woman, and those elements of bodily substance.”]

when it became flesh in a woman, those elements of bodily substance also—that is, moisture and blood—would naturally be fitted together within the very vessel in which those elements are situated.

The mother, therefore, of our Lord Jesus Christ was promised already then in that woman. [Note: [Col. 0940D] Manuscript: “She was set in opposition to the serpent’s enmity.”] She was placed in opposition to the serpent’s enmity: “I will put,” he says, “enmity between you and the woman” (Gen. III). He certainly does not say, “I put,” lest this should seem to pertain to Eve. It is the word of a promise, transmitted into the future.

“I will put,” he says, “enmity between you and the woman”—that woman, certainly, who would bear the Savior, not the one who would give birth to a fratricide. “I will put,” he says, “enmity between you and the woman”—the woman who, having rejected the ease of believing, would not merely refuse to listen to you if you displayed the sweetness of fruits as a way of opening her eyes, or promised that she would become like the gods; she would also, when Gabriel himself brought the word, demand an explanation of the novelty of the promise, saying, “How shall this be, since I have not known a man?” (Luke I).

That woman whom golden modesty made tremble at the sight of the angel was nevertheless made bold to inquire into the matter by the ardor of her faith and a steadfastness incapable of slipping. She gave to the one who came what modesty had kept silent about, yet she did not yield to the one who promised because of her astonishment. Indeed, concerned about what was being announced, she sought an explanation. The angel, accordingly, did not rebuke her for unbelief, as he did Zechariah, [page 131] but instructed her concerning the novelty of the divine action, saying: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I).

Behold the seed of the woman, which would not be poured into the womb through the passage of genital functions and the union of the two sexes, but would be found within the closed enclosure of an undeflowered virgin.

[Note: [Col. 0940D] Manuscript: “is found in the womb of an undeflowered virgin.”]

Accordingly, when the prophet promises a new thing full of wonder, he sets it forth in a new expression: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. VII).

Certainly, every day we both see and hear of the necessity of procreation; yet of no woman is it said, “she conceived in the womb,” since the substance of the future human being, poured out through the man, grows together in the woman, and the woman’s womb is not the beginning of the human being who is to be born, but the place where what has been deposited is nourished.

Mary, however, was not merely the first but the only woman to conceive in the womb; and the inviolate condition of her modesty brought forth the conception of the womb without damage to her virginity. She alone bore for us what she had not received from us, as the Lord says: “You are from below; I am from above” (John VIII). She alone is mother of a son while remaining a virgin in relation to her husband; her virginity, unaware of conception, acknowledged childbirth; she alone was called a woman not by conceiving but by giving birth.

From her, therefore, the seed of the woman was promised: according to humanity, our Lord and God, who was not infused into the womb but found there, as the evangelist confirms when he says of Mary: “She was found to have [a child] in the womb” (Matt. I).

[Note: [Col. 0940D] Manuscript: “Behold, also, with the prophet’s preceding wording.”]

Behold, the announcement does not depart from the preceding prophetic utterance: “A virgin shall conceive in the womb”; but, in the novelty of the mystery, it also agrees in the similarity of its wording, and by that same style the history of the event is marked—

[Note: [Col. 0940D] Manuscript and edition: “by which the prophet announces that it is to be done. Isaiah says …”]

the style by which the prophet announces that it is to be done. The prophet Isaiah says, “A virgin shall conceive in the womb”; Matthew reports, “She was found to have [a child] in the womb” (ibid.). The effect corresponds to the very word of the promise: the evangelist speaks no differently from the prophet, nor is he confused by the difficulty of finding an expression to convey the novelty of the work.

Where are the grammarians? Where are the counselors? What school produced these men, so that they speak outside ordinary usage? [Note: [Col. 0941D] Manuscript and edition: “which so clearly showed the novelty of the doctrine.”] What school showed so clearly the marked novelty of the doctrine? [Note: [Col. 0941D] Manuscript: “Let them not speak according to human understanding.”] They do not speak according to human understanding, because what they proclaim is not a human work.

[Note: [Col. 0941D] Manuscript and edition: “And although it was a new thing, never before done …”]

And yet they indicate a new thing, never done before, in such a way that you understand that, together with a wondrous work, a wondrous utterance was also born.

Let us return, then, to the holy women of the patriarchs, and see whether anything like this was written of any one of them. We read of Sarah: “And the Lord visited Sarah, as he had said. And God did for Sarah as he had spoken to her, and she conceived and bore Abraham a son” (Gen. XXI).

In the case of Isaac, divine benevolence is shown in these words: “And God heard him, and Rebecca his wife conceived” (Gen. XL). Likewise, concerning Jacob’s wives, it is written: “And Leah conceived and bore a son to Jacob” (Gen. XXIX), and so forth.

Certainly, of none of these women is it written that she conceived in the womb. Yet whatever they conceived, they could not conceive anywhere other than in the womb. But because they knew that they conceived through intercourse with a man, and because conception could not occur while virginity remained intact, Mary alone conceived in the womb: with the seminal entrance unopened, she conceived while her womb remained closed.

For the seed of this conception, if we reason correctly and examine divine matters inwardly, that sentence which, according to the figure appropriate to the time, bound the firstborn to blessings or obligations preceded it: “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exod. XIII).

What is this male that opens the womb, when it is not the necessity of childbirth but marital intercourse that opens the wombs of all women? Indeed, no virgin is said to be “after her husband”; that name, apparently closed off, seems to suit future mysteries.

We have shown above that Scripture says of Rachel: “And God heard her, and opened her womb, and she conceived.” It certainly did not first say, “she conceived,” and afterward, “he opened her womb”; rather, it says first, “he opened it”—namely, so that the husband, having opened the doors of the womb, might enter a field prepared for seed, as one about to sow.

Then it adds, “and she conceived.” Thus it was not childbirth but conception that was indicated; indeed, conception was made possible. The passage did not designate the one who was to be born as he was being born, but the one who was to sow what would be born.

And if, even before conception, she was opened so that she might conceive, certainly the one who was born could not have opened her for long, when he is described as about to be born—he who could not even be conceived while she was closed: “Every male,” he says, “that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Luke II).

What kind of reasoning is this, which does not appear to have been fulfilled according to the literal sense? Jacob fraudulently seized the place of his firstborn brother, yet he was not prevented by the order of birth, nor condemned for his deceit. The sons of Joseph were marked out by their grandfather’s blessing in an order contrary to their rank by birth; nor did the blindness of the one who foresaw the future prevent the son from directing the parent’s right hand, which watered the younger with the sap of the richer blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0942D] Manuscript and edition: “which watered the younger.”]

All these things are plainly contradictory if we think that the statement—“Every male that opens the womb”—refers to those who are born first from women through male seed. [Note: [Col. 0942D] Manuscript and edition: “Every male that opens the womb: one who is born from male seed from among women.”]

But since that sentence has another inward meaning, for this reason such firstborn sons yield their place and lose their blessings.

Jesse’s son David was not the first, second, or third, but the very last of all to be anointed by the prophet, and he was chosen as king though despised above all the others. Nor did the legal sentence promulgated concerning the firstborn flatter either the first or the second son against David, since it would surely have judged the greatest if it judged the wombs of their mothers to have been opened by them. When, then, and in whom do we say that this was fulfilled—a thing that plainly could not fail to be fulfilled?

Whose womb is opened by a fetus, not by a husband? What virgin conceives without ceasing to be a virgin in order to conceive? Certainly not the one of whom Scripture says, “Adam knew his wife, and she bore him a son” (Gen. IV), but the one of whom the evangelist declares, “Joseph did not know her until she had borne a son” (Matt. I).

Therefore, in Mary this was fulfilled without doubt: her womb was opened not by the violation of virginity but by the issuing forth of childbirth. She bore as a virgin, conceived as a virgin, and became a mother before she became a wife. From her came forth that male who truly ought to be called holy, and who opened the womb according to the promise of childbirth, not according to the common custom and nature of conception through a man’s seed.

## CAP. VI.

But since we cannot quickly unfold the rich meanings of God, with so many massive passages of Scripture presenting themselves in support of a single interpretation that it is easier to grow weary than to escape them—since all Scripture is one path through all its meanings, who could travel it in human speech, even if the spirit were to assign angelic wings to mortal tongues?—it is fitting to return to the subject at hand. Let us not set our sails into the deep in a small boat, lest boldness run into danger; rather, for the relief of our weakness, let us sail within sight of the shore, so that if anything frightening arises, there may at least be hope that what we see can easily be grasped.

We were saying that the Lord is the holy seed of the woman, because according to the flesh he would have no human father, and that he was already hostile to the serpent: in the womb of the virgin, the Spirit of God, not material moisture, would generate him. [Note: [Col. 0942D] Manuscript: “would generate him, not virile moisture.”]

Indeed, what follows produces an even greater result through the virgin-born man: “She herself shall crush your head” (Gen. III). Who doubts that, apart from our Lord, no one has crushed the serpent’s head? For he alone walked upon dragons and scorpions; he led captivity captive. And “you shall watch his heel”—to whom else do we believe this pertains?

The heel is the extremity of the footstep. And the Lord, after John’s baptism and a forty-day fast, when he was tempted by that same serpent, already victorious over the third of its deceits, cries out: “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. IV). What else does he command the serpent to watch but what has been placed or left behind? He commands it to watch his heel.

I have said these things above, and from there the argument itself has led us to this point: the inner man, when he thinks—not in this world but above this world—seems to live with that maker of all things and his own Maker, as David says: “Blessed are those who search out his testimonies” (Ps. XI). If it is permissible to say so, this is almost to become God: to meditate on divine things.

That Lord of ours had already revealed the mystery of our salvation at that time; hence he says in the Psalms: “In the heading of the book it is written concerning me” (Ps. XXXIX). The heading of the book is the beginning of Genesis, since all Scripture is one book, and it is one book concerning him of whom it is written, God. We see that the promise concerning him is at its beginning; and the heading of our life is hope. Therefore the heading of the living book is hope made through God.

That Creator, as we have often said, when the world was already growing old, fulfilled what he had promised in the first age of the world. Hence the prophet says: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. XXII). The rod is the mother of the Lord, from whom this staff came forth to sustain the world, already wearied by age.

Let us therefore retrace the whole history of our redemption: he descended into the virgin’s womb and, through his birth, showed himself to be human for the sake of humanity; he made his own creature from the Creator. He took the form of a servant, but emptied himself by the will of his power, not by the nature of his divinity—for through that nature he could not fail to be what he had been.

He earned curses for his saving miracles. He endured spittle, blows, a crown of thorns, and finally the cross. He penetrated the realms below; on the third day he rose again in the body that had been fastened to the cross. As a human being after death, he went to heaven as the living God and victor, sat at the right hand of God, and will come at the appointed time to execute judgment. He is celebrated by the Spirit of God through the mouths of his saints.

To think upon these things is to live. This thought is nourishment for the soul. To fall back or return to these things with the Lord is to be joined to him; through them, to be humbled with him is to suffer with him, to die with him, and also to be raised with him.

What shall I say about the resurrection itself, in which, though we are mocked by the nations, we are not separated from Christ? Even many who call themselves Christians exclude the resurrection of the flesh. Let those who are perhaps granted such a condition be without bodies—if it is permissible to say so—and appear before the Lord in some other way than the Lord returned to the Father, as we believe and proclaim.

## 134 CAP. VII.

What, I say, could be more joyful than this thought? What could be more uplifting than this hope? It ought to remain fixed and cling more firmly to our minds: someday, when we have departed from here, we shall return to our bodies. The separation of soul and body in the meantime does not make us utterly nothing, but serves for our reformation as better beings through the Spirit of God, since we have received the promise that the Lord already gave us this pledge here.

And this body, which by its nature is perishable, weighed down by the merit of its former transgression, and said to be subject to the divine curse, will go to the earth (Gen. III). Again, after a long time—that is, at the end of the ages—when only the smallest, perhaps no, part of it remains as ash, it will be restored by that same earth which corrupts it into nothingness—for the earth itself is to be freed from the slavery of corruption—to the complete solidity of its limbs and renewed into a state of beauty and loveliness.

Whom would such a thought not delight with wonder? The remains of our bodies, I say—either none or certainly only the smallest remnants, however slight, and nevertheless filthy, which the mind has never looked upon without horror—will be restored to their own human form, not, as Pythagoras falsely and deliriously imagined, [Note: [Col. 0943D] Manuscript and edition: “so that it might be believed to be Euphorbus.”] believed to be Euphorbus, but to their own body and identity, reassembled through bones and sinews, through veins, through every vital part, [Note: [Col. 0943D] Manuscript and edition: “not merely formed, but also articulated.”] indeed, joint by joint.

This is not an implausible thing, since the seeds of all crops and plants return greater and more beautiful in the grasses than they were when sown in the earth by human beings or when they fell there of their own accord. [Note: [Col. 0943D] Manuscript and edition: “Who would not rejoice in these seeds, so to speak?”]

Who would not rejoice, so to speak, that he is sown in the earth, which will return us better than it received us, as the Apostle says: “The resurrection of the dead is sown in corruption; but it will rise in incorruption” (1 Cor. XV). [Note: [Col. 0944D] Manuscript and edition: “But it will rise in incorruption.”]

What possession of present things could be compared with this hope? Or what else could raise us to contempt for death except this meditation, unfolded through divine promises and the voices of the prophets?

What had Cleombrotus of Ambracia learned of such a thing in Plato’s book, when he did not fear becoming his own murderer and threw himself from a high wall, believing that after death there would be no judgment and that all souls, without distinction of merits, were carried equally to heaven? So universally did they all hold this as true, and so completely did one cloud of this error envelop all the wise men of that age, that Socrates himself—himself such a praiseworthy teacher, as they think—killed himself privately, so that he would not be killed publicly.

The blessed Apostle had meditated upon and conceived something very different: he had received what he taught “not from human beings, but through a revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. I). He was instructed not beneath the shadowy coverings of the wooded Academy, but illumined by heavenly light; not in some literary school among yawning boys, but in the third heaven among shining angels. He cries out, in contempt of the present life: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. I).

Certainly, he does not seek a wall from which to throw himself to his death, but Christ the Lord, through whom this mortal condition may be swallowed up by immortality. For he understands that dying is gain for the one whose future life is with Christ. Without the Lord, however, nothing profits, even if one gains the whole world, while suffering the loss of one’s soul.

That man, therefore, the vessel of election, believed that through Christ our Lord he would be transformed from this earth—which never returns without interest what it receives, but with a lesser or often greater increase, thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold, as the Lord himself reads in the Gospel concerning the shoots he had planted—from this earth, I say, which also held the truth unknown to Pilate and unseen by any of the rulers of this age: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. XXVIII). The Apostle says that from this earth he would return transformed into the glorious body of the Lord, with his members made radiant.

Wisdom, through Solomon, likewise promises this when it says: “The righteous will shine, and like sparks they will run through the reed-bed” (Wis. III). And so, secure in this declaration—“For me to live is Christ” (Phil. I)—he burst forth into it; in that declaration, whatever merits there were will live, while those who, in their ignorance, were far from him will likewise be unknown.

Now, if it seems good, let us inquire what that Solomonic sentence promised: “The righteous will shine, and like sparks they will run through the reed-bed.” Why, when the brightness of flames is granted to these people, is such a lowly and despised place offered for them to run through, so that those who have grown in the light of their bodies seem to diminish through the contemptibility of the place? What, I ask, is meant by their flying among the reeds in comparison with the stars, and traversing the wretched growths of the earth in the form of starry radiance, when reeds and radiance are so incongruously mingled?

Attend, I beg you, to the words of the divine mystery. Just as God is not concerned with oxen, so he is not concerned with a reed-bed. Or what do reed-beds do in the resurrection, except represent us through the forms of all animals and plants? Hence, as the Apostle says, everything was written for our sake (Rom. XV).

Understand that, through the images of the reed-bed, faithless and unbelieving people are signified: their bodies are pleasing on the surface but inwardly empty of virtues.
