When the spirit of vanity first blows upon them, they imitate the hissing of the serpent, and, as offspring of vipers, serve sound and healthy births. [Note: [Col. 0944D] Manuscript and edition: “and the native sounds of vipers, etc.”]

“They will run as sparks through the reed-bed,” he says. Thus the saints will be among sinners, since not all flesh is the same flesh. “Through the reed-bed,” he says—that is, through bodies empty of light and destined to burn with another’s radiance, for whom the brightness of the saints will be future punishment. For God is a consuming fire, and the righteous will come into the likeness of the Godhead.

For God made the human being; he made him in his own image (Gen. I). And the Apostle bears witness that he believes humanity will necessarily become like him. For if he was like God when he was made, he will also be like him when he rises again. Whatever now appears unlike our Maker in us has all been impressed upon us by the fault of transgression. The craftsman of falsehood distorted the living form of truth through swollen deeds and, after corrupting our minds, inscribed his depravity even upon our limbs. Through the glory of the resurrection, what was wrongly added or diminished will be washed away, and only that which reflects the Maker of all things as in a mirror will shine forth. Thus the one who tampered with the work will grieve that he has lost it, while humanity will at last glory in being whole.

Yet not all of us, as we have already said, will be in the light, but only the righteous. For we will all rise, but we will not all be changed (1 Thess. IV); the diversity of merits will make a distinction among persons. Even among the saints there will be some difference in their works, as the Apostle says: “Star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. XV). How much more shall we perceive such diversity among the ungodly and sinners, some of whom rise for judgment and others for the counsel of the saints?

And although they are separated at the very time of the resurrection, what shall we say of their appearance and form? These, as I think, will not be found in some woven garment or in the elaborate handiwork of women, but in their own merits and prayers. Blessed John shows this in the Revelation, where he says that he saw the saints clothed in linen (Rev. XIX). And lest we should seek threads or material under the covering of linen, or imagine that anything material, corruptible, and fleeting is being fashioned in the heavenly realms, he added: “The linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.”

Then, as I understand it, what is now hidden beneath the body will appear on the surface of our bodies. Then each person’s conscience will become his garment—wretched me! Then what each person has built upon that foundation, than which no other can be laid (1 Cor. III), will stand forth, so that the one who established what will endure may receive a reward, while the one who built what will burn may suffer loss.

Why should I now recount what follows, all of which belongs to the saints? Flesh without earth, a body without the sensation of pain, a soul without fear, life without end, age without time, light without night, blessedness without end? I see a human being, and in the human being, God, “because God is all in all” (1 Cor. XV).

Everything that now appears impossible for a human being will then occur through the munificence of the eternal King: it will be veiled and revealed, liquefied and made solid again. The human being will become one whom the disciples did not perceive entering to them through solid, bodily walls and doors, yet whom they all saw standing within before them. And the body, together with the Spirit of God, will accomplish everything that the Spirit of God had nurtured without this body. [Note: [Col. 0945D] Manuscript and edition: “to be with the Spirit of God. Christianity cannot be satisfied with the delight of these thoughts.”]

Christianity cannot be satisfied with the delight of these understandings. This is its rest, this its pleasure, this its delight: to go in thought into the dwelling of God and there claim for itself a place and a share in his throne, not by presumption but by the promise of the Godhead. Nor does this seem difficult to it, once it recognizes that its own human being is already there in Christ the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0945D] Manuscript: “recognizes that the Lord is its own.”]

It claims for itself a rightful status through kinship with God by means of the flesh he assumed, because we are of his flesh and of his bones. For he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning of every principality and power, as the Apostle proclaims: “From him the whole body, being joined together, brought forth through its connection, and knit together, grows into the increase of God” (Col. II).

What, then, shall I say about the coming judgment, and the day of the Lord, desirable to the devout and to be fled by the ungodly? What shall I say about that fiery flood—not of waters—with the earth smoking, the sea fleeing, and heaven folded up like a book? [Note: [Col. 0946D] Edition: “These things are sorrowful to the rich of this age, but …”]

These things are sorrowful to the rich of this age, but they are to be awaited by the poor of Christ, for whom the Lord sighs in the Psalm, saying: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise” (Ps. XII).

What shall I say about that immense tribunal, awesome in the majesty of its Judge and in its twelve seats, and about the great power given by the Son, so that in judging they may have even the angelic beings assigned to them, as though by their Creator, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. VI). And what will be thought not to be subjected to those to whom that spiritual nature of wickedness is also to be made subject?

What, then, will those do who now glory in honors, who through terrifying prefectures, fasces, and eternal—so they suppose—consulships strive to make themselves equal to God by seizure, not by nature? What will he do who joins house to house? Who, having thrown the state into confusion and broken all the boundaries that hemmed it in on every side, leaping over mountains, rivers, and seas, wishes, so far as it concerns him, that the one earth common to all should become a single possession? Driven by insatiable desire beyond the breadth of the immense world, he spreads himself into the anxiety of Alexander of Macedon and the innumerable worlds of the Epicureans. Having acquired, through his greed, the narrow limits of this world, he burns with credulous expectation of another, without considering what his own body can bear; he thinks he will suffer loss of his rightful possession if he does not lend credence to his madness.

What will those do who, as correctors of morals, rebuke and harass the household of the Lord when it lives with greater attention and discipline—whether in garments of humble color, in the dry austerity of food, or in the wakeful sobriety of vigils? [Note: [Col. 0946D] Manuscript and edition: “or in humble clothing, etc.”] They attack them as though they were pampered by softer clothing, fattened by more abundant banquets, or drowsing on warmer beds, not knowing that, in the holy martyrs and confessors of God, his eye is struck as the pupil of the eye.

They will surely perish; on that day all their thoughts will perish. Neither Lucius Crassus nor Marcus Antonius nor Tullius, more eloquent than these men, will defend them before that tribunal, because then every tongue of this age will fall silent. Only justice will be eloquent in its humble places—the justice that made the mouths of infants articulate and loosed the tongues of the mute into a new song, acquiring for itself, through its mercy, a heavenly harmony from its little sheep.

Even if human efforts should cease in celebrating his glory, the condemned stones are displayed as an accusation bringing confusion upon the human race.

[Note: [Col. 0946D] Manuscript: “But how have I exceeded the subject before me …”]

But I have strayed from the subject, as though rebuking human wickedness. Like a public accuser of uniform evil, I have not spared worldly vices, while pitying certain people. Yet even if it were the time for judging, I would not dare to throw a stone at the adulterer; and even if authority armed me with a purer conscience for an innocent judgment, I ought nevertheless to have waited for the proper time. The Apostle teaches that he did not take judgment away from the saints, but postponed it. He says: “Do not judge before the time” (1 Cor. IV).

He indicates that we must await the time of the resurrection, when, through the glory of incorruption, the restored flesh will appear in wonder before the judgment; when steadfastness will already abide in eternity, while fear concerning falling away will be present. Then one will not tremble to pass judgment on another when one has deserved to be secure concerning oneself.

For now, however, everything is uncertain and wavering, as the Apostle says: “Considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. VI)—for one who does not know the condition of his own standing may easily judge another’s ruin. And what if God gives confidence to the wretched, as to the blessed? Let us praise instead the rewards of the saints—that is, let us praise what is true—lest we be marked as reckless or untimely, whether because of our conscience or because of the time.

## CAP. VIII.

Let us therefore return to those most noble and joyful thoughts of the saints; for nothing is more joyful than for a mortal to meditate upon the inheritance promised to him. Let us place before our eyes the one whom we have mentioned, since it is safer to celebrate what is true than to condemn what is pitiable—although truly blessed things cannot be related without also relating the misery of sinners. [Col. 0946D]

Let us see, then, as we have determined, the saints of God flying everywhere with torches and brandishing double-edged swords, their right hands flashing forth for vengeance. For this is the glory of God’s saints; this is the military service despised in this world; this is what has been scattered by the tongues of all in their slanders. Then the fruit of our patience, then the reward of our endurance, will be this—these will be the rewards for [bearing] the name “blasphemers”: to have every proud soul and every person who exalts himself subject to them; to have the once most powerful kings of the world, worshiped throughout the whole earth, brought forward with iron handcuffs and fetters; and to have their nobles, bearing the monstrous weight of chains upon their necks and throats, presented before the brilliance of that august tribunal to those whom they had once despised, scorned, and mocked.

For the order of things will be changed: this age is for the wealthy, but another is to come for the wretched. For “woe to the rich, because they have received their reward”; but woe to those rich men to whom it will have to be said: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink” (Matt. 25). Woe, certainly, to those rich men who did not wish to make friends for themselves from unjust wealth; who, with their abundance bearing fruit, planned in their thoughts to build new storehouses of immense capacity, in which they would not know where they would eat on the following day. [Col. 0947A]

[Note: The Codex reads: “in which they did not know where they would store it.”] [Col. 0947D]

Their soul was being demanded of them at that very time, while they were occupied throughout a single night with empty anxiety; for they did not cease to hoard treasure, nor did they neglect to keep watch over their buried wealth. Hence poor Lazarus, together with that patriarch who lived as a stranger in the world, rejoices in his resting-place. But the rich man, on the contrary, burns in eternal fires; stripped of every honor and possession, he implores the divine assistance of the poor man whom he had once despised, and longs to be touched by the very tip of that man’s finger, whose poverty he had not supported even with crumbs falling from his table amid his sumptuous dishes and abundant banquets.

Since, then, the judgment prescribed above is to be celebrated by us—that is, by the saints—“vengeance upon the nations and upon the peoples” has been given to us. [Col. 0947B] When this is considered, what state of mind, what ardor of spirit, what longing for the future, and what contempt for the present arise in us can more easily be felt than expressed? Who is there who, hastening toward these things, would not desire to be released and to be with Christ (Phil. 1)? And what great thing is it if death is despised for the sake of such great and such excellent blessings, for the sake of which this life too ought to be despised? For “whoever loses his life for these things will save it; but whoever saves his life here will lose it.”

Indeed, when most people in this world are so inflamed by the ambition of their minds, as though by frenzied fires, that they spare neither hoarded wealth, nor inheritances, nor even their own children—whom, when accused of avarice, they are accustomed to set forward as their excuse—while they purchase prefectures and consulships, offices which death takes away and a successor excludes, what madness is it not rather to obtain, at every expense and even at the cost of life itself, those things which would make the promoted either secure concerning the eternity of life or glorious in the everlasting dignity of judgment?

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0947C]

The time admonishes us, and the place itself suggests it; nor does the subject seem unrelated, since we have begun to discuss the merits of the saints. We should therefore refute the blasphemies of most miserable misery, which seem to belong to this matter.

[Note: The Codex reads: “of most miserable unbelief.”] [Col. 0947D]

For there have been people who, when outstanding and heavenly works were already being performed through the relics of the saints, almost in our own time, preferred to wound them with detraction rather than receive them with veneration. They vomited forth against the servants of God that ancient poison of Jewish unbelief which those people once poured out against the Lord himself with viperous tongues and deadly hissing, saying: “By what authority are you doing this? And who gave you this authority?” (Matt. 25).

For they recited to us, while we were standing nearby, what foolish unbelief was saying about the divine and blessed Gervasius and Protasius. While attempting to snatch something from Pope Ambrose, they did not fear to violate the martyrs with sacrilegious words, seeking an explanation for the miracles in this fashion:

“What is this? Because they are martyrs, have they deserved the gifts of miraculous powers? Why is what was granted to them long ago being exercised only so late? Or, if they did not display these powers at the time when they suffered, how have they now performed them? What is this that they seem now to display? Or did Ambrose make them greater by revelation than by the dignity of martyrdom?”

[Note: The Codex reads: “greater by the dignity of martyrdom than by favor.”] [Col. 0947D]

Do you recognize, though in different words, the same falsehood which we have reported as having been directed against the martyrs concerning the Lord: “By what authority are you doing this? And who gave you this authority?” (Matt. 21)?

It is, as I think, a lukewarm consolation, born of envy: to ask whether what you see to be divine is truly divine, and to demand a reason when it is necessary to believe. And since the Apostle says, “Love believes all things” (1 Cor. 13), who doubts that those who have not applied faith to such great works are without the love of God? [Col. 0948A]

But the person who investigates as though testing the matter denies faith, asking, “From where does this authority come?”—as though it were not clear that the holy martyrs now perform miracles in the spirit by that same authority by which they previously overcame their adversaries in the flesh and in their passion.

Let us set our foot against these people—if it is lawful to say so—these children of the Jews; and just as recently we crushed their ancestor, that is, the Jew who thought himself excessively wise in his sacrilege,

[Note: The Codex and printed editions read: “who considered himself wise in the sacrifice.”] [Col. 0948D]

by the gift of divinity, so let us also destroy this offspring of blasphemies under a Christian name, through him who said: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the intelligent” (1 Cor. 1). Thus we may glory through the Lord in a double triumph, and they may recognize that understanding of divine realities is established in the Catholic faith, not in the wisdom of the world. The Lord warns us: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7).

Thus it may become clearer that the obscurities of unbelief are open to the faithful, while even what is plain in faith cannot be seen by unbelievers.

Perhaps, in your concern, vigilance, and life-giving diligence, you may ask what that dispute was in which the Lord granted us a trophy over a false Israelite. I shall recount it and not remain silent, since you love to have the page extended by such matters. Although it may seem inappropriate to insert a new subject before the earlier one has been completed, I prefer, for your sake, to speak of some matters even out of their proper order rather than pass over what has now been granted to me through your prayers. [Col. 0948B]

One of the enemies of the cross of Christ—indeed, one of the household of God and even a teacher—attacked the Lord in a spirit of blasphemy. Because of the scandal of his people, which they had taken upon themselves against our Lord, he produced examples from the Law. Just as his murderous father once tested the Lord on the pinnacle of the Temple and shamelessly proclaimed what had been promised concerning him in the Law, so this man, lest his perfidy seem less learned or his falsehood appear exposed as unsupported by greater authority, said:

“Our prophet Elisha performs more miracles than your Lord Christ. For when you report that Lazarus was restored to life as a great deed (John 11), what more can you say than that a dead man was raised by a living man? I shall produce something which even by your own confession is considered true. For our Elisha, already dead, revived another dead man through contact with his bones (2 Kings 13)—a man whom a crowd, fleeing because of the arrival of raiders and abandoning the duty of burial, had thrown beside Elisha’s body. Elisha brought him back to life, pouring vital warmth from his cold bones and bloodless body into another corpse. He did not give what he possessed; rather, he granted to another what he himself did not then possess.

“I believe this seems to you greater than all other miracles: that a dead man was sent back into the air of life through a dead man, and that, at the very time when he himself was bound by the law of nature, he dissolved nature’s law. If this surpasses all other works, why is he not considered the greater one, whom nevertheless we confess to be prophet and Lord?” [Col. 0948C]

[Note: The Codex and printed editions read: “whom nevertheless we confess to be prophet and Lord.”] [Col. 0948D]

“Or, if you know anything similar to this, declare it, so that the one who was superior in the excellence of his deed may also surpass him in honor.”

At these words our leaders were stunned. They gave no answer and produced no weapon with which to strike back; almost overcome beneath the empty machinery and useless battering ram of their adversary, they nearly collapsed—so much so that the man who, as they say, ought to have been the fugitive from all people carried off the glory of victory without a contest. [Col. 0948D]

When this was reported to me, I groaned that such negligence existed among us that we could not even establish the truth, while others were able to thrust falsehood forward in place of truth. I asked the Lord—since nothing belongs to us—that he supply his own weapons, by which the reproach of his cowardice might be removed.

[Note: The Codex reads: “by which the reproach of his cowardice might be removed.”] [Col. 0948D]

“Give me,” I said, “this man who speaks great words: ‘Our lips are our own; who is our lord?’ (Ps. 11). I shall bring forward an answer through him who destroys the tongue that speaks great things, so that they may understand that a servant must not be equated with his lord, although the Jews themselves know that the ancient prophets performed no miracles by their own powers.”

Indeed, when Elisha himself inherited the spirit of his master and came, as though somewhat insolent, in return for the reward of his gifts, he still could not divide the waters except under invocation of God (2 Kings 2). [Col. 0949A]

But I admit that, for the moment, this was the virtue of the matter proposed: it would bring greater glory to our faith if, while believing, we also overcame the temptation.

“What do you say, blasphemer of the Lord?”

“Elisha himself,” he replied, “being dead, raised another dead man by contact with his body.”

Here, so that the prophet’s power may rise fully to the level of his Lord in every respect, consider what happened with the Lord Jesus Christ. When your unbelief fortified his tomb with stones and soldiers surrounded the stone, I suppose this was done because his resurrection required reliable witnesses. For if you wished to believe, you knew that he would rise. Then, when the hinges of the underworld and the earth were suddenly shaken, amid the soldiers’ astonishment and the stones’ collapse, he did not raise someone else into the light, but himself.

If these had been Elisha’s own gifts, he would have preferred to give them to himself; nor could he provide another with what he himself needed. Indeed, even your ancestors showed that this was the greater deed when they mocked the Lord on the cross, saying: “He saved others; let him save himself. Let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. 27). [Col. 0949B]

Therefore we conquer by the judgment of your own people. Your people promised that they would believe if he supplied for himself what he had been accustomed to supply for others. Why do you not believe what you admit to be greater? Certainly no one else possessed this authority. Indeed, the Lord himself says concerning his soul: “I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10).

Review the proud images of your ancestors and unfold again the virtues of the patriarchs, and you will find who possessed such authority. Why should I not believe that he can free my soul, who was able to free his own?

As I was about to say more, the recollection of the matter suggested that the volume was growing, and therefore that the course of this discussion should be recalled, since the earlier matter still stands at the door and deserves its own space, even if under tighter reins, still untouched. In truth, it was not necessary to say much on this point, lest he grow as well—unless he thought he had produced something great and was seeking victory through an extended dispute. We have broken not his wisdom, which was nonexistent, but his pride, which abounded. [Col. 0949C]

## CHAPTER X

Having dismissed this Israelite, lest he boast that he had fought—for what we have said was offered chiefly to instruct our own people, not for a contest and struggle with those who refuse to believe even when they are defeated—we must return to the place from which I wandered here, almost cutting across the paths of meaning. Otherwise we might be judged to have rashly given what is holy to dogs or scattered pearls before swine (Matt. 7).

The sheep of the house of Israel must be visited more carefully, since, if the love of God is in us, “who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (1 Cor. 11). They must be taught, moreover, lest they speak even to the point of blasphemy, if perhaps they do not grasp or understand what has been prophesied.

They ask whether the divine power now appearing in the martyrs is truly divine. What people, belonging to what law, ask this? Surely people of the Christian law, which has been so equipped with prophecies that nothing so new or unexpected can arise in our times that the more discerning faith will not admire it, or the weaker faith will not blaspheme it. [Col. 0949D]

The ancient prophets foretold everything up to the Lord. The apostles prophesied everything that remained after the Lord. Blessed Paul, through the freedom of the Holy Spirit, did not remain silent when he said: “We know in part and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13). This does not mean that he does not know all things or prophesy all things, especially since Christ speaks in him; rather, he prophesies from a part of the whole and knows from a part of the whole.

He prophesies to us what he knows belongs to that time which was to come. Whatever he prophesies, he certainly prophesies for the age that is to come. He prophesies the whole, although he prophesies in part. For he prophesies those things whose disclosure was needed by the portion of that age which remains until the end.

Therefore he prophesies in part because part had already been prophesied; and for that reason the prophet knew the things that he prophesied were to come. The fullness of time, as he himself said, has abolished the portions of that prophecy in this way: “When what is perfect has come, what is in part will be destroyed” (ibid.)—that is, when, at the conclusion of the world, neither greater knowledge nor further prophecy will remain to be sought. [Col. 0950A]

Finally, to demonstrate the power of this understanding more clearly, he added: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (ibid.). For the present, everything exists through figures and is shaded by certain outlines of images, so that the weakness of our flesh and our earthly substance might stretch itself toward the truth of spiritual things; so that, shown only faintly through a mirror, the beauty of that truth might arouse desire in us; and so that it might teach us how great that truth itself is in its substance, since it appears so wondrous even in riddles reflected by its light.

Therefore we do not yet behold what has been promised through the mirror, nor do we possess it on account of the merits of our powers. We marvel at it through an obscure light, but we do not yet hold it as something delivered into our hands. [Col. 0950B]

Then prophecy and knowledge will cease, when we have entered into the very power of all the promises that was being promised.

This is also why prophecy is always obscure: it is sung at one time and seen at another. What is spoken while it is not seen is almost not believed to have been foretold. Thus Isaiah, when he had been granted to recognize our redemption long beforehand in the Virgin’s womb and displayed it to the people as though it were already present, saying, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7), disturbed the age of the unbelieving Israelites by speaking of what was both present and future.

The earlier Israelites killed their own prophet because they did not see what he showed them; and these later Israelites killed him who had been prophesied to them because they did not receive the prophecy.

[Note: The Codex and printed editions read: “because they did not repeat the prophecy.”] [Col. 0949D; Col. 0950D]

We must take care that the same thing does not happen to us, if our own age blasphemes those whom the earlier age persecuted. [Col. 0950C]

And since, as we have said, what was foretold has come, there is nothing still to come that was not previously foretold, the Lord himself saying: “Behold, I have foretold everything to you” (Mark 13).

Let us rather see whether these things were ever poured into the ears of our ancestors, which now seem to us to be imagined as fulfilled before our eyes. Let us see whether “the one and same Spirit” performs all these things (1 Cor. 12). Finally, let us see whether even an angel from heaven should proclaim anything other than what has been proclaimed to us.

Even though the Lord’s miracles themselves bear witness through the torments of demons, Satan does not cast out Satan, because the uniformity of wickedness, naturally formed by an undivided association, does not fear that an accession of likeness will harm it, but receives an increase from it.

For the power of wicked spirits had gathered many into the form of a single legion, and the confederation of serpentine iniquity had massed them together. Their multitude did not hinder them; just as, joined together by their miserable weakness, they acquired a kind of strength, so they feared incurring the emptiness of a divided and dispersed substance.

[Note: Another reading omits “spirit.” The Codex and printed editions read: “the wickedness of the spirits of a legion,” and so forth.] [Col. 0950D]

[Note: The Codex and printed editions read: “the emptiness of an insubstantial separation,” and so forth.] [Col. 0950D]

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0950D]

But for the moment setting aside this part of the argument, let us prove, as we proposed, that what we admire in the churches of the Lord and in the cemeteries of the saints is believed to occur by divine power, provided that it has been prophesied.

In this matter, so difficult and arduous, and previously treated by no one, we ought to consult the Lord, if we were not afraid that our lack of merit might be rejected because of our boldness; for no one outside the Lord himself can explain what belongs to him. [Col. 0951A]

Indeed, it is astonishing from where such confidence has flowed into wretched people, and from where such intimate familiarity in addressing the Lord has arisen, that we dare to burst forth in this voice: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1).

Who conceived so great a desire? Who, neglecting to measure his own worth, sighed with such lofty prayers that he longed to touch the Lord’s mouth face to face? And would that he deign to kiss us with the kiss of those whom he himself has deigned to kiss, so that, standing among the second and third ranks, we might deserve to draw some portion of knowledge from the lips of those who learned the fullness of wisdom from the mouth of the Lord himself.

Yet even if we were supported by the privileges of great merits, examples had been set before us as certain lofty foundations repeatedly laid for modesty, lest the presumption of light-minded disorder dare anything improper.

Who was more chosen than blessed Peter? Who was more lifted up in hope? What was freer in faith than the Lord’s promise that he would kiss him with the kiss of his mouth, when he said: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” and again: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16)?

Yet Peter, bending under a certain weight of modesty, submits the confidence that he possessed through his merit to a more modest form of inquiry. At the Lord’s supper, he does not ask directly who is going to betray the Lord; instead, humble and bashful, he asks for the Lord’s kiss through another’s mouth.

He did have confidence before the Lord, so that afterward he would presume unshaken confidence even before a human being; as when, while the Lord was walking across the sea, Peter dared to ask that he too be supported by the waters, whose backs had been made firm beneath the Lord’s footsteps. Yet in this he was somewhat less confident but more prudent toward us, for by his action he placed before us, as in a mirror, forms that we might imitate.

If, through an intermediary, he cautiously investigates the Lord’s foreknowledge, what could be more worthy than this instruction? What could be subtler than this art of consulting?

[Note: The Codex and printed editions read: “What ought we to do?”] [Col. 0951D]

We, whose confidence has no merit, ought at least to possess the modesty of this example. Let us imitate blessed Peter even in this respect, for he showed not only with what humility, but also by what means, we may reach what we desire. Let us seek from the one whom Peter himself was not ashamed to question the resolution of this question.

Let us seek it from the one who, resting upon the Lord’s breast as though upon the ark of the New and Old Testament, approached not merely the threshold of certain divine oracles as a diligent inquirer, but entered the innermost chamber of the hidden dispensation like a familiar priest. For this reason he alone saw the Word in the beginning, when he was entrusted with measuring the interior sanctuary, just as the outer altar of the most holy Temple was entrusted to others. [Col. 0951C]

May he himself lead us from that book which he wept over when it was sealed with seven seals, and over whose opening he rejoiced, not through some false likeness but through open doors, into his own breast, the dwelling of truth.

## CHAPTER XII

But lest we linger while consulting him, he anticipates those who inquire, by the shortcut of his foreknowledge, and illuminates what he saw would at some point be a source of trembling for our minds. He also gives, as though questioned, answers from Patmos—from that place, certainly, where the secrets of heaven, closed even to Caesar, were entered by one who was no stranger; where, driven away from human society, he came to know the mysteries of angels.

For he says:

[Note: This reading differs in many respects from the Vulgate.] [Col. 0951D]

“I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been killed because of the word of God and because of the testimony of Jesus, which they possessed; and individual robes were given to them. And they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?’ And individual white robes were given to them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers who would later be killed in imitation of them should be completed” (Rev. 6). [Col. 0951D]

[Note: The Codex reads: “O truly divine Apocalypse, revealed by so great an apostle at the fitting time of confession, so that they might be made more steadfast for endurance when the merits of those who had suffered were shown to them,” and so forth.] [Col. 0952D]

O truly divine Apocalypse, revealed by so great an apostle at the fitting time of confession, so that they might be made more steadfast for endurance when the merits of those who had suffered were shown to them!

We must not therefore wander through the leaves of the Sibyls. Just as their pages struggled against the uncertain evils of the spirits of the world, so their places were disturbed by the winds of this air.

[Note: The Codex and printed editions read: “through the leaves of syllables, whose pages, like the Sibyls’, struggled with the uncertain evil spirits of the world,” and so forth.] [Col. 0952D]

Behold, the apostle most clearly unfolds what he possessed and brings light to an exceedingly obscure question. He had perceived that these things would one day be said—things which a more hostile tongue now hurls toward the destruction of its hearers and itself through words artfully softened as with oil.

Therefore, he says, “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been killed.” No one doubts the testimony of the witness concerning the faith; let the testimony be examined and the meaning of the answer be uncertain, but not the authority of the speaker. [Col. 0952A]

## CHAPTER XIII

First of all, this must be observed: the apostle testifies that he saw the souls of the martyrs who had been killed. Thus, when we begin to discuss the gifts granted to them, no one may say that these gifts must be assigned to the martyrs only after the resurrection, since the text teaches that they have already been granted to their souls—especially because their complaint about the delay of judgment supports our position. The one who will rise complains of delay; not the one who has already risen. For it is one thing to ask that you may possess something, and another thing already to possess it.

The martyrs’ army is given robes, and, as though ungrateful for such great freedom, it strikes heaven with a great accusation concerning the delay of vengeance. With no slight weight of words it reproaches the delay, saying: “How long, Lord?” That is to say: How long will you not avenge those whom you ought to have avenged at once? “How long, Lord?” That is to say: Will you delay us beyond the end of the ages? For we have already reached the end, and you do not speak of our vengeance. [Col. 0952B]

They add this with astonishing force: “Will you not avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” Therefore they do not say “How long?” if those mortals are still living on earth who persecuted the servants of the Lord with clubs, stones, claws, whips, lead, iron, wild beasts, and fire.

For “how long?” is a charge of prolonged duration: either “how long?” is without end, or the persecutors still remain in the flesh; or they have departed this life, even though they dwell on earth, if “how long?” is not false.

But nothing false is brought forward by witnesses of the truth. Therefore what is required is interpretation, not faith; the meaning is somewhat obscure in expression, but it is not excluded—it is veiled.

When they say, “How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” they do not desire the blood and deaths of those mortals who once raged against them in popular uprisings or, supported by tribunals, pronounced capital sentences. Nor is it right that the dead be accused, since while they lived they were defended by these words: “Do not hold this sin against them; for they do not know what they are doing” (Acts 7). [Col. 0952C]

If, amid the tortures of their passions and the bitter struggles of death, the martyrs prayed so piously for the unjust, the impious, the bloodstained, and the blasphemers; if, finally, at the very time when the extreme sensation of suffering could have stirred any one of them to cursing, a prayer for human beings was poured forth, who does not understand that it was not the minds of the martyrs but the persons of their persecutors that were indicated?

The martyrs sought those whom it must be believed still dwell on earth at that time—those whom ignorance did not defend—not those who had ceased, by the condition of their natural substance, to dwell on earth, and whom the martyrs themselves had long ago excused on the ground of ignorance.

We are not ignorant who these people are. They are without doubt the spiritual powers of wickedness and darkness, which still dwell on earth and did not sin against the servants of God through ignorance. [Col. 0952D]

For when those powers said to the Lord himself, “Why have you come to torment us before the time?” (Matt. 8), how could they have been ignorant of his servants? They would not have persecuted his servants if they had been ignorant that they were his servants. Therefore, when they persecuted them, they knew whom they were attempting through torments to tear away from their Lord.

Consequently, when the blessed martyrs intercede for human beings and defend them by excusing their ignorance, it follows that those powers are held guilty knowingly—those who themselves poured the darkness of ignorance over human beings, whose fury even excuses human impieties.

Who else could these be than those who are not even friendly toward their own, since they do not allow them to be good; who are also enemies of God’s servants, since they persecute those who do not know what is good? [Col. 0953A]

## CHAPTER XIV

Let us examine what follows the complaint of these holy souls: “And individual white robes were given to them.”

What does this mean—that they are clothed a second time? For previously, as it is written, they received garments from God; and now they are given garments with a double freedom.

[Note: The Codex and printed editions read: “and now, with liberty doubled in their garments,” and so forth.] [Col. 0953D]

Since these garments are spiritual, we need not fear that the garments first given might be seen outwardly; nor, indeed, has the complaint arisen from this. Therefore, since the difference and significance of the garments are not without mystery, we must understand them as varieties of gifts and riches of operations, because one and the same Spirit supplies them.

They first receive garments when, through confession, they laid down their bodies—I suppose, so that they might be found clothed, not naked. Again they receive other garments after their appeal, or rather after the transformation of such prolonged patience and endurance.

When they receive these, who does not understand that they are infused not only with a new garment but also with the power by which they now shine and appear? If they had asked for one thing and received another, they would have been mocked either for rejecting the gifts or for asking for more.

But since it is not characteristic of God to mock those to whom he has made great promises, and since they do not complain after the second act of generosity, should we doubt that this manifestation, granted to those asking for vengeance, pertains to the consolation of their complaints?

[Note: The Codex reads: “that that hope pertains,” and so forth.] [Col. 0953D]

But if it pertains to their consolation, what greater consolation could be found than this power, by which they pursue demons—that is, their own persecutors?

For if we compare these robes with our own clothing, let us search for some other robes as well, lest the martyrs lack something in which to store them. But this is ridiculous, as is immediately evident, because it departs from the true and necessary interpretation.

The complaint was generated by the delay of vengeance, until the end of the times—that is, our own; for upon us the ends of the ages have come. To dispel this delay, the souls are clothed with robes, lest they be thought entirely naked and without greater protection.

The condition of souls stripped of their bodies is one thing; the condition of human beings still living in the flesh is another. For us, sheep’s wool and the work of women provide garments; for them, merits make their clothing. [Col. 0953C]

When, therefore, after the martyrs’ complaint, the souls are clothed with robes, they are granted divine protection—the same protection with which that chosen vessel also desired to be clothed. When Adam had lost that garment, he was found naked even in paradise.

Finally, the action itself indicates what we ought to understand by the robes. If we believe that the martyrs asked for vengeance, then we believe that, for their consolation, they received something in the meantime. If their complaint was quieted because of the robes, as though because of gifts of clothing, did they not deserve these first gifts as well?

But since, as I have said, the varieties of powers by which the illustrious souls are divinely strengthened are signified by the robes, the text shows, after the second generosity and in accordance with the form of their request, what they seem to have obtained against those persecutors who dwell on earth and what they will still obtain, while those persecutors will kill their fellow servants in a like persecution until the predetermined number of witnesses is completed.

Here too we must not pass over the fact that, between the two periods of persecution, this voice of the martyrs came first. It indicates those who blaspheme when they are astonished that the martyrs have obtained something new in our time.

For since we see that there have been cruel persecutions and believe that more are to come, the intervening period in which the martyrs who preceded us are rewarded is our own time. Therefore they now perform these works—not because of merit, which they have always possessed, but because of the power which they have recently acquired.

## CHAPTER XV

[End of supplied source.]

Perhaps someone may wonder what it is for which they are ordered to wait: if the virtue that would bring judgment upon the demons has already burst forth to the maturity of punishment, they are nevertheless admonished to await the resurrection [Col. 0954A]. Moreover, this glory had also been promised to them in David’s songs in these words: “They will rejoice in their beds” (Ps. 149). While they are buried, they will indeed rejoice. He used “beds” for graves, from which they will also rise when they have been roused by the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God (1 Thess. 4). They are therefore truly called beds, in which they now rest. Even if “they will rejoice in their little chambers” was first intended to refer to the future, namely, when they would rise from their graves, it has been fulfilled to such an extent that we can see without doubt that they rejoice in their beds. For what other such exultation could enter their souls than when, before those very beds—that is, as we have said, the graves of the saints—their enemies, whom they once thought they had killed, now acknowledge, not without the bitterness of torment, that they both live and avenge themselves? These are the benefits that those robes, which a special generosity has repeated, have conferred upon them: through them those who were not named are invoked, those who were unknown are celebrated, and those who were not seen appear. As we read, they did not have these robes until now [Col. 0954B], but they have now begun to possess them.

In this form the woman is praised in Solomon, who makes double garments for her husband: one in the endurance of suffering, the other in the power of vengeance. It is holy and devout for us to read it in this way; otherwise we ought not even to speak, lest either our unbelief or our ignorance descend into the darkness of paganism through blasphemous argument, since the prophecy preceded this event in order to bring light to what was to come.

Now it remains that we believe that the things we have proved were promised—and not merely promised, but also requested—are brought about by God. If they were both requested and granted to none other than those who asked, what is surprising if they do not conceal either what they had requested or what they rejoice to have received beforehand? They demand punishments from those who dwell on earth: those whom the accusation encompasses are attacked by the power of the saints. For they dwell on earth who possess the minds of people who possess earthly things; and when the martyrs [Note: [Col. 0953D] Other copies: *martyria*.] demand punishment for them, they also plead on behalf of those whom they had possessed.

Finally, they pursue their own desires in such a way that they exclude them from earthly habitation—that is, from earthly people who are possessed. Or do they bring a false accusation because the demons are tortured, and do we favor our enemies? The martyrs rise up against them with an almost envious indignation and complain that they are being allowed to remain for so long a span of ages [Note: [Col. 0954D] Manuscript: *and we do not pretend*.]; yet we pretend to wonder what this means, as though they ought not, or ought not even in our own time, to pay what they have deserved since Adam.

As for the fact that this miracle seems to have first arisen at Milan, or to have been granted to the good Ambrose, who does not see that our faith was approved by divine testimonies because of the Arians’ unbelief? For when the Catholic faith in Italy had endured intolerable tyranny under Auxentius, at last, when the Lord granted back its ancient liberty, it breathed again, although by then Ambrose had been appointed in Auxentius’ place. Yet, for the confusion of the adversaries and, certainly, for our hope, all the glory of heaven and all the martyrs assented to this very faith. Although they had long had opportunity to appear, they were seeking a man through whom they might make themselves known: one to whom they might be revealed under the faith by which they had become martyrs [Col. 0954D].

Thus Ambrose was granted what had been denied to Auxentius, because what Auxentius blasphemed, Ambrose preached. But although this power of the martyrs will pass through all the provinces [Note: [Col. 0954D] Manuscript: “for it must be granted to all martyrs without respect of persons”]—for it must be granted to all, without respect of persons, not to Ambrose alone—it nevertheless necessarily first appeared in Italy, where Arian unbelief had held dominion. For signs are given not to believers but to unbelievers (1 Cor. 14). Those who ask the Lord for a sign are unbelievers: the scribes ask, the Pharisees ask; the apostles are silent, believe, and follow.

Therefore it is not surprising that divine power works through the graves of the saints [Col. 0955A], since the heretical mind could not be healed even by its own remedies, so that at last it might follow that bishop whom the martyrs themselves had deigned, through the revelation of their powers, to see worthy even to share communion with them.

## CHAPTER XVI

Now let us return to the meditation of the perfect man, from which this entire accumulation first grew before his measure had been filled. [Note: [Col. 0955D] Manuscript and edition: “And although this discussion concerns the meditations themselves.”]

Behold, this discussion concerns those very meditations of which David says: “Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. 1). Indeed, it is difficult, when entering the forest of the law, to separate the material of individual questions, since one touches another through the fellowship of instruction like branches, so that what has been begun cannot be explained without beginning with the other.

How beautiful it is to recognize this very man of ours, who alone, amid such matters, does not become bewildered, whereas such things move all others as though they were merely chance occurrences】【：】【“】【},{ to distinguish the kinds of actions; and because the demons also act, to understand their natures; to know what is true and what is false; not to be deceived or to err; not to assign to the enemy what belongs to God, nor to attribute to God what belongs to the demons; to know the times; to recognize the signs; to understand the Lord’s will; and, with thanksgiving, to venerate some of God’s wondrous works, while avoiding others with deserved abhorrence.

Even worldly people have praised such a man, as Virgil says:

> Fortunate is he who has been able to know the causes of things.

A good sentiment, if he had reached it by the proper path, so that it would be evident that he did not understand what he praised. He omitted the first things and celebrated what comes second. For, by placing the order backward, he also distorted the task of the wise man: the Creator of things must be sought, not merely the causes of things. Through him, if we have learned to know him, we shall enter into the causes of things.

Otherwise, with him omitted, how could we know the causes of things, since one must first ask who made these things and only afterward why he made them? Once the author of things has been found, we shall also find their causes. Virgil failed to see this to such an extent that he proclaimed as the chief position the one that could recognize the causes of things; then he added that one should worship the gods, as though carrying out a lesser task. Thus anyone may recognize that they were not the creators of things, since knowledge of things is distinguished from them as something foreign and they ought not to be worshiped if they cannot provide, as the first and highest things, what is praised.

They do not know the things of which they were not the makers. Finally, having taken the invention of these things away from their gods [Note: [Col. 0955D] Manuscript: “they attribute human discoveries to their gods through human ingenuity.”], they assign it to human intelligence—namely, to those who excel in wisdom and therefore do not worship idols. Thus man has become more powerful than their gods, if he reaches through deeper thought what their gods themselves do not know.

Yet he commanded that the gods be worshiped by those who, in their utter foolishness, cannot discover the causes of things and whose innermost hearts, to use his own words, contain “cold blood.” Our man, however, knows both that worshiping God is the principal wisdom and that he possesses knowledge of the causes of things [Note: [Col. 0955D] Manuscript: “he has discovered them; not by the wisdom of the world from Syracuse” [Col. 0956D].]. He does not seek to excel through the reasoning of the worldly wisdom of Syracuse, but through the teaching of the one whom he worships and whom he sought before seeking the causes of things, since the Creator of things precedes the things themselves. He warned him what things would come at what times; no one recognized his arrangement except the one who arranged it, because no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.

But we, as the Apostle says, “have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God” (1 Cor. 2). Therefore, we know what belongs to him [Note: [Col. 0956D] Manuscript: “not instructed by the words of human wisdom”], not taught by the words of human wisdom, but through the Spirit of God and by his favor poured over us.

This is the foolishness of worldly people; this is the wisdom of those who have been called: always to think in the heart, “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” [Col. 0956A] (Ps. 116); always to have him in one’s mouth, because he is the Word; to hunger for him, because he is bread. Through his Spirit also to become intoxicated in the mind and go beyond oneself, because he is the cup of the New Testament and the wine from the vine that he had previously brought out of Egypt—the vine that was the people of Israel, whose fathers were the ancestors according to the flesh of the Lord Jesus Christ.

To speak of him at all times, because his Spirit brought us new tongues. What are these new tongues, except these: to be in the world and not to possess the speech of the world; to speak to the people in languages other than those in which the people themselves are accustomed to speak among themselves?

Moreover, to speak in other tongues means to confess the one God by someone who had been accustomed to confessing many gods; to speak and profess him as one in our faith through new tongues; and to believe the Trinity.

We must also love him because he intercedes for us; fear him because the Father has given all judgment to the Son; worship him at every moment; and ask from him what we need and what pleases him, since he wishes to be asked through himself. Indeed, he shows the one who asks these words, and—something new among us—he alone loves those who ask him. [Note: [Col. 0956D] Manuscript and edition: “For he alone also, which is remarkable, …”] He alone also, remarkably, becomes angry unless he is asked.

For it is unbelief to expect nothing from God. One who does not ask for what he judges God capable of doing believes that God can do nothing.

This is that narrow way, dearest son; this is that eye of the needle through which those burdened with baggage do not enter, nor animals loaded with weights. For narrow and small entrances not only fail to admit misshapen beasts carrying burdens [Note: [Col. 0956D] Edition: “For these openings do not merely fail to admit beasts with their burdens”], but also frustrate the sight of our own eyes if it is distracted in many directions. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Be still and see” (Ps. 46). And when will it be possible to enter what, through the occupations of the world, has not yet begun to be discovered?

## CHAPTER XVII

We have completed, in their several divisions, the questions we set forth, by showing the outer and the inner man. We have shown what the holy life is, in what activity it consists, with what devotion it is maintained, and by what substance it is nourished; and we have briefly carried its entire course to the end—more by leaps, if one may say so, than by steps, because of our haste.

Now hear why this man is not also seen by the people of this world, since you take pleasure in my verbosity, though you judge it rather carelessly while you attend more diligently to divine matters.

When the one who first introduced the seed of death into us had subdued this world—that is, the suffering of humanity—by conquering man for himself, and had seized his kingdom beneath his feet and under his dominion once its king had already been captured, using everything in the world as though it were his own property and the spoils of his victory, he feared that at some time man might seek the wisdom he had lost or the testament of life owed to him. Therefore he so infected everything with the juices of his art that he clothed foolishness in the color of wisdom and overshadowed death with the allurements of a deceptive life, so that those who did not perceive better opposites would not flee from evils.

From that time onward the human race has proceeded everywhere in this manner: foolishness is regarded as wisdom. The Psalmist says: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the unjust man is blessed” (Ps. 10). [Col. 0956D] Then what is death is thought to be life, and evils deceive under the appearance of good, when, in order to defraud the understanding, the power of all good is concealed by deceit.

Riches that will not follow a person after death are loved. The honor of the fasces, which will fade through succession, is sought. To have done an injury is considered virtue; to possess another’s property is considered power; to deceive an innocent person is considered cleverness; not to know Christ is considered wisdom; to dread the prophet is considered eloquence.

Thus everything is full of errors; thus darkness is poured through human minds, as one person attacks another; the world is wrapped in obscurity. Truth is darkened to such an extent that lying in the lap of death is called blessedness.

When God, who is always thinking of us and of what belongs to us, saw that his wisdom had been abandoned because of the wisdom of the world—the world having found collaborators and corruptors for itself—it pleased him, in opposition to the craft of the deceiver, to employ his wisdom against innumerable vices and to veil his wisdom, as it truly is, with what would be called foolishness, and to hide his life under a certain obscurity of death. Thus no one who had fled the reputation of foolishness in this world could reach wisdom, nor could anyone approach his life who had not held death in contempt.

Therefore he sent his Son, our Savior, in human form: that is, he clothed his Wisdom in flesh, which is foolishness. He made his way undergo the cross, which is death. Thus, by opposing opposites, he destroyed them; and through dissimilar works, performed ages ago, he shattered the contrivances of that ingenious artificer, so that the deadly marks left by him might be erased by certain saving traces, even though they had been impressed upon them.

But unless we desire this—that “what is foolish in God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1)—we shall not hold fast to his wisdom. Unless we love this death, which is the cross, because “what is weak in God is stronger than men,” we shall not be able to enter his life.

What follows, then, except that, abandoning both the wisdom and the life of the world, we should allow ourselves to be considered fools and always desire to die with the Lord, so that in the hope of his coming—which will reveal both realities—we may deserve to have some share?

Then, when all veils have been torn apart, each and every thing will be seen as it truly is. The foolishness of the world, stripped of the coverings of false wisdom, will stand exposed; and death, which has pretended to be blessedness, its veil uncovered, will be revealed as the enemy of life, always gaping with open mouth and throat exposed toward the abyss.

Then heavenly wisdom, which is called foolishness in worldly terms, will enter without any laborious effort into the height of the knowledge of God; and true life, obscured by no darkness of death, will shine forth through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER XVIII

You see, son, with what illness the mind of one who does not consider these things is afflicted. I applied consolations to the little body; had I neglected it, the soul would have been stronger, for it becomes weak when the outer person is strengthened.

But may the soul I have described as corrupted by the disease of foolishness be healed by the frequency of your prayers; for a soul undefiled by the crimes of the world can help others. A sick person cannot apply a remedy to those pierced by sickness [Note: [Col. 0957] Manuscript: “cannot apply a remedy to those pierced by illness”], nor can one gasping beneath the height of his wounds heal the wounds of others. Certainly, the healthy person will care for the sick; the sighted person does not lead the blind over precipices.

Therefore, as one who is wise, supplicate the Lord that I may become wise in what I have not understood; and through your intercessions, as through certain remedies, make me be healed.

Someone might criticize me for proceeding so far in a delightful discussion that I had no awareness of my own merits, or for suddenly and unworthily ascending the narrow chair of Moses as a disputant of such matters. But I truly did this out of love for you, not out of self-assertion. For I had read the command addressed to the sinner that he should not dare to proclaim the Lord’s righteousness with his mouth.

If, contrary to that prohibition, I presumed to do so out of affection for you, your grace will deign to compensate for it: do not bring these little writings, which have not been fully corrected—as the very letters with which they were written show—too readily into public view. And although I was unable to be as modest on my own behalf as I ought to have been, may your modesty spare my embarrassment.

And since the fact that they are badly written is attributable to me, let their concealment be attributed to you. Farewell, and love us in the Lord, in whom we are loved by you.

# INDEX OF MEMORABLE SUBJECTS AND STATEMENTS CONTAINED IN THE TEXT

[Note: [Col. 0957C] In this index, Arabic numerals refer to the column numbers printed in bold type in the text.]

## A

Aaron was chosen and anointed by Moses as priest, 717.

Abel, killed by his brother Cain, is a figure of Jesus Christ crucified by the Jews, 173. He signified the chosen Christian people, just as Cain signified the Jewish people, who were to be rejected, 735.

Abijah, a priest of the temple from the lineage of Aaron, from whom descended Zechariah, father of St. John the Baptist, 550.

Abraham was justified by faith, not by circumcision; he himself and his seed of faith received a blessing from God, 742. In spirit he rejoiced that he had seen the day of the Lord, 37. When three men appeared, he hurried to meet them, fell on his face, and prayed that they would turn aside to his tent, 645. He fathered two sons: Ishmael, the elder, by the slave-girl Hagar, and Isaac, the younger, by the free woman Sarah. Ishmael represented the Jewish people; Isaac, the faithful Christian people, 735. God appeared to him by the oak of Mamre, 737. Abraham wrestled with the Angel and became lame in one foot. What does this signify? 494. He addresses the rich man placed in torment, 774.

Renunciation, to be made by those being baptized, is called the surest pledge, 715.

Abstinence from eating meat during the Lenten fast is most ancient in the Church, 445.

All our acts must be performed with Christ either as companion or as witness, 297. Whatever we do must be done in God’s name, so that we may receive its fruit, ibid.

Every sex, age, and rank is summoned to do good, 337.

Adam, the first human being, was formed by God’s hands from clay. The second Adam, Christ, was formed by God’s Spirit in the womb of a virgin. Both arise from God the Father; both are born from a virgin mother; both are sons of God. But Adam is God’s creature, whereas Christ is his substance, 445.

When Adam had been placed in paradise, he was forbidden to taste from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, 440. He did not know how to guard against the devil’s ambushes laid through Eve, 42. Preserving the dignity of angelic purity, he was indeed naked of worldly garments, but clothed in the splendor of immortality, 286. Through the intervention of intemperance, he was expelled from paradise and knew Eve, 445, 451.

In Adam the first-formed man there is a figure of Christ’s resurrection: just as Adam, rising after sleep, recognized Eve formed from his side, so Christ, rising from the dead, formed the Church from the wound in his side, 477.

When Adam is asked, “Where are you?”, this does not mean that Adam could hide from the Lord’s sight, but that no place is safe for a guilty conscience while it fears being discovered, 165.

What harm did Adam do to the human race by sinning? 385.

Aeneas, a paralytic, was healed by Peter at the Beautiful Gate of the temple; this was Peter’s first miracle, 354, 577.

At the autumnal equinox, in the seventh month, St. John was conceived in his mother’s womb; in the first month, at the spring equinox, the Lord Savior was conceived in the womb of his virgin mother, 551.

Hagar bore the figure of the Synagogue, 342. She was expelled from Abraham’s house with her son Ishmael, 741.

The field purchased with the price of Christ’s betrayal provides rest for strangers, not for sinners who have taken possession of it, 148.

The martyrdom of St. Agnes, and her praises, 538.

The Agnoetae impiously said that Christ progressed in inner holiness and wisdom, 57, in the note.

The Philistines were called foreigners (*allophyli*), enemies of the Israelites; under this name Maximus understands the barbarians devastating Italy, 20, 58, 119, 722.

Amaon and Cleophas, disciples to whom Christ joined himself as a companion on the road, were inflamed with divine love, 363. [Col. 0959]

The love of God is kindled through faith and longing for the Savior, 581. The whole sum of the virtues and the fullness of all righteousness arise from the love by which God and one’s neighbor are loved, 587. Anyone can make God his friend, 637. For love of the heavenly kingdom, the honors and dignities of this world are to be despised, 634.

Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, the boys enclosed in the furnace of Babylon, walked unharmed amid the balls of fire, 582.

The sudden death of Ananias is recalled because he defrauded Peter of the price of the field he had sold, 322, 354.

The martyrs of Anaunia—Alexander, Martyrius, and Sisinnius—are celebrated, and the cause of their martyrdom is related, 607.

At the birth of the Lord, the angels announced glory in heaven and peace to human beings on earth, 32, 55, 61, 402. After Christ had completed his fast, they ministered to him, 128. Those who imitate the angels will deserve their companionship, 311.

The angel Gabriel was sent by God to announce to Mary her divine motherhood, 31, 556, 565. He also foretold the birth, name, and merit of John the Baptist before he had been conceived in the womb, 213, 556, 565.

In the Angel who wrestled with Abraham, an image of Christ is to be discerned: Christ struggled with death and conquered it for the life and salvation of humanity, 494.

The faithful soul is corrected by fear and rejoices in correction, 29.

How is the soul that has been lost for Christ to be found? 567.

The immortality of the soul and the eternal recompense of works are demonstrated, 733.

Some people reckoned the beginning of the year from the day of the Lord’s birth, 403, in the note.

The story of Antaeus is hinted at with the name suppressed. Maximus used it to explain Christ’s victory over death through his own death and resurrection, 494.

The Antichrist will reign in the world before Christ comes a second time to earth to judge all human beings, 6. Christ will overcome him, flashing with his supreme majesty and power, 7.

King Antiochus raged against the seven Maccabean brothers and their mother because they refused to violate the holy law by eating forbidden meats, 606.

The Apollinarians blasphemously claimed that the divine Word fulfilled the function of the soul or mind in Christ’s nature, 57, in the note.

The apostles are fountains overflowing with the grace of preaching. Christ is learned only through their mouths and through the teaching of the disciples, 124. Christ calls them the salt of the earth because they were sent to season all peoples, 314. Persevering unanimously in prayer, they were filled with the Holy Spirit and received the gift of tongues, 525. How they are the light of the world, 767. They were represented by the twelve baskets of fragments, 668. Through the sincerity of their faith and divine works they healed all illnesses, 723. Gathering together, they established the creed, 271. Their names are explained, 779.

How the waters of the river Mara were made sweet, 124.

The miraculous transformation of water into wine at the wedding feast of Cana in Galilee, 69.

The resurrection of the dead is shown to be possible, 419. Its mystery is contained therein, 420.

When Christ was baptized, the whole substance of the waters was consecrated for our baptism, 63, 95.

What is to be understood by the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? 465.

Noah’s ark preserved unharmed in the shipwreck of the world all whom it had received, 641. It is a figure of the Church, ibid.

The error of the Arians is refuted, 146, 246. Why they oppose the Gospel of John, 248.

Christ ascended into heaven while his disciples watched; he took with him the righteous captives liberated from the captivity of the demons, 192.

At the Lord’s Ascension the revelation of the sacraments written in the Law and the Prophets was completed, and the book that no one except the Lamb of God could open was opened, 520. What difference there is between the Lord’s Ascension and Elijah’s being taken up, 377.

The harshness of masters toward slaves is rebuked, 459.

How vain it is to attend to omens, since God distributes prosperity and adversity to mortals by the power of their free choice, 48.

Avarice is the root and origin of all evils, 112, 128, 219, 223, 250, 354. How many hardships the miser endures in vain while amassing riches, 628. Misers may say to gold: “For your sake we are killed all day long,” ibid.

In unleavened bread the Pasch of truth is celebrated whenever we approach the Church of God chaste, sober, righteous, peaceful, and full of brotherly love, 505.

## B

Balaam, priest of the nations, prophesied that Christ would be born, so that the nations would not lack testimony concerning the birth of the Lord, their Restorer, 53. The same prophecy of Balaam is announced, 55, 76.

John’s baptism preceded Christ’s baptism, just as his preaching did, in order to fulfill the order of a forerunner, 551.

Christ’s baptism was foretold in Psalm 28; its explanation, 422 ff.

Christ wished to be baptized by John in order to pass through all the sacraments of humanity, 92. In his baptism the whole Holy Trinity intervenes and acts, 98, 425, 430. The heavenly powers and angelic authorities marveled that Christ was baptized by John, 98. When he was about to command baptism, he taught by his own example that it must not be omitted, 89.

The sacrament of baptism is useful and necessary because forgiveness of sins is granted in it, 402. Why is Christ’s baptism to be regarded as more perfect than John’s baptism? John’s is called the baptism of repentance, whereas Christ’s is called the baptism of life or of grace, 99.

John’s baptism of repentance was emptied of its force when Christ’s grace arrived, 406.

Baptismal water, which is called Christ’s water, both removes sins and confers the grace of justification, 329.

Why is baptism called burial? 150. Its benefits are declared, ibid.

The effect of baptism, which remits sins, proceeds from God’s grace and power; for the Holy Spirit acts in that water, 713. Its benefits are signified, 625.

Those being baptized were immersed with their whole body, 714. Before baptism they made an explicit profession of faith; this was called “handing over the creed,” 714. Triple immersion was celebrated with the signification of a twofold mystery, 716. Baptism must in no way be repeated; one may be washed only once, 717.

Here baptism produces not only the remission of sins but also the inner renewal of righteousness, 441. Baptism was administered on the solemnity of Easter, 194. The sacred death of the Son of God earned for the baptized the efficacy of conferring grace, 625. The baptism of blood regenerates and consecrates souls.

The goodness of God the Father is to be admired: he prepared as judge for unbelievers the one whom he sent beforehand as redeemer for believers, so that mercy might forestall the severity of the coming judge, 30.

Bethlehem, in which Christ was born, is called the city of the supreme God and “house of bread”; it brought forth for us Christ, the heavenly bread, 23. It is also called the city of David, 20, 24. The prophecies concerning Christ’s birth in Bethlehem are reviewed, 52, 54.

How grave a sin blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is, 530. It is not forgiven either in this age or in the age to come, 351.

By the gift of his indulgent goodness, God’s goodness does not arm us for guilt but washes us for glory, 273.

How goodness is to be tempered with severity in those who rule, 553.

No one is good who is good only for himself, 587.

## C
## C

Kadesh: what is to be understood by it in Psalm 28, 423. Cain’s sacrifices rejected by God, 735. The cup so often mentioned in Scripture signifies the Passion of Christ the Lord, as well as that of the martyrs, 155. The way of Christian life is expressed in the cup, 755. The passion of the brothers Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla is described, 615 ff. Captivity subjects one to the devil’s slavery, but Christ’s captivity restores one to freedom, 189. Love for Christ is to be preferred to the world, 628. Nothing ought to separate us from it, 241. Love of neighbor is necessary for every virtue, 204. The duties of Christian charity are set forth, 677. The resurrection of the flesh is the end of our religion and the supreme object of belief, 273. Chastity is to be loved above all things; for Christ showed how pleasing it is to him by choosing a virgin as his mother, 36. It is the adornment of our soul; how carefully it must be guarded! 679. The benefits of baptism are explained to catechumens, 91. When persecution threatened, baptism was hastened, 625. Not all the mysteries of the faith were entrusted to them for knowledge, 709. After baptism the mystery of the Trinity was disclosed to them, so that they might become steadfast in its confession, 96. They were likewise urged to hasten to baptism, 441. When persecution threatened, the period of the catechumenate was shorter, so that they might be prepared to fight for the faith, ibid. “Your taverners mix water with wine”: these are the words of Isaiah, chapter 1, to be understood of priests, to whom the care of souls has been entrusted, 340. The warmth of earthly love yields when the flame of divine charity has kindled the Christian mind, 593.

[Col. 0961] Chaldaea rejoiced at the Lord’s birth, while Jerusalem, together with all its rulers, was tormented, 85. The Canaanite woman who begs Christ for the salvation of her daughter represents the Gentile people imploring the Lord to have mercy on them, lost as they were in idolatry, 671, 673. In the Canaanite woman’s daughter every sinful soul is represented: each day it is tormented by the devil and subjected to every vice and evil, 673. Her great faith is commended by Christ, ibid.

All Christians are Christ’s body and members, 182. In the time of the apostles everything was held in common among them, and they possessed nothing privately, 319. They should be simple as doves and shrewd as serpents, 384. Christians of later times are very unlike the first believers, 421. Those who truly observed Lent abstained from banquets, pleasure, and wives, 446. The more ready they are to imitate Christ, the nearer they will be to grace, 637. The Christian who does not possess the world possesses the whole Savior, 130. The whole life of a Christian, if he lives according to the Gospel, is a cross and martyrdom, 265.

Christ’s conception from a virgin was foretold by Isaiah, 17. When the Holy Spirit came upon the womb of holy Mary and the Most High overshadowed it, Christ was generated, 19. That immaculate Spirit—that is, the Son of God, pure, holy, and secure in himself—assumed human flesh from holy Mary and by his own power and capacity made it flesh, 738. He who from eternity was God became man and was born in time from an immaculate virgin, in order to free human beings from the devil’s slavery, 20. Christ’s flesh was born from a woman whom God had made; nor can Christ’s majesty be defiled in the flesh. For if the shining sun is not polluted by contact with anything, much less could the Lord of the sun be polluted, 739. In Bethlehem, the city of David, Christ was born according to the prophecies and, wrapped in swaddling clothes, was laid in a manger, 20. He had no place in the inn, because when Christ entered the world he did not find faith in which he could rest, 32. At the end of the ages a man was born who, before all ages, had proceeded as the Only-begotten from the Father, 24. There are two generations in Christ: one eternal, by which he was born God, and the other temporal, by which he was born man, ibid. Christ was human in the tenderness of his limbs, but God, proceeding from God, was born from the conception of his undefiled mother, 24, 558.

It is not contrary to nature that Christ was born from a virgin without the intervention of human action; rather, the power of the Most High overshadowing her was present. God, for whom all things are possible, exercised his power and joined both the divine and human natures to one person, 34, 511. According to prophecy, Christ was born from the seed of Jacob and, according to the flesh, from the royal blood of David, 55. Angelic choirs bear witness to the birth of the heavenly King, 36, 74. Although after his birth in the flesh he is a little child in body, he is nevertheless God in majesty, 58. The shepherds seek the newborn Lord, 61. The varying opinions of chronographers concerning the time of Christ’s birth, 329.

Christ, born from the virgin Mary, was dedicated by the sign of circumcision, either to show the unquestionable reality of his flesh or lest Judaea, nourished by circumcision, reject him as a foreigner, 99. The commemoration of Christ’s circumcision is shown to be older in the Church than the sixth century, 43.
