Christ was worshiped by the Chaldaean Magi, preceded by a new star, and gold, frankincense, and myrrh were offered to him; these gifts contain many mysteries, 49, 51, 54, 61, 64, etc. The worship offered to the newborn Jesus by the Magi was not merely civic but religious, 67. To fulfill the commandment of Moses’ law, a burnt offering was offered for him in the Temple, 100. The meaning of the Gospel passage, Luke 2, “The child grew,” and so forth, is explained, 58.

Jesus came to the Jordan in the thirtieth year of his age to be baptized by John, and, when John refused, commanded him to administer baptism to him, 87, 95, 552. For he wished first to carry out what he commanded others to do, so that, like a good teacher, he might impress his teaching not so much by words as by practicing it himself in deeds, 89. At Christ’s baptism the revelation of the Holy Trinity took place. The Father is heard in the voice, the Son is manifested in the man, and the Holy Spirit is recognized in the dove, 98. The presence of the Holy Spirit, the authority of the Father’s voice among the whole human race, and John’s testimony confirmed both the truth of the Son and the sacrament of baptism, 102. Christ’s consecration is the consecration of the greater element. For when our Savior is washed, then already all water is cleansed in our baptism, and the font is purified, so that afterward it may provide the grace of washing to succeeding peoples, 90.

Christ preceded his preaching with a fast, as Moses did when he received the commandments to be delivered to the people of Israel. Moses is the author of the old law; Christ is the founder of the New Testament, 433, 442. The difference between the two—Christ and Moses—is indicated, ibid. After fasting forty days and forty nights, Christ is tempted by the devil in the desert [Col. 0962], 106. Tempted three times, he defeated the tempter with a threefold triumph, teaching that the one God must be worshiped and served alone, 38, 130. He was hungry after the forty-day fast so that, although by nature he was the Son of God, he might reveal that he had assumed the fragile nature of a true human being, 129.

He performed his first sign at a wedding feast in Cana of Galilee, and his disciples believed in him, 70, 72. By his presence he sanctified marriage, 50. During the time of his preaching he gave his disciples the teachings they were able to bear; he reserved others to be received from the Holy Spirit, 200. He bears witness that the revelation of his divinity was granted to Peter not by human beings but received from the Father, 217. He asked his disciples what they believed about him, 373. In return for the merit of his confession he gave Peter the keys of the heavenly kingdom—that is, the power of judging—and entrusted him with feeding his sheep, 218–219.

He sent healing to the absent servant of the centurion and restored three dead persons to life: the son of the widow of Nain, the daughter of the chief priest, and Lazarus after four days, 513, 568. Throughout his whole manner of life, just as he revealed himself to be true God, so he showed himself to be perfect man, 495. In his transfiguration he gave the disciples a foretaste of heavenly glory, 769.

Christ was handed over to the Jews by Judas, the false apostle, 145. It is a great testimony to the Lord’s innocence that his accuser both confesses his crime and is guilty concerning the payment, 146. Accused before Pilate, he is declared innocent and nevertheless condemned to crucifixion, 144, 148. While hanging on the cross, he grants the repentant thief forgiveness of his crimes and paradise, 158, 162. His lament on the cross—“My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?”—from Psalm 21 is explained, 138. Christ dies and by his Passion frees human beings from death, 153. His words to the Father, “Forgive them, for they know not what they do,” are adorned with various interpretations, 503. The division of Christ’s garments after his crucifixion, and the seamless garment woven from above, which was not divided, 140.

Christ, who was at once victim and priest, brought every shadow of the old priesthood and sacrifice to an end by revealing their figures and enigmas; for the new people he inaugurated a new priesthood and a new sacrifice, 476. He was “free among the dead,” because alone among mortals he had no cause for dying, 504. Christ descended into hell, 510. His resurrection was all the more certain and astonishing because the Jews’ diligence in guarding the tomb was all the greater, 471. Christ’s resurrection must be held among the articles of faith, 716. He appeared to Mary Magdalene and rebuked her because she doubted his resurrection, 177. With the doors shut he entered among the apostles and showed himself to them risen again, 480, 510. He invited Thomas to touch his wounds, ibid. He wished to retain the marks of the nails after the resurrection so that the memory of his Passion would not be erased in us, 510.

As he was about to ascend into heaven, he promised the apostles that he would send the Holy Spirit to them, 197, 199. He likewise promised his perpetual presence to the apostles and the Church, 520. He sent his apostles to enlighten the nations as rays of truth, 137. After the resurrection he lived with the disciples for forty days, teaching them with complete maturity of wisdom; then he ascended into heaven, to the Father, presenting the fruit of the flesh and leaving in the disciples the seeds of righteousness, 188. He is called the victor over death and sin, 513. His promise to send the Holy Spirit upon the apostles is shown to have been fulfilled, 294, 197, 199, etc. We must believe that Christ reached the Father when we see that the Paraclete descended upon the apostles, 197. Christ and the Holy Spirit proclaim one another by reciprocal testimonies, because they know themselves to reign in undivided majesty, 530. Christ’s will to save all human beings is demonstrated by the diversity of languages entrusted to the apostles, ibid. His clemency and mercy are celebrated in his sparing others, 503.

In Christ the distinct operation of humanity and divinity is established against Eutyches, 669. Christ is represented in the mountain seen by Daniel, 767.

Christ’s various titles: why he is called the Word and will of the eternal Father, 517. The Sun of righteousness, 137. King of the nations, 17. Lamb of God, 546. Lord of all ages, 24. The New Adam, 23, 35, 445. The Bread that came down from heaven, 436. Why Christ is called Lord, king, priest, and sacrifice, 744. Christ the Prophet, Son of God, foretold in the Old Testament, 746. He is called the Father’s Word, the Father’s power and wisdom, in whom and through whom the Father made all things, 748. The Only-begotten Son of God, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit has one and the same divinity and omnipotence, 53. Christ is life, 757. “Christ is the same yesterday and today,” Hebrews 13: these words of Paul to the Hebrews are explained, 471, 491.

Christ sits at the right hand of the Father, not because he is greater than the Father, but so that he may not be thought less than the Father, 190. The reason is given why Saint Stephen said that he saw the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God the Father, and not rather the Son of God [Col. 0963], 202. He holds primacy over all things and is ruler of the whole earth, 505. He is compared to leaven, and the comparison is explained in many ways, 370. He is not a respecter of persons, but according to the quality of merits he repays the affection of love, 380. Christ daily observes our harmful wills and draws and urges us toward saving remedies even against our will. This saying of Maximus is explained in the note, 359. Christ’s grace perfects human freedom, 504. The meaning of Christ’s being sent by the Father into the world is explained in various ways, 498. He is believed to go or come when he deigns to reveal himself, ibid. He governs the ship of his Church and does not permit it to be destroyed by the waves of the age, 357. One must not depart from the worship and obedience of Christ, 334. In the sacrifice of the Mass Christ is both victim and priest, 600. Christ’s body becomes condemnation for those who receive it unworthily, 138. The necessity of eucharistic food for eternal life, 138. Desire for food was Adam’s first cause of transgression, 431.

Circumcision, given as a sign of descent, was not necessary for salvation. The righteous Abel, Enosh, Enoch, Noah, and Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God—all righteous—were not circumcised according to the flesh, 741. Saint Clement, a disciple of Peter, 733. Commerce is forbidden to clerics, and their function in the Church is explained, 347. How they ought to perform their office, 378. The twelve apostles are signified by the twelve baskets of fragments, 678. The apostles Peter, James, and John are called the pillars of the Church, 769. Adam and Peter are compared: both sinned after being ensnared by a woman, 665. Who were the *competentes*? 466. Maximus derives the calculation of the years from the creation of the world to Christ’s coming from the reckoning of the Septuagint interpreters, 328.

The sacrament of confirmation was conferred on the newly baptized through anointing with chrism, 711, 717. This anointing was performed on the head. What this anointing of the head signifies, ibid. The very ancient custom of the Church of placing ashes on the foreheads of the faithful on the Wednesday before the first Sunday of Lent, 103. The conversion of water into wine performed by Christ at the feast in Cana of Galilee contains the mystery of the resurrection, 420. Drunken banquets are condemned, 62.

Cornelius the centurion was inspired by the Holy Spirit before he received baptism, 554. He became the first Christian from the Gentiles, 578. How great his faith was, 684. A crown of thorns is placed on Christ—not by bloody hands, as among the Jews, but by wicked thoughts and depraved deeds, 598. The precepts of fraternal correction are set forth, 675. The creation and regeneration of human beings are compared with each other, 533. Not only those who do evil but also those who consent to its perpetrators are guilty, 656.

The mysteries of the cross are indicated, 155. What the tree is in the ship, the cross is in the Church, ibid. It is the distinguished trophy of Christ’s victory, 506. Crosses are appointed as ornaments of triumphs and are carried on the forehead by kings, 414. It is a sign of faith and salvation, 290. Its power is declared, 156, 506. The guilt of the first parent benefited humanity more than it harmed it. How is this saying of Maximus to be understood? 515. Saint Cyprian is celebrated not so much for the glory of martyrdom as for the greatness of his wisdom and the zeal of his faith, 255 ff., 591 ff.

## D

Demons are not expelled from the possessed except through fasting and prayers, 118. By fasting Daniel merited knowledge of future events, 452. He foretold the overthrow of the city of Jerusalem, ibid. His judgment concerning Susanna is compared with Pilate’s judgment concerning Christ, 142. The persons and judgments of these judges are compared, ibid. He is said to have been filled with the Holy Spirit, 145.

King and prophet David foretold Christ’s resurrection, 179, 185, as well as his ascension into heaven, 289. He struck down the proud Philistine not with an iron weapon but with a spiritual sword, 290. He laid aside his weapons and entered the battle armed with faith in God, ibid. When he dealt with the structure of the Temple and its function, he divided the whole offspring of the sons of Aaron into twenty-four groups and chose from each group priests who would minister in turn and in order in the Temple sanctuary, 595. Christ was born from his bloodline, 55.

[Col. 0964] God is incomprehensible, 28. He is the creator and governor of the world, 732. He is incorporeal and invisible, for he is Spirit, as the Lord says: “For God is Spirit,” John, chapter 4, 198. Through his innate divinity God is omnipotent, and through omnipotence he is Father, 269. How greatly God’s wisdom shines forth in the restoration of humanity, 440. Only God can be born from God; therefore there is no doubt that he is God who proceeds from God, 524.

God created heaven, the sun, and the stars from nothing; he himself created the earth, seas, animals, and the whole adornment of this spectacle, the world, 22. Therefore he could make a virgin a mother, ibid. He animated the human being, formed from the mud of the earth, with the breath of his Spirit, 149. He is called the Potter; why? ibid. God formed us with his hands for life; Christ re-formed us for glory, ibid. If God is wonderful in his saints, how much more wonderful is he in himself? 26.

Why God, although good and merciful, did not wish to relax the punishment inflicted for original sin, 439. His decrees are immutable, 440. Knowledge of future things belongs to God alone, 47. Because in his greatness all things are present to him, all time is today for him; hence the Psalmist says in Psalm 89: “A thousand years in your sight are like one day,” 72, 491. He must be loved above all things, 730.

God’s dealings with human beings: he is merciful and just—just because he did not remove the punishment of sin by which humanity was held after the fall; merciful because through Christ he bestowed the gift of forgiveness and resurrection, 441. He forgets no one, but we make him seem forgetful when we sin, 338. By chastising us in this world he heals us and prepares us to merit eternal life, 469. He is our Father when we do good; our judge when we sin, 395. He does not permit himself to be mocked, since he hears and sees everything, 730. The whole course of our life must be referred to God, 62. It lies within our power to make him our friend, 367. The works of divinity are not to be investigated by words but believed with devotion, 511. In God is the whole fullness of goodness and the whole tranquility of goodness, 743. Our devotion must not trust in its own strength but commend to divine grace the accomplishment of its good purpose, 571.

The devil, changed into a serpent, deceived the pious and inexperienced innocence of the new human beings with deceitful tongues, 740. The devil, uncertain whether something beyond humanity was present in Christ besides his human nature, attempted to discover this through various temptations. But he achieved nothing: always expelled and rejected, he departed, 109, 126, 130. Christ responded to all the enemy’s temptations in such a way that the devil could not discover the mystery of heaven in the one who was both God and man, 132, 434, 437 ff. He recognized the vessel of his deceit in the gatekeeper woman, because he customarily attacks faithful men only through a woman, 165. The devil has nothing to seize from a human being who is occupied day and night in doing God’s will, 596. He tries to deceive Christ’s faithful through crafty temptations, 634.

The lengthening of the day at Christ’s birth and its shortening at the birth of John the Baptist are said to contain a mystery, which is explained, 400 ff. Christ’s day is without night, a day without end: everywhere it shines, everywhere it radiates, everywhere it does not fail, 180. Those days are better on which we are reborn to eternal life than those on which we are born into this temporal life, since the gifts of grace are greater than those of nature, 493.

On the Lord’s Day it is the duty of the Christian to assemble in the Church. On that day laws are silent and judgments are still, so that the salvation of humanity may receive the place of devotion, 638. Those are rebuked who on the Lord’s Day, because of a worldly banquet, disdain the heavenly meal and abandon Christ’s table while delighting in a human table, ibid. Love of enemies is commanded by God, 293, 674. Christians ought to love one another, 744.

The universal Flood, which occurred in the days of Noah, was a figure of baptism, through which all the sins of the world are washed away, 448, 461. The fiery Flood upon the two cities, Sodom and Gomorrah, 749. During the Savior’s Passion all the disciples trembled; nearly all abandoned him when he was betrayed, 164. The seventy disciples, figured by the seventy palm trees, hold a rank below the apostles and are sent by the Lord for the salvation of humanity, 124. Christ’s examination of all human beings at the final judgment, 272.

The rich, compared with a camel, undertake the way of the heavenly kingdom with difficulty, 386. Many are rich in gold in their houses, yet beggars in righteousness in the Church, 322. Wealth does not hinder the attainment of Christ’s glory but helps it, provided that those who possess it do not squander it in wantonness but distribute it for salvation. The fault is not in possessions: wealth is fuel for wickedness in fools, but nourishment for salvation in the wise, 654, 656.

[Col. 0965] The teachers of the Church, bishops and parish priests, must always admonish and rebuke those who perform the works of the devil, and pray for them, 674. To teach by one’s deeds is greater than by one’s voice, 587. A special privilege of teaching is that, although it is communicated wholly to others, it feels no deficiency in itself, 595. What *Domnedius* signifies, 657, in the note. The gift of tongues was bestowed on the apostles by the Holy Spirit so that the diversity of nations might learn the unity of faith through speech of many kinds, 524.

## E

The Church flows from Christ’s side, of which Eve, brought forth from the rib of the first man Adam, was a figure, 172, 486. Its salvation comes from Christ’s death, 174. Because of the excellence of its properties it is called paradise, 433. It shines not by its own light but by the Savior’s, and radiates not with its own brightness but with the Father’s, 338. It cannot stand without the cross, just as a ship is weak without a mast, 154. It grows when it is crowned with martyrs, 338. It is adorned by their triumphs, 528. It is compared with Noah’s Ark, which saved all who were in it, 641. Its holiness must be believed, 272.

The Church to which Christ will bring the joy of peace after the final judgment is called Peter’s Church, 640. It was called barren because before Christ’s coming it could not produce children of God, 314. How it became fruitful, ibid. As a cause of joy, and because Christ lived with the apostles, the Church abstained for a time from fasting between the resurrection and Pentecost, 193. The Church of Milan was destroyed by Attila’s army and restored through the work of Saint Eusebius, bishop, 315. Its dedication is celebrated, ibid.

The merit of almsgiving is commended, 97, 325, 665. The fruits of almsgiving are enumerated, 258. A small almsgiving can receive a great reward from God, 765.

While Elijah was fasting, the elements served him, 451. An angel brought him bread so that he might be refreshed, 452. By fasts and prayers Elijah brought rain down from heaven, 465. After a forty-day fast he was carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot, 312, 442. Just as Elijah divided the waters, so the Spirit of the Lord effected in that same Jordan the separation of sins, 426. Because of the merits of chastity and faith he was lifted to heaven in a flaming chariot and with fiery horses, 513.

Elim: to this place the people of Israel came after departing from Egypt. There were twelve springs of the purest water and seventy flourishing palm trees. What is to be understood in these things? 122. Though advanced in years and with a womb already barren, Elisabeth miraculously bore John, the Lord’s forerunner, 207. After hearing the greeting of the virgin Mary, she confessed that the infant in Mary’s womb had leaped, 543, 546, 547, 553, 559.

The prophet Elisha is commended for his outstanding faith. Though surrounded by the weapons of Ahab, king of Syria, he feared nothing, knowing that God was with him, 308. He struck the whole army of the king with blindness, 310. He asked that a double portion of Elijah’s spirit be given to him, 312, 555. His wonders are described, 313. Scripture reports that he became renowned for twenty-four miraculous signs, 555. His raising of a dead man by contact with his body in the tomb was a figure of Christ’s resurrection, 556. Elisha did not surpass Elijah in holiness, although he had asked for a double portion of his spirit, but only in the number of miracles; nor was he greater than John the Baptist in inward righteousness, ibid.

The name Emmanuel, interpreted as “God with us,” means God in man, the Word in flesh, majesty in a body, 738. Purchase: things bought from plunder do not constitute a legitimate contract, 324.

Epiphany, or Theophany, means the same as manifestation or appearance of the Savior Christ, 48, in the note. From the Fathers it is demonstrated that the solemn celebration of that day is a very ancient rite in the Church, ibid. The day is also called the day of Epiphanies, or of appearances and lights, ibid.

Bishops are urged, by the duty and necessity of their office, to preach the Gospel to the people, lest by keeping silent about others’ sins they incur the charge of negligence, 659. The letters of blessed Paul the apostle are praised as flowing with honey and milk, 579. Esau lost the honor of primogeniture for a lentil, 436.

The Eucharist: the true body of Christ is contained in the Eucharist, and its true offering is made in the Mass, 600. Whoever neglects to eat the Eucharistic food cannot have life in himself, 138. How great a purity of conscience is required, ibid. For those who receive it unworthily, that heavenly bread becomes condemnation, ibid. Although the faithful are refreshed and satisfied by it, what has been received remains entire. Those who frequently partake of the Holy Eucharist approach the heavenly banquet and the Lord’s table, 745.

The virtues of Saint Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, are adorned with praises [Col. 0966], 245 ff. His Passion is compared with the martyrdom of the Maccabees, 611 ff. Catholic doctrine is opposed to the Eutychian heresy, 53. The distinct operations of divinity and humanity in Christ are likewise established, 669. The teaching of the Gospel is divinely inspired, 679. If the Gospel had not been given, the law would have been entirely unnecessary, 10. The evangelists deposited the deeds of Christ the Lord in their writings as an eternal treasure, 182. The evangelists are compared with the four rivers of paradise, watering the Church with the purest teachings, 434.

Excommunication is separation from the assembly of the faithful, 146. Examples of heavenly punishment inflicted on those who speak wickedly are enumerated, 682. The spies of the land of Canaan—Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh—who carried a cluster of grapes on a pole upon their own shoulders, presented a figure of the Savior’s coming, 255. Ezekiel, chapter 1, presents a figure of the two Testaments in two wheels joined together, 11. His words in chapter 3 concerning the watchman appointed over the house of Israel are explained, 660 ff.

## F

Deeds are proved by words; words without deeds are of no benefit, 611. Christ healed the sick servant of the centurion while absent, sending healing; he visited him with the eye of his divinity, 512.

What is fate? Its influence and necessity are refuted, 121 ff. How many opinions philosophers held about it, ibid. Felicitas, the mother of the Maccabees, is celebrated with the highest praises because she stood present with unconquered spirit at the martyrdom of her sons, 601, 606.

Woman, who through Eve had been the source of iniquity, through Mary became the minister of righteousness, so that through the one by whom death opened an entrance into this world, life might through her gain entrance to us, 42. The outstanding virtue of women is celebrated: stronger than the men who tortured them, they conquered tortures for Christ, 632.

The properties of faith are described, 363. The early faithful brought all their possessions to the feet of the apostles, 320. The faithful are urged to observe modesty and guard chastity, 669 ff. Following Christ’s example, they are instructed to wash one another’s feet, 719. Faith is proved by deed, not by speech or tongue but by the heart, 72. How great is the excellence of the Christian faith? 162. Its triumph is proclaimed, 570. How damnable are those who still doubt it, 624. Faith makes great progress when it conceives of its God as greatly as speech cannot express, 27. Those who are of faith are sons of Abraham, 597. Faith in the Creed is necessary for eternal life, 372. Faith is the mother of martyrs, 624. On account of our faith, at Christ’s baptism the heavens were opened, the Spirit descended to Christ, the Father to the Son, and the Voice to the Word, 425.

The faith of the thief who, from the cross, confessed the Lord crucified with him and begged for pardon is commended, 158, 162. All his sins were forgiven on account of his exceptional faith and love, and he himself was admitted to fellowship in the heavenly kingdom, ibid. We ought to have confidence in divine mercy, because Christ descended from heaven for this reason: that through his insults and injuries he might always grant pardon to sinful mortals, 687.

The Son of God became man not to live for himself but by his death to redeem the dead to life, 42. The Son of God was born for us from Mary so that, produced through the true conception of our flesh, he might grant to the human being created by him both paternal affection and brotherly love, 33. Through the undivided substance of divinity he was never separated from the Father; for while the one remains in the one, this always signifies that the Father and the Son exist together, 77. “Although he was in the form of God,” and so forth: these words of the apostle concerning Christ in Philippians 2 are illuminated by various interpretations, 512. The Son of God alone frees sinners, because he alone is free from sin, 504.

The baptismal font is honored by many names, 713. Courage, especially conceived from love of Christ, is admirable, 587. The strength of the believer is not to yield to a threatening persecutor, 572. What are the fruits of the Spirit? 755. Flight during persecution accords with the teachings of the Gospel and is not contrary to them, 572.

## G

True joy was not, is not, and cannot be in this world, 584. Two generations of Christ must be acknowledged: one eternal, from God the Father, and the other temporal, from the virgin Mother, 27, 558.

[Col. 0967] The nations came to Christ through faith and the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit, 672. The Gentiles are opposed when they deny that the divine incarnation is possible, 34. Those who accuse Christ’s birth and death as unworthy of him are also refuted, 509. To the Gentiles, for whom the priest Balaam had prophesied the coming of a new king, a new star appeared as a testimony to him, 55. The Gentile people are represented in the one whose neck bears a millstone, 288. The Gentile world is invited to exultation by the announcement of the Lord’s birth, 37. Devoted to the altars of idols and always weighed down upon the earth by the burden of its faithlessness, it is enlightened, 77. Invited by the new star in the Magi, it comes to adore the newborn Redeemer, 49, 51, 61, 86, etc. The whole philosophy of the Gentiles vanishes in the investigation of the mystery of the Lord’s birth, 53.

Bending the knee: the reason is given for the Church’s custom of not bending the knees in prayer during the Easter season, 191 ff. How Goliath was struck down and killed by David, 290, 721.

The grace of the Holy Spirit is not restricted by the law and is not bound by necessity: he breathes as he wills, and likewise freely distributes his gifts to those whom he wills, 554. The greatness of the grace of baptism instituted by Christ is explained, 419 ff.; its abundance is declared, 514. The assistance of grace was also given to those living under the former Testament for their justification through faith in the coming Redeemer, 15, 16, in the note. Its necessity for every good work is established, 531. The distinction between grace received *ex opere operato* and grace received *ex opere operantis*, 430. Thanks are to be given to God daily, 295. The same thanksgiving is especially to be offered before one goes to bed and immediately upon rising in the morning; and all the works of the day are to be performed under the sign of the Savior, 298. How many injuries the vice of gluttony causes, 436.

## H
### Heresies

Apollinaris denied that Christ possessed a human mind and taught that the Word performed its functions, 57. The error of the Agnoetans, who said that Christ advanced to the highest holiness and wisdom through daily progress, ibid. Arius, denying that the Word or Son of God was God, impiously asserted that he was a creature. Jovinianus said that Mary did not give birth to Christ as a virgin; Helvidius blasphemously asserted that she bore other sons after Christ, 25. Nestorius introduced two persons into Christ and denied that Mary was the Mother of God. Eutyches did not admit the distinction between the divine and human natures, but introduced a third nature composed from them, 53. He was likewise an opponent of the distinction between the two operations of the same Christ, 498, 670. Heretics corrupt the sacred Scriptures, 140. After one and a second admonition, they are to be avoided, 146. They embrace the darkness of the devil and shudder at the light of the Savior, 300. They are compared with foxes, and their cunning is noted, 292. They secretly lie in wait for the Church, 383. They tear Christ’s garment—that is, the Church—with false doctrines, 140. The scandal of heretics is a very great evil, since by the perversity of their teaching they harm all the faithful, 690.

The Hebrews are said by the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 12 to have been baptized in the cloud and in the sea: how this passage is to be understood, 92. Among them the Church had its beginning, but among the Gentiles it grew to full strength, 51. Many things concerning Christ had been foretold to them, but they neither heard nor understood them, 56, 82.

King Herod, deceived and scorned by the Magi, became exceedingly angry and killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem, 81. Through Herod the devil acted, either to destroy Christ or, by the slaughter of the children, to sadden the one whose entrance into the world had been most joyful, 182. John the Baptist reproved him because he had taken the wife of his brother Philip and married her himself, 551. His crime is described in the killing of Saint John, 756.

The formation of humanity is threefold: first, Adam formed from clay; second, the woman brought forth from Adam’s rib; third, the heavenly one belonging to Christ, born from a virgin, 34. The best course for a human being is to yield to the author of the mind in matters that cannot be grasped by the mind, 498. Christ placed in the heavenly homeland the human being whom the envy of the malignant enemy had driven and expelled from that first dwelling in paradise, making him a stranger in this world’s mire; he made the exile from paradise a citizen of heaven, 514. A human being consists of soul and body; separated and dispersed, one without the other is a disordered nature, 567. Uprightness cannot be bought at a price but is acquired by virtue, 266. Honors, riches, health, and the good things of this life do not come through merit but happen by chance, 344. [Col. 0968]

The duties and characteristics of Christian hospitality are indicated, 332. Hospitality is commended by the example of Abraham, who invited three men to turn aside to his tent, 642. The humility of Christ’s birth shone forth marvelously through the loftiness of its mystery and the splendor of its wonders, 38, 39, 40.

### I

How greatly the worshipers of idols suffered from blindness, and how detestable idolatry is and must be rejected, 562. Idols must be removed from villages and fields. Whoever permits them defiles himself through superstitious religion, 659. Imperial laws were issued for their destruction, 610.

The impious dread death in sickness; the righteous, however, rejoice, since they hope for an everlasting inheritance and believe in a passage rather than an end, 631. Examples of God’s indulgence toward sinners are given, 502. Bodily illnesses, if endured patiently, make the spirit purer, 8. Some reckoned the beginning of the new year from the day of the Lord’s birth; hence it was called the new sun, 404.

Enemies are to be loved because of God’s commandment, for our own benefit, and following the example of the saints, 208. Christ made the Innocents, who suffered on their own account, participants in his passion and glory, 82. The renewal of the human being through righteousness; hence the newly baptized are called *neophytes*, because they have cast off the stains of oldness through a certain newness and assumed the grace of simplicity, 186. It is not irreligious to do what is commanded to be done through religion, 103.

Isaac is a figure of Christ offering himself on the cross for the salvation of the world, 173, 741. Esau and Jacob had two sons, from whom two peoples arose, ibid.

### J

Jannes and Jambres, the magicians, were convicted by Moses of wickedness, 385.

The fast of Lent was not established by human beings but commanded by heavenly majesty, 110. Its beginning on Wednesday, before the first Sunday in Lent, is very ancient in the Church. See the admonition to Homily 36, 103. It is said to have been instituted as preparation for the paschal solemnity, 112. Christ gave us an example of this fast, 113. Whoever omitted abstinence for even one day violated the whole of Lent, 114. Fasting is a certain wall for the Christian, impregnable to the devil and unbreachable by the enemy, 117. It sanctifies the human being and grants great grace, 118. Christian fasting is compared with the forty-two encampments by which the Israelites, after completing them, reached the Promised Land from Egypt, 114. The difference between Christ’s fast and Moses’ fast is indicated, 133. Through fasting for forty days and forty nights, Moses deserved to receive the tablets written by the finger of God, 453. We must imitate Christ fasting. The various ways in which fasting is sanctified, 109, 292. The fast of hypocrites is rejected, 104. Why there is no fasting for forty days after Easter, 192. One cannot be fasting who is refreshed by the Savior’s grace, ibid.

Jesus Christ was contemptuously called by the Jews the son of Joseph the carpenter, 641. Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh carried on their own shoulders to the Israelites on a pole a cluster of grapes; this event is explained mystically, 256.

John the Baptist was foretold by Isaiah as the angelic forerunner of the Lord, who was to prepare his ways, 20, 557, etc. A son was promised to the priest Zechariah, advanced in years, and to Elizabeth, already aged and barren, 212, 214. The time of his conception, 551. Holy prayer, not pleasure, brought John into being, 561. While still in his mother’s womb, he revealed the Savior by prophetic exultation, 207, 559. He was born greater than all those born of women, but not greater than Christ born of a virgin, 214. At his birth the bond of his father’s tongue was loosened, and he was called John, in accordance with the angel’s prophecy, 207, 596. As the herald and magnificent announcer of the new grace, he did not need to be cleansed by circumcision, 554. Nevertheless, he fulfilled the law of circumcision, 550.

In his thirtieth year from birth, John began to baptize those who came to him and to preach to the people the baptism of repentance, 551. He is called the lamp prepared for Christ, and the reason is explained, 405. He deserved to see with his own eyes and announce as present Jesus Christ, whom the other prophets had foreseen as coming in the distant future, 213. He bears witness that Christ is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world, 91. He asked to be baptized by Christ but did not obtain it, 92. He himself refused to baptize Christ. His humility is praised, 87. Obedient to Christ, he administered baptism in the Jordan, 63, 87, 97, 100, etc. He saw the Holy Spirit standing over Jesus in the form of a dove and heard the voice of the Father from heaven addressing the Son, 88, 91, 98, 101, etc. Many were converted to the Lord through his preaching and repented of their sins, 551. What the desert was in which John cried out, 564 ff. How severe his way of life was, 212, 560. He is called greater than the other prophets and endowed with a greater gift of grace, 546, 549. He was holier than Elisha, although Elisha possessed a double portion of Elijah’s spirit, 556. He was the end of the Law and the Prophets, 554. Herod had him beheaded because John had reproved him for his unlawful marriage with his brother’s wife, 212, 552, 560.

Job’s statement in chapter 2—“If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why shall we not also endure evils?”—is explained, 295. Jonah was a type of the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, 174, 180. Although Jonathan was unaware of his father’s command, since he had violated the fast he was declared liable to death, 120.

Joseph, by heavenly dispensation, was always a betrothed husband and never a husband. The angel said to him: “That which Mary has in her womb is from the Holy Spirit.” Innocent and just, he believed the angel who affirmed Mary’s virginal purity, 533. He was called a young bridegroom, ibid. Joseph of Arimathea buried Christ in his own new tomb, 280. Provision was made for the sanctity of Christ’s body when a new tomb was prepared for him, ibid.

For the Jews in the desert, God rained down manna from heaven as food and brought forth water from the rock, 37. From their own scrolls the Jews knew that the Lord and Redeemer would be born according to the flesh from a virgin, 54. Therefore they are without excuse, because despite so many figures and prophecies of the sacred Scriptures and so many visible signs warning them, they refused to believe that he had been born, 74. Their execrable cruelty is condemned: they brought upon themselves and their children guilt for the shedding of Christ’s blood, 479. The more carefully they guarded the tomb in which Jesus’ body had been laid, the more clearly it is established that he himself rose from the dead, 472. Association with the Jews is to be avoided, 412.

Judas Iscariot became guilty of impiety through the sale of Christ’s blood, 146. After losing faith, he lost the innocence of apostleship; for he became guilty of every offense once he denied the Lord of all virtues, 162. Repenting of his deed, he returned the money to the Pharisees, but, despairing of pardon, judged himself worthy of death, 147.

How effective meditation on the Last Judgment is for the correction of morals, 388. The righteous are called mountains and hills because, leaving behind the low things of the world, they have raised the summit of their faith toward the higher things of heavenly life, 507. Juvencus the presbyter adorned with verses the gifts offered to Christ by the Magi, 64.

### L

How powerful Peter’s tears were, 167. They benefit all penitents in obtaining pardon for their offenses, ibid. Lust is a corruption of the Christian, 433. Lustful looks are very sinful and therefore must be restrained with every effort, 680, 754.

The marvelous conversion and faith of the thief crucified with Christ. The Lord’s wounds were for him the cause of love. Paradise was granted to him not so much because of his faith as because of his love for God, 157 ff., 502, 743.

Saint Lawrence, archdeacon of the Roman Church, an outstanding distributor of the Church’s funds among the poor, rejoiced at the prophecy of Saint Sixtus, the supreme priest, as he went to martyrdom, concerning his own approaching passion, 237. How admirable his courage was in enduring the punishment of the flames, 240 ff. Heavenly fire was more intense than earthly fire in Lawrence, 242. Placed upon a heated gridiron, he mocked his torturer, offering his other side to be burned, 582, 586. He did not yield to the tyrant’s savagery; the firmness of his spirit arose chiefly from the love of Christ, 581, 587 ff.

Lazarus is restored to life, 766. Through reading the divine Scriptures we acquire the food of everlasting eloquence, 436. Imperial laws were enacted against the heresies of Jovinianus and Helvidius, 25. Also against idols and their worshipers, 610.

How heavy the burden of the Old Law was, 10. Its letter is bitter without the mystery of the cross; when the sacramental realities of Christ’s passion are joined to it, all its bitterness is spiritually seasoned, 116. This is explained at greater length, 122. The law of Christ is spiritual, and spiritual things must be compared with spiritual things, 137. [Col. 0970]

Secular laws and rights are sold and corrupted through long-established wickedness, 378. Following the example of Saint Paul, who appealed to Caesar, it is lawful for God’s servants to defend themselves against unjust laws, 572. Pope Saint Leo III extended the lesser litanies, or rogations, to the whole Church: see the admonition to Homily 90, 301.

Leporius the monk, who had said that Jesus Christ, according to his humanity, was ignorant of something, abandoned and anathematized his error: see the note to Homily 21, 58. Free will, given to the human being by God, is not infringed by him, 761. It is perfected by Christ, 504. Its captivity is freedom, 515.

The variety of languages introduced among the builders of the tower of Babel deterred them from their undertaking and separated them from one another. The same variety, granted to the apostles on the day of Pentecost, gathered different peoples throughout the world into one Church, 530. In various languages the apostles proclaimed the unity of the Godhead, 525, 527. Their speech was manifold, but one Spirit spoke through them all, 527, 528, 597. The vices of the tongue are identified and reproved, 351.

The prophecies concerning Christ preserved in the sacred Scriptures became present realities when he came, 71. Lot alone, by his merits, saved the city of the Sodomites from destruction, 265. The washing of feet is to be performed by Christians following the Lord’s example, 718. In the earliest times of the Church it was administered to adults who had recently been baptized, ibid. Profit acquired from evil is condemned, 265. The Saturnalia, which Christians attended on the Kalends of January, are rejected, 343. Stage games were first brought from Greece into Italy by the Romans, 727, in the note.

The Moon. When the moon was eclipsed, Saint Maximus sharply rebuked the people who raised cries and noises, 334. What effects occur as the moon waxes and wanes, and what benefits it provides to the earth, 337. The Church is compared with the moon, and the reason is explained, 338. The *lustrum* (pagan lustration), a superstitious religious observance, is condemned, 609. Luxury is always joined to satiety, 451. It is a companion of drunkenness, 461, 660. Through luxury the devil subjected the whole world to himself, 107.

### M

The brothers Maccabees were outstanding in virtue and courage because, in defense of their ancestral laws, they endured the most bitter punishments in the presence and at the exhortation of their mother, 601 ff.

Three Magi set out from Chaldea, led by a new star, and came to Jerusalem seeking the king of the Jews who had been born, 74. They proceeded as far as Bethlehem after learning from the prophecies the place of his birth, 52. Although they found the infant Christ lying in a humble manger, they worshiped him as God and Lord, 67. They offered him gold, frankincense, and myrrh—precious yet mystical gifts, 51, 53, 54, 56, 73, 74, 78, etc. The Magi came by one road to worship the Lord and returned to their homeland by another; it is shown that this happened not without a mystery, 54, 64. In the Magi all the nations were called to the knowledge of the true God, 49, 51, 53, 56, etc. The Magi were the first fruits of the Gentiles in the Christian faith, 51. According to tradition, the arrival of the Magi at the Lord’s manger occurred on the eighth day before the Ides of January, 55, in the admonition.

Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne in Gaul, is regarded as the first institutor of the rogations, 301, in the admonition. The manifestation of the Holy Trinity took place at Christ’s baptism, 90. Manna was given to the Hebrews from heaven, 37. When they gathered more than the daily ration contrary to the divine command, it was changed into worms, 138.

Christ heals the withered hand; its mystery is explained, 383 ff. The pearl mentioned by Matthew in chapter 7 is Christ, to be acquired through generosity toward the poor, 389.

Mary the Virgin, Mother of God. Isaiah’s prophecy that a virgin would bear a son whose name would be Emmanuel was fulfilled in her, 17. Mary is called a suitable dwelling place for Christ, not because of bodily condition but because of original grace, 18. For Christ to be conceived according to the angel’s announcement, Mary was filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit and overshadowed by the power of God the Father, ibid. She was a virgin when she conceived, a virgin when she gave birth, and a virgin after giving birth, ibid. She was betrothed to the just and youthful Joseph, 534. Christ was born from Mary so that the female sex might also give birth to a human being, while virginal integrity might reveal God, 42. She preserved the uncorrupted seals of her undefiled womb, 534. Mary, indeed, the daughter of Eve, gave birth to Christ, yet she did not conceive him from Adam, 166. [Col. 0971]

At Mary’s request, Christ performed the first of his signs at the wedding feast in Cana of Galilee, changing water into wine, 68. She represented a certain type of our souls, 61. Mary is mystically called a rod, because through the integrity of her body she brought forth Christ like a flower, 112. In the same sense she is also called manna, because, radiant, sweet, and virgin, she descended as if coming from heaven, flowing to all the peoples of the Churches as food sweeter than honey, 158. She is compared with the Ark of the Old Testament, 604.

Mary Magdalene came to Christ’s tomb and was reproved by the risen Lord for her unbelief, because she was seeking him among the dead, 176. She wept because she had not found Christ, 177. Christ’s words to Mary Magdalene—“Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father”—are explained, ibid. She represents the person of the faithful Church, 753. She approached Christ reclining at the Pharisee’s banquet; what she did and what the Lord said to her are explained, 766 ff.

The excellence of martyrdom is commended, 122. It is not punishment that is praiseworthy in martyrs but faith, 599. The deaths of martyrs are honored in the Church of God as a genuine birthday, because through a new order of birth they are born to a new life in heaven, with death serving as the midwife, 593. Their bodies are rightly placed beneath the altar, because Christ is placed upon the altar; thus those whom the cause of the passion had bound together with Christ might also be joined by the religious significance of one place, 600. The martyrs would never have willingly relinquished this life unless they had believed that another was incomparably happier, 624. They die with joyful courage, to be restored to something better, ibid. For while they endure death without hesitation, they clearly affirm the hope of immortality, 524. They are therefore to be honored above all, 626. The Taurinensian martyrs Octavius, Adventius, and Solutor are commended, 261.

The memory of the holy Fathers was celebrated in the religious gatherings of Christians, recalling their virtues to mind, 245. No soldier who commits extortion and plunder is excused, 376. Military service is not itself a crime, but abusing military service to the destruction of one’s neighbor is counted as guilt, 376. Christian warfare requires what kind of faithfulness, 506.

Ecclesiastical ministry is to be carried out not to acquire money but to gain souls for God, 339. The ministry of the sacraments must not be undertaken without a confession of faith, 102. The ministers of God who are placed in charge of divine functions must abstain from human concerns, 341. Christ’s miracles are enumerated, 522 ff. How does God’s mercy—that is, his grace—precede us? 680. Mercy toward the poor is pleasing to God and useful for obtaining pardon for sins, 58.

The sacrifice of the Mass is performed daily, 600. In it the memory of Christ’s passion and death is proclaimed; the Lord’s body is offered and Christ’s blood is poured out. In the sacrifice of the Mass Christ is both victim and priest, ibid.

The millstone of an ass tied around the neck of one who causes scandal is understood mystically: what does it signify? 690. Evil habits are worse enemies than hostile foes, 312. They are the cause of every calamity, 210. Good habits, however, are like wings that lift us to the heights of heaven, 438.

Death saddens the minds of unbelievers but gladdens Christian hearts, 593. Death must be met with courageous spirit, 295, in the note. Death was not present in nature but was turned into nature, ibid. Human nature is not destroyed by death; when the Savior’s grace breathes upon it, it receives the immortality in which it was created, ibid. Why the death of the saints is precious in the sight of the Lord, 200, 259, 591, 756, etc. To die for Christ is to reign with Christ, 556. Not to avoid death when one can do so is rashness; but not to yield to the one who is killing is the courage of a believer, 572.

Moses, prince of the Israelite people, concealed in the cloud, spoke alone with the Lord on the summit of the highest mountain, 37. He received two tablets of the Covenant, namely the commandments of God, which the Hebrews were to obey, 12. He brought the Israelites out of Egypt and, after completing forty-two encampments on the journey, led them to the Promised Land, 442. He fasted for forty days and forty nights and received the law from God, ibid. While he fasted, he deserved to see God; the people, indulging in intemperance, cast idols for themselves, [lacuna]01. He raised up a bronze serpent in the desert, which represented a type of Christ’s cross, 152. Waging war against Amalek, he conquered not with weapons or iron but with hands raised to God, 155. When he brought his hand out from his bosom shining with a new radiance, he convicted the magicians Jannes and Jambres of wickedness, [Col. 0972] 385. When God told Moses that he could not see his face, this is to be understood of the Godhead, which cannot be seen by bodily eyes, 28.

The Canaanite woman, touching the fringe of the Lord’s garment, is healed of an issue of blood, 673 ff. Worldly cares choke the word of God in the heart: one who is concerned with the world cannot be concerned with Christ, 598. Lovers of the world endure many things to no purpose; those, on the contrary, who despise it earn an eternal reward for themselves in that very contempt, 629. Some held the opinion that the world would last seven thousand years, 652, in the note. The world was made from nothing, 28. The mystery of the cross, on which Christ deigned to humble himself, is explained, 506.

### N

The nostrils of those being baptized were anointed, and the mysteries contained in this anointing are explained, 742. How one should approach the nativity of the Lord and Savior, 1 ff., 15, 393 ff.

There are two natures and one person in Christ, 511. See *Christ*. No one can change nature except the Lord of nature, 419. The mystery of the boat into which the Lord entered and crossed over is explained, 357. He himself does not need a boat, but the Church does, so that it may deserve to reach the heavenly harbor across the sea of the world, ibid. The boat left by Christ on the lake of Gennesaret represented the Synagogue abandoned in its unbelief and obstinacy, 639 ff. Peter’s boat is the Church entrusted to him to govern, 641 ff. It suffered a storm because Judas the betrayer was found in it, ibid. It will preserve unharmed all who persevere in it while the world burns, ibid.

The necessity of our remedy demanded that Christ be born as a human being, 499. Those who have recently been regenerated through baptism are called *neophytes*, and why? 185, 486. The error of Nestorius was condemned at the Second Council of Ephesus, 29, in the note. Nineveh was saved from destruction because of the repentance of its citizens and its king himself, 173, 301, 308, 761.

Those who receive the rest of night in Christ are kept under God’s protection until the light, 298. The name Noah signifies rest among the saints, 487. Before the Flood he did not preach repentance with his mouth but through his works; his tongue was silent, but his building cried out, 451. In the cloud that received Christ as he ascended into heaven, God the Father is to be understood, 194. Marriage, instituted by God, is sanctified by Christ’s presence, 67. Spiritual nourishment is drawn from reading the Scriptures, 436.

### O

The offering of frankincense to the newborn Jesus signified that the superstition of demons would cease; gold signified royal dignity, and myrrh mortal nature, 78. The death of martyrs is regarded in the Church of God as their birthday, 593.

Careful guarding of the eyes is commended, 754. We received them so that they might provide light for the body, not bring harm to the soul, 680. Their unrestrained license is condemned by Christ’s testimony, 679, 780.

Hatred of one’s neighbor. “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer”: this statement of Saint John in his First Epistle, chapter 3, is explained, 204. Hatred opposes all virtues, and no good works performed with hatred can please God, ibid. Even the sacrifice must be left aside so that we may first be reconciled with our brother, ibid.

A manner of life is prescribed as the pattern for all duties, 377. The operation of the Most Holy Trinity is undivided: in the working of divine powers, the unity of the persons cannot be absent, 87. The distinct operations of each of Christ’s divine and human natures are asserted against Eutyches, 512. For one and the same deed we cannot both seek the praise of the flattering world and acquire the reward of heavenly life, 144.

Many oracles existed in the sacred books foretelling that the Lord would be born from David’s offspring; the Jews neglected them at the Savior’s coming, 54. The Sibyl’s oracle concerning Christ, 730. How effective prayer to God is, 309 ff. The example of the Canaanite woman teaches that one must persevere in prayer, 674. The qualities by which prayer excels and the virtues with which it must be joined, 353. [Col. 0973]

The East. Just as the East was illumined by the passion of Christ the Lord, so the West can glory in the martyrdom of the apostles Peter and Paul, 232. Original sin was remitted under the Old Law through circumcision, 554. Under the New Law, however, it is washed away through the baptism of water or of blood, 625. Christ’s birth should rather be called the birth of the world, 17. Christ did not refuse Judas Iscariot’s kiss, and why, 492. The lost sheep, which the good shepherd found, he carried back to his flock on his own shoulders, 440.

### P
Pagans said that everything happens by fate, and that the entire human race is fixed and immovable, 722. They raved by imagining and worshiping such a vast progeny of gods and goddesses, 724. Palm branches are offered to Christ as he sits upon the colt of a donkey and enters Jerusalem, 123. Their blessing and distribution on the Sunday of Holy Week is an ancient practice in the Church, 135, in the admonition. The bread is the Lord himself, who descended from heaven, 436. The miraculous multiplication of the five loaves and two fish is examined, 668, 735. The other multiplication, of seven loaves and a few fish, is discussed, 670. In the seven loaves are understood the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which the Church is defended and restored, 757. The Gospel parable about two men in one bed and two women grinding, Luke XVII, Matthew VIII, 371, 387. About the Publican and the Pharisee, Luke XVIII, 762. About the father who received his younger son, repentant of his deed, back into favor, Luke XV, 773. The Paraclete came from the Father, so that we may not doubt that all the gifts of eternal salvation are conferred upon us by the disposition and will of the omnipotent Father, 525. The same Paraclete is manifold in speech, omnipotent in power, diverse in languages, and one in all, 536. What spiritual paralysis is, ibid. The paralytic carried on a bed to Jesus is healed, 318. Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and the other nations hear the mighty works of God in their own languages, 529. *Pascha* is called in Hebrew; in Latin it is called “passing over,” or “advance,” because through this mystery, with Christ rising again, one passes from worse things to better, 183. Christ’s Passion was prefigured and foretold from the very beginning of the world, 171. Nothing base is to be observed in it, since the glory of his resurrection was so great, 449. The Good Shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine little sheep, sought the wandering sheep and, when he found it, carried it back to the flock on his own shoulders, 440. The shepherds, warned by the angel, hastened to the Lord’s manger and worshiped the newborn Redeemer, 94. It is the duty of the shepherd of souls to rebuke those who conduct themselves negligently in fulfilling Christian works, 373. The divine Father is called the Voice, the Son the Word; why? 425. How the Father is seen in the Son, 246. How it is also to be understood that the Father receives the Son beneath the shadow of a cloud, 194. To abandon one’s homeland in danger is the greatest injustice and ingratitude, 306. Paul, formerly Saul, while hastening toward Damascus, was struck and blinded by God and, from being a persecutor, became a teacher of the Church, 219, 223, 469. As a reward for his virtues, he was caught up to the third heaven and learned heavenly secrets, 220. And he learned what he was to teach on earth, 224. Paul showed that he was protected by divine power when he punished a magician, a deceiver of the people, with blindness and freed a woman possessed by a demon, 562. He ordered a Corinthian guilty of incest to be removed from the fellowship of the saints and received him back when he repented, 354. So that he would not be beaten with rods by the Gentiles, he appealed to Caesar. In this he used the privilege of the nations and apostolic prudence, 572. His Epistles nourish the peoples of the Churches unto salvation, 579. Paul’s statement in 1 Corinthians II concerning the Holy Spirit, who searches the depths of God, 524. His words in Ephesians IV—“Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth”—are expounded at length, 681 ff. Glorious Paul, who by contending with great struggle for the faith of Christ among diverse nations had fought countless battles, was received by Rome, like a conqueror of the world, for a triumph after his head had been cut off, 221. From his neck, when the persecutor struck it with a sword, a stream rather than blood is said to have flowed, 578. To whom the peace of Christ was announced, 61. Although a sinner may appear to live, nevertheless he is devoted to death by his crimes, 576. Sins must be removed so that we may make God favorable toward us, 439. No one can forgive sins except God alone, 412. If sinners conceal their sins in confession, they become more guilty, 381. They must not despair of God’s grace whenever they implore his mercy and place their hope in Christ’s merits, 502. Adam’s sin brought death upon the whole human race, 385. The strangers for whose burial the potter’s field was bought at the price of Christ’s betrayal are to be understood as Christians who have renounced the cares and riches of the world, 150. The distinction of the Persons must be believed in divine matters; it introduces no difference in nature. When the Father and the Son are said to be one, their inseparability and unity are proclaimed, 246. We hold and believe in three Persons—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—of one power, one substance, one eternity, one will, and also one divinity; and we venerate the whole Trinity under the designation of one God, 714. How those statements concerning the divine Persons are to be understood—“They speak to one another, they send one another, they obey one another,” 526. Although the three divine Persons work inseparably, certain actions are nevertheless attributed particularly to each. For the remedy of our life, the Father bestowed the Son upon us; the Son granted the grace of regeneration; the Holy Spirit supplied power, 523. Masked persons who disfigure the image of God in themselves are detested, 46. Peter, by profession a fisherman, is called by Christ to fish for human beings, 227, 567, 643. He was the first to confess Christ as the Son of the living God, 217. The Savior himself declared the greatness of this confession when he said that he had received that revelation from the Father, made Peter the rock—that is, the foundation—of his Church, and entrusted to him the keys of the heavenly kingdom, 218, 375, 467, 641. Peter is therefore called “rock,” because he was the first among the nations to lay the foundations of faith and, like a stone, holds together the immovable structure and form of the entire Christian work. Peter is called *petra* (“rock”) on account of devotion, and the Lord is called *petra* on account of power. He rightly deserves a share in the name who deserves a share in the work, 169, 578. Peter’s righteousness was so approved by God that the power of judgment was assigned to him, heavenly judgment was placed in his decision, and the governance of the whole Church was entrusted to him, 226. The fact that he trembled while walking on the sea occurred so that human weakness might recognize how great is the difference between master and servant, 218. Nothing is higher than his faith, 222 ff. When Peter desired to die with Christ, the same Lord told him that he could not then follow him, because he was being reserved to establish the Church, 161. Peter denied his Master three times; but scarcely had the Lord looked upon him when he burst into the bitterest tears, which cleansed him from his offense, 166. When he repented of the crime he had committed, why he remained silent and shed tears silently, 167. The example of his defection teaches that no one ought to presume upon himself, 391. Peter did us no harm by denying, and benefited us greatly by making amends, 168. Christ foretold to Peter by what kind of death he would have to die, 570. His vision of the vessel descending from heaven like a linen cloth containing animals of different kinds is expounded, 573 ff. After he had thrice protested his love for the Lord, he accepted responsibility for feeding his sheep and lambs, 219, 354. Heavenly providence brought Peter and Paul to Rome so that, through the preaching of the Gospel—which held primacy over the whole world—Rome might become the head of the holy religion, 216. When Simon Magus was deceiving many people in Rome by magic and false wonders and had even attempted to fly through the air, Peter by his prayers brought Simon headlong from on high to the ground, and when he fell his legs were broken, 232. This, indeed, was the reason why Nero condemned Peter to crucifixion. On the same day and in the same city Paul was crowned by the cutting off of his head, so that those who had been companions in spreading the true faith might not be separated in undergoing the glorious contest for it, ibid. Pilate declares Christ innocent, but thereby becomes even more guilty of unjust condemnation, 142. Owners of estates are rebuked because they still allowed idolatry to be practiced on them, 656. The command of the Lenten fast is urged, 462. God’s commandment is not the law of one place but of the world, 446. The divine commandment must be observed everywhere, because the one who commands is everywhere, ibid. The ministry of preaching has necessarily been imposed upon bishops or priests as part of their office, 659. Its condition is that the one who wishes to avoid his own sins must not conceal the sins of another, ibid. How Christian preparation for the Lord’s Nativity ought to be undertaken, and with what virtues, 1 ff. The real presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist is asserted most explicitly, 600. Prayers are to be offered to God in the morning after we rise and in the evening before going to bed, so that he may deign to keep us safe by day and by night, 298. The privileges of the first birth, lost through original guilt, are restored in human beings by Christ’s holier birth, 35. Peter’s primacy in the Church is established, 169, 461. His prerogatives are enumerated more explicitly, 642 ff. It is not divided between him and Paul but established in one Peter, 233, in the note. The princes of this world reward their servants while they live; God, however, generally reserves the reward of his chosen ones until after death, in eternal life, 569. Judas’s betrayal was foretold in David’s prophecy, 145. The prophecies of the prophets were brought forth into the world before Christ’s light like a certain radiance, 405. Prophecies concerning the coming of the Lord and Savior are brought forward against the Jews, 737. All the prophets, holy through the merit of their faith, performed many virtues and many wonders, 729. The whole exposition of Psalm XIII concerns Christ’s resurrection, 179. The words of Psalm XVIII, “Day pours forth the word to day,” are interpreted, 180. Also Psalm XXI, “My God, my God, look upon me,” 137. Psalm XXVIII is expounded as referring to Christ’s baptism, 422. The words of Psalm LXXI, “He shall descend like rain upon a fleece,” 409. And Psalm CIX, “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand,” 197. Also of the same psalm, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you,” 748. The prerogatives and merits of chastity are celebrated, 141. The simplicity and innocence of children are to be imitated by those who aspire to the kingdom of heaven, 689. How precious purity of mind is, since through it God is possessed, 658.

## Q

The institution of Lent. See “Lenten fast.” By restraining carnal desires through a forty-day fast, we shall be victors over the devil, 119. From what Christians ought to abstain during Lent, 446. Holy meditation on the virtues must be joined to fasting, 132. Questions of secular wisdom must be refuted, and the faith received through revelation must be held, 509.

## R

Avarice is the root of all evils. See “Avaricious,” “Avarice.” Reconciliation with the neighbor from whom we have received an offense is the Lord’s commandment, 204 ff. The regeneration of the human being is compared with his creation, 533. The Christian religion is not to be called into dispute after the prophecies of the prophets, the testimony of the apostles, and the wounds of the martyrs; nor is the ancient faith, as though it were new, to be subjected to examination, 624. Religious men are subjected to heavier temptations, 437, 453. The relics of the holy martyrs are placed on altars by the institution of the Church, 599. Concerning the honor and veneration to be shown to the sacred relics, 623, 627. The forgiveness of sins which Christ earned for us must be believed, 277. It has been reserved to Christ’s grace, 95. The world will be renewed according to God’s faithful promise, and the soul must be restored to the body and the body to the soul, 567. How God provided for the restoration and salvation of human beings while the law of death remained, though the law of their condemnation was altered, 440. The resurrection of Christ. God willed this mystery, revealed from the beginning of the world’s birth and repeatedly prefigured in the Old Law, so that he might show that throughout each successive age of the passing world the hope of the saints continually tended only toward him who is the expectation of all nations, 486. Figures of Christ risen from the dead found in the Old Testament are brought forward, 173. The possibility of Christ’s resurrection is demonstrated by the fact that, while living, he raised several dead persons, 514. At his resurrection, not only angels and disciples but even his enemies bore witness, 472. Christ’s resurrection filled the holy patriarchs with joy, from whose stock the Son of God himself was born, 501. We ought to rejoice over it, and why, ibid. The risen Christ appeared to Mary Magdalene when she sought him in the tomb, 176. He also appeared to Thomas and gave him the marks of his Passion to touch, 482. He joined the disciples traveling to the town of Emmaus, 363. Christ’s resurrection is life for the dead, forgiveness for sinners, and glory for the saints, 179. When he rose, many bodies of the saints also rose, 619. The resurrection of the dead. This was the principal purpose for which the Son of God assumed flesh: to grant flesh perpetual existence, 273. The resurrection of the flesh must be believed, since it is the end of our religion and the highest object of belief, ibid. The whole hope of Christians rests on faith in the resurrection, 715. The future human being rose beforehand in Christ, before he received his lot of life in the world, 474. Resurrection is the reward of the righteous, 478. Unbelievers and sinners, however, and those who do not obey God’s commandments, will rise for this purpose: that their flesh, made immortal, may be assigned to eternal fires, so that it may burn forever and never cease by burning, 716. The reward of good works prepared by Christ for the righteous in the future life is established, 569. The person who is condemned by the judgment of his own conscience is guilty without excuse, 143. The revelation of the future Redeemer awakened desire for him in all the saints throughout the successive ages of the world, 486. The Church’s custom of praying not on bent knees but standing from Easter to Pentecost is mentioned, 192. The institution of the Rogation observances: it is discussed, 301, in the admonition to Homily 90. Rome glories in the special patronage of Peter and Paul, 226.

## S

The queen of Sheba, from the South, who came to hear Solomon’s wisdom, 760. The Jewish priests are rebuked because they did not receive the Lord and Savior as God but judged him as a human being, 341. Priests are compared with bees, 371. They are soldiers of Christ and receive pay and gifts from him, 379. Priests concerned for their people on account of Christ are compared with shepherds keeping watch over their flock by night at the Lord’s Nativity, 409. Reverence is owed to priests and the ministers of God, 285. What the ministry of a priest requires, ibid. The sacrifice of praise is truly martyrdom, 630. Since the memory of the Lord’s death is renewed daily in the Mass and mystically represented, it is proved that the Mass is a true sacrifice, 600. For sinners it is a propitiatory offering, ibid. The dignities of the world are not to be sought by evil arts, 151. The Savior, sent under the Law, born under the Law, and brought up according to the Law, is neglected by the Jews and received by the Gentiles, 396. Why the Savior was placed in another’s tomb and had no burial place of his own, 282. In the Savior we all rose, all came back to life, and all passed over to heavenly things, 472. Christ grants the Samaritan woman the water of everlasting life and forgiveness of sins, 326, 396, 667. She herself represents a type of the Church, 328. Samson sent foxes armed with burning torches into the field of the Philistines, 382. By killing more of his enemies when dead than he had killed while alive, he prefigured Christ obtaining the salvation of the world through his death, 493. The prayers of the saints are more powerful than human weapons, 310. Whoever honors the saints honors God, and whoever despises the saints despises the Lord, 580. What divine wisdom and human wisdom are, 140. Human wisdom is foolish when it refuses to believe that God could be born human; it belongs to those who do not understand a mystery of such depth, 21. The Gentiles who deny the possibility of the divine Incarnation are refuted, 34. All human wisdom becomes foolish in examining heavenly matters and is foolishness with God, 508. The wise person understands that this life was not given to us for rest but for labor, 293. King Saul of Israel, while waging war against the Philistines, imposed a fast upon the entire army and publicly declared Jonathan guilty of death, although he had violated the fast innocently, 119. Occasions of scandal are to be avoided according to Christ’s command, 754. Why a millstone should rather be fastened around the neck of one who causes Christians to stumble than any other stone, 297. How diligently scandal must be avoided: the gravity of its guilt is shown, 286 ff., 690. Heretics who disseminate wicked doctrine cause scandal to the whole Church, 690. The knowledge of God is compared with the five loaves and two fish multiplied by Jesus Christ in the desert, 667. Reading the divine Scriptures is necessary, 71. The Scriptures call us back from the enticements of the world, 151. They supply the food of enduring eloquence, 436. Their riches are so great that they can never be exhausted, 667. The divine Scriptures preserved by the Hebrews bear witness against the Hebrews themselves to the truth of the Gospel, 172. The wickedness of the elders who slandered Susanna’s innocence is exposed and condemned, 143. The meaning of that statement of Maximus, Sermon 42, 515a—“The fault benefited the human being more than it harmed him”—and how it is to be understood, is explained, 316, in the note. Undisciplined license in speech is censured and shown to be the cause of many evils, 681 ff. The bronze serpent hung upon a tree in the desert was a figure of Christ hanging upon the wood, on which he sacrificed himself for the salvation of all human beings, 152. Slaves and household servants are to be treated as brothers, 459. The sign of the cross is commended to the faithful and is the emblem of our victory, 506. Silence concerning the higher mysteries of the faith was maintained in the presence of catechumens, 709. Simon Magus was cast from the heights of the air to the ground through the prayers of Saint Peter, and his legs were broken, 233, 340. What constitutes Christian simplicity, 183. It is called infancy, and why, ibid. The power of the mustard seed, to which faith is compared, 361, 365. What “the bosom of the Father,” in which Christ is said in John I to exist, signifies, 416. Maximus used the story of the Sirens to signify the enticements of desire and the snares of the world, 152. Association with an innocent person teaches innocence; association with a perverse person leads to depravity, 647. The sun was darkened during Christ’s Passion, 681. No one who is concerned with the world is concerned with Christ, 598. Who is the watchman appointed over the children of Israel, as in Ezekiel III, 659. Those who consume all the reward of their works in the present age through ambition for temporal wealth can have no hope of future recompense, 106. Christ rejects the faithless Synagogue and takes up the faithful Church, 640. The Holy Spirit came upon Mary and filled her with his power so that she might conceive Christ, 18, 33, 531. How the Holy Spirit united human flesh in the Virgin’s womb to the Father’s Only-Begotten is explained, 530, 534. He descended upon the apostles to demonstrate that Christ had reached the Father, 197. He strengthened the hearts of the apostles with heavenly power and enriched their tongues with a new utterance, 522 ff. He bore witness to Christ’s divinity, 530. Christ and the Spirit proclaim one another by their testimonies, because they know themselves to reign with an undivided majesty, ibid. The Holy Spirit came into the hearts of those whom the blood and teaching of Christ had first purified, 528. There must be no doubt that the Holy Spirit is God, whose glory with the Father and the Son is inseparable. His divinity is therefore established against heretics and Jews, 532. It is argued from the unity of the teaching that he taught through the Apostle that he is of one substance with the Son of God, 200. Since all things between the Father, the Son, and the Spirit are shared, they must have the same nature in all things, 523. Their will and power in every work must likewise be believed to be one, ibid. He is said to have been sent by both, namely by the Father and the Son, 535. In the Holy Spirit there is the full power of regeneration and the authority to forgive sins, 532. “He breathes where he wills,” and freely distributes his gifts to whom he wills, 554. His cooperation in our salvation is shown, 523. The Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and promised by the Son, deigned to pour the gifts of his glory into Christ’s apostles, so that they might speak of his sufferings and kingdom in the language of all nations. Through this dispensation, since the whole human race was called to life, the whole world everywhere was to hear the mysteries of God, 532. The Holy Spirit is true God; Christ testifies with equal confession both that he proceeds from the Father and that he is to be sent by Christ himself, 535. The Holy Spirit inspired Cornelius the centurion before he was baptized and, while Peter was speaking, not only fell upon some who were still Gentiles but also instructed them to speak in tongues, 554. Through the power of his strength the martyrs are fortified to undergo torments, 528. The faithful are filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit—that is, with his seven gifts, 672. A newly risen star led the Magi to the Lord’s manger, 50. It revealed Christ’s majesty and heavenly origin, 38. Only three men from the Gentiles understood what this star signified, ibid. Saint Stephen was assigned to the ministry of widows and earned testimony to the holiest chastity, 648. Ordained deacon by the apostles, he preceded the apostles themselves in a blessed and triumphant death, 201. He gave an illustrious example of love for enemies, ibid. The heavens were opened to Saint Stephen, and he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God, 197, 202, 466. The superstition of the people shouting and making a commotion during an eclipse of the moon is rejected, 45. Saint Susanna was vindicated from the accusations of wicked elders by Daniel as judge, and her chastity is commended, 142. An exposition of the Creed is provided, 272. Unless someone professes the faith expressed in the Creed, he will not be saved, ibid.

## T

Those marked with the letter tau—that is, with the figure of the cross—were preserved unharmed from the angel’s destruction, 414. Temperance is exceedingly useful; conversely, how great are the evils of intemperance, 445. What fruits do those who use time well obtain? 596. Demonic temptations are overcome by fasting and prayer, 118. When people cry out to God in temptations, he does not deny them help, 172. The devil deceives Christ’s faithful through crafty temptations, all the more dangerously because he does so secretly, 634. The two Testaments perfect one another. The Law of Moses was given as a testimony to the Law of Christ; and if the Gospel had not been given, the Law would not have been necessary at all, 10.
